permission-gate.summary: Category: hooks that turn Jev's typed probabilities into allow, ask or deny decisions on Claude Code tool calls. Most of the 60 members are young, single-author alpha repos, 0 to 5 stars. Most are hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai. OpenRouter-native ones are toolgate, blastgate, Rahul's jev-auto-mode, jevexec, failproofai and leepokai's jev-guard (HEAD only). Several others switch with a one-line or env change (nafiurrahmanniloy jev-guard, greghavens jev-scope-control, yanmad27 ask-jev, agent-reflex). Evidence is self-reported and small-n. For this user (defaultMode auto, frequent bypassPermissions, Anthropic's classifier already in place) the value is a cheap, low-latency second opinion that can only add prompts or denials. It is not a prompt-remover. The wrong event is the PermissionRequest cookbook and several 'auto-approver' repos, because that event does not fire in the user's normal modes.
permission-gate.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already has: allow/ask/deny rules; the auto-mode classifier (Sonnet 5 by default). The classifier sees user messages, tool calls and CLAUDE.md, but never tool results, and blocks exfiltration, remote-code-execution style actions and pushes to untrusted remotes. It also has deterministic PreToolUse command hooks (the user's no-secret-leak.cjs), prompt and agent hooks (an LLM yes/no with no extra infrastructure), PermissionDenied and PermissionRequest events, and critical-path rm protection. Jev is far cheaper and faster (about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, p50 about 200 ms, p95 about 600 ms). Independent evals put it roughly at parity with a frontier LLM on bounded action gates (100/111 vs 102/111, and 55/60 vs Sonnet 5), with clearly worse calibration. It is overconfident on unanswerable inputs, steerable by injected text in state, and on the /alpha endpoint with no SLA. Its edge is being a fast, cheap, typed extra vote on top of the native classifier. It cannot be a better one, and the user's static rules and no-secret-leak hook cover most of the same ground with no egress.
permission-gate.worthItReason: Anthropic's classifier plus the user's deny rules and no-secret-leak hook already gate most risk, and Jev is not a better judge (accuracy a bit below mid-price LLMs; 1.0 probability on 56% of answers, 9 of them wrong). Most 'auto-approver' repos remove prompts, which the user in auto and bypass modes mostly does not have, and PermissionRequest hooks and gates keyed on default/acceptEdits mode do nothing there. What remains is Jev as an add-only layer: deny or ask on things like out-of-scope commits, pushes, deploys or unrequested edits, especially in bypass sessions where a hook deny is the only certain brake. Costs are real. Every judged call adds about 0.3 to 1 s and sends commands, prompts and sometimes code to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which needs a data-policy check for client projects. Every candidate is days to weeks old, and no study measures the false-approve rate on real Claude Code traffic. Worth a shadow-mode trial on personal projects with a narrow scope. Not a daily must-have, and not something to run on client repos without a data-handling decision.

bestPick.name: RiskAverseTech/toolgate
bestPick.reason: Least-bad verified option, not a strong endorsement. It is the only one that is automatic, natively OpenRouter (verified), can deny in bypass, and is actively maintained. Trial it in a narrowed setup: gated_tools set to Bash and Write only, unattended.ask set to ask, backend.provider pinned to openrouter, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to no-secret-leak first. Run it for 1 to 2 weeks on personal repos only, checking its log against your own decisions before enforcing. Everything in the category is a days-old alpha.

permission-gate.runnerUp: stas4000/blastgate (https://github.com/stas4000/blastgate) as a vendored copy with JEV_MODEL pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13 and hook timeout 10. It is the smallest ask-only hook. Alternatively nafiurrahmanniloy/jev-guard in watch mode (with the ENDPOINTS one-line patch) if the goal is catching unrequested commits and pushes.
permission-gate.recommendationForUser: Do not install a Jev 'auto-approver': in auto and bypass modes it removes prompts you rarely see, and the cookbook PermissionRequest hook mostly never fires. If you want Jev here at all, run it as an add-only PreToolUse layer. Either trial toolgate in a narrowed, shadow-first setup (Bash and Write only, provider pinned to openrouter, personal repos only), or write the ~60-line hook described above (ask/deny only, fail-open, pinned model). Before enabling anything, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak.cjs, decide whether client code may go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and test whether a hook ask prompts under bypassPermissions. Skip it on client projects until that decision is made.

security-guard.summary: Security-guard is the largest and most Claude-Code-native Jev category: about 12 real hook/plugin integrations plus a long tail of scanners, gateways and libraries that do not fit. The useful ones are harness-run PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks that send a redacted command or tool output plus typed Noul/Choice questions to Jev and return allow, ask or deny, or an injection warning. Every candidate is 1 to 12 days old, single-author, 0 to 21 stars and unreviewed. Only a few can reach OpenRouter without patching. None has been shown to work with an OpenRouter key end to end.
security-guard.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already ships a layered stack. Permission rules and deny/ask rules are evaluated first. Auto mode has a Sonnet-class server-side classifier that sees the user messages, tool calls and CLAUDE.md, blocks exfiltration, RCE-style actions and untrusted pushes by default, and never sees tool results, so it resists injection. Hooks can be command, http, mcp_tool, prompt or agent type; a prompt or agent hook on PreToolUse or PermissionRequest gives an LLM judge without any Jev. The user's own no-secret-leak.cjs already covers secret paths. Compared with these, Jev adds a cheap and fast typed probability ($0.042/M input, p50 about 200 ms). Independent evals show it about equal to Claude on bounded action gates (100/111 vs 102/111, small n) but overconfident on unanswerable input, steerable by text in state that reads as evidence (96.5% to 26.5% accuracy in one test), and it runs on an alpha endpoint with no SLA. It also sends code off-machine to a third party. It does not beat the native classifier on safety; it only offers cheaper judging for allow/skip decisions, and the native classifier already covers that.
security-guard.worthItReason: The idea fits the "automatic, no prompting" goal. Hooks are the one mechanism that fires without saying "use jev". But the evidence for this user is thin. (1) In bypassPermissions there are no prompts to save, and the audited plugins' tripwires only defer (verified for jev-bouncer), so only a Jev deny at p>=0.95 or an ask adds anything. The dr-dimitru plugin even suppresses ask in bypass mode. (2) In auto mode the Sonnet classifier is already a stronger judge and cannot be injected through tool results. A Jev allow would replace it for that call, weakening a layer. (3) Jev is documented as injectable and overconfident: exactly 1.0 on 56% of answers, wrong on 9 of them, and one test moved accuracy from 96.5% to 26.5% with an appended line. No study measures the false-approve rate on real Claude Code Bash traffic against an adaptive adversary. (4) Client-project code, commands, edits and MCP output go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, and none of the tools has a real per-project opt-out. (5) Latency is one round trip of 0.2 to 0.8 s or more per non-allowlisted call, and it stacks on the gitnexus hooks. (6) Every tool is under two weeks old. It becomes worth it only as an audit-first, deny-side or shadow-mode layer on personal projects, or as a small self-written cookbook-style hook you fully control.

bestPick.name: jev-bouncer (alsoleg89)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad of an immature field, not something I would trust yet. It is the only one adversarially verified as automatic, config-only switchable to OpenRouter (/api/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13), zero context cost, and it defaults to dry mode with a local log and calibrate tooling for the shadow rollout the evidence recommends. Use it only after reading the 81 KB bouncer.py yourself, in mode=dry then mode=guard (never on), with edits, mcp and scan turned off for client projects, and with OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to no-secret-leak.cjs's protected list first.

security-guard.runnerUp: Reflex (ursuciprian/reflex) if you want native OpenRouter support with no key or model renaming, but it is unverified and fail-closed in enforce mode. Otherwise the ClemensSchartmueller Go jev-guard (best tests and CI, but it hard-denies in bypass).
security-guard.recommendationForUser: Category verdict: situational, and not yet worth wiring into every session. Because you run auto and bypassPermissions, the native auto-mode classifier plus your no-secret-leak hook already do the job. A Jev allow would only replace a stronger judge, and in bypass a Jev tripwire mostly changes nothing. If you still want to try, first add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak.cjs, then install jev-bouncer after reading bouncer.py, run it in dry mode on personal projects for 1 to 2 weeks, and check its log against what you would have approved. Consider moving to mode=guard, deny only, with scan, edits and mcp off for client work. For an allow-side saver, I would instead build the small PermissionRequest cookbook hook described above, fail-open to the normal prompt, and skip anything that runs a plugin daemon or checks every tool result.

decision-mcp.summary: Decision-MCP servers wrap Jev's Noul/Choice/Score primitives as MCP tools (classify, check, score, rank, verify, gate) that Claude may call. Of 126 members reviewed, roughly 90% are model-discretion tools and about 70% are 0 to 5 star repos under 3 weeks old. Around 12 have real OpenRouter routing in code. Nothing in this category makes Claude call Jev on its own. The only candidates that fire automatically ship hooks (jevwire, master-jev-hook, jev-use gate) and are young and invasive.
decision-mcp.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already has the auto-mode classifier (Sonnet-class, sees user messages, tool calls and CLAUDE.md). It also has deterministic PreToolUse regex and deny rules, and prompt and agent hooks that return {ok, reason} using a background model you can set. Opus can also do any judgment inline, or in a cheap Haiku or Sonnet subagent via CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL, with free-text reasoning and better accuracy. Jev is faster (p50 about 200 ms), very cheap ($0.042 per 1M input tokens) and returns typed probabilities. It is also a bit less accurate than mid-price LLMs, overconfident on unanswerable inputs, movable by injected text in state, on an alpha endpoint with no SLA and a 32k context, and it sends data to a third party. For a strong main model doing coding decisions, the built-ins win. Jev's niche is cheap bulk triage and scoring of many items, or a low-latency yes/no gate you build yourself.

bestPick.name: FrancoisChastel/jev-code
bestPick.reason: Highest verified score (7). Native OpenRouter routing, small tool surface, no hooks to wedge a session, fail-visible errors, large test suite. Least-bad rather than trustworthy: it is 3 days old, has no npm provenance, is discretionary only, and needs TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-1.13 and a doctor --live check first.

decision-mcp.runnerUp: itsmostafa/system-one-connector (verified 6.5): single read-only tool, Go binary, OpenRouter native, 337 stars. Register it by hand with an env wrapper, pin a tag, use --no-update-check, and pass model explicitly to avoid the floating alias. jkudish/jev-mcp (verified 6.5) is the richer alternative with 12 tools but heavier schemas.
decision-mcp.recommendationForUser: Skip this category as an always-on layer: no MCP here makes Claude use Jev automatically, and Opus plus the built-in auto-mode classifier and your own regex hooks already cover the judgment work with better accuracy. If you want to experiment, hand-register FrancoisChastel/jev-code (with TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-1.13 and a doctor --live check) or itsmostafa/system-one-connector on personal projects only, pinned, with a capped OpenRouter key. Before that, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY and mcp__jev__* to your no-secret-leak matcher. Keep it off client repos. If you truly want automatic gating, write the small fail-open PermissionRequest script described above and run it in shadow mode first, remembering it will rarely fire under your auto and bypass habits.

task-mcp.summary: Task-specific Jev MCP servers and skills are small wrappers that take a diff, test log, file set or claim, send it to Jev as typed questions, and return scores or verdicts (review scoring, claim verification, injection screening, bulk relevance filtering, CI triage). About 29 candidates were reviewed. Nearly all are 1 to 14 days old, single-author, alpha, and 0 to 90 stars (the 231-star niazmorshed2007/jev-review is a TypeSafe-only outlier). They are advisory tools that Claude calls at its own discretion. None gives deterministic automatic use, and none has been tested against real Claude Code traffic. OpenRouter support is native in only a few (tracecheck, jev-judge-mcp, paulrobello, jev-funnel). Most others are TypeSafe-only but switchable through OpenRouter's documented TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or QUICKSILVER_API_BASE overrides.
task-mcp.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already provides: the auto-mode classifier (Sonnet-class, sees user messages and tool calls, blocks exfiltration and risky actions), prompt and agent hooks (a Haiku-class or chosen model as a single-turn ok/reason judge), Stop and PostToolUse hooks with additionalContext, the /code-review and /security-review skills, subagents for review, and Claude itself running tests and reading logs. Jev is cheaper (about $0.042/M input tokens) and faster (p50 about 200 ms), but independent evals put it at or slightly below mid-price LLMs, poorly calibrated on unanswerable inputs (overconfident) and steerable by injected text. Opus 5.5 running the test suite and reading its own diff is more accurate for review and triage. A prompt hook on Haiku is a similar-cost, more accurate second opinion with no third-party code or off-machine hop beyond Anthropic. Jev's only real edge is cheap bulk relevance filtering and sub-second yes/no gating.
task-mcp.worthItReason: The user's goal is Jev used automatically with no prompting. This category cannot meet that: every MCP or skill option is model-discretion, and the hook options are narrow or unusable as shipped. The project's own bench shows 0 of 150 auto-calls, and an agent-outcome study shows no accuracy gain and +4.6 s median. Jev quality is a poor fit for review and verification: Noul ECE is 0.169 and Choice 0.226 on 4,995 coding-agent decisions, and vulnerable-code accuracy is 71.5%. One appended line can flip accuracy from 96.5% to 26.5%. Diffs, logs and files go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the alpha endpoint has no SLA. That matters for client projects, and the existing no-secret-leak hook does not cover MCP or CLI egress. In auto and bypass modes the Opus 5.5 main model and the classifier already make these calls, so a Jev advisory adds a turn without gating anything. There is value in two narrow places: bulk closed-set triage of many files or log lines (quicksilver-style, cost about $0.006 for 500 items), and a deterministic rules-first test-failure hook. Use them only on personal repos, pinned, after a shadow period.

bestPick.name: uditakhourii/quicksilver
bestPick.reason: Least-bad rather than trustworthy. It is the lowest-overhead verified option (no MCP, no hook, about 190 tokens always-on, config-only OpenRouter switch) and it targets Jev's real strength, bulk relevance triage. Use it only from a locally pinned, read-through copy with jev-1.13 pinned, a Bash allow rule for the exact qs.mjs path, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY plus the JEV_API_KEY alias added to the no-secret-leak list. Skip client repos, and do not trust qs status on OpenRouter. It will not fire automatically in any guaranteed way.

task-mcp.runnerUp: bmccarn/tracecheck for native OpenRouter support and the most disciplined review-verification design (local secret screen, size cap, fail-closed on screen hits), or PyModel/jev-judge-mcp as a reference kit. Among verified items, buchmark/claude-jev is next. All three stay model-discretion advisory tools.
task-mcp.recommendationForUser: Treat this category as optional and mostly skippable. Your Opus 5.5 main model and the auto-mode classifier already do review, triage and gating better than Jev, and no candidate here makes Jev fire automatically. If you want one, use quicksilver on personal repos only, as a pinned local copy with jev-1.13, a Bash allow rule for the exact script path, and the key names added to no-secret-leak first, accepting that it triggers only on bulk triage. For anything automatic, write a small rules-first PostToolUse test-triage hook that returns additionalContext JSON and fails open, with shadow logging, rather than installing a third-party gate, and never let Jev alone allow or deny an action in your bypass sessions.

prompt-steering.summary: Prompt-steering Jev integrations sit in Claude Code hooks. A small typed Jev call (Noul, Choice or Score) classifies a prompt, an edit diff or a turn. The result becomes injected context, a block, or a repair request. Of 24 members, only a handful are automatic and fail-open. Most are advisory labels (task type, coaching, skill routing) that add cost with little value for a senior dev on Opus 5.5. The two worth a look are abide (edit and turn rule checks against AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, config-only OpenRouter route) and claude-jev (rules and compaction). Both are about 12 days old, single-team, and untested against OpenRouter in practice.
prompt-steering.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already has several native routes. The auto-mode classifier (Sonnet-class, sees CLAUDE.md and tool calls) decides permissions. Prompt and agent hooks run an LLM judge with a JSON verdict. CLAUDE.md, skills and path-scoped rules steer Claude directly. Opus itself can judge any of these questions. Compared with these, Jev is cheap ($0.042/M input, output free) and fast (p50 about 200 ms, p95 about 600 ms), and it returns typed probabilities that code can threshold. But it is no more accurate: independent tests put it a bit below mid-price LLMs, overconfident on unanswerable input (KoBBQ fell from 0.95 to 0.00 accuracy when "unknown" was removed), and injectable through text in state. It is on an /alpha endpoint with no SLA, and it sends code and commands to a third party. A native prompt hook on a small model gives similar judgment with no new vendor. Jev wins only on latency and cost for high-volume, bounded yes/no checks.
prompt-steering.worthItReason: Nothing here covers general daily coding. The value is narrow: enforcing prose rules from CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md that linters cannot check (for example "don't commit unless asked"), or a shadow-mode permission helper. The independent evidence supports Jev only for bounded, text-recoverable decisions. Action gate was 100/111 vs 102/111 for Opus. Tool-call risk was 55/60. The p>=0.85 band was right in sec-bench. It fails on ambiguous or unanswerable input, out-of-distribution shift (a dependency auto-merge gate had 15 unsafe merges), and injected approval text. Every gating design must therefore be allow-side or advisory, with deterministic rules owning safety. Your habits make the case weaker. In auto and bypass modes the classifier and bypass already skip prompts, so a Jev "skip the prompt" helper has almost nothing to do. PermissionRequest rarely fires there. Only PreToolUse deny/ask and Stop/PostToolUse feedback still bite, and those add unattended repair loops driven by an overconfident model. Privacy is the second cost. Diffs (up to 24k chars), commands and the last prompt leave the machine, unredacted, to OpenRouter and its provider. That is a problem on client projects, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not yet in your no-secret-leak protected list. Latency of about 1 s per edit stacks on gitnexus. None of these tools has been measured against real Claude Code traffic with an adaptive adversary. Adopt one integration, in shadow or project-scoped mode, on personal repos only, if you have many prose rules. Otherwise skip the category.

bestPick.name: coldteadotai/abide
bestPick.reason: Highest verified score (7). It is automatic, fail-open, bounded, near-zero context cost, project-scopable, and reaches OpenRouter with env vars only (bare jev-latest is mapped by OpenRouter docs). Use it only on personal repos, and only after fixing these gaps. First, install it globally at a stable path with an absolute node path. Second, keep the base URL only in ~/.abide/.env, never a repo .env. Third, add TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak list. Fourth, run it in observe or report mode for 1-2 weeks and check `abide report`. It is not proven: 12 days old, v0.0.7, not tested on OpenRouter by its authors. If you have few prose rules in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md, it will do little.

prompt-steering.runnerUp: 0x7067/claude-jev, with promptRouter and subagentRouter off and only rules (and optionally compaction) on. First fix its bare-node hooks and the unconditional per-Bash git snapshot, and add Edit/Write coverage to your secret hook. Otherwise, doronp/jevc for a single observe-mode commit-consent gate using model jev-latest.
prompt-steering.recommendationForUser: Treat this category as optional, not core. Your auto and bypass modes leave a Jev permission helper with little to do, and none of these tools has an independent track record. If you have many prose rules in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md that lint cannot check, try abide with --project on one personal repo. Use the env-only OpenRouter route and an absolute node path. Keep the base URL out of repo .env files. Add the OpenRouter and TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY names to no-secret-leak first. Run it in report-only mode for 1-2 weeks and keep it off client repos until you have read what it sends. Skip the prompt-router and skill-router plugins. If you want Jev to "just work" as a permission helper, write the 80-line PermissionRequest hook from the cookbook in log-only mode and validate it on your own labeled history before it can allow anything.

skill-tool-router.summary: This category asks Jev, before or during a turn, which installed skill, agent, MCP tool or model/effort setting fits the current prompt. It then injects a one-line hint, a skill pointer or a routing override. Most of the 52 members are UserPromptSubmit hooks (Jev Choice over a skill roster plus Noul gate questions). A few are MCP servers or CLIs the model must call itself, one is a local proxy on ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, and one is a function-hooks plugin. Most are days to weeks old, single-author, and 0-10 stars. The high-star items (jev-gateway 267, jevrouter 301, skillbox 255, skillranker 125) are not proof of quality, and only two of them are hook-based. The category answers a problem this user barely has: 13 personal skills, a 2% listing budget, and Opus 5.5 that already reads skill descriptions well.
skill-tool-router.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already lists every non-disabled skill with its description under skillListingBudgetFraction (2% here), and Opus 5.5 picks from that list. Beyond the budget, descriptions are dropped least-used first while names stay. Native levers cost nothing and send nothing off-machine: skillOverrides (name-only, off), disable-model-invocation, `paths:` frontmatter on skills, MCP tool search (deferred by default), and per-agent model frontmatter or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL. The auto-mode classifier and prompt/agent hooks cover approval decisions natively. Jev is cheaper and faster (~$0.042/M, p50 ~200-400 ms) than a Haiku/Sonnet prompt hook. Its accuracy is a bit below mid-price LLMs, though, and it cannot see the conversation beyond what the hook forwards. Authors' own data show 24% needless suggestions and confident wrong picks, and 3 suggestions in 34 turns for another hook. The one unusual Jev strength here is cheap, many-way Noul gating over a very large roster (100+ skills), which this user does not have.
skill-tool-router.worthItReason: Benefit is marginal and unproven for this setup. Opus 5.5 already selects skills from native descriptions, and the user has only ~13 personal skills. Plugin skills (caveman, anthropic-skills) are often not even scanned by these tools. Every hook adds 0.3-2 s of synchronous latency to every prompt, stacked on the caveman UserPromptSubmit hook and the gitnexus hooks. Every prompt (and often recent transcript and skill descriptions) leaves the machine, which is a real confidentiality problem for client projects. The existing no-secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit and does not list OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Jev's known weaknesses hit exactly this task: overconfidence when no option is right (a "none" option is mandatory), a tendency to invent a tool (76% of When2Call no-tool cases), and prompt injection when the state contains hostile text (the prompt itself is the state). Nobody has measured an improvement in task outcomes on Claude Code with Opus. jev-pilot's own changelog says Opus 5.5 was already correct with or without the advice on its quality tasks. A hook never blocks under bypassPermissions, so safety is not the issue. The issue is cost, latency, egress and unproven gain. The better Jev use for this user is the OpenRouter cookbook PermissionRequest gate (a different category). Situational only if the skill library grows past what 2% of context can describe.

bestPick.name: jev-pilot (Akramovic1)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad, not trustworthy enough for a global default. It is the only verified candidate that is automatic and native to OpenRouter (/api/v1/systemone), and it fails open with a 1.5 s race timeout. Use it only as a cautious trial. Install by hand and pin the reviewed commit e61f801. Skip curl|bash and the claude-jev proxy. Set hideListing=false, designPack=false and routeMainEffort=false. Set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, keep the key in the plugin credential store, and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak protected list. It routes effort, model and skills rather than only suggesting skills, so review its other defaults, such as routeSubagentModel, before enabling.

skill-tool-router.runnerUp: holstered (tupe12334): verified, native OpenRouter and fail-open, and the narrowest and safest of the group. Run it only from a user-level settings.json hook with an absolute binary path (built from source), HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS near 2000, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY loaded from a 0600 file by a wrapper. Its value is small because it only scans ~13 personal skills.
skill-tool-router.recommendationForUser: Skip this category as a daily default. With about 13 personal skills, a 2% listing budget and Opus 5.5, native skill selection is already good, and every prompt-time hook adds latency and sends prompts (including client-project prompts) to OpenRouter for an unmeasured gain. If you still want to try one, use jev-pilot with the conservative settings, or holstered from a user-level hook with an absolute path. Run either in shadow or advise mode first, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to your no-secret-leak list, and disable it in client repos. Spend your Jev effort on the OpenRouter cookbook PermissionRequest gate for Bash instead.

stop-verifier.summary: Stop-verifier category: 29 members reviewed (10 audited from source, 2 deep-audited, 17 README-triaged), all Claude Code or Codex hooks or wrappers. Every serious one is a Stop hook. On turn end it sends the final reply (and sometimes tool calls, diffs or transcript excerpts) to Jev as Noul yes/no questions such as "claims something unverified", "stopped early", "violates a rule". Above a threshold it exits 2 with stderr, or returns decision:block, so Claude continues with the flagged point. This is the one category that satisfies "automatic, no 'use jev' prompt". The hook is deterministic, runs in auto and bypassPermissions alike, and costs no standing context. The evidence is thin, though. Every repo is 1-3 weeks old with 0-20 stars (Canny has 106 and only a minor Jev role), and none has been shown to improve Opus-class output. The one honest A/B (jevwatch, 28 runs) showed no gain. Limpet's own numbers show AUROC 0.50-0.64 and only 5-12% of bad stops caught at 5% false positives. Almost none has been tested on OpenRouter by its author. Egress is the main cost: every turn ships prose, tool output or diffs of your code to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, with regex-only or no redaction.
stop-verifier.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already offers: (1) type "prompt" and "agent" Stop hooks, where a Claude model reads the transcript and returns ok/reason, so an LLM verifier with no external egress; (2) a plain command Stop hook that checks deterministically (git diff shows edits, a test command ran, exit codes), with no model at all; (3) TaskCompleted and PostToolBatch hooks; (4) Claude itself, via CLAUDE.md "verify before claiming done", the /code-review skill, and a verifier subagent. Prompt hooks use the background model (Haiku-class) and stay inside your subscription, with no third-party data flow. Jev's edge is only price and speed: about $0.0002-0.0015 per check, p50 about 0.2-0.6 s, and a calibrated-ish number rather than free text. Its weaknesses are accuracy slightly below mid-price LLMs, overconfidence on unanswerable inputs, susceptibility to injected text in the state, and a 32k context on the alpha endpoint with no SLA. Deterministic checks (did tests run after the last edit) beat Jev for "done" criteria, which is why Canny and Belay gate on them first. Note the built-in alternatives cost subscription quota rather than cents.
stop-verifier.worthItReason: Upside: a Stop-time honesty check is the only place Jev integrates fully automatically. It is cheap, adds no per-tool-call latency (unlike your gitnexus hooks), works unattended in bypassPermissions sessions where a false "tests pass" claim costs most, and can be fail-open. Downsides: (1) Value is unproven. The only controlled A/B (jevwatch) showed no gain, Limpet's AUROC is 0.50-0.64, and independent evals show the high-probability band is reliable (p>=0.85 was right 100% in sec-bench) but calibration is poor, with 1.0 saturation and overconfidence on unanswerable inputs. That means false-positive extra Opus turns (subscription quota) and misses on the cases that matter. (2) Privacy is the blocker for client work. Every turn ships assistant prose, tool output, commands or diffs to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, redaction is regex-only or absent, and your no-secret-leak hook does not cover this channel. The OPENROUTER_API_KEY also needs adding to its protected list. (3) The stack is days old, single-author, mostly unlicensed or 0-star, and untested on OpenRouter, so the plugins would run with full privileges in bypass sessions. (4) A deterministic Stop hook (edited but no test run) plus a Claude prompt hook already covers most of the value without egress. Worth it only as a shadow-mode trial on personal repos, or as a cheap second layer over a deterministic gate. Not worth it as a default on client projects.

bestPick.name: greghavens/jev-no-bullshit
bestPick.reason: Highest verified score (7). It is a deterministic, fail-open, stdlib-only Stop hook that is OpenRouter-compatible with just TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key in ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env (the hardcoded 'jev-latest' is accepted by OpenRouter). It has real tests and CI, and needs no prompting. It is least-bad rather than trustworthy: no LICENSE, unredacted default-on egress, a week-old repo. Run it from a pinned local copy after reading the script, disable it per project (enabledPlugins false) on client repos, and start in personal repos only.

stop-verifier.runnerUp: valentynkit/jev-belay (score 5.5 verified). It has the narrowest egress, fires only when files were edited and no check passed, and has MIT and 20 stars. Use it only with JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13, shadow mode first, and after the pytest -q false-negative issue is fixed or accepted. If you want a code-quality gate instead of a claims gate, haystackeditor/stop-rules on one personal repo.
stop-verifier.recommendationForUser: Treat this category as an optional experiment, not a default. First add OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and any key file path) to no-secret-leak.cjs's protected list. Then try greghavens/jev-no-bullshit from a pinned local copy on one personal repo, with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, and count useful vs noisy flags over 1-2 weeks. Keep it off on client projects (enabledPlugins false there). If the flags are mostly noise, replace it with a deterministic Stop hook (edited but no test run) plus a Claude prompt hook, which give most of the benefit with no third-party egress.

compaction-memory.summary: The compaction-memory category uses Jev as a cheap yes/no scorer at two points. One is compaction, where Jev decides which old tool calls and results to keep, truncate or drop. The other is memory, where Jev decides which stored notes or facts are worth writing or recalling. About 40 repos exist. Most are forks or ports of tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction (7.2k stars). Many target other hosts (Pi, Codex, OpenCode, Cursor), use TypeSafe-direct or Vercel gateway only, or need the model to choose to call them. In Claude Code 2.1.285 the only way to replace the compaction summary is the undocumented, early-access "function hooks" API. That API needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, and the code in this space was written against 2.1.274 to 2.1.278. Documented hooks cannot do it: PreCompact can only block, PostCompact is read-only, and SessionStart(compact) can only add context. Every automatic candidate is days old and single-author, with 0 to 99 stars on the real ones. All of them send transcript or prompt excerpts to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe.
compaction-memory.builtInAlternative: Natively, Claude Code has: the built-in LLM compaction and auto-compact (Opus 5.5 with a large window rarely hits it); /compact with a focus argument; a "Compact Instructions" section in CLAUDE.md; SessionStart with matcher "compact" returning additionalContext to re-inject pinned notes (the only documented steering route); auto-memory, CLAUDE.md and MEMORY files; and PreCompact, which can only block. Jev pruning keeps text verbatim and is fast (about 0.5 s and $0.0003 per compaction in one self-reported session, against a multi-second LLM summary). It also does not hallucinate a summary. The costs: it silently drops tool results Jev scores low; Jev is overconfident on unanswerable inputs and steerable by injected text in tool output; there is no narrative summary of decisions and progress; and the transcript leaves the machine. On a subscription login the money saved is negligible, so the only real benefits are latency and verbatim fidelity. For memory, native auto-memory and CLAUDE.md already cover most of what jevmem does. Jev adds only relevance filtering per prompt.
compaction-memory.worthItReason: The narrow upside is faster, verbatim compaction and per-prompt memory recall. The downsides for this user are heavy. (1) Every real compaction integration depends on the undocumented function-hooks flag, and nothing has been verified on 2.1.285. It may break silently on update. (2) They send tool inputs (bash commands, diffs, Write content, file paths) and prompts to a no-SLA /alpha OpenRouter endpoint and then TypeSafe, with only regex secret masking. That is a real client-confidentiality issue under auto and bypassPermissions sessions, where many unreviewed commands run. Only ingebyd pins zdr:true and data_collection:deny. cc-mod-jev sends none. (3) Jev's independent quality evidence is weak where it matters: injection-flippable answers, overconfident on unanswerable input, and calibration ECE around 0.17 to 0.23 on coding-agent decisions. A wrong low score deletes the one tool result you later need, and that is hard to notice. (4) Evidence of benefit is thin: fast-compact's own bench shows only about +2 points over "keep the newest", within CI. cc-mod-jev's headline (314k to 11.4k tokens) is one best-case session. (5) Compaction is rare with Opus 5.5's window. Latency is not an issue, since none of them touch per-tool hooks. It is worth trying only on personal projects, with a pinned commit and shadow logging.

bestPick.name: jevmem (avinash-jetwani)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad and best fit, not trustworthy enough for client work. It is the highest verified score (6.5) and the only automatic integration on stable documented command hooks, with no function-hooks flag. It is opt-in per project, fail-open, and has a documented OpenRouter base-URL swap. Use it only on personal, trusted repos with a pinned version. Do not enable it in client repos because of the per-prompt egress and the project .env endpoint-override risk.

compaction-memory.runnerUp: JayDoubleu/cc-mod-jev (jev-context), score 6. Use it if you want Jev in compaction rather than memory: OpenRouter-native and the most restrained egress at compaction time. Keep the gate off, pin commit 9c526c2, put the key in the plugin's sensitive apiKey option (not settings env), and try it on personal projects only.
compaction-memory.recommendationForUser: Treat this category as optional and experimental. The one thing worth trying is jevmem on a few personal, trusted repos: pin the version, use a dedicated low-limit OpenRouter key placed in a 0600 file (and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak's protected list), and run it for a week with a check on what it injects. If you want Jev-guided compaction, try cc-mod-jev with the gate off on personal projects only; it needs the function-hooks flag and a pinned commit, and you should confirm it loads on 2.1.285 first. Keep both off client repos. For everything else, the free native route (CLAUDE.md Compact Instructions plus a SessionStart(compact) re-injection hook) already covers most of the value.

dev-skill.summary: The dev-skill category is about 62 skills, docs, CLIs and SDK wrappers that teach Claude how to write code that calls Jev. Most are inert knowledge skills (SKILL.md and references) that load only when the task mentions Jev or TypeSafe. A minority ship a small stdlib CLI (okooo5km/jev, jevify, Barba-Tech jev.py, decide, lazniak) that Claude can call through Bash. Only a few ship hook code (KHAEntertainment/jev-skill gate template, dariofontanel prompts), and none installs a hook on its own. Nothing here makes Claude Code use Jev automatically during ordinary coding, which is your core goal. I read the 23 audits, the 5 deep audits, the 34 triage rows and the adversarial verifications. I ran nothing and cloned nothing.
dev-skill.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already covers most of this natively. The auto-mode classifier (Sonnet 5 by default) makes permission decisions with server-side review. Prompt and agent hooks (prompt hooks return {ok,reason}) and plain command hooks can gate tool calls. Opus 5.5 itself does the judgment at far higher accuracy than Jev on open-ended and code-related questions. Independent evals put Jev a bit below mid-price LLMs, with ECE around 0.17 to 0.23 on coding-agent decisions and injection sensitivity. Jev's edge is roughly 200 ms latency and $0.042 per million input tokens, which matters only for high-volume bounded decisions. It does not matter for a single interactive session. For your auto and bypass modes, the native classifier and PreToolUse deny hooks already exist. Jev adds a second, weaker opinion.
dev-skill.worthItReason: The category does not deliver what you want, which is automatic Jev use. All 62 members are either knowledge skills or model-discretion CLI wrappers, and Opus rarely reaches for Jev in ordinary coding. The hook-shaped items are templates, not integrations. A PermissionRequest hook is the official cookbook pattern, but it fires only when a permission prompt would show. That means never in bypassPermissions, and in auto mode only for ask rules or hook-forced asks. A PreToolUse gate can only deny or ask in practice, so it adds latency and prompts and removes none. Jev quality also caps the upside. Bounded action-gate accuracy is comparable to Opus on small n (100/111 vs 102/111, p about 0.75). Out of distribution it is overconfident, probabilities saturate at 1.0 on 56% of answers, and appended evidence-like text flipped accuracy from 96.5% to 26.5%. Commands and diffs would leave the machine to an /alpha endpoint with no SLA, which is a real concern for client projects. The category is worth using only as reference material when you hand-build one narrow hook, not as an installed capability.

bestPick.name: okooo5km/jev
bestPick.reason: Least-bad option, not a real answer to your goal. It is the most auditable OpenRouter-native, zero-dependency, well-tested client (verified). Vendor the single file, pin JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter in the settings env block, and use it as a building block for your own hook, with --timeout 3 --retries 0. It does not make Claude use Jev automatically.

dev-skill.runnerUp: altryne/jevify (https://github.com/altryne/jevify). It is the only member explicitly written to auto-trigger without the user mentioning Jev, at about 110 tokens of context. It is a soft, model-discretion nudge whose scan.py fits bulk log and document shortlisting, not daily coding.
dev-skill.recommendationForUser: Do not install anything from this category expecting automatic Jev use, because none delivers it. If you want OpenRouter Jev in the loop, vendor okooo5km/jev (read the single file, set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter in the settings env block, and pin typesafe/jev-1.13) and write the small PermissionRequest hook from the OpenRouter cookbook. Only allow when both Noul answers are at least 0.95, fail open to the prompt, and run it in shadow mode first. Expect it to matter only in auto mode on ask-path calls, never in your bypass sessions. Add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak.cjs before exporting it. Optionally install the single OpenRouter openrouter-decisions skill via gh skill install as a design helper, and skip the rest.

model-router.summary: The model-router category has about 100 Jev tools. They use Jev to decide which Claude model or reasoning effort a turn or subagent gets. It splits into three groups. (1) Local ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxies or launchers (switchboard, dirien/jev-router, automodel, jevcc, alexei-led) that rewrite model and effort in the upstream request. (2) Hooks and plugins (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse on Agent) that rewrite the subagent model or inject an advisory hint or effort directive. (3) Skills, libraries and clones aimed at Codex, Pi, OpenCode or OpenAI, which are irrelevant to Claude Code. All of them answer one narrow question: which tier or effort to use. None gives Claude a general "ask Jev when it adds value" capability, and none does permission gating. Most are 1 to 14 days old, single-author and have 0 to 15 stars. Few call OpenRouter natively.
model-router.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already offers most of this natively and deterministically. You have /model and /effort. Subagents take a `model` argument or frontmatter, and CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL sets a default. You can write an agent file with a fixed cheap model for exploration. Prompt hooks (single-turn, background model) and Claude itself can also judge "is this task hard" for free inside the turn. Auto mode already runs a server-side classifier for permissions. Compared with these, Jev has real strengths: a typed, probabilistic answer, about 200 ms latency, roughly $0.00002 per call, and no reasoning tokens. Its weaknesses are large. Accuracy is below mid-price LLMs. It is overconfident on unanswerable inputs (short follow-ups like "yes, do it"). Injected text in state can move answers. And a router can only downgrade an Opus 5.5 user, which saves nothing on a flat subscription and risks quality. The built-in options never leave your machine.
model-router.worthItReason: For this user the category is mostly not worth it, and it is not what the user asked for. Opus 5.5 is already the top tier and the login is a flat-rate subscription. So routing can only downgrade quality (Sonnet or Haiku on a real task) or lower effort, and cost savings barely matter. Jev's independent evals show accuracy a bit below mid-price LLMs, overconfidence on short or ambiguous prompts, and steerability by injected text. Those are exactly the weaknesses a prompt classifier meets. The proxy tools (switchboard, dirien, automodel, jevcc) put a single-maintainer, days-old binary in front of ALL Claude and OAuth traffic. That includes client work and the auto-mode classifier, and it disables tool search and Remote Control. The dirien verification also found that auxiliary requests (including the classifier) may be re-routed to Haiku. Prompt text also goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which is a problem for client projects. Latency is +0.2 to 3 s per prompt, on top of your gitnexus and caveman hooks. The only defensible slice is subagent-only routing, where the main model and prompt cache stay untouched. It is a hook on Agent that downgrades read-only exploration to Sonnet or Haiku, with a fail-open path and a shadow period first. That is a nice-to-have. It does not deliver "Jev used automatically whenever it adds value", which fits the permission gate and action-review categories better.

bestPick.name: davila7 claude-code-templates: jev-model-router mod (subagent routing only)
bestPick.reason: This is the least-bad option, not a strong one. It is the only automatic Jev router that needs no ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy, keeps OAuth traffic direct to Anthropic, and is verified fail-open on the router half. Use it with routeMainEffort off, run it in observe mode first, put the key in via /config, copy only the jev-model-router mod folder, and skip the sibling skill-suggestion mod. It rests on an early-access hook API, has no OpenRouter or live tests, and sends prompts to OpenRouter, so treat it as an experiment.

model-router.runnerUp: psadventure/jev-model-router. It is a 176-line OpenRouter-native PreToolUse hook on Agent that you can audit in minutes and use as a template for a self-written version. stas4000/claude-subagent-router (score 4) is a good reference implementation of the pattern, with a Choice question, regex fallback and 12 s deadline, but it needs its own agents and denies Sonnet overrides. Neither is a plug-and-play install.
model-router.recommendationForUser: Skip the proxy and launcher routers. They add a single point of failure and an OAuth trust surface for a benefit you do not need, since you already run Opus 5.5 on a flat subscription. If you want to try the category, use only subagent-level routing: install just the davila7 jev-model-router mod, or write the small PreToolUse Agent hook described above. Start in shadow mode, keep main-effort routing off, use client-safe privacy settings, and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak protected list first. To have Jev help automatically, you would get more from a PermissionRequest gate or an action-review hook (the OpenRouter cookbook pattern, fail-open to the normal prompt) than from a model router, so evaluate those categories before this one.

routesLegend.claude: picks or suggests a Claude tier (Haiku/Sonnet/Opus/Fable) for the main turn or subagents; the service used to decide (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) does not matter
routesLegend.mixed: picks between Claude tiers and other vendors (Codex, GPT, Gemini, OpenRouter models)
routesLegend.provider-pool: picks from an OpenRouter, LiteLLM, gateway or YAML pool of models from several providers
routesLegend.effort-only: sets or suggests reasoning effort, never switches model
routesLegend.other: routes between agents, apps or another harness (Pi, OpenCode, Hermes, Cursor...), or is not a model router

code-search-nav.summary: This category is Jev used as a relevance judge for code search: it turns a query into many yes/no (Noul) questions over files, chunks, functions or diff hunks, then ranks or filters by probability. Nothing here is a hook on Grep. The integrations are CLIs called through Bash and driven by a skill description or CLAUDE.md nudge, or MCP servers, or, in two cases (oko, the Read-narrowing jev plugin), MCP plus hooks. Every one uploads the judged source text to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. Jev's accuracy is a bit below mid-price LLMs, it is overconfident on unanswerable inputs, and instructions injected in file text can shift answers. Claude Code already has Grep/Glob/Read, Explore subagents and your gitnexus graph tools, so the marginal value is concept-level 'where is X handled' queries and diff filtering in unfamiliar repos. All ten candidates are 2 to 12 days old and single-maintainer. Only oko and jegrep were adversarially verified.
code-search-nav.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already does file discovery with Grep, Glob, Read and Explore subagents, and you have gitnexus (graph query/context/impact, plus your seconds-long PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook) on top. Opus 5.5 is a far better judge of code relevance than Jev, which scores a bit below mid-price LLMs and is overconfident on unanswerable queries. Opus costs tokens on a subscription, but no client code leaves the machine. Jev's real edge is cost and parallelism: about $0.0015 to $0.005 per search, a p50 of about 200 ms per call, and it can screen thousands of functions or chunks without spending Claude context. That is useful for broad behavioural discovery in a repo you do not know, and for filtering big diffs. It does not replace exact-symbol Grep or gitnexus, and it is worse on precision.
code-search-nav.worthItReason: The value is real but narrow. Jev is cheap (about $0.042 per 1M input tokens) and fast (p50 about 200 ms), and semantic screening of many files or hunks is something Grep cannot do. Against that: Opus plus gitnexus already answers most 'where is X' questions better, and Jev's independent evals show accuracy below mid-price LLMs, overconfidence (exactly 1.0 on 56% of answers) and vulnerability to injected file text. The larger blocker is privacy. Every tool uploads source chunks to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on the /alpha endpoint (no SLA), most with only filename-based secret filtering, and in your bypassPermissions sessions nothing prompts before a bulk upload. That rules it out for client projects without consent. Nothing here is truly automatic (only oko and the Read-narrowing plugin are near it), and all candidates are under two weeks old. It is worth a shadow trial on personal repos only.

bestPick.name: oko (bartlomein)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad and the only near-automatic option: alwaysLoad MCP tool plus non-blocking hooks, verified to work on OpenRouter by setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL alone. Still 12-day-old single-author alpha code that uploads snippets and installs per project, so pin a release, try it on a personal repo first, and never on client repos.

code-search-nav.runnerUp: jegrep (can1357): best engineering and secret handling, native OpenRouter, zero standing context. Pass --model typesafe/jev-1.13 --only openrouter --json, and add your own CLAUDE.md line, since it is not automatic.
code-search-nav.recommendationForUser: Category is situational, so do not wire Jev into your default workflow. First add OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and any key files these tools create) to no-secret-leak.cjs. Then trial jegrep (pinned release binary, --only openrouter --model typesafe/jev-1.13 --json) on personal repos only, with one CLAUDE.md line limiting it to concept-level 'where is X' questions and diff screening. If you want the automatic-use experience, pilot oko per project on a personal repo and watch how it interacts with your gitnexus hook. Keep client repos off every one of these and skip the Read-narrowing hook entirely in bypass mode. Your PreToolUse hooks are the deterministic layer, and Jev should never replace them.

library-harness.summary: The library-harness category is building blocks (SDKs, clients, gate libraries, hook installers) for calling Jev, not ready-made Claude Code integrations. Almost none can make Claude Code use Jev automatically without glue code. The few with a Claude Code surface are hook installers (oh-my-harness, yfe404/jev-harness) or skill-plus-CLI bundles (onesie, jevkit CLI, fuzzy-jev). The rest target Pi, Codex, Spring, Rust, Go or Ruby apps, or need a base-URL swap to reach OpenRouter. The only OpenRouter-blessed path is the official @typesafe-ai/sdk plus OpenRouter's own cookbook hook. I ran nothing; this is from static reading and the adversarial verifications.
library-harness.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already has the auto-mode classifier (Sonnet 5 by default, sees user messages, tool calls and CLAUDE.md, never tool results), allow/ask/deny rules, prompt and agent hooks (single-turn LLM judgment with a background model), and Claude itself. Jev is cheaper ($0.042 per 1M input tokens, output free) and faster (p50 ~200 ms, p95 ~600 ms) than a Sonnet call, and returns typed probabilities. It is not more accurate: independent evals put it around Sonnet 5 / Opus 5 on bounded action gates (100/111 vs 102/111, 55/60 vs the same as Sonnet 5), with imperfect calibration (overconfident on unanswerable inputs, p=1.0 on 56% of answers) and injection sensitivity. A built-in prompt hook gives similar gating with no new vendor, no egress to OpenRouter's alpha endpoint, and no extra secret. Jev's only real edge is latency and cost on a high-frequency hook.
library-harness.worthItReason: Nothing here delivers "automatic when it adds value" out of the box. Most members are SDKs for other stacks, and the Claude Code ones are per-project, alpha, days old, and self-benchmarked. In your auto mode the native classifier already decides most Bash calls, and PermissionRequest hooks only see the residual ask-path, so the friction Jev could remove is small. In bypass sessions there are no prompts to remove, so the only useful role is a deny/ask PreToolUse tripwire, which deterministic regex already does better. Jev's limits matter: 89.7-96.5% injection detection with context, accuracy 71.5% on code with ECE 0.19, saturated p=1.0, false approvals out of distribution, and injected text in state can flip answers. Every command leaves the machine to a 32k-context /alpha endpoint with no SLA, which matters for client projects, and your no-secret-leak hook does not yet protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It is worth building only as a small shadow-mode, allow-side, fail-open hook after 1-2 weeks of logged would-allow data. Adopting a packaged harness is not worth it.

bestPick.name: @typesafe-ai/sdk (official TypeScript SDK), as the base of a self-written hook
bestPick.reason: Least-bad, not trustworthy as a packaged integration. It is the only verified item that is vendor-blessed for OpenRouter (baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api, model jev-1.13 pinned), dependency-free, telemetry-free and gives typed errors for clean fail-open. Nothing in the category is safe or calibrated enough to install as an off-the-shelf gate. A plain fetch hook following the OpenRouter cookbook is an equally good alternative.

library-harness.runnerUp: onesie (frodi-karlsson/onesie), verified score 5: native OpenRouter, static binary, --print-request/--mock and timeout flags make it a decent CLI to call from your own hook wrapper. Do not use its shipped shell-safety gate as-is (it asks on every network command) and do not install its skills. oh-my-harness is the pattern to copy, not the package to install.
library-harness.recommendationForUser: Do not install any packaged harness from this category. If you want Jev in the loop, write the small dependency-free PermissionRequest (or allow/ask-only PreToolUse) hook described above, following OpenRouter's cookbook: regex never-gate list first, two Noul checks at >=0.95, 1.5-2 s timeout, and fail open to the normal prompt. Run it in shadow mode for 1-2 weeks and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to your no-secret-leak protected vars before anything else. Given your auto and bypass habits, the native classifier and your existing deterministic hooks cover most of the value, so expect a small gain; skip it for client projects unless egress is acceptable.

suite-plugin.summary: Suite plugins bundle several Jev-backed behaviours into one Claude Code install: PreToolUse and PermissionRequest-style risk gates, UserPromptSubmit routing hints, PostToolUse injection screening or output pruning, Stop "did you really finish" checks, subagent model routing, and experimental compaction replacement. Some also add a skill, an MCP tool or a CLI. About 55 repos were reviewed. Nearly all are 1 to 12 days old, single-author, 0 to 30 stars and unreplicated. Roughly half are TypeSafe-only, and a few of those are trivially switchable through a base-URL variable. No suite has independent field evidence that it helps an Opus-main user. The one field report (klukacin) says it cost more time than it saved and the author abandoned it.
suite-plugin.builtInAlternative: Auto mode already runs a server-side classifier (Sonnet 5 or better) that sees the user messages, tool calls and CLAUDE.md, and it has deny and fallback logic. bypassPermissions removes prompts entirely. PreToolUse deny still wins in every mode. Native `prompt` and `agent` hooks can ask Claude a yes/no question on Stop, PermissionRequest and similar events, with a configurable model. Opus 5.5 itself does classification, routing, done-checks and injection awareness with much better accuracy, and it can be pointed at a cheaper model by native subagent `model` frontmatter or CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL. Jev is faster (p50 about 200 ms) and about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, but its accuracy is a bit below mid-price LLMs, its calibration is imperfect, and injected text in state can move its answers. Its only real edge is cheap, typed, low-latency yes/no gating on the allow side, for example the OpenRouter cookbook PermissionRequest gate. That gate would sit in front of prompts that auto mode or the user would otherwise see. It never fires on actions the classifier auto-approves or that bypass mode skips.
suite-plugin.worthItReason:
As installable suites, mostly no. As a building block for a small self-written hook, situational. Against installing one:
- Evidence is thin. The only end-to-end benchmark (Gilbert09, 1,176 sessions) is haiku/sonnet only, shows no gain on Sonnet and never tested Opus. klukacin logged about 18,000 decisions, found 126 minutes of added Bash-gate latency and no prevented incidents, then abandoned the plugin. griffinwork40/claude-jev measured 9.3% false blocks on real accepted edits.
- The user's habits neutralise most of the value. In bypassPermissions there is no prompt for a gate to save. A hook "ask" is undocumented there, and dansya's harness turns ask into a silent pass in bypass. In auto mode the Sonnet classifier is already the arbiter. The PermissionRequest hook only fires on the ask path, so it helps only where a prompt would otherwise appear.
- Jev quality limits matter for safety gating. It is overconfident on unanswerable inputs, its probabilities saturate at 1.0 on 56% of answers, and it is injection-sensitive. It is fine for a bounded allow-side gate behind deterministic rules and only at p >= 0.95, but not for anything that should deny or protect.
- Privacy is the biggest cost. Most suites send prompts, diffs, tool outputs (up to 40 KB per read in Gilbert09, 4 KB in truthsayer) or Bash commands to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. Redaction is regex best effort, and several suites have none. That is a problem for client work. The /alpha endpoint has no SLA.
- Cost of stacking: extra synchronous hooks on Bash/Read/Edit add latency on top of gitnexus, plus fail-closed no-secret-leak, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not yet in the protected-vars list.
Worth using only as a deliberate, shadow-mode, allow-side prompt reducer on personal repos.

bestPick.name: garygentry/system1
bestPick.reason: Least-bad, not trustworthy enough for unattended use. It is the only suite that is both verified OpenRouter-native and fail-open with near-zero context cost. Use it only with SYSTEM1_ENDPOINT pinned in the environment, a dedicated low-limit OpenRouter key, and .system1/config.yaml reviewed in every freshly cloned repo, or kept off client repos. Without the pin, a cloned repo can redirect your OpenRouter key.

suite-plugin.runnerUp: danielhirt/truthsayer, run in log mode only. It has the safest trust boundary (a project file cannot redirect the endpoint or key) and a shadow-first rollout that matches the recommended 1 to 2 week trial. Install it pinned with `cargo install --rev`, set the model explicitly to typesafe/jev-1.13, and keep mode=off on client repos. Nasrallah-AL/jevctl is the pick if you would rather build your own hook on a tested CLI.
suite-plugin.recommendationForUser: Don't install a whole suite. It buys little for an Opus 5.5 user in auto or bypass mode, and it egresses client code. If you want Jev involved, write the small PermissionRequest allow-gate from the cookbook (see customAlternative) and run it in shadow mode on personal repos for 1 to 2 weeks. Add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak first. If you'd rather trial something ready-made, use system1 with SYSTEM1_ENDPOINT pinned and a dedicated low-limit key, or truthsayer in log mode with a pinned commit, mode=off for client repos and an explicit jev-1.13 model. Either way, use absolute node/python paths in hook commands, avoid all compaction and function-hook features and subagent model routers, and use jevctl only as a CLI building block.

review-ci.summary: The review-ci category covers Jev used as a cheap typed yes/no or score judge on diffs, edits and commits. It appears in three forms. First, Claude Code hooks (PostToolUse or PreToolUse on Write|Edit, Stop, or PreToolUse on `git commit`) that ask Noul questions and return additionalContext, a deny, or a block. Second, CLIs or skills that Claude runs through Bash (supercov, perch, jev-codes, leanest). Third, CI-only GitHub Actions and git hooks that never run inside Claude Code. Of 57 members, only about 8 are hook-driven and automatic inside Claude Code. Almost all of those send full source to a third party through a young, single-author repo that is weeks old. Only a few can reach OpenRouter without patching: jevgate has native support, and supercov and patdown work by environment variables only. jev-hooks, jev-lint and jev-gate need URL config or a patch. The best of them are useful second opinions, not gates.
review-ci.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already offers /code-review and /security-review, the /simplify skill, the auto-mode classifier (which sees tool calls but not tool results), prompt and agent hooks (a Claude-model judge, multi-turn with tools), the caveman-review skill, and the gitnexus detect_changes and impact tools. Opus 5.5 itself reviews a diff better than Jev. Independent data shows Jev accuracy a bit below mid-price LLMs. It was overconfident on unanswerable input. In one benchmark, vulnerable-versus-secure code pair accuracy was 71.5% absolute, and ECE was 0.17 to 0.23 on coding decisions. A fake pre-approval line in state moved answers sharply. Jev's real advantage is narrow: a p50 ~200 ms / p95 ~600 ms call at about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, with typed probabilities. That makes it suitable for per-edit or per-commit checks that would be too slow or costly with an agent hook. Against that: /alpha endpoint, no SLA, 32k context, and every checked file leaves the machine. A `type:"prompt"` hook with a Haiku-class model gives similar per-edit checking, stays on your existing Anthropic data path, and has no third-party egress.
review-ci.worthItReason: The category is worth a bounded trial in personal repos, not a global install. Pro: hook-driven tools genuinely satisfy "automatic", fire under bypassPermissions (PreToolUse denies and PostToolUse still run), and cost about $0.0001 per check with 200-600 ms latency. Con: (1) Jev is measurably weaker than Opus or Sonnet at code judgment and is overconfident, so it produces both false alarms and misses, and injection in the code being judged can suppress findings. (2) Every checked edit or commit sends full source to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, which is a consent and NDA problem for client projects and a silent risk in bypass sessions. (3) The only tool with native OpenRouter support (jevgate) is 12 days old, single-maintainer, force-pushed, and saw 50-63% 503s on the OpenRouter path. Most others are TypeSafe-only and need a patch. (4) Failure modes are mixed: jevgate and jev-lint fail open, but patdown fails closed and denies every Write/Edit. (5) Existing Opus review, /code-review and gitnexus already cover most of the value. No study measures false-approve rates on real Claude Code traffic. It can work only with shadow mode, fail-open behavior, a project-scoped install, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the no-secret-leak hook first.

bestPick.name: JevGate (Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad rather than trustworthy. It is the only tool that is both fully automatic (hooks fire with no prompting, fail open, verified against v0.32.0 source) and natively OpenRouter-capable. But it is 12 days old, has a single maintainer and a force-pushed main, had 50-63% 503s on OpenRouter, writes Git objects into every repo, and has a bare-'jevgate' PATH problem. Use it only project-scoped in personal repos, with hand-written absolute-path hooks and 'jevgate auth login' instead of an env key.

review-ci.runnerUp: jev-hooks (7hemas7er): commit-only PreToolUse hook with secret redaction and fail-open behaviour, OpenRouter by config; safer scope, but unverified and 3 days old. supercov is the pick if you accept a manual, skill-triggered CLI with a tested OpenRouter path.
review-ci.recommendationForUser: Do not install any of these globally. If you want a trial, run jevgate or jev-hooks in one personal repo, in shadow mode, and first add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak protected list. For jevgate, use `jevgate auth login` and a hand-written hook with an absolute path. Keep Jev advisory (additionalContext only) and never in the Bash permission path for client work. For daily review value, keep using Opus with /code-review and gitnexus detect_changes; the typed Jev call earns its place only as a cheap second opinion on commits.

context-pruning.summary: Context-pruning integrations use Jev as a cheap, typed relevance classifier. It decides which lines, chunks or old tool results of a large tool output Opus does not need to see. Nearly all of the 37 members are days-to-weeks old, single-author and unreplicated. Only a handful run as real Claude Code hooks, and just three (compactio, jev-lens, maxkimambo/jev-mcp) were verified to work with OpenRouter with little or no patching. The rest either target other harnesses (Pi, Codex, OpenCode, DeepSeek Harness, omp), hard-code api.typesafe.ai, or depend on Claude Code's early-access "function hooks", which are not among the five documented hook types in 2.1.285 (command, http, mcp_tool, prompt, agent). Expected payoff is context savings only, not better decisions. Independent evidence says Jev is overconfident, injectable through text in state, and its drop decisions are silent when wrong.
context-pruning.builtInAlternative: Claude Code already bounds tool output natively. Bash output is truncated, Read takes offset/limit, and MCP output has a 25k-token cap (raisable with MAX_MCP_OUTPUT_TOKENS) with overflow saved to a file. Tool search defers MCP schemas, and auto-compaction plus subagents keep noisy work out of the main context. The user already has a subagent option (caveman:cavecrew investigator/builder/reviewer) that compresses returns by about 60%. Opus 5.5 with a large window makes raw context pressure modest. Deterministic head/tail/error-line filters, RTK-style, do most of the safe pruning with no network call, and compactio and jevprune already run rules first. Jev adds only a judgement layer for the ambiguous middle. It is fast (p50 ~200 ms) and cheap ($0.042/M input). But independent evals rate its calibration imperfect, and dropped lines are invisible to Opus. The author-reported harm in jev-lens is a 2.2% dropped-identifier-later-used rate, and 2 of 26 later edits missed their block. Claude itself, or a Haiku-class subagent, is a more accurate relevance judge but costs subscription tokens and latency.
context-pruning.worthItReason: The payoff is small and the risks are real for this user. Safe operating points hide little. Winnow's author data shows 2-5% of text hidden at the safe threshold. jev-lens gets 79% overall but only 31% on code, and its 88% on command output is mostly the kind that rule-based head/tail filters already handle. Opus 5.5 does Read-then-Edit work, where a lossy view is the costly failure. Jev is overconfident (exactly 1.0 on 56% of answers, 9 of them wrong) and injectable, so a hostile log or file can hide lines from Opus. The larger cost is data egress. Every large Bash, Read, grep or MCP result (playwright, gitnexus, git diff) goes to OpenRouter and its upstream on an /alpha endpoint with no SLA. Your no-secret-leak hook guards tool input, not tool output, and it does not yet cover OPENROUTER_API_KEY. That is a client-NDA problem. Worst-case hook latency adds seconds to a stack that already has slow gitnexus hooks. In bypassPermissions or auto sessions there is no human catching a bad edit that follows a bad drop. It is worth a shadow-mode trial on personal projects, particularly for log-heavy Bash output. It is not worth enabling by default, and it should not be enabled on client work.

bestPick.name: compactio (RamaAditya49)
bestPick.reason: Least-bad option, not a trustworthy default. It is the only verified candidate that is a plain command-hook PostToolUse integration using OPENROUTER_API_KEY natively, fully automatic and fail-open. It has tight timeouts (1.5s Jev, 5s hook), never cuts Read of code files, and redacts what it sends to Jev. Use it hooks-only on personal projects: replace bare `node` with an absolute path, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak, pin COMPACTIO_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, and never run /compactio:setup or sweep. It is 5 days old with an untested real Jev-drop path.

context-pruning.runnerUp: jev-lens (dizk), score 6, verified. It has a good recall tool and stats view, but it is lossy on code Reads (31% saving with 2.2% dropped-identifier harm), silently falls back to a mock classifier, and keeps plaintext prompt and output logs for 90 days. Use it after compactio, on personal repos only, checking /jev-lens:stats for mock=false.
context-pruning.recommendationForUser: The category is situational. It is not a daily-driver win for Opus 5.5 on a subscription, since the savings are modest, lossy drops interact badly with Read-then-Edit, and client output would leave the machine. If you want to try it, use compactio in hooks-only mode on personal repos, in shadow or log-only behaviour first if you can. Before that: add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak's protected list, put an absolute node path in the hook command, pin typesafe/jev-1.13, and set OPENROUTER_API_KEY="" in client repos. Never use the proxy or Sweep modes. For client work, or if you want a lower-risk path, skip Jev here and use a rules-only head/tail/error filter as a PostToolUse hook. That is the custom alternative described above. Jev fits better in the PermissionRequest and allow-side cookbook (not this category), which does not rewrite what Opus sees.
