entries.name: bgivenb/flick-computer-use (Flick)
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Playwright, Swift macOS AX helper) that runs a whole browser or macOS "computer use" goal autonomously. The host agent hands over a goal, exact inputs and completion conditions. Flick then loops observe (DOM or AX tree), then a Jev typed decision (Choice questions bundled into one /v1/systemone request), then execute and verify. It is a GUI automation agent that uses Jev as its per-step policy. It is not a coding-assistant integration or a general Jev decision tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude calls computer_execute or computer_run when a task needs GUI automation, guided by the server instructions and tool descriptions. It is not a hook, skill trigger or proxy. Even used well, Jev here only drives the browser or desktop and never advises Claude on coding decisions, so it does nothing to serve the user's goal of Jev being used automatically for coding.
security: API key is read from a .env.local file in the install dir via process.loadEnvFile (src/config.ts:10-13) and sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. It is not in argv. The key does not appear in the MCP launch entry, which is good practice.
Redirects are blocked: redirect:'error' (typesafe.ts:236). Response size is capped at 2 MB on the fallback path (typesafe.ts:213).

Inputs whose names look like password, secret, token, api key, pin or otp are filtered out of the verification payload (typesafe.ts verificationInputs). Other inputs, page text and typed values are sent to TypeSafe. The README warns that task traces can contain input values.
No postinstall hooks. Setup runs npm ci, a Chromium download and an optional Swift build. There is no curl|sh.
No telemetry found. The only network calls are to api.typesafe.ai and the optional Cerebras, Groq and OpenAI endpoints.

Prompt-injection surface is large: page and app text feeds Jev's decisions and the writing helper, and Jev drives real clicks, typing and form submits. The system prompt says interface text is evidence and not instructions, but a 15-tool server that clicks, types and submits on the user's browser or (on macOS) desktop is a high-risk primitive, particularly in bypass mode.
entries.dataEgress: Sent to api.typesafe.ai on every decision: the goal, supplied inputs (except keys that look secret), selected interface text (element names, roles, values, page title, URL), task memory and retained text artifacts, recent action history, and milestone evidence (up to 72 KB for the whole-goal check). If a text-helper key is set, the goal, current page text, the observed form and error history go to Cerebras, Groq or OpenAI. Screenshots stay local. OCR is local, on macOS only. Nothing from the user's code repo leaves the machine unless the browser goal displays it. There is no path for Claude Code transcripts, diffs or tool outputs to reach Jev.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the task, and the failure is contained. Each Jev call has a 15 s timeout (typesafe.ts:237) and up to 5 attempts, with backoff on 429/503/529 and transient network errors (150 ms x 2^n, 300 ms x 2^n). The last attempt uses a fresh HTTPS connection. After that the run throws a 'TypeSafe request failed' or 'retry budget exhausted' error and the task errors. Individual guarded driver actions have a 10 s timeout (server.ts:44). It is not a hook, so a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code's normal tools. Only computer_* calls fail. Direct inspect and act tools work without a key (server.ts:53).
entries.contextCost: 15 tools registered in src/server.ts and src/app-guide-tools.ts (server.ts:85-262), plus a very long server 'instructions' string of about 2.4k chars (server.ts:33) and long tool descriptions and zod schemas. My estimate is 5-7k tokens (about 27k chars of TS source for the tool definitions, and a good part of that is prompt text that is not exposed to Claude). That is heavy for an MCP that overlaps with the already-installed playwright MCP (about 25 tools). There are no hooks and no injected text per turn. Claude Code's MCP tool search may defer the schemas.
pros: Real, readable, tested source (about 3.5k lines of TS, about 25 test files, CI on Linux and macOS). It is a serious reference for how to build Jev Choice/Noul decision contracts (decisionContract in typesafe.ts:56 onward): options keyed by element IDs, per-field value questions, and probability/choice validation.

Batches several related questions into one /v1/systemone request and validates that the returned choice exists in the criteria. Its retry, backoff and fresh-connection fallback handle 429/503/529 sensibly.
MIT licensed, no postinstall, no telemetry, key kept out of argv, redirects blocked.
Runs on Linux for dedicated Playwright browser sessions (CI does this on ubuntu). The INSTALL notes mention the Ubuntu AppArmor Chromium setup.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It is browser and macOS GUI automation, and the user is on Linux doing coding. The native macOS control, existing-Chrome attach, Apple Vision OCR and user-input interruption are all macOS-only. On Linux only the generic Playwright path works, and playwright MCP is already installed.

No OpenRouter support: the URL https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone is hardcoded (typesafe.ts:235), and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_MODEL exist (config.ts:13-14). The user wants OpenRouter as the Jev provider, so this needs a private fork.

It cannot make Claude Code use Jev automatically for coding. Jev is buried inside a sub-agent loop, and Claude only decides whether to call computer_execute. There are no hooks, no gating of tool calls and no use of Jev for code decisions.
Heavy context footprint: 15 tools plus a roughly 2.4k-char instructions block, for an MCP that duplicates the existing playwright server.

Security posture is risky for a bypass-permissions user: an autonomous agent that clicks, types and submits in a real browser, driven by untrusted page text, with client-project browser sessions in scope. The server instructions also tell Claude to run post-mortems and write local guide files after every run.

Immature: 6 days old, 1 author, 24 commits, 23 stars, no releases, private package. The author's own README says 'early developer release' and 'native macOS control is experimental'. It is also 'independent, not affiliated with TypeSafe'.
Its tests stub the Jev calls. The only live checks (test:live) need a real TYPESAFE_API_KEY. I found no evidence that the OpenRouter route works with this schema.
The README install prompt tells the coding agent to star the repository on the user's GitHub account. That is an unrequested social action embedded in the install text.
entries.verdict: Not suitable as the Jev integration for this user. It is a macOS-centric GUI computer-use agent hardwired to api.typesafe.ai, not a way to have Claude Code consult Jev during coding, and it duplicates playwright MCP at a 5-7k token cost. Treat it only as a reference implementation for building Jev Choice/Noul contracts and a robust client.

entries.name: askjev-mcp (AskJev)
entries.what: Browser-automation MCP server (npm askjev-mcp 1.7.3, 15 tools) plus a Chrome extension. askjev_do runs a Playwright/CDP autopilot loop. Each step it snapshots the page (URL, title, up to 60 interactive elements with role, name, href and current input value) and sends one fan-out POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. That call asks a Choice (next action), a Choice (target element), a Noul (irreversible) and a Score (progress). It then executes the chosen click or type. It stops when P(irreversible) is 0.65 or higher. Jev drives web browsing here. It is not a coding assistant and does not help with code, diffs or tests.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. Claude calls askjev_do only when the task involves a website or browser. It is aggressively worded (REQUIRED for any website request) but never triggers during ordinary coding, so it is not a deterministic hook and never runs by itself.
security: Key handling: the API key is read from env or ~/.askjev/api-key (mode 600, written by the extension's Auto-connect). It is not passed in argv. The extension's Auto-connect writes the key into Claude's MCP config env, which would put it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or the Claude Desktop config.

Instruction hijack: server `instructions` and the askjev_do description say 'ONLY browser automation', 'REQUIRED for any website request' and 'Do NOT use any built-in browser pane... or other browsing tools'. In this user's setup this would fight the existing playwright MCP and is the opposite of a neutral integration.

Prompt-injection surface: page element names, hrefs, titles and read_page text flow into Jev state and into Claude's context. Jev is a typed classifier, so it cannot be told to run arbitrary shell commands. The single-action tools (askjev_act, click, type, navigate) have no guard, and a Claude that has been injected can drive a logged-in browser.
The guard is only a probabilistic P(irreversible) >= 0.65 inside the autopilot loop. It is not a security boundary.

No shell execution of user input. It spawns a browser with --remote-debugging-port, or attaches to ASKJEV_CDP_URL (default 127.0.0.1:9222). An open CDP port gives any local process browser control. Launched browsers use a persistent Playwright profile, and the code comments mention a past profile-corruption incident (cdp-browser.ts ~line 99).

Supply chain: root package.json has a postinstall (`npm install --prefix mcp`) but it belongs to the extension repo. The published npm package has no postinstall. Dependencies are @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, playwright-core, ws and zod. No curl|sh installer was seen. One maintainer, 4 versions published within 2 days.
entries.dataEgress: On each autopilot step, sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone: the goal text (the user's words), page URL, page title, the last 6 actions, and up to 60 interactive elements (role, accessible name, href, input_type, and current_value truncated to 80 chars for form fields). Values typed into form fields, including possibly passwords or PII, can appear in current_value. No source code, diffs or Claude prompts are sent, because it only ever sees what is in the browser tab. Screenshots are returned to Claude, not to Jev. Everything goes to TypeSafe directly, not through OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-loud for the multi-step tools. Without a key, askjev_do returns a missing_api_key error. There is a 15 s per-attempt timeout and 2 retries with exponential backoff on network errors, 429 and 529. 401 and 422 fail fast. On failure the tool returns an error to Claude rather than silently degrading. Single-step tools never call Jev and keep working. It does not block Claude Code itself, because there is no hook. The failure only affects browsing tasks.
entries.contextCost: 15 MCP tools. The descriptions, zod schemas and server instructions add up to roughly 2-3k tokens (estimate from the sizes of index.ts's tool registrations, about 16.8k chars including code, and the instructions string of about 700 chars). It is always loaded, or deferred if tool search is on. No hook-injected text. The instructions text tries to steer Claude away from other browser tools, which would bias against the user's playwright MCP.
pros: Real, working Jev integration in code: a System One fan-out with Choice, Noul and Score questions. It uses structured criteria, confidence gating (ASKJEV_MIN_CONFIDENCE 0.45), an irreversible-action Noul guard at 0.65, and stuck/oscillation detection. It is a good reference for how Jev is meant to be used.
Has tests (6 files in mcp/test, including jev-client and autopilot-loop) and a GitHub Actions CI that runs typecheck and tests. MIT license. Fetch timeouts and retry logic are present.
Key kept out of argv (env or a 0600 file). No telemetry. Only one outbound host.
Single-step tools (navigate, snapshot, read_page, screenshot) need no key and never call Jev.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It uses Jev to drive a browser, not to improve coding decisions in Claude Code (which model to route to, whether to run tests, whether a change is risky). It offers nothing for the daily coding loop.
Hardcodes api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev-client.ts:16) with no OpenRouter or base-URL env override. Using OpenRouter needs a fork and a response-shape check.
Duplicates the playwright MCP that the user already has. The server instructions explicitly tell Claude not to use other browser tools, so installing it would cause conflicts.
The Jev browser loop is slower and less reliable than Claude planning directly. Jev has no reasoning trace and re-decides every step from a 60-element list.

Sends page URLs and form field values to a third party. Security posture is weak for client work: an open CDP port, unguarded act/click/type tools, and the extension writing the key into Claude's config.

Very immature. Repo created 2026-09-17, 128 commits, 2 contributors (apparently one person under two names), 9 stars, 4 npm versions in 2 days, last push 2026-09-18. No changes since. Extension-centric README (Options, Auto-connect flow) aimed at Claude Desktop and Cursor, not Claude Code.
entries.verdict: Not recommended. It is a genuine Jev client, but for browser autopilot on api.typesafe.ai only, with no OpenRouter path. Its instructions also fight the existing playwright MCP, and it adds nothing to Claude Code's coding workflow. Keep it as a reference for the System One request format only.

entries.name: Friedjof/jev-mobile
entries.what: Python (uv) durable Android sub-agent. A SQLite-backed worker drives a USB Android phone through an observe, decide, mutate, verify loop. Jev (via the typesafe-sdk System One Choice primitive) picks the next action from a catalogue of pre-validated candidate actions. It exposes a stdio or HTTP MCP server with six task-delegation tools (start_task, get_task, get_task_events, cancel_task, answer_task, get_device_status) so an orchestrator such as OpenClaw can hand off phone tasks. It has nothing to do with coding: it is for Android UI automation (Google Keep notes and the like).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, and only if Claude is asked to do phone automation. It would never be triggered by coding work.
security: TYPESAFE_API_KEY comes from an env var or a *_FILE secret file (config.py:73), and the file variant is preferred for services. It is not passed via argv.
MCP HTTP mode has a TrustedHost allowlist, optional origin allowlist and optional bearer token (mcp_server.py:718-727). The bearer token is optional.
adb runs via create_subprocess_exec with an argument list, not shell=True (portal_adb.py:174, cli.py:96).
Errors are summarised without headers or credentials (jev.py:_safe_error_summary).
The Android bridge binds to loopback only, over an adb forward tunnel.
The task text is a prompt-injection surface, because it comes from the orchestrating agent and drives a real phone. The README states that payments and account changes are out of scope.
entries.dataEgress: Only Android screen semantics leave the machine for Jev. Each request carries the goal, app name, screen hint and up to 16 UI elements (label, value, resource_id and so on) plus candidate action labels (jev.py:build_jev_state). That goes to the TypeSafe API. It never touches Claude Code source, diffs or file contents unless you point it at those, and it isn't wired to them. If the optional LLM planner is configured, it also sends data to LLM_BASE_URL.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed, but only for its own Android tasks. With no key, or if Jev fails, ProviderUnavailable is raised and the task goes to recovery or a failed state with a PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE category. The Claude Code session is not affected, because tasks are asynchronous via a separate worker. Timeouts are the SDK defaults, and I did not verify their values.
entries.contextCost: Low. 6 MCP tools, roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens of tool defs from short descriptions plus schemas including the subtasks list. No hooks and no injected text. All of it would be dead weight for a coding session.
pros: It is a real, working example of the Jev pattern: a Choice question over a validated closed action list, with probabilities and a probability margin used to decide when to escalate (providers/jev.py:decide). That is a good reference for designing your own Jev hook or gate.
It shows how to build a compact state payload (build_jev_state) and use Jev confidence to fall back to a bigger model. Good design material.
Careful engineering: durable SQLite tasks, idempotency keys, secret-file support that fails closed, redacted logs, about 30 test files, CI and MIT licence.
The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so the TypeSafe SDK route to OpenRouter is plausibly a base-URL and key swap (unverified).
cons: It is Android UI automation, not a coding tool. It needs a physical USB phone plus adb, and gives Claude Code nothing for editing, reviewing or testing code.
It cannot be used automatically for coding. The tools only make sense if you ask Claude to operate a phone.
The code only supports the TypeSafe-direct SDK path (TYPESAFE_API_KEY). No OpenRouter code or env var exists in the repo. The OpenRouter path would need an unverified SDK base-URL trick.
Early and single-author: 37 commits over 2 days (2026-09-17 to 09-18), 8 stars, v0.1.2, no activity since 2026-09-18.
Heavy footprint: a worker process, SQLite, an Android companion APK and an accessibility service. Over-scoped for the user's goal.
Adds 6 tools of context that would never be used in coding work.
entries.verdict: Not an option for the user's goal. It is a Jev-driven Android phone controller, not a coding integration, and it targets TypeSafe direct only. It is worth reading as a reference for a confidence-gated Choice design, but should not be installed in Claude Code.

entries.what: Experimental Python framework: Jev chooses Android actions from accessibility trees, executed via ADB/UIAutomator2 with permissions and budgets. Bench 314 ms median, 78.6% accuracy.

entries.name: Teylersf/WindowsJev
entries.what: Windows-only (.NET 8 WPF, UI Automation) stdio MCP server. It does two things. (1) Desktop automation: a deterministic router opens URLs and Google searches; any other goal is turned into a bounded action list from the foreground accessibility tree, and Jev (Choice plus a completion Noul) is called once per step to pick an action. (2) Durable background web-research jobs that write Markdown and JSONL evidence files, with optional Jev evidence reranking and claim verification. It has no coding-workflow functionality (no code review, commit, diff or test decisions).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. There are no hooks or skills. The tool descriptions target 'Windows desktop' and 'web research', so Claude would call them only for those tasks and never on coding tasks. The README itself says to prompt 'Use WindowsJev to open the browser...'.
security: API key sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS, not in argv. It is read from the env or a .env.local found by walking up parent directories from the exe location (EnvironmentFile.cs), and errors redact it.

Controls the local desktop through UI Automation and can launch processes (Process.Start in WindowsAutomation.cs:97,107). The action space is limited to deterministic candidates, and text typed must be a literal span from the goal.

Prompt-injection surface: window titles and accessibility labels go into the Jev prompt, but Jev can only choose among predefined IDs. Its keyword blocklist is substring-based and crude ('pay', 'buy', 'delete').
Research fetcher blocks private and loopback hosts by hostname preflight only. SECURITY.md admits a DNS-rebinding and redirect gap. Downloads are capped at 3 MB and 15 s, with cookies disabled.
The binary is unsigned, has no releases, and comes from a 1-commit, 2-star, 8-day-old repo.
No telemetry or curl|sh installer found. The install scripts are PowerShell that copy local files. There are no npm postinstall hooks.
entries.dataEgress: Only to api.typesafe.ai (direct, not OpenRouter): the goal text, the foreground process and window title, up to 8 recent actions, the labels of offered UI candidates (from the accessibility tree), and for rank/verify the claim, objective and up to 40 saved web-page excerpts. Research page fetches go to arbitrary public URLs. Page contents are not sent to Jev except through the explicit rank/verify tools. Nothing from Claude Code source code, diffs or prompts would leave the machine, because the tool never sees them.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: it returns a JSON status of configuration_required or failed, or throws, and Claude continues. The Jev HTTP timeout is 15 s (JevClient.cs:12) and 30 s for research, with up to 3 attempts and backoff on 429 or 529. The agent loop stops on low confidence, a blocked action or a stall. It does not block Claude Code, and it is never on the critical path since it is not a hook.
entries.contextCost: 12 MCP tools. Approx 2,700 characters of descriptions plus parameter schemas, so about 1.5 to 2k tokens of tool definitions per session, with no server instructions and no hook-injected text. The cost is pure overhead for a Linux coding workflow because the tools are irrelevant to it (and the server cannot start on Linux).
pros: Real, MIT-licensed, readable, small codebase (about 1.9k lines of C#), with a clear safety model in SECURITY.md and CI on Windows.

Concrete working example of the System One request/response schema: Choice with criteria, Noul, and reading probabilities, confidence and usage (JevClient.cs:35-81). It is useful as a reference for how to build the request body.
Uses Jev in the intended way: the model only picks among deterministically generated options, and validation rejects choices that were not offered.
Sensible cost hygiene: deterministic fast paths use zero Jev tokens, and rank/verify are explicit opt-in calls.
cons: Windows-only (net8.0-windows, UseWPF, UI Automation). It cannot run on the user's Linux machine, so it is unusable as-is.
Not a coding tool: no decisions on code, diffs, permissions, commits or routing. Nothing here automates 'use Jev when useful' inside a coding session.
Direct TypeSafe only: the endpoint is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai and the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY. There is no OpenRouter support and no config hook.
Invocation depends on the model reading tool descriptions, and the README expects the user to say 'Use WindowsJev...'. That contradicts the user's requirement of no prompting.
Very immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, an unsigned binary, and the repo is 8 days old. The author admits gaps (DNS rebinding, and the 'does not yet' list).
Adds 12 irrelevant tools (about 1.5 to 2k tokens) to every session if registered.
Crude substring keyword blocklist ('pay', 'buy') and desktop control via bypass permission mode could be risky.
entries.verdict: Not usable and not relevant for this user: it is a Windows-desktop-automation and web-research MCP that is Windows-only, TypeSafe-direct (no OpenRouter), and model-discretion only. Skip it as an integration; at most read JevClient.cs as a reference for building a System One request body.

entries.name: kofanlabs/typesafe-computer-use-windows
entries.what: Windows-only desktop GUI automation agent (fork of awlevin/typesafe-computer-use). Captures a selected native window, runs local Windows OCR and UI Automation, and sends the resulting screen text and controls to Jev through typesafe-sdk to pick the next click, type or scroll operation. A Node MCP wrapper (mcp.mjs) spawns the Python CLI and hands free-text and final-screen checks back to the host agent. It does not help with code editing, review or routing.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. It only fires when the user asks for native desktop GUI automation. It has no hook and no proxy behaviour, and does nothing for code-related turns.
security: Shell execution is intentional: mcp.mjs spawns the Python CLI with the goal string as argv; the goal is not passed through a shell. The API key is not in argv, it is passed through the environment.
Install-Windows.cmd and scripts/*.ps1 are PowerShell installers; they were not run.
Keys are stored with Windows DPAPI, which does not apply on Linux; on Linux only the TYPESAFE_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY env vars would work.

Prompt-injection surface is high: OCR and UI text from arbitrary windows goes to Jev and to the host agent, and the tool can click and type. SKILL.md and mcp.mjs tell the host to treat screen text as untrusted data.
The project refuses password fields, has a top-left mouse abort gesture and a STOP file, and states that authentication and terminals are out of scope.
Screenshots, OCR text and traces are stored unencrypted under runs/.
entries.dataEgress: Selected-window OCR and UIA text plus the goal and previous actions go to the Jev provider (TypeSafe direct or Vercel AI Gateway). The text-writer step goes to the host agent, meaning Claude. Standalone mode can send content to Anthropic if ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is set. Screenshots stay local. Nothing here reads source code, but any window on screen could leak text to the provider.
entries.failureMode: The client timeout is 20 s per Jev call (runner.py:78). A missing key makes the CLI exit with an error (cli.py:28). Runs are bounded by a steps limit (default 20, max 100). If Jev fails, the run ends with an error or crashed outcome, and mcp.mjs surfaces the process tail. This only affects the explicit desktop task and never blocks normal coding, so it is effectively isolated. The whole server does not work on Linux.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Descriptions plus zod schemas total roughly 2.5k characters, so about 700-900 tokens. No server-level instructions. SKILL.md is a separate skill with a short description (about 60 tokens) but is written for Windows GUI tasks. No hooks.
pros: Real, MIT-licensed code that genuinely uses Jev Choice/Noul primitives (decide.py:364, 422) in a working agent loop, so it is a useful reference for how Jev is consumed as a typed-decision engine.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL are read from env (runner.py:78), so the endpoint is configurable in principle.
Host handoff design (typesafe_respond, needs_host) is clean: Claude supplies free text and verifies the final screen, and screen text is labelled untrusted.
Safety features: act=false preview by default, STOP file, mouse-corner abort, refuses password fields.
6 tools with a small context footprint; nothing is injected on non-desktop turns.
cons: Windows-only runtime. It needs Windows.Media.Ocr, UI Automation, PrintWindow and .venv\Scripts\python.exe (mcp.mjs), so it cannot run on the user's Linux box.
Solves GUI automation, not coding decisions, so it never adds value in a daily Claude Code workflow (no routing, permission, review or classification use).

No OpenRouter support: no 'openrouter' string in the repo. It uses typesafe-sdk 0.6.0 with a TypeSafe or Vercel AI Gateway base URL. It is unverified whether the SDK's wire format matches OpenRouter's Decisions API.
Brand new (created 2026-09-20), 1 star, 30 commits of which 26 are inherited upstream, single-fork maintainer, alpha status, and the README itself lists many untested scenarios.
Requires an unused-by-user provider key (TYPESAFE_API_KEY or Vercel AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY), and DPAPI key storage does not work on Linux.
Automatic invocation would be undesirable: the tool clicks and types on the desktop, with high prompt-injection risk from screen text.
Screenshots, OCR and traces are stored in plaintext under runs/.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this user: it is a Windows-only desktop GUI automation agent with no OpenRouter path, and it does not address coding decisions. At most it is a reference implementation of Jev Choice/Noul in an agent loop.

entries.name: @compootor/jev-bot
entries.what: macOS-only computer-use MCP server (2 tools: js, reset). The agent writes JavaScript against a persistent 'cua' API that drives native Mac apps through the external Cua Driver (accessibility tree, screenshots, clicks, typing). app.act(goal) sends the window's accessibility elements to Jev, which chooses the next UI action via a Choice primitive. Built for Codex and ChatGPT desktop. It is not a coding-assist tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code would call js only when a task involves native Mac GUI control, which is never true for a Linux coding workflow. Nothing is automatic and there are no hooks or skills.
security: Keys are read from an --env-file or the environment, not argv. The README says to keep them out of chat.
The js tool lets the agent run arbitrary JavaScript in a persistent REPL (src/repl-worker.ts). It is annotated destructive and open-world, and it is high-risk under bypass or auto permission mode.

It controls the whole desktop through Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions. UI content is a prompt-injection surface. The code marks window text as untrusted and redacts secure fields ('[secure field]', '[redacted]') before sending to Jev.
The installer is curl|bash from cua.ai for a third-party driver. No npm postinstall script; a prepare script exists only for dev (effect-tsgo patch).
No telemetry seen in the sources I read.
The dependency chain is a personal npm scope (@compootor) with two maintainers, an Effect release candidate, and a 0.0.4 SDK. The npm tarball is signed with provenance attestations.
entries.dataEgress: On app.act, Jev receives the goal, app name, window title, and every accessibility element (role, label, value, enabled, actions) up to about 120k characters, plus the last 8 actions as JSON. Secure fields are redacted. Screenshots stay with the host agent and do not go to Jev. Nothing about code or repos leaves unless it appears in an app window. The server's tool results, including screenshots, go to the MCP client's LLM.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for Jev actions. provider.ts uses an 8s timeout and 0 retries, and throws if the key is missing or the response is invalid or off-table. The js tool wraps errors as isError results, so the agent falls back to deterministic element-number actions. Missing Cua Driver or a non-macOS platform fails at startup or in the driver connection. This is a tool, not a hook, so it can never block Claude Code turns.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools (js, reset). The js description is long, roughly 150-200 tokens in total. The server 'instructions' string is about 90 tokens. The JSON schemas are small, so the total is about 500-700 tokens. It would also inject API guidance into cua.getState() output, on demand. No hooks.
pros: Real, well-built reference for calling Jev System One from code. The Choice primitive is used with per-candidate descriptions, strict validation of probabilities (sum ~1, keys match candidates), and untrusted-content framing (src/provider.ts:60-100).
Clean, small codebase (about 2.7k lines of TS) with tests and CI on Linux and macOS, and actions pinned by SHA. MIT licensed and published to npm with provenance.
The provider base URL is overridable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and the model via TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, so OpenRouter routing is likely a config-only change.
Secrets come from an env-file, not argv. Secure fields are redacted before egress. Failure is bounded (8s timeout, no retry, fallback to deterministic actions).
cons: macOS-only computer-use tool and the user is on Linux. It needs Cua Driver (macOS Accessibility and Screen Recording), so it cannot work here at all.
Not a coding aid. Jev picks UI controls, not code decisions, so it adds nothing to editing, testing, review or routing in Claude Code.
Entirely model-discretion. There is no hook or skill, so it cannot deliver the requested 'automatic use without prompting'.
The js tool grants arbitrary JS and desktop control, which is dangerous under bypass or auto permission mode, and it needs a curl|bash third-party installer.
Very immature: 1 star, 1 contributor, 7 commits, created 2026-09-18, versions 0.1.0 to 0.1.3 in 2 days, on an Effect RC and a 0.0.4 SDK. README targets Codex and ChatGPT desktop, not Claude Code.
OpenRouter is not documented or tested. The default model ID 'jev-1.13.0' differs from OpenRouter's 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.
entries.verdict: Skip. It is a legitimate but macOS-only computer-use MCP for Codex and ChatGPT that uses Jev to pick UI controls, so it cannot run on this Linux machine and does nothing for coding. Its only value is as a reference implementation of a validated System One Choice call and of the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override pattern.

entries.name: huaaudio/jevsim (@huaaudio/jevsim)
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server that runs bounded (1-10 step, 60 s) iOS Simulator (via XcodeBuildMCP) and Android (via Appium/UIAutomator2) UI workflows in a single tool call. Jev is used only as a Choice-primitive selector: it picks which accessibility control matches a natural-language target description (or 'none'); a 0.90 probability threshold gates the action. It is a mobile-app UI test-automation tool, not a general coding aid.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. Claude would call it only if a task involves driving an iOS Simulator or Android device, which the tool descriptions and README explicitly scope to.
security: API key read from env only; sent as Bearer header (src/jev.ts:40), not in argv unless user puts it there; docs say never put creds in command-line args. Key is not passed to the XcodeBuildMCP or adb child processes (env allowlist per docs/configuration.md, docs/privacy.md).
fetch uses redirect:'error' (src/jev.ts:39) so key is not forwarded on redirects; upstream error text is reduced to stable codes to avoid leaking key or UI text (src/types.ts:62).

Prompt-injection surface: screen labels/values are sent to Jev as data; Jev can only return one of the offered refs or 'none', with sum-to-1 and argmax validation (src/jev.ts:12-24), so injection can at worst mis-select a control. Relevant only to mobile UI.
Launches child processes: npx -y xcodebuildmcp@2.7.0 (pinned version but fetched from npm at runtime) and adb; JEVSIM_XCODE_COMMAND/ARGS can be overridden by env (executed without a shell).
No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no curl|sh; only prepack build. Appium is a separate, unpinned-by-this-repo server that may log full UI text and installs helper APKs on the device.

Very new single-author package (npm maintainer with a student email, 0 stars, 1 release), so no supply-chain track record; the README is written to instruct an installing agent ('give your agent this repo URL'), which is a mild prompt-injection-style pattern if an agent ingests it.
entries.dataEgress: Only when semantic selection is used (no exact identifier): the normalized accessibility snapshot of the mobile screen (all target roles/labels/values/identifiers/state, page text, device id, screen hash), the requested target description and action type, and the per-candidate criteria JSON, to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (src/jev.ts:49-55, docs/privacy.md). Typed text and assertions are omitted; screenshots never sent. No source code, diffs, prompts, or file contents from the developer's repo leave the machine. Traffic goes directly to TypeSafe, not OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per workflow but bounded: Jev connection error, non-2xx, or invalid response throws Stop (jev_connection_failed / jev_http_N / invalid_jev_response, src/jev.ts:43-46) and the run stops with partial progress reported; missing key gives credentials_missing but exact-identifier steps still work without any key. Whole run has a hard 60 s deadline via AbortSignal.timeout (src/runner.ts:81, workflow timeoutMs max 60000); no separate per-request Jev timeout or retry. Never automatically replays uncertain actions. It cannot affect other Claude Code operations since it only runs when its tool is called.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Descriptions total ~900 chars plus zod-derived JSON schemas (workflowSchema with 5-way discriminated step union, 10 predicates, device fields) roughly 3-4k chars, so about 1.0-1.5k tokens of tool definitions. No server 'instructions' field (server created with only name/version, src/server.ts:86). No hooks and no injected text. Full agent guidance lives in docs, not in context.
pros: Genuine, non-trivial use of Jev's Choice primitive with strict output validation (sum to 1, argmax, key set equals criteria, src/jev.ts:12-24), a 'none' abstain option, and a 0.90 probability gate: a good reference design for a Jev integration.
Careful safety design: no automatic replay of uncertain actions, redacted results, key not passed to child processes, redirect:'error', stable error codes, pinned dependencies and backend version.
Costs almost no context (3 tools, ~1-1.5k tokens, no hooks, no server instructions) and adds zero latency to normal coding turns.
MIT, no postinstall scripts, no telemetry, reasonable test suite with mock backends and CI.
Reported 3.3x speedup on an iOS Settings navigation task (vendor-run, 3 runs) if the user ever does mobile UI automation.
cons: Wrong domain for this user: it automates iOS Simulator / Android UI, not code editing, search, review, or general development; it would rarely or never be auto-invoked on a Linux dev box.
iOS backend (XcodeBuildMCP + Xcode simulator) requires macOS; README says Linux hosts and physical Android devices are unvalidated; Android needs a separately run Appium 3 + emulator.

No OpenRouter support: api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone is hardcoded (src/jev.ts:38) with no base URL override; using OpenRouter would require forking the package, and TypeSafe direct key is needed as shipped.
Not automatic: it is only a model-discretion MCP tool, and the agent must supply the plan; nothing decides 'when Jev adds value' across general coding.
Extremely immature: created 2026-09-21, 9 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, single 0.1.0 release, 9 days old; Node pinned to exactly >=24 <25; vendor-authored benchmarks (n=3) on a single simulator.
Sends app accessibility text and field values (potentially client data) to TypeSafe on every semantic selection; Appium may log full UI text locally.
Runtime fetches xcodebuildmcp via npx -y for iOS, adding a second unaudited supply-chain hop.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered but off-target: a mobile-UI-automation MCP that uses Jev as a control selector, hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, useless for general Linux daily coding and not automatically invoked. Skip it for this setup; at most read src/jev.ts as a reference for validating Choice responses.

entries.name: kofanlabs/jev-browser-chrome
entries.what: Fork of browser-use/jev-ultrafast: a browser-automation agent. Python MCP server (chrome_mcp.py, MCPServer from mcp>=2) plus a Chrome MV3 extension bridge (loopback websocket, host_permissions <all_urls>) that drives the user's existing signed-in Chrome/Edge tabs. Jev (System One /v1/systemone) picks CLICK/TYPE_TEXT/SELECT/SCROLL/DONE and a target element from a numbered DOM element table; TYPE_TEXT text comes from a separate text LLM (OpenRouter mercury-2.5 by default) or the MCP host. It is a browser agent that uses Jev as its policy head, not a coding-workflow helper.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only (plus an optional skill description that says 'for user-requested browser tasks'). No hooks, no proxy, no deterministic trigger. It would fire only when Claude decides to do a browser task, which duplicates the already-installed playwright MCP.
security: Chrome extension requests host_permissions <all_urls> plus tabs and scripting: it can read and act on every page in the user's signed-in profile (banking, client admin panels, etc.). SECURITY.md itself warns about this.

Prompt-injection surface: visible page text (state.page.text, element labels) goes into Jev questions and into the text-helper context (page text up to 6000 chars); Jev output is constrained to choice IDs validated against observed elements (model.py validate_choice), which limits injection, but the text LLM and the MCP host receive untrusted page content via needs_host requests.
Bridge uses a random 32-byte token in a websocket path on 127.0.0.1 (extension_daemon.py:41-116), token file created 0600; loopback demo server at 127.0.0.1:8766.
API key is sent as Bearer header from env var, not in argv; MCP config passes no key on the command line. Windows uses DPAPI, macOS a 0600 file; Linux path is env var only.
act=false by default, allowed_origins required, password/payment/upload/hidden fields not filled, per-mutation recheck of live page.

No curl|sh installer, but Install-Windows.cmd / Install-Mac.command / PowerShell scripts run local setup; not audited in depth. browser-harness pinned dependency, unknown upstream. No telemetry found in grep; README carries a Browser Use Cloud waitlist marketing banner.
entries.dataEgress: To TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai) or Vercel AI Gateway per action step: page URL, title, visible page text, the numbered element table (labels, values, roles), the goal, and last 10 recent actions. To the text-helper provider (OpenRouter by default, TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY) on TYPE_TEXT: goal, field info, up to 6000 chars of page text, recent actions. Screenshots and traces stay local. No source code or repo files are sent by design, but any signed-in page content (emails, dashboards) visible in a controlled tab is.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per run: post_json (model.py:33-48) retries 429/503/529 up to 3 attempts with 0.5/1 s backoff, httpx client timeout 25 s, then raises 'Model unavailable; no action executed'. Runs bounded by max_steps=30 and max_seconds=180 with a stop tool. It only fails a browser task, never blocks Claude Code's coding flow, since it is an opt-in tool.
entries.contextCost: 8 MCP tools. Server instructions about 250 chars (about 60 tokens). jev_browser_run has a very long docstring (>3000 chars) plus a 9-parameter schema including free-form text_inputs; estimated total tool defs about 2,500-3,500 tokens. No hooks inject text. SKILL.md (about 1-2k tokens) is a Codex/Grok skill telling the model to use it only for user-requested browser tasks.
pros: Genuine, non-trivial Jev integration: uses System One choice heads with per-option probabilities and confidence, and validates them strictly (model.py validate_choice), so it is a good reference for how to build a Jev question payload.
Request format (model, state, questions -> answers{choice,probabilities,confidence}) is exactly the System One shape, so an OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone swap is plausible with a small patch.
Sensible safety design: act=false default, required allowed_origins, loopback-only token-authenticated bridge, no password or payment filling, output limited to observed element IDs.
MIT license, decent test suite (about 91 pytest tests and node tests), CI with ruff and build.
Uses the user's real signed-in Chrome, which playwright MCP does not do, useful for authenticated-app QA if ever needed.
cons: Not a coding aid: it automates browsers; Jev never sees code, diffs, errors or repo state, so it adds no value to daily coding decisions.

No OpenRouter support for Jev: model.py:141 hard-rejects any endpoint except api.typesafe.ai or the Vercel gateway; key loader only reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. Needs a source patch, which conflicts with the user's OpenRouter-only requirement.
Windows and macOS only: docs, installers and CI cover no Linux, and the user is on Linux; the Chrome extension must be loaded unpacked manually.
Not automatic: only model-discretion MCP tools, and it duplicates the already-installed playwright MCP; the SKILL.md wording restricts use to explicit user-requested browser tasks.
Very large blast radius for a 10-day-old, 0-star, single-fork project: an <all_urls> extension in the profile used for client work, plus sends visible page text to third parties.
Extra context cost (8 tools, huge jev_browser_run docstring) for a capability the user rarely needs, and TYPE_TEXT requires yet another LLM key (TEXT_MODEL_API_KEY).
Requires the extra sub-dependency browser-harness==0.1.13 and mcp>=2, plus a heavier install for zero coding benefit.
entries.verdict: Really a Jev-powered Chrome browser agent for Windows and macOS, not a coding integration. It lacks OpenRouter support, has no Linux path, is not auto-invoked, and overlaps with playwright, so skip it for the goal of automatic Jev use inside Claude Code. It is useful only as a reference for the System One request/response schema.

entries.name: avishekjana-89/playwright-jev
entries.what: A Python agent framework (not an MCP server) that drives Playwright MCP (spawned via npx @playwright/mcp@latest over stdio) for autonomous browser automation. Every step (which Playwright tool, visual check needed, complexity, which accessibility ref to click, which variable to type) is decided by Jev System One calls through the typesafe_sdk client, with a URL deny-list guardrail. It is an app you run from the CLI or import, and it has no MCP server, hook or skill interface for Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a standalone Python script or library that a human runs. Claude Code has no path to it: no MCP server, no hook, no skill.
security: The API key is read from .env or env vars and passed to the SDK in-process, so it does not appear in argv.
@playwright/mcp@latest is run through npx with an unpinned version, which is a supply-chain risk.
typesafe-sdk>=0.2 is unpinned and third-party.
decision_engine.py:60-64 and 75-79 log the full page state and the raw Jev request and response at DEBUG level. Logs may contain page content, including credentials typed into forms.
The guardrail is a URL substring deny-list only. The README says Noul-based safety is used, but the guardrail is static.
No license, so reuse rights are undefined.
entries.dataEgress: Page context sent to Jev on every step: the task goal, the Playwright accessibility tree (up to 25k tokens, config max_context_tokens), the URL, and task variables such as search queries and possibly credentials. This goes to openrouter.ai or Typesafe. It sends nothing from Claude Code sessions, because it is not integrated with Claude Code. The Playwright browser fetches the target sites.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to a safe default. decide() catches every exception and returns safe_fallback() (decision_engine.py:68-70). decide_dynamic re-raises. If typesafe_sdk is missing, a MockJevClient is used silently, with a log warning only. The timeout_ms=30000 parameter is documented but not visibly enforced, since asyncio.to_thread has no timeout. Not applicable to Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools and zero server instructions, because it is not an MCP server, hook or skill. To use it from Claude Code you would have to write a wrapper. Claude Code already has a Playwright MCP, and this would duplicate it.
pros: It shows a working pattern for calling Jev with batched Choice/Noul questions in one system_one call (decision_engine.py:67).
It has OpenRouter switching logic: an OPENROUTER_API_KEY makes the base URL https://openrouter.ai/api (config.py:73-84).
It fails open to a safe fallback when Jev errors (decision_engine.py:68-70).
Small codebase, about 1.8k lines, easy to read as a reference.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook or skill. Claude Code cannot invoke it, so the automatic-integration goal is not met.
It only automates browser flows and does nothing for coding tasks.
It is a 2-day-old proof of concept with 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no license, no tests and no releases.
It replaces Playwright MCP's LLM-driven agent with a Jev-driven one, duplicating the Playwright MCP the user already has.
It logs full page state and Jev payloads at DEBUG level.
npx @playwright/mcp@latest and typesafe-sdk are unpinned.
The OpenRouter path depends on the SDK's URL handling, which is unverified. The README documents only TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
The README's claim of 15 ms latency is unsupported, and the timeout is not enforced.
entries.verdict: This is a standalone Python browser-automation demo that uses Jev through typesafe_sdk, not a Claude Code integration. It has no MCP, hook or skill surface and is a proof of concept, so it is irrelevant to the user's goal. At most it is a reference for the OpenRouter env/base-URL pattern.

entries.name: @legostin/jev-browser
entries.what: Browser-automation MCP server plus skill (not a coding-assistant helper). You give a goal; Jev picks browser actions via the OpenRouter Decisions API, and Playwright or a Chrome extension executes them. The npm package (3 files, 32 KB) is only an installer/launcher shim. It git-clones the real engine from github.com/legostin/jev-browser main, and that repo now returns 404 (private or deleted). The npm package is therefore a dead installer. A sibling public repo, legostin/jev-mcp (MIT, 94 commits, 1 star, created 2026-09-23), holds the same author's earlier browser MCP with the same purpose.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. No hooks and no transparent proxy. It fires only when Claude decides that a browser task needs it, which is unlikely in daily coding. It is not a general Jev integration.
security: Install-time supply chain risk. bin/jev-browser.mjs:44-46 does `git clone --depth 1 --branch main` of an unpinned repo and then runs its scripts/setup.mjs with node. Any main-branch content, including a hijacked or recreated legostin/jev-browser repo, executes on the user's machine. Nothing is pinned or checksummed.
README offers `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash` and a `gh api ... | bash` installer, both curl|sh style. Those are unauditable now because the repo is 404.

Background auto-update is on by default. README: 'MCP starts, checks for updates in the background, at most once a day' from main. Validated builds become current, so unreviewed remote code runs on every MCP launch.
Persistent background service. It survives terminal close and is not tied to the Claude session. Local dashboard link contains an access token.

Chrome extension uses the `debugger`, `tabs`, `nativeMessaging`, `webNavigation` permissions. It gives CDP-level control of the user's real logged-in Chrome, and a Native Messaging host is registered. This is a large attack surface, especially on client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: web page content is fed to Jev, and results and findings are returned to Claude. Passwords can be passed through MCP args into the Claude transcript. README admits: 'MCP arguments may remain in the calling conversation's history'.
entries.dataEgress: Only to OpenRouter (Decisions API), per README. Per step it sends a compact page structure (DOM/ARIA groups, labels, field values except password/secret-typed fields), the goal, planned values, browserContext (URLs, clicked elements, typed text, up to 14 KB), and the saved findings. It does not send source code, diffs or Claude prompts, because it is unrelated to the repo. The risk is browsing-session content. It uses the user's real Chrome with existing sign-ins, so private pages, client portals and form data go to OpenRouter and Jev. Local history under ~/.local/share/jev-browser also stores page-derived data. It cannot be exercised or audited for coding tasks, because it has no code-editing surface at all.
entries.failureMode: Unverifiable in code. README says it fails closed and safe on ambiguity. Below minConfidence (default 0.55) or on an uncertain result it stops with needs_review or needs_input and returns alternatives. It never auto-lowers the threshold and never auto-replays mutations. If GitHub or npm is down, the auto-update keeps the working release. Timeout values for Jev calls are not documented. Tool calls block for up to 25 s (jev_run) and 45 s (jev_wait), so a slow Jev stalls the Claude turn. If the engine repo cannot be cloned, `install` throws and nothing works (bin/jev-browser.mjs:27).
entries.contextCost: 8 MCP tools. README-derived estimate of about 1.5-2.5k tokens for names, descriptions and schemas. jev_run and jev_resume have large schemas (goal, values, secrets, plan, checks, limits, sessionId). Plus an installed skill (the sibling skill is about 11 KB, or about 2.8k tokens, when loaded). No hooks and nothing injected per prompt. MCP server instructions are unknown. The tools are only useful for browser tasks. The user already has Playwright MCP loaded, so this duplicates and competes with it.
pros: Uses OpenRouter as its native Jev provider. The README describes `jev configure` with an OpenRouter key and the Decisions API, which matches the user's chosen provider.

Thoughtful design per README: confidence threshold (default 0.55) with alternatives and probabilities surfaced, stale-target revalidation, and passwords kept out of the model context by design. Sound principles for browser use.
API key handling looks good: hidden-input configure, 0600 .env, and the key not in argv or the extension.
Cheap per run, according to the README (about $0.001-0.002 per 5-step task), and an explicit Claude Code install path exists (`--client claude`).
No npm postinstall script, and the 32 KB shim is small and easy to read.
cons: Engine repo legostin/jev-browser returns 404 (gh repo view and git clone fail), so the package cannot be installed or audited. The npm shim clones that repo, so `install` fails or, worse, would run whatever a re-created repo contains.

Solves the wrong problem. It is a browser-automation agent, not a coding-assistant decision layer. It has no hook, no routing, no permission or classification role, and nothing to make Claude Code use Jev for code tasks. It scores near zero against the user's stated goal of automatic, prompt-free integration.
Not automatic. It relies on Claude's discretion to call browser tools. The user already has Playwright MCP, which overlaps.

Runs unpinned code from main and auto-updates daily. It also uses curl|bash installers, a persistent background service, a Native Messaging host and a Chrome extension with `debugger` permission over the real signed-in browser. This is a heavy trust and attack surface for a developer handling client projects.
Prompt-injection and data-egress exposure: page content from signed-in sessions goes to OpenRouter and results go back to Claude. Secrets can land in the conversation history.
Immature. Two npm versions published on one day (2026-09-18), single author, no discernible stars or community, alpha dependency on the OpenRouter Decisions API, and a missing license.

Duplicates a sibling from the same author (legostin/jev-mcp), which is public, MIT and inspectable. If a Jev browser MCP is wanted at all, that repo or another public alternative is better to evaluate.
entries.verdict: Not recommended. The GitHub repo the npm shim depends on is 404, so it cannot be installed or audited. Even if it worked, it is a browser-automation MCP that duplicates Playwright and does not give Claude Code automatic Jev decisions for coding. It also runs unpinned auto-updating code with heavy Chrome-debugger permissions.
entries.license: Unknown. No license field in package.json, no LICENSE in the npm tarball, and the source repo is inaccessible. (Sibling legostin/jev-mcp is MIT.)

entries.name: abeatrix/cline-plugin-jev-browser
entries.what: Cline plugin with isolated Playwright browser; jev_run loops Jev choices over indexed DOM targets via Vercel AI Gateway, with screenshots and jev_stop.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion tool (Cline)
pros: Jev picks actions from structured DOM observations, no free text; smart split with a text model for TYPE_TEXT
Tests present, single-step-comparison design
cons: Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY), not OpenRouter; Cline plugin only
Redundant with playwright MCP already installed; 1 commit, 0 stars

entries.name: jegrep (crates.io)
entries.what: Rust CLI (~18.6k lines incl. 5.1k vendored walker) for semantic grep. It walks the live tree respecting .gitignore, sends batched file listings and file/passage content to Jev as Noul/Choice questions, and prints files with P(yes) and line ranges. Output is human, --json, or --compact tab-separated. It has 13 exploration strategies (default cascade). No index, daemon, MCP server, hook or skill is shipped.
entries.autoInvocation: Manual only. Nothing is shipped for Claude Code, so automatic use depends entirely on the user's own CLAUDE.md rule or a small skill saying to run 'jegrep "<query>" --compact' via Bash for conceptual 'where is X handled' questions. A PreToolUse hook on Grep could in theory redirect fuzzy queries to it, but that is custom work and would stack on the existing seconds-long gitnexus hook.
security: Key handling: the key is read from the process env, then from ~/.env (env.rs:6-35). It goes only into an Authorization Bearer header (jev.rs:101), never argv, so nothing appears in ps. It reads ~/.env whole-line for the requested variable only.

No telemetry or analytics found (grep for telemetry/analytics/proxy in src is empty). The only network calls go to the openrouter.ai, api.typesafe.ai or configured local URL. The one subprocess-like call is process::exit; there is no shell exec. The code has an unsafe/libc/windows-sys path in the vendored walker only.

Secret withholding: src/tree.rs SECRET_FILES/SECRET_EXT never lists or reads .env, .netrc, .npmrc, id_rsa, *.pem, *.key, *.tfvars, *.tfstate and similar, even with --hidden. src/secrets.rs also does a content check before send (PEM blocks, GCP service-account JSON, AWS keys, ghp_/xoxb-/sk- tokens). --allow-secrets disables it. This is a safety net only; an unfamiliar token pasted into config.yaml is sent.

Prompt-injection surface: repo file contents are placed in Jev 'state'. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so an injected instruction cannot execute anything. It can only skew ranking (independent evals show that risk). Output text pasted back into Claude is paths and numbers, plus a snippet in the human format. --compact has no snippets, which limits the injection channel into the Claude context.
Privacy: code from client repos is sent to OpenRouter and its upstream provider. That is a policy concern, not a bug.

Supply chain: the crate is 11 days old and has 3 contributors. Prefer the release binary with SHA256SUMS, or build from a pinned tag. The tag build is CI-gated, actions are SHA-pinned, and there is no release secret.
entries.dataEgress: Leaves the machine over HTTPS to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai on failover if both keys are set): the directory and file listings of the searched tree (paths), the query text, and file/passage content. Defaults are 8 KB per passage for cascade and 32 KB per file for the whole-file strategies. Credential-looking files are withheld by name and by content. Files matching .gitignore, lockfiles, build dirs, binary extensions and dot-files are not sent. Nothing else leaves the machine. A search over a few thousand files is about 36k tokens, about 9 requests. The Bearer key goes in the header only. Failover to a second provider is silent unless --only is used.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft and non-blocking. The process exits 2 if no key resolves, the query is empty, the strategy is unknown or the path is bad. Otherwise it retries 429/529/5xx with backoff, max_retries 6, backoff capped at 20 s (jev.rs:449-454), with a 120 s global HTTP timeout per request (jev.rs:247). Failed requests are logged and counted, and the run still completes with whatever was judged (README on local endpoints, applies generally). So a provider outage can look like zero hits. Claude could read that as 'nothing exists', so the footer's error counts need checking. The worst-case wall time is minutes, and a Bash timeout is needed. It never blocks tool use, because it is only a called CLI and not a hook.
entries.contextCost: Zero standing cost: no MCP tools, no hook injection, no skill listing entry. Adding a CLAUDE.md snippet or a small skill costs roughly 150-300 tokens (a skill description in the 0.02 budget). Per call, --compact output is about 10-20 rows, roughly 300-600 tokens. Much cheaper than gitnexus MCP tool definitions.
pros: Native OpenRouter: /alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY preferred by default (jev.rs:43,82). No patching, and --only openrouter forbids silent billing on a second account.

Real agent ergonomics: --compact gives tab-separated path, score and spans, with a root-relative trailer. It is stable to parse, has no snippets (a small injection surface), and costs roughly 300-600 tokens.
Zero standing context and zero hook latency. It is a plain CLI called on demand via Bash, so it does not touch the existing no-secret-leak or gitnexus hooks.
Solid secret hygiene for a tool that uploads code: credential files skipped by name and by content (tree.rs, secrets.rs). Key goes only in a header. No telemetry, no shell exec.

Engineering quality above typical for age: 83 unit tests including failover and retry against local TCP servers, strict clippy, SHA-pinned CI on 5 platforms, release binaries with SHA256SUMS, benchmark harness on postgres/linux/kubernetes/cpython.
Cheap (about $0.0015-0.005 per search) and index-free, so results are never stale, unlike an indexed tool.
cons: No Claude Code integration. Claude does not use it unless told by CLAUDE.md or a skill, which is a partial fit for the 'never prompt use jev' goal. The user must author and maintain the trigger rule, and Claude may still prefer Grep or gitnexus.

Model default is 'jev-latest' (main.rs:86), and the brief's OpenRouter id is 'typesafe/jev-1.13'. Whether OpenRouter's alpha endpoint accepts the alias is unverified statically. A --model override may be needed.

Reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from ~/.env as a fallback (env.rs). This is a wider read path than the env only. The user's no-secret-leak.cjs hook does not protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY yet, so it should be added. The key must also be in the environment of Claude's Bash tool.

Privacy: uploads file content of client repos to OpenRouter and its upstream. Secret detection is heuristic. In bypassPermissions sessions it runs without any prompt, so client repos should be excluded by rule.

Failure mode can look like emptiness. Request errors are counted and the run continues, so a 429 or outage yields few or no hits with exit 0. Claude may wrongly conclude the code does not exist. Worst-case wall time is several minutes (6 retries, 20 s backoff, 120 s per request).

Very young (created 2026-09-19, v0.1.3, 19 commits, about 99 crates.io downloads, 3 contributors). Linux release binaries need glibc >= 2.39 (Debian 13 is fine). Only the Jev /alpha endpoint with no SLA, 32k context, and a calibration record that is only fair.
Overlaps the installed gitnexus and plain Grep. Value is mainly for concept-level questions in unfamiliar repos, so it is not a daily driver for every task.

--compact output hides request errors and failover. The trailer has no error count and no 'failed over' flag, and the process exits 0 even if every request failed. The audit's own mitigation, checking footer error counts, is not possible in compact mode, so an outage looks like '0 hit(s)'. Claude would need --json or stderr to tell them apart.

The default model 'jev-latest' is not in OpenRouter's public /api/v1/models listing. That listing only shows typesafe/jev-router, a different product, and Jev itself is an unlisted alpha model. The default alias is unverified on OpenRouter, so a wrapper or the CLAUDE.md rule should always pass --model typesafe/jev-1.13 explicitly.

Silent failover to TYPESAFE_API_KEY happens whenever that key is present in the env or in ~/.env. Failover triggers on 401/402/403/408/429/5xx, transport errors and invalid responses. Client code can then reach a second vendor account. Use --only openrouter.

Env lookup also reads JEGREP_ENDPOINT_URL and the API keys from ~/.env. The JEGREP_DUMP env var prints request bodies, which include file content, to stderr. If it is set in a session, that content ends up in the Claude transcript. This is minor.

Static reading only: nothing was built or run, and there is no live-API test in the repo. The request and response shape is shared between /alpha/decisions and api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, and OpenRouter acceptance is unverified.
entries.verdict: Best-quality OpenRouter-native Jev tool in the set: it is well tested, has a clean --compact agent mode, sends no key in argv, has good secret withholding, and costs nothing in standing context or per-tool latency. Full automation still needs a user-written CLAUDE.md rule or skill, since no MCP, hook or skill ships. Use pinned release binaries with --only openrouter, --model set explicitly and client repos excluded. Add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the secret-leak hook.

verification.note: Verified from source. The OpenRouter endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and OPENROUTER_API_KEY are at src/jev.rs:35,43 (via Endpoint::url and key_name). OpenRouter is preferred by default (jev.rs:82). The Bearer header is sent only in the Authorization header (jev.rs:101 region). The retry list (429/529/5xx, max_retries 6, 20 s backoff cap, 120 s global timeout) is correct. Live repo metadata matches the audit: 101 stars, 9 forks, MIT, not archived, pushed 2026-09-26, created 2026-09-19, 19 commits, v0.1.3, 5 release assets plus SHA256SUMS, glibc >= 2.39 stated in the README. crates.io shows 4 versions and 99 downloads. There are 83 #[test] functions. There is no telemetry, and no Command::new anywhere except a subprocess-free code path (only process::exit); unsafe appears only in src/walker/cache.rs and src/walker/mod.rs. No MCP, hook or skill is shipped, which the audit states correctly. The secret file and extension lists in tree.rs:140-175 and the content check in secrets.rs are real. The main issues are that OpenRouter acceptance of the 'jev-latest' alias is unverified (Jev is not in the public OpenRouter models list), that --compact hides error and failover information (so an outage reads as zero hits), and that there is no Claude Code integration. I lowered the score from 7 to 6.5: the tool is good, but the failure signal is missing in the mode meant for agents, and auto-invocation needs custom work.

judge.why: Cleanest engineering of the set: Rust single binary, 83 tests, SHA-pinned CI, SHA256SUMS on releases, real secret withholding, no telemetry, no shell exec. It ships no Claude Code integration, so use depends on your own CLAUDE.md line or skill.
pros: --compact output is token-lean (about 300 to 600 tokens per call), with no snippets, which limits the injection channel into Claude's context
Credential files are withheld by name and by content before upload (tree.rs, secrets.rs); key goes only in a header
Zero standing context and no hook latency; index-free so never stale; about $0.0015 to $0.005 per search
Retries are bounded (6 retries, 20 s backoff cap, 120 s request timeout)
cons: --compact hides errors and failover: an all-requests-failed run prints '0 hit(s)' and exits 0, so an outage looks like 'nothing exists'. Use --json or check stderr
Silent failover to TYPESAFE_API_KEY if that key is in env or ~/.env; use --only openrouter
Not automatic: needs your own CLAUDE.md rule or skill and Bash allow-rule, and Opus may still prefer Grep or gitnexus
Uploads passage content of client repos; secret detection is heuristic; 11 days old, v0.1.3, about 99 downloads; glibc >= 2.39

entries.name: bartlomein/oko
entries.what: Local Rust binary (oko) that runs an MCP stdio server exposing a single code-search tool (mcp__oko__search). It does local ripgrep/BM25/tree-sitter retrieval to build up to 60 candidate snippets (max 32,000 bytes per request), then asks Jev via the System One API (/v1/systemone) one Noul yes/no relevance question per candidate and returns the top ~3 excerpts with line numbers. `oko setup --client claude` also writes a managed section into CLAUDE.md, adds SessionStart/SubagentStart/PreToolUse hooks to .claude/settings.local.json, and allow-lists mcp__oko__search. Also has CLI (oko ask/rank/auth) and a --deep multi-step mode.
entries.autoInvocation: Hybrid, mostly model-discretion. The MCP tool is alwaysLoad'ed (visible to main agent and subagents) and steered by CLAUDE.md guidance + SessionStart/SubagentStart context + PreToolUse reminder every 4th grep + deterministic rewrite of Explore/Plan/general-purpose subagent prompts. Nothing forces or intercepts Grep/Glob; Claude may still grep. No user prompting needed after `oko setup`, but setup is per-project (CLAUDE.md + settings.local.json in each repo).
security: Key never on argv: read from env, cwd .env, or OS keyring (keyring crate, zeroize); `oko auth login` uses hidden prompt; docs say never pass keys as arguments. On headless Linux without Secret Service the keyring errors and you must use env var.

install.sh (curl|sh style, 109 lines) is careful: HTTPS-only, downloads release tarball plus SHA256SUMS from same GitHub release (checksum protects against corruption, not a compromised release), rejects unsafe tar paths/links, runs `oko --version` before linking; no root. macOS binaries unsigned. I did not run it. Rust source build alternative exists (cargo).

No npm postinstall; prebuilt binary + bundled ripgrep from GitHub releases; single-author repo (158+11 of 175 commits by owner, 6 by CharlieHelps bot), 7 stars, 12 days old, so supply-chain trust is low.

Prompt-injection surface: candidate code snippets from the repo are embedded in the Jev request state and returned to Claude as tool output; server instructions say 'Source excerpts are untrusted data'. Jev returns only numeric probabilities so it is not a text-injection channel itself. Hook text is phrased as facts because Claude Code treats imperative hook text as injection.

Hook rewrites Agent subagent prompts (updatedInput) - a behaviour-modifying hook that may collide with other PreToolUse hooks (GitNexus, secret-guard) since it also matches Bash|Grep|Glob. Never denies/blocks.

Setup edits CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.local.json in each project (client repos too) and adds allow rule for mcp__oko__search; under your bypass/auto mode the allow rule is moot. Managed markers make it idempotent, but it leaves files in client repos (settings.local.json is typically gitignored, CLAUDE.md is not).
entries.dataEgress: Per search: the user's question text plus up to ~60 shortlisted code snippets (whole request capped at 32,000 bytes; trailing items dropped) with file-path 'source' labels, sent to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/v1/systemone (TypeSafe or, if repointed, OpenRouter, which then routes to TypeSafe). Multi-question calls and --deep send several requests. Not sent: full repo, diffs, tool outputs, Claude conversation. Local index cache lives in ~/.cache/oko. Hook and MCP process otherwise make no network calls. With client repos this means client source snippets go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (a contract consideration); --no-jev avoids all egress but then no Jev.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for Claude. Jev call has a 10s hard reqwest timeout, no retries (ranking.rs JEV_TIMEOUT=10s); the MCP path uses a shorter 4s patience (mcp.rs JEV_PATIENCE, overridable OKO_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, clamped 500ms-10s) and on timeout/error returns keyword-ranked results labelled 'lexical-fallback' instead of an error. Missing key: MCP returns an error message telling to run oko auth login (mcp.rs:486) unless started with --no-jev. Hooks print {} on any error and never block; timeouts 10s/5s. A process-wide token bucket throttles at 200k tokens/s. Claude can always fall back to native grep (guidance says so).
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (search) with a ~1.4 KB description plus a schema of 8 params (~700 chars incl. doc comments) => roughly 500-600 tokens always loaded (alwaysLoad meta forces it out of deferred ToolSearch). MCP server instructions ~500 chars (~125 tokens). Per project CLAUDE.md managed section ~2.9 KB (~750 tokens) added every session. SessionStart hook ~600 chars (~150 tokens) once; subagent-start hook ~500 chars per subagent; PreToolUse reminder ~250 chars every 4th grep/Glob; ~200 chars appended to each exploring subagent prompt. Total baseline about 1.5k tokens per session per project, plus tool results up to 16,000 bytes (~4k tokens) per search (MAX_MCP_RESULT_BYTES).
pros: Only Jev integration found whose whole purpose is automatic use inside a coding agent: Jev is on the hot path of every search and the user never has to say 'use jev'.

Correct use of Jev's strengths: independent Noul yes/no relevance per candidate, numeric output only (ranking.rs:261-330), no free text from Jev, cheap at ~$0.042/1M input tokens with 32KB caps per request.

Provider layer is one function: base URL, model and bearer key are all env-configurable, path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so OpenRouter is likely a pure config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY).
Fail-open design: 4s patience then labelled lexical fallback, hooks never block, native grep remains available; no dependence on Jev availability.
Key handling is good: OS keyring/env/.env, hidden prompt, zeroize, nothing in argv; no telemetry endpoints; only one outbound call site.

Sophisticated auto-adoption: alwaysLoad meta, subagent prompt rewriting, grep reminders, guidance in CLAUDE.md; tool results returned as exact current file text with line numbers so Claude can edit directly; result stub dedup and 16KB result cap.

Substantial test suite (~330 #[test], big tests/mcp.rs 2.7k lines) and CI with build workflow; published benchmarks with raw results (author claims 17-27% fewer tokens, 32-53% fewer tool calls); MIT license; MCP works with Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode; single static binary, no Node/Python runtime.
Supports TS/JS/Python/Go/Rust/Ruby/Java/Kotlin via tree-sitter for caller/usage queries.
cons: Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-18, 175 commits in 12 days, 7 stars, 0 forks, 6 releases; v0.6.0 'prerelease' per README. Expect breaking changes and bus-factor 1.

Not natively OpenRouter: only TYPESAFE_* env vars; OpenRouter compatibility is my inference from matching path/schema, not tested (I did not run it). BASE_URL/MODEL are not read from .env so must go in the MCP env block; the key variable name is misleading (OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY).

Sends user questions and up to 32KB of code snippets per search to OpenRouter and TypeSafe: a real client-confidentiality issue for the user's client projects, with no redaction and no per-project allowlist besides --no-jev.

Overlaps with existing GitNexus (graph query/context/impact) and Claude Code's own Grep/Glob; the user now has two code-navigation MCPs competing for the agent's attention, and oko's PreToolUse matcher (Bash|Grep|Glob|Agent) stacks on GitNexus and the secret-guard hooks on the same events. Its Agent-prompt rewrite may fight GitNexus guidance.

Setup is per project and mutates repos: CLAUDE.md managed section (committed file), .claude/settings.local.json hooks, `claude mcp add-json --scope local`; must be repeated for every repo and can leave diffs in client repos. --no-hooks/--no-instructions reduce this but also reduce auto-invocation.
Auto-invocation is still model-discretion: nothing intercepts Grep; adoption depends on guidance text. Under Opus 5.5 it may or may not prefer it; the author's benchmarks are self-run.

Jev only reranks a lexical shortlist, so recall is bounded by BM25/ripgrep retrieval; skeptics' claim that Jev is a router-ish model is irrelevant here but quality of Noul vs a local reranker is unproven independent of author benchmarks.
install.sh is curl|sh style with checksum from same release origin; unsigned macOS binaries; needs glibc>=2.35 (fine on Debian 13). Linux keyring needs Secret Service/D-Bus, else must use env var.
Context tax of about 1.5k tokens per session per project plus up to ~4k tokens per search result.

4xx failures (revoked/invalid OpenRouter key, 402 no credits, wrong model id) are NOT covered by the lexical fallback and surface as mcp__oko__search errors; Claude must notice and grep instead (main.rs:246-254).

`oko setup` copies an env-provided TYPESAFE_API_KEY into the OS keyring without being asked (auth.rs:90-100); combined with using an OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY this persists it and it then silently overrides nothing but also survives env changes.

Default setup target is codex, and --client claude installs only local-scope (per-project) MCP entry in ~/.claude.json plus per-repo CLAUDE.md and .claude/settings.local.json; there is no user-scope install, so 'automatic everywhere' requires repeating setup for every repo, including client repos (committed CLAUDE.md diff).

Hook is a PreToolUse process on every Bash/Grep/Glob/Agent call and rewrites Agent prompts via updatedInput; it runs in parallel with the user's gitnexus PreToolUse and no-secret-leak hooks on the same matchers, so updatedInput/additionalContext interplay with gitnexus guidance is untested. Benign per docs (updatedInput without permissionDecision is valid) but adds a third context-injecting layer.

Scope is code search only: it does not give the user's other requested Jev uses (permission gating, routing, classification), so 'whenever it adds value' is narrow and the value overlaps gitnexus query/context and Claude's own Grep/Explore.
Very high release churn (v0.6.0 on 09-28, 0.6.1 on main 09-30, guidance text changing daily) plus zero forks and a single maintainer; pinning a release or vendoring is advisable.

File discovery via ripgrep respects ignore rules but no secret redaction: tracked config files containing keys/tokens can be shipped as snippets to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, and the user's no-secret-leak hook does not cover the MCP server's egress.
entries.verdict: Best candidate found for genuinely automatic, everyday Jev use in Claude Code: a real, well-tested, fail-open MCP server with hooks and guidance whose provider layer looks repointable to OpenRouter with three env vars. Adopt it cautiously (try with --no-hooks first, verify the OpenRouter /v1/systemone response shape on a scratch repo, and keep it off client repos unless snippet egress to OpenRouter/TypeSafe is acceptable), given its age, single maintainer and overlap with GitNexus.

verification.note: Repo re-queried 2026-09-30: 7 stars, 0 forks, MIT, not archived, pushed today, Cargo 0.6.1 on main. entries.name: jev-grep (jgrep)
entries.what: Python CLI (PyPI jev-grep 0.6.0, command jgrep) that turns each input line, paragraph, file, JSONL/CSV field, text chunk, Python/Go/C function, or unified-diff hunk into one Jev yes/no (Noul) question built from a plain-English description. It prints matches in input order with probabilities. Answers are cached in SQLite and a $1 budget applies by default. It ships one SKILL.md (skills/jgrep/SKILL.md) but no MCP server, no hook, and no plugin.json or marketplace.json. Provider plumbing (URLs, keys, retries, cache, budget) lives in a separate shared package, jevkit-runtime 0.4.2 (github.com/keltokhy/jevkit-core, MIT, 0 stars, same author).
entries.autoInvocation: Skill-description trigger only (model discretion). The description is 'Filter text, records, code functions, or complete diff hunks by a plain-English description using Jev.
