Use for semantic filtering and code navigation...'. It says nothing about when Claude should pick it over Grep, and it is not framed as a proactive default. Nothing forces it: no hook, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no permission allow-rules are provided. The SKILL.md starts with 'Check command -v jgrep', so the CLI must be installed first. To make it automatic, the user would need their own CLAUDE.md rule or a rewritten skill description, plus Bash(jgrep:*) in the allowlist.
security: Key handling is good. The Bearer key goes in an HTTP header (jevkit-core client.py:205-209), never argv. It is read from env or ~/.config/jev/openrouter.key. SECURITY.md says keys are never written to the cache or logs. I did not audit every logging path.

This user's existing no-secret-leak hook does not list OPENROUTER_API_KEY. An env-var key would be visible to any Bash command Claude runs (env, printenv). A key file at ~/.config/jev/openrouter.key is also readable by Read or cat unless the hook is extended.

No shell exec: diff_context.py:71 and :101 call git via subprocess with fixed argv lists. GIT_NO_LAZY_FETCH, GIT_NO_REPLACE_OBJECTS and protocol.ext.allow=never are set to blunt hostile repos. -W confines paths to the repo root. The README says it is not a sandbox. A worker-process pool exists in jevkit-core workers.py; I did not review it in depth.

No telemetry found: the only outbound hits are the provider endpoint (plus an X-Title 'jev tools' header) and the optional gateway or local URLs. The X-Title header lets OpenRouter attribute traffic to 'jev tools'.

Prompt-injection surface: every judged line, hunk or function is untrusted text placed in the Jev state. The README admits 'text in the input can try to steer the answer. Do not use jgrep as a security boundary'. Output is only a probability, so Jev cannot inject instructions into Claude, and matched lines are echoed verbatim to Claude's context, which is normal grep behaviour.

Supply chain: this is a single-maintainer, one-person project created 2026-09-18. Publishing uses PyPI Trusted Publishing from a GitHub workflow with actions pinned by SHA. The runtime dependency jevkit-runtime is a second package from the same author, at version 0.4.2. The repo is only 12 days old, so it has no track record.
entries.dataEgress: Every judged unit is POSTed to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That is the full line (up to 8000 chars by default), the -C neighbour lines, the whole paragraph, file or chunk, the full function body for --functions, and each full diff hunk plus the enclosing function up to 8000 chars with -W. The description question goes along with it, plus the model name and the Bearer key. Cached answers are not re-sent. A recursive search over a client repo therefore uploads its source text to OpenRouter, and from there to TypeSafe as the model provider. A large run is one request per unit (32 in flight), which is an easy way to send a lot of client code without a prompt. No file paths or telemetry are sent beyond what the state text contains. The local backends (--api diffusiongemma, laya or gliner) keep everything on the machine but need a self-run server.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the tool itself, not for Claude Code. There is no hook, so a jgrep failure cannot block anything. Bad key: JevFatal stops the run at once, exit 2. Timeout: the default is 15 s per line with 4 attempts, exponential backoff, and Retry-After honoured for 408/429/5xx/529 (transport.py:16,52). Failed lines are reported as errors and exit 2. Budget: at $1 the run stops with 'stopped at the budget' and exits 2 while printing partial results. Distinguishing 'no match' (exit 1) from 'error' (exit 2) is well handled, but Claude has to read the exit code and stderr. On the alpha endpoint with no SLA, a large tree at 32 concurrency can hit 429s and produce partial results.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no hook-injected text. As a skill, the description is one line of about 190 chars (about 50 tokens against a skillListingBudgetFraction of 0.02). The SKILL.md body is about 4.5 KB (about 1.1k tokens), loaded only when the skill is invoked. Output goes to Claude only for what it pipes back, e.g. 'jgrep ... | head'.
pros: OpenRouter is first-class and working out of the box: jevkit-core providers.py:84-91 uses /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ~/.config/jev/openrouter.key is auto-selected when it is the only key. No patching.

Real code-oriented modes rather than only text grep: --functions (Python AST; Go/C via tree-sitter), --diff for git diff/log -p hunks, and -W for enclosing-function context. All are usable as a review filter, e.g. `git diff | jgrep --diff "removes error handling"`.

--estimate is genuinely offline (no key, no network) and reports call count, tokens and cost. A hard $1 default budget, reserved per request before sending, guards against a stray recursive run. The cache makes repeats free.

Safety-conscious engineering: git is invoked via fixed argv with hostile-repo env flags, -W paths are confined to the repo root, key goes in a header, and no telemetry was found. The README and SKILL.md openly state that model output is not a security boundary and that flagged code needs manual inspection.

Broad tests: about 146 test functions across 10 files, offline against a fake API and a local HTTP server. There are benchmarks (SMS spam F1 0.91, AG News 86.6%, a 20-example code-review experiment) and honest caveats. The license is MIT, and releases (v0.4.1 tag, PyPI 0.6.0) are published via trusted publishing.
Tiny context footprint: no MCP tools, a roughly 50-token skill listing entry, and a roughly 1.1k-token body loaded only on use. Cost is about $0.0000126 per typical line.
Pipe-friendly with grep-style exit codes and --json output, so it can be chained in Bash or wrapped in a user-written hook.
cons: It is a filter over text Claude already has or a file set, not a decision gate and not a replacement for real Grep or gitnexus. Claude will still default to Grep/gitnexus unless the description or a CLAUDE.md rule pushes it. The skill description contains no 'use proactively when...' guidance, so the user's 'never prompt use jev' goal is not met by the repo as shipped.

Every judged unit is uploaded to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. --functions -r or --diff -W on a client repo sends source code out, one request per function or hunk, at 32 concurrent. There is no allowlist, secret redaction, or per-project opt-in. For client projects this needs a policy decision, or a local --api backend.

Cost is per unit, not per file: a large recursive run means thousands of parallel calls to an /alpha endpoint with no SLA and 32k context, risking 429s and partial results (exit 2). The $1 budget caps spend but not egress volume.

Accuracy limits apply: TypeSafe itself documents weak spots (counting, numeric comparison, double negatives, long inputs). Jev's overconfidence on unanswerable inputs and injection steering are amplified when the input is untrusted repo text. The tool's own code-review experiment used only 20 handwritten examples.

Brand new and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18, 52 commits in 12 days (47 by keltokhy, 4 by Claude, 1 by Neel Patel), 4 forks, and a runtime split across two repos (jevkit-core has 0 stars). The GitHub release tag is v0.4.1 while pyproject and PyPI are at 0.6.0, and a 0.5.x/0.6.0 breaking change to --budget semantics already happened. Expect API churn.

Install and setup are manual: `uv tool install jev-grep` (PyPI, not vetted by this audit), the key must be placed in env or a file, the skill has to be copied into ~/.claude/skills, and Bash(jgrep:*) must be allowed. OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not covered by the user's no-secret-leak hook.

Fit to the workflow is narrow. Many daily tasks (find a symbol, read a file) are better served by ripgrep/gitnexus at zero cost and zero egress. The best fit is the semantic review filter on diffs, and that is an occasional rather than daily use.
Known open limitations documented in the README: CRLF patches and quoted paths with spaces give spurious errors, and C with macros is often skipped.
entries.verdict: The strongest OpenRouter-ready Jev CLI found so far. It is well engineered, tested and cost-guarded, and works with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY, with a small context footprint. It is still an opt-in filter, not an automatic integration: nothing makes Claude reach for it, it uploads client source to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and it is a 12-day-old single-author project. Worth installing as a manually or CLAUDE.md-nudged semantic diff/function filter for personal repos, not as the automatic Jev backbone.

judge.why: Strongest code-oriented modes (--functions, --diff with -W enclosing function) plus an offline --estimate and a $1 default budget. It is an opt-in filter, not automatic, and it is new and single-maintainer.
pros: --diff and --functions are useful as a semantic review filter (git diff | jgrep --diff "removes error handling")
--estimate works offline; hard $1 budget; SQLite answer cache makes repeats free
Key in header only, git called with fixed argv and hostile-repo env flags, no telemetry found
About 146 tests, MIT, trusted publishing, about 50-token skill listing
cons: Not automatic: skill has no 'use proactively' framing; the CLI must be installed via uv tool and the skill copied by hand
Uploads full lines, functions and hunks (up to 8000 chars) at 32 concurrent; a recursive run on a client repo exfiltrates a lot of code silently
Two packages by the same author (jevkit-runtime 0.4.2); GitHub tag v0.4.1 vs PyPI 0.6.0; a breaking --budget change already happened
Local cache may hold derived data; OPENROUTER_API_KEY not covered by your secret hook

entries.name: sufianetaouil/every
entries.what: `every` CLI (pip every-cli): asks a yes/no question of every function in a codebase via Jev, returns ranked hits with cost and a local cache; usable by an agent as a semantic grep. Plugin wrapper included.
entries.autoInvocation: manual / skill or model discretion via Bash
pros: Unique capability: question-shaped grep over all functions (thousands for cents, seconds), JSON output, cache keyed by hash
Stated cost/latency data (gin 1302 funcs 3.7s $0.018); 21 test files; selftest reports AUROC
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override in reference/sweep.py
cons: Sends all function source to a third party: unacceptable for many client repos
Not auto-invoked: needs skill or model choice; requires pip install (uv tool)
Overconfidence on unanswerable questions means noisy hits; created 2026-09-17 with single push

entries.name: Bentlybro/siftr
entries.what: Stdlib-only Python CLI plus stdio MCP server exposing four read-only tools (semantic_search, focused_read, pick_relevant, filter_output). Each tool packs code outlines or chunks into batches, asks Jev a `noul` question ("is this relevant to the query?") per item through hundreds of parallel requests, and ranks or filters the returned P(yes). It is a real, purpose-built Jev integration: Jev is used as a cheap relevance judge, not as a chat model. `siftr agents install` also rewrites the MCP config files of many coding agents.
interface: semantic_search(query, path?, top?, files_only?, glob?, include_tests?)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill or proxy. Claude will call semantic_search only if its description, plus the optional CLAUDE.md snippet from docs/agents.md, convinces the model to prefer it. Its descriptions do say 'Use it FIRST when you don't know the exact identifiers', which nudges usage. The project itself recommends adding a CLAUDE.md block to make agents use it, so unprompted usage is probabilistic and not guaranteed. With existing GitNexus and Grep/Glob tools, Opus 5.5 may often pick those instead.
security: API key handling is good. The key is read from env or from a 0600 file (config.py:64), sent only as a Bearer header (jev.py:71) and never put in argv. `siftr agents install` writes only command=siftr and args=[mcp], with no key in the MCP config, so nothing shows in ps or ~/.claude.json.

config.load_env (config.py:40-48) runs at CLI start and loads the first `.env` found in the CWD or any parent directory into os.environ via setdefault. Under Claude Code the CWD is the project, so a client project's .env containing OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY would be picked up, and the key used would depend on the project. Real env vars win over it. Setting the real env or the user config avoids the surprise.

No secret redaction before upload. scan.py TEXT_EXT includes .json/.yaml/.toml/.ini/.cfg/.conf/.sh/.tf. .env itself is skipped (no extension match) and dot-directories are skipped, but config files with embedded credentials can be sent as chunks (up to 1600 chars each). The existing PreToolUse secret guard does NOT cover this, because the MCP server reads files itself and does not go through the Read tool.

The MCP tools are read-only and accept arbitrary absolute paths (semantic_search path, focused_read path, filter_output path) with no root confinement (mcp.py:131, 150-155). A prompt-injected agent could point them at ~/.ssh or ~/.aws text files, which would upload contents to OpenRouter. Extensions like .json/.conf/.txt are only filtered in the directory scan, not in focused_read/filter_output, which read any file.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Jev returns only probabilities, so tool output is scores and file:line ranges plus the first line of chunk text as a preview (search.py:110-111), which is repo-controlled text echoed to the agent (minor).

Installer risks: curl|sh for siftr and, transitively, for uv. The default source is the unpinned main.zip, so a compromised repo or account gives code execution at install time. No npm-style postinstall. Runtime shell use is limited to `git ls-files` (scan.py:104).
entries.dataEgress: Yes, code content leaves the machine. Per semantic_search: (1) every file's relative path plus its symbol-name outline, in batches of up to 150 files or 24k chars, for the whole tree minus gitignored and skipped dirs; (2) the top 30 files' chunks, up to 1600 chars of raw source each, sent verbatim, plus the query text. focused_read sends chunks of the target file. pick_relevant sends the item strings. filter_output sends log chunks. Everything goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, which forwards it to TypeSafe (README 'Privacy and cost' warns not to use it on code you can't send to a third party). Nothing goes out for diffs, prompts or tool outputs unless the agent passes them as query/items. Outlines are cached locally in ~/.config/siftr/cache/. This conflicts with client-project confidentiality unless the client permits OpenRouter and TypeSafe processing; OpenRouter data policy and ZDR settings should be checked.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and bounded. Per-request timeout is 6s (engine.py:24), with 2 retries (RETRIES=2, so up to 3 attempts) and a hedged duplicate after 2s (engine.py:63-91). A request that still fails becomes {} and its items get None scores, which are dropped from results (search.py:78). In the worst case a search can take about 18s or more before returning 'No confident matches', which is misleading because it does not say Jev was down. A missing key raises JevError, surfaced as an isError tool result (mcp.py:223-224). An HTTP 401/403 gives 'API key rejected'. The server itself never crashes, since exceptions are caught in the serve loop. Claude falls back to Grep/Read because each tool description says to. There is no stalling or blocking of the main flow because these are opt-in tool calls, not hooks. The 64-thread fan-out can hit OpenRouter rate limits on large repos, and that would appear as silent partial results.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. Tool definitions total about 4,000 chars (about 1,000 tokens), and the server `instructions` string adds about 430 chars (about 110 tokens), for about 1.1k tokens always resident, or less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Tool results are compact: 10 hits at about 100 chars each.
pros: Only candidate found so far that ships a working, benchmarked Jev to OpenRouter path: correct OPENROUTER_URL and typesafe/jev-1.13 model, OPENROUTER_API_KEY preferred (jev.py:26-53). It needs no patching to match the user's provider choice.

Uses Jev for what it is actually good at, cheap parallel calibrated yes/no relevance judgments, rather than as a chat replacement. The batching design (150 items per request, 64 threads, hedged duplicates) fits Jev's 70-500ms latency.
Directly addresses a real daily-coding token sink: semantic 'where is X' search and partial reads of large files, at about 1-2 cents per big-repo search and under a cent for read/pick.

Zero dependencies, stdlib-only, about 2.8k lines of readable Python. The auditing burden is small and the runtime footprint is tiny (no npm, no build). Only ~1.1k tokens of always-resident tool definitions and no hook overhead.

Well-documented fail-open behaviour and honest limits: docs say to use grep when exact strings are known, and filter_output is labelled experimental. Results are suggestions with a map of omitted sections, so a wrong answer costs one extra read.
API key is never in argv or MCP config. It sits in a 0600 file or the env. The MCP server does not execute shell commands (deliberate design noted in mcp.py:7-10).
Frozen dev/test benchmark methodology on SWE-bench Lite, with raw result JSONs in bench/results, is more rigorous than typical for a repo this small. It is still Python-only and self-reported.
MIT license. Manual install is easy and reversible with `claude mcp add -s user siftr -- siftr mcp` and `claude mcp remove`.
cons: Not automatic. It is model-discretion only. The author's own docs say to paste a CLAUDE.md block to get agents to use it, and there are no hooks. It cannot satisfy 'Claude must use it without my prompting' deterministically, and it competes with the built-in Grep/Glob and the user's GitNexus graph tools.

Sends raw source (up to 1600-char chunks) plus all file paths and symbols to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every search. There is no redaction, no path allowlist and no project opt-out. This is a real problem for client projects under NDA, and the existing secret-leak hook never sees these reads because the MCP server reads files itself.

MCP tools take arbitrary absolute paths with no project-root confinement (mcp.py:131, 150-155), so a prompt-injected agent could exfiltrate any text file to a third party via focused_read/filter_output.
Project `.env` in cwd or parents is auto-loaded into the environment (config.py:40-48), so a client repo's own OPENROUTER_API_KEY could silently override the intended key or billing account.

Very immature: 11 days old, 8 commits all on 2026-09-19, 1 contributor, 5 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, and mid-rename (jgrep to siftr, legacy cleanup code). Expect API churn. Depends on the OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, which is alpha and could change.
Install path is curl|sh (twice: siftr, then uv) against an unpinned main.zip. `siftr agents install` edits many agent configs. Use a pinned git commit and add the MCP by hand instead.

Search cost and latency scale with repo size: about 2s and 1-2 cents per search on 4k files, and every call re-sends the full outline of all files (cached only locally). A heavy day of searches costs cents but not zero. Silent partial results under rate limiting look like 'No confident matches'.

Benchmarks are self-reported, Python-only (SWE-bench) and unverified by third parties, so quality on the user's TS/JS/other stacks is unproven. Redundant with GitNexus (which already gives graph and semantic query context) for indexed repos.

Skeptic caveat about Jev itself (possible 'flash router' behaviour, unverified) applies because the whole tool's quality depends on Jev's relevance probabilities. The benchmark was run on jev-1.13, which is the model the code pins.
entries.verdict: Best-fit Jev-on-OpenRouter integration found so far: a small, readable stdlib-only MCP server that already targets /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and it uses Jev sensibly for relevance ranking. It is still model-discretion (needs a CLAUDE.md nudge, not truly automatic) and uploads raw code chunks to a third party without redaction or path confinement, so adopt only on personal or approved repos, pinned to a reviewed commit and installed by hand rather than via curl|sh.

judge.why: Small, readable, stdlib-only Python MCP server that already targets your provider and uses Jev for cheap parallel relevance judgments. It is model-discretion only and needs a CLAUDE.md block.
pros: Correct OpenRouter endpoint and model out of the box; stdlib only, so a small supply-chain surface
Fail-open and bounded: 6 s timeout, 2 retries, hedged duplicate after 2 s; bad key gives an explicit 'API key rejected'
Batching (150 items per request, 64 threads) fits Jev's latency; about 1 to 2 cents per big-repo search
Also supports partial reads of large files to save tokens
cons: Not automatic; the author's docs tell you to paste a CLAUDE.md block; competes with Grep and gitnexus
Sends raw chunks (up to 1600 chars), all file paths and symbols to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no redaction or path allowlist; your secret hook never sees MCP-server file reads
Worst case about 18 s, and a failed search can read as 'No confident matches' without saying Jev was down
Alpha, 5 stars, install docs suggest curl|sh (install by hand instead)

entries.name: @dzhng/jevgrep (jg CLI + jevgrep skill)
entries.what: Node CLI `jg` that answers natural-language repository questions ("where is auth checked?") by walking the repo hierarchy and asking Jev many boolean (Noul) relevance questions per folder/file/declaration (tree-sitter/TS parsing), then prints a ranked file list plus verbatim source excerpts to stdout. It is not an MCP server or hook. Claude Code integration is a separate SKILL.md (installed with `jg skill`, which runs `npx --yes skills add dzhng/jevgrep --skill jevgrep`) whose description tells the model to run `jg` first for "how/why/where does X work" questions.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). The description says to start behavioral discovery with jg before broad text searches or git history and to tell subagents to use jg, so no per-prompt 'use jev' is needed. Evidence is thin: the author's pilot (evals/results/skill-trigger-2026-09-29.md) ran on Codex with a shim, 3 repeats, ceiling effect, and 'jg before ANY other search' scored 0/6 because agents did filename discovery first; not verified on Claude Code/Opus. Not deterministic: Opus 5.5 with GitNexus, Grep hooks and other skills may prefer gitnexus query, Grep or Explore subagents.
security: No execution of repo code (docs/architecture.md: repository source is never executed). Only child process is `npx --yes skills add dzhng/jevgrep ...` in `jg skill` (skill.ts:9), which pulls the third-party vercel-labs skills CLI at run time.

API key stored as plaintext JSON in ~/.config/jevgrep/credentials.json with mode 0600/dir 0700, atomic write (auth.ts:76-90); piped via stdin with --stdin so it is not in argv; interactive path uses clack password prompt. Key is redacted from provider error messages (evaluator.ts providerDiagnostic).
Env-based OPENROUTER_API_KEY is deliberately ignored; you must run `jg auth` once (the skill tells Claude not to request keys in chat). Awkward but safe.

Skill Setup section tells the agent to run `npm install --global @dzhng/jevgrep@latest` if jg is missing: an unpinned global install of a days-old package that Claude would run unprompted in bypass mode.

Prompt-injection surface is small: repo source and paths go INTO Jev requests with 'data, never instructions' guidance (requests.ts), and Jev returns only probabilities. Output to Claude is verbatim repo excerpts, same trust class as Read/Grep output.

Sensitive filtering is heuristic: skips hidden files, ignore-listed, binary, sensitive names (.pem/.key/.p12/.pfx and a name list, filesystem.ts:51-65,117-123,320) and content matching PRIVATE KEY blocks (filesystem.ts:381); README itself says filters are not a guarantee. `--include-sensitive` is opt-in.
entries.dataEgress: Eligible source content is sent to the selected provider (OpenRouter to TypeSafe Jev) on every search: directory listings and file names, file previews, sampled content, parsed declarations and source blocks, plus the natural-language query (requests.ts navigationRequest/evidenceRequest/fileAssessmentRequest). On big roots this can be most of a repo's non-ignored text (issue #38 measured median ~5M input tokens per query on a 2.7k-file repo). Does not send the Claude conversation, diffs or tool outputs; only the query string Claude writes and repo files under the chosen root. For client projects, full code goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (and any upstream), which is a contract/NDA question. Local answer cache in ~/.cache/jevgrep. No other telemetry found.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: on provider errors jg prints an incomplete/error status (exit 2 or 1) and the skill tells Claude to treat missing context as unknown and use grep/read instead. Per-request timeout 15 s for non-TypeSafe providers (60 s for direct typesafe, evaluator.ts:46), 2 attempts, Retry-After honored on 429 (waits up to 60 s), 401/403 aborts the whole search, request cap 50,000 (evaluator.ts:85-89). No global wall-clock limit: a large-repo search runs ~65-80 s (issue #38) with up to 32 concurrent requests, so failure mode is slow rather than blocking forever; HTTP 402 (out of credit) surfaces mid-query. If jg is missing or the model ignores the skill, it silently falls back to grep.
entries.contextCost: Very low. No MCP tools, no hooks. Only the skill frontmatter name+description (~490 chars, ~120 tokens) sits in the skills list permanently; the ~2.9 KB SKILL.md body (~750 tokens) loads only when triggered. The real cost is the search output itself: verbatim excerpts to stdout, capped by --max-source-bytes (render.ts) but issue #41 reports a 5 MB output for a no-match query; a typical invocation adds several thousand tokens.
pros: Only candidate audited that is actually wired to the Jev System One API through OpenRouter out of the box: `jg auth --provider openrouter --stdin` calls https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with model typesafe/jev-1.13 (providers.ts:12-16; SDK typesafe-ai-evaluation-model.ts:109). No patching needed.
Uses Jev as designed: many parallel typed boolean (Noul) probabilities, no free text, so no hallucinated answers and injection cannot alter output beyond scores.
Solves a real daily-coding task (finding relevant code in unfamiliar repos) and is passive: skill description auto-triggers on how/where questions and excludes exact-symbol lookups.
Near-zero standing context cost (one ~120-token description, no MCP tools, no hooks), so no conflict with the secret-leak guard or GitNexus hooks.

Fail-open, timeouts, retry/backoff, 401 abort, key redaction, 0600 key file, stdin key entry; unit tests plus Docker installed-package tests; SHA-pinned CI with tag-based npm release; MIT; 1.8k stars; 13 releases in 4 days.

Author benchmark on 10 SWE-bench tasks: same 8/10 solves at ~25-30% lower total cost including Jev (evals/results/total-cost-2026-09-28.md, speed-2026-09-28.md); small repos cost cents (~$0.002-0.018 per query at $0.042/M).
Filesystem filters respect .gitignore, skip hidden/dependency/binary/obvious credential files and PRIVATE KEY content; `jg files` gives an offline scope estimate; `--exclude` for sensitive paths.
cons: Sends repository source (previews, declarations, blocks) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every search; for client projects this is a real data-egress/NDA problem, and sensitive-file filtering is heuristic (README admits it).

Scales poorly: issue #38 measured median ~65 s, ~5M tokens, ~$0.22 and 215-1,483 requests per query on a 2.7k-file repo, with 19/20 runs ending 'discovery incomplete'; issue #41 reports 5 MB output and 40% of files marked relevant when nothing matches. No spend readout in CLI output.

Auto-invocation is only a soft skill trigger; author's evidence is from Codex with a shim and a tiny sample, none from Claude Code/Opus. With GitNexus hooks, Grep and Explore available, Opus may not choose jg; nothing is deterministic.
Ignores OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var by design; needs one interactive/stdin `jg auth` writing a plaintext key file. Cannot be configured via Claude Code settings/env.

Overlaps with existing GitNexus (graph query/context) and Grep/Glob, adding a second retrieval path with a different cost profile. Quality claims come from the author's tuned Python SWE-bench tasks plus one user report, not independent tests.

Very young: created 2026-09-26, 179 commits in 5 days, 174 by one author, 9 open issues, 0.1.0 to 0.7.0 in 3 days; GitHub latest release v0.6.0 vs npm 0.7.0. Needs global npm install; skill may run unpinned `npm install --global @dzhng/jevgrep@latest` unprompted in bypass mode; `jg skill` executes `npx --yes skills add`.

Uses only Noul (boolean); does not use Choice or Score, so it does nothing for other Claude Code decisions (routing, permission gating, classification). No total wall-clock limit, so one search can stall a turn for over a minute.

Output has no default size cap (DEFAULT_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES = 0). A successful query on a 6k-file root printed 10k lines; a no-answer query printed 5.4 MB. That would flood or overflow Claude Code's context or its Bash output limit, and issue #40 (spend and output budgets) is still open.

Latency and timeout mismatch with Claude Code: large-root queries take 65-385 s (issues #38, #41), versus a 120 s default Bash timeout. The SKILL.md instructs 'wait on that session/process ID', wording that does not match Claude Code's Bash tool, so long searches risk timeout or partial output.

OpenRouter path is unproven live. All author benchmarks and the #38/#41 numbers used the native TypeSafe provider. The OpenRouter preset had a wrong model id until issue #11, and OpenRouter rate limits at 32 concurrency across hundreds of requests are untested. The 15 s per-request timeout applies to it.

Sensitive-file filtering is filename-based. Secrets inline in normal source files (hardcoded keys, .env-style constants) are still uploaded to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. For the user's client projects this is a contractual and NDA problem, and the tool has no allowlist or 'refuse in this repo' switch; the only control is choosing the root and --exclude, which the model chooses, not the user.

The OpenRouter key is stored in plaintext at ~/.config/jevgrep/credentials.json (0600). It is separate from the existing no-secret-leak.cjs protected-vars list, so that guard does not cover this file or the env var. The tool ignores OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the user needs a second, unmanaged copy of the key. Piping the key via printf in a Claude-run Bash command would put it in a tool call, so it should be run in the user's own terminal.

Skill's Setup step says to run `npm install --global @dzhng/jevgrep@latest` when jg is missing. The model would run it unprompted, unpinned, under bypassPermissions. jg skill uses `npx --yes skills add` from the repo tip (issue #21 open to pin it).

bypassPermissions plus a tool that uploads repo contents means a prompt-injected repo file could steer the model to run jg on a broad root, or to pass --include-sensitive, --include-dependencies or a parent root. Only the query and files are sent, but the flags are model-controlled.
Version drift: GitHub latest release v0.6.0, npm 0.7.0, 13 versions in 4 days, repo 4 days old (created 2026-09-26), so an unpinned install may change behaviour between sessions.
entries.verdict: The only audited option that genuinely runs Jev through OpenRouter's System One endpoint out of the box and is auto-triggered by a skill description, with tiny context cost and fail-open behavior. Treat it as a supplementary code-discovery tool for small/medium personal repos (pin the version, use `jg files` and --exclude, avoid client code and big monorepos until the ~65 s/5M-token scaling and egress issues are addressed), not a core integration.

verification.note: Repo metadata re-queried on 2026-09-30. Stars 1851, MIT, not archived, last push 2026-09-29T07:30Z (commit 82ef1fd, which matches the clone), 179 commits with 174 by one author, npm 0.7.0 vs GitHub release v0.6.0, os darwin/linux, engines node>=22, no postinstall script. All confirmed. OpenRouter wiring is real in code (providers.ts:12-16 baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, model typesafe/jev-1.13; SDK tarball @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai@3.0.8 dist/index.js:126 POSTs ${baseURL}/systemone with Bearer, boolean mapped to noul). But it is selected only through `jg auth`, no env var is read, and no live OpenRouter benchmark exists. The audit's interface claims are correct: it is a CLI plus SKILL.md, not an MCP server or hook, and the `jg` subcommands exist. The Claude Code hook question is moot; the only Claude Code surface is a skill, and the frontmatter is valid. The audit is mostly accurate, and its main misses are these: (1) issue #29 does give Claude Code/Opus auto-trigger evidence (5/5 vs 0/5 with a stronger description than the one shipped); (2) the default output cap is unlimited; (3) filtering is filename-only, so inline secrets are uploaded; (4) OpenRouter is not exercised live by any eval; (5) Bash timeout and output-limit mismatch with 65-385 s and MB-scale runs. Score lowered from 6.5 to 5.5. It is a genuinely Jev-on-OpenRouter, low-standing-cost, skill-triggered tool, but it is 4 days old, uploads repo source (a real problem for client projects), scales badly, is unproven on OpenRouter, and only uses Noul for one task. It should be offered as an opt-in tool for small personal repos with a pinned version and the user's own hand-copied SKILL.md, not as a general integration.

judge.why: Most popular and the most thoughtfully skill-triggered, with third-party evidence (issue #29) of Claude Code/Opus auto-triggering. Output is uncapped and slow, and it is only proven on native TypeSafe.
pros: Only candidate with Claude Code/Opus trigger evidence: a rewritten description scored 5/5 vs 0/5 on 'how/where' prompts, and exact-symbol queries stayed on grep
No hooks or MCP tools; about 110 to 130 tokens of skill listing
Filters .env, keys, netrc and similar by filename; 1848 stars and active maintenance
cons: The shipped SKILL.md description is weaker than the one tested in #29, so the 5/5 result is unproven for what you would install
No default output cap (DEFAULT_MAX_SOURCE_BYTES=0): issue #41 shows 10k lines on success and 5.4 MB on no-answer; large roots take 65 to 385 s against a 120 s Bash timeout
Filtering is by name only; inline secrets in source files are uploaded; needs a second plaintext copy of the key, which your hook does not cover
Skill tells the model to run an unpinned npm install -g @dzhng/jevgrep@latest; 13 versions in 4 days; OpenRouter path never exercised live

entries.name: kyu1204/jgrep (npm: jevgrep)
entries.what: A zero-dependency Node CLI (`jgrep`, npm package `jevgrep`) that does semantic grep. It splits files (git ls-files) or git diff hunks into 5-60 line chunks and packs 16 chunks plus 16 Noul yes/no questions into one System One request ("does this code match: <description>"). It prints file:line hits above a probability threshold. It also has --diff (lint a diff with English rules), --tests (predictive test selection, name + import graph in code, rest via Jev) and --rows (score CSV/JSONL). A bundled SKILL.md (also a Claude Code plugin via .claude-plugin/) teaches the agent when to call the CLI through Bash. There is no MCP server and no hook.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, i.e. model discretion. The description (skills/jgrep/SKILL.md frontmatter) says to use jgrep when locating code by behavior, before opening many files, and as a self-check of the diff before committing. Claude Code would load the skill and then run the CLI through Bash. There is no hook, no MCP tool and no proxy, so there is no deterministic trigger. With Opus 5.5 and built-in Grep/Glob/Explore plus the user's GitNexus MCP and hooks, the model may often prefer those, and the reliability of the skill trigger is unproven. To make it deterministic, the user would need to add their own PreToolUse/Stop hook or a CLAUDE.md rule, which is not shipped. The skill depends on a globally installed npm binary and a key in ~/.config/jgrep/env or the env.
security: No shell string execution: git is called via execFileSync with array args (src/jgrep.ts:91,103) and xdg-open via execFile. No postinstall script in package.json. The npm tarball ships dist/skills/README/LICENSE, published via OIDC trusted publishing.

The API key is sent only in the Authorization header and never in argv, so it is not visible in the process list. It comes from the env var, ./.env, or ~/.config/jgrep/env (written 0600, dir 0700). readVar also reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from the cwd's ./.env, so a client repo's .env could inject a key or JGREP_ENDPOINT (mitigated: non-loopback http:// is rejected; an https endpoint attacker-controlled by a malicious repo's .env would still receive the key, and this is a real but narrow risk).
jgrep init can append the key to ./.env in a project (only if the user picks it) and warns if .env is not gitignored.
No telemetry beyond the API call. OpenRouter attribution headers (Referer/Title jgrep) are sent, which identifies the app, not the user. init asks to open the GitHub star page (opt-in).

Prompt-injection surface is small: the model returns only probabilities, never text, so injected text in scanned code can bias a score but cannot make the tool run commands. The bigger risk is the SKILL.md instructing the agent to trust or ignore hits. The SKILL.md itself is benign and says not to install anything.

No secret filtering. The file walker uses `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` (tracked plus untracked-not-ignored) and skips only binaries and files over 1 MB. An unignored .env, key file or credentials JSON inside the scanned path is chunked and uploaded. The user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard only sees the Bash command line and will not stop jgrep from reading files itself.
entries.dataEgress: Raw source text leaves the machine: every 5-60 line chunk of every scanned file (or every diff hunk with +/- lines and 3 context lines), plus file path, line range and the English query. It goes to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai, or JGREP_ENDPOINT) in request bodies of about 16 chunks (src/jgrep.ts buildRequest, :131-141). For --tests it also sends the compacted source diff and each test file's imports and test names. --rows sends full CSV/JSONL rows. Nothing is sent for cache hits. The local cache is ~/.cache/jgrep/cache.json, a plain JSON of sha1(query+chunk text) mapped to probability, with no code stored. Scanning a whole client repo means the whole repo goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. This matters for client NDA projects and for anything with unignored secrets.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense that nothing is in Claude's critical path: it is a CLI the model chooses to call. The CLI is resilient: 5 attempts, full-jitter backoff (500 ms base, 30 s cap), a per-batch deadline of 15 s including retries, a per-attempt timeout of 30 s, and a circuit breaker after 3 consecutive fatal errors. On failure it exits 2 (distinct from 1 for no match), keeps partial hits, and prints a typed error summary on stderr. The SKILL.md says never to treat exit 2 as clean. If jgrep is missing, the skill tells Claude to ask the user to install it. A missing key gives a 'No API key' message and Claude is told not to work around it. Worst case is a wasted Bash call of up to about 15 s, and there is no hang.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens and no server instructions. No hook-injected text. The skill frontmatter (name plus description, about 509 chars) adds roughly 130 tokens to every session. The SKILL.md body (4.1 KB, about 1.1k tokens) loads only when Claude invokes the skill. Results are compact file:line lines, and the skill tells Claude to Read only the listed ranges. Output tokens are small compared with a multi-file grep/read exploration.
pros: It is the only candidate here with real OpenRouter support in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with model ~typesafe/jev-latest (src/jgrep.ts:18-19,345-346). The user needs no patching or proxy.
Zero context overhead: no MCP tools and no hook text. It costs about 130 tokens of skill description per session, unlike MCP servers that add tens of tool schemas.

Uses the 'System One' strength directly: batched Noul yes/no questions (16 chunks in one request) at $0.042/M input, about $0.01 per 900 chunks, with output free. This is a sensible use of Jev, whose decision output is cheap and typed.

The self-lint idea (`jgrep --diff --staged "<rule>"` before commit) gives a second-model check on Opus's diffs, and `--tests <ref>` narrows test runs. Both are workflows that built-in grep and GitNexus do not cover.

Robust engineering for a 11-day-old tool: typed errors, retries with jitter, per-batch deadline, circuit breaker, exit 2 distinct from 1, and a cache. About 120 offline tests plus CI that smoke-tests under Node. The key is never in argv, the config file is chmod 600, there is no postinstall, execFile is used with arrays, and non-loopback http endpoints are refused.

Non-invasive integration: a plain skill copied to ~/.claude/skills or installed as a plugin, with no settings.json edits. It does not interfere with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks, and it is trivially removable.
Has a `--estimate` dry-run that shows requests, tokens and cost without a key or a call. The SKILL.md tells Claude to stop and tell the user rather than install software or work around a missing key.
cons: Not deterministic. It is a skill-description trigger via Bash, so it does not meet 'Claude Code must use it when needed'. With GitNexus (graph/semantic query), the built-in Grep/Glob and Explore agents already available, Opus will often pick those. Nothing forces Jev use, and there is no hook to make it automatic.

Sends raw source to a third party (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe): every scanned chunk, file path and diff hunk (src/jgrep.ts buildRequest). There is no .env or secret filtering; `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard` includes untracked non-ignored files, so an unignored .env or key file is uploaded. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover file reads made by the CLI itself. This is a real problem for client projects.

Chunks are judged in isolation by a heuristic column-0 splitter (a 'ponytail' comment in the code admits tree-sitter is not used), so cross-file or flow questions do not work (README Tips). The probability quality (p>=0.9 reliable) is self-reported, and the bench covers only --tests, with no precision/recall for grep. The Theo 'flash router' skepticism is untested here.

Very young: created 2026-09-19, 23 commits, 2 committers (effectively one author, 22 commits), 57 stars, v0.6.0 and 5 versions in 11 days. Expect churn. The System One endpoint is beta. The README says it 'appears in OpenRouter's app rankings' (attribution headers are sent by default), and init nags for a GitHub star.

Requires a global `npm i -g jevgrep` binary and a separate key file (~/.config/jgrep/env or ./.env), so there is a second place for the OpenRouter key to live. The cache key uses the constant MODEL 'jev-latest' (src/jgrep.ts key()) rather than the resolved model id, so the README claim 'cached per model id' looks inconsistent for JGREP_MODEL or OpenRouter runs. A project ./.env can also supply the key or JGREP_ENDPOINT (a supply-chain risk on untrusted repos).

Scope mismatch with 'Jev decides things in the workflow': this is a grep replacement and a diff linter, not a general router or decision layer for Claude Code (permission decisions, task routing, and so on). It also scans whole directories, so cost and time grow with repo size (600+ requests on a 10k-chunk monorepo; a 15 s batch deadline).
entries.verdict: A well-built, low-footprint skill and CLI with genuine OpenRouter support, and the best 'drop-in' Jev candidate for optional semantic search, diff self-lint and test selection. But it is model-discretion only (not automatic), it uploads raw code with no secret filtering, and it competes with GitNexus and built-in Grep. Use it as a complement (skill plus a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge you add yourself, restricted to non-client repos), not as the core Jev integration.

judge.why: Low-footprint skill plus CLI with real OpenRouter support and good retry hygiene, but it is manual, uploads raw code without secret filtering and overlaps gitnexus.
pros: OpenRouter works with only the key; about 130 tokens of context, no MCP tools or hooks
Batched Noul questions (16 chunks per request); about $0.01 per 900 chunks
Resilient CLI: 5 attempts with jitter, 15 s batch deadline, circuit breaker; exit 2 on failure and partial hits kept
cons: Skill-trigger only; Opus will often pick Grep or gitnexus
No secret filtering: git ls-files -co --exclude-standard includes unignored untracked files such as a stray .env
Uploads raw code to a third party; your hook does not cover its key
Young, single-maintainer, no adversarial verification

entries.name: BorisLeMeec/jev (Claude Code plugin + Go CLI "jev")
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (skill + one PreToolUse hook) around a Go CLI that calls the TypeSafe System One API with Noul/Choice primitives. `jev find` ranks files/lines by natural-language description, `jev ask` sweeps yes/no questions across files, and the hook rewrites Read calls on files of 400 lines to 80 KB into a window of about 1/5 of the file centred on the line Jev picks for the user's last message. It also has an opt-in lint (not wired into hooks.json), plus scan/probe/gain helpers.
interface: hook: PreToolUse matcher=Read (hooks/hooks.json), command `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/jev hook read`, timeout 20
entries.autoInvocation: Hybrid. (1) Deterministic PreToolUse hook on Read, which runs with no prompting and transparently rewrites offset/limit. (2) A skill whose description triggers at Claude's discretion to run `jev find` or `jev ask` through Bash; there is no MCP tool and no CLAUDE.md nudge, so the trigger rate is uncertain. Opus 5.5 tends to prefer Grep, and you have the GitNexus graph hook already steering search.
security: Key handling is good: read from env, sent only in an Authorization Bearer header (client.go:247), never in argv. The `Debug` writer prints raw response bodies, not the key. Request bodies are not logged.

No shell execution in the Go code (no os/exec). No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry. The only network call is the hardcoded POST to api.typesafe.ai. Local writes: ~/.jev/usage.jsonl (command, token counts, bytes; disable with JEV_NO_STATS).

Data egress bypasses your secret-leak guard: the Read hook itself reads the file (os.ReadFile) and sends its contents to a third party. Claude Code runs matching PreToolUse hooks in parallel, so the secret guard's deny does not stop jev from having already uploaded a 400+ line file. Sensitive large files (dumps, key bundles, client code under NDA) are exposed on every Read.
The hook also reads transcript_path (the full session JSONL, up to 8 MB per line) and takes the last user message (first 600 chars) as the 'goal' sent to the API.

Prompt-injection surface: file content is sent as model state, but Jev returns numbers only, so injection cannot produce instructions. The worst case is a manipulated ranking or window, which could hide the relevant part of a file from Claude. additionalContext is generated locally from numbers and the file basename.

Integrity risk: the Read hook silently rewrites tool input, so Claude sees only about 1/5 of a large file. It can miss code (author measured 50/50 targets kept, but on small samples and Go repos only), and Claude may edit with incomplete context. Only partially mitigated by the note and the ability to re-read with offset.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter once patched): for the hook, the full contents of every file the agent Reads that is 400 lines to 80 KB with no explicit offset/limit, cut into chunks with the file's basename and the user's last message (600 chars max, from the transcript). For `find`, code skeletons of every file in scope, then full contents of the top candidates. For `ask`, whole files in scope. Not sent: Bash output, diffs (unless lint is enabled), other tool outputs, or the whole transcript. Local: ~/.jev/usage.jsonl.
entries.failureMode: Hook fails open. Any error, missing key, unreadable payload, low confidence, or a Jev failure returns an empty decision, so the Read proceeds unmodified (hook.go:53-58, 125-130). If the binary is missing, the hook command errors non-blockingly. The client retries 429 and 5xx up to 5 times with exponential backoff and jitter (client.go:190-213), with a 120 s HTTP timeout (client.go:69) but a 20 s hook timeout in hooks.json, so a slow or down Jev can stall a Read for up to 20 s before Claude Code kills the hook and continues. Normal cost is +1.25 s per qualifying Read (the author's number). `find` and `ask` are CLI calls where errors are surfaced to Claude as text and it can fall back to grep.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens. The skill description costs roughly 170-200 tokens in the always-on skills list (about 700 chars). The full SKILL.md body is about 6.5k chars, roughly 1.7k tokens, loaded only when the skill is invoked. The hook adds about 60 tokens of additionalContext only on a narrowed Read (and top-level additionalContext may not even be honored by Claude Code, since it sits outside hookSpecificOutput, hook.go:40-43). `find` and `ask` output is a few lines, and the README claims about 40 tokens per search. The net effect on context is negative, by design: it shrinks large reads.
pros: The only Jev candidate with a genuinely automatic mechanism: a PreToolUse hook that fires on every Read without any prompt. That matches your 'never say use jev' requirement more literally than skills or MCP tools.
Hooks fail open by design (every gate returns the read untouched on error, timeout or doubt), and JEV_HOOK_DISABLE=1 is a clean kill switch. Explicit offset/limit reads are never altered.
No MCP servers, so no schema-token tax and no extra process. Small footprint of a skill description plus one hook.
Clean, readable Go with no shell exec, no telemetry and no curl|sh. Bearer auth via env only. Easy to audit in an hour (about 1.5k lines).

Real, honest benchmarks with harnesses in-repo, including a candid TIMING.md that admits the median wall-clock effect is a wash. `find` P@1 0.96 vs grep 0.08 on vocabulary-gap queries and `ask` precision 1.00 are useful specifically when names are unknown, such as unfamiliar client codebases.

Uses the same System One endpoint shape that OpenRouter exposes, so porting to OpenRouter is a one-line endpoint change plus a key env, and the client already handles 429/5xx backoff and the 32k-token limit (80 KB cap).
Cost is negligible ($0.042/M input, roughly $0.0016 per ask).
cons: No OpenRouter support today (endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, no base-URL override). You would have to fork and maintain a patched copy, and the marketplace install would pull upstream.

Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 6 commits in a single day, one author, no releases, no CI, about 10 tests, no issues or activity since 2026-09-18. Benchmarks are self-reported, small (tens of queries) and on Go/Flutter/React repos only.

Install looks broken for a plain marketplace install: bin/ is gitignored and nothing builds the binary, so hook and skill probably have no `jev` to run until you build it yourself. go.mod requires Go 1.26.1 while the README says 1.22+.

The Read hook is the dangerous part: it hides about 80% of a large file from Claude, and Claude edits code that way. The author admits recall was measured only on 50 targets, and in your bypass/auto mode nobody reviews those reads. On client work a silently missed guard clause is costly.

Sends full contents of every large file Claude reads, plus your last prompt, to a third party. It runs in parallel with your secret-leak guard, so the guard cannot prevent the upload. This matters for client NDA code.

The hook pays about 1.25 s on every big-file Read and returns no turns, so on the Read hook alone it is pure latency; the token saving mostly matters for API-billed users, and you are on a subscription where the win is only context and rate-limit headroom.

`find` and `ask` depend on the model choosing to invoke the skill, with no MCP tool or hook to force it. `find` takes about 13 s repo-wide and makes one request per file, which is heavy for big monorepos. This overlaps with the GitNexus graph search you already use and with Grep.

The hook's `additionalContext` is emitted at the top level, not inside hookSpecificOutput, and it uses updatedInput without a permissionDecision. I could not verify how Claude Code 2.1.285 treats either; the narrowing note may be dropped, so Claude may not know its Read was cut short.

Goal quality: the hook uses the last typed user message as the search goal. In long agentic runs with subagents or 'continue' style messages, that goal is stale or vague, so the window can point at the wrong region (it then passes through only if confidence is under 0.60).
entries.verdict: The most 'automatic' Jev integration found (a real PreToolUse hook plus a skill), and it is easy to patch to OpenRouter with a one-line endpoint change. But it is a 1-day-old single-author POC whose install does not obviously ship the binary. Its headline hook silently truncates Reads and uploads file contents past your secret guard, so use it only as a forked, audited, pinned build, ideally with the Read hook disabled or limited and the skill/`ask` used for repo-wide audits.

entries.name: jev-claude-plugin (barretg)
entries.what: Go CLI (jev find/ask/scan/lint/probe/gain/hook) packaged as a Claude Code plugin. It has one skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) and one PreToolUse hook on Read (hooks/hooks.json, timeout 20 s). The hook reads the whole file, sends it to Jev with the user's last transcript message as the goal, and rewrites the Read to a narrowed offset/limit window (about 1/5 of the file, minimum 150 lines) for files of 400 lines to 80 KB. When confidence is below 0.60 it denies the Read up to twice per file and asks the agent to run `jev hook goal` first. find/ask send one request per file with skeletons and full contents, so the model is queried instead of the agent reading the files. An opt-in PostToolUse lint command exists in code (internal/run/lint.go) but is not wired in hooks.json.
interface: PreToolUse hook, matcher Read: `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/jev hook read`
entries.autoInvocation: Yes for the Read hook: deterministic, fires on every Read without an offset or limit and needs no prompting. The find/ask CLI is model-discretion via the skill. The skill's description triggers are concrete but compete with gitnexus semantic search and Grep, and the model may prefer gitnexus, so the actual find/ask usage is uncertain. Nothing is wired for Bash permission gating, PermissionRequest or Stop.
security: Key handling: read from env only and sent as a Bearer header (client.go:122). It is never put in argv and never written to disk. `jev probe` prints raw response bodies (not the key).

Egress path: the URL is env-overridable via JEV_BASE_URL (client.go:34). A poisoned project env could redirect all file contents and the API key to another host. This is low risk for the user's own env.
Local writes: ~/.cache/jev/hook/<session>.json (0600, contains file paths and goal text, 30 min TTL) and ~/.jev/usage.jsonl (0644; counts only, no content). No telemetry beyond the OpenRouter call.

Shell exec: none in Go code (no os/exec). The deny message asks the agent to run a Bash command containing a %q-quoted absolute path and session id. The session id is validated against [A-Za-z0-9_-] (hook_retry.go:52-62), so path traversal is prevented.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents and the user's last message go into the Jev state. Jev returns only numbers, so the direct impact is limited to steering which window a Read shows, or forcing a deny. Injected text in a file could bias the located line and hide the real target. The additionalContext text is plugin-authored and constant.

Secret exposure: the hook does not exclude sensitive files. Any Read of a 400-line-plus file sends the whole content to OpenRouter, including a large secrets/config file the agent reads. The existing no-secret-leak PreToolUse hook may deny first, but hooks for the same event run in parallel, so ordering is not guaranteed. The scan for find/ask skips dot-files and dirs (scan.go:38-56, :122-130) but not credentials.json, *.pem, id_rsa or secrets.yml.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or JEV_BASE_URL) on every Read of a file of 400 lines to 80 KB that has no offset/limit set. The request carries the full file content (up to 80,000 bytes), the file basename, and the last user prompt (up to 600 chars) as the goal. Each find/ask request carries one file's skeleton or full contents, per file, across the whole scanned tree except skipped dirs and dot-files. The client sends the OpenRouter key in the Authorization header. The unit is roughly 30 tokens of instructions plus file content per question, and the result is numbers only. Client code and any secrets inside large source files therefore go to OpenRouter and on to TypeSafe. Source files under 400 lines are never sent by the hook, but find/ask sends everything.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open for the Read hook. Unreadable payload, a missing key, a decode error, an API error or a low goal all call passThrough, which prints an empty decision and exits 0 (hook.go:103-168). Main errors exit 1 (non-blocking in Claude Code). Latency worst case is bad. The client has a 120 s HTTP timeout and 5 retries with backoff (client.go:65-88), but the hook's own limit is 20 s, after which Claude Code kills it and proceeds. That is up to 20 s of stall per Read during an OpenRouter/alpha outage. Two fail-closed-ish behaviours: on locate confidence under 0.60 the hook DENIES the Read up to twice per file (hook_retry.go:137-155), which costs extra turns and needs the agent to run a Bash command. This deny fires under bypassPermissions and auto modes as well. A narrowed Read silently hides about 80% of a large file. The agent is told via additionalContext, but an Edit based on a partial view is a real risk. There is no cap on total denies per session beyond 2 per file, and state is keyed on the session id. If the model id 'jev-latest' is rejected by OpenRouter, every call returns 4xx and the hook passes through with cost ~0 and benefit 0.
entries.contextCost: Very low: 0 MCP tools and no MCP instructions. The skill listing entry is about 590 chars (about 150 tokens) against the 0.02 skillListingBudgetFraction. The full SKILL.md is 6.5 KB (about 1.6k tokens) when triggered. The hook adds about 60 tokens of additionalContext per narrowed Read. A deny reason is about 150 tokens per event. Net context effect is negative (saves) on large-file reads.
pros: The Read hook is genuinely automatic (hooks.json PreToolUse Read, updatedInput offset/limit + additionalContext). It is the only candidate found that needs no 'use jev' prompt. It is well gated and fails toward passthrough (hook.go:99-141, 168, 183-185, 201).

OpenRouter is the default endpoint (client.go:27) with OPENROUTER_API_KEY read first (client.go:44). It is pure Go stdlib with no third-party dependencies, so the supply-chain surface is small. No os/exec, no argv secrets, no telemetry.

The author committed reproducible benchmarks (bench/RESULTS*.md, hook cases on public Hugo/Prometheus repos). Claimed numbers: find P@1 0.96 vs BM25 0.33 vs grep 0.08, ask F1 0.97, Read hook 50/50 targets kept and -41% billed tokens in paired runs. They are the author's own measurements and sample sizes are small, but the methodology is sensible (labellers forbidden from running jev, near-miss cases).

Sensible safeguards: explicit offset/limit is never overridden, files over 80 KB are refused because sectioned recall was measured worse (hook.go:138), the window is generous (min 150 lines), the agent is told how to re-read, there is a session-id validator, and JEV_HOOK_DISABLE is a one-line kill switch.
Negligible context cost: no MCP tool schemas, a 590-char skill description.
Cost per use is trivial ($0.042 per 1M tokens, about $0.0001 per narrowed read, $0.0025 per 434 KB find scan).
cons: Unverified OpenRouter compatibility: DefaultModel remains 'jev-latest' (client.go:29) while OpenRouter's slug is 'typesafe/jev-1.13'. The fork commit changed only URL and key names. The benches (bench/hook/measure_band.py:34) still use jev-latest, and there is no evidence of any OpenRouter run. The fix is trivial (JEV_MODEL), but it means the 'beta' label is optimistic.

Silent code hiding while editing: narrowing a Read to about 20% of a large file is dangerous for a user running bypassPermissions with the main model editing heavily. The agent sees only a note. The deny-retry loop can also block Reads, and with 'auto' or bypass modes there is no human to notice a miss.

Privacy: the whole content of any Read file of 400 lines or more, plus the user's last prompt, goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. There is no exclusion for secrets or client-confidential files. This conflicts with the client-project rules and with the no-secret-leak hook, and the user would need an allowlist/denylist wrapper. The mixed-parallel hook ordering with no-secret-leak is unspecified.

Latency: +1.25 s per qualifying Read per the author's own bench, two or more sequential API calls, the whole transcript re-scanned per Read, and up to 20 s when OpenRouter's /alpha endpoint (no SLA) is slow. Wall-clock benefit is described as a wash.

Requires building and installing an unaudited third-party Go binary. The fork has 0 stars, 8 commits, 3 committers and no releases. It was created 2026-09-26. bin/ is not committed, so `claude plugin install` from GitHub alone yields a broken hook, and rebuilds need `make sync`.

Thin tests (12 tests, none for the client, find, ask or lint). The find/ask query sets are private and unreproducible. Benchmarks are Go/Flutter-centric, so the author himself says other stacks are not covered.

Overlaps with gitnexus semantic query for find, and Claude Code's own subagents/Grep. The skill's find/ask relies on model discretion and is slow on big trees (linear per-file requests). The token-saving thesis targets API-billed context; the user is on a subscription where the saving is less directly valuable.
The retry deny asks the agent to run a bare `jev hook goal` command. This depends on jev being on the Bash PATH, and the user's PATH override in settings env may make that fail, wasting turns.
entries.verdict: Best-executed automatic Jev integration seen: it is a real deterministic Read hook with conservative gates, small context cost and OpenRouter as the default endpoint. Two things hold it at 6 for this user. The model id is unverified against OpenRouter. The hook hides ~80% of large files from an agent that edits in bypass mode, and it ships raw file contents to a third party with no secret or client-code filter. It is worth a read-only pilot (fork, set the model to typesafe/jev-1.13, add a path denylist, JEV_HOOK_NO_RETRY=1) before trusting it on client projects.

judge.why: The only deterministic integration: a PreToolUse Read hook that narrows large-file reads by goal. It is also the riskiest for an editing agent in bypass mode, and it ships whole files to a third party.
pros: Fires on every qualifying Read with no prompting (updatedInput offset/limit plus additionalContext); explicit offset/limit is never overridden; JEV_HOOK_DISABLE kill switch
Fails to passthrough on error; pure Go stdlib, no os/exec; reproducible Hugo/Prometheus hook bench (author's numbers: -41% billed tokens, 50/50 targets kept)
Negligible context cost
cons: Silently hides about 80% of files of 400 to 2000 lines from an agent that edits in bypass mode; the low-confidence deny (twice per file) also fires in bypass/auto
Uploads the whole content of any large Read file plus your last prompt; no secret or client exclusion; runs in parallel with no-secret-leak, so ordering is undefined
+1.25 s per qualifying Read (author's bench), up to 20 s when /alpha is slow; the transcript is re-scanned on each Read; wall-clock benefit called 'a wash'

Must be built locally (make build, make sync after every rebuild); 0 stars, 8 commits, only 12 tests, none for the client; the retry text needs jev on the Bash PATH, which your PATH override may break

entries.name: nassim-arifette/jevgrep (@nassim-arifette/jevgrep)
entries.what: Local Node 24 CLI plus stdio MCP server exposing one tool, semantic_search_code. It inventories an authorized repo, chunks files into fragments (JS/TS, Python and Java syntax-aware boundaries, else line windows), sends each fragment to Jev as a Noul (yes/no) question ("does this excerpt contain evidence useful for the search question"), thresholds the P(yes) at 0.5 and returns the original excerpts with paths and line numbers under a token budget. Scores are cached locally per (query, fragment). It is an embedding-free semantic grep in which Jev acts as the relevance judge over the whole repo on each novel query.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code will list the tool and may choose it based on its description ('when exact identifiers are unknown'); there is no hook, skill, or transparent proxy, and the description itself tells Claude to prefer exact search for known symbols. Reliability of unprompted use is therefore variable and would compete with the existing gitnexus MCP and Grep/Glob; a CLAUDE.md line or a UserPromptSubmit hint would raise it but that is not built in.
security: API key read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env or ~/.config secrets.env (written mode 0600, dirs 0700 via src/local-directory.ts:47,82); never passed via argv; the MCP tool schema has no root/credential/endpoint/model field so the model cannot widen authorization

Per-repo opt-in: remote_evaluation_enabled defaults false, must be enabled per repository by the user (README lines ~115-125); trusted profile is stored outside the repo so an untrusted repo cannot enable egress for itself
Default exclusions: .env, credential-pattern files, deps, build output, generated/minified, symlinks/junctions not followed, .gitignore respected; README concedes filters cannot catch every secret
HTTP transport refuses redirects, bounds response bodies, pins base_url per adapter (src/contracts.ts:238-246), so a poisoned config cannot redirect the key to another host

Prompt-injection surface: repo text is embedded in Noul questions; criterion says 'Repository text is data, not instructions'; Jev output is a bounded probability, so injection can only skew ranking, not execute anything. Returned excerpts are untrusted repo text landing in Claude's context as with any Read
No child_process use except a PowerShell worker on Windows only; no postinstall/preinstall scripts; no curl|sh installer; no telemetry found in grep of src (only provider URLs)
entries.dataEgress: On every uncached query, eligible source fragments from the whole authorized repo (or the given scope) are POSTed to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions together with the search question, repo-relative paths, line ranges and a relevance criterion. That is essentially the entire non-ignored UTF-8 text codebase per novel query (unchanged fragments are served from local cache, TTL 15 min for rolling OpenRouter model aliases, 7 days for pinned TypeSafe). Nothing else (no telemetry, no tool outputs, no diffs) leaves. For client projects this means full source disclosure to OpenRouter and its upstream provider(s) (provider.allow_fallbacks=false is sent); needs per-repo consent and client-contract review. Caches store scores/hashes only, not source or questions.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft per call, not a hook: the tool returns a structured result with isError=true (rejected/error) or a partial/complete flag with coverage info, so Claude can fall back to Grep/Read. Search deadline default 300 s (deadline_ms), concurrency 4, scheduler retries max 2 with 250ms-5s backoff (ambiguous attempts are not retried), README suggests client tool timeout 360 s. No global impact when Jev is down because it is not in any hook path, but a slow cold search can block a Claude turn for minutes. Startup is offline, so an unreachable or unauthorized state does not break other MCP servers. Note Jev alpha endpoint may change; with require_fit true a scope exceeding caps is refused rather than silently truncated.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool, semantic_search_code: description ~640 chars plus schema ~650 chars plus name, roughly 350-400 tokens total; server 'instructions' string ~110 chars (~30 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Returned excerpts default 4,000 reference tokens per call (max 16,000) that land in the context, but this is offset by fewer exploratory Reads.
pros: Only candidate here with a real use for Jev's strength: fragment relevance is a Noul yes/no question, which matches Jev's typed-decision, calibrated-probability design instead of misusing it as a chat model
OpenRouter is a first-class provider: exact endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13, allow_fallbacks:false (src/evaluation/openrouter.ts, src/init.ts:147)
Zero setup friction for Claude Code: `claude mcp add ... jevgrep mcp`, single tool, ~400 tokens of context, no hooks that could slow every Bash/Grep call

Safety-conscious design: per-repo opt-in for remote evaluation (default off), profile stored outside the repo, pinned base URLs, no redirects, key never in argv or cache, offline `inspect`/`doctor` to preview exactly what would be sent

Good engineering hygiene for a 12-day-old repo: ~10k lines of TS, ~50 test files, strict response validation (invalid answers never coerced to 0), CI on Ubuntu and Windows, MIT, honest README limits, fail-loud partial/coverage reporting
Score cache per (query, fragment) makes repeat and follow-up questions on unchanged code cheap; cost at ~$0.042/1M input tokens is small
Returns exact excerpts with line ranges, not summaries, so Claude can Read the right file directly; complements gitnexus (graph) and Grep (lexical)
cons: Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 108 commits, ~96 by one author, 91 stars, 11 forks, no GitHub releases; npm latest is 0.1.1 while repo is at 0.2.0 (unreleased to npm), so `npm i -g` gets older code

OpenRouter path is explicitly untested live: README says no live OpenRouter request or automated test was run; TypeSafe direct also untested on a real account. Only Vercel Gateway was checked, on a tiny example. Alpha endpoint could break it

Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code (Opus) already reaches for Grep/Glob and gitnexus, so unprompted use of it is uncertain; README admits Claude Code/Codex sessions are not yet qualified

Brute-force architecture: no persistent index, every novel query re-scores every eligible fragment of the repo through the API and re-reads/hashes all files each time; cold latency of seconds to minutes on big repos and per-query token cost scales with repo size, versus embedding/graph search (gitnexus) that is instant

Heavy data egress for client work: essentially all source (minus ignore/credential filters) goes to OpenRouter plus upstream per novel query; secret filters are pattern-based and admittedly incomplete; needs per-client consent, and the existing PreToolUse secret guard does not cover it
Setup is per-repo and manual: `jevgrep init` in each repo, absolute --config path per MCP server, one server process per repository, so a single global MCP entry does not cover all projects
Hard-pinned model typesafe/jev-1.13: cannot use ~typesafe/jev-latest or Jev Router without patching; Node engine pinned >=24 <25 (matches user's Node 24 but brittle)

Noul probabilities are thresholded at a fixed 0.5 and quality is unproven: benchmarks are on synthetic sources (benchmarks/README.md) and the Theo 'flash router' skepticism about Jev's calibration is unaddressed
entries.verdict: Best-fitting Jev integration found for a coding workflow: a real OpenRouter-capable MCP tool that uses Jev's Noul primitive for a legitimate task (behavioural code search), with sensible opt-in and egress controls. But it is alpha (12 days old, OpenRouter path never run live), only model-discretion rather than automatic, brute-force per query, and ships client source to a third party; a reasonable optional add-on for personal repos after a manual test, not a core piece and not for client repos without consent.

judge.why: Sensible per-repo opt-in and egress controls, one small MCP tool. It is 12 days old and the OpenRouter path is untested live.
pros: Per-repo opt-in for remote evaluation (default off); single tool of about 400 tokens; startup is offline
Structured partial/complete results with isError, so Claude can fall back
Uses Noul for fragment relevance
cons: OpenRouter never run live; npm latest 0.1.1 is older than repo 0.2.0
Model-discretion only; brute force per query, up to 300 s search deadline
Ships source to a third party; single maintainer, no releases

entries.name: romeromarcelo/jev-retrieval (jevr)
entries.what: Rust CLI (jevr) doing stateless local BM25 recall over a repo, then sending 100-line file windows to Jev System One as many concurrent Noul questions (plus one listwise Choice rerank per lane) to return ranked path:start-end + calibrated score. Ships a Claude Code plugin/marketplace with one skill (using-jevr) whose description tells Claude to use jevr instead of grep/glob for conceptual code search. Not an MCP server and no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). Description explicitly says 'even when the user doesn't name the tool', so Claude may auto-invoke on conceptual location questions. Not deterministic, and competes with GitNexus graph hooks and native Grep/Glob/Explore; nothing intercepts grep.
security: API key read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var only and sent as bearer over rustls HTTPS; not put in argv (good). Env var must be exported into the shell Claude Code spawns.

Data egress of source content is the whole design: windows of candidate files are sent to a third party; no secret redaction found in walk.rs (only gitignore + hidden-file skipping + a skip list), so .env-like non-hidden files or config files with secrets that are not gitignored could be uploaded. Conflicts with client-project confidentiality and with the user's existing secret-leak guard hook philosophy (that hook guards Bash|Read|Grep but cannot see what the jevr binary reads).
Prompt-injection surface: file content becomes Jev state, but Jev returns only typed probabilities so injection can only skew rankings; the skill itself allows Bash(jevr:*) only.
Local response cache in ~/.cache/jevr/ stores raw JSON responses keyed by sha256 of request body (keys not stored; responses contain scores only, not code).

install.sh is local script (claude plugin add + copy); no curl|sh; no npm postinstall; Rust build from crates.io. Telemetry: none found. Single-author, no CI, no signed releases; supply-chain trust rests on one new maintainer and cargo install of a 1-week-old crate.
No cargo-audit/CI; deps are mainstream (tokio, reqwest rustls, clap, ignore, serde).
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (not OpenRouter): the natural-language query, and for every BM25/git-grep candidate file (up to ~30 per lane per variant) overlapping 100-line windows of raw file contents plus whole-file text, as Jev state; plus a rerank request containing candidate file heads (~25 lines each). Repo-wide code chunks leave the machine on every cold query (cached responses avoid repeats). No diffs, no Claude prompts or tool outputs, no conversation context.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the search itself but harmless to Claude Code: missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY exits 2 immediately with a clear message; network errors retry 3x with exponential backoff 250/500/1000 ms on 408/429/5xx (non-retryable 4xx bail); no explicit request timeout set on reqwest::Client::new() (default no total timeout), so a hung connection could stall the Bash call until Claude Code's own Bash timeout. Rerank failure falls back to score order. Claude can fall back to grep/rg as the skill itself states.
entries.contextCost: Very low: zero MCP tools, no hooks, no server instructions. Only the skill description (~700 chars, ~175 tokens) sits in the always-on skill list; full SKILL.md (~5 KB, ~1.3k tokens) loads only when triggered. Tool output is small (path:range score lines; --snippets up to 25 lines per file, top-10).
pros: Only candidate so far that is truly 'automatic' via the standard mechanism: a skill whose description invites use without the user naming it, zero MCP/hook context overhead (~175 tokens).

Targets a real daily task, conceptual code location, with grep-shaped output and exit codes and a claimed SWE-bench Lite file-localization any-gold@10 of 0.90 (author-run, 50-sample, unverified by me).
Uses Noul and Choice primitives correctly, with pinned model, 3x retry, sha256 response cache (content-keyed so never stale), gitignore-aware walking, stateless (no index dir).
Apache-2.0, small readable Rust codebase (~30 files), 30ish unit/integration tests including captured wire-format replay (tests/wire.rs), cargo-installable binary, no shell exec or telemetry.
Fail-safe for Claude Code: if it errors, Claude simply uses grep; no hooks that could block tool calls.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read; user wants OpenRouter as provider, so needs a fork/patch (likely small but schema equivalence unverified).
Uploads raw source windows of many files to a third party on each cold query, with no secret redaction; risky for client projects and only partially aligned with the user's secret-guard hooks.
Brand new and single-author: repo created 2026-09-23, 7 commits, 1 contributor, 4 stars, v0.1.1, no CI workflows, crates.io stats not checkable; benchmarks are self-reported small samples.

Skill triggers are model-discretion and overlap with GitNexus (query/context) and native Grep/Glob/Explore; Claude may often ignore it, and it is not a real 'automatic' interception. Also requires installing Rust 1.88 toolchain and the binary; skill alone does nothing.

Cost/latency amplification: fan-out of many requests per query (concurrency 32) with no reqwest timeout; on OpenRouter at ~$0.042/M input it is cheap in dollars but could hit rate limits; Jev is a router-like 'System One' model, so quality claims (rerank beating cross-encoders) rest on author benchmarks only.
Solves search, not the broader 'decision' use cases (e.g., routing, permission triage, commit/PR classification) where Jev's typed decisions could add value in Claude Code.
