entries.verdict: A well-built, low-overhead, skill-triggered semantic search CLI that is Jev-specific and genuinely auto-invocable, but it is TypeSafe-direct only (hardcoded URL and key), ships source code off-machine, and is a week-old single-author project. Worth considering only as a forked OpenRouter-patched extra for non-confidential repos, not as the core Jev integration.

entries.name: tonyzdev/pijev
entries.what: Pi-based terminal coding agent: Jev ranks repo file excerpts, shortlists skills and triages tool failures; main model writes code. Has SWE-bench and unfamiliar-repo experiments.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic in-agent (pre-task briefing, search ranking, failure triage)
pros: Strongest evidence in batch: 46 paired tasks, tool calls -20% (CI 11-28%), sign test p=3e-6, same resolve rate
Clean designs to copy: file-excerpt ranking, skill shortlisting, failure triage, all advisory and fail-open with deadlines and no retry loops
cons: Separate agent on Pi, not a Claude Code plugin; ideas would need porting to an MCP or hook
Endpoint is api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone or Vercel AI Gateway; OpenRouter needs a code change

entries.name: @opengeni/genigrep (ggr)
entries.what: Code-search tool for agents (CLI `ggr`/`genigrep`, stdio MCP server `ggr mcp` with a single `code_search` tool, library, and an Agent Skill). Given a question plus 6-15 agent-chosen keywords, it runs one ripgrep pass, then uses Jev (Choice/Noul/Score-style probability answers via POST /v1/systemone) to triage up to 240 candidate files, verify up to 80 line-numbered passages, follow definitions one level, and rate the final evidence. It returns verbatim passages with path:line. Jev only scores; it never writes text. It is a port of the code_search engine from Cloudgeni's OpenGeni harness (packages/jev).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, nudged by the server instructions (a directive that says to start with one code_search call instead of several searches/reads) and the tool description. Optionally also a skill (description-triggered). No deterministic hook and no transparent proxy: Claude decides. It also competes with the user's existing GitNexus hooks/MCP and native Grep/Glob, so real invocation frequency is uncertain. It is best treated as an opt-in via the instructions, not guaranteed.
security: API key: read from GENIGREP_JEV_API_KEY or a 0600 config file in a 0700 dir; sent only as a Bearer header; never logged; `ggr auth` prompts without echo, so the key never appears in argv. Warns if the config file is world-readable (config.ts:~160). The MCP server re-reads the key on every call (it does not go into .mcp.json).
HTTPS enforced for the base URL, with http only for localhost (config.ts:66-77).
No telemetry found: grep shows no analytics. The only network destination is the configured Jev base URL (plus GET /healthz warm-up to the same host).
No postinstall scripts (package.json scripts: build/typecheck/test/check/prepublishOnly only). The npm package is published with provenance (publishConfig.provenance=true). No curl|sh installer.

Shell execution is limited to spawning ripgrep (src/workspace/local.ts:285) with --no-config and a flag allowlist (no --pre, no symlink following, no absolute or .. paths) and `rg --version` in doctor. ripgrep is the bundled @vscode/ripgrep binary, which is downloaded from GitHub at that package's postinstall (a transitive supply-chain step to note).

Reads honor .gitignore/.ignore/.rgignore, skip binaries, dependency/build dirs and lockfiles, and skip a list of secret files (.env*, keys, *.tfvars, .npmrc, .netrc, .ssh, .aws, etc., case-insensitive; src/workspace/excludes.ts). It refuses ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.gnupg and ~/.kube as the search root. The MCP server confines calls to configured or client roots.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured Jev endpoint only (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if overridden, and then also OpenRouter and its upstream). Per docs/how-it-works.md:173-186 and README Privacy: the question and sub-questions; paths of up to 240 candidate files each with up to 3 matching lines (160 chars each); up to 80 passages plus 6 followed definitions of up to 8,000 chars each (verbatim source code) with path, line numbers and enclosing declaration; up to 60 identifier names with their line text; and up to 60,000 chars of the final packed passages. The keywords, whole files and gitignored/secret files are not sent. Secrets in ordinary source files can be sent. Not sent: prompts or conversation history, diffs, or other tools' outputs, because the agent only supplies a question and keywords. A single search can therefore send on the order of hundreds of KB of client source code to a third party. Per the user's client-project context, check the contracts.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the tool but non-blocking for Claude Code. There is no keyword-only fallback; the README says this is deliberate, because keyword-only ranking lost 7.7 quality points. On error the MCP tool returns isError text ending with 'Search with rg, grep or file reads instead', so Claude falls back to native tools. Per-request timeout is 10 s (GENIGREP_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, 1-120 s), with 2 retries on network/429/5xx (backoff 250 ms base, retry-after capped at 2 s). 401/402/403 fail immediately and are surfaced as key/billing problems. The circuit breaker (src/engine/circuit-breaker.ts, 3 consecutive failures, cooldown of minutes, auth cooldown longer) then refuses fast, so an outage costs one quick refusal per call. There is no total wall-clock cap besides per-request timeouts times the stages. A worst-case stall can be several tens of seconds before the first breaker trip. A missing key returns a setup error without any network call.
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (code_search). Tool description about 1,150 chars plus input schema (5 properties with descriptions) about 1,500 chars, plus title/annotations, so about 700 tokens. MCP server `instructions` (CODE_SEARCH_DIRECTIVE) about 900 chars, about 225 tokens, injected into the system prompt on every session. Total about 900-1,000 tokens fixed per session; deferred tool loading may hide the schema until needed. The optional skill adds about 100 tokens of description, with the body loaded only when triggered (about 900 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injection. Each call returns up to a 12k-token evidence pack (default budget 12000), typically 5-10k tokens, which is a big per-call cost when the answer is small.
pros: Only candidate seen that does real Jev work: it uses Jev's probability answers as a ranker (src/engine/client.ts POST /v1/systemone), with Jev never producing free text, so it fits Jev's 'System One' design.

Configurable base URL and model by env vars (config.ts:10-13,174-175), so pointing it at OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/api + typesafe/jev-latest) is plausibly a config-only change; the endpoint suffix /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's documented System One path.

Ships an MCP server with one small, read-only, well-annotated tool (~1k tokens of context, no hook overhead per turn) plus server instructions that tell Claude to prefer it for 'where is X decided?' questions. This is the closest thing to automatic use short of hooks.

Good engineering for a 3-day-old repo: circuit breaker, bounded retries, fail-to-rg messages, 0600 key storage, no key in argv/logs, HTTPS enforcement, ripgrep flag allowlist, secret-file skip list, root confinement, no postinstall, npm provenance, Apache-2.0, big test suite and CI.

Honest documentation: publishes measured results with CIs (about -6.6%/-7.5% cost and -9%/-10% time on 26 investigation questions with equal quality, and no effect on bug-fixing) and explicit limitations. It also tells the agent not to over-trust the rating.
No bundled telemetry; egress goes only to the configured Jev endpoint; the exact fields sent are documented.
cons: Extremely new and single-author: 18 commits in 3 days, 3 stars, 1 contributor, no releases on GitHub, npm 0.1.0/0.1.1 published 2026-09-28. Expect churn and bugs.

Evidence applies only to the OpenGeni harness with GPT-6-class agents on one TypeScript monorepo; the README says the CLI, MCP server, skill and derived keywords were not part of the evaluation. Zero measurement with Claude Code / Opus. The reported gain is modest (7-10%) and its 2nd run's CIs include zero.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs (no 'openrouter' string anywhere). Schema parity with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified, and the auth/doctor verification flow and warm-up /healthz assume TypeSafe. Needs a smoke test with a real OpenRouter key before trusting it.

Sends verbatim source code (up to 80 passages x 8k chars, plus 60k chars of evidence) to a third party per search, and does not scan for hard-coded secrets. Risky for client projects with NDAs, and it bypasses the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard because the MCP tool is not in the Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit matcher (the guard only sees the Grep/Read that genigrep replaces).

Not deterministic: it depends on Claude choosing the tool. Claude Code already has native Grep/Glob and the user's GitNexus MCP/hooks (graph context) that overlap heavily; it is likely to be under-used, or duplicate GitNexus's function.

Requires the agent to supply 6-15 good keywords per call, and the results are only as good as those; each call returns up to about 12k tokens, which can inflate context when only a small fact is needed. It is not exhaustive (rg is still needed for renames and counting), and language tuning is TypeScript-only.
Fail-closed with no fallback ranking: if Jev/OpenRouter is slow, calls can take several seconds to tens of seconds before failing over to rg. Beta model plus an alpha tool.
Bundled ripgrep binary is fetched at @vscode/ripgrep install time (network at install), a small supply-chain step.
entries.verdict: The best, and about the only, working Jev-as-ranker integration for Claude Code: a small single-tool MCP server whose instructions make Claude reach for it on 'where is X decided' questions, and its base URL and model are env-configurable, so OpenRouter is probably a config-only switch. It is 3 days old, evaluated only outside Claude Code with modest gains, sends real source code out per search, and leaves auto-invocation up to the model, so try it in a sandbox project with an OpenRouter key and a smoke test of the response schema before adopting it globally.

judge.why: A single small MCP tool whose instructions push Claude to use it. Evidence comes only from a non-Claude harness, and it is 3 days old.
pros: Env-configurable base URL and model; about 1k tokens of context; read-only annotated tool
Circuit breaker and explicit error text telling Claude to use rg
cons: 3 days old, 18 commits, 3 stars; gains modest (7 to 10%), CIs include zero; no Claude Code measurement
No keyword fallback (fail-closed for the tool); OpenRouter schema parity unverified
Sends source out per search

entries.name: JevTrace (123wwwa/JevTrace)
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) that, given a plain-language JS/TS coding task, uses the TypeScript compiler (call hierarchy, references, types, tests) plus Jev Noul/Choice judgments to select the relevant functions and their callers/callees/types/tests within a token budget, returning source text to the agent instead of grep/read loops. Multi-stage pipeline: scope check (is the task specific?), directory/file/symbol discovery via Jev, compiler expansion, Jev context ranking. Falls back to lexical/structural ranking if Jev stages fail. JS/TS/Vue only.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Tool description ('Use first when a JS/TS task needs code you have not located yet') and server instructions nudge Claude, but there is no hook or skill. The repo's own pilot benchmark found that without an explicit CLAUDE.md line the agent skipped the tool in 2 of 5 sessions (and used it with 4 Grep/searches median, tokens 120k vs 50k when guided). The README recommends adding a CLAUDE.md line ('call mcp__jevtrace__retrieve_dependency_context ... before using Grep, Glob or Read'). A deterministic hook could be layered on top (e.g. a PreToolUse Grep/Glob nudge) but the repo ships none, and it would collide with the user's existing GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hook.
security: API key: stored in ~/.jevtrace/config.json (chmod 0600, dir 0700) by setup, or read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env; not passed via argv when using setup (docs recommend nothing secret in Claude Code MCP config). Plaintext at rest, though.
Key is only sent as Bearer header to the configured endpoint; but JEVTRACE_ENDPOINT / config endpoint can redirect it to any URL (user-controlled, not remote-controlled).

No child_process/exec/spawn found in src or package.json scripts; no postinstall/preinstall/prepare hooks (only prepack). Node deps only, but npm install pulls a large tree (vite, TS 6, MCP SDK) and must be built locally from an unreviewed 1-day-old, 1-contributor repo; supply-chain risk is normal npm risk.

Prompt-injection surface: repository source and the task are placed in the Jev 'state' JSON, with guidance saying source is data; Jev returns only typed probabilities/choices (no free text), so injection can at most bias which code is returned. Returned context is repo source text delivered into Claude's context (attacker-controlled repo content is already readable by Read).

Local telemetry: appends task text + project path to ~/.jevtrace/usage.jsonl on every call (src/usage-log.ts) - unbounded log, local only, disable with JEVTRACE_USAGE_LOG=off. No phone-home telemetry found.
The repo removed its .claude/ and skills/jevtrace directories in commits, so no bundled hooks/skills to review.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured provider (OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions by default when chosen) on each retrieval: the task text; a repository tree of file paths (up to 20,000 chars) and lexical hints; and per candidate source code truncated to 3000 chars per node, 4000 for an entry, 600 per supporting-context item, 1200 for choice candidates (src/judges.ts:114-149, 258-262), in batches of 16. So real source snippets from client projects leave the machine to OpenRouter and its upstream (TypeSafe). Nothing else observed leaving; no other network calls in src. Local: usage log with task+project path.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open with degradation. postJson uses 30 s default timeout (15 s for scope and choice calls), one retry on 408/425/429/5xx/network error (decision-backends.ts:87-121). Discovery stage failure -> falls back to lexical top-k leads with a warning (discovery.ts:540-544); scope-check failure -> treated as specific (task-pipeline.ts:136-140); Stage 4 ranking failure -> structural order (task-pipeline.ts:409-411). Missing API key or no provider configured -> tool returns isError with 'run jevtrace setup' (judges.ts:334-336), not a crash; there is no automatic offline fallback (--offline is CLI flag only). Worst case a single tool call can block for tens of seconds (up to 30 s x2 attempts per batch stage) before degrading; the agent can still fall back to Grep.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools + 2 MCP-app UI resources. Tool definitions: source text of descriptions + zod schemas is ~4.7k chars for the fragments I measured; JSON-schema serialization of 17+16+7 params with defaults/ranges plus ~900-char server instructions puts it at roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens of always-on context (deferred tool loading in Claude Code 2.1.x can reduce this). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Each call returns up to maxChars=30000 (~7.5k tokens, default tokenBudget 8000) as BOTH content text and structuredContent.context (server.ts:139-149) - Claude Code passes one of them to the model, but the duplicate payload may inflate transcript size. Result also carries a 'Session so far' savings line.
pros: Natively supports OpenRouter Jev (Decisions API, typesafe/jev-1.13) with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, with the wire format implemented (noul/choice) and OpenRouter used in the author's own benchmarks; no patching needed.
Actually uses Jev for what it is good at (typed Noul relevance probabilities and Choice), not as a chat replacement; Jev cost is tiny (~$0.002-0.008 per retrieval, per the repo's benchmark tables).
Fails open in the retrieval pipeline: Jev discovery/ranking failures degrade to lexical/structural results with warnings; 30 s/15 s timeouts and one retry.

Server instructions plus tool description are written to steer Claude to call it before grep; user-scope registration follows CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR so it works across all projects without per-project config.
Key handled reasonably: setup writes 0600 config, nothing secret in claude mcp add argv; no exec/spawn, no postinstall scripts, no phone-home telemetry seen.

Self-reported pilot: 50k vs 120k agent tokens and 0 repo searches on 5 focused tasks when guided; retrieval 98.2% of labelled code vs 70.6% for jevgrep on 19 tasks (author-labelled, so treat as directional).
cons: Very immature: repo created 2026-09-29, 12 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, not on npm, no CI for tests; benchmarks are author-labelled and the agent benchmark is a 5-task single-run pilot on small repos (Ky, Hono).
JS/TS/Vue only (no Python, Go, Svelte, Astro); the user also uses Python 3.13, so it helps only on TS/JS client/personal projects.

Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool; the repo's own data shows the agent skips it in 2 of 5 sessions without a CLAUDE.md line, and it would compete with the user's existing GitNexus graph-context hook and MCP for the same 'find the code' job (overlapping, possibly conflicting guidance).

Sends real source snippets (up to 3-4 KB per candidate, batches of 16) and a file-path tree to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every retrieval; for client projects this is a confidentiality/contract issue, and the server's file reads bypass the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard (only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) and no .env/secret exclusion is applied in file scanning.

Adds 3 tools + 2 UI resources (~2.5-3.5k tokens of always-on context) and returns up to ~7.5k tokens per call, duplicated in content and structuredContent; latency 1-9 s per call vs a ~100 ms local grep, and first-call indexing on large repos.
Must be cloned and built locally (npm install + vite build, TS 6) from an unaudited fresh repo; no version pinning or releases, so upgrades are git pulls of a fast-moving main.
Uses OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), which may change; Jev itself is beta and Theo-style skepticism about what model sits behind it is unresolved.
entries.verdict: The only candidate I inspected that genuinely and natively integrates OpenRouter-hosted Jev (Noul/Choice) for a real coding-agent task and is decently engineered (fail-open, 0600 key file, no exec), but it is a 1-day-old single-author POC, JS/TS-only, still needs a CLAUDE.md nudge or hook to be used reliably, and ships client source snippets to OpenRouter outside the user's secret guard. Worth trialing on personal TS projects with JEVTRACE_USAGE_LOG on, not as a default on client repos.

judge.why: Well-designed multi-stage retrieval that degrades gracefully, but it is a 1-day-old POC limited to JS/TS.
pros: Native OpenRouter with tiny per-retrieval cost ($0.002 to $0.008)
Fails open at each stage (lexical or structural fallback, warnings); 0600 key file; no exec
Server instructions written to steer Claude
cons: Created 2026-09-29, 12 commits, not on npm, no releases, 5-task single-run pilot
JS/TS/Vue only
Still model-discretion; skipped in 2 of 5 sessions without a CLAUDE.md line; overlaps gitnexus
Source snippets go out beside your secret guard

entries.name: WanLanglin/jev-skills
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also usable from Codex) with 3 Python skills that call Jev's System One API: jev-shortlist (rank Grep/Glob/rg candidate paths by P(agent needs to open it) via Noul, includes a PostToolUse hook that reorders Grep/Glob filenames), jev-triage (batch Choice classification with confidence and an escalate-below threshold), jev-logscan (collapse a long log to templates, score them against a goal, return the relevant lines in original order). Shared zero-dependency client scripts/jev.py batches up to 256 questions per request (Jev bills shared state once). Ships an eval harness and a self-measured calibration study (Noul ECE 0.169 on 4,995 decisions; Choice ECE 0.226). Not an MCP server.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed and weaker than advertised. (1) Skill description triggers: model-discretion; Claude may invoke jev-shortlist/triage/logscan when descriptions match, but the skills run through Bash scripts and Opus will often just read results itself. (2) The PostToolUse Grep|Glob hook is defined in skill frontmatter, so it registers only after jev-shortlist has been invoked in that session (SKILL.md: 'for the rest of the session'); it is not installed by plugin.json and there is no hooks/hooks.json. For a truly automatic hook the user must copy it into ~/.claude/settings.json (or a fork's hooks/hooks.json) as a global PostToolUse matcher Grep|Glob. The user's existing GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks fire on the same tools; two PostToolUse hooks both emitting updatedToolOutput may conflict (ordering unspecified, unverified).
security: API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), sent as Bearer header; never placed in argv, so not visible in the process list.

No shell execution, subprocess or os.system anywhere; pure urllib + stdlib; no npm postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev call itself. Whole codebase is about 1,000 lines of Python and easy to audit (jev.py, shortlist.py, triage.py, hooks/rerank_search.py read fully; logscan.py partly).

Hook output is constrained: it only permutes an existing string array in filenames, so a hostile payload cannot inject text into Claude context through the hook. Jev returns numbers, no free text, so prompt-injection surface via the model response is minimal.
Prompt injection into Jev itself is possible (file names or log lines placed in state could bias ranking), but the worst effect is a mis-ordering; nothing is dropped.
Egress of possibly sensitive data (see dataEgress); logscan and triage do no secret redaction.

No LICENSE file in repo (GitHub licenseInfo null) although README and plugin.json say MIT; legal ambiguity for client work. Single author, 1 star, no releases: supply-chain trust is low, though pinning a commit SHA and reading the 1k lines mitigates it.
entries.dataEgress: Hook (automatic path): on every Grep/Glob with >=12 results, sends to Jev the last user prompt text (first 600 chars, from transcript) plus the full list of matched file paths (indexed). No file contents, no match lines. Manual scripts: shortlist sends the task sentence plus paths (grep match lines only with --context); triage sends up to 1500 chars of each item plus optional context (may include code or diffs); logscan sends one raw representative log line per template (up to 300 chars, unredacted, may contain tokens, hostnames, emails). All goes to the configured BASE (if patched, OpenRouter and its upstream TypeSafe see it). File paths and user prompts from client projects leave the machine, which may matter for client NDAs.
entries.failureMode: Hook fails open: no key, unparseable payload, non-dict response, <12 files, no user message, any exception -> exit 0 with no stdout so the original output is kept (hooks/rerank_search.py:33-36, 66-102, 116-121). Harness timeout is 15 s, but jev.py uses urlopen timeout=120 with 3 attempts and 2s/4s sleeps and calls die() (sys.exit(1)) on 401/403/other 4xx/unreachable; the 15 s hook timeout caps worst-case added latency at about 15 s per Grep/Glob during an outage (not 0). Manual scripts fail closed with an error message and non-zero exit (no fallback ranking except logscan --no-jev). A bad OpenRouter key means every big search pays a wasted round trip, then exits.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, no server instructions. Three skill entries (name plus multi-line description, about 700 to 900 chars each, roughly 2.3k chars total, approx 550 to 650 tokens) in the skill listing permanently. Invoking a skill loads its SKILL.md body (about 3 to 4k chars each, roughly 800 to 1000 tokens). The hook injects no text; it only permutes filenames. Script output adds a small block per use.
pros: Only candidate so far that actually turns Jev into an automatic, deterministic-capable hook in Claude Code (PostToolUse on Grep|Glob with updatedToolOutput), matching the 'no prompting' requirement once installed globally.

Same wire schema as OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone: pure env-var switch (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), no code patch needed.
Small (~1k LOC), stdlib-only Python, no shell exec, no installers, key via env not argv: easy to audit and safe to run.
Hook is conservative: reorder only, never drops or rewrites content, preserves schema, fails open on all errors, MIN_RESULTS=12 avoids wasteful calls.
Uses Jev where it fits (Noul relevance, batched shared state at ~$0.042/M input, output free): cost is negligible.

Unusually honest evidence: ships eval harness and a measured calibration curve (Noul ECE 0.169, Choice ECE 0.226, recall@10 0.69 vs 0.53 search order), reports negative results and corrected its own default from 0.7 to 0.9.
Zero context bloat compared with an MCP server: no tool schemas, roughly 600 tokens of skill descriptions.
cons: Measured benefit is modest: reordering Grep/Glob file lists improves recall@10 from 0.53 to 0.69 on the author's own 102 cases; Opus 5.5 with ripgrep and GitNexus graph context rarely reads whole file lists blindly, so real gain for this user is doubtful.
The 'automatic' hook only activates after the jev-shortlist skill is invoked (skill-scoped frontmatter hook); out of the box it is not automatic. Needs manual copy into settings.json to be always-on.

Likely overlap or conflict with the user's GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash pre/post hooks and secret-leak guard: another PostToolUse rewriting Grep output may clash, and GitNexus already enriches search context.

Sends the user's last prompt (600 chars) and all matched file paths to a third party on every big search; client-project paths and prompts leave the machine; no redaction, allowlist or per-project opt-out. logscan sends raw log lines.
Task relevance signal is only the last string user message from the transcript; in long agentic turns or slash-command flows it may be stale or empty, degrading ranking.
Outage behaviour is not zero-cost: up to the 15 s hook timeout per Grep/Glob during slow or failed API; a wrong key wastes an HTTP call every time; no circuit breaker.
Jev is unreliable mid-range (author's own numbers: says 0.45 when reality is 11%); Choice confidence separates only above 0.9, so jev-triage has limited use for code-review-type judgments.

Weak maturity: created 2026-09-21, 5 commits, 1 author, 1 star, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file despite claiming MIT, unaffiliated with TypeSafe; '360x cheaper' marketing compares against a use Opus would not need for such tasks.
OpenRouter path untested by the author; TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming is confusing when holding an OpenRouter key.
entries.verdict: The most concrete Jev integration for Claude Code so far (real PostToolUse hook, stdlib-only, repointed to OpenRouter by three env vars), but it is a small single-author POC whose gain (reordering Grep/Glob results) is marginal for an Opus + GitNexus workflow, and its hook is only auto-registered after the skill is invoked. Worth cherry-picking the hook and jev.py into a self-owned global hook (with an allowlist/redaction and a circuit breaker) rather than installing the plugin as is.
entries.license: None in repo (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null). README and plugin.json claim MIT.

entries.name: Lagnajit09/sgrep
entries.what: Python CLI semantic grep: chunks repo (tree-sitter), local Model2Vec+BM25 prefilter, then one Jev yes/no call per chunk ranked by confidence; Claude Code plugin skill adds call-graph trace/impact.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger (model discretion)
pros: Prefilter keeps Jev calls bounded on big repos; chunk and verdict caches, daemon mode, Vercel gateway fallback
Claude Code marketplace plugin with SKILL.md, BENCHMARK.md and DECISIONS.md documenting evaluation
cons: Default endpoint typesafe /v1/systemone; SGREP_JEV_URL override exists but model id for OpenRouter unverified
Fan-out of 1 call per chunk sends source code to provider; overlaps with existing gitnexus MCP
Requires pipx install and downloads embedding model on first run; skill-triggered rather than hook

interface: plugin manifests for Claude and Codex
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger (model discretion)
pros: Concrete coding use: filter git ls-files by relevance before reading, with measured bench
Node script with mock tests and CI; Claude plugin manifest
Batch of many questions in one call
cons: Endpoints only api.typesafe.ai and Vercel gateway; needs code patch for OpenRouter
Korean docs; TypeSafe key required
No hook, not deterministic

entries.name: zbush/jev-context
entries.what: Node stdio MCP server (search_code): runs ripgrep, asks Jev a yes/no relevance noul per passage, returns only relevant passages with token-savings receipts; Codex plugin but generic MCP.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP with skill trigger
pros: Stdio MCP server plus SKILL.md, portable to Claude Code via .mcp.json; ripgrep-based so local and predictable
Auditable per-call receipts, hashes, judgments and latency; expand_result for withheld passages
Tests for core, context, expansion and MCP

entries.name: uehaj/sys1grep (formerly uehaj/jev-semgrep, npm @uehaj/sys1grep) + /uehaj:sys1grep skill
entries.what: The candidate URL jev-semgrep redirects to the repo renamed uehaj/sys1grep. It is a single-file Node CLI (sys1grep.mjs, about 2,100 lines, no runtime dependencies) that does "grep by meaning". Each input line (or commit, sentence or function) is sent in chunks of 30 to the /v1/systemone endpoint as a Jev "noul" question ("Does line L000 match the meaning: ...?"). Lines are kept when P(yes) passes a threshold. It supports AND, OR and NOT across meanings, mixed with regex terms. It also has auto-scope, dedup, optional --rank and --summarize (which pipes matches to `claude -p` haiku by default). The Claude Code integration is a separate skill, `uehaj:sys1grep`, in the uehaj/uehaj-marketplace plugin. The skill description tells Claude to reach for sys1grep before Grep or reading whole files. The repo itself contains no MCP server, no hooks and no SKILL.md.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, at the model's discretion. There is no deterministic hook and no proxy. The description asks Claude to use it before Grep or before reading whole files, when Grep returns too many or zero hits, and after failed commands with an unclear error. Whether Opus 5.5 follows that is probabilistic, and it competes with the existing Grep, GitNexus hook and MCP habits. The author's skill-eval measured wording effectiveness with claude -p Sonnet on synthetic logs, not on real coding work.
security: API key is read from env or ~/.config/sys1grep/.env. sys1grep.mjs:21-23 states it never reads ./.env, so an untrusted checkout cannot redirect the key.
The key is sent as `Authorization: Bearer` to whatever SYS1GREP_URL is configured (sys1grep.mjs:1278). It warns when the URL is plain http and not localhost (sys1grep.mjs:559-560).
--sys1-api-key on the command line is visible in `ps` and shell history. The README warns about this and recommends the .env file. The skill does not pass the key on argv.
No telemetry found: grep for telemetry, analytics and sentry returned nothing. Network calls go only to the configured Jev URL, plus the optional --summarize target.

Shell execution is limited to execFileSync/spawn with argument arrays for git and for the --summarize tool (sys1grep.mjs:2019). There is no shell string interpolation in what I read. No postinstall script exists (npm view shows none).

The skill runs `npx -y` at run time, so each session can fetch and execute npm code. It is version-pinned to 0.5.0-next.1, but the author's npm account is a supply-chain trust point. Installing the plugin also trusts the marketplace repo.
entries.dataEgress: Every searched line is sent to the configured endpoint, which would be OpenRouter here and then TypeSafe/Jev. A request is JSON {model, state, questions}. It holds up to 30 lines of file or stdin content per chunk, plus file names and question text such as the meanings you typed. Lines are truncated to 2,000 characters. Blank lines are not sent. It also sends auto-scope questions about the meaning, dedup and rank questions containing match text, and git commit metadata and diffs with -g. README.md:923 says "Every searched line is sent to api.typesafe.ai. Do not run it over files you would not upload there." With --summarize (the default tool is `claude`, model haiku) the matched lines are also sent to Anthropic or to any URL configured as summarizer, and the skill's own text says so. OpenRouter is an extra intermediary, and its logging and privacy settings apply. Nothing leaves unless a search runs. For client code this needs client approval and an OpenRouter zero-data-retention or privacy setting.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the tool, but harmless for Claude Code. Each request has a 60 s timeout (sys1grep.mjs:1280). Connection errors, timeouts, 429, 529 and 5xx are retried up to 6 times with exponential backoff (500 ms x 2^n, about 63 s of sleep in total). After that it throws and prints a one-line error with exit code 2. A missing or malformed answer is an error, not a silent 0 (sys1grep.mjs:1289-1295). Claude sees a failed Bash call and can fall back to plain Grep. Nothing is blocked, because this is an optional skill and not a hook. Worst case is a slow call of about a minute or more before the failure shows. The cost guard --max-cost (default 1 USD) asks a question on a terminal. Under Claude Code Bash there is no TTY, so the skill has to pass -y or narrow the search.
entries.contextCost: Very low and static. It adds 0 MCP tools and no server instructions. The only always-loaded cost is one skill listing entry: name plus a description of about 700 characters, roughly 200-300 tokens (Japanese text tokenises worse). The SKILL.md body (about 6.9 KB, roughly 2-2.5k tokens) loads only when the skill fires. No hook-injected text. Command output enters context only as matched lines, or a summary with --summarize, which can shrink context.
pros: Real, working OpenRouter path today: sys1grep.mjs:555 has a configurable URL, and README.md:273 lists openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. Only three env vars are needed and there is no code patching.

Zero context cost. No MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook text. It only adds one skill listing entry (about 250 tokens), so it will not bloat the existing gitnexus, playwright and caveman setup.

Well-engineered and security-aware for its size. It never reads ./.env, warns about http URLs, sanitises server output and control characters, skips secret-like files with -r, and has a cost guard (--max-cost 1 USD) and --dry-run to preview what would be sent.

Model-invoked skill with a description written to fire on 'no fixed search term' questions, Grep returning too many or zero hits, and cause-hunting in noisy logs. This is close to the automatic behaviour the user wants, with no 'use jev' prompt needed.

Real use case for a semantic probability judge: log triage with --dedup, finding customer tickets by intent, and finding commits by meaning with -g. --summarize keeps bulk output out of Claude's context.
Solid test discipline for a 12-day-old project: an offline fake-Jev suite, CI on Node 20.16, 22 and 24, gitleaks, a scope eval with a holdout set, and a reported P/R of 0.94/0.98.
MIT license, zero runtime dependencies, one readable .mjs file. That is easy to audit (I did) and easy to fork and pin.
cons: It covers one narrow slice of daily coding, search. Code search is already served by rg, Grep and the GitNexus graph, which are local, free and instant. Paying per line and adding latency for a semantic grep beats them only in edge cases such as logs, tickets and free-text prose.

The skill needs the user to name a target (files, a directory with -r, or stdin) and all of it goes over the network. Recursive semantic search over a real repo means sending source to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. That conflicts with client-project confidentiality, and the secret-file skip list is best effort.

It uses only the Noul primitive, one question per line. It does not use Choice or Score, or the /api/alpha/decisions endpoint. It is not a general 'let Claude Code ask Jev for decisions' bridge (routing, permission, triage decisions). It is only a grep front-end.

Auto-invocation is probabilistic. The trigger is a skill description in Japanese that competes with Claude's strong Grep and GitNexus habits. In bypass or auto permission mode nothing forces it. No evidence was found that Opus 5.5 fires it reliably on real repos. The author's eval uses Sonnet on generated logs.

Supply-chain surface. The skill runs `npx -y @uehaj/sys1grep@0.5.0-next.1` at run time, so it depends on a prerelease tag and on npm availability. npm `latest` still points to 0.5.0-next.0. The plugin also lives in a third-party marketplace whose maintainer can change the skill text later.

Repo is 12 days old with 3 contributors, one main author, version 0.5.0-next.1 and a large Unreleased list. It was renamed from semgrep to sys1grep, the old repo URL and the /uehaj:semgrep skill are deprecated, and the option surface is churning. The CLI has about 100 flags, which is heavy for a skill.

Model id and OpenRouter compatibility are not verified. The default model is 'jev-latest', not OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13. The response shape it requires (answers.*.noul plus usage.cost) was assumed to match OpenRouter's /v1/systemone and I did not test it live.

Failure cost. A downed or throttled endpoint can burn about a minute of retries inside a Claude Bash call before failing. The cost prompt cannot be answered without a TTY. --summarize also sends matched lines to Anthropic haiku, which adds another egress path and a prompt-injection path.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here with a proven, documented OpenRouter Jev path and near-zero context cost, but it is a semantic-grep skill and not a general Jev integration. It fits log, ticket and commit triage better than everyday code editing, and the data-egress and latency cost is not worth it as the main Jev integration. Treat it as an optional add-on, enabled per non-confidential project, and not as the answer to 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically'.

Tiny codebase (src/search.ts, walkers.ts), easy to wrap as MCP or skill
From Ellipsis, credible authors
