entries.name: JayDoubleu/cc-mod-jev (plugin jev-context)
entries.what: Claude Code function-hooks plugin (TypeScript, no runtime deps). On session.compact (manual /compact, engine auto-compaction, or its own turn.complete trigger at >=60% context) it pairs every tool_use/tool_result, sends an abridged whole-conversation state (20k-token cap) plus two Noul questions per call (keep call? keep full result?) to OpenRouter's Jev decisions endpoint, then returns the transcript with stale results truncated to a 300-char head or stale calls dropped, everything else verbatim and no summary written. Falls back to the built-in summary on missing key, Jev error, or <20% reduction. Optional tool.call gate (off by default) asks Jev whether an oversized Bash/Read output is needed in full and cuts the middle if P<0.3. /jev prints config and decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic once installed with the env flag: session.compact intercepts /compact and engine auto-compaction; turn.complete requests compaction at 60% context; optional gate on tool.call. Model never has to be told to 'use jev'. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in env (can go in settings.json env) and Claude Code >=2.1.278 (user has 2.1.285).
security: No shell exec, spawn, child_process or eval anywhere in src/ or hooks/ (grep). Only network is $.http.fetch to the configured URL; scripts/smoke.ts uses plain fetch but is a manual dev script.

Key handling: sent in an Authorization header via engine $.http.fetch (not argv, not a subprocess). Plugin option apiKey is marked sensitive. Key can also be read by the hook from settings.json env via $.settings.read(). Not logged; /jev prints only key=set/MISSING (src/config.ts:170).

Prompt-injection surface: tool results (up to 120-char head each at stage 0), tool inputs (1000 chars), user/assistant texts (2000 chars) go into the Jev state; adversarial file/web content can push Noul answers to drop/truncate needed context (Jev is known to be steerable by injected state). Output is only numeric probabilities, so no code execution path, worst case is lost context or wrongly kept context.
Gate is a tool.call hook and can silently alter what the model sees from Bash/Read (cut middle with a note), a correctness risk (e.g. test failures in the middle of output); off by default.

Function hooks run in-process in Claude Code's runtime with $ access to settings, session messages, http; the plugin is 372+ lines of readable TS but a broad-capability early-access API. Single-author, 1 star, days old: supply-chain trust is the main risk; pin to a commit.
Does not touch the existing no-secret-leak PreToolUse hook; OPENROUTER_API_KEY should still be added to its protected list (the plugin's own hook reads it, the model should not).
entries.dataEgress: Only to openrouter.ai (default URL, src/openrouter.ts:3), and only when compaction runs (or gate is on). Compaction: goal (last 3 user prompts, 500 chars each), the entire conversation oldest first with user/assistant texts abridged to <=2000 chars (down to length-only at later stages), every tool_use input abridged to <=1000 chars (Bash commands, file paths, edit snippets may contain secrets or client code), and per tool result a note 'ok, N chars' plus a <=120-char head; plus question text per call. Capped at ~20k state tokens, 28k per request. Gate (if enabled): last 12 messages abridged (600 chars text, 200 chars per call input), goal, and up to 1500-char head and 800-char tail of the Bash stdout or Read file content per gated output, i.e. actual file/command contents. No ZDR/provider pinning or data-collection:deny set in the request body (body is only model,state,questions), so OpenRouter/TypeSafe retention policy applies to client-project content. model IDs and base URL configurable.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe for compaction: missing key, HTTP error, malformed JSON, missing answers, state not fitting, or reduction below 20% all fall back to the built-in summary (manual/auto) or skip (plugin-triggered) via noteFallback (hooks/jev-context.ts session.compact). Gate fails open (errors return the original outcome, 'gate skipped'). turn.complete errors are logged and swallowed. No explicit per-request timeout or AbortSignal in the plugin code (grep found none); it relies on $.http.fetch defaults, whose time does not count toward the 10 s hook budget per CLAUDE.md, so a hung OpenRouter request could stall a compaction; alpha endpoint has no SLA. Residual risk is semantic, not availability: overconfident Jev may truncate or drop a result still needed (model can re-run tools; truncation notes say so), and pruning leaves user/assistant text untouched so reduction may be small on chat-heavy sessions.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no skills, no SKILL.md, no MCP instructions, no additionalContext injection. Only /jev slash command description (one line). Gate adds a short '[jev-context cut N chars ...]' note only when it cuts; truncated compacted results carry a short note. Negligible standing context; its purpose is to reduce context (README claims 96% on one session, measured with 8 large file reads).
pros: Native OpenRouter: default URL https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/openrouter.ts:3-4, 37), no patching.
Truly automatic with zero context footprint (no tools, no skills, no injected text), matching the user's 'never prompt use jev' requirement.
Compaction is fail-safe: every error path falls back to the built-in summary or skips (session.compact handler); reduction floor of 20% prevents pointless prunes.
Cheap and fast: README measured 1 request, 7.8k tokens, $0.00033, 503 ms vs an LLM summary; state capped to 20k/28k tokens under Jev's 32k window with 5-stage fitting.
Verbatim pruning never rewrites user/assistant text and keeps tool_use/tool_result pairing intact; first message and newest 6 messages pinned; pairs <300 chars kept without a question.

Clean, small, readable code with no shell exec, no runtime dependencies, MIT; sensitive apiKey userConfig; 31 tests with a fake OpenRouter through the engine, evals, live smoke scripts, honest Limitations section and documented gate eval blind spot.
Config is rich (thresholds, env overrides JEV_CONTEXT_*) and gate is opt-in per tool; /jev gives visibility into every decision.
Works with subscription/OAuth login since it uses no Anthropic key; user's 2.1.285 exceeds the >=2.1.278 requirement.
cons: Depends on the early-access function-hooks API behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; the author says the API may change and typings are pinned to 2.1.278, so a CC update could break it silently.

Privacy: whole-conversation abridged state (tool inputs up to 1000 chars, text up to 2000 chars, result heads) is sent to OpenRouter with no ZDR / provider-data-policy pinning in the request body (src/openrouter.ts:41); a client-project concern, and the gate would also send real file/command output heads and tails.
Not on the user's protected-vars path: OPENROUTER_API_KEY would live in settings.json env or the plugin config, and the no-secret-leak hook must be updated so the model cannot read it.
1 star, 1 author, 4 commits all on one day (2026-09-19), no releases, no CI; unreviewed by others; supply-chain risk for a plugin with broad in-process access.

Jev quality limits apply: overconfident on unanswerable inputs, steerable by injected text in tool results; wrongly dropped results can degrade the session, and state is abridged so decisions on long sessions are coarse (README Limitations).
No explicit request timeout in the plugin code; alpha endpoint has no SLA, so a slow OpenRouter call can stall a compaction.

Replaces the summary with no summary: only tool results are pruned, so chat-heavy or thinking-heavy sessions get little reduction (then falls back), and it defeats prompt-cache reuse like any compaction; the gate tool.call result is not verifiable in evals and can hide the middle of test/build output.
Only helps at compaction time, so it is an occasional benefit rather than a per-prompt daily one; with Opus 5.5 large context windows the trigger at 60% may rarely fire.

Key exposure path: if OPENROUTER_API_KEY goes into settings.json env (as the README suggests), Claude Code exports settings env to the Bash tool's child processes, so the model could `printenv` it. Under bypassPermissions the no-secret-leak hook is the only barrier. Prefer the sensitive plugin `apiKey` option (which takes precedence, src/config.ts:136) and still add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the protected list.

The always-on `session.compact` `{trigger:'precompute'}` hook returns skip. It disables the engine's background precompute of the built-in summary for every session. Whenever Jev fails, is missing a key, or reduces less than 20%, the fallback summary must then be computed synchronously, so the fallback path is slower than stock Claude Code (d.ts ~8523: precompute result is 'kept for the compaction that comes').

The session.compact hook also receives subagent transcripts when the engine compacts them (README Limitations), so subagent content (tool inputs and results) egresses to OpenRouter too, not only the main conversation.

Reduction is judged in characters, not tokens, and chat/thinking-heavy transcripts are barely reduced. Every such compaction still costs a Jev round trip, then falls back to a full LLM summary, and plugin-triggered attempts are retried every +10 context points.

Function hooks are documented in the 2.1.285 binary and d.ts as needing CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 (verified), but the plugin's types are pinned to 2.1.278 and the README says the API may change. A silent CC update break is plausible. Hook failures are skipped and reported by name, so the failure mode is benign (built-in compaction).

The gate's Read cut discards the entire remainder of a file after about 4000 chars, not just the middle. A wrong P<0.3 call on a file to be edited silently hides the code being edited, though the note gives the offset to re-read from. This is riskier than the audit's description of 'cut the middle'.
entries.verdict: Best-fitting automatic, OpenRouter-native Jev integration found: hook-driven, zero context cost, fail-safe fallback to built-in compaction, clean code with real tests. Held back to 6 by the early-access function-hooks flag, a days-old one-star single-author repo, and sending abridged transcripts (and optional gate output slices) to OpenRouter with no ZDR pinning, so try it on personal projects with the gate off and pin a commit before touching client work.

entries.name: kunchenguid/compact-adviser
entries.what: Multi-host plugin (Pi, Claude Code, Codex, Grok). The Claude Code part (packages/claude-mod) is a "function hooks" mod, not a normal command hook. After each finished answer in an interactive session it checks local gates (context >= 40k tokens, idle session, cooldowns, key present). If they pass, it sends a bounded snapshot of the conversation to Jev's System One API with two Choice questions: "is the latest unit of work finished" and "hands-on vs coordinating". It combines the probabilities into one score and compares it with a floor that slides from 0.90 (context <=10% used) to 0.50 (>=90% used). On a pass it shows a status-line hint "work appears completed or recorded. Run /compact to save tokens." Optionally (mode=auto, after a first-use confirmation) it runs $.session.compact() itself. The output is a hint or a compaction only. It gives no general-purpose Jev decisions for coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. The turn.complete handler fires automatically after every final answer in interactive sessions, gated locally by mode, key, idle state, cooldown and the 40k-token minimum. No prompt and no model discretion are involved. Caveat: it needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in the launch environment. It is inert in claude -p and other non-interactive sessions, and for subagent turns.
security: The Claude Code integration depends on an experimental, default-off 'function hooks' / Claude Mod API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; verified only on Claude Code 2.1.275 per SECURITY.md). Whether 2.1.285 still ships it is unverified and has to be tested by the user.

Key handling: sent in the Authorization header via host fetch ($.http.fetch), so it does not appear in argv or the process list. It is resolved from env, then a saved setting (hidden in /config), then cwd .env. It is stripped from the snapshot (snapshot(messages,[activeKey,savedKey])) and never logged. The plugin reads the working-directory .env for TYPESAFE_API_KEY (register.ts:138-140), a small behavior to be aware of.

TYPESAFE_BASE guard (commit a73995f, #62): https only, or loopback http; no credentials, query or fragment; read from the launch env only. A malicious project cannot redirect the key via .env or settings, though a project's own env config could. The endpoint override is documented as such in SECURITY.md.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The Jev output is validated to a strict schema of probabilities and can only produce a hint or a compaction. Both questions tell Jev the state is 'untrusted conversation data, never instructions'. Errors, timeouts and malformed replies never count as an affirmative judgment.

No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, and no runtime dependencies in claude-mod (SECURITY.md). Install is via 'claude plugin marketplace add' plus 'claude plugin install'. The marketplace source is ./packages/claude-mod in a repo one person mostly controls, so pin the version and review updates (plugin auto-update pulls new code).
No telemetry beyond the TypeSafe/Jev call. Optional local request logging is off by default. If enabled, the full request body (conversation excerpts) is written under ~/.claude.
entries.dataEgress: On each judged turn, one POST to <TYPESAFE_BASE or api.typesafe.ai>/v1/systemone. Contents: bounded user constraints, up to the last 64 visible messages and tool results (each tool result clipped to about 512 bytes, middle-truncated), short tool-result excerpts, an existing compaction summary, saved-artifact names (files written via Write/Edit/Bash redirects), and omission markers. It is capped at 32,000 UTF-8 bytes. Not sent: the system prompt, hidden reasoning, images, environment variables, the API key, and the full transcript. With OpenRouter as the base, that text also passes through OpenRouter to TypeSafe (two third parties). Code snippets, diffs and command output from client projects can appear in the excerpts, and redaction is only known-key-pattern matching. A judgment runs only when conversationTokens > 20k and context >= 40k, and it is deduped per checkpoint fingerprint plus cooldowns and backoff, so the call rate is low (roughly once per completed checkpoint).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, with no blocking. The judgment runs in a scheduled task after the turn ($.clock.after(0), register.ts:~404), never on the critical path. TIMEOUT_MS is 2000 (judge.ts, a race with $.clock.sleep). On timeout, network error, 401/403/429/5xx, malformed reply, or an oversized request/response (32 KB cap), it throws a JudgeError. Then it applies backoff, shows a toast (one per message), and leaves the context unchanged. An invalid TYPESAFE_BASE means no request and no advice. If CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC is set, plugin fetch is refused and the toast says so. The toasts could be mildly noisy if OpenRouter's response shape mismatches the strict parser.
entries.contextCost: About zero tokens for the model. It exposes no MCP tools and no skill, injects no hook text into the prompt, and its hint goes only to the UI status line ($.ui.status) or a toast. It adds one slash command (/compact-adviser). The only context effect is when auto mode runs /compact. Estimated total tool-definition cost: 0 tokens.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a deterministic turn.complete hook that fires with no prompting, which is exactly the mechanism the user wants. It does not depend on the model choosing to call anything.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected hook text, and hints go to the status line only. It does not add to the existing gitnexus, playwright, caveman and hook overhead.
Fail-open by design. The judgment runs after the turn with a 2 s timeout, a backoff, and no blocking of the session.

A good fit for Jev's design: two calibrated Choice questions composed in code with a usage-dependent floor, and it never asks Jev for text. It is an honest example of Jev doing a job that Opus should not spend tokens on.

TYPESAFE_BASE support (added 2026-09-29, #59/#62) makes OpenRouter routing a two-variable change: TYPESAFE_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api yields /api/v1/systemone, and OpenRouter maps bare 'jev-latest' to typesafe/jev-latest. The request and response fields match the OpenRouter docs.

Careful engineering: strict response validation, a documented threat model, an https-only base URL guard, and key redaction from the snapshot. It also has real tests, an eval harness and a CI matrix, and it is very active (5 contributors, 10 releases in 2 weeks).
Hint mode is the default and safe. Auto mode needs an explicit confirmation, and the user can opt out at any time with /compact-adviser off or COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1.
cons: Narrow: it only answers 'should I /compact now?'. It gives no Jev decisions for coding itself (routing, permission decisions, review triage, test selection). The user's core wish, Jev used whenever it adds value in daily coding, is met only for context compaction.

Depends on Claude Code's experimental function-hooks / 'Claude Mod' API behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. It was verified only on 2.1.275, and the user runs 2.1.285. The API may have changed, be removed, or be gated. The env var must be set at every launch (e.g. shell alias or settings env), which is one more thing to keep working.

Egress on client projects: up to 32 KB of conversation, tool-result excerpts and file names goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe on every judged checkpoint, protected by best-effort redaction only. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover this channel. Needs a per-project COMPACT_ADVISER_DISABLE=1 for sensitive clients.

Using it with OpenRouter is not a supported path. It is undocumented in the repo, the strict parser could reject a response that has extra fields, and the OpenRouter key has to live in a variable named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, in the launch environment or a saved setting. The user must verify this with a real run; I did not execute the code, per the rules.

Value is modest. Claude Code already auto-compacts, and the user is on a subscription where saved tokens are not billed per token. The main win is compaction timing and quality. Auto mode is lossy and is 'experimental'.

Also reads a working-directory .env for the key, keeps the saved key in the plugin's settings store, and can write request logs (with conversation text) to ~/.claude if logRequests is turned on. The Jev claims are unverified (skeptics say it acts like a small router model), and the eval is the author's own, on a 96-checkpoint set.
entries.verdict: The cleanest true-automatic Jev integration found so far: a zero-context, fail-open turn.complete hook that works with OpenRouter by setting TYPESAFE_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key. Its scope is only compaction timing, it relies on an experimental Claude Code hooks API that must be re-checked on 2.1.285, and it sends conversation excerpts off-machine. Worth a hint-mode trial on personal projects, disabled on client projects, but it is not the main Jev integration.

It only helps with compaction timing.

entries.name: ingebyd/fast-jev-compaction-openrouter
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (early-access "function hooks" module, plus npm library) that hooks session.compact. It sends the whole stripped transcript to Jev on OpenRouter with two Noul questions per non-pinned tool call (keep call, keep result verbatim). Tool calls and results Jev scores below 0.5 are dropped or truncated to a 300-char head. User and assistant text stays verbatim. If the reduction is under 25% or anything fails, it falls back to the built-in summary. A turn.complete hook also triggers /compact-equivalent at 60% context.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic once installed: session.compact fires on /compact and on Claude's auto-compact, and the turn.complete hook self-triggers compaction at 60% context. Needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 in the env. The installed 2.1.285 binary still gates function hooks behind that variable (strings: 'hooks modules are not turned on for installed plugins ... set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1'). The checked-in types are from 2.1.274, and API drift on 2.1.285 was NOT verified (the code was not executed).
security: No shell exec, no child_process, no installers or install scripts, and no telemetry in src/ or hooks/. The only network call is $.http.fetch to the fixed openrouter.ai URL (the hook cannot change the URL).

Key handling: apiKey is a sensitive userConfig, or the key comes from $.env.get / merged settings env (hooks/fast-jev.ts:227-243). It goes in a Bearer header, not argv. The hook reads all merged settings via $.settings.read() but only takes env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

The hook is a TypeScript module that runs in Claude Code's sandboxed plugin engine (no fs or network of its own; the network goes through the host's $.http.fetch). Function hooks are a very new, early-access surface, so the trust model is less battle-tested than command hooks.

Prompt-injection surface: the full conversation, including tool inputs and text, is the Jev state. Injected text inside a tool input or file content Claude echoed could sway keep/drop scoring and cause important calls or results to be dropped (integrity risk, not exfiltration). Jev is documented as injectable.
The Jev question strings interpolate only the tool name, id and char count, not user content. Answers are validated as finite numbers (request.ts:117-131).

Fork provenance: 3 commits by one new contributor (Vladislav Rzhevicky, bitstarz.com) on top of tamaratran's Devin-generated code. The fork's diff is small and reviewable (ZDR block, URL, key name). The marketplace.json owner is this fork.
entries.dataEgress: Every compaction sends the ENTIRE session transcript to openrouter.ai, and the same state is resent once per request batch, up to 25k estimated tokens each. It contains all user prompts, assistant text, tool inputs (file paths, bash commands, diffs, Edit/Write content) and, for the first/pinned messages, full text. Tool results are replaced by 'ok, N chars (omitted)' notes in the state, so file contents and command output are not sent. Secrets pasted in prompts or written in commands or Write inputs would still be sent (inputs are truncated to 1000/200/60 chars only when the state does not fit). The provider block {zdr:true, data_collection:'deny'} restricts routing to ZDR endpoints, and OpenRouter errors if none exists. OpenRouter itself still sees the request, and 'zdr' only covers upstream provider retention. The existing no-secret-leak hook does not cover this path, because the request is made by the hook engine and not via Bash/Read.
entries.failureMode: Fails closed to Claude Code's built-in summary. Any exception (no key, non-2xx, including a ZDR routing rejection, malformed JSON, missing answer, state cannot be fitted) is caught in the session.compact handler (fast-jev.ts:283-289) and returns next(event), with a toast and ui.log 'fallback to built-in summary (...)'. It is also a fallback when the reduction is under 25%. There is NO request timeout, and no retry logic in the fetch path (JevClient uses plain fetch, and the hook uses $.http.fetch without a timeoutMs), so a hung OpenRouter call would stall compaction until the host's own limit. The turn.complete auto-trigger has no cooldown: if compaction falls back to the built-in summary or the context stays above 60%, it can retrigger on every turn (in-flight flag only). Effectively this changes when auto-compaction happens (60% versus Claude's default), which is a behavior change independent of Jev. Risk of silent semantic loss: dropped tool calls and results are removed without a summary, so a wrong low score deletes needed context (mitigated by keepThreshold 0.5 and model re-runnability).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, skills or hook-injected additionalContext, so nothing is added to the prompt or skill listing. Positive effect: compaction keeps verbatim messages instead of a summary, so it removes large stale tool results but keeps much more text than a summary would (post-compact context is bigger). Cost is external: ~25k-token state x N requests per compaction on OpenRouter (about $0.001 per request at $0.042/M).
pros: Genuinely automatic: hooks session.compact and turn.complete, so the user never has to say 'use jev'. Zero context/token cost in the prompt, no tool list bloat.

Natively OpenRouter (src/request.ts:2-3,82) with the hard-coded provider {zdr:true, data_collection:'deny'} (request.ts:54), the only candidate that treats the whole-transcript egress as a privacy problem. This matters for client projects.
Fails closed to the built-in summary on every error path (fast-jev.ts:283-289) and on <25% reduction. Missing key or ZDR rejection just means normal compaction.

Small, readable code (~1.9k lines incl. tests), no shell exec or telemetry, MIT. Uses Noul questions correctly, batches under the 32k limit and fits the state into staged budgets (compact.ts, state.ts). Tool results are NOT sent to Jev (only length notes), limiting egress of file contents.
Uses Jev for what it is good at (many cheap, well-defined yes/no probabilities per item, ~$0.042/M input), and keeps user/assistant text verbatim, avoiding a lossy LLM summary.
cons: Depends on the early-access function-hooks API (needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1). Types were generated for 2.1.274, the user runs 2.1.285, and compatibility is unverified. A breaking change will disable it silently or loudly.

Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-18, 33 commits (17 by Devin AI, 12 by upstream owner, 3 by fork author), 2 stars, 29 test cases in 2 files, all using a fake Jev. It has never been shown to run on real sessions here, and there is no release.

Replaces the summary with pruned raw history: no summary of decisions or progress, so post-compaction context can stay large, and a mis-scored drop (Jev is overconfident on unanswerable input and injectable) silently loses needed tool calls. State is limited to 25k tokens while Opus contexts can be far larger, so on long sessions the state is heavily abridged and 'cannot fit' throws, giving the fallback anyway.

turn.complete forces compaction at 60% context with no cooldown. If reduction is <25% or the built-in fallback leaves the context still >= 60%, it can compact repeatedly. It also changes the user's auto-compact timing.

No request timeout or retry. The whole transcript (prompts, commands, diffs, tool inputs) leaves the machine on every compaction, and no-secret-leak does not cover it. OPENROUTER_API_KEY would have to sit in settings env or the plugin keychain option; adding it to the env also makes it visible to Bash subprocesses (add to the protected-vars list).
Narrow: it only covers compaction, not permission or routing decisions. It is a fork with upstream drift risk (tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction moves daily) and a single-maintainer, unknown-org fork.

The hook never filters on event.trigger or event.agentId, so it also runs on the engine's speculative 'precompute' compactions (binary logs 'precomputed compact ... attempt N') and on subagent/fork transcripts. Whole-transcript egress and Jev cost can happen without a user-visible compaction, and possibly several times per session.
$.http.fetch (HttpInit) offers no timeout option, so the missing timeout cannot be fixed inside the hook, only by the host.

Compaction is atomic across batches: Promise.all means one failed batch (ZDR reject, 429, malformed answer) discards all Jev work and falls back to the built-in summary. On transient OpenRouter errors the user pays latency for nothing, and there is no retry.

Given defaultMode 'auto' and frequent bypassPermissions sessions, tool inputs (bash commands, Write/Edit content, diffs, file paths) for client projects leave the machine to OpenRouter. The hook sends them without user-visible consent or a per-project opt-out, and the hook has no allow/deny list.

Reduction is measured in characters (messageChars), not tokens, and uses a fixed 25% floor. If the context stays above 60% after a kept-history compaction, turn.complete retries with no cooldown. Each retry re-sends up to ~25k-token states, so a long session can burn repeated OpenRouter requests and toasts.
Upstream popularity (7.2k stars) does not transfer to this fork: it is a 3-commit detached copy pushed once, with 0 issues and 0 releases and nothing run on real sessions.
entries.verdict: A well-scoped, safe-failing, genuinely automatic OpenRouter+ZDR Jev integration, but it targets only compaction, relies on an early-access hooks API unverified against 2.1.285, and is days old with fake-only tests. It is a reasonable opt-in experiment (pin a commit, set the flag, watch the toasts) and not something to depend on as the main Jev integration.

judge.why: An OpenRouter-only fork of tamaratran's plugin. It prunes tool calls and results at compaction and triggers compaction at 60% context. It is the only one that sends provider {zdr:true, data_collection:'deny'}. Verification lowered its score from 6 to 5.

entries.name: jevcomp/jevcomp
entries.what: Replaces Claude Code's model-written compaction summary. A plugin function hook (session.compact, early-access, needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1) shells out to node dist/cli.js claude-compact with the transcript on stdin. For each completed tool call, Jev gets two Noul questions (drop_<id>, truncate_<id>: would deleting or shortening lose needed info). Outputs with risk below 0.5 are dropped or cut to 300 chars, and user/assistant text stays verbatim. It falls back to native compaction on any error, on a reduction under 15%, or when the transcript is unsupported. A SessionStart hook starts a detached local dashboard on 127.0.0.1:43127 and edits ~/.claude/settings.json. It also proxies Codex and Antigravity, which are irrelevant here. This is compaction pruning, not a general Jev decision helper.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic, and it needs no prompting: the session.compact function hook fires on every auto or manual compaction (except 'precompute' triggers, which are skipped). It does nothing else during coding, so it is not a general 'use Jev when useful' integration. It is one narrow decision point (which old tool outputs to keep at compaction) and adds no per-tool-call value.
security: Key handling is mostly OK. The plugin apiKey goes to the child process over stdin JSON (hooks/claude.js), not argv. The key file is written 0600 in a 0700 dir (provider.ts:46-59). The key can also come from env. The child node process inherits the full environment. The repo's own no-secret-leak hook does not cover it, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY should still be added to your protected-vars list.

Modifies user config without asking. The SessionStart hook rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json to add env CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 (hooks.ts:75-91), re-serialising the whole file. That is a risk to your hand-managed settings.

Depends on an early-access Claude Code function-hook API (`session.compact`, `$.process.run`, `$.session.id`). I could not verify it in Claude Code 2.1.285: the web search hit a rate limit and no repo doc cites Anthropic documentation. If the flag or API is absent, the compaction part does nothing and only the dashboard nagging remains.

Supply chain: README install is `npm install -g --install-links github:jevcomp/jevcomp`, unpinned from a 0-star, 8-day-old repo. dist/ is committed, so the shipped JS may differ from src/, and there is no dependency lockfile. It has no runtime dependencies, which is a plus. The plugin path (claude plugin marketplace add jevcomp/jevcomp) also runs committed dist/ JS.

Spawns a detached, long-lived local HTTP server (dashboard). It binds only 127.0.0.1, checks the Host header, and has a token plus Origin check on POST. GET /api/history and /api/stats are unauthenticated to any local process.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs go into Jev state. compact.ts:33 tells Jev that tool outputs are untrusted. Worst case, injected text tricks Jev into dropping or keeping evidence, so it degrades context rather than executing anything. Per the brief, injected instructions can move Jev answers.
entries.dataEgress: To https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions only, on each compaction: the last 3 user messages (as goal, up to 500 chars each), the full history of user/assistant text, and tool call names, inputs (truncated) and result previews (80-420 chars). All of it is regex-redacted and capped at about 24k state tokens and 30k request tokens, in batches with up to 4 requests in parallel. Because pinned recent messages and older assistant text are included, client code, file paths and command outputs will leave the machine, and the regex redaction is incomplete. Nothing goes to TypeSafe or anywhere else if the OpenRouter provider is chosen. History and metrics are stored locally in ~/.jevcomp/history.jsonl.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design and tested. Any error in cli.js, a key or network failure, a timeout (20s per request, 1 retry, 300s outer), a state too large for Jev, a reduction under 15%, or a conversation with fewer than 2 messages returns {apply:false}, and hooks/claude.js calls next(e) for native compaction. The function-hook module also catches all errors. A worst case is a delayed compaction of up to about 20-40s. Jev misjudging (overconfidence, label swap) could drop a tool result that was still needed. Protection against that is only the 0.5 loss threshold, the 6 pinned recent messages, and the fact that user messages are never touched. It fails quietly toward less-informed context. No fail-closed risk to tool execution.
entries.contextCost: Adds no MCP tools. The SKILL.md description is about 190 chars (about 50 tokens) against a listing budget of 0.02, so negligible. The SessionStart hook only emits a short systemMessage, and it stays silent when everything is configured. It injects no additionalContext. Compaction output is verbatim conversation minus dropped or shortened tool results, and it removes the summary request. The saving is real but only when compaction triggers.
pros: Native OpenRouter support with correct endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, Bearer key, x-openrouter-title header and model/url env overrides (provider.ts:24-25,126-133,198-202). Key via stdin, env or plugin sensitive userConfig, never argv.

Genuinely safe failure mode: every failure path returns to native compaction (hooks/claude.js, claude-compact.ts, cli.ts:294-300). User messages are never removed, recent 6 messages are pinned, and outputs are only kept, shortened or dropped when Jev risk is below 0.5. The prompt tells Jev tool outputs are untrusted data.

Uses Jev well as a typed-decision engine (Noul questions per tool call with criteria), batched and budgeted, with zero third-party runtime dependencies and 2000+ lines of tests using a fake Jev (tests/claude.test.mjs covers registration, settings edit, and cut application).
Fully automatic once installed: no need to prompt 'use jev'. It also saves the summary request, and dropped commands are re-runnable. Dashboard and local audit give observability of what was cut.
cons: Depends on unverified early-access Claude Code function hooks (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, session.compact, $.process.run). I found no confirmation in Claude Code 2.1.285 docs, since web search was rate-limited. If it is unsupported or changes, the value is zero. The plugin also auto-edits ~/.claude/settings.json without consent (hooks.ts:75-91).

Sends transcript content (user and assistant text, tool inputs and result previews) to OpenRouter's alpha endpoint (no SLA). That is client data for a user with client projects, protected only by an incomplete regex redaction. It needs a client-consent decision.

Value is narrow for this user: it only affects compaction and never helps decide permissions, routing or risk. With a subscription login there is no per-token saving, and Opus 5.5 context loss from Jev's overconfident pruning is a quality risk that is hard to detect (irreproducible outputs, e.g. one-off test failures).

Supply-chain and hygiene issues: brand-new repo (created 2026-09-22, 0 stars, 69 commits in 8 days, one author), committed dist/ with no lockfile, unpinned GitHub npm install, a persistent detached dashboard server on a fixed port, and about 560 KB of code (58 KB dashboard.ts) for what is a small idea. Codex and Antigravity code is dead weight for this user.

Stale SKILL.md contradicts the code (mentions Codex PreCompact/PostCompact hooks that were removed), and the default model alias '~typesafe/jev-latest' is unpinned so Jev version drift can change cut behavior silently. When both keys exist TypeSafe is preferred unless JEVCOMP_PROVIDER=openrouter is set.
entries.verdict: Well-built, fail-open, OpenRouter-native compaction pruner, but a narrow use of Jev that rides an unverified early-access function-hook API. It sends redacted transcript data to an alpha endpoint and edits settings.json on its own. Worth a look only if you can confirm function hooks exist in 2.1.285 and accept client data going to OpenRouter. Not a general 'Jev when it adds value' integration.

judge.why: An automatic compaction pruner built as a plugin function hook that spawns a Node CLI. Its failure paths are fail-open and tested (15 test files). It has too much side-effect baggage for what it does.
pros: Fails open to native compaction on every error; 20 s per-request timeout and 1 retry; user messages never removed and the last 6 pinned
Zero runtime dependencies; OpenRouter endpoint and key handling are correct (key over stdin, not argv)
cons: SessionStart hook edits ~/.claude/settings.json without asking (re-serialises the whole file) and spawns a detached dashboard server on 127.0.0.1:43127
Needs the unverified function-hooks flag; unpinned GitHub npm install; committed dist/ with no lockfile; 0 stars, 8 days old; Codex and Antigravity code is dead weight for you
Redaction is regex-only; the default model alias ~typesafe/jev-latest is unpinned; TypeSafe is preferred over OpenRouter when both keys exist

It has a local no-network ruleset classifier (40 ms), so it can run with no Jev at all. It has the strongest safety design for pruning: deterministic protections and a snapshot before compaction.

entries.name: tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction
entries.what: Claude Code function-hook plugin (early-access, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, types generated from CC 2.1.274) plus an npm-style library. It hooks session.compact: pairs tool_use/tool_result, sends Jev the whole conversation as state (tool results replaced by "ok, N chars (omitted)"), asks two noul questions per non-pinned call (keep call? keep result verbatim?), and drops/truncates tool calls/results below keepThreshold 0.5. It replaces the built-in LLM summary with the original messages minus stale tool calls. A second hook, turn.complete, auto-triggers $.session.compact() when context reaches 60%. It falls back to the built-in summary on any error or if reduction is under 25%.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: session.compact (manual /compact and auto-compaction) and turn.complete (proactive compaction at 60% context). No prompting is needed, and it is fully automatic once installed. It needs the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS flag.
security: No shell execution, no child_process, no postinstall, no telemetry, no curl|sh installer (grep finds none in src/ and hooks/). Only network egress is via host $.http.fetch to the configured URL.

Plugin sandbox per types/claude-code.d.ts:21: no fs, network or exec of its own, and everything goes through the host. This limits blast radius, but the function-hooks API is early access and can change.

API key is sent as an Authorization Bearer header inside the host fetch, so it is not in argv or the process list. The apiKey plugin option is marked sensitive: true. But the hook also reads $.settings.read() env (hooks/fast-jev.ts:236-243) to fetch the key. The key would live in ~/.claude/settings.json env, and that env is also exported to every Bash tool call, so the existing secret-leak hook should watch for it.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns only numeric noul probabilities and the parser rejects anything else (request.ts:96-122). But adversarial text in the transcript could steer the score, so an injected page could cause a tool result about a constraint or instruction to be dropped. Dropped results are irreversible within that session context (the original messages are replaced).

Integrity risk: it deletes tool calls and results with only a probabilistic 0.5 threshold. There is no user confirmation. Truncated results keep 300 chars plus a note. Context loss can cause silent regressions such as forgotten error details or file contents, though the assistant can re-read files.

Repo is 13 days old with 17 AI-authored commits and 7.2k stars in a day; a supply-chain risk for a plugin that runs in-process on every compaction. Pin a commit and audit before install (and re-audit any update: marketplace add tracks the default branch).
entries.dataEgress: On each compaction, one or more requests (the full state is resent per request) go to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. The state contains: all user and assistant text (long ones abridged to 400 head + 150 tail chars, pinned messages likely full), the goal (last 3 user prompts), and each tool call's name and input (Bash commands, file paths, Edit/Write inputs and grep patterns, truncated to 1000, then 200, then 60 chars). Tool RESULT contents are NOT sent (only 'ok, N chars (omitted)', src/state.ts header + README step 2). So file contents read via Read/Bash output are not sent, but Bash commands (may contain inline secrets or tokens), paths, client project names, and pasted prompts are. That matters for client projects: the data goes to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if patched), with no redaction. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover this channel.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for correctness: any Jev error, HTTP failure, malformed JSON, missing key or non-fitting state throws, and the hook catches it and calls next(event) to use Claude Code's built-in summary (hooks/fast-jev.ts:283-289). There is no explicit timeout or AbortSignal anywhere in the repo (grep for timeout/AbortSignal finds only the toast timeout), so a hung request depends on the host $.http.fetch default and could stall the compaction. turn.complete errors are swallowed. The hook is not on the per-tool path, so a Jev outage does not block coding.
entries.contextCost: None added: no MCP tools, no skills and no hook-injected text into the model context (it is a function hook, not a prompt injection). A toast and a ui.log decisions line appear only in the UI. The plugin actually reduces context: compaction keeps the original messages minus stale tool calls/results instead of an LLM summary, and it triggers at 60% context (versus the default of about 90% or so). Side effect: the pruned history is likely larger than a summary, so it may compact more often. Its hidden cost is cache invalidation on rebuilt messages.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks session.compact and turn.complete, so the user never prompts for Jev (hooks/fast-jev.ts:263, 292).
Uses Jev for what it is designed for: typed noul yes/no probabilities with no free text (src/request.ts noulAnswer), and it maps well onto Jev's calibrated decisions.
Fail-open design: any error, missing key or low reduction falls back to Claude Code's built-in summary (fast-jev.ts:283-289), so it cannot block work.
Zero context-token overhead, no MCP tool definitions, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry; runs in the CC function-hook sandbox with network only via the host fetch.
Tool RESULT contents are never sent to Jev (only length notes), which limits egress of source code and file contents.
Compaction is verbatim: user and assistant text is kept unmodified, so there is no lossy summary, and it compacts at 60% instead of near the limit.
Has a library baseUrl option (request.ts:60,67), so retargeting to OpenRouter is a small patch; MIT license; the tests mock Jev so the logic is covered.
cons: No OpenRouter support: hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; the hook does not even pass baseUrl (fast-jev.ts:94,171), so OpenRouter use requires a fork or local patch, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema compatibility is unverified (docs pages 404, not in llms.txt).

Depends on the early-access, unstable CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS feature; types were generated from CC 2.1.274 and the user runs 2.1.285, so behavior on the current version is untested and may break on any release.
Only helps at compaction time (rare in a day of coding, and the user runs Opus 5.5 with a large window). It does not give Jev a role in routing, permission decisions, or code review.

Irreversible probabilistic deletion at 0.5 threshold with no confirmation; context loss can silently drop constraints or error detail, and prompt-injected tool text can bias which calls get dropped. Jev claims (per Theo) may just be a fast flash router, and no benchmark of compaction quality is in the repo.

Sends prompts, assistant text and Bash commands and file paths (inputs up to 1000 chars) of client projects to a third party with no redaction, every compaction, up to N times per compaction (state is resent for each request).

Immature and hype-driven: 13 days old, 30 commits (17 by Devin AI), no CI, no release, version mismatch (0.2.0 vs 0.3.0), an unrelated macOS SwiftUI demo bundled, no timeout on the fetch, and a 7.2k-star/463-fork count reached in one day.

May conflict with the user's existing setup: replaces built-in compaction wholesale, does not interact with the GitNexus and secret-guard hooks, and the sensitive key would need to sit in settings.json env, which is exposed to Bash subprocesses.
entries.verdict: The only candidate that is fully automatic (deterministic session.compact and turn.complete hooks, zero context cost, fail-open), but it is narrow, not OpenRouter-ready without a patch, and built on an early-access feature and an untested 13-day-old repo. Worth a pinned, audited fork (baseUrl plus OPENROUTER_API_KEY plus typesafe/jev-latest) as an optional experiment for compaction only, not as the main Jev integration.

judge.why: The original Devin-assisted plugin (session.compact and turn.complete at 60%) that most of this category forks. It has the highest star count, but the star count does not transfer to the forks. It is TypeSafe-only as shipped, so it is only a reference implementation for this user.
pros: The reference design: pruning at compaction, fail-open, zero context cost, about 464 forks
Unit and hook tests present
cons: No OpenRouter support without a patch; TypeSafe-only key
Early-access hooks; idle since 2026-09-18; replaces a good Opus summary with destructive pruning

entries.name: fast-compact (nodardavituri)
entries.what: Claude Code function-hooks plugin (TypeScript, no deps) registering /fc and /fast-compact. On invocation it schedules the built-in /compact with a "[fast-compact] <focus>" marker (hooks/fast-compact.ts:88,155-160) and answers that compaction from a session.compact hook. The hook plans which old tool outputs (>~1950 chars, older than the newest 10 calls) to cut, asks Jev one Noul question per output ("will the assistant need something from this again?") via POST to /api/v1/systemone, keeps the top-ranked ones whole (max 25% of old chars, score >= 0.45), and cuts the rest to 1000 head + 500 tail chars. Full originals are saved first to ~/.claude/fast-compact/<session>/ and the cut is then applied. Long old tool inputs and host notices are also trimmed. No tool call is ever deleted. It does not touch built-in /compact or auto-compaction (session.compact only acts on marker-prefixed manual/plugin triggers, hooks/fast-compact.ts:176-178).
entries.autoInvocation: Manual only. The user must type /fc; nothing triggers it on context thresholds. The design (marker-based /compact scheduling) exists specifically to leave built-in auto-compaction alone. It does not meet the user's 'automatic use' goal. Making it automatic would need a separate mechanism, e.g. a Stop/UserPromptSubmit hook that nags to run /fc, or a fork that hooks the auto trigger, and the code deliberately passes auto triggers through (hooks/fast-compact.ts:174-178).
security: No shell exec, child_process, eval or process.env use anywhere in src/ or hooks/ (grep clean); runs in Claude Code's sandboxed function-hook environment using $.http, $.fs, $.env, $.settings.

Key handling: Bearer key in an HTTPS header via host $.http.fetch, never argv. But the hook can read arbitrary env by literal name and reads the whole settings.json (`$.settings.read()['env']`, hooks/fast-compact.ts:199) to find the key; it only extracts OPENROUTER_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The plugin apiKey option is marked sensitive (stored by Claude Code securely).

Secret masking (src/redact.ts) is regex-only (sk-/ghp_/AKIA/JWT/Bearer/PEM/NAME=value URLs). The author calls it a safety net, not a guarantee. It would miss free-form secrets, client-confidential source, or business data.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs (samples of first 200 + last 100 chars, plus one-line notes) and conversation text go into Jev's state. The injection could only shift Noul scores, i.e. change which outputs stay whole. Impact is bounded to what is cut or kept, because the full text is archived and Claude is told where to read it. It is not a tool-execution vector.

Unsalted local archive: full cut outputs (which may contain secrets that the redactor did not mask) are written in plaintext to ~/.claude/fast-compact/<session>/ with no auto-cleanup. File names are sanitised to [A-Za-z0-9._-] (hooks/fast-compact.ts:243).
Hidden effect: resumeSafe (default on) drops hidden reasoning and image-only messages. Unknown behavior on CC 2.1.285 because it was built and tested on 2.1.283 against an early-access API.
entries.dataEgress: On each /fc run only, to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai): the user's and Claude's messages (long ones abridged to ~400 head + 150 tail chars), shortened tool inputs, a one-line note per tool output, and with sendSamples (default true) the first 200 + last 100 chars of each output being ranked, plus a 'goal' (last user request) and optional focus. Regex-masked for credentials first (src/redact.ts). State is bounded around 32k tokens (src/jev.ts:21). Nothing is sent unless the user types /fc, and nothing is sent when there is no key. Client-project code and conversation snippets would go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which matters for client work. No data goes to the author.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe, and better than most: Jev timeout is 6 s per request and is capped by the hook's 10 s budget minus a 2.5 s reserve (hooks/fast-compact.ts:101-104,210-211). 2 retries with backoff on 429/5xx/transport (src/jev.ts:158,172,196). Any Jev error or missing key falls back to keeping the newest outputs whole (decide() catches; jevSkipped is reported). Any hook exception returns {skip}, so it never triggers the slow built-in summary. If the archive write fails, that item is not cut. Because it acts only on its own marker, a plugin failure cannot affect normal /compact or auto-compaction. A risk: the function-hooks module load failure is silent in the TUI (CLAUDE.md), and the feature is early-access.
entries.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server and no tool definitions, no SKILL.md, so the skill listing budget is unaffected, and no hook-injected additionalContext. It adds two slash-command descriptions (about 60 tokens). It only reduces context when run: the example shows 103k to 81k chars (-21%), and cut markers of about 200 chars replace the middles. The compaction leaves a '/compact [fast-compact]' line in the transcript.
pros: OpenRouter is the native default provider (src/jev.ts:14, hooks/fast-compact.ts:38), with the key read from env, plugin option or the settings.json env block. No patching is needed, and a key held in the settings env block works.

Safest failure design of any Jev integration seen: 6 s cap, retries, fallback to newest-kept, and {skip} on any error. It never falls to the slow summary and never touches built-in /compact or auto-compact.

Non-destructive: every cut is written to disk first, with a marker telling Claude the path, tool calls are never deleted, and an item whose archive write fails is left uncut. Directly fixes the failure mode of the upstream fast-jev-compaction project.
Zero context cost, with no MCP tools, no skill or hook injected text, and no per-tool-call latency. It suits the user's low skillListingBudget.

Real evidence: a 122-moment, 59-session replay bench (bench/RESULTS.md) with CIs, with per-run cost reporting; 4 test files (core spec plus plugin host tests, about 48 tests); credential-shaped strings are masked before send.
cons: Manual only (/fc), so it violates the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told. Auto-compaction is deliberately not intercepted, and the user gets no benefit on the long unattended auto/bypass sessions where compaction actually happens.

Depends on an early-access, undocumented function-hooks API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, tested only on CC 2.1.283, user on 2.1.285). Silent load failure, and it runs the built-in /compact with a marker as a hack (README Limits). It may break on any update.

Marginal measured value: bench shows Jev-keeps-whole 75% needed-usable vs 73% for just keeping the newest and 69% for head_tail at the same size. Jev adds only about 2 points over a no-Jev rule, which is within the confidence intervals (RESULTS.md), and only 48% of history is cuttable. Author says the measurements come from one person's sessions.

Sends conversation text and 300-char output samples to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on each run, with only regex masking, which is a concern for client projects. The full-text archive holds unmasked outputs in plaintext under ~/.claude/fast-compact/ indefinitely. OPENROUTER_API_KEY would need to be added to the settings.json env block (and to no-secret-leak.cjs protected vars), and the hook itself reads settings.json env.

Very young and unproven: created 2026-09-26, 5 stars, no release, 37 commits (shared with a forked history), and a 'Devin AI' co-author. The default model 'jev-latest' is unverified against OpenRouter; use 'jev-1.13'. It only shrinks tool output and does not summarise the conversation, so it complements rather than replaces /compact, and resumeSafe drops thinking blocks and image-only messages.
entries.verdict: Well engineered, safe on failure, and OpenRouter-native, but it is a manual /fc command built on an early-access function-hooks API, and its measured benefit over a simple keep-the-newest rule is only about 2 points. It fails the user's core 'automatic, never prompt' requirement, so it is a niche optional tool rather than a daily integration. Try it only if manual pruning of tool output is wanted, and set model=jev-1.13.

judge.why: A manual /fc command that trims old tool outputs and archives full originals to disk first. It is the best-engineered fail-safe design in the group. It fails the 'automatic' requirement by design and leaves auto-compaction alone.
pros: Non-destructive: originals are archived before any cut and no tool call is ever deleted; 6 s cap, retries, fallback to keeping the newest outputs, and {skip} on any error
A replay bench (122 moments, 59 sessions) with CIs; zero context cost
cons: Manual only (/fc), so no benefit on unattended auto or bypass sessions where compaction actually happens
Measured gain over keeping the newest is about 2 points, within CI; needs the flag and was tested on 2.1.283 only
Archive of unmasked outputs stays in plaintext under ~/.claude/fast-compact/ with no cleanup; 1 day old, 5 stars

entries.name: Kevthetech143/super-jev
entries.what: A third-party "decision-to-action harness" built on TypeSafe Jev (single-maintainer, created 2026-09-17). It is mostly a retrieval/memory layer for agents: Python skills (ask.py, dispatch.py, superjev.py) and Node 24 TS CLIs (navigate, permit, sweep, fetch, skill-search, catalog) that use Jev as a yes/no and which-one judge over connected local folders. It caches user-approved answers. It also ships three EXAMPLE Claude Code hooks (Stop claim gate, PostToolUse Agent-report verify, UserPromptSubmit teammate-report verify) that you copy into settings.json by hand. There is no MCP server, no plugin.json and no marketplace.json. The install path is manual (clone, setup.py, symlink skills into ~/.claude/skills) or `curl | bash` install.sh for a "superjev" terminal chat CLI. It is a knowledge-base/claim-checking product, not a general coding accelerator.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. The Stop hook (if the user pastes the snippet into settings.json) is deterministic and automatic, but it only judges the finished reply for unsupported claims. It is the sole real "Claude Code uses Jev without prompting" element. Everything else (ask, check, permit, skill-search) is a skill triggered by description at model discretion, or a manual CLI. The docs give a "retrieval rule card" to paste into CLAUDE.md to make the model prefer ask/skill-search. No PreToolUse/permit hook is shipped, so the permit gate is not automatic.
security: No API key in argv: key is read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (docs suggest export TYPESAFE_API_KEY="$(cat file)") and sent only as an Authorization header. There is a key-provider file option for hooks.
Key exfil guard: the URL override is refused unless it is the same host as the profile or loopback (lib/jev_client.py _key_may_go_to; src/jev.ts:206). Redirects are disabled (_NoRedirect).

Outbound secret scan: every request is scanned (payload_has_secret) and refused with SecretBlocked before sending. This is a heuristic, not a guarantee, and it is separate from and additional to your own secret-leak hook.

install.sh is a curl|bash installer that clones the repo's default branch and runs `npm install --omit=dev` (only 2 deps: @clack/prompts, picocolors). It has no pinned commit or checksum, so you trust the moving `main` branch. Do not use it. Read-only cloning and manual symlinking is the safer path.

The stop hook parses the model's own last message and tool outputs, so it processes untrusted tool-result content (prompt-injection surface) and feeds it to a classifier that can BLOCK a turn. Blocking requires confidence >= 0.80 and no stop_hook_active.
Shell execution: the verify path runs git, gh and test commands DERIVED from a worker report's text (run twice); this is a command-injection style surface if the report is attacker-influenced.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (not OpenRouter, as shipped): with the Stop hook enabled, EVERY turn end sends the assistant's final reply text plus the content of the last ~8 tool results (file reads, grep and bash output, diffs), up to about 8000 judge tokens, along with the user's last prompt when no tools ran. Secret-scan heuristics filter some of it. With ask/connect: the text of connected files (to describe and check them), descriptions and questions. With check: the claim plus the evidence files. The README states this. On a client project this means code and client data leave to a third party on every turn, which is outside any client-confidentiality boundary unless authorized.
entries.failureMode: The Stop gate mostly fails open: a missing SUPERJEV_GATE_CMD is a no-op, a budget overrun (default SUPERJEV_GATE_BUDGET_S=15s, timeout 90s) prints "budget exceeded, not judged" and exits 3 (advisory), and a Jev error is a typed error with no verdict (not a pass, not a block). It FAILS CLOSED in one case: a confident (>=0.80) NOT_SUPPORTED/CONTRADICTED/REJECT verdict returns exit 2 and forces Claude to continue the turn. With Jev's calibration only measured on the TypeSafe model, and false-positive misfires documented in the code comments (HAS_LEAKS on plain notes), this can annoy in daily coding. A stop_hook_active loop guard exists. Client retries on 429/529 (4 attempts, 1s doubling) can add multi-second delays. In bypass mode the blocking is the only friction.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 MCP tool definitions and 0 server instructions. Skills: super-jev SKILL.md is ~22 KB (~5.5k tokens), loaded in full when the skill triggers. The frontmatter description is about 300 chars (~75 tokens) always resident, plus skill-search (5.5 KB) and super-jev-connect (12 KB) if linked. The Stop hook injects at most one advisory line, or a block reason, into the transcript, so it is negligible normally. The lookup protocol pushes every question through ask.py and Python output with OUTCOME lines, which costs tokens per use. The SKILL.md prose is extremely dense and hard for a model to follow.
pros: Only candidate here with a real, documented Claude Code hook integration (Stop hook that reads last_assistant_message and transcript_path per the actual hooks payload, honors stop_hook_active to avoid loops, fail-open budgets). It is the one place Jev fires automatically with no user prompt.

Serious hardening for a 2-week-old repo: outbound secret scan before every request, API key locked to same-host or loopback (lib/jev_client.py), no redirects, typed errors so a failure is never reported as a pass, and pinned GitHub Action SHAs.
Judge is abstracted behind judge_profiles.json (typesafe-jev + local laya), so adding an OpenRouter profile is a small JSON edit rather than a rewrite. The Node twin reads the same table.

Large test surface: about 107 Python tests in skills/super-jev/tests, about 45 Node tests, CI on Node 24 plus pytest, gitleaks config and a scorecard workflow. MIT licensed, 275 commits, a release v1.0.12, 113 tags, active daily pushes.
Honest maturity table and 'what 1.0 does not do' in the README, and data-egress documented in a 'What this tool touches' section.
cons: No OpenRouter support. The URL override refuses anything except api.typesafe.ai or loopback, so the user's OpenRouter key and endpoint cannot be used without patching judge_profiles.json and keeping a fork. The calibrated thresholds (0.8/0.9) are measured for TypeSafe direct only, and OpenRouter's alpha endpoint may differ.

Wrong problem domain. It is a document-retrieval, cache and claim-verification system for agent 'brains' (connect folders, approve answers, principals, pointers, ledgers), not a coding router. Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives are used for 'which file answers this?' and 'does this text support this claim?', not for coding decisions such as model routing, permission decisions or test selection. Setup burden is high (setup.py, connect, prepare_bulk, principals, state dir).

Egress risk on client work: the recommended Stop hook ships the final reply plus recent tool outputs (code, diffs, file contents) to a third-party API every turn. It is heuristic secret scanning only, and it duplicates what the user's secret-leak hook guards against.

Can block. Stop-hook exit 2 forces extra turns on a confident NOT_SUPPORTED, and the source itself documents false positives (HAS_LEAKS/SELF_CONTRADICTORY misfires in hand tests 2026-09-24). On a coding session 'tests pass' claims need a trace and the gate derives evidence only from the last 8 tool results, so long sessions get judged on partial evidence.

Two of the three hooks depend on an external 'worker-verify' tool that is NOT in the repo (SUPERJEV_VERIFY_CMD), and the PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit hooks target multi-agent team workflows the user does not run. The permit gate (the only coding-relevant primitive) has no hook wiring.

Complexity and churn: superjev.py is about 10k lines, docs are dense internal changelog prose, SKILL.md is 22 KB, package.json version 1.0.6 vs release v1.0.12, 203 of 275 commits by one author (72 more by 'admin'), age 13 days. It is a one-team daily driver made public, with no plugin manifest or marketplace entry. install.sh is curl|bash from a moving branch. Sole live evidence for Jev is one recorded call on 2026-09-17 (test/fixtures/live-score-2026-09-17.json).
entries.verdict: Not recommended as the integration. It is a genuine, well-tested Jev harness, but it targets agent knowledge retrieval and claim verification, hard-locks TypeSafe direct (OpenRouter needs a forked profile), and its only automatic Claude Code piece is a Stop-hook claim gate that ships every turn's replies and tool outputs to a third party and can block turns. Treat it as a reference for a fail-open Stop hook and for keeping the key on the same host, and borrow those ideas rather than installing it.

entries.name: romiluz13/jevmory
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also stdio MCP server + CLI) providing per-project agent memory. A SessionEnd hook ingests transcripts into a local SQLite store (secrets regex-redacted). Sentence candidates are extracted, and only after an explicit per-project opt-in (jevmory init --enable-grading, TYPESAFE_API_KEY) are they graded by Jev via the /v1/systemone endpoint (Choice/Noul/Score questions: durability, category, significance, support, contradiction). A SessionStart hook injects up to 12 top verbatim facts into context. Three read-only MCP tools (status/recall/fact) search the local store. `jevmory audit MEMORY.md` grades memory-file lines as VERIFIED/STALE/WRONG/UNSUPPORTED. It is a memory tool that uses Jev as a judge, not a general "decision at the point of coding" integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. Deterministic hooks: SessionStart auto-injects facts, SessionEnd auto-ingests (both need no prompting). MCP tools recall/status/fact are model-discretion, nudged by server instructions ('Call recall before re-deriving project conventions'). Jev grading itself is NOT automatic: requires manual `jevmory distill`/`audit` runs after opt-in; no hook calls Jev.
security: No shell exec of untrusted input found in hooks; commands are fixed python3 -m jevmory.* with PYTHONPATH set from CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT
API key read only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY and sent as Bearer header via urllib (client.py); not passed in argv, so not visible in process list
No telemetry, no curl|sh, no postinstall (stdlib-only, no build deps at runtime)
Hooks always exit 0 (never-die contract) and log errors to ~/.jevmory/hooks/*.jsonl

Secret redaction at rest is regex-based (sk-*, AWS, GitHub tokens, JWT, PEM, password=/token=, high-entropy) and best-effort; docs/PRIVACY.md admits paths, hostnames, names stay in quotes that are sent to the API. Relevant for client projects

Prompt-injection surface: SessionStart hook re-injects stored verbatim quotes from past sessions (user prompts and assistant text; tool_result skipped per claude.py docstring) into fresh context as plain text; a poisoned or misgraded quote could steer a future session, though sources are limited to the user's own and the assistant's statements
entries.dataEgress: Default plugin install: nothing leaves the machine (hooks and MCP are local, MCP is read-only). Only when a project is opted in (init --enable-grading) AND TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set, distill/audit send to api.typesafe.ai redacted candidate quotes (<=600 chars), verbatim context (<=800 chars) and the project name; never whole transcripts, file contents, diffs or tool outputs per PRIVACY.md. Quotes can contain non-secret paths/hostnames/names. distill/audit are manual CLI calls, not triggered by hooks.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: hooks catch all exceptions and exit 0; recall stays silent on any error; client raises typed errors (401/422/transport fail fast, 429/529 retry with 1/2/4s backoff x3 then give up) and callers leave candidates queued. Per-request timeout 30s (thresholds.py:60); hook timeouts 15s (SessionStart) and 60s (SessionEnd) in hooks.json. Jev latency is irrelevant to interactive turns because grading is offline/manual and off the hot path.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools (status, recall, fact): roughly 350-450 tokens for names, descriptions and schemas (about 1.4-1.8k chars), plus server 'instructions' string (~330 chars, ~80 tokens). SessionStart hook injects up to 12 fact lines (~600-1500 tokens per session, only when the store is non-empty). Slash command file adds nothing until invoked. Total roughly 0.5k tokens fixed plus up to ~1.5k per session.
pros: Genuinely plug-and-play Claude Code plugin with valid hooks.json/.mcp.json/plugin.json and a marketplace entry (README claims validate --strict; I read manifests, did not run)
Zero runtime deps, stdlib-only, no install scripts, no telemetry: small audit surface (~2k lines in top-level modules, readable in minutes)
Fail-open by construction: hooks always exit 0, recall silent on error, Jev out of the interactive path, so no latency or availability risk to daily coding

Jev is used for a sensible System One task (calibrated grading of candidate facts with Noul/Choice/Score) and client already parses the exact /v1/systemone {state, model, questions} envelope, which matches the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone path
Default install egresses nothing; grading is per-project opt-in with documented, capped payload (<=600+800 chars) and honest privacy caveats
Client is injectable with endpoint/model args, so pointing at OpenRouter is a ~10-line patch
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (cli.py:138-141); needs fork/patch of a vendored plugin, and OpenRouter parity of envelope/model IDs is unverified

Jev is NOT called automatically: no hook triggers distill/audit; without manual CLI runs the plugin is just a local transcript-to-FTS store and never uses Jev, failing the user's 'Claude must use Jev when needed' goal
Solves agent memory, not coding decisions: it does not use Jev for routing, permission classification, commit/PR gating, test selection or similar per-action decisions where System One adds value
Very young and single-author: 11 days old, 27 commits, 1 contributor, 11 stars, 0 issues; 'Development Status: Beta' claims not battle-tested

Overlaps with Claude Code's built-in CLAUDE.md/auto-memory and the user's existing hooks; adds another SessionStart injector alongside GitNexus/caveman, and adds a plaintext store of all sessions (client code discussion) under ~/.jevmory
Recall injects stored verbatim quotes as context every session, a persistent prompt-injection/poisoning vector and possible stale-fact noise; the redactor misses paths/hostnames of client projects
Memory quality depends on unverified Jev grading; Theo's 'flash router' skepticism about Jev applies, and no benchmark of value over plain FTS is provided beyond a self-authored planted-truth fixture
entries.verdict: A tidy, safe, fail-open memory plugin that only uses Jev in an opt-in, manual, TypeSafe-direct-only grading step, so it does not deliver automatic OpenRouter Jev in Claude Code. Consider it only as a reference for the /v1/systemone client and question shapes, or as an optional low-priority memory add-on after patching the endpoint to OpenRouter.

entries.name: carryforward (Dharundp6/jev-carryforward)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (MCP server + skill + SessionStart hook) that keeps a per-project append-only JSONL ledger (~/.carryforward/<project>.jsonl) of constraints, corrections, decisions, measurements and parked threads. On recall(task), Jev scores each non-pinned entry with a boolean question (P that the entry is still live for the task); >=0.60 is injected in full, 0.30-0.60 as one line, below is omitted. It is a session-memory relevance filter, not a coding-assist router. Jev is used only for scoring ledger entries.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. Deterministic: SessionStart hook (startup|clear|compact) auto-injects pinned rules and unscored one-line entries without the model, but without Jev. Model-discretion: recall/record MCP tools plus skill description trigger. The author's own eval found the agent called recall 0 of 4 times even with tools and skill present, so the Jev-scoring path is not reliably auto-invoked. Not a transparent proxy.
security: Ledger is plaintext, unencrypted, at ~/.carryforward/<slug>.jsonl (slug = cwd basename + sha1 prefix); if the model records a secret it persists (SECURITY.md warns)
Key passed via `claude mcp add -e AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=...` lives in ~/.claude.json, not in argv of the server; hook uses npx with inherited env, no key in argv

`npx -y carryforward` runs unpinned latest npm code at every session start (hook) and MCP launch; supply-chain risk, single-maintainer npm account; version in plugin.json is 0.1.1 but npm shows only 0.1.0 published at review time, so the plugin/hook may resolve a different version than the repo
No shell execution, no postinstall/preinstall script, no curl|sh, no telemetry found in src/

Prompt-injection surface: recall output (ledger text) is injected into context via hook/tool result; any injected text recorded earlier (record is model-discretion) would be replayed as trusted 'Always' rules
Pinned constraints/corrections never sent to Jev (recall.ts pinned filter); husk is that the model decides what to record
entries.dataEgress: Only `recall` with a non-empty task and AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY set. Sent to Vercel AI Gateway (then TypeSafe Jev): the task sentence plus text/ref/refresh/kind/obtained/date/id of every non-pinned (decision, measurement, thread) entry, in batches of 25 (recall.ts:263-272). Constraints and corrections are never sent. `record` and the SessionStart hook (no task) make no network calls. No source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent automatically, only what the model chose to write into ledger entries (which may include file paths, commands, branch names, PR refs).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. No key, no task, or any scorer exception returns the full ledger with an explanatory note (recall.ts:286-300, 312-319). Entries missing from Jev's answer default to 'inject'. No explicit request timeout is set in gateway.ts, so a hung scorer relies on AI SDK defaults and the MCP client's tool timeout; the hook has a 25s timeout (hooks.json) but does not call Jev. Ledger corruption lines are skipped and counted, never deleted.
entries.contextCost: Low. 2 MCP tools (record, recall); descriptions ~870 + ~600 chars and schemas ~900 chars, roughly 600-700 tokens total; no server-level 'instructions' field. Skill description ~450 chars (~110 tokens) always listed. SessionStart hook injects the brief (empty ledger prints nothing only with --quiet; the plugin hook.json omits --quiet, so it prints 'The ledger is empty' text every start/clear/compact). Ledger size grows unbounded, so hook output grows with all non-pinned entries one line each.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for what a calibrated boolean scorer is good at: ranking ledger entries per task with thresholds exported as constants (recall.ts:245-248)
Excellent fail-open design: every error path returns the whole ledger with a note, so Jev outages never cost information
Hook does the important part deterministically (re-injects rules after compaction) and is honest in the README that the tools alone were not called (0/4 in author's eval)
Small, readable, 2 tools, ~800 lines src, no shell execution or postinstall, MIT, CI on 2 OS x 2 Node versions, pluggable Asker interface makes an OpenRouter scorer a small patch
Pinned constraints/corrections never leave the machine; nothing sent unless a task is given and a key is set
Low context footprint (~700 tokens tools + ~110 skill)
cons: No OpenRouter support: hard-wired to Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, model typesafe-ai/jev, AI SDK experimental_evaluate), so it needs a fork to use the user's OpenRouter key, and the OpenRouter Decisions API schema is not implemented anywhere here

The Jev call happens only in recall(task), which the model must choose to call; the SessionStart hook passes no task so Jev is never used in the only deterministic path. The author's own eval showed recall was not called even with skill installed
Solves cross-session memory, not daily coding decisions; user already has gitnexus graph context, CLAUDE.md and auto memory, so overlap is high and Jev adds little
Very young and tiny (created 2026-09-18, 6 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars), no accuracy evidence (README says only 9 entries x 3 tasks), npm shows only 0.1.0 while repo/plugin is 0.1.1

Depends on the model diligently calling record with well-worded text; ledger is plaintext and could capture secrets or client-project details, replayed as trusted rules in future sessions (injection / client-confidentiality concern across projects sharing the home dir)
`npx -y` unpinned at each session start adds a network-dependent supply-chain hop and cold-start latency on top of the user's existing hooks; hook without --quiet prints 'ledger is empty' noise
Jev is beta and skeptics say it may be a flash-model router, so ranking quality of a 4-line boolean question over free-text notes is unproven
entries.verdict: Well-engineered but tiny alpha memory ledger whose Jev use is confined to model-invoked recall and is hard-wired to Vercel AI Gateway, not OpenRouter. Not a good fit for automatic Jev use in daily coding; useful only as a design reference for a fail-open Jev relevance scorer (the Asker interface could be repointed at OpenRouter's Decisions API in a fork).
