pros: Reversible design: original history intact, /jev off restores; latest 5 tool pairs protected
CI, unit tests, MIT, no runtime deps; branch-aware cache
cons: Pi-only; Claude Code has no context-filter hook, so it is not portable
Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter path
Sends code and tool output to a third party; threshold 0.8 is aggressive and breaks prompt cache

entries.name: Smith2912/jev-context-mcp
entries.what: Local Node MCP server (v0.10.0) built for OpenAI Codex CLI on Windows, not Claude Code. It calls TypeSafe's System One API (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13.0) with Score-type questions to (a) rerank redacted log/file chunks before loading them into context (triage_log, select_file_context), (b) score generated files against criteria (check_file_output), (c) recommend a model/effort/skill/execution profile for a prompt (route_task), and (d) run an optional registered-workflow and Computer Use decision mode. Everything is advisory. A deterministic local fallback works without a key. Extra machinery includes a disk cache, a 6-requests-per-minute limiter, a usage ledger and a native Codex runner.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The descriptions push Claude to call select_file_context before loading large files ('Before loading a large code, document...'), and triage_log before raw logs. Nothing deterministic ships for Claude Code. The shipped hook is a Codex hook for an explicit 'jev: workflow=' prompt prefix. The route_task hook mode has no script, so a user would have to write a wrapper that speaks MCP or reimplement the call.
security: Key handling: TYPESAFE_API_KEY comes from the MCP process env or a Windows DPAPI file. It is not passed on argv, and launch.mjs deletes it from process.env after import. Under Claude Code the key would sit in the .mcp.json env block, or be inherited from the shell.

Data leaves only if the per-call boolean shareWithTypeSafe is true. That is a tool argument the model chooses, so under bypass or auto permission mode nothing stops Claude from setting it to true. The README says redaction is best effort.
Redaction: regex cleanText/redact strips private keys and password/token/apikey/secret JSON fields. It is not a guarantee, and client code and secrets could still be sent.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted passages and prompts go into Jev's 'instructions' fields, with wording that tells the model to treat them as data. The output is typed scores only, so injection impact is limited to biasing rankings. A wrongly low score could hide relevant evidence from Claude.
File reads are confined to allowedRoots and contextRoots from a private settings.json. The shipped example grants no roots, and SHA-256 checks bind ranges to a selection.

launch.mjs can execFileSync python (refresh-catalog.py) and powershell only if configured. The native runner spawns detached Codex processes. No postinstall script, no curl|sh, no telemetry found. The only outbound URL is api.typesafe.ai.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only, and only when shareWithTypeSafe=true and a key is present. Contents: redacted question text plus up to 24 passages of at most 900 characters each (log or file chunks), or the redacted prompt (max 4000 characters) plus skill names and descriptions for route_task, or a file's content for check_file_output. Workflow mode adds compact evidence and observations. Nothing goes to OpenRouter. Local disk holds a cache of validated typed responses only (not requests), a usage ledger and run artifacts.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, and timeouts are bounded. Any provider error, bad schema, oversized response (over 100 KB) or missing key falls back to local-only results, or to {continue:true} for route_task. Timeouts are 6 s for route_task, 20 s for rank and 15 s in the workflow policy. A local limiter allows 6 paid requests per minute, and 429s get 1 retry. If the MCP process fails to start (for example a missing settings.json, which launch.mjs and server.mjs read unconditionally), the tools are simply absent.
entries.contextCost: 10 tools if the workflow mode is enabled, otherwise 6. Tool names, descriptions and schemas together are about 6 KB of source for all 10, so roughly 1.5-2k tokens. With the default 6 tools it is about 1k tokens. There is no server 'instructions' field, and no hook-injected text unless the user builds a hook themselves (route_task adds at most 800 characters of additionalContext).
pros: It uses Jev in the way the brief describes: Score questions over typed criteria, and the response validation is strict (score range, confidence 0-1, size cap). Good reference code for the request and response shape of /v1/systemone.
The select_file_context idea (rerank chunks before they enter context) is a sensible System One use, and a small file skips Jev entirely. The file tools work locally with no key.
Fail-open design with a cache, a 6 requests per minute limiter, per-run token ceilings, a usage ledger and SHA-bound retrieval. Little risk of runaway spend or of blocking the session.
Pinned dependencies, SHA-pinned CI actions, MIT license, an extensive test suite (14 test files), and no postinstall or telemetry. The sharing opt-in is per call.
It has a tiny context footprint in the default mode (6 tools, roughly 1k tokens).
cons: Built for Codex CLI on Windows. The install docs are `codex mcp add` and PowerShell, the DPAPI credential path is Windows-only, and the hook and its output projection target Codex's parser. The native runner is Codex-only. Roughly 10-15 of about 50 files are Codex or Windows specific, so it needs a rework for Claude Code on Linux.

No OpenRouter support. The TypeSafe URL is hardcoded in 3 places, the env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the model 'jev-1.13.0' is checked by strict equality in decision-engine.mjs:25. Switching to OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-1.13, /api/v1/systemone) needs a fork patch, and the schema match is unverified.

The auto-invocation the user wants doesn't exist for Claude Code. It relies on the model deciding to call tools and setting shareWithTypeSafe=true. The route_task hook mode has no script, and the native-global-hook only fires on the explicit prefix 'jev: workflow='.

It leans on a narrow pipeline: rerank files or logs, route models. route_task recommends models that Claude Code cannot switch mid-task, and its tier table and skills come from a local catalog that is empty in the tracked template. The docs are DayZ-flavored (triage_log is for .rpt logs). The value for general daily coding is small.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-25, 4 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 2 contributors (Smith2912 and a second identity 'The Songsmith'). CI runs on Windows plus one Linux test file (remediation.test.mjs) only. Treat it as alpha.

Client-code privacy risk: the sharing flag is a model-controlled argument, and redaction is regex-based best effort. In bypass or auto mode Claude can send file chunks to a third party without a prompt. The prompt-injection surface goes into Jev instructions, though the effect is limited to biasing rankings.
Dense minified single-line code style makes it hard to audit or maintain a fork.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this user as is. It is a Codex/Windows advisory toolkit hardwired to api.typesafe.ai, with no Claude Code hook and no OpenRouter path. Its request and response handling for the System One Score primitive is useful reference code to crib from if you build a Claude Code hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: raj8525/universal-jev
entries.what: Hand-rolled Node (zero-dependency) stdio MCP server plus CLI and a Codex-only PostToolUse hook that use Jev decisions to (a) 'dehydrate' long command output into a 'verified receipt' (jev_receipt), (b) compact conversation transcripts (jev_compact), (c) expose raw Choice/Noul/Score primitives, (d) an LLM 'guard' for shell commands. Also contains an unrelated Ego browser-automation engine. Not a Claude Code plugin: no plugin.json, no hooks.json, no SKILL.md, no .mcp.json. Despite the 'hooks' label in the candidate summary, the only hook (bin/codex-hook.js) targets OpenAI Codex.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only, for Claude Code. Nothing forces Claude to call them; tool descriptions are generic ('Fast, calibrated multi-option classification...') and do not tell the model when to use them, so it will rarely or inconsistently call them and never on its own with the output it already received. The only deterministic component (codex-hook.js, PostToolUse output rewriting) is Codex-only and not wired for Claude Code; Claude Code hooks can only rewrite MCP tool output via updatedMCPToolOutput, so it could not rewrite built-in Bash results anyway (my understanding of Claude Code's hook API, not verified here). Not a transparent proxy, no skill triggers.
security: API key sent as Authorization Bearer header via fetch; key is read from env or plaintext JSON config files, never put in argv (good). Caveat: keys placed via 'claude mcp add -e' land in ~/.claude.json in plaintext.

Data-exfil surface is the core function: the receipt path sends the head 1000 + tail 1500 chars plus an error anchor of arbitrary command output (and the command string) to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe/upstream). Hook has NO secret redaction. It would ship .env dumps, tokens in logs, client code snippets from test output to OpenRouter. Conflicts with the user's existing secret-leak guard hook and client-project confidentiality. jev_guard sends the full command + context; jev_decide_* send whatever state the model passes.

Correctness/safety risk: a 4 s-budget probabilistic classifier decides whether to DELETE tool output from the context. 'success' + P(error)<0.15 replaces the entire output with the last 4 lines. Warnings, skipped tests, or deprecation notices in the middle of a long run can be lost. Exit-code path is deterministic but the Claude Code Bash tool result has no reliable exit-code field for the hook to use (regex on trailing text only).

Prompt-injection: command output is passed as Jev 'state' and instructions strings; a malicious log line could push the classifier toward 'success' and hide errors. Jev is typed-output so no text injection into the agent, but suppression of real errors is possible. Receipt text itself is generated locally (last 4 lines) and returned to the agent.
No shell execution in the MCP path (no child_process in mcp-server/receipt/client). Only bin/ego-browse.js spawns a hardcoded macOS path.

install.sh: no curl|sh, no npm postinstall. But it does 'git pull --ff-only' from origin on every run (auto-running unreviewed upstream code, symlinked so a later git pull silently changes executed code), appends to ~/.codex/config.toml and edits other agents' JSON configs, and creates ~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json and ~/.agents/mcp.json even if those agents are not installed. Single anonymous author, 0 stars, created 12 days ago: high supply-chain risk for client work.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions) or api.typesafe.ai: for jev_receipt/hook, tool name, command string, output length/lines, first 1000 + last 1500 chars of output, and up to ~1200 chars of a mid-output error anchor; for jev_decide_*, whatever 'state' string the model chooses (could be code, diffs, file contents); for jev_guard, the full shell command plus context; for jev_compact, likely tool-result and message text from the transcript (compactor decides per tool result). No redaction step anywhere. Local: telemetry.json with command prefixes.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design in the receipt path: on API error/timeout receipt.js:238-253 falls back to mechanical head/tail truncation with error isolation (which still deletes output, silently 'Fallback Mode'). Codex hook catches all errors and emits '{}' (passthrough). Timeouts: default 15000 ms per request (client.js:56); the receipt code passes {timeout:4000} (receipt.js:186) but JevClient.decide ignores options.timeout (client.js:141-142 only reads options.model), so the effective budget is 15 s, and with two keys primary+fallback can stack to 30 s per tool call. Missing key: JevClient constructor throws (client.js:80) -> MCP tool call returns isError text. MCP server itself starts fine without a key since client is lazy. jev_guard is fail-closed only in the sense that it throws; it is advisory, not enforcing.
entries.contextCost: 7 MCP tools. Tool defs in bin/mcp-server.js lines 18-125 are about 3.6k chars, roughly 900 tokens (plus Claude Code's mcp__jev__ name prefix). No server 'instructions' field returned by initialize (mcp-server.js:220-231). No hook-injected text in Claude Code, since no Claude Code hook exists. jev_compact and jev_receipt are the costly ones in practice: the model must pass the entire raw output/transcript as a tool ARGUMENT, meaning the tokens are already spent in context (output was read, then re-emitted as output tokens) before any 'savings', so it increases rather than decreases token use.
pros: Only candidate seen so far where OpenRouter is a first-class, coded provider: src/client.js:5-6 uses https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest and works with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY (client.js:59).
Small and auditable: ~3.1k lines total, zero npm dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no child_process in the MCP path; one afternoon to fully review.
Clean generic primitives (jev_decide_choice/noul/score) in src/primitives.js that map directly onto Jev's Choice/Noul/Score API, usable as a reference for building your own thin MCP.

Thoughtful protections in the receipt path: diff/patch and source-code immunity (compactor.js isProtectedCall), non-zero exit-code fast path with zero API calls, mid-output error anchor sampling, passthrough under 1200 chars.
Fail-open error handling in receipt path and hook; MCP key is lazy so server starts without a key and does not break Claude Code startup.
MIT license, local-only telemetry, key never in argv.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: install.sh configures OpenCode, Codex, Antigravity and Pi only; the single hook (bin/codex-hook.js) is Codex-format and unregistered for Claude Code. The README's Claude Code support is one line saying 'connect via MCP'. You would get 7 tools the model may never call, i.e. fails the user's core requirement of automatic use.

Wrong use of Jev for coding: main value proposition is 'prune command output' (receipt) and 'compact history' (jev_compact), which duplicates caveman-shrink / Claude Code's own compaction, and via MCP requires the model to re-send the whole log as an argument, costing more tokens, not fewer. No Jev-based code decision (e.g. routing, permission triage, commit-message or test-failure classification) is provided.
Lossy and unsafe by design: a classifier decides 'success' and the whole output is replaced by 4 lines; fallback mode silently truncates on any API failure. Risky for debugging on client projects.
Sends command output to a third party with no redaction, contradicting the user's secret-leak-guard setup and client-confidentiality constraints.
Timeout bug: JevClient.decide ignores options.timeout (client.js:141-142), so the advertised 4 s budget in receipt.js:186 is really 15 s (up to 30 s with fallback).
jev_guard is advisory, not a hook; it cannot block anything, and is redundant with your PreToolUse guards. It also adds an LLM round trip for a task where deterministic checks are better.

Ships unrelated and broken code: browser engine hardcoded to /Users/yangyu/.local/bin/ego-browser (bin/ego-browse.js:53), Pi extension, Chinese/English mixed README with marketing claims ('95%+ token savings', '100% transparency') and no benchmarks; 'Codex (GPT-6)' claims suggest the README is largely AI-generated.

Very immature and single-author: 14 commits over 1 day (2026-09-18 to 09-19), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, not on npm, tests need live keys. install.sh auto git-pulls and symlinks, so upstream changes execute unreviewed.

Request schema (state string + questions map) is the author's own; I could not confirm it matches OpenRouter's documented Decisions API, and the TypeSafe URL (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) is not in the brief.
entries.verdict: Not recommended: it is a 1-day-old, single-author Codex/OpenCode-oriented package with no Claude Code hook or skill, so nothing would invoke Jev automatically, and its headline feature (LLM-based output pruning without redaction) is risky and token-negative via MCP. At most, mine src/client.js (OpenRouter Decisions call) and primitives.js as a reference for writing your own minimal MCP plus a Claude Code PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook.

entries.name: ctxjev (ctxjev-mcp + ctxjev-claude plugin)
entries.what: Monorepo (ctxjev-core, ctxjev-cli, ctxjev-mcp, plus a Claude Code plugin "ctxjev-claude") that uses Jev only for one job: asking a "noul" question per history entry ("is this still relevant to state.goal?") to rank or prune agent context. The MCP server exposes score_relevance and prune_history. Both take history entries as tool arguments, so Claude would have to write its own history into the call. The Claude Code plugin is a separate, hook-based piece. It scores the transcript at PreCompact (offline keyword overlap by default, Jev only if CTXJEV_SCORER=jev) and re-injects the top few entries at SessionStart(compact). The README itself says Jev did not beat plain truncation on held-out tasks.
entries.autoInvocation: Two different things. (1) ctxjev-mcp is a model-discretion MCP tool. Claude would have to decide by itself to serialize history into arguments for score_relevance, and nothing in the tool descriptions or server instructions prompts it to. The README itself says this does not save tokens in Claude Code. In practice it will almost never fire automatically. (2) The bundled plugin is a deterministic hook (PreCompact and SessionStart compact), which runs automatically, but only around compaction events, and it is offline (keyword overlap) unless the user sets CTXJEV_SCORER=jev. It is not a per-edit or per-tool-call integration.
security: MIT license. Repo created 2026-09-21, so it is 9 days old at the audit date; 234 commits at depth 200. Contributors are x96x64 (84), 'Claude' (124), 'Re:COO' (24) and dependabot. In practice it is a single maintainer with a heavily AI-authored history. 0 stars, 0 forks.

npm ctxjev-mcp: 22 versions in 9 days (0.1.0 to 0.7.1), published by GitHub Actions via npm OIDC (trusted publishing). Dependencies are only zod, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and ctxjev-core, which in turn pulls @typesafe-ai/sdk. I found no postinstall, preinstall or install scripts in package.json. The MCP package has no curl|sh installer.

The API key comes from an env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and is never passed in argv. The .mcp.json variants use ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} expansion. The SDK sends it as a Bearer header and redacts headers in debug logs (redactHeaders).

Secret masking: packages/core/src/redact.ts (redactSecrets) masks common key formats, passwords in URLs, private keys, JWTs, card numbers and values of API_KEY/SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD-like names. It runs in jevClient.ts buildJevRequest on goal, content and toolName, and entry ids are replaced with e0, e1. The README calls it best-effort. There are blind-corpus dev/holdout redaction tests, which is unusual diligence, but any masking is still not exhaustive.

Prompt-injection surface: with the MCP tools, Claude sends entries as tool arguments, and the results are numeric scores only (JSON), so the injection risk is low. The plugin's SessionStart digest re-injects verbatim excerpts of past tool output into context, which is a small replay-of-untrusted-content surface. The sessionStart output and the skills explicitly say to treat the content as data.

Shell execution: the plugin hooks run only bundled node scripts (dist/*.js committed to git, with CI checking that the bundle matches src). The cache in ~/.claude/ctxjev/ holds session excerpts, mode private to the user, with the 50 most recent sessions kept. No telemetry found beyond the Jev call; the SDK adds X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers.
entries.dataEgress: MCP path: nothing leaves the machine unless a tool call uses scorer 'jev', and that is the default for the tools. Then the goal (max 2000 chars) and each entry (role, toolName, content up to 4000 chars each, up to 500 entries, secrets masked best-effort) go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter as the System One `state`. Because Claude must supply the entries itself as tool arguments, the data sent is only what Claude chooses to pass, and it also costs Claude output tokens. Plugin path: no egress by default. With CTXJEV_SCORER=jev plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY, every compaction sends excerpts of the whole transcript since the last compaction: user messages, assistant replies, and tool calls with their outputs (file contents, command output), goal included. For client projects this is a real confidentiality issue on top of the OpenRouter/Jev provider chain.
entries.failureMode: The MCP server starts without a key (index.ts:216) and returns an isError result telling Claude to use scorer 'local' when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is missing (server.ts:15-27). It fails open at the connection level, but a Jev call error simply surfaces as a tool error, and the SDK default timeout is 10s with retries on 408/429/5xx. The plugin is fail-open by design: PreCompact always exits 0, uses a 20s Jev deadline inside a 25s hook timeout, and falls back to offline keyword scoring. The UserPromptSubmit hook swallows all errors. Nothing here blocks the user's prompt.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 2 tools (score_relevance, prune_history). Descriptions plus zod-derived JSON schemas (entries array with 6 fields, scorer enum, thresholds, with .describe text) come to about 1.2-1.8k tokens (estimated as chars/4 from server.ts and schemas.ts, about 3.8KB of schema source). I did not read any server 'instructions' field; the McpServer is created without one. Plugin: no per-turn injected text except after a compaction, when the SessionStart digest of about 5 entries is added. Two skills have short descriptions (set-goal is a model-invocable skill; status is disable-model-invocation). The UserPromptSubmit hook adds one node process start (roughly 30-60 ms, estimated, not measured) to every prompt.
pros: It is the only candidate so far with a real, working design for a hook-based automatic path in Claude Code (PreCompact plus SessionStart compact). It fails open: it always exits 0, has a 20s deadline, and falls back to offline scoring.

Honest, evidence-based README. The author preregistered a holdout eval and reports that Jev did not beat plain truncation (0 points, CI [0,0]) and kept less than a random ordering on the secondary measure. It is rare for a project to say this, so the claims can be trusted more than most.

Good hygiene: npm OIDC trusted publishing, pinned action SHAs, no install scripts, key kept in env and not in argv, secret redaction with blind-corpus tests, private cache in ~/.claude/ctxjev, and an offline default that sends nothing.

OpenRouter reroute looks near-trivial on paper: the SDK builds `${TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone` with a Bearer key, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and the OpenRouter key is put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY (unverified; the model id may also need a change).
cons: The MCP server cannot be invoked automatically in a useful way: it needs Claude to copy history into tool arguments, costing output tokens, and the README admits it saves nothing in Claude Code. There is no instruction or hook that makes Claude call it.

The Jev use case is context pruning/scoring for compaction, not coding decisions, and its own eval says Jev ranking adds nothing over truncation or keyword overlap. The plugin therefore defaults to offline, so the automatic part does not use Jev at all unless CTXJEV_SCORER=jev is set.

With Jev enabled in the plugin, excerpts of every session (user messages, assistant replies and tool outputs including file contents) go to a third party at each compaction. Redaction is best-effort only, which is risky for client projects.

No OpenRouter support in code; it needs an untested env-var trick and possibly a model-id change; only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is checked in the MCP server, so an OpenRouter key would have to be placed in a variable named for TypeSafe. The default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id.

Very young (9 days), 22 npm releases in 9 days, 0 stars, effectively one maintainer with a mostly AI-authored history, and the audit documents are in Japanese. It could conflict with the user's existing compaction handling (caveman plugin hooks) and adds a PreCompact/SessionStart injection of replayed tool output.
entries.verdict: Not a fit for the goal of Jev used automatically during daily coding. The MCP tools are model-discretion and will not be called on their own, and the deterministic plugin only touches compaction, is offline by default, and its own eval shows Jev does not help there. Skip it, or at most consider the offline plugin for compaction, which has nothing to do with Jev or OpenRouter.

entries.name: @turnprune/core (TurnPrune)
entries.what: Agent-neutral library that, once per user turn, sends the previous turn's tool outputs to Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via the OpenRouter Decisions API, one Noul question per output: "is this needed for the current request?") and replaces outputs with relevance below 0.4 by a fixed placeholder to cut context cost and preserve the prompt-cache prefix. The only shipped adapter is for OpenCode 2 (@turnprune/opencode). The Claude Code adapter is only listed as "planned" in docs/architecture.md and the README. So the core is not usable in Claude Code today.
interface: Config: enabled/TURNPRUNE_ENABLED, timeoutMs/TURNPRUNE_TIMEOUT_MS (500-5000, default 1500), pricingFile, diagnostic
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent in-process context hook, fully automatic in OpenCode 2 (no user prompting). For Claude Code there is no integration. The only route would be a custom local proxy pointed to by ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL that rewrites /v1/messages bodies with the core. That is not built, and the user's subscription/OAuth login makes a base-URL proxy awkward.
security: MIT license (LICENSE present).
API key from env var only, sent as Bearer header over HTTPS. Not in argv, so not visible in the process list.
No runtime dependencies in core. opencode package depends only on @turnprune/core. No postinstall/preinstall scripts (grep of package.json files).
No child_process, exec or telemetry found in packages/*/src.

Secret handling: regex redaction (private keys, api_key/token/password=..., Bearer, sk-/ghp_/github_pat_, AKIA) and a sensitive-path blocklist (.env, .npmrc, id_rsa, *.pem, ~/.aws, ~/.ssh) that pins such tool work and never sends it. Pattern-based only, so secrets in unusual formats can still leak.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output content (untrusted file/log/web text) is embedded in the Jev request as candidate.content. Jev returns only numeric probabilities, so injection can at worst bias a keep/drop decision. It cannot execute anything. A drop can hide needed context from the main model, though.
entries.dataEgress: Per README Privacy section and selector.ts: to openrouter.ai only, the candidate tool outputs (redacted, capped 20,000 chars each, up to 60 per batch, 200 kB, 20 batches), the user's current message (redacted, capped) used as current_request and active_goal, and the repository path. Anything matching secret patterns or credential-file paths is not sent. This means source code, logs and test output from client projects go to OpenRouter and Jev on every user turn. That may conflict with client confidentiality terms. The main model provider still gets the whole context.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. The Jev call has a 1500 ms timeout (configurable 500-5000). Missing key, HTTP error, timeout or invalid answer means the context goes out unchanged, or with the already-frozen prefix. The tool loop adds about 1 ms and makes no Jev call. Once per user turn the hook blocks for the Jev round trip (README: p95 0.9-1.6 s). Under context pressure (80% of window) it re-judges on every request.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool or MCP context cost, because it is not an MCP server or skill (no tool defs, no server instructions, no hook-injected text). Its effect is the opposite: it removes stale tool outputs from the prompt. It replaces them with a 95-character placeholder. But this only works where the host allows rewriting the message list before each model request (OpenCode's context hook). Claude Code has no equivalent hook today (PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit can add context or block, but cannot rewrite prior tool_result content already in the transcript). So even a Claude Code adapter would need an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy in front of the API.
pros: Real, working use of Jev on OpenRouter: the correct endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions), a correct noul request shape, the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var, and typesafe/jev-1.13 (selector.ts:7-8, 227-233). It is a useful reference for the request format.

Well-thought-out safety design: fail-open on every error, 1.5 s hard timeout, secret redaction plus credential-file pinning before anything is sent, a kill switch, content-free state storage, no runtime dependencies and no postinstall.
Cache-aware policy (prune only behind the cached prefix, reuse in tool loops, cost check before refresh) and a reproducible metric replay. This is more careful than a naive context trimmer.
Honest README with measured numbers: about -21% billed cost on a 200k-token session, and an explicit warning that short sessions can cost more.
CI on ubuntu Node 22 and 24, macOS and Windows; about 1,400 lines of tests (core.test.ts, pruner.test.ts, stats.test.ts, plugin.test.ts, cli.test.ts). Jev cost is about $0.004 per session.
cons: No Claude Code adapter exists. docs/architecture.md says 'Claude Code / Codex: planned', and no Claude Code file, hook config, plugin.json or .mcp.json exists in the repo (grep for 'claude' returns only planning text). It cannot be installed into Claude Code today.

Claude Code has no context-rewrite hook. Integrating would need an ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy that mutates /v1/messages requests. That is a new project, it conflicts with subscription/OAuth login, it breaks prompt-cache assumptions if done wrong, and it is risky for client work.

Mutating the transcript changes what Opus sees. Jev only sees the new user message, so a short 'ok continue' can drop something needed later. The README admits this, and the cost is extra tool re-runs.
Sends tool outputs (source code, logs) and the repo path to OpenRouter every user turn. Redaction is regex-based and could miss secrets, and it may not be acceptable for client projects.

Savings claims come from a single OpenCode session on cheap models (glm-5.3-flash, gpt-5.6-luna) with 16 prompts. Claude with an already-efficient cache and auto-compaction may see much less benefit. Added latency of about 1 s per turn.

Very immature: created 2026-09-25, 12 commits by one author in 2 days, npm 0.1.0 to 0.1.3 published within 4 hours on 2026-09-26, 0 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases. It targets the alpha Decisions endpoint, which may change.
It solves a narrow problem (pruning old tool output). It is not a general Jev integration for routing, permission decisions or code-review classification.
entries.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code: only an OpenCode adapter ships, the Claude Code adapter is unbuilt, and Claude Code offers no hook to rewrite prior tool results without a custom API proxy. Treat it as a well-engineered reference for the OpenRouter noul request shape, fail-open design and secret redaction, not as something to install.

entries.name: Takamasa045/ctxfilter-jev
entries.what: A personal, Mac/Codex-specific proof-of-concept that adds an MCP server (Python stdio, one tool classify_records). It reads an allowlisted local JSONL file, extracts bounded excerpts via a separate ctxfilter tool, and sends them to a locally cached jev-mcp@0.4.0 process (tool jev_ask) to label each record relevant, irrelevant or needs_context for a given goal. It does not talk to Jev over HTTP itself. The README says it is not a distributable package and does not work after a plain clone.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills, plugin manifest or proxy. The description says it is opt-in and that ordinary literal search should use ctxfilter without Jev, so Claude would rarely pick it. Its input is a JSONL file path that must be allowlisted, which is not a normal coding-loop input.
security: Design is security-conscious: allowlist keyed on path plus hash, default deny, byte/time/record bounds, excerpts capped at 240 to 400 chars, a fixed untrusted-evidence notice, and secret env stripping for the child process (strip_secret_env).
Launcher is pinned to a cached jev-mcp dist and its sha256 is recorded (provenance.py:60-70). The key is read from a file, not argv, and the code only checks file existence.
The Jev child is spawned as a subprocess with a list argv (no shell), start_new_session=True and stderr discarded. Spawn is bounded by a 20 s timeout and a process-group kill.
Fetched JSONL record text goes into the Jev state, so there is a prompt-injection surface. It is mitigated, since Jev returns typed choices, but it is not eliminated.

No LICENSE, hardcoded /Users/takamasa paths, no npm postinstall and no curl|sh installer, no telemetry seen. The registration scripts rewrite ~/.codex/config.toml, which is invasive for a foreign environment.
entries.dataEgress: Only for allowlisted JSONL files: excerpts (default 240 chars each, max 400) of up to 8 to 16 records, plus the goal (max 400 chars) and up to 4 criteria rules (200 chars each), sent as a state payload of at most 64 KB via jev-mcp to TypeSafe. The tool does not transmit source code, diffs or general tool outputs. Nothing leaves without an allowlist entry, and the README says the goal and rules need separate approval.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe and defer. Timeout (default 25 s runtime, 20 s Jev), malformed reply, transport error, provenance mismatch or file change during the call all yield a deferred or error result, never a false negative. In Claude Code the tool would simply return an error and Claude carries on. It never blocks like a hook. However, when the launcher check fails (the case on every machine except the author's Mac), Jev is never called at all.
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (classify_records). The description is about 1,000 chars and the schema about 1,600 chars, so roughly 650 to 700 tokens. No server instructions are set that I saw, and no hooks inject text. The optional AGENTS-block.md is Codex-only (about 150 tokens if copied).
pros: Careful, well-bounded design for sending untrusted local data to an external inference call: allowlist by hash, size limits, defers on uncertainty instead of guessing negative.

Uses Jev's typed Choice-style answer (relevant, irrelevant, needs_context) with a confidence threshold (ACT_ABOVE 0.8, REVIEW_ABOVE 0.5) as a gate. This is a reasonable pattern to copy for log triage.
Has a mock-based test suite and written verification and rollback docs.
Small footprint of one tool and about 700 tokens if it were ever registered.
cons: Does not work outside the author's Mac: hardcoded /Users/takamasa paths, /opt/homebrew python3.14, an npx cache hash directory, and a sibling ctxfilter repo that is not included. The README states it does not run after a clone.
No OpenRouter support anywhere. It delegates to jev-mcp@0.4.0 and a ~/.config/typesafe/key file, so it is TypeSafe-direct at best. Porting means a rewrite.
Codex-oriented: registration edits ~/.codex/config.toml, and there is no Claude Code .mcp.json, hook, skill or plugin.
Use case is narrow (classifying records in an allowlisted JSONL file) and needs manual allowlist-add steps per file, so Claude Code would not use it in normal coding work.
No automatic invocation is possible: only a model-discretion MCP tool. It fits the user's stated goal of automatic use poorly.
No license, 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no CI, 10 days old. Depends on an unmaintained-looking jev-mcp@0.4.0 pin.
Every call spawns a Python process and then a Node child, which adds latency.
The README is in Japanese, and the design docs are largely AI-generated Codex and Grok artifacts.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this user: it is a Mac-and-Codex-specific proof of concept that wraps the third-party jev-mcp@0.4.0 for JSONL relevance filtering, with no OpenRouter path, no license and no Claude Code integration. Its allowlist and bounded-excerpt pattern is worth reading as a design reference for safely calling Jev, but do not install it.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; licenseInfo is null, so all rights reserved by default)

entries.name: DihRJ/claude-code-jev-compaction
entries.what: Guide plus LiteLLM config: gateway between Claude Code and Anthropic API where a Jev guardrail drops stale tool results before they reach the main model. Requires API billing, not subscription.
entries.autoInvocation: proxy
pros: Honest warning that the setup moves the session off Pro/Max subscription to per-token API billing
Cuts whole tool results all-or-nothing (no paraphrase), so kept context stays auditable
cons: Incompatible with this user's OAuth subscription login (needs ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN/BASE_URL); would raise cost and break prompt caching
Only docs and a config example, no tests; TypeSafe key only; Portuguese primary

entries.name: FrancoisChastel/jev-code
entries.what: Node/TypeScript MCP stdio server (npm @french-castle/jev-code@0.3.0, launched via npx) exposing 5 tools (jev_classify, jev_check, jev_score, jev_rank, jev_ask) over POST {base}/v1/systemone, plus a bundled Agent Skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) whose description tells the model when to reach for Jev. Also ships a CLI (setup/doctor/classify/...), Pi and OpenCode adapters, and works as a Claude Code plugin marketplace (plugin.json + .mcp.json + skills/). Tools batch many items into one request and post-process probabilities into local auto/review and yes/no/uncertain decisions with tunable thresholds.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion. The MCP tools sit in the tool list and the /jev skill has a long description with explicit triggers ('labelling or routing many items', 'yes/no checks', 'ranking candidates', 'prefer over eyeballing, regex, one frontier-model call per item') plus MCP server instructions and per-tool descriptions written as 'use instead of X' nudges. There is no deterministic hook, so Opus 5.5 decides; it will fire on batch-triage-shaped tasks (CI failures, many files, issue labelling) but never automatically on ordinary edits, and Opus may often judge it can do the classification itself. README's own example still prompts explicitly ('Triage the failing tests...'). For a stronger guarantee the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or their own hooks.
security: No postinstall/preinstall/prepare scripts in package.json; only prepublishOnly. Runtime deps are just @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod (small surface).
Runtime server makes exactly one outbound HTTPS POST per tool call to the host the key belongs to; never reads files, git state or session on its own (SECURITY.md, client.ts). No telemetry found.

Key routing guard: key sent only to the host matching its prefix; a mismatched TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is refused; custom proxy needs JEV_CODE_PROVIDER for non-TypeSafe keys (config.ts:292-303). Good design.

Key exposure: `setup` copies the key into `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-...` (src/setup/index.ts:329,296) so the key appears in argv (visible in ps for the moment the child runs) and is stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. Redaction is applied to printed output only (index.ts:311-318). Avoid by using the plugin route + shell-exported env, or --no-env.

Tool results are JSON of numbers/labels computed locally from the model's typed answer; no free text from Jev returns, so Jev itself is a weak prompt-injection channel. Class labels/ids echoed back come from the agent's own input. Injection-into-Jev risk (untrusted text making it label wrongly) exists but consequences are limited to bad decisions; skill says keep destructive actions behind confirmation.

Tools annotated readOnlyHint/idempotentHint but openWorldHint true (server.ts:46); with bypass permissions they run without prompts, so any content the agent chooses to classify (code, diffs, logs, possibly secrets) is sent to OpenRouter -> TypeSafe with no gating.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model puts in tool arguments (items[].text up to 4000 chars each, state/diff/log excerpts, class/question text, candidate excerpts; up to ~120k chars per request, src/core/limits.ts) is POSTed to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with Bearer key plus HTTP-Referer/X-Title attribution headers (identifies the app as jev-code to OpenRouter). Passes through OpenRouter to TypeSafe. Nothing is read from the repo, session or files automatically; no telemetry. Note the skill actively encourages sending raw diffs, logs and file excerpts, which for client projects means client code leaves the machine via two third parties (OpenRouter, TypeSafe); check client NDAs and OpenRouter data policy settings.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: client errors are caught and returned as an MCP isError text result "jev_x failed: ..." (server.ts:52-57), so the agent just continues and falls back to its own reasoning; no hook blocks anything. Client is lazy: a missing key surfaces as a tool error, not a server crash (server.ts:32-37), but an MCP server that fails to start (e.g. npx offline on first run) just leaves the tools absent. Default per-attempt timeout 30 s with 2 retries on 408/425/429/5xx/timeouts and exponential backoff (500 ms to 8 s, honours Retry-After capped at 30 s) (client.ts:30-33,99-103), so worst case a single tool call can stall ~90+ s before failing (tune JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES=0/1 for interactive use). Local input validation rejects oversized requests before spending a call.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools always present in the tool list (deferred loading via ToolSearch may reduce this in Claude Code 2.1.x). Estimate from source: tool descriptions ~550-800 chars each (~3.3k chars) plus zod-derived JSON schemas for 5 tools (src/tools/schemas.ts 6.8k chars plus per-tool schema code; generated JSON schema with descriptions likely 8-12k chars) -> roughly 3,000-4,500 tokens for tool defs. MCP server 'instructions' = USAGE_GUIDANCE, 6 sentences ~1.2k chars (~300 tokens), injected into system prompt every session (server.ts:30). Skill: name + ~1,000-char description always in the skill listing (~250-300 tokens); full SKILL.md (~7.5k chars, ~1.9k tokens) loads only when triggered, references on demand. No hook-injected text (no hooks). Total steady-state overhead about 3.5-5k tokens/session.
pros: Native OpenRouter support verified in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY / sk-or- prefix auto-routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (providers.ts:42-55, client.ts:27,93), no patching needed, and the correct System One surface is used.

Best-fit packaging for the 'automatic, no prompting' goal among file-based options: MCP tools plus a skill whose description is written as concrete triggers, plus server-level instructions and 'use X instead of Y' tool guidelines; installs as a Claude Code plugin marketplace (single command, auto-updatable) or `claude mcp add`.
Zero hook overhead: no latency on normal turns, and no interference with existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, GitNexus graph hooks or caveman hooks (none installed).
Thoughtful key safety: key never sent to a host that didn't issue it, proxy override rules, masked logging, backups of edited configs, no shell in setup, no postinstall script.

Well-designed local policy layer: batching (64 items/250 candidates per request), local input validation and size budget before spending a call, thresholded auto/review decisions, any_relevant on rank so a top hit isn't mistaken for an answer; fail-open errors returned as tool results.
Tools annotated readOnlyHint/idempotentHint, sensible for permission modes; retries with Retry-After honoured; version-pinned npx launch.
Large test suite with CI across Node 20/22/24, npm provenance, active same-day releases, responsive single maintainer; MIT license; Node 24 on user's machine is supported.
Jev's use cases (CI failure triage, rank candidate files, verify PR claims, injection screening of fetched pages) map to real coding-agent chores; cost ~$0.04/M input tokens is negligible.
cons: Not truly automatic: purely model-discretion (skill/tool description). No hook, so Opus 5.5 will frequently just do the triage/ranking itself; auto-invocation will be inconsistent and only for batch-shaped tasks. True guarantee needs extra CLAUDE.md rules or custom hooks.

Very young and single-maintainer: repo created 2026-09-19, npm package created 2026-09-27 with only 2 versions, 23 commits, 1 human contributor, 32 stars, unofficial and unaffiliated with TypeSafe. API/tool shapes may churn (0.x).

Key handling in setup: passes key via `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` (argv briefly visible; stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json). Plugin route avoids this but then the key must be in the environment Claude Code inherits; whether Claude Code forwards that env var to the plugin MCP process was not verified (README itself warns some harnesses filter env).
Sends raw code/diffs/logs to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no confirmation under bypass permission mode; relevant for client projects under NDA. Skill actively encourages passing raw evidence.

Sends bare model alias 'jev-latest' to OpenRouter rather than documented IDs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest; unverified live here. Easy override via TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL but a possible first-run 400.
Default failure timing is generous (30 s x 3 attempts) so a degraded Jev could stall a turn ~90 s; should set JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES.

Context tax of ~3.5-5k tokens/session (5 tool schemas + server instructions + long skill description) for tools that may fire rarely; jev_rank/jev_ask overlap with GitNexus/grep for code search, and skeptic claim that Jev is 'a flash router' means classification quality is unproven on code.
Jev is classification only (no free text), so value in daily coding is narrow (triage, gating, ranking); it does not replace any editing/reasoning workflow.
Uses npx at each MCP start: needs network/cache; cold start latency and supply-chain exposure to npm for a young package.

No npm provenance attestation exists on either published version, and the publish appears to be manual from a laptop. Combined with `npx -y` on a 3-day-old single-maintainer package that receives the user's OpenRouter key, this is a real supply-chain concern. Mitigation: pin 0.3.0 (already the default) and read the tarball diff before bumping.

The plugin .mcp.json uses bare `npx` and no env block. It is fragile with the user's overridden PATH, and the key must reach the MCP process by inheritance. There is no `${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}` expansion in the shipped config. The user will probably need a hand-written .mcp.json entry with an absolute npx path and an env block that references the variable, not a literal key.

Under bypassPermissions (and probably auto), the tools carry readOnlyHint=true and openWorldHint=true, and they send arbitrary agent-chosen content to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe with no gate. The skill and USAGE_GUIDANCE push the agent to 'pass raw evidence' such as diffs, logs and pages. Client-project code can leave the machine without any prompt, and the user's no-secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not inspect MCP tool arguments (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). A secret read earlier in the session can therefore be forwarded in a jev_check state.

The OpenRouter Jev endpoint is /api/v1/systemone and the brief calls /alpha experimental with no SLA. An outage returns tool errors that the agent must handle. The tools are non-blocking for other work, but a 30 s x 3 default can stall a turn for about 90 s or more. The user must set the env vars.

Independent evals show Jev is overconfident on unanswerable inputs and that injected instructions in state can move its answers. jev_check on untrusted content, which the skill recommends for injection screening, is therefore a weak guard. The audit mentions the injection channel but not that the recommended screening use case is itself attackable.

The SKILL.md description is ~1000 chars. With the user's skillListingBudgetFraction of 0.02 it may be truncated in the listing, which weakens the skill's own auto-trigger. No evidence this was tested.
entries.verdict: Best-packaged and most complete option for using OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code: native OpenRouter routing, MCP tools plus a trigger-rich skill, no hooks, fail-open behavior, good tests. Its limits are that invocation is model-discretion only (not deterministic), it is a 3-day-old single-maintainer package, and the value is limited to batch-classification chores. Install via the plugin route with OPENROUTER_API_KEY exported in the shell and short timeouts, and add a CLAUDE.md nudge or a small custom hook if you want stricter automatic use.

verification.note: Re-queried facts match the audit: 32 stars, 3 forks, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-19, last push 2026-09-30 (v0.3.0), 23 commits, one human maintainer under two identities plus dependabot, npm versions 0.2.1 and 0.3.0 only. package.json has no install scripts, and the tools and skill exist as listed. Source confirms native OpenRouter routing (baseUrl https://openrouter.ai/api, path /v1/systemone, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, sk-or- prefix, Bearer auth). It is an MCP server plus a skill with no hooks, so use is model-discretion only. The audit's claims about the key-in-argv and plaintext ~/.claude.json exposure, retry/timeout defaults, and single-POST egress are confirmed. Main weaknesses of the audit: (1) it treats 'jev-latest' on OpenRouter as probably fine on the strength of a mocked test, but the repo's own docs say `jev-1.13` for OpenRouter, so the safe move is TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-1.13 and a `doctor --live` check before relying on it; (2) it counts npm provenance as a positive although no attestation exists for either version; (3) it under-weights the bare `npx` and env-inheritance fragility given the user's PATH override, and the ungated egress under bypass mode. Score stays at 7. It is still the best-packaged option, but it fits the 'automatic use' goal only weakly (no deterministic trigger) and is very young and unverified against live OpenRouter.

entries.name: jkudish/jev-mcp (@jkudish/jev-mcp)
entries.what: Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server (optional stateless HTTP mode) wrapping TypeSafe Jev as 12 typed judgment tools: verify claims against evidence, screen text for prompt injection, noul probabilities, find/rerank/classify/decide/compare/extract/audit, plus jev_review (score a diff) and jev_gate (patch review plus completion-claim verification). Ships a companion skills/jev/SKILL.md that tells the agent when to call each tool. Provider is auto-selected from env (TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Vercel, or a compatible endpoint); OpenRouter is a first-class path. Not a proxy or hook: Claude Code only uses it when the model chooses to call a tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. The bundled SKILL.md is aggressive ('Call the matching tool ... even when the answer looks obvious', 'Gate before done') and its description keyword-matches verify/screen/review/gate/extract/rank/classify tasks, so Claude will call jev_screen after WebFetch, jev_review/jev_gate before declaring done, etc. only if the skill is copied to ~/.claude/skills (not auto-installed by the MCP add). Even then it is probabilistic; with Opus 5.5 and 12 tool descriptions in context it will be used inconsistently. Getting real automation requires adding your own hooks (for example a Stop or PostToolUse hook that reminds the model, or a CLAUDE.md line), which the repo does not provide.
security: API key is read from process.env only (src/provider.ts:304) and is never in argv, provided it is injected via env and not `claude mcp add -e` written to ~/.claude.json in plaintext (that stores it on disk).
Client-visible errors are fixed strings (provider and status only) and error bodies are redacted, so a reflecting endpoint cannot leak the key (CHANGELOG 0.6.0, 0.10.0; src/provider.ts:316-324).
Bounded retries (408/409/429/5xx only, no retry on ambiguous network failures), 1 MB response ceiling, whole-request deadline.

No telemetry, no child_process usage in src (grep clean). SECURITY.md states it makes no other network calls than to the configured provider; the only extra header sent to OpenRouter is HTTP-Referer/X-Title identifying jev-mcp.
Only shell-ish surface: jev_extract runs caller-supplied regexes in a node:worker_threads Worker (src/lib.ts:472) as a ReDoS sandbox with timeout; not shell execution.

No npm install scripts in the 43-package lockfile (hasInstallScript count 0); `prepare` builds only on git installs. Runtime deps: @jkudish/jev-agent-tools 0.1.3 (same author, small), @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, MCP SDK, zod. `npx -y` fetches latest of a single-maintainer package on every start unless version is pinned: supply-chain risk, pin @0.11.0.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes as tool arguments leaves the machine, sent to openrouter.ai (POST /api/alpha/decisions) as {model, state, questions}: claims, evidence text, fetched page text for screen, candidate lists, and for jev_review/jev_gate the diff, request text, test output and completion claims. The server never reads files itself (SECURITY.md); egress is entirely model-driven, so the model can send client code or diffs to OpenRouter/TypeSafe if it decides to call review/gate. Per-tool truncation limits exist (e.g. jev_noul 150k chars, rerank 100k chars, decide evidence 12k chars). Your existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__jev__* calls unless its matcher is extended. OpenRouter also sees the key holder identity and content per its own logging policy; check OpenRouter data-policy settings for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level: it is an optional tool call, not a gate. If OpenRouter is down/slow, the tool call errors (fixed string like 'OpenRouter decisions API 503') after up to 3 attempts with jittered backoff within a 60 s whole-request deadline (JEV_MCP_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS default 60000, JEV_MCP_MAX_ATTEMPTS default 3; src/provider.ts:40-42), so a bad outage can stall one tool call up to 60 s; lower the timeout to about 10000 for interactive use. Malformed model answers fail closed per judgment (invalid_response, action review, never a clean pass). Missing/invalid key: configuration error at call time. Nothing blocks Claude Code startup except normal MCP spawn cost (npx cold start).
entries.contextCost: 12 tools. Tool descriptions plus zod schema descriptions I extracted total about 11.3k characters of literal text (about 2.8k tokens); with JSON-schema structure, property names and enums the realistic tool-definition load is about 5-7k tokens if fully loaded (jev_gate, jev_review and jev_decide are the largest, each 2.4-3.1k chars of source schema). No MCP server 'instructions' string (McpServer created with only capabilities, src/index.ts:105). No hook-injected text. The SKILL.md (7.9KB, about 2k tokens) adds only its ~70 token frontmatter description until triggered, then about 2k tokens plus reference/tools.md on demand. Claude Code deferred MCP tool loading (ToolSearch) reduces the upfront cost to names only.
pros: OpenRouter is supported in code with the correct alpha Decisions endpoint and only OPENROUTER_API_KEY needed (src/provider.ts:293-336); no patching required.

Only candidate seen with tools aimed at coding-agent moments: jev_review/jev_gate score a diff and verify 'tests pass' claims against evidence before done, and jev_screen checks fetched pages for prompt injection, which is useful when WebFetch/Playwright ingest untrusted pages.

Ships a real agent skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) with routing policy and per-tool reference, which is the closest thing to automatic invocation in this repo; description triggers on realistic coding-agent tasks.

Careful engineering: strict zod input schemas, per-judgment fail-closed invalid_response, bounded retries/deadline/1MB body cap, redacted errors, regex worker sandbox, static tool list, sizeable mock test suite plus CI.
No install scripts, no telemetry, no shell execution, key never in argv; small dependency tree (43 lockfile packages).
Active and popular: 463 stars, 53 forks, 12 releases in 12 days, contributor PRs merged, responsive changelog; MIT licensed.
No MCP instructions string and only 12 tools, so context cost is moderate, and Claude Code's deferred tool loading lowers it further.
Cheap: about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, so tool calls cost fractions of a cent even at heavy use.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP; the user's requirement of Claude Code using Jev without prompting is only met probabilistically via the skill, and the skill must be installed separately (manual copy).

Jev cannot read code: jev_review/jev_gate require Claude to serialize the diff and evidence into tool arguments, costing Opus output tokens and 1-3 s per call, and it sends client code diffs to OpenRouter/TypeSafe (data egress on client projects, and it bypasses your Bash/Read/Grep-matcher secret guard).

Jev judgments are calibrated probabilities from a small router-like model (Theo's claim unverified); a passing jev_gate is weak evidence and could give false assurance next to real tests; the README itself says 'not infallible' and thresholds are untuned defaults.

OpenRouter path is alpha and adds a hop; on OpenRouter 'jev-latest' is hardcoded to typesafe/jev-1.13 in code (src/provider.ts:296) so it will not follow new releases without JEV_MCP_MODEL; usage tokens are not documented for the Decisions API (falls back to 0), so cost reporting is unreliable.
Silent provider precedence: if TYPESAFE_API_KEY exists in env it wins over OpenRouter; must set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter to be explicit.
OpenRouter key must be provided as sk-or- env var; `claude mcp add -e` stores it plaintext in ~/.claude.json, so use env inheritance or a wrapper instead.
Failure can stall up to 60 s with default retries/timeouts; `npx -y` unpinned means every start trusts the latest publish of a 13-day-old single-maintainer package.

Twelve tools is broad: much of it (classify, rerank, extract, compare, audit, find) is retrieval/data-pipeline oriented and duplicates what Claude, rg and gitnexus already do in daily coding; only about 4 tools (screen, verify, review, gate) matter.
Aggressive skill wording ('even when the answer looks obvious') can make Claude call Jev on every finish, adding latency and cost with low marginal value.

Input caps exceed the 32k-token OpenRouter context. Limits are MAX_GATE_EVIDENCE_CHARS 200,000, MAX_REVIEW_FILES_TOTAL_CHARS 200,000, MAX_NOUL_TOTAL_CHARS 150,000 and MAX_RERANK_TOTAL_CHARS 100,000 chars (roughly 25-50k tokens). A large diff or test log accepted by the schema can be rejected upstream, so review/gate on big patches will error rather than judge (src/lib.ts:177-273).

No tool annotations (readOnlyHint/openWorldHint) are set on any of the 12 tools (grep of src/index.ts is empty). In default permission mode every jev_* call prompts. In auto mode, the classifier may block or ask when Claude ships diffs or evidence to an external service. Users need explicit mcp__jev__* allow rules, which also means the egress is not vetted per call.
Provider precedence is silent: any TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment overrides OpenRouter under JEV_PROVIDER=auto, so data would go to TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter.

The bundled SKILL.md is written for Amp (frontmatter mcpServers/includeTools), so the Claude Code wiring is manual: register the MCP server, copy the skill, extend the no-secret-leak matcher to mcp__jev__*, and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to its protected vars. Nothing in the repo provides hooks, so 'automatic' still depends on the model's discretion.

Dependency chain: runtime relies on two more packages from the same author or vendor (@jkudish/jev-agent-tools 0.1.3, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0), so the effective supply-chain surface is broader than 'single small package'. jev-1.13 is also absent from OpenRouter /api/v1/models (only typesafe/jev-router is listed), so the alpha decisions route is undiscoverable and may change without notice.
entries.verdict: Best-fit ready-made option so far: real, maintained, OpenRouter-native, with a skill and coding-relevant tools (screen, review, gate). It still relies on model discretion (no hooks), so treat it as the base layer: install via env-injected OPENROUTER_API_KEY with JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, pin the npm version, copy the skill globally, and add your own thin Stop or PostToolUse hook if you need deterministic triggering. Restrict or gate jev_review/jev_gate on client repos because diffs leave the machine.

verification.note: Core facts hold up. OpenRouter support is real: src/provider.ts:293-336 POSTs https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY, body {model:'typesafe/jev-1.13', state, questions}, and /v1/systemone is used only by the 'compatible' provider. All 12 tool names exist (src/index.ts registerTool at 168-1863). I found no child_process, eval or new Function in src, and no telemetry. Retries cover only 408/409/429/5xx, the deadline is 60 s, and there are 3 attempts. Repo stats re-queried on 2026-09-30: 463 stars, 53 forks, MIT, not archived, last push 2026-09-29, 78 commits, 2 open issues, npm 0.11.0 with 12 versions in 12 days. The audit's errors are minor (sk-or- gate location, skill install path and Amp-only frontmatter, description token count). The audit understates three points. First, there is no automation: it is model-discretion only. Second, Claude must serialize diffs into tool args, so client code leaves the machine, the existing secret guard does not cover it, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in its protected list. Third, the tools carry no readOnlyHint annotations. Input caps of 100-200k chars also exceed the 32k-token context on OpenRouter. The user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev automatically without prompting) is only probabilistically met, and the project is 13 days old with one maintainer, so I lower the score from 7 to 6.5. It is still the best-fit ready-made candidate.

entries.name: itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp (renamed: itsmostafa/system-one-connector), binary "evaluate"
entries.what: Single static Go binary ("evaluate") that runs as a stdio MCP server exposing ONE tool, `evaluate`. The tool POSTs {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} to Jev and returns the typed JSON (probabilities, confidence). Local extras: criteria validation, stable option ordering, client-side min_confidence abstain (`__uncertain__`), and an `items` fan-out (up to 500 records, 8 concurrent, one billed request each). Also has `setup mcp` (auto-registers with claude/codex/hermes CLIs and Claude Desktop), `setup pi`, `update` (self-update with SHA-256 check) and `version`. Routes: TYPESAFE_API_KEY -> api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (wins if both set), otherwise OPENROUTER_API_KEY -> openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest. The repo was renamed from typesafe-mcp to system-one-connector; the old URL redirects.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The trigger is the tool description (`Use for classification, routing, scoring, extraction, branching, guardrails/judging...`) and the server instructions, which the model reads at session start. Nothing is deterministic: there are no hooks, no skill, and no proxy. Real-world firing in coding sessions is likely rare, because Opus 5.5 can classify or branch inline at no extra cost and there is no cue in normal coding work that says to call Jev. To get reliable automatic use you must add your own steering, for example a CLAUDE.md paragraph or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook that nudges use in defined situations (triaging many issues/logs/files with `items`, gating risky actions with a noul such as `does this diff touch auth/payments`). The user said they do not want to prompt it, so a CLAUDE.md rule is the practical lever.
security: API key handling: `evaluate setup mcp` runs `claude mcp add ... -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<value>` (setup.go:226-232), so the key sits in argv, visible in `ps` and /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the moment setup runs. It is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (user-scope mcpServers.evaluate.env). This is avoidable: register by hand and use `${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}` expansion in .mcp.json or an env-wrapper, so the key is never written to disk by the tool.
At runtime the key is read from the env and sent only as a Bearer header to the fixed OpenRouter URL (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). It is not logged; no `log`/print of the key is visible in the source.
No shell execution at runtime. The only exec.Command calls are in `setup` (claude/codex/hermes CLIs, with fixed args). Nothing runs during normal MCP operation.

Install: README pushes `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | sh`. The script (install.sh, 61 lines) is short and sane: it downloads the release tarball and SHA256SUMS.txt from the same GitHub release, verifies the hash, and installs to ~/.local/bin. The checksum is same-origin, so it does not defend against a compromised release. Safer path for you: `gh release download` and inspect it, or `go install` at a pinned tag and audit the source (about 1.3k lines of non-test Go). I did not run the installer.

Self-update (`evaluate update`) replaces the binary from GitHub releases with the same same-origin checksum. Releases are built by GitHub Actions with pinned action SHAs (release-please.yml), which is good hygiene. There are no signed releases and no provenance attestation.
No npm postinstall (Go binary). Dependencies are minimal: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.7.0, cobra, and their transitive deps.
entries.dataEgress: Everything Claude puts in the tool-call arguments (`state`, `items`, `questions.instructions`/`criteria`, optional `model`) goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your OpenRouter key, and then to TypeSafe's hosted Jev via OpenRouter (or to api.typesafe.ai on the direct route). It is only what the model chooses to send, not automatic capture: no hook reads your files, prompts or diffs. In practice that means code snippets, diffs, error logs, ticket or issue text, and anything else Claude decides to pass as `state`. There is no client-side redaction, and the secret-leak PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover MCP tool calls, so a mcp__evaluate__* call could carry a secret it has read. Provider-side data retention and logging follow OpenRouter's and TypeSafe's policies (not checked here), which matters for client projects under NDA. A second egress is the GitHub API call at every server start (IP and version only).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Errors come back as an MCP tool result with IsError, and Claude just carries on without Jev. HTTP client timeout is 60 s per attempt (main.go:168); 429 and 529 are retried up to 3 times with 1s/2s/4s backoff (client.go). A hung endpoint could therefore stall a single tool call for up to about 4 minutes. A non-JSON 2xx body or a response over 16 MiB is rejected. If neither key is set, `evaluate mcp` exits at startup (route() error, main.go:164), so the MCP server shows as failed and no tool is registered, with no impact on other Claude Code functions. At server start the update check adds up to 2s, and if it fails it silently adds nothing. There is no circuit breaker, so a slow provider costs 60s per call. In items mode, one failed item does not fail the batch.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Rough size, chars/4: server instructions about 2.9k chars (~730 tokens; Claude Code may truncate long server instructions, so the tail, including the score/confidence notes, might be cut, which I could not verify), tool description about 1.3k chars (~320 tokens), JSON schema property descriptions about 2.3k chars (~580 tokens) plus schema scaffolding (~200 tokens). Total is about 1.8-2k tokens of always-present context if the tool is loaded eagerly. With Claude Code's MCP tool-search/deferral, only the name is present until the tool is needed, but the server instructions are still injected. No hook-injected text, since there are no hooks. Small compared with gitnexus (17 tools) or playwright (~25 tools).
pros: Is the one, Jev-specific integration that already supports OpenRouter in code: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` set and `TYPESAFE_API_KEY` unset routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest (main.go:152-158). It fits your setup with no patching.
Tiny footprint: one tool, no runtime dependencies, one static Go binary with a small dependency tree, and no telemetry or hooks. Very little context cost next to gitnexus or playwright.

Well-engineered client behaviour for its size: 429/529 retry with backoff, 16 MiB response cap, rejection of non-JSON 2xx, local validation that gives clear errors, exact preservation of numbers (UseNumber), and stable option ordering.

Useful extras for agent use: `min_confidence` abstain, which turns a shaky Jev answer into `__uncertain__` so Claude escalates rather than acts; and `items` batching for cheap bulk triage (e.g. classify 200 log lines or issues in one call).

The instructions and tool description are unusually good prompt-engineering for Jev (evidence not verdicts, no-match option, do not do arithmetic). They raise the chance that Claude will use the tool correctly.

Actively maintained: 121 commits in 13 days, 8 releases (v0.4.8 on 2026-09-30), release-please with pinned action SHAs, checksummed release archives, MIT. 337 stars and 37 forks show real adoption. Tests exist: 24 Test funcs in a 940-line evaluate_test.go.
Fail-open and read-only. It cannot modify files or run commands, so a bad Jev answer costs little unless Claude acts on it blindly.
Can be installed with tighter security than the README suggests: build from a pinned tag with Go, use env expansion in .mcp.json, and pass `--no-update-check`.
cons: Only auto-invoked at the model's discretion (no hook, no skill), which is not the guaranteed 'Claude Code uses it without me asking' behaviour you want. Left alone, Opus 5.5 will probably seldom call it; you would have to add CLAUDE.md steering or a hook yourself.

Jev has no code-specific strength and no reasoning. Daily coding (edit, debug, refactor) rarely needs a calibrated classifier, and Claude can decide the same things inline. The realistic wins are narrow: bulk triage, routing, guardrail-style gates. Vendor latency and quality claims are unverified, as is the skeptics' 'DeepSeek flash router' claim.

Sends whatever Claude passes as `state` (code, diffs, logs) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. That is a compliance question for client projects. Your secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls, and there is no redaction.

`setup mcp` puts the OpenRouter key in argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. `setup` also silently re-registers with codex, hermes and Claude Desktop if they are present. Avoid `setup` and configure manually.

README's `curl | sh` installer and the self-update use a same-origin checksum only, no signatures. Sole maintainer is an individual account, so it is a supply-chain trust decision on a 13-day-old repo (contributors: itsmostafa/Mostafa are the same person under two identities, plus 2 one-off contributors and a bot).

Depends on OpenRouter's `/api/alpha/` path, which the docs say may move. The default model is hardcoded to ~typesafe/jev-latest, so pinning a version needs per-call `model` unless you patch it. The tool uses /decisions, not the /api/v1/systemone endpoint.

No CI test workflow: only release-please.yml exists, so the 940 lines of tests run only if a contributor runs them (Taskfile); a release can ship without a test gate. No timeout budget for the LLM route beyond a flat 60s, and no circuit breaker, so a slow provider can freeze a turn.

Blocking GitHub call (up to 2s) on every server start, and an 'update available' string injected into instructions for the model to relay. That is harmless, but it is unrequested outbound traffic and a prompt-adjacent channel from a third-party release feed.
`items` with ReadOnlyHint true can burn 500 billed requests per call; you need an OpenRouter spend cap. Instructions may be truncated by Claude Code's server-instructions limit (unverified).

The binary has no non-MCP query mode. Its only subcommands are mcp, setup, update and version (main.go:103-113), so hooks cannot call it as a CLI. Claude Code 2.1.x does support `type: "mcp_tool"` hook handlers (server, tool, input with ${tool_input.command} substitution), but the tool's text output is treated as hook stdout. Jev's raw JSON is not a valid PermissionRequest decision (hookSpecificOutput.decision.behavior allow/deny), so replicating the OpenRouter cookbook gate needs a wrapper script that calls the API directly. This connector does not deliver that deterministic path.

Hardcoded floating alias ~typesafe/jev-latest (main.go:156) and no env override on the OpenRouter route. Probabilities and any thresholds you tune (e.g. 0.9 gates) can silently shift when TypeSafe bumps the model, and pinning typesafe/jev-1.13 requires passing `model` on every call.

OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in the existing no-secret-leak.cjs protected list, and `setup mcp` writes the key into ~/.claude.json in plaintext. Any Read/Grep of ~/.claude.json by Claude is a leak path unless that file is protected. Add the key to the hook's list, or better, keep it out of ~/.claude.json via an env wrapper.

The MCP call is not a hook and is not deterministic. In defaultMode auto, a first call to mcp__evaluate__evaluate may still prompt, or an auto-mode classifier may object to sending code or logs to a third party. In bypassPermissions it runs silently, so client-project code and diffs can leave the machine with no gate. Add a permission allow/deny rule deliberately and decide per client project whether this MCP is enabled (unverified: how the auto classifier treats external-egress MCP calls).

Blocking update check plus GitHub API call at every MCP server start (up to 2s, update.go:146-158) sits on the session-start path alongside the gitnexus and caveman startup costs. It is avoidable with --no-update-check, which is a hidden flag.

Go toolchain requirement go 1.27.1 (go.mod:3) makes `go install` from source non-trivial on a machine without that toolchain. The audit mentions it but does not weigh it against its own 'build from source' recommendation.

Sole-maintainer, unaffiliated individual account for a component that will receive client code. The audit says affiliation is unverified, and I confirmed the GitHub profile carries no company or affiliation ('I build stuff').
entries.verdict: Best-fit Jev integration for you and the reference implementation to use: it already speaks OpenRouter, is tiny and fail-open, and has strong usage guidance. Two caveats: auto-invocation is model-discretion only (so pair it with a CLAUDE.md rule or a thin hook), and Jev's value for coding itself is narrow (bulk triage, gating, routing). Install it by building from a pinned tag and registering manually with env expansion and `--no-update-check`, not with `curl|sh` or `setup mcp`.

verification.note: Re-queried and verified the key facts. Repo is itsmostafa/system-one-connector (renamed from typesafe-mcp), 337 stars, 37 forks, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-17, last push and v0.4.8 on 2026-09-30, 12 releases. OpenRouter support is real in code: main.go:152-158 POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model ~typesafe/jev-latest. TYPESAFE_API_KEY takes precedence if both are set (main.go:135). The endpoint answers (401 without a key, not 404), and openrouter.ai/~typesafe/jev-latest exists (HTTP 200). There is one tool, `evaluate`, ReadOnlyHint true (tools.go). No shell exec outside setup (exec.Command only in setup.go), no telemetry, and the only extra egress is the GitHub releases check. The key-in-argv and plaintext ~/.claude.json claims are confirmed (setup.go:231 `-e kv`). The audit was largely accurate, with these errors: the 4-minute hang claim is wrong (max 60s per hang, since only 429/529 are retried), the release count is 12 not 8, the contributor count is inflated by a duplicate identity, and the update-notice channel is a slightly bigger injection surface than 'harmless'. Score lowered from 7 to 6.5. It is the best fit for Jev and OpenRouter, small in context, and fails open. But it does not meet the user's headline requirement of automatic use without prompting. That would need CLAUDE.md steering, or a hook that Claude Code's `mcp_tool` handler cannot turn into a valid PermissionRequest decision without a wrapper. It also has a floating model alias, a 13-day-old single-author repo, no test gate in CI, and no egress control for client code, notably under bypassPermissions. Recommended install stays as the audit says: pinned tag, manual registration with the key kept out of argv and ~/.claude.json, --no-update-check, TYPESAFE_MAX_ITEMS low, and an OpenRouter spend cap on the key. Files: <scratch path>,client.go,setup.go,update.go,tools.go}.

entries.name: shaharia-lab/jev-cli
entries.what: Unofficial, Rust (2 crates: jev-client, jev-cli) command-line tool for TypeSafe Jev. It does three things. (1) CLI: `jev noul|choice|score|eval|validate|batch run` sends state plus typed questions to POST {base}/v1/systemone with Bearer auth and returns probabilities. Exit codes make it usable as a semantic `if` (0 = ok, 10 = gate false, 11 = abstain band). (2) `jev mcp serve`: a hand-written stdio JSON-RPC MCP server with 6 tools (7 with --allow-dir). (3) A Claude Code plugin and skill (skills/jev-cli/SKILL.md, .claude-plugin/marketplace.json) that teaches the agent the workflow. It ships no hooks and no proxy. It is not affiliated with TypeSafe.
entries.autoInvocation: The MCP tools are model-discretion: Claude calls noul, choice, score or evaluate only if it judges they fit. The descriptions are well written for this ('Choose noul for an absolute judgment', 'ask one snap judgment per question'), and the server-level `instructions` explains when to use it. The optional plugin skill is a description-triggered skill, so it fires on 'semantic judgment about content (classify, route, detect, rate, verify)' tasks. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no CLAUDE.md wiring. Real auto-use will be sparse and unpredictable, because Opus 5.5 can classify text itself for free with the reasoning it already has, and nothing in a coding session specifically calls for a calibrated probability.
