The most reliable way to make it fire more is to add a short CLAUDE.md rule, or to put the calls in a PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook that runs `jev noul ... --fail-under` (a CLI call, deterministic, but you must build the hook yourself).
security: API key handling is good: it comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or a 0600 credentials file in a 0700 dir (credentials.rs). It is never accepted as an argv value, so it does not appear in `ps` or shell history. It is held in a zeroize-on-drop type with a redacting Debug, and response bodies are scrubbed of the key. Redirects are never followed, so the Authorization header cannot be replayed to another host. HTTPS is enforced except for loopback, and TLS uses rustls with the platform verifier. There is no project-local config, so a repo cannot redirect the key.

MCP file access is deny-by-default. batch_run exists only with --allow-dir, paths are canonicalized (symlinks and .. resolved), and the output file must not already exist. Without --allow-dir the server touches no files.
No telemetry. The two hosts contacted are the API base URL and GitHub Releases for self-update (docs/development/threat-model.md, README).

Self-update: a detached background `jev update --background` runs at most once every 24h. It downloads a release from GitHub, verifies it against minisign keys compiled into the binary (crates/jev-cli/keys/*.pub) and swaps the binary in on the next run with a rollback self-test. This is a supply-chain surface (a compromised release key or repo would give code execution on a dev machine). It can be turned off with `jev config set update.auto false` or update.pin_version. On a client-work machine, turn it off and pin the version.

The installer is curl|sh, but the script is verified: SHA-256 always and minisign only when minisign is installed (--require-signature enforces it). Prefer cargo install --locked, or a manual download of the release plus checksum, over piping to sh.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are numeric JSON (probabilities), not free text, so a Jev response cannot carry injected instructions. The inbound direction is the risk: the agent chooses what to send as `state`, so injected content in a file could steer what gets sent. The blast radius is small, because it is read-only, has no shell execution and no file writes unless --allow-dir is set.
entries.dataEgress: On every noul, choice, score or evaluate call: the `state` text or JSON, plus the question instructions and criteria, plus the model name. All of it is chosen by Claude as tool arguments, so it can be code snippets, diffs, logs, file contents or a tool output. It goes over HTTPS to {base_url}/v1/systemone, which is OpenRouter and then TypeSafe as the inference provider, so it crosses two third parties. The Authorization header carries the API key. `validate` sends nothing. `list_models` sends only the GET with the key. The auto-updater makes a request to GitHub Releases at most once a day and sends no code. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry. Bodies are logged only with --debug-bodies. For client projects this is a real consideration, because the model decides what to send and no hook or allowlist restricts it. OpenRouter's data-policy setting for the account should be checked.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice. The MCP server starts even without a usable key, and each evaluating call then returns a tool error (JSON error object with code and hint, e.g. no_api_key, exit class 3). Claude sees the error and carries on. Nothing blocks the session and there are no hooks to hang. Per attempt the HTTP timeout is 30 s with a 10 s connect timeout (retry.rs:65, http.rs:32), and there are 2 retries with 0.5 to 5 s backoff. Timeouts are retried and Retry-After is honoured up to 60 s. So a hung or slow Jev could stall a single tool call for about 90 s plus backoff before erroring. This can be tightened with --timeout and --max-retries or a profile. A 429 or 5xx becomes a tool error. Validation errors are caught offline before any request is spent.
entries.contextCost: There are 6 tools by default (evaluate, noul, choice, score, validate, list_models) and 7 with --allow-dir. A static estimate from the source is about 5 to 7k tokens (about 22 to 28k chars) if the tool definitions are loaded in full. The evaluate, validate and batch_run descriptions are 0.9 to 1.6k chars each and embed the full request JSON schema (schemas/request.schema.json is 6.5k chars). The noul, choice and score tools carry smaller per-question schemas plus a shared ~600-char JEV_LIMITS/RESULT boilerplate in each description. The server sends an `instructions` string of about 800 chars (mod.rs INSTRUCTIONS). Claude Code here defers MCP tool schemas behind ToolSearch, since deferred tools appear by name only, so the resident cost drops to a few hundred tokens of names plus the ~800-char server instructions. The plugin skill adds only its description line (~800 chars) to the skill listing, and its ~16.5 KB body loads only when triggered. No hook-injected text.
pros: Best-engineered Jev integration found so far. It is the only candidate here that combines an MCP server, a CLI (usable from hooks and CI), a skill/plugin, offline validation and batch mode, all Jev-native. It has a real test suite (~493 tests, fuzzing, 3-OS CI, nightly live smoke test).

OpenRouter works with config only. The client builds `{base}/v1/systemone` with Bearer auth, and OpenRouter documents `https://openrouter.ai/api` plus `/v1/systemone` as TypeSafe-compatible with the same body (state, model, questions -> answers, usage). So: `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api` with the OpenRouter key. `jev-latest` maps server-side to ~typesafe/jev-latest.
A profile (`jev profile create openrouter --base-url ...`) plus `jev mcp serve --profile openrouter` keeps the OpenRouter settings and key out of ~/.claude.json.

Safe by default: read-only tools, no shell execution, file access only via --allow-dir, key never in argv, no telemetry, results are numbers (no injection channel), and failure never blocks Claude (tool error only).

Tool descriptions and server instructions are written so that a model knows when to pick a tool (prefer evaluate for several questions, always include an escape option, Jev cannot count). Because MCP schemas are deferred in this Claude Code setup, the resident context cost is small.

Offline `validate` catches the API's silent failure modes (unknown fields inside questions are silently accepted and bill you) before spending money. The CLI is scriptable: `jev noul ... --fail-under 0.8` gives a hook-friendly exit code, so a deterministic PreToolUse or PostToolUse hook (e.g. 'does this diff touch auth/secret handling?') is possible.
Apache-2.0/MIT license, signed releases, cargo-deny and audit in CI.
cons: Automatic use is the weak point. It is pure model-discretion. Nothing makes Claude reach for Jev during coding, and a frontier model can usually answer 'is this a bug fix?' at zero marginal cost. Expect it to be called rarely unless you add CLAUDE.md rules or build your own hooks.

The OpenRouter path is untested by the project. The repo never mentions OpenRouter. It depends on OpenRouter's compat shim, which is beta. `list_models` and `models list` will break because the OpenRouter models shape differs, and cost estimates come back null. `--max-cost-usd-per-call` only knows the id `jev-1.13.0`, while OpenRouter expects `jev-1.13`, so the spend cap needs the pricing override in config.toml or a small patch. The response-parsing assumption (extra OpenRouter fields tolerated) comes from a lack of deny_unknown_fields, not from a test.

It is a new (11 days), 33-star, community, single-maintainer project (55 of 67 commits from one person, the rest bots) that is explicitly unofficial. If TypeSafe changes the API the tool may lag, though the nightly live smoke test helps. The API itself is beta.

The background self-updater (daily GitHub check, staged binary swap) is a supply-chain and surprise-behavior risk for a machine that holds client work. It must be disabled with `update.auto false`. The recommended installer is curl|sh, and its signature check is skipped when minisign is not installed.

Data egress goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the agent picks the payload. On client projects, code, diffs and logs could be sent to third parties with no hook to filter them. It bypasses your secret-leak guard, because the guard matches Bash, Read, Grep and NotebookEdit, not `mcp__jev__*`. You would need to add an MCP matcher.
Worst-case stall is about 90 s for one call (30 s timeout x 3 attempts) unless you set --timeout 5s --max-retries 0 in the profile.

No hooks are shipped. This is the audit's main gap against 'automatic': the skill and MCP server are advisory. The 16.5 KB skill body is heavy if it triggers often, and its install text tells the agent to run a curl|sh install (it does say to ask the person first).

Two Jev surfaces exist on OpenRouter (Decisions API at /api/alpha/decisions and System One). jev-cli only speaks System One, so it does not cover the Decisions API or 'Jev Router' semantics beyond the model id.
entries.verdict: The strongest Jev-specific building block found, and the best MCP server to use if you want Jev at all: `jev mcp serve --profile openrouter` with base URL https://openrouter.ai/api and your OpenRouter key should work with no code changes, but this is unverified live. It will not make Claude 'use Jev automatically' on its own. Auto-use needs your own CLAUDE.md rule or a CLI-based hook. Before using it on client work, turn off auto-update, pin the version and add an mcp__jev__* matcher to your secret guard.

entries.name: @goldjunge91/jev-code
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (plus Claude Code plugin/marketplace, Agent Skill, CLI, Pi/OpenCode adapters) exposing five Jev tools (jev_classify, jev_check, jev_score, jev_rank, jev_ask). It batches items into one POST to OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone (model hard-coded to typesafe/jev-1.13) and turns Jev's probabilities into auto/review decisions and yes/no/uncertain verdicts using local thresholds. A bundled SKILL.md tells the model when to call the tools. It is a fork by goldjunge91 of FrancoisChastel/jev-code (32 stars, TypeSafe-direct). The fork's only substantive change is switching the backend to OpenRouter (commit db79fd2).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, plus a skill-description trigger. There are no hooks and no proxy. Claude Code (Opus) sees the 5 tool descriptions and the MCP server instructions in every session and can call the tools on its own, which meets the 'no need to say use jev' goal in the loosest sense. In practice the description and skill text ('when you notice yourself about to label more than a handful of items...') is a soft nudge that Opus may often ignore in favour of reasoning inline or Grep/Read. There is no deterministic guarantee. Making it reliable would need a CLAUDE.md rule, or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook that you write yourself.
security: No install hooks. npm package has no preinstall/postinstall/prepare scripts. Only the 'prepublishOnly' script exists, and it runs at publish time. Runtime deps are just @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod.

No telemetry and no analytics. The only network call is the POST to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. grep of src found child_process only in setup/exec.ts, which spawns claude/codex/pi with fixed args and no shell. There is no eval.

API key handling: read from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, sent as a Bearer header, and masked in doctor. BUT `jev-code setup` by default bakes the key into harness config. src/setup/index.ts:189-212 builds `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key> ...`, which puts the key in argv (briefly visible in the process list) and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. `--no-env` avoids this. The plugin route (.mcp.json) has no env block and relies on inheriting the shell env, which is cleaner.
Do not run `setup` blindly. Register the server yourself with an env reference, or use the plugin, to keep the key out of argv and config.

Supply chain: the .mcp.json and setup use unpinned `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp`, so every Claude Code start resolves the latest version from npm. That is a single-maintainer third-party package (v0.1.0, 4 days old) that runs with your full env. Pin the version, e.g. @0.1.0, or vendor it.

npm dist shows only a registry signature, no provenance attestation, despite publishConfig.provenance:true. The 0.1.0 tarball was evidently published outside the release.yml workflow. The package.json author is still 'François Chastel', while the maintainer is goldjunge91 ([email removed]), so attribution is confusing. SECURITY.md still points to the upstream author's email.
entries.dataEgress: Only the payload the model puts in a tool call leaves the machine: items[].text (each truncated at 4000 chars), classes, questions, context or state, sent as JSON to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the Bearer key. The whole request is capped at about 120K chars. Nothing is read from disk, git, the session or the environment by the tool itself, so whatever code, diffs, logs or file excerpts Opus chooses to pass goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe/its upstream provider. That matters for client projects under NDA, and the secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* calls (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). The OpenRouter account's data and logging policy applies, and the response contains only usage plus the model id.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level. It is an optional MCP tool, not a hook or proxy, so nothing blocks if it fails. A missing key surfaces as a tool error (isError:true, 'jev_x failed: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not set...'), because the client is built lazily (mcp/server.ts:9,23). Each attempt has a 30 s timeout (JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS) and up to 2 retries (JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES) on 408/425/429/5xx/529, timeouts and connection errors, with exponential backoff of 0.5-8 s and Retry-After honoured up to 30 s. Worst case is roughly 90 s or more of stall on a hard-down endpoint, which is long for a 'fast classifier'; lowering the env vars to ~3000 ms and 0-1 retries fixes that. The model then sees the error and proceeds by itself. If the server fails to start (npx offline), the tools are simply absent and the skill falls back to a `jev-code` CLI that does not exist, so it just tells the user to run setup.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Estimated at chars/4: tool descriptions about 2.9k chars (~730 tok), JSON schemas including field descriptions about 8-9k chars (~2.2k tok), MCP server instructions (6 sentences) about 1.1k chars (~280 tok). Total is roughly 3.2-3.5k tokens of tool definitions, or about 12-14k chars, if tools are not deferred (Claude Code 2.1.x tool search can defer them and cut this to the names). The skill adds a ~1.4k-char description always listed (~350 tok); the SKILL.md body (8.5 KB, ~2.1k tok) loads on trigger, and the references (~30 KB) load only if read. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Net always-on cost is about 3.5-4k tokens, moderate, and larger than the value of a tool that is called rarely.
pros: It is the only candidate found here that is wired to OpenRouter by design. Base URL and model are hard-coded to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13 and a Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (config.ts:6-13, client.ts:104,148,181), so it works with just one env var and no TypeSafe account.

A tool set shaped for coding work: batch classify (64 items), check (64 yes/no), score, rank (250 candidates, with any_relevant to avoid trusting a false top hit) and a raw jev_ask escape hatch. Thresholds and decisions are computed locally, so the model gets auto/review flags rather than raw probabilities.

Fully automatic install is possible via the Claude Code plugin marketplace (`claude plugin marketplace add goldjunge91/jev-code`), which bundles the skill and .mcp.json. It is user-level, and you never have to type 'use jev'. Tool descriptions are written as triggers ('triage CI failures', 'pick which files to open').

Sane client engineering: retries with backoff and Retry-After handling, a lazily built client so a missing key is a tool error rather than a crash, local validation of duplicate ids and request size before spending a call, and read-only/idempotent annotations. 81 test cases across tests/ (client, config, tools, MCP server, setup), a CI matrix on Node 20/22/24 and a smoke script.

Small and auditable: about 2.9k lines of TypeScript, 2 runtime deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell execution beyond fixed-argument spawns in setup. MIT licensed, and Jev's calibrated outputs mean it fits the typed-decision design.
cons: Not really automatic. It is a model-discretion tool, so Opus decides whether to call it, and for a strong reasoning model most triage of small lists is cheaper inline. Expect it to be called rarely unless CLAUDE.md nudges it. It only helps in bulk-judgment situations (CI failure triage, many files to rank), which are a small part of daily coding.

Brand-new and single-maintainer. The repo was created 2026-09-26, has 11 commits (8 by the fork owner, 3 by upstream), 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues and no GitHub release. npm 0.1.0 is 4 days old, has no provenance attestation, and carries a mismatched author and SECURITY contact (still the upstream author). It is a fork of a 32-star upstream (FrancoisChastel/jev-code) that could be pulled from directly with a 2-line OpenRouter patch, which would remove trust in a second party.

The default `setup` bakes OPENROUTER_API_KEY into `claude mcp add -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...`, so the key lands in argv (transiently visible in the process list) and in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (src/setup/index.ts:189-212). The `npx -y @goldjunge91/jev-code mcp` launcher is unpinned, so a compromised or updated package would execute with your environment on every session start. Register manually with a pinned version.

Rides on the beta System One endpoint, and there is no way to select ~typesafe/jev-latest, the Jev Router, or the alpha Decisions API, because model and URL are constants. If the doc-cited endpoint changes, the tool breaks until a new release. The retry defaults (30 s x 3 attempts) can stall the tool for over a minute on an outage, so tune JEV_CODE_TIMEOUT_MS and JEV_CODE_MAX_RETRIES.

Code egress to a third party with no guard. Whatever excerpts Opus classifies go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which is a real concern on client projects. Your existing secret-leak hook matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it will not inspect mcp__jev__* payloads; add a matcher for it. About 3.5-4k tokens of always-on context (5 tools with long schemas, server instructions, skill listing) for occasional use, unless tool-search deferral applies. The stated Jev quality is unverified (the Theo/t3.gg 'flash router' skepticism), and its output is an unexplained probability, so review-band items still need Opus.
entries.verdict: Best-fit OpenRouter-native, well-scoped Jev MCP found so far: safe to try as a user-scope plugin (pinned version, key kept in shell env, short timeout) for bulk triage and file-ranking. However it is a day-old single-maintainer fork whose automatic use is only a soft model nudge, not a deterministic hook, and it needs a hook matcher and vetting before use on client code.

entries.name: jevwire (wesleydionisio fork of Brainwires/jevwire)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (v0.6.0) + stdio MCP server (6 tools) + embeddable TS library around Jev. The plugin hooks (SessionStart cmd; UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd as type:http posts to a self-spawned loopback daemon on 127.0.0.1:10522) run a deterministic bash/path prefilter, then ask Jev typed questions for: tool-call gate notes (additionalContext) and a deny-once "tripwire" (hard regex shapes like rm -rf ~, force-push main, DROP TABLE, plus Jev-scored destructive/outward/out-of-scope calls), prompt-injection screening of WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__ results, stop-short and false "tests pass" detection at Stop, optional per-prompt task classification. Never emits allow, never prompts the user unless ask_on_trip. It is a fork of Brainwires/jevwire (original author Josh Guyette); Wesley Dionisio added the OpenRouter provider in 4 commits on 2026-09-18 (a27d59c, d9d9f58, 0f852ef, 92bf204). Upstream Brainwires has since moved to 0.6.3 (pr_scope commit lint, staged-secret trip) and its tree has no src/jev/provider.ts, so the OpenRouter support exists only in this fork.
entries.autoInvocation: Yes, without prompting: hooks fire deterministically on prompt submit, gated tool calls, mcp/web results, and Stop, and nothing needs the model to decide to call anything. This is the only candidate style that satisfies 'automatic without saying use jev'. Caveat: hook output is advisory, PreToolUse notes arrive after the call ran, and only the tripwire deny and one Stop block can change behavior. The 6 MCP tools rely on model discretion via the jev-decisions skill (rank-glob-before-read is a genuinely useful nudge but unprompted use is unreliable).
security: Key handling: OpenRouter key read from env or plugin userConfig (sensitive). hooks.json passes it as HTTP headers X-Jev-Env-Key-OpenRouter: $OPENROUTER_API_KEY / Authorization Bearer to http://127.0.0.1:10522 on every hook call (allowedEnvVars lists it). Loopback only, timingSafeEqual auth, but a different local user who squats port 10522 first receives payloads AND the key; SECURITY.md admits this and says multi-user hosts unsupported. Fine on a single-user box.

Key is not on argv (configure-openrouter.mjs reads env), but that script writes the plaintext key into ~/.claude/settings.json env (mode 600). The user's no-secret-leak hook does not yet protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the key is also in every Bash child env and readable by the model via env/printenv unless added to the protected list.

Daemon is a detached long-lived node process (control.ts spawn detached+unref, stdout to daemon.log), idle exit 30 min; /v1/health unauthenticated but carries no secret; no shutdown endpoint; keyless install runs unauthenticated.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev answers can be moved by injected text (independent evals). Tripwire is soft: the deny text tells Claude to re-issue with '# jev:intended <reason>' and then it passes without judgment, so a compromised/injected agent can self-override; Claude Code's own permission rules still apply. Stop hook can block once per prompt (a wrong Jev answer just costs one extra turn). Notes are declarative to avoid tripping Claude's injection defenses.

Redaction is best-effort regex (sk-, ghp_, AKIA, Bearer, JWT, key=value, PEM, long hex) applied before send and before local logging; misses unshaped secrets. Sensitive-path predicate (src/util/sensitive-path.ts) blocks .env, keys, .ssh, .aws, .claude/settings*.json for jev_rank/jev_verify file reads, realpath-confined to project root.

No telemetry found in src (grep for telemetry/analytics returned nothing); only outbound is the Jev API plus OpenRouter attribution headers (HTTP-Referer https://github.com/Brainwires/jevwire, X-Title jevwire). Local decision log and session files written to the plugin data dir (deletable, described in SECURITY.md).
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and onward to TypeSafe as model provider) only when the prefilter decides to judge: tool name plus redacted excerpt of arguments (<=4,000 chars) for Bash/Write/Edit/NotebookEdit/mcp__ calls that are not plainly read-only or in-project edits (in advisory mode: writes outside project, sensitive paths, unrecognized shell commands, MCP tools with unknown effects); last 3 user prompts (<=2,000 chars each) and captured subagent task prompt; Claude's final assistant message (tail 6,000 chars) at every Stop when stop_check=true; the FULL text of every WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__* tool result in 16,000-char chunks up to 8 chunks (about 128k chars) when screen_results=true (default) - this includes gitnexus and playwright outputs (code snippets, page snapshots) for client projects; file contents only if jev_rank/jev_verify MCP tools are pointed at paths. Regex redaction is best-effort. Also OpenRouter sees the account key and attribution headers. Memoization (5 min) avoids repeated identical calls. For client/NDA projects this is a real third-party (OpenRouter + TypeSafe) egress of code and tool output.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: every command hook exits 0 with empty stdout on error; http hooks get 200 {} even on auth failure (never non-2xx), refused connection is a non-blocking error in Claude Code; hook Jev deadline 1.5 s (JEV_HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS), hooks.json timeout 5 s (2 s SessionEnd); no key or provider mismatch means judgment hooks inactive and a once-per-session notice; port conflict means hooks inactive for the session. Handlers cannot emit permissionDecision allow (tests/hooks/never-allow.test.ts). The only blocking outputs are the tripwire deny (works in bypassPermissions, one-time, self-overridable via marker) and the Stop block (max once per prompt). MCP tools retry (3 retries, 30 s deadline). Pinned-model retirement would look like silence. If daemon is down, UserPromptSubmit falls back to a node command hook (about 160 ms).
entries.contextCost: MCP: 6 tools. Description/param text I could measure statically is roughly 5-6k chars in describe() strings plus longer tool descriptions and JSON schemas: estimate about 2.5-4k tokens of tool definitions per session (deferred behind ToolSearch in recent Claude Code if tool search is on). Skill: jev-decisions description about 100 tokens always in listing (with skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02 it competes for a tiny budget); SKILL.md body 11.7 KB (about 2.9k tokens) plus references/question-writing.md 3.4 KB only when invoked. Hook-injected text: SessionStart once-per-session note only when unconfigured; [jev] notes at most 5 per prompt (each about 60-100 tokens), typically zero for ordinary work; injection flags and stop-block messages rare; route_prompts is off by default, so no per-prompt line. Six slash commands are disable-model-invocation.
pros: Only candidate that actually delivers automatic, prompt-free use: hooks.json wires SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse (Bash|Write|Edit|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit|Agent|Task|mcp__.*), PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd; deterministic prefilter (src/hooks/prefilter.ts) keeps ls/git status/reads/in-project edits at about 3 ms with zero model calls

OpenRouter is a first-class, explicit provider: src/jev/provider.ts + client.ts:159 POST /api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and Bearer key; explicit provider never silently falls back to TypeSafe; OPENROUTER_BASE_URL override; tests/openrouter.test.ts

Safe failure modes by design: fail-open everywhere, cannot emit permissionDecision allow (never-allow test), never prompts unless ask_on_trip, 1.5 s per-hook deadline, kill switches JEV_HOOKS_DISABLE=1, gate=off, stop_check/screen_results toggles, /jev:off, JEV_DAEMON_DISABLE=1

Tripwire deny works under bypassPermissions where the user has no prompts: hard code rules (rm -rf ~, force push main, DROP TABLE, mkfs, dd of=/dev, chmod -R 777, fork bomb) fire without any model call, so this part has value even with Jev offline; Stop hook catches 'tests pass' claims contradicted by a verification ledger (evidence-based, not only model opinion)

Engineering quality above typical for a 0-star repo: 44 test files incl. http/command hook byte conformance, daemon lock/contention tests, redaction tests, CI with Node 20/22 and bundle freshness check; honest docs (SECURITY.md lists exactly what leaves the machine and the port-squatting residual risk; skill has a 'when not to use it' section); local decision log plus /jev:calibrate to tune thresholds on the user's own data
Cheap per-call cost (about $0.0045 per 108k input tokens reported for jev_rank), tool defs small (6 tools), no per-prompt context injection by default
cons: Broad egress with default settings: screen_results=true sends the full text (up to about 128k chars) of every WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__* result (gitnexus code, playwright snapshots) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, and Stop sends the final assistant message every turn; on client projects this is third-party code egress; regex redaction is best-effort. Would need screen_results=false and possibly gate=off/limited matchers for client work

Latency stacking: synchronous PostToolUse on every mcp__ result and PreToolUse on all mcp__.* plus Stop calls, on top of gitnexus (seconds) and no-secret-leak; README latencies are measured on macOS against TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter alpha

Weak enforcement: notes for PreToolUse arrive after the call already ran; tripwire is answerable by Claude re-issuing with '# jev:intended <reason>' so it is a speed bump not a guard, especially under prompt injection; Jev evals show overconfidence and injection sensitivity. In bypassPermissions the plugin deliberately cannot prompt the user, so value is mainly the 8 regex rules plus Stop nudges

Key exposure surface: OPENROUTER_API_KEY sent as HTTP headers to the loopback daemon on every hook call and becomes visible in the process env; configure-openrouter.mjs writes it plaintext to ~/.claude/settings.json; user's no-secret-leak hook does not yet cover OPENROUTER_API_KEY; loopback port squat by another local user leaks payloads and key (fine on single-user machine)

Provenance risk: the OpenRouter support lives only in a 0-star personal fork (wesleydionisio) that is 4 commits ahead of Brainwires 0.6.0 and now behind upstream 0.6.3 (which lacks provider.ts); 12 days old, no releases/tags, runs 1.7 MB of committed minified bundles; OpenRouter Decisions API is alpha with no SLA; fixed port 10522 (hardcoded in hook URLs) and a resident daemon; MCP tools rely on model discretion (skill only) so unprompted use of rank/verify is unreliable

Overlap and noise with the user's existing setup: Stop hook can force an extra turn on a false positive; PreToolUse matcher on Agent|Task and mcp__.* adds hook invocations for every subagent spawn and every gitnexus/playwright call; the user's caveman UserPromptSubmit and plannotator hooks are independent but /jev commands run through Bash (sandbox loopback quirk documented)

Fork base is upstream 0.5.1, not 0.6.0: it is 18 commits behind upstream and misses 0.5.2 (hook-post auth by session id), 0.6.0 (rank/pick/stop-claim verification), 0.6.1 (semantic lint) and 0.6.2/0.6.3 (staged-secret trip, pr_scope). The fork's '0.6.0' version string collides with upstream's different 0.6.0, which will confuse any plugin update or merge. Getting the upstream fixes requires a manual rebase and rebuild of the 1.7 MB bundles.
Bare `node` in all hook and slash-command invocations conflicts with the user's overridden PATH. Failure is silent: SessionStart never starts the daemon, so all http hooks post to nothing.

SECURITY.md and README security prose were not updated for OpenRouter. SECURITY.md says egress is to api.typesafe.ai only and that the key is never written to a settings file, but the fork's script does exactly that. Documented guarantees are unreliable for the fork's own feature.

PostToolUse screening has no prefilter: every mcp__ result of 200 chars or more, including read-verb tools like gitnexus query, goes to OpenRouter. Read, Bash and Grep results are not screened, so a prompt injection arriving via file contents or curl output is not covered even though the default posture suggests broad coverage.

Playwright tools are all judged at PreToolUse, because 'browser_*' does not match the read-verb skip list. Tool arguments such as URLs and typed form text for client sites go to OpenRouter, and each call takes a synchronous Jev round trip.

Retries are 0 in hooks, and screening fires up to 8 concurrent requests per result. Under OpenRouter alpha rate limits or 429s, coverage silently degrades. The user gets no signal beyond the local decision log.
The OpenRouter attribution referer credits Brainwires/jevwire, so this user's traffic is attributed to a third party repo on OpenRouter dashboards.

The daemon is spawned with the SessionStart hook's full environment, so it holds OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and any other env passed to that hook) in /proc/<pid>/environ for up to 30 min idle. This is same-user only, but larger than a per-call process.
entries.verdict: The strongest fit for an automatic, OpenRouter-hosted Jev: real hook coverage, explicit OpenRouter provider, fail-open and never-allow by design, and unusually good tests and honest docs. Adopt only pinned to a reviewed commit and with screen_results off (or matchers narrowed) and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the secret-leak list, because default egress of MCP/web results and the fork-only, alpha, 0-star provenance are the real risks.

verification.note:
Verified. The OpenRouter provider is real and correct in code: src/jev/provider.ts sets OPENROUTER_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha, and src/jev/client.ts:159 posts to /decisions with body {state, model, questions} and a Bearer key at client.ts:294. OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_PROVIDER and the OPENROUTER_BASE_URL override are read in src/config.ts and src/hooks/config.ts. Model typesafe/jev-1.13 is resolved from jev-1.13.0. OpenRouter's own Jev docs (openrouter.ai/docs/guides/community/jev, per web search) confirm POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and the alternative /api/v1/systemone. This was a static read only, and no live call was made. Both dist bundles contain the alpha URL.

Other checks. All 6 MCP tools exist: jev_rank, jev_verify, jev_evaluate, jev_gate_action, jev_next_step and jev_list_models. All 7 hook events are in hooks.json, and 6 slash commands plus the skill are present. There are 44 test files (14,328 lines) and a CI workflow. Stats re-queried today: fork 0 stars, 0 forks, MIT, not archived, created and last pushed 2026-09-18, 18 commits (Josh Guyette 14, Wesley Dionisio 4). Upstream Brainwires/jevwire has 22 stars and 5 forks, and was last pushed 2026-09-21. There are no telemetry strings in the source or the dist bundles. Defaults confirmed: screen_results=true, stop_check=true, gate=advisory, route_prompts=false, 1.5 s timeout, 0 retries. Hard patterns and the PROMPTLESS_MODES deny under bypassPermissions are as described. Stop checks the final message on every turn, capped at 1 block per prompt. The audit's egress, chunk-size (16k x 8), Stop tail (6000) and fail-open claims are accurate.

Score 7 -> 6.5. The main errors are the wrong fork base (0.5.1, ahead 4, behind 18, with a colliding 0.6.0 version), the stale and contradictory SECURITY.md, the overlooked bare-`node`-versus-overridden-PATH silent-inert risk, and the fact that all playwright and most gitnexus tools are judged, not just a subset. The recommendation still stands: it is the only candidate style with automatic invocation. Adopt it only if pinned to a reviewed SHA, with screen_results off or narrowed matchers, an absolute node path patched in, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the secret-leak list. Better still, cherry-pick the ~600-line provider.ts / client.ts change onto current upstream 0.6.3. I did not verify Claude Code 2.1.x behavior live: http hook headers with allowedEnvVars, PreToolUse additionalContext timing, and the stop_hook_active, permission_mode and agent_type input fields are taken from the repo's own spike doc (docs/SPIKE_HTTP_HOOK.md) and tests.

entries.name: tumf/jev-cli
entries.what: Unofficial community Python package (PyPI jev-cli 0.6.3) that installs two commands: `jev` (CLI for noul/choice/score/run) and `jev-mcp` (stdio MCP server exposing the same four operations as tools). Also bundles an Agent Skill (`jev install-skills --claude [-g]`). Thin urllib client over the System One request schema (state + questions map) with selectable providers: official TypeSafe, Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter, custom. No hooks, no auto-invocation logic. The README calls it 'dependency-free' but that only holds for the CLI; the MCP server depends on `mcp>=2.2.0,<3` (pyproject.toml).
interface: MCP tool noul(state, question, [provider, model, endpoint])
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus an optional skill description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. The tool descriptions are generic ('answer one yes/no question about the state'), with no guidance on when a coding agent should use them, so Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for them unprompted. Achieving the user's 'automatic' goal requires adding your own steering (a CLAUDE.md rule, a custom skill, or a hook) on top.
security: API key never in argv: `auth set` reads from a hidden prompt or stdin, and MCP takes the key from env. Credential file is written atomically with 0600 in a 0700 dir (__init__.py:117-138). It is plaintext JSON.
Only if you put OPENROUTER_API_KEY in `claude mcp add -e` or in .mcp.json, it sits in ~/.claude.json or the project file; use env expansion or export it in the shell instead.
Env var wins over the credential file. The key is sent only as a Bearer header to the selected endpoint.

Per-call `endpoint` and `provider` tool arguments exist. A prompt-injected model could point the `custom` provider at an attacker URL, but it would send JEV_API_KEY (not the OpenRouter key) and the state. With `endpoint` overridden while provider=openrouter, the OpenRouter key would go to the arbitrary endpoint (call() uses api_key(provider) with whatever endpoint is passed, __init__.py:280). This is a real key-exfiltration vector via injected tool args, and is not mitigated by the code.

No shell execution, no subprocess, no eval; the MCP server calls the library directly. No telemetry. No postinstall. Pure Python wheel from PyPI, published from a single maintainer account; release workflow uses no trusted-publishing step that I could see (upload done outside the visible workflow).
install-skills copies files into ~/.claude/skills with a managed marker and rmtree only on directories it marked. Low risk.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly what Claude puts in the `state` and `question`/`criteria` arguments is POSTed as JSON to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or the chosen endpoint), verbatim. Nothing is read from disk by the MCP server (no @file or stdin expansion in MCP mode). Nothing leaves automatically beyond what the model chooses to pass, so code, diffs, or file contents are sent only if Claude puts them in `state`. The CLI does read @file/stdin. OpenRouter also sees the model ID, key and usage.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level: any HTTP error, timeout or bad JSON raises a ToolError returned to Claude, which can continue without it. Fixed 60 s urllib timeout (__init__.py:288), no retry and no circuit breaker. No hook is involved, so a Jev outage never blocks a tool call or the session. A hung call can stall a turn for up to 60 s, and there is no tunable timeout. If the MCP process fails to start (uv/python/mcp version) the server just shows as disconnected, as caveman-shrink does now.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (noul, choice, score, run). Estimated about 6,500-7,000 chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas, roughly 1.6-1.8k tokens if loaded eagerly. Server instructions add about 330 chars (about 80 tokens). Smaller if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch (only names loaded). The `run` schema is the heaviest (nested QuestionSpec with extra=allow). Bundled SKILL.md: the description is about 1 line always in context, and the body loads on trigger. No hook-injected text.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code, with the correct endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions), OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and model typesafe/jev-1.13 (__init__.py:29-33). Works with the JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter env only, no patching.
Exposes all three primitives plus batched `run`, with sensible validation (>=2 options/levels), giving Claude a ready MCP surface for Jev in an hour.
Small and auditable: about 740 lines of source, only stdlib plus the official `mcp` SDK. No shell exec, no telemetry, no postinstall.
Key handling is careful: no key in argv (env or hidden prompt), 0600 credential file, MCP stdout kept for protocol only.
Tools return errors as ToolError instead of crashing, and never block the session (no hooks). Fail-soft.

Ships a Claude-targeted SKILL.md (`install-skills --claude`) that tells the model to send minimal state and not to send secrets, which is a useful base to extend into a proper 'when to consult Jev' skill.
Has tests and cross-OS CI, and the openspec change history shows deliberate design, which is unusual for a 1-week-old repo.
Vercel and custom providers give a fallback if OpenRouter's alpha endpoint changes.
cons: Does not solve 'automatic': no hook, no routing, no trigger guidance. The user must add their own steering, so as-is Claude will use it only rarely.

Tool descriptions are generic ('the text or JSON value to judge') and say nothing about coding scenarios such as commit risk, test-need classification, or PR triage. There are no ready-made decision templates or presets.

Per-call `endpoint` and `provider` arguments let a prompt-injected model redirect the request, and call() attaches the selected provider's key to whatever endpoint is given (__init__.py:274-284), so the OpenRouter key could be sent to an attacker URL. Under bypass or 'auto' permissions this matters. Mitigate by denying/removing those args, which needs a fork or a wrapper, or by a scoped low-limit OpenRouter key.
Key must be provided through MCP `env` or the shell. `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plain text in ~/.claude.json unless you use ${VAR} expansion.

Requires Python >=3.13 and the `mcp>=2.2.0,<3` package; 'dependency-free' in the tagline is false for the MCP path. Fine for this user (Python 3.13 and uv installed), but cold start pulls a dependency tree.
Single maintainer, 14 stars, created 2026-09-17, unofficial, version 0.x alpha; the OpenRouter alpha API and the beta model may change. Default model is pinned to jev-1.13, not ~typesafe/jev-latest.
Fixed 60 s timeout, no retries, no per-call timeout config; a hung call can stall a turn far beyond the claimed 70-500 ms.
No urllib connection reuse, no usage/cost reporting except through the raw response, and only /alpha/decisions (not /v1/systemone).

Sends `state` verbatim, so the only guard against leaking client code or secrets is the model's judgment (SKILL.md text), and the user's existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* by its matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
entries.verdict: Best-in-class as a plain MCP transport for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (native OpenRouter provider, small auditable code, fail-soft), so it is a reasonable building block, but it gives no automatic invocation on its own. To meet the goal you would pair it with your own CLAUDE.md rule, a custom skill or a hook, and ideally fork or wrap it to drop the `endpoint`/`provider` overrides before running it in bypass mode with a real OpenRouter key.

entries.name: molis-ai/jev-workbench
entries.what: Local service to define, test and publish versioned Jev judgment functions; exposes them over HTTP and an MCP bridge (jev_list_functions, jev_describe_function, jev_invoke) with scoped tokens and a skill telling agents to list functions first.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP + skill trigger
pros: Claude Code is a first-class target (MCP stdio, skill, diff-confirm installer); vendor key stays local behind scoped client tokens
Versioned, fixed decision functions with demo mode, tests, playwright, CHANGELOG, security doc
cons: Upstream https://api.typesafe.ai hardcoded in apps/server/src/provider.ts, needs patch for OpenRouter; v0.1.0 only
Heavy setup (pnpm 11, Node 24, web UI, SQLite service) for a per-machine daemon; model-discretion only

entries.name: rtf6x/jev-mcp
entries.what: Local Node/TypeScript MCP server (plus Tauri tray app and Claude Desktop .mcpb bridge) exposing 12 Jev judgment tools (jev_verify/screen/noul/find/rerank/classify/decide/compare/extract/audit/review/gate). Each tool builds Choice/Noul/Score questions, POSTs one {model,state,questions} request to a single configurable JEV_URL with a Bearer JEV_API_KEY, validates answers fail-closed, and returns JSON verdicts+probabilities+action (auto/review/escalate). A port of jkudish/jev-mcp (MIT) with the endpoint made configuration. Ships a skill (skills/jev) whose description is a mandate to prefer the tools over the model's own reading.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by a skill description trigger (the resident skill description mandates calling jev_* by default). Not a deterministic hook and not a proxy: Claude Code decides whether to call, so invocation is probabilistic; the author himself notes MCP instructions are not delivered in Claude Code and relies on the skill alone. No hooks/settings snippets are provided to make it automatic (e.g. Stop/PreToolUse hooks calling jev_gate). The user must copy skills/jev into ~/.claude/skills manually.
security: Key handling: JEV_API_KEY read from env or .env only (config.ts:63-83), sent as Bearer header (forward.ts:31), not in argv; /health returns endpoint+model but not key. Plan doc claims key never logged.
Zero shell execution in the MCP server path (grep: no child_process/exec/eval in mcp-server/src or mcpb/server); Tauri app only spawns sidecar and open/xdg-open on log paths.

HTTP transport binds 127.0.0.1:18791 with NO authentication and no Origin/Host check (server.ts); any local process (or DNS-rebinding page, since no Host validation) can POST /mcp and spend the user's OpenRouter key by invoking tools; multi-user machine risk. stdio mode avoids this.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are JSON of numbers/enums from Jev, not free text, so low; server adds anti-injection framing to questions (questions.ts). But the skill/instructions push the agent to send text to third party by default.

Skill description is an aggressive mandate ('reach for them by default', 'even when the answer looks obvious', jev_screen every fetched page, jev_gate/jev_review at end of every non-trivial task, irreversible steps) - behavioural steering text from a 1-day-old repo; also 'never substitute your own reading for a failed call' and 'Start it in the jev-mcp checkout (npm start)' could cause the agent to run npm start/npm install for you.

Supply chain: deps are @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod only (runtime); no postinstall/preinstall scripts found in package.json files; private:true, not on npm - must git clone and npm install (dev deps esbuild, postject, sharp, typescript, plus Tauri/Rust for the app). Release binaries are macOS-notarized; Linux build exists in CI matrix but README install is macOS-centric (AppTranslocation, Applications, xattr).
entries.dataEgress: Everything the agent passes as tool arguments goes verbatim (after per-tool truncation, e.g. 2000 chars/candidate/item, review/gate docs up to 200,000 chars aggregate evidence) to JEV_URL (OpenRouter) as JSON {model,state,questions}: full diffs and file excerpts (jev_review/jev_gate), test logs, fetched web page text (jev_screen), claims and evidence, candidate lists. Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself; it is model-driven, so egress volume depends on how aggressively the skill mandate makes Claude call tools. For client projects this means client source diffs go to OpenRouter -> TypeSafe. Local-loopback hop only for MCP transport. No telemetry to rtf6x.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at tool level, fail-open at Claude Code level. Default JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=60000 (AbortSignal.timeout, forward.ts:35) - a hung OpenRouter alpha endpoint can stall a tool call up to 60 s unless lowered. No retry, no fallback: HTTP errors and transport errors become isError tool results (call.ts:70-90); malformed answers become status invalid_response with action review (never a pass). HTTP transport is stateless per request; if the server process is not running, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools simply are absent - the skill tells the agent to start it (npm start) and never substitute own reading, which is friction rather than a hard block. Nothing blocks Claude Code's own tool calls since it is not a hook.
entries.contextCost: 12 tools. String literals in descriptions plus .describe() text total ~12.9k chars (~3.2k tokens); with JSON-schema overhead (property names/types/enums/strict objects) realistic estimate ~4.5-5.5k tokens of tool definitions (with Claude Code tool search/deferral, names only until used). Server sends an ~900-char INSTRUCTIONS string (server.ts:12) but the repo itself states Claude Code does not pass it to the model (issues 23808/41834). The skill adds ~150-200 tokens resident (long mandate description) and ~2.5k tokens body/ref when opened. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
pros: Only candidate here with a native, config-only OpenRouter path: JEV_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, question type noul, matching the brief exactly (.env.example, config.ts, forward.ts).

Tool set is coding-relevant: jev_review (diff scored on correctness/spec match/test gap/blast radius with safe_to_apply), jev_gate (diff + 'tests pass' claims vs evidence), jev_screen (injection check for fetched web content), jev_classify/rerank/find for triage, jev_decide with ask_user/investigate escape hatches.

Solid fail-closed design: unknown args rejected (strict schemas), malformed answers -> invalid_response + review, no retries so no double-billing, explicit timeout, key not in argv and not logged; small dependency footprint (MCP SDK + zod), no postinstall, no shell exec, no telemetry.

Ships a skill whose resident description is written to trigger automatic use ('reach for them by default', four 'not optional' moments), which is the closest thing to 'Claude uses Jev without being told' among MCP options; stdio mode available (npm run stdio) so no port/daemon needed.
MIT; 39 commits with CI (typecheck, ~1.8k lines of tests over all 12 tools, bundle + stdio smoke test), tagged releases v0.1.1-v0.1.5.
Tools return only enums/probabilities/usage JSON so results add little context and carry little injection surface; usage/cost reported per call.
cons: Extremely young and unproven: repo created 2026-09-29, 0 stars, 0 forks, single human author (34 of 39 commits by 'Alex', 5 bot), 5 releases in ~1 day; ported from jkudish/jev-mcp (463 stars) so a more-followed upstream exists. No evidence of a live end-to-end run against OpenRouter: tests use a stub endpoint and OpenRouter is only 'fixtures from docs'; OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions is itself alpha.

Automatic use is only probabilistic (model discretion via skill text); no hook-based deterministic integration (no Stop/PreToolUse hook to run jev_gate/jev_review). Author admits Claude Code drops MCP server instructions, so everything rests on a skill description that must be copied manually.

Skill mandate is aggressive and expensive for daily coding: 'even when the answer looks obvious', screen every fetched page, review/gate at the end of every non-trivial task and before pushes; Jev is a small System One model with claimed router-like quality (unverified), so it may add latency (70-500 ms claimed, but 60 s timeout) and noisy false-positive review/escalate actions that Opus 5.5 must then reason around.

Data egress risk for client projects: diffs (up to 200k chars aggregate for gate), test logs and fetched pages are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe whenever the model calls tools; the existing secret-leak guard hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* arguments, so secrets in diffs could be forwarded.

Unauthenticated localhost HTTP endpoint (no token, no Origin/Host validation) that spends the user's OpenRouter key; safer stdio config would avoid it but README steers toward the macOS tray app (Tauri, Rust 1.77+, macOS-centric docs and xattr/AppTranslocation notes), which is a poor fit for a Linux user. Must git clone + npm install (Node >=22.18) and keep a checkout path; not published to npm.

Key naming friction: uses generic JEV_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY; real env beats .env so shell exports can silently override; 12 tools cost ~4.5-5.5k tokens of definitions (mitigated by MCP tool search) and many tools (find/rerank/extract/audit/classify) are of marginal use in ordinary coding.

Skill body tells the agent to run 'npm start' in the checkout if tools are missing - an agent-initiated process start driven by third-party text; Claude Code's bypass/auto mode would follow it without asking.
entries.verdict: Best-fitting concrete MCP candidate found so far for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (config-only endpoint, coding-relevant review/gate/screen tools, sane fail-closed code), but it is a 1-day-old single-author fork with no proven OpenRouter run, and 'automatic' is only skill-nudged, not a hook. Use stdio mode (not the HTTP tray app), pin a commit after reading it, restrict to jev_review/jev_gate/jev_screen, and pair with a Claude Code hook if deterministic invocation is required.

entries.name: CodeCampusCo/jev-mcp
entries.what: Minimal stdio MCP server (TypeScript, ~430 LOC, plain fetch, one runtime dep: @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) exposing a single tool `evaluate`. It forwards {model, state, questions} unchanged to the TypeSafe System One endpoint and returns the raw JSON (per-answer probabilities). Retries twice on 408/429/529/5xx with backoff, has a 10s per-attempt timeout and a 4MB response cap. Has optional Axiom logging, off unless AXIOM_API_KEY is set. Not published to npm: requires git clone, npm install and npm run build.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, skill or proxy. The tool description is written to make the model use it mid-task ("Reach for this mid-task, the way you would read a file... classifying, routing, scoring, gating") and also says when NOT to. There is no deterministic trigger, so how often Opus 5.5 actually calls it is unpredictable and likely low, since Opus can answer small classification questions itself at no extra cost. To raise the rate you would add a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill, which is contrary to the user's wish for no explicit prompting but is a one-time global setup.
security: API key handling is good: read from .env resolved relative to the package (client.ts:7) or from the environment, so it never appears in argv or the process list; sent only as a Bearer header to TYPESAFE_API_URL (client.ts:55-56); never logged.
No shell execution, no child_process, no postinstall/preinstall/prepare scripts (package.json checked), no curl|sh installer, nothing written to disk.

Telemetry is opt-in only: Axiom logging fires only if AXIOM_API_KEY is set (log.ts:52-53). If set, it ships full state, instructions, criteria and the hostname to Axiom (README Logging section, SECURITY.md). Leave it unset.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the response is a typed JSON blob with probabilities and no free text. But an API error body is passed back verbatim (index.ts:258), and the `state` the agent sends can contain attacker-controlled repo text that influences the decision. Do not let a Jev decision gate a destructive action.

Outbound channel: anything the agent puts in `state` leaves the machine, including code or secrets from client repos. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and will NOT cover mcp__jev__evaluate.

Single-maintainer, 2-week-old repo, zero stars, so supply-chain trust is low. The code is small enough to audit fully (I read all of it), and dependency surface is just the official MCP SDK. Pin a commit and use package-lock (npm ci).
entries.dataEgress: On every `evaluate` call the entire `state` (whatever the model chose to include: code snippets, diffs, file text, tool output, plus questions/criteria) and the API key go to the endpoint in TYPESAFE_API_URL, by default api.typesafe.ai, or openrouter.ai if reconfigured. With OpenRouter, the request is subject to OpenRouter's logging and data-policy settings. Nothing is sent when Claude does not call the tool. Axiom receives a full copy plus hostname only if AXIOM_API_KEY is set. No other telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: errors come back as an MCP tool error (isError), never a crash, so Claude Code carries on and the model reasons itself. Worst case is about 31s per call (10s timeout x 3 attempts plus backoff) while Claude waits, which is a noticeable stall if Jev is down or hanging. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the server exit at startup with code 1, so the tool silently disappears (a failed MCP connection, not a session failure). There is no circuit breaker, so a dead endpoint costs up to 31s each time the model tries it.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate). Tool name plus description plus schema is about 4,000 chars, roughly 1,000 tokens (DESCRIPTION alone is about 1,550 chars, and the schema property descriptions about 2,300). The server sends no MCP `instructions`. It adds no hooks and injects no text. Claude Code may defer tool loading, in which case only the name is in context until searched for. Each answer adds about 100-400 tokens of JSON. The tool is cheap in context versus e.g. playwright.
pros: Smallest, cleanest way to expose Jev to Claude Code: one tool, about 1k tokens of context, no server instructions, no hooks, so it will not collide with the existing secret-guard, GitNexus or caveman hooks.
Whole source is about 430 lines and I read all of it. No shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry by default, key never in argv (loaded from .env or env).

The tool description is the best I've seen at telling the model when to use Jev (bounded classification, routing, gating, claim-support check) and when not (prose, code, arithmetic, open answer space), including 'add a none-of-these option'. This gives real model-driven auto-use without prompting.
Provider URL, model and key are env-configurable (client.ts:36-37), and the endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's, so an OpenRouter switch is likely config-only.
Robust client: 10s per-attempt timeout, 2 retries with jitter and Retry-After support, a 4MB response cap, and tool errors returned instead of crashes (fail-open).
MIT, CI on Node 20/22/24, 14 stubbed-fetch tests, signed merge commits, CLAUDE.md/SECURITY.md documenting what leaves the machine.
Batch design: multiple typed questions per call against a single state, which saves round trips.
cons: Not really 'automatic': it is a model-discretion tool. Opus 5.5 can answer most bounded questions itself for free, so it will likely rarely call Jev, and there is no hook forcing it. It also needs the model to build a good state/criteria payload each time, which costs output tokens and a turn.
Not on npm: needs clone, npm install, and manual npm run build after every pull; `claude mcp add` needs an absolute path. No npx one-liner and no release tags.

Very new and single-maintainer (30 of 32 commits by one person, 2 by a bot; 0 stars, 0 forks, 12 days old, version 0.1.0). The project is by CodeCampusCo, not TypeSafe, so it is not the official integration.

OpenRouter is not first-class: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_URL exist, the key var is misnamed for an OpenRouter key, and the default model is jev-1.13.0 (a code comment says the TypeSafe API rejects jev-1.13) whereas OpenRouter uses typesafe/jev-1.13. OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified by me (docs URLs returned 404).

Data egress risk on client projects: whatever Claude puts in `state` (code, diffs) goes to a third party. The user's existing secret-leak hook does not match the mcp__jev__evaluate tool, so it would need a new matcher.
Worst-case stall of about 31s on a hanging endpoint with no circuit breaker. The 10s x 3 retry policy is fine for a batch job but bad for an interactive agent.

Inherits Jev limits and beta status: no 'don't know' answer, poor on arithmetic and dates, accuracy drops with noisy state, 32k limit; the value for coding is niche (routing/triage/claim checks) rather than a daily driver. The Theo/t3.gg skepticism (it may just be a small routed model) is unverified but relevant to how much decisions can be trusted.
entries.verdict: The best-built and lowest-overhead way to expose Jev to Claude Code (one tool, about 1k tokens, clean and auditable code, config-only OpenRouter path), but it is only a model-discretion tool, so it won't reliably fire on its own. Worth using as the base layer if paired with a CLAUDE.md/skill nudge, a secret-guard matcher for mcp__jev__evaluate, and a check that the OpenRouter endpoint and model id work.

entries.name: pyck-ai/jev-cli
entries.what: Single static Go binary (`jev`) that exposes TypeSafe Jev via OpenRouter's System One endpoint as 14 MCP tools over stdio (`jev mcp`, optional `--tools a,b,c` subset) and the same 14 as a Unix CLI. Tools wrap the noul/choice/score primitives with fail-closed parsing, thresholds, batching, retry, USD budget caps and a hashed-input JSONL audit log. It is only an MCP server and CLI. There is no plugin manifest, no hooks, no SKILL.md and no .claude-plugin directory, so the "plugin" in the discovery summary is wrong.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tool descriptions have "Use jev_X instead when..." routing text, but no hook, no skill trigger and no proxy, and the server sets no instructions. Claude will call a tool only if it decides to. To make it reliable the user would need to add a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a hook (for example PostToolUse on Edit, or Stop, calling `jev review` via the CLI). Those are user-authored, not provided by this repo. The CLI mode (`jev review --json ...`, exit code equals verdict) is a good building block for a deterministic hook, but the repo ships none.
security: API key comes from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY, or from opencode's auth.json as a fallback (read-only). The key is never read from the config file or logged, and is sent only as a Bearer header. It is not in argv unless the user puts it in `claude mcp add -e`, which stores it in ~/.claude.json. Reading another tool's credential file is a mild surprise, but it is skipped if absent.

No os/exec and no shell execution anywhere (grep: the only net/http user is internal/openrouter/client.go). The only outbound host is openrouter.ai. No telemetry and no postinstall script; the install is a source build via `go install`. The README's `go run ...@main` fetches and builds unpinned main at every start, which is a supply-chain risk. Pin a commit or build locally after reading.
Audit log at ~/.local/share/jev-cli/audit.jsonl (dir 0700, file 0600) stores only SHA-256 of the input, plus tool, model, score, tokens, cost and latency. No raw content is stored.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Outputs are structured numbers and enums, and tool descriptions are static. Unsanitized text in the `state` sent to Jev could sway a verdict, but Jev cannot emit instructions. jev_screen is advisory only.

Tools carry no readOnly/destructive annotations (grep for Annotations found none), so permission prompts may fire on each call in non-bypass modes. The user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover mcp__jev__* calls, so diffs or content the model passes to jev_review could include secrets and be sent to OpenRouter without inspection.
Single anonymous-ish maintainer (Michael Krupp, pyck-ai org), 3 days old, 0 stars, no releases. Code quality looks careful, but it has had no external review.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone as JSON {model, questions, state}. For jev_review and jev_gate that is the request text, the full diff and the test output, each truncated at 50k chars. For verify, check, match, rerank, classify, compare and extract it is the claims, evidence, passages and documents supplied. The tool itself reads no files and runs no commands. Only what Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine, and it goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe/its upstream providers, with OpenRouter's logging and privacy settings applying. This matters for client code under NDA. Nothing else is sent (no telemetry).
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at tool level, and non-blocking for the session. Timeout is request_timeout_ms=30000 total (default) across all attempts. Retries: 3 attempts with jittered backoff (500 ms to 8 s), on HTTP 408, 409, 429 and 5xx only. Network errors are never retried. If the endpoint is down or slow, the tool returns an error or `invalid_response` and Claude carries on. A hang could cost up to 30 s of waiting per call. There is no fail-open verdict, and malformed answers become status=invalid_response with action=review, never a fabricated pass. Missing key makes `jev mcp` exit at startup, so the MCP server shows as failed and nothing else breaks. Default budget caps are $0.01 per call (flag only) and $1.00 per session (hard refusal).
entries.contextCost: 14 MCP tools, or fewer with `--tools`. The server sets no `instructions`, since mcp.NewServer is called with nil options. Each description is about 600-900 chars (14 x ~750 = ~10.5k chars), and there are 79 schema fields with jsonschema descriptions (~12k chars of description plus JSON-schema structure), so about 25-30k chars, or roughly 6-8k tokens for the full set. Trimming to `--tools review,verify,check` cuts that to about 1.5-2k tokens. No hook-injected text. Claude Code's MCP tool search/deferral may reduce the standing cost.
pros: Native OpenRouter support: it calls /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so no code change is needed for the user's chosen provider (types.go:84, credentials.go:21).

Only jev_review/jev_gate are directly coding-relevant (diff versus request on correctness, spec_match, test_gap and blast_radius, with auto/review/escalate). jev_screen (prompt-injection screen), jev_classify and jev_verify are useful as secondary tools.
The `--tools` flag (commit f59398c) lets the user expose only 2-4 tools and keep context cost near 2k tokens. Otherwise the 14-tool surface is heavy.
Strong safety design: fail-closed parsing, budget caps ($1/session default), a hashed-input audit log, no shell exec, no telemetry, only openrouter.ai contacted, and SHA-pinned CI actions.

Single static Go binary, and the same logic is exposed as a CLI with exit codes, so it can be wired into deterministic hooks (for example a Stop or PostToolUse hook running `jev review`) that make invocation automatic. This is the only way to meet the user's no-prompt requirement.
Broad test coverage with fake-server integration tests and a real MCP session test; MIT license.
It documents a live end-to-end call on 2026-09-26 that fixed the model alias (~typesafe/jev-latest), a sign that at least the score path was exercised for real.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a plain MCP server with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, so Claude calls it only at its own discretion. That fails the user's core requirement unless the user builds a hook or rule layer.
It is very new (created 2026-09-26, 18 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases or tags), and the README itself says schemas and thresholds may change. Installing from `@main` is unpinned.

Most wire shapes are transcribed from docs and not verified live (types.go header). Only the score path and the model alias are noted as live-tested, so choice/noul tools such as review and verify may have edge-case bugs.

The 14 tools mostly target document, RAG and ops workflows (rerank, match, extract, classify), not coding. Only review/gate/screen/decide are relevant, and the rest is context clutter (~6-8k tokens) unless trimmed with `--tools`.
Requires a Go 1.25 toolchain, which the user's Node/Python/uv stack does not include.

Data egress: diffs and code that Claude passes are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. This is a concern for client projects. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse matcher does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and the server does no secret redaction.
It has no MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint) and no server instructions, so it may prompt for permission outside bypass mode and gives Claude no guidance on when to use it.
It uses only the /api/v1/systemone endpoint, with no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions), no direct TypeSafe path, and the endpoint URL is hardcoded.

Jev's value for review is unproven (calibrated probabilities but no reasoning trace), and the author's own docs flag it as beta. Rubric weights, thresholds and default 0.8/0.7 gates are the author's invention (comments in verify.go say the 64 cap is invented).
entries.verdict: This is the most complete and best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev MCP server, with fail-closed behavior, budget caps, an audit log and a `--tools` subset. It is still only a tool menu and gives no automatic invocation. Use it as the OpenRouter backend (ideally `--tools review,verify,check,screen` from a pinned, locally built commit) and add your own hook or CLAUDE.md rule to trigger it. Do not expect it to fire on its own, and be careful about sending client diffs.

entries.name: nshcr/jevs
entries.what: Bun/TypeScript stdio MCP server wrapping the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (src/index.ts, src/server.ts). Exposes 7 tools (classify, score, check, assess_structure, assess_batch, jev_list_models, jev_guide) that map to Jev Choice/Score/Noul questions and return typed probabilities. src/provider.ts injects a custom fetch that rewrites the SDK path /api/v1/systemone to /api/alpha/decisions when the origin is openrouter.ai. It also adapts OpenCode Zen, Vercel AI Gateway and Cloudflare. It is packaged as a Codex plugin with a prebuilt 800 KB dist/index.js on the release branch. It includes a jev-mcp skill and local guide resources. It has no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP tool plus a model-discretion skill (jev-mcp). MCP server instructions tell the model to use the tools for focused judgments, but nothing forces or triggers it. There is no hook, so 'automatically whenever it adds value' depends on the model choosing it, and the user would likely still have to nudge it, or add a CLAUDE.md rule or their own PermissionRequest/PreToolUse hook. It can be layered under a separate hook script (the cookbook pattern) but does not provide one.
security: No shell exec, telemetry or installer in runtime code. Runtime grep shows only process.env reads and the SDK fetch. Bun.spawn appears only in build/publish/audit scripts.

Key handling is clean: the key comes from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and is sent only as a Bearer header by the SDK. It is never in argv or tool args. The docs say not to put credentials in tool parameters. src/index.ts sets logLevel off. Errors keep the provider error code but do not echo the full body (README).
providerFetch rewrites only for exact origins and paths (openrouter.ai, opencode.ai, ai-gateway.vercel.sh, api.cloudflare.com). Non-OK responses are passed through unmodified.

Prompt-injection surface: any content sent to Jev is untrusted data, and Jev is reported to be movable by injected instructions in state. Tool outputs are numeric or label only, with no free text. The main risk is a model treating a probability as permission. SKILL.md says 'Confidence is not proof or action permission'. MCP tool annotations are readOnlyHint true and openWorldHint true.

Supply chain: 3 runtime deps pinned exactly (@modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.30.0, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 with npm provenance attestation, zod 4.6.5). bun.lock exists, CI uses --frozen-lockfile --ignore-scripts. The release branch ships an 800 KB prebuilt bundle with CHECKSUMS.sha256 and third-party-notices. I did not audit the bundle itself, only the source. The repo is 8 days old with 1 author, so the trust surface is a single new maintainer. Pin a release commit.
Installation for Claude Code is manual: clone or vendor the release branch and add an .mcp.json entry with command bun. Do not use the Codex marketplace commands.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `content`, `question`, options and levels goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and on to TypeSafe via OpenRouter), together with the Bearer key and model name. Only agent-selected content is sent, and only when a tool is called. Nothing is sent automatically, and jev_guide and startup make no network call. For client projects the model can pass source code, diffs or commands as `content`, so this needs a policy. OpenRouter/TypeSafe retention terms apply. The README claims the service does not persist input, but that is unverified. The README says a timeout or cancellation does not mean the remote side did not run or bill.
entries.failureMode: Tool-level fail-visible and never fail-open into a decision. Errors return isError with JSON {error:{code,action,retry}} (src/errors.ts). Codes seen: NOT_CONFIGURED (missing key or bad base URL), INVALID_REQUEST, INVALID_RESPONSE. The SKILL says never to treat an error as a negative judgment. The SDK timeout is 30 s per attempt (src/index.ts:19) with SDK default retries, so worst-case latency is well above 30 s when OpenRouter is down. The local scheduler admits 4 concurrent requests, queues 32, and rejects after a 1000 ms queue wait. A missing key does not crash the server: it starts, and tools error on first call. Startup errors give exit code 1 with a generic message. Since there is no hook, a failure just yields a tool error in the transcript and never blocks Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools. An estimate from the source, not measured: tool descriptions total about 2.3k chars, plus JSON schemas for five nested tools (item arrays with options/levels and descriptions) of roughly 10-14k chars, so about 3-4k tokens of tool definitions. Server instructions are about 640 chars (about 160 tokens). The skill jev-mcp is small (description about 170 chars; body 4.3 KB loaded only on trigger). Guide resources add about 22 KB but are read on demand. In Claude Code, MCP tools are deferred behind ToolSearch, so the resident cost is names plus instructions, and the full schema loads when used. There is no hook-injected text. Skill listing budget 0.02 is barely affected (one skill).
pros: Real OpenRouter adapter in code: rewrites to /api/alpha/decisions, filters the typesafe/jev- catalog, sets the default model typesafe/jev-1.13, and rejects the null inputs OpenRouter disallows (src/provider.ts). Setup is env-only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a key mapping.
Clean key handling (env only, Bearer header, never argv or tool args), no shell exec or telemetry in runtime code, exact-pinned deps, SDK with npm provenance.

Broadest generic tool surface: classify/score/check/assess_structure/assess_batch cover Choice, Score and Noul. It has concurrency limits (4 in flight, queue 32, 1 s queue timeout), strict zod validation and response-contract checks that turn malformed responses into INVALID_RESPONSE instead of fake numbers.
Well written caller guidance (SKILL.md and jev_guide) that tells the model not to treat probabilities as permission or errors as negatives, which suits a discretionary-use tool.
Fail-visible tool errors with structured retry hints. No blocking behaviour in Claude Code sessions. Prebuilt dist on the release branch means no npm install at runtime (Bun only).
MIT licence. About 47 test cases across 11 files, plus audit and governance scripts and CI on ubuntu and macos.
cons: OpenRouter path is untested live. The author's own docs say 'mock adapter tests only; not really called', and the /alpha endpoint has no SLA. The assumption that the SDK's TypeSafe-shaped body/response matches alpha/decisions is unverified by the author.
No hook and no permission-gating logic. It gives the model a tool but not automatic use, which misses the user's core goal. Nothing implements the cookbook PermissionRequest flow.

Requires Bun >= 1.4.2 (package.json engines), which is not in the user's stack (Node 24). Install is Codex-oriented (marketplace commands, .codex-plugin/plugin.json, env_vars key which is Codex-specific), so Claude Code needs a hand-written .mcp.json and a cloned release commit.

Env var name is hard-coded to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so OPENROUTER_API_KEY needs the ${VAR} mapping. The mapped key is then in the MCP child env, which is exposure to consider alongside the no-secret-leak hook's protected-vars list.
Brand-new and tiny: created 2026-09-22, 10 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no topics or description. Docs and code comments are largely Chinese. Version 0.1.3.

Model-chosen content leaves the machine to OpenRouter/TypeSafe with no redaction or size guard in the server. Client-project code could be sent by discretion. Independent evals say Jev is overconfident on unanswerable inputs and can be swayed by injected instructions in state.
Worst-case latency is unbounded-ish (30 s timeout times SDK retries). assess_batch sends N requests, and 32k context limits mean no large diffs.
Tool schemas are heavy for occasional use (about 3-4k tokens estimated when loaded) relative to a single-purpose Noul gate.
entries.verdict: This is the cleanest and most configurable Jev MCP server, and OpenRouter works by env config alone (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key mapped to TYPESAFE_API_KEY). But it is only a discretionary tool with no hook, its OpenRouter path has never been called live, and it needs Bun plus a hand-made Claude Code config. It is useful as the Jev tool layer under a separate PermissionRequest/PreToolUse hook, but on its own it does not deliver automatic use. Pin a reviewed release commit and add a data-egress rule for client repos.

entries.name: shitianfang/jev-use (npm jev-use 0.8.0)
entries.what: Claude Code / Codex / pi plugin plus npm package that wraps Jev behind two MCP tools (jev_judge for batched noul/choice/score judgments, jev_gate for allow/deny risk-check of one action), a routing SKILL.md that tells the model when to hand decisions to Jev, an optional zero-LLM-token PreToolUse hook (`jev-use hook gate`) that risk-checks every Bash/Write/Edit call, and a `jev-use judge` CLI for bulk data. Adds client-side escalation logic: confidence thresholds (0.5 reported / 0.4 estimated), oversized-state and unreachable handling, credential redaction of gated actions. Backends: TypeSafe direct, OpenRouter, Vercel AI Gateway, mock.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. (1) Model-discretion: jev_judge/jev_gate MCP tools, nudged by the description and by the jev-use skill (skill-description trigger) when installed as a plugin; Claude Code may or may not choose to call them, and no permission mode auto-allows MCP tools so the user must add `mcp__jev` to permissions.allow (in bypass mode this is not needed). (2) Deterministic: the optional PreToolUse `hook gate` runs automatically on every Bash|Write|Edit call, but is not enabled by install and the user must merge gate.hooks.json into settings.json.
security: API key read from env only; never written to disk/logged per SECURITY.md; passed as Authorization header over HTTPS, not in argv (good). MCP server started via `npx -y jev-use@0.8.0 serve` inherits env from Claude Code.
No telemetry/analytics/phone-home claimed (SECURITY.md) and none found in http.ts/backends: only outbound calls are to the configured provider.
