Every run uses `npx -y jev-use@0.8.0`: network fetch of npm package (pinned version, good) with transitive deps; package has a `prepare` script (tsc build) and open issue #3 about `prepare` failing on production installs (npm error 127); no postinstall found. Supply-chain trust rests on a single anonymous maintainer 11 days old.
install.ts uses spawnSync with `shell: false` on Linux and fixed args (no user-controlled interpolation); no curl|sh.

Gate redacts credentials from the proposed ACTION only (src/redact.ts: URL passwords, auth headers, credential flags, secret-name=value, sk-/ghp_/AKIA/xox/AIza/JWT shapes); regex-based, best effort. The surrounding state and anything the model puts into jev_judge `state` is sent verbatim (judge.ts:188-190).

Prompt-injection surface: jev_judge takes state assembled by the LLM from tool output/file contents; verdicts are typed JSON (no free text back except fixed hints), so return-path injection is low. The gate is advisory only-tightening (never auto-allows) so an injected 'allow' just falls through to normal permission flow, but in bypass mode fall-through means nothing checks it.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured provider (OpenRouter https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, or TypeSafe/Vercel if their keys are set and take priority): for jev_judge, whatever `state` string the model chooses to paste (tool output, file excerpts, diffs, logs, up to 30k tokens) plus the questions. For the optional gate hook, on EVERY Bash/Write/Edit call: cwd, permission mode, optional JEV_GATE_STATE, tool name and the full tool_input JSON (entire shell command, and for Write/Edit the full file content / old_string / new_string) after regex secret redaction (hook gate, src/cli.ts:170-176; judge.ts:198-201). No truncation of tool_input found before send except the 30k-token oversized check. Client source code from personal and client projects therefore flows to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on each write when the gate is on; retention/training policy is the provider's.
entries.failureMode: Timeout per attempt 10s, 2 retries with 0.5-5s jittered backoff, honors Retry-After up to 60s (src/backends/http.ts:11-16,34-83). Worst case ~31s+ can exceed the hook's 30s timeout, in which case Claude Code treats the hook as a non-blocking error (effectively fail-open). MCP tools: provider failure becomes escalate:true reason 'unreachable' ('proceed as if Jev didn't exist'), so the model continues. Gate hook: fail-open (exit 0, no output) if stdin invalid or credentials missing/backend construction throws; but if the provider is unreachable at call time the engine returns an escalate verdict, which the hook maps to permissionDecision 'ask' (cli.ts:158,182-186), meaning a Jev outage/429 would prompt the user on every Bash/Write/Edit call (issue #1 raises the doc/behaviour mismatch). Not fail-closed, but not silently open either.
entries.contextCost: Two MCP tools (jev_judge, jev_gate). Description+schema text in src/server.ts is ~7.4 KB source, roughly 4.5-5 KB of model-visible text, approx 1.2-1.6k tokens always loaded (if MCP tool search/deferred loading is on, only names until needed). Plugin form also adds the skill: front-matter description ~1 KB (~250 tokens) always in the skill list, body ~3.4 KB (~900 tokens) loaded only when triggered. No MCP server-level 'instructions'. The gate hook injects no text into context (silent on allow; short reason on deny/ask). Total steady-state overhead roughly 1.5-2k tokens. Also every jev_judge call pays context tokens for state pasted as tool input plus verdict JSON back (SKILL.md admits it is a rate win, not a token win).
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class backend in code: /api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY and default model typesafe/jev-latest (src/backends/openrouter.ts:16-50); user only needs to export OPENROUTER_API_KEY (and not have TYPESAFE_API_KEY set, since auto-detect prefers it) or set JEV_BACKEND=openrouter.
Only project found offering a truly automatic path: skill description trigger plus a real deterministic PreToolUse hook, matching the user's 'Claude must use it without being told' requirement.

Gate is designed to only tighten (deny/ask, silent on allow), never bypasses the existing permission flow, and costs zero LLM tokens; useful safety net in the user's bypass/auto permission modes where nothing else asks.

Careful engineering of failure semantics: typed escalate reasons (unsure/oversized/unreachable/writing), separate confidence thresholds for reported vs estimated confidence, retry/backoff, 30k-token state cap, server starts without credentials and reports a named error.

Credential redaction for gated actions (src/redact.ts) with its own test file; SECURITY.md is explicit about what leaves the machine; no telemetry; version pinned in .mcp.json/hook (jev-use@0.8.0); mock backend for keyless dry runs; MIT; small readable codebase (~2.6k lines TS).
Ships a bulk path (`jev-use judge` CLI) so large lists of items can be classified without passing through the conversation.
cons: Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-19, 18 commits, 1 contributor, 31 stars, last push 2026-09-22; README admits it is substantially AI-written; performance numbers are self-reported and measured through Vercel AI Gateway, never through OpenRouter, and uses the alpha endpoint that may move.

Gate hook sends the full tool_input of every Bash/Write/Edit call (entire file contents being written, commands) to a third party; redaction is regex best-effort and applies only to the action, not the state. Risky for client projects under NDA.

Gate hook launches `npx -y jev-use@0.8.0 hook gate` for every Bash/Write/Edit call: added latency (npx startup plus ~0.25-0.7 s network) per tool call on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks; provider outage/429 turns into an 'ask' prompt on each such call rather than fail-open.

Its safety judgment is generic (state given to Jev is just cwd + permission mode + the action) so it duplicates and is weaker than the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard; 'allow' falls through to bypass mode, so the gate mainly adds a probabilistic deny on destructive commands, with unknown false-positive rate on real dev work (author tested only 12 commands for accuracy).

The MCP tool path is model-discretion, not deterministic: Jev is a rate win, not a token win (SKILL.md), pasting state into jev_judge costs Opus context both ways, and for a coding session most steps (edit, refactor, debug) are generation which the tool explicitly excludes; realistic value is limited to occasional triage/classification/verification steps.

Adds ~1.5-2k tokens of tool/skill definitions to every session; CI shows action_required (not really run), open unmerged external fix PRs (#2, #3), and `prepare` build script issue on production installs; supply-chain exposure via npx on every hook invocation.
Dependence on Jev quality itself is unverified (Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim), and beta Decisions API on OpenRouter.
entries.verdict: The most complete and OpenRouter-ready Jev integration for Claude Code, and the only one with both a skill trigger and a deterministic hook, but it is a 10-day-old single-author project whose real daily benefit is narrow (optional gate plus occasional batched triage) and whose gate sends every Bash/Write/Edit payload to a third party. Reasonable to try MCP + skill with OPENROUTER_API_KEY; enable the gate hook only after reviewing data-egress, per-call npx latency and outage-becomes-ask behaviour, ideally pinned and scoped to personal projects.

entries.name: gecm0/jev-judge-mcp
entries.what: Single-tool stdio MCP server (`judge`) that POSTs typed Choice/Noul/Score questions plus a caller-supplied `state` to TypeSafe's direct System One API and returns the validated JSON answers. It is packaged as a Claude Code plugin (`typesafe@jev`) that bundles the MCP server and a `jev` skill on how to design questions. It is entirely model-discretion: it has no hooks and no proxy.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a skill description trigger. The tool description says 'Reach for it on a close call you cannot settle by running code: choosing among candidate files, symbols or fixes, ... reranking hits, scoring against a rubric, triage', but it also says 'Run the test or the grep where one exists'. Opus 5.5 will only occasionally choose to call it, because it must author state and typed questions itself. There is no deterministic hook, so it does not fully meet the 'Claude Code must use it when needed, without prompting' requirement. The README's own usage example starts with 'Use Jev to...'. It can be strengthened with a CLAUDE.md rule or a custom hook, but that is not provided here.
security: The API key is read from the env var and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv (.mcp.json has no key), and it is validated as printable ASCII (server.mjs:129). The fetch catch deliberately swallows the error, because Node embeds the header value in the TypeError (lines 144-150).
Error bodies are never echoed into the transcript (lines 152-157). This is a good practice.
Hardcoded HTTPS endpoint with redirect:"error". There is no user-controlled URL, so no SSRF or redirect exfiltration.
No shell execution, no file reads, and no .env loading. The only filesystem write is the truncated result at mkdtemp(tmpdir()/jev-*)/result.json with mode 0600, which can contain echoed evidence.
No postinstall script. The package scripts contain only `test`. No telemetry in the code (grep found no analytics).

`npx -y jev-judge-mcp` in .mcp.json is unpinned, so each start can pull a new version from a single-maintainer, 10-day-old package. That is a supply-chain risk, mitigated by npm provenance and by the small dependency set (MCP SDK + typebox). Pin the version, or vendor and read it.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into `state` and the question `instructions` and `criteria` goes to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, with the key as a Bearer token. That can include code snippets, diffs, file contents and tool outputs, at the model's discretion. The server never reads files or forwards session history on its own (README:144-147). Nothing goes to OpenRouter as shipped. Sending client code to TypeSafe raises a per-client data-sharing question, and the user's secret guard does not cover this channel.
entries.failureMode: Fail-loud and fail-open for the workflow. There is a 30 s AbortSignal.timeout (server.mjs:131), no retry and no fallback model. Failures surface as a tool error such as 'Could not reach TypeSafe', 'TypeSafe HTTP 429', or 'Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY' (checked before any network call). Claude sees the error and simply proceeds without Jev, so nothing blocks the session. The tool stays listed even with no key. A hung Jev can stall a turn for up to 30 s, but only when the model chose to call it. It honours MCP cancellation.
entries.contextCost: One tool. Description is about 1,900 chars (~475 tokens). The inputSchema (a typebox union of three question kinds plus record and array descriptions) is roughly 1,500-2,000 chars (~400-500 tokens). The server sets no MCP `instructions`. The skill's frontmatter description is about 550 chars (~140 tokens), always loaded. The SKILL.md body (~113 lines, ~1.5k tokens) loads only when triggered. Total always-on cost is about 1,000-1,200 tokens, which is very cheap. No hook-injected text.
pros: The most complete and best-designed Claude Code packaging of Jev found here: plugin + marketplace + MCP + skill, install is two `claude plugin` commands.

Careful engineering: strict typebox schema validation before the network call, per-question response validation, no error-body echo, key never in argv, redirect:error, 30 s timeout, cancellation, and a private 0600 temp file for large output (server.mjs:85-199).
Tiny always-on context footprint of about 1k tokens for one tool plus a skill description, so it fits alongside gitnexus, playwright and caveman without bloat.
Fail-open: any Jev outage or missing key becomes a tool error and Claude carries on. It cannot wedge sessions or block hooks.

The SKILL.md is high quality: the one-second test, decomposition, fan-out (cites a 11.5x cheaper, 9.6x faster figure from TypeSafe's cookbook), and probability-to-decision thresholds (>0.9 for destructive actions). It teaches Claude to make good calls.

The tool description explicitly targets coding use cases: choosing among candidate files, symbols or fixes, reranking hits, triage. MIT license, small (245-line) server that is easy to audit and fork, and CI with trusted publishing and provenance.
TYPESAFE_MODEL lets you pin a version such as jev-1.13.0.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter. The endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read (server.mjs:125,137). Using OpenRouter needs a small fork, the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified, and the fork then has to be maintained.

Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool: no hook, no proxy, and nothing forces use. Opus tends to solve close calls by running grep or tests, and the description itself says to do that first. The README example even starts with 'Use Jev to...'. It does not meet the 'never prompt Claude to use jev' goal on its own.
Very new and thin: created 2026-09-19, 8 commits over 2 days, 1 star, 0 forks, one maintainer, no GitHub releases, no live-API test and no accuracy evidence. It is version 0.5.2 for a beta model.
Unpinned `npx -y jev-judge-mcp` in .mcp.json pulls whatever the latest version is on every start, from a single new maintainer. Pin the version or vendor it.

Data egress to a second vendor (TypeSafe direct) with only advisory guidance. Nothing scrubs secrets, and the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover mcp__ tools. Sending client code needs a per-client decision.

Model-authored questions are the bottleneck. Claude must spend output tokens and reasoning to build state and typed criteria, so for most everyday coding it is cheaper to just decide. The value is niche: reranking, triage, rubric scoring.
The tool is currently 'a DeepSeek flash router' per skeptics (unverified), and 32k context caps the state size.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered off-the-shelf Claude Code wrapper for Jev, with a tiny context cost and safe failure behavior, but it is TypeSafe-direct only and purely model-discretion. Fork it (about 5 lines) to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, pin the version, and pair it with a CLAUDE.md rule or hook if you want reliable automatic use.

entries.name: sophia-phillipa/master-jev-hook
entries.what: Local Node/Hono HTTP gateway (127.0.0.1:8795, systemd user service) that turns Jev Choice/Score/Noul calls into 5 MCP tools via a thin stdio adapter (master-jev-mcp.mjs), plus a Python hook script (claude_jev.py) installed into ~/.claude/settings.json. Hooks inject a mandatory "consult Jev before any decision with explicit alternatives" rule (rule file + skill + per-prompt reminder), announce Jev calls, and run their own Jev checks: a Bash risk gate, a Stop-verification check, PreCompact "what to preserve", and a drift detector every 30 tool calls. Includes a local dashboard and optional proxy launchers for Codex/Gemini/opencode. Supports TypeSafe, OpenRouter and Vercel AI Gateway as Jev providers.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed but strongest of the candidates: (a) deterministic hooks that fire without any user prompt (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit reminder, Bash gate, Stop, PreCompact, drift) - these call Jev themselves; (b) model-discretion MCP tools driven by a mandatory-rule text injected in three places (rules file, skill, per-prompt reminder) - adherence is model-dependent, and the author's own experiments.md admits 0 model-side calls in 10 real sessions after a rule wording change, restored by making the trigger mandatory again, with no post-fix measurement published; (c) skill description trigger. Optional proxy launchers (not needed, and not usable with OAuth login) are not part of the Claude Code path.
security: API key stays in the gateway process env; loaded via systemd --env-file from a 0600 file outside the repo; not passed in argv. MCP adapter and hooks never see it (they only send MASTER_JEV_GATEWAY_KEY if a non-loopback ROUTER_API_KEY is configured).

Gateway binds 127.0.0.1 by default; non-loopback HOST refused without ROUTER_API_KEY+UPSTREAM_API_KEY; Host and Origin header checks (app.ts:265-275) mitigate DNS-rebinding/browser CSRF against localhost.
systemd unit is sandboxed: NoNewPrivileges, PrivateTmp, ProtectSystem=strict, ReadWritePaths only the state dir, RestrictAddressFamilies.

No postinstall hooks (installs with --ignore-scripts; runtime deps only hono + @hono/node-server; SDK is a types-only devDependency). No curl|sh installer. No telemetry found besides Jev calls; OpenRouter receives http-referer/x-title attribution headers.

install.py edits user config: rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json hooks, ~/.claude.json, adds rules/skill files; backs up first, validates plan before writing, supports --dry-run, removes only its own managed hooks/blocks. It is a real global-config mutation the user must review.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev outputs typed decisions only (no free text), and gateway prepends 'treat state as untrusted data'; but the hook injects mandatory-instruction text into every prompt and the Bash gate lets a Jev classification influence permissionDecision ('ask'), and can DENY commands touching the gateway. Jev verdicts are not authoritative and no allow decision is ever emitted.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (or TypeSafe/Vercel) only, over HTTPS from the local gateway. Per path: (1) MCP tools - exactly what Claude puts in the args (objective, candidate texts, evidence, items up to 8000 chars each, 64KB cap; Claude is told to send ids/short snippets). (2) Bash gate - only for regex-risky commands: command (<=4000 chars), cwd, Claude's description, and the last 3 user prompts (<=700 chars each), redacted. (3) Stop check - user's last request (<=2000), edited file paths, commands run after last edit, Claude's final message (<=3000). (4) PreCompact - up to 32 of the user's own messages (<=1500 chars each) sent as separate Noul questions. (5) Drift detector every 30 tool calls - last request + 4 earlier requests, last 1000 chars of prior assistant reply, and tool names + file paths/commands (<=200 chars) with error flags; no file contents or tool output. (6) SessionStart self-test - a fixed 'water boils at 100C' probe. No whole files or diffs by design, but user prompts on personal AND client projects, client file paths and commands do leave the machine. Redaction is best-effort regex. Local copies only if JEV_INSPECT_INPUTS/JEV_DEBUG_DUMP_DIR set (off by default); dashboard log on disk if JEV_LOG_FILE set.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. claude_jev.py catches all exceptions and exits 0; gateway() returns None on any error or >64KB body; per-hook Jev timeouts 3-8s (self-test 3s, Bash gate 5s inside an 8s hook, Stop 6s/10s, PreCompact 8s/12s, drift 5s/8s); gateway->Jev timeout default 8s (max 15s), retries only on 429/503/529/connection-refused (x2, honoring retry-after up to 5s); low confidence -> abstain -> continue locally. MCP adapter returns 'Gateway unavailable. No decision was applied.' isError with a 17s fetch timeout. Only fail-closed behavior: a Bash command that does systemctl stop/disable/mask/kill master-jev-hook is denied unless Jev says the user requested it (abstention also denies). If gateway is down, SessionStart still adds a status line and instructs Claude to print an error block, and each hook silently degrades.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools, all marked alwaysLoad (per-tool _meta plus server-level alwaysLoad:true written to ~/.claude.json): tool names+descriptions+schemas approx 3.7k chars = ~920 tokens; MCP server instructions 783 chars = ~200 tokens; rule file ~/.claude/rules/master-jev-hook.md 2.4k chars = ~590 tokens always loaded; skill SKILL.md description ~100 tokens (body 7.7k chars ~1.9k tokens when triggered); UserPromptSubmit reminder ~900 chars = ~230 tokens injected on EVERY prompt (duplicates the rule); SessionStart adds ~1.5k chars (~400 tokens) for tool-load request + print-status instruction + status block, and asks Claude to run a ToolSearch turn and print a verbatim status block at the top of the first reply. Roughly 1.7k tokens standing overhead plus ~230 tokens per prompt (cached mostly), plus 'announce with 🔷 lines' text before and after each Jev call. Author measured ~2.8k extra cached tokens per turn.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code (providers.json:11-17, jev.ts) with unit tests; switching from TypeSafe is two env vars in the gateway.env, no code patch. Model typesafe/jev-1.13 and endpoint /api/alpha/decisions match the brief.

Only candidate here that delivers true 'no prompting needed' automation: hooks fire deterministically and the rule is injected on every prompt, so Claude is pushed to call Jev without the user saying so.

Sensible Jev use-cases mapped to real Claude Code events: triage of 3+ grep hits/files (jev_rank), risky-Bash second opinion tuned to bypass/auto workflows (asks only at >=0.80 confidence that a command is severe, irreversible and beyond the request), completion-without-verification check, compaction 'what to keep' scoring.
Fail-open design with bounded timeouts and a hook that swallows all exceptions; never emits an 'allow' decision so it cannot widen permissions.

Good local engineering: typed input validation, 64KB caps, Host/Origin checks, loopback default, hardened systemd unit, keys not in argv, --ignore-scripts install, no runtime deps beyond hono, idempotent installer with backup and --dry-run.
Substantial tests (~190 vitest cases, 51 Python) and a candid experiments.md documenting failures and cost-weighted measurement; local dashboard gives visibility into every Jev call and cost.
Jev cost is negligible (~$0.042/M input, small queries ~600-950 tokens) so paid hook calls are not a budget concern.
cons: Heavy, invasive footprint for a 4-day-old, 0-star, single-author, no-CI, alpha project: requires building a Node service, running a systemd daemon, and rewriting global ~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude.json, rules and skills. Must be reviewed line by line.

Spawns a Python process on every tool call (PostToolUse with no matcher) and every prompt just to count to 30, on top of the user's existing GitNexus/caveman/secret-guard hooks; small but constant latency tax on a heavy all-day workflow.

Sends user prompts (last 3-32 messages), commands, file paths and Claude's final message to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on hooks the user never triggers manually; regex redaction is best-effort. Client projects with confidentiality obligations need explicit sign-off; the guide even states 'by installing, you authorize paid queries'.

Permission-mode interplay uncertain: the Bash gate can return permissionDecision 'ask' (and 'deny' for gateway-off commands), which may interrupt bypass/auto sessions; whether 'ask' overrides bypass mode in Claude Code 2.1.285 was not verified. The Jev's 'routine vs confirm' verdict comes from a probabilistic model (Theo's 'flash router' skepticism applies) and gates only regex-flagged commands, overlapping the user's existing secret-leak guard.

The model-side tool value is questionable for Opus 5.5: Claude must spend output tokens writing structured candidates/evidence, wait 0.7-1.7 s per call, and then only gets a probability; author's own log shows Claude ignored the tools entirely (0 calls in 10 sessions) when the wording allowed opt-out, and the mandatory wording can force calls where Claude's own judgment would be cheaper and better.

Standing context overhead ~1.7k tokens plus a ~230-token reminder on every prompt (duplicating the rule), a forced ToolSearch turn plus a verbatim '🔷 status block' printed in the first reply of every session, and 🔷 announcement lines around each call: noisy and counter to the user's own strict CLAUDE.md efficiency rules.
SessionStart makes a blocking live paid self-test (up to 3 s) every startup/resume/clear/compact/fork.

Drift/stop/compact hooks' benefit is speculative: Jev is a typed-decision model with a 32k window judging transcript summaries; no published evidence they improve outcomes. Stop check is limited to 3 nudges and skipped if any test/lint command ran.

Not packaged as a Claude Code plugin/marketplace or npm package: no update path, manual clone/build/systemd setup, Claude Desktop-oriented workarounds (deferral bugs) add complexity; the OpenRouter alpha endpoint schema was not verified live by me, only via mocked tests.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed candidate that natively supports OpenRouter (JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter + OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and truly auto-invokes Jev via hooks, with solid fail-open engineering and tests, but it is a 4-day-old single-author alpha that installs a daemon, rewrites global Claude Code config, adds a Python spawn on every tool call, and ships transcript snippets to a third party. Worth a sandboxed trial (install with --dry-run, disable the drift/UserPromptSubmit/SessionStart hooks, keep the MCP tools plus Bash-gate/Stop only), not a drop-in all-day default, especially for client projects.

entries.name: jfrader/jev-mcp
entries.what: Zero-dependency Go stdio MCP server (single main.go, 822 lines) that wraps the System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone) and exposes four tools: ask (batched typed questions), choose, score, noul. It validates inputs, retries 429/529 with backoff, adds a 'reliable' flag against a min_confidence threshold, and rejects state over 120 KB locally. It ships a SKILL.md with frontmatter that describes when an agent should use Jev. It is unofficial and not affiliated with TypeSafe.
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only, via the MCP tool descriptions and the optional SKILL.md description trigger. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy, and no forced trigger. Opus decides case by case whether a closed-set decision merits a Jev call, and in practice it will rarely choose to call an external classifier for decisions it can make itself, unless CLAUDE.md contains explicit routing rules. That is the weakness against the user's 'automatic' requirement: it is only as automatic as the model's own habit, and a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge is needed to make it reliable.
security: API key is read from the environment only (main.go:173), never from argv, so it does not appear in the process list. With claude mcp add -e the value is written in plaintext to ~/.claude.json; use a wrapper script that sources a 0600 file to avoid that.

No shell execution or os/exec, no telemetry, no file reads or writes, and no network calls except the single POST to baseURL/v1/systemone. There is no install script or postinstall; the only build step is make build.

TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is unrestricted (any http or https URL), so a poisoned env would send the key and state elsewhere. That is normal for env-configured clients, and http:// is allowed, so keys could go in cleartext if misconfigured.

The tool result is Jev's typed JSON only (no free text), so returned data has a small prompt-injection surface. The input surface is the state that Claude chooses to pass, which can contain untrusted repo content. SKILL.md itself warns that adversarial content can steer answers, so Jev output is a hint and not a guard.
Error bodies are truncated to 300 chars (main.go:257-259) and returned to the model. This is low risk.

Supply chain: brand-new repo, 0 stars, one anonymous-ish maintainer, no releases, and you must build from source. Pin a commit hash and review the ~800-line main.go before building; I read all of it and found nothing malicious.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the 'state' argument plus the question text and criteria. This is an arbitrary JSON or text payload of up to 120 KB, and it could be code snippets, diffs, logs, or file contents that Claude chooses to include. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background, because it is a pure request/response server that only acts on tool calls. It goes to the configured base URL: OpenRouter if you set it, otherwise api.typesafe.ai. With OpenRouter, that traffic is subject to OpenRouter's data policies and to TypeSafe as the model provider. The README says TypeSafe does not train on customer data, which is unverified. For client projects, Claude may forward client code or secrets unless an instruction or a hook stops it. The existing secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__*, so it would not scan Jev payloads, and a matcher for mcp__jev__.* would need adding.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level, because Claude Code just sees an isError tool result and continues. The HTTP client timeout is 30 s (main.go:36), with up to 3 attempts on 429/529 only, and backoff of 0.5 s then 1 s or Retry-After capped at 15 s. Worst case is roughly 30 s per attempt on a network hang, but the retry only triggers on 429/529, so a hang fails after 30 s without retrying. Other 5xx errors are not retried. The process exits at startup if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset, which shows up as a failed MCP connection, but Claude Code itself works normally. It is a synchronous single-threaded loop (run(), one request at a time), and there is no circuit breaker. A slow Jev blocks the server, but not other tools.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. The tool definitions (names, descriptions and JSON schemas in main.go, about lines 668-735) are about 6-8k characters, which I estimate at roughly 1.5-2.2k tokens when loaded. Claude Code's tool search defers MCP tool schemas, so only the names sit in context until a tool is needed. The server sends no MCP 'instructions' field (initialize returns only protocolVersion, capabilities and serverInfo, main.go:410-415). There are no hooks and no injected text. If SKILL.md is installed, add roughly 100 tokens for the always-listed description, and about 1.4k tokens when the skill is invoked (5.4k chars). Overall a low context footprint.
pros: OpenRouter works with config only. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api produces the exact /v1/systemone path that OpenRouter documents for the TypeSafe SDKs (main.go:221 versus typesafe-sdk.md). The request schema matches, and bare model IDs such as jev-latest are mapped to typesafe/ by OpenRouter.

Small, auditable and dependency-free. It is one 822-line Go file with no exec, no filesystem access and no telemetry, so I could read all of it. The key comes from env, not argv, and the binary is trivially pinned.

Well-shaped tool surface. Batched ask amortises one request over many questions, and the reliable/min_confidence flag gives the model an act-or-escalate signal. Local guards include a 120 KB state limit, validation, and retry with Retry-After.
Low context cost: 4 tools, no MCP instructions field, no hooks, and it adds nothing to turns that don't use it. Failures are non-blocking (fail-open).

SKILL.md is a well-written trigger for closed-set decisions and includes honest limits (not a calculator, literal, steerable, English-strongest), which suits Jev's real strengths. The tests are offline and cover the retry and 401 paths.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain tool and skill, so Claude Code calls it only if the model decides to. Opus 5.5 can already route, classify and triage in its head, so the tool will likely sit unused unless you add CLAUDE.md rules or a hook. There is nothing deterministic in this repo that fires it.

Very immature: 0 stars, 6 commits in 1 day, one author (git identities 'Fran' and 'fran'), no releases, no tags, no prebuilt binaries. It needs a Go toolchain to build. It is explicitly unofficial and was born as an OpenCode integration ('Initial commit: ... for opencode'), so it has not been tested against Claude Code (README lists OpenCode, Claude Desktop and Cursor). The tools are standard MCP and should work.

Leaks nothing on its own, but the payload is model-chosen, so client code or secrets can flow to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. Your secret guard does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and you would need an extra PreToolUse matcher.
The env var naming is confusing (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holds an OpenRouter key). claude mcp add -e writes the key in plaintext into ~/.claude.json, so use a wrapper script instead.

Built for System One's typed decisions only. It does not use OpenRouter's /alpha/decisions API or the Jev Router, and it has no code awareness, so 'which file holds the bug' still depends on Claude passing sufficient state. State beyond 32k tokens or with unrelated detail degrades accuracy, per its own docs. Value versus just letting Opus decide is unproven, with Theo's 'flash router' claim untested.
Sync and single-threaded with a 30 s timeout and no circuit breaker. A stall blocks the Jev tools and adds an extra model turn per decision, which can cost more time than it saves.
entries.verdict: The best plain MCP building block found for Jev: tiny, readable, and switchable to OpenRouter with three env vars and no code changes. It is only model-discretion, though, so on its own it will not meet the 'Claude Code uses it automatically' goal. Use it as the tool layer, build from a pinned commit after review, and pair it with CLAUDE.md routing rules or a hook (plus an mcp__jev__ matcher on the secret guard) to make invocation reliable.

entries.name: burnigtm/jev-mcp
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Node >=20) exposing 9 jev_* tools plus 8 pack resources. Each tool sends a state plus typed Choice/Noul/Score questions to TypeSafe System One through @typesafe-ai/sdk, then applies local TypeScript policy to produce an action of auto, review or escalate. Tools cover step routing, prepared tool-call selection, patch review, claim verification, untrusted-content screening, candidate ranking and a free-form evaluate. It never edits files, executes anything or generates text. It ships a SKILL.md that tells the host when to call the tools, but no hooks and no plugin manifest. It is not published to npm: the npm package named jev-mcp belongs to a different author (rashedInt32, v0.5.1). Install means clone, npm ci, npm run build.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There is no deterministic hook and no proxy. Claude may call jev_review or jev_step if the SKILL/tool descriptions persuade it, but nothing forces it. The main flow (jev_step with candidates) requires Claude to prepare structured call candidates and host-fact flags first, which costs extra Claude turns and tokens and is unlikely to happen naturally in Claude Code. The user's requirement of automatic use is therefore only weakly met.
security: Built by a Cursor cloud agent: 16 of 33 commits are by 'Cursor Agent', 8 by 'Serhii Leshchynskyi @ISD' and 8 by burnigtm. The repo also contains .github/workflows/notify-jev-mcp.yml, which posts PR events to a Cursor Cloud Agent, and Windows helper scripts. This is a personal Cursor-workflow project, not something official from TypeSafe.

Not on npm, so no registry supply-chain hop: git clone, npm ci and build. Runtime dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (author evinism, MIT, created 2026-09-12) and zod. There are no postinstall scripts or curl|sh installers. The npm package named jev-mcp is an unrelated package by another author, so `npx jev-mcp` would run the wrong code (typosquat-like risk).

API key comes from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and can go in the MCP env block or shell, so it does not appear in argv. The docs say the server does not log state, diffs, claims or keys. The SDK is created with logLevel off. fetch uses redirect:error, which prevents redirect-based key leakage.

The base URL is strongly hardened: HTTPS only, HTTP allowed only for loopback, custom hosts need an explicit opt-in flag, and userinfo, query strings, obfuscated IPs and private, link-local and metadata addresses are rejected (config.ts). This is unusually careful code.

Prompt-injection surface: it returns typed probabilities only, with no free text from the model. Host-supplied flags (authorized, schema_valid, preconditions_met) gate executable call dispatch, and the SKILL says never to derive them from untrusted content. jev_screen is a probabilistic injection filter, and Jev is a small classifier, so its detection quality is unmeasured.
No shell execution and no telemetry in the server. Calls go only to the configured TypeSafe or custom base URL.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to pass as tool arguments leaves the machine, sent to api.typesafe.ai (or to openrouter.ai if reconfigured). That means the task text, observations (command output, test results), diffs, claims and evidence, candidate tool-call descriptions and argument shapes, and candidate text (capped at 2000 characters each). State is truncated to about 32k-64k tokens. Raw host arguments stay local unless the call is selected. The server reads no files itself and has no ambient collection. Nothing is sent unless Claude invokes a tool, and no telemetry goes to any third party. Client-project code and diffs will go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter whenever jev_review or jev_gate is called. That matters for client confidentiality and OpenRouter data-policy settings.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft and advisory. There is no hook, so a Jev failure or timeout cannot block Claude Code. The default deadline is 30 s per tool call (JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS) and it is shared across retries. There is no fabricated verdict, and errors return isError with code CONFIG_ERROR, TIMEOUT or API_ERROR plus a retryable flag. A missing key returns CONFIG_ERROR. In the worst case Claude waits up to 30 s, so lower the timeout to about 3 s. When the SKILL guidance is not followed, nothing happens at all.
entries.contextCost: Nine tools registered eagerly. Descriptions total about 2.8k chars (roughly 700 tokens). Input schemas are zod with nested candidate/execution objects (step.ts and tool-route.ts are about 11k chars each of source), so I estimate about 4-6k tokens of tool definitions in total. That is heavy for a marginal helper, though Claude Code's deferred tool loading (ToolSearch) reduces the standing cost. The server sets no MCP `instructions`. It has no hooks, so there is no per-turn injection. The optional SKILL.md adds only a short description (about 100 tokens) until it is triggered, and its body is about 1.4k tokens.
pros: Most complete Jev toolkit found: 9 recipes (review, verify, gate, screen, rank, step and tool routing) with pre-built question packs and local policy thresholds (auto, review or escalate). It also refuses to auto-approve when the context is truncated.

Solid engineering for a 2-week-old repo: 19 test files (about 3.3k lines) against 3.5k lines of source, an MCP stdio transport test, an offline packed-install test, a benchmark, and CI on Node 20 and 22 across Windows and Linux. MIT licence.

Security-conscious code: env-only key handling (not in argv), a strict base-URL validator, redirect:error, logging off, and no shell execution, telemetry or postinstall. Fail-explicit errors never invent a verdict.

Config-only OpenRouter path is plausible: the SDK calls {baseURL}/v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MCP_ALLOW_CUSTOM_BASE_URL=1 and JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 would target it.
The docs name Claude Code as a supported stdio host (docs/install.md:54). jev_review and jev_gate are concrete, useful pre-completion checks that a senior dev could plausibly want.
Read-only, idempotent tools with readOnlyHint annotations, so they can be auto-allowed in the user's permission mode without prompt friction.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code. The variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the user would have to put an OpenRouter key there plus enable the custom-URL flag. Schema parity with OpenRouter is unverified, and the `doctor` models.list call may break.

Not on npm. The npm package jev-mcp is a different project (rashedInt32), so `npx jev-mcp` would run the wrong code. The user must clone, npm ci, build and pin an absolute path. There are no releases or tags and the version is 0.1.0.

Automatic invocation is weak. It is model-discretion tools only, with no hooks. jev_step needs Claude to prepare candidate calls and set host-fact flags (authorized, schema_valid, preconditions_met), which is awkward in Claude Code's native tool loop. The skill is Cursor/Codex-oriented and must be copied by hand.

Bloated for a helper: 9 tools with heavy nested schemas (about 4-6k tokens) and overlapping tools (jev_step vs jev_coding_loop vs jev_tool_route, and review vs verify vs gate). Much of its 'reduce partner-model turns' premise does not apply, because Claude Code with Opus 5.5 has no cheaper partner model to route to.

Client-project diffs and observations get sent to a beta third-party model on every review or gate. The README admits live quality and cost savings are unmeasured. Jev has no reasoning and outputs probabilities only, so its review verdict is a weak signal next to Opus's own reasoning.

Immature and single-vendor: created 2026-09-17, last push 2026-09-21, about 33 commits, 62 stars, 10 forks, and about half of the commits authored by a Cursor cloud agent. The repo carries Cursor-specific workflow/dashboard scaffolding and Windows scripts that add noise. Bus factor is roughly one person.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and most complete Jev MCP found (nine recipes, tests, hardened config), but it is TypeSafe-only in code, must be built from source, and relies on Claude choosing to call it. That is not the automatic, hook-driven integration the user wants. Usable as an opt-in review/gate helper after a small env-only or forked OpenRouter tweak, but not as the core integration.

entries.name: rashedInt32/jev-mcp (npm jev-mcp)
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (TypeScript, wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing six tools that call Jev's System One endpoint (Choice/Score/Noul). Also ships as a Claude Code plugin (plugin.json inlines mcpServers -> npx -y jev-mcp@0.5.1) plus a skills/jev/SKILL.md describing when to call the tools. Answers are validated against the question sent and gated into act/review/abstain and yes/no/uncertain. jev_triage reads files server-side (confined to roots, credential-name deny list) so file contents go to Jev but not into the agent context.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There are no hooks and no proxy, so nothing is deterministic. The skill's own trigger text and body are deliberately conservative: 'Prefer an ordinary answer for a single judgment in conversation', 'Do not reach for a tool to look rigorous', and 'Do not call a tool to prototype what will become shipped code.' It steers Claude toward Jev only for repeated judgments over many items (triage of dozens of files, ranking candidates). In daily Opus coding that is rare, so expect Claude to rarely call it on its own. It will not run without the user asking, and rewriting the skill or adding a CLAUDE.md nudge is needed to make usage frequent.
security: API key is never a tool argument (README design rule 3); read from env or a key file, so it does not appear in argv/ps. With `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` the key would sit in ~/.claude.json, so the 0600 key-file route (JEV_KEY_FILE) is better.

jev_triage file reads: paths must be below JEV_FILE_ROOTS (default = the cwd of the server, i.e. the project Claude Code was started in), checked lexically and after realpath. Credential-name deny list in src/files.ts:57-65 (.env*, .ssh, .aws, .npmrc, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa, credentials/secrets, ~/.config/typesafe|gh, the server's own key file). It is name-based only, so secrets in ordinary source files, config.json, or hard-coded tokens still go out. Only regular text files, no truncation, 200k chars max per item.

Prompt-injection surface: the model chooses which paths to send, and file contents go to a third-party API. The tool result never echoes file contents, only answers, so injected text cannot flow back through this tool. Result strings such as verdict and action are computed locally. The SKILL.md tells the agent to treat files as untrusted.

No shell execution, no child_process, no telemetry in the repo code. The SDK sends only User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers. No postinstall/preinstall script in package.json. `prepare` exists but does not run for registry installs.

Supply chain: plugin runs `npx -y jev-mcp@0.5.1` at every start, so it pulls an unpinned transitive tree from npm from a sole maintainer with an 8-star repo. The version is pinned but the dependency ranges (^) are not lockfile-pinned for npx users. Pin and review, or vendor it. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__ tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so jev_triage bypasses it.
Debug logging: SDK logger at TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs request bodies (state) to stderr. Headers are redacted. Default level is not debug.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state`/`question`/`options` (diffs, code snippets, file text, tool outputs) for jev_classify/score/check/ask, plus full file contents for every `path` item in jev_triage (up to 50 files x 200k chars per call, one request each), minus the credential-name deny list. Sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone by default, or to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says (OpenRouter would then receive it and route it to TypeSafe, which matters for client projects under NDA). Nothing else leaves the machine: no telemetry, no repo metadata. The API key goes in the Authorization header only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors come back as isError results with a classified kind (no_api_key, authentication, rate_limit, server_error, timeout, connection, malformed_response, file_access) and retryable flag, so Claude just continues without Jev. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), SDK retries 2x on 408/429/5xx with 500 ms to 5 s backoff, so worst case is about 45 s+ for a single stalled call, not the claimed 70-500 ms. Nothing blocks the session and there is no hook. If the npx download fails or the key is missing the server still starts (lazy client) and each tool returns a clear error. A missing MCP connection is simply an absent tool.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Tool descriptions total about 2.4k chars, but the JSON schemas with long .describe() strings (state, question, options, levels, threshold params, the nested QuestionSpec union in jev_ask and jev_triage) push it to roughly 14-16k chars, which I estimate at about 3.5-4.5k tokens for names, descriptions and schemas. That is well below Playwright's 30+ tools. The server sets no `instructions` field (src/index.ts:252 `new McpServer({name, version})`). The skill adds a ~700-char description to the skills listing (~150-200 tokens) and the 203-line SKILL.md body (~2.5k tokens) loads only when triggered. No hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred-tool loading (ToolSearch), the schemas may only load on demand.
pros: Best-engineered Jev MCP I inspected: answer validation against the question sent (malformed_response instead of trusting a bad label), caller-owned option sets, confidence gating, classified errors with retryable flag, stderr-only logging (src/index.ts:80-85).

Runs on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, and the base URL is read from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (SDK index.mjs:58,513) with path /v1/systemone (index.mjs:554), which lines up with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Switching to OpenRouter is env-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, key, JEV_MODEL) with no fork needed, in principle.

jev_triage keeps file contents out of Claude's context and screens up to 50 files per call for about $0.04 per 1M input tokens. This is the one workflow with a plausible coding payoff (find which files matter before opening them).

Real safety design for the file-reading tool: root confinement, symlink re-check after realpath, FIFO guard, no truncation, credential-name deny list, no file content in errors or results (src/files.ts).

Solid hygiene: MIT license, CI on Node 20/22/24 with `npm ci --ignore-scripts` and npm audit, about 67 tests including an offline stdio integration suite, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec, key never in argv, and low context footprint (6 tools, no server instructions, no hooks).
Fail-open, and adds zero latency or tokens on turns that do not use it. Compatible with the user's existing hooks because it adds none.
cons: Not automatic in the deterministic sense the user wants. It is model-discretion, and its own SKILL.md and README tell Claude to answer itself for one-off judgments, so Claude will seldom call it during ordinary coding. There is no hook, transparent proxy or auto-trigger; Opus 5.5 is a better judge than a 'System One' classifier for single decisions.

No OpenRouter support in the repo: no OpenRouter env var, doc or test. The OpenRouter route depends on the OpenRouter System One schema matching the TypeSafe SDK's request and response bodies, which I could not verify statically. The wrong default model id ('jev-latest') must be overridden with JEV_MODEL, and jev_models likely misbehaves on OpenRouter's /v1/models. The plugin ships no env block, so you must hand-register the server with -e flags or a key file instead of the one-command plugin install.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-17, 10 commits, 2 contributors (9 by the author), 8 stars, 1 issue/PR, no GitHub releases, four npm versions in 9 days. Formally beta on a beta model, and the plugin runs `npx -y` at each session start, which is a live supply-chain fetch on a machine with client projects.

Data egress on client projects: jev_triage ships whole file contents to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter then TypeSafe). The deny list is name-based only, and the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not see mcp__jev__ calls. Client NDAs may forbid it; JEV_FILE_ROOTS=off or a narrow root is required.

Jev is a one-pass chooser with no reasoning and cannot compute, count or compare dates (README 'When not to reach for this'), and confidence is only distribution concentration, not correctness. This restricts it to screening and ranking, which are the least critical steps of coding work.

Failure timing is worse than the marketing: 15 s per-attempt timeout with 2 retries means a slow API can stall a tool call for tens of seconds. In the plugin, using it inside the jev-mcp checkout itself fails (README dev note).
entries.verdict: Best-built Jev MCP and the one to use if you want Jev tools at all. It is easy to point at OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL and a key file (unverified against OpenRouter's schema, so smoke-test with jev_models and one jev_check). But it is opt-in model-discretion by design: Claude will rarely reach for it unprompted, so it does not deliver the automatic, hook-like integration the user asked for. Pin the version, restrict JEV_FILE_ROOTS, and treat it as a niche triage add-on rather than the core integration.

entries.name: freepik-company/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Go stdio MCP server (~2.3k lines incl. tests/docs) wrapping the OpenRouter/TypeSafe System One endpoint. Exposes generic 'decide' (choice/noul/score questions over arbitrary state) plus three convenience wrappers (classify, verify, rerank) and list_models. Validates that provider answers match the asked questions; returns the raw provider response with usage.cost. It only acts when the model chooses to call a tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, skills, CLAUDE.md snippet or plugin shipped. Claude Code will call classify/verify/rerank/decide only if the tool descriptions persuade Opus to do so; descriptions are generic ('Evaluate named, typed questions...') with no coding-workflow triggers and MCP tools may be deferred behind ToolSearch, so real-world auto use will be rare unless the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill/hook on top. Does not meet the 'never say use jev' bar on its own.
security: API key read only from server env (config.go:37-39), never a tool argument, not in argv of the server process; but `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` (README) writes the literal key into ~/.claude.json plaintext, and the `-e OPENROUTER_API_KEY="$OPENROUTER_API_KEY"` form puts the key in the shell/argv of the `claude mcp add` command once. Docker variant inherits env without argv exposure.
Provider error bodies are never surfaced, only HTTP status (client.go:151-153); transport errors sanitized (:144-148) so an echoed key cannot reach the model.
HTTPS enforced, plain HTTP only on loopback, no userinfo/query in BASE_URL (config.go:51-62); redirects refused (client.go:104); 1 MiB request / 2 MiB response caps; 30s timeout.
No os/exec, no telemetry or analytics in server code (grep clean; only os/exec in a test file). Static binary, tiny dep set (go-sdk v1.8.0, segmentio/encoding, oauth2 indirect).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is typed JSON (choice/probabilities), so limited free-text return; but inputs are model-chosen text, and BASE_URL/API_KEY env can redirect key if the MCP config is tampered.

Supply chain: Apache-2.0, GitHub Actions pinned to SHAs, govulncheck in CI, dependabot, SHA-256 checksums for release archives, GHCR image, MCP Registry entry. No curl|sh installer, no postinstall. Install requires downloading a third-party binary or `go install ...@latest` (unpinned, needs Go 1.26.4 toolchain per go.mod which user may not have; Docker or release binary avoid this). Single maintainer (Mario Campos, Freepik) org account, 4 stars, unaudited.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model puts into tool arguments: 'state' (arbitrary JSON), question instructions/criteria, or classify/verify/rerank items/claims/evidence/candidates (up to 1 MiB) go via HTTPS POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with Authorization Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: no code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs leave unless Claude copies them into a call. No telemetry to other hosts. Data is subject to OpenRouter (and downstream TypeSafe) retention/terms; matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but non-blocking overall: on timeout (30s hard, http.Client.Timeout), non-2xx (only status reported), invalid JSON or inconsistent answers, the tool returns an MCP error and Claude carries on without Jev. No retries. If the API key is missing the process exits at startup (main.go:185-188) so the MCP shows as failed to connect, harmless to the session. It is not in the hot path of any built-in tool, so Jev being down never blocks work. 30s worst case wait is long versus claimed 70-500 ms typical.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. Descriptions ~1.7k chars; embedded schemas: input 2.0k, output 1.2k (output schemas are attached per tool and duplicated for classify/verify/rerank via taskOutput incl. $defs), tasks 1.7k (with $defs copied into each of 3 tools) -> est. 9-12k chars of tool defs total, roughly 2.5-3k tokens when loaded (fewer if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch; only names load until needed). No MCP 'instructions' field set (server.go passes nil options). No hook-injected text.
pros: Only candidate-type that already targets OpenRouter by default with the correct System One endpoint (client.go:95, config.go:24) and the OpenRouter decisions-model catalogue (models.go:159); works with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY, no patching.

Very clean, small, readable codebase (~700 lines of Go non-test), no shell execution, no telemetry, hardened HTTP client (no redirects, size/time caps, sanitized errors) and answer validation that fails on inconsistent probabilities.
Ships a prebuilt binary or Docker image so no npx/uvx and no toolchain needed; static Go binary starts instantly and adds little RAM; Claude Code registration is one line (README).
Low context footprint (5 tools, ~3k tokens, none in hot path) and read-only annotations; safe to leave enabled globally at negligible risk; fail-open in practice because nothing depends on it.

Generic 'decide' exposes all three Jev primitives (choice, noul, score) so it can be reused for arbitrary coding decisions (e.g. is this diff risky, which file is relevant) if the user adds prompting/rules; rerank and classify are plausible for triage of search hits, log lines, issue routing.
Tests present for config, client, models, tasks, server, main; CI with govulncheck, SHA-pinned actions, release checksums, MCP Registry publish.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool, no hook/skill/CLAUDE.md; the generic descriptions don't tell Opus when in a coding session to prefer Jev over its own reasoning, so it will mostly go unused; violates the user's core requirement unless paired with additional glue (CLAUDE.md rule, skill, or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook).

Extra tool-call round trip via Opus costs more time and tokens than the ~cents saved; Opus is far stronger at code judgment than a 'System One' router-like model, so value for daily coding is marginal (classify/rerank use cases are generic support-ticket style per README examples, not code-centric).

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-21, 9 commits, 1 human contributor, 4 stars, 0 forks, 7 issues/PRs, 3 releases in 8 days; API churn likely (Jev itself is beta). Note server.json still says version 0.2.0 while latest is 0.3.1.

Does not use the OpenRouter alpha /decisions API; uses /api/v1/systemone only. Bare default model 'jev-latest' vs OpenRouter's '~typesafe/jev-latest' / 'typesafe/jev-1.13' ids; depends on OpenRouter accepting the alias (README claims yes; not verified by running); pin JEV_MODEL explicitly.

Key storage: Claude Code stores `-e` env in ~/.claude.json in plaintext; data sent to OpenRouter is a concern for client projects when the model decides what to put in 'state'/'text' fields (no redaction, no allowlist, no size guard beyond 1 MiB). Existing secret-leak guard hook only covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* calls.
go install needs Go 1.26.4+ (go.mod), unpinned @latest; the safe route is the release binary + checksum or Docker (adds container startup latency and docker dependency).
No Jev-specific prompt/rules for coding tasks, no caching, no batching guidance; 30s timeout too long for interactive use.
entries.verdict: Best-quality plain MCP wrapper found for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (correct endpoint, safe defaults, tiny context cost), but on its own it is discretionary tool availability, not automatic integration. Use it only as the transport layer, and pair it with a CLAUDE.md/skill or hook so Claude actually invokes it; do not expect it to add value for daily coding without that.

entries.name: clouatre-labs/decisions-judge-mcp (npm: decisions-judge-mcp)
entries.what: Single-tool stdio MCP server (Node >=20, ESM, ~360 lines server.mjs plus 2 provider files). Exposes one tool, `judge`, that forwards {state, questions} (noul/choice/score) to the TypeSafe System One API via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk and returns typed answers, model and usage. Any failure returns a {fallback:true,error} envelope instead of an MCP error. Optional Cloudflare Workers AI provider and optional unauthenticated HTTP transport. Its flagship consumer (clouatre-labs/agentic-coder-skill) uses it only inside a scripted Scout/Build pipeline for tier classification and premise gating, not as an ambient helper.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces Claude to call it: no hook, no skill trigger, no CLAUDE.md snippet shipped. The tool description says what it is but gives no guidance on WHEN a coding agent should use it, so Opus 5.5 will rarely call it unprompted. Making it automatic would require the user to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a custom skill/hook, which is exactly what this candidate does not provide.
security: API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY*), passed by `claude mcp add --env` so it lands in ~/.claude.json, not in argv; SDK redacts Authorization in debug logs and server pins logLevel 'off' so nothing corrupts stdout (typesafe-api.mjs:44, audit F1)

Run with `npx -y decisions-judge-mcp` (unpinned) fetches latest npm release on every launch; single-maintainer package, 12 days old, so supply-chain exposure unless pinned to an exact version. No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json; 3 runtime deps

Input hardening: __proto__ key stripping, 256 KiB payload cap, question-spec validation before any request (server.mjs:126-160); no shell execution, no filesystem access, no telemetry beyond SDK headers X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime

Prompt-injection surface is low: the tool only returns probabilities/option names, no free text; but the model (Claude) chooses what state to send, so injected content in state could steer questions, and answers could steer Claude's decisions
Optional HTTP transport is explicitly unauthenticated (README warning); irrelevant unless enabled
Apache-2.0, REUSE compliant, SECURITY.md with private advisory process, OpenSSF scorecard workflow
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the `state` and `questions` arguments of a judge call (up to 256 KiB per call) goes to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai/api if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is set), plus the bearer key and SDK User-Agent/runtime headers. The server itself reads no files, diffs or tool outputs; egress is model-chosen, so summarized repo state, file paths, diffs or code snippets could leave if Claude includes them. The flagship skill's own docs flag this as third-party transit (agentic-coder-skill SKILL.md item 9). Matters for client projects; no allow/deny filter exists and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools unless matcher is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every error (network, 4xx/5xx, bad key, missing key, oversize payload, malformed question) returns a normal tool result {fallback:true,error} with exit 0 (server.mjs:143-176; typesafe-api.mjs:116-143). Missing key only prints a stderr warning at startup, server still handshakes. Timeout: caller-supplied timeout_ms up to 60000, otherwise the SDK default timeout (not read from source here), SDK retries 408/5xx up to 2 times with backoff (retry list typesafe-api.mjs:45, DEFAULT maxRetries 2, backoffInitialMs 500); 429/529 rotate across configured keys with no delay. Worst case a slow Jev stalls one tool call, never the session. Because the tool is model-invoked, a fallback envelope simply makes Claude proceed without it.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`judge`). Approx tokens (chars/4): description about 330 chars, MCP server instructions about 400 chars, JSON schema of inputSchema (zod unions for state, entryType, criteria, nested records) plus outputSchema about 2000-2500 chars. Estimated 650-800 tokens total, and lower if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via tool search (then only the name and short description are always present). No hook-injected text, no skill text. Small.
pros: Only candidate here that is a thin, readable wrapper (about 690 lines total) around the OFFICIAL @typesafe-ai/sdk, and I verified from SDK source that TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + bearer key is enough to point it at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, no fork needed (sdk index.mjs:58, 514, 555, 581)
Exposes all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) in one call with arbitrary JSON state, so it is a reusable generic building block for any hook/skill/CLAUDE.md rule that the user later writes
Genuinely fail-open: fallback envelope on every error, missing key does not break MCP startup, no stdout pollution (logLevel pinned off), client abort propagates

Good hygiene for a 12-day-old repo: Apache-2.0, SHA-pinned Actions, zizmor/scorecard/REUSE, SECURITY.md, three self-audits that found and fixed real issues, releases v1.5.0, no postinstall, minimal deps, readOnlyHint annotation
Small context footprint (one tool, roughly 700 tokens or less) so it costs almost nothing to keep installed
Has a documented real consumer (agentic-coder-skill) showing the intended pattern: propose inline, validate with judge, deterministic fallback, so it demonstrates safe use of noul thresholds
cons: Does NOT meet the core requirement: no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, and the tool description gives no trigger conditions, so Claude Code will use it only when the model happens to think of it; the only 'automatic' usage in the ecosystem is inside another repo's bespoke Scout/Build pipeline skill

Not OpenRouter-native: OpenRouter support is only possible through an undocumented env-var trick (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) with a TYPESAFE_* variable holding an OpenRouter key; schema parity with OpenRouter's /v1/systemone and model-id mapping (jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-1.13) are unverified and could fail closed into fallback envelopes silently

Extra model-driven step per use: Claude must author state plus questions, so gains over just letting Opus decide are unclear for ordinary coding decisions (Jev returns probabilities, no reasoning; a 'DeepSeek flash router' skeptic claim is unverified)

Data egress is model-chosen and unfiltered: whatever state Claude serializes (paths, diffs, snippets) goes to a third party; for client projects this needs an explicit rule, and the existing secret guard hook does not match mcp__ tools

Very young and single-maintainer (79 of 82 commits by one person, remainder a bot; 4 stars, 1 fork, 30 issues/PRs total, created 2026-09-20, 5 releases in 6 days), README already had wrong example output fixed in audit F2; moving API surface (SDK 0.6.0, MCP server SDK ^2.0.0 with spec 2026-07-28)
npx -y unpinned on every start means silent supply-chain updates and npm resolution latency; must pin exact version or install globally
Silent degradation: fail-open returns success-shaped results, so a bad key or wrong base URL looks fine to Claude and it just ignores the answer; no health signal to the user
entries.verdict: Best available MCP transport layer for Jev: tiny, sound, fail-open, and via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL it can hit OpenRouter's System One endpoint with no fork. But by itself it gives zero automatic invocation, so it is only useful as the plumbing under a user-authored CLAUDE.md rule, skill or hook that tells Claude exactly when to call `judge` (pin the version and add a data-egress rule).

entries.name: walidboulanouar/jev-agent-kit (jevkit)
entries.what: Unofficial zero-dependency Node CLI plus stdio MCP server (@walidboulanouar/jevkit 0.2.0) wrapping the Jev System One API in 11 tools (check, choose, score, judge, route, triage, guard, grep, rank, compact, ask). Also ships a SKILL.md and a `jev guard --hook` PreToolUse hook mode. Nothing is installed automatically: MCP, skill and hook each need manual setup.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger (SKILL.md must be copied manually), so Claude decides when to call them; README even says "then ask Claude to use it". Only jev guard --hook is deterministic (PreToolUse), and it must be added manually to settings.json. The README itself says a single quick judgment is better done by the LLM, so model-discretion use will be rare for daily coding. Nothing is a transparent proxy.
security: API key never printed; sent only over https (localhost http allowed), redirect:'error' set, URL credentials refused (src/client.js:87-91, 125-133)
Key passed via `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` lands in ~/.claude.json env and in argv of that one-off command; server itself takes key from env or ~/.config/jev/key, so not in the server's process argv
No child_process, spawn, eval, telemetry or postinstall found in src/bin (grep clean); no install scripts, zero dependencies (small supply-chain surface); npx -y pins version 0.2.0

MCP path reading is hardened (src/files.js): confined to cwd/JEV_ROOT, dotfiles/dot-dirs and secret-looking names refused, extension allowlist, hard-link check, home dir refused as root, 5 MB cap. Weak spot: JSON/MD/HTML/no-extension files anywhere in the project are readable and get shipped to the provider, and the CLI --file is unrestricted

Prompt-injection surface: text sent to Jev (logs, diffs, commands) can steer probabilities; jev_compact/jev_grep results feed back into Claude context, and a poisoned log could hide lines (error-looking lines are pinned by regex, which mitigates). Tool results are JSON only (no free text from model), so injection back into Claude is limited
jev_guard is explicitly not a security boundary; docs admit obfuscated commands pass, thresholds untuned, eval non-adversarial
entries.dataEgress: MCP tools send only what the agent passes (text, log lines, items, action strings) or what path-reads from the project folder, clipped: 1500 chars per item, 600 per line, 8000 for check/choose/score/judge, 4000 for guard action/route task, up to 5000 lines for grep/compact (up to 5 MB file read). Endpoint is api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if overridden (then OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see the data). Hook mode sends every matching tool call to the provider: full Bash command lines (which may contain inline tokens, passwords, client hostnames), Write/Edit file path plus first 800 chars of content, other tools first 1500 chars of JSON input. Nothing else (no telemetry). SKILL.md itself warns text goes to api.typesafe.ai. Sending client code/diffs to a third party is a compliance question for the user's client projects.
entries.failureMode: Client: 20 s timeout per attempt, 2 retries on 429/5xx/network with 0.4-0.8 s backoff (retry-after honored up to 10 s), so worst case about 60+ s before error (README says about a minute). MCP tools: return isError with message (Claude carries on). Guard hook: fail-closed toward 'ask' (any API failure, unreadable payload, incomplete answer prints permissionDecision ask); safe verdict prints nothing so normal permissions apply. Consequence: an OpenRouter outage stalls every matched Bash call up to ~60 s and then prompts the user, which in bypass/auto mode is disruptive. No circuit breaker or short hook timeout in the kit; user must set a hook timeout in settings.json. Batch tools fail open in sensible ways (compact keeps lines, route abstains).
entries.contextCost: 11 MCP tools; tool names+descriptions+schemas about 7.1k chars, roughly 1.8k tokens (measured from src/mcp.js:15-90, run lambdas excluded). No MCP server 'instructions' field (initialize returns only capabilities and serverInfo). SKILL.md is 3.8k chars (about 950 tokens) but only the description line (~330 chars) is always loaded, body loads on trigger. Guard hook injects no text into context unless it emits ask/deny. Could be trimmed via Claude Code tool allow/deny lists, but that is manual.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with zero code changes: JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL and JEV_API_KEY env vars (src/client.js:66-68, 23-33), and the answer parsing (answers.q.noul/choice/score) matches OpenRouter's System One schema
Best-in-class hardening for a young repo: https-only, redirect:'error', file path sandbox with secret-name and dotfile refusal, guard never emits allow, all failures in hook mode fall to ask
Zero dependencies, no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry; version-pinned npx invocation; MIT

jev_compact and jev_grep read files server-side via path, so Claude does not spend tokens pasting logs; error lines are pinned by regex so Jev misses cannot drop them (author's eval: 100% of relevant lines kept with defaults)

Guard hook is a real deterministic auto-integration: no user prompting needed, prints nothing when safe so it does not override Claude Code permissions; hard-deny/ask regex floors work offline without any API call
Honest docs and measured.json; states limits of Jev (literal, weak at math) and of guard
Small context footprint (about 1.8k tokens for 11 tools)
cons: Not OpenRouter-aware and never tested against it by the author; default is api.typesafe.ai, so user must set 3 env vars and avoid a stray TYPESAFE_API_KEY (takes precedence). Default model 'jev-latest' unprefixed relies on OpenRouter mapping it into the typesafe/ namespace

Automatic invocation is weak: MCP tools and skill are model-discretion, README says to explicitly ask Claude to use them; only the guard hook is automatic and it needs hand-written settings.json. No plugin.json/marketplace.json/.mcp.json/hooks.json shipped

Guard hook overlaps the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, sends every Bash command (may include secrets or client data) to a third-party API, and adds a network call to each Bash/Write/Edit; false positives ask the user even in bypass/auto mode; its eval is 30 non-adversarial commands and thresholds are 'untuned starting points'

Hook has no built-in short timeout: 20 s x 3 attempts per call, so an OpenRouter/Jev outage can freeze Bash calls for about a minute each before falling to ask; fail-closed is wrong for a bypass-mode workflow

Most tools (triage, rank, route, check, choose, score) solve problems Opus 5.5 already solves inline and better; compact/grep are conservative (grep found only 33% of relevant lines in author's fixture); semantically compressing tool output can silently drop needed lines, and per-line calls cost many requests on large logs

Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 12 commits in one day by one author, 3 stars, no CI, no releases, npm 0.2.0 only; unofficial, maintainer is commercially promoting (AY Automate); hand-rolled MCP JSON-RPC
Data egress on client projects: logs, diffs and commands go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (two parties); no redaction beyond path/name filtering
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and most complete Jev wrapper for Claude Code, and it can point at OpenRouter purely via env vars, but auto-use is limited to an optional guard hook (which duplicates the user's existing guard and needs a timeout wrapper) while the other 10 tools depend on Claude's discretion and rarely beat Opus itself. Worth using as a pinned, narrow integration (compact/grep/judge MCP plus optionally a short-timeout guard hook), or better as a reference for a custom minimal hook, not as a drop-in fulfilling the no-prompt goal.

entries.name: jbt95/jev-toolkit
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (Bun + Effect + @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing three Jev tools: typesafe_ask (raw choice/noul/score questions over arbitrary state), typesafe_rank (orders 1-20 supplied text candidates via one Noul question per candidate), typesafe_verify (labels claims supported/contradicted/unrelated/insufficient vs supplied evidence, using an evidence-matrix question pack plus a numbers-missing-from-evidence check). Writes a local JSONL event log (~/.local/share/jev/events.jsonl). Includes 'jev install claude-code|opencode|pi|omp' which registers the server (claude mcp add --scope user jev-toolkit -e JEV_HARNESS=claude-code -- bun .../jev.ts mcp). Server 'instructions' tell the model to call the matching tool before answering.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Server instructions ('call that tool before answering') and tool descriptions ('Use whenever you need to order or prioritize...', 'especially before presenting evidence-based conclusions') nudge Claude to call it without user prompting, but there is no hook, skill trigger or proxy; behavior depends on Opus deciding a task matches. Not deterministic; not integrated into file editing, code review or routing flows.
security: API key read from env at call time (src/cli/jev.ts:91), never in argv; installer passes only JEV_HARNESS via -e, so key is inherited from Claude Code's environment and not written to ~/.claude.json unless the user adds it.

No postinstall scripts; no curl|sh; scripts/install.sh only mkdirs and symlinks into ~/.local/bin. Pi target runs 'pi install npm:pi-mcp-adapter' (irrelevant for Claude Code). Only child processes are 'claude mcp add/remove' and pi (install.ts:41-110).
No telemetry code; the retired Prometheus/telemetry surfaces were removed in the last commit. Only outbound calls are to the configured JEV_ENDPOINT via the SDK.

Credential redaction is a heuristic regex (src/core/text.ts:8-15) applied to rank and verify only; typesafe_ask state is sent as supplied with no redaction (docs/mcp.md: 'callers must redact'). Existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard hooks do not cover mcp__ tools (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).

Code/diff/transcript regex reject for rank (server.ts:96-106) is bypassable prose-only heuristic (README admits it); typesafe_verify has NO such reject, so Claude can pass test output, diffs or source as 'evidence' to a third party.

Prompt-injection surface: claim/evidence/candidate text is passed inside Jev questions; rank tells Jev to treat text as data. Jev outputs are only numbers/labels (no free text) so injected output risk is low; the larger risk is the server 'instructions' text pushing the model to call tools.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (default) or JEV_ENDPOINT: the Bearer API key; for rank: query + up to 20 candidate texts (credential-redacted, regex-filtered against code/diff/transcripts, max 40k chars); for verify: claims + evidence (credential-redacted, up to 40k chars, no code filter); for ask: arbitrary state JSON and questions exactly as Claude supplies them (no redaction). Model name and question definitions also sent. No file reads, no automatic capture of prompts, diffs or tool outputs: only what Claude explicitly puts in tool arguments. Local only: event log with metadata. With OpenRouter as endpoint, OpenRouter also sees this traffic (subject to its data policy settings).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: every failure (missing key, API error, timeout, decode mismatch) is returned as MCP text with isError:true, logged locally, and Claude continues (server instructions say to report the limitation). SDK path timeout is 10 s per attempt with maxRetries 2 (SDK index.mjs:74,518), so a hung upstream can block a single tool call roughly 30 s+ backoff; the 120 s TIMEOUT in client.ts:21 is only for the legacy fetch transport. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY does not stop server startup; tools then error per call. Server startup failure (e.g. bun missing) only drops the MCP server. Never blocks tool execution as it is not a hook.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Approx chars: ask schema+desc ~1.9k, rank ~2.5k, verify ~1.7k, server instructions ~1.4k, plus annotations/titles ~0.4k = ~7.9k chars = ~2.0k tokens per session (with Claude Code tool search deferral, tool schemas load lazily but the instructions text stays). No hook-injected text.
pros: Genuinely Claude Code-aware: 'jev install claude-code' registers a user-scope MCP server automatically, adding no key to argv or config.

Model-discretion auto-use is the closest available to the user's wish: server 'instructions' (directives.ts:2-9) and tool descriptions tell Claude when to call ask/rank/verify without the user saying 'use jev'.

Sensible primitive mapping: rank = per-candidate Noul, verify = 4-way claim labelling with a deterministic numbers-not-in-evidence check (server.ts:456, evidence-matrix.ts), ask = raw Choice/Noul/Score passthrough; all return numbers/labels only.

Endpoint is env-overridable (JEV_ENDPOINT, paths.ts:28) and the SDK uses Bearer auth on /v1/systemone, so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the OpenRouter key should need only env vars plus a one-line default-model patch.
