Privacy-conscious design: credential redaction on rank/verify, code/diff/transcript rejection for rank, no raw claim/evidence/candidate text in the local event log, key read at call time, no telemetry, no postinstall, small auditable codebase (~2.7k src lines), MIT.
Fail-open with typed errors and bounded SDK timeout; no hook so it can never wedge Claude Code; only ~2k tokens of context; plays well with existing hooks (no hook overlap).
Good test discipline (offline fakes, e2e CLI, MCP protocol tests) and strict pinned deps.
cons: No OpenRouter support as shipped: hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY and default model 'jev-latest'; OpenRouter use is an undocumented env hack plus a source patch, and schema compatibility of OpenRouter's /v1/systemone with TypeSafe's is unverified by the repo.
Uses only System One /v1/systemone; ignores OpenRouter's Decisions API.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21, one author, 2 stars, no release, no CI, no npm publish, last commit is a large rewrite (Node to Bun, TS 7, retired most features) so churn/breakage risk is high; depends on effect 4.0.0-rc.112.
Requires Bun (not part of the user's Node/Python/uv stack) and a live git checkout executed on every session; updating means git pull + bun install with no signed releases.

Scope is narrow and not core to coding: relevance ranking of prose, claim-vs-evidence labelling, and ad hoc typed questions. It does not do code review, commit/permission gating, model routing, or edit decisions; rank explicitly rejects code-like text, which is most of a coding session.
Automatic use is only probabilistic: Opus 5.5 may rarely call it, or over-call verify on every conclusion (each an extra turn, network hop, and paid call); no hook-level determinism.

Privacy gaps for client projects: ask state is unredacted, verify has no code filter, and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools; readOnlyHint:true means in bypass/auto mode nothing prompts before data leaves the machine.
Worst-case latency 10 s x 3 attempts on a stalled endpoint; no user-configurable timeout via env.
Skeptic caveat from the brief (Jev may behave like a small router model) means verify/rank verdicts are not obviously better than Opus judging the same text itself, while adding cost and latency.
entries.verdict: The most Claude Code-native and cleanest Jev MCP wrapper so far (auto-registers, model-discretion tool routing, small, MIT, privacy-aware), and OpenRouter is reachable via JEV_ENDPOINT plus a key alias and a default-model patch, but it is a week-old single-author Bun project whose three tools (prose rank, claim verify, ad hoc ask) add little to daily coding and whose auto-use is only best-effort. Worth forking/pinning as the MCP layer if you want Jev in Claude Code at all, but do not expect deterministic or high-value automatic behavior from it alone.

entries.name: ctmx/openrouter-jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Python 3.13 stdio MCP server (plus importable JevGateway client) that wraps OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint (model ~typesafe/jev-latest). It exposes Jev's Noul, Choice and Score primitives as MCP tools with input validation, bounded retries and a local diagnostic log. It is OpenRouter-only: a TYPESAFE_API_KEY is explicitly rejected. It is purely a model-discretion tool. It has no hooks, skill or plugin, and the README tells the user to prompt the agent to use it ("How to Prompt Your Agent").
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill, plugin, CLAUDE.md snippet or transparent proxy in the repo. The README's 'How to Prompt Your Agent' section prescribes explicit prompts ('Use jev_classify to evaluate...'). With bare tool descriptions such as 'Evaluate a Noul proposition against string, object, or list state', Opus 5.5 will rarely call it unprompted, so it does NOT meet the 'never say use jev' requirement on its own. Making it automatic would need the user's own additions: a CLAUDE.md policy block, or a PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook that has Claude call the tool (hooks cannot call MCP tools directly; a hook would need to call the gateway class or the OpenRouter API itself).
security: The API key is passed via env (claude mcp add -e), not argv, so it is not in the process list. However, Claude Code stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. Prefer launching through a wrapper or shell env that reads the key from a secrets file.
gateway.py:104 also reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the environment and only uses it to emit an error message. It is never sent anywhere.

The key is added to the log redaction list (gateway.py:120), and diagnostics redact keys matching authorization/api_key/token/secret/password/credential/cookie (diagnostics.py:21,248-259). This is best effort, as the README admits.

Default-on local logging of every successful call's full STATE and answers to ~/.local/state/jev-gateway (0700 dir, 0600 files, O_NOFOLLOW, 24h retention, 20 MiB cap: diagnostics.py:61,134,182-184). For client projects this puts code, diffs and log snippets on disk in plaintext for 24h. There is no env switch to disable it. Only JEV_LOG_DIR can redirect it, e.g. to /dev/null or tmpfs.

No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh in the code I read. The only network destination is openrouter.ai (hard-coded). Response size capped at 256 KiB; content-encoding forced to identity.

Install via uvx from unpinned git HEAD is a supply-chain risk: the sole maintainer can change the code, and it runs with the key in env. Pin a commit SHA or vendor a clone. Single anonymous-ish maintainer, 1 star, 1 day old at first commit.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the Claude model puts into the `state` argument (arbitrary strings, objects or lists such as code, diffs, logs, commands, test traces) plus the question text and options is POSTed to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the model ID and Authorization: Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (gateway.py:161-163,212,221). Payload cap is 256 KiB. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool, so it is model-controlled and unfiltered. logging_exclusions does NOT strip fields from the outbound payload (README). Secret filtering exists only in the local log copy. The secret-leak PreToolUse guard the user has covers Bash/Read/Grep/NotebookEdit and will not see MCP tool arguments, so a matcher on mcp__openrouter-jev-mcp__.* would be needed. OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe (a third party), which matters for client-project NDAs. Even for client code, only a single hop to OpenRouter is added.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level. Every JevGatewayError is caught and returned as a normal result {"error":{"category","message"}} (server.py:17-21), and the README says to treat this as 'no judgement'. Claude Code is never blocked and no hook can deny anything. Timeouts: an overall asyncio.timeout of 20 s covering up to 3 attempts, with retries on 408/429/502/503/504, connect errors and timeouts, and exponential backoff from 0.25 s or Retry-After (gateway.py:213-244). At most 8 concurrent requests; excess calls error immediately. Worst case adds about 20 s to a single tool call when the API is down. A missing key returns a configuration error per call (and the MCP server still starts). The one real risk is that an error result costs a tool round-trip of context. This is the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint, so contract breakage would surface as provider_response errors.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. The descriptions are short one-liners (about 100 chars each, server.py:24-47). The schemas are generated from type hints (state: Any, question: Any, options: dict[str,str|None], levels: list[str], logging_exclusions: list[str]|None), with no per-parameter descriptions. Estimate: about 5 x 130 tokens = 600-900 tokens of tool defs. The FastMCP-style server passes description=... to MCPServer, but I saw no long 'instructions' text, so there is no instruction overhead. It injects no hook text. With ToolSearch-style deferral, the cost drops to just the tool names. The cost is very low, but there are also no usage instructions to steer the model.
pros: The only candidate I saw that targets OpenRouter natively: the hard-coded alpha Decisions URL, ~typesafe/jev-latest, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY match the user's chosen provider exactly (gateway.py:19-20,101).
Cheap in context: 5 tools, about 600-900 tokens, no server instructions, and no hook injection into every Grep/Bash call, unlike the user's existing GitNexus hooks.
Covers all three Jev primitives, plus jev_evaluate to batch several questions into one call (fewer round trips, up to 64 questions).
Fail-soft design: errors are returned as data, a 20 s hard deadline, bounded retries, an in-flight cap of 8, and 256 KiB request/response caps. A Jev outage cannot block or break Claude Code.
Sane engineering for a 1-day-old repo: ~51 offline tests including a stdio subprocess test, pinned dependencies, and owner-only 0600 log files with O_NOFOLLOW.
Small (about 1.1k lines of source), so it is easy to audit, fork and modify. MIT licensed. It supports uvx, and mcp==2.2.0 resolves on PyPI.
Egress is explicit and limited to openrouter.ai; no telemetry, no shell execution, no installers.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain MCP tool, so it needs a prompt or a CLAUDE.md rule for Claude to use it, which fails the user's core requirement. Nothing in the repo (no hooks, skill or tool-selection guidance) makes Claude call it.
Tool descriptions are generic one-liners with no guidance on WHEN to call them, and the parameters are untyped `Any`. The model has no cue for when Jev adds value in coding.
Unpinned `uvx --from git+...` recommended in the README: an unreviewed HEAD of a 1-star, single-maintainer repo would run with the OpenRouter key in its env. Vendor it or pin a SHA.
Default-on plaintext logging of full state to ~/.local/state/jev-gateway with no off switch. This is a concern for client-project data. Redirect JEV_LOG_DIR to tmpfs or /dev/null as a workaround.

Model-controlled, unfiltered egress: code and diffs can go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. logging_exclusions only affects the local log. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tools and needs a new matcher.

Hard-coded to the alpha /api/alpha/decisions (the contract may change, README admits this). There is no env var for the base URL or model (JevGateway() takes no arguments in server.py:14), and TYPESAFE_API_KEY and /api/v1/systemone are unsupported.

Python 3.13 only (<3.14 pin) and package name `src`; a git-only distribution with no PyPI release, no tags, no CI, and no verification of the request schema against the live API was possible from the source. Test claims about the live API are unverified and I did not run anything.
Each tool call costs an extra Opus turn, so it will not save time or tokens when Jev is merely 'advisory'. It is a weak fit for the coding loop unless a hook makes gating decisions deterministic.
Wide-open API key handling on the host side: `claude mcp add -e` writes the key in plaintext to ~/.claude.json.
entries.verdict: The best OpenRouter-native Jev MCP wrapper I've audited: small, readable and fail-soft, with a cheap context footprint. But it is a passive model-discretion tool with no auto-invocation, default-on plaintext logging and an unpinned git install. Use it (vendored or pinned to a SHA, JEV_LOG_DIR pointed at tmpfs) only as the transport layer, and add your own CLAUDE.md or hook-based trigger policy on top. As shipped it does not satisfy the 'automatic without prompting' requirement.

entries.name: tphakala/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Go stdio MCP server (optional loopback Streamable HTTP) exposing one tool, jev_evaluate, which sends a state plus 1-64 typed questions (choice/score/noul) to Jev via POST {base}/v1/systemone on either TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai) or OpenRouter (openrouter.ai/api), with retry, jittered backoff and provider fallback. Also has a `doctor [-probe]` preflight CLI command.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Server instructions and tool description nudge Claude to use jev_evaluate for routing/classification/gating, but nothing is deterministic: no hooks, no skill, no proxy. Coding tasks rarely present 'pick one option with calibrated probabilities' questions, so Claude will seldom call it unprompted; would need a CLAUDE.md rule or hook to be reliably used.
security: API key read from env only, never argv (good; `claude mcp add -e` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, no process-list exposure)

Keys trimmed and rejected if blank/control chars; doctor never prints keys; provider-supplied error text sanitized (control chars, bidi, invalid UTF-8) and capped at 512 bytes -- reduces prompt-injection via error messages (CHANGELOG, internal/jev/errors.go)
Response body capped (maxResponseBytes) and per-attempt timeout 10s (client.go:33, ReadAll with LimitReader ~line 280)
No shell execution, no telemetry/analytics, no calls other than the configured provider base URLs (grep for http.Get/Post, telemetry: none)
HTTP mode refuses non-loopback bind, optional bearer token, rejects cross-origin non-GET; stdio mode (default) has no network listener

Prompt-injection surface is small: output is typed numbers/enum keys, no free text from the model; but tool input (state) is attacker-influenceable if Claude pastes untrusted file content, and any secret Claude includes is sent to OpenRouter
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts in jev_evaluate arguments: `state` (arbitrary text/JSON up to 1 MiB, could include code snippets, diffs, file contents, tool outputs if the model chooses to) and question instructions/criteria, plus model id, sent over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (and to api.typesafe.ai if a TypeSafe key is set / as fallback in auto mode). Nothing is sent automatically from Claude Code's transcript; Claude decides per call. Server instructions tell Claude not to include secrets, but this is advisory only. Note: with both keys set, fallback would also leak the same payload to TypeSafe; use JEV_MCP_PROVIDER=openrouter plus JEV_MCP_FALLBACK=false to pin to OpenRouter. Client sends only Authorization, Content-Type, Accept, User-Agent headers; logs go to stderr.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft from Claude's point of view: on error the tool returns an MCP tool error (isError) after retries (default 2 retries per provider, jittered exponential backoff, honours Retry-After up to 20s) within a total budget JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT default 30s, per-HTTP-attempt cap 10s. Claude sees the error and simply continues without Jev. Worst case a single call can block ~30s (default budget) with retries; should be lowered (e.g. JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT=5s, JEV_MCP_MAX_RETRIES=0) for interactive use. Missing key makes the server exit at startup, so the MCP server shows as failed but Claude Code continues. No caching.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. Approx tokens (chars/4): server instructions ~1.1k chars (~280 tok) + tool description ~700 chars (~175 tok) + input schema with per-field descriptions (state, questions, name, type, instructions, criteria, model, detail, plus output schema fields) ~5-6k chars (~1.3-1.5k tok). Total roughly 1.8-2k tokens of always-on context (less if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via tool search). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
pros: Genuinely supports OpenRouter from code: default base https://openrouter.ai/api + /v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY (provider.go:19,44-47; jev/provider.go:18); OpenRouter-only setup works with just the key and JEV_MCP_PROVIDER=openrouter

Best-engineered candidate seen for the wire protocol: full validation of choice/score/noul limits, exact raw-argument passthrough to avoid float64 rounding of large ints (tools.go:~225-245), handles OpenRouter-specific fields (id, provider, usage.cost)
Single, well-described read-only tool with sane annotations; low context cost (~2k tokens) and no hooks so no per-turn latency
Solid security hygiene: env-only keys, no argv exposure, sanitized provider text, response size caps, loopback-only HTTP, no telemetry, no shell exec, Apache-2.0
Robust reliability features: retry with Retry-After, budget timeout, optional provider fallback; doctor -probe eases setup
Strong test/CI/CodeQL/govulncheck/Scorecard posture for a 9-day-old repo
cons: Not automatic: only model-discretion MCP tool; the user's requirement (Claude uses Jev without being told) is met only weakly via server instructions; Claude will rarely find typed-probability questions in ordinary coding, and Jev cannot help with code generation, review or search
No hook, skill, or proxy integration, so it cannot gate Claude Code's own decisions (e.g. permission classification, tool routing, subagent choice) transparently

Install friction: requires Go 1.27 toolchain (not installed here); README advertises release binaries and ghcr image 0.1.0 but GitHub shows 0 releases/0 tags and CHANGELOG is [Unreleased], so must build from source and trust a 1-star, single-maintainer, 9-day-old repo (10 commits)

Egress risk in bypass permission mode: Claude could pass code, diffs or secrets from tool outputs as `state` to a third party; only advisory instructions prevent it, and default auto mode may also fall back to TypeSafe if both keys are set
Default 30s budget with 2 retries can stall a turn if OpenRouter is slow; must tune env vars
Beta upstream model of unverified quality (skeptics claim it is a routed flash model), and costs nothing meaningful but adds an extra Opus turn per use; net latency benefit unclear
OpenRouter key would be stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json if added via `claude mcp add -e` (use a wrapper reading from a secrets file or env inheritance instead)
entries.verdict: Best available MCP surface for OpenRouter-hosted Jev (correct /v1/systemone + OPENROUTER_API_KEY, careful, safe, cheap on context), but it is only an on-demand tool, so it does not deliver the fully automatic integration the user wants; use it as the transport layer only if paired with a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook, after building it from source (no release exists yet) and pinning JEV_MCP_PROVIDER=openrouter, JEV_MCP_FALLBACK=false and a short JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT.

entries.name: @sidearker/vex-mcp (Vex + jev CLI)
entries.what: TypeScript package (npm @sidearker/vex-mcp 0.1.1, bins `vex` and `jev`) with a stdio MCP server and a CLI, both on a shared engine that calls Jev over OpenRouter (/api/alpha/decisions) or TypeSafe direct (/v1/systemone). It exposes 4 MCP tools: vex_choose (bounded 2-12 option choice with an abstain option and 0.70 confidence / 0.15 lead thresholds, plus an optional forced 'routing' mode), vex_tool (pick a tool from candidates), vex_gate (destructive / escalate / risk noul+score questions) and vex_verify (completion-evidence gate). It is advisory only. Nothing hooks into Claude Code; the model must choose to call the tools.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills or plugin manifests, and it is not a proxy. The repo ships only integrations/codex/AGENTS.example.md, a 7-line 'use only when choosing among plausible skills' snippet. For truly automatic use in Claude Code you would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule, or write your own PreToolUse/Stop hook that shells out to `jev gate` or `jev verify-diff`, which this repo does not provide. Claude, an Opus-class model, already reasons well, so it will often skip a 'ask a tiny classifier' tool that returns abstain often.
security: No shell execution: grep of src found no child_process, exec or spawn use. The only outbound calls are the decision POST and, in `stats` only, GET openrouter.ai/api/v1/auth/key and /credits (src/core/stats.ts:209,224).

API key comes from env or ~/.openrouter_key, ~/.typesafe_key and ~/.jev_key. There is no --api-key CLI flag, so no key in argv/ps. The key is sent as a Bearer header only to the configured URL. The base URL is overridable via env, so a hostile env could redirect the key; that is a normal risk.

No telemetry beyond the provider call. It writes a local stats file (~/.agents/jev_stats.json, path from VEX_STATS_PATH) holding op name, provider, elapsed time and token usage, not prompts (stats.ts:62-64,182-183). A failed stat write is swallowed with .catch(() => {}).

package.json has `prepare: npm run build`. That runs on git installs and local npm install, not on registry installs. The published tarball ships prebuilt dist/ (27 files) and has no postinstall script. The dist matches the 4 tools in src. The tarball was reviewed statically only; no `npm pack` or install was run.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is small structured JSON (choice ids, numbers), so it is a low injection channel in the return direction. But the input is model-authored free text that the model must summarise. The LLM decides what to send, and the docs tell it to sanitise secrets, which is only a prompt-level control. vex_gate and vex_verify results are advisory and the agent can ignore them, so they are not a security control.

Supply chain: single anonymous maintainer (sidearker, Radoslaw Sowa), package published 2026-09-26, only 2 versions, 1 star, no CI, no provenance attestation seen. `npx -y` with no version pin would auto-pull any later malicious release. Pin the version.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into the tool arguments leaves the machine, sent over HTTPS to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai). For vex_choose that is question, context (string or object), constraints, and the option ids and descriptions. For vex_tool it is the task, the tool descriptions and the context. For vex_gate it is the proposed action text and the context. For vex_verify it is the task, the acceptance criteria and the evidence text, which may include test output or diffs if the model pastes them. Nothing is read from disk or captured automatically. There are no hooks, so no automatic capture of prompts, files or tool outputs. Keys are never in argv. OpenRouter sees the requests under the user's account; the HTTP-Referer 'https://github.com/typesafe-ai/jev' and X-Title 'Jev' headers are hard-coded and are not the user's app. The client-side abstention logic runs locally.
entries.failureMode: There is no hook, so nothing blocks Claude Code. If the server is missing or the key is absent, the tool returns isError JSON, or the MCP server simply does not connect, and Claude carries on. It is effectively fail-open. A default 45 s fetch timeout (AbortSignal.timeout(45_000) at engine.ts:241, overridable via EngineOptions only, and the .env.example JEV_TIMEOUT_MS is not read by the engine, so it may be dead config) means a hung call can stall one tool call for up to 45 s. Timeouts, HTTP errors, bad JSON and schema-mismatched responses all become error results with no retry. Because the alpha endpoint and the beta model are volatile, expect occasional error results. Abstention is common by design (<0.70 confidence returns null), so the model must handle 'no answer' well.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Tool names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas total about 3-3.5k chars, so roughly 800-1000 tokens of tool definitions, loaded into every session (or deferred behind ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.1.x if MCP tool search is enabled). The McpServer sets no `instructions`, so it adds no server-instruction text. No hooks, so no injected text. Each call costs the model tokens to author the options and context (typically 150-400) plus a ~100-token JSON result. The only discovery signal is the terse tool description; without a CLAUDE.md rule the model will rarely call it.
pros: Works with OpenRouter today: sk-or- key auto-detected, default model typesafe/jev-1.13 and endpoint /api/alpha/decisions match the brief (schemas.ts:5-7, engine.ts:53-64,119-120). Set OPENROUTER_API_KEY and it works. TypeSafe direct also works, giving a fallback.
Small and readable: 4 tools, about 1.5k lines of TS, only 2 runtime deps, no shell execution, no postinstall, no key in argv, no telemetry. Static review found nothing dangerous.

Good client-side safety layer: options validated against caller ids, reserved abstain id, probability-key checks, and the confidence/lead abstain logic (engine.ts decide()). This reduces the risk of a hallucinated route.

Covers the sensible Jev use cases for a coding agent: vex_gate (destructive / escalate / risk with Noul and Score) and vex_verify (done-ness gate) map well onto Jev's Noul/Score primitives. vex_choose has a forced routing mode.
The npm tarball has prebuilt dist that matches src, and MIT is the licence. The `jev` CLI could be reused inside your own hooks (e.g. `jev gate` from the existing PreToolUse setup) if you write them.
Costs are trivial (about $0.042/1M input tokens, output free) and the local stats file with `vex stats` gives usage tracking.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a pull-style MCP tool; Claude Code will not call it unless the model decides to. There is no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet for Claude Code (the only guidance is Codex-specific). This directly misses your 'never say use jev' requirement without extra glue.

The README claims Claude/Cursor support but only Claude Desktop, Cursor and Antigravity config examples are given; there is no Claude Code `claude mcp add` recipe or hooks. Docs reference `vex_workflow`, which does not exist in the 0.1.1 code (agent-integration.md section 3), and the docs are partly stale or Codex/Pace-specific (e.g. model names like gpt-6-luna).

Very immature: created 2026-09-24, 36 commits in 2 days, single contributor, 1 star, 2 npm versions, no CI, no releases. Alpha endpoint plus a beta model plus a 3-day-old wrapper is three unstable layers.

Fail-soft but blunt: there are no retries, no circuit breaker and a 45 s timeout that cannot be set from env in the MCP path (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS in .env.example is not read). The README's 'mathematical guarantee' is only a threshold heuristic on model outputs, not a proof.

Fit with an Opus-class main model is weak: asking a tiny System-One classifier which tool to use (vex_tool) or whether the task is done (vex_verify) adds a round trip and a possible false 'done' or false 'destructive' signal versus Claude's own judgement. vex_gate duplicates your existing secret-guard and permission flow and is not a security boundary.

Data egress is model-authored: evidence and diffs pasted into vex_verify or vex_gate go to OpenRouter under client projects. That needs a client-NDA decision, and sanitisation depends on the LLM obeying docs. `npx -y` without a pinned version is a supply-chain risk for a single-maintainer, new package. The hard-coded HTTP-Referer 'github.com/typesafe-ai/jev' also misattributes usage in OpenRouter analytics.
entries.verdict: The safest and most complete off-the-shelf way to get OpenRouter-hosted Jev into Claude Code as MCP tools (works today with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, no code execution beyond HTTP), but it is only a model-discretion tool with no hooks, so it does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' goal alone. Use it, version-pinned, as the transport and pair it with your own CLAUDE.md rule or a small PreToolUse/Stop hook that calls `jev gate` / `jev verify-diff`. Treat the package itself as alpha.

entries.name: rahulrajaram/jev-mcp
entries.what: Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server (v0.5.0) exposing TypeSafe Jev as 5 typed-judgment tools (classify=Choice, score=Score, check=Noul, batched ask, models). Fork of rashedInt32/jev-mcp 0.4.0 that adds a native OpenRouter Decisions API client (POST /api/alpha/decisions), fixes Score cap to 10 levels and state cap to about 32k tokens. Ships as a Claude Code plugin (inline mcpServers via npx github spec) plus one skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) with a three-way scope test. Validates every answer against the question sent and adds act/review/abstain gating.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. There is no hook, proxy or deterministic trigger. Worse, the tool descriptions and SKILL.md explicitly tell Claude NOT to use Jev for one-off judgments and to prefer its own reasoning, so for normal coding turns Claude will rarely invoke it. It only fires when Claude decides a repeated-judgment or calibrated-threshold task is at hand (e.g. triaging 40 files).
security: No install-time shell: package.json has only a prepare script (tsc build); CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts and npm audit; no curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry found (grep clean).

Plugin launches `npx -y github:rahulrajaram/jev-mcp#main` (.claude-plugin/plugin.json): unpinned floating branch, code fetched from a 0-star personal repo and built on first run, so any future push to main runs on the user's machine with the user's env and key. Pin a commit SHA or use a local checkout (README option 1) for client work.

API key never a tool argument and not in argv; read from env or key files (~/.config/openrouter/key, ~/.openrouter). Plugin deliberately ships no env block. Sent only as Authorization Bearer to OPENROUTER_BASE_URL (default openrouter.ai); OPENROUTER_BASE_URL is overridable so a poisoned env could redirect the key.
Sends X-Title=jev-mcp and HTTP-Referer=repo homepage to OpenRouter (app attribution, benign).

No shell execution or file reads beyond key files; MCP server only makes HTTPS calls. Prompt-injection surface: tool result is structured JSON with validated shape (answers checked against the question sent), the model cannot emit free text.

No secret scrubbing of the state: Claude decides what to put in state, so code or secrets Claude pastes go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user's existing PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tool args (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the tool's `state` and question/option text: diffs, file excerpts, claims, candidate lists, up to about 150k chars (JEV_MAX_STATE_CHARS) per call, sent via HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (which routes to TypeSafe's Jev; OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see it). Nothing is sent automatically or in the background: only on model-initiated tool calls. Also GET /api/v1/auth/key and /models/.../endpoints on jev_models. Plus API key as bearer. No telemetry. Client-project code can leave the machine, which needs a client-policy check.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice: tool errors come back as isError with classified kind/retryable/hint (authentication, rate_limit, timeout, connection, insufficient_credits, malformed_response, invalid_request), so Claude just proceeds without Jev. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), 3 attempts on 408/429/5xx/connection with 500 ms doubling backoff capped 5 s and Retry-After honoured up to 60 s, so worst case can be roughly 45+ s stall on a single call. Missing key at startup: server still starts and every call errors (does not block Claude Code). No hook involved, so nothing can block tool execution.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Approx 16-18k chars of tool names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas, about 4-4.5k tokens loaded per session (each of 4 judgment tools carries a roughly 1.3k-char SCOPE_GUIDE plus long state/question/thresholds descriptions; jev_ask has the largest schema). Estimate from source, not measured. No MCP server `instructions` field (new McpServer({name,version}) only). Skill adds about 150 tokens of description in the listing (body loads only on trigger, about 1.9k tokens). No hooks, so nothing injected per turn. Could shrink by deferring tools via tool search.
pros: Native OpenRouter support against the exact endpoint in the brief (POST /api/alpha/decisions), default model ~typesafe/jev-latest, per-call dollar cost surfaced from OpenRouter usage: works with the user's OpenRouter-only setup with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY + JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.

Best-in-class safety design among Jev wrappers: caller owns option set, every answer validated against the question sent (malformed_response otherwise), local enforcement of real limits (10 score levels, 255 options, about 32k tokens), classified errors, retries with Retry-After, act/review/abstain gating.
Ships both the MCP server and a skill in one Claude Code plugin; skill and tool descriptions carry honest scope guidance (no computing, no dates, filter state, batch via jev_ask), reducing misuse.

Fail-open by construction (errors returned as tool results; no hook can stall a Claude Code turn); no telemetry, no postinstall, key kept out of argv and tool args, CI with ci --ignore-scripts and audit, about 1.7k lines of tests (unit + local stand-in, live e2e opt-in).
MIT, small readable code (about 1.5k lines src), easy to fork/pin/audit.
cons: Does not meet the core requirement of automatic use: it is model-discretion only, and its own SKILL.md and tool descriptions tell Claude to prefer its own answer for single judgments, so in normal edit/debug/refactor turns it will almost never fire. There is no hook or router that puts Jev in the loop.

Supply chain risk: plugin runs `npx -y github:rahulrajaram/jev-mcp#main` (unpinned branch head) from a brand-new personal fork (created 2026-09-18, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 13 commits, 2 authors in 2 days); on client projects pin a SHA or use a local build.

Repo is 12 days old, jev 'beta' upstream, and the OpenRouter Decisions endpoint is /api/alpha/: two layers of instability; the fork tracks upstream only manually and the README says npm jev-mcp is the inferior 0.4.0 without OpenRouter.
Context tax of roughly 4-4.5k tokens for 5 tools every session (long repeated SCOPE_GUIDE text) for a capability Claude is told to seldom use; jev_models is only a diagnostic.

Data egress with no guard: Claude-chosen state (diffs, code) goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; the existing secret-leak PreToolUse matcher does not cover mcp__jev__* tools, and client-confidential code may not be allowed off-machine.

Tool-call overhead: each use costs an extra Claude turn to construct a large JSON call plus the state tokens re-emitted as output by Opus; worst-case failure stall about 45 s (15 s x 3 attempts). Provider auto-selection prefers TypeSafe if any TypeSafe key exists, so must pin JEV_PROVIDER.
Jev is a fixed-option chooser that cannot count/compute/compare dates; few daily coding tasks fit (triage many files, rank candidates), and Opus already handles those with an explainable answer.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and the only one found here with first-class OpenRouter support, plus a plugin and skill, but it is a passive, model-discretion tool that deliberately discourages use for one-off judgments, so it will not deliver the 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' goal alone. Reasonable as the tool layer (pinned to a commit SHA, JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter) only if paired with a hook or CLAUDE.md routing rule that deterministically triggers it for batch triage or gating tasks.

entries.name: louis-szeto/open-jev-bridge
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node (>=22.16) stdio MCP server plus Claude Code command hooks, provider-neutral for any service speaking the System One contract (POST {base}/v1/systemone with {model,state,questions}). Exposes 14 system_one_* MCP tools (verify, screen, find, classify, decide, rerank, compare, extract, review, gate, query, compact, belay, status) and installs 10 lifecycle hooks: it records a per-session ledger of edits and check results, runs a Stop/SubagentStop/TaskCompleted completion check that can block with a follow-up request (belay heuristic, then a Jev gate review), screens WebFetch and MCP fetch/search results for prompt injection, injects a "use system_one_* proactively" policy on every SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit and SubagentStart, and writes PreCompact checkpoints. It also ships local-model adapters (Kev, Laya, Decider, Shisa, OpenJev GGUF via llama.cpp), which are irrelevant to an OpenRouter user. Repo is 8 days old, one author, 0 stars, 0 forks.
entries.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks, which matches the user's requirement, plus model-discretion MCP tools nudged by injected policy and skill descriptions. Deterministic without model choice: Stop, SubagentStop, TaskCompleted completion check and gate review, PostToolUse external-content screen, PreCompact checkpoint, evidence recording. Model-discretion: the other tools (find, rerank, classify, decide, compare, extract, verify, review). The authors say explicitly that there is no deterministic event for semantic tool selection. It is the only candidate I have seen that installs real automatic hooks, but its uses are review and safety nets, not "make Claude's decisions with Jev".
security: API key is read from env (SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY) or from a 0600 regular non-symlink key file (config.mjs readSecret, lines 98-109), so it is never in argv. install.mjs:79 deliberately never persists an env key to config.json. Key is sent only as a Bearer header. redirect:'manual' is set, so redirects are refused (client.mjs:181).

Upstream error bodies are never echoed back (client.mjs:186). Request and response byte caps, concurrency and queue limits and a circuit breaker exist. The circuit breaker is per process, so it does not persist across hook invocations, which are each a fresh node process.

No telemetry, and no curl|sh or postinstall (no npm dependencies, package private). Shell execution is limited to execFile of 'claude'/'codex' CLIs during install (install.mjs:15-16). MCP tools are readOnlyHint and never execute commands.

Writes to ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.claude/skills (install.mjs:24). It merges rather than replaces and has rollback, but it is still a global settings edit with a hard-coded absolute path to the checkout.

Prompt-injection surface: the PostToolUse hook injects 'additionalContext' built from Jev's action label (a fixed template, not model free text), so the risk is low. The policy strings injected at SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/SubagentStart are static. Screening is documented as advisory only (SECURITY.md).

Local state: ledgers and checkpoints under ~/.local/state/open-jev-bridge (0700/0600). They hold verbatim tool inputs and results and user prompts (prompts are passed through redact(); tool inputs in ledger are stored raw), so they may contain secrets or client code at rest. redact() is a best-effort regex (pure.mjs:34-41).
entries.dataEgress: With hosted Jev via OpenRouter and defaults (autoVerify/autoReview/autoScreen/autoCompaction all true), the following is sent to OpenRouter and on to TypeSafe: (1) Stop gate after passing checks: the redacted original user task, the edit tool inputs (diffs, i.e. Write/Edit contents), check commands and their output, and the final assistant message (hooks.mjs:110, automation.mjs:295-299, up to 50k chars per field). (2) Belay on Stop when verification is missing or stale: the message ledger with tool uses and results. (3) PostToolUse screen: WebFetch and MCP fetch|search|read_resource results up to 3000 chars. (4) PreCompact: historical tool calls and results of the whole session in batches of up to about 7.6k tokens, which is the largest leak of file contents and command output. (5) Any explicit system_one_* tool call, which carries whatever the model supplies. Redaction is regex-only, and the docs admit it. Nothing is sent to anyone other than the configured URL. For client projects with confidentiality obligations this is a real problem, because OpenRouter's own routing and logging policies then also apply. Everything can be turned off with SYSTEM_ONE_AUTO_*=false but that removes the point of the plugin.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for hooks. Every hook error, timeout, invalid response or lock conflict is caught and returns {} with a stderr note, and main() also prints '{}' on any config error (hooks.mjs:130-136, bin:63). Unavailable review returns only a systemMessage saying that no verification was certified. Default request timeout is 20 s (config timeoutMs, must be <=20000 for install) inside a 25 s host hook timeout, retries 0, so if OpenRouter or Jev hangs, each Stop, SubagentStop or PreCompact can stall the session by up to 20 s; connection refusals or HTTP errors fail fast. There is no persistent circuit breaker across processes. MCP tool calls fail closed with an explicit isError result and action 'review'. The Stop hook can also fail 'closed' in a productive sense: it returns decision:block up to 3 times per session when Jev's probabilities cross belayThreshold 0.7, which could cause spurious continuation requests, especially in bypass mode where the user is not watching.
entries.contextCost: 14 MCP tools (about 4.4k chars of schema source, expanding to roughly 8-12k chars of JSON schema and descriptions, so about 2-3k tokens if loaded, less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind tool search) plus a one-line server instruction (~150 chars). 3 skill descriptions (~150 tokens total). Hook-injected text: about 480 tokens at SessionStart, again after each compaction, and at each SubagentStart; about 85 tokens on every user prompt; occasional one-line notes after fetch results. Overall about 3k tokens up front and about 100 tokens per turn, which is moderate. It also adds pressure toward proactive tool calls ("use system_one_* proactively") that can waste turns and tokens.
pros: Genuinely automatic: 10 lifecycle hooks fire without the user ever saying 'use jev' (Stop/SubagentStop completion gate, WebFetch and MCP fetch/search injection screen, PreCompact checkpoint). This is the exact integration style requested (hooks.mjs:11-13, hooks/claude.json).

OpenRouter works with configuration only: SYSTEM_ONE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api resolves to /api/v1/systemone (endpoints.mjs:15-19), and any bearer key works, so a separate TypeSafe account is unnecessary (wire envelope compatibility still unverified).

Robust fail-open design: every hook error, timeout, bad JSON or lock conflict returns {} and never blocks the host (hooks.mjs:130-136); the evidence ledger refuses to certify a pass when events are missing or oversized; it never auto-approves or rewrites tool calls, so it does not conflict with the user's existing secret-guard or GitNexus hooks.

Good hygiene for a young project: zero dependencies, key never in argv and never persisted by the installer, no redirects followed, error bodies not echoed, byte limits, owner-only state files, clean uninstall that preserves other hooks, MIT license, offline CI on 2 OS and 2 Node versions.

Uses Jev for what it is actually designed for: typed Noul/Choice/Score decisions (is the completion claim supported, should this tool output be kept, is this text an injection), with no free-text generation.
Can be trimmed: SYSTEM_ONE_AUTO_VERIFY/REVIEW/SCREEN/COMPACTION each toggle a hook family, and SYSTEM_ONE_BELAY_SHADOW=1 gives a shadow mode that logs would-be blocks without enforcing.
cons: 8 days old, single author, 0 stars, 0 forks, 10 commits, no releases, apparently AI-generated dense one-line code; the docs record a red CI run on the day of the latest release. No evidence anyone has run it on a real Claude Code session with hosted Jev.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs: the only tested hosted target is api.typesafe.ai /v1/systemone. Response envelope on OpenRouter is unverified, and the GET /v1/models expectation (a 'models' array, providers.mjs:275) does not match OpenRouter's 'data' list, so 'doctor' and system_one_status will fail even if judgments work.

Data egress is heavy and on by default: edit diffs, test output, fetched web content and whole-session tool results at each compaction go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a problem for client projects, and redaction is regex-only. Ledgers on disk also store raw tool inputs and results.

The value is narrow: Stop-time gating of 'is this done' with a probabilistic model can produce false blocks (up to 3 forced continuations per session, at belayThreshold 0.7) that burn Opus tokens, especially in bypass or auto mode where the user is not watching. Screening only covers WebFetch and MCP fetch/search, not Read, Bash curl, or Grep.

Hook overhead on the hot path: PreToolUse and PostToolUse spawn node for every Bash, Write, Edit and every mcp__* call, on top of the user's existing Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus). Stop or PreCompact can stall up to 20 s if the provider hangs, because the circuit breaker is per process and retries are 0.

Broad global footprint for a 0-star project: edits ~/.claude/settings.json, installs 3 skills, and injects a 'use system_one_* proactively' policy on every session, prompt and subagent, which pushes Opus into extra tool calls that add context and cost; 14 tools add about 2-3k tokens of definitions.

Most of the repo (Kev, Laya, Decider, Shisa, OpenJev GGUF adapters, Python sidecars, Codex support, function-hook plugin) is irrelevant to an OpenRouter-hosted Jev user, increasing the audit surface. The install is tied to a git checkout path (not on npm).
entries.verdict: The closest fit so far to "Claude Code uses Jev by itself", because it works through real lifecycle hooks, and pointing it at OpenRouter is only a config change. But it is an 8-day-old, unproven, single-author project with no OpenRouter testing, default-on egress of diffs and tool output, and a narrow use (completion gating, injection screening, compaction), so I would treat it as something to trial with only AUTO_SCREEN and shadow-mode AUTO_VERIFY on personal projects, not as a default for client work.

entries.name: derwells/sieve
entries.what: Local Python MCP server (stdio or loopback HTTP; mcp 2.x + typesafe-sdk) exposing 8 Jev-backed tools. jev_ask is the general one: the agent writes a question plus yes/no, choose or score criteria and gets calibrated probabilities per item. jev_grep, jev_rank, jev_search, jev_verify, jev_route and jev_triage_* are shortcuts over the same core, which batches 8-40 items per request, caches answers in sqlite, validates answers client-side and enforces a USD budget. Jev never generates text; the agent reads the survivors itself. jev_grep (rank repo files/functions against a plain-language question) is the coding-relevant tool. Also ships a sieve-ask shell CLI and SearXNG/Brave/codex/claude web-search backends for jev_search.
interface: jev_ask(question, items, kind=judge|choose|score, yes/no/options/levels, top_k, threshold, max_chars=4000, budget_usd=0.50)
jev_grep(question, path, mode=files|functions, top_k=20, threshold=0.5, budget_usd=0.50)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The server instructions text and tool descriptions are the sole nudge; there are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no PreToolUse interception. Claude Code will call jev_grep/jev_ask only if Opus judges it better than its native Grep/Glob/Read and gitnexus, which in practice it often will not, and the instructions do not say 'prefer over Grep'. It could be raised by adding a CLAUDE.md rule or a UserPromptSubmit hook yourself, but that is not part of this project. The README claims Claude Code was 'verified headless', but only for registration and a live jev_ask.
security: bin/sieve-mcp:12-16 sources ~/.config/sieve/env AS SHELL CODE with set -a, and values in it override the environment. Fine if the file is mode 600 and yours, but it is code execution from a config file.

API key is never in argv: read from env or env file, so it is not visible in ps. It is sent as Bearer to the base URL only. The claude/codex search backends strip ANTHROPIC_*/OPENAI_* routing env before spawning children (backends/base.py:120-145).

Side effect on user repos: jev_grep appends '.sieve-cache/' to an existing .gitignore in the searched repo (cache.py:19,43-54), otherwise writes to ~/.cache/sieve/<hash>/. Modifies client repos without being asked, though it is documented.

No secret filtering in the walker (enumerate.py:67-68 ALWAYS_SKIP only .git/.hg/.svn/.sieve-cache; rely on .gitignore + binary sniff). Untracked or ignore-missed files such as .env.local, keys or config with tokens would be previewed and sent to the API. The user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tools.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are only ids and probabilities (no free text back), which is a small surface. But jev_search and jev_verify fetch web pages/PDFs (2 MB/25 MB caps, PDF parsed in a child with 30s/1GB limit) and jev_search can spawn `claude -p`/`codex exec` children as search backends (not default unless configured; default falls back to `claude` when no SearXNG/Brave is set).

Install path: git clone + `uv sync` pulls typesafe-sdk, mcp>=2.2.0, tree-sitter-language-pack, pypdf (uv.lock pinned, 130 KB). No curl|sh, no postinstall. No telemetry found in sieve code. Optional bin/sieve-searxng runs a digest-pinned Docker container on loopback.
entries.dataEgress: To the TypeSafe API (or OpenRouter if re-pointed): the question text and item payloads. For jev_grep that means the relative path, line range and preview of EVERY non-ignored text file in the searched directory (first 40 lines plus a line-numbered outline for files over 80 lines, up to 6000 chars each; whole file if shorter), so effectively a large fraction of the repo source goes out per call; functions mode sends function bodies. jev_rank/jev_ask send whatever the agent passes (2000/4000 chars per item). jev_verify sends fetched passages from cited files/URLs. jev_search sends only the query and result snippets to Jev; the query also goes to the chosen search backend (Brave / SearXNG upstream engines / claude or codex child). Not sent: chat history or Claude Code prompts, unless the agent puts them in items. Cached locally in ~/.cache/sieve or repo/.sieve-cache (includes hashes, probably question and answers). Relevant for client projects under NDA: every jev_grep uploads client source to a third party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter; check OpenRouter data policy).
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per tool call but harmless: errors raise a ToolError (SieveError) that the model sees and can work around with native Grep/Read. SDK retry policy: up to 4 retries with backoff 0.5-8s on 408/429/5xx, honors Retry-After, total timeout 300s, per-request timeout 90s (client.py:14-28). So a hung or down Jev can stall a call for up to about 5 minutes before the agent sees an error. Missing key raises MissingAPIKeyError with a clear message. No circuit breaker. Since it is not in a hook path, Claude Code is not blocked overall, only that tool call. The budget cap (default $0.50) returns partial results with budget_exhausted=true, but uses estimated token costs, so actual spend can exceed it.
entries.contextCost: 8 MCP tools. I measured the decorator title/description text at about 3.8k chars, plus parameter schemas (jev_ask alone has 11 parameters with Field descriptions; jev_verify, jev_triage_threads and jev_grep also have long ones), so roughly 3.5-4.5k tokens of tool definitions (my estimate, chars/4; the mcp SDK also adds JSON-schema overhead). Server 'instructions' block is about 830 chars, or roughly 200 tokens, and it tells the model that 'anything you were about to eyeball item by item is a jev_ask', which is an aggressive nudge. Total about 4-5k tokens always in context if not deferred via ToolSearch. jev_triage_paseo/jev_triage_threads are dead weight for a Claude Code user, and there is no config to disable individual tools. It adds nothing via hooks.
pros: Most complete and well-designed Jev MCP found: general jev_ask (judge/choose/score = all three Jev primitives) plus purpose-built jev_grep/jev_rank; the closed-set design matches what Jev is actually good at (sieve/jev.py, validate.py).

Real cost controls: per-call budget_usd (server.py), answer cache keyed on (model, question, item, criteria), client-side validation of probability sums and Choice-argmax (validate.py), cost reported in every result.

Endpoint is env-configurable through the SDK: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key should route it to /api/v1/systemone with roughly zero code change (SDK path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One path).

Actual evals with honest, mixed results committed in evals/: recall eval strict 3/5 fail, relaxed 5/5 pass; jev_verify 18/20 four-way verdicts; triage explicitly marked as not beating a baseline. It documents its own limits.

Shared loopback HTTP mode (127.0.0.1:8723, stateless, Host/Origin check) via systemd user unit avoids one Python process per Claude Code session and the uv start-up cost; also `claude mcp add --scope user` is documented.
Good offline test suite (about 22 test files, live tests marked and skipped by default), MIT license, uv.lock pinned, no postinstall or curl|sh, no telemetry, key not in argv.
Very cheap when used: about $0.008-0.054 per whole-repo jev_grep, $0.00005 per small rank.
cons: Purely opt-in by the model: no hook or skill trigger, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic use without prompting; Opus with native Grep/Glob and gitnexus will rarely pick jev_grep.

jev_grep uploads previews of every non-ignored text file in the target dir to a third party per uncached call (enumerate.py has no secret or sensitive-path filter beyond .gitignore); this is a serious problem for client projects and bypasses the user's PreToolUse secret guard (not matched to mcp__ tools).
Side-effect writes: appends '.sieve-cache/' to the target repo's .gitignore (cache.py:43-54), which dirties client repos.

Not built for OpenRouter: no OpenRouter mention anywhere; it needs a hand-edit of DEFAULT_MODEL (client.py:12) to 'typesafe/jev-1.13' (model ID differs) and depends on OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone being body-compatible with the TypeSafe SDK (unverified); the alpha decisions API is not used.

Only jev_grep and to some extent jev_rank/jev_ask matter for coding; jev_search (needs SearXNG/Brave or spawns claude/codex children), jev_verify, jev_route and two Paseo triage tools are bloat, about 4-5k tokens of always-on tool schema with no way to disable tools.
Immature: created 2026-09-22 (8 days old), 34 commits, one contributor, 0 stars, no CI, no releases, depends on beta SDK 0.7.x; mcp>=2.2.0 is a brand-new major that may conflict.

Recall for its headline use case is only marginal: strict recall@10 gate failed (3/5), and ranking with a 'preview + outline' is not clearly better than ripgrep + gitnexus for a senior dev's normal repos; README itself says the agent must still open and read survivors.
Failure latency: SDK retries up to 4x with 300s total budget, so an OpenRouter alpha outage can stall a tool call for minutes.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered Jev MCP and the only one where OpenRouter routing is nearly free (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + key + a model-ID tweak), but it is model-discretion only, so it will not fire automatically, and jev_grep ships repo previews to a third party with no secret filter, which is risky for client work. Worth using as the Jev tool backend (ideally with a small trimmed fork, a CLAUDE.md or hook nudge, and use limited to personal repos), not as a drop-in automatic integration.

entries.name: arbitype (formerly typesafe-mcp / typesafe-codex-mcp)
entries.what: Dependency-free Python STDIO MCP server that wraps TypeSafe's /v1/systemone endpoint. It exposes 9 read-only tools (evaluate, classify, score, check, verify, gate, route, review, health) that turn Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives into higher-level helpers, e.g. gate/review thresholds pass/review/fail and route to pick a next action. The repo was renamed from typesafe-mcp to arbitype. The candidate's PyPI typesafe-mcp 0.5.2 is stale; the canonical package is arbitype 0.7.0, and the old names are kept as aliases. It has no hooks, skills or plugin. It only works if Claude decides to call a tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Every description uses 'USE WHEN / DO NOT USE WHEN' phrasing and the server instructions carry a routing guide, so Opus may call them unprompted. Nothing deterministic guarantees it: there are no hooks, no skill, and no CLAUDE.md snippet. Real-world trigger rate for Opus 5.5 is likely low, because Opus can classify or review directly and has no reason to ship a diff to an external classifier. To make it reliable, add a CLAUDE.md or hook layer yourself.
security: API key is read from the environment only and never put in argv; the generated Claude config uses a ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} env reference, so it does not appear in the process list or in a checked-in file. It is redacted from error output (core.py:531-565).

Sends the bearer token only over HTTPS (HTTP only for loopback) and disables redirects (core.py:56-78), so the key cannot be forwarded to another host. Request and response size limits apply (512 KB / 4 MB) and STDIO frames are bounded.

No subprocess, shell exec, eval, telemetry or analytics in the code (grep found none). Zero third-party runtime dependencies, which keeps the supply-chain surface small. Tools carry readOnlyHint=true annotations.
'arbitype setup' edits ~/.claude.json, which is a sensitive file, although it uses a diff, confirmation and backup. Avoid it and add the server manually with 'claude mcp add'.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev output is numeric or label only, so it cannot inject free text back. The model chooses what state to send, so an injected instruction in repo content could cause it to be sent, which is standard MCP risk. openWorldHint=true.

The uvx launch pulls an unpinned PyPI package on every start unless pinned. PyPI publishing is done from GitHub Actions, and docs/SUPPLY_CHAIN.md exists. It is a single-maintainer project created 9 days before the audit, so a supply-chain takeover risk is non-trivial.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the 'state' argument, plus the question and option text, is POSTed to {base_url}/v1/systemone (TypeSafe or OpenRouter). That can be diffs, code, plans and test output, up to 120k state chars (about 30k tokens) per call by default (core.py DEFAULT_MAX_STATE_CHARS), and the tool description explicitly invites diffs and release artifacts for review. The model id and a User-Agent of arbitype/0.7.0 are also sent. Nothing else leaves the machine: no telemetry, and nothing is read from disk by the server itself. For client projects, this means code is sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, so check client confidentiality and OpenRouter data-policy settings.
entries.failureMode: The failure is per-call and non-blocking. It is not a hook, so Claude Code is never stalled or blocked. Timeout is 10 s per attempt with 2 retries on 408/429/5xx/529 and network errors, exponential backoff 0.5 s base capped at 20 s with jitter, and Retry-After honoured. Worst case is roughly 30-60 s inside one tool call before an error is returned to the model, which then continues without Jev. A missing key gives a ConfigError only when a tool is called. The MCP server starts fine without a key, and 'health' works. Redirects are treated as errors. This is fail-open for the workflow but can waste tokens if Claude retries. Timeouts are tunable through TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS and TYPESAFE_MAX_RETRIES.
entries.contextCost: 9 tools. Estimated tool definitions come to about 14k characters, roughly 3.5k tokens. That is about 2k chars of shared schemas, about 6.6k chars for the 9 tools with their input schemas, about 1.5k chars of annotations, and about 3k chars of outputSchemas. Server 'instructions' add about 0.5k chars (about 120 tokens, core.py-adjacent SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS at mcp.py:99-105). Zero hook-injected text. Claude Code's tool search can defer schemas, which would reduce the cost. Small relative to gitnexus and playwright, but every session pays it whether or not Jev is used. This is an estimate from static reading, since the server was not run.
pros: Zero-dependency, stdlib-only Python server with a small, clean, well-read code base (core.py 728 lines, mcp.py 1158 lines) that is easy to audit, and no subprocess or telemetry.

OpenRouter works with config only: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api gives exactly /v1/systemone (core.py:145,649), and TYPESAFE_MODEL can be set to typesafe/jev-1.13. No fork is needed if the OpenRouter response matches.
Sound key handling: env-only, ${VAR} forwarding in the Claude config, redaction, HTTPS-only, and redirects disabled so the bearer token cannot leak.
Good error semantics: bounded retries with Retry-After, size caps, response validation (probability maps, score consistency), and per-call errors that never wedge the session.

Useful semantic layer over raw primitives: gate/review with pass_at/review_at thresholds, route for next action, verify for multiple claims. It maps to concrete coding moments (PR risk, does the change satisfy the spec, is this test failure flaky).
Tool descriptions are unusually well written for model routing (USE WHEN / DO NOT USE WHEN), so Opus will pick the right tool if it decides to use Jev.
Tool count is small (9) and the estimated cost of about 3.5k tokens is modest.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion only, with no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md wiring. This does not satisfy the user's core requirement without extra glue (a CLAUDE.md rule or a PostToolUse/Stop hook that calls it).

Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-21, 28 commits, 1 contributor (two git identities), 0 stars, 0 forks, one release line (v0.7.0). Renamed twice in about a week, with the 'typesafe-mcp' name now stale on PyPI at 0.5.2, so 'uvx typesafe-mcp' would pull the wrong, older build.

Unofficial: the README states it is not a TypeSafe AI product. No OpenRouter support is documented, the env vars are TYPESAFE_* only, and OpenRouter compatibility is inferred from the URL path, not tested.

State must be serialized by Opus as tool-call arguments, so sending a diff costs output tokens and seconds each time. That erodes Jev's 70-500 ms advantage and works against the point of a cheap router.

Sends code and diffs to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) at the model's discretion. That is a real concern for client projects, and secret-leak guards on Bash|Read|Grep would not inspect MCP tool arguments.
Worst-case retry latency inside one call can reach tens of seconds. The 96.67% tool-selection benchmark measures Jev picking the tool, not Claude, and is self-reported and unreplicated.
Adds about 3.5k tokens of tool definitions to every session, for tools Opus will seldom need. The 'setup' command edits ~/.claude.json and is best avoided.
entries.verdict: The best-engineered MCP wrapper of the set for safety and simplicity, and it should work against OpenRouter by setting only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (untested). Alone it does not meet the 'automatic, never prompt' requirement, because it is only a model-discretion tool from a nine-day-old solo repo. It is usable as the transport layer if paired with a CLAUDE.md rule or hook that makes invocation deterministic.

entries.name: Renwang-Huang/arbitype
entries.what: Zero-dependency Python (stdlib only) STDIO MCP server, independent and not official TypeSafe. It exposes nine read-only tools (evaluate, classify, score, check, verify, gate, route, review, health). Each wraps a Jev System One request (Choice / Noul / Score) to POST {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone. It validates request and response strictly. It never executes actions. The agent host must decide to call it.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. There are no hooks, no skill and no proxy. Claude Code calls them only if Opus decides to. The USE WHEN descriptions and the 495-char instructions nudge selection. The repo's own benchmark (96.67%, 120 cases) measures Jev picking among Arbitype's tools, not Claude Code choosing to call them, and the README says so. Opus 5.5 will often prefer its own reasoning over an opaque probability call, so uptake is likely low. Anything deterministic would need a separate hook or CLAUDE.md rule.
security: API key is read from the process env only, is not an argv argument, and is never printed. It is redacted from error details (core.py, _safe_error_detail(secret=api_key)). Settings repr excludes the key. Host setup writes '${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}' rather than the literal key.

HTTP redirects are disabled (_NoRedirectHandler, core.py:57-82), so the bearer token cannot leak via redirect. HTTPS is enforced except for loopback. Request and response size caps are enforced (512 KB / 4 MB) and STDIO frames are capped at 16 MB.
No subprocess, os.system, shell=True, or telemetry/analytics found by grep in arbitype/. Zero third-party runtime dependencies (pyproject 'dependencies = []'), so the supply-chain surface is small.

Publishing looks OIDC/registry based (publish.yml, publish-mcp.yml) with pinned action SHAs, CodeQL and dependabot. I did not verify the PyPI sdist matches the git source. The install path is 'uvx arbitype' from PyPI, which is unpinned unless the user pins ==0.7.0.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are plain probabilities and labels, with no free text from the model. The main risk is the calling agent putting untrusted repo content into 'state'. SECURITY.md itself says it is not a prompt-injection firewall.
'arbitype setup claude' modifies ~/.claude.json. It shows a diff and asks for confirmation and makes a backup, but you can just add the mcpServers entry by hand instead.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts into the 'state' and 'instructions'/'criteria' tool arguments. That could be diffs, code snippets, file contents or plans, up to 120k chars of state and 512 KB per request. It goes over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to openrouter.ai when TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is set. The Bearer key, model id and User-Agent 'arbitype/0.7.0' are also sent. Nothing is collected automatically: the server does not read files or the repo itself. No telemetry to the maintainer was found. The secret-leak guard hook does not cover what the model chooses to send in MCP arguments.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for the workflow. Errors come back as an MCP tool error (ConfigError / APIError) and Claude Code carries on without blocking. Each HTTP attempt has a 10 s timeout (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, range 1-300 s). Up to 2 retries (max 6) on 408/429/5xx/529 and on network errors, with exponential backoff (0.5 s base, jitter) that honors Retry-After. Worst case is about 3x10 s plus backoff, roughly 31 s, before an error. A missing API key raises ConfigError at call time. The server still starts and lists its tools. It is single-threaded STDIO with a blocking urllib call, so a slow provider stalls that MCP call only.
entries.contextCost: Nine tools. I measured the JSON of name+description+inputSchema+annotations at about 8,978 chars, roughly 2.2k tokens, on every session while the tools are loaded (Claude Code may defer them via ToolSearch, which lowers the cost). evaluate alone is about 2,065 chars. Server 'instructions' is 495 chars (about 125 tokens) and lists when to use each primitive. Descriptions carry USE WHEN / DO NOT USE WHEN wording. No hook-injected text.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with no code change: core.py:649 builds {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone and core.py:657 sends a Bearer key, which matches OpenRouter's System One endpoint. Three env vars in the mcpServers entry are enough.

The decision-primitive tools map cleanly onto coding checks: check/verify for 'does this diff satisfy X', gate for pass/review/fail, route for next action, classify for triage. They return typed probabilities, and model output is never free text.

Strong hygiene for a 9-day-old project: key only in env and redacted from errors, redirects disabled, HTTPS enforced, size limits, argument validation against schemas, and strict validation of the provider response including a top-probability consistency check (core.py:449-489).
Zero dependencies and stdlib urllib. No subprocess or telemetry, and the code is small (about 2.7k lines) and readable, so it is easy to audit or fork.
Bounded retry and timeouts are configurable. It fails open, so a Jev outage never blocks Claude Code.
Tests and CI: about 85 test functions on local fakes, CI on 3 OSes x 4 Python versions, CodeQL, dependabot and pinned action SHAs. Eval assets are published (BENCHMARK.md and the eval datasets).

Read-only, idempotent annotations on every tool, so bypass or auto permission mode is unlikely to prompt or cause side effects. It is also cheap: Jev is about $0.042 per 1M input tokens and output is free.
cons: Not automatic. It is an MCP toolbox that only fires if Opus chooses to call it. It fails the user's requirement 'Claude Code must use it when needed' unless it is paired with a hook or CLAUDE.md routing rules.

No OpenRouter documentation or tests anywhere. The compatibility is inferred from the URL shape and from search results. The 'jev-latest' default alias may not resolve on OpenRouter, and 'arbitype setup claude' will not write TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or TYPESAFE_MODEL.

Costs about 2.2k tokens of tool definitions per session (evaluate alone is about 2k chars), and nine near-overlapping primitives add tool-choice ambiguity. Only 2-3 of them (check, verify, route) are useful for daily coding.

Egress is model-controlled: Claude will paste diffs or code into 'state', sending client-project code to a beta third-party model via OpenRouter. The user's secret-guard hook does not inspect MCP tool arguments.

Very immature: 0 stars, 0 forks, one maintainer, 28 commits, and created on 2026-09-21, only 9 days old. It has had 7 minor releases in about 1 week (v0.7.0), plus registry renames (typesafe-mcp -> arbitype) that suggest churn. It is unofficial, and the benchmark is self-run and measures Jev, not Claude Code uptake.

Each call adds an extra agent turn and network round trip (a full model turn overhead) for a probability that Opus can usually judge itself. Jev is described as beta, with 32k context and unverified skeptic claims of being a router.
Worst-case blocking of about 31 s inside a tool call when the provider hangs (10 s x 3 attempts plus backoff). Python and uvx cold start also adds startup work.
entries.verdict: The best-engineered and simplest Jev MCP wrapper for OpenRouter. Point TYPESAFE_BASE_URL at https://openrouter.ai/api and use an OpenRouter key, with no code patch. It is safe and fail-open, but tool availability alone will not make Opus use it, so it needs a companion hook or rule to meet the 'automatic' goal, and it is very young, unofficial and untested against OpenRouter.

entries.name: Alberto-Codes/judgevet
entries.what: Unofficial Python client (httpx, pydantic) for TypeSafe's Jev System One API, plus a CLI (`judgevet`) and an optional stdio MCP server (`judgevet-mcp`). The MCP server exposes 4 tools: ask_noul, ask_choice, ask_score and evaluate_policy. evaluate_policy runs a local pass/fail acceptance policy over Jev's probabilities. It is a plain request/response wrapper: Claude must decide to call the tools. There are no hooks, no skill and no plugin manifest.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code loads the four tools and Claude may call them if the descriptions look relevant. There is no hook, no skill trigger, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no server instructions telling Claude when to use Jev. In practice it will rarely or unpredictably call ask_noul and friends unless the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook wrapper. That misses the user's goal of Claude Code using Jev when needed with no prompting.
security: API key: read from env, file or `!command` into SecretStr; sent only in the Authorization Bearer header. Never in argv when using `--env 'JEV_API__KEY=${JEV_API__KEY}'`, though docs show the key held in the launching shell env. The CLI explicitly warns against putting keys in command arguments.
Base URL validator rejects non-loopback http://; redirects disabled (SECURITY.md). A configured replacement host receives the same data and key.

`!command` credential source runs argv directly with no shell (credential_command.py), bounded stdout, stderr discarded, and a timeout. It is a trusted-config feature, not an attack surface unless the env is attacker-controlled.
No telemetry or phone-home (SECURITY.md); logs are quiet by default and exclude state and question text. Tracebacks and error envelopes may contain content.

No curl|sh installer and no npm postinstall. It is a PyPI package run via uvx; the docs pin ==0.15.0 but transitive dependencies are not pinned. There is a supply-chain workflow (SBOM, uv audit, CodeQL, Dependabot).

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs come from Claude, so injected file content can be steered into a Jev call. Jev returns only typed probabilities, no free text, so the return channel is low-risk. The main risk is exfiltration by sending content to a third-party host.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude passes as `state` and `instruction`/`criteria` in each tool call. Nothing is sent automatically: Claude decides what to include, which could be code snippets, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. It goes as JSON {state, questions, model} to the configured base URL, i.e. OpenRouter and then the TypeSafe or Jev provider. The Bearer key goes in the header. evaluate_policy rules stay local. No telemetry. Retention and training policy of the remote service is not established (SECURITY.md says so). Client work needs a check against OpenRouter data policies and client NDAs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, and it never blocks the session. A missing key makes the server exit 2 at startup, so the tool shows as failed in /mcp. At call time errors are typed and returned as an MCP error result: JevAuthError, JevRateLimitError, JevServiceError, JevBudgetExceededError. Timeouts are 30 s read and 5 s connect (settings.py:302, http.py:404). Retries default to max_attempts=3 with 0.5-5 s backoff on retryable HTTP errors. Transport-error retry is off by default (retry_transport=False). Worst case a single call could take about 90 s, so tighten timeout_seconds and max_attempts. Since Claude is the caller, it can ignore a failed call and carry on. There is no fail-open hook semantics because there is no hook.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Input-side definitions (names, descriptions, inputSchema) come to about 6-9k chars, roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens. evaluate_policy dominates because it embeds the closed policy JSON Schema and nested question schemas (mcp_schemas.py, 314 lines, 11.3k chars including docstrings). Output schemas (mcp_output_schemas.py, 253 lines) are also declared but Claude Code does not use them. No MCP server `instructions` text (grep found none) and nothing injected by hooks. Tool descriptions say what each tool returns but not WHEN Claude should call it, which weakens discretionary use.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with no code change: `TYPESAFE_BASE_URL`/`JEV_API__BASE_URL` aliasing plus the `/v1/systemone` path match OpenRouter's `https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone`, and the response parser ignores OpenRouter's extra fields (settings.py:116-118, http.py:497, response_parser.py:65-74).

The only candidate found with all three Jev primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) exposed as typed MCP tools with output schemas, plus a local policy layer that turns probabilities into pass/fail. That fits a 'gate' use of Jev.
Careful key handling: SecretStr, key file and `!command` sources, https-only base URL, no redirects, no telemetry, and debug logs that exclude state.
Real engineering hygiene for a 10-day-old repo: 148 test files, CI with lint, docs checks, uv audit, SBOM, CodeQL, release-please and a signed publish workflow. MIT licence.

Includes a CLI that could back a deterministic hook (e.g. a PreToolUse or Stop hook gating on `judgevet` exit status) if the user builds one. `examples/staged-review` shows the pattern for `git diff --cached`.
Claude Code was already tried by the author (STATUS.md: v2.1.280 connected and discovered 3 tools; calls blocked only by the author's account spend limit).
cons: Not automatic: no hook, no skill and no server instructions, so Claude uses Jev only if it happens to pick a tool. This directly fails the user's 'never say use jev' requirement without extra glue such as a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook.

OpenRouter was never tested by the author: docs and tests target api.typesafe.ai only, and the evidence in STATUS.md is TypeSafe-direct with jev-1.13.0. OpenRouter error bodies (not `detail.error_type`) degrade to bare status lines.
Ignores OpenRouter's Decisions API (`/api/alpha/decisions`) and the 'Jev Router' model. Only System One is supported.

Solo maintainer, 0 stars, created 2026-09-20, daily releases, pre-alpha classifier, docs marked 'draft'. High churn and bus-factor risk. The pin `==0.15.0` will need bumping, and the MCP path is verified only on the legacy handshake.

No redactor in the MCP path: Claude-chosen state, which could contain client code or secrets, goes to a third party unredacted. The only guard is Claude's judgement, and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover these mcp__ tools unless its matcher is extended.

Generic tools (ask yes/no, choice, score) with no coding-specific presets. Claude must design the question each time, and Jev is not a chat model, so value for edits, refactors or code search is weak.
Adds ~1.5-2.5k tokens of tool definitions to every session for a rarely-called tool. Long worst-case timeouts (30 s x 3 attempts) unless tuned.
Requires Python 3.12+ and uvx cold start, and the transitive dependency set (mcp>=2.2, pydantic-settings, structlog, typer) is not pinned.
entries.verdict: The most complete and best-engineered Jev client/MCP found, and it works on OpenRouter by setting only JEV_API__BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and the key. But it is a passive toolbox, not an automatic integration: use it as the transport layer (MCP or the CLI called from a hook) rather than a standalone answer to the 'Claude must use it by itself' requirement. It also has a solo-maintainer, 10-day-old, pre-alpha risk profile.

entries.name: @maximem/jev-mcp (with @maximem/jev-core)
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (11 tools) wrapping Jev's System One API. Five generic primitives (jev_classify, jev_score, jev_check, jev_rank, jev_ask), jev_health, and five "harness" tools (jev_plan_gate, jev_action_gate, jev_verify, jev_screen, jev_select). Each harness tool bundles fixed Noul/Score/Choice questions into a single call and applies local threshold logic (deny/ask/allow, verified, safe, abstain). The "automatic checkpoints" in the README are only the tool descriptions telling the model when to call them. There are no hooks, skills or slash commands. Decisions are logged to a local JSONL ledger.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. No hooks, skills or transparent proxy. 'Automatic' behavior depends on the descriptions ('Run this BEFORE planning any non-trivial task', 'Call BEFORE any irreversible action', 'BEFORE telling the user it is done'), which Opus may follow inconsistently, and which conflict with the user's bypass/auto permission mode: the model must voluntarily consult it. Ends up mostly firing on planning and verification prompts, not deterministically.
security: GitHub repo maximem-ai/jev_mcp returns 404 (the org's 6 public repos do not include it), so it is unauditable beyond the 4-file npm bundle. The only source I could read is the minified/tsup-built dist. No provenance attestation, only registry signatures. Publishers are maximem.ai (a memory/context company), not TypeSafe. The npm 'directory' fields point to packages/mcp-stdio and packages/core.
npx -y always pulls the latest 0.1.x from the registry: supply-chain exposure on every session start unless pinned (@maximem/jev-mcp@0.1.5).
