No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no child_process/exec/spawn, no telemetry or analytics calls (grep of both dist files). The only network call is fetch to ${JEV_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone.

API key is read from env only, never a tool argument. redact() strips key-shaped strings from error messages (jev-core:156-162). The key is visible in argv only if passed as `claude mcp add --env KEY=...` on the command line, and it is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
JEV_BASE_URL is not validated: any value receives the Bearer key. Only the local env can set it, so this is low risk.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are numeric or enum (structured), which is good. But tool text is model-authored and untrusted content (diffs, web pages) is forwarded into Jev state. jev_screen is itself a model call and is bypassable. A misjudged jev_action_gate 'allow' could lull the agent, so it must not replace real permission controls.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments is sent to ${JEV_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe as the provider). jev_plan_gate sends the user's task verbatim plus context (file names, constraints). jev_action_gate sends the literal shell command plus context. jev_verify sends the claim plus raw evidence (test output, diffs). jev_screen sends full untrusted text (web pages, issue and PR bodies). jev_rank/jev_ask/jev_check/jev_select send arbitrary state, candidates or options. Nothing is read from disk by the server itself (no file scanning, no hook capture); only what Claude chooses to pass leaves. That still means client-project code and diffs can reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe, so check OpenRouter's data-retention and logging settings for client work. Requests carry Authorization: Bearer <key> and a JSON body only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice, but only because it is advisory and model-mediated. A Jev error, timeout or budget error returns an isError MCP result ('Jev call failed (kind): ...'), and the agent proceeds. Client timeout is 5s per attempt with 2 retries (jev-core:204-205) and backoff of 250ms and 500ms ±25%, honoring Retry-After. Worst case is about 15.8s of stall on a hard outage or a black-holed network for a single call. Auth (401/403), request and schema errors are not retried. Claimed 'failOpen' in the harness config schema (jev-core:369) is dead config: never read anywhere. CallBudget (maxCallsPerTask=8) is only enforced if opts.enforceBudget is set, and main() calls createServer() with no opts, so it is never enforced. Nothing can block a tool call, because there are no hooks and only the model decides whether to obey a 'deny'. JEV_HARNESS=off (README: disables automatic checkpoints) is also effectively a no-op in 0.1.5: harnessDisabled/checkpointEnabled are exported but never called by the server code. With no key set, the server registers only jev_health, so it does not crash.
entries.contextCost: 11 tools, mcp__jev__*. Tool descriptions total about 6.6k chars (12 description strings, 522-758 chars each; the largest are jev_plan_gate, jev_check and jev_action_gate) plus input and output zod schemas with .describe() text. My estimate is about 3k tokens for names, descriptions and schemas (about 12k chars / 4), which is heavy for a single MCP. Claude Code's MCP tool-search deferral can cut the always-on cost. No MCP 'instructions' field is set. There is no hook-injected text, and results are compact (a few lines of text plus structuredContent with full probabilities and a duplicated 'answers' object, about 150-400 tokens per call).
pros: Only candidate here that is a working, typed, complete MCP wrapper around System One: all three primitives are exposed (jev_classify/jev_score/jev_check plus jev_ask for mixed batches), and I verified the wire format matches OpenRouter's documented System One request/response shape.

OpenRouter switch is config-only, with no fork: JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_API_KEY (or TYPESAFE_API_KEY) = OpenRouter key, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13. Response parsing uses passthrough, so OpenRouter's extra id/provider/usage.cost fields are fine.

Harness tools encode useful coding-agent patterns in a single batched call each (action pre-flight with allow/ask/deny thresholds, verify-claim-against-evidence, injection screen, choose-between-approaches) with abstention. This matches the OpenRouter 'auto-approve permission prompts' cookbook idea, though as tools rather than a hook.

Small, dependency-light, readable dist (about 1.4k lines total); no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry; key redaction in errors; structured content carries full probabilities so the model can see uncertainty.

README candidly lists when NOT to use Jev (deterministic checks, trivial work), and tool descriptions repeat it, which limits over-calling. Retry/backoff/jitter and a 5s timeout are implemented; when there is no key it degrades to a single diagnostic tool instead of crashing.
Cheap: about $0.042/M input tokens, so gate calls cost fractions of a cent.
cons: Not deterministic: fully dependent on Opus 5.5 choosing to call the tools, which contradicts the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev automatically without prompting. There is no PreToolUse hook, so jev_action_gate cannot actually block anything, and in bypass/auto mode the model can ignore or skip it.

Source repo is 404/private: unauditable, no visible commits, tests, CI, issues or contributors. 6 versions in 6 days (0.1.0-0.1.5, all 2026-09-20/21), by maximem.ai rather than TypeSafe. It is an alpha third-party package, run via npx -y unpinned.

Documented safety knobs do not work in 0.1.5: JEV_HARNESS=off is never checked by the server, harness config 'failOpen' is never read, and CallBudget is never enabled (enforceBudget unset). This is the README behavior versus the code.

11 tools (about 3k tokens of definitions) is heavy for a tool that fires rarely, and jev_plan_gate/jev_verify get called on non-trivial turns only if the model complies. Each call also costs an extra Opus tool-call turn (seconds), so the '~100ms replaces seconds of deliberation' claim is unproven for Claude Code.

Data egress of task text, shell commands, diffs and test output to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on client projects, at the model's discretion and unfiltered. Nothing redacts secrets or code, so it overlaps badly with the user's secret-leak guard hook.

Writes .jev/decisions.jsonl into every project cwd by default (dirties client repos, needs global gitignore or JEV_LEDGER_PATH), and reads an untrusted repo's jev.harness.json, which can loosen thresholds or crash startup with invalid JSON.

Default model 'jev-1.13.0' is not an OpenRouter-documented ID, so JEV_MODEL must be set explicitly. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is unsupported. Jev is unproven: the Theo/t3.gg 'DeepSeek flash router' skepticism means the calibrated-probability gating is unvalidated on real coding work.
entries.verdict: Best-shaped plain MCP wrapper for Jev and easy to point at OpenRouter with three env vars (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL), but it is model-discretion only. It cannot deliver the guaranteed 'automatic' behavior wanted here, its safety toggles (JEV_HARNESS, failOpen, budget) are inert, and the GitHub source is not public. Use it as an optional tool layer (pinned version, trimmed to 3-4 tools) beneath a deterministic PreToolUse/PermissionRequest hook that calls OpenRouter directly, not as the primary integration. Process note: I ran one `node -e import()` of the candidate dist that failed at module resolution (missing @modelcontextprotocol/sdk) before any of its code evaluated. Nothing from the package executed, and every other check was static.
entries.license: MIT (npm metadata; GitHub repo not visible)

entries.name: @y0usaf/typesafe-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (index.js, ~220 lines) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, evaluate(state, questions, model?), which POSTs to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone with a Bearer key and returns Jev's typed answers (noul/choice/score) as JSON text plus structuredContent. It also ships server "instructions" and a typesafe://guide resource with recipes (tool-call verification, intent routing, decomposition, confidence gating). It is a thin pass-through: there is no hook, no caching, no local logic.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. There is no hook and no proxy. Claude Code decides whether to call evaluate based on the tool description and server instructions, which say to use it for "classification, detection, scoring, routing, verification, ranking, context selection". Nothing in the package forces invocation. Coding turns rarely have a natural "typed decision" step, so real-world call rates are likely low unless CLAUDE.md or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook reinforces it. That would be extra work outside this package, and it would conflict with the goal of never having to prompt for it.
security: API key is read from the environment (index.js:152), not argv, so it is not exposed in the process list. `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, so use a scoped, low-limit OpenRouter key.

No child_process, no shell execution, no filesystem access, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, and no telemetry in the 220 lines of code. The only network call is the fetch at index.js:163 to BASE_URL.

Supply-chain risk: an unaffiliated single maintainer (y0usaf), a package 2 weeks old with 85 downloads/week, and no public repo. `npx -y @y0usaf/typesafe-mcp` without a version pin re-resolves on every start, so a later malicious 0.1.x could run with the key in its environment. Pin the exact version, or vendor the 220-line index.js and run it with node.

Prompt-injection surface: the JSON result is returned as text, and Jev output is typed numbers and labels, which is low risk. The risky direction is outbound, since Claude may put untrusted file content in state. Jev cannot act on it.
Bug at index.js:176-178: response.json() consumes the body, so the later response.text() fallback always yields an empty string. Error detail is lost on non-JSON errors. This is minor.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is unvalidated. If it is set to an attacker's host, the key goes there. It is only set by the user's own config.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts into the evaluate `state` and `questions` arguments goes out: HTTPS POST to openrouter.ai (then to TypeSafe as upstream provider) or api.typesafe.ai. There is no automatic collection of files, prompts, or diffs. The model decides what to send, and per the built-in instructions this will typically be code snippets, diffs, user requests, and tool traces. With client projects, that content can be client source code going to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user should check OpenRouter's data-policy and ZDR settings and avoid sending secrets or NDA code. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool calls unless its matcher is extended to mcp__typesafe__evaluate.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by construction. It is an optional tool: a missing key, a network error, an HTTP error or a timeout returns an isError text result (index.js:154-179) and Claude continues without Jev. It never blocks the turn as a hook would. The default timeout is 30 s (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS), so a hung API can stall one tool call for up to 30 s. Set TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS=3000-5000. There are no retries and no circuit breaker, and if Jev is down Claude may retry the tool repeatedly. If the server crashes at startup (for example an npx fetch failure), the tools are unavailable but the session continues.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate). Tool definition is about 1.1k chars of description plus about 2k chars of JSON schema, roughly 800 tokens. Server instructions are about 1.7k chars, roughly 430 tokens, added to the system prompt. Total is about 1.2-1.3k tokens per session, or somewhat less if tools are deferred via ToolSearch. The 3.4k-char guide resource is not auto-loaded. No hook-injected text. Cost per call is small: the state Claude serializes into the call, plus about 100-300 tokens of JSON back.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with zero code change: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> (index.js:11,152,163 match OpenRouter's documented System One path and body).
Tiny and auditable: one file of about 220 lines, MIT, one dependency (official MCP SDK), no shell, filesystem or postinstall, no telemetry.
Only about 1.2k tokens of context and 1 tool, so it is cheap next to gitnexus and playwright (tens of tools).
Fail-open: errors come back as isError results and never block Claude Code.

Exposes all three primitives (choice/score/noul) generically through one batched call, and ships a useful typesafe://guide with recipes, including tool-call verification, intent routing and injection detection.
Configurable model, base URL and timeout via env, so it can pin typesafe/jev-1.13.
cons: Not automatic: invocation is left to Opus's discretion. No hook or proxy forces use, which fails the core requirement of automatic use without prompting, unless reinforced with CLAUDE.md text or a custom hook.
Very immature: v0.1.0, published 2026-09-16, one maintainer, 85 downloads/week, no public repo link, no tests or CI. The declared scripts/review.mjs is missing from the tarball.

Generic tool: the model must write the questions and criteria every call, which costs Opus tokens and time and needs prompt engineering to be reliable. There are no ready-made coding recipes (lint triage, commit classification, and so on).

Default timeout of 30 s is too long for a 100 ms model, and there are no retries. The default model 'jev-latest' is not OpenRouter's canonical id form (docs say it is accepted, but pin it explicitly).
Data egress to third parties: client code in `state` goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The existing secret-leak hook does not match mcp__ tools by default.
`npx -y` without a version pin is an unnecessary supply-chain exposure for an unknown single-maintainer package that holds the API key.
Minor bug: error body handling at index.js:176-178. Jev is a System One decision model, and for most coding turns Opus 5.5 reasoning is better and already free of extra hops.
entries.verdict: The best available minimal bridge: it is clean, safe by inspection, and works with OpenRouter through env vars only. But it is only a model-discretion tool, so it will not give the "automatic, never-prompted" integration on its own. Use it as a pinned or vendored transport, not the answer to auto-use: pin the exact version or copy index.js locally, set TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS=5000 and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, and pair it with a deterministic PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook or CLAUDE.md rules for real automation.

entries.name: sebastianbugal/jev
entries.what: Claude Code plugin bundling a zero-dependency Node stdio MCP server (jev_decide, jev_check), two slash commands (/jev:ask, /jev:check) and a jev-decisions skill. The server POSTs {model, state, questions} to OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, validates the three primitives locally, retries transient errors, and annotates answers (noul 0.5 = cannot tell, confidence near 0 = flat distribution, choice contract_violation). It is a generic ask-Jev toolbox for Claude to call on demand. It has no policy layer and no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. The skill description is broad ('classification, routing, triage, yes/no judgement, severity rating, ranking') and could trigger, and the jev_decide tool description says to use it for those. But there is no hook and no CLAUDE.md nudge, so in practice Opus will rarely choose to send code to a third party for its own coding decisions, and it is unlikely to fire automatically in ordinary coding. Deterministic automatic use (e.g. a PermissionRequest hook) would need to be built separately on top of this or the OpenRouter cookbook.
security: Key handling: .mcp.json passes the key in the child's env (${user_config.openrouter_api_key}), not argv, so there is no argv exposure. plugin.json marks it sensitive:true. On Linux, whether the OS keychain (libsecret) is actually used or Claude Code falls back to a plaintext file in ~/.claude is Claude Code behaviour, not verified here.

The fallback credentials file ~/.config/jev/credentials.json is read on every call. There is a mode check (:111-115) that warns if group or other can read it. The key is never logged. jev_check returns only a masked preview (first 6 and last 4 chars, fully masked under 20 chars).

OPENROUTER_API_KEY is still absent from the user's no-secret-leak protected list. The server process has the key in its env, and the fallback file path is not covered by that hook's Read/Grep guard, so the list should be extended before use.

No shell exec, no child_process, no eval, no file writes, no telemetry. grep found no exec/spawn in jev/server. The only network call is fetch to baseUrl/decisions. It sends HTTP-Referer https://github.com/sebastianbugal/jev and X-Title 'Claude Code jev', which is OpenRouter app attribution, not telemetry.
JEV_BASE_URL env override: if an attacker could set it, the Bearer key would go to that host. This is an env-control risk only.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever state Claude sends (diffs, files) goes to Jev, and per the brief, injected instructions in state can move answers. Answers are typed numbers and labels, so the return channel cannot inject prose. The one free-text pass-through is error body text, capped at 800 chars.
entries.dataEgress: Only the `state` and `questions` that Claude composes, plus model and an optional session_id, plus the Bearer key, go over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, where they are served by TypeSafe. That can include diffs, file contents and tickets. Content is chosen by the model, and there is no redaction, allowlist or path filter. The local size guard is 110k chars. The README has an honest disclosure ('do not install if terms forbid third-party inference'). There is no telemetry to the author. For client projects, the model's discretion over what to send is the main risk.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft by design. Tool errors return as isError text with hints, not as protocol errors. Timeout is 60s per attempt, and there are up to 3 attempts with 500ms exponential backoff or Retry-After (capped at 30s) on 408/429/5xx. That gives a worst case of about 3 minutes if OpenRouter hangs, which is too long for anything inline. There is no hook, so nothing blocks tool execution and nothing can wedge the session. A missing key does not stop the server starting, but every call errors. A 200 without answers throws. Local validation rejects malformed questions before any billed call.
entries.contextCost: Two tools. The tool source is about 4.7k chars, and QUESTION_SHAPES (about 1.2k chars) is embedded twice in jev_decide (in the tool description and in the questions property description), so expanded JSON is roughly 6.5k chars, about 1.6-1.7k tokens per session (deferred if tool search is on). The skill listing entry is a long description (about 480 chars, roughly 120 tokens against the 0.02 budget). The skill body is about 8.7k chars (roughly 2.2k tokens) once loaded. Each command adds a listing entry. There is no MCP `instructions` field and no hook-injected text. Each call's output includes both interpreted answers and raw_answers, which duplicates data.
pros: Native OpenRouter: baseUrl https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha, path /decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, and a plain OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so no patching (jev.mjs:27-28, :413).
Clean, dependency-free code. jev.mjs and index.mjs are about 41KB total, readable in minutes, with no exec, no writes and no telemetry. The key travels via env, not argv.

Solid client engineering: local schema validation (255 choices, 10 score levels, both noul branches), a payload guard, 408/429/5xx retries honouring Retry-After, handling of 402 in-flight budget, and detection of a 200 with an error envelope.

Good answer interpretation: labels noul 0.5 as cannot tell, flags flat distributions, and adds contract_violation if a choice answer is not one of the offered options. This matches the independent evals' calibration caveats, and the skill says 'policy belongs in code'.
58 offline tests including a stub-endpoint integration test, and an API contract doc verified against the live endpoint.
Honest privacy notice, and Jev's model slug is overridable (JEV_MODEL / ~typesafe/jev-latest).
The tool wrapper is reusable: a custom PermissionRequest hook or the cookbook pattern could call the same decide() via a small script, and the validation and retry logic is worth borrowing.
cons: It does not deliver the user's stated goal. There is no hook and no automatic path, so use relies on Opus choosing to invoke a skill or tool, or on the user typing /jev:ask, which is the 'use jev' prompting the user wants to avoid.
Sends code to a third party at the model's discretion with no allowlist or redaction. With client projects, defaultMode auto and bypassPermissions sessions, this is the biggest risk.

Missing files fits neither the PreToolUse secret guard nor the fail-closed posture. OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not yet in no-secret-leak's list, and the plugin's fallback credentials file is not covered either.

Very immature: 0 stars, 5 commits in about 1 day, a single author, no releases, no tag pinning, and a README/test-count inconsistency (43 vs 58). The README also documents short forms (/jev, /jev-check) but the command files are ask.md and check.md, which resolve to /jev:ask and /jev:check.

Heavy per-call cost for a small win: Opus has to write 1-4 typed questions plus state (seconds of model time), and results carry both interpreted and raw_answers. Jev's accuracy is a bit below mid-price LLMs, so it adds little for a strong main model doing coding decisions.
Timeouts are generous (60s x 3 attempts) with no fast-fail option for interactive use. Duplicated QUESTION_SHAPES text bloats the tool definition by about 1.2k chars. The alpha endpoint has no SLA.
Not a permission gate or safety layer: it offers nothing for the Bash risk classification use case beyond what the skill teaches Claude to do manually.
entries.verdict: A well-built, dependency-free and safe-to-read OpenRouter-native Jev MCP plugin, but it is a manual /jev:ask toolbox with no hook, so it will not give the user automatic use of Jev, and it can send client code to a third party at the model's discretion. Worth borrowing its client and validation code for a custom PermissionRequest hook, and worth installing only if on-demand /jev:ask is enough; otherwise it is a moderate fit for this user.

entries.name: darwintechlab/claude-jev
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace "openjev", plugin "claude-jev" v0.1.1) bundling a local stdio Node MCP server "jev" with 5 tools (jev_choice, jev_noul, jev_score, jev_ask, jev_doctor) that POST {model,state,questions} to the TypeSafe System One endpoint, plus a skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) that tells Claude to prefer Jev for bounded decisions. Adds client-side validation, retries, confidence gating (auto/escalate), criteria linting, head+tail truncation at 60k chars and a stderr audit log (state hash only). It is a mirror of the author's opencode-openjev; no hooks, no proxy. Built plugin/runtime/*.mjs is a committed esbuild bundle (about 950 KB total, dominated by the MCP SDK and zod/ajv chunks).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: an MCP tool set plus a description-triggered skill. There is no hook, proxy or router, so nothing is deterministic. Whether Opus 5.5 calls jev_* for a given decision depends on it judging the skill description/tool descriptions relevant; for a general coding agent, bounded classification decisions rarely arise as explicit steps, so calls will be sporadic. Could be made deterministic only by adding your own PreToolUse hook that calls Jev (not provided; gateGuardrail is exported but unused).
security: API key handled well: marked sensitive userConfig, passed to the MCP process via env CLAUDE_JEV_API_KEY (plugin.json mcpServers.jev.env), never in argv; no .env auto-load or fallback to shell keys in the shipped runtime; errors do not print the key (client.ts:129 prints only status and up to 800 chars of the response body).

No child_process/spawn/exec in the shipped runtime (grep of index.mjs and chunk-A3CL7OOL/LX7VSNGJ/QTEOOZ7M found none; the only fetch is client.mjs chunk line 125 to baseURL). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the configured endpoint. Bundled node_modules code is minified-free but large (about 750 KB of vendored MCP SDK/zod/ajv), hard to audit; THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES included.
base_url is user-configurable and receives both the Bearer key and all decision text; a wrong/malicious base_url exfiltrates key + state. Default is the legit typesafe host.

Prompt-injection surface: tool result is model-authored-free JSON (choice/probabilities) so low; but `state` is attacker-influenceable content (repo text, tool output) and Jev has no reasoning trace, so a gate decision on injected text is manipulable. SKILL.md encourages Claude to auto-act on 'auto' results; the README itself says keep irreversible actions behind human approval.
Audit log goes to MCP stderr (Claude Code debug log) and uses a 32-bit FNV hash of state: not a security hash, weak for low-entropy text but no raw state is logged.
Release files are committed generated bundles (no reproducible-build CI), so the runtime cannot be trusted to match TS source without rebuilding; spot-check of endpoint/env/tool text matched source.
entries.dataEgress: On every jev_* call the full `state` string (up to 60k chars; whatever Claude puts in it: code, diffs, commands, file contents, ticket text) plus the question schema (instructions, criteria) and the API key are sent over HTTPS to base_url (default api.typesafe.ai, or openrouter.ai if reconfigured). Nothing is sent automatically by the plugin itself; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool. No telemetry elsewhere. README warns not to send secrets, but nothing in the code scrubs secrets; the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tool inputs unless its matcher is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: on error/timeout the tool returns isError JSON {ok:false,error} (index.ts:168-170) and Claude just continues with its own judgment; no hook is in the path so nothing blocks. Client timeout 15 s per attempt, 2 retries with exponential backoff on 429/529/5xx/timeouts/network errors (client.ts:39-41,121-163), so the worst case for a hung endpoint is about 45 s plus backoff of one stalled tool call. Missing key throws immediately 'API key is required'. Invalid JSON in criteria/questions strings throws (caught).
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Tool names+descriptions+schemas total about 2.9k chars, roughly 700-800 tokens permanently in the tool list (unless Claude Code tool-search defers them). No server-level 'instructions' field. Skill adds only its frontmatter description (about 400 chars, about 100 tokens) always; the SKILL.md body (about 3.3k chars, about 850 tokens) loads when triggered. Zero hook-injected text. Each result is pretty-printed JSON (JSON.stringify(...,null,2)), typically 150-600 tokens; jev_ask echoes the full answers map.
pros: Cleanest integration mechanism of the kind: proper Claude Code plugin with userConfig, sensitive key storage, and a stdio MCP server; base_url and model are user-configurable (plugin.json userConfig), so pointing at OpenRouter needs no code change if OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body.

Reasonable engineering: input validation before network, retry/backoff, 15 s timeout, head+tail truncation, confidence gating with asymmetric fail-closed guardrail helper, key never on argv, no shell execution, no postinstall, MIT license.
jev_ask batches up to 32 typed questions in a single call, which suits a future hook that asks several safety/routing questions at once.
Small footprint: 5 tools (about 750 tokens) and a short skill; no per-call hook overhead so it cannot slow normal coding.
Ships a skill description that explicitly nudges Claude to reach for Jev on bounded decisions without the user saying 'use jev'.
cons: Only model-discretion invocation: no hook, so it does not satisfy 'Claude Code must use it when needed' deterministically; in practice Opus will mostly decide inline and rarely call jev_* for routine editing/search tasks.

No OpenRouter support in code (zero references); works only via manual base_url override to an endpoint whose schema I could not verify; key must be typed into a plugin config dialog, OPENROUTER_API_KEY env is ignored, which is awkward for headless/scripted setups. Does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) or model ids beyond a free-text model field.

Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-24, 7 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, no CI; README and marketplace instructions reference a different repo (claude-openjev), and the description calls itself a 'mirror of opencode-openjev', so upstream provenance is confusing.

Benchmarks are self-authored (115 cases, vendor-adjacent), README claims of 90% accuracy, 'calibrated' probabilities and 1/128 cost vs Opus are unverified; author's own severity scoring accuracy is 67%. Latency claims are inconsistent (307 ms vs 223 ms).
Unused value: guardrail gate (gate.ts:200-218) that would be the most useful piece for a PreToolUse safety check is not wired to anything; user would have to build the hook himself.

Sends full state (code, diffs, command text) to a third party with a beta model; no secret scrubbing; on client projects this is a data-handling/NDA concern and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* inputs.
Each Jev call costs an extra Opus turn to write the call and read JSON, so net latency and tokens are usually worse than letting Opus decide inline; up to about 45 s stall if the endpoint hangs.
Committed 950 KB bundled runtime is hard to audit and not reproducibly built in CI; 32-bit FNV 'hash' in audit log.
entries.verdict: A tidy, safe-looking but very new and self-benchmarked MCP plugin that gives Claude typed Jev tools; it is only model-discretion (no hook), has no native OpenRouter support (needs a base_url override that is unverified against OpenRouter's schema), so it does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' requirement on its own. Useful as a transport/reference for a custom PreToolUse hook or as an optional MCP tool, not as the primary integration.

entries.name: MarkChu-git/typesafe-mcp (npm: typesafe-mcp)
entries.what: A working stdio MCP server (Bun, TypeScript, about 880 LOC of src) that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk and exposes Jev's three primitives as 5 typed tools (jev_check/Noul, jev_classify/Choice, jev_score/Score, jev_ask/batch, jev_models). The server, not Jev, computes a threshold-gated act/review/abstain verdict from certainty (default act_above 0.8, review_above 0.5). The discovery summary "research/scaffolding" is outdated: the repo also has a published npm package (v0.1.0 and v0.1.1 on 2026-09-21), MIT license, CI, and about 18 test files. It is a third-party wrapper by an individual, not a TypeSafe official project.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code will call jev_* only if the model decides the tool descriptions fit the current situation. The descriptions are generic (an "ask Jev a yes/no question about state"), with no coding triggers, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no skill, and no hook. So it will rarely fire on its own for daily coding, and a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill would be needed to make it fire reliably. The user's requirement "without me prompting" is only weakly met.
security: API key is read only from env (src/config.ts:23) and never placed in argv. The README config passes it via the MCP `env` block, so it is not visible in the process list. It does end up in plaintext in the Claude config file if pasted.

Errors redact keys (README says so; src/errors.ts handles the mapping). The SDK's logLevel is forced to 'warn' (src/client.ts:27), so the request body is not logged (SDK debug level would log bodies and redacted headers).

No shell execution, child_process, eval, or telemetry found in src/. The published bundle (mcpnpm dist/typesafe-mcp.js, 22.5k lines) contains no eval, child_process, or spawn calls. No postinstall scripts in typesafe-mcp or @typesafe-ai/sdk package.json. No curl|sh installer.

Supply chain: 2 runtime deps that matter (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0, published 2026-09-15 by the TypeSafe maintainers; @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0) plus zod. Releases use OIDC trusted publishing with provenance. The author is an individual (1 contributor, 1 star), so the trust is in one unknown maintainer plus a very new npm package. Pin the version.

Prompt-injection surface is low: outputs are numeric probabilities and echoed ids, with no free text from the model. The model's answer is constrained. But the tool inputs (`state`) are arbitrary text the agent chooses to send to a third party.

Repo contains committed .claude/.cursor skills and a .claude/settings.json with teamai hooks. These are the author's own dev tooling in the repo, are not shipped in the npm package (files: dist, examples), and are irrelevant unless someone opens the repo in Claude Code.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in the `state` and `question`/`options`/`levels`/`criteria` fields of a tool call goes to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is changed), as JSON POST to /v1/systemone with Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: the server never reads files, diffs or transcripts on its own, and only the text Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine. Extra headers sent: User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK / X-TypeSafe-Runtime (SDK version and runtime name). With OpenRouter, the provider also sees the payload and may apply its own logging or data policies, which matters for client projects. The state limit is about 32k tokens.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft per call and not blocking. This is an MCP tool, not a hook, so a Jev outage only returns an isError tool result with a category prefix (TIMEOUT, NETWORK, RATE_LIMIT, OVERLOADED, UPSTREAM, AUTH, CONFIG, VALIDATION) and Claude carries on. Timeout is 10 s per attempt (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS in src/config.ts:13, override via TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS). The SDK retries up to 2 times with backoff (index.mjs:73-74), so the worst case is about 30 s of hang for one tool call. Without a key the server still starts and lists tools, and calls return a CONFIG error. Note that Claude might waste turns retrying or reasoning about the error.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. Tool descriptions total about 1.9k characters. The zod schemas with long .describe() text (state, question, model, thresholds, and a discriminated union in jev_ask) plus outputSchemas add roughly 8-10k characters more. My estimate is about 2.5-3.5k tokens of tool definitions, and it is not measured. No MCP server `instructions` (createServer only sets name and version, src/server.ts:11). No hook-injected text. Loaded lazily via ToolSearch if the user has deferred MCP tools enabled.
pros: It is the only candidate here with a real, tested, MIT-licensed Jev MCP server that exposes all three primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) plus a batch `jev_ask`, with strict zod input/output schemas and outputSchema on every tool (src/tools/*.ts).

OpenRouter switch is env-only in theory: the official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and sends Bearer to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (sdk index.mjs:58,513,554,581), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key should reach OpenRouter's System One endpoint with no fork.

Sensible engineering hygiene for a week-old repo: pinned GitHub Action SHAs, CodeQL, zizmor, dependency review, OIDC npm provenance, recorded error fixtures for 401/422/429/529, key redaction, stdout kept clean for stdio.

Server-computed act/review/abstain gate with echoed thresholds (src/gating.ts) makes the output easy for an agent to act on deterministically, and `jev_ask` batching keeps calls to one upstream request.
Low risk profile: key via env not argv, no shell exec or postinstall, no telemetry in src or the bundle, readOnlyHint on tools, data sent only when Claude passes it.
Small footprint of 5 tools (about 3k tokens of context), and fail-soft errors so an outage never blocks coding.
cons: Does not meet the core requirement of automatic use: pure model-discretion tools with generic descriptions and no coding-specific triggers, no skill, no hook and no CLAUDE.md snippet, so Claude will seldom reach for it unless told. Integration would need extra glue (a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill written by the user).

OpenRouter is not supported in code or docs (docs/research-jev-typesafe-mcp.md:182 says unconfirmed). The base-URL trick depends on OpenRouter's /v1/systemone schema matching TypeSafe's, and I did not verify that. jev_models will very likely fail because it expects `{models:[...]}` from GET /v1/models (sdk index.mjs:368-371), and the default model ids (jev-latest, jev-1.13.0 hints in src/config.ts:11-12 and schema text) are not OpenRouter ids (typesafe/jev-1.13), so the user has to override the model everywhere.

Requires Bun, which is not in the user's stack (Node 24, uv). The npm bundle is built with `--target=bun`, so npx/node use is not supported by the README. Adds a runtime to install for one small server.

Very immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-21, 15 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 1 fork, v0.1.1 only, SERVER_VERSION constant still says 0.1.0 (src/config.ts:2) although the package is 0.1.1. Roadmap items (HTTP transport, Jev-specific coding tools like jev_gate) are not implemented. Depends on an SDK that is itself only about 2 weeks old (0.6.0, 2026-09-15). Jev is beta.

The MCP server asks for a decision, but for coding the tool result is only a probability. Claude still has to spend a model turn to decide to call it and to read the result, so it is slower and more expensive than just deciding. The Opus main model answers a typed choice in one thought. Value only appears for routing or gating logic in the user's own apps, or for calibrated abstain thresholds.

Sends `state` text (potentially client code or ticket content) to TypeSafe or OpenRouter. No per-project allowlist or redaction, and the user's existing secret-leak guard only covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* tool inputs, so a leak would be possible if Claude passes secrets in `state`.
Failure worst case is a 30 s hang per call (10 s timeout x 3 attempts) with no circuit breaker, and there is no fast-fail mode.
Adds 5 tool definitions (about 3k tokens) to every session for a tool that will rarely be called, unless deferred tools are used.
entries.verdict: The best-built Jev MCP wrapper found so far and almost certainly switchable to OpenRouter with just TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus an OpenRouter key and typesafe/* model ids (inferred from code, not tested), but it is a passive, generic tool that Claude will rarely call unprompted, needs Bun, and comes from a one-week-old single-maintainer repo. Use it at most as a pinned, optional building block behind a CLAUDE.md rule or skill, not as the automatic integration the user wants.

entries.name: Djancyp/oido-typesafeai-mcp (oido-typesafe MCP extension)
entries.what: Small Go stdio MCP server (about 240 lines plus a 90-line HTTP client) written as a plugin for Oido Studio. It exposes four tools (typesafe_choice, typesafe_noul, typesafe_score, typesafe_ask) that wrap TypeSafe's System One API. Each tool POSTs {state, model, questions} to <BASE_URL>/systemone with a Bearer key and renders the typed answer (choice, probabilities, noul, score, confidence) as plain text. It has nothing Claude-Code-specific: no hooks, skills or plugin.json. It is a plain MCP server that works with Claude Code once built.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills or CLAUDE.md snippets in the repo. Whether Claude calls it depends on the tool descriptions, which are written in a generic 'routing/classification/policy' style aimed at agent builders rather than coding workflows. With no reinforcing instruction, Opus will rarely reach for it in ordinary coding. It would be reliably used only if the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule (which the user does not want to do per prompt, though a one-time global rule is not a per-prompt instruction).
security: API key is read from an env var (config.go:17), so it is not in argv by default. The --config JSON flag (main.go:12-31) would put the key in argv and the process list if used. Avoid it and use env only.
No shell execution, no postinstall and no curl|sh in the repo. The build is a plain go build.
No telemetry. The only network call is the configured BASE_URL, so if the base URL is misconfigured the bearer key goes to that host. There is no allow-list or https enforcement.
Error paths return the raw response body to the model (client.go:81), so any upstream error text ends up in context (a minor prompt-injection surface, only from the configured endpoint).
Tool output is a small typed numeric summary, so the injection surface is small. The main risk is the opposite direction: the model chooses what state to send.
Dependencies are only go-sdk v0.2.0 and uritemplate. No lockfile problems are visible (go.sum is present), but the SDK is pre-1.0.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts into the 'state' and 'instructions' tool arguments leaves the machine. That is not a fixed set: it can be code snippets, diffs, file contents or ticket text, whatever Claude decides to pass. It goes to the configured endpoint (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe/Jev if the base URL is switched; api.typesafe.ai by default). The server itself reads no files and hooks nothing, so nothing is sent automatically. There is no redaction and no size cap, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__ tool arguments unless its matcher is extended. That is a concern for client code.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in effect. The HTTP client timeout is 30 s (client.go:47), with no retry. Any failure (non-200, network error, or parse error) returns an isError tool result 'Error: ...' (mcp_server.go:235-240) and Claude simply continues. If the API key is missing, the server exits at startup (log.Fatalf, mcp_server.go:52), so the MCP server shows as failed to connect and Claude Code carries on without the tools. A 30 s hang on a slow call would stall the turn, as the timeout is far longer than Jev's claimed 70-500 ms. There is also a nil-pointer risk: if the response lacks the 'q1' key, answers[answerQID] is a zero Answer and renderAnswer returns an empty string, so the model sees an empty success.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools (typesafe_choice, typesafe_noul, typesafe_score, typesafe_ask). Descriptions total about 1.9k chars. Arguments use jsonschema tags, and 'state' and 'criteria' are 'any' and free-form maps, so the schemas are loose and add about 1.5-2k chars. Total is roughly 900-1,100 tokens per session if the tools are eagerly loaded (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch). No MCP server 'instructions' are set (server built with nil options), and no hook-injected text. The OIDO.md auto-trigger guidance is not loaded by Claude Code, so the model gets only the tool descriptions, which say when to use each primitive but never say 'proactively use this when coding'.
pros: Smallest correct thin wrapper over the System One schema: about 330 lines of Go, easy to read and audit in full, with no shell, postinstall or telemetry.

Config-only switch to OpenRouter (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 plus the model slug), because the client appends /systemone and sends a standard Bearer key. The request schema matches OpenRouter's System One API.
Exposes all three Jev primitives plus a batch tool (typesafe_ask), so one call can score several dimensions over shared state, which saves round trips.
Only 4 tools and about 1k tokens of context, so it is cheap to keep loaded.
Tool errors are returned as isError results and the server never blocks Claude; API key is passed via env, not argv.
OIDO.md has sound anti-misuse guidance (do not use for exact or rule-based answers; confidence is not correctness).
cons: Built for Oido Studio, not Claude Code. The auto-trigger guidance (OIDO.md), the TOML slash commands and oido-extension.json are all ignored by Claude Code, so the 'automatic' behavior the user wants is not delivered.
Purely model-discretion invocation. Nothing deterministic (no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook, no skill), so Opus will only occasionally call it and it can silently never fire.
1 commit, 0 stars, 1 contributor, no tests, no CI, no releases and no LICENSE file (README claims MIT), on a 7-day-old repo. It needs a Go 1.24 toolchain to build and uses the pre-1.0 go-sdk v0.2.0.
30 s HTTP timeout with no retry, and an empty-answer edge case if the q1 key is missing (renders as a blank success).

Not OpenRouter-aware: the env var names say TYPESAFE/OIDO, the default model 'jev-latest' is probably not a valid OpenRouter slug, and it cannot use the /api/alpha/decisions endpoint or the Jev Router model.
The model chooses what to send as state, with no redaction, so code from client projects may go to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, and the existing secret guard hook does not cover this tool.
Random Go map ordering makes probability lines and batch answers come out in a different order each time.
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal, auditable MCP wrapper that can be pointed at OpenRouter by changing env vars alone, which makes it a reasonable primitive. As a stand-alone answer to 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' it falls short: it is Oido-oriented, invocation is left to the model, and it is a 1-commit, untested, unlicensed prototype. Its best use is as a base or reference (or to fork with a Claude-Code-aware description and hooks), not as the daily-driver integration.
entries.license: None detected by GitHub (licenseInfo null; there is no LICENSE file). README says MIT, but no license file is present, so legally it is unlicensed.

entries.name: gnapse/jev (@gnapse/jev)
entries.what: Third-party (individual author Ernesto García, not TypeSafe) TypeScript CLI plus local stdio MCP server that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0. Exposes Jev Choice/Noul/Score requests as 4 MCP tools (jev_ask, jev_batch, jev_models, jev_validate) and a `jev` CLI, plus an Agent Skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md). The MCP server is purely model-discretion; nothing hooks into Claude Code events. It is a thin generic transport, with no coding-specific logic (examples such as CI triage and diff labels exist only as CLI scripts in the repo).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude would call jev_ask only if it judges the tool description fits (generic: 'Ask typed questions about text or JSON using Jev'). There is no hook and no proxy, so nothing deterministic. The optional skill's trigger is tied to 'working with @gnapse/jev or adding classification... to scripts', which is not a general coding trigger. Auto-use in daily coding would be rare and unpredictable unless CLAUDE.md or a hook adds policy (e.g. 'before X, call jev_ask with Choice to classify Y'), which the user explicitly does not want to hand-prompt.
security: API key never accepted via argv or tool arguments (docs/mcp.md, SKILL.md). It comes from env or a credentials file (~/.config/jev/credentials.json, dir 0700 and file 0600, O_NOFOLLOW, perms enforced on read: src/cli/credentials.ts:45-60). This is good hygiene.
Key is stored unencrypted (README says so). For OpenRouter use, an env var in the MCP config is the practical route, and it lands in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
Diagnostics purposely omit bodies and credentials (api.ts:38-40; logLevel 'off'). Logs only origin and retry count.
No telemetry found (grep telemetry|analytics returned nothing in src). SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers with the version, which is benign.
No shell execution or eval in the MCP path. A base URL override accepts any http(s) host, so a malicious env could redirect state and key elsewhere, but that needs control of the env.

Prompt-injection surface: the MCP output is only numeric probabilities and option labels, with no free text from the model, so the return path is a low injection risk. The input path is whatever Claude chooses to send (code, diffs, tool output).
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude places in `state` and `questions` arguments of jev_ask/jev_batch leaves the machine: POST to <base>/v1/systemone with the bearer key, sent to api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (and then TypeSafe as its provider) if the base URL is overridden. Nothing is sent automatically: no hooks, no file scanning, no transcript access. Claude decides content per call, so client code, diffs and file contents are sent whenever the model chooses to include them. With the secret-leak guard hook only on Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, MCP calls to jev_* are not covered, so secrets in state would pass through unguarded. OpenRouter's prompt-logging/ZDR settings then apply.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's point of view: errors come back as an MCP tool result with isError:true and a structured error body (code, retryable, http_status), and Claude simply proceeds without Jev. Defaults: per-attempt timeout 10 s (settings.ts:69), total deadline 120 s (settings.ts:70), SDK retries maxRetries 2 with backoff (settings.ts:79), concurrency 4, max 32 outstanding calls. Worst case for a slow or down backend is a call stalling the turn for up to ~120 s (retries x 10 s), unless timeout_ms/deadline_ms are tuned via a config file or CLI flags. Those cannot be set through MCP env vars, only via the `config` file or `jev mcp` flags. If the key is missing, the tool returns an AUTH_ERROR without crashing the server.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Estimated ~1.5-2k tokens for tool names, descriptions and inputSchemas (descriptions about 1.3k chars, input schemas about 5k chars, roughly 6-7k chars/4). outputSchema is also declared, but it is likely not sent to the model. Server `instructions` are about 300 chars (~75 tokens). No hook-injected text. If the optional SKILL.md (6.4k chars, about 1.6k tokens) is installed, only its description line sits in context until it triggers. This is a small, static cost, and lower still if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch.
pros: Wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, which POSTs `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` with a Bearer token (dist/index.mjs:554,579). That path matches OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, so OpenRouter should work via env only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (settings.ts:63) with an OpenRouter key.

Well-engineered for a v0.1: strict AJV request validation offline, jev_validate needs no key, bounded concurrency, request deadlines, cancellation, structured errors with retryable flag, secrets excluded from logs.
Tiny context footprint (4 tools, about 1.5-2k tokens, no hook text), and no hooks, so no interference with the existing secret-guard/GitNexus/caveman hooks and zero per-turn latency.
Tools declared readOnlyHint, so no permission prompts in auto or bypass mode.
MCP-only path returns only numbers and labels (no free text), so it is a low prompt-injection risk on the return path.
MIT licensed, cross-platform CI on Node 22/24, semantic-release pipeline; also ships a CLI usable from Bash by Claude or scripts, and a SKILL.md.
Includes typed request examples for CI-failure triage, diff labels and claim verification. These show concrete uses to model an auto-invocation policy on.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with a generic description. Nothing makes Claude Code reach for Jev during coding, so the user's core requirement (no 'use jev' prompting) is not met without extra glue (CLAUDE.md policy or own hooks).

Hard-wired to TypeSafe: no OpenRouter code path, docs or tests; OpenRouter works only by an unverified env override. Default model name 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter slug (needs TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL). jev_models likely breaks on OpenRouter's /models shape.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21 (9 days old), 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, v0.1.1; not TypeSafe-official. API and behaviour may churn, and it is a supply-chain trust decision (pin the version).

Timeouts/retries default to 10 s x 3 attempts and 120 s deadline, and are not configurable via MCP env vars, so a slow Jev could stall a turn for a long time. Would need a config file or wrapper flags.

Silent egress: jev_* calls are readOnly so auto/bypass mode sends whatever state Claude chooses (code, diffs) with no prompt, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not match MCP tools. Would need a PreToolUse matcher for mcp__jev__.*.

Jev is a decision-classifier, not a code model; this package adds no coding-specific integration (no PreToolUse routing, no diff/permission classification hooks), so daily-coding value is speculative.

Key handling: for OpenRouter the key has to live as plaintext env in the MCP config (~/.claude.json) or be exported in the shell; `jev auth login` stores it only for TypeSafe verification and may reject an OpenRouter key when verifying before save (unverified).
entries.verdict: A clean, safe-ish thin MCP/CLI wrapper that can probably be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is a generic manual-use tool: it gives Claude Code the ability to call Jev, not any automatic trigger. Useful only as the transport layer beneath a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy, or as a reference for the request format; pin the version and treat it as alpha.

entries.name: mcp-server-jev (bin: jev-mcp)
entries.what: Generic stdio MCP server that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (systemOne call) and exposes Jev's three primitives as tools: batched jev_evaluate, single-question jev_choice / jev_score / jev_noul, and jev_models. Not coding-specific: no hooks, no skill, no code/diff awareness. The model must decide to call it and must build the typed question and the self-contained 'state' itself. Ships a short server 'instructions' string telling the model to ask atomic questions, batch them, and read confidence as a second axis.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, skill, or proxy. Claude will call it on its own only if the tool descriptions and server instructions look relevant to the current task. Those texts are generic: 'routing, classifying, gating an action' (not coding-specific), and they say nothing like 'before committing / after tests fail'. Expect rare and inconsistent use unless a CLAUDE.md rule or hook/skill supplies concrete triggers. So it does not meet 'Claude must use it when needed' by itself. It is a good transport layer under a hook or skill, not the automation.
security: npm package published 2026-09-24 by a single individual maintainer (mark-haedal <[email removed]>), not a typesafe-ai account; package.json has no repository/homepage/bugs field, so there is no auditable source repo, CI, or issue tracker. Tarball contains only dist/index.js (bundled, deps external), README, LICENSE, package.json (4 files, 30.9 KB). README says releases are manual 'npm publish' with no CI or Git remote. Tests described in README are not in the tarball, so I could not verify them.

No install/postinstall scripts; only prepack/prepublishOnly (publisher side). Dependencies: @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.1.0, @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 (official, MIT, repo typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js), commander, zod. Unpinned `npx -y mcp-server-jev` would auto-pull any future malicious version from an anonymous single maintainer: pin the exact version (mcp-server-jev@0.1.0) or vendor dist/index.js.

Read dist/index.js in full (377 lines): no shell execution, no filesystem access, no telemetry of its own, only the SDK HTTP call. SDK sets X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers and User-Agent (harmless metadata) and redacts headers in debug logs.

Key handling: the env-var names are unusual and case-sensitive (jevApiKey, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY). README recommends env block over --jevApiKey because argv shows in ps; via claude mcp add --env the key lands in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, so use a dedicated low-limit OpenRouter key. Could be sourced from shell env instead of a literal.

Prompt-injection surface is small: tool output is just numbers and labels (no free text from Jev). The main risk is the reverse: Jev's low-confidence or wrong probabilities could steer the model's decisions. Tool result echoes user-supplied option labels and legend text only.
Error logging goes to stderr (console.error), never stdout, so the protocol is not corrupted. Server warns on start if no key is set.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts in the tool arguments (state, instructions, criteria/options/levels, optional model) is JSON-POSTed to jevBaseUrl/v1/systemone (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe/its provider) with the bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: no hooks, no file scanning. But 'state' is free-form, so if Claude passes code, diffs, file contents, tool output or secrets into it, all of that leaves the machine to OpenRouter and its upstream. This matters for client projects. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools unless its matcher is extended. The SDK adds SDK version/runtime headers.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice: any error is thrown as a tool error with an actionable message (dist/index.js:255-262, 119-150) and Claude simply continues. Nothing blocks the session. However the latency worst case is bad: SDK timeout is 10 s per attempt (index.mjs:518) with maxRetries 2 on timeouts, connection errors, 408, 429 and 5xx (index.mjs:74-88), with backoff 0.5-5 s and Retry-After up to 60 s, so a down or slow endpoint can stall one tool call for about 30-40 s or more. Claude's MCP tool timeout applies on top. No option to tune this through the server's config (only jevApiKey, jevBaseUrl, jevModel are exposed). Missing key: server starts, every call errors.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. Estimated tool definitions ~9-11k chars, about 2.5-3k tokens (jev_evaluate has the largest schema: discriminated union of 3 question types with long describe() strings; each shortcut tool ~1.2-1.8k chars; jev_models tiny) if all loaded eagerly. Claude Code's MCP tool search can defer them to names only. Server 'instructions' text ~1.3k chars (~330 tokens) is injected every session. No hook-injected text. Adds one more always-on stdio process (Node, ~50-80 MB). A cheaper setup exposes only jev_evaluate via permissions/allow lists.
pros: Only needs config to use OpenRouter: jevBaseUrl=https://openrouter.ai/api hits the correct /v1/systemone endpoint, verified in SDK code (index.mjs:554,581), and reuses OpenRouter's key as Bearer.
Small and readable: one 377-line bundled file with no shell, fs, or telemetry code, no install scripts. Statically auditable in minutes.
Built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so request/response schemas match TypeSafe's, with built-in retries and typed errors mapped to actionable messages.

Good tool ergonomics: jev_evaluate batches mixed noul/score/choice questions in one call; structuredContent plus a readable text line; probabilities truncated to keep output small; server instructions teach atomic questions and confidence use.
Fits the 'gate an action' idea: jev_noul can be a cheap yes/no check (for example 'does this diff touch auth?') when something else triggers it.
MIT licensed; the same server also works on TypeSafe direct if OpenRouter is dropped.
cons: Does not satisfy the core requirement: invocation depends on the main model's judgment. There is no hook or skill trigger, and the generic descriptions do not say when to consult Jev during coding, so Claude will mostly ignore it without extra CLAUDE.md prompting, which the user explicitly does not want.

Provenance risk: released 6 days ago (0.1.0, single version), an anonymous individual maintainer, no repository link, no CI, and README-described tests that are absent from the tarball. Unpinned npx would auto-update from that account.

Odd, non-standard env names (jevApiKey/jevBaseUrl/jevModel, case-sensitive) instead of OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The key ends up in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or must be exported in the shell. jev_models is broken on OpenRouter.

Data-leak channel: free-form 'state' can carry code and client data to OpenRouter. The existing secret-guard hook does not cover it without a matcher change, and there is no redaction or size cap in the server (32k context limit is left to the API to reject).
Poor failure bounds: 10 s x 3 attempts plus backoff (up to about 30-40 s) with no config knob to shorten it, and Retry-After up to 60 s honored.

Every question costs an Opus turn to author the typed schema plus its output tokens, likely more than a Jev call saves for typical coding decisions. Jev returns no text or reasoning, so it does not help write, debug or review code directly.

Adds 5 tool defs and about 330 tokens of server instructions to every session for a tool that will rarely fire. Overlaps with the other community Jev MCPs (burnigtm/jev-mcp, jkudish/jev-mcp, Brainwires/jevwire) that appear to target coding loops or ship hooks; this one has no source repo to compare.
entries.verdict: Clean, small, OpenRouter-compatible transport for Jev (config-only, verified in code), but it is a bare model-discretion MCP with no hook or skill triggers and an unauditable one-week-old single-maintainer npm release, so it will not give the user's 'Claude uses Jev automatically' behavior on its own. Usable only pinned (@0.1.0) and paired with a hook or skill that supplies the triggers, or as a reference implementation to vendor.

entries.name: arunav25/jev-mcp (@arunav25/jev-mcp)
entries.what: Node (ESM) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards typed Jev questions (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe's System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone) and returns the raw JSON of probabilities. Also ships `jev-eval`, an offline harness (Brier, ECE, AUC, McNemar, latency/cost) for comparing Jev vs OpenAI/Anthropic baselines on labelled noul datasets, plus `jev-mcp install` which registers the server in Claude Code/Desktop/Codex.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no plugin, no CLAUDE.md snippet. The tool description ('Use it wherever you would otherwise ask a model for an answer and then parse the reply') and server instructions are the only nudge; Opus will rarely choose it for ordinary coding since it has no coding-shaped use case (classifying tickets/urgency is the example domain). Meets the 'no prompting jev' requirement only weakly and unreliably; would need a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook to make it deterministic.
security: API key handling: `jev-mcp install` passes `-e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<value>` as argv to `claude mcp add` (install.js:130-131), so the key is visible in the process list during install and is stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (and Desktop/Codex configs, mode 0600 only for the Desktop temp file). It also copies every TYPESAFE_* var. Mitigation: register by hand or use env passthrough.

No shell execution beyond execFile (no shell) for `which`, `claude`, `codex` in install.js; no postinstall/preinstall scripts (package.json scripts only start/test/eval); no curl|sh; no telemetry found in src/ (only fetch is client.js to the configured base URL and eval/http.js for baseline LLMs).
Response cap 8 MB streamed-reject (client.js:106,268-297); timeouts via AbortSignal (90 s per attempt); 401/422 not retried.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is raw API JSON of numbers/labels (no free text from Jev), so low injection risk from output; input is whatever the agent puts in `state`, which is untrusted repo content sent off-machine.

Supply chain: single-author, 8-star repo, install from git HEAD (unpinned unless a commit is specified), 95 transitive npm packages; server name `jev` written with user scope. Baseline `bare jev-mcp` on npm is an unrelated project (README warns), a typosquat-style confusion risk.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put in `state` and `questions.instructions/criteria` (could be code, diffs, logs, ticket text, file contents) plus the model id, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default api.typesafe.ai; would be openrouter.ai with override) with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically from the machine; no telemetry, no file scanning, and it does not read hook events or transcripts. On OpenRouter, provider logging/retention settings apply; client code must be considered egressed to TypeSafe via OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level, never blocks Claude Code: transient errors (429/502/503/504/529/network) retried up to 4 attempts with jittered exponential backoff from 700 ms and Retry-After honoured (client.js:103,157-165,249-253); per-attempt timeout 90 s (client.js:161), so worst case a single call can stall roughly 5-6 minutes if the service hangs (4 x 90 s + backoff), which is long for a synchronous tool call, though it honours the abort signal. After exhaustion it returns an isError tool result the model can ignore. Missing key makes serve throw at startup (config.js:25-33) so the MCP server shows as failed to connect but Claude Code continues. No circuit breaker, no lower configurable timeout without editing code.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`mcp__jev__evaluate`). Tool description ~380 chars plus zod-derived JSON schema with long .describe() strings (~2.2k chars total, ~550 tokens) and server `instructions` ~3.6k chars (~900 tokens; config.js:53-91). Roughly 1.4-1.6k tokens permanently in context; zero hook-injected text. Small compared with the existing playwright and gitnexus servers.
pros: Genuinely wraps the Jev System One endpoint with all three primitives (noul/choice/score) and pre-validates criteria (tool.js:63-89), saving wasted 422 round trips.

OpenRouter is one env var away: the path /v1/systemone (config.js:7) and Bearer auth match OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api; patch is at most a one-line default-model change.

Small, readable, dependency-light code (about 900 LOC in src/), MIT, no postinstall, no telemetry, execFile not shell, response size cap, sane retry/Retry-After handling, tests plus CI on Node 20/22/24.
Single tool with ~1.5k tokens context cost; readOnly/idempotent annotations may let permission modes auto-approve it.
Server instructions contain unusually good guidance for avoiding self-confirming state (config.js:59-65), which matters for a calibrated classifier.

jev-eval offers a statistically careful way (Brier, ECE, McNemar, perf on unlabelled data) to test whether Jev beats Opus/Haiku on the user's own decisions, which is the honest way to test the 'router' skepticism.
cons: Not coding-oriented: example domain is support tickets; nothing maps to Claude Code events (edit, test failure, diff, PR risk). Automatic use is left to model whim, so the user's core requirement (automatic, no prompting) is not met.

Only OpenRouter via undocumented-in-repo override; model default jev-latest is not a valid OpenRouter id, so calls without an explicit `model` may 4xx unless patched; OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
`jev-mcp install` leaks the API key into argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and stores it plaintext in ~/.claude.json; also blanket-copies TYPESAFE_* env.
Not published to npm, unpinned git install, single author, 5 commits over 4 days, 8 stars, no releases, v0.1.0: alpha-quality supply-chain trust for client projects.
No timeout/retry configuration surface: 90 s x 4 attempts can hang a turn for minutes when Jev (beta) is down; no fail-fast for a latency-sensitive 70-500 ms model.

Every call requires the model to hand-write a typed schema and put code/context into `state`, costing Opus output tokens and time that likely exceed the value of a decision Opus could make itself; sends client code off-machine to a third party.
Eval harness scores only noul questions and needs hundreds to thousands of labelled items; large surface (about 400+ LOC of eval) unrelated to the integration goal, and pulled in by the install.
entries.verdict: The most complete existing Jev MCP wrapper and safe to read/fork, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an explicit model id, but it is only a model-discretion tool with no coding-specific triggers, so it will not give the automatic, hook-driven Jev use the user wants. Best used as a base to fork (fix default model, add OPENROUTER_API_KEY, shorter timeout/fail-fast) behind a hook or CLAUDE.md rule, or as the eval harness to test Jev; register manually rather than via `jev-mcp install` to keep the key out of argv.

entries.name: ajensenwaud/hermes-jev-plugin
entries.what: Hermes Agent plugin exposing jev_evaluate/jev_check/jev_route/jev_score with coding-agent recipes (failure triage, review gate) and a jev-questions skill on question design and confidence gating.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion tool plus skill
pros: Clean 4-tool decision surface (Noul/Choice/Score/mixed) with coding recipes and gating guidance skill
Thin httpx client, easy to port to an MCP server and repoint to OpenRouter
cons: Hermes plugin format only; endpoint constant hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
Single commit, minimal tests, model-discretion only

entries.name: thehan-co/jevriel
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + skill + zero-dependency stdio MCP server, node ESM) bundling a "jevriel" skill and 9 MCP tools that call TypeSafe Jev through a selectable provider (OpenRouter Decisions API, TypeSafe direct, Cloudflare, custom HTTPS endpoint, local adapter). Tools wrap Jev's primitives as route/rank/extract/verify/judge helpers and write a local usage ledger. Its "Deep" adoption mode appends a pointer block to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md telling the agent to assess each task for Jev-suited decisions. It also ships a Python benchmark ("Flight Test") comparing Jev vs LLMs. It is designed mainly to help you build Jev into apps and agent workflows, not to accelerate Claude Code's own coding loop.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. Light (default): the skill triggers via description only when the user talks about Jev/integration/benchmarks, and MCP tools are called only if the model decides. Deep (opt-in): a CLAUDE.md pointer instructs the model to read the policy and 'assess every workflow' and use Jev when useful; docs/adoption.md states plainly this is prompt-guided, 'not interception of every tool call, a daemon, or a scheduler'. No deterministic hook, no proxy, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse. So it cannot guarantee automatic use and will often not fire in pure coding turns.
security: API key never in argv: setup rejects keys as arguments (bin/jevriel.mjs:42), hidden TTY prompt; env OPENROUTER_API_KEY takes precedence. Positive.
Saved key is plaintext JSON at ~/.config/jevriel/provider.json (0600, dir 0700); SECURITY.md admits plaintext. --key-command (argv, no shell) supports secret managers.
fetch uses redirect:'error' (providers.mjs/runtime.mjs:153) so the bearer token cannot be redirected; compatible endpoint must be credential-free HTTPS (providers.mjs:32).
Error handling deliberately hides provider response text and input content (runtime.mjs:174-176). Ledger stores metadata only (no prompts/answers), 0600.
Adapter/key-command run local executables from config with your env (spawnSync shell:false, timeouts 30s/15s); trusted config, low risk unless provider.json is tampered with.

Deep mode edits ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md (writes .jevriel-backup, 0600 mode on writeFileSync) and points the model at a policy file under ~/.agents/skills; this is a persistent prompt-injection/instruction surface owned by the plugin and would load in every session including client projects. Note writeFileSync mode 0600 only applies on creation.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put into tool arguments: state / candidates / evidence / source / claim / route rubrics (any code, diffs, file text, notes the agent decides is relevant) go via HTTPS POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your OpenRouter key, and OpenRouter forwards to TypeSafe. Payload capped by assertPayloadSize (judge.mjs). Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself; there is no telemetry and no hook that captures tool traffic. Setup sends one 'green/red' connection-check request. Local ledger records metadata only. With Deep mode, the agent is encouraged to send excerpts autonomously, so a secret-leak guard hook would not see these MCP calls (your guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jevriel__*), meaning client code could reach OpenRouter/TypeSafe unreviewed.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, by design: one attempt (maxAttempts:1, no retries), 30 s AbortSignal.timeout in judge.mjs:111, HTTP errors mapped to short messages returned as MCP isError text (runtime.mjs:154-176); skill policy says report once and fall back to code/LLM/manual. Nothing blocks Claude Code because it is not on the critical path (no hook, no proxy). Downside: a hung Jev can stall a single tool call for up to 30 s, and the ledger must be writable or the call is refused before sending (runtime.mjs:137-138). Missing config yields 'Provider setup required' error. Invalid/unnormalised responses are rejected by validateAnswers (server/validation.mjs).
entries.contextCost: 9 MCP tools; tool defs measured at 7,455 chars (about 1,860 tokens) via JSON size of definitions, plus namespace overhead, so about 2k tokens if not deferred; Claude Code 2.1.x tool search defers MCP tool schemas so real baseline is less. Server 'instructions' string about 60 tokens (tells model to run jevriel_status first, which itself is an extra call per session). Skill: frontmatter description about 60 tokens always loaded; SKILL.md body ~1.3k tokens plus references when triggered. Deep mode adds a CLAUDE.md block (~100 tokens) and forces reading adoption.md (~700 tokens) each task. No hook-injected text.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class, code-verified provider: hits /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (providers.mjs:12,16,30); no TypeSafe account needed.
Safe secret handling for a hobby-grade project: no key in argv, hidden prompt, redirect:'error', errors scrubbed of content, key-command support for secret managers.
No hooks, no proxy, no telemetry, no postinstall: it cannot break or slow existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.

Response validation is rigorous (validateAnswers checks answer IDs, normalised distributions, choice/argmax consistency, score vs expectation) so malformed Jev/OpenRouter output is rejected rather than trusted.

Only real attempt at the 'automatic' requirement in Claude Code so far: Deep mode gives persistent CLAUDE.md-level policy with an explicit skip-trivial rule and code/LLM/human/Jev triage, plus local metadata ledger for auditing what fired and what it cost.
Useful as a design/evaluation aid when you want to add Jev decision points to an app you build (opportunity map, shadow test, Flight Card); benchmark scaffolding is reusable.
Zero-dependency Node server is easy to read and vendor; Apache-2.0.
cons: Does not deliver truly automatic invocation: Deep is a prompt pointer in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, explicitly not enforcement (docs/adoption.md, SECURITY.md); Opus 5.5 will decide case by case and mostly skip Jev on ordinary coding.

Its job is 'help you build Jev into apps', not 'make Claude Code faster'. Tool set (route/rank/extract/verify) is generic; there is no coding-specific decision (e.g. which files matter, whether a command is safe, commit-message routing) shipped.

Deep mode writes to your global CLAUDE.md, so the behaviour applies to client projects too, and it will encourage sending excerpts of client code to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; your secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jevriel__* tools.

Each use costs an extra model turn (tool call + result) that likely exceeds the latency and cost of Opus deciding directly; Jev is only worth it for bulk/batched semantic classification, not per-step agent decisions.

Immature: 12 commits over ~9 days, one author, 6 stars, v0.2.0, alpha OpenRouter endpoint, tests are all mocked/offline; README's own 429-document benchmark shows Jev had 12 invalid batches of 489 vs 2 for GPT, and no accuracy result yet (human scoring pending, frontier eval 'pending').
Install path is unpinned `npx github:` HEAD plus setup that stores the API key plaintext on disk; the setup verification call is billed.
Default model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13 (no jev-latest); .mcp.claude.json passes no env, so env must be exported in the shell that launches Claude Code or a plaintext file used.
~1.9k tokens of tool definitions plus skill and policy reads for something that will fire rarely; server instructions demand a jevriel_status call each session.
Dense one-line JS style and vendored code from a community connector make audits/upgrades harder.
entries.verdict: Best-documented OpenRouter-capable Jev package and safe enough to read and try, but it is a builder/evaluation kit with prompt-based 'Deep' adoption, not a deterministic Claude Code integration, so it will not reliably give you Jev without prompting. Use it at most as a pinned, Light-mode skill+MCP for experiments; do not enable Deep globally and do not rely on it as the daily integration.

entries.name: BYK/jev-mcp (npm: jev-eval-mcp)
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (Node/TS, ~48 KB source) wrapping TypeSafe's System One endpoint. Exposes 3 tools: jev_ask (prototype typed questions on one state), jev_map (run a question set over many items from a JSONL/JSON file, filter/sort, save full results to disk), jev_eval (evaluate question variants against labeled data: accuracy, Brier, ECE, AUC, threshold sweep, worst misses). It is an offline-workflow/eval tool for building and calibrating Jev classifiers and for bulk triage. It is not a runtime gate or routing layer inside Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tools describe prototyping, bulk triage and eval workflows, not gating routine coding actions. Claude may occasionally reach for jev_map when triaging hundreds of items, but nothing here makes Claude Code use Jev on ordinary coding turns, and the server's own instructions tell it not to use Jev for decisions it can make itself. Not a hook, skill or proxy.
security: README install puts the key in argv via `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...`. That value is stored in ~/.claude.json, not in the process list. The server process reads it from its environment. Prefer the config-file env block or `${VAR}` expansion.

`npx -y` without a version pin runs whatever latest is on npm on every start, which is a supply-chain risk for a process holding an API key. The dependency set is small (MCP SDK and zod, pinned exactly) and there is no postinstall script.

Arbitrary filesystem access via tool args: dataset_path is read with readFile (src/schemas.ts:83) and save_path is written with writeFile (tools/map.ts:194, evaluate.ts:331), with no path sandboxing.
