A prompt-injected agent could write JSON to any path, but the content is fixed-format results. The written data is not attacker-controlled shell code, so the risk is low but real.

Read path: the dataset file's contents are sent to the remote API. A prompt-injected agent could point dataset_path at ~/.ssh or .env files that are valid JSON or JSONL and exfiltrate them to the Jev provider. This is limited to JSON-parsable files (invalid JSON throws an error that quotes only the line number). It is still a hole in the existing secret-leak guard, which only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would not see MCP calls.

No shell execution, no eval, no telemetry (grep for process.env shows only 3 vars). Calls only the configured base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is fully user-controlled, so if the env is poisoned the key goes to an arbitrary host.

Tool results contain only numeric/typed model output (no free text from the model), so the prompt-injection surface via responses is minimal. Injection inputs (state) go to Jev, whose output is typed, which is a good property. Error messages echo up to 500 chars of the API response body.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` (or in the dataset file items) plus the question instructions/criteria is POSTed as JSON to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone, for example file contents, diffs, tickets, or logs. That is entirely model-discretion, because nothing is sent automatically. With OpenRouter as the provider, the payload goes to openrouter.ai and then to TypeSafe. Nothing else leaves the machine: no telemetry, and the API key is sent as a Bearer header. Client and personal code is exposed only when Claude chooses to pass it, which is relevant for client NDAs, and that choice is not gated by the existing secret guard.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design, because it is a tool. On error the tool returns isError text and Claude carries on. Client retries: up to 4 attempts on 408/425/429/5xx/529 and on network errors, with exponential backoff (250ms*2^n, max 8s, plus Retry-After up to 20s), and a 60s per-request timeout (typesafe.ts:88-156). Worst case a single hung call blocks that turn for about 4x60s plus backoff, which is a bad tail for interactive use. The timeout is not configurable through env. A missing key makes the server exit(1) at startup, so the MCP connection fails visibly. No hook or gate exists, so nothing can block Claude.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Estimated tool defs: names, descriptions and zod-derived JSON schemas total about 6-8k chars, so roughly 1.5-2.2k tokens. The schema is inflated by the repeated discriminated-union question schema (noul/choice/score) in each tool, plus the dataset fields. Server `instructions` is about 420 chars (about 105 tokens). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Total is about 2k tokens of standing context, which is moderate for what is a niche capability. Claude Code's MCP tool search/deferral may reduce this when many tools are configured.
pros: Only real Jev-specific MCP found here with a clean, honest design: read-only annotations, typed output, and instructions explicitly warning against oracle-style use.

OpenRouter switch is config only: baseUrl + '/v1/systemone' (typesafe.ts:130) with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and model override via JEV_MODEL, so OpenRouter can be used without patching (schema parity still to be confirmed).

jev_eval gives real calibration metrics (Brier, ECE, AUC, threshold sweep, worst misses), which is the right way to decide whether a Jev question is trustworthy and where to set a threshold before wiring any gate. That directly addresses the 'is Jev just a flash router?' skepticism with the user's own data.
jev_map keeps bulk triage (files, findings, tickets) out of Claude's context via save_path, filter and sort. It fits one-off large triage jobs.
Small, readable codebase (~48 KB), MIT, pinned exact deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec. It was easy to audit statically.
Retry and backoff logic is sane, and there is CI with lint and typecheck. Runs on Node 24 without changes.
cons: Does not deliver the user's stated goal. No hooks, skill or proxy exists, so Claude Code will not use Jev automatically on routine coding; it only appears when Claude decides an MCP tool fits, and the tool descriptions target eval and bulk triage, not everyday decisions like permission classification, commit-type choice or test triage.

OpenRouter support is undocumented and unverified. Env naming (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding an OpenRouter key) is confusing, the default model 'jev-latest' would not resolve on OpenRouter (needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest), and the Decisions API is not used.

Very young and thin: created 2026-09-17, 7 commits, 4 stars, one release, 12 days old, a single human author, 5 tests that cover only the metrics math and none of the HTTP client or tools. No issue history to judge responsiveness.

Unbounded file access: dataset_path reads and save_path writes any path with no sandbox. Because the MCP call bypasses the existing secret-leak hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), a JSON-parsable secret file could be sent to a third party without a guard firing.
Retry policy up to 4 x 60s can stall an interactive turn on a slow or down provider, and the timeout and attempts are not configurable via env.
Standing context tax of about 2k tokens for three tools, mostly repeated question schemas, for a niche feature; `npx -y` cold start on each session unless pinned.
Privacy: anything Claude passes in state (client code, diffs) leaves the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, at the model's discretion, which is not ideal for client projects.
entries.verdict: A well-built, safe-to-read eval and bulk-triage MCP for Jev, useful when building or calibrating a Jev classifier and worth keeping as an optional, pinned side tool. It cannot give the automatic, no-prompt integration the user wants, because nothing in it triggers on its own in Claude Code. Use it (via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api) to measure whether Jev is good enough on your own data, then put the measured questions into a hook or proxy.

entries.name: Ravinder82/jev-flash-router
entries.what: Single-file stdio MCP server (TypeScript, about 317 lines) exposing one tool, evaluate_decision, which POSTs a model-authored state, question, type (noul, choice or score) and criteria to the OpenRouter Decisions API using ~typesafe/jev-latest. It returns the answers.eval object plus a hard-coded telemetry block. It also bundles a SKILL.md with a "MUST call before reasoning" directive and an install-skill CLI subcommand.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, plus a skill-description trigger only if SKILL.md is copied manually into ~/.claude/skills (the bundled installer does not). There is no hook, no proxy and no deterministic path. Whether Claude calls it depends on Opus following the tool description ('Use this BEFORE generating long reasoning plans') or the skill directive. That is unreliable, and it may over-trigger and add friction.
security: No third-party binary and no postinstall script (only prepublishOnly). Runtime deps are just the MCP SDK and dotenv. But the recommended `npx -y jev-flash-router` runs unpinned code from a 4-star, single-author package at every start, so pin the version or use a reviewed local clone.

The API key is read from the env var, so it is not in argv when passed via the MCP env block. The tool also accepts an apiKey argument (src/index.ts:139, 163-166), which would put the key in the model context, the transcript and tool-call logs. The README examples embed the key literally in JSON config.

dotenv.config() (:18) loads a .env from the process cwd. Claude Code launches stdio servers in the project directory, so a project .env is parsed into the server's env. It only uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY, but a client project's .env key could silently be used and billed instead of the intended one.

The prompt-injection surface is moderate. The model chooses the state, so untrusted repo, log or web content can flow into it. The output is only probabilities, which limits injection back into the agent, but the SKILL.md 'you MUST call' directive is an injected instruction and would drive frequent calls.

No shell execution and no eval. install-skill writes SKILL.md files into home directories, which is benign but writes outside the project. It calls process.exit(0) whenever the install-skill arg appears anywhere in argv.

No telemetry is sent. The 'telemetry' in responses is local. output_tokens:0 and cost:"$0.00 output" are hard-coded strings (:263-267), not read from the API, so they are marketing rather than measured.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model puts into `state`, `question` and `criteria` is sent (any code, diffs, logs or task text Claude chooses to include) to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the Bearer key and Referer/X-OpenRouter-Title headers. Nothing else leaves the machine. Nothing is sent to TypeSafe directly or to the package author. There is no redaction or size cap. The secret-leak guard hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not MCP tools, so it will not inspect what goes into state. Sending client code to OpenRouter and TypeSafe is a data-policy question for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice but with no timeout. The fetch (:233) has no AbortSignal or timeout, so a hung OpenRouter connection would block the tool call until the client's MCP timeout. HTTP errors and network errors are caught and returned as isError text, so Claude simply continues without Jev. There is no retry and no fallback. A missing key returns an error message on every call, and the server still starts fine.
entries.contextCost: One tool, evaluate_decision. The description is about 250 chars and the schema (5 properties, each with a description) is about 1.2k chars, so roughly 400-450 tokens of tool definition, or even less if the tool is deferred via ToolSearch. The server sends no MCP instructions. If SKILL.md is manually installed, the frontmatter description adds about 60 tokens permanently, and the 4.2k-char body (about 1k tokens) loads whenever the skill triggers. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
pros: OpenRouter is the native and only provider: it hits /api/alpha/decisions with an OPENROUTER_API_KEY and ~typesafe/jev-latest, exactly the requested setup, with no patching (src/index.ts:214,233).
Tiny surface: one tool, about 317 lines, two dependencies, no postinstall or shell exec. It is easy to audit and vendor in minutes, and the ~450-token context cost is small.
Supports all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) with a correctly shaped questions.eval payload and a clean unwrap of answers.eval.
MIT license, a package that reads sensibly, and stderr redirection of console.* to protect the stdio handshake.
Ships a SKILL.md with a valid Claude Code frontmatter and examples that can be reused as the basis of a home-grown skill.
cons: Automation is weak. It is a model-discretion tool only, and the bundled install-skill writes to ~/.gemini and ~/.agents, not ~/.claude (src/index.ts:40-47), so out of the box Claude Code has no trigger. That fails the user's 'never say use jev' requirement.

Hard-coded fake telemetry (output_tokens:0, cost string) and 'zero-token' marketing are misleading. Claude must generate state, question and criteria as output tokens on Opus, so it costs more than it saves.
No timeout, no retry and no fallback on fetch. There is no model or base-URL override, and no TypeSafe direct or System One endpoint support.
The apiKey tool argument invites keys into transcripts. dotenv loads the cwd .env, which is risky across client projects.
Immature: created 2026-09-18, 4 stars, 16 commits, no tests, no CI, no releases, a backdated changelog (1.0.0 dated 2025-09-15), and it is the work of a single author.
All egress goes through model-chosen free text with no redaction, so the existing secret-guard hook does not cover MCP calls. It is a concern for client code.

The 'MUST call before reasoning' skill directive risks over-triggering, adding an agent step (1-3 s) to trivial decisions, and giving Jev's calibrated probabilities false authority over Opus's own judgement.
entries.verdict: A small, correct and OpenRouter-native wrapper around the Decisions API that is fine as a reference or a vendored starting point, but not something to install as-is. It cannot deliver the automatic, no-prompt integration wanted: it is only a discretionary MCP tool, its skill installer misses ~/.claude, and its claims of zero cost and telemetry are cosmetic. Prefer a self-owned copy with a timeout, a fixed key path and a hook or skill wired for Claude Code.

entries.name: y0usaf/typesafe-mcp (@y0usaf/typesafe-mcp)
entries.what: A ~220-line single-file stdio MCP server exposing one tool, evaluate(state, questions, model?), which is a thin pass-through to POST {BASE_URL}/v1/systemone with a Bearer key. It returns Jev's typed answers (noul, choice, score) as JSON text plus structuredContent. It also ships server "instructions" and a typesafe://guide resource that teach the agent to batch atomic questions and gate on confidence. There is no hook, skill, or proxy. Everything is left to the model's discretion.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description and server instructions nudge Claude to use it for 'classification, detection, scoring, routing, verification, ranking, context selection', but nothing enforces it. The instructions are generic and not coding-specific, so Opus 5.5 will rarely call it unprompted, because it can make those judgments itself for free. To reach the user's 'automatic' goal you would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a hook on top, or write your own wrapper, and this repo provides none of that.
security: The API key is read from the environment, never from argv (index.js:152). `claude mcp add -e` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. Use a dedicated, spend-limited OpenRouter key. Note that -e appears in the shell history of the `claude mcp add` command.

Supply-chain risk: `npx -y` runs the latest published code from a single-maintainer, 4-star, two-week-old package. It has no postinstall script and no shell execution (index.js does not use child_process). The only outbound call is fetch to BASE_URL. Pin the version (@0.1.0) or vendor index.js, and audit the transitive deps of @modelcontextprotocol/sdk.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is fully overridable, so a poisoned env would redirect the state and key to any host. That is normal for this pattern, but there is no allowlist.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns only numbers and option names, with no free text (the error path echoes the API error body verbatim, index.js:178-179). Answer option keys come from the model's own criteria. The real risk is Claude trusting low-quality probabilities for gating.
No telemetry. No secret handling beyond env. Unsigned commits.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude itself puts into the `state` field (and the question text) of an evaluate call goes to openrouter.ai, along with the OpenRouter key. If Claude passes file contents, diffs or tool outputs as state, those leave the machine. Nothing is sent automatically, and there is no background traffic. OpenRouter's own logging and retention policy applies, and this matters for client code under NDA. Also check whether the OpenRouter account's data policy allows routing to TypeSafe.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Missing key, network error, timeout or non-2xx becomes an isError text result (index.js:153-180) and Claude just continues. It never blocks tool use, since it is not a hook. Weaknesses: the default timeout is 30s (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS), which is far above the claimed 70-500 ms and could stall a turn if OpenRouter hangs. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. A bad or garbled `questions` shape is only caught server-side.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate). By my estimate: description ~1.0k chars, input schema ~1.6k chars, and server instructions ~1.3k chars, roughly 3.9k chars or 1.0k tokens always resident. The typesafe://guide resource (~3k chars, about 750 tokens) is only loaded if Claude reads it. Hooks inject no text. That is cheap and one of the lightest options.
pros: Works with OpenRouter by env vars alone. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus the /v1/systemone path matches OpenRouter's documented TypeSafe-SDK-compatible System One endpoint exactly (index.js:11,163).
Tiny and fully auditable: a single 222-line file, one dependency, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry, and the key is passed via env rather than argv.
Low context cost: about 1k tokens for one tool, and no hook-injected text on any turn.
Fail-open: errors are returned as tool errors and never block the session.

Faithful, generic pass-through of all three primitives (noul, choice, score) with configurable model and timeout. The batching and atomic-question guidance in the instructions is sensible for how Jev is meant to be used.
MIT license, and it is a usable building block that can be forked or vendored in minutes.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain MCP tool, so Claude only calls it if it chooses to. Opus can do these judgments itself, and the instructions give no coding-specific triggers, so expect near-zero organic usage. It fails the user's central requirement without extra glue (a hook, CLAUDE.md rules or a skill).
Very immature: 3 commits, 1 contributor, 4 stars, created 2026-09-16, one 0.1.0 release, no tests, no CI, no changelog.

No OpenRouter awareness: the docs, env var names and defaults all say TYPESAFE_* and default to api.typesafe.ai. The OpenRouter key must be put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the default model 'jev-latest' relies on OpenRouter's bare-ID mapping.
Default 30s timeout with no retry. A hung upstream would stall a turn, versus the claimed 70-500 ms latency.

Leaves the hard part to the model: Claude must author well-formed question schemas each call (extra Opus output tokens and a round trip), which usually costs more than the judgment is worth. Nothing gates or verifies the answers.

Data egress depends entirely on what Claude sends as `state`, with no redaction or size cap. With client code this needs a policy, and the existing secret-leak guard hook matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not MCP tools like evaluate.
`npx -y` on an unpinned single-maintainer package is a supply-chain risk. The key would sit in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
entries.verdict: This is a clean, minimal, OpenRouter-compatible pass-through, so it is a decent thing to vendor or pin as the transport for Jev. On its own it won't give the user automatic use, because it is a discretionary tool with generic instructions and no hooks. Treat it as a building block: pin it or fork it, then pair it with a PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hook or CLAUDE.md routing rules if real automation is wanted.

entries.name: anasbekheit/typesafe-jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Rust stdio MCP server (rmcp 3.4, reqwest/rustls) exposing a single tool `evaluate` that forwards state + typed questions (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe's direct Jev endpoint and returns the typed probabilities. Ships an installer that downloads the binary, stores the key, drops a `jev` SKILL.md into ~/.claude/skills and runs `claude mcp add jev -s user`. Unofficial ("Not affiliated with TypeSafe").
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: MCP tool description plus server instructions plus the description-triggered `jev` skill nudge Opus to call `evaluate` for classify/route/score/verify tasks. No hook, no transparent proxy, so no deterministic automatic use; in normal coding (edit, debug, refactor) Opus will rarely find a reason to call it, so real-world usage will be sporadic. Does satisfy 'no need to say use jev' only in the weak sense that the model may choose to.
security: API key handling is decent: header marked sensitive (jev.rs:112), Debug redacted (secret.rs:48-52), and the installer avoids putting the key in Claude config by registering TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND (`cat ~/.config/typesafe-jev-mcp/key`, file 0600 in 0700 dir, install.sh:122-128). The key is NOT in argv; but the env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND is stored in ~/.claude.json and, if the plain TYPESAFE_API_KEY env is used instead, it is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ of the server process (same user only).

TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND is executed via `sh -c` at startup (secret.rs:19-29): anyone who can write to that env/config value gets code execution. Acceptable for a user-scoped config but a notable pattern.

Installer is curl|sh of a script that itself fetches and pipes a second script (`download_text "$DIST" | sh`, install.sh:292) from GitHub releases 'latest' (unpinned, no checksum verification shown in the wrapper), also downloads SKILL.md from raw main branch (mutable, install.sh:10,217) and writes it into ~/.claude/skills. Supply-chain risk: a future push to main changes a skill the model follows. Do not use the installer; per hard rules it was not run.

npm package `typesafe-jev-mcp` is a cargo-dist npm wrapper (0.1.0-0.1.2, single maintainer) that downloads a prebuilt binary; `npx typesafe-jev-mcp` would run unaudited binary. Building from source (cargo, 5 direct deps: rmcp, tokio, reqwest, serde, schemars) is the safer route; CI has rustsec audit + dependabot (ci.yml:35-41).

Prompt-injection surface: state is arbitrary content the main model chooses to send (files, issue text); Jev output is numeric/enum only so the return channel is low-risk (typed floats and an option key chosen from caller-supplied criteria). Response is size-capped 1 MiB (jev.rs:179).
No telemetry in code; only outbound call is to api.typesafe.ai. User-Agent carries name/version.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions`/`criteria` is sent verbatim as JSON over HTTPS to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe, NOT OpenRouter) with the API key as Bearer. Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself: no file scanning, no hooks, no diffs unless Claude decides to paste code, diffs, file contents or tool output into `state`. With client projects this means Claude-selected code/text can leave to a second vendor (TypeSafe; even via OpenRouter it would be a third party plus upstream provider). The existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not inspect MCP tool inputs (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so nothing prevents secrets in state from being sent.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, non-fatal to the session: errors are returned as tool error strings (tool.rs:68 `Result<_, String>`), so Claude just sees a failed tool call and can proceed without Jev. Timeouts: overall 60 s deadline (jev.rs:14,132), 4 attempts with 1s/2s/4s backoff honoring Retry-After on 429/529 and connect/timeout errors (jev.rs:15,143,164,198); no per-request timeout set on the reqwest client, so a hanging connection can stall a tool call up to 60 s. Bad/missing key: server exits with code 1 at startup (main.rs:30-33), so the MCP shows as failed to connect (as caveman-shrink currently does) rather than degrading gracefully.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Estimated always-on cost (or deferred via ToolSearch if tool-search is on): tool name+description ~470 chars (~120 tok) + JSON schema for state/questions/model with enum variants and descriptions ~1.8k chars (~450 tok) = ~570 tok; MCP server `instructions` ~2.4k chars (~610 tok) injected into system prompt; skill `jev` frontmatter description ~430 chars (~110 tok) always listed, body ~1.7k chars (~430 tok) loaded only when triggered. Total ~1.3k tokens baseline, ~1.7k when skill loads. No hooks, so zero per-turn injected text. Modest compared to gitnexus/playwright.
pros: Tiny, readable, single-purpose codebase (~4 Rust files, ~17 KB) that can be fully audited in minutes; no shell execution except the optional key command.
Clean typed interface: noul/choice/score with client-side validation of criteria sizes (tool.rs:95-131) and good retry/backoff with Retry-After handling (jev.rs:137-151).
Good key hygiene design: sensitive header, redacted Debug, key file 0600, key kept out of Claude config via TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND.
Low context footprint (~1.3k tokens, one tool) and non-fatal per-call failures; no hooks so it cannot slow or break existing PreToolUse/GitNexus hooks.
Well-written server instructions that steer the model toward correct use (state = evidence, batching, no-match option) and ships a Claude Code skill for description-based auto-triggering.
MIT license, CI with clippy+audit+dependabot, multi-platform release artifacts, MCP registration via `claude mcp add -s user` so no manual settings editing.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev.rs:11), key env is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. User wants OpenRouter as provider, so a fork/patch and local cargo build is required; released binaries and npm wrapper cannot be pointed at OpenRouter.

Not automatic: purely model-discretion tool plus skill; no hook or proxy, so Claude will call Jev rarely in day-to-day coding, and never deterministically. Fails the user's core 'must use it when needed' requirement beyond a weak nudge.

Jev is a classifier/router, not a coding assistant; the tool description itself says 'Not for prose or code'. For a solo senior dev on Opus 5.5, realistic uses (triage issue severity, route tickets, screen text) are rare in coding sessions, and Opus can judge most of these itself at similar cost in a turn.
Data egress to a third party is model-controlled and unguarded: client code/diffs pasted into `state` go to TypeSafe with no hook filtering (existing secret guard does not cover MCP tools).

Very immature and single-maintainer: 5 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, repo 10 days old, 0.1.2, no tests, explicitly unaffiliated with TypeSafe; API drift risk on a beta model (strict serde Response struct will hard-fail on any schema change, jev.rs:73-77,186).

Installer is curl|sh chaining a second curl|sh from 'releases/latest' and pulls SKILL.md from mutable main into ~/.claude/skills; server exits on missing key (main.rs:30), which would show as a failed MCP like caveman-shrink currently does.
No per-request timeout: a stalled connection can block a tool call up to 60 s.
entries.verdict: A clean, auditable but very young and unofficial MCP wrapper that only speaks to TypeSafe directly and relies on model discretion, so it does not meet the OpenRouter or automatic-use requirements without a fork; best treated as a reference implementation to copy (base-URL/key patch) rather than something to install as-is. Useful only as an opt-in, low-cost tool for occasional triage/classification tasks.

entries.name: askjev (pZacca/askjev)
entries.what: Unofficial stdio (npx askjev) or hosted-HTTP (jev.zacca.dev/mcp on Cloudflare Workers) MCP server exposing one tool, `ask`. The agent passes `state` (string/object/array) plus free-text `questions` (optional `options`). The server uses @typesafe-ai/sdk to make 2 Jev systemOne calls (3 if a scale question has no options): a routing call that classifies each question as noul, score or choice, an optional call that picks one of 7 built-in rubrics, then an answer call. It returns raw probabilities, confidence and routing metadata. It has no thresholds or verdicts, and per-question errors are returned as `kind: error` entries.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The description says 'Use it for a quick second opinion, a classification, a rating, or a yes/no check instead of reasoning it out yourself or spawning a sub-agent', which is a soft nudge. Opus 5.5 will rarely call a probabilistic classifier for coding work unprompted. There is no hook or skill trigger, and no transparent proxy. To meet the 'never say use jev' requirement, it needs a one-paragraph rule in the global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, or a separate deterministic hook or skill layered on top.
security: No postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json). Runtime deps are only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk and zod. There is no child_process or shell use in src (grep clean).

Release workflow publishes to npm with `--provenance` (release.yml). MIT license. Single maintainer, so npx -y pulls whatever he publishes next, and the account or package is a supply-chain point. Pin the version, e.g. askjev@0.2.0.

Key handling: stdio mode reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from the env, so it is not in argv. `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, but the process list only shows `npx -y askjev`. Hosted mode puts the key in a header, and the operator of jev.zacca.dev could see the key and state if malicious. Never use hosted mode with client code.
SDK debug logging redacts headers (redactHeaders, index.mjs), but debug logs print the request body (the state) to stderr. Leave TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL unset.

No telemetry in askjev source. Tool output is JSON of numbers and short strings, with label echoes only from the caller's own options. Prompt-injection surface is small, but the `state` text sent to Jev could contain injected content that skews probabilities. The `note` field is server-authored.
Not audited by a third party. The hosted worker is a personal Cloudflare deployment, and CI auto-deploys every push to main, which makes it a moving target.
entries.dataEgress: In stdio mode, whatever `state` Claude chooses to pass (code snippets, diffs, error text, ticket text, anything) goes to OpenRouter, then to TypeSafe/Jev. Also sent are the question texts and options, and a routing call whose state is the question text. Nothing leaves automatically beyond what the model puts in `state`. There is no file scanning or hook capture. The existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it will NOT inspect mcp__askjev__ask inputs. Hosted mode would additionally send everything to jev.zacca.dev (a third party) and should be avoided for client work.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level. The SDK default is timeout 10s and maxRetries 2, with retry on 429/5xx/connection errors and backoff (index.mjs:74, 518). Worst case is roughly 10s x 3 per Jev call, and ask() makes up to 3 sequential calls, so a hung upstream could block one turn for tens of seconds (~90s worst case). Nothing lowers the timeout except SDK config, and askjev exposes no timeout env var, so it is not tunable without patching. On failure it returns an MCP result with isError:true and a readable message (src/server.ts:100-112). Claude sees the error and continues. Auth failure gives 'Jev rejected the API key'. There is no fail-closed behaviour, and no session-blocking hook is involved.
entries.contextCost: One MCP server with one tool (`mcp__askjev__ask`). The tool description is about 1.1k chars (server.ts:34-42 plus the describeOutput and key-hint lines), and the input and output schemas add roughly 2.5k chars of zod descriptions. Total is about 900-1,000 tokens of tool definition, or fewer when tools are deferred via ToolSearch. No MCP server-level `instructions` field is set. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. This is very light next to playwright or gitnexus.
pros: Works with OpenRouter with no code change, because it uses the official TypeSafe SDK (whose baseURL and key come from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and OpenRouter documents that exact path (/api/v1/systemone). Config is env only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest.
Tiny and auditable: 734 lines of TS across 10 src files, no shell execution, no postinstall, and only 3 runtime deps. Verified in the tree, not just the README.
Very small context footprint: one tool, about 1k tokens, no hooks and no per-turn injection.

Clean output design: raw probabilities and confidence, with no invented thresholds. Per-question errors do not fail the batch. Routing metadata makes misclassification visible. The tool description tells the agent to read the confidence and fall back to its own reasoning when it is low.

Good engineering hygiene for a young project: 35 unit tests across 5 test files, CI on lint, typecheck, tests and a 3-OS smoke run, a weekly live router eval with a human-labelled dataset (claims 42/42 routing, 16/16 rubric), npm provenance, and clear architecture and eval docs.
Fail-soft: errors surface as isError tool results and Claude continues. Batching several questions into one ask costs the same number of Jev calls.
stdio mode keeps the key in an env var, not argv, and keeps the request off any third-party host.
cons: Only model-discretion invocation: no hook, no skill, no proxy. It will not be used 'automatically when it adds value' without a CLAUDE.md rule. Even then, invocation is probabilistic and each call adds a model turn.

Wrong shape for coding. It is a generic free-text question router meant for support-ticket-style triage. It has no coding-specific rubrics, and the built-in rubrics (sentiment, frequency, agreement...) are not code-review concepts. Its own routing layer costs an extra Jev round trip on every ask, which is 2-3 sequential calls where a direct SDK call needs 1.

Ecosystem maturity is poor: 2 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor (Pedro Zaccaria), 40 commits, created 2026-09-17, only 2 npm versions (v0.1.0 and v0.2.0, the latest published 2026-09-18), and no push since. It is unofficial and not affiliated with TypeSafe. Single-maintainer supply chain, so pin the version.

Not tunable for reliability: SDK timeout 10s with 2 retries is not exposed as an env var, so a slow OpenRouter could stall a turn for up to ~90s across the 3 sequential calls. Fixing it means forking or patching.

The secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover mcp__askjev__ask (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so source or secrets Claude puts in `state` go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe unfiltered. That matters for client projects. A matcher extension would be needed.

The env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY but must hold an OpenRouter key, which is confusing. Hosted mode (jev.zacca.dev) would send code and the key to a personal third-party Worker, so it should not be used.

Uses the System One (/v1/systemone) surface, not the Decisions API. If OpenRouter's Decisions alpha is the endorsed path, that limits future alignment. Jev's quality is itself unverified, since skeptics call it a router-like model. A 5-level 'severity' score from a 32k-context model is weak evidence for code decisions.
entries.verdict: This is the cleanest and lowest-risk way to get Jev into Claude Code as an MCP tool, and it works on OpenRouter with env vars only: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-latest. On its own it fails the 'fully automatic' requirement, because Claude has to choose to call it. It also spends 2-3 round trips per question on generic routing that a coding-specific hook or skill could skip. Use it only as an opt-in second-opinion tool with a CLAUDE.md nudge (pin askjev@0.2.0, run stdio only), not as the core integration.

entries.name: E-FL/typesafe-as-a-judge
entries.what: Unofficial community Claude Code / Codex plugin: a zero-dependency Node stdio MCP server plus 3 skills wrapping the TypeSafe System One endpoint. Exposes 8 MCP tools (route, rank, extract, verify, judge, usage_summary, session_mode, escalation_gate) that turn a bounded decision into Choice/Score/Noul questions and return probabilities, confidence and a proceed/review recommendation. Claude itself decides when to call them, guided by skill descriptions. Tools are read-only; no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus skill description triggers. There are no hooks and no proxy. The tools are read-only and Claude Code will call them when the skill description (or tool descriptions) match. The 'auto' policy in the session-control skill encourages Jev for bounded semantic decisions. Nothing is deterministic, so invocation reliability depends on Opus choosing to call it. With Opus 5.5, expect it to mostly do these micro-decisions itself (file ranking, claim checks) and rarely call Jev. The skills also explicitly steer away from open-ended coding work, which is most of a daily session.
security: Key handling: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or ~/.config/typesafe-as-a-judge/token (chmod 600, setup.sh uses hidden prompt). The key is never in argv; .mcp.json passes it via env_vars.
Setup token validation makes a live call (validate-token.mjs).
No child_process, exec or shell use in server or scripts (only tests/mcp.test.mjs spawns node). Zero runtime dependencies. package.json has no install or postinstall scripts, and no curl|sh.
No telemetry to third parties. Usage stats are in-memory only. The only network destination is api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool arguments are composed by Claude, so any injected repo content can flow into the request. The output is typed probabilities and a recommendation only, so there is little to inject on return. There is no redaction, only a 256KB payload cap (judge.mjs:3) and a 'don't send secrets' instruction in the skill. That instruction is not enforced in code, and the user's secret-leak hook would not cover MCP tool args.
Apache-2.0. Sole maintainer, unofficial, no security audit. The SECURITY.md is only a policy.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the tool args goes to api.typesafe.ai (or openrouter.ai after a patch): 'state', 'source', 'evidence', 'claim', candidate lists and criteria. Sizes are capped at 256KB. In practice this means code excerpts, file paths, test output and diffs that Claude chooses to include. Nothing is sent automatically, since there are no hooks, and there is no redaction. The model name and a Bearer key go with each call. Client work sent to a third-party beta model may breach client NDAs, so decide this per project.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. On network error the code retries up to 3 attempts total with 250/500 ms exponential backoff, and only on network errors, HTTP 429 and 529 (judge.mjs:4, 101-118). Each attempt has a 30 s AbortSignal timeout (judge.mjs:111), so the worst case is roughly 90 s of stall on a hang. A final failure returns an isError text result to Claude, which just carries on without Jev. A missing key returns an error immediately. Nothing blocks the session. There is no circuit breaker, so a slow API can stall turns. The 30 s timeout is too generous for a 70-500 ms service.
entries.contextCost: 8 tools. The tool definitions are about 8.3k chars in server/index.mjs (lines 1-98), so roughly 2.1k tokens of names, descriptions and schemas, some of it repeated per tool (comparison_model appears 5 times). Server instructions are one short sentence (about 30 tokens). The 3 skills add about 150-250 tokens of descriptions. Total is about 2.3-2.5k tokens of always-on context, which is moderate. Claude Code may defer MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch, lowering the constant cost. No hook-injected text.
pros: Purpose-built for the exact use case (Claude Code decides when to call Jev). It is the only candidate found that ships both MCP tools and a skill trigger, with no need for the user to say 'use jev'.
Typed, calibrated outputs with a proceed/review recommendation and a deterministic escalation gate. Sensible guardrails: refuses to be an authority for security, permissions, or destructive actions.

Clean, small codebase: zero dependencies, no shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry, and all network I/O funnels through one function (judge.mjs:83), so it is easy to audit and patch for OpenRouter (about 5 lines).
Sound token handling: setup.sh uses a hidden prompt and a 0600 token file, and the key is not in argv. Retries with backoff on 429/529. Input validation and a 256KB payload cap.
Session-mode tool gives an in-session kill switch (disabled), and the local usage summary is honest about 'theoretical' savings.
Apache-2.0 license, with tests (9 test cases across 4 files), a CHANGELOG and a v0.1.0 release.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and no env override. The user must fork or edit locally (about 5 lines), and the OpenRouter response shape is unverified.

Very immature: repo created 2026-09-21 (9 days old), 11 commits all on one day by one author, 2 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues, no CI workflows (no .github/workflows), and only about 9 tests. The unofficial status is stated in the README.

Value for daily coding is doubtful. The README's own benchmark is a single hand-picked case (which file to inspect first) that Opus would answer inline for free. Extra tool-call round trip plus 0.86 s API call, so it is likely slower and costs money (a separate Jev API bill) while the main model is on a subscription. The savings claims are self-declared 'theoretical'.

Invocation is at the model's discretion, so it is not deterministic. Opus is unlikely to route trivial choices through an external tool, so the 'automatic' integration would be weak and hard to observe.
Costs about 2.3-2.5k tokens of constant context for 8 tools, 3 of which (usage_summary, session_mode, escalation_gate) are meta or local-only and add no Jev value in daily coding.

Data egress risk on client projects: no redaction (only a prompt-level 'do not send secrets'); the existing secret-leak guard hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would not see MCP tool arguments. Code, diffs and test output would go to a third-party beta model.
30 s per-attempt timeout with 3 attempts (up to ~90 s stall) is badly tuned for a sub-second service, and there is no circuit breaker.
The declared 'comparison_model' savings narrative is Codex/GPT-centric (gpt-5.6-luna) and irrelevant to Claude Opus.
entries.verdict: The closest thing to an agent-facing Jev integration, and clean, dependency-free code that could be patched for OpenRouter in about 5 lines. It is a 9-day-old, single-author PoC whose model-discretion tools add context and latency for micro-decisions Opus already handles well. Worth forking as a low-risk experiment, but not a solid basis for automatic daily use.

entries.name: reiswaffel78/jev-agent-toolkit (skill + npm MCP bridge jev-agent-toolkit-mcp)
entries.what: Two independent parts. (1) A portable Agent Skill (skills/jev-agent-toolkit/SKILL.md, ~9.3 KB plus 11 reference files) that teaches an agent when and how to use Jev as a bounded judgment layer (decision gate, Choice/Score/Noul, batching, confidence thresholds, limitations) and adds generic guidance on browser research, tool orchestration, Blender, Unreal and multi-agent work. (2) An optional stdio MCP server (npm jev-agent-toolkit-mcp 0.1.0, TypeScript, ~340 lines) exposing exactly one tool, jev_evaluate, which forwards {state, questions, model?} to POST /v1/systemone through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. It is not a hook or router: nothing intercepts Claude Code traffic. Automatic use depends entirely on the model deciding to call the tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. The MCP tool is just available, and the skill description triggers when the task looks like building a classifier/router or mentions Jev/TypeSafe. Neither contains a mechanism that makes Claude Code call Jev during ordinary coding. The bundled coding.md only suggests ideas (triage, change risk, review property checks, test-failure classification) and itself says most work should stay deterministic. Expect rare organic invocation; getting consistent use would require adding your own CLAUDE.md rules or hooks.
security: API key read only from env (index.ts:48), never a tool arg; no shell/child_process code; tool schema has no url/endpoint field so the destination is fixed at startup by TYPESAFE_BASE_URL; single POST /v1/systemone only.
redact() applied to logs and error text; 401 bodies never echoed; debug logging refused unless JEV_MCP_ALLOW_BODY_LOGGING=1 (index.ts:29-43) because the SDK logs raw bodies at debug.

No postinstall/preinstall scripts in mcp/jev/package.json or in @typesafe-ai/sdk package.json; no telemetry found in SDK dist grep. Runtime dependency surface is small (3 deps) but @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0 is a very new major.

npx -y fetches latest matching version at each launch (supply-chain exposure); single-maintainer, 1 contributor, npm publisher handle (bastidd84) differs from GitHub owner (reiswaffel78); package 10 days old; version not pinned in shipped configs. Pin exact version or vendor a clone if adopted.

Key visible in argv only if the documented `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$TYPESAFE_API_KEY` form is used; the .mcp.json ${VAR} interpolation form avoids it. Key does appear in the child process environment (normal for MCP).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is bounded numeric/enum-like JSON (choice key is echoed from caller-supplied criteria), so return channel is low risk. The skill text instructs 'never install anything silently' and treats state as untrusted data, which is benign. Skill contains generic behavioural instructions (e.g. 'batch speculative questions', 'confirm before destructive') that would sit in Claude's context whenever loaded.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model chooses to put in the jev_evaluate `state` and question instructions/criteria goes to the configured base URL (TypeSafe direct by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden), plus the API key as a Bearer header. Nothing is sent automatically: no prompts, diffs or tool outputs are forwarded unless Claude copies them into `state`. The skill's own guidance says to keep state minimal. Local logs on stderr contain metadata only (duration, model, token counts, question ids). Through OpenRouter, the request would additionally be subject to OpenRouter and upstream provider data-retention policies, which matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: SDK default timeout 10 s (index.mjs:518, overridable by JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS) with maxRetries 2 (index.mjs:74), so worst case could stall a single tool call for tens of seconds before returning an isError result with a retryable hint; Claude then just continues without Jev. If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset the server process exits at startup (index.ts:49-52) and appears as a failed MCP connection, again non-blocking. Nothing in the flow can block or deny Claude Code actions since it is not a hook.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 1 tool. Description ~1.5 KB plus zod-generated JSON schema (nested union of 3 question types, descriptions on state/questions/model) roughly 2.5-3 KB total, so about 700-900 tokens; no MCP server `instructions` field is set (server.ts constructs McpServer with only capabilities.tools). In Claude Code 2.1.x MCP tools are typically deferred and loaded via ToolSearch, so the eager cost is closer to a tool-name line. Skill: frontmatter description ~0.7 KB (~180 tokens) always listed; full SKILL.md body ~9.3 KB (~2.3k tokens) loaded only when the skill triggers, with 11 reference files (~1,900 lines total) loaded on demand. No hook-injected text.
pros: Cleanest and most auditable Jev MCP bridge found here: one tool, ~340 lines of TS, no shell, no arbitrary URL, key from env only, metadata-only logging, 401 bodies suppressed, SHA-pinned CI with npm audit.

Works with OpenRouter with zero code changes in principle: it delegates to @typesafe-ai/sdk which honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and hits /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, matching OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone (config: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key=OpenRouter key, model typesafe/jev-1.13).
Fail-open, non-blocking design: errors come back as isError tool results, so a slow or down Jev never blocks Claude Code; timeout tunable via JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT_MS.
Small context footprint (1 tool, no server instructions, skill body loads on demand) and honest documentation of limitations (literal reading, counting, dates, adversarial state).
Ships a Claude Code .mcp.json using ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} interpolation so the key stays out of files; 35 offline tests including an MCP protocol round-trip.
The batching advice (many questions per call, questions are parallel) and the decision-gate guidance are practical and match Jev's primitives.
cons: Not automatic: no hook, no proxy, no CLAUDE.md snippet; Claude only calls jev_evaluate if it chooses to. This fails the user's core requirement ('Claude Code must use it when needed, without prompting') unless supplemented with custom CLAUDE.md rules or a hook.

Documented coding use cases (triage, diff risk score, review Noul questions, test-failure classification) are illustrative only; Claude Opus can answer these itself at similar cost in a single turn, and Jev adds a 1-5 s round trip and a second failure point. No evidence anywhere of accuracy gains.

Zero OpenRouter awareness: no string 'openrouter' in repo, no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) support, default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID, and the OpenRouter path was never tested by the author. Schema/response compatibility with the SDK's parser is assumed, not proven.

Very immature and single-author: 10 commits over 2 days, 2 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub release, one npm version published by a maintainer handle different from the repo owner, dependent on a brand-new @modelcontextprotocol/server v2 and an SDK at 0.6.0. npx -y at each launch means unpinned supply-chain exposure.

Bridge-level retries (SDK maxRetries 2 with 10 s timeout) can stall one call for ~30 s in the worst case, and the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not match mcp__ tools, so state contents are unguarded and would go to a third party (OpenRouter plus provider) on client projects.

Much of the repo is generic non-Jev agent boilerplate (Blender, Unreal, browser research, multi-agent) that would bloat context if the skill triggers and duplicates behaviour Claude Code already has; README itself defers to TypeSafe's official skill (typesafe-ai/skills) as canonical.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and safest Jev MCP bridge candidate so far, and re-pointable to OpenRouter purely through env vars (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key and model typesafe/jev-1.13), but it is only a model-discretion tool plus a Markdown skill, so it will not deliver automatic Jev use in daily coding. Use it as the transport layer, pinned to an exact version, and pair it with your own CLAUDE.md rules or a hook if you want real auto-invocation.

entries.name: moisesfilho/typesafe-jev-opencode
entries.what: Tiny local stdio MCP server (mcp/index.mjs) with a single jev_decide tool (noul/choice/score) plus a confidence-gated Developer-agent policy doc, written for OpenCode but usable in any MCP client.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Single small file on official MCP SDK, native fetch, key from env, easily forked to point at OpenRouter /alpha/decisions
Includes usable conservative policy text for when to trust Jev
cons: Endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, no base URL or OpenRouter env; needs a patch
2 stars, no tests, model-discretion only so Claude may rarely call it

entries.name: ieee0824/jev-mcp
entries.what: Rust stdio MCP server (rmcp 3.4, reqwest/rustls) that exposes TypeSafe Jev's System One API as four tools (jev.noul, jev.choice, jev.score, jev.batch). The caller (an agent) supplies `state` evidence and a closed question; the server POSTs {state, model, questions} to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, validates the response, and adds a deterministic `policy` block (accept/verify/reevaluate by confidence thresholds 0.90/0.60). Ships a Codex-oriented `jev-decisions` SKILL.md with 7 recipe references (action selection, hypothesis ranking, evidence sufficiency, trace monitoring, context selection, safety advisory, multi-axis), an offline/online JSONL eval CLI, and optional input-free JSONL telemetry to stderr. It does not read repos, collect history, or execute anything: the model must decide to call it and must hand-assemble the evidence.
interface: jev.noul (exposed by Claude Code as mcp__<server>__jev_noul or similar)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus (optionally) skill-description trigger. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no proxy. Claude will only call jev.* if the tool descriptions/instructions/skill description persuade it in-context; the skill's own description is weakly worded ('when the user requests a Jev judgment, or when several related judgments share the same evidence') and the SKILL says 'Use Jev only when the judgment justifies an additional network call', so with Opus 5.5 it will rarely call it unprompted. To meet the user's 'never say use jev' requirement one would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule or rewrite the skill description, and even then invocation stays probabilistic.
security: API key from env var only, never argv (good: not visible in process list); wrapped as sensitive HeaderValue; error messages never include remote bodies or the key (README + client.rs:263 message text).

No shell execution, no file reads, no tool execution in the server; tools annotated read_only/non_destructive/open_world. No curl|sh installer, no postinstall (Rust, source build only). Cargo.lock committed; deps are mainstream (reqwest, rmcp, tokio, serde, schemars, wiremock dev).
Redirects disabled, 8 MiB response cap, 10s connect timeout, rustls (no OpenSSL).
Telemetry is off by default; when JEV_TELEMETRY=1 it writes only counts/timing/model/tokens to stderr, not to any remote service. No phone-home found.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever the model stuffs into `state` (logs, diffs, file contents) is forwarded verbatim to the remote API; response is typed probabilities only, so injection influence on Claude is limited to numeric/option outputs, and the SKILL tells the agent to treat embedded instructions as data. Real risk is data egress, not injection.

Single-maintainer, 1 star, no releases, no signed binaries; you would be building and trusting a one-person week-old codebase (I found nothing malicious in client.rs/server.rs/main.rs). Small unofficial project, not TypeSafe-official (name 'ieee0824', README says built for Codex).
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into `state`, `instructions` and `criteria`, plus model id, sent by HTTPS POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (would be openrouter.ai if patched). By design that is model-selected excerpts: diffs, stack traces, test output, file snippets, work traces (the skill recipes explicitly send tool results and work history for context-selection/trace-monitoring/safety-advisory). Nothing is sent automatically; the server never reads the repo. No client-side secret redaction: the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook does NOT cover MCP tool calls (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so a secret that appears in a log the model relays into `state` would leave the machine. For client projects this is a contract/confidentiality question (routing through OpenRouter adds a second third party; OpenRouter privacy/ZDR settings apply).
entries.failureMode: Fail-explicit at the tool layer, fail-open at the agent layer. Missing key: tools still list, calls return isError with kind authentication. Timeouts/429/529/network/invalid response all return structured isError results with error.kind + retryable and policy `reevaluate/evaluation_failed`; never fabricates an answer. Profiles: `reliable` (default) 30s per attempt / 60s total, retries 429/529 up to 2x, no timeout retry; `interactive` 1.5s per attempt / 3s total, one retry incl. timeouts (profile.rs:59-69). Set JEV_PROFILE=interactive for a coding loop, else a hung Jev can stall a turn up to 60s. Claude must decide to continue without Jev; nothing blocks tool use or permissions (it is not a hook).
entries.contextCost: 4 tools always loaded (unless Claude Code tool search defers them). Estimated static cost: 4 descriptions ~1.1k chars + JSON schemas from schemars (Context untagged enum with Text/Object/Array, Question tagged enum with 3 variants, NoulCriteria, profile enum, repeated in $defs for batch) roughly 6-9k chars total, approx 2-2.5k tokens, plus server `instructions` ~470 chars (~120 tokens). Total about 2.2-2.7k tokens per session (estimate, I did not build the binary to dump tools/list). Optional skill: frontmatter description ~430 chars always visible (~110 tokens); full SKILL.md is 8.7 KB (~2.2k tokens) loaded on trigger, plus reference files 1-3 KB each on demand. No hook-injected text (no hooks).
pros: Best-engineered Jev integration found so far in terms of hygiene: key via env only (not argv), sensitive header, no redirects, 8 MiB cap, explicit typed errors, never fabricates results, MIT license, CI with SHA-pinned actions, clippy -D warnings, mock-server + stdio integration tests.

Correct semantics for Jev: closed decision space, exposes all three primitives plus batch, preserves raw probabilities and adds a deterministic accept/verify/reevaluate policy layer (configurable thresholds) that suits Claude acting on calibrated output.

Has an `interactive` profile (1.5s/3s budget, one retry) purpose-built for coding loops, plus opt-in privacy-preserving telemetry to stderr (no state/keys) that would let you measure real latency and call rate.

Same wire path (/v1/systemone) and body ({state, model, questions}) as the OpenRouter System One endpoint in the brief, so retargeting to OpenRouter is a ~3-line const/env patch, no schema translation expected.
No shell execution, no repo reads, no install-time scripts: static analysis found nothing risky; read-only/non-destructive tool annotations.

Recipe library (action selection, hypothesis ranking, evidence sufficiency, context selection) gives concrete design ideas for where Jev could plausibly add value in agent loops, and SKILL.md is a valid Claude Code skill format after copying.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tools with no hook or proxy. Directly conflicts with the user's core requirement; Opus will seldom call a decision tool when it can answer itself, and the bundled skill explicitly discourages routine use.

Hard-coded TypeSafe endpoint (client.rs:15), no OpenRouter support: requires a local fork and Rust >=1.88 toolchain build, with no releases or prebuilt binaries. OpenRouter response envelope compatibility is unverified.
Written for Codex, not Claude Code: README documents only ~/.codex/config.toml, skill ships agents/openai.yaml, no plugin.json/.mcp.json/hooks. Claude Code setup is DIY.

Calling LLM must serialize the evidence into `state` itself: burns Claude output tokens and a full extra tool round trip per decision, so net latency/cost is likely worse than letting Opus decide; Jev's 70-500 ms advantage is swamped.
Data egress of code/diffs/logs to third parties (TypeSafe/OpenRouter) at model discretion, with no redaction and outside the existing secret-guard hook's matcher; sensitive for client projects.

Adds ~2.2-2.7k tokens of tool schema context every session for a tool that will rarely fire; README itself states real-model quality, cost and latency are unmeasured ('Evaluate ... separately') and that Jev-vs-token-savings benefit is a future question.

Immature: created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 1 star, 0 forks, 1 contributor (two alias names), no releases, self-declared 'experimental'; 'host-specific model or session routing for Codex, Claude, or other agents' is explicitly not implemented.
entries.verdict: Cleanest and safest Jev MCP code I inspected, and retargetable to OpenRouter with a 3-line patch plus a Rust build, but it is only a model-discretion tool set for Codex, so it cannot satisfy 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being asked'. Useful as a building block (client + policy layer) behind a hook/proxy, not as the integration itself.

entries.name: MattiooFR/mcp-server-jev
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (Node, ~440 LOC) exposing two tools, jev_evaluate (mixed noul/choice/score typed questions over a supplied state) and jev_classify (batch classification of up to 100 items against predefined classes plus a mandatory none class, with review flags from probability/margin thresholds). It POSTs to the TypeSafe native /v1/systemone endpoint. Its server instructions tell the agent to 'use Jev proactively' for narrow semantic judgments, but it is purely model-discretion, with no hooks and no skill.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The server 'instructions' text and tool descriptions nudge 'Use Jev proactively' for classification, relevance and triage. There is no deterministic trigger: Opus 5.5 decides, and for a coding workload it will rarely see a narrow semantic-classification need, so real usage would be near zero unless CLAUDE.md rules or a hook direct it.
security: API key handled well: read from env, sent only as Bearer to a hardcoded HTTPS host, redirect:'error', errors never echo URL/content/key (client.mjs:73-78). Documented env-file pattern keeps the key out of argv and ps.

No shell execution, no file reads, no URL fetching, no telemetry, no logging of content (grep and SECURITY.md consistent with source). Deps are pinned; the CI and install guidance use --ignore-scripts, so no postinstall.

Prompt-injection surface is small: tool has readOnlyHint and returns only numbers and ids. The main risk is the calling agent trusting probabilities. classify wraps item text as data with 'evidence not instructions' notes (classify.mjs:60-64), which is only a soft guard.
Response body capped at 1 MiB and requests at 256 KiB; strict zod validation of response with sum-to-1 check (schema.mjs:45-64) so malformed output fails closed as a tool error.

Supply chain risk: single anonymous-ish maintainer, 4 commits, 1 star, no npm release, no signed tags. A fork should be pinned to a reviewed commit SHA. Also the README links a French article, which is untrusted data.
entries.dataEgress: Only the explicit tool arguments (state, questions, item contents, class definitions and context) serialized as JSON, plus the model name and the Bearer key, go to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (would be openrouter.ai if patched, which then also sees it and its logging and retention policy applies). The server never reads project files by itself. However, because the model chooses what to put in state, Claude could send code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. Tool args and results also stay in the Claude Code transcript. Nothing is sent when Claude does not call the tool.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, because it is an optional MCP tool: errors return isError JSON with codes (MISSING_API_KEY, TIMEOUT, NETWORK_ERROR, RATE_LIMITED, HTTP_xxx, INVALID_RESPONSE) and Claude just proceeds without a decision. There is no substitute model. The per-attempt timeout is 30 s (client.mjs:40) and there are up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx with short Retry-After honored (a delay above 5 s returns RATE_LIMITED). Network errors and timeouts are not retried. Worst case is about 90 s or more of blocking on repeated 5xx, and the README advises a 120 s MCP client timeout. If the process fails to start (bad env-file path), the MCP server shows as failed and the rest of Claude Code is unaffected (as with caveman-shrink now).
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. Estimated about 6,000 chars total, roughly 1.5-2k tokens: server instructions about 1.3k chars (server.mjs:126) which are always injected into the system prompt; jev_evaluate description about 700 chars and jev_classify about 640 chars; JSON schemas from zod with nested unions and describe() strings about 3-4k chars. Under Claude Code tool search/deferred MCP tools, only the names are loaded until needed. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn.
pros: Cleanest code of the candidate types: small (about 440 LOC), readable, pinned deps, 3 concurrent calls cap, strict input and output validation, fail-closed on malformed answers, and the tests are offline.
Good security hygiene: key via --env-file (not argv), fixed host, no redirects, no logging, no shell, no postinstall; readOnlyHint set.
jev_classify batches up to 100 items into one upstream request with a required none class and review thresholds, which is sensible design for Jev's calibrated-probability strengths.
Tool descriptions and server instructions already encode when-to-use guidance ('use proactively'), which is the only auto-invocation lever available for an MCP tool.
MIT licensed; the native /systemone shape matches what OpenRouter says it accepts, so an OpenRouter fork is a roughly 3-line patch.
Tiny context footprint (2 tools, about 2k tokens) and no per-turn hook cost.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter as shipped: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model regex rejects typesafe/ IDs, and the default jev-1.13.0 is not an OpenRouter-style ID. It needs a fork, and the OpenRouter response compatibility of the strict zod schema is unverified.

Automatic use is not guaranteed: it is model-discretion only. The instructions say 'proactively', but daily coding rarely presents narrow, pre-defined-class semantic judgments, and Claude must write a full rubric each call, which costs tokens and seconds and is often slower than deciding itself. It does not meet the goal of Claude Code using Jev automatically when needed, unless supplemented by CLAUDE.md rules or hooks.
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, v0.1.0, not on npm, so you would install from a git clone and maintain it yourself. Jev is beta and the vendor is unaffiliated.
Data egress is model-chosen: Claude may send code or client file contents to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on client projects. It needs an explicit policy for client repos.

No coding-specific features (no commit or diff triage, test-failure routing, or PR risk scoring recipes), and a generic tool needs the model to design good criteria. Interplay with existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks is neutral, but there is no hook integration.
Permission friction: without an allowlist entry or bypass mode each call prompts; timeouts up to 30 s x 3 attempts could stall a turn on bad days.
entries.verdict: A well-written, safe, minimal generic MCP wrapper, and the best MCP-shaped starting point because an OpenRouter fork is nearly a 3-line patch (URL, key env, model regex). But it is TypeSafe-only as shipped, brand-new and single-maintainer, and being model-discretion it will not deliver the truly automatic, hook-like Jev use the user wants. Use it, if at all, as a forked, SHA-pinned tool paired with deterministic hooks or CLAUDE.md routing rules.

entries.name: Afloat16/jev-mcp
entries.what: Unofficial TypeScript stdio MCP server (v0.5.0) wrapping TypeSafe's System One API /v1/systemone with four read-only advisory tools (jev_decide, jev_route, jev_risk_score, jev_gate). It bundles multi-client installers (including claude-code via 'claude mcp add --scope user'). Server instructions tell the host model to call Jev only after inspecting context, and only for bounded, genuinely uncertain decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The server instructions and tool descriptions deliberately ask for restraint ('only after inspecting enough context... genuine uncertainty... do not call merely because a task is complex'). It has no hooks, no skill triggers and no proxy behaviour. Claude Code will therefore call it rarely and unpredictably, and there is no deterministic trigger. It cannot be forced without editing the SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS or adding a CLAUDE.md or hook policy outside this repo. It has only the Codex-flavoured AGENTS.jev-conservative.md, which is also conservative.
security: Created 2026-09-28, two days before the audit date. v0.5.0 is the only release. 43 commits, all on one day. 1 star, 0 forks, 1 open issue. 2 author identities (Afloat16, Afloat), effectively a single maintainer.
License MIT. package.json marks the package private, and npm publishing is intentionally disabled.

API key is read from the process env or a plaintext ~/.jev-mcp/.env (mode 0600, dir 0700) written by the installer (installer.ts:287-301). The key is never placed in argv or in the client MCP config; the claude mcp add call has no -e flag. This is good for the process list, but the key sits in plaintext on disk, and env-file loading also reads a checkout-local .env (index.ts:44).

Recommended install is curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/.../v0.5.0/scripts/install.sh | bash. It clones the repo at a tag (a tag, not a commit SHA, so it is mutable) and runs 'npm ci' and 'npm run build'. That executes the dependency tree's install scripts on the machine. Dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/server ^2.0.0 and zod ^4.3.6, and the lockfile is committed. Do not use the curl|bash path; audit and build manually instead.

installer.ts uses spawnSync with fixed argument arrays, plus 'sh -lc command -v <fixed literal>' (installer.ts:187). I found no shell injection surface. The runtime MCP server itself does no shell execution and no file writes, only fetch. No telemetry found. Its only outbound call is fetch to the configured base URL, and there is a User-Agent jev-mcp/0.5.0.

Prompt-injection and exfiltration surface: 'state' is free-form, chosen by the host model, and forwarded to the remote API. A prompt-injected model could ship repository content out, but only to the configured endpoint. If TYPESAFE_BASE_URL were tampered with, the bearer key would go to another host, and the code accepts any http/https URL, including plain http (core.ts:75).
entries.dataEgress: The only egress is the 'state' argument (free-form string, object or array) plus the question, options, criteria and model name, POSTed as JSON to ${TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (index.ts:141-153). The host model decides the content. The server instructions say to send a minimal, redacted summary, but nothing enforces it. The server does not read files itself and does not see the transcript, diffs or tool outputs unless the model copies them into 'state'. With OpenRouter as the base URL, the data goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe/upstream, and OpenRouter's logging and privacy settings apply. That matters for client code. No telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Each tool wraps callJev in try/catch and returns isError:true with the message, so the host model just proceeds without the Jev signal (index.ts:223, 173-179). The timeout is 15 s by default, configurable from 250 ms to 120 s via TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS (core.ts:81-88). There are no retries and no circuit breaker. A missing API key throws at call time, not at startup, so the server still starts and the tools appear. A bad key produces an error only when a tool is used. Nothing blocks a turn, because the call is model-initiated.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Estimated static cost is about 1.7k tokens: server instructions about 3.7k chars (roughly 930 tokens, injected every session, index.ts:56-116), tool names, descriptions and zod-to-JSON schemas about 3k chars (roughly 750 tokens). With Claude Code's MCP tool search the tool definitions may be deferred, but the instructions block still loads. No hooks and no hook-injected text. Each call returns a JSON payload of a few hundred tokens with an advisory wrapper (about 60 tokens).
pros: Small, readable, auditable code (about 500 lines of runtime logic). The request format matches OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone body and answer shapes, so OpenRouter works with three env vars and no patch.
Fail-open by design. Errors return isError text and never block the coding flow. The timeout is configurable and defaults to 15 s.

Good hygiene for secrets. The key is never in argv or in the Claude config, the .env file is 0600 with a 0700 dir, and tool annotations are readOnlyHint. It has no shell or filesystem access at runtime.
Sensible tool taxonomy. Risk score with 4 fixed levels, gate with a threshold, and choice for routing map cleanly onto Jev's Choice/Score/Noul primitives.
It has a claude-code installer target and a documented MCP-only setup, and it ships instructions that push the model toward privacy-minimal state.
cons: It does not deliver the user's core requirement. Invocation is model-discretion and deliberately conservative ('prefer zero Jev calls'), with no hook or skill to trigger it automatically. In daily coding Claude Code will almost never call it. Forcing more usage means editing the instructions or CLAUDE.md.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2 days ago, one day of history, 1 star, tests only for helpers. Pre-1.0, with tool schemas that may change in minor releases (README says so).

The default path is curl|bash, which does git clone plus npm ci plus build, and the installer targets nine clients and writes to their configs. There is no npm package, so updates are manual. Use the manual build instead.

OpenRouter is undocumented and unsupported by name. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY hold OpenRouter values, the installer writes the TypeSafe default URL into ~/.jev-mcp/.env, and JEV_MODEL must be set to an OpenRouter ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). There is no live-call verification here.

Only the /v1/systemone endpoint is used, with no Decisions API, no session_id, no trace and no provider routing. The 15 s timeout with no retry is far longer than Jev's 70-500 ms claim. Anything in 'state' goes to a third-party API, which is a client-confidentiality risk. Nothing scrubs secrets or code, and the server relies only on the model following instructions.
About 1.7k tokens of standing context per session (instructions plus tool schemas), for a tool the instructions say should rarely be used.
entries.verdict: A clean, small, fail-open MCP wrapper that works with OpenRouter via env vars only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). It is an opt-in second-opinion tool that is deliberately rarely called, so it cannot give the automatic, hook-level Jev use the user wants. Build it from source after review if you want an MCP baseline, but pair it with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md policy, and treat it as young and unproven.

entries.name: marceloatoledo/JEV-MCP-REST
entries.what: C#/.NET 10 port of jkudish/jev-mcp (Node stdio). Runs as a long-lived ASP.NET Core HTTP service (Docker or dotnet run, port 10022) exposing 10 read-only Jev judgment tools over MCP Streamable HTTP at /mcp and the same tools as REST at /api/jev/{tool}. Each tool decomposes a task into atomic typed questions, calls Jev, validates the output and applies threshold policy in code (auto/review/block/escalate). It also ships a Blazor admin UI (dashboard, audit log, playground, settings, token management) and a SQLite call-audit DB. Provider auto-detect order is TypeSafe, then OpenRouter, then Cloudflare, then Vercel, then compatible.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no server instructions in this repo. Claude will call jev_review or jev_gate only if it decides to from the tool descriptions, for example 'before the task is called done' and 'before an agent reads it'. It is not deterministic. The user's requirement of firing without being asked would need a separate Stop or PreToolUse hook, or a CLAUDE.md rule, which this repo does not provide.
security: API key handling: the provider key is read from env or appsettings by the server process (Docker env_file or dotnet appsettings.Development.json), not passed in argv. Secrets.cs and JevClientBase.Failure redact the key from errors, and the README says keys never go to SQLite, the browser or logs.

The Claude Code client authenticates with a static Bearer token (jevmcp_...), issued once, stored SHA-256 hashed (McpBearerMiddleware in AccessControlMiddleware.cs). It would sit in ~/.claude.json headers in plaintext. Env interpolation such as ${VAR} is available in Claude Code .mcp.json, so this is manageable.

Opens a network listener (0.0.0.0:10022 in Docker). It refuses to start on a non-loopback bind without a token, admin login or explicit anonymous mode. AllowAnonymousMcp is available but off by default. /health, /scalar and /openapi are always anonymous.

Blazor admin UI plus cookie login plus /api/setup and /api/tokens is a large attack surface for a local dev tool. There is a loopback-only first-run /setup bootstrap. Any local process or container reaching the port can hit it.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall. The Dockerfile builds from source on mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet images; the runtime image apt-installs curl. Stateful MCP session mode is enabled for initialize clients (Program.cs:106).
No telemetry found. Grep for analytics, telemetry and AppInsights hit nothing in src. The only outbound calls are to the chosen Jev provider.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude passes as tool arguments leaves the machine (via the local service) to the chosen Jev provider, here openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That means diffs (up to 50k chars), the request text, test output, claims, evidence documents (up to 200k chars for gate), candidate lists, and any text given to screen, extract, compare or classify. Only tool-call arguments are sent, so the MCP tool descriptions ask Claude to pass diffs, evidence and text. There are no hooks, so nothing is sent automatically beyond what the model chooses to pass. OpenRouter headers include the fixed Referer https://github.com/jkudish/jev-mcp and the X-Title jev-mcp. Locally, the SQLite audit DB (data/jevmcp.db) logs metadata per call (tool, latency, tokens, cost, outcome, token identity). Payload capture is off by default (CALLAUDIT__CAPTUREPAYLOADS=false); if enabled it stores up to 4096 chars per payload for 30 days. For client projects, code and diffs would reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which needs client consent.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open for the Claude Code workflow, because there is no hook. If the service is down, the MCP connection fails like caveman-shrink did this session and the tools simply vanish, so Claude proceeds unchecked. If Jev is slow, the HttpClient timeout is 60 s (JevProviderServiceCollectionExtensions.cs:26), with up to 3 attempts and exponential backoff (0.5 s base, 5 s cap) on 429 and 529 only (JevRetryHandler.cs, JevProviderOptions.cs:8-13). A worst-case stall on one tool call is therefore a long block, with no short-timeout circuit breaker. Internally the tools are fail-closed on the verdict: malformed model output becomes invalid_response and truncated input never returns auto. With no credentials the app still starts and /health reports degraded (Program.cs comment, JevProviderResolver.cs:27), and tools then error.
entries.contextCost: 10 MCP tools. Tool titles, descriptions and parameter descriptions total about 10.5k chars of string literals in src/JevMcp.Tools/Mcp/*.cs. With JSON schemas (snake_case params, JsonElement evidence unions) I estimate about 3.5-5k tokens always loaded, and less when Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search. I found no MCP server 'instructions' field (grep for Instructions and ServerInfo in the App returned nothing). No hook text injection. Roughly 2-3x the token cost of a 3-4 tool server, because only 2-4 of the 10 tools are useful for coding (review, gate, verify, screen).
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code: OpenRouterJevClient posts to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with an sk-or- key, mapping jev-latest to typesafe/jev-1.13.
