It is the only candidate that fits the user's 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' requirement with no patching, just JEV__PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Tool set is coding-relevant. jev_review (score a diff: correctness, spec match, test gap, blast radius, safe_to_apply) and jev_gate (review plus verification of 'done' claims against test evidence) map directly to a pre-completion check. jev_screen targets web-fetch prompt injection. Its descriptions say 'before the task is called done'.

Policy is in code, not model text: typed thresholds, auto, review and escalate actions, and fail-closed invalid_response handling. The output is compact typed JSON and does not add reasoning noise to context.
All tools are marked ReadOnly = true, so they are safe under the user's bypass and auto permission mode. Nothing is executed or applied locally.
Retry only on 429 and 529, with capped backoff (JevRetryHandler.cs). The provider key is redacted from errors (Secrets.cs). Bearer tokens are hashed at rest. No telemetry found.
Same tool names, schemas and payloads as upstream jkudish/jev-mcp, so it can be swapped for the stdio original later. MIT licence. Sizable test suite (359 tests) for a 4-day-old repo.
Local audit dashboard shows per-call cost, latency and outcomes, which is useful for judging whether Jev adds value (README pricing seed of 0.042 USD per 1M tokens matches the brief).
cons: Wrong deployment shape for Claude Code: a heavy .NET 10 web app (Blazor admin, MudBlazor, EF Core SQLite, cookie login, token store, Scalar, ECharts) that must run as a persistent Docker or dotnet service. A stdio server started by Claude Code (upstream jkudish/jev-mcp via npx) has none of that. The user has Node, Python and uv but no .NET 10, and needs a background service and open port for a 10-tool wrapper.

No automatic invocation of any kind. There are no hooks, no skill, no server instructions and no CLAUDE.md snippet. Firing depends on the model choosing to call jev_review or jev_gate, so it fails the user's core 'automatic, without me prompting' requirement. Opus with 10 unfamiliar tools will often skip them.

Very immature: created 2026-09-22 (8 days old), 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, no CI, no published image. Depends on a beta upstream API. The port's own .cursor/mcp.json is empty. The README says Windows PowerShell 5.1 is the dev gate.

Uses the OpenRouter alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), not /api/v1/systemone. The endpoint is a compile-time const, so it is an alpha surface that can break. The OpenRouter alias is pinned to the hard-coded jev-1.13 and will not follow ~typesafe/jev-latest.

Adds a network service and static Bearer token on the developer machine, with an anonymous /health, /scalar and /openapi and a setup and login surface. That is more attack surface and secrets-in-config (token in ~/.claude.json headers) than a stdio process gives.

Token bloat: 10 tools (about 3.5-5k tokens of schema) are loaded for a coding workflow that would use 2-4 of them. Tools such as jev_find, jev_rerank, jev_classify, jev_decide, jev_compare and jev_extract are generic and mostly redundant with Claude and GitNexus.

Fail-open silently: if the container is down the tools disappear (as caveman-shrink did this session). Worst-case latency is a 60 s timeout with 3 retries, with no short circuit breaker, which can stall a turn.
Sends diffs and evidence (up to 200k chars) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe through model-chosen arguments. This is a data-handling concern for client projects, and there is no path or secret filtering.
Skeptic risk remains. Jev's value as a code-review gate is unproven (calibration claims, the 'DeepSeek flash router' claim), and thresholds are only 'starting points' from cookbooks per the README.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed candidate with native OpenRouter support and a coding-relevant tool set (jev_review, jev_gate, jev_screen), but it is a heavy, days-old .NET web service with no hooks, skill or instructions, so Claude only uses it if it decides to. It cannot deliver the automatic integration the user wants on its own. Better to take its tool contract (or the upstream stdio jkudish/jev-mcp) and add a Stop or PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter directly.

entries.name: decide-mcp
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Vercel AI SDK 7) exposing one `decide` tool: the calling agent supplies a decision string, context (string/JSON, up to 100k chars) and 2-64 choices with descriptions; the server calls Jev's Choice primitive via AI SDK experimental_evaluate and returns the selected choice plus per-choice percentages (Jev's native probability distribution). Optional config adds bias/policy profiles with a 2-stage router (a first Jev call picks a profile, a second evaluates), optional per-profile tools (decide-default, decide-<profile>), and a language-model fallback (generateText with structured output) that yields model-estimated, non-calibrated percentages. Only the Choice primitive is used; Noul and Score are not exposed.
interface: decide-<profile-id> (MCP tool, one per configured profile)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no proxy and no server instructions. Claude calls `decide` only if the tool description (generic: 'Evaluate a decision, context, and choices') persuades Opus 5.5 to do so, so unprompted use will be rare and inconsistent. The design assumes the agent formulates the question and options itself. To get the user's 'use it whenever it adds value' behaviour you would have to add a CLAUDE.md rule, such as 'when choosing between 2+ concrete options call mcp__decide__decide', or wrap it in a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. That is outside this package.
security: API keys are read only from env vars named in config (apiKeyEnv) and never from argv or committed config files (src/providers.ts:27-31; readme 'Credentials stay in environment variables'). An env-based key is safe from ps output. However, `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` writes the key in plaintext to ~/.claude.json.
Startup is fail-fast: if apiKeyEnv is set but the variable is missing, the server throws and exits (providers.ts:30-31, cli.ts:52-57), which Claude Code shows as a failed MCP connection.
Provider errors are swallowed and replaced with a generic message, so no auth headers or response bodies leak into Claude's context (server.ts:161-171). An e2e test covers redaction.

Prompt-injection surface is small: context is JSON-stringified data and the policy instructs the model to treat it as data (scoring.ts:7-8, 104), but the README admits this is not a security boundary. The output is a choice ID and numbers, with no free text from the provider, so injection into Claude via the return value is minimal. A malicious repo could steer what Claude puts into `decision` and `choices`, and the tool result then biases Claude's next action.

No shell execution. `custom` provider kind does dynamic import() of an operator-configured module (providers.ts:57-77). This is local trusted code, and the config comes from the operator, not from tool input. Do not use it with an untrusted DECIDE_CONFIG_JSON.

No postinstall script; only `prepack` builds (package.json). No telemetry code in src. Dependencies are exact-pinned (ai 7.0.105, @ai-sdk/*, MCP SDK 1.30.0, zod), but the install pulls 5 provider SDKs you do not need (openai, anthropic, google, gateway, openai-compatible), which widens the supply-chain surface. `npx -y` fetches from npm at every start unless the package is pinned and cached.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts in the tool arguments is sent to the configured provider: the `decision` string (up to 16k chars), the `context` (string, JSON object or array, up to 100k chars), and each choice id and description (up to 8k chars each, max 64 choices). It goes as the `state` and `questions` body of POST {baseURL}/systemone with a Bearer key (typesafe-evaluation-model.ts:52-63). If profiles and routing are enabled, the same full input is also sent in a first routing call (decision-service.ts:95-115). Nothing is read from disk or the repo automatically and no hook captures tool outputs, so egress is limited to what Claude chooses to include. In practice that can be code snippets, diffs, error text or client details, and there is no redaction or filtering layer in the server. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this: it matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__decide__decide. No telemetry beyond the provider call itself.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's point of view: a provider error, timeout or invalid output returns an MCP tool result with isError true and the text 'Decision failed... No recommendation was produced' (server.ts:161-171), so Claude continues without a recommendation. Defaults: timeoutMs 30000, covering routing, retries and evaluation together (config.ts:100, decision-service.ts:80); maxRetries 2 (config.ts:101). A dead Jev could therefore stall a single call for up to 30 s before it errors. Client cancellation is propagated. Router errors fail the request rather than silently switching policy. Server start is fail-closed: a missing key env var or bad config prevents the MCP server from starting, and the tool is simply absent.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool in the default 'routed' mode. With tools=separate|both it adds 1 + 1 + N profile tools. The `decide` description is 260 chars (server.ts:178-179). The input schema (decision, context union, choices array with id regex and constraints, with output schema) is roughly 1.5-2.5k chars and the outputSchema adds another ~1.5k. Estimate about 700-1000 tokens for the tool definition (chars/4), a single tool. The server sets no `instructions` field (server.ts:126 only name and version), and no hook injects text. Because nothing tells Claude when to call it, effective use needs a CLAUDE.md or rule paragraph (adds ~100-200 tokens per session). Under Claude Code MCP tool search / deferred loading, the definition may only cost its name until needed.
pros: Smallest workable surface for Jev in Claude Code: one read-only tool (readOnlyHint true), ~1k tokens of context, no hooks that can interfere with the user's existing PreToolUse guards or GitNexus hooks.

Uses real Jev probabilities: the percentageSource 'provider-distribution' path passes Jev's native Choice distribution through unmodified (scoring.ts:83-88) and refuses to invent numbers when they are missing ('unavailable'). It is honest about non-calibrated estimates in language mode.

OpenRouter path is a pure config change: kind 'typesafe' plus baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 plus apiKeyEnv OPENROUTER_API_KEY yields POST /systemone (typesafe-evaluation-model.ts:109), which is exactly the OpenRouter System One route. No fork needed, though it is untested.
Secrets are handled correctly: key only via env var name in config, generic error strings, MCP stdio only, no telemetry, no postinstall, exact-pinned deps, MIT.

Good input hygiene: strict zod schemas, unique choice IDs, size caps, timeout that covers retries, abort propagation. Reasonably thorough unit and e2e tests (real MCP client against local HTTP fixtures) for a 1-commit project.
Profiles and routing (bias policies such as 'reliability' or 'cost') are a neat way to encode team risk preferences if wanted, and language-mode fallback lets the same tool work with other models.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with a generic description and no server instructions, so it fails the user's core requirement (Claude Code must use Jev without being told). Getting closer needs CLAUDE.md nudging or your own hook.

Only the Choice primitive. There is no Noul (yes/no) or Score (ordered scale) tool, and no way to feed real app state. `state` is just the model-written decision/context/choices, so Jev is asked to judge Opus's own summary of the situation. The value over Opus deciding directly is unproven, and Jev returns no reasoning trace.

Data egress is unfiltered and model-controlled: up to ~100k chars of context per call can go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, including client code. The user's secret-leak guard does not match this MCP tool's name, so a PreToolUse matcher for mcp__decide__decide must be added before use on client projects.

Immature: 1 commit, 1 star, 1 contributor, no CI, no GitHub release, 13 days old, tied to experimental AI SDK 7 `experimental_evaluate` APIs that the README says may change in patch releases. The @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai adapter is also days old.

OpenRouter is not documented or tested. The default is Vercel AI Gateway, and the OpenRouter routing is inferred from reading the adapter. The only unverified point is whether OpenRouter's /v1/systemone response matches the AI SDK's zod response schema and accepts the model id 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Installs five unused provider SDKs (openai, anthropic, google, gateway, openai-compatible) and an npx cold start, and Node 22+ (Node 24 fine). The default 30 s timeout with 2 retries can stall a turn if Jev is down.
Optional 2-stage routing doubles Jev calls, and the router judges the full payload again, sending it twice. Bias profiles add configuration complexity with little value for coding decisions.
entries.verdict: A clean, honest, minimal Jev-Choice MCP wrapper, and the best off-the-shelf way to reach OpenRouter's System One route from Claude Code by config alone (untested). It is only a manually-invoked model-discretion tool, though, so it does not satisfy the 'automatic' requirement without extra CLAUDE.md or hook glue. Egress control is also needed for client work. Treat it as a low-risk experimental add-on, not a core integration.

entries.name: angrysky56/jev-mcp
entries.what: A TypeScript stdio MCP server ("jev-capability-runtime" v0.2.0) that wraps Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives in a programmable "capability" runtime. The connected agent authors typed questions (jev_judge), saves versioned multi-stage workflows with conditional stages, composite scores, routes and ranking (define_capability), runs them over up to 20 items (run_capability), evaluates them against caller-written examples, and stores records in a local SQLite FTS5 store. It ships five starter capabilities (claim_router, inference_warrant, evidence_stance, formalization_fidelity, tool_router) and one SKILL.md. It is a research and experiment lab (inquiry studies, continuity studies, a Graph-of-Thoughts scorer comparison), not a coding-workflow integration. It has no hooks and no code-specific judgments (no commit, diff, test or permission triage).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a description-triggered skill. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic path. Nothing in the repo makes Claude call Jev on ordinary coding. The tool descriptions say 'Ask agent-authored Choice, Score, or Noul questions... Use this to try a new semantic predicate', so Claude would call it only when it decides to author a question. The suggested habits (run tool_router before substantial tasks, claim_router before reporting findings) live in a resource the model must first fetch (jev://guide), and in a skill that triggers on 'create/test/compose Jev capabilities'. Getting real automatic use would need your own hooks or CLAUDE.md rules, i.e. exactly the prompting you want to avoid. The bootstrapped starter capabilities target research-claim reasoning, not code.
security: No license file: licenseInfo is null, so it is all-rights-reserved by default. That matters for client projects.

Key handling is decent. The key comes from env or a project-root .env (loaded via process.loadEnvFile, src/server.ts:12-13). It is never in argv. The Codex config forwards env var names only. Error bodies are scrubbed with replaceAll(apiKey,'[REDACTED]') (provider.ts:114). fetch uses redirect:'error' and fixed endpoints, and non-Jev slugs are rejected.

Data on disk: every request (state) and response is persisted in SQLite at <repo>/.jev/jev.sqlite via startRun/event, including exact per-stage requests. Anything the agent sends to Jev, such as code or diffs, is retained in plaintext locally. The .jev directory is gitignored.

No child_process, exec, spawn or telemetry found in src/*.ts (grep). Runtime dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 and zod 4.6.5; devDeps are typescript 7.0.2 and the MCP client. It uses built-in node:sqlite.

No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall. Install is a manual git clone + npm ci + mcp:configure, which writes an absolute-path .mcp.json inside the repo. It cannot be run via npx because Node refuses to run TS from node_modules.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev returns only typed numbers or labels, so the model cannot inject text. The stored-record and guide text is agent-authored. Jev outputs are model judgments that could be mistaken for permission, though the guide says they are not permission. Its tool_router and claim_router outputs steer the agent, a soft-influence vector if you trust them blindly.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling agent puts in jev_judge state / run_capability items+context, plus the question instructions, goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai). There is no automatic collection of prompts, files, diffs or tool outputs: the server is passive and sees only what Claude chooses to pass. Requests are capped at 40 KB (provider.ts:101) and batches at 250 KB. Because the state is arbitrary JSON, Claude can send code or client data to OpenRouter (and on to TypeSafe) at its own discretion, and nothing screens it. Your existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Locally, everything is also saved unencrypted in .jev/jev.sqlite. The jev_judge description says 'never include API credentials', which is advisory only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and advisory. The server never sits in the tool-call path, so an outage does not block Claude's own tools. Each call has a 20 s timeout (AbortSignal.timeout, provider.ts:111) and at most one retry for 429/500/502/503/529 when Retry-After is 5 s or less (provider.ts:119). 401/402/403/404 mark the run fatal and stop remaining calls (capability-runtime.ts). Failures return an MCP isError result with status failed or partial, so Claude just sees an error and continues. A missing key returns a 'missing_key' RuntimeError on each call, and the server still starts. The worst case is a wasted tool call of up to about 40 s. There are 4 concurrent calls server-wide and a 32-call default budget per run. Response validation is strict, so malformed responses are rejected.
entries.contextCost: 10 tools. tool_defs: description text is about 7.2 KB (src/mcp-server.ts lines 77-93). The Zod schemas (runtime-contracts.ts, 14 KB, 49 .describe() calls) are nested unions for questions, rules, composites and routes. My estimate of total tool names+descriptions+schemas is 18-24k chars, roughly 4.5-6k tokens (chars/4), always resident unless Claude Code's MCP tool search defers them. The server 'instructions' string is short, about 300 chars (~75 tokens). The 9 KB guide (~2.3k tokens) is a resource read on demand, and the SKILL.md is 3.9 KB, and only its name and description are loaded up front. No hook-injected text. Note that the tool-count and schema footprint is heavy for what you would use it for.
pros: Genuinely OpenRouter-native: default provider is openrouter, endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions and default model ~typesafe/jev-latest (src/provider.ts:3-10, .env.example). It works with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so no patching is needed.

Most thorough client of the Jev API seen: strict response validation (probability sums, choice equals argmax, score equals expectation, label match, provider.ts:49-88), bounded concurrency, per-call cost reporting, pinning of model slug/hash, and floating-alias warnings. This is a solid reference implementation for building your own thin Jev wrapper.

Safe by construction on the write side: it makes no generative calls, calls only fixed Jev endpoints, has no shell execution or child_process, and has a small dependency set (MCP SDK + zod). The key is redacted from stored responses.

Expressive: composites, confidence-gated routes, conditional stages and speculative fan-out map to TypeSafe's documented patterns, so a coding-specific triage capability (for example 'is this diff risky?', 'route this error') could be defined and reused via define_capability and run_capability.

Has tests (5 test files under test/ using node --test), reproducible study artifacts and honest self-reported limitations, including the key-order sensitivity finding (0.1-0.2 shifts on borderline cases).
Reference material: starters/tool-catalog.example.json and the tool_router study (20-server catalog, about 800 chars per routing) is a relevant idea for your MCP-sprawl setup.
cons: Not automatic. It is a passive tool set that Claude must choose to call. The repo has no hooks, and the useful behaviors (tool_router before a task, claim_router before reporting) are 'suggested habits' in a resource the model must read first. That fails your core requirement of Claude using Jev without you asking.

Not built for coding: the bundled capabilities target research reasoning (claim routing, inference warrants, evidence stance, formalization fidelity). None is for code review, test triage, commit-risk, permission decisions or file relevance. You would author the coding capabilities yourself, and the effectiveness is unvalidated.

Heavy footprint for the value: 10 tools with deeply nested schemas (~5k tokens estimated) on every session, in addition to gitnexus and playwright; plus a SQLite record store, run history and versioning machinery that a daily coding flow does not need.

No license (licenseInfo null): all rights reserved. Using or modifying it in client projects has legal ambiguity. A single-author repo (1 contributor, 5 commits in 3 days, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI) and it is very young (created 2026-09-20, last push 2026-09-23). Effectively abandoned-on-arrival risk.

Manual install: git clone + npm ci + a generated absolute-path .mcp.json (gitignored). It cannot be run via npx, must live in a cloned directory, requires Node >=24.12, and stores .jev/jev.sqlite plus a .env in the clone directory. Claude Code reads .mcp.json only when opened in that folder, so you would have to copy the entry into user-scope config with an env block.

Extra data path: any code or diff Claude chooses to judge goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe and is stored plaintext in .jev/jev.sqlite. The mcp__jev__* tools are outside your secret-leak guard matcher. That is a client-confidentiality concern.
Model-discretion tool calls cost a full LLM turn (Opus tokens + latency) per judgment, which cancels most of Jev's 70-500 ms / $0.042 per 1M advantage.

Inherits Jev's beta limits, and its own docs report order and transport sensitivity for borderline cases, so it is unfit for safety or permission decisions (the guide itself says to keep those in code).
entries.verdict: Best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev client found, but it is a research capability workbench with no hooks, so it does not deliver the requested automatic in-Claude-Code use, and it has no license and a single author. Treat it as a reference implementation (provider.ts validation, endpoint and schema) for your own small hook plus minimal MCP wrapper rather than something to install.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null)

entries.name: hangarbay/jev.mcp
entries.what: Go stdio MCP server (v0.1.0, MIT) wrapping TypeSafe's System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone, GET {base}/v1/models). Exposes 5 tools (classify, score, check, ask, models) that return typed Jev decisions with probabilities and confidence, plus a same-binary CLI (classify/score/check/ask/models/serve). Purely a passive tool: no hooks, no skills, no proxying.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code will call classify/check/score/ask only if the model judges the tool descriptions relevant. The descriptions target app-building (intent routing, moderation, guardrails, labels) and say nothing about coding workflows, so Opus will rarely invoke it unprompted in daily coding. There is no hook, skill trigger, CLAUDE.md snippet or proxy shipped. To get automatic use the user would need to add their own CLAUDE.md policy or hooks.
security: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (typesafe.go:72), sent only as Bearer header to configured base URL (:516); not in argv when using docker '-e TYPESAFE_API_KEY' (inherit form) or claude mcp add -e (env). Only the CLI has -state on argv (user data, not key).

No shell execution, no file writes; CLI reads -state-file / stdin only. No telemetry code found; only outbound host is the base URL. Response body capped 4 MiB, error body 400 chars (typesafe.go:43-45).
Base URL is env-controlled: whoever can set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL exfiltrates key and state; not an issue when user controls the env.

Supply chain: solo author (org 'hangarbay', 0 stars), single commit, Docker image built by CI with secrets from Dockerhub, mutable :latest, unsigned, pulled without digest pinning. Building from source at a pinned SHA mitigates this. Deps are few and mainstream (modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk, google/jsonschema-go, segmentio, x/*).

Prompt-injection surface is low: tool output is numeric/typed (choice string is echoed only from caller-supplied option names), so a Jev response cannot carry free-text instructions. The dangerous vector is the reverse: Claude passing code/secrets as 'state' (the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools).
Dockerfile: static CGO-free build, alpine:3.22, non-root uid 10001.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly the 'state' field plus instructions/criteria that Claude chooses to put in each tool call, POSTed as JSON to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (OpenRouter -> upstream TypeSafe if routed there). That means whatever code, diff, log, or file contents the model decides to pass as state, and it is passed verbatim (state may be string/object/array; ParseState). Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself: no file scanning, no background traffic. GET /v1/models sends only the auth header. On OpenRouter, prompt logging/data policy settings of the account apply. On client projects this is third-party egress of client code, so per-project enable is advisable.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, non-fatal to the session: errors become MCP isError tool results and Claude can continue without Jev. Per-request timeout 60s default (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT), retries default 3 after first attempt on 429/529 and presumably network errors, exponential backoff 0.5s doubling capped 30s, honoring Retry-After (typesafe.go:41,551-560). Worst case a slow endpoint blocks one tool call ~4 min (4x60s + backoff) unless TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT=5s and TYPESAFE_MAX_RETRIES=1 are set; recommend those. Other 4xx fail immediately. Missing key: server starts, tools error.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools always present (deferred/searchable in Claude Code 2.1.x MCP tool search, else loaded). Estimated from source: descriptions ~1.9k chars plus JSON schemas with jsonschema tags and nested ask/classify schemas ~4-5k chars, so roughly 1.5-2k tokens total when all schemas are loaded (chars/4). No MCP server 'instructions' set (mcp.NewServer options nil, main.go:116-121). No hook-injected text. Per-call cost: state echoed in tool call args and result JSON plus a text rendering (structured content duplicates as text), small.
pros: Only real, direct Jev MCP found here with all three primitives (Choice, Noul, Score) plus batched ask, matching System One request/response schema (typesafe.go:179-306).
OpenRouter works by config alone: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives exactly /api/v1/systemone (typesafe.go:36,129) with Bearer auth (:516) and model override via TYPESAFE_MODEL.
Small, readable, dependency-light Go codebase (about 2.4k non-test lines), MIT, no shell exec, no telemetry, no postinstall, key via env not argv.
Solid unit/e2e tests (61 funcs) with httptest stubs, sensible retry/backoff and configurable timeout and retries.
Typed structured-content outputs and short descriptions keep context cost small (about 1.5-2k tokens) and there are no hooks adding per-turn latency or injected text.
Also a CLI (jev-mcp check -json etc.), which could be called from a user-authored hook or script for deterministic gating.
cons: Does not solve the user's core requirement: no auto-invocation mechanism. It is a passive tool the model may ignore; descriptions are aimed at app developers (routing, moderation), not coding tasks.
Immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 0 stars, 13 days old, no releases, no prebuilt binaries; CI builds an unsigned Docker :latest but never runs tests.

OpenRouter not explicitly supported or documented: env vars are TYPESAFE_*; default model alias 'jev-latest' differs from OpenRouter IDs; 'models' tool hits GET /v1/models which on OpenRouter has a different, huge payload/schema; OpenRouter parity of /api/v1/systemone body is assumed, not proven (and the Decisions API alpha endpoint is unsupported).
Default reliability settings are poor for interactive use: 60s timeout x 4 attempts can stall a tool call for minutes when the endpoint is slow, needs TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT/TYPESAFE_MAX_RETRIES tuning.

Sends whatever code/diff Claude passes as state to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) on client projects; existing secret-leak hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover mcp__jev__* calls.

Jev has no reasoning or code understanding claims (32k context, beta, skeptic claims of being a small router), so decisions on code-quality questions are unvalidated; every call also costs Opus output tokens and latency to compose state/options.
entries.verdict: Best available MCP wrapper for Jev and OpenRouter-compatible through env config alone (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus OpenRouter key and model ID), but it is a bare model-discretion tool with no automatic trigger and app-oriented descriptions, so on its own it will not meet the 'Claude uses it without being told' goal. Useful only as the transport layer if paired with user-owned hooks/CLAUDE.md policy, and build from a pinned commit rather than pulling the mutable Docker :latest.

entries.name: nirvana124/typesafe-mcp (npm: system-one-mcp)
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server exposing a single tool, `evaluate`, that forwards {state, model, questions} (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe System One direct (via @typesafe-ai/sdk), OpenRouter's alpha Decisions endpoint, or Vercel AI Gateway. Thin pass-through adapter by a third-party individual (not TypeSafe). Published to npm as `system-one-mcp` because `typesafe-mcp` was taken.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. The tool description says what it does but gives no guidance on WHEN a coding agent should call it (no 'use before X' triggers), so Opus will rarely call it unprompted. Getting auto-use would require adding CLAUDE.md rules or a companion skill/hook. Does not satisfy 'used automatically without prompting' on its own.
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts (npm scripts are only build/dev/test/typecheck); published dist contains the openrouter URL matching the repo (checked tarball).
API key comes from env, not argv, if set via the MCP `env` block (README config). The README's `TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... npx` form is also env-based. No key in the process list.

dotenv loadEnv({quiet:true}) at src/index.ts:27 reads .env from the MCP server's cwd, which for Claude Code is the project directory. A client repo's .env (or a hostile cloned repo's) can inject OPENROUTER_API_KEY, JEV_BACKEND, OPENROUTER_BASE_URL/AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL, so the key could be sent to an attacker-chosen host, or an unrelated project OPENROUTER_API_KEY could be used silently. Real risk on client projects. Host-injected env wins (dotenv does not overwrite).
OPENROUTER_BASE_URL is used as the full POST URL with the bearer key, no host allowlisting (openrouter.ts:36).
npx -y with no version pin runs whatever is latest on npm from a solo maintainer with a brand-new account/package: supply-chain exposure. Pin system-one-mcp@0.1.0 or vendor the source.

Tool output is returned as JSON of numeric probabilities only, so the prompt-injection surface from responses is small; the state sent is model-authored so exfiltration risk is via what Claude chooses to send.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and `questions.instructions/criteria` on each evaluate call goes to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe/Jev), plus the bearer key. It could be code, diffs, file contents, or tool output, because the model decides what to pass; nothing is sent automatically. Client-code confidentiality depends on OpenRouter/TypeSafe data policies. Nothing else leaves the machine (no telemetry in the repo).
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup: the process exits 1 if no credential resolves (src/index.ts:29-40), so Claude Code shows the server as failed with no tools. At runtime, errors are returned as isError tool results (index.ts:75-77), which Claude can read and carry on from, so the agent flow is not blocked. The hand-rolled HTTP path (openrouter/vercel) has a 10s timeout per attempt and 2 retries with 0.5-5s backoff on 408/429/5xx/network errors (http.ts:9-12, 27-56), so worst case is about 30s+ before an error. If OpenRouter relocates the alpha path, every call fails with HTTP 404 (README and code note this).
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. Tool description 486 chars plus inputSchema, total src/tools/evaluate.json 2230 chars, about 550-650 tokens of tool definition in context (fewer if tool search defers it). The server sets no `instructions` field (Server constructed with capabilities.tools only, index.ts:47-50). No hooks, so no injected text.
pros: Only candidate-type that already has a first-class OpenRouter path: correct alpha Decisions URL https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY (openrouter.ts:11,37), and JEV_BACKEND=openrouter forces it.
*_API_KEY_ENV redirect (index.ts:21-28) lets you keep a dedicated OpenRouter key var without colliding with other tools; useful with existing secret-leak hook setups.
Tiny surface (1 tool, about 600 tokens, no hooks, no postinstall, no telemetry, Apache-2.0), easy to audit (about 400 LOC) and to vendor or pin.
Exposes all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) with multi-question parallel calls in one request, matching the Jev brief.
Sensible error handling: 10s timeout, 2 retries with Retry-After, tool errors returned as isError rather than crashing; backend switching to TypeSafe direct later needs only a key change.
cons: Model-ID trap: `model` is a required tool arg (evaluate.json:45) with example "jev-latest", but OpenRouter's IDs are typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest; the OpenRouter default (openrouter.ts:12, lacking the ~) is bypassed and itself likely wrong. Claude will likely hit 4xx on the first call.
Only model-discretion invocation and no guidance on when to call it, so it fails the core requirement 'Claude Code must use it automatically'. You would need CLAUDE.md prompts or hooks anyway.
dotenv loads the project's .env from cwd (index.ts:27); on client repos that can silently swap the OpenRouter key/base URL (key exfiltration or wrong billing). Needs cwd isolation or removing dotenv.

Very immature: 3 commits over about 1 hour, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases or CI, single npm version 0.1.0, third-party (not TypeSafe or OpenRouter official); never verified against the live alpha API (tests only use a mock).

Uses alpha /api/alpha/decisions (may move), not the more stable /api/v1/systemone; no `response_format`-style normalization; returns raw probabilities with no thresholds or decision policy, so Claude must interpret them.
Sends whatever code/diffs Claude puts in `state` to a third party; on client projects that needs contract review. `npx -y` unpinned adds a supply-chain risk.
No Claude-Code-specific value: no code-review, commit-gate or permission-gate recipes; Jev's typed decisions are just exposed generically.
entries.verdict: Cleanest existing OpenRouter-capable Jev MCP wrapper and a reasonable base to fork or vendor (pin version, drop dotenv, fix model ID to ~typesafe/jev-latest, make model optional). By itself it is not automatic: it is a bare model-discretion tool with no invocation guidance, so it needs a hook or CLAUDE.md layer to meet the goal.

entries.name: miskakaskinen/typesafe-mcp (evaluate)
entries.what: Single static Go binary `evaluate` that runs as a stdio MCP server exposing one read-only tool, `evaluate`. The tool forwards {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} to Jev and returns the raw typed JSON. It picks its backend from env: TYPESAFE_API_KEY goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, otherwise OPENROUTER_API_KEY goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest. It also has `setup mcp` (registers with Claude Code, Codex and Claude Desktop), `setup pi`, `update` and `version`. It is only a thin transport: the host model still has to decide when to call it and what state and questions to send.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no proxy. Claude will call `evaluate` when its description ("classification, routing, scoring, extraction, branching, guardrails/judging") seems relevant, but for ordinary coding turns it almost never does, since Opus decides itself and the tool says "Not for prose, code". There is no deterministic trigger. The desired "Claude Code uses Jev automatically when it adds value" is only weakly met, with no code-level rules for when to call. Realistic use is limited to explicit classification or triage tasks.
security: API key handling: `evaluate setup mcp` calls `claude mcp add ... -e OPENROUTER_API_KEY=<key>` (setup_hosts.go:121-125), so the key is visible in argv and the process list briefly. It is then stored in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. This can be avoided by running `claude mcp add` by hand, or by using an env reference or wrapper.
At runtime the key is read from the process env and sent only as a Bearer header to the hardcoded HTTPS endpoint (client.go:82). It is not logged and there is no telemetry in the code I read.
No shell execution in the server path. The only exec.Command calls are the setup adapters, which run `claude` and `codex` with fixed argv (setup_hosts.go:28-30).

The install.sh in the README is a curl|sh installer. It does verify a SHA256SUMS.txt fetched from the same GitHub release, so the checksum protects against corruption but not against a compromised release. The install URL points at PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which returns 404. This repo has no releases at all (releases API returns []). The install.sh and `evaluate update` paths would therefore fail as documented, and the only working path is building from source with Go.

README badges and install URLs reference github.com/PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which does not resolve (404 via gh api). The clone under miskakaskinen is not a fork (fork=false) and has 0 stars. Provenance is muddy: the README says it is maintained by elkaix under PyModel, and nearly all commits are by author elkaix. A future PyModel org could be squatted, and install.sh/update would then fetch binaries from whoever owns that org.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is JSON of probabilities, not free text, so returned content is low-risk. The state the host sends is untrusted repo or tool content that goes to a third party.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the host model puts in `state` and in the question `instructions`/`criteria`, sent as JSON to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai). This can include code, diffs, logs, tickets and file contents that Claude chooses to pass. It is not automatic, since the server sees nothing except what Claude passes in a tool call. The OpenRouter key goes in the Authorization header. No telemetry was found in the code. `evaluate update` and install.sh contact api.github.com and github.com. On OpenRouter the data is subject to OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies, which matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by nature, since it is a model-discretion tool. The HTTP timeout is 60s (client.go:35). 429 and 529 are retried up to 3 times with exponential backoff starting at 1s, or Retry-After capped at 60s (client.go:101-110). Worst case is about 60s x 4 plus backoff before a tool error is returned to Claude, which then just carries on. Other errors come back as an IsError tool result. If no key is set at startup the server exits and Claude Code shows it as a failed MCP server, but the session continues. There is no hook, so a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code. The 60s timeout is long compared with the claimed 70-500ms latency, so a stalled call would hang a turn.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Tool description is about 690 chars (tools.go:51-56). The input schema with jsonschema tags is about 1.3k chars (tools.go:58-68). Server instructions are about 2.1k chars of guidelines (tools.go:30-43), which the MCP client injects into the system prompt. Total is about 4.1k chars, roughly 1,000 tokens, always present in every session. There is no hook-injected text. That is small compared with playwright and gitnexus.
pros: Native OpenRouter support with the exact endpoint the user wants: OPENROUTER_API_KEY only gives /api/alpha/decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest (client.go:45-52). No patching needed.
Tiny context footprint: one tool, about 1k tokens including instructions. Much cheaper than the user's existing playwright and gitnexus servers.

Well-engineered wrapper: local criteria validation with JSON-path errors (tools.go:114-146), 429/529 backoff, 16 MiB cap, 60s timeout. 117 tests exist (evaluate_test.go, 34 KB, roughly 22 top-level Test funcs by grep). CI runs gofmt, vet and go test -race with SHA-pinned actions.
Single static Go binary, MIT licensed. No Node or Python runtime, and no npx cold start.
Good agent guidance is baked into the server instructions: do not put your verdict in state, batch independent questions, and read noul near 0.5 as uncertain. This reduces misuse of Jev.
The tool is read-only and returns typed JSON only, so the prompt-injection surface from the response is small.
No telemetry found. Failure is fail-open, because a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code.
cons: Not an automatic integration. It is a plain MCP tool that relies on Opus choosing to call it. There is no hook or skill trigger, and the description itself excludes code and prose, so it will rarely fire on daily coding. This directly misses the user's goal of Claude Code using Jev without being prompted.
Very young: repo created 2026-09-20, 62 commits in about 2 days (most commits by one author, elkaix), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases and no tags on the GitHub repo. Maturity is proof-of-concept.

Broken distribution: README, install.sh and `evaluate update` point to github.com/PyModel/typesafe-mcp, which returns 404, and this repo has no releases. The curl|sh installer and updater cannot work as documented. It must be built from source (`go build`, and go.mod may demand a very new Go toolchain, which was not verified). It must also be reviewed and built by the user, since running it here is forbidden.

`evaluate setup mcp` puts OPENROUTER_API_KEY on argv (`claude mcp add -e KEY=...`) and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json (setup_hosts.go:121-125). It is better to register by hand with an env reference, or a wrapper that reads the key from a secrets store.

Hardcoded alpha endpoint (client.go:47) with no base-URL or model env override. If OpenRouter moves /api/alpha/ the binary must be rebuilt. It does not use the newer /api/v1/systemone route on OpenRouter.

Data egress is model-chosen: Claude decides what code, diff or log to send to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That may violate client confidentiality unless the user restricts it, and the existing secret-leak guard does not cover mcp__ tools (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).

Adds a round trip and Claude authoring tokens for each use. For most coding decisions Opus 5.5 is both faster and better than authoring a Jev question. The 60s timeout with 3 retries is far above the claimed sub-500ms latency.
Documentation is inconsistent about ownership (miskakaskinen copy, PyModel org, elkaix maintainer). A supply-chain risk if the PyModel org name is claimed by someone else.
entries.verdict: The best-written Jev MCP wrapper I inspected for OpenRouter: it supports OPENROUTER_API_KEY natively, has a small context footprint and fails open. It is still a model-discretion tool with no automatic trigger, so it will not deliver "Claude uses Jev when it is useful", and it is a two-day-old repo with no releases and dead install links. Build it from source after review and register it manually so the key stays off argv. Treat it as an optional building block for explicit routing or classification, not as the automatic integration.

entries.name: sf-stav/mcp_typesafe
entries.what: Unofficial single-file Rust MCP server (rmcp 0.8, stdio or SSE) that wraps TypeSafe's System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone, GET {base}/v1/models) and adds 10 higher-level tools: bulk filter/rank/classify/dedupe with chunking, choose_one (skim then verify, with rejection), stability_check, verify_output, verify_tool_calls, check_claims, extract_fields. Thresholds, aggregation and clustering are computed deterministically in Rust. Default model "jev-latest".
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The server ships no hooks, no skill and no plugin. The server 'instructions' and tool descriptions steer Claude to use bulk filter/rank tools "instead of reading long lists yourself", but nothing deterministic makes Claude call it. For daily coding, Claude with Opus would rarely reach for these, since typical coding work (edit, grep, test) has no Jev-shaped judgment step.
security: Apache-2.0. Single 1839-line src/main.rs, 0 tests in the repo (README claims e2e testing against a mock API, but no test code or CI is committed), no .github directory.

API key is passed via env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or the --typesafe-api-key CLI flag. The flag exposes the key in argv and the process list, and start.sh does this. Use the env form in the MCP 'env' block, which stays out of argv.
Key is only used as an Authorization Bearer header (src/main.rs:493). tracing::info! calls log tool names and counts, not content or key. Log level is info to stderr by default.

No shell execution, no file writes, no Command::new. Egress is only the configured base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is an env override, so a poisoned env could redirect data, but this is standard for a client.

Install requires cargo build --release from source: no prebuilt binaries, no releases (latestRelease null), no crates.io publish found. Building compiles about 200 transitive crates (Cargo.lock), which is a supply-chain surface. No npm/pip postinstall and no curl|sh.
start.sh binds SSE to 0.0.0.0:3391 with no auth. Do not use it; use stdio.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the tool arguments leaves the machine, sent verbatim to {base}/v1/systemone: the state (strings, JSON, items lists, draft outputs, code snippets, sources, claims, tool-call schemas) and the question text, plus model name. That is up to 64k chars per chunk. Nothing is read from disk or intercepted automatically. Only what Claude chooses to pass. With the base URL pointed at OpenRouter, this goes to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe. verify_output sends the draft and sources, which may include client code or secrets if Claude passes them, so this must be considered for client projects. No telemetry from the server itself. It sends the User-Agent mcp-typesafe/0.1.2.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open (see above): MCP tool error, 30 s HTTP timeout, no retry.
entries.contextCost: 12 tools. Tool descriptions total about 5.5k chars on one-line #[tool] attributes (some are multi-line), and the 66 schemars field descriptions total about 10k chars. With JSON schema structure overhead, roughly 21k chars for the tool defs, plus about 2.9k chars of server 'instructions' text (src/main.rs:1502-1530), for about 24k chars, or roughly 6k tokens permanently in context per session (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search, in which case only the names load until needed). No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. Tool results are pretty-printed JSON, and bulk tools return the full probability vector, so results can be large.
pros: Only candidate found so far with a typed, tested-by-author wrapper over the full System One primitives (choice/score/noul) plus useful compositions: filter_items/rank_items/classify_items for triaging long lists (logs, search hits, issues) and verify_output/verify_tool_calls/check_claims as an independent second opinion.

OpenRouter path is config-only for the main tool: base URL is a runtime flag/env (src/main.rs:96-97) and the path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One API path, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key should work (schema match unverified).
Deterministic server-side math (thresholds, ranking, clustering, chunking); returns only numeric or typed output, so little prompt-injection surface and small results relative to reading lists.
Low-risk runtime: no shell, no file access, no writes, 30 s timeout, fail-open, Apache-2.0, apart from the one HTTP egress.
Small ~6k-token footprint, no per-turn hook cost or latency, so it does not compete with the existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tools, no hook or skill trigger. Violates the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told, unless paired with a CLAUDE.md nudge or a custom hook (which the repo does not provide).

Default model is 'jev-latest', which is not an OpenRouter model ID (OpenRouter uses typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Without a patch, Claude must pass model on every call, or the call likely fails. list_models on OpenRouter would dump the full OpenRouter catalogue.
OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified (docs 404'd during this audit); the server has no OpenRouter test, so any field difference would surface as runtime errors.

Extreme immaturity: repo created 2026-09-19, 4 commits (3 by sf-stav, 1 by Stav Katsoulis), 1 human contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, no test code in the repo, self-described AI-assisted, unofficial, and the maintainer solicits paid work.

Build-from-source only: needs a Rust >=1.85 toolchain and compiling ~200 crates; no binaries, no crates.io or npm package, and you must not run it blindly as an audited artifact. A default_model patch means owning a fork.
--typesafe-api-key flag and start.sh put the key in argv (env form avoids this). start.sh SSE binds 0.0.0.0 unauthenticated.

Everything Claude passes as state, drafts or sources goes to a third-party API, which is a concern for client code, and verify_output's 'safe_to_share' check would itself require sending the possibly-secret text out.

Use case mismatch for coding: Jev is a judgment engine; most of the 12 tools solve list-triage and agent-pipeline problems that rarely arise in an editing session, and Claude must spend an Opus turn to compose the typed questions, which erodes the latency and cost advantage.
entries.verdict: The most complete Jev MCP wrapper in the discovered set and pointable at OpenRouter by env (plus a model override), but it is a brand-new, untested, one-person Rust project, and being a pure model-discretion tool it cannot deliver the "automatic, without prompting" integration by itself. It is worth using only as a building block (optionally with a pinned fork and a hook or CLAUDE.md nudge) rather than as the solution.

entries.name: codeChap/mcp-server-jev
entries.what: Small Rust (rmcp, stdio) MCP server wrapping OpenRouter's Decisions API (POST /api/alpha/decisions, default model typesafe/jev-1.13). Exposes 8 tools: 3 raw primitives (noul, choice, score), a batch (decide), and 4 opinionated composites built from fixed noul/score questions (rank, screen, verify, gate). A companion skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md) describes when an agent should call them. Every tool is pure model-discretion; nothing intercepts tool calls automatically.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a description-triggered skill. Nothing is deterministic: no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks, no proxy. Claude will call it only if it judges a tool description relevant; with Opus 5.5 that is rare for tasks like 'noul: does this diff touch auth' because it can answer directly. The bundled SKILL.md is written for Grok's search_tool/use_tool flow and references Fable/Grok, so it needs rewriting for Claude Code. Making it truly automatic (e.g. gate before every Bash, screen after WebFetch) would require adding your own hooks that call the API or the binary, which this repo does not provide; note the README itself says gate/screen never execute or block anything.
security: API key: read from config.toml or OPENROUTER_API_KEY env (config.rs:115-119); never in argv, so not visible in ps. Registering via 'claude mcp add -e' stores it in ~/.claude.json plaintext instead; the config.toml route avoids that. Key is sent only as a Bearer header to base_url.
base_url is user-configurable and the bearer key goes to whatever it points at; low risk since config is local.
Error path returns raw upstream response body / decode body to the model (api.rs:245,247), which is tool-result text but comes from OpenRouter, low injection risk.

No shell execution, no file reads/writes of user code, no subprocess spawn; server only reads its own config files and makes one HTTPS POST per call. No telemetry beyond OpenRouter attribution header X-Title=mcp-server-jev.
Fallback silently reads ~/.config/mcp-server-open-router/config.toml for a key (config.rs:118), an undocumented-by-default cross-tool credential read that could pick an unintended key.

Prompt-injection surface: 'screen' and 'gate' send untrusted text to a model, and 'gate'/'screen' results are advisory and are themselves a classifier a crafted payload could evade; SKILL.md itself warns not to trust them for enforcement. Relying on gate to catch destructive commands is weak compared with deterministic hooks.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into the tool arguments: state/question text for noul/choice/score/decide; query + up to 32 item strings for rank; full text of fetched/pasted content for screen; claim + evidence (diff/log/passage) for verify; proposed command + optional task/policy for gate. All sent verbatim (except rank's local index preview truncation) to openrouter.ai, which forwards to TypeSafe (response 'provider' field). Nothing is harvested automatically from the repo or transcript, but in practice Claude will paste diff hunks, commands and file snippets, so client code can reach OpenRouter/TypeSafe; no redaction or secret stripping is done server-side (SKILL.md only says 'strip env files first'). Client-project NDAs and OpenRouter data-retention/provider policy should be checked. Cost: about $0.042/M input tokens.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by construction: API errors (HTTP, non-2xx, decode) are returned as a normal isError tool result with the message (server.rs:45, api.rs:243-247), so Claude just sees a failed tool call and continues. Missing key makes the process exit at startup (main.rs:418 config::load()? -> Err), so Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools are absent, again not blocking anything. Timeout is 60 s per request (api.rs:210), no retries, no circuit breaker, no cache. A hung Jev could stall one turn up to 60 s if the model chose to call it; in a hook this would matter, but here it is model-discretion only. No hook means no fail-closed path exists.
entries.contextCost: 8 tools always in the tool list. Estimated from source: descriptions about 2.3k chars, JSON schemas from params.rs (about 4.3k chars of source with per-field descriptions, schemars output about 5-6k chars incl. structure) plus server instructions about 700 chars (server.rs:357-364), total roughly 8-9k chars, about 2.0-2.5k tokens. If Claude Code's MCP tool search defers tool defs, only names are loaded until needed. No hook-injected text (no hooks). SKILL.md adds only its description (about 400 chars) to the skill list until triggered; full body about 2.3k chars (about 600 tokens) when loaded.
pros: Genuinely OpenRouter-native and code-verified: hits https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.rs:8-12,117; api.rs:170), matching the Jev brief exactly. Zero patching needed for the user's chosen provider.
Small, readable codebase (about 1.1k lines Rust, about 64 KB source excluding lock); auditable in 10 minutes. No shell exec, no file access, key never in argv when config.toml is used.

Good tool design for typed decisions: decide batches many atomic questions in one request; rank/verify/screen/gate are sensible pre-baked prompts for coding-agent use cases (retrieval reranking, claim vs diff, injection screening, tool-call risk).
Fail-open and non-blocking: errors surface as isError tool results; missing key just disables the server; adds no per-turn cost or latency when unused.
MIT licensed, pinned model default with an explicit comment that jev-latest moves (config.toml.example), and CI runs fmt/clippy/test.
Cheap: ~$0.042/M input tokens; even heavy tool use is pennies.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion. Opus 5.5 has little reason to delegate a yes/no to another model, so it will seldom call these tools unless CLAUDE.md or hooks force it; that directly fails the user's 'Claude Code must use it without being told' requirement.

No Claude Code integration at all: no hooks, no plugin.json/.mcp.json/marketplace entry; README documents only Grok; SKILL.md targets Grok/Fable (search_tool, use_tool, 'Keep Fable/Grok for that') and would need rewriting.

gate and screen are advisory and never enforce; thresholds (secrets>=0.30, injection>=0.75, etc.) are hardcoded guesses (format.rs:138-166) with no calibration evidence. Using an unverified beta model as a security classifier is weaker than the user's existing deterministic secret-leak PreToolUse hook and would add no real protection.

Data egress risk on client projects: diffs, commands and file content that Claude chooses to pass go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no redaction; the user's existing secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool arguments unless its matcher is extended.

Extreme immaturity: 1 commit, 1 author, 0 stars/forks, created 9 days before audit date, no releases, no prebuilt binaries (must cargo build), one mocked round-trip test and no live-API tests, uses alpha endpoint that may change (/api/alpha/).
Extra Opus round trip per use (~seconds) outweighs Jev's 70-500 ms; ~2-2.5k tokens of always-on tool-def context for 8 tools, most of which overlap what Claude does natively (verify, rank, screen).

Silently falls back to reading ~/.config/mcp-server-open-router/config.toml for an API key (config.rs:118), and the sample 'site_url' attribution defaults to the author's domain example; minor hygiene issues.
Only System One Decisions API; no TypeSafe direct key support, no System One (/api/v1/systemone) path, no Jev Router model support beyond overriding default_model.
entries.verdict: The only OpenRouter-native, code-verified Jev MCP found so far, and safe to read and build, but it is a Grok-oriented proof of concept whose tools Claude will rarely call on its own, so it fails the 'automatic' requirement unless you add deterministic hooks or CLAUDE.md rules yourself. Best used as a reference implementation or a low-cost opt-in tool (fork it, build locally, add a Claude Code hook layer), not as a drop-in solution.

entries.name: douglance/jevon (jev CLI + MCP server)
entries.what: Rust binary `jev` (alias `typesafe`) built on the incurs CLI framework. One command graph is exposed as a CLI and as an MCP stdio server (`jev mcp add` registers it) and can generate skill files (`jev skills add`). Each command wraps the TypeSafe Rust SDK's System One call (POST {base}/v1/systemone) with Choice/Score/Noul questions over a text state. No hooks, no proxy. Purely model-discretion tools.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description says 'Use when code needs a judgment — choosing the next action, filtering or ranking, routing, or gating — rather than generated prose', which is aimed at app code, not at an agent editing code, so Claude Code will rarely pick it unprompted for daily coding. Not a hook, not a proxy, not a skill trigger (`jev skills add` can write skill files, but those are also description-triggered and the same mismatch applies). Cannot deliver the 'Claude Code uses it automatically' requirement by itself.
security: API key is read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY); `jev mcp add` deliberately writes no key into agent config; no --api-key CLI flag found, so not visible in argv. Key masked in `doctor` output and redacted in SDK debug logs (typesafe-sdk-headers/src/redact.rs). Caveat: Claude Code must have the key in its own environment, so it also reaches every Bash tool call and other MCP children; use claude mcp add --env instead to scope it.

No shell execution, no subprocess spawn in library code (Command::new appears only in tests/mcp_stdin.rs), unsafe forbidden, no build.rs/postinstall in jevon (SDK runtime crate has a build.rs that only records rustc version), no curl|sh installer.

Local file read primitives: --state-file, --items-file, --questions-file take arbitrary paths (crates/typesafe-sdk-cmd-kit/src/input.rs read_file, no path allowlist). A prompt-injected agent could send any readable file (e.g. .env, ~/.ssh) to the API endpoint. Tools are flagged read-only, so with auto/bypass permission mode they run without any prompt. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, NOT MCP tools, so it would not catch this path.
Hint text in tool descriptions points the agent to docs.typesafe.ai/*.md URLs to fetch (ask/src/lib.rs:118-121); external content pulled into context = minor prompt-injection surface.

Telemetry: SDK sends User-Agent/X-TypeSafe-SDK/X-TypeSafe-Runtime (rustc/os description) headers to whatever base URL is configured; no separate analytics endpoint found. Dependency tree is large (reqwest/hyper/tokio via SDK), from crates.io, unaudited; 0 stars, single-author (35 of 37 commits), SDK repo maintained by same person (douglance, appears to be a community project; a typesafe-public-bot[bot] and one other contributor exist) — supply-chain trust is personal, not vendor.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the `state` argument (or reads from --state-file/--items-file) plus the question text and labels, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai/api when redirected) with the bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: no hook or background capture. Content is entirely model-chosen, so it can include code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. Via OpenRouter the payload additionally passes through OpenRouter's logging/routing policy and TypeSafe as upstream provider. Also SDK identification headers.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the session level (it is an optional MCP tool; an error is just an isolated tool result with stable codes TIMEOUT, CONNECTION_ERROR, RATE_LIMIT, AUTHENTICATION_ERROR, etc. from kit lib.rs:46-72). But a single call can block a turn for long: SDK default per-attempt timeout 10 s, 2 retries, backoff 500 ms to 5 s with jitter, honours Retry-After up to 60 s (typesafe-sdk-retry/src/policy.rs:7-50), so worst case ~30+ s before an error is returned. Missing key returns 'No API key was provided' rather than crashing. Timeout is settable in the SDK but I found no env var for it in jevon. If the server binary fails to start, Claude Code just shows the MCP server as failed.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools (ask, classify, eval, doctor, models_list). Source text for descriptions/hints/examples/schemas is ~18 KB across ask/classify/eval libs (ask HINT alone ~1.9 KB of prose, includes 5 docs URLs); after schema generation with option docs I estimate roughly 9-12k chars, about 2.5-3k tokens always resident (or deferred behind ToolSearch in recent Claude Code). No MCP server-level 'instructions' seen. No hook-injected text. Moderate footprint, larger than a single-purpose tool, mostly wasted for coding since eval/classify/models/doctor are rarely wanted.
pros: Works against OpenRouter with zero code changes: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> gives POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (client.rs:27, send.rs:35), matching OpenRouter's own doc for the TypeSafe SDK; default model 'jev-latest' is auto-mapped to ~typesafe/jev-latest.

Cleanest available wrapper for the System One (Choice/Score/Noul) API: full primitive coverage, parallel multi-question requests, batch classify with concurrency and min-confidence, eval command for threshold calibration.
Key never written to config by `jev mcp add`; no key in argv; redacted logging; no shell exec, unsafe forbidden.
Tools annotated readOnly so no approval prompts (matches bypass/auto workflow); stable structured error codes; sane 10 s timeout and bounded retries.

Very disciplined codebase (strict clippy/pedantic, size limits, CI, MCP stdin regression test that drove a real bug fix), MIT license, and the docs/when-to-use.md is honest that Jev is for decisions with known options, not general coding.
Also useful as a manual/scripting CLI (`jev ask ... --format json`) and as a reference for how the SDK talks to the endpoint.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tool whose description targets app developers building decision logic, so Claude Code (Opus) will seldom call it unprompted, which fails the user's core requirement. There is no hook, proxy or per-turn integration.

Young and thin: repo created 2026-09-19 (11 days before audit date), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, 37 commits with 35 by one author, version 0.8.0 alpha; SDK dependency (typesafe-sdk-rs 0.6) is a separate community repo. API surface may churn.

Install requires cargo build from source (`cargo install jevon`, rust 1.98 toolchain, big reqwest/tokio tree); no prebuilt binary, npm or uvx path, and I cannot verify the crates.io artifact matches the GitHub source.

Data exfiltration path: --state-file/--items-file/--questions-file read arbitrary local paths and send content to a third party, marked read-only so auto/bypass mode runs it unprompted; the user's secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tool calls. Client projects make this a real concern.

Everything sent is model-authored text; ask needs the agent to serialise code/context into a string argument, costing Opus output tokens and a full extra turn per decision, which usually exceeds what Jev saves.
Context tax: 5 tool definitions (~3k tokens) mostly for commands (eval, classify, models list, doctor) irrelevant to coding.

`models list` likely breaks on OpenRouter (different /v1/models envelope); Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported; retry policy can stall a turn ~30 s worst case; API key must sit in Claude Code's own environment (leaks to all child processes) unless passed via claude mcp add --env.
Jev itself is a decision model with 32k context and no reasoning; skeptics call it a small flash-router; no evidence in this repo it improves code-editing decisions.
entries.verdict: Best-quality, lowest-risk generic wrapper for reaching Jev through OpenRouter (just set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api), so it is a fine building block or manual/scripting tool, but as a plain model-discretion MCP it will not fire automatically in daily coding and it adds a file-read egress path under bypass mode. Use it only as the transport behind a deterministic hook or a purpose-written narrow skill, not as the integration itself.

entries.name: blakestone-x/jev-mcp
entries.what: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP/mcp>=2.2) wrapping the official typesafe-sdk. Seven model-discretion tools (jev_ask, jev_classify, jev_score, jev_check, jev_match, jev_screen, jev_health) that send caller-supplied state plus a closed answer set to Jev's System One endpoint and return a normalized envelope with choice/probabilities/confidence/band, usage and estimated cost. Adds request-size budgets, a client-side rate limiter, windowed matching with an abstention Noul, an optional two-call order-ensemble for classify, and an untrusted-text screening verdict.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no server instructions. The only steering is tool descriptions that say what the tools are not for ('not for text generation or numeric extraction'). Claude Code will rarely pick these on its own for coding, because there is no coding-oriented trigger; matches the user's requirement only weakly and would need extra steering (CLAUDE.md rule or a hook) that this repo does not provide.
security: Key in argv: README states the key 'is briefly visible in the process list while claude mcp add runs' (scripts/register.sh:96 passes -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=${api_key}); the key is then stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json mcpServers env. Avoid register.sh; use an env-var-from-secret wrapper.

The server itself reads the key only from environment (client.py:41-49); it does not log it. It sets TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=warning at import (jev_mcp/__init__.py:8) so SDK request bodies are not logged, and _failure returns state-free error envelopes with truncated loc/details (server.py:140-187, SECURITY.md).

No shell execution or subprocess in the runtime package; no telemetry beyond calls to the configured base URL. Egress goes only to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL resolves to (default api.typesafe.ai). Because TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is honored by the SDK, a mis-set env would send the bearer key and state elsewhere.

Supply chain: uvx installs from a git tag (mutable, no release artifacts, single-author brand-new repo, 26 stars, 3 commits in one day) plus transitive deps mcp>=2.2, typesafe-sdk, httpx2 (unusual package name to vet). Runs unsandboxed with the user's privileges on every session start. Pin a commit SHA and review deps.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are numeric/label envelopes, but jev_ask/jev_classify echo caller-supplied labels and mapping keys back in results; jev_screen is explicitly a filter, not a security boundary (SECURITY.md, README). Output validation rejects answers outside the submitted options (server.py:374-390, 502 envelope).

Dangling risk in helper scripts: register.sh/register.ps1 write plaintext key into ~/.codex/config.toml and the Claude user config; they do validate key characters and back up configs, but apply mode modifies user config files.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the state/questions/labels/candidates/text tool arguments is serialized and sent to the Jev endpoint (up to 120,000 chars per request, JEV_MCP_MAX_REQUEST_CHARS). Nothing is collected automatically: no hooks, no file scanning. Claude Code decides what to pass, so code snippets, diffs, log text, ticket text or file contents can leave the machine if Claude includes them. With OpenRouter as the base URL that data goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe (OpenRouter's data policies apply). Also the bearer key and model name. jev_health sends only an authenticated model-list request. jev_match fans out ceil(n/window)+1 requests carrying all candidates.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to the agent, not fail-closed to the workflow: every error is caught and returned as an {ok:false,status,error} tool result (server.py:140-187); Claude just sees a failed tool call and proceeds. Timeouts: 8 s HTTP timeout, 20 s SDK retry budget with 3 retries and 1 s to 20 s backoff honoring Retry-After (client.py:107-125), so one call can block about 30 s when degraded (README); ensemble classify about 60 s (two sequential calls); jev_match up to 45 s deadline. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY does not stop the server from starting; each call returns a 401 envelope (ConfigurationError). No circuit breaker, so a down provider makes each attempted call cost up to 30 s of wall time. It is not in the hook path, so it cannot block tool execution.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools, all deferred-capable (Claude Code 2.1.x loads MCP tool schemas lazily via ToolSearch when many tools exist, but names appear in the deferred list). Approx tokens of names+descriptions+schemas by chars/4: docstrings about 300-500 chars each (about 100 tokens each incl. the repeated cost/confidence sentences) plus pydantic-derived input schemas (jev_ask with nested Choice/Score/Noul question unions is the biggest) for roughly 2.5k-3.5k tokens when fully loaded. No MCP server 'instructions' are set (MCPServer(name, version, description) at server.py:74-79). No hook-injected text. Small compared to playwright (26 tools) and gitnexus (17 tools) already installed.
pros: Real, readable, well-structured code: strict pyright, ruff, offline tests (about 59) and CI on two OSes; errors are state-free envelopes; out-of-set model answers are rejected (server.py:374-390).

Uses the official typesafe-sdk, whose base URL is env-configurable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and whose paths are /v1/systemone, exactly the path OpenRouter exposes at /api/v1/systemone, so pointing it at OpenRouter is plausibly config-only (unverified, needs a live test).

Sensible engineering for Jev's real quirks: token-per-minute 429 backoff with Retry-After, order-ensemble to detect position bias (README says 32 of 200 choices flipped on reversal), windowed matching with abstention, confidence bands (act at 0.90, verify at 0.50).
Key is read from env, not tool arguments; SDK logging forced to WARNING so bodies are not logged; MIT licensed; no shell exec or telemetry in runtime code.
Small footprint (about 3k tokens) and errors never crash the session; it is off the hook path so it cannot block edits.
cons: Not automatic: nothing triggers Jev unless Claude chooses to call a tool; there is no coding-specific profile (README says 'Jev intentionally does not load profiles for you'). The user's 'never prompt use jev' requirement is not met without extra CLAUDE.md steering or a custom hook.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; env override is undocumented and jev_health (GET /v1/models) likely breaks on OpenRouter's different model-list schema; model IDs differ (jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-1.13).

Very new and thin: created and last pushed 2026-09-16, 3 commits, 1 author, no release, 26 stars; 'Development Status :: 3 - Alpha'. The README performance numbers come from one unnamed field-service company's ticket data, not code tasks.

Installs via uvx from a mutable git tag at every session start; unpinned transitive deps (mcp>=2.2, httpx2) widen supply-chain exposure; a different unrelated 'jev-mcp' exists on PyPI (name-confusion risk).
Plaintext key in ~/.claude.json and briefly in argv when registered via claude mcp add or scripts/register.sh (README admits it); with OpenRouter that is a general-purpose OpenRouter key.
Degraded-provider behaviour is slow: up to about 30 s per call (60 s ensemble, 45 s match) with no circuit breaker.
Any code or diff text Claude passes as state leaves the machine to a third party; the design encourages passing raw text (jev_screen, jev_classify) to be judged.

Use cases (support-ticket classify, entity match, injection screen) are generic decision primitives, not code-review, routing-of-tasks or tool-permission decisions; Opus 5.5 already answers these better in-context for small inputs.
entries.verdict: Clean, honest, small MCP wrapper that is probably repointable to OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus JEV_MCP_MODEL, but it is only a model-discretion toolbox with no coding triggers, so it fails the 'automatic, never prompt' requirement on its own. Useful only as a transport layer if paired with your own hook or CLAUDE.md policy (pin the commit, keep the key out of argv).

entries.name: wangkuangkuang/jev-mcp-server
entries.what: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, mcp>=1.9, httpx[http2]) wrapping TypeSafe System One. Exposes 7 tools: choice, score, noul (1:1 with the official question types) plus compare (A/B choice), verify (claim vs evidence noul), classify (batch choice, sequential per item, up to 100), and setup (verify and store a key at ~/.config/jev-mcp/key). Also ships an `install <client>` subcommand for claude-code, cursor, codex, opencode and pi. It POSTs {model, state:{}, questions} to a configurable base URL with a Bearer key, validates the response (probabilities sum to about 1, choice in ids, and so on), and returns compact JSON with latency and usage. It has no hooks, skills or proxy. Claude has to decide on its own to call the tools.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The sole trigger is the tool descriptions, which say things like 'triage, routing, classification' and 'is this change breaking?'. There is no hook, skill, CLAUDE.md snippet or proxy, so nothing guarantees Opus will call them unprompted. Opus will mostly answer such questions itself unless CLAUDE.md, a skill, or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook nudges it. A README-style prompt ('Which of these is safest? Show me the probability split') is what triggers it in practice.
security: The key is read from the env var or from ~/.config/jev-mcp/key (dir 0700, file 0600, atomic write; config.py:106-113). The installer's `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key>` puts the key in argv, so it is briefly visible in the process list (installer.py:108-121). It then persists in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, and codex and cursor configs get the same treatment.

The `setup` tool takes the API key as a tool argument. That routes the secret through the model context and the transcript, and a prompt injection could invoke it. Setting the env var means it never needs calling.

There is no shell execution at runtime. subprocess is used only in the installer, for `claude mcp add`. There is no postinstall hook and no curl|sh in the code; the README only suggests the astral.sh uv installer as an option.

There is no telemetry. The only network destination is config.base_url(), and the User-Agent header names the repo. Overriding JEVMCP_BASE_URL sends the Bearer key to whatever host is set, so it must be set correctly.

Supply chain: this is a solo-maintainer 8-day-old package, and `uvx jev-mcp-server` without a pin pulls the latest release on each run. The publish workflow uses a PYPI_API_TOKEN secret and a mutable @release/v1 action ref. Errors return only the first 200 chars of the response body, and there is no logging of the key.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Tool outputs are numeric JSON plus echoed input; classify echoes the items it was given. Jev returns no free text. The risk sits in what the model chooses to send out as context.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts into tool arguments leaves the machine: question, options, levels, context, a and b, claim and evidence, or classify items. The `verify` tool is designed to carry log excerpts and diffs as `evidence`, and `context` is free text.
