Everything goes to the endpoint in JEVMCP_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter after an override) together with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically from the repo or from tool outputs; the model decides. Under OpenRouter, the OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies apply. That matters for client-project code, and the payload can contain snippets of it.
entries.failureMode: Failures are per call and non-blocking, so Claude Code keeps working. The client uses a 25 s httpx timeout, up to 3 attempts on 429, 503 and 529 with 0.5 s then 1 s backoff, and then raises RuntimeError ('TypeSafe unavailable after retries; no decision made', client.py:34-45). Connection errors raise immediately with no retry. Other HTTP errors raise with the first 200 chars of the body. FastMCP turns the exception into an isError tool result, so the model sees the failure and can proceed without Jev. There is no circuit breaker: with a dead endpoint the worst case is roughly 3 x 25 s plus backoff on each call. Malformed responses raise ValueError ('no decision returned'). classify is sequential, so one failure aborts the whole batch.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools (mcp__jev__choice, score, noul, compare, verify, classify, setup). The docstrings from server.py come to roughly 6.5k chars, and the JSON schemas add about 1.5-2k chars, so roughly 2-2.5k tokens of tool definitions. The server sets no MCP `instructions`, and there are no hooks, so nothing else is injected. Dropping `setup` (or denying it via permissions) trims it a little. If Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch, only the tool names sit in context until they are needed.
pros: Uses the official question types 1:1 (choice, score, noul). It validates responses strictly (server.py:48-97), so garbage or out-of-range output becomes an error and never silently misleads Claude.

OpenRouter is a config-only switch. JEVMCP_BASE_URL and JEVMCP_MODEL are both overridable, the auth is a plain Bearer header, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone forwards the TypeSafe body unchanged, so no fork is needed.

Small and auditable. About 17 KB of server code and no shell exec at runtime, no telemetry, and no hooks or proxy that could break the existing PreToolUse chain. It is MIT and has an offline test suite plus a cross-OS CI.

Compact JSON output and a small tool surface (7 tools, about 2k tokens). Probabilities are sorted, so near-ties are visible. compare and verify are well-shaped for code-review-style checks, such as claim vs log or A/B of two error messages.
Fails gracefully: tool errors are visible to Claude and never block the session. The cache is off by default, and the response includes latency and usage.
cons: Not automatic. It is a pure MCP toolset with no hook or skill, so it fails the user's core requirement. Claude would call it only rarely unless a CLAUDE.md rule or hook is added on top.

Has no OpenRouter support in code or docs. The key env var is hard-named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which is confusing when it holds an OpenRouter key. The default model id 'jev-latest' is wrong for OpenRouter, which needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest. This is untested against OpenRouter.

A weak value proposition for a subscription-based Opus 5.5 workflow. Jev is a classifier, not a reasoner, and most coding decisions (what to edit, why a test fails) are not enumerated-option problems. In that workflow it saves few tokens and adds a network hop, an API key and a data-egress path to a third party.

Very immature: created 2026-09-22, 8 commits, 3 stars, 5 releases in 1 day. The 0.2.3 fix corrected an installer bug that crashed on every non-`--key` path, and the earlier BOM handling could wipe a user's whole client config. That does not inspire trust in the installer, so do not use it and register the MCP by hand.

The `setup` tool lets the model take an API key as an argument (a secret in the transcript, and an injection target). The installer puts the key in argv. Unpinned `uvx` means unreviewed updates run automatically on the user's client projects.

Data egress on client projects: `context`, `evidence` and `items` are free text that Claude may fill with code, diffs or logs. No redaction is applied, and the user's secret-leak guard hook covers only Bash, Read, Grep and NotebookEdit, not MCP tool args.

classify is sequential (about 1 min per 100 items) and has no concurrency. There is no circuit breaker, so a dead endpoint blocks each call for up to about 75 s. The client also cannot use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) or the Jev Router, only /systemone.
entries.verdict: A clean, small, well-validated Jev MCP that would work with OpenRouter by env vars alone (JEVMCP_BASE_URL, JEVMCP_MODEL, and the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY). But it is purely model-discretion, with nothing that makes Claude Code call it automatically, and it is very new. Useful only as a thin transport layer if paired with a CLAUDE.md rule or hook, and pinned by version.

entries.name: agent-fastpath (abhishekswe/agent-fastpath, npm: agent-fastpath)
entries.what: Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server that wraps TypeSafe Jev (System One) behind opinionated presets (ship_gate, risk, severity, ambiguity, relevance, verify_claim, classify, intent, rank, compare, extract_fields). Deterministic regex rules run first (failing test logs, git push --force, rm -rf, DROP TABLE); otherwise one Jev call, then a local confidence gate maps the answer to accept/review/escalate. It also offers server-side file triage (reads up to 500 files locally, sends 4,000-char redacted excerpts to Jev, returns top-N snippets) and a Playwright headless browser with SSRF proxy and an irreversible-action gate. It is a caller-driven decision tool, not a router or a transparent proxy.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions ("Answer typed questions about a piece of text...", "Rank files... without reading them into your context") are the only trigger. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no proxy. Opus will call them only when it judges them useful, and in practice it is unlikely to volunteer a ship-gate/risk call on its own, especially when it can read a log directly. Reliable automation would need a user-written PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook or CLAUDE.md rules, which this project does not provide.
security: The API key is passed by env (`-e TYPESAFE_API_KEY`), stored in ~/.claude.json, and sent as a Bearer header. It does not appear in the npx argv. It is redacted from state by the TypeSafe key pattern in deterministic_engine.ts:210.

Redaction is regex-based (deterministic_engine.ts:169-247): private keys, ts_/apikey_ keys, sk-ant, sk-, ghp_, AKIA, xox, Bearer, *_API_KEY= assignments and JSON password fields. It does not cover an OPENROUTER key format (sk-or-v1-... matches the generic sk- rule only if 32 or more chars, which is likely) or arbitrary proprietary secrets. The docs admit it is not DLP.

No postinstall or preinstall scripts and no telemetry found by grep. `npx -y` runs the latest published version unpinned, so a compromised release would auto-execute. Pin agent-fastpath@0.2.0 to mitigate.

cli/src/index.ts:13-22 calls process.loadEnvFile on ./.env in the cwd, so a project's .env is loaded into the server process env. It is not sent anywhere, but it can pull in a client project's TYPESAFE_API_KEY or FASTPATH_* overrides. This is odd behaviour for client work.

Prompt-injection surface: the browser tool feeds page text to the judge (acknowledged in SECURITY.md) and triage feeds file content. Impact is limited to skewing a decision, and the confidence gate escalates on low confidence. Filesystem access is confined to FASTPATH_ROOTS with symlink resolution. Browser SSRF is enforced by a per-session egress proxy. Chromium runs with its sandbox on, unless FASTPATH_BROWSER_NO_SANDBOX=1.
Single maintainer, 3 stars, project 9 days old. The supply-chain trust level is low for use on client code.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone only (hardcoded, client.ts:31): the redacted `state` string the calling agent passes to fastpath_evaluate (logs, diffs, requirements, up to 262,144 bytes by default) plus the question definitions. fastpath_triage sends the first 4,000 redacted chars of each ranked file, up to 500 files per call, read from disk by the server. That is source code excerpts leaving the machine, though they stay out of Claude's context. Browser page text may go to Jev for choose/check. Deterministic verdicts stay local. No prompt/conversation data is sent unless Claude puts it in `state`. Playwright itself does normal web browsing. There is no other telemetry. For client projects, note that source excerpts go to a third-party (TypeSafe today, OpenRouter after a patch).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, advisory. Retries: 2 with 100/200ms backoff on timeout, 429 and 5xx. A 4xx fails immediately (client.ts:62-110). Default timeout is 5000ms per attempt, so worst case is about 15s plus backoff unless the caller sets deadlineMs. On failure or a missing key, the tool returns status 'error' (PROVIDER_ERROR) or 'escalate' (JUDGMENT_PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE) with recommendedAction 'fallback_large_model' (capability_router.ts:103-129). Claude just proceeds on its own. Nothing blocks the session and there are no hooks to hang. Deterministic rules keep working offline. A dead Jev costs Claude a wasted tool call and up to about 15s.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools, all always loaded (no MCP server instructions, no hooks, no skill). Estimated 2,000-2,800 tokens for names, descriptions and zod schemas. fastpath_evaluate has a large schema (discriminated union of questions, policy object, presets) at about 900 tokens, fastpath_browser about 600, triage about 400, evidence and capabilities about 100 each. Each call's result is compact JSON, but the evaluate result carries full answers and traces. Claude Code may defer these via ToolSearch, lowering the idle cost. Compared with the existing gitnexus (17 tools) and playwright (26 tools), this is small, but fastpath_browser duplicates the playwright MCP already installed.
pros: It is the only candidate here that is a real Jev consumer with a working, tested wrapper: presets, normalization of choice/score/noul into one confidence scale (questions.ts:42-76) and a margin/confidence gate (escalation_gate.ts). This is a sensible pattern for using System One.
Deterministic rules run before any API call (deterministic_engine.ts). `git push --force`, rm -rf, DROP TABLE and failing test logs cost nothing and never leave the machine.
Fail-open, honest degradation: missing key or outage yields escalate/error with 'fallback_large_model' and never a fabricated answer (capability_router.ts:103-129). No hook can hang the session.
Small tool surface (5 tools, about 2-3k tokens), no postinstall and no telemetry found. Secret redaction runs before egress. Triage roots are confined by symlink-resolving checks.
MIT licensed, small readable codebase (about 4.4k lines TS) with CI on Node 20/22/24, CodeQL and dependency-review. Easy to fork and patch for OpenRouter.
The JudgmentProvider interface (docs/providers.md) is a clean seam for adding an OpenRouter provider.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and there is no env override (client.ts:31, server.ts:43). It needs a TypeSafe key, or a fork to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. The wire-schema equivalence is unverified.
Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool, with no hook or skill. Claude must decide to call it, which the user explicitly does not want to depend on.

Value proposition is thin for a senior dev on Opus. The typical Claude Code workflow already reads test output directly and has permission and secret-guard hooks. Ship-gate and risk regexes duplicate what Claude sees, and a Jev call adds a network hop and trust in a beta model (Theo's 'flash router' claim is unverified).

fastpath_triage sends 4,000-char source excerpts per file, up to 500 files per call, to a third party. That is a real code-egress path that is a problem for client projects (redaction is regex-only), and it contradicts the 'keeps files out of context' framing (README acknowledges this).
fastpath_browser duplicates the already-installed playwright MCP and adds a second Chromium.
Immature and single-maintainer: 9 days old, 3 stars, 24 commits, 2 npm versions, no releases. `npx -y` is unpinned, and cli/index.ts:15-21 loads the cwd .env into the server process.

Worst-case failure latency is about 15s (5s timeout x 3 attempts) unless deadlineMs is passed, wasted whenever Jev is down. Score dimension is 0-based and preset outputs are opinionated, so custom needs mean writing question schemas anyway.
entries.verdict: A decent, honest, fail-open Jev wrapper, but it is TypeSafe-only (needs a fork for OpenRouter) and depends entirely on Claude choosing to call it, so it does not meet the 'automatic, no prompting' goal. It is a reasonable code reference or fork base for an OpenRouter-backed hook or MCP, but I would not install it as-is for daily client work because of triage code egress, unpinned npx and overlap with existing tools.

entries.name: RudyJunyu/Jev-MCP (Jev MCP Hub)
entries.what: Small Go (1.26.4, official modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.8.0) MCP server that wraps TypeSafe's System One API (POST {base}/systemone). Exposes four MCP tools (jev_noul, jev_choice, jev_score, jev_evaluate). Runs either as a stateless Streamable-HTTP gateway (per-request Bearer token forwarded upstream) or as a stdio server (token from TYPESAFE_API_KEY). Includes an installer that writes the "jev" entry (with the token in an Authorization header) into ~/.claude.json and ~/.codex/config.toml, plus Docker/compose, Prometheus /metrics and JSON logs.
interface: CLI init / install --client codex|claude|all / healthcheck / version
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The server ships no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet; the only steering is the generic 'instructions' string and short tool descriptions. Claude (Opus) will rarely reach for a probability oracle unprompted, so the user's 'never say use jev' requirement is not met by this repo alone; it would need an external CLAUDE.md rule or skill/hook to make invocation reliable.
security: API key handling in HTTP mode: the installer writes 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' in plaintext into ~/.claude.json (install.go Merge, mcpServers.jev.headers), file mode 0600 enforced, timestamped backup files also contain it; key is not in argv. Claude Code header values in ~/.claude.json are not encrypted.
Stdio mode: key comes from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (main.go:119), not argv - good, but Claude Code's .mcp.json/~/.claude.json env block still stores it in plaintext (or use ${VAR} expansion).

Good hygiene in upstream client: Authorization header only, redirects disabled so key never follows a redirect (client.go:198-202), upstream error bodies never echoed, https enforced except loopback, 4 MiB response cap, 1 MiB request cap, bounded retry (429/529, max 3 attempts, <=30 s delay), Origin header rejected on /mcp, token validated to printable ASCII.

No shell execution in Go code; installer uses only file I/O with lock file and atomic write. scripts/install.sh just builds with go and execs the binary; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry (GOTELEMETRY=off in Dockerfile). Logs contain tool name, success, duration only - no tokens or content (observability.go, server.go:346).

HTTP-mode default bind is 0.0.0.0:8080 (main.go:102, JEV_ADDR); compose binds to loopback, but a bare `serve` exposes an unauthenticated-relay /mcp (any bearer string is accepted and forwarded upstream) plus /metrics to the LAN. Use stdio for local single-user use.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is a JSON of numeric probabilities/choice labels (option labels are chosen by the caller), so returned text is low-risk. Bigger risk is the model itself deciding what state (code, secrets) to send; the repo's secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* tools unless its matcher is extended.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the `state` and `instructions`/`criteria` arguments of a tool call (arbitrary text/JSON: could be code, diffs, file contents, logs) goes to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai if repointed) together with the API key. Nothing is sent automatically by the server; only on tool calls. In HTTP mode there is an additional hop: Claude Code -> your hub -> upstream, so a remotely hosted hub would also see the content and key. No telemetry, no content logging.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level: every failure (bad/missing token, 401/403/422, 5xx, timeout, network error) is returned as an MCP tool result with isError=true and a short sanitized message, so the agent just continues without Jev. Not a hook, so it can never block a tool call. But the default total timeout is 45 s including retries (main.go:105) with retries on 429/529 sleeping up to 30 s, so a degraded upstream can stall a single tool call for tens of seconds; --timeout should be lowered (e.g. 5-8 s). If the stdio process cannot start (no Go build, missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY exits with error, main.go:121) the MCP server just shows as failed to connect.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools; est. ~1.0-1.5k tokens of tool names + descriptions + JSON schemas (jev_evaluate has a oneOf with three variants and is the largest, ~1.5-2k chars; each single tool ~0.8-1k chars incl. criteria schema; descriptions ~200 chars each) plus a ~300-char server instructions string (~75 tokens). No hooks, no injected text per turn. Cheap (with Claude Code tool search deferral, near zero until used).
pros: Cleanest available primitive mapping: exactly exposes the three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) plus a batch tool, with strict client-side validation (choice 1-255 options, score 2-10 levels, noul true/false) that mirrors the documented System One schema (client.go:127-180).

Stdio transport exists and reads the key from env, and base URL is overridable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so pointing to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 is a config change plus a model-ID workaround, not a rewrite (main.go:104,119).

Solid security hygiene for a young repo: no redirects with key, sanitized errors, size caps, https enforcement, no content or token logging, no shell exec, SHA-pinned CI actions, 0600 config writes with backups.
Fail-open behavior: errors surface as isError tool results, never block Claude Code; tiny context footprint (~4 tools, ~1-1.5k tokens, no hook injection).
Compact, readable code (about 1.6k non-vendored lines) that is easy to fork and patch (DefaultModel, add OpenRouter base, add a hook wrapper).
cons: Not automatic: nothing forces or even strongly encourages Claude to call it; pure model-discretion tools with a generic instruction blurb. Fails the user's primary requirement without extra hook/skill/CLAUDE.md glue.

OpenRouter not supported by design: hardcoded DefaultModel "jev-latest" (client.go:103) is not an OpenRouter model ID; README/installer are TypeSafe-key-only ('TYPESAFE_API_KEY'); OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone response-shape compatibility with the 'answers' check is unverified; no OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) at all.

Installer path is poor for this user: writes the API key in plaintext into ~/.claude.json and uses HTTP transport requiring a running gateway (Docker, 0.0.0.0:8080 default bind); the stdio route requires a manual Go build (Go 1.26.4, not in the user's stated toolchain of Node/Python) and manual config, since no release binaries exist.

Very immature and low-trust: created 2026-09-17, 6 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no license, no releases, module path github.com/jev/mcphub suggests a mimic namespace; Docker images routed through a third-party Chinese mirror. Unlicensed code cannot legitimately be forked/redistributed for client work.

Usefulness for coding is inherently limited: Jev returns only probabilities, so the agent has to author a well-formed state + criteria for each call (extra Opus tokens and 2-6 s latency), and with 32k context and beta-quality quality/skeptic claims it is a poor substitute for Opus judgment on real code decisions; risk that the model dumps code/secrets into `state` to a third party, unguarded by the existing secret-leak hook (matcher does not cover mcp__jev__*).
Default 45 s total timeout with up to 30 s retry sleeps is far too lenient for an interactive coding loop; must be lowered by flag.
entries.verdict: A tidy, reasonably secure but brand-new (5 days, 1 star, unlicensed) wrapper whose stdio mode could be pointed at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model-ID fix. It is an on-demand tool only, so it does not deliver 'automatic' use, and it would need an external CLAUDE.md, skill or hook layer for that. Treat it as a reference implementation, or write your own ~150-line MCP/hook against OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone rather than adopting it as-is.
entries.license: None (GitHub licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file). All rights reserved by default, so legally unclear for client-project use or patching/redistribution.

entries.name: aimcc-org/aimcc-jev-mcp (codex-jev-mcp)
entries.what: A Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server ("decision kernel") that turns 6 coding-agent questions into batches of Jev Choice/Noul/Score primitives, sends them to a System-One provider (TypeSafe SDK, OpenRouter /alpha/decisions, generic endpoint, or a local 0.48 GB DeBERTa ONNX model), validates the typed answers, and applies deterministic threshold policies (config/policies.json) to return an accept/reject/collect_evidence/system_two_review/ask_user envelope. It returns advice only. It runs nothing and finishes no task itself.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no proxy. Claude will call it only if a tool description matches its judgment. The Chinese one-line descriptions plus nothing telling Claude to call it after tasks make automatic use unlikely without adding your own CLAUDE.md rule or a Stop/PostToolUse hook. Hooks would still need to build the JSON evidence themselves.
security: Key is read from env vars only; it is not put in argv. With a `command`/`args`/`env` MCP entry the key stays out of the process list, though it is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ to the same user.
Redacts the API key in HTTP error text (src/providers/http.ts:92-94, 138, 164).
Fail-closed response validation and a response byte cap (1 MB) are implemented. Retries are limited to 408/409/429/5xx.
No shell execution, child_process or telemetry in src (grep clean). Only outbound calls are the provider endpoint and the Hugging Face model download for the local provider.

Supply chain is heavy: needs a local `pnpm install && build` (a pnpm workspace allowBuilds for onnxruntime-node and protobufjs runs native build scripts) and pulls @huggingface/transformers, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (real, published 2026-09-15) and the MCP SDK. Not published to npm, so it is git-clone only. Repo is 8 days old with 2 commits by one author, and the git author email is a personal QQ address. The pnpm allowBuilds rule means build scripts run at install time.
Playground binds to 127.0.0.1 by default (PLAYGROUND_HOST overridable) and has no auth. It is only started manually.
entries.dataEgress: On every call the whole `state` goes to OpenRouter (then to TypeSafe): claims, evidence text (diffs, test/build logs, file contents, up to about 96k chars per call after reduction), task descriptions, capability descriptions and rule text. Because Claude must fill these arguments, nothing is sent unless the model chooses to call a tool, but each call can include client code and diffs. Headers include HTTP-Referer https://github.com/aimcc-org/codex-jev-mcp and X-Title, so OpenRouter sees an attribution to the repo author. With provider=local (auto without keys) nothing leaves the machine except a one-time Hugging Face download of about 0.48 GB. This is a concern for client projects with confidentiality obligations.
entries.failureMode: Provider timeout or error is caught per tool and returned as a normal (non-isError) text envelope with status provider_error and action `escalate` (src/mcp/server.ts:28-51, 72-74). It never throws to Claude and never blocks a tool the way a hook could, so it is effectively fail-open advisory. Default timeout is 60 s (JEV_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS, max 300 s) with up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx inside one shared deadline (http.ts:15-33, 119-158). A hung Jev can therefore stall a turn for up to 60 s unless the timeout is lowered, and the smoke test does not cover this. In the local fallback the first call waits for a 0.48 GB download. Missing required env (e.g. provider=openrouter with no key) makes startup fail with an exit code, so the MCP shows as failed to connect.
entries.contextCost: 6 tools, no server `instructions`, no hook text. Estimated at about 12k chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas, roughly 3k tokens permanently in context (completion_gate and verify are the largest, with enum lists, nested evidence objects and min/max constraints). Descriptions are in Chinese, which is cheap to read but gives Claude no English cue about when to call. Every actual call also costs Opus output tokens to serialize claims and evidence (can be thousands of tokens for diffs), plus about 1-3k tokens of returned JSON with signals and meta.
pros: Only candidate-type project with a real OpenRouter Decisions API provider: POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/ model prefix (openrouter.ai/api default), so OPENROUTER_API_KEY works with no code patching.
Sound design: Jev is a sensor, deterministic policy decides; strict zod schemas, fail-closed response validation of probabilities and winners, and bounded responses.
Deadline plus limited retries plus key redaction are implemented, and errors return as data instead of crashing the session.
Env-only secrets. No shell exec, no telemetry, no install scripts of its own, MIT.

completion_gate is the one tool with a plausible daily-coding use: a 'is this really done' sanity check that treats failed or not_run checks deterministically and does not let the model grade test results.
Local OpenJev fallback lets you avoid sending client code to any cloud, if you accept a weaker English-only 512-token model.
cons: Not automatic. It is a model-discretion MCP tool only, with no hooks or skill, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told. The Chinese-only tool descriptions make spontaneous calls unlikely.

Marginal value for an Opus 5.5 main model: tools like assess_task, rank_candidates and verify just re-ask a small classifier what Opus already judges better, at the cost of Opus writing large structured inputs.
Sends diffs, logs and file contents to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, which is a data-egress risk on client projects, and the beta Jev model is scored by unvalidated bootstrap thresholds (ARCHITECTURE.md).
Very immature: 8 days old, 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no CI, no release, not on npm; OpenRouter request/response schema not confirmed by a live test in the repo.
Default 60 s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn if Jev is slow. It must be lowered by env.
Silent provider drift: auto mode prefers TYPESAFE_API_KEY over OPENROUTER_API_KEY and falls back to a 0.48 GB local model download when no key is set, so pin JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.
Costs about 3k tokens of context permanently for 6 tools, most of which are irrelevant to routine coding (screen_content, select_capability).
entries.verdict: A well-structured but brand-new proof of concept that supports OpenRouter properly, yet it only exposes model-discretion tools and nothing that makes Claude Code use Jev on its own. It is worth reading as a reference for wiring Jev primitives (especially completion_gate), but not as the primary always-on integration for this user.

entries.name: echohello-dev/jev-mcp
entries.what: Tiny hand-rolled stdio MCP server (about 500 lines of TypeScript, no deps, no MCP SDK) that wraps the Jev Decisions API in five tools: jev_verify, jev_classify, jev_screen, jev_decide and jev_extract. Each tool builds a {state, questions} body, POSTs it to the provider, and returns the probabilities as JSON text. The optional fail_on argument turns a matching result into isError:true. It is a manual, model-discretion tool: nothing in the repo makes Claude Code call it on its own.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, no skill, no server `instructions`, no CLAUDE.md snippet, and no proxy. Opus will call jev_* only if it judges a tool description relevant, and the descriptions ('Decide whether the evidence supports the claim...') are generic. In practice Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for a probabilistic classifier when it can just reason, so it would be used only occasionally. Deterministic auto-use would require adding your own hooks, a CLAUDE.md rule, or a skill on top of this server.
security: The API key is passed through the MCP `env` block, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. It does end up in plaintext in ~/.claude.json or settings.
No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry. The only network call is the provider fetch (provider.ts:34), and there are no runtime dependencies to attack.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The server returns only numbers and labels, but a classify/decide choice string comes from the caller's own input. Provider error text (first 200 chars) is echoed back in the tool result (provider.ts:45), which is a minor channel.

The build uses `bun-version: latest` and softprops/action-gh-release@v2 with unpinned tags, so the supply chain is weak. The release artifact is not signed, and there is no npm provenance because it is not on npm.
No input validation beyond the JSON schema shown to the model. Args are cast blindly (index.ts:418-426), so malformed args cause a caught TypeError and an isError result, not a crash.
Unparseable JSON lines are silently dropped with no response (index.ts:366-369).
entries.dataEgress: Everything the model puts in `state`, `claim`/`evidence`, `text` or `options` is sent verbatim to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. With this server that means whatever Claude Code chooses to pass: code snippets, diffs, file contents, fetched web content or tool outputs. The server sees nothing else. It does not read files and does not hook into Claude Code events. Key and model ID go in headers and body. OpenRouter/TypeSafe may log requests, and the user works on client projects, so client-confidentiality and zero-data-retention settings matter. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY would silently reroute traffic to TypeSafe direct.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft per call. Any HTTP error, timeout or parse error is caught and returned as a tool result with isError:true and {error: message}. Claude Code sees an error and can continue. The default timeout is 30 s, up to 120 s per call via timeout_ms (tools.ts:75). That is generous compared with the claimed 70-500 ms latency, so a hung provider could stall a turn for 30 s. There is no retry, no circuit breaker and no cache. A missing key gives a JSON-RPC -32603 error on each call, not a startup failure (the server starts fine and only logs to stderr). Caveat: isError is used both for real failures and for a matched fail_on, so the model cannot tell an outage from a verdict without parsing the message.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. tools.ts:59-168 defines them in about 4,000 chars of source, so the schemas the client receives come to roughly 1,000-1,300 tokens (chars/4) including the mcp__jev__ name prefixes. There is no MCP `instructions` field (index.ts:375 returns no instructions), and no hook-injected text. That is small and cheap. But the descriptions are terse and do not tell Claude WHEN to use the tools, which matters for auto-use.
pros: Works with OpenRouter today: it uses the right endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), model ~typesafe/jev-latest and Bearer auth, and the request and response shapes match the OpenRouter API reference.
Very small (about 500 lines) and easy to audit or fork. No dependencies, no telemetry, no shell execution, and the key travels via env, not argv.
Cheap on context: 5 tools, about 1k tokens, no injected instructions.
The jev_screen idea (relevance plus risk of fetched content) and fail_on gating are a sensible fit for guarding web or MCP content. It is a useful pattern to copy into a hook.
MIT license. It is a good reference implementation of the wire contract, and forking to add a hook wrapper is easy.
cons: Cannot trigger automatically, which was the user's core requirement. It ships only MCP tools, with no hook, skill or usage instructions, so Claude would use it only if it decides to.
Not installable the easy way: it is not on npm (E404) and needs bun to build. The docs/brief.md claim of `npx -y @echohello/jevmcp` is false today.
Very immature: 9 days old, 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, and no tests. The last commit was refactored with an AI agent. CI runs only on tag push, so nothing runs before a release.

Concrete bugs: jev_screen sends 4 risk levels (safe/low/medium/high, handlers.ts:243), so the score runs 0..3. But the tool description and schema say '0..2' and cap min_risk at maximum 2 (tools.ts:104,119). A 'high' verdict can never be gated by schema-valid input. jev_extract only tests for field presence (the brief promised verbatim extraction). It reads noul confidence, which the API does not return (always undefined).
The state input is typed as a plain string only. The API also accepts an object or array, so structured app state has to be stringified by the caller.

The TypeSafe-direct URL (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) is unverified. If the user later sets TYPESAFE_API_KEY, traffic silently switches provider. The OpenRouter URL and model are hard-coded, so there is no env override, and floating on ~typesafe/jev-latest can change behavior without notice.
Default 30 s timeout with no retry. isError conflates outages with fail_on verdicts. Key in plaintext in the MCP config.
Generic Jev caveats also apply: alpha endpoint, no reasoning trace, and Jev is a classifier and not a coding aid. Of the five tools, only screen/verify have any plausible daily coding value.
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal and correct-enough OpenRouter wrapper, but it is only five passive tools, so Claude Code will almost never use it without being told, which fails the 'automatic' requirement. Treat it as reference code for the wire contract, or fork it and pair it with hooks and a CLAUDE.md rule. It is not worth adopting as-is, given no npm package, no tests and a few bugs.

entries.name: synthet/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small (about 600 lines) Python stdio MCP server that wraps the official typesafe-sdk (pinned to a 0.7.x-era >=0.1,<1 range, lock has 0.7.1) and exposes four tools: jev_choice, jev_score, jev_noul, and jev_system_one (multi-question). It validates the input, builds SDK Choice/Score/Noul objects, calls POST {base_url}/v1/systemone, and returns a normalized {ok, result|error} envelope. It also ships a Claude Code skill (.claude/skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md) with a description-based trigger, plus a workstation installer script. The rest of the repo is unrelated agent-scaffolding boilerplate seeded from the author's synthet-code-framework (dozens of skills, commands, agents, memory and wiki tooling).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description trigger. There are no hooks, so it is not deterministic. Claude decides to call jev_* only if it judges the task to be a typed classification/ranking/verification and the skill or tool descriptions match. In normal coding (edit files, run tests, debug) there is almost no natural trigger, so it would rarely fire without the user asking. The skill's trigger list (reranking, verifying evidence, routing text) is aimed at LLM-app builders, not IDE-style coding. To make it fire automatically for coding you would have to write your own CLAUDE.md or hook policy, which this repo does not provide.
security: API key is read from env vars only (client.py:26-39) and never placed in argv; the SDK sends it as a Bearer header over HTTPS. Good.

dotenv_util.py:64-70 loads JEV_ENV_FILE / DOTENV_PATH / <project>/.env without overriding the process env. It does not log values. The project_root path computation looks off (parents[1] of src/jev_mcp/cli.py resolves to src/), which is a minor bug.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no file reads or writes in the server code. Network egress is only via typesafe-sdk to base_url.

Third-party dependency surface: mcp>=2,<3 and typesafe-sdk (0.7.1 per uv.lock). The SDK adds X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers and a User-Agent. I saw no telemetry beyond that, and I did not read all the SDK code.

Prompt-injection surface: state and instructions are model-authored, so injected file content could be forwarded to Jev. The output is only typed probabilities and labels, so there is no free-text channel back, which is low risk. The tool result echoes error details, but the messages are static.
Installer script edits ~/.claude.json and user-level configs of several tools and copies files into sibling repos (hardcoded Windows paths). Do not run it; wire the entry by hand.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes in the tool arguments leaves the machine: the `state` (string, object or string array), the question `instructions`, the criteria text, and the model name, sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if repointed) with the API key in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent automatically from hooks or the filesystem, and there is no whole-transcript egress. Data is limited to what the model chooses to include, so code snippets, diffs or file contents could be sent if Claude puts them in `state` (32k context limit). The response size cap is 512 kB. On a client project this is a third-party data-processor disclosure via TypeSafe and OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking at the harness level. Any SDK error, including timeout, 5xx and auth failure, is caught (client.py:224-237) and returned as {ok:false, error:{code:'typesafe_error', retryable:true, next_steps}}. A missing key gives {code:'missing_credential'}. The model just sees an error result and continues. The worst case is a stalled turn: the MCP-level timeout defaults to 30 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_SECONDS, client.py:13, 47-66) and the SDK has its own retry policy (RETRY_AFTER headers, so roughly 30 s or more per hung call, not verified). No circuit breaker or caching. A new SDK client is opened per call (client.py:218). A missing key is also detected lazily at first call, not at startup, so the server connects fine and every call fails. That means a silently useless tool until OPENROUTER/JEV key is configured.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. Tool defs (names, docstrings, schemas from type hints) are about 500-800 tokens total by my chars/4 estimate: the docstrings are one line each, but jev_system_one uses `questions: dict[str, Any]` and `state: Any` with no per-field descriptions, so schemas are compact but the model gets little guidance. No MCP server `instructions` field is set (MCPServer('jev-mcp') only). The skill adds about 90 tokens of always-loaded description plus a body of about 500 tokens loaded on trigger. The repo also ships 40+ unrelated skills, commands and agents under .claude/, .cursor/ and .agents/. These load only if the user opens Claude Code inside this repo, or via the installer. Do NOT copy those; take only .claude/skills/jev-mcp. No hooks, so nothing is injected into prompts.
pros: Genuinely Jev-specific and minimal: 4 tools map 1:1 to the Choice, Score and Noul primitives plus a batched multi-question call, all built on the official typesafe-sdk (client.py:201).
Small, readable server of about 600 lines with no shell exec, no file access, no telemetry of its own; easy to audit and to fork in an afternoon.
Key handling is safe: env only, never in argv, .env loader does not override the process env or log values (dotenv_util.py, client.py:26-39).

OpenRouter is reachable without code changes in principle: the SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone (sdk constants.py, transport.py:134), which matches the OpenRouter System One route; only JEV_TOKEN and JEV_MODEL need swapping.
Structured error envelope with retryable and next_steps; a 512 kB response cap; input validation before any network call (client.py:69-165).
Model pinned by default (jev-1.13.0), which is good for calibration-sensitive use; overridable per call.
Mocked unit tests (14 test functions) plus CI (ruff, pytest, CodeQL, dependency-review) in .github/workflows.
cons: Very immature: created 2026-09-22 (8 days old at audit), 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no LICENSE, and no description or topics. Bus-factor of one; the README says it was 'seeded from synthet-code-framework'.

No OpenRouter support in the repo: no base_url parameter, and the default model name (jev-1.13.0) is the TypeSafe name rather than OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13. The OpenRouter path via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is my inference from SDK code and is unverified against OpenRouter's actual response schema. It targets the System One API only, not the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions).

Not automatic: only model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill description. There are no hooks and no pre-tool or post-tool integration, so Claude will rarely call Jev during ordinary coding, which is the user's core requirement. Nothing here decides 'when it adds value' for code work.

The skill's example use cases (reranking, evidence verification, routing) target building LLM apps, not editing code. The skill also carries approval_required: true and 'remote_write' metadata, which nudges Claude to ask before use; in bypass or auto mode this is unenforced, so behaviour is inconsistent.

Adds a round-trip through Opus (tool call plus result) for each judgment; Jev's claimed 70-500 ms is dwarfed by model turn time. A 30 s default timeout can stall a turn; no caching or circuit breaker; client is rebuilt per call.

Repo is bloated with unrelated scaffolding (40+ skills, commands, agents, .agent-memory, wiki lint scripts). Installing it 'as a plugin' or opening Claude in it would import that noise. Not a plugin: no plugin.json or marketplace.json. Only the server and one SKILL.md are useful.

Installer script hardcodes D:\Projects Windows paths and the author's sibling repo names (scripts/install_jev_mcp_workstation.py:16-45), and edits ~/.claude.json; unusable as-is on Linux and better avoided.

Data-egress risk on client projects: the model chooses what goes into `state`, so code or confidential content can reach TypeSafe and OpenRouter with no filter and no hook-level secret guard (the user's own PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tool args because its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
Missing-key failure is lazy: the server starts and connects, and every call fails with missing_credential, so it appears healthy in /mcp while doing nothing.
Dependency on mcp>=2,<3, a very new major API (from mcp.server import MCPServer), which may break on ecosystem drift.
entries.verdict: A clean, tiny, safe-looking MCP wrapper around the official SDK and the best raw material found for exposing Jev tools to Claude Code, but it is a day-old single-commit POC with no license and no OpenRouter awareness, and as a model-discretion tool it will not give the user automatic Jev use during coding. Use it (or a small fork with an explicit base_url/OpenRouter key and a rewritten skill or hook policy) only as the tool layer, not as the automatic integration.

entries.name: nandansrikrishna/jev-agent-tool
entries.what: Small community (non-official) Python package (PyPI jev-agent-tool 0.1.0b1) giving a CLI (jev), a Python API and a local stdio MCP server (jev mcp) on top of the official typesafe-sdk. The MCP exposes 3 tools that let the agent author Choice/Score/Noul questions at runtime and send a state to Jev's System One endpoint; CLI adds JSONL batch evaluation with resume. Total code ~350 lines.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, skill, plugin or proxy. Claude will use it only if the tool descriptions and context convince it; the descriptions are generic ('Evaluate context against typed questions') with no coding-specific triggers, so with Opus 5.5 as main model it will rarely or never call it unprompted. Getting 'automatic' behaviour would require adding a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill with a trigger description, or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook that calls the CLI, none of which ship here. AGENTS.md in the repo is for developing the repo itself and is not loaded in user projects.
security: API key: read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or ~/.config/jev/api-key (0600, atomic write via mkstemp+replace, credentials.py:12-24). Key never passes through MCP args or argv unless the user uses `claude mcp add -e`, which stores it in ~/.claude.json in plaintext. jev auth uses getpass or stdin, so no argv exposure.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no eval in the ~350 lines; no telemetry in this repo (README states none; SDK grep found no analytics, only X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers).
Errors deliberately strip upstream bodies and inputs (core.py:47-50).

Prompt-injection surface: tool returns only typed numeric/enum answers (no free text), so injected content cannot flow back as instructions; however Claude authors the questions and state, and Jev output could sway Claude decisions if trusted blindly.

Supply chain: brand-new single-maintainer, 0 stars, 1 commit; dependency mcp>=1.30,<2 and typesafe-sdk 0.7.x (official, github typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-python). Pin exact version and review before install. Not an official TypeSafe product (README says so). No curl|sh, no npm postinstall; pure-Python setuptools build.
evaluate_batch uses a ThreadPoolExecutor, up to 50 records inline, so bounded but could burn quota if the model loops.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the LLM puts in `state` and `questions` (and record states in evaluate_batch) is sent as JSON over HTTPS to the base URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL overridden) with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically: only content Claude chooses to copy into the tool call (could be code snippets, diffs, tool outputs, prompts, so client code could leave the machine if Claude passes it; the existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__ tools unless matcher extended). No local file scanning by the server; no telemetry beyond SDK version/runtime headers. Via OpenRouter, OpenRouter's data policy also applies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's view: errors raise ValueError with sanitised message and Claude continues without Jev. Client timeout 60s (core.py:33) plus SDK 2 retries with backoff on 429/5xx (retry.py:52), so a slow/down Jev can stall a single tool call up to ~3 minutes worst case, longer than the claimed 70-500 ms; MCP client tool timeout applies. Missing key raises 'Set TYPESAFE_API_KEY or run jev auth' at call time, not at startup, so server still starts. evaluate_batch does not catch client-construction errors. No circuit breaker.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools (question_schema, evaluate, evaluate_batch). Tool names+descriptions+JSON schemas approx 2.0-2.8k chars ~ 500-700 tokens (server.py docstrings: evaluate ~430 chars, evaluate_batch ~190, question_schema ~80, plus schema for state:str|dict|list, questions:dict, records:list[dict], model). FastMCP created without `instructions` (server.py:4), so no server instructions. No hooks, so no injected text. Very light. Note question_schema output when called is a large pydantic JSON schema (maybe 1-2k tokens) that Claude must call before authoring questions unless it guesses format.
pros: Thinnest viable path to OpenRouter: the official SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone (config.py:61, constants.py:5), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api maps onto OpenRouter's System One URL with zero code changes.
Tiny, readable (~350 LOC), MIT, no subprocess/eval/telemetry; key kept in env or 0600 file; error sanitising avoids leaking bodies.
Only 3 tools and about 600 tokens of context, no server instructions, no hooks, so it won't slow or pollute the existing GitNexus/secret-guard hook stack.
Uses the official typesafe-sdk (typed responses, retries, timeouts), so it tracks the real wire schema rather than reimplementing it.
Dynamic question authoring (Choice/Score/Noul) supports arbitrary coding classifications like 'is this diff risky' or 'which file is relevant'.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with generic descriptions; no hook/skill/CLAUDE.md trigger shipped, so it fails the user's core 'never prompt for jev' requirement without extra glue.

Default model hardcoded as 'jev-latest' in server.py/core.py; OpenRouter needs 'typesafe/jev-1.13' or '~typesafe/jev-latest', and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL does not help because the tool passes model explicitly. Needs a one-line fork or Claude passing model every call.
OpenRouter is undocumented and untested here: no reference to openrouter anywhere in the repo; schema parity of /api/v1/systemone with api.typesafe.ai is assumed.
Extremely immature: created 2026-09-19, 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases besides PyPI 0.1.0b1, README calls it a community beta with interfaces likely to change.

Each use costs an extra Opus turn to hand-write question JSON (and possibly call question_schema first), likely exceeding Jev's 70-500 ms benefit; Jev is a decision primitive, not something that speeds up code edits.
Worst-case stall: 60 s timeout x 3 attempts per call, no circuit breaker; batch tool doesn't wrap client-init errors.
Data egress is at Claude's discretion: code/diffs it pastes into `state` go to a third party, and the existing secret guard hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover this MCP tool.
Fits no clear daily coding loop (edit/test/debug); useful mostly for classification of records/tickets, not developing software.
entries.verdict: A clean, small, safe-looking wrapper that can plausibly be pointed at OpenRouter with just TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model-id patch, but it is a brand-new one-commit beta whose plain MCP tools Claude will almost never call unprompted, so it does not deliver the requested automatic integration by itself. Useful at most as a low-cost transport layer under a custom hook or skill.

entries.name: tacticocc/Jevbridge (@tactico/jevbridge)
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node 22+ TypeScript project (run via --experimental-strip-types, about 4.1k lines) that provides (a) a stdio MCP server with 4 tools (jev_decide, jev_gate, jev_computer_use, jev_recipe), 3 resources and 2 prompts, and (b) an ACP (Agent Client Protocol) sidecar/proxy for Zed/JetBrains-style hosts that can wrap claude-agent-acp or codex-acp and gate their tool calls with Jev. It POSTs {model,state,questions} to a System One endpoint and post-processes the typed answers with a local confidence gate (execute/confirm/escalate/abort). If no TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set it silently falls back to another LLM (whichever provider key is in env) posing as System One, or to a keyword heuristic. Mostly a generic wrapper and demo, not a Claude Code-native integration.
interface: MCP resources jevbridge://recipes and jevbridge://recipe/{id}; prompts jev_decide, jev_computer_use
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by server 'instructions' and tool descriptions ('Use this instead of asking the generating model to classify, route...'). NOT deterministic: no Claude Code hooks (no PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit), no plugin manifest and no proxy for the CLI. The strongest automation (ACP proxy interception of tool calls) only works in ACP clients like Zed/JetBrains, since Claude Code CLI is not an ACP host. The user's requirement of 'Claude Code must use it when needed without prompting' is only weakly met, and there is no clear coding use case for Claude to reach for it (the tools target support routing and GUI clicks).
security: No API key in argv, since keys come from env vars. In the README's Claude Desktop config the key sits in the MCP 'env' block. In claude mcp add, use -e or a settings.json env block.
No shell execution in the MCP path and no postinstall or curl|sh scripts. package.json has only prepublishOnly (tests). No telemetry found.

Proxy mode spawns 'npx -y @agentclientprotocol/claude-agent-acp' (src/acp/upstream.ts), which fetches and runs unpinned third-party code at runtime. It also honors JEVBRIDGE_ACP_COMMAND/ARGS. Not used in the MCP path.

envLlm() (src/env.ts:12-21) picks up ANY of JEVBRIDGE_API_KEY, XAI_API_KEY, OPENAI_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or OPENCODE_API_KEY from the environment. With 'auto' and no Jev key, state is silently sent to that provider. Default provider is xai, so an OPENAI_API_KEY in env could be sent to api.x.ai as a Bearer token (key/provider mismatch leak).

'auto' silently degrades to a keyword heuristic that the README itself says is not a safety signal (question text overlaps state). A misconfigured key therefore yields fake 'execute' decisions rather than an error.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever the model passes as 'state' goes to Jev, and the output is only numbers. A gate 'execute' is advisory, and Claude can ignore or game it. The ACP proxy can genuinely deny tool calls, but only inside ACP hosts.
entries.dataEgress: MCP path: only what Claude chooses to put in the 'state' and 'questions' arguments of jev_decide/jev_computer_use/jev_recipe leaves the machine, sent to the endpoint from TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (default api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if overridden), plus the key as a Bearer header. jev_gate sends nothing. Nothing is sent automatically, but because Claude authors the state it can include code snippets, diffs, commands or paths. If no Jev key is set, the same payload goes to whichever LLM provider key exists in the environment (xAI, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenCode or a custom base URL). ACP proxy mode would send the user prompt, cwd, tool name and full tool input for every tool call (src/acp/intercept.ts toolCallState), meaning shell commands and file edit contents. That is irrelevant to the Claude Code CLI but a large egress on client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design at the tool level: the MCP tool never blocks Claude Code, because errors come back as isError text results (callMcpTool catch) and Claude proceeds. There are no timeouts, retries or AbortSignal anywhere in src (grep found none), so a hung Jev/OpenRouter connection makes the tool call wait until undici's default timeouts (minutes), stalling the turn. Because MCP tools are model-discretion, a slow Jev only hurts when Claude calls it. Misconfiguration (no key) falls back silently to heuristic or another provider rather than failing loudly, which is a fail-wrong mode. In ACP proxy mode a Jev failure behavior is more complex, but that mode does not apply to Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools (jev_decide, jev_gate, jev_computer_use, jev_recipe): tools array is about 4.3k chars of names, descriptions and schemas, roughly 1.1k tokens. Server 'instructions' string about 480 chars, roughly 120 tokens, and it aggressively says 'Call jev_decide before routing or acting on a closed set. Call jev_gate before executing a tool, shell command, or GUI click', which nudges Claude to add extra calls before shell commands. Total about 1.2-1.3k tokens per session (deferred/ToolSearch reduces it further). Resources and prompts add no context unless used. No hook-injected text. The SKILL.md description is about 60 tokens if the skill were installed separately.
pros: MIT-licensed, readable, zero-dependency 4.1k-line codebase that I could fully audit statically. There are no postinstall scripts, no shell exec in the MCP path and no telemetry.

Env overrides TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEVBRIDGE_JEV_MODEL (src/env.ts:7-8) plus a Bearer-auth POST of {model,state,questions} make OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone usable with zero code changes, if the schema matches.

Genuinely Jev-specific building blocks worth borrowing: the choice/noul/score question builders, coerceAnswers normalization, and gate.ts thresholds (execute >=0.72, confirm >=0.46, abort <0.18, independent destructive noul >=0.62) map well to a 'should this Bash command run' gate.
The MCP server is protocol-clean (negotiates 2025-11-25 down to 2024-11-05), tools carry readOnlyHint annotations, and there are tests and CI with typecheck.
Small footprint, about 1.2k tokens of context; jev_gate is a local no-network pure function.
The intercept design (src/acp/intercept.ts: choice next + noul is_destructive + score risk over tool_name/tool_input) is a reasonable reference for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls Jev.
cons: Not automatic in Claude Code: only model-discretion MCP tools. The ACP proxy that could deterministically gate tool calls needs an ACP host (Zed/JetBrains), and Claude Code CLI 2.1.x is not one. There is no hooks.json or plugin.json to hook PreToolUse.
Not published: npm 404 for @tactico/jevbridge, no GitHub releases. Install is a manual clone with an absolute path to run unreviewed-upstream code, and later pulls change it.
Very young and thin: 9 commits over 3 days (2026-09-18 to 09-21) by effectively 1-2 people, no tags, 5 issues and 4 PRs total. 46 stars come from Jev hype rather than track record.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; it only works via the undocumented TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env trick, and the OpenRouter response schema equivalence is unverified. The Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is unsupported. The variable name TYPESAFE_API_KEY holding an OpenRouter key is confusing.

Silent fallbacks are dangerous: with no or wrong key, 'auto' uses the keyword heuristic (self-declared 'not a safety signal') or ships state to any of XAI/OPENAI/ANTHROPIC/OPENCODE keys found in env (default provider xai even with an OpenAI key) — a leak risk on client projects.

Coding value is thin: recipes target support routing, GUI clicks and destructive gating, which duplicate Claude Code's own permission system and the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook. Instructions push Claude to call jev_gate before every shell command, adding latency and tokens for little benefit under bypass/auto permission mode where the gate cannot actually block anything.
The gate is advisory and computed on Claude-authored state, so it is not a real security boundary. There are no timeouts on fetch, so a slow OpenRouter call can hang a turn.
Adds 4 tools, 3 resources and 2 prompts, including computer-use tools irrelevant to coding, and the tool surface is mostly noise beyond jev_decide/jev_gate.
entries.verdict: Only usable as a manual MCP server that the model may or may not call, and it is not yet on npm. It works with OpenRouter only through an undocumented env override (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and JEVBRIDGE_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). It has silent multi-provider fallbacks, no timeouts and computer-use-oriented tools. It is better mined for its gate thresholds and question shapes to build a small, deterministic PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter System One directly than adopted as-is.

entries.name: jev-layer (typakon4)
entries.what: Node.js stdio MCP server plus CLI (npm jev-layer 0.2.0) that lets an agent harness ask Jev to pick ONE option from a closed candidate set the host supplies (jev_route), plus advisory extras (supervision, model-route, shadow-compaction, browser step), with JSONL replay receipts. It never executes anything; on any error it returns a fallback status. Adapters exist for Hermes, OMP and Codex only. There is no Claude Code adapter, hook, or plugin; the string "claude" does not appear anywhere in the repo. The generic MCP snippet would work with Claude Code as a plain MCP server.
interface: jev install / init / add / doctor / mcp / cli (CLI)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no Claude Code hook, no skill, no plugin and no transparent proxy. The only trigger prose is the tool description plus a Codex-specific SKILL.md and AGENTS.md, which cannot be used as-is in Claude Code. The user's goal of never having to prompt 'use jev' is NOT met. You would have to add a Claude Code skill or CLAUDE.md rule, and even then the invocation depends on Claude's judgment. A UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook could be added by the user, but the hook would need its own code to build the candidate list, since the tool cannot discover Claude Code's capabilities by itself. There is a src/discovery.mjs that has explicit capability discovery for skills, MCP, CLI and so on, which I did not verify against Claude Code's layout.
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts and no runtime dependencies (package.json), so npm supply-chain surface is small; no curl|sh installer.

API key is read from environment only (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and sent in an Authorization header, so it never appears in argv; the generated MCP snippets carry only JEV_LAYER_PROVIDER. Caveat: with Claude Code the key must be exported in the shell or in the .mcp.json env, and the second option would put it in a plain file.
No shell execution in the core. child_process is used only in the OMP adapter (integrations/omp/extension.js) to spawn node. No telemetry found by grep.
Egress goes only to the configured endpoint. The endpoint is overridable via OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_ENDPOINT, so a poisoned env could redirect the key and payload.

Prompt-injection surface: the request intent, context and capability descriptions go to the model. The model output is an ID chosen from the closed set, and the host validates it against eligible[] (route.mjs:81-97). Data flowing back is bounded, but a wrong pick is possible. SECURITY.md itself says it is not a security boundary and that it does not detect injection.

Writes plaintext JSONL receipts at ./.jev/replay/cases.jsonl in the cwd. They can contain intent, context and host results (result is bounded to 8000 bytes, receipts.mjs:5). In client repos this means sensitive data on disk and a risk of committing it, so it needs .gitignore. src/context-filter.mjs has a sanitizeContext redactor, but I did not audit its coverage.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, per call: model id, and state = {intent string, context object projected/capped to about 6,000 bytes by projectState (route.mjs:16, maxContextBytes 6_000), actor/permissions}, plus questions.tool.criteria = {id: {name, kind, description, risk}} for each eligible candidate. Nothing is sent unless the calling agent (Claude) chooses to call jev_route and passes intent/context, so what is sent depends entirely on what Claude puts in the arguments. There is no automatic capture of files, diffs or tool outputs; the tool takes only what the model supplies. The Codex SKILL says "never send secrets or full transcripts", which is prompt guidance only. If supervision, shadow_compaction or browser_step are used, host-supplied observations and context (which can include page text and file content) are sent too. The demo provider sends nothing. Locally it appends to .jev/replay/cases.jsonl.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Any provider error, timeout, HTTP non-2xx or malformed answer returns a status 'fallback' envelope with fallback.type (route.mjs:70-79), and confidence below policy.min_confidence also gives fallback. No retries. Timeouts: 5s OpenRouter, 2s TypeSafe via AbortSignal.timeout. A missing key returns fallback without an HTTP call. JEV_LAYER_ENABLED=0 disables it. Caveat: the fail-open only means the MCP tool returns a fallback JSON; whether Claude then proceeds normally depends on Claude reading it. MCP-level failures (server crash) surface as a failed tool call. The server has no per-tool-call timeout beyond the fetch timeout. Note that a server startup failure only produces an MCP connection warning, not a blocked session.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Tool definitions are about 4.1k chars, roughly 1,000 tokens of names, descriptions and schemas (src/mcp-server.mjs lines 15-123). The server declares no 'instructions' field. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. The schemas are loose (capabilities: array of object), so Claude gets little guidance on how to build valid inputs. If you rely on CLAUDE.md or a skill to trigger it, add a few hundred more tokens.
pros: Native OpenRouter support that matches the Decisions API contract: endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and optional HTTP-Referer / X-Title headers (typesafe.mjs:59-125). No patching needed for the user's chosen provider.
Fail-open by design with tests: every error path returns a fallback envelope, there are no retries, and the timeout is 5s. A dedicated fail-open-smoke script runs in CI.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry and no shell exec in the core. The key comes from env, not argv. MIT license.

Host-side policy is deterministic (risk levels, permissions, min_confidence, and the selected ID must be in the eligible set), so a Jev answer cannot escalate privileges; it can only pick among options the host offered.
Standard stdio MCP with JSON-RPC 2024-11-05, so it loads in Claude Code via a plain .mcp.json entry. The context cost is small at 6 tools (about 1k tokens).
Receipts and replay (.jev/replay/cases.jsonl) allow offline evaluation of whether Jev's routing choices were any good, which is useful for testing the Theo 'flash router' skepticism.
cons: No Claude Code integration at all. Adapters exist for Hermes, OMP and Codex only, and 'claude' appears nowhere in the repo. There is no hook, skill or plugin.json for Claude Code (the only plugin.json is for Codex).

Invocation depends on Claude's discretion, so it cannot satisfy 'use Jev automatically without me prompting'. The Codex SKILL.md even restricts it to closed-set capability routing and forbids open-ended planning, coding, research or recovery.

The use case is routing among capabilities the host already knows. Claude Code already picks tools and skills natively with a strong model, so routing through a second model adds a hop and two extra model turns to build and read the candidate list, with no gain in coding quality. The sweet spot (Noul/Score/Choice calibrated probabilities on daily-coding decisions such as 'should I run tests now', 'is this a risky edit') is not addressed.

Only the Choice primitive is used by the router. The Decisions API's Noul and Score primitives, which are Jev's more interesting outputs, are not exposed as a generic tool. The tools are opinionated wrappers, not raw Jev access.

Very immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-19, 15 commits, 2 authors, 4 stars, 1 fork, 2 releases, and the MCP serverInfo still says version 0.1.0 while the package is 0.2.0. Several features are marked experimental or shadow-only (browser step, model route, shadow compaction). The tests are offline-only, with no live OpenRouter validation.

Plaintext receipts with intent/context are written to the cwd (.jev/replay/cases.jsonl). On client projects this creates sensitive artifacts inside repos, and the user's global secret-leak guard does not cover this file.
Unused surface: the model-routing, compaction, browser and supervision tools duplicate things Claude Code already does, and add attack/confusion surface and tool-name noise for little value here.
Uses the alpha OpenRouter endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) which may change, and the 5s default timeout can stall a tool call in the worst case.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, fail-open Node MCP wrapper that already speaks OpenRouter's Jev Decisions API, but it is a router for Codex, Hermes and OMP and has no Claude Code hook or skill, so it only fires when Claude chooses to call it. It fails the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement and adds little for daily coding. At best it is a reference for the request/response shape (a provider class you could crib) or an opt-in experiment behind a custom hook, not something to install as the main Jev integration.

entries.name: codaaiteam/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (about 250 lines) Node stdio MCP server that wraps one Jev call (POST {model, state, questions} with a Bearer key) as 5 tools: jev_classify, jev_score, jev_check, jev_gate and jev_decide. It only acts when Claude decides to call a tool. It has no hooks, skill or plugin manifest, so nothing runs automatically. The README says it is by an independent third party (jevtypesafeai.com, CODEFASHION TECH LTD), not TypeSafe AI, and it promotes that party's paid hosted gateway.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skill triggers or proxy. Claude would call the tools only if it judges them useful from their descriptions, and in practice it rarely picks a niche classifier tool unprompted. That fails the user's 'automatic' requirement unless it is paired with a hook or a CLAUDE.md instruction.
security: Key is read from env and sent only as a Bearer header, which is fine. The README's `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=key` example stores the plaintext key in ~/.claude.json; the key itself is not in the server's argv.

The unpinned `npx -y github:` install is a supply-chain risk. A 2-star repo by a single author could change at any time, and npm may run install scripts on git dependencies. There is no postinstall script today, but the code is not pinned.

Any jv_live_ key auto-routes to jevtypesafeai.com, which says it is not affiliated with TypeSafe AI and whose logging and retention policy is undocumented in the pages I saw. A hosted key would send all state to that reseller.
No shell execution, no file reads and no telemetry in the code. Only fetch to BASE_URL.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are raw JSON of typed numbers and enums, so it is small. jev_gate is advisory only, and a model following injected instructions could skip it or misreport the action.
stderr logs the endpoint and whether the key is set, not the key.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the state, action, context or instructions arguments of each tool call is sent to BASE_URL. That is typically shell commands, code snippets or diffs the model chooses to include. There is no automatic capture of prompts or files. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, jevtypesafeai.com for jv_live_ keys, or the OpenRouter URL if you set JEV_BASE_URL. That could include client code, so client confidentiality and OpenRouter/TypeSafe data policies need checking.
entries.failureMode: Fails open. Errors return isError tool results (timeout, unreachable, or HTTP error with the body). There is a fixed 20s AbortController timeout and no retry. A missing key throws an error on the first call, but the server still starts. Because it is not a hook, a Jev failure never blocks Claude Code, and there is also no enforcement.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. Descriptions are about 1.3k chars and schemas (including the z.describe strings) about 2k chars, so roughly 800-1000 tokens of tool definitions per session (schemas are deferred if ToolSearch is active). The server sets no MCP `instructions` and no hook injects text.
pros: Tiny, readable, dependency-light single file (src/index.js, about 250 lines) that is easy to audit and fork completely.
Covers all three Jev primitives (choice, score, noul) plus jev_decide for arbitrary multi-question calls, matching the brief's API shape.
Generic JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL overrides mean OpenRouter is reachable without code changes if the OpenRouter systemone schema matches (src/index.js:29-30).
Fail-open, 20s timeout, no telemetry, and MIT licensed. Tool outputs are small typed JSON, so little context is used.
The jev_gate concept (risk-score a shell command) is a useful pattern to lift into a PreToolUse hook.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion tools only, with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, so the user would still need to prompt or rely on Claude choosing it.

The default endpoint is api.typesafe.ai and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read. OpenRouter requires manual JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest, and the OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and schema compatibility with /api/v1/systemone is unverified.
Promotes a third-party reseller (jevtypesafeai.com, CODEFASHION TECH LTD, explicitly not affiliated with TypeSafe AI). jv_live_ keys route state there, and its retention and logging are undocumented.
Very immature: 3 commits over 3 days, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, not on npm, no version pinning. Installing via unpinned `npx github:` is risky for client work.
jev_gate is advisory and depends on Claude calling it, so it is no real guardrail compared with a PreToolUse hook. It would also duplicate the existing secret-leak guard hook.
No key-file support: the README's -e KEY=value approach stores the plaintext key in ~/.claude.json.
Sends whatever code, commands or diffs Claude puts in state to an external API, which is an egress concern for client projects.
entries.verdict: A small, readable, MIT-licensed wrapper that is useful mainly as a reference implementation. It is a manual model-discretion tool with no hooks and no OpenRouter support out of the box, so it does not give the user automatic integration. Fork or copy the ~250 lines, pin it, and point it at OpenRouter yourself rather than adopting it as-is. If used at all, pair it with a hook and avoid jv_live_ keys.

entries.name: rajasekharponakala/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (server.py, 193 lines) FastMCP stdio server that exposes TypeSafe's Jev System One endpoint as 5 MCP tools (generic batch evaluate, noul, choice, score, list models). It is a thin httpx wrapper: it POSTs {state, model, questions} to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or OpenCode Zen) with a Bearer key, and returns the answers. It contains no hooks, no skill and no auto-invocation logic. Claude only calls it if it decides to.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or nudges Claude to use it: there is no hook, no server `instructions`, and no SKILL.md. The tool descriptions are terse ("Yes/no judgment...") and do not say when to use them. Without a CLAUDE.md rule or a companion hook or skill, Claude will rarely call it, which conflicts with the user's goal of use without prompting.
security: API key: read from the env var, or from a .env file next to server.py by _load_dotenv (server.py:30-53; it fills only unset vars). The README's `claude mcp add ... -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...` puts the key in the shell history and in ~/.claude.json in plaintext, and with `-e` the value also shows in the `claude mcp add` argv. The server itself takes the key from env, not argv, so it does not appear in the server's process list.

Key forwarded only as an Authorization Bearer header to hard-coded HTTPS hosts (api.typesafe.ai, opencode.ai). No key logging is present in the code. Error messages echo up to 500 chars of the response body (server.py:82,86), and that text goes into Claude's context.

No shell execution, no eval, no file access other than the .env read. No telemetry. The only dependencies are fastmcp and httpx. uv.lock is pinned (392 KB), but fastmcp>=4 is unbounded. The dependency tree is large and not audited.
No curl|sh installer and no postinstall. The `endpoint` parameter chooses only between two fixed URLs, so it is not an arbitrary-URL SSRF.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the outputs are numeric or enum values from a typed model, and only error strings carry free text. The bigger risk is the reverse: Claude can pass any file content or secret into `state`, and nothing filters it. Your secret-leak PreToolUse hook matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does NOT cover mcp__jev__* calls, so secrets Claude read earlier could be sent out through `state`.
Single-author repo created 9 days ago with 2 commits and 2 stars. It is a supply-chain trust risk if you run it via uv from a moving git checkout, so pin a commit.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the `state` and `instructions` arguments goes to api.typesafe.ai, or to opencode.ai for zen. It is not restricted: code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs or secrets could all be sent, because the model chooses the content. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background, and the server never reads project files itself. Requests go directly to TypeSafe, not through OpenRouter, unless patched.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice, because it is an optional tool: HTTP errors become RuntimeError, so the MCP tool call returns an isError result and Claude carries on. There are no retries, and the timeout is a long 60 s for POST (server.py:75) and 30 s for the models GET. A hung Jev call can therefore stall a turn for up to a minute. A missing key raises a ValueError at call time, while the server still starts fine. If the process cannot start (uv or fastmcp problems), Claude Code shows the server as failed and loses only these tools, as with your caveman-shrink failure.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. The generic jev_evaluate schema is loose (state: str|dict|list, questions: dict). The estimated total is about 1.0-1.5k tokens for tool names, descriptions and the FastMCP-generated JSON schemas (about 4-5k chars). The server sets no `instructions` string (FastMCP("jev") with no instructions arg), and no hooks inject text. The cost is fixed unless the tools are deferred through ToolSearch, which is Claude Code's default for MCP tools when many are configured.
pros: Small enough to audit completely: 193 lines, one file, no shell, no telemetry, no postinstall. It can be reviewed in five minutes.
Full coverage of the three Jev primitives, plus a batch tool with parallel questions and a models-listing tool, all in the documented request shape {state, model, questions}.
The key comes from env (with the .env fallback never overriding real env), and it goes only to hard-coded HTTPS hosts.
The design is easy to patch for OpenRouter: an existing Zen branch shows exactly where a third endpoint goes (server.py:56-66), and the /v1/systemone suffix is shared across gateways.
Also usable as a model-callable building block if you write your own hook or skill on top (the tools give the typed answers to a routing decision).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and OPENCODE_API_KEY (server.py:56-66). It requires a patch or fork, which turns you into maintainer of an AGPL fork of a 2-commit, 2-star repo.

No automatic invocation: no hook, no skill, no server instructions. It only ever runs when Claude chooses to call it, and nothing in the tool descriptions tells Claude when Jev is useful. This does not meet the requirement 'Claude must use it without me prompting'.
The 60 s no-retry timeout (server.py:75) could block a turn if Jev or the gateway is slow, and there is no circuit breaker.
Zero tests, no CI, no releases; 9 days old, one author; fastmcp>=4 is an unbounded dependency.
Nothing constrains what goes into `state`, and your secret-leak guard hook matcher does not cover MCP tools, so a secret could be exfiltrated in a Jev call.

Even when called, the value for coding is thin: Jev returns probabilities for classification or routing questions, not code, and Claude Opus's own judgment is already available for those at no extra tool round trip. Every call costs a tool turn.
