AGPL-3.0 license is unusual for a tool you would use on client projects (fine to run, but avoid embedding).
The README `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` pattern stores the key in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
entries.verdict: A clean, auditable but tiny and brand-new proof-of-concept wrapper. It has no OpenRouter path (needs a roughly 5-line patch whose schema compatibility I could not verify) and, more importantly, no automatic-use mechanism, so alone it does not satisfy the user's goal. It is only useful as a reference or base for a fork paired with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md routing rule.

entries.name: Songokou1983/jev-mcp
entries.what: Python FastMCP server (stdio or Bearer-authed streamable HTTP) wrapping TypeSafe's direct System One API (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) as 6 MCP tools: classify (Choice), check (Noul), rate (Score), batch_judge, system_one_raw, health. Adds server-side confidence gating (act/confirm/escalate), 32k-char state cap, $0.10 per-process budget, in-memory LRU cache, tenacity retry on 429/529, and a JSONL decision log. It is a personal project whose default deployment is a home server reached over Tailscale.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tool descriptions are the sole trigger; there are no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin manifest, and no CLAUDE.md snippet for the user's projects (the repo's own CLAUDE.md is for developing the project). The NEGATIVE text in each description actively discourages use unless the case is fuzzy, so Claude will call it rarely and unpredictably. Not deterministic and not transparent. This does not meet the user's requirement of use without prompting, other than by chance.
security: API key handling is sound: TYPESAFE_API_KEY comes from env or ~/.jev/.env (server.py:599-615), never argv. Under `claude mcp add`, the key would sit in ~/.claude.json env unless you use ~/.jev/.env. A hand-rolled .env parser strips quotes only.

HTTP mode enforces Bearer auth with hmac.compare_digest (bearer.py:165-174) and refuses to start without a token (server.py:579-584). But the token travels over plain http:// on Tailscale, and if you use the README's --header form the token appears in ~/.claude.json and the claude process argv.
stdio mode has no auth, which is fine because it is a local child process.
transport_security allowlist hard-codes the author's Tailscale IP 100.86.140.31 (server.py:500-505) and issuer_url 127.0.0.1:8765, so HTTP mode on another host needs code edits. stdio is unaffected.
httpx trust_env=False (jev_client.py:93,114) deliberately ignores HTTP(S)_PROXY and NO_PROXY, so it breaks in proxied or corporate networks and bypasses any egress policy.
No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, and no telemetry in the code. Its only outbound host is api.typesafe.ai.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the tool's text/state or in system_one_raw's state and questions goes over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter). That means arbitrary code snippets, commands, diffs or file contents that Claude chooses to pass. Nothing is sent automatically from hooks, since there are none. Capped at 32000 chars per call (state_cap.py). health() sends only a GET with the key. With the HTTP deployment, the same payload first crosses Tailscale (plain http) to the home server. No third-party telemetry. Client-side text is not filtered for secrets, and the user's secret-leak guard hook covers only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* calls.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level and not fail-open at the workflow level. The client has a 30 s timeout per attempt (jev_client.py:53) with up to 3 retries on 429/529 (base 0.5 s, max 4 s), so a bad case can stall a call for about 2 minutes. Other errors (401, 422, 5xx except 529, connect errors) raise JevAPIError or httpx errors, which surface as an MCP tool error to Claude. Claude can carry on without Jev, so it is effectively soft. Nothing blocks Claude Code itself. batch_judge is sequential (about 20 x 300 ms), and a mid-batch failure loses all results. Once the $0.10 session budget is hit, tools raise BudgetExceeded. No circuit breaker. trust_env=False ignores proxies, so a network that requires one fails.
entries.contextCost: 6 tools. Descriptions total about 5,600 chars (about 1,400 tokens: classify 903, check 844, rate 736, batch_judge 1391, system_one_raw 1028, health 695), plus JSON schemas for parameters (options, descriptions, criteria, state, questions), roughly 400-700 more tokens. That is about 2,000 tokens in total, always loaded unless Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch (which the environment shows it does for MCP tools). The FastMCP instructions field is not set (no instructions kwarg at server.py:508-525). No hook-injected text. The tool descriptions are written in English as [POSITIVE]/[NEGATIVE]/[EXAMPLE]/[CONTRACT] blocks. They are wordy and tell the model when not to use the tool.
pros: Cleanest primitive mapping of the three Jev primitives: classify=Choice, check=Noul, rate=Score, with typed results and per-option probabilities (server.py:119-160).
Hard cost and abuse limits: 32k-char state cap, $0.10 per-process budget, LRU cache, so a runaway loop cannot burn much money (budget.py, cache.py, state_cap.py).

stdio mode works locally with no Tailscale, no bearer token and no server to run. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no shell execution, and the only egress is api.typesafe.ai. Python 3.13 and uv are already on the machine.
Sensible engineering for a PoC: retry/backoff on 429/529, health probe that costs nothing, decision log stores hashes rather than content by default, 142 tests including regression tests.
Useful pattern to steal: the action gate (act/confirm/escalate) and effective_confidence=|noul-0.5|*2 to convert Noul into a confidence. It works as a reference for writing your own thin wrapper.
Descriptions include explicit NEGATIVE guidance (do not use for regex, arithmetic, deterministic checks), which avoids paying for trivial calls.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: base URL https://api.typesafe.ai is hard-coded and never overridable (jev_client.py:51, server.py:546), key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (server.py:599-615), and the model is pinned to the TypeSafe ID jev-1.13.0. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider, so a fork is needed to switch.

Not automatic. It is a pure model-discretion MCP tool set with no hooks or skill. The NEGATIVE text deters use, and Claude Code will rarely reach for a probability tool while coding. Directly conflicts with the no-prompting requirement.

Designed for support-ticket/agent-routing use (examples: refunds, billing, customer anger) rather than coding work. Nothing in it targets code review, diff triage, test selection or command safety, so the user would have to author all the coding-specific criteria in every call, and Claude must serialise code into the text argument each time.

Every use costs a full extra Opus tool round trip (Claude decides, formats, calls, reads), which is usually slower than Jev's 70-500 ms and often slower than Claude just deciding itself. Net latency gain is negative.

Egress is uncontrolled: whatever Claude puts in text (code, diffs, secrets) goes to a third party. The existing secret-guard hook does not match mcp__jev__* tools, and there is no redaction in the server.
Sequential batch_judge, echoing items back, 30 s timeout x 4 attempts, and a per-process $0.10 cap that raises BudgetExceeded mid-session. There is no circuit breaker.

HTTP deployment code is tied to the author's home Tailscale IP (server.py:500-505) and is plain http; trust_env=False breaks proxied networks. Author's own machine paths (/home/son_goku) in the README.
Very young and single-author: 5 commits all on 2026-09-22, 2 stars, no CI, no LICENSE file, unsigned commits, docs largely in Chinese. Unverified against the current OpenRouter alpha API.
entries.verdict: A tidy, well-tested weekend PoC that maps Jev's three primitives to MCP tools, but it is TypeSafe-direct only, takes no OpenRouter key, and relies on the model choosing to call it, so it fails both the OpenRouter and the automatic-use requirements as shipped. At best, use it as a reference or fork base (about 30 lines to retarget) and pair it with hooks or a skill, since it has neither.
entries.license: No LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo is null. pyproject.toml declares MIT in metadata only, so the legal position is ambiguous.

entries.name: Ashfaqbs/jev-mcp-spring
entries.what: Java/Spring Boot MCP server over HTTP exposing jev_classify, jev_score, jev_check, jev_gate (patch merge-risk), jev_health via jev-spring-boot-starter.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Clean typed tool set incl. jev_gate for diff/completion-claim review, Apache-2.0, CI
Errors returned as isError with safe messages
cons: Needs a running JVM 17 service and a Spring starter; heavy for a local CLI user; TypeSafe key only, tests hit api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
OpenRouter only if starter baseURL is overridden (unverified); single test file

entries.name: CodeIA-Academy/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (313 lines), stdlib-only Python stdio MCP server exposing two tools: ask_jev (POST {BASE_URL}/v1/systemone with state + typed choice/score/noul questions) and list_jev_models (GET /v1/models). Hand-rolled JSON-RPC (protocol 2025-06-18). run.sh sources a local .env and execs python3 server.py. Defaults to TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai) but base URL, model, key and timeout are env-driven.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The instructions string and tool description nudge Claude to use ask_jev for classify/route/check judgments, but there is no hook, no skill trigger, no transparent proxy. For coding tasks Opus has no natural reason to delegate to a classifier, so it will rarely call it without being told; achieving 'automatic' would need CLAUDE.md rules or a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook written by the user, none provided here.
security: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.py:47); run.sh sources ./.env with set -a (a file with shell syntax is executed, low risk since user-owned) so key is NOT in argv/process list; README's alternative 'claude mcp add ... -- python3 server.py' or JSON env block puts the key in ~/.claude.json plaintext
Spoofs a macOS Chrome User-Agent (server.py:32-35) to get past what is presumably Cloudflare/WAF on api.typesafe.ai; harmless but a smell, and OpenRouter may not care
No telemetry, no shell execution, no subprocess, no eval, no postinstall, no curl|sh, zero dependencies; ~300 lines easily auditable

Prompt-injection surface: whatever the agent puts in `state` (file contents/diffs) is sent to a third party; Jev output is structured numbers/enum choices so return-side injection surface is small, but summarize() echoes API error bodies and choice strings into agent context (server.py:164-168)
Client-side validation mutates the caller's question dicts (server.py:98) but no security impact
stderr log prints base URL and model, not key (server.py:294); key absent only warns
entries.dataEgress: Only the `state` and `questions` the agent passes to ask_jev, sent over HTTPS to BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default; openrouter.ai if repointed). That is whatever Claude chooses to include: arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, commit messages, tool outputs, plus the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically (no hooks, no ambient capture); egress only happens when the model calls the tool. Secret-leak guard hook does not cover mcp__ tool inputs unless matcher extended. If routed via OpenRouter, OpenRouter (and its upstream provider) also sees the payload; client work code would leave to two third parties.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open and non-blocking to the workflow: every HTTP/network error is caught (server.py:64-82) and returned as an MCP tool result with isError=true and a Spanish hint, so Claude sees an error and carries on. But synchronous single-threaded stdio loop with default 90 s timeout (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT) means a hung Jev call blocks the server (and the model's tool call) up to 90 s; no retries, no backoff (despite hints advising it), no circuit breaker. Missing key -> server starts, warns on stderr, every call returns 401/403 error. Set TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT to ~5-10 if used.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. ask_jev description ~780 chars + inputSchema ~1,400 chars (nested descriptions in Spanish) + list_jev_models ~140 chars + server instructions ~250 chars = ~2.6k chars, roughly 650-750 tokens always resident (less if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via tool search). No hooks, so zero per-turn injected text. Each ask_jev result is verbose: text summary plus the full raw JSON pretty-printed (server.py:174) plus structuredContent, so probably 400-1,000 tokens per call, duplicated output.
pros: Tiny, auditable, stdlib-only, no install step (no npx/pip), no telemetry, no shell exec: easy to vet and vendor at a pinned commit
Clean, minimal 2-tool surface (~700 tokens resident); server instructions plus 'send all questions in one call' guidance are sensible for Jev's parallel typed-question model
Base URL, model, timeout are env-configurable, so OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/api + typesafe/jev-1.13) is a config-only switch if body schema matches; hooking it up is 3 env vars
Errors are always caught and returned as tool errors; server never crashes the session on API failure
run.sh keeps the key out of argv and out of ~/.claude.json, and .env is gitignored
Client-side validation of choice/score/noul question shapes catches 422s before spending a request
structuredContent returned alongside text, so a future hook/agent could consume typed probabilities
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool; nothing makes Claude Code invoke it, and Opus 5.5 has little reason to for ordinary coding; user's explicit requirement (no prompting) is not met

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; body schema for OpenRouter System One is unverified; list_jev_models would hit GET /v1/models on OpenRouter (global model list, wrong semantics); env vars named TYPESAFE_* for an OpenRouter key
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 5 commits in one afternoon, 2 authors, 1 star, no releases, no CI, no unit tests (only live-API shell scripts), weakly Spanish-only docs and tool descriptions
Default 90 s blocking timeout, no retry/backoff, no connection reuse; a slow Jev stalls the tool call
Verbose duplicate result payload (summary plus full JSON plus structuredContent) burns context per call
Sends arbitrary code/diffs from client projects to third parties; no redaction, no allowlist, and the existing secret-leak guard matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover this MCP tool
Spoofed Chrome User-Agent to bypass edge filtering is fragile and a mild integrity concern

README limits claim 64k tokens per request vs 32k context in brief: undocumented drift; Jev's typed decisions (classify/route/score) have few real daily-coding use cases and no reasoning trace, so low value even if invoked
entries.verdict: A clean, safe-to-read 300-line reference wrapper that gives Claude an ask_jev tool, but it is only a manually-invoked model-discretion tool, TypeSafe-direct by default with OpenRouter reachable via env-var repointing (schema unverified). It does not satisfy the 'automatic, never prompt' requirement on its own; at best it is a base to fork (pin a commit, add OpenRouter defaults, wrap with hooks/CLAUDE.md rules).

entries.name: cbruyndoncx/AskJev-MCP
entries.what: Small (about 250 LOC) stdio MCP server wrapping the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. Exposes a batched `ask` tool (one state plus N choice/noul/score questions, one call to POST /v1/systemone) and `list_models`. The model must decide to call it; nothing is automatic.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code invokes it when the model judges it useful, based on the tool description, which is written for classification and rating of business state (tickets, frustration, routing). Nothing pushes Claude toward coding-loop uses, and no CLAUDE.md snippet, hook or skill trigger is shipped. This is the weakest form of the user's "automatic" requirement; it would need a CLAUDE.md rule or hook added on top.
security: API key comes only from the env var and is never logged. The README's `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...` puts the key in shell history and argv of the add command, but the running server gets it through env, not argv.
The server does no shell execution, no file access and no telemetry of its own. The SDK sends a User-Agent header of typesafe-sdk/VERSION and redacts authorization and x-api-key headers in its logs.
Prompt-injection surface is low. Tool output is JSON probabilities, and Jev returns no free text. The `state` and `instructions` fields are model-supplied and go straight to the API.

The MCP tool exposes no safety controls: no size cap on `state` (a large state means large token cost), no redaction, and the secret-leak guard hook cannot see MCP payloads because its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit.
Supply chain: brand-new single-author repo with 1 star, no license file, and an unpinned ^ range on a pre-1.0 SDK and the MCP SDK v2. Low bus factor.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in `state` and `instructions`/`options` of an `ask` call goes to api.typesafe.ai (or the overridden base URL, for example OpenRouter), plus the API key. Claude chooses the content, so it can include code, diffs, file contents or tool output, up to 32k context. Nothing else leaves the machine, since the server reads no files itself. For client projects this is a risk, because OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see the content, and the secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. API errors return an isError tool result (src/index.ts:45-55) that Claude can ignore. The SDK retries 408/429/5xx and connection errors twice with 0.5-5s backoff and honors Retry-After up to 60s. The per-attempt timeout is 10s with no total budget (README), so worst case is roughly 30s+ of blocking a tool call. A missing key makes the server exit at startup (shows as a failed MCP connection). Because it is model-discretion, a slow Jev only stalls turns where Claude chose to call it.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. Estimated size: `ask` description (about 1.2k chars) plus a zod-derived JSON schema (state, a discriminated union of 3 question types, options and levels, all with descriptions, about 2.5k chars), `list_models` (about 0.3k chars), and server instructions (about 0.55k chars). That is roughly 4.5k chars, or about 1.1k tokens, always loaded (or deferred behind ToolSearch in recent Claude Code). No hooks and no injected text.
pros: Thin, readable MCP server (src/index.ts is 122 lines and schemas.ts 126), so it is easy to audit and fork. It uses the official TypeSafe SDK for retries, errors and wire format instead of a hand-rolled client.
The batched `ask` design (one state, many typed questions) matches Jev's per-input-token billing and gives choice, noul and score in one call, with rubric-style option descriptions.
The base URL is overridable through the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api probably reaches OpenRouter's /v1/systemone with no code changes, though this is unverified.
Fail-open behavior: errors come back as isError results, with sane SDK retry defaults and no shell or file access.
Small context footprint (about 1.1k tokens, 2 tools) compared with big MCP servers.
Handles both MCP protocol eras (2026-07-28 and the older initialize handshake) via serveStdio.
cons: Not automatic. It is a plain tool the model may or may not call. There are no hooks, no skill and no CLAUDE.md guidance for coding use, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told.
The tool description is framed around support tickets, customer frustration and app state routing, not coding decisions, so Opus is unlikely to reach for it during normal coding.

Not OpenRouter-native. It requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY (the variable name is misleading when it holds an OpenRouter key), a manual base-URL override and TYPESAFE_MODEL. The OpenRouter schema and model ID are untested, and list_models will hit OpenRouter's whole-catalog /v1/models.

No tests, no CI, no releases, no npm package, no LICENSE file (MIT is declared only in package.json), and a single author at 1 star. The repo is 12 days old and the SDK is pre-1.0 with a ^ range, so breakage on upgrade is likely. Users must clone and build it.

Data egress is model-controlled: Claude can put code, diffs or file contents into `state`, with no redaction or size cap. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover MCP calls, which matters for client projects.
The 10s per-attempt timeout with 2 retries and no total budget can stall a turn for 30s+ when Jev is degraded.
The README's install example passes the key on the command line, and the scripts are hardwired to the author's private vault paths.
entries.verdict: A clean but tiny, unproven personal MCP wrapper for the TypeSafe direct API. It is a reasonable template to fork (rewrite it to be OpenRouter-native, add a coding-oriented description and a CLAUDE.md or hook nudge), but as shipped it is not automatic, not coding-focused and not OpenRouter-ready, so it does not satisfy the user's goal.
entries.license: Declared MIT in package.json, but no LICENSE file in the repo and GitHub reports no license

entries.name: miaopj0325-collab/jev_mcp (jev-mcp)
entries.what: Minimal single-file (307 lines) Node CommonJS stdio MCP server exposing 4 tools (jev_noul, jev_choice, jev_score, jev_batch_decisions). Each tool wraps caller-supplied context plus an instruction into a POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and returns the JSON result. It is a passive tool that Claude must decide to call; it has no hooks, no skill and no proxy.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The descriptions are generic ("Ideal for verification, assertions, bug detection"), and there is no server instructions field, hook, or skill. Opus 5.5 has no reason to prefer a remote classifier over deciding inline, so it will rarely or never call these unprompted. Achieving the user's "automatic, never say use jev" goal would need extra glue: a CLAUDE.md rule, a PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook, or a skill. This repo provides none of that.
security: API key is read from env, never logged, and sent only as Bearer to openrouter.ai over HTTPS (src/index.js:18,36). The README example puts the key in the MCP config `env`, so it sits in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. It is not in argv.

The `npx -y github:...` install runs unpinned, unaudited third-party code with the key in its environment. Any later push to the repo, or a compromise of the account, executes on the next start. Pin a commit, or vendor and clone the code.

package.json has no postinstall or install scripts and there is no shell execution. The only network call is the one fetch (src/index.js:33). There is no telemetry beyond the HTTP-Referer and X-Title headers, which OpenRouter uses for attribution and which advertise this repo.

npm name collision: package.json names the package jev-decision-mcp, but that npm name is registered by a different author (amidabuddha/jev-decision-mcp). The two codebases are unrelated. Confusion or typosquat risk if someone runs `npx jev-decision-mcp`.

No input validation on args (e.g. destructuring undefined args would throw, though it is caught). There is no timeout or AbortController on fetch, and the full upstream error body is returned verbatim to the model (src/index.js:44-47).

Prompt-injection surface is low: responses are numeric or typed JSON from Jev (probabilities plus echoed option keys). But the option keys are chosen by Claude, and the verdict is only as trustworthy as the caller's framing.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `context` (log, code snippet, diff, file contents, tool output) plus the instruction and criteria, sent as JSON to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and then to TypeSafe as the model provider). Nothing is sent automatically. Only Claude-composed arguments leave the machine, and only when a tool is called. There is no filtering or redaction, so it bypasses the existing secret-leak guard unless that hook also matches mcp__jev__*. Client-project code is a compliance concern under OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies. The key is sent as the Bearer header.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft per call, and only because Claude sees the error and carries on. Errors are caught and returned as isError text "[Jev MCP Error] ..." (src/index.js:286-296), so a missing key or HTTP failure does not crash the session. There is no fetch timeout or retry: a hung OpenRouter request blocks that tool call until Claude Code's own MCP tool timeout. A missing key does not fail at startup, only on the first call. The tools/list response is served regardless. With a wrong or beta-changed schema, noul silently falls back to probability 0.5 and verdict true (src/index.js:188-189), which is a misleading default.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Tool defs are about 3.9k chars in src/index.js:65-166, i.e. about 1.0k tokens with schemas, or roughly 1.3k with the MCP wrapper names (mcp__jev__jev_noul, etc.). No server `instructions` field is set (capabilities: {tools:{}} only). No hooks, so no injected text. Cheap. With Claude Code tool search, tools are deferred anyway.
pros: Uses OpenRouter natively: the correct Decisions API URL, model typesafe/jev-1.13, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, with a JEV_MODEL override for ~typesafe/jev-latest (src/index.js:8-9,18,25). It works with the user's chosen provider with no patching.
Tiny, readable and auditable: one 307-line file, one dependency, MIT licence. It can be fully read in 5 minutes, and vendoring or pinning it is easy.
Covers all three primitives (noul/choice/score) plus a raw batch passthrough. Since every primitive maps to a single question named `decision`, the tools are easy for a model to call.
Very low context cost (4 tools, about 1k tokens) and no hooks, so it adds no per-turn overhead and cannot break the existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).
No shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry, and errors are caught and surfaced as isError instead of crashing.
cons: It cannot deliver the automatic goal. It is a pure model-discretion tool with generic descriptions and no instructions, hook or skill. Claude will not reach for it unprompted, which is the exact failure the user wants to avoid.
It is a 10-day-old, 1-star, 1-author PoC with 5 commits all pushed within 20 minutes. It has no tests (deliberately deleted in a2735bd), no CI, no lockfile and no releases.
The recommended `npx -y github:...` install runs unpinned HEAD code on every start with the API key in its env. That is a supply-chain risk for a user working on client projects.

The package.json name jev-decision-mcp collides with an unrelated npm package by another author (amidabuddha, 0.1.3). It is not published to npm from this repo, so the install path must stay GitHub-based or a local clone.

The request and response schema was not verified against the live OpenRouter Decisions docs, which could not be read via curl. The fallback `answer?.noul ?? 0.5` silently yields verdict true at p=0.5 if the shape differs, which would fail without any visible signal.
No fetch timeout or retry, and no use of v1/systemone or the TypeSafe direct API (so no fallback provider). The Opus round trip to call the tool usually costs more than the 70-500 ms Jev call saves.

Sends arbitrary code and log context off-machine with no redaction, and is auto-approved in bypass mode. This is a data-handling issue for client projects, and it sits outside the existing secret guard's matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
entries.verdict: This is a correct, small, OpenRouter-native wrapper, and it is fine as a low-risk reference or a base to fork and pin. It is not an automatic integration: it is just four passive tools that Opus will almost never call unprompted. To meet the user's goal it would need a deterministic layer on top (hooks or skill/CLAUDE.md routing) and a pinned local copy rather than `npx github:`.

entries.name: charliepgarcia/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (202 lines) Python stdio MCP server that wraps OpenRouter's Decisions API (POST /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13). It exposes 4 tools: jev_decide (raw multi-question call), and convenience wrappers jev_noul, jev_choice and jev_score. It is a thin passthrough. The model (Claude) must decide to call a tool and must write the state text, the question and the options itself. There are no hooks, no skill and no coding-specific logic. The README says it was written for Hermes Agent and shows a Windows path.
interface: jev_score(state, question, levels:str JSON array of 2-10)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing in the tool descriptions steers Claude toward coding use cases. The examples are 'Is this text sarcastic?', 'What is the sentiment?' and 'Rate the writing quality', so Claude will rarely call these unprompted during coding. There is no deterministic hook, skill trigger or proxy, so it does not meet the requirement of automatic use without prompting. It would need extra CLAUDE.md rules, or a hook or skill layered on top, to trigger reliably.
security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from env only (server.py:18) and is never placed in argv. It can be passed through the Claude Code MCP env block. The key is used only as a Bearer header to the hardcoded openrouter.ai host (HTTPS), so the endpoint cannot be redirected.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, no curl|sh installer, no postinstall. Install is only `pip install -r requirements.txt` (mcp>=1.0.0, httpx>=0.27.0, unpinned, no lockfile or hashes).

Compatibility bug: `from mcp.server import MCPServer` (server.py:8) exists only in mcp 2.x (verified in mcp-2.2.0 src/mcp/server/__init__.py). requirements.txt allows >=1.0.0, so it breaks on 1.x. Run it in a uv-managed venv with mcp>=2.

Non-200 responses return resp.text verbatim to the model (server.py:47-52), a minor path for upstream text to reach context. Jev output is numeric only, so the prompt-injection surface of responses is small. Inputs are model-chosen text, so the tool can exfiltrate any text Claude passes as `state` to OpenRouter. This matters for client code under NDA.
No license file (licenseInfo null), so the code is technically all-rights-reserved. Single anonymous-ish author, one commit, 1 star, 0 forks.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever string Claude puts in `state` (up to 32k context), plus the question and criteria text, goes to openrouter.ai and on to TypeSafe. In practice this could be code, diffs, file contents or tool output, depending on what the model chooses to pass. Nothing is sent automatically. There is no filtering, redaction or size cap, and the existing secret-leak hook only guards Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* calls. Usage and cost metadata come back. OpenRouter's data-retention and logging policy for typesafe/jev applies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft but not deliberately designed. There is a 30 s httpx timeout (server.py:12, 37), which is very long against the claimed 70-500 ms. A non-200 becomes an {error:true,status_code,detail} JSON string. A missing key raises RuntimeError inside the tool, which MCP surfaces as a tool error. Timeouts and connection errors are not caught (only JSON decode is), so httpx exceptions surface as tool errors. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. Because the tool is model-invoked and optional, an outage costs at most one failed call and never blocks the session (fail-open). The README suggests timeout: 60 in Hermes, which is not needed for Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. The tool names, docstrings and JSON schemas (all params are plain strings) total roughly 2.4k chars of docstrings plus schema overhead, about 800-1000 tokens per session (estimated as chars/4). No MCP server `instructions` string is set. There are no hooks and nothing is injected per turn. With Claude Code's deferred-tool loading, the schema cost can drop to names only. The contextCost is low, but jev_noul, jev_choice and jev_score are redundant with jev_decide.
pros: Correct OpenRouter Decisions API usage with the exact endpoint and model ID from the brief (server.py:10-11), so it is a working reference implementation of the payload and response shapes for noul, choice and score.
Tiny (202 lines), fully auditable, with no shell, file or telemetry surface. The API key is env-only and never in argv.
jev_decide allows batching several typed questions in one request, which is useful if you build a router or hook on top of it.
Low context cost (4 tools, about 1k tokens) and no hooks, so it cannot slow down or break the existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks.
Fail-open by construction: it is an optional tool, so a Jev outage cannot block coding.
cons: Not automatic. It is a passive, model-discretion tool with generic sentiment/writing-quality examples. Nothing makes Claude Code call it while coding, which is the user's core requirement.

Jev returns only probabilities, and the server offers no coding decision templates (for example 'is this bash command destructive', 'does this diff touch security-sensitive code' or 'does this need a plan'). Claude would have to author the question and criteria JSON as escaped strings on every call, which costs more tokens and time than it saves.
No use of the hook system, where Jev would actually add value: PreToolUse risk classification, permission auto-decisions, and routing or triage.

Hardcoded model typesafe/jev-1.13, so it does not use ~typesafe/jev-latest or the Jev Router. It has no configurable base URL, no TYPESAFE_API_KEY path and no /v1/systemone. The 30 s timeout is far too long for a latency-critical decision.
Only mcp>=2 works (the MCPServer import) although requirements.txt says >=1.0.0. There are no tests, no CI, no release, no license, and one commit from 2026-09-21, hence very immature.

The README is Hermes-specific (Windows path, config.yaml) with no Claude Code instructions. It has no input size cap and no redaction, and its egress bypasses the secret guard hook because the guard's matcher does not cover this MCP tool.
Unhandled httpx timeout and connect exceptions, plus raw upstream error text returned to the model.
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal, OpenRouter-native reference wrapper. It is useful as a starting template for a custom Jev hook or MCP server, but on its own it is a passive generic-classification tool that Claude will rarely call while coding. It fails the requirement of automatic use, so use it only as a base to fork, with a configurable model ID, a short timeout and coding-specific hooks.
entries.license: None (no license file; GitHub licenseInfo null)

entries.name: baize7815/jev-mcp-open-source
entries.what: Self-hosted Cloudflare Worker (D1 for encrypted key store + /admin UI) that exposes a streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint at /mcp with 9 tools. Eight are workflow wrappers (route_intent, rerank_candidates, batch_judge, select_values, verify_evidence, evaluate_options, classify_hierarchy, decide_next_step) that decompose into System One Choice/Noul/Score calls, plus a raw system_one pass-through. The Worker calls api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with model jev-latest, using TypeSafe API keys stored AES-GCM encrypted in D1 and rotated round-robin. Also ships a Codex-style skill (skills/jev-workflows/SKILL.md, in Chinese) and a call-mcp.mjs fallback client.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools. Tool descriptions are explicitly written for autonomous use ('Call proactively ... the user need not mention Jev', 'even if the user never mentions Jev') and the server instructions reinforce it, so Claude Code may call them unprompted, but it is not deterministic: no hook, no proxy. The bundled SKILL.md is a Codex-style skill (frontmatter name/license/description only, Chinese description) that could load as a Claude Code skill by copying to ~/.claude/skills, but its trigger text is Chinese and oriented to KB/RAG/ticket workflows.
security: /mcp is deliberately UNAUTHENTICATED (README.en.md and src/index.ts:72-76): anyone who learns the workers.dev URL can burn your TypeSafe/OpenRouter quota; only /admin needs ADMIN_TOKEN. workers_dev:true in wrangler.example.jsonc makes a public *.workers.dev URL by default. Mitigation requires adding Cloudflare Access/service tokens yourself, and then Claude Code's MCP config must send the header.

API keys are AES-GCM encrypted in D1 with KEY_ENCRYPTION_SECRET (src/keys.js), only last-4 hint shown; decent design. Secrets set via wrangler secret put interactively, not argv. Keys never sit on the user's machine or in Claude Code argv (client only needs the Worker URL).
Admin token is sent as Bearer from the browser page; a login form in an inline HTML page; small surface, but no rate limiting seen and no MFA.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are JSON of probabilities/IDs (no free text from Jev), so injection back-channel is small; but inputs are model-composed from repo content and forwarded off-machine. Tool descriptions themselves are benign.
Deployment requires npm ci + wrangler (deps @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0, agents 0.24.0, zod, wrangler 4.136.0); no postinstall or curl|sh seen. Not executed by me.
Worker observability enabled (logs head_sampling_rate 1) in wrangler.example.jsonc, so request metadata may be logged in your Cloudflare account.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in tool arguments (request/context strings, candidate excerpts up to 128 KB, records, claims and evidence, goals and observations) goes Claude Code -> your Cloudflare Worker -> api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe, not OpenRouter as shipped). Nothing is sent automatically by the server itself; content is model-chosen, so code snippets, file excerpts and client-project text can leave the machine to two third parties (Cloudflare, TypeSafe) beyond Anthropic. Instructions say 'never secrets' but nothing enforces it; the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover mcp__ calls (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Usage counters (token counts, status) are stored in D1. No telemetry to the author was found in the code.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the model level: tool errors return isError with message text (src/index.ts:15-18), SKILL/instructions say 'unavailable -> continue, do not retry'; Claude simply proceeds without Jev. Upstream timeout is 30 s (src/typesafe.js judge default timeoutMs=30000), which is long: a hung upstream would stall a tool call up to 30 s (call-mcp.mjs uses 60 s). No automatic retries (avoids double billing). No caching. Batch items fail individually and are marked failed. If Worker is down, Claude Code MCP connection shows failed and tools vanish; no hard block.
entries.contextCost: 9 tools; my estimate ~3-4k tokens of tool definitions (descriptions 300-600 chars each, ~4.5k chars, plus zod-derived JSON schemas in src/workflows.ts, which is the bulk: nested routes/candidates/items/questions/criteria) and a ~1k-char server 'instructions' string (src/index.ts:12, ~250 tokens) injected every session. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Tool results are compact JSON. If MCP tool search/deferral is active in Claude Code, the cost drops further.
pros: Only candidate so far whose tool descriptions and server instructions explicitly tell the model to call proactively without the user mentioning Jev (src/index.ts:12,24,29,34), which matches the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement as closely as an MCP-only approach can.
Keeps the API key off the workstation and out of argv/process list; keys are AES-GCM encrypted in D1 and the client only needs a URL.

Well-designed typed workflows: rerank_candidates and verify_evidence map onto genuine Jev strengths (typed decisions with confidence), with deterministic weighting in code, failed items marked 'not judged', no auto-retries, and 'never authorizes actions' guard rails.
MIT, small readable codebase (~50 KB source), no postinstall or curl|sh, privacy-check script, clear README in English and Chinese.
Fail-open behavior: errors return isError and the guidance says to continue without Jev.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and model jev-latest (src/typesafe.js:28,33). Directly contradicts the user's requirement; needs a fork and redeploy, and OpenRouter response/usage compatibility is unverified.

Requires running your own Cloudflare Worker + D1 for a single-user tool: a whole infra layer, a second vendor seeing your data, and an unauthenticated public /mcp endpoint by design (anyone with the URL spends your quota). Making it safe needs Cloudflare Access plus header config in Claude Code.

Conceptually aimed at RAG/knowledge-base/ticket triage (default routes answer/search_files/search_knowledge/search_web; examples about photography tutorials, refunds), not code work. Claude Opus 5.5 already routes, ranks and verifies well for coding; the tools duplicate what grep/GitNexus plus the main model do, and add a tool round trip per use.

Model-discretion only: Opus will often skip or over-use the tools; no deterministic hook, so 'automatic' is unreliable. Adds ~3-4k tokens of tool defs plus instructions to every session for marginal use.

Data egress is model-composed and unfiltered: code excerpts and client-project content would go to Cloudflare and TypeSafe; the existing secret-leak hook does not match mcp__ tools, and the worker has full logging enabled in the template.

Very immature: 1 star, 1 author, 7 commits in 2 days, no releases, no CI, version 0.3.0; claims about accuracy are unvalidated (eval:check only validates case format). Skill is Codex-oriented with a Chinese description, not a Claude Code plugin.
Composite tools multiply upstream calls (batch of 10 with concurrency 3, level-by-level taxonomy walk), raising latency and cost versus a single decision call; 30 s upstream timeout is generous.
entries.verdict: Not recommended as-is: it is TypeSafe-direct only (no OpenRouter), needs a personal Cloudflare Worker with an intentionally unauthenticated /mcp, and targets RAG/KB workflows rather than coding. Its proactive-use tool descriptions are a useful pattern to copy, but you would be better off with a small local stdio MCP or hook pointed at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: amidabuddha/jev-decision-mcp
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (TypeScript) exposing one tool, jev_decide. Takes a state blob plus a batch of named choice/score/noul questions, calls TypeSafe's System One endpoint through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 and returns validated probabilities, confidence and token usage as structured content. Strict response validation. Errors are returned as isError tool results, never invented decisions. Written and documented for Codex; the model must call the tool itself.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skill, CLAUDE.md snippet or proxy. The description says what it does but nothing tells Claude Code when to call it, and Opus will rarely reach for a probability classifier on its own without a routing rule. Meeting the user's goal of automatic use would need extra glue such as a CLAUDE.md rule, a SessionStart hook or a skill, which this repo does not provide. It is not deterministic.
security: API key is passed via env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), never argv, unless the user puts it in `claude mcp add -e`, which stores it in plain text in ~/.claude.json. Claude Code can inherit it from the launching environment.
Base URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai, so tool input cannot redirect the key (src/decision.ts:35). SDK logLevel is 'off'. Upstream error bodies are suppressed (decision.ts:62-68).
No postinstall or lifecycle scripts in the package (only prepack). The npm tarball contains just dist, LICENSE, README, examples and server.json. No shell execution or child_process in src.
No telemetry in this server. Source build reads a .env beside the project via loadEnvFile (config.ts:8); the npm install does not read the caller's cwd .env.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Output is numeric probabilities and label keys validated against the requested criteria (schema.ts:55-79). Free text from Jev is not returned, although the legend echoes the caller's own criteria.
Supply chain: single anonymous-ish maintainer, 11 commits, package about 1 week old, 1 star. Pin the version (0.1.3) and read dist before use. @typesafe-ai/sdk is MIT and from the typesafe-ai org.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly what the model puts in the jev_decide arguments: the state and the question instructions and criteria (plus the optional model name), sent by HTTPS POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with the API key as a Bearer header. Nothing is sent automatically from the machine. Claude Code decides what excerpts of code, diffs, tool output or prompts to include, so it can include proprietary or client code. Nothing is persisted locally (README). Client projects would need TypeSafe's data-handling terms checked (unverified). There is no path to OpenRouter as shipped.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level. Failures (MISSING_API_KEY, API_ERROR, CONNECTION_ERROR, TIMEOUT, INVALID_RESPONSE) come back as isError tool results, so the agent proceeds without Jev. The server starts even without a key. Overall deadline JEV_TIMEOUT_MS defaults to 30000 (1-120000). Per-attempt SDK timeout is min(that, 10000) ms with SDK maxRetries 2 (decision.ts:38, sdk index.mjs:74), so worst case is about 30 s of blocking per call. README suggests a host tool timeout above that (Codex 45 s). Slowness is visible to the user only as a pending tool call. A bad config value for JEV_TIMEOUT_MS makes the server exit (index.ts:36-39), so Claude Code shows it as failed to connect.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. The description is about 690 chars, about 175 tokens. The input schema is zod-derived JSON schema with discriminated union, descriptions and 255-option and 2-10 level constraints, roughly 900-1500 chars, about 300-400 tokens. The output schema is also advertised, about 250 tokens. Total about 700-900 tokens always resident, or lower if Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via tool search. No MCP server 'instructions' field is set (server.ts constructs McpServer with only name and version). No hooks inject text.
pros: Small, readable, auditable codebase (about 170 lines of src) with strict output validation (schema.ts:55-79) and no invented decisions on failure.
Thoughtful security posture: hardcoded origin, error-body suppression, no lifecycle scripts, npm trusted publishing with OIDC, MIT license.
Batching many choice/score/noul questions in one call matches Jev's design and cuts round trips.
Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, whose /v1/systemone path and Bearer auth line up with OpenRouter's System One API, so a fork to OpenRouter is a few lines.
Fail-open error handling and a configurable overall timeout; readOnlyHint annotation avoids permission prompts.
Tool description is careful about how to use the tool (independent questions, include a none option, caller owns thresholds).
cons: Does not support OpenRouter: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and the README explicitly rejects gateway keys. The user's stated requirement (OpenRouter-hosted Jev, no OPENROUTER_API_KEY today) means it works only with a separate TypeSafe key or after forking and maintaining a patch.

No automatic invocation mechanism. It is a bare model-discretion tool, and the user must not say 'use jev', but nothing makes Claude Code call it. There is no hook, skill, CLAUDE.md rule or instructions field.
Documented and tested for Codex, not Claude Code. There is no Claude Code config or guidance.

Sends whatever Claude assembles into state to a third party. Client-code confidentiality is on Claude's discretion, and there is no redaction or allowlist. It cannot see local files or the conversation.

Very new and thin project: 1 star, 1 contributor, 11 commits, first published 2026-09-23. Likely to change or be abandoned. Depends on the beta Jev model, whose value for coding is unproven (Theo claims it is a router).
Worst-case blocking of about 30 s per call with retries. npx cold start on first use. Passing the key via `claude mcp add -e` puts it in plain text in ~/.claude.json.
Jev returns probabilities only, with no reasoning, so it does not help coding tasks directly. Use cases such as cheap triage or routing rarely justify a tool call by a strong main model.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, well-validated single-tool Jev MCP, but it is TypeSafe-direct only (OpenRouter explicitly unsupported and hardcoded out) and offers no auto-invocation, so it fails both of the user's core requirements. Only worth considering as a base for a forked OpenRouter variant plus a separate routing rule or hook. It is not a drop-in answer.

entries.name: Fuwn/typesafe-mcp
entries.what: Tiny (~200 line) Node stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards {state, questions{noul|choice|score}, model} verbatim to POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY and returns the raw JSON (answers, probabilities, confidence, usage) as tool text. Validates question shapes with Zod before sending and checks each returned answer type matches the question type. Nothing else: no hooks, no skill, no routing.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or triggers a call: no hook, no skill, no system prompt or CLAUDE.md text. Claude will call `evaluate` only if it judges the description relevant, and the description is written for classification/scoring of evidence, not for coding decisions, so on typical coding turns it will almost never be picked. Getting the 'automatic without prompting' behaviour requires adding CLAUDE.md rules, a skill, or hooks around it (not provided by this repo).
security: API key read from env only, never argv; sent only as Bearer header to a hardcoded HTTPS host (server.js:160-162). Redirects disabled (`redirect: "error"`), so key cannot be bounced to another host.
Error text has the key replaced with [redacted] (server.js:184) and upstream error bodies are never echoed (server.js:168-171), which is good hygiene and tested.
No shell execution, no child_process in server.js, no fs access, no postinstall scripts in package.json, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry beyond the single API call.
Exact-pinned dependencies plus a package-lock.json (42 KB); dependency surface is just the MCP SDK and zod.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool returns only numeric/enum JSON from Jev (no free text), so returned content is low-risk. But the tool description asks the caller to 'supply evidence', so the model decides what data goes out; injected text in a repo could steer what gets sent, though egress is only to TypeSafe.

Tool has no output-size or input-size cap client-side (32k context limit is enforced upstream). One-person, 1-star, 8-day-old repo: supply-chain trust rests on Fuwn, so pin a commit or fork after reading (the file is small enough to audit fully, which I did).
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions`/`criteria` (arbitrary text or JSON: could be code, diffs, file contents, logs, tool outputs, prompts). Sent over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe) as-is. The full request body is JSON.stringify(input) (server.js:163), so also the `model` string. Only the API key in the Authorization header besides that. Nothing is sent automatically; egress happens only when the model chooses to call the tool. Client projects: contents leave to TypeSafe's direct API (would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe if patched), so check client confidentiality terms.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level: every failure (missing key at startup exits 1 so the MCP server shows as failed; HTTP non-2xx, bad JSON, mismatched answers, network error, 60 s timeout) is returned as an isError tool result and the model simply carries on without Jev. 60-second deadline (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MILLISECONDS, server.js:5) is long relative to the 70-500 ms claim, so a hung upstream would stall a turn for up to 60 s before failing; no retries; honours MCP cancellation (Esc). Nothing blocks tool use.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Description about 450 chars (~110 tokens); input schema (Zod discriminated union of three question types with nested criteria, generated JSON Schema, no per-field descriptions except `state`) roughly 1.5-2.5k chars (~400-600 tokens). Estimate total ~500-700 tokens per session (deferred via ToolSearch if MCP tool search is on, so likely only the name). No MCP `instructions` field is set (McpServer created with only name/version, server.js:145). No hooks, so zero per-turn injected text.
pros: Smallest possible correct wrapper: single file (server.js, 199 lines) that I read completely; easy to audit and to fork for private use.

Covers all three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) with proper Zod validation (choice 1-255 options, score 2-10 levels) and answer-type verification, so malformed calls fail locally without spending money.
Good security hygiene: key via env, not argv; redirect:'error'; key redaction; no upstream body echo; no postinstall/shell/telemetry; exact-pinned deps with lockfile.
Fail-open behaviour: errors come back as isError results and never block Claude Code; cancellation propagates to the fetch.
Tiny context footprint (one tool, ~0.5-0.7k tokens, no server instructions, no hooks).
Test suite with mocked transport is meaningful (7+ cases), plus an opt-in live check that verifies probabilities sum to 1.
Patch to OpenRouter is two-line and MIT permits it; the endpoint path /v1/systemone already matches OpenRouter's System One API path.
readOnlyHint:true annotation makes it low-friction in permission modes.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: base URL hardcoded (server.js:160), key env fixed to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter slug. Must be forked/patched; compatibility of OpenRouter's response envelope is unverified.

No automatic invocation mechanism: purely model-discretion. It does not meet the user's requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told. Needs CLAUDE.md rules, a skill, or hooks written separately.
Not published to npm (private:true), no releases, no CI, 2 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 8 days old: version 0.1.0 alpha with bus-factor 1 and no maintenance track record.

Nothing in it is tailored to coding: no code-oriented question templates, no diff/file gathering, no risk/permission-classification helper. The model has to compose questions and evidence itself each time, costing an extra Opus turn that likely outweighs Jev's 70-500 ms benefit.
60 s timeout is far too generous for a 70-500 ms model; a slow upstream would stall a turn. Not configurable via env.

Data egress is model-chosen and unfiltered; in bypass/auto mode with the secret-leak hook not matching mcp__typesafe__* tools, sensitive/client code could be sent out. Would need the hook matcher extended.
Returns the raw JSON blob as text with no summarisation; adds tokens to context per call (answers + probabilities + usage).
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, minimal reference wrapper worth forking (two-line change to OpenRouter) as the transport layer, but on its own it is a bare model-discretion tool with no auto-invocation and no coding-specific logic, so it will not deliver the 'Claude uses Jev by itself' goal. Use it, if at all, as the MCP backend under a hook/skill layer you write, not as the integration.

entries.name: altregubov/jev-antigravity-mcp (jev-mcp-proxy)
entries.what: Small Python (~535 LOC) stdio MCP server built on the mcp SDK (imports mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer, i.e. mcp 2.x). Exposes 4 tools that forward a caller-supplied state plus typed questions to TypeSafe System One (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, Bearer auth) and return typed answers: jev_evaluate (batch), jev_choice, jev_noul, jev_score. Retries 429/529 with backoff. Written for Google Antigravity; README has a generic Claude Code/Cursor config snippet. Pure passive tool: no hooks, no skills, no routing logic.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The sole nudge is a generic server-instructions string ('use whenever a skill needs fast, structured decisions...'), which is written for agent skills, not coding. Nothing deterministic: no hooks, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no skill. Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for a classifier tool during normal coding, because it has no concrete coding use case (no 'is this diff risky', no 'which file is relevant', no 'should I run tests'). Achieving the user's 'never prompt use jev' goal would require adding your own CLAUDE.md rules or hooks on top.
security: API key from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (good, not in argv), but the --api-key CLI flag would expose it in the process list, and every tool takes an optional api_key argument, so the model can put a key into tool-call arguments and transcripts (server.py:52, 90, 128, 164).
No shell execution, no eval, no postinstall or curl|sh. Only outbound httpx POST to the configured endpoint (client.py:320).

Logs to stderr at INFO by default (JEV_DEBUG defaults to '1', client.py:228): endpoint, model, question ids, latency, token counts. On non-200 it logs the full response.text (client.py:349), which could echo request content on 4xx. State content itself is not logged.
No telemetry beyond the User-Agent 'jev-mcp-proxy/0.1.0'.
Prompt-injection surface is small: outputs are numeric or typed labels. The risk is the reverse, since the model decides what state to ship out.
Supply chain: single-author, 1-star, 4-commit repo installed from unpinned git HEAD, no signed releases, no CI. An arbitrary-code-execution trust decision for a client-project machine.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly what the model puts in the tool arguments: the 'state' (any text or JSON: could be code, diffs, logs, file contents, tool outputs), plus 'instructions' and 'criteria', sent over HTTPS to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe direct by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden, and then OpenRouter and the upstream Jev host both see it). The Bearer key goes in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, but it does not crash the session. Errors (401/422/429/529/network) become ToolError 'Jev routing error: ...' (server.py:74-75), and Claude sees the error and can continue without Jev. Timeout is 30 s per attempt (client.py:265), and max_retries=3 for network errors and 429/529 with backoff 0.5, 1, 2 s or Retry-After, so the worst case is about 2 minutes of blocking on a hung endpoint. 401/422 fail immediately. The timeout is not configurable via env. No circuit breaker, so repeated calls during an outage each pay the full penalty. It never blocks tool use the way a PreToolUse hook could.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools plus server instructions. Estimated ~1.2-1.6k tokens always loaded in the session: 4 tool descriptions (~230 chars each) plus JSON schemas with nested Union[str, dict, list] types on state/instructions, plus the ~330-char instructions string (~0.3k). Unless Claude Code tool search defers MCP tools, this is loaded every turn. No hook-injected text.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related and minimal: one small file set (~535 LOC) that is easy to audit; I read all source (server.py, client.py, models.py) and found no shell exec, no telemetry, no installer hooks.
Exposes all three Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) plus a batch tool, so the typed-decision surface is complete for building your own gating logic.
Base-URL normalization (client.py:272-275) makes 'TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1' resolve to the OpenRouter /v1/systemone path, so an OpenRouter route is close to env-only.
Key comes from env by default; sane retry and Retry-After handling on 429/529; errors surface as clean ToolErrors so Claude continues without Jev.
MIT licensed; tests exist (client, server, stdio handshake); uv.lock pins deps.
Server-instructions text explicitly tells the model when to use it, which is the only auto-invocation lever an MCP server has.
cons: Age 12 days, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no releases, no CI: PoC-grade for a beta model.

No OpenRouter awareness: default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id, no OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var (must abuse TYPESAFE_API_KEY), and no support for the /api/alpha/decisions API. Schema parity with OpenRouter System One is unverified.
Not automatic: pure model-discretion tools with a generic instruction. Fails the user's core requirement ('Claude Code must use it when needed') without extra hooks or CLAUDE.md rules.

No coding-specific design: it is a generic pass-through, so Claude must compose state and rubrics itself each time, and Jev's 32k context and no-reasoning design gives little value to an Opus 5.5 session doing agentic coding.
Unpinned uvx-from-git install of a 1-star single-author repo is a supply-chain risk on client projects; pyproject 'mcp>=1.3.0' conflicts with the 2.x-only import, so a non-lock resolve may break.

Exfiltration risk: the model can send arbitrary code, diffs or file contents as 'state', and the existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools. The api_key tool parameter lets keys leak into transcripts.
Timeouts/retries up to about 2 minutes per call with no env config or circuit breaker; a new HTTP client per call (no connection reuse); stderr logging on by default.
~1.2-1.6k tokens of always-on tool and schema context for a tool that will rarely be called.
entries.verdict: A clean, small, honest passthrough MCP for Jev, but a 12-day-old one-author PoC that is TypeSafe-direct only, has no auto-invocation beyond a generic instruction, and no coding use cases. Useful at most as a reference, or as a base to fork with OpenRouter defaults and pair with your own hooks or CLAUDE.md gating; not something to install as-is for automatic Jev use.

entries.name: bestagentkits/typesafe-demo-mcp (typesafe-mcp-server)
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (TypeScript, built on @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0) exposing two tools: typesafe_ask (send a state plus noul/choice/score questions to POST /v1/systemone, get typed probabilities back as markdown or JSON) and typesafe_list_models. Purely model-invoked tools; no hooks, no proxy. Repo also bundles the official typesafe-ai SKILL.md under .agents/skills (empty .claude/.pi skill dirs).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or triggers use; Claude Code would call typesafe_ask only if the description/instructions convince Opus to do so mid-task. Instructions are written for app-builders ("route a request", "rank items"), not for coding-agent workflows, so unprompted use during ordinary coding would be rare. No deterministic hook, no skill trigger for coding (the bundled SKILL.md triggers on 'building AI-powered software with TypeSafe').
security: API key read from env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY only; not in argv if registered via claude mcp add -e / settings env block (docs/typesafe-mcp-server.md:24-60). Key is never logged by server code (src/index.ts logs only a warning about a missing key).
No shell execution, no file access, no fs reads; only outbound HTTPS via SDK fetch. Build is plain tsc; no postinstall scripts found in package.json or package-lock.json; no install.sh or curl|sh.
No telemetry in server code; SDK 0.6.0 was only grep-checked for endpoints, no telemetry endpoint seen (only api.typesafe.ai base URL).

Not runnable via npx: package.json 'files: [dist]' and 'bin' exist but the package is not published to npm (unverified), so user must git clone, npm install, npm run build and point Claude Code at node dist/index.js. Supply chain = npm deps @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, @typesafe-ai/sdk (0.6.0, MIT, created 2026-09-12), zod, all reasonable.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is a numeric distribution plus question labels echoed back; low risk. Bigger risk is the model deciding what state (possibly code/secrets) to send; the existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover MCP tool args by matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
Repo has no license file (licenseInfo null), so legally all rights reserved despite being a demo; bundled SKILL.md is MIT.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts into the 'state' and 'instructions'/'criteria' arguments of typesafe_ask (arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, prompts) is sent over HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if repointed, then routed onward by OpenRouter to TypeSafe). Nothing is sent automatically; the server has no hooks and reads no files. Also sends Bearer key. No caching, no server state (src/index.ts:5-7). For client projects, code would leave the machine to OpenRouter plus TypeSafe on each call.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: every error is caught and returned as an isError tool result with an actionable message (src/tools/ask.ts:106, src/typesafe.ts:97-140), so Claude just continues. Missing key does not crash startup (warning only, src/index.ts:32-36). Per-attempt timeout 30 s (src/constants.ts:155) with SDK default 2 retries, backoff 0.5-5 s on 408/429/5xx/connection/timeouts (SDK index.mjs:72-88), so a hung Jev could stall a single tool call up to ~90 s plus backoff. Not a hook, so it can never block a tool call or the session.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. Approx chars: typesafe_ask description 4.5k + input schema descriptions ~4.5k (src/schemas.ts, 5.7k source incl. code), typesafe_list_models ~1.2k, server instructions 1.9k => roughly 11-12k chars = about 3k tokens always-resident (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch, then only names until loaded, though server instructions are still injected). No hook-injected text.
pros: OpenRouter switch is config-only: SDK appends /v1/systemone to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (sdk index.mjs:513,554), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api hits the exact OpenRouter System One endpoint with a Bearer key.
Genuinely tiny and auditable: ~16 KB of source, 2 tools, no shell/file/network code beyond the SDK, no postinstall, no telemetry, key only via env.
Fail-open by construction: all SDK errors mapped to isError tool results (src/typesafe.ts:97-140), missing key does not crash Claude Code startup.

Clean, accurate tool schema with per-primitive Zod validation (score needs >=2 levels), and good guidance on interpreting probabilities/confidence; gives a working reference for how Jev requests are shaped.
Low always-on context cost (~3k tokens, 2 tools) and read-only annotations, so it will not trigger extra permission prompts.
cons: Not a coding integration: labeled a demo; generic 'ask a typed question about state' tool with no coding-specific use (routing, commit classification, risk scoring) and nothing that Claude Code would call unprompted, which fails the user's core 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement.
Purely model-discretion: no hook, no proxy, no skill trigger for coding. Opus would have to spend a turn composing question JSON, which usually costs more than just deciding itself.

Not published to npm; must be cloned, installed and built and pinned by hand. 1 commit, 1 star, 0 forks, age 13 days, no CI, no license file (usage rights unclear for client projects), authored by a third-party 'bestagentkits' account rather than TypeSafe.

OpenRouter path unverified end to end: default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID (must set typesafe/jev-1.13), list_models will hit OpenRouter's global /v1/models and likely error, and OpenRouter body/response parity with the SDK is assumed.
Data egress is model-controlled: Opus could pass source code or secrets as 'state' to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on client projects; existing secret-guard hook matcher does not cover this MCP tool.
Retry policy (30 s timeout x 3 attempts) can stall a turn for over a minute if Jev hangs; no circuit breaker.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, tiny reference MCP wrapper that can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is a one-commit third-party demo whose tools only fire if Opus chooses to call them, so it does not deliver the automatic, unprompted integration the user wants. Useful as a base or template for a custom hook-driven wrapper, not as the daily integration itself.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null). Bundled skill file is MIT.

entries.name: @mokei/mcp-system-one
entries.what: Tiny stdio MCP server exposing a single tool, predict, that forwards a typed System One request (state + choice/score/noul questions map + optional model) to an HTTP backend at POST {SYSTEM_ONE_URL}/v1/systemone with Bearer auth, validates the response, and returns answers+usage as structuredContent. It is a generic System One protocol client written against the Laya (laya-serve) backend, not Jev-specific; no OpenRouter or TypeSafe code or docs anywhere in the repo.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description ('Classify text with System One typed questions (choice/score/noul)') is generic and gives Claude no guidance on when to use it; without a CLAUDE.md rule or skill it will almost never be called spontaneously, and Claude must construct a valid typed question map each time.
security: API key read from SYSTEM_ONE_API_KEY env var (config.ts:56), not argv, so not visible in process list; but stored in plaintext in MCP config env if added via claude mcp add -e
No shell execution, no postinstall/preinstall scripts (package.json scripts only build/test/prepublishOnly), no telemetry found in grep of server+client src

Prompt-injection surface is low: tool returns only numeric probabilities/labels, but 'choice' labels and criteria keys echo caller-supplied strings; error messages include up to 300 chars of backend error body (http.ts:93-99)
Single maintainer (Paul Le Cam), 1 star, brand-new npm package with only 2 versions; supply-chain risk of unpinned npx -y; npm tarball has provenance-style signatures but no repo README
Manifest (manifest.json) is an MCPB bundle spec pointing SYSTEM_ONE_URL to localhost:8000
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in the predict tool's state and questions arguments is sent to SYSTEM_ONE_URL/v1/systemone (with model name and bearer key). Nothing is sent automatically; Claude must decide to call the tool and choose what state to include (could be code, diffs, tool output). No other outbound traffic found.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude level: errors are thrown as MCP tool errors (config.ts:92-97) and Claude just sees a failed tool call and proceeds. Default is no retry (resolveClient passes no retry policy, config.ts:54-58) and no explicit timeout (falls to ky default, ~10 s unless overridden); connection errors mapped to SystemOneConnectionError, 401/403 to auth error, 404 to model error, 429/529 to rate limit. If the MCP process fails to start the server is simply unavailable.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__system-one__predict). Definition includes the full recursive question-map JSON schema (anyOf choice/score/noul, instructions anyOf string/object/array) plus outputSchema; estimated ~600-900 tokens. No server-level instructions field set. No hooks, no injected text.
pros: Minimal, readable, MIT-licensed wrapper (3 source files, ~130 lines server + ~850 lines client) that is easy to audit and does exactly one thing
Endpoint path v1/systemone and Bearer auth match OpenRouter's System One API, and base URL/key/model are env-configurable, so OpenRouter-hosted Jev is plausibly a config-only change
Strong schema validation of both inputs and responses (choice/score/noul with probabilities, confidence, act_probability) and structuredContent output with outputSchema
No shell exec, no postinstall, key via env not argv, no telemetry
Actively developed (commits through 2026-09-30) and low context cost (single tool)
cons: Not Jev-specific: built for Laya/laya-serve (default localhost:8000, model 'english'); zero mention of OpenRouter, TypeSafe or Jev in code or docs, so OpenRouter compatibility is inferred, not proven
No deterministic trigger: a bare model-discretion tool with a generic description; Claude will not use it automatically, which violates the user's core requirement
Every call requires Claude to author a full typed question map, costing an extra main-model turn, tokens and latency; poor for routine coding steps
README is thin (npm README empty), only 1 star, single maintainer, package 6 days old (0.13.0 on 2026-09-24), no GitHub releases

No default timeout/retry configured in the MCP server, no fallback behavior; send-what-Claude-chooses egress with no redaction, and would sit beside the existing secret-leak guard without integrating with it
Requires storing the OpenRouter key in MCP env config (plaintext in ~/.claude.json) and npx -y of an unpinned young package
entries.verdict: A clean but generic System One MCP client aimed at Laya; it can probably be pointed at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone by env vars alone, but as a discretionary MCP tool it cannot deliver the automatic, no-prompt Jev usage the user wants. Useful only as a reference implementation or as the transport underneath a hook/skill that decides when to call it.

entries.name: thesammykins/jev_ampcode
entries.what: Amp plugin exposing an advisory tool that compares supplied alternatives against supplied evidence and priorities via Jev Choice, returning typed choices with probabilities.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Careful usage guidance (not reassurance or authorization); no runtime dependencies (two small files)
Eval cases and tests; pattern easy to port into a Claude Code MCP
Clear secrets handling
cons: Amp-only plugin API; not usable from Claude Code as is
Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, uses JEV_KEY, no license
Relies on model discretion, no deterministic trigger

entries.name: LeddoEngano/jev-eyes
entries.what: Local OCR plus spatial layout turns images/screenshots into Jev-ready text state; CLI, Python lib, MCP server (see, ask tools) and skill. Jev calls via typesafe_sdk.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: see() needs no key and runs locally, transparent about what Jev sees
MCP server plus skill and tests; includes accuracy benchmarks
cons: Image/OCR niche; rarely relevant to daily code work
ask() uses typesafe_sdk with TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no OpenRouter support found
Not yet on PyPI; OCR deps (rapidocr/tesseract) are heavy

entries.name: darthzen/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (157 LOC) Python FastMCP 3 server exposing one tool, `evaluate`, that forwards the exact body of POST /v1/systemone (state + questions + model) to TypeSafe and returns the raw JSON response. Runs only as a streamable-HTTP server (designed for a k8s deployment behind a Cloudflare tunnel with a URL path secret), not stdio.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The server `instructions` (server.py:46-51) say to use `evaluate` 'before any decision', which nudges Opus to call it, but nothing deterministic forces it, and Claude Code often truncates or deprioritises MCP instructions. No hook, no skill, no proxy. Whether Claude actually calls Jev is unreliable, and each call requires the model to compose a large typed payload, which is the opposite of the transparent System One use case. Would need a companion CLAUDE.md rule or a hook to be reliable.
security: API key read from env or *_FILE (server.py:54-67); never in argv, which is good, and never logged. The key lives in the server process, not in Claude Code config.

Server does NOT authenticate callers (README); with the default bind 0.0.0.0 (server.py:139) and allowed_hosts=['*'] (:152), anyone on the LAN can spend the key's credits unless JEV_BIND_HOST=127.0.0.1 is set and a path secret used. Without JEV_MCP_PATH_SECRET it serves unauthenticated on /mcp with only a warning (:124-126).
No shell execution, no file access beyond reading the key file, no postinstall or curl|sh. Dependencies pinned exactly.

Upstream error text (first 500 chars of response body) is returned to the model as a ToolError (:113): a small prompt-injection surface only if the upstream is compromised. Response JSON is passed through unchanged and is typed numbers/keys, so injection risk from Jev output is low.
No telemetry in code. Dockerfile runs as non-root uid 10001.

Bigger risk is the content Claude chooses to put in `state`: arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, secrets could be sent; the user's secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover this MCP tool (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in `state` and question `instructions`/`criteria` (code snippets, diffs, error logs, file contents, tool outputs, possibly client code) goes from the local server process to api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter if repointed). Also the API key (Bearer) and model name. Nothing else; no telemetry. The model decides the payload, so the volume and sensitivity are unbounded (32k ctx limit upstream). With OpenRouter, data additionally passes through OpenRouter and its provider policies, which matters for client projects under NDA.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude Code level: on timeout (default 60 s, JEV_MCP_TIMEOUT), network error or HTTP >=400 the tool raises ToolError with a message and Claude continues on its own. But there is no retry, no circuit breaker, and 60 s is far above the claimed 70-500 ms, so a hung upstream can stall a turn for up to a minute per call. If the local server process is down, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tool is simply absent (fail-open, silent). Startup fails fast if no key (:138). Tool is stateless HTTP (stateless_http=True), so restarts are harmless.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (`evaluate`). Tool description ~1,250 chars, input schema roughly 350 chars (state union, questions dict, model), plus server instructions ~560 chars: about 2,200 chars = roughly 550 tokens. Cheap. No hooks and no injected text. Deferred tool search may reduce it further.
pros: Very small, readable, auditable (157 LOC, pinned deps, Apache-2.0), no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry.
Exposes the full Choice/Noul/Score contract via one tool, mirroring the raw System One body, so nothing is lost.
Switching to OpenRouter needs only env vars (JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL, JEV_API_KEY_FILE) with no code patch (subject to schema parity).
Key handled via file/env, never argv; fail-fast on missing key; ToolError on failures so Claude is not blocked.
Tiny context cost (~550 tokens, one tool).
cons: Built for the author's homelab: HTTP-only, no stdio mode, must run a long-lived local process yourself (no PyPI, no npx/uvx one-liner); defaults bind 0.0.0.0 with unauthenticated MCP.
Purely model-discretion: does not meet the 'automatic without prompting' requirement; no hook or skill layer; the user would need CLAUDE.md nudges or a custom PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook on top.
Default model 'jev-latest' and default URL are TypeSafe-only; the repo has never been tested against OpenRouter and is not aware of OpenRouter model IDs (~typesafe/jev-latest) or headers.
