Brand new (created and last pushed 2026-09-22, 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no CI); one commit already fixed an API-shape bug, showing the tool description is hand-maintained against a beta API.
60 s timeout with no retries; new HTTP client per call.

Claude must author the whole typed payload with state, so cost is Opus output tokens plus seconds of latency per decision, and it can leak code/secrets to a third party via `state` with no redaction and outside the existing secret-guard hook matcher.
Not really a coding accelerator: Jev returns probabilities, and in a coding agent the LLM already decides; benefit is unproven.
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal, safe-to-read wrapper that would work against OpenRouter by env vars alone, but it is a homelab-shaped, HTTP-only, day-old PoC that relies entirely on Claude choosing to call it, so it does not deliver the automatic integration wanted. Useful at best as a raw building block (run locally on 127.0.0.1) beneath a hook or CLAUDE.md rule, or as a reference for a purpose-built stdio/hook integration.

entries.name: tmbmartell/jev-mcp
entries.what: Tiny (about 250 lines of Python) stdio MCP server that wraps the OpenRouter Decisions API (and optionally TypeSafe direct) as two tools: jev_decisions (state + typed questions -> noul/choice/score answers with probabilities and confidence, plus client-side contract validation and cost) and jev_health. It is a generic pass-through: Claude must author the questions itself. It has no coding-specific questions, no hooks and no skills. Text is in Portuguese, with English payloads passed through unchanged.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude sees the tool and the Portuguese server instructions ('use when you need semantic judgment that ordinary code cannot do'). Nothing pushes it to call jev_decisions during ordinary coding: there is no hook, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet. Opus 5.5 already handles classification internally, so it will almost never choose to author a typed-question payload and pay a round trip, unless the user adds a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill. It does not meet the requirement of 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically without me saying so'.
security: API key: read from env var, else from a plaintext file under ~/.hermes/secrets. The README's Claude Code snippet puts the key in the mcpServers env block, which lands in plaintext ~/.claude.json. Use `claude mcp add -e` or inherit from the shell environment instead. The key is never on argv in the recommended setup, and no code logs it.
No shell execution and no eval in the server. HTTP goes through urllib to hardcoded HTTPS URLs only. No telemetry. No npm postinstall.

scripts/install.sh is not curl|sh. It is local, idempotent and does `pip install --upgrade mcp` into whichever Python it finds. It writes /tmp/jev-install.log at a predictable path (minor symlink and tmp risk). It does not write the key.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever Claude passes as `state` (code, file contents, issue text) goes to Jev. Jev returns only typed numbers and enums, so the response channel is a very low injection risk. Error text `raw_error` is truncated to 500 chars and comes from the provider.

Retries: up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff, and a 120 s timeout per attempt (jev.py:77,93). A hung provider can block one tool call for a very long time (about 8 min worst case). This is a reliability risk, not a vulnerability.

Unpinned dependency (`pip install mcp`) and a brand-new single-author repo with no releases or signing. It is small enough to audit in 10 minutes, but nothing ties a future git pull to what was audited, so pin a commit.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and in each question's `instructions` and `criteria` goes to openrouter.ai over HTTPS with a Bearer key. That means arbitrary code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs if the model chooses to pass them. Nothing is sent automatically, and there is no hook that harvests content. Responses come back with model, provider, cost and request_id. jev_health sends the fixed string 'Teste de conectividade.'. OpenRouter and TypeSafe see and may log the payloads. Check OpenRouter's data-policy settings before using this on client code under NDA.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the MCP layer: config errors, HTTP errors and network errors all return a JSON {ok:false,...} tool result rather than raising, so Claude Code continues. The problem is latency. Retryable statuses (429, 500, 502, 503, 529) and URLErrors are retried 4 times with backoff of 1, 2 and 4 s, and each attempt has a 120 s timeout (jev.py:77-107). A stalled Jev can therefore hang a tool call for minutes. There is no circuit breaker and no short timeout option exposed to the tool. Non-retryable errors such as 400 or 401 return immediately. If the key is missing, the tool still registers and only fails when called.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. Rough count: server instructions about 1.3k chars (about 330 tokens), jev_decisions description about 750 chars, jev_health about 300 chars, plus schemas (state: Any, questions: dict, route) and tool names, about 500 chars. Total about 2.9k chars, or about 700-800 tokens permanent. In Claude Code 2.1.x with tool search deferral, the schemas may be deferred and only the names shown, and the instructions text is always injected. Very cheap. The Portuguese description is a small quirk.
pros: Correct endpoint, default route and model for the user's setup: OpenRouter POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY read from the environment (jev.py:37-39). No patching is needed.
Small and auditable: about 250 lines in mcp_server.py plus jev.py, stdlib HTTP, no shell execution, no telemetry and no postinstall. Static read shows no exfiltration beyond the declared call.

Pre-validates question contracts (choice criteria as dict, score criteria as ordered list) before spending a call, and validates response probabilities (sum to about 1, range checks), so malformed Claude-authored questions get a corrective error. This handles the trickiest part of the Decisions API.
Fail-open: all errors are returned as data, not exceptions.
Returns cost_usd, tokens and request_id per call, which is useful for auditing spend. About 700 tokens of permanent context for 2 tools.

Ships the honest guidance 'policy stays in code, low confidence is information', and a README that lists real API gotchas (no /v1, not in the models catalog, /chat/completions returns 400, noul has no confidence field).
cons: Cannot satisfy the core requirement. It is only a model-discretion tool with no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md rule, so Claude Code will not use Jev 'when needed' on its own. Opus 5.5 will normally just decide things itself.

Generic pass-through with no coding-specific value: no prebuilt questions for 'is this diff risky', 'which file matches this task', 'does this test failure look flaky', and so on. The only example is customer-ticket triage. The user or Claude must invent schemas each time, which costs more Opus tokens and time than the decision saves.

Extreme immaturity: 0 stars, 3 commits in one day, 1 contributor, no CI, no releases, no unit tests, no pyproject or lockfile. It is Hermes-first (install.sh, ~/.hermes/secrets, HERMES_HOME) with Claude Code treated as an afterthought.

TypeSafe direct route (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model 'jev-latest') is unverified in the code, and the repo has no evidence it ever worked. The /api/v1/systemone OpenRouter endpoint is not supported. Only the alpha Decisions API is used, and 'alpha' may change or break.

Retry and timeout policy is hostile to an interactive session: 4 attempts, 120 s timeout each, no way to shorten it. A Jev outage or 429 storm would stall the tool call for minutes with no circuit breaker.

README example puts the API key in the mcpServers env block, which is plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The key-file fallback lives under ~/.hermes, which is irrelevant to this user. The `mcp.server.mcpserver` import needs the v2 SDK, with no version pin, so it can break on install.

The repo's own benchmark (6 ticket cases, 5/6, tied with gpt-4o-mini) does not show Jev outperforming a plain LLM, and says nothing about code tasks. It offers no evidence for the 'router' claims, and the author admits calibration is unproven.

Client code sent as `state` leaves the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the server has no allow/deny filtering or redaction. This matters for client projects even though the existing secret-leak hook guards only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit tool inputs, not MCP calls.
entries.verdict: A clean, honest, OpenRouter-native reference wrapper that is worth copying as a starting point. But it is a passive tool that Claude will basically never call unprompted, it has no coding-specific questions, and it is a one-day-old single-author POC with an aggressive retry and timeout policy. Use it, if at all, as the transport layer, and add your own PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hook or skill (with fixed coding questions and a short timeout) to get the automatic behaviour the user wants.

entries.name: seb4ez/jevguard-mcp
entries.what: Zero-dependency Python stdio MCP server (PyPI jevguard-mcp) that wraps TypeSafe's System One endpoint. It exposes 7 tools: 3 atomic ones for command safety, patch verification and option choice, plus 4 low-level ones for generic evaluate, calibrate, prune_state and cache_fingerprint. It prunes state, injects an UNRESOLVED_OR_OTHER escape option, caches results in local SQLite, and applies its own calibration thresholds. The repo also ships an Antigravity-style SKILL.md that tells the agent to call the tools before risky shell commands and large diffs. It is not a hook. The tools are only called if the model decides to call them, or if the skill is copied in and triggers.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The tool descriptions tell the model when to use them, and the optional SKILL.md description triggers on 'evaluating terminal command safety, verifying code diffs, making architectural decisions'. There is no deterministic hook and no PreToolUse integration, so it is not guaranteed and not automatic. The user would have to write their own PreToolUse hook to force it.
security: The API key is read only from the env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv, but it sits in the MCP env config in ~/.claude.json.

Good hygiene in the code: NoRedirectHandler blocks redirects to prevent Authorization leakage (tools.py:64-70), https only, no userinfo in the URL, and a host allowlist with wildcards rejected. The response is capped at 10MB. Unknown tool arguments are rejected.

The endpoint can be changed through env (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT or JEVGUARD_ENDPOINT), but only to allowlisted hosts. Adding hosts requires JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS, which is env-controlled, not model-controlled.

No subprocess or os.system, and no shell execution. It never executes the commands it evaluates; it only classifies them. No telemetry beyond the upstream call. The 'telemetry' field in results is local latency data.

The local SQLite cache at ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db (TTL 3600s default, JEVGUARD_CACHE_PATH and JEVGUARD_CACHE_TTL) stores the full wire_payload in plaintext. That includes evaluated shell commands, diffs and states, so pasted secrets in commands or diffs would persist on disk for an hour. The cache also keys on the tenant (a SHA-256 prefix of the API key).
A mock_answers argument is refused unless JEVGUARD_TEST_MODE=1. This is fine in production but is a test-only bypass toggle.
entries.dataEgress: On a cache miss, the full JSON {model, questions, state} is POSTed over HTTPS to api.typesafe.ai (or the configured endpoint). For command_safety, state is the command, working_dir and elevated flag. For verify_code_patch, it is the complete patch content and the target file path. For evaluate_decision, it is the context text, the question and the options. For jevguard_evaluate, it is whatever the model puts in state. Only what Claude chooses to pass leaves the machine; the server does not read files. Cache hits send nothing. Anything in a command or diff is sent to a third party, including secrets and client code, which is a real issue for client projects, and the existing secret-leak guard would not see this MCP traffic unless its matcher covers mcp__jevguard__ tools.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for the workflow but fail-closed in the advisory verdict. On timeout, HTTP error, missing key or network error, a tool returns isError JSON with verdict/fallback_action MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED, and the stdio connection stays up. The default per-call timeout is 10s (parameter up to 300s). _dispatch_upstream retries up to 3 times on 429/5xx/timeouts with exponential backoff inside that total deadline. Client-side rate limit is 120 requests/min. Because nothing is enforced at the harness level, a failure can only make Claude ask you for confirmation (per SKILL.md) or ignore the result. In bypass mode there is no hard block. In the worst case a slow or down upstream stalls a turn for up to about 10s per checked command.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools. The tool definitions (names, descriptions, JSON schemas, lines 1268-1560 of tools.py) come to about 15.8k characters, or roughly 3.9k tokens, and that is loaded into every session unless tool search defers it. Tool descriptions are long, disambiguation-style ('Use ONLY for... Do NOT use for...'). The server sends no MCP 'instructions' field (server.py:270-310 has only the tools capability). No hooks and no injected text. If SKILL.md is installed, add about 100 tokens for the description at discovery, and about 1.2k tokens when loaded. Each actual call costs a model turn for the tool call plus a JSON result with echoed wire_payload, calibration and telemetry, so it is verbose.
pros: Only candidate here whose code and SKILL.md are aimed at coding-agent use: command safety, diff verification, and decision choice map directly onto Jev's Noul, Score and Choice primitives.
Zero dependencies, pure stdlib Python 3.10+, and no postinstall or shell execution; the source is small enough to read and even pin (one 2.6k-line tools.py).
Endpoint hardening is better than typical MCP servers: https only, host allowlist, redirects blocked, response size cap, key only in env and never in argv.

Endpoint and key are env-overridable, and a JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS=openrouter.ai plus TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone gets past the allowlist with the same Bearer scheme. So a patch to reach OpenRouter is small.

Local SQLite cache with 1h TTL and volatile-key masking avoids repeat spend for identical commands. It also has a 134-test suite, and failures come back as structured errors and never crash the stdio session.
Escape-option injection (UNRESOLVED_OR_OTHER) and dispersion checks are a reasonable defence against a forced-choice classifier.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code: model is hard-coded 'jev-latest' with no env override, no openrouter references, and TypeSafe direct is the only documented path. The OpenRouter wire format is unverified for this payload.

Not automatic. Pure model-discretion tools plus an optional skill; nothing runs unless Claude decides to. No hooks.json, no plugin.json, no PreToolUse integration, which is exactly what the user asked for (automatic use without prompting).

Duplicates what Claude Code already does. Claude Code has its own permission system, and the user runs bypass or auto mode with an existing secret-leak hook. A probabilistic classifier's advisory verdict cannot block anything in bypass mode, and judging 'is this command destructive' with a 32k-context router model is weaker than the main model's own judgment.

Sends every checked command and full diff to a third-party endpoint on cache miss, which conflicts with client-project confidentiality. The cache also keeps the payloads in plaintext on disk for 1 hour.
Costs about 3.9k tokens of tool definitions per session, plus a whole extra model turn per check, and the verbose output echoes wire_payload.

Provenance and maturity risk: brand-new (created 2026-09-20), one anonymous author, 0 stars, no CI, no issues, and versions inconsistent (PyPI 1.0.2, repo 1.1.0, latest release tag v1.0.1). It claims to be 'Official' while calling itself independent. The author churned about 4 'hardening' commits in one day (2026-09-25), so the code is still changing.

Custom calibration thresholds (0.40, 0.15, 0.12) are admitted heuristics rather than fitted, and the README benchmark measured only 5 hand-picked cases against TypeSafe direct, with a 730-750 ms latency far from the claimed 70-500 ms. The safety claims are unproven.
Prompt-injection risk: the untrusted diff or command is what gets judged, so an adversarial patch can bias the verdict, and the harness does not enforce the outcome.
entries.verdict: A small, reasonably hardened but very young and unaffiliated MCP wrapper that only supports TypeSafe direct. Reaching OpenRouter would need env tweaks plus a model-name patch, and it is model-discretion only, so it does not deliver the automatic, no-prompt integration the user asked for. It is worth using only as a reference for wire format and calibration ideas, or as a base for a custom PreToolUse hook. It is not worth installing as-is.

entries.name: yuyang2230/jev-agent-skill
entries.what: A Claude Code / ZCode skill (SKILL.md plus a 108-line stdlib-only jev.py) that calls Jev's System One endpoint through OpenCode Zen, using the free model jev-1.13-free. The SKILL.md description tells the model to use it automatically for classify/route, batch screen, score/rank and verify tasks. The author adapted it from the official typesafe-ai/skills SKILL.md. Its examples and showcase are about triaging e-commerce comments for the author's Taobao shop, and the README links that shop.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill-description trigger only. It is model-discretion, and Claude decides from the description whether a task matches. There is no deterministic hook and no transparent proxy. The triggers (tickets, comments, batch screening, scoring, verifying claims) are generic and business-flavored, so Claude will seldom hit them during normal coding work.
security: API key is sent in the Authorization header from a file or env var. It never appears in argv, so there is no process-list leak. There is no file permission check on ~/.jev/zen.key.
jev.py:63 deliberately spoofs the User-Agent 'curl/8.9.1' to get past the gateway WAF. That is a smell, and it only matters for the Zen route.
There is no telemetry, postinstall, curl|sh installer or shell execution in jev.py. It is stdlib only with a single HTTPS endpoint, and the ENDPOINT is env-overridable.

The prompt-injection surface comes from the skill's design. It tells the agent to feed raw untrusted content (comments, logs, messages) to Jev and consume the probabilities, which are typed and cannot carry free text. That is lower risk than a free-text model, but the agent decides what goes into 'state'.
The SKILL.md and README promote the author's Taobao shop (self-promotion). It is not malicious, but it is the marketing of an unrelated business.
The free tier depends on a claimed loophole: the /v1/systemone endpoint bypasses the free-tier client fence that applies to chat endpoints (api-notes.md:70-74). It could be closed at any time.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in the 'state' and 'questions' JSON goes to opencode.ai/zen, or to openrouter.ai if you override the endpoint. That could be code snippets, logs, diffs, commit messages or file contents if the model chooses to send them. There is no built-in redaction, size cap or allowlist. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background. Data leaves only when the agent decides to run jev.py. With the free Zen route, data goes to a third-party gateway on a free tier, which is a client-confidentiality concern.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the process level. jev.py returns {'error': ...} after 3 attempts (backoff 1s, 2s, 3s, 60 s timeout each, so worst case is about 3 minutes plus sleeps). It exits 1 on API error or 2 if there is no key, and Claude just sees the error text. Nothing blocks the session because there is no hook. A stalled call can hold a Bash tool call for up to 3 minutes, though. There is no circuit breaker.
entries.contextCost: There are 0 MCP tools and 0 hook-injected text. Cost is the skill listing entry, which is the name plus a description of about 900 characters, roughly 225 tokens per session. SKILL.md (about 5.3 KB, roughly 1.4k tokens) loads only when the skill is invoked.
pros: Zero-dependency 108-line jev.py that is easy to audit. I read the whole thing: no shell execution, no telemetry, and the key stays out of argv.

The endpoint, model and key can be pointed at OpenRouter with no code change: JEV_ENDPOINT=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, ZEN_API_KEY=<openrouter key>. A hard-coded key lookup is the only oddity.
Context cost is tiny, about 225 tokens for the listing, and there are no MCP tools. It also does not touch the existing PreToolUse, GitNexus or caveman hooks.
It uses Claude Code's native skill mechanism, so the trigger is truly automatic and needs no user prompting. That is the user's stated wish, and it is done in the least invasive way.
It has practical retry and backoff logic, and it merges several questions into one request for parallel execution.
The batch pattern (raw items stay in the script, only conclusions return to context) is a sensible use of the skill if a bulk task ever arises.
cons: Wrong domain for coding. Triggers are ticket/comment/log triage, candidate screening and claim verification. Examples and showcase are Chinese Taobao shop comments, so Claude will rarely or never match it during real coding tasks, or will match it on the wrong things.

Provider is hard-wired to OpenCode Zen. Nothing in the code mentions OpenRouter, so the user must know about the env overrides. The default model jev-1.13-free is a Zen-specific name that does not exist on OpenRouter.
The free tier relies on an unofficial loophole (api-notes.md:70-74). Sending client code and logs to a free third-party gateway is a confidentiality risk if it is left on the default endpoint.

It never says what to give Jev in a coding session (for example diff classification or test-failure triage). It offers no coding-specific question templates, and the model would have to hand-build the JSON each time.
Single author, 4 commits in a single day, 0 stars, no tests or CI, no releases. It is a personal utility that advertises the author's shop.
No timeout budget or fail-fast: 3 retries with a 60 s timeout each can block a Bash call for up to about 3 minutes if the gateway hangs.
Spoofing the curl User-Agent to get past the WAF is fragile and ethically dubious.
Adds nothing beyond the official typesafe-ai/skills SKILL.md apart from the Zen workaround, since the author adapted that skill.
entries.verdict: This is a thin, safe-to-read wrapper adapted from the official skill, and it is tuned to shop-comment triage on OpenCode Zen. It works on OpenRouter with three env vars, but the triggers rarely match coding work, so it is marginal for this user. If the user wants a Jev skill, fork it and rewrite the description around coding judgments, or use the official typesafe-ai/skills version, rather than adopting this one as is.

entries.name: henrykey/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Python/FastMCP service exposing four Jev (System One) tools (jev_choice, jev_score, jev_noul, jev_decide) over Streamable HTTP at /mcp with a shared bearer token. It is a thin wrapper that POSTs {state, model, questions} to {TYPESAFE_API_BASE}/systemone. Designed to be deployed as a Docker + Caddy remote service (Tailscale or public VPS), not as a local stdio server.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet shipped. Instructions say 'gather evidence first, then pass as state', which does not tell Claude when in a coding workflow to prefer Jev. Claude will rarely call it unprompted for coding; to get auto use you must add your own CLAUDE.md rule or a skill/hook on top.
security: Auth: single static shared bearer token, hmac.compare_digest (src/auth.py:32); /health exempt. Token lives in Claude Code MCP config headers (plain in .mcp.json / ~/.claude.json unless ${VAR} expansion used); not in argv since transport is http, not a spawned process.

MCP_HOST default 0.0.0.0 (config.py:108); Docker binds app to 127.0.0.1:9020 and exposes Caddy :8443 to all interfaces, so on a machine with a public IP the endpoint is internet-reachable unless firewalled.
Default caddy config uses tls internal (self-signed) so clients must skip verification or install root CA; README suggests -k / verify=False.
Upstream API key kept server-side, never logged or returned; error detail truncated to 500 chars (jev_client.py:265-276).
Logging: state never logged unless JEV_LOG_STATE=true (config.py:111, logging_setup.py:66-68); per-call JSON line with tool, latency, usage, confidence.

No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall. deploy/deploy.sh + bootstrap_remote.sh do SSH/rsync, install Docker from download.docker.com via apt (only relevant for remote deploy). Dockerfile installs curl, runs as non-root uid 10001.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude places in the `state` argument (arbitrary text/JSON: code snippets, diffs, file contents, logs, error messages, requirements) plus question/options/criteria, sent over HTTPS to the jev-mcp host you run (extra hop, its logs), then to TypeSafe/OpenRouter (and OpenRouter's upstream provider). Nothing is sent automatically by the server; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool. No hooks, so no passive capture of prompts/tool outputs. For client projects, code snippets in `state` leave the machine to two extra third parties (your relay VM if remote, OpenRouter/TypeSafe); the existing secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tool args (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level: all Jev errors (auth, 429, timeout, connection, bad JSON) are caught and returned as {ok:false, error:{type,message}} (server.py:161-163, 392-394), nothing fabricated. Upstream timeout defaults to 30 s (config.py:106, connect 10 s), which is long if Jev stalls; no retries, no fallback. If the jev-mcp service itself is down or the cert is untrusted, Claude Code marks the MCP server failed and the tools just vanish (no session block). Missing env vars: server refuses to start (main() SystemExit) though module loads with _startup_error and tools return error.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools plus server instructions. Approx: 4 tool descriptions (docstrings ~377+942+667+688+1193 chars including module doc, so ~3.5k chars of tool docs) + JSON schemas (state: Any, nested dict/list params, ~1.5k chars) + server instructions ~640 chars = roughly 5.5-6k chars = ~1.4-1.8k tokens per session when tools are loaded (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch). No hook-injected text.
pros: Genuine Jev wrapper with all three primitives and a batch tool (jev_decide) that maps 1:1 to the native multi-question System One request (server.py:297-394, jev_client.py:204-262).
OpenRouter switch is env-only: TYPESAFE_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (config.py:104) + OpenRouter key; body schema state/model/questions is what OpenRouter's System One API documents.
Clean, small, readable code (~700 LOC); honest error handling that never fabricates confidence (jev_client.py, server.py:161); state not logged by default.
Typed numeric outputs limit prompt-injection from tool results; constant-time token compare; non-root container; MIT.
Batching guidance in tool docs reduces round trips.
cons: Built as a remote Docker+Caddy service for Open WebUI/Tailscale/Oracle VM; for one dev laptop it is heavy: needs Docker, self-signed CA trust or -k equivalent, hardcoded host IP list in Caddyfile, or you must hand-run python -m src with MCP_HOST overridden (undocumented path).
Zero auto-invocation machinery: no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md guidance for coding. Directly conflicts with the user's 'Claude must use it without me asking' requirement.
Requires an extra relay hop: code snippets in `state` pass through the relay before OpenRouter; client-project data egress and an additional secret (MCP_AUTH_TOKEN) to manage.
Immature and unproven: created 2026-09-23, 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no CI, README admits the public deploy flow was not run live in its current form; no live verification against OpenRouter.
Env names TYPESAFE_* and default base api.typesafe.ai/v1; no native OPENROUTER_* vars; pinned to /systemone (not /alpha/decisions).
30 s default timeout, no retry/fallback, sync in the model loop; 4 tools with permissive `state: Any` schema add ~1.5k tokens of context each session.
Author's own README targets non-coding use (stock picking, support routing); nothing about diffs, code review, or test triage.
Tool args bypass existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard (matcher excludes mcp__ tools).
entries.verdict: A correct but generic, day-old Jev wrapper whose only path to OpenRouter is a base-URL env override; it gives Claude Code discretionary tools but no automatic-trigger mechanism and its Docker/Caddy remote-deploy design is overkill for a local dev workflow. Useful only as a reference for the tool schema; better to write a tiny local stdio MCP or hook that calls OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone directly.

entries.name: Mokusei-Hana/Jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, one 241-line server.py) written for Codex that wraps TypeSafe's System One API. It exposes four tools (jev_choose, jev_judge, jev_score, jev_decide) that POST state plus typed questions to a hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone endpoint. It validates the response strictly (answer IDs, probability keys, sum-to-1, choice equals argmax) and adds local needs_review hints from thresholds: confidence below 0.7, or Noul probability between 0.2 and 0.8. There is no hook, skill or proxy layer. README and comments are in Chinese.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. Claude Code will call them if the tool descriptions and server instructions persuade it. There is no deterministic trigger: no hook, skill or proxy. The repo's AGENTS.snippet.md is a Codex-oriented nudge, and an equivalent CLAUDE.md snippet would be needed to raise call frequency. Opus 5.5 rarely delegates small judgments to an external classifier without a strong prompt, so this does not deliver truly automatic use.
security: API key is read from the process environment (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put on argv. The Codex example passes it via env_vars, which suits Claude Code's .mcp.json env expansion.
httpx redirects are disabled to protect the key (server.py:96). Error bodies are not surfaced, so state and key are not echoed back (server.py:149-155).

The only network egress is the single hardcoded HTTPS POST. No shell execution, no file reads, no telemetry, no postinstall. Source is 241 lines and easy to audit. Dependencies are mcp, httpx[socks] and pydantic, all reputable.

The install is git clone + uv sync from an unpinned default branch, with no release tags. Running uv run executes whatever is on disk, so the user should pin a commit hash and review it before trusting it.

Prompt-injection surface is low: the server returns only numeric or label decisions with no free text. Model-controlled inputs (state, options) are sent outward. The response is strictly validated, and the README states that output is advisory and never authorization.
No license file (licenseInfo null). Default copyright applies, so the code is legally unlicensed for reuse or forking, which matters for client projects.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes in the tool arguments: state (any JSON: error text, code snippets, diffs, facts), question text and option descriptions. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai; through a patched OpenRouter route it would go to openrouter.ai and then TypeSafe. The server itself reads no files and runs no commands. Nothing is sent automatically. Egress happens only when the model chooses to call a tool, but on client projects Claude can pass proprietary code inside state. The existing secret-leak guard hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it would not cover mcp__jev__* arguments unless the matcher is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for Claude, no hang. There is a 15 s total deadline (asyncio.timeout plus httpx timeout, configurable up to 120 s) and no retries (server.py:96,138). Timeout, network error, non-200 or an invalid response becomes an MCP tool error with a short message telling the model to keep reasoning (server.py:144-160). A missing key gives a tool error, not a crash. The Codex example sets tool_timeout_sec=25. In Claude Code a slow Jev only costs one failed tool call, but 15 s is long if it stalls. A missing key only errors at call time, so the server still starts.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. The tool schemas are dominated by the nested Question model in jev_decide (JsonValue unions), roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens for all tool names, descriptions and schemas (estimated, not measured). Server instructions add about 140 tokens. There are no hooks, so no per-turn injection. Total is roughly 2k tokens resident, which is moderate for a low-utility toolset. Tool search or deferred loading in Claude Code 2.1.x may reduce this.
pros: Small, readable, well-defended adapter: 241 lines, strict schema validation (server.py:52-86), no redirects, no error-body leakage, and no shell or file access. Realistic to audit in 10 minutes and safe to run locally.
Explicit fail-open design: 15 s hard deadline, no retries, and errors told to the model as 'continue reasoning'. It cannot block a Claude Code session.
Uses the native System One schema (state/questions/answers), which OpenRouter also serves, so the OpenRouter switch is a 3-line patch. jev_decide batches up to 64 questions into one call.
Local needs_review thresholds (confidence under 0.7, Noul 0.2-0.8) give Claude a sane 'don't trust this' signal. The README states plainly that this is not authorization.
Tests use MockTransport (tests/test_server.py) and require no API key.
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint (server.py:140) and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, so it does not work with OpenRouter without editing source. The user has no TypeSafe direct key and wants OpenRouter.
Not automatic in Claude Code. It is MCP-tool-only, so it depends on model discretion. The only nudge is a Codex AGENTS snippet in Chinese, and there is no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md integration.
Built for Codex, not Claude Code: no .mcp.json, no plugin manifest, no Claude Code docs. The user would write the config and patch the code themselves.
Very immature: created 2026-09-22, 2 commits from 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE (legally unusable for client work), and an empty repo description. Unpinned uv sync from main.
Data egress is model-controlled: Claude can put code or diffs from client projects into state. The existing secret guard hook does not cover mcp__jev__* calls.

Marginal value for an Opus-class agent: each call costs an extra turn plus about 2k resident context tokens for choices Opus can make itself. The output has no reasoning trace, and the Jev quality claim is disputed (unverified 'flash router' skepticism).
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, well-validated but tiny and unlicensed Codex-oriented MCP wrapper. It is TypeSafe-only with a hardcoded URL, and it offers no automatic invocation in Claude Code beyond model discretion. It is usable as a reference implementation of the System One client and response validation, but a poor turnkey pick. If the user wants an MCP, a 3-line OpenRouter fork of it (or a clean rewrite) is realistic, though the license gap means rewriting is safer.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo is null)

entries.name: masaki-shinkawa/jev-mcp
entries.what: Minimal stdio MCP server (TypeScript, ~150 LOC) exposing one tool, jev_decide(context, question, choices). It POSTs a single-question 'choice' request to {JEV_API_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone with model 'jev-latest' and returns {choice, confidence, scores}. README is largely about running it behind OpenAI's Secure MCP Tunnel Client (author-specific /home/ms paths), which is irrelevant to Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool description is a one-liner ('Ask Jev to choose among the supplied options...') with no guidance on when to use it, so Claude will rarely call it unprompted. Would need a CLAUDE.md rule or a companion skill/hook to trigger reliably; nothing in this repo provides that.
security: API key read only from process env; sent solely as Bearer header; never in argv if registered with env (claude mcp add -e). Not logged.
No shell exec, no postinstall script, no telemetry, no curl|sh; only deps are MCP SDK and zod (lockfile present).
JEV_API_BASE_URL is fully attacker/user-controllable: if pointed at a wrong host, the key and context are sent there; no https enforcement.
Prompt-injection surface small: returns only a choice label + numbers, but the model-supplied 'context' is free-form and forwarded verbatim; upstream error bodies are not surfaced (only HTTP status).
No fetch timeout/AbortSignal (jev-client.ts:90), so a hung request blocks the tool call until the MCP client timeout.
README/deploy files reference OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel Client and a systemd unit for the author's account; irrelevant and unused for local stdio use.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude passes as context/question/choices in the tool call (arbitrary JSON: could be code snippets, diffs, file contents, tool output) is sent to the configured base URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if overridden). Nothing is sent automatically; only what the model chooses to put in the call. No secret filtering, so the existing secret-leak guard hook would not cover MCP tool args unless its matcher is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: errors (missing key, non-2xx, invalid JSON, schema mismatch) are returned as isError text without crashing the server, so Claude just proceeds without Jev. Weakness: no client-side timeout or retry, so a slow/hung Jev stalls the call until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout; and if the server fails to start, the MCP shows as failed (nothing blocks). Missing key only errors at call time, not startup.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. Approx 90 chars description + name + JSON schema (context any-JSON union, question, choices record) roughly 700-900 chars, so about 200-250 tokens always loaded (or deferred behind ToolSearch). No server 'instructions' field, no hook-injected text, no resources/prompts.
pros: Tiny, fully auditable (about 150 LOC), MIT, no postinstall/telemetry/shell; only two deps.
Points at the same /v1/systemone path that OpenRouter exposes; base URL and key are env-configurable, so JEV_API_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api is nearly a drop-in (jev-client.ts:84,90).
Fail-open design: errors returned as isError results, never crash; returns compact structured {choice, confidence, scores} that Claude can branch on.
Cheap context footprint (one tool, ~200-250 tokens).
Zod validation of the response and unit tests with a stubbed fetch.
cons: Does not satisfy the 'automatic, never prompt' requirement: a bare MCP tool with a vague description gives no deterministic trigger; no hook, skill, or CLAUDE.md guidance included.

Hard-coded model 'jev-latest' (jev-client.ts:98) is a TypeSafe-direct name; OpenRouter needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest, so a code patch is required, and OpenRouter schema equivalence is unverified (docs fetch 404).
Only the Choice primitive; no Noul (yes/no) or Score, and no Decisions API, which are the more useful primitives for gating decisions (e.g. 'is this a risky change?').

Age 5 days, 0 stars, 2 commits, 1 author, no releases/CI, not on npm; needs clone+build and own maintenance. README is mostly OpenAI Secure Tunnel instructions with hard-coded /home/ms paths (noise for Claude Code).
No fetch timeout or retry; a slow upstream stalls the tool call. No https/base-URL validation.
Sends model-chosen context (potentially code/diffs) to a third party with no redaction and outside the existing secret-guard matcher (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
Jev has no reasoning trace and is a 32k-context beta classifier; as an on-demand tool it adds a model turn and 1-3 s latency for a decision Opus could usually make itself.
entries.verdict: A clean but very thin single-tool PoC whose only value is as a reference/starting point: with JEV_API_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and a one-line model patch it would probably talk to OpenRouter System One, but it offers no automatic triggering, only the Choice primitive, and has no maturity. Fork it for own wrapper (add Noul/Score, timeout, model env) and pair with a hook/CLAUDE.md rule rather than adopting as is.

entries.name: tijo95/jev-mcp
entries.what: Single-file (458 lines), stdlib-only Python stdio MCP server. Exposes 6 jev_* tools that each translate a small typed argument set into a TypeSafe System One request (state + one Choice question with hard-coded criteria) and POST it to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone using a spoofed Chrome/Windows User-Agent to dodge the Cloudflare WAF (Error 1010) on the official remote MCP (jevai.org/api/mcp). Returns the raw JSON (probabilities) as text plus structuredContent. jev_decide is a raw pass-through for arbitrary choice/noul/score questions.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no server instructions, no CLAUDE.md snippet. Claude will call jev_* only if the terse tool descriptions ("Immediately before a consequential tool call...") persuade Opus to do so; in practice Opus rarely calls advisory tools unprompted, and jev_guard_tool_call relies on the model self-reporting its own action, so it is not deterministic and not enforced. Would need extra scaffolding (PreToolUse/Stop hook or CLAUDE.md rules) to meet the user's 'automatic' requirement.
security: API key read from env only, never logged (log line at :428-433 prints only key_set yes/no); not in argv if passed via env. Note `claude mcp add -e` stores the key in ~/.claude.json plaintext.

Sends Bearer key with a deliberately spoofed Chrome-on-Windows User-Agent (:49, :197) to evade Cloudflare WAF; TypeSafe/Cloudflare may treat as bot-evasion and could block it; not a vulnerability but ToS-adjacent and fragile.
If key is empty, it still sends the request unauthenticated (:198 `if API_KEY`), producing 401 rather than a clear local error.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, no eval, no postinstall; only one outbound host (api.typesafe.ai). Single 458-line file, easily auditable, low supply-chain surface (no deps).

Prompt-injection surface: response is model-generated JSON of probabilities; low injection risk, but the jev_decide `state` is free-form and `criteria` strings are attacker-influenceable if the calling model copies untrusted repo text into them. Advisory guard verdicts (allow) could be steered by injected content, so it must not be treated as a security boundary.
Unpinned: a git clone with later `git pull` runs whatever the author pushes; 1 anonymous maintainer, 0 stars. Pin to a commit hash if used.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model puts into tool arguments: task descriptions, claims, evidence strings, action/side-effect/policy summaries, completed_work/known_gaps text, candidate model descriptions, or arbitrary `state` JSON in jev_decide. Nothing is collected automatically (no file reads, no diffs, no transcript access). Because the model composes the args, it can include code snippets or client-confidential text if it chooses; the existing secret-leak guard hook only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* tools, so secrets in args would not be scanned. Destination: api.typesafe.ai (direct), not OpenRouter as shipped.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: any HTTP error, network error or timeout is returned as an MCP result with isError=true and the raw text (:205-214, :365-375); the server never blocks Claude Code. 30 s urlopen timeout (:202) is far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms, so a hung endpoint stalls the calling turn up to 30 s per call, with no retry, no backoff, no circuit breaker; synchronous single-threaded loop means calls serialize. Missing key yields 401 errors on every call rather than startup failure. Because it is an advisory tool, an error just means Claude proceeds without a verdict.
entries.contextCost: 6 tools. Tool defs (names + descriptions + JSON schemas) are about 3.6k characters, roughly 900-1,000 tokens; in Claude Code 2.1.x with MCP tool search/deferred loading, only names cost until fetched. No MCP `instructions` field and no hook-injected text, so nothing else. Results are pretty-printed JSON (indent=2) duplicated in both content text and structuredContent, modest (a few hundred tokens per call).
pros: Tiny, fully auditable single file with zero dependencies, no shell exec, no telemetry, no install scripts; can be read in 5 minutes and vendored.

Payload already matches System One (state/model/questions with choice criteria) and uses Bearer auth, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone is a ~4-line patch (URL, env var, model id, UA).
jev_decide passthrough exposes all three primitives (choice/noul/score) so a custom-question workflow is possible, and `model` can be overridden per call.
Preset tools map well to real agent decision points (guard a tool call, review completion, route task), which is the right use for a System One model.
Dependency-free Python 3.10+ runs on the user's Python 3.13 without uvx/pip; fail-soft (never crashes Claude Code, returns isError).
cons: Does not support OpenRouter as shipped: URL and key env var are hardcoded to TypeSafe direct (:45-46); the user would have to fork/patch and maintain it.

Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool with no hook, skill or instructions. Fails the user's core requirement ('Claude Code must use it when needed') unless combined with separate hook/CLAUDE.md scaffolding.

guard_tool_call is advisory and self-reported by the same model that may be prompt-injected; does not block anything and is not wired to PreToolUse, so gives false assurance in bypass/auto permission modes.
Immature: 3 days old, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file despite README claiming MIT.
Spoofed browser User-Agent to evade Cloudflare is a hack that may break or violate TypeSafe terms; irrelevant/unneeded on OpenRouter.
30 s timeout with no retry, plus synchronous serial loop; a stalled call freezes a turn far longer than Jev's advertised sub-second latency.

Outputs are raw probability JSON with no thresholds/interpretation, and the 5 presets are generic (not coding-specific like 'is this diff safe to commit', 'should tests run'); little concrete daily-coding value from Opus 5.5 self-invoking them.
Secrets or client code the model puts in args bypass the existing secret-leak hook (matcher does not cover mcp__* tools), and it sends data to a third party on client projects.
Duplicated payload (text + structuredContent) wastes context tokens per call.
entries.verdict: A clean, readable 458-line proof-of-concept wrapper that is TypeSafe-direct only and purely model-discretion, so it does not meet the 'automatic, no prompting' goal on its own. Useful mainly as a reference/patch base (change 4 lines for OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone) for a hook-driven integration; not recommended as-is for daily coding or client work.
entries.license: README says MIT, but no LICENSE file and GitHub licenseInfo is null (effectively unlicensed/ambiguous)

entries.name: resumocast/jev-mcp
entries.what: Zero-dependency Go stdio MCP server exposing one tool, evaluate (noul/choice/score typed judgments), plus an opt-in select_evidence tool behind --enable-selection. It POSTs to a hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone using a key read only from a 0600 file. The main deliverable is a Pi coding agent extension (adapters/pi/jev.ts, 3.3k lines TypeScript). Claude Code is not a supported target. The README says other MCP hosts need their own setup. It is a community client, not from TypeSafe, and derives from itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp.
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. Claude decides whether to call the MCP tool, guided by the tool description and server instructions. Nothing is deterministic (no hook, skill trigger or proxy). The README says 'the model will pick this tool' is not established. The tool description is written defensively ('Do not call it merely to confirm your conclusion'), which likely lowers the call rate in Claude Code. This does not meet the user's 'automatic without prompting' requirement, except in the weak sense that the tool is always visible.
security: Key handling is unusually careful: file only, mode exactly 0600, owned by the user, opened with O_NOFOLLOW|O_NONBLOCK and checked via the descriptor (key_unix.go). It is never read from env or argv, so it cannot leak to `ps`. This conflicts with an OpenRouter workflow, where the key normally comes from OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Network is fixed to one URL. Proxy is nil, so HTTPS_PROXY is ignored. Redirects are not followed, so the bearer token cannot be replayed elsewhere (client.go:57-88). TLS 1.2 or newer. Errors omit HTTP bodies.
Resource bounds: 16 questions, 64 KiB request, 128 KiB response, depth 8, 30s deadline, at most 2 retries and only on 429/529. Child env is HOME, PATH and LANG only.
No postinstall, curl|sh, telemetry or self-update. Zero Go dependencies. Dev-only npm deps are pinned. The MCP server runs no shell.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are structured numbers only, with no free text, so the surface is small. The model does choose which state to send out, and the tool description tells it not to include secrets, but nothing enforces that on the server side.

Provenance risk: 1 author, 0 stars, 10 days old, history-free 'public snapshot' export. Release binaries are darwin-only with SHA256SUMS, unsigned. You would have to audit the code and compile it yourself. The maintainer uses 'ACTION-7' and 'CONTROL-N' internal tags. No SECURITY policy.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts in evaluate.state and the question instructions and criteria, or the items of select_evidence. In practice that means code snippets, diffs, logs, file excerpts and issue or commit text the model chooses to send. This goes to api.typesafe.ai, a direct TypeSafe account, not OpenRouter, so it means a second vendor relationship. That matters for client projects under NDA. Nothing is sent automatically or in the background. Each call is paid and transmits the content. There is no telemetry, and jev.ts in Pi may retain tool args and results in the session transcript.
entries.failureMode: Fails closed and per call. Any error, timeout (30s API deadline, 40s tool-call bound in server.go:73), invalid response, model mismatch or bad distribution returns an MCP tool error (isError) with a generic message. It never returns a guess. The main model sees the error and continues without Jev, so nothing hangs the session. But an invalid or missing key file makes the server exit at startup (main.go run() returns a 'credential:' error), which shows as a failed MCP server. One in-flight evaluation per runner, no queue. The 30s worst case blocks that turn.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (evaluate), or 2 with --enable-selection. Approximate token counts are chars/4 estimates. evaluate description is about 1.0k chars and the schema about 2.3k chars, roughly 800-900 tokens. The server 'instructions' are about 1.5k chars, roughly 400 tokens. That is about 1.2-1.4k tokens per session for evaluate alone. With select_evidence add about 2.2k chars, roughly 550 tokens. Claude Code may defer MCP tool schemas via tool search, which would cut the schema part. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text.
pros: The best-engineered security posture among Jev clients I can imagine: 0600 key file with O_NOFOLLOW, key never in argv or env, fixed endpoint, no redirects, no proxy, bounded sizes, fail-closed validation, and zero Go dependencies (only stdlib).
Small, readable Go server: about 2.9k non-test lines of Go, easy to audit and fork. The wire schema (state, model, questions) matches System One, so an OpenRouter port is a small patch.
The MCP server is a real, standard stdio server (initialize, tools/list, tools/call), so it can be registered in Claude Code with `claude mcp add` even though only Pi is documented.
Honest README: says workflow value is unproven, lists limits, warns against using Jev for authorization, arithmetic or code generation. Tool descriptions steer away from misuse.
MIT license. Only 1-2 tools, so context cost is modest (about 1.3k tokens). Extensive offline test suite including fuzzing.
cons: No OpenRouter support by design. The README says 'No OpenRouter... no endpoint or model override' and 'alternate providers' are out of scope. It requires a TypeSafe direct account and key, which contradicts the requirement to use the OpenRouter-hosted Jev. An OpenRouter port means maintaining a fork, and the model-pin validator would also need patching (response.go:134).

Target is the Pi agent, not Claude Code. The main adapter is Pi-only and no Claude Code config, plugin, hook or skill ships. Release binaries are darwin only, so on Linux you must build with Go 1.27.1 yourself (the Makefile targets darwin only).

Cannot be automatic. It is a model-discretion tool with a defensive description, and the README says whether the model will pick it is not established. There are no hooks and no deterministic trigger, so it does not meet the 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so' requirement.
Key must be a 0600 file. No env var support, so the OPENROUTER_API_KEY workflow does not fit. Starting the server without the file makes it exit and show as a failed MCP server.
Immature and unproven: 7 commits over 2 days, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no CI, history-free public export, no Linux artifacts, no evidence of real-world value or cost savings.

Data egress to a second vendor (TypeSafe) whenever it is called. The model decides what code or context to send, which is a concern for client projects. There are still no hard guards beyond a prompt-level 'no secrets' rule.

Judgments are only as good as the state Claude writes into the question, and Claude must spend output tokens composing state and rubrics. That can cost more than a direct main-model decision for the small coding tasks Jev suits.
entries.verdict: A well-built but Pi-first, TypeSafe-direct-only, model-discretion MCP with no OpenRouter path and no Claude Code integration, so it fails the two core requirements: OpenRouter hosting and automatic invocation. Worth reading as a reference implementation (its key handling and validators are good) or forking as a base. I would not install it as-is for daily Claude Code use.

entries.name: kevinqpeng/jev-mcp
entries.what: Tiny (82-line, zero-dependency) hand-rolled stdio MCP server exposing one tool, jev_ask, which forwards {state, questions, model} to TypeSafe's direct System One endpoint and returns the raw JSON body as text. Header comment says it was written so Codex can delegate decisions to Jev. Not published to npm; installed by git clone + npm install --global ./jev-mcp.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. Claude Code will only call jev_ask if the model judges it useful from the tool description. The description does say 'Use it for judgments and decisions: classify or route, rate on a rubric, check whether something holds', which is a reasonable nudge, but there are no hooks, no skill and no CLAUDE.md snippet, so Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for it in ordinary coding, because it can decide such things itself. Achieving 'automatic when it adds value' would need extra scaffolding (CLAUDE.md rules or a hook) that this repo does not provide.
security: The whole server is one 82-line file with no dependencies and no postinstall script, so it is trivially auditable, and I read all of it. It contains no shell execution, no filesystem access, no telemetry and no extra network calls; the only outbound call is the fetch to api.typesafe.ai (server.mjs:40).

The API key is read from process.env inside the server (:39, :42), so it is not in argv if supplied via claude mcp add -e. It is not logged. The server would return the upstream error body to the model (:46), which could echo request details.
No fetch timeout or AbortController (:40), so a hung upstream can block the tool call indefinitely.

The tool returns the raw upstream JSON text to the model. Jev output is typed probabilities, so the prompt-injection surface from the response is small. The main injection risk is the reverse: whatever the model puts in state is sent to a third party.

Provenance risk: a brand-new personal repo by one author with 2 commits, no license and no release. Pin a commit SHA or vendor the file rather than tracking it. Global install runs npm install --global from a clone, which links the bin; there are no install scripts in package.json.

Protocol robustness is minimal: silent drop of malformed JSON lines (:59-62), and initialize echoes the client's protocolVersion without negotiation. It works for basic tools but is not spec-complete (no ping, no resources or prompts).
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the state and questions arguments goes to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe directly, not OpenRouter as shipped). That could be code, diffs, file contents or tool output if the model chooses to include them. Nothing is sent automatically; the server only forwards what Claude passes in the tool call. Also sent: the bearer key and the model id. After patching to OpenRouter, the data would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. For client projects, the user should consider NDA and confidentiality implications, since the model decides what goes into state.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense that the tool simply returns an error to Claude (isError, or JSON-RPC -32603 when the key is missing or the fetch throws) and Claude continues without Jev. Nothing is blocked because there are no hooks. There is no timeout, retry or fallback, though, so a slow or hung upstream stalls that tool call until the MCP client's own tool timeout fires. The MCP server itself never crashes on network errors (they are caught at :79-81).
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. Tool definition is about 1.6k characters (description about 570 chars plus schema and property descriptions about 1000), so roughly 400 tokens (chars/4) in the tool list. No server instructions field is returned (initialize returns only capabilities and serverInfo). No hook-injected text. If Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas via ToolSearch, only the name is loaded until needed. Very light.
pros: Smallest possible attack and context footprint: one file of 82 lines, zero dependencies, no postinstall, about 400 tokens of tool definition. I fully audited it, and forking it costs nothing.

The tool description is well written for model-discretion use: it states what Jev is for (classify/route, score, noul), what it is not for (no code, no prose), and tells the model to batch independent questions in one call. It is the best of the small MCP wrappers in this respect.
OpenRouter switch is about 3 lines: swap the endpoint constant (server.mjs:6), key env var (:39, :42) and model id (:7), assuming the OpenRouter System One request schema matches (unverified).
The key stays in the server process env, not on the command line, when registered with claude mcp add -e.
Errors are surfaced to the model as isError rather than crashing the server.
cons: Hardcodes api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, with no OpenRouter support and no base-URL override, so it does not meet the user's stated OpenRouter requirement without patching.
No license, so legally you cannot fork or redistribute it, and for client work vendoring unlicensed code is a compliance smell. In practice the file is trivial enough to rewrite from scratch.
Zero maturity: 2 commits in one day, one author, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, and no npm package. It was written for Codex, not Claude Code, so nothing is tested against Claude Code.
No timeout on fetch (:40), so a slow Jev can stall a turn.
No automatic integration: purely a model-discretion tool with no hook, skill or CLAUDE.md guidance. Opus 5.5 will seldom call it unprompted, which contradicts the user's core requirement.

Passes model output straight through with no formatting or validation, and passes arbitrary questions through with additionalProperties: true, so a malformed question surfaces only as an upstream 4xx string.

Nothing prevents the model from sending sensitive code or client data to a third party. There is no redaction and no interplay with the user's existing secret-leak guard hook, which matches only Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__*.
Protocol implementation is hand-rolled and minimal (no ping, no protocol negotiation, silent drop of bad JSON), which could break with future Claude Code MCP versions.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe-to-read 82-line proof of concept that shows the minimal shape of a Jev MCP tool, but it is TypeSafe-direct only, unlicensed, untested and has no auto-invocation mechanism. Use it at most as a reference to write your own OpenRouter-pointed wrapper (3-line patch plus a timeout), not as the integration itself.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file, GitHub licenseInfo null, package.json has no license field), so all rights reserved by default

entries.name: ThePFMind/jev-mcp
entries.what: Minimal Python stdio MCP server (mcp SDK 2.x MCPServer, httpx, pydantic) with two tools that POST to TypeSafe System One (/v1/systemone). jev_evaluate takes state plus any mix of noul/choice/score questions. jev_route takes one choice question plus a confidence threshold and returns choice, confidence, probabilities and an escalate flag. It is a generic wrapper with no Claude Code specific logic, hooks or skills, so it runs only if Claude decides to call the tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The descriptions say to use it for classification, routing, urgency scoring or yes/no checks, but Claude Code (Opus) has no natural reason to call a small classifier during coding, so it will rarely if ever fire without being told. The generic 'not for text generation' framing gives no coding trigger. No hook, no skill, no proxy. It does not meet the requirement of automatic use without prompting; that would need a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a hook layered on top.
security: API key is read from env or a plaintext .env in the repo root (chmod 600 advised); never placed in argv, which is good. The README registration carries no secrets. The key is sent as a Bearer header to jev-ai.pro, a host other than the documented docs.typesafe.ai; the user must trust that domain (it answered with a JSON 404 to HEAD on 2026-09-30).
No shell execution, no postinstall or curl|sh. Pure Python; dependencies mcp>=2.0 (2.2.0 exists on PyPI), httpx, pydantic, all unpinned (>=).

No telemetry in code. Not published to PyPI; a different, unrelated PyPI package named jev-mcp (Aitejiu, jev-harness-lab) exists, so a naive uvx jev-mcp or pip install jev-mcp would fetch the wrong package (typosquat/name-collision risk). Must be installed from a local clone or a git URL.
Prompt-injection surface: the model output is only numeric probabilities and enum labels, which is low. The main risk is what Claude chooses to send as state.
API errors return resp.text verbatim to Claude (client.py:111,113), which is untrusted-ish content in context. Retries only on 429/529 (up to 3 with exponential backoff).
No license file (licenseInfo null), so the code is technically all-rights-reserved; forking or patching for client work is legally unclear.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude passes in the state and questions arguments of a tool call goes to https://jev-ai.pro/api/v1/systemone (or the OpenRouter URL if repointed) along with the Bearer key. Nothing is sent automatically, no repo scanning and no hooks. In practice this means whatever code, diff, log or ticket text Claude decides to put in state, with a 32k limit for state plus the longest question (README:67). This matters for client projects. There is no redaction.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the MCP sense. Each JevError is caught and returned as a JSON {"error": ...} string, so Claude just sees a tool error and continues. Timeout is httpx 30s, with up to 3 retries on 429/529 (sleeps of 1s, 2s, 4s), so the worst case is roughly 30s+ per attempt or more than 1.5 minutes stalled on repeated 429s. A missing key raises JevError inside get_client() (server.py:25). Line 102 is inside the try, so it returns an error string rather than crashing the server. jev_route does result["answers"]["route"] outside the try (server.py:135), so a malformed or changed response raises an unhandled KeyError or TypeError, which MCP reports as a tool error.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools plus a 1-line server instruction. Approx 700 to 1000 tokens: nested pydantic JSON Schema ($defs Question with type/instructions/criteria anyOf, plus RouteInput) and two multi-line descriptions, roughly 3 to 4k chars. Modest, and an acceptable one-time cost; no hook-injected text.
pros: Smallest possible surface: 2 tools, about 250 lines of Python, a readable client, no shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall.
Key never appears in argv or the MCP config (loaded from env or .env), unlike most stdio MCP examples.
jev_route gives a ready confidence-gated escalate flag, which is the right primitive for gating decisions.
Correct request path (/v1/systemone) and Bearer auth that match OpenRouter's System One API, so repointing via JEV_AI_API_BASE is nearly config-only.
Tests use respx mocks for the happy path, escalation, validation and the dotenv edge cases (BOM, CRLF), plus a 3-OS x 3-Python CI matrix and a v0.1.0 release.
Works in Claude Code with a one-line 'claude mcp add jev -s user' and about 1k tokens of context.
cons: Does not satisfy the core requirement: nothing triggers it automatically. Pure model-discretion tool with generic non-coding descriptions, so Opus will almost never call it.

Not OpenRouter-native: default host is jev-ai.pro with JEV_AI_API_KEY and model jev-latest. Model ids on OpenRouter need the typesafe/ prefix; the model default is hardcoded in the pydantic schema, so JEV_DEFAULT_MODEL does not work for tool calls (server.py:71,83,105,131).
Response contract on OpenRouter is unverified; jev_route has an unguarded dict index (server.py:135).
Brand-new one-person repo: 6 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, created 2026-09-21 and last pushed the same day. No issues, no maintenance history.
No license (all rights reserved by default) which is a problem for client work.

No install-from-registry: the PyPI name jev-mcp belongs to a different project (Aitejiu/jev-harness-lab), so the user must clone and run a local venv (or uv --from git+URL) and must not run uvx jev-mcp.
Sends whatever Claude puts into state to a third-party host with no redaction, on top of existing client-confidentiality concerns; no allowlist or size cap (32k model limit only, README:67).
Extra Claude turn per Jev call makes it slower and costlier than just letting Opus decide; no batching, and the example use cases are ticket triage, not code work.
Retry loop sleeps in the request path (1+2+4 s) with a 30 s per-attempt timeout, so degraded upstream can stall a tool call for more than a minute.
Dependency pins are only lower bounds (mcp>=2.0 on a fast-moving SDK 2.x).
entries.verdict: A clean, tiny and safe-looking reference wrapper, but it is a manually-invoked classifier tool with no automation layer and no native OpenRouter support (needs JEV_AI_API_BASE plus a model-id patch). Useful as a base to fork (add a license, OpenRouter defaults, hook/skill triggers), not as the automatic integration on its own.
