entries.name: danna-zhou/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (TypeScript, 145 lines) exposing jev_ask (POST {JEV_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone with state + choice/score/noul questions) and jev_health (GET /v1/models). Also ships two optional Claude Code hooks: a PreToolUse Bash guardrail (regex pre-filter for git push/terraform apply/DROP TABLE etc., then Jev risk judgment -> deny/ask) and a Stop hook that scores every final assistant message for quality/accuracy and logs it to ~/.claude/jev-quality-log.jsonl (display-only). Targets TypeSafe Jev or a local Kev server.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. jev_ask/jev_health are model-discretion MCP tools; the description tells Claude to use them for reliable classification/scoring/yes-no, but nothing in the repo tells Claude WHEN in a coding workflow, so it will rarely call it unprompted. The hooks (PreToolUse Bash for a regex set of high-stakes commands; Stop every turn) are deterministic and truly automatic, but their use cases (risk gating, self-scoring of replies) are weak fits for a classifier model and Stop scoring is purely a dashboard.
security: API key read from env only; not in argv when set via 'claude mcp add -e' (stored in ~/.claude.json). Bearer sent only to JEV_BASE_URL; no logging of the key.
No shell execution in MCP server; hooks only call execFile('osascript') on darwin (irrelevant on Linux). No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh, no telemetry found.
Default JEV_BASE_URL is plain http://127.0.0.1:8009 with API_KEY 'local'; a missing/typo env silently points at localhost rather than failing loudly.

Prompt-injection surface: jev_ask returns Jev JSON only (typed probabilities), low injection risk; but state/criteria are model-authored and hook inputs (commands, assistant text) go to a third-party model. Hook stdout is trusted by Claude Code, so a compromised/impersonated endpoint could emit permissionDecision 'allow'-like output only if code were changed; current code only emits deny/ask.
No fetch timeout in the MCP server (index.ts:53) - a hung endpoint hangs the tool call; hooks have 8s AbortController timeout (lib.mjs:168).
Stop hook writes message previews of every assistant turn (may contain client code/secrets) to ~/.claude/jev-quality-log.jsonl unbounded, no rotation.
entries.dataEgress: MCP: whatever Claude puts into jev_ask state/questions (arbitrary code, diffs, file contents, tool output - model discretion) goes to JEV_BASE_URL (OpenRouter/TypeSafe). PreToolUse hook: full Bash command string, only for regex-matched high-stakes commands (may embed tokens/URLs/creds in args). Stop hook: the entire last assistant message of EVERY turn (can include code, file paths, client details). No egress of user prompts or files by the hooks themselves. On OpenRouter this also passes through OpenRouter's logging policy. Nothing else leaves the machine (no telemetry).
entries.failureMode: Hooks fail open: catch -> failOpen() emits systemMessage + additionalContext and exit 0 (lib.mjs:197-205); 8s timeout via AbortController. Bug risk: failOpen emits hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext even for the Stop event, which the author's own comment (stop-guardrail.mjs:191-195) says forces Claude to continue another turn, so an unreachable endpoint / 4xx (e.g. message exceeding 32k context, missing key) could trigger extra continuation turns after every stop (stop_hook_active guard stops loops but wastes a turn). Also uncaught TypeError if response shape differs (e.g. answers.risk undefined) is inside try so fail-open too. MCP tool: errors returned as isError text; no timeout, so a slow endpoint stalls the call. Also SDK-level MCP connect failure just drops the tools.
entries.contextCost: 2 MCP tools; approx 450 tokens total (jev_ask description ~640 chars + permissive zod schema with passthrough record/union types ~700 chars; jev_health ~250 chars). No MCP server 'instructions' field. Hooks inject nothing on success except Stop systemMessage summary (display only, ~100 chars); on failure additionalContext line (~120 chars) per event.
pros: Smallest possible integration: ~145-line server, env-only config, so pointing it at OpenRouter is just JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 (index.ts:16-18,53), no fork needed.

Ships real deterministic hooks (settings.json snippet in README:125-145) - the only pattern in this repo that gives 'automatic' use without prompting; PreToolUse regex pre-filter keeps non-risky Bash calls at zero API cost.
Fail-open with 8s timeout in hooks (lib.mjs:168,197) so a Jev outage won't block work in bypass/auto mode; low context cost (~450 tokens, 2 tools).
Clean, readable, dependency-light hooks (.mjs, no build) that are easy to audit and adapt; permission decision output uses correct hookSpecificOutput schema and 'ask' rather than only 'deny'.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh; API key only in env.
cons: Brand-new, 0 stars, 4 commits in one day by one author, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file; not published to npm so must clone+build; package-lock.json resolves to a private Skyscanner artifactory, so npm install may break.

Zero OpenRouter awareness: no OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling, hard-coded /v1/systemone path, default model 'kev-latest'; OpenRouter compatibility relies on unverified schema equivalence and users must set three env vars correctly (wrong/missing silently falls back to localhost:8009).

Value proposition for daily coding is thin: the hooks judge shell risk (which the user's existing secret guard and Claude Code's permission system already cover; a 'DeepSeek flash router'-class classifier is a weak safety judge) and score Claude's own replies (Stop dashboard is display-only and pointless for a subscription user).

Stop hook sends every full assistant message (client code included) to a third party each turn and stores previews in an unrotated local log; no truncation for the 32k context; adds latency at every turn end; macOS notification does nothing on Linux.

Probable bug: failOpen emits additionalContext for Stop events which the author himself notes forces a continuation turn; so endpoint failures can cause an extra Claude turn (token cost) rather than a clean skip.

jev_ask is passive: tool description gives Claude no coding-specific triggers, and the schema is loose (z.record(z.any()), passthrough), so the model must invent question schemas itself; likely rarely invoked.
MCP fetch has no timeout; hook overlaps/duplicates existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard on Bash, GitNexus) adding another node spawn per Bash call.
entries.verdict: Tiny, readable, env-configurable reference wiring (MCP tool plus Bash risk and Stop-score hooks) that could talk to OpenRouter with just JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL, but it is a week-old zero-star POC with no tests, a possible Stop-hook failure bug, and use cases (risk-gating, self-scoring) that add little for this user. Best treated as a code template to copy and harden (custom hooks, OpenRouter endpoint, truncation) rather than installed as-is.
entries.license: README and package.json say MIT, but no LICENSE file and GitHub reports no license (licenseInfo null)

entries.name: elyal2/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small (about 600 LOC Python) stdio/streamable-http MCP server wrapping the TypeSafe System One decision endpoint. It exposes 3 tools: health, decide (one state, several typed Choice/Score/Noul questions) and classify_batch (same questions across many items, with concurrency control). Retries with exponential backoff. Nothing beyond the MCP tools: NO hooks, NO skills, NO plugin manifest, NO .mcp.json. The discovery claim of "hook/skill docs" is wrong; the README only mentions Amazon Quick skills as motivation and shows a Claude Code registration snippet in OpenCode-style JSON, not Claude Code's mcpServers format.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook or skill ships with the repo, and the descriptions never tell Claude WHEN to consult Jev in a coding workflow (they talk about triaging documents/emails), so Claude will almost never call it unprompted. To get automatic use the user would need to add their own CLAUDE.md rules/skill/hook on top.
security: API key read from env or a relative '.env' file (config.py:22 env_file='.env' resolves against process CWD); when Claude Code launches the server the CWD is the project dir, so a project's own .env could be parsed for JEV_/TYPESAFE_ vars (extra='ignore' limits it to those names, but a client repo's .env with a different JEV_BASE_URL could redirect the key/state). Mitigate with 'uv run --directory' or explicit env.
Key sent only as Authorization Bearer header via httpx; not in argv if configured via env. health tool exposes masked key hint (4+2 chars) to the model.
No shell execution, no curl|sh, no postinstall; deps mcp>=2.2,<3, httpx, pydantic, pydantic-settings (uv.lock pinned).
Error messages include up to 500 chars of upstream response text returned into model context (client.py:147): minor prompt-injection surface only from the API host.
JEV_BASE_URL is an unrestricted URL: state is posted to whatever host is configured; no allowlist or TLS enforcement.
No telemetry. Logs are JSON to stderr; logs 'usage' and error strings, not state (logger.info decide.usage), item ids logged in batch.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts into the `state` argument of decide/classify_batch plus question instructions/criteria, sent to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if repointed). Nothing is sent automatically: no diffs, files or tool outputs unless Claude chooses to paste them into a call. Response usage metadata logged locally to stderr.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-slow then fail-closed-for-that-call. Per attempt timeout 30 s (config.py:32); retries 5 on network/timeout/429/5xx with backoff 2,4,8,16,32 s (+10% jitter) (retry.py, config.py:40-42). Worst case a single decide blocks about 6x30s + 62s = roughly 4 minutes before returning an MCP tool error. 4xx fails immediately. Since it's an MCP tool (not a hook), Claude just gets an error and continues, so nothing is blocked permanently, but the turn stalls. Tunable via JEV_TIMEOUT and JEV_RETRY_MAX_ATTEMPTS (should be set to about 5-8 s and 1 retry for interactive coding).
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. decide/classify_batch schemas embed a union of 3 pydantic models (Choice/Score/Noul) with descriptions in Spanish; estimated about 1,000-1,400 tokens total for tool names+descriptions+schemas (docstrings in server.py lines 48-110 about 2.5k chars plus JSON schema about 2.5k chars, /4). No MCP server 'instructions' set (MCPServer("jev") with no instructions), no hooks, no injected text. Tool descriptions are Spanish and describe email/document triage, not coding.
pros: Thin, readable, dependency-light wrapper (about 600 LOC); correct thin transport: Bearer auth + {model,state,questions} body matches the TypeSafe contract in client.py:131-142.
JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL env-configurable, so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a config change (no fork needed) if response shape matches.
Proper typed schemas for Choice/Score/Noul (models.py:162-186) so Claude gets constrained tool inputs; errors are real MCP errors, not disguised successes.
classify_batch is useful for bulk triage (e.g. classify many issues/log lines/files) with bounded concurrency.
Has 3 test files (about 234 lines) covering client, retry and server; mypy --strict, ruff, pre-commit config; uv.lock present; no shell/postinstall.
Small context footprint (3 tools).
cons: Not a hook or skill despite the discovery summary: no automatic-invocation mechanism at all; user's core requirement (Claude uses Jev without being told) is not met by this repo.

Repo is 6 days old (created 2026-09-24), 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE, empty description; author's paths hardcoded (/Users/install4/...) and README motivated by Amazon Quick, not Claude Code.

No OpenRouter support in code: default model 'jev-latest' is wrong for OpenRouter (needs typesafe/jev-latest), the alpha Decisions API is unsupported, and the client requires an 'answers' key that may not match OpenRouter's response.
Default retry policy (5 retries, 30 s timeout) can stall an interactive turn for about 4 minutes when Jev/OpenRouter is degraded.
Relative .env loading from CWD means project-level .env files in client repos can influence the server config (key/base URL) when launched without --directory.

Tool descriptions are Spanish and doc/email oriented; nothing coding-specific (no pre-built questions for e.g. 'is this change risky', 'should I run tests'), so the model must compose the typed question itself every time, costing tokens and reliability.
Jev returns only probabilities, so its coding value depends on someone wiring specific decision points; this MCP offers no such wiring.

Requires 'mcp>=2.2,<3' and Python 3.12+: fine for the user's 3.13 but pins to a new MCP SDK major that could conflict with uvx resolution; README registration snippet is not Claude Code's native .mcp.json format.
entries.verdict: A tidy but very young, unlicensed proof-of-concept MCP wrapper that gives Claude manual access to Jev's Choice/Score/Noul primitives; it is repointable to OpenRouter by env vars but has no hook, skill or auto-invocation logic, so it does not satisfy the "Claude uses Jev automatically" goal. At best a code reference or base to fork (add OpenRouter defaults, shorter timeouts, coding-specific descriptions plus a hook/CLAUDE.md trigger).

entries.name: devnolife/copilot-jev
entries.what: Copilot-CLI-oriented Jev bundle (Indonesian docs): a Python stdio MCP server (mcp_server.py) exposing 5 tools (jev_ask, jev_choice, jev_score, jev_noul, jev_usage) over the official typesafe-sdk; a Claude Code plugin/marketplace that ships ONLY a SKILL.md (+3 reference files) teaching agents Jev's API and patterns; plus a standalone chief.py task router, a demo, and doctor/measure scripts. The MCP server is not bundled into the plugin (no .mcp.json), it must be registered manually.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. MCP tools with 'delegate every repeated structured decision' instructions and an SKILL.md description trigger ('closed-list choice, rubric scoring, true/false doc check, or writing code using typesafe-sdk'). No hook, no proxy, no deterministic trigger. In a coding session those trigger conditions rarely arise organically, so Claude will mostly ignore it; when it does call it, it must synthesize state and rubric itself, costing extra output tokens and a turn.
security: API key read from env or repo-root .env via python-dotenv (config.py:18,35); never in argv, so not visible in process list. .env is gitignored.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no curl|sh, no postinstall; pure Python static reading showed only httpx calls via SDK.

Telemetry writes JSONL (timestamp, model, question_ids, latency, tokens, cost, error) to <repo>/telemetry/calls.jsonl (telemetry.py:42-43); no state text stored, but error strings are stored. Writes into the plugin/clone dir, not project dir.
Repo warns TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug makes SDK log request/response bodies unredacted (README Keamanan, .env.example:17-19).

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs are model-authored state; tool output is numeric/typed JSON (low injection risk), but skill/instructions text is Indonesian, ~9KB, and would steer the main model to call Jev.
1 contributor, 0 stars, 6 days old, unaudited, single-maintainer supply chain (repo plus PyPI typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 + mcp). Pin commit if used.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in the 'state' argument of each Jev tool call (arbitrary text: could be code snippets, diffs, file contents, tool outputs, error logs, prompts) plus instructions/criteria text, sent via HTTPS to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default; would be openrouter.ai if repointed). Nothing is sent automatically; egress happens only when Claude decides to call a tool. Client-project code could leak into state; the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__* tools, so it would not cover these calls unless the matcher is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for the session: errors are caught and returned as a JSON dict {error: config|api, message} (mcp_server.py:73-80), so Claude continues. Missing key surfaces as ConfigError at first call (client is lazily constructed, mcp_server.py:66-70), server still starts. SDK RetryPolicy max_retries=3, backoff 0.5-5s, timeout 30s (client.py:71): worst case a single tool call can block on the order of 1-2 minutes on a hung API before returning an error. Non-API exceptions (e.g. network/httpx errors not wrapped as TypeSafeAPIError) are not caught and would surface as an MCP tool error. No circuit breaker.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 5 tools; tool names+descriptions+schemas approx 3.5k chars (~900 tokens) plus server instructions ~1.1k chars (~300 tokens) always loaded (deferred by ToolSearch may reduce). Skill: frontmatter description ~480 chars (~120 tokens) always listed; full SKILL.md 8.7KB (~2.2k tokens) + reference 12KB (~3k tokens, on demand) when invoked. No hooks, so no injected per-turn text. Total steady-state approx 1.3k tokens, with an overwhelmingly Indonesian-language payload.
pros: Real, readable MCP server (277 lines) with well-formed typed tools; jev_ask batching design and Noul-has-no-confidence handling (mcp_server.py:102-112) reflect correct understanding of Jev primitives.
Uses official typesafe-sdk, whose base URL is env-configurable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and appends /v1/systemone, so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs env vars only (untested).
Safe hygiene: key from env/.env, no argv exposure, no shell exec, no installers, MIT, errors returned as data (fail-open), local telemetry of cost/latency, tests + CI.

SKILL.md is a decent primer on the three primitives, confidence gating and fan-out that helps when the user is BUILDING apps that call Jev (typesafe-sdk code); useful as a reference skill for that only.
Cheap steady-state context (~1.3k tokens), no hooks that could conflict with GitNexus/secret-guard/caveman hooks.
cons: Wrong tool for the goal: it gives Claude Code tools it may call, not a mechanism that makes Claude Code consult Jev automatically; no hooks, no routing/proxy, so no deterministic auto-use. README itself says Jev is a 'partner' and the model is not swapped.

Copilot CLI/Windows-first: README paths are D:\ PowerShell, MCP registration example targets ~/.copilot/mcp-config.json; the Claude Code plugin installs the skill only and never registers the MCP server (no .mcp.json in .claude-plugin or plugin.json) so 'install' does not deliver the tools; manual venv + claude mcp add required, and key lives in a .env inside the plugin/clone dir.

Zero OpenRouter support in code or docs; the direct TypeSafe endpoint and TypeSafe key only. OpenRouter route relies on the user's own untested base-URL trick; hardcoded pricing (mcp_server.py:117) and TypeSafe-specific error hints remain. Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) unsupported.

Immature: 0 stars, 1 contributor, 2 commits over one day (2026-09-24), no releases; claims (e.g. '2.4x cheaper') are the author's own single-machine measurement. mcp>=1.2 pin vs import of mcp.server.mcpserver.MCPServer is a possible install-time breakage (unverified).

Docs, tool descriptions, server instructions and skill are all Indonesian; the prompt steering text for the model is not in English, and the skill/MCP are oriented to agent-orchestration (research/write/review routing), not day-to-day coding decisions.

Every use requires Claude to author a state blob and rubric (output tokens + a round trip), and can ship code/diffs to a third party; existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__jev__* calls. Realistic coding use cases (which file next, is this test flaky, is this diff risky) are not addressed by ready-made questions.
Retry policy of 3x with 30s timeout can stall a turn for over a minute when the API is degraded.
entries.verdict: A tidy but tiny, Copilot-CLI-first proof of concept: a usable 5-tool Python MCP server plus a skill-only plugin, with no hooks and no OpenRouter support in code (repointing via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is plausible but untested). It cannot deliver the user's 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically' goal on its own; at best treat mcp_server.py as a reference/fork base, not something to install as-is.

entries.name: Chrishow2/mcp-jev
entries.what: Tiny Python MCP server (about 200 lines of source) exposing one tool, jev_decide, that forwards {model, state, questions} to TypeSafe's POST /v1/systemone and returns the answers and usage as pretty-printed JSON. It validates question shapes locally (noul, choice, score). It runs over stdio or streamable-HTTP, and the README pushes a Docker container on 127.0.0.1:8000. There are no hooks, skills or routing logic; the author says threshold and routing logic belong in the agent prompt.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no proxy. Claude calls jev_decide only if its own judgment says a calibrated yes/no, choice or score fits, and it must also construct the questions JSON itself each time. The generic instruction text gives Claude little reason to reach for it in normal coding turns, so in practice it would fire rarely. To make it automatic the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or a UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hook on top, which this project does not provide.
security: Created 2026-09-22, 8 days old; 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases or tags. Effectively a weekend proof of concept.
MIT license; unofficial, with a disclaimer in the README.

API key is read from the environment and sent only as a Bearer header to JEV_API_BASE. It is not logged, and error paths return only response text (first 500 chars) and JSON body. Stdio mode with 'env' in the MCP config keeps the key out of argv. The recommended HTTP mode keeps it in the container env or .env instead.

Recommended mode is an unauthenticated HTTP MCP endpoint on 127.0.0.1:8000 (the compose file binds 127.0.0.1). Any local process or browser-origin request to localhost can call it, spending the user's key and sending arbitrary state. Inside the container it binds 0.0.0.0, which is safe only because of the 127.0.0.1 port mapping. The README's 'docker run -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000' is also safe.
JEV_API_BASE is unvalidated: a poisoned env or .env could redirect the key and state to another host. Only a local trust issue.

env.py:9-18 loads a .env from the package's repo root via python-dotenv. With a non-editable pip install this resolves to site-packages parents and is harmless. Under uv/editable use it loads the repo .env.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude puts in the jev_decide arguments: the 'state' JSON or string and the question instructions and criteria. That goes from the local MCP process (or Docker container) to JEV_API_BASE (TypeSafe by default, or OpenRouter if patched). Nothing is sent automatically, and there is no telemetry and no persistence in the server. Whatever Claude decides to classify (code, diffs, tool output, file contents) is exposed to TypeSafe/OpenRouter and their upstream providers. Client-project code therefore needs an explicit data policy. The user's global secret-leak PreToolUse hook does not cover the mcp__jev__ matcher unless it is extended.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level and blocking-heavy in time. Every error path returns a structured error JSON string and never raises, so Claude just sees {error:true}. Missing key returns a 401-style error. Timeout is 30 s per request (JEV_TIMEOUT_SEC), with retries only on HTTP 429/529 (up to 3, sleeps of 1, 2, 4 s or Retry-After) using synchronous time.sleep. A network timeout or connection error (httpx exception) is not retried and is caught by the generic handler as a 500. Worst case is about 4x30 s plus backoff on repeated 429s. If the Docker container is down, the MCP server shows as failed to connect in Claude Code and its tools are simply absent; it does not break other work. There is no circuit breaker and no fallback.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (jev_decide). Estimated tool definition about 900 chars, roughly 225 to 300 tokens, covering the name, a one-line description, and schema for state (anyOf string/object/array), questions (object) and model. Plus about 230 chars (about 60 tokens) of server instructions. Total about 300 to 350 tokens per session (less if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch). No hook-injected text.
pros: Small enough to audit fully: about 200 lines of source, one tool, no shell exec, no telemetry, no install scripts, no hooks that could interfere with the existing secret-guard/GitNexus/caveman hooks.

Uses the same System One /v1/systemone request and response shape as OpenRouter's documented endpoint. Switching to OpenRouter is env-only (JEV_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), with no fork needed.
Supports stdio transport. Claude Code can launch it from .mcp.json with an env block, with no Docker and no open localhost port, once the user has vetted the code.
Local validation of noul/choice/score shapes (choice up to 255 options, score 2-10 levels) gives fast, readable errors to Claude, and all failures come back as structured JSON, not crashes.
Negligible context cost (one tool, about 300 tokens) and no effect on any hook.
cons: Not automatic. It is a single model-discretion tool with a generic 'use when you need calibrated probabilities' hint. The user's requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told) is not met, and nothing routes tool calls, prompts or diffs through Jev. The user would have to write the automation (CLAUDE.md rules or hooks) themselves.

Claude must hand-write a full questions JSON (instructions plus criteria) on every call, costing tokens and an extra Opus turn. There are no preset gates such as risky-command check, commit-message classification or test-failure triage.

Only TypeSafe is coded in. OpenRouter works only via the misnamed TYPESAFE_API_KEY variable and JEV_API_BASE. Nothing in the repo or tests covers OpenRouter, and the Decisions API and Jev Router are unsupported. I verified schema parity from docs, not by running it.

Immature: 8 days old, 5 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no releases and no PyPI/npm package. The Docker image tracks floating :latest with no signing. Dependency mcp>=1.0 is inaccurate because the code needs mcp 2.x.

The recommended deployment (an always-on Docker container on an unauthenticated localhost HTTP port) is heavier and less safe than a stdio server. Any local process can spend the key. If Docker is stopped, the MCP server shows as failed in Claude Code.
Synchronous retry loop can block a tool call for minutes on repeated 429s, with no client reuse or circuit breaker.
Sends whatever state Claude passes (possibly client code) to a third party with no redaction, and the existing secret-guard hook would not cover it.
entries.verdict: A clean but thin proof-of-concept wrapper. It is safe to read and trivially repointable at OpenRouter via JEV_API_BASE, but it gives Claude Code nothing beyond a manual jev_decide tool and no auto-invocation. It is only useful as a low-cost, on-demand building block, or as a base for a custom hook that calls Jev, not as the integration itself.

entries.name: Aether-254/ask-jev
entries.what: Small stdio MCP server (Node/TS, esbuild bundle committed as mcp/dist/index.js) that wraps the Jev System One endpoint POST {base}/systemone with 3 tools (jev_evaluate, jev_batch_evaluate, jev_ping), plus a Claude/Codex plugin manifest, a .mcp.json and one SKILL.md. Purely a thin HTTP client: no hooks, no proxying, no auto-routing. Everything is model-discretion or explicit-request.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions do hint at when to use them ('classifying, triaging, filtering or ranking dozens to hundreds of items') but nothing forces or nudges Claude to call them during ordinary coding, and the skill trigger is explicitly conditioned on the user asking 'with Jev'. There is no deterministic hook. Opus 5.5 will rarely reach for a 3-tool typed-classification server unprompted while editing code; a CLAUDE.md rule or a separate hook would be needed for reliable auto-use.
security: License MIT (LICENSE, GitHub licenseInfo).

API key read from env only (client.ts:55) and sent as Bearer header over HTTPS; never put in argv (server launched as 'node ./mcp/dist/index.js' with no args), so not visible in ps. jev_ping reports only hasApiKey boolean. Error messages include upstream body slice(0,500) (client.ts:67), which could echo server text to the model.

No shell execution, no child_process, no telemetry/analytics in app code (grep of dist: only undici/zod/MCP SDK vendored code; undici's sqlite cache store code is bundled but unused). No postinstall: mcp/package.json is private with no install scripts; plugin runs a committed bundle, so no npm install is needed.

Supply-chain risk: the plugin entrypoint is a 1.8 MB committed esbuild bundle (mcp/dist/index.js, 47.5k lines) that cannot be audited by reading; only lines ~47285-47498 are app code and match src/. CI has a 'git diff --exit-code -- dist/index.js' check but it's only a rebuild-consistency check by the same author. Pin a commit SHA if used; ideally rebuild locally from source with npm ci.
Single-author personal account (Aether-254, created 2020, 57 public repos), 0 stars, 0 forks, repo created 2026-09-24 (6 days old). No reviews, no security policy.

Prompt-injection surface: tool returns only numeric/keyed JSON from upstream, low risk; but upstream error body text is passed through to the model. The model could be induced to send arbitrary file content as 'state' if a prompt-injected file instructs it (generic to any MCP tool that sends data out).
entries.dataEgress: Exactly and only what the model puts in the tool call: `state` (arbitrary text/JSON the model chooses, could be code snippets, diffs, file contents, error logs) plus the question definitions and model id, sent to {baseUrl}/systemone (TypeSafe by default, OpenRouter if reconfigured). Nothing is sent automatically: no hooks, no prompt/transcript capture, no telemetry. If used via OpenRouter, that content also transits OpenRouter (their data-policy/logging settings apply); for client projects the user must decide what may be put in state.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but non-blocking to the session: it is a model-invoked tool, so a failure just returns isError text to Claude and the model continues without Jev. Defaults are slow: 30 s timeout per attempt (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), 3 retries on 429/5xx/network errors with exponential backoff 0.5/1/2 s (client.ts:98-120), so a hung backend can stall a single turn for about 2 minutes (4x30s + 3.5s) unless JEV_TIMEOUT_MS / JEV_MAX_RETRIES are lowered. Note bug-ish: JEV_MAX_RETRIES parsed with Number(), a non-numeric value gives NaN so attempt >= NaN is false, causing unbounded retries. JSON.parse on 200 body is inside try, so malformed 200s are retried too. No circuit breaker, no caching.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Estimated ~1.8-2.5k tokens of tool definitions when loaded: descriptions about 1.2k chars (jev_evaluate ~610, batch ~300, ping ~150) plus two large Zod-derived JSON schemas (discriminated union of choice/score/noul with .describe() texts, appearing in both evaluate and batch, ~3-4k chars each) => roughly 8-10k chars / 4. No MCP server 'instructions' field. No hook-injected text. Plus the ask-jev skill description (~330 chars, about 80 tokens) always in the skill listing; SKILL.md body (~2.4k chars, about 600 tokens) loads only when triggered. With Claude Code tool search/deferred MCP tools the schema cost is deferred.
pros: OpenRouter switch is config-only: client.ts:54-56 honors JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_KEY/JEV_MODEL and posts to `${base}/systemone` (client.ts:102), which is exactly OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone path; no fork needed.
Small, readable (~300 lines of app code), no shell exec, no telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh, key never in argv; MIT.
Exposes all three Jev primitives (choice/score/noul) with sensible Zod validation (2-255 options, 2-10 score rungs) and returns raw probabilities/confidence, so Claude can threshold on calibration.
Batch tool with bounded concurrency and per-item error isolation suits bulk triage (e.g. classify 200 issues/log lines/commits) better than serial calls.
jev_ping gives a cheap diagnostic of base URL, model, key presence and latency.
Configurable timeout/retries and proxy support; CI with unit tests and a smoke test.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion MCP tools; the skill is gated on the user saying 'with Jev' (SKILL.md frontmatter), no hooks. Fails the user's core requirement of Claude using Jev without being told.
Little natural daily-coding use: typed classification of a state is rarely something Opus needs to outsource mid-edit, and each call costs an extra Opus round-trip that dwarfs Jev's 70-500 ms.

Sends whatever the model puts in `state` to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe); no redaction and no allow/deny of paths, which matters for client code and interacts with the user's secret-guard hook only for Bash/Read/Grep, not for MCP tool payloads.

Default retry policy is bad for interactive use: 30 s x 4 attempts plus backoff (about 2 min stall) and JEV_MAX_RETRIES=non-numeric yields NaN and unbounded retry; must set JEV_TIMEOUT_MS/JEV_MAX_RETRIES.

Claude Code packaging looks Codex-first and probably broken as a plugin: .mcp.json uses Codex 'env_vars' and relative './mcp/dist/index.js' with cwd '.' rather than ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}; no marketplace.json; README examples are PowerShell.

1.8 MB opaque committed bundle as entrypoint; 6-day-old, single-author, 0-star repo with 4 commits and no releases beyond v0.1.0 means no track record and unaudited maintainer trust for running code with the API key.
Adds about 2k tokens of tool schema (duplicated union schema in two tools) to context if not deferred.

Uses OpenRouter's System One API only if that schema matches TypeSafe's exactly; untested here and README never mentions OpenRouter, so model slug/response differences are the user's risk. Does not offer the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions).
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal but brand-new (6 days, 1 author) MCP wrapper that can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, and is a reasonable low-effort building block for explicit typed-classification/batch tasks. It does nothing to make Claude Code use Jev automatically (no hooks; skill requires the user to say 'with Jev'), so for the stated goal it is at best a transport layer to combine with a hook or CLAUDE.md rule, and its Claude Code plugin packaging needs fixing.

entries.name: @donbee/jev-mcp (repo saahmadnejad/cline-option-scorer)
entries.what: Dependency-free stdio MCP server (plus CLI) that exposes one real tool (score_options, with a duplicate alias score_cline_options). It POSTs a Jev "choice" question to a /systemone endpoint and returns per-option probabilities and confidence. The repo is a monorepo whose main target is Cline: its PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks and SKILL.md only work with Cline's ask_followup_question and Cline's ~/.cline paths, not Claude Code. The MCP server is the only part that is portable to Claude Code, and it is a thin wrapper around a single Choice call.
interface: Cline-only parts in the repo, not in the npm package
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. The tool description says 'Use BEFORE presenting choices to the user or making a decision', but Claude Code (Opus 5.5) has no mandatory trigger and no deterministic mechanism to call it. The Cline hooks that make it deterministic in Cline (PreToolUse on ask_followup_question) have no Claude Code equivalent in this repo. Claude Code's AskUserQuestion is not covered by anything here. With autoAnswer the tool tells the model to answer for the user, which is a behavior override, not an automatic integration.
security: No npm postinstall script or lifecycle install hooks. The package has zero dependencies and ships only src/, README and LICENSE. The scripts are check, test and smoke, and the smoke script runs only in prepublishOnly.

API keys live in plaintext in jev.json, cline-jev.json or ~/.config/jev/jev.json. There is no env-var path, so the keys cannot come from a secrets manager. They are not put in argv. Keys are read from config and sent as a Bearer header.

Config discovery walks up from cwd to the nearest package.json, .git or .cline and reads jev.json there first (jev-config.js:131-166). A cloned client repo can therefore ship a jev.json that redirects baseUrl to an attacker host and captures state text, or sets autoAnswer:true. This is a real config-injection risk for a user working on client repos.

Prompt-injection and behavior-steering surface: the tool result can append a directive 'DO NOT ask the user ... Treat X as the user's answer and continue' when autoAnswer is true, which can come from a repo-level config file. The output is a probability distribution from a remote model, so a decision could be made on behalf of the user without asking.
The default provider is zen-free, which is an anonymous free endpoint on a third-party host (opencode.ai). Everything in `state` goes to that host with no key and no agreement about retention.

No telemetry, no shell execution and no curl|sh installer in the MCP package. Its CI and publish workflows use OIDC trusted publishing. The npm package was hand-published by a single maintainer, so provenance is minimal.
entries.dataEgress: The `state` string (which the model chooses, and can include task context, repo facts, code or diffs), the `question` and every option label. All of it goes over HTTPS to opencode.ai/zen (the DEFAULT, anonymous, with no key) or api.typesafe.ai, or to a custom baseUrl from the config file. No file reads or tool outputs are collected by the server itself, and only what the model puts in the arguments leaves the machine. No telemetry. The Cline decision-trail logs (~/.cline/data/logs) are NOT written by the MCP package.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Timeout is 10 s by default (jev-config.js:124, AbortSignal.timeout at jev-client.js:64). On error, timeout or a missing key, the MCP tool returns isError:true with the text 'Jev scoring unavailable ... Proceed without percentages.' (mcp-server.js:329). Nothing blocks Claude Code. The worst case is one tool call stalling for up to 10 s. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. Because it is a model-called tool, a Jev outage only wastes a turn.
entries.contextCost: 2 MCP tools with an identical schema. Approximately 350 chars of description per tool plus about 800 chars of JSON schema, so about 1,100 chars per tool, or roughly 550 tokens total for both (estimate at chars/4). There are no server instructions. There are no hooks and nothing is injected per prompt. Each call's result is small, about 100-200 tokens.
pros: Tiny, readable, zero-dependency code (about 400 lines in the npm package), so a full audit takes minutes and there is no supply-chain surface beyond the package itself.
Correct fail-open behavior: errors come back as isError text that says to proceed without percentages, with a 10 s timeout.
Criterion IDs are positional (opt_N) so the option labels cannot collide, which is a real bug fix in 0.3.1 (jev-client.js:17-29).
Has a baseUrl override and a model override, so pointing it at OpenRouter is possible in principle (jev-client.js:60,49).
MIT license, real tests (node --test) and CI with a drift guard between the copied files.
Low context cost: about 550 tokens for two tools and no hooks.
cons: No OpenRouter support: three hard-coded providers, and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY or any env var. A custom baseUrl needs a plaintext key in a JSON file, or a fork.
Exposes only Choice for option scoring. There is no Noul (yes/no) or Score (ordinal) primitive, so it covers the smallest part of Jev.

Automatic use is not achievable. It relies on model discretion, and the real automation (hooks, SKILL.md) is Cline-specific (ask_followup_question, ~/.cline). It does not meet the user's requirement that Claude Code uses it without being told.
Default provider is the anonymous free Zen endpoint at a third party, and `state` would carry client project context to it. A poor default for client work.
A project-level jev.json is trusted and searched first from cwd upward, so a cloned repo can redirect baseUrl or set autoAnswer:true. It is a config-injection risk on client repos.

autoAnswer tells the model to 'DO NOT ask the user' and to treat Jev's top option as the user's answer. That is the opposite of what a careful senior developer wants for code decisions, and a probability model with no reasoning trace should not be answering for the user.
Duplicate tool alias (score_cline_options) wastes context in Claude Code. The server version string is 0.3.0 while the package is 0.3.1.

Very immature: created 2026-09-21, single author, 42 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, first npm version published 2026-09-25, package hand-published by one maintainer. No response-schema check against the OpenRouter API.
The MCP protocol is hand-rolled JSON-RPC (protocol version 2024-11-05, no ping, no cancellation), which risks incompatibility with newer Claude Code clients.
entries.verdict: This is a small, honest, fail-open wrapper around one Jev Choice call, but it targets Cline's UX. It has no OpenRouter path except by editing config or forking, and nothing in it makes Claude Code use it automatically, since that depends entirely on the model deciding to call it. It is useful only as a reference for the Choice request/response shape, and a fork or a custom hook would be needed for any real integration.

entries.name: jev-mcp-server (npm, weeeeekdy)
entries.what: Tiny (about 85-line, 3.5 KB, 3-file) stdio MCP server exposing three generic tools that wrap TypeSafe's System One endpoint: jev_noul (yes/no probability), jev_choice (pick one from a criteria map, with confidence and per-option probabilities), jev_score (ordered levels, with score, confidence and probabilities). Claude must build the `state` string itself, because Jev reads nothing on its own. It is a passive judge tool with no hooks, skills, or policies.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces or prompts Claude to call it. Its descriptions say nothing about when to use it, and the README's 'gate on noul >= 0.8' guidance is not shipped as a skill or CLAUDE.md snippet. Achieving the user's 'automatic' goal would need extra glue: a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a hook that instructs Claude to call jev_* at certain moments. There are no deterministic triggers.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. The README's `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...` form puts the key in argv at install time and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, and no postinstall script. Runtime dependencies are only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk and zod.
Ships compiled dist only, with no source or repo, so the published JS cannot be compared against a public git history. It is short enough to read in full, and I found nothing malicious.

Single anonymous maintainer (weeeeekdy, gmail address), package created 2026-09-21 and unclaimed by TypeSafe. This is an unofficial third-party wrapper, so there is a supply-chain and typosquat risk. If you use it, pin the exact version 1.0.0 or vendor the file.

No error handling: an API error message body is thrown verbatim into the tool error. An uncaught fetch failure or a missing `answers` field throws inside the handler, and the MCP SDK returns it as a tool error.
Prompt-injection surface is small because the server only relays text. The `state` Claude sends is whatever it chooses, and the returned probabilities are numbers only.
entries.dataEgress: Only the `state` string, the `instructions` string, and the criteria/levels that Claude passes in each tool call go to api.typesafe.ai (the direct TypeSafe API, not OpenRouter, as shipped). Whatever code, diff, or text Claude puts into `state` leaves the machine. The server never reads files by itself. There is no telemetry and no other network calls.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup: the process exits 1 if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset, so the MCP server shows as failed to connect. At call time there is no timeout (plain fetch with no AbortSignal), no retry, and no fallback. HTTP errors and network failures raise a tool error to the model, which is non-blocking for Claude Code since it is a model-invoked tool, not a gate. A hung connection could stall a tool call until the undici default timeouts.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. The tool names, descriptions and schemas total about 830 chars of quoted strings plus zod schema structure, roughly 350-500 tokens with JSON-schema overhead. The descriptions are in Chinese, which is token-heavier per character and not ideal for an English workflow. The server sets no MCP `instructions`. No hooks inject text. Claude Code 2.1.x with MCP tool search defers these schemas anyway.
pros: Very small and easy to audit: one 3.5 KB file with no shell exec, no file reads, and only two runtime deps (dist/server.js).

Exposes the three real Jev primitives (Noul, Choice, Score) with a generic `criteria` map, so it is flexible enough for diff-review gates, error-class routing, and 'does the evidence support the claim' checks.
Cheap context footprint (3 tools, roughly 400 tokens), no MCP instructions, and no hook text injected into every turn.
MIT license, and the README states plainly that Jev is a judge and not a generator.
Simple enough to fork and point at OpenRouter by editing 3 constants.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter. The URL api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY are hard-coded (dist/server.js:5-6), with no env override. It needs a TypeSafe console key, which contradicts the user's OpenRouter-only plan unless the file is patched.

No source, no repo, and no git history on npm (package.json has no `repository`; the guessed GitHub URL is 404). The build script needs src/, which is not published, so a patch has to be made in dist/, and updates cannot be tracked.
Model-discretion only, so it fails the core requirement of automatic use without prompting. Claude has no reason to call jev_* unprompted, and the tool descriptions do not say when to.

No timeout, retry, or graceful fallback, and it crashes on startup without a key. Error handling is minimal, with no validation of the response shape (data.answers.judgment.noul is dereferenced blindly).
Tool descriptions are in Chinese and the error message is in Chinese, which is odd for an English-language workflow and may confuse both the model and the user.

Extra hop with a real per-call model-turn cost (Claude must compose `state`), and Jev only judges what Claude feeds it. There is no automatic diff or file access, so most 'gating' value is redundant with Claude's own judgment.

Brand-new (published 2026-09-21), version 1.0.0 only, a single anonymous maintainer, no tests, no CI, no releases, and no stars or community. There is no evidence the schema is correct against live TypeSafe or OpenRouter, since the response fields (answers.X.noul and others) are unverified.
Unofficial: not affiliated with TypeSafe, and there is a name collision with the PyPI jev-mcp-server, so pin the package name and version.
entries.verdict: A minimal, readable but unofficial wrapper that only talks to TypeSafe's direct API and is purely model-invoked, so it fails both the 'OpenRouter' and 'automatic' requirements as shipped. It is useful at most as a reference or a base to fork (change the URL, env var and model id, then add a hook or skill for automatic triggering), not as a drop-in install.

entries.name: @livx.cc/mcp-jev
entries.what: Tiny stdio/HTTP MCP server exposing one tool, post_jev_evaluate {state, questions[], provider?}, which forwards to Jev via Vercel AI Gateway, OpenRouter Decisions API (alpha) or TypeSafe direct, normalizes the answers (choice / score / boolean) and falls through providers on failure. Also ships an MCP resource skill://mcp-jev/workflow (SKILL.md text) and a library export. Purely a model-discretion tool: Claude must decide to call it and must author state + questions itself.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no Claude Code skill is registered (the SKILL.md sits inside the npm package and is an MCP resource, not installed to ~/.claude/skills). Claude would call it only if its own judgement says a probabilistic decision is useful, which for daily coding is rare, and it must hand-build a state + questions payload each time. To make it 'automatic' the user would need to add CLAUDE.md rules or write own hooks; this package provides none.
security: API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header to the chosen provider (src/providers/openrouter.ts:24); not in argv if supplied via env; but cli.ts:7-8 loads a .env from the package root (in bunx cache) or --env-path, so best to pass keys via the MCP config `env` block instead

No shell exec, no postinstall/preinstall scripts, no telemetry, no curl|sh; only fetch to provider URLs. URLs overridable by env (OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_URL, TYPESAFE_API_URL, AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL) so a hostile env could redirect the key
Logging is stderr-only and logs failure messages (HTTP body first 500 chars), not keys

Transitive deps are heavy for a 1-tool server: edge.libx.js pulls express 4, libx.js, selfsigned, body-parser, @vercel/edge, @whatwg-node/server, isomorphic-fetch, ua-parser-js; same single maintainer (Elya Livshitz, also ships shraga/agentx); version 0.1.0 published 2026-09-25, 5 days old, no repository field, no tests in tarball, no provenance link to source (gitHead 2a916ae only)
Runs TypeScript directly with Bun-only APIs (import.meta.dir, #!/usr/bin/env bun); bun is not installed on this machine, so it cannot run under Node 24 as is
HTTP mode binds 127.0.0.1 only, no auth on REST/MCP endpoint (any local process could spend the key) - avoid HTTP mode
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude puts in `state` and each question's `instructions`/`criteria` leaves the machine as JSON to openrouter.ai (and, with default JEV_PROVIDERS, on failure to ai-gateway.vercel.sh and api.typesafe.ai if those keys exist; unconfigured providers are skipped). Nothing is sent automatically: only what the model chooses to serialize, which can include code, diffs, file contents or ticket text. No hook reads user prompts or tool outputs. Client projects: OpenRouter data-policy/ZDR settings apply; TypeSafe/Jev is a third-party model behind OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level: errors are caught and returned as {ok:false,error} (src/app.ts:27-29), so Claude Code sees a normal tool result and continues; in stdio mode it is not a blocker for the turn. However there is NO fetch timeout or AbortSignal in postJson (src/types.ts:53-62), so a hung OpenRouter connection can stall the tool call until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout. Provider fall-through (src/jev.ts:42-56) can add extra latency and unintended egress to other providers if their keys are set. Not a hook, so no fail-closed risk to normal work.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__mcp-jev__post_jev_evaluate). Tool description about 900 chars plus body-param description about 250 chars plus name/schema, roughly 350-450 tokens; server `instructions` string about 330 chars (~85 tokens); total about 450-550 tokens always loaded (less if MCP tool search defers it). SKILL.md (~1.9k chars, ~480 tokens) only loaded if the resource is read. No hooks, no injected text per turn.
pros: Correct OpenRouter Decisions API wire format (POST /api/alpha/decisions, boolean->noul mapping, model typesafe/jev-1.13) implemented in about 30 lines (src/providers/openrouter.ts) - useful as a reference or to vendor
Small, readable surface: 520 lines total, one tool, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry
Response normalization gives identical choice/score/boolean shape across providers; client-side validation of question shapes gives clear errors to the model
Tool-level failure returns {ok:false,error} instead of crashing the session; keys can be passed via MCP env block
Only ~500 tokens of always-on context, cheap to keep loaded
Can be pinned to OpenRouter only with JEV_PROVIDERS=openrouter, matching the user's stated provider
cons: Requires Bun (shebang #!/usr/bin/env bun, import.meta.dir, TS entrypoint shipped uncompiled); user has Node 24/uvx only and bun is not installed, so npx will not work

Not automatic: single model-discretion tool, no hook, no CLAUDE.md fragment, no installed skill; Claude must invent state and questions schema every call, which contradicts the 'never prompt to use jev' requirement without extra glue
Default provider order tries Vercel then OpenRouter then TypeSafe, so failure can leak the same payload to other vendors if their keys exist; must set JEV_PROVIDERS
No fetch timeout/abort; hung upstream stalls the tool call
Very new and unproven: v0.1.0 published 2026-09-25, single maintainer, no repository link, no tests shipped, no CI/provenance visible; heavy transitive tree (express, libx.js, etc.) for one POST call
Uses the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint with hardcoded model default typesafe/jev-1.13 rather than ~typesafe/jev-latest; alpha API can change
Jev is a decision model with no coding-specific value proposition; a generic 'state + questions' tool gives Claude little reason to prefer it over its own reasoning for code tasks
entries.verdict: Correct but thin proof-of-concept wrapper: it proves the OpenRouter Decisions API call shape, but it is a Bun-only, model-discretion tool with no hook or trigger, so it does not deliver the 'automatic' integration and is not worth running as-is. Best used as a reference for a small custom Node hook/MCP against openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions.

entries.name: jev-incur-cli
entries.what: Node/TypeScript CLI + stdio MCP server built on the incur framework. It wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (POST /v1/systemone) and exposes Jev typed questions (noul/choice/score) to agents. It also ships 5 authored Jev "workflow" skills (plan validator, completion gate, metric decomposition, subagent orchestrator, grill-with-docs) that are installed via a wrapper around `npx skills@1.7.0`. It is a generic question-asking tool. It has no hooks and no automatic invocation. The caller supplies the state text and the question.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. It is an MCP tool behind progressive discovery plus optional skill description triggers. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic trigger. Because the tools are hidden behind search_tools, Opus has no standing cue that a Jev tool exists, so auto-use is unlikely unless a CLAUDE.md line or a skill description nudges it. The bundled skills trigger on 'plan validation', 'task completion', 'subagent routing' and 'metric decomposition' phrasing. They fire rarely in ordinary coding and are workflow-heavy.
security: No install-time scripts in the published package. package.json has only a dev-side `prepare: husky`, which does not run on a registry install. Runtime deps are incur ^0.5.1, cross-spawn 7.0.6 and @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. The SDK is MIT, from github.com/typesafe-ai/typesafe-sdk-js, created 2026-09-12.

API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header (SDK index.mjs:581). The key never appears in argv. The MCP env block should forward it as `${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}`, but the README says registration does not add this automatically. The user must hand-edit the .mcp.json.
The SDK logger defaults to the console at a configurable level (TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL). debug logs bodies (index.mjs ~line 620), so keep it at the default.

Shell execution is limited to `skills add`, which runs `npx --yes skills@1.7.0` through cross-spawn without a shell. That fetches and runs a third-party installer (Vercel Skills) at install time. The recommended MCP registration also uses `npx --yes --package=jev-incur-cli@latest`, which runs unpinned latest code on every Claude Code start.

Prompt-injection surface: Jev returns only numbers and labels. No free text returns except the criteria labels the caller supplied. That is a low surface. The bundled skills are long instruction documents (29-83 lines each plus references) that steer the agent to run subagents, which is a moderate behavioural-influence surface.

Single-maintainer package. npm publisher stevennevins. Versions 0.1.0 to 0.3.0 were published between 2026-09-18 and 2026-09-22. npm signatures are present. The GitHub source repo is not publicly reachable (gh returns 404 for the repo and the README itself says 'this private Git repository'), so the published dist cannot be checked against source. I read the compiled JS directly.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly what the agent puts in the `state` and `question` fields is POSTed to TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is redirected). The README instructs agents to 'read the relevant files yourself, then pass each file's contents inline as an item state'. The typical payload is therefore code and file contents, plans and diffs, and one full copy per question, because the fan-out sends the same file once per item (the README example is 126 concurrent calls with the same file). Choice questions expand to up to 8 permutations. Nothing is sent automatically. Everything is model-authored. The existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool inputs (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so secrets in a file the model chooses to forward would go out. A client-project NDA implication exists: client code would go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter, and OpenRouter data policy applies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, but non-blocking for Claude Code. The SDK defaults are 10 s timeout and 2 retries (index.mjs:74, 518). Worst case is about 30 s or more before the tool returns c.error with a typed code such as TIMEOUT, RATE_LIMITED, AUTH_FAILED or CONNECTION_FAILED and a `retryable` flag (dist/jev/errors.js). AskJevQuestions is all-or-nothing: one failed item discards all results, and in-flight siblings are not cancelled (README and ask.js:80-98). A missing key errors at first use, not at startup. If the MCP server itself fails to spawn (npx fetch on a bad network), the tools are simply absent and the session proceeds normally.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 4 top-level tools (search_tools, get_tool_details, call_read_tool, call_write_tool). Their descriptions and schemas are about 1.5-2k chars, so roughly 400-600 tokens in the tool list. This is small thanks to progressive discovery, and there is no server `instructions` string in cli.js. The 5 real Jev tools cost nothing until fetched. Each full schema fetched (AskJevQuestions with its nested union) is roughly 500-800 tokens, added mid-conversation. If the 5 skills are installed, each adds a ~300-char description to the skill listing, so about 400 tokens standing. Invoking one loads 30-80 lines of workflow plus references, several thousand tokens. Hooks: none, so no injected text.
pros: Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The wire shape is exactly POST /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, so OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone should work by setting only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY (an OpenRouter key) and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL. No fork is needed (index.mjs:513, 554, 581).

Covers all three Jev primitives (noul, choice, score) plus batching. Choice questions get permutation averaging (up to 8 orderings) to cancel option-order bias (permutation-choice.js), which is a real quality feature for a calibrated-probability model.

Low standing context cost (about 500 tokens) because incur's progressive discovery hides the schemas. All tools are marked readOnlyHint, so they should not trigger permission prompts under the user's auto or bypass mode.
Typed error codes with a retryable flag let the agent back off or skip cleanly (errors.js). No install hooks in the published package, MIT license, npm provenance signatures present.
The bundled skills show sensible Jev usage patterns (thresholds left to the caller, 'raw model signals not verified facts'). They are the only agent-usage guidance found so far.
cons: Not automatic. It only offers tools, with no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook and no router. The user's stated requirement, that Claude Code uses Jev without being told, depends entirely on Opus deciding to call it. Progressive discovery makes that less likely, because the model must search_tools, then get_tool_details, then call_read_tool before it can use it.

Not built for the daily coding loop. Its own README example is checklist triage (126 concurrent noul calls against one Solidity file) and 'metric decomposition' and 'plan validation' skills. There is no built-in coding-specific use such as command risk or 'should I run tests' classification.

Sends whatever state the agent passes, and the README tells agents to pass whole file contents inline. The fan-out repeats that content per question. Client-project code would leave the machine, and the existing secret guard does not match mcp__ inputs.

Unpinned npx registration (`--package=jev-incur-cli@latest`) means code from a single new maintainer runs at every session start. It needs manual pinning (jev-incur-cli@0.3.0) and preferably a vendored install.

Source repo is not publicly accessible (GitHub 404; the README calls it private). It is 12 days old with 3 versions and one maintainer, and its tests are not shipped. The README references release availability quirks ('0.1.1 release does not contain this skill' although the registry lists 0.1.0/0.2.0/0.3.0). Maturity is alpha.

`models` command breaks on OpenRouter (different /v1/models response shape). The key must be hand-added to .mcp.json env, and the SDK's 10 s timeout with 2 retries can stall a tool call for 30 s or more. An all-or-nothing batch discards partial results.

The 5 skills are heavy orchestration prompts (routing subagents, gating completion). They add process overhead and could conflict with the user's existing caveman, GitNexus and context-efficiency workflows.
entries.verdict: A competent, thin wrapper around the official SDK that can talk to OpenRouter with env vars alone, but it is an on-demand tool box, not an automatic integration. With progressive discovery and no hooks, Claude Code will rarely call it unprompted. Use it at most as the transport for a custom deterministic hook, and prefer a small direct OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone hook or wrapper of your own that you control.

entries.name: jevguard-mcp (PyPI: jevguard-mcp / GitHub: seb4ez/jevguard-mcp)
entries.what: Zero-dependency Python stdio MCP server (JSON-RPC, MCP 2024-11-05) wrapping TypeSafe's System One API. It exposes 6 tools: 3 canned task wrappers (shell-command safety, code-patch verification, option choice) and 3 generic ones (evaluate, calibrate, prune_state, cache_fingerprint). Each wrapper sends a hard-coded noul/score/choice question set to the endpoint. It then post-processes the answer with local heuristics: neutral-escape injection, dispersion/ambiguity thresholds, and a SQLite SHA-256 result cache in ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db with a 1h TTL. Third-party single-author project, not official TypeSafe. README says "Official" but it is by Seb4Ez. Repo seb4ez/jevguard-mcp, created 2026-09-20; PyPI 1.0.0 to 1.0.2 (2026-09-22 to 09-23); GitHub HEAD is 1.1.0, unreleased on PyPI.
interface: skills/jevguard/SKILL.md (repo only, not in the PyPI sdist)
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. The tool descriptions say 'Use ONLY to ...', and the optional SKILL.md nudges Claude to call safety/patch/decision tools. There is no deterministic hook, no PreToolUse integration and no transparent proxy. In bypass or auto mode, nothing forces the model to call these tools, and Claude would rarely do so for routine Bash. Wiring the safety tool into a PreToolUse hook would need your own script.
security: Good: the API key is read only from env and never from tool args (tools.py:1534). HTTPS-only endpoint allowlist that rejects userinfo and wildcards (tools.py:82-105). Redirects blocked to avoid Authorization leakage (NoRedirectHandler, tools.py:63). mock_answers verdict forgery is refused unless JEVGUARD_TEST_MODE=1 (tools.py:1359, 1541).
Key never appears in argv if passed through the MCP env block. Stdlib-only, no shell/subprocess/eval/exec, no telemetry, and the only network egress is the configured endpoint.

Local plaintext SQLite cache at ~/.cache/jevguard/decision_cache.db stores answers keyed by hash. It stores hashes and results, not prompts, so the leak risk is low. The wrapper tools set bypass_cache=true for commands.

Prompt-injection surface: the command and diff text is placed as raw 'state' in a request to a classifier, and the verdict (ALLOW_AUTONOMOUS / APPROVE) is then trusted by the agent. An attacker-controlled diff or command comment could steer the classifier. The output is not a security boundary.

Trust: a 3-day-old single-author package with 0 stars, no CI, no signed releases and a self-declared 'Production/Stable' label. The README claims 'Official', which is misleading (author Seb4Ez, not TypeSafe). Supply-chain risk on `uvx` because it always pulls the latest version unless pinned. Pin ==1.0.2.
entries.dataEgress: Per call to the configured endpoint (TypeSafe or OpenRouter): the full shell command string, working_dir and sudo flag (safety tool). The full unified diff and target file path (verify_code_patch). Free-text context, question and options (evaluate_decision). Arbitrary state/questions (evaluate). Whatever Claude passes is sent, which can include secrets that appear in commands or diffs, and client code. On OpenRouter the key and payload go to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe (or a routed model). The retention policies of both apply, and this matters for client projects under NDA. Nothing leaves without the model choosing to call a tool. There is no telemetry to the author.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level: on missing key, timeout or HTTP error the tool returns isError=true with verdict/fallback_action MANUAL_REVIEW_REQUIRED (tools.py:1613-1617, server.py:254-275). There are 3 retries with exponential backoff (about 0.5+1+2 s) and a default 30 s timeout per attempt (tools.py:2071-2128), so the worst case is over 2 minutes of blocking on a hung endpoint. 400/401/403/404 fail immediately. Because it is a model-called tool, failure only stalls that single tool call and the agent can continue. The SKILL.md rule 'status==error -> REQUIRE_HUMAN_APPROVAL' would cause an approval prompt in bypass mode. If the MCP process fails to start (uvx fetch), Claude Code just marks the server disconnected, as with caveman-shrink.
entries.contextCost: 6 tools. The tools/list JSON in tools.py:1051-1326 is about 8.8k chars, so roughly 2.2k tokens of tool definitions on every session (less with Claude Code's deferred MCP tool loading). No MCP `instructions` field is returned (server.py:153-169 has none). No hooks, so no injected text per turn. The SKILL.md (about 4k chars) costs only its ~50-token description until triggered, but it is not shipped on PyPI.
pros: Only Jev-specific MCP found that is installable in one line, with no dependencies, no shell exec, no telemetry, and a small readable codebase (about 2.5k lines) I could audit fully.
Sensible security hygiene: key from env only, HTTPS host allowlist, redirects blocked, mock forgery blocked, fail-closed error payloads (tools.py:63-105, 1534-1551).

Endpoint is env-configurable (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT + JEVGUARD_ALLOWED_ENDPOINTS), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs no fork for the generic jevguard_evaluate tool with model='~typesafe/jev-latest'.
The task-shaped wrappers (command safety, patch verify, choice) map to Jev's noul/score/choice primitives and give ready-made question sets.
Local calibration and caching add value where Jev is noisy: escape option, ambiguity thresholds, 0.1 ms cache hits for repeated state.
cons: Not OpenRouter-native and not official: only TypeSafe and its allowlist are supported. The wrapper tools hard-code model 'jev-latest', which is not an OpenRouter id, and the OpenRouter response shape compatibility is unverified. Real use needs a fork or patch.

No automatic integration: it is model-discretion MCP tools only. There is no hook, and the SKILL.md is not in the PyPI package. This misses the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told). Claude Code is not even in the README.

Poor fit for Claude Code semantics: it duplicates your PreToolUse secret guard, and a Jev classifier cannot judge 'is this Bash command safe' or 'does this diff regress' from a diff alone. The prompts are generic canned rubrics, so results are shallow and vulnerable to prompt injection. Its verdict could create false confidence in bypass mode.

Data egress: full diffs, commands and context go to a third-party endpoint (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe), which is a real NDA problem on client projects. Secrets in commands are sent too, and there is no redaction.

Immature: 3 days on PyPI, 0 stars, one author, no CI, tests are all mocked, 'Production/Stable' and 'Official' are overclaimed, PyPI lags GitHub (1.0.2 vs 1.1.0), and version churn is heavy. `uvx` unpinned pulls whatever is latest.

Worst-case stall of over 2 minutes (30 s x 4 attempts) on a slow endpoint; roughly 2.2k tokens of tool definitions per session for 6 tools, 3 of which (calibrate, prune_state, cache_fingerprint) are local utilities the LLM never needs.
entries.verdict: Skip it as the primary integration. It is a tidy, safe-looking, stdlib-only MCP, but it is a discretionary-tool wrapper for TypeSafe's own API, written by a single unofficial author, with a 3-day history and no hook or OpenRouter support. If you want to experiment, pin ==1.0.2, set the OpenRouter env overrides and call only jevguard_evaluate with an explicit OpenRouter model id. Do not rely on it to gate Bash or diffs, and do not send client code through it.

entries.name: @sunchojack/jev-cli
entries.what: Tiny (about 160 LOC) unofficial npm package with two bins: `jev` (CLI that builds a single-question request) and `jev-mcp` (stdio MCP server exposing one tool, `judge(state, questions)`). Both POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with model `jev-latest` and return `data.answers` as JSON text. Published 2026-09-21 by an individual (sunchojack), 2 versions in 20 minutes, no repository field, no tests, no hooks or skill.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The description actively suppresses auto-use: 'Call ONLY when ... explicitly required', 'Use it when the caller names Jev'. There is no hook, skill trigger or proxy, so it will rarely fire without you naming Jev. It could be made more proactive by editing the description, but Claude would then still be choosing when to spend an extra round trip.
security: API key is read from env only, never placed in argv; sent as Bearer header over HTTPS. Not printed. Good.
CLI accepts --state on argv, so state content is visible in the process list (not the key).

No shell execution beyond execFileSync('security', [...]) with fixed args and process.env.USER as an argument (no shell, so no injection). On Linux this call just fails (ENOENT) and yields the 'key not found' error.

No postinstall or install scripts; only dependency is @modelcontextprotocol/sdk ^1.30.0 (caret range, no lockfile shipped). `zod` is imported (index.js:5) but not declared in package.json, so it relies on the SDK hoisting it (works with npm/npx today, fragile).

No repository field or provenance link. Single anonymous-ish maintainer (gmail address), package about 9 days old, two versions 30 minutes apart. Supply-chain risk is moderate for a tool that holds an API key; pin an exact version or vendor the 53-line file.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever `state` Claude passes (files, diffs, tool output) goes to Jev, but the output is a numeric structure with no free text, so the injection blast radius on return is small.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly the `state` and `questions` that Claude Code chooses to put in the judge call, sent to api.typesafe.ai (direct TypeSafe, not OpenRouter). This could be code, diffs or file contents if the model decides to pass them. The server never reads files or hooks anything itself. The CLI --file option reads a local file and sends it whole. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at startup without TYPESAFE_API_KEY: the top-level throw crashes the MCP server, so Claude Code shows it as failed to connect (same status as the caveman-shrink failure you see now). Not a blocking hook, though, so Claude Code keeps working. At call time, HTTP errors and network errors throw and become an MCP tool error, which the model just sees and continues from. There is no timeout, no AbortController and no retry on fetch, so a hung connection would rely on Claude Code's MCP tool timeout (very long by default). Effectively fail-open for the session but with a possible long stall.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool (mcp__jev__judge). Description about 680 chars plus schema (state unknown, questions record with nested union types, generated JSON schema roughly 1.0-1.5k chars) gives roughly 400-550 tokens in the tool list. No MCP server `instructions`. No hook-injected text. Very cheap.
pros: Smallest possible surface: one tool, about 500 tokens of context, no hooks, no prompt-rewriting, no proxying. Cannot break existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.
Whole implementation is 53 lines (index.js) and readable in a minute; easy to audit, vendor and fork into an OpenRouter version.
Sends the key as a Bearer header from env, not argv; no install scripts; no telemetry.
Tool schema mirrors the real System One contract (noul/choice/score with instructions and criteria), and README examples show the response shapes, so it is a correct thin client.
Batch-friendly: the questions record lets Claude ask several independent typed questions about one state in a single call.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL, model and env var are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (index.js:7-11). It fails your stated requirement unless you fork or patch it.
Uses jev-latest and the TypeSafe direct endpoint; OpenRouter model IDs (typesafe/jev-1.13, ~typesafe/jev-latest) are not accepted without editing.
Description tells the model to use it only when Jev is named, which is the opposite of your goal. Nothing deterministic (hook, skill or proxy) makes it fire automatically.
Linux-hostile key path: the fallback is the macOS `security` command; on Linux the only working path is the env var, and if it is unset the server crashes at import time (index.js:19).
No timeout or abort on fetch; no retries; errors surface as raw thrown text including the response body.
Maturity is very low: created 2026-09-21, 2 versions in 30 minutes, single individual maintainer, no repo link, no tests, no CI, no license field in package.json. Not affiliated with TypeSafe.
Undeclared `zod` dependency and a caret-ranged SDK with no lockfile, so installs are not reproducible.

Offers no coding-specific value on its own: it is a generic judge call, and any code-related question (is this test flaky, which file to edit) requires Claude to hand-write the question schema each time, costing tokens and a round trip.
entries.verdict: A correct but throwaway 53-line TypeSafe-direct wrapper that cannot use OpenRouter without a fork, and whose tool description tells Claude not to use it unless you name Jev. At most, copy index.js as a template for your own OpenRouter-backed MCP or hook. Do not install it as-is.

entries.name: noetion/dsh-jev
entries.what: DeepSeek Harness (DSH) plugin registering jev_ask tool (noul/choice/score) posting to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, plus a bundled jev skill.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion tool in DSH
pros: Clean jev_ask schema mixing noul/choice/score over one state
MIT, CI workflow, client/config tests
cons: Only for DSH (DeepSeek Harness) rc runtime, not Claude Code
Hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint, TYPESAFE_API_KEY only; model decides when to call
Install requires pnpm allowBuilds prepare script

entries.name: nanami-0713/dsh-jev-decide
entries.what: Plugin for DeepSeek's DSH agent (cordis) registering a jev_decide tool (noul/choice/score); configurable baseUrl and credential lookup order.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion (DSH tool)
pros: Clean tool signature and clear guidance on when to use Jev; baseUrl configurable
Published on npm with tests
cons: DSH runtime only, not an MCP server; posts to {baseUrl}/systemone, which is not OpenRouter's /alpha/decisions path
Chinese docs, 3 stars

entries.name: wangBoYi972/typesafe-mcp
entries.what: Single-file Python stdio MCP server (server.py, 343 lines) with 3 model-discretion tools that POST to the TypeSafe System One endpoint with a hardcoded question set. One generic tool (typesafe_classify) plus two hardcoded Chinese-language templates: support-ticket triage and content moderation. Nothing here is aimed at coding work.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, skills or CLAUDE.md snippets. The tool descriptions are Chinese-language and describe ticket triage and content moderation, so Claude has no reason to call them during coding unless the user prompts it. That is exactly what the user wants to avoid.
security: API key is passed through the MCP env block (README), not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. Bearer header only.
No install script, no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry. Only deps are mcp and requests (unpinned: mcp>=1.0.0, requests>=2.31.0).
requests.post has no timeout (server.py:61), so a hung upstream blocks a worker thread indefinitely.
The tool result is the raw upstream JSON dumped as text (server.py:191-196), with no sanitizing. Risk is low because Jev returns typed output, not free text.
Errors are caught and returned as 'Error: <exception>' (server.py:168-175). A requests exception message can include the endpoint URL but not the key.
Single-author repo created 2026-09-23 with 1 star and no releases or CI. Supply-chain trust is low, but the code is small enough to audit in 5 minutes, and I did.
entries.dataEgress: On each tool call, only what the model puts into the 'content' or 'questions' arguments (or title/content for the ticket tool) leaves the machine. It goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to OpenRouter if the endpoint is overridden. The server has no hooks and never reads files, diffs or tool outputs itself. Whatever code or text Claude chooses to pass is sent to a third party, and client-project code would be included if Claude passes it.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in effect. Errors are returned to Claude as an isError tool result, so Claude carries on without Jev. The real risk is that there is no HTTP timeout (server.py:61): a slow upstream can hang the tool call for as long as requests waits. Startup is fail-closed for this server only: it exits with code 1 if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset (server.py:25-28), which shows up as a failed MCP connection.
