Under mcp 1.x it would also crash, because the code uses the 2.x Server(on_list_tools=...) constructor. requirements.txt allows mcp>=1.0.0, so a pinned 1.x install would fail; I confirmed against mcp 2.2.0 sdist source that those kwargs exist there.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Approx 500-700 tokens of tool names + descriptions + schemas (about 2-2.5k chars of JSON schema). The descriptions are in Chinese, so token counts run higher per character and Claude gets weak triggering signals from them. No MCP server 'instructions' and no hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred MCP tool loading, the cost is lower still.
pros: Small (343 lines) and easy to audit. No shell exec, no telemetry, no installers.

The System One payload shape (state/model/questions, choice criteria dict, noul instructions) matches OpenRouter's documented schema, so pointing it at OpenRouter is one env var (TYPESAFE_API_ENDPOINT) plus the key.
The API key goes in via the MCP env block, not argv.
The generic typesafe_classify tool lets Claude build its own choice/noul/score questions, so it could serve as a raw System One passthrough (e.g. 'is this diff risky?').
MIT license. The 3-tool footprint is light on context.
cons: Wrong domain for this user: the two purpose-built tools are Chinese-language support-ticket triage and content moderation, which have no use in coding.

No auto-invocation: it is a plain MCP tool, and the descriptions never mention code, diffs, commits, or PRs. Claude will rarely call it unprompted, so the user's core requirement is unmet. It would need extra CLAUDE.md text or a hook.
No timeout on requests.post (server.py:61), so a hung upstream can stall a tool call.

Score questions are malformed: the ticket/moderation templates pass criteria as 3 strings ('影响范围评分','1=个别用户','10=全站影响') plus a 'score':{min,max} field (server.py:247-251, 292-299). The OpenRouter docs describe score as an ordered criteria list of levels, so 3 strings would be read as 3 levels, not a 1-10 scale. Results are likely wrong or misleading.
Requires the mcp 2.x lowlevel API (on_list_tools kwargs); requirements.txt says >=1.0.0, so a pinned 1.x install crashes.
'codex-latest' in the model enum is unexplained and unvalidated.
Not battle-tested: 1 commit, 1 star, created 7 days before audit, no tests or CI. The commit message shows it was AI-generated, and the repo description is just 'typesafe-mcp'.
Anything Claude passes is sent to a third party. On client projects that means code egress at Claude's discretion, with no allow/deny filter.
No caching, retries or rate-limit handling.
entries.verdict: A tiny, honest, OpenRouter-patchable wrapper, but it targets Chinese ticket triage and moderation, and it is an opt-in MCP tool with no auto-trigger. It would not deliver 'Claude uses Jev automatically'. At most, borrow the typesafe_classify passthrough idea, and write your own coding-focused hook or tool with a timeout and coding-oriented question templates.

entries.name: Obrais-cloud/typesafe-mcp
entries.what: Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP) written for one person's private agent fleet (openclaw/hermes, Mac mini, Tailscale IPs). It exposes 7 tools over the TypeSafe direct API (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-1.13.0): judge (NL request compiled by a private Ollama fleet LLM into a typed noul/choice/score request), rerank, systemone (raw passthrough), quality_judge, compare, classify_push_failure, job_fit (shells out to a personal career-ops script). Also includes cron triage/ledger/router-shadow scripts, launchd plists and a vendored copy of the official TypeSafe SKILL.md. Not a Claude Code plugin, no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hook, no skill trigger, no proxy. The author achieved 'automatic' use by hand-adding a Jev block to CLAUDE.md (docs/INTEGRACION-2026-09.md:194-201), which is prompt steering, not deterministic. Nothing in the repo makes Claude Code call Jev on its own for coding events.
security: Key read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or plaintext ~/typesafe-mcp/.env or a .env next to the module (core.py:86-105); not passed in argv, so not visible in the process list when set via env. Never logged per docstring.

Hardcoded private Tailscale IPs and an internal 'ollawake' host in source (core.py:30,37-42): user prompts/content sent to compile step go to hosts the user does not control if the default chain is left in place (connect will normally just fail, but it is a data-egress footgun on shared tailnets).

Committed stray file 'remotework@100.94.117.48' (a copy of triage.py) and deploy scripts leaking the author's SSH user/hosts; docs describe the author's tailnet topology and a bearer-token HTTP MCP endpoint at 100.70.244.85:11451.
HTTP mode disables DNS-rebinding protection and relies on an optional bearer token (server.py:143-146); optional, off by default (only when TS_MCP_HTTP_PORT set).
job_fit runs a subprocess (node typesafe-job-fit.mjs from ~/career-ops); posting data written to a temp file; fixed argv, no shell string, but an unrelated attack surface.

Optional Supabase ledger POSTs metadata (caller, model, tokens, latency, SHA-256 of state, error text up to 500 chars) if SUPABASE_* env are present; silent no-op otherwise. Uses service-role key when configured.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever Claude decides to pass as tool args: state/content/text/responses/error_text go to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if URL swapped). For judge/rerank the same text is FIRST sent to the hardcoded private Ollama fleet (100.x Tailscale hosts) for compilation. Ledger (only if SUPABASE_* set) sends metadata + state hash, not content. Nothing is sent automatically; only what the model chooses to put in a tool call. Direct TypeSafe API, not OpenRouter, by default.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call (tool returns an error to Claude; no Claude Code blocking since it is a model-discretion tool, not a hook). TypeSafe call timeout 60 s (core.py:270; jevkit 60 s), fleet compile 90 s per host plus 4 s reachability probes across 4 dead hosts and a 10 s wake call, so judge/rerank on a non-fleet machine can burn tens of seconds before failing with 'no fleet host compiled the request'. Ledger is fire-and-forget with 2 s timeout and never raises. job_fit degrades to decision='manual' with 20 s timeout. Missing key raises RuntimeError at first call, not at startup.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools (mcp__typesafe__judge, rerank, systemone, quality_judge, compare, classify_push_failure, job_fit). Docstrings plus FastMCP-generated JSON schemas roughly 5-6k chars, about 1.3-1.6k tokens of tool definitions (less if deferred via tool search). No server 'instructions' field, no hooks, no injected text. The author's optional CLAUDE.md 'Juicios con Jev' block is not shipped in the repo (only referenced in docs). 3 of 7 tools (job_fit, quality_judge, compare) are irrelevant noise for this user.
pros: Uses the real v1 System One contract with sensible local validation (score 2-10 levels, choice <=255 options, noul true/false criteria) at core.py:145-186, and pins model to jev-1.13.0 instead of moving alias.

systemone and jevkit tools are plain httpx/urllib code with no fleet dependency; the URL is env-overridable (TS_MCP_TS_URL) so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13 is a config-only change for those tools.

Compiler prompt (core.py:44-83) encodes TypeSafe's official question-design rules; vendored official SKILL.md (skill/, MIT) is a useful reference, and README documents installing the official typesafe-ai/skills plugin.
classify_push_failure is a small, real dev-workflow example of a typed Jev decision; small tool surface (~1.5k tokens).
Key handling avoids argv (env or .env file), ledger cannot block or fail a call, no postinstall or curl|sh.
cons: Not built for this use case: it is one person's private fleet glue (Tailscale IPs, Mac mini, launchd, career-ops job-fit, Supabase ledger, openclaw/hermes). judge and rerank, the headline tools, fail on any other machine because compilation needs the author's Ollama hosts (core.py:37-42) and Ollama-format payloads.
No OpenRouter support at all (0 grep hits); only TypeSafe direct. Response-shape parity on OpenRouter is unverified, and judge/rerank would need code changes.

No automatic invocation: model-discretion tools only, no hooks/skill triggers; relies on CLAUDE.md prompt steering, which is exactly what the user does not want. Claude has no reason to call 'systemone' with hand-built typed questions during normal coding.
Tools are mostly non-coding (job_fit, quality_judge/compare for LLM-eval, rerank tickets); only classify_push_failure is coding-adjacent and marginal.
No license (all rights reserved), 1 commit author, 1 star, 33 commits in 11 days, no releases/CI/packaging, tests cover only jevkit and ledger; leaks author's infra details in tree.
Extra dead-host latency: up to 4 unreachable probes + 10 s wake before erroring.
Requires Jev to be called through Claude as a tool: an Opus turn to build the request then read probabilities, so cost/latency far exceeds the 70-500 ms Jev call itself.
entries.verdict: Not suitable as the Claude Code integration: it is a private-fleet MCP wrapper for TypeSafe direct, with headline tools that depend on the author's Ollama hosts, no OpenRouter path, no license and no automatic triggering. At most, reuse its validation rules and the systemone URL override idea as reference material for a custom minimal hook or MCP.
entries.license: None (GitHub reports no license; only the vendored skill/ dir carries MIT). Unlicensed = all rights reserved by default.

entries.name: wr0x00/jev_mcp
entries.what: A small FastMCP (Python) server, about 700 lines. It exposes 4 tools over Streamable HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8800/mcp: jev_route_task, jev_tool_gate, jev_verify_done and jev_ask. Each tool sends fixed Chinese-language Noul/Score/Choice questions to a Jev endpoint. It then applies threshold policies from config.yaml and returns auto_execute, human_review, block, pass or continue. The design is an "agent control loop" (route, then gate before a tool call, then verify at the end). Nothing in Claude Code invokes it; the calling model has to choose to call the tools. The README calls it "just a demo".
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no SKILL.md and no CLAUDE.md snippet. The tool descriptions say what they do but not when Claude must call them. The README's control-loop pseudocode assumes an external harness that calls route/gate/verify around the LLM, which Claude Code is not. Automatic use would need extra work: hooks (PreToolUse calling the gate, Stop hook calling verify) or CLAUDE.md rules. A hook cannot call an MCP tool, so it would need a separate script that reimplements the HTTP call, which makes the MCP server pointless.
security: The MCP HTTP server binds to 0.0.0.0:8800 by default (server.py:226, config.yaml JEV_MCP_HOST, Dockerfile, docker-compose port 8800:8800). It has no authentication in code: FastMCP is created with no auth provider. The README shows a 'Bearer <your-mcp-token>' header, but nothing validates it. On a laptop this exposes an unauthenticated tool endpoint, which is a LAN risk; it would have to be changed to 127.0.0.1.

The API key is read from an env var or from config.yaml, so it is not in argv. The config.yaml `env` section invites putting the key in a file next to the code, and .gitignore does not exclude config.yaml. The shipped defaults have the key and URL fields swapped (config.yaml:8-9).

The prompt-injection defence is weak: sanitize_text (templates.py:110-126) strips control characters, truncates to 8000 chars, and only warns on five regexes without blocking. The gate's `proposal` text is written by the LLM being gated, so a compromised or injected agent can write a benign-looking proposal. The gate is also advisory: nothing enforces it.
Timeouts and failures return human_review, but the calling model can simply ignore that.
No shell execution in the server. No npm postinstall, curl|sh or telemetry. start.sh is a plain venv bootstrap. Dependencies are unpinned.
Docker image runs as root (no USER) on python:3.12-slim.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever text the model puts into the tool arguments, up to 8000 chars per call (safety.max_context_chars). That means the user request, the proposed action, tool name and target, and result summaries. The data goes to JEV_BASE_URL, and the server never checks that the URL is TypeSafe or OpenRouter. The server does not read files, diffs or tool output on its own. Since the args are written by the model, code and secrets can reach the endpoint if the model pastes them in, and there is no secret redaction. The server itself has no telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-conservative but not fail-open. Client timeout is 4000 ms with 1 retry (config.yaml client, client.py:268-281), so the worst case is about 8 s per call. On any error or when unconfigured, the tools return degraded=true with action human_review (or block if configured). That is a returned value, not an exception, so Claude just sees text. With the shipped config the server starts unconfigured and every call returns 'not_configured'. In practice it soft-fails: it wastes a tool call and adds nothing. Because MCP is a separate daemon, a missing daemon means Claude Code shows the server as failed to connect and the tools are absent, which is harmless.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. The description text is Chinese with English Args blocks, about 2,000 chars in total. JSON schemas are small except for jev_ask (list of dicts). Estimate about 800-1,000 tokens of tool definitions (Chinese text tokenizes poorly). It sets no MCP server `instructions` (the FastMCP("jev_mcp") constructor has no instructions argument). No hook-injected text. It is cheap on context, but it is only worth having if it is called.
pros: MIT licence, small (about 700 lines), and readable in 10 minutes, so it is easy to audit or fork.
The three-part control-loop framing (route, gate, verify) maps sensibly onto Noul/Score/Choice, and templates.py has reusable questions for destructive, exfiltration and scope_breach checks.
Degrades to human_review on timeout or misconfiguration instead of auto-approving. The client timeout is 4 s with 1 retry.
Low context footprint: 4 tools and about 1k tokens, with no injected hook text.
Includes /health, Docker and cross-platform start scripts, and policy thresholds are in YAML.
cons: It does not work with OpenRouter, and probably not with TypeSafe directly either. It posts an invented {context, questions[]} payload to {base}/v1/ask, while the real API takes `model`, `state` and a `questions` dict with instructions/criteria. It also parses a single scalar `p` per field, which does not fit the real per-option probabilities (client.py:271-302). The README's own default URL would produce .../v1/systemone/v1/ask. There is no evidence anywhere in the repo that it was ever run against a live endpoint.
Shipped config.yaml has the API key and URL swapped (TYPESAFE_API_KEY holds the URL, JEV_BASE_URL is empty), so it starts unconfigured and every call returns not_configured.
It never fires on its own. It is a plain MCP tool with no hook or skill. Claude Code would have to choose to call it, which is the opposite of the user's requirement for automatic use.

Per-action gating through an LLM tool call adds seconds of turn time on every Bash or Edit call. Quality is unproven: the thresholds (exfiltration 0.1, destructive 0.05) are uncalibrated guesses, and the prompts are written in Chinese.
The gate is advisory, and its input `proposal` is authored by the model being gated, so it gives little real protection against prompt injection.
Server binds to 0.0.0.0:8800 with no authentication (the README's Bearer token is never checked), and the design needs a separately managed daemon instead of a stdio server.
Very immature: 0 stars, 1 author, 6 commits all on one day, no tests, CI or releases. The author calls it a demo and points to a sister project (nanojev_mcp) for local use.

The hard-coded question set targets a generic agent loop (support-ticket style task_type). There is nothing specific to coding workflows such as tests, diffs, git or refactors, so it would rarely add value in daily development.
entries.verdict: Do not use as is. It does not match the real Jev/OpenRouter API, the shipped config is broken, and it has no hooks or skills, so Claude Code would never call it automatically. At most it is a source of question templates (route/gate/verify) to port into a purpose-built hook or a small MCP server that calls openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions.

entries.name: keysersoft/jev-mcp-server
entries.what: Not an MCP server in itself: a 15-file "satellite" repo containing only a declarative connector definition (adapter/jev.json, synced daily from HelpCode-ai/anythingmcp) plus docker-compose/install/smoke scripts. The definition is loaded into AnythingMCP (a separate AGPL gateway: Docker + Postgres, or the cloud.anythingmcp.com SaaS) which then exposes 6 MCP tools (jev_playbook, jev_yes_no, jev_classify, jev_rate, jev_ask, jev_list_models) that proxy to TypeSafe's POST /v1/systemone. Targeted at claude.ai/ChatGPT connector use and support-ticket triage, not coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Descriptions are written for support-ticket triage/lead scoring ('START HERE' playbook, 'routing, labelling, intent, triage'), nothing about coding, so Claude Code will rarely pick them unprompted; no hook, skill or proxy component to force use.
security: No server code in the repo; all runtime trust sits in the AnythingMCP gateway (632 stars, AGPL, separate project) and its Docker image helpcodeai/anythingmcp:latest (unpinned tag, amd64 only).

README 'claude mcp add ... --header "X-API-Key: <MCP_API_KEY>"' puts the MCP gateway key in argv/process list and in ~/.claude.json; install.sh also prints it. TYPESAFE key itself stays in the gateway, stored AES-256-GCM encrypted, never shown to the model.

install.sh is a local bash script (not curl|sh) that writes .env (chmod 600), runs docker compose, writes admin password into .env with default admin@example.com, and writes temp auth JSON to /tmp/amcp-auth.json (briefly, world-readable default umask, contains admin JWT). docker-compose uses default postgres password 'amcp' but binds ports to 127.0.0.1 only.
Stack: gateway + Postgres containers running 24/7 for a tool that costs $0.04/M tokens; large attack surface (SSO/RBAC/SCIM/web UI) for a single-user workflow.

No npm postinstall; package.json has only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk for smoke test. GitHub Action sync-adapter opens PRs rather than pushing. Adapter is auto-synced from upstream, so tool descriptions can change under you.

Prompt-injection surface: jev_playbook itself warns that instruction-like text in state can steer Jev; all 6 tools annotated readOnlyHint/openWorldHint false. AnythingMCP audit log stores every input/output (i.e. code/state you send) in its Postgres.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in `state` and `questions` (arbitrary text/JSON: could be code, diffs, tickets) goes claude -> local/cloud AnythingMCP gateway (logged in its audit DB with input/output) -> https://api.typesafe.ai. With AnythingMCP Cloud (Frankfurt, helpcode.ai) the data additionally transits and is logged by a third party. Nothing is sent automatically; only when Claude chooses to call a tool.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by nature (it is an optional MCP tool; if the gateway container is down, claude shows the server failed and simply the tools are unavailable). Adapter states 429/529 retry with backoff (README claim, retry config inside the gateway not in this repo); no client-side timeout config visible. Gateway crash at startup would only lose the tools, not block Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 6 tools; tool names+descriptions+JSON schemas approx 7.7k chars, roughly 1.9k tokens (incl. ~2.2k chars server instructions ~550 tokens, so ~2.3k total). jev_playbook is ~4k chars returned on demand. No hooks, no skill files.
pros: Clean, typed tool surface mapping 1:1 to Jev primitives (noul/choice/score) with good playbook and parameter docs; only 6 tools and ~2k tokens of context.
All tools annotated read-only, no write/shell surface exposed to Claude.
TypeSafe key stays in the gateway, never enters Claude's context or argv (only the gateway key does).
Adapter definition is readable JSON, so the request shape (/v1/systemone body, response selects) is a useful reference for writing your own OpenRouter client.
Works with Claude Code out of the box over HTTP transport for TypeSafe-direct users.
cons: Contains no MCP server code: requires running a full third-party gateway (AnythingMCP + Postgres in Docker, or sending data to a SaaS) just to proxy one $0.04/M-token endpoint.
No OpenRouter support at all; hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai with TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Patching means editing gateway DB config and fighting the daily sync PR.

Not automatic: pure model-discretion tools with triage/lead-scoring descriptions and example prompts that all start 'Use Jev to...'; nothing in it makes Claude Code call Jev on its own for coding decisions. Directly contradicts the user's requirement.
Brand new (created 2026-09-27, 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no tests, no CI beyond sync); AGPL-3.0 may matter for client projects if embedded.
Every call costs an Opus tool-call round trip (compose state JSON, read result) that is far slower and pricier than the 300 ms/$0.04 Jev call itself.
Sends whatever Claude puts in state to a gateway that audit-logs input/output in Postgres; with Cloud variant to a third party, a concern for client code.
Gateway key passed via --header on argv/config; unpinned docker image :latest; default admin@example.com and postgres password 'amcp'.
Extra always-on Docker stack (2 containers) on the dev machine for marginal value.
entries.verdict: Not an MCP server but a packaging of a declarative AnythingMCP connector for TypeSafe-direct, aimed at ticket triage, with no OpenRouter path and no automatic invocation. Skip it for this setup; at most read adapter/jev.json as a reference for the /v1/systemone request schema when building an OpenRouter-native hook or tiny MCP.

entries.name: opsiaadi/opnroute-jev
entries.what: Two tiny (about 5.7 KB and 8.2 KB) single-file Python MCP servers, one stdio and one Streamable HTTP, written for the Hermes agent. They wrap OpenRouter's POST /api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev via urllib. The exposed tools are classify, classify_batch and health. The default question set is a hardcoded chat-message classifier (is_crypto, is_support, is_spam, category, urgency, sentiment_score). Nothing in it is coding-specific, and nothing in it triggers automatically.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no routing. The server instructions describe a generic text classifier and never mention coding. Opus would almost never call it unprompted for coding tasks, since the tool descriptions and defaults are about crypto, spam and sentiment. It does not meet the user's 'automatic' requirement.
security: No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry. Only outbound call is to openrouter.ai (urllib, jev_classifier.py:77-88).

Stdio variant: the key can be passed via env, so it stays out of argv (good). The README example for Hermes uses `--env OPENROUTER_API_KEY=...`, which puts the key in the Hermes command line. Claude Code's `claude mcp add -e` avoids that.
Fallback silently reads ~/.hermes/.env (:28-35). The parser only picks the OPENROUTER_API_KEY line, but it is an odd hardcoded path for a non-Hermes user.

HTTP variant: a default of 127.0.0.1 is safe, but the README pushes 0.0.0.0 with no auth by default. MCP_AUTH_TOKEN is optional (jev_classifier_http.py:36-45), and the check is `!=` string compare, not constant-time. transport_security=None disables DNS-rebinding protection (:193). Anyone who reaches the port can spend the user's OpenRouter credits. The HTTP variant is not needed for Claude Code, so use stdio only.
Prompt-injection surface is small. Tool output is JSON probabilities, so it cannot carry free text back into the model, except the raw OpenRouter error body (first 500 chars, :90).
Data sent to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) is whatever text the model passes as 'text', with no redaction and no allowlist. For client projects that is a compliance concern.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever string Claude passes as the `text` argument, sent as `state` to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (and on to TypeSafe), plus the question definitions. Nothing else. There is no automatic capture of prompts, diffs, files or tool outputs. The scope depends on what Claude chooses to send, and unlike a hook it is not filtered by the user's secret-leak guard, because that guard only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and MCP tool inputs are not covered. Headers include the OpenRouter key and a Hermes HTTP-Referer.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level. Errors (missing key, HTTP error, URLError, bad JSON) are returned as {"error": ...} JSON and not raised. The timeout is 30 s per call and blocking. The stdio server is synchronous inside async tools, so a slow Jev call blocks the server event loop. classify_batch is sequential, so N texts can take up to N x 30 s. TimeoutError and socket.timeout raised while reading the response body are not caught (only HTTPError, URLError and JSONDecodeError are), so the tool can raise. There is no retry and no circuit breaker. Since nothing calls it automatically, failures only affect turns where Claude chooses to use it.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Names, descriptions and schemas come to about 250-350 tokens in the HTTP variant, which has docstrings. The stdio variant has no docstrings at all, so its tools are described only by name and args, which is worse for model discretion. Server instructions add about 55 tokens ("JEV Classifier MCP - structured classification ... noul, choice, score"). Total is about 300-400 tokens, negligible. Nothing is injected by hooks.
pros: Very small and fully auditable (about 14 KB of Python), with no shell execution, no postinstall and no telemetry. The only network destination is openrouter.ai.

Uses OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL defaulting to ~typesafe/jev-latest. Model id and env var match the user's chosen provider directly, and the stdio variant can be registered with `claude mcp add -e`.
Custom `questions` passthrough (JSON with type noul/choice/score, instructions, criteria) makes it a usable raw System One client if you supply your own coding-oriented questions.
Errors are returned as data instead of crashing the server in the common cases. MIT license, tiny context footprint (about 300-400 tokens).
cons: Not automatic. Pure model-discretion tool with generic-classifier descriptions (crypto, spam, sentiment). Claude Code will not use it without being told to, which is the exact thing the user wants to avoid.
Default questions are a hardcoded crypto/support/spam chat classifier (jev_classifier.py:45-66) with no coding use case such as risk-gating a Bash command, triaging a diff or picking a test scope.

Built for Hermes. README has no Claude Code instructions, hardcodes the Hermes Referer and X-Title headers and reads ~/.hermes/.env. Depends on `mcp.server.MCPServer` from an mcp 2.0+ API that is not verified and has no pinned version, so a plain `pip install mcp` may fail to import.
Zero tests, no CI, no releases, 0 stars, 4 commits in one day, and an unverified request/response schema that has not been checked against OpenRouter docs. The stdio tools have no docstrings.

Sends arbitrary Claude-chosen text to a third party with no redaction, outside the coverage of the user's secret-leak hook. No timeout tuning, no retry, sequential batch, and a blocking call inside an async server.
Uses only the System One endpoint and not the Decisions API. It offers no Choice-over-tool-calls or permission-hook integration.
HTTP variant encourages an unauthenticated 0.0.0.0 bind that would let others spend the user's credits (transport_security=None). The user would not need it.
entries.verdict: A harmless but tiny Hermes-oriented proof of concept that proves the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone call shape (model + state + questions). It is not an automatic Claude Code integration and has no coding-relevant behavior. Use it at most as reference code for a custom hook or MCP, and do not adopt it.

entries.name: mcp-jev
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (Node, @modelcontextprotocol/sdk + zod) that forwards typed Jev questions (noul/choice/score) to TypeSafe's /v1/systemone endpoint or to a local Laya server. The candidate summary is stale: v2.0.x (latest 2.0.1) replaced jev_decide/jev_list_models with four tools: decide_predict, decide_preset, decide_status, decide_list_models. Presets (triage, guard, moderation, router, email) are hard-coded question sets aimed at support-ticket, moderation, email and LLM-routing use cases, not coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude calls it if the tool description convinces it to. The description says to call it to "classify or route text", "check a true/false condition" or "rate content on a rubric", which rarely arises in coding work. Opus 5.5 can classify or route text itself for free, so it has little reason to call an external classifier and will mostly ignore it. There is no hook, skill, or proxy, so it will not be used automatically in the sense the user wants unless CLAUDE.md or a hook forces it, and that would be the user telling Claude to use it.
security: No install scripts: package.json has no preinstall/postinstall. The `prepare: tsc` script does not run for registry installs.
Runtime dependencies are only zod and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No child_process, fs or eval in dist/*.js. Only fetch() calls, to the configured base URL.
No telemetry found: outbound requests go only to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (or LAYA_BASE_URL) at /v1/systemone, /v1/models and /health.
API key is read from env (factory.js:108) and sent only as a Bearer header, so it stays out of argv if placed in the MCP `env` block. It is not logged; stderr only shows startup lines.
Any base URL is trusted: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is not validated, so a mis-set URL would send the key and state to another host. The default is HTTPS api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is raw JSON of numbers and enum keys (no free text from the model), which is small. But question text and state are chosen by the calling LLM, so file contents pass through it.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the LLM puts in `state` and `questions` (up to 200k chars each call) goes to the provider. With OpenRouter that is the text the agent chooses to send: possibly code, diffs, file contents, user prompts or tool output, plus the OpenRouter key. Nothing is sent automatically. Claude Code's own prompts and tool results are not intercepted, so egress is model-driven and opt-in per call. Client code would reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe only if Claude decides to call the tool with it. This matters for client projects under NDA.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors are caught and returned as an isError text result ("Error: ..."), so Claude continues. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the server call process.exit(1) at startup (index.js:31), so it shows as a failed MCP connection, which is harmless but noisy. Each request has a 30 s timeout (lib.js:6) and 3 attempts on 429/500/502/503/529 with backoff (1 s, 2 s, capped at 60 s total). The worst case is therefore about 90 s plus about 3 s of waits on one call, while a healthy call takes roughly 70-500 ms. There is no circuit breaker. Because it is a tool call, a slow Jev blocks only that call and not other turns.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Descriptions total about 2.3k chars. The JSON schemas from zod (a question discriminated union, state union, model) add roughly 2-3k chars. Estimated total is about 1.2-1.5k tokens of tool definitions per session (chars/4), less if Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch. No server-level `instructions` field is set. No hook-injected text, since it has no hooks. It is a small footprint, but it pays for tools whose presets are irrelevant to coding.
pros: Small, readable, benign code: about 30 KB of dist JS, two dependencies, no shell exec, no postinstall, no telemetry, MIT.

Uses the same /v1/systemone path as OpenRouter's System One API and sends a Bearer key, so the base-URL override TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api will probably work with no code change (wire format unverified).

Exposes all three Jev primitives generically through decide_predict, with limits enforced by zod (max 100 questions, 255 choices, 2-10 score levels), so Claude can build custom noul/choice/score questions.
Good errors: 401/403 and 400/422 are not retried, retries are bounded, and there is a 30 s timeout. Failures come back as isError results, so Claude keeps working (fail-open).
Small context cost of about 1.2-1.5k tokens for four tools.
Key stays in the MCP env block and does not show up in argv.
cons: The candidate description is stale. It lists jev_decide and jev_list_models, but the current 2.0.1 has decide_predict, decide_preset, decide_status and decide_list_models. The old v1 tool names would no longer match.

The GitHub source repo and author account return 404, so provenance, commit history and tests cannot be verified. The package is about 9 days old with 7 releases in a week, one anonymous-looking maintainer, and the tarball ships no tests or source.

No OpenRouter support in code. It has no OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The key has to be smuggled in via TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the hard-coded default model "jev-latest" is probably not a valid OpenRouter ID (typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). There is no env to change it, so the LLM must pass `model` every time or you must fork the package.

The response parser is strict (zod requires answers, model, and usage.input_tokens/output_tokens). Any difference in OpenRouter's response envelope breaks every call with ParseError. I could not confirm the shape because the OpenRouter doc URLs I tried gave 404.
decide_status never calls the API and always reports status "ok" for Jev, so it is useless for diagnosing a bad key or an outage.

Presets are built for support tickets, moderation, phishing and email, plus an LLM 'router', and none is for coding. The router preset's model-routing idea does not apply to Claude Code, which can't switch its main model per prompt through MCP.

It is a passive tool that only fires when the model chooses to call it. Opus has no reason to hand simple classification to an external model, so this fails the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement. Forcing it would take CLAUDE.md instructions or hooks, both outside this package.
Data sent is whatever the LLM puts into `state`, so client code could leave the machine to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The tool's own advice is to send only relevant fields, which nothing enforces.
Worst-case retry time of about 90 s per call, with no circuit breaker, and `npx -y` without a version pin runs whatever is latest on the registry at each session start.
entries.verdict: A clean, small, generic Jev wrapper, but young, of unverifiable provenance (GitHub repo gone), and not OpenRouter-native. Even patched, it is a model-discretion tool with support/moderation presets that Claude Code has no reason to call, so it will not deliver the automatic integration the user wants. It is at best a building block: if used, pin mcp-jev@2.0.1 or vendor the 30 KB and set the base URL and default model. A hook-driven approach fits the goal better.

entries.name: aiex/Jevcodex
entries.what: Local Python MCP for Codex: jev_decide, jev_classify_file (JSON/JSONL/CSV), jev_review_evidence; macOS Keychain key storage and delegation skill.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Batch-classify records and review line ranges without returning text to the agent
Small, tests exist
cons: macOS-only installer (Keychain, Install Jev.command) and Codex-specific; user is on Linux
TypeSafe key only; no OpenRouter

entries.name: Olli0103/openclaw-typesafe-ai
entries.what: OpenClaw plugin registering one optional typesafe_decide tool that posts typed questions to TypeSafe /v1/systemone with SecretRef credentials and strict validation.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion tool in OpenClaw
pros: Strict response schema validation, explicit opt-in, no hooks or background services
Includes verification report and host smoke test
cons: OpenClaw-only, version-pinned to 2026.9.4
TypeSafe endpoint hardcoded, no OpenRouter
Explicit invocation only, adds nothing over a generic MCP

entries.name: jevx-mcp
entries.what: Tiny (about 10 KB source) stdio MCP server exposing 3 tools that wrap the third-party jevx.org gateway (README states it is an independent playground, not affiliated with TypeSafe). Model-invoked `decide` POSTs state + up to 16 typed questions (choice/noul/score) to https://jevx.org/api/decisions/run using a Bearer JEVX_API_KEY, and formats the returned probabilities as text. Not a hook, skill or proxy, so nothing is automatic.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions never tell Claude WHEN to use Jev (for example, no "use this before branching on X"). Claude would rarely call `decide` unprompted, and it must author a whole question schema each time. It does not meet the user's "automatic without prompting" requirement. There are no hooks, no skill, and no CLAUDE.md snippet in the repo.
security: Key is passed via env (JEVX_API_KEY), not argv, so it does not show in the process list. It is sent only as a Bearer header to BASE_URL (client.ts:138).
JEVX_BASE_URL env override is unvalidated. If it is ever set to an attacker-controlled host, the Bearer key and state leak. Low risk for this user, who controls their own env.
No postinstall or install scripts (package.json scripts: build, start, prepublishOnly, test only). No child_process or shell exec in dist. Zero dependencies beyond the MCP SDK and zod.
No telemetry beyond the jevx.org call itself. The utm_source=mcp link is returned as tool text only.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is only formatted numbers plus model/request id, so it is small. But `decide` input is model-authored text sent to a third party.

Supply chain: brand-new single-maintainer npm package (kavel, [email removed]), 1 version, 0 stars, unaffiliated with TypeSafe. `npx -y` without a version pin means a later malicious publish would run with the user's shell privileges.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever `state` and `questions` Claude puts in the `decide` call (arbitrary text or JSON, so code snippets, diffs, or file contents if Claude includes them) is POSTed to https://jevx.org/api/decisions/run, a third-party site that is not OpenRouter or TypeSafe, with the JEVX_API_KEY. Nothing is sent unless the model calls the tool. No background collection. For client projects this creates a new, unvetted data processor.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open only in the trivial sense that the tool returns isError text on failure (missing key, non-JSON, code!=0, network throw is caught at index.ts:232). There is NO fetch timeout or AbortController (client.ts:136), so a hung jevx.org could stall the tool call until the MCP client's own tool timeout. No retries. Because the tool is model-invoked, not hook-based, it cannot block Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Approximate tool-definition text is 3.5k characters, so roughly 900 tokens: the decide description of about 430 chars, the decide schema of about 1.2k chars with nested questionSchema (duplicated in validate_questions), and the small open_in_jevx. No MCP server `instructions`. No hook-injected text. Cost is paid every session, and the tools are likely deferred under Claude Code's tool search, which reduces it.
pros: Very small and auditable: about 10 KB of source, no postinstall, no shell exec, and the published npm dist matches the git source (verified by grep of the tarball).
Key passed by env, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
`validate_questions` is a free local schema checker that could be useful to a developer prototyping Jev question shapes.
Surfaces the useful semantics: the API's HTTP-200-with-code!=0 refusals become tool errors, and a noul of exactly 0.5 is flagged as 'declined' (index.ts:229; client.ts:150).
cons: Wrong provider: hardcoded to the unaffiliated jevx.org gateway and its own credits (client.ts:136). No OpenRouter or TypeSafe endpoint, and it needs a separate jevx.org account and key. Not the OpenRouter-hosted Jev the user wants.

Not automatic: model-discretion tool with no trigger guidance, so it fails the core requirement. It would need a CLAUDE.md nudge or a wrapping hook or skill, and the user does not want to prompt for it.
Sends model-chosen state, which may include client code, to a third-party site with an unknown privacy policy. That is a serious concern for client work.
No fetch timeout or retry (client.ts:136), 1 commit, 0 stars, 1 unaffiliated maintainer, brand-new (8 days old), a single test file, no CI. Effectively a proof of concept.
`open_in_jevx` is just a referral link and wastes context tokens. The tool schemas cost about 900 tokens per session for minimal gain.
`npx -y` unpinned means a future malicious publish auto-runs. The LICENSE text is nonstandard (GitHub shows 'Other').
entries.verdict: Skip. It is a small clean wrapper, but for a third-party gateway (jevx.org), not OpenRouter or TypeSafe. It is a discretionary MCP tool with no auto-trigger, and it sends prompts to an unvetted 8-day-old service. If the user later builds their own integration, the only reusable idea is the question-shape validation and the code!=0 error handling, and it is easy to reimplement.

entries.name: okooo5km/jev
entries.what: Unofficial single-file stdlib-Python CLI (jev/scripts/jev, ~2170 lines) plus an Agent Skill (SKILL.md) for TypeSafe Jev. Verbs: yes (Noul), pick (Choice), score, filter (semantic grep per line), run SPEC (multi-question specs: mail, feedback, signal, commit, route), raw, auth, provider. Talks to TypeSafe api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone by default or OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions. Not an MCP server, not a hook. Meant to be invoked by the model via Bash when SKILL.md description matches. Built-in specs are in Chinese. No PermissionRequest hook recipe is shipped.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at model discretion. It fires when the model reads a task as classify/triage/route/filter. Opus will rarely reach for a Jev call in ordinary coding, so it is not reliably "automatic". No hooks, no PermissionRequest recipe, no CLAUDE.md snippet. The user would have to write his own hook or CLAUDE.md rule that shells out to `jev yes` or `jev run`. Use for hooks: `JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter /abs/path/jev yes "..." --timeout 3 --retries 0 --json`.
security: Key handling is good. The key is read from env, then $JEV_ENV_FILE, then ~/.config/jev/.env (jev:196-228), and sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (:350-351). It is never taken from argv. `auth set` needs a TTY with hidden input and writes 0600 via O_EXCL and chmod (:1582-1617). SKILL.md explicitly tells the agent never to read or print key files or pass keys as args.
`auth set --stdin` exists, so a key could be piped in. SKILL.md forbids the agent from doing so, but that is only an instruction.
JEV_DEBUG=1 prints the full request payload (state) to stderr (:697-701). The Authorization header is not printed in the code I read, but not exhaustively verified.
No subprocess, os.system, eval or exec found in the CLI (grep returned nothing). Pure stdlib http.client and urllib. Proxy support exists (test_proxy.py).
No telemetry. Only static X-Title: jev-cli and HTTP-Referer github header on OpenRouter calls, which is OpenRouter's normal app attribution.

Installer is decent: version regex check, refuses symlinked home, sha256 verify before extract, atomic swap, main() wrapper against truncation. The checksum comes from the same release host, so it guards integrity but not a compromised repo. The user does not need the installer: the single file can be read and copied.
entries.dataEgress: The state text, the question text and criteria, and the model name go to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, plus the Bearer key and a static User-Agent/X-Title/Referer. For filter and -l, every input line is sent, and one request is made per line. For `jev run commit`, `git diff --cached` content leaves the machine, which matters for client code. The CLI does no redaction beyond a SIZE_WARN_TOKENS=30000 warning. OpenRouter's own logging and provider policies apply.
entries.failureMode: Not a hook, so it fails per call. A network error or HTTP 4xx/5xx gives exit code 2 with a message on stderr after retries with backoff on 429/5xx (default --retries and --timeout 60 s, jev:2020 and 2067). Exit 1 means a legitimate "no", so a naive script that treats non-zero as "no" conflates error with no. The caller must distinguish 2 from 1. The default 60 s timeout with retries is far too long for a hook, and a hook would need --timeout 3 --retries 0. If used inside a PermissionRequest hook wrapper, fail-open-to-prompt has to be written by the user. The alpha endpoint may move (SKILL.md acknowledges this, and JEV_BASE_URL is the escape hatch).
entries.contextCost: Low. One skill. The frontmatter description is about 1.2k chars (~300 tokens) and is always in the listing, which is noticeable with skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02 (may get truncated). The body is 9.1k chars (~2.3k tokens), loaded when triggered, and references/cli.md (~24k chars, ~6k tokens) only if read. Zero MCP tools and zero hook-injected text.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (jev:65-73), with correct model normalization to typesafe/jev-1.13 and ~typesafe/jev-latest, and the request body matches the alpha/decisions schema. It works with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY, with no changes.

Well-engineered key handling for this user: keys stay out of argv, files are written 0600, and there is a status/check command that never prints a key. That suits a setup with a fail-closed secret hook.
Zero dependencies (stdlib only, Python 3.9+), a single readable 2.1k-line file with no subprocess or eval, and no telemetry. It is easy to audit and vendor, so it can be used without the installer.

Substantial test suite: about 190 test functions across 15 files (test_providers 52, test_auth 29, test_provider_admin 31), a mock server, and CI on Python 3.9/3.11/3.13 on Linux and macOS with pinned action SHAs and shellcheck.
Useful primitives for shell pipelines: filter as a semantic grep, -l batch with concurrency, --json output, and exit codes usable in shell tests. It also handles retry/backoff and connection reuse.
Ships a `commit` spec (type, secret leak, breaking change, risk) and a `route` spec that map onto real dev workflows. Users can add JSON specs in ~/.config/jev/specs.
Low context cost (no MCP tool defs, one skill) and the Apache-2.0 license.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a skill plus CLI with no hooks, and it provides no PermissionRequest hook (the official cookbook pattern), Stop hook or CLAUDE.md snippet. Reaching the user's goal (Claude Code uses it without being told) requires writing the hook glue himself, so this is a building block, not the integration.

Auto-invocation depends on Opus choosing the skill from the description. That description is long (~1.2k chars), partly Chinese, and aimed at classify/triage/email/feedback, not coding, and it may be truncated at a 0.02 skill listing budget.
Default provider is TypeSafe. With both keys present, auto picks TypeSafe (jev:274-279). The user must pin openrouter (JEV_PROVIDER or `jev provider default openrouter`).
Default 60 s timeout and retries make it unsuitable for a hook as-is. Exit code 1 (no) versus 2 (error) must be handled carefully in glue code.
Built-in specs and error messages are in Chinese, and the main README is Chinese (an English README.en.md exists). Spec instructions must be rewritten for an English coding context.
Very new and low-adoption: created 2026-09-18, 12 commits by a single author, 11 stars, 1 fork, and it is unofficial. It depends on an alpha endpoint that may move.
Data egress of diffs and commands to a third party. `jev run commit` sends the staged diff, which is a concern for client repos. No redaction is offered.
Jev calibration and prompt-injection weaknesses apply unchanged, and the CLI adds no mitigation.

A PermissionRequest hook is skipped entirely in bypassPermissions sessions. It fires in auto mode only for calls that would prompt. The main automatic-use design (allow when Jev is confident) therefore does not cover the user's frequent bypass sessions.
The default model alias ~typesafe/jev-latest floats to whatever Jev version is newest. Gate behavior and calibration can change silently, so pin typesafe/jev-1.13.

There is no wall-clock cap. --timeout is a per-socket timeout with default retries of 3 and backoff, so worst-case hook latency can far exceed one timeout. A hook needs --retries 0 and an outer `timeout` or a hook timeout setting.
Everything is hardcoded in Chinese: help text, error messages (e.g. 'jev: API 错误 (HTTP n)') and all five built-in specs. An agent parsing stderr sees Chinese.
The 32k context limit on OpenRouter combined with the CLI's 30000-token SIZE_WARN_TOKENS means large diffs will fail or be truncated, and the CLI does not truncate them for the caller.
Author-declared Unofficial: it defers to the official `typesafe-ai` skill for app integration, so treat it as a community wrapper.
entries.verdict: A well-built, OpenRouter-native, auditable CLI, and the best ready-made client available for shell-level Jev calls. It is only a building block: it ships no hook or automatic trigger, so the user would still write PermissionRequest/PreToolUse glue (calling it with JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, --timeout 3 --retries 0) and adapt the Chinese specs. Vendor the single file instead of running the installer.

verification.note: Re-queried and mostly confirmed. Repo: created 2026-09-18, pushed 2026-09-19, v0.3.2, Apache-2.0, 11 stars, 1 fork, not archived, 0 open issues, 12 commits, single author. Source: PROVIDERS table at jev/scripts/jev:56-73 has OpenRouter at https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The payload is {model,state,questions}, Bearer auth, no subprocess/eval/exec, no telemetry beyond X-Title/HTTP-Referer, and defaults are --timeout 60 and --retries 3. Auto provider selection prefers TypeSafe when both keys are present. All ten claims the audit cites for this were confirmed, including the key handling and the pin order. The audit's only real errors are minor: the description is partly coding-relevant (git diffs, logs, guardrail), commit-spec egress is caller-driven because the CLI never runs git, and it missed that PermissionRequest hooks do not fire under bypassPermissions. Score 6 is retained. It is OpenRouter-native, zero-dependency and auditable, but it is a two-day-old single-author beta with no hook, no auto-trigger and no English specs, and the user must write the glue. The score would rise to 7 only with a shipped hook recipe. Nothing was executed; static review only.

judge.why: Best auditable ready-made OpenRouter client: a single stdlib Python file with a Bash-callable CLI (yes, pick, score, filter, run). It ships no hook or auto-trigger, so you write the glue yourself.
pros: Native OpenRouter; key from env or 0600 file, never argv; no subprocess, eval or telemetry (verified)
About 196 test functions with CI on Python 3.9/3.11/3.13; zero dependencies; Apache-2.0

Very low context cost (one skill, about 300 tokens)
cons: Not automatic: no hook, no PermissionRequest recipe; model-discretion skill only

entries.name: altryne/jevify
entries.what: Community (ThursdAI, Alex Volkov) agent skill, not an official TypeSafe product. SKILL.md tells the agent to use Jev as "System One" during its own work: sift large documents or tool outputs, select evidence from many candidates, check many items against criteria, and rank or score them. It says to do this even if the user never mentions Jev. It ships stdlib-only Python helpers (scan.py ranks text/JSONL, run_cases.py runs request packs, jev_client.py is a concurrent client with cache and retries) plus about 160KB of reference docs on question design and the Choice/Noul/Score primitives. It also covers "Jevify this" product discovery. It is prompt-level: it makes no API calls until the agent chooses to run the scripts.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion), the closest thing to the requested 'Claude decides itself' behavior. The description explicitly says 'Trigger when sifting large documents or tool outputs ... even if the user never mentions Jev'. But README:40 states 'installation does not intercept tool outputs automatically', and SKILL.md concedes 'activation depends on the host agent'. Opus 5.5 may often prefer grep/GitNexus/its own reading. Nothing is deterministic.
security: No install script, no postinstall, no curl|sh. Install is 'npx skills add altryne/jevify' (vercel-labs skills CLI, third-party but standard). Manual copy into ~/.claude/skills also works.
Python helpers use only stdlib (http.client to a fixed HTTPS host); no shell execution or subprocess found by grep in scripts/.
API key goes in an Authorization header via env var or a .env file (jev_client.py:47-61, 134). It is never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.

find_key() reads NAME=value lines from ./.env in the cwd (default env_files=('.env',)), a project file that may hold many secrets. It only extracts the named key, but the user's secret-leak guard hook on Read/Bash may interfere or be triggered.
Error bodies are deliberately omitted so submitted data is not echoed (jev_client.py:163-164). Timeout is 30s per attempt.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill tells the agent to run Jev over untrusted documents and tool outputs. Jev only returns typed probabilities, so it is not an instruction channel, but answers used for filtering can be gamed by adversarial text (a missed-evidence risk).
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves at install or load time. On a live run, the JSON body {model, state, questions} goes over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set). The state is whatever text the agent chooses: chunks of documents, tool outputs, log excerpts, candidate code or diffs, chunked in about 4000-char pieces by scan.py with excerpts. The OpenRouter key goes in the Authorization header. There is no automatic capture of prompts or tool calls, and only what the agent explicitly feeds the scripts is sent. The optional --cache-dir cache writes responses locally, keyed by request hash.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft and at the agent's discretion, because there is no hook in the path. jev_client.py defaults to a 30s timeout per attempt, 3 retries with jittered backoff (0.25*2^n s up to 8s) on network errors, and 429/529 with Retry-After up to 30s. Non-retryable HTTP errors return {error, status}. Malformed or partial answers are flagged as 'unjudged', never treated as negative. SKILL.md says to report partial coverage and use the task fallback. A missing key means the agent explains setup once and continues locally. Worst case, one call could stall roughly 30s x 4 attempts, but only inside a script the agent chose to run. Claude Code itself never blocks on Jev.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions. There are no hooks and no injected text. Always-on cost is only the skill listing entry: name plus a description of about 620 chars, roughly 150 tokens. When triggered, SKILL.md loads at about 10.8KB, roughly 2.7k tokens. References load on demand (the largest are field-notes at about 14KB and question-design at about 14KB, each around 3.5k tokens). A full task typically costs 3-8k tokens of skill text.
pros: It is the only found candidate whose skill description is explicitly written to auto-trigger without the user naming Jev, which matches the 'do not make me prompt' requirement.

OpenRouter is natively supported in code (jev_client.py:36-39, 83-97, 125-126), with the correct model mapping to typesafe/jev-1.13 and tests for key selection. The fallback path is already there: set only OPENROUTER_API_KEY and it works.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, no hooks, about 150 tokens always-on. It coexists with the existing gitnexus/playwright/caveman hooks without conflict.
Stdlib-only Python 3 (works with the user's Python 3.13), no npm or pip dependencies, no installers, no telemetry, key never in argv, error bodies deliberately withheld.
Good failure semantics: failures are 'unjudged', not negatives, with retry/backoff/pacing and an atomic cache. Includes unit tests for the client and scanner.

Encodes useful usage doctrine (bulk semantic filtering of logs, tool output, candidate lists; per-item Noul/Score; audit low-ranked samples) that fits large-log and large-search triage in Claude Code.
MIT license, small readable codebase of about 1.4k lines, easy to fork and patch.
cons: It is not a real integration. Claude uses Jev only if it decides to shell out to scan.py. There is no hook or transparent routing, and the README admits it does not intercept tool outputs. Auto-trigger reliability is unproven; evals/evals.json exists but no results are published.
Opus 5.5 already handles grep, GitNexus and file reads well. The bulk-semantic-filter niche (big logs, hundreds of docs) is uncommon in typical daily coding, so real hit rate is likely low.

The skill's prose is aggressive and salesy: 'Default to Jev', 'Assume it is faster and cheaper', and instructions to skip cost comparison. It nudges the agent to use an unvalidated beta model (Theo claims it's a cheap flash-router) for judgments whose errors can silently drop relevant evidence.

Privacy and consent risk on client projects: 'reuse task or session authorization for external inference, data'. In bypass or auto mode the agent may send client code or documents to OpenRouter without an explicit prompt. Needs a deny rule or a CLAUDE.md boundary.

Provider selection is implicit. TYPESAFE_API_KEY wins over OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and a leftover key routes to TypeSafe directly. There is also no way to select the Decisions API, ~typesafe/jev-latest or the Jev Router model without patching. The model is pinned to jev-1.13.0.
The helpers read ./.env in the cwd by default, which on client repos contains unrelated secrets. Safer to export the key in the shell environment. May also trip the user's secret-guard hook.

Young and small: 6 commits, 2 contributors (Wolfred 4, Alex Volkov 2), created 2026-09-17, last push 2026-09-26, no releases, no CI, 36 stars, 2 forks. Vendor docs may drift from its hardcoded price and limits (last verified 2026-09-21).
It is third-party: not the official typesafe-ai/skills. Unit tests are not run by CI, and I did not run them (static review only).

The bundled scan.py handles a single local UTF-8 text or JSONL file, ranks it with a fixed generic 4-level relevance Score, and returns a shortlist. It does not search code repositories, diffs, or command output. For a coding agent with grep and GitNexus, the practical use cases (huge logs, exported conversations, long docs) are narrow, so the real trigger rate in daily coding is low.

Provider precedence includes cwd .env files. A client repo's .env with TYPESAFE_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY can override or replace the user's key (see jev_client.py:47-95), which risks billing or leaking across client boundaries. The user should always export OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY must stay unset in every project .env.

The client is raw http.client with no proxy handling and no retry on 500/502/503/504. On the alpha-flagged OpenRouter endpoint a transient 5xx becomes an 'unjudged' failure with no retry. Under a Claude Code network sandbox or proxy the calls may fail outright. The agent then continues locally, so the harm is wasted turns rather than blocked work.

The skill pushes the agent hard: 'Default to Jev for bulk semantic judgments', 'Assume it is faster and cheaper', and 'Ordinary use needs ... not a cost comparison first' (SKILL.md:17-19). This is the vendor-community-marketing tone and could cause over-triggering on tasks where Opus reading is more accurate. The brief says Jev accuracy is a bit below mid-price LLMs, and injected instructions in the state can move answers. Independent evals note the overconfidence and injection weaknesses, and the skill only says to 'test with injected text'.

OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in the user's no-secret-leak protected list. Exporting it into the environment that Bash tools inherit makes it readable by the agent (echo $OPENROUTER_API_KEY, env). It also means the key sits in the process environment of every Bash call, and the hook would not block that. Add it to the protected list before use.

The scripts' token limits (64k state plus questions, 32k state plus longest question; running-jev.md and run_cases.py) come from the direct TypeSafe docs. The brief says OpenRouter offers 32k context. scan.py's 24,000-byte request heuristic fits, but run_cases.py estimates could pass a request that OpenRouter rejects.

The repo is one week old (created 2026-09-17), and issue #2 ('Give Jev Choice a state-appropriate way out') is open. All 6 commits were within 9 days and there is no CI. Stars re-queried now: 36, forks 2, MIT, not archived, last push 2026-09-26T23:42:37Z. Those figures match the audit.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed option that is truly zero-friction and zero-context and already speaks OpenRouter, but it is a soft, model-discretion nudge, not a deterministic integration. It is worth installing globally as a cheap complement (with OPENROUTER_API_KEY exported and no TYPESAFE_API_KEY set) but it will not by itself deliver reliable automatic use, and it needs a data-egress guardrail for client repos.

verification.note: OpenRouter support is real in code. jev_client.py:36-39 sets openrouter.ai and /api/v1/systemone, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read at :38 and :87-92. The model id typesafe/jev-1.13 is mapped at :39 and :125-126. Tests at test_jev_client.py:84-100 cover the selection with mocked HTTP. Stars (36), MIT, not archived, last push 2026-09-26, 6 commits, 2 forks, and no CI are all confirmed. The repo has no hooks, no MCP server, no install scripts, no subprocess or shell exec, no telemetry and no key in argv. Claude Code correctness is fine: the frontmatter has only valid fields (name, description, license), and there are no hook events to misuse. The audit's main weakness is calibration, not fabrication. I corrected the description length (443 chars, not about 620), the reference count (12 files, about 93KB, not 11 files or 160KB), the code size (827 lines, not 1.4k), and the consent con, which omits the 'a key alone does not establish authorization' caveat. I added gaps it missed: terminal 5xx handling, no proxy support, cwd .env key override, OPENROUTER_API_KEY missing from the secret-guard list, and the low relevance of the single-file scan.py to coding work. Score goes from 5.5 to 5.0. It is a safe, cheap, non-blocking soft nudge that the user could not get from a hook. But auto-use is model-discretion only, the fit to daily coding is narrow, and there are several edge risks on client projects. I could not run anything, so the auto-trigger rate is unmeasured. The repo's evals have no published results.

judge.why: Closest thing to a zero-friction automatic nudge: a 443-character description that says to trigger even if the user never mentions Jev. The bundled scan.py fits only bulk shortlisting of a single log, JSONL or doc file.

entries.name: lazniak/jevskill
entries.what: Agent Skill (skills/jev/SKILL.md, Claude Code plugin marketplace "jevskill" plus npx skills) that teaches the model when and how to call Jev for bounded decisions (route, triage, classify, gate, rank, and a reversible REDUCE that shortlists large logs/data before they reach the main model). It bundles a stdlib-only Python caller (scripts/jev_query.py), a bigger optional pip package/CLI (jevskill: ask/batch/plan/doctor/stats, ledger, disk cache, localhost web console, hot-loop client, Windows-only computer-use module), and a lot of reference docs. Jev is called via OpenRouter (default) or TypeSafe vendor API. It is NOT an MCP server and installs no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger: Claude Code loads the skill when its description matches the task (keywords like classify, triage, gate, rank, too many logs, is it safe to), then the model decides to run python scripts/jev_query.py. Not deterministic: no hook, no MCP tool, no proxy. Reliability of firing without the user saying 'use jev' is uncertain and unmeasured; the model must also judge Jev worthwhile vs. just grepping, and the skill itself says to prefer regex/grep when possible.
security: API key: read from env only (no --api-key CLI flag found in jev_query.py or cli.py grep), sent as Authorization Bearer over HTTPS via urllib; not visible in argv/process list. Skill instructs the agent to check key presence only via `jevskill doctor` (8-hex fingerprint), never print it.

Redaction by default: regex scrub of private keys, sk-/sk-or- keys, AKIA, gh*_ tokens, slack, JWT, bearer, password=/token= params before state leaves the machine (jev_query.py:88-100, jevskill/redact.py). Credential-shaped only; no PII/source-code protection; emails opt-in. Regex coverage is limited (e.g. no generic high-entropy secrets, .env style values under other names).

Prompt-injection surface: log/diff/ticket text goes into the state sent to Jev; SKILL.md itself warns Jev is advisory and manipulable by state content and must not authorize irreversible actions. Since Jev only returns typed decisions, injection can bias REDUCE (hide the relevant line) but cannot produce text/commands. Risk is silent omission of important lines.

Shell exec: skill declares allowed-tools Bash(python:*) Bash(python3:*) Bash(jevskill:*) which pre-approves arbitrary python execution when the skill is loaded (broad); in bypass/auto mode moot. No subprocess/os.system in package (grep clean).

Writes to disk in the CURRENT PROJECT: REDUCE stores rejected items under <cwd>/.jevskill/recovery/*.json; ledger and optional cache also at <cwd>/.jevskill/ (jev_query.py:626-631, stats.py:58-83, cache.py:57-64). On client repos this leaves log/state copies in the working tree unless gitignored; ~/.jevskill/config.json and global ledger also used.

No telemetry found; only network destinations are openrouter.ai / api.typesafe.ai (plus HEAD warm-up). OpenRouter requests send HTTP-Referer/X-Title attribution headers naming the project. Web console binds 127.0.0.1 only with Host/Origin checks.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in --state / --state-file: log lines, diffs, ticket text, file contents, tool output, plus the question text and option criteria, after regex credential redaction (on by default). Sent to openrouter.ai (default) or api.typesafe.ai; OpenRouter routes to TypeSafe. Also a client-identifying Referer/X-Title header. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when the model chooses to run the script. For client projects, code/diffs/logs leave the machine to two third parties (OpenRouter + TypeSafe); check client NDAs. No local file is uploaded outside what the agent selects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in effect but soft: nothing blocks Claude Code because there is no hook. Script: default 60 s read timeout, 2 retries with 0.25-2 s backoff on 429/5xx/transport (jev_query.py:671-672, 395-430), so a hung/slow Jev can stall a Bash tool call up to roughly 3 minutes worst case; errors raise SystemExit exit 1 with a message. Package hot path uses 1.5 s read timeout, 0 retries, hedged request (config.py:123-135) but that is only for the optional Python API, not the skill default. Exit 3 means nothing sent because state exceeds token budget (default 8k). SKILL.md says API errors must be reported, not simulated. Missing key: skill tells the agent to STOP and ask the user (A get a key / B judge yourself), which is an interactive interruption, not silent.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. Always-on: skill frontmatter name + description = about 660 chars description (~165 tokens) plus name/listing, roughly 200 tokens per session. On load: SKILL.md is 11,595 chars (~2.9k tokens) each time the skill triggers, plus optional reference files (api.md 26 KB, act.md 47 KB, patterns.md 30 KB etc.) if the model opens them. No hook-injected text. The skill's trigger words are very generic ('should we', 'is it safe to', 'rank', 'route') and may cause frequent loads of the 3k-token body.
pros: Only candidate in this class that is genuinely OpenRouter-first: default provider openrouter, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, key OPENROUTER_API_KEY (config.py:36-45; jev_query.py:60-66). Drop-in for the user's setup.
Zero-install path: the bundled jev_query.py is stdlib-only Python, no npm/pip needed; Python 3.13 present. No required dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh (Linux path).
Skill approach costs almost no context when idle (~200 tokens) and adds no MCP tool schema tax; no hooks so it cannot interfere with the existing secret-guard / GitNexus / caveman hooks.

Sound Jev usage guidance codified in SKILL.md: decision-not-text, fan out many questions in one call, name the target value (avoids flat ~0.74 output), budget state to 8k tokens, escape-hatch options, thresholds as policy, never authorize irreversible actions from Jev output. Encodes Jev pitfalls accurately relative to the brief.

Default-on credential redaction of state before egress (private keys, sk-*, AKIA, gh tokens, JWT, bearer, password=) - meaningful for client projects, and a reason it complements the user's secret-leak guard.
REDUCE for big logs/test output is a plausible real use for daily coding: shortlist 900 log lines to ~8 before the Opus context sees them; reversible via jev_recovery.py.

Honest docs: README publishes a YAML failure, says grep/regex ties Jev on its own benchmark (18/18 both), labels savings modelled vs measured, and says use a regex if one suffices. Large offline test suite (1533 test functions counted; CI on py3.9/3.11/3.13; suite fully offline).
MIT license, key handled via env with fingerprint-only doctor; no telemetry; no key in argv.
Unpinned upgrade path is mitigated by Claude Code plugin marketplace/skill install being git-based, so a commit can be pinned.
cons: Not automatic in the deterministic sense the user asked for: it is a description-triggered skill, so Claude may or may not load it, and even then must choose to shell out. No hook or MCP tool means no guaranteed use; e.g. it will not intercept a big Bash/Read output before it enters context (REDUCE only helps if the model already decided to run it, after the tokens were often already read or must be piped through the script).

Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 26 commits in 10 days, 2 stars, 1 fork, effectively single author (24 commits lazniak + 2 Paul Lazniak), 4 issues total, latest release v0.10.2 while pyproject/marketplace say 0.15.1. Rapid churn; pin a commit before trusting it with client repos.

Sprawl: much of the 3.3 MB tree is off-topic for a Linux coding user (Windows-only UIA computer-use `cu/` module ~300 KB Python, web console, install.ps1, 47 KB act.md, benchmark fixtures). Marketing-heavy README (YouTube live banner, modelled $ savings per year, '99.3% fewer tokens' from n=3 per cell, one cheap answering model).

Broad tool permission: frontmatter allow-list Bash(python:*) Bash(python3:*) Bash(jevskill:*) pre-approves arbitrary Python when loaded; combined with bypass/auto mode it widens blast radius if the repo is ever compromised.

Data egress on client projects: logs/diffs/file text go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe; redaction is regex credential-only, no PII/source protection. Also writes .jevskill/recovery, ledger, cache into the current project working tree (not the home dir), which can leave copies of client log data and dirty git status.

Default provider selection is name-based and can silently flip to the vendor if a JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY exists; must set JEVSKILL_PROVIDER=openrouter to pin. Model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13, not ~typesafe/jev-latest or Jev Router.

Failure/latency: default 60 s timeout x 2 retries can stall a Bash call for minutes on a hung endpoint; no circuit breaker across calls. Each use costs an extra LLM turn (write command, read output), so for Opus 5.5 the seconds cost far exceeds Jev's 300 ms; benefit is only for large-data cases.

SKILL.md body is ~2.9k tokens on every load and trigger words are generic ('should we', 'rank', 'is it safe to'), risking frequent irrelevant loads; 'no key' path makes the agent stop and ask the user, an interruption.

Value is unproven for this user: the primary benefit (context reduction) matters less if grep/head/GitNexus already narrow the data; author's own benchmark shows a structural filter equals Jev. Jev cannot help with code, summaries, or reasoning, which is most of daily coding.
Jev is beta, and Theo's skeptic claim (cheap router in disguise) is unaddressed; the repo's accuracy evidence is self-reported.
entries.verdict: Best-in-class as a low-friction, OpenRouter-native starting point (skill only, no hooks/MCP, near-zero idle context, default redaction), but it is not the deterministic automatic integration requested: firing depends on model discretion and the payoff is limited to large-log reduction and gating. Try it pinned to a commit with JEVSKILL_PROVIDER=openrouter and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and expect to pair it with a hook (e.g. PostToolUse on big Bash output) if real automation is needed.

judge.why: OpenRouter-native skill with default redaction and near-zero idle context. Audit called it best-in-class as a low-friction starting point, but it is still model-discretion only.
pros: OpenRouter-native; default redaction of state
Skill only, no hooks or MCP, tiny idle cost
cons: Not deterministic or automatic
Alpha, 2 stars, no adversarial verification (audit score used as is)
