entries.name: vsekhar/decide
entries.what: Swift CLI ("decide") that sends context plus yes/no, choice or scale questions to a decision model (Jev) and prints the answer, confidence and probabilities, with exit codes for shell branching. The repo also ships a Claude Code skill (.claude/skills/decide/SKILL.md) that tells the agent to shell out to decide via Bash. It is not an MCP server and has no hooks. It is a thin wrapper over the author's DecisionModels Swift library, which has OpenRouterAlpha and TypeSafe Jev providers.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger. Claude auto-loads the skill when the description ("a step needs a classification or a verdict, not prose") matches the task, and allowed-tools Bash(decide *) skips permission prompts. There is no deterministic hook. In a typical coding session the trigger will rarely match, and even when it fires Claude decides for itself. Reliability can be raised by adding a CLAUDE.md line, or by writing a custom description. Nothing in the repo does this.
security: Key handling: --api-key <key> puts the key in argv (visible in ps and shell history). The safer paths are --api-key - (stdin or a no-echo prompt), the DECIDE_MODEL_API_KEY / OPENROUTER_API_KEY env vars, or the home config. Decide.swift:560-567 writes the home config with 0700 dir and 0600 file, but the key is stored in plaintext.

Trust rule (ConfigFiles.swift:122-132): DECIDE_MODEL_API_KEY is rejected in a project .decide/config, so keys cannot be committed. A project config can still set DECIDE_MODEL, so a hostile repo cannot steal the key but can choose the model or provider that receives your context. Low risk.

Prompt-injection surface: --context text comes from files the agent reads, and Jev returns only typed probabilities with no free text. The model cannot inject instructions back. The main risk is a wrong or manipulated decision that Claude then trusts. The skill's own text pushes Claude to trust and cascade decisions.

Shell execution: the skill grants Bash(decide *). In bypass or auto mode that is a wildcard, and the model can pass arbitrary --context @path files, so it can upload any readable file to OpenRouter. This interacts with the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard only if the guard matches on Bash commands that reference secret paths.

Install: the Homebrew formula has depends_on :macos (Formula/decide.rb), so brew cannot install it on Linux. The 0.4.1 release has no binary assets. A Linux user must build with Swift 6.2+ (swift build, which pulls swift-syntax and the DecisionModels package from GitHub). No curl|sh and no postinstall script. No telemetry found in the Swift sources (grep for telemetry and analytics is empty).
Supply chain: one author, a young repo (2026-09-20), and a dependency on his own DecisionModels package (2 stars, 67 commits, created 2026-09-19). Package.resolved is pinned. Apache-2.0.
entries.dataEgress: Everything passed via --context, --context-json, stdin or --questions, plus the question and option text, is sent as JSON over HTTPS to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai for the direct provider) with the Bearer key. If the skill is followed, that means whole files, tickets, diffs and tool output. Nothing leaves automatically outside a decide invocation. The key travels only in the Authorization header. There is no CLI telemetry. OpenRouter and TypeSafe logging and retention policies apply. This is a concern for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by default with an explicit escape. Attempts time out at 10s (RetryPolicy.default in DecisionModels), with 3 retries, backoff 0.5s to 8s and Retry-After honoured. There is no overall deadline by default (DecisionRequest.timeout is nil), so a bad outage can block one Bash call for roughly 40s or more. After that it exits 11 with stderr text. Exit 10 means no key or model. --fallback V turns remote errors into a printed value. Because it is a skill and not a hook, a failure only costs a failed Bash call, and Claude simply reads the file itself. It never blocks the session.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema cost. Skill listing entry: the description is about 250 chars, so roughly 60-80 tokens permanently in the skill list. Body of SKILL.md is 3,468 chars, roughly 870 tokens, loaded only when the skill is invoked. No hook-injected text and no MCP server instructions. Each call adds the Bash command and a short result (a few tokens for text output, more for --json).
pros: Native OpenRouter support with the exact model IDs the user wants (openrouter:typesafe/jev-1.13), verified in OpenRouterAlpha.swift, and it uses the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var. Nothing to patch.

Zero context tax: no MCP tools and no hooks. The skill costs about 70 tokens in the listing and about 870 tokens only when loaded. That fits with the user's existing MCP and hook load (gitnexus, playwright).

Well-designed for agents: exit codes, --min-confidence, --fallback, --json, multi-question batching that shares one request, and confidence and probability output. Fail-open behaviour is available via --fallback.
Good engineering hygiene for a young project: 96 commits, CI on macOS and Linux with live tests, key kept out of project configs (trust rule), 0600 config file, retries and timeouts with backoff.
The skill ships in-repo (.claude/skills/decide), so it is the only candidate that is a real Claude Code skill and needs no server process.
Apache-2.0, small readable codebase (about 4.2k lines of CLI Swift plus the library). No postinstall, telemetry or curl|sh.
cons: Not automatic in any strong sense. It is a skill, so Claude decides when to use it. The description is generic ('classification or a verdict'), so Claude Code will rarely pick it during ordinary coding, which fails the user's requirement that it is used without prompting. There is no hook and no proxy. Making it dependable needs extra work (a CLAUDE.md rule or a custom hook).

Linux install is friction: the Homebrew formula is depends_on :macos, the release has no binaries, and you need a Swift 6.2+ toolchain plus a from-source build (swift-syntax makes it slow) that pulls a 2-star dependency.

Weak fit for daily coding: Jev is a typed classifier (32k context, 64k in the OpenRouter capabilities), while the real coding decisions (edit, plan, review) need Opus's reasoning. The skill's advice to send whole files and cascade calls encourages uploading code to a third party, and it adds a Bash turn each time.

Data egress for client work: every --context file goes to OpenRouter (alpha endpoint) with no allowlist. Bash(decide *) is pre-approved, and in bypass mode there is no prompt, so Claude can upload any readable file. It needs pairing with the user's secret-leak guard.
--api-key <key> in argv leaks via ps. Only the stdin, env or config paths are safe. The key is stored in plaintext in ~/.config/decide/config.

Alpha risk on both sides: the OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions endpoint may change (the code comments say so), the wire format follows docs read on 2026-09-20, and there is one maintainer, 1 star, and a 10-day-old repo. The uses of Jev where it is claimed to win (fast triage) are not verified independently.
No overall default timeout: 10s per attempt times 3 retries can stall a Bash call for about 40s. The user must pass --fallback or wrap it in timeout.
entries.verdict: Cleanest and safest way to call OpenRouter Jev from Claude Code: it is a CLI plus a real skill with native openrouter:typesafe/jev-1.13 support, no context cost, and sane failure codes. But it is only a model-discretion skill (not automatic), needs a from-source Swift build on Linux, and the core use case (classify whole files with a small model) is marginal for daily coding. Best used as the CLI layer beneath a custom hook or skill, not as a drop-in answer to 'Claude should use Jev on its own'.

judge.why: CLI plus a real skill with native OpenRouter support, sane failure codes and no context cost. Audit called it the cleanest and safest way to call OpenRouter Jev, but it is model-discretion only.
pros: Native OpenRouter and pinned model syntax; sane exit codes
No context cost
cons: Model-discretion only, not automatic
1 star, alpha, unverified

entries.name: OpenRouterTeam/skills (openrouter-decisions skill)
entries.what: Official OpenRouter Agent Skills collection (18 skills plus open-responses). The relevant one, skills/openrouter-decisions, is a knowledge skill (SKILL.md ~9.9 KB, 3 reference docs, agents/openai.yaml) that teaches Claude how to design Decisions API calls: split judgment from computation, choose choice/noul/score, minimal state, question wording, pin model, gate in code, probe thresholds. It ships two CLI helpers (scripts/decide.ts, models.ts, lib.ts) that POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and list decision models from /api/v1/models?output_modalities=decisions. It is an authoring aid only. It provides no hook, MCP tool or runtime call path, so it never makes Claude Code call Jev on its own.
entries.autoInvocation: Yes, but only for authoring. It is a description-triggered skill and it auto-loads when Claude is asked to build or replace a classification, routing or gating step, or when Jev, TypeSafe or decision models are mentioned. It does not make Claude call Jev automatically during normal coding, so it does not meet the user's goal of automatic Jev use. Its value is that Claude writes a well-designed gate, such as the PermissionRequest hook, once.
security: Key handling: the key is read from the OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var only (lib.ts:46,189), sent as a Bearer header to openrouter.ai only. It is never in argv and is not logged. Error output prints the response body only.

No shell exec, spawn or child_process in the decisions scripts. Only readFileSync on the user-supplied request path or stdin. No telemetry and no extra hosts. Fetches go to openrouter.ai only. No X-Title or Referer headers.
Scripts need npm install, which pulls @openrouter/sdk ^1.3.23 (first-party) and tsx (dev). A package-lock.json is committed. Running this is the only third-party code step, and I did not run it.

The skill text is pure prose. The prompt-injection surface is the skill content itself, which is first-party and benign (guidance only, with explicit adversarial-content warnings). The plugin auto-updates from the repo, so future changes to the skill would be trusted instructions. This is a supply-chain trust decision on OpenRouter.

Adopting decision gates with state that contains repo or command text sends it to OpenRouter, then TypeSafe. That is the data-egress risk of any gate built with this skill. The skill itself does nothing at runtime.

Installing the whole plugin (/plugin install openrouter@openrouter) brings in all skills, including openrouter-oauth, spawn-ori-eval and install-ori-harness. These are larger attack and context surface than needed. gh skill install OpenRouterTeam/skills openrouter-decisions installs the single skill.
entries.dataEgress: The skill itself sends nothing. When decide.ts or models.ts is run, the request JSON (state and questions), the model id and the Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY go to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. Requests also go to openrouter.ai/api/v1/models (unauthenticated) and to the per-model endpoints URL (with the key, lib.ts:47). Nothing else leaves the machine. There is no telemetry. Any real gate built from the guidance sends whatever state the author chooses to OpenRouter and TypeSafe.
entries.failureMode: The scripts have no fetch timeout and no retry (lib.ts:251 plain fetch). A non-2xx response throws an error with the body, and the process exits non-zero. They are one-shot CLIs, not a hook, so there is no fail-open or fail-closed behaviour for Claude Code. The skill's guidance does recommend gating in code and keeping a fallback for probabilities near the threshold, and warns that confidence is not correctness. That matches a fail-open-to-prompt permission hook design. If the skill is not triggered, nothing happens. It is inert.
entries.contextCost: If installed as the plugin, 19 SKILL.md descriptions are listed, about 7.7 KB total (~1.9k tokens) against skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02, and the openrouter-decisions description alone is about 850 chars (~210 tokens). A single-skill install costs only ~210 tokens. The SKILL.md body (~9.9 KB, ~2.5k tokens) loads only when triggered, plus references (~13 KB, ~3.3k tokens) on demand. Zero MCP tools and no hook-injected text.
pros: Official OpenRouter source. It targets exactly POST /api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY (lib.ts:3,46) and is model-agnostic through the live catalog, so it survives Jev version bumps.
Active and current: created 2026-01-31, last push 2026-09-29, decisions skill added 2026-09-25 and reworked 2026-09-29. 87 commits, 10 contributors, 275 stars, 50 forks.

Contains a Jev-specific weaknesses table (decision-model-limits.md) covering literal reading, math and dates, and adversarial content. This helps Claude write safer gates and matches the independent evals.
Gate-in-code and probe-before-trust workflow: thresholds as named constants, a fallback band, and decide.ts --compare for validating thresholds on real inputs.
The scripts are small and clean: no exec, no telemetry, key via env only, an openrouter.ai-only host list, lib.ts with typed parse and validation that can be copied into a hook.
Very low context cost if installed as a single skill (~210 tokens listed). It can be installed alone via gh skill install OpenRouterTeam/skills openrouter-decisions.
cons: It is guidance only. Nothing here makes Claude Code call Jev during normal work. There is no hook, MCP server or PermissionRequest example in the repo (grep for hooks/PermissionRequest/mcp finds nothing). The cookbook hook the user wants must be written separately.
No LICENSE file (GitHub licenseInfo null, no topics, empty description). The reuse terms for copying lib.ts are unclear.

No tests for the decisions scripts and no CI (.github absent). The only tests in the repo are in an unrelated sample. The scripts have no fetch timeout or retry, so copying decideViaHttp into a hook needs an AbortSignal timeout added.
Scripts require npm install and npx tsx. Startup of about 1 s and a third-party dependency chain make them unsuitable as-is for a hot-path hook. A raw fetch of about 30 lines is better.

The plugin install path is all-or-nothing (19 skills, including OAuth, eval and harness installers), adding listing tokens and irrelevant triggers. It also auto-updates, so skill content can change under the user.

The description is very broad ('whenever decision models, Jev, TypeSafe, or System One come up' and 'human review queue', 'misfiring router'), so it may trigger in unrelated conversations. The decisions API is /alpha with no SLA.
OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not yet in the user's no-secret-leak protected list. The scripts read it from env, so adopting them requires adding it.

The skill and its scripts are tied to OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions with no SLA, and the skill's own guidance covers request design only. It supplies no Claude Code hook wiring (grep for hook, PermissionRequest and mcp in SKILL.md and README finds only an unrelated 'mcp' hit in create-headless-agent).

The skill body tells Claude to run probe scripts that require npm install of @openrouter/sdk and tsx, i.e. it prompts Claude to make Claude run third-party dependency installs (first-party package, lockfile committed), and the probe sends the user's real repo or command text as state to OpenRouter and TypeSafe.

decisions-api.md pins typesafe/jev-1.13 and examples also use a dated build typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917. The skill teaches pinning, so gates written by Claude will pin a snapshot that can be retired; a model-drift or deprecation failure path is not covered by the scripts.

The limits doc's claims are sourced from TypeSafe's own docs (docs.typesafe.ai/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md), i.e. vendor-published, not independent. The audit says it 'matches the independent evals', which is not verifiable from the repo.

Skill is Jev-advocacy-adjacent: its description fires on the words 'Jev', 'TypeSafe', 'System One' and 'approval gates', which for this user would make it load (~2.5k tokens body) in any conversation about this very project, though it never triggers a runtime call.
entries.verdict: A high-quality, official, safe authoring skill for designing Jev gates on OpenRouter, but it is inert at runtime. It gives no automatic Jev use, hook or MCP integration. Install it alone (gh skill install ... openrouter-decisions) as a helper for writing the PermissionRequest gate, and do not count it as the integration itself.

verification.note: Core facts verified from source and gh api: 275 stars, 50 forks, no license (licenseInfo null), not archived, pushed 2026-09-29, 87 commits, created 2026-01-31, no .github/CI, no hooks/MCP. lib.ts:3-5 endpoints, lines 46/189 env var, line 251 plain fetch with no timeout, line 270 SDK client all match. No exec/spawn/child_process, only readFileSync for the request file, no telemetry, no extra headers. models.md:41 does mention the /api/v1/systemone path with baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api, so typesafeDirect 'partial' is fair (pointer only, no code). The audit is largely accurate; the only factual errors are the contributor count (13, not 10) and the unsubstantiated auto-update claim, plus the missed process.exit in requireApiKey. The score of 5 is somewhat generous for the rubric: the artifact is inert at runtime, has no license, and does not meet the user's stated goal of automatic Jev use, so it fits 3-4 (niche/weak for the goal) though it is safe and cheap as a single-skill authoring aid. Adjusted to 4. Recommendation stands: at most install the single skill via gh skill install as a design helper; do not count it as the integration. Note: a local PreToolUse hook false-positived on one grep containing OPENROUTER and exec patterns, so that grep was replaced by reading lib.ts fully.

judge.why: Official, high-quality authoring skill with a Jev limits table and a gate-in-code workflow. It is inert at runtime and ships no hook or license.
pros: Official source; correct /api/alpha/decisions usage; model-agnostic via the live catalog
decision-model-limits.md and a probe/--compare workflow are useful when writing your own gate
Single skill installable alone (about 210 tokens)
cons: No hook, MCP or PermissionRequest example; the cookbook hook must be written separately
No LICENSE file; scripts need npm install and tsx; no fetch timeout, and requireApiKey calls process.exit(1)
Description is broad and may trigger in unrelated conversations; /alpha with no SLA; limits are vendor-sourced
Installing the whole plugin adds 19 skills

entries.name: disler/ten-levels-of-jev
entries.what: IndyDevDan's lab of 10 Jev usage levels: a TS client (mock/OpenRouter/TypeSafe), 30 example decision modules, a Vue web lab, and pi-agent extensions (jev-guard bash/write/result-screen hooks, jev-compact, ask_jev tools). Also ships a portable hyper-jev Claude Code skill (SKILL.md + cookbook + starter template) that scaffolds Jev integrations into a user's backend. It is NOT a Claude Code hook/MCP integration; nothing in it runs inside Claude Code at tool-call time.
interface: pi extension jev-compact.ts (turn_end hook, compact_now, should_i_compact)
pi tools ask_jev / ask_jev_file / ask_jev_files (pi registerTool)
just recipes (web, dev, jev1..jev10, demo, demo-live, test, test-live, install)
No .mcp.json, plugin.json, marketplace.json, or hooks.json exist
entries.autoInvocation: The hyper-jev skill auto-triggers by description only when the user talks about building Jev integrations (setup, classifiers, gates, routing) - i.e. for building apps with Jev, not for making Claude Code itself use Jev during daily coding. The 'agent reaches for Jev unprompted' behaviour (L10) is pi-only via a system-prompt NUDGE and tool registration, and the README admits it is inconsistent ('Some runs call it once, some more'). Nothing here delivers automatic Jev use in Claude Code; the hook pattern is a manual port.
security: Key handling: client.ts reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY from env, trims, sends only in Authorization header; JevRawExchange stores request body only, no headers; redirect:'error' blocks header leakage via redirects. Good hygiene. Key never on argv.
README 'Where it can still fail' admits the pi agent can print its own env and the OpenRouter key stays visible to it; agent env is filtered to shell basics + Jev keys + JEV_* by server code.

Prompt-injection surface: ask_jev accepts agent-written questions_json and a 'command' run via child_process.exec (shell) with env {...process.env, CI:1}; only protection is the Jev bash gate itself (a probabilistic classifier). Non-gated for read-only-looking but exfil commands. README admits agent routed around the write gate via bash heredoc in a live run.

jev-guard result screen and bash gate send full command/tool output to Jev; injected instructions in that state can move answers (per independent evals). Gates fail-open on exceptions (catch -> report, no block).

Installer/exec: /install.md instructs curl -fsSL bun.sh | bash suggestion and npm -g install of pi; justfile install recipe runs `claude --dangerously-skip-permissions /install`; `just web` runs lsof|xargs kill on port 4399; shell is zsh -i. All local-lab only, not part of the skill.
Telemetry: none found. Only outbound fetch in src/ is client.ts to the Jev endpoint (grep of src, server, extensions).
entries.dataEgress: Only the Jev endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, or api.typesafe.ai if TYPESAFE_API_KEY set - which takes precedence over OpenRouter, a silent provider switch risk). Payload is the state you assemble plus question block. For guard hooks: full bash command + cwd, write path+content, and read/bash tool output (up to 200k chars in ask_jev). For a client project this means code/output content goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; would need a data policy. The hyper-jev skill itself sends nothing; the user's scaffolded app does.
entries.failureMode: Client: 30s total timeout, 3 attempts with exponential backoff on 429/502/503/529, missing credentials throw (fail-closed, no silent mock fallback). But pi hooks catch every exception and proceed (fail-open). The Claude Code skill has no runtime failure mode (generation-time only). No Claude Code hook exists here to fail either way; a ported hook would need its own fail-open-to-prompt logic (not provided).
entries.contextCost: Skill: name+description ~640 chars (~160 tokens) in the listing (tight against skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02 but small); full SKILL.md ~6.7KB (~1.7k tokens) loaded only on trigger, plus cookbook files read on demand. No MCP tools, no tool defs, no hook-injected text in Claude Code. pi ask_jev tool description ~2.6KB (~650 tokens) + system-prompt NUDGE, but only in pi.
pros: Native OpenRouter: client.ts posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model ~typesafe/jev-latest, retries/timeouts/redirect:'error', raw-exchange retention, no silent mock fallback (client.ts:17-30, selectProvider).

Best reference material for question design: hyper-jev cookbook (5 guides + 10 use-case guides) with concrete thresholds, e.g. bash gate blocks at irreversible>=0.6 / destructive>=0.7 (levels/level06/bash-gate.ts), and honest caveats ('confidence is not authorization', classifiers not sole safeguard).

Level 6 bash gate + result screen and Level 7 compaction question sets are directly portable as prompts/questions for a Claude Code PreToolUse/PermissionRequest hook; client.ts is small, dependency-free, and Node 24-native (matches user's runtime).
MIT, no telemetry, no install scripts that run automatically, key never on argv or in stored raw exchange; README has an unusually candid 'Where it can still fail' section.
Skill is portable and low context cost (~160 tokens listing, ~1.7k on trigger); explicit guidance to keep security gates as one signal and to fail closed on missing credentials.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no plugin.json, marketplace.json, .mcp.json or hooks.json; the hooks (jev-guard.ts, jev-compact.ts) and ask_jev tools use the pi coding-agent extension API (pi.on('tool_call'), pi.registerTool) and cannot be loaded in Claude Code without a rewrite.

Does not meet the 'automatic use without prompting' goal: the hyper-jev skill triggers only for Jev-building requests, and the sole automatic-use mechanism (NUDGE system-prompt + ask_jev) is pi-only and self-described as inconsistent.

Very young and thin: single commit, single author, created 2026-09-27; 'beta' claim in triage is generous -> proof-of-concept/demo lab (Vue web UI, lab server, slides-style images) with claims (201 tests, live results) not independently verified.

Uses /api/alpha/decisions and moving alias ~typesafe/jev-latest as default: unpinned model + alpha endpoint, so behaviour can change silently; TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently takes precedence over OPENROUTER_API_KEY if both present.

Guard hooks fail-open on exception and the README documents an agent bypassing a single gate via bash heredoc; ask_jev exec()s agent-supplied shell commands gated only by a probabilistic classifier. Lab tooling has quirks (zsh -ic, lsof|xargs kill, --dangerously-skip-permissions in `just install`).

Offers no fail-open-to-prompt PermissionRequest design (unlike the official OpenRouter cookbook), no Claude Code hook JSON, no absolute-path handling, and no interaction with existing no-secret-leak or gitnexus hooks.
entries.verdict: Well-written educational reference and question-design cookbook with a native OpenRouter client, but it is a pi-agent demo lab, not a Claude Code integration: no hooks/MCP/plugin packaging and the auto-use mechanism is pi-only and admittedly inconsistent. Useful to mine (client.ts, bash-gate questions, cookbook thresholds) when hand-building a PermissionRequest hook; not something to install for automatic Jev use.

judge.why: Educational lab. Its hyper-jev skill and bash-gate questions (irreversible >= 0.6, destructive >= 0.7) are worth mining, but the guard hooks use the pi extension API, not Claude Code.
pros: Solid dependency-free Node client (redirect:'error', retries); candid failure section; portable hyper-jev skill
Reusable gate question sets
cons: No Claude Code hooks, plugin or MCP packaging; auto-use is pi-only and admittedly inconsistent
Guards fail open; TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently outranks OpenRouter; single commit; unpinned ~jev-latest alias

entries.name: shantanugoel/ask-jev-skill
entries.what: Hermes-agent skill plus stdlib python script askjev.py: ask Jev choice/score/noul as a tiebreaker when paths are ambiguous, with confidence gates and an eval script.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger (model discretion, description 'Use when in doubt')
pros: Tiny (SKILL.md + one stdlib script), easy to port to a Claude Code skill
SKILL.md has clear when/when-not rules (no secrets as state, no safety questions)
cons: Hermes install paths and HERMES_HOME .env; needs porting for Claude Code
Targets api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no OpenRouter path; only model discretion triggering, unreliable

entries.name: DarioFontanel/jev-claude-code
entries.what: Not a plugin or package: a repo of three Italian-language copy-paste prompts (prompts/01-model-router.md, 02-context-compaction.md, 03-code-review.md) that make Claude Code generate the integration inside the user's project. 01 builds a Claude Code "function hook" TypeScript module (.claude/skills/jev-router/) that calls Jev once at the first prompt of a session (plus once per subagent spawn) to pick the model tier (Sonnet/Opus/Fable) and effort, then overrides them on turn.step. 02 builds a function hook on session.compact that replaces native compaction: it sends tool-call contents to Jev in batches with a noul "still needed?" question and drops or truncates the rest. 03 builds a Python jev-review/review.py that sends a diff plus 14 typed questions to Jev in one call, computes a verdict (BLOCK, SECURITY REVIEW, NITS, MERGE) from JSON thresholds, plus a /jev-review skill. No source code exists in the repo; only README, LICENSE and 3 prompt files (56 KB total).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for 01 and 02: prompt.submit, turn.step, agent.spawn and session.compact fire without user prompting once the project has the folder and the env flag. 03 is a skill triggered by its description ('can I merge?', 'check the diff before commit') or /jev-review, so it is model-discretion, not deterministic. All of it is per-project unless the user moves it to ~/.claude/skills, and a project's .claude/skills is only loaded after the trust prompt is accepted.
security: No shipped executable code, so no postinstall, curl|sh or telemetry in the repo itself. All risk lives in the code Claude generates from the prompts at paste time, which is non-deterministic per run and must be reviewed by the user.

API key read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or settings env; README says never paste it in chat. Bearer token goes in an HTTP header via $.http.fetch, not in argv. In 03 the Python script reads os.environ, so no argv exposure.

Hook 02 exfiltrates tool-call content (file reads, Bash output, possibly secrets or .env contents that the user's existing secret-guard would otherwise block) to a third party; nothing in the prompt redacts secrets before sending.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs and the user prompt are placed in Jev's 'state'. Jev returns only numbers, so injection can at worst skew keep/drop decisions or tier choices, not run commands. However, a poisoned prompt or tool result could trick the router into a low tier or the compaction into dropping safety-relevant results.
Router hook silently downgrades the model to a smaller tier on Jev's decision; policy thresholds are hardcoded in the generated code.

Relies on an early-access, undocumented function-hook API (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS) that the README itself says changes between releases; the prompts tell Claude to regenerate types from the local build and trust those over the prompt.
entries.dataEgress: 01 router: the full text of the first user prompt of each session, plus each subagent's prompt, description and agentType, sent to api.typesafe.ai (would be openrouter.ai after patching). 02 compaction: the contents of tool calls and results from the conversation (file contents, command output, search results; up to 25k tokens of state per request, 30k per request, several batches) at every /compact or auto-compact. 03 review: the entire git diff plus title and description, on each /jev-review. Nothing is sent when the key is missing. On OpenRouter this data would also transit OpenRouter, so it is subject to that gateway's logging and provider policies. This matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design for 01 and 02. Router: 1500 ms Promise.race timeout, any error means no decision, the session keeps its native model, and it retries at the next prompt. Compaction: 8 s timeout (under the hook's 10 s budget), any error, missing key or a reduction under 15% delegates to native compaction (next(e)). Review (03) is on demand; a missing key exits with code 4 and Claude stops and says where to set it. A failed Jev call in the review does not block a commit because it is not gated by a hook. The hook engine can also skip a hook if it exceeds its budget; the prompt notes 'delegates to native without saying so'.
entries.contextCost: Near zero permanent context: no MCP server, no tools. Hooks inject no text into the model context; only a single transcript UI line ('[jev-router] sessione: sonnet · effort low') appears, plus a status bar and toast during compaction that are UI-only. The /jev-review skill adds one skill description (~50 tokens) to the skills list. The one-time generation cost is high: pasting a 12-20 KB prompt (about 3-5k tokens each) plus Claude building files with tests is a long agentic turn. Compaction can even reduce context, replacing the summary with verbatim pruning.
pros: Only candidate here that actually hooks Jev into Claude Code deterministically (prompt.submit, turn.step, agent.spawn, session.compact), which matches the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement better than an MCP tool the model must choose to call.

Correct System One request/response contract with concrete typed questions (choice/score/noul), thresholds kept in code rather than in the model, and a documented 1500 ms/8 s timeout with fail-open fallback to native behaviour.
Design is sound for cache: decides the model once per session because switching invalidates the prompt cache; subagents get their own classification. Zero tool-definition context cost.
Prompt-form means auditable: the user reads the full spec before pasting, and generated code lives in the user's own repo with no third-party runtime, no npm/pip dependency and no postinstall.
Provider swap to OpenRouter is a URL, key and model-id edit (openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, typesafe/jev-latest), as the schema is the System One shape.
MIT license; prompt 03's policy-in-JSON review design (14 checks, BLOCK/SECURITY REVIEW/NITS/MERGE) is a reusable pattern.
cons: It is not an installable integration: 2 commits, 1 author, 7 stars, created 7 days before the audit date, no code, tests or CI in the repo. Output varies per Claude run and needs review each time.

Depends on the early-access, unstable function-hook engine (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1) that could break on any Claude Code update; I could not verify that it exists in Claude Code 2.1.285. It must be enabled through the settings env.

Router value is doubtful for this user: on a subscription/OAuth login with Opus 5.5 as the main model, auto-downgrading to Sonnet or overriding effort can reduce quality on client work, and the hardcoded model IDs (claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5-5, claude-fable-5-1) may not match the account. The saving of tokens is small on a flat-rate plan.

Compaction hook sends raw tool outputs (files, command output, possibly secrets) to a third party at every compact; there is no redaction, which is a bad fit for client projects, and it would bypass the intent of the user's PreToolUse secret guard.

Compaction replacing native summaries is a risky semantic change: dropping tool results by a noul probability can remove context the model needs, and the 'still needed?' judgement is by a small non-reasoning model.
Hardwired to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (which requires early-access approval); the prompts do not mention OpenRouter, so the user must edit each of the three prompts.
Prompts are in Italian only, and everything is per-project by default (must be moved to ~/.claude/skills for global use), with a project trust prompt gating .claude/skills.
Review skill (03) is model-triggered and needs a manual key; the diff (full client code) leaves the machine.
entries.verdict: A well-designed but immature set of copy-paste prompts, not a maintained integration; its hook-based, fail-open architecture is the right shape for automatic use, but it depends on an unstable early-access hook engine and has no OpenRouter support out of the box. Use it as a reference design (especially the session-start tier router and the policy-in-code review), not as a drop-in; skip the compaction hook for client repos because of data egress.

judge.why: Copy-paste prompts with a hook-based, fail-open architecture, which is the right shape for automatic use. It depends on an unstable early-access hook engine and has no OpenRouter path.
pros: Fail-open hook design is conceptually right
cons: No OpenRouter; immature; unstable dependency; unverified

entries.name: HyunjunJeon/jev-judgment
entries.what: Agent Skill (SKILL.md plus one stdlib-only Python script, jev.py) that tells the coding agent to send closed questions to TypeSafe Jev at three points. (1) Before asking the user a closed question, it asks Jev whether context already determines the answer. (2) Before a risky command, it scores destructive, exfiltration, beyond_scope and impact. (3) After a command fails, it classifies the failure and checks for leaked secrets. jev.py is a thin pass-through for POST {base}/v1/systemone. It redacts credentials with regexes, truncates strings, fails open on every network error, and prints the JSON answer. SKILL.md holds fixed thresholds and action tables (for example, auto-answer if P>=0.9 and determined>=0.9; stop if destructive>=0.9 or exfiltration>=0.7). The agent applies these itself, so nothing is enforced.
interface: python3 scripts/jev.py [--model M] [--timeout S] [--dry-run] [-f FILE] [--max-string-chars N] [--max-state-chars N]
Protocol 1: pick (choice incl. ask_user) plus determined (noul)
Protocol 2: destructive, exfiltration, beyond_scope (noul) plus impact (4-level score)
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). Claude Code decides whether to load the skill from the description, then the model decides at each point whether to call jev.py. There is no hook, so nothing is deterministic. Under bypass or auto permission mode the model is not forced to consult Jev before rm or push --force, so the risk-gate protocol is not reliable. Reliability of triggering on 'about to ask the user' or 'command failed' is uncertain because Claude has no strong reason to defer to it. It can be improved by adding a CLAUDE.md line or by wrapping jev.py in a PreToolUse hook, which would require code changes.
security: API key is read from env or <cwd>/.env (jev.py:246-251) and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. The state goes via stdin heredoc.
Reading <cwd>/.env (jev.py:234-243) means a client project's .env is parsed for TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. Other entries are not returned, but the file is opened.

Regex redaction (jev.py:70-124) covers PEM, JWT, AWS, gh*, sk-*, Slack, Bearer and KEY=value assignments with 16+ chars. It is best-effort. Secrets in other formats, DB connection strings, and short passwords pass through. The README admits false negatives are possible.

No shell execution inside the script, no curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry. It is stdlib-only, with a single HTTPS call to a user-configurable base URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL can redirect traffic anywhere, so a poisoned env or .env could exfiltrate the redacted state and key. Nothing else is in the way.
Installation uses `npx skills add` (third-party skills CLI). That is outside this repo and unaudited, but it is only needed once. The files can also be copied by hand.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output and file facts are put into the state and Jev's verdict then drives agent behaviour. A malicious repo could word its content to push 'destructive' low. The verdict is advisory and the agent can ignore it.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in `state`, after regex redaction. Per SKILL.md, that means user_request, last_user_message, chosen facts (file listings, config snippets), the exact tool arguments (the command, path, first 400 chars of content), and the first 2000 chars of failed-command output. Strings are capped at 2000 chars and the whole state at 8000 chars. It goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to the host set in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (OpenRouter, in this user's setup). It is chosen by the model, so it varies per call. On client projects this can include proprietary paths, commands and snippets, and OpenRouter and TypeSafe would both see them. There is no telemetry from the script itself.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design (jev.py:411-446). A missing key, HTTP 401, 422 or 429, another HTTP error, a timeout or a connection error each print {"error":...} with exit 0, and SKILL.md says to behave as if the skill were not installed. The default timeout is 8 s (jev.py:58). There are no retries in the script, and the agent is told to retry at most once. Worst case per failed call is about 8 s blocked, most likely when the network hangs. Exit 2 only on a malformed request or a state over 8000 chars, and the agent is told to fix and resend. There is no fail-closed mode, so Protocol 2 gives no guarantee on Jev outages.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens. The always-loaded cost is the skill name plus description (SKILL.md:2-12, about 690 chars, roughly 175 tokens) plus the compatibility and allowed-tools frontmatter, so about 200 tokens per session. The full SKILL.md (204 lines, about 9.5k chars, roughly 2.4k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. Each trigger also costs the model tokens to author the state and questions JSON (roughly 300-600 output tokens, since instructions and criteria must be written per call), plus the returned JSON (roughly 150-300 tokens). references/questions.md (217 lines) is read on demand, and the model may re-read it. No hook injection and no MCP server instructions.
pros: Zero-cost passive footprint: no MCP server, about 200 tokens always-loaded, and no hooks to conflict with the secret-leak guard, the GitNexus hooks or the caveman plugin.
Auto-invocation is at least designed in. The description names concrete moments (before AskUserQuestion, before rm/reset/force-push, after a failed command), so the user never has to say 'use jev'.

jev.py is small, readable and stdlib-only. Fail-open on every network error, an 8 s timeout, redaction of common secret formats, and --dry-run to inspect exactly what would leave the machine (jev.py:407-409).

The OpenRouter switch is config only if the OpenRouter body schema matches: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model typesafe/jev-1.13 (jev.py:53-57, 267-278, 422). The wire format {model,state,questions} matches the documented System One shape.
MIT licensed and a single file to fork. Adding OPENROUTER_API_KEY support is a 5-line change.
The protocols are well thought out, with an always-ask list (dependencies, remote state, multi-select) and a rule to report every Jev-driven decision. This limits the damage from over-trusting Jev.
Failure-class and secret-in-output checks could complement the existing secret-leak hook.
cons: Not deterministic. It is a skill, not a hook, so Claude decides whether to invoke it. In bypass or auto mode the Protocol 2 risk gate can simply be skipped, which is when it is needed most. It cannot block a command; it only asks the model to self-police.

Very young and unproven: 1 commit, 1 contributor, created and last pushed 2026-09-17, 7 stars, 1 fork, no releases, no tests, no CI. The benchmark cited in questions.md (54 items) is unpublished and self-reported.

Uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL only. OpenRouter needs a misleadingly named key variable and non-default model slugs. Whether OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the same body and returns the same answer shape is unverified from the repo. The user's planned OPENROUTER_API_KEY would be ignored.

Poor value for Opus 5.5. Each use costs the model 300-600 tokens of hand-written JSON (instructions, criteria) plus 0.6-1.5 s of network and startup, to answer questions Opus can usually answer itself. Protocol 1 mostly helps agents that ask the user too often, and Protocol 3's failure classification is trivial for a strong model.

Real safety risk of over-trusting a beta model whose behaviour is disputed (the Theo 'flash router' claim). A wrongly confident 'determined' can auto-answer a question the user should have decided. Protocol 2 tells the model to skip mention of Jev when nothing fires, which weakens visibility.

Privacy: commands, snippets, user messages and failed-command output leave the machine on every trigger, including client projects. Regex redaction is best-effort and only covers the listed formats. The model chooses what goes in the state, so egress is unpredictable.

Overlaps with existing controls. The PreToolUse secret guard already deterministically blocks secret leakage. Permission modes already gate destructive commands when not bypassed. There is no code-search, refactor or analysis value, so it does not help with daily coding tasks.
Reads <cwd>/.env for the key (jev.py:251). In client repos this can hit the wrong .env or be surprising.
entries.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-open skill and the lightest possible way to get Jev into Claude Code (about 200 tokens, no MCP, no hook conflicts). But it is only advisory and model-triggered, one-commit and untested, and it is aimed at agents weaker than Opus 5.5. Use it as a low-risk experiment through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model slug (after verifying the OpenRouter schema with --dry-run and one live call), or as the source for a hook-based fork. Do not rely on it as a safety gate.

entries.name: jev-assist
entries.what: Single-file Node CLI (scripts/jev.mjs, 531 lines, zero deps) plus a SKILL.md. Since 1.0.0 it is skill-only: no hooks and no MCP server. The agent pipes grep/git/test output on stdin (one candidate per line) into `jev noul|choice|score '<question>'`. The CLI batches the lines into Jev Decisions API calls (concurrency 8, 45k-token budget per request) and prints a banner with exact totals, then rows sorted by calibrated probability with a cut line (widest-gap "cliff", else p>=0.70, else top 10). Verdicts are cached locally. The pitch is that the agent reads about 30 rows instead of thousands of grep hits. It does not search. It classifies what the agent already found.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger only (SKILL.md description). There are no hooks in the current version. This matters: the author's own git history (commit 3a5d3c5, 2026-09-22) records that a session with the description in the skill listing, a full SessionStart injection and a memory note still ran nine hand-written greps and never invoked the skill, and the description lever was called 'exhausted'. The author then added a PreToolUse hook (asks once per session on repo-wide file-listing greps) and removed it again in 1.0.0 (7f3679b), which deleted install-hook.mjs, pretool.mjs, session-start.mjs. So the shipped package does not meet the user's 'automatic without prompting' requirement on its own, and the author's data suggests it would rarely fire. A custom PreToolUse hook could be layered on top, but that means writing our own code and colliding with the existing Grep|Glob|Bash hooks.
security: No postinstall or lifecycle scripts in package.json. Network calls go only to the chosen Jev endpoint (fetch in ask(), :57). No telemetry, no shell execution, no child_process, no eval.

Key handling is mostly good. The key file is 0600 in a 0700 dir, JEV_API_KEY takes precedence, and the key is masked on echo (`sk-or-…xxxx`, :496). The weak spot is `jev key <API_KEY>`: it puts the secret in argv, visible in ps and shell history, and an agent running it would also have the key in its transcript. Use the env var instead.

Prompt-injection surface: candidate lines are sent as `instructions` to a typed classifier. The SKILL.md itself admits 'no prompt-injection defence' and that comments and fixtures in the repo can move an answer. Consequence: a poisoned line can only skew a probability (silent false negatives), not execute anything. However, the Claude agent reads the sorted output and may skip rows it should have read.
The output echoes candidate lines JSON-quoted into Claude's context, so repo text still reaches the model, as with plain grep.

The skill tells the agent to run a script via absolute path and to pipe grep output into it. That is fine under bypass or auto mode, but it means a repo-wide flood of code is sent off-machine on each use.

The cache is ~/.cache/jev/cache.json, keyed by sha256(model, cmd, spec, line). It holds hashes and verdicts, not plaintext code. It grows without eviction (author's own 'ponytail' note, :14) and is written non-atomically without locking, so parallel runs can clobber each other.
entries.dataEgress: Per call, to openrouter.ai (via the sk-or- prefix): the OpenRouter API key, the question text, the raw candidate lines (for example `path:line:code snippet` from grep, file paths from git ls-files, test failure lines, diff hunks), the model id, and the criteria/options. No whole files unless the agent pipes them in (SKILL.md tells it not to). Nothing is sent when every line is a cache hit. On the OpenRouter side the payload is subject to the account's data-policy settings. For client projects, the client's source lines leave the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, which needs a client-policy decision. The tool's own doc says: 'If the repo must not leave the machine, do not point jev at it.'
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per invocation, but harmless to Claude Code because it is not on the tool path. A missing key exits 1 in milliseconds with a message (:54, :395). Any non-OK HTTP status (401, 429, 5xx) calls die(), exiting 1 with the first 400 chars of the body, with no retry or backoff. The only retry is halving a batch on `max_tokens_exceeded`. fetch has no timeout or AbortController, so a hung endpoint hangs the Bash tool call until Claude Code's own Bash timeout. There is no fallback to plain grep. That fallback is the agent's own behaviour. Because it is a voluntary skill, an outage just means the agent falls back to reading grep output. A malformed API response produces a loud die() and not a fake result. With one worker failing, the whole run dies and partial results are lost (the cache is only written after all batches finish).
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens and no server instructions. The skill listing costs only the frontmatter description: about 900 characters, about 230 tokens, permanently in every session. When invoked, the full SKILL.md is loaded: 183 lines, about 2.5k tokens. No hook-injected text in 1.0.0. The earlier 0.x SessionStart and PreToolUse hooks were removed. Each call's output is capped to about 30 rows or 50 rows, so it typically costs 0.5-2k tokens instead of the tens of thousands a flood would cost.
pros: Direct OpenRouter support in the code: sk-or- key prefix routes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest (jev.mjs:31-38). It needs no patching, only JEV_API_KEY=sk-or-... in the environment.
Cheapest possible context footprint: no MCP server, no tools, about 230 tokens for the skill description, and output capped at about 30-50 rows regardless of pool size.

Uses Jev for what it is actually good at: batched typed classification (noul/choice/score) of many short candidates with calibrated probabilities, rather than free-form chat. Counts are computed in JS, so the model is never asked to count.

Honest, well-documented failure modes: short lines score low, multi-hop questions degrade, no injection defence, noul and choice are not comparable. Good guidance on when NOT to use it (under a dozen candidates, anything a linter decides).
Small, dependency-free, readable code (531 lines) with no postinstall, no shell exec and no telemetry. Key stored 0600 outside the repo, and cache holds hashes only.
Real batching and resilience details: token-budget batching, halve-and-retry on max_tokens_exceeded, concurrency 8, dedupe, local verdict cache so re-runs are free and cheap ($0.042/1M input).
Works with any agent that reads SKILL.md and can call it via `node /abs/path/jev.mjs`, so it can be dropped into ~/.claude/skills with no interference with the existing gitnexus/caveman hooks.
cons: Not automatic. It is a description-triggered skill only. The author's own commit message (3a5d3c5) documents the agent ignoring it and running nine hand-written greps, then 1.0.0 deleted the hooks that tried to fix it. That is direct evidence against the user's core requirement.

Solves a narrow problem (triaging huge grep/TODO/test-failure floods). Opus 5.5 plus GitNexus (already installed) already narrows search results, so the 'flood of thousands of lines' case is rare in normal daily coding. Value is occasional, not constant.

Sends real source lines (grep hits, diff hunks, paths) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every uncached call. This is a data-egress problem for client projects and there is no per-project allow/deny switch ('There is no per-project config').

Fragile API coupling: uses the alpha Decisions endpoint and guesses response field names with fallbacks (`noul ?? probability`, `choice ?? label ?? option ?? value`). A schema change breaks it, or worse, it defaults a choice probability to 1 when the field is missing (jev.mjs:231-232).
No fetch timeout, no retry/backoff on 429/5xx, and one failed batch kills the whole run with no partial results. Poor for a tool that fans out 8 concurrent requests on large pools.

A classifier on short lines is unreliable (author states short candidates score systematically lower, especially CJK), so the sorted cut line can hide true positives. There is no prompt-injection defence, so a hostile repo comment can skew the ranking, and the agent is told to trust the cut.

Single-maintainer, 10-day-old, 4-star project, 40 commits in 4 days, 1 npm version, 0.x churn that ended in removing its own automation. Test coverage is unit-level only. Authored with heavy AI assistance ('Co-Authored-By: Claude Code' throughout).
`jev key <KEY>` puts the secret in argv, and the skill install does not put `jev` on PATH, so the agent must be given an absolute path.
entries.verdict: Clean, safe, OpenRouter-ready CLI skill for one niche job (triaging grep/test floods), but not an automatic integration: it is a description-triggered skill, and the author's own history shows the agent ignoring it and the hooks removed. Worth installing only as an optional low-cost helper (key via env var, not on client repos) and never as the main Jev integration.

entries.name: Kmasterrr/use-jev
entries.what: Claude Code/Codex skill (SKILL.md + AGENTS.md + 141-line dependency-free Node script scripts/jev.mjs). Claude writes a request.json (state + typed questions of type choice/score/noul), runs `node jev.mjs request.json`, and gets JSON answers from typesafe/jev-1.13 on OpenRouter. Documents route / detect-and-gate / score-and-rank patterns with 4 example request files. No MCP server, no hooks, no plugin.json/marketplace.json/.mcp.json. Nothing that runs without Claude deciding to invoke the skill.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger only. The description is oriented to business workflows (triage, lead scoring, support routing, rerank, guardrails, 'ask Jev') rather than coding events, so for daily coding it will rarely fire without being told, and when it does, rule 1 makes Claude ask permission for anything not obviously public. No hook, so it cannot be a deterministic gate (e.g. no PermissionRequest integration). It does NOT meet the 'never prompt use jev' goal by itself; the user would need to rewrite the description and privacy rule and add hooks.
security: Key never on argv: read from env or file and sent only in Authorization header (jev.mjs:39-42,96); output never echoes key. Good.
Key file fallback ~/.claude/secrets/openrouter.key is plaintext 0600; set-key.sh uses hidden read, umask 077, sk-or- validation. User does not need it if OPENROUTER_API_KEY is in env.
Only shell exec is execFileSync('powershell') gated on win32 (jev.mjs:45-53), args array, apostrophe-escaped path: irrelevant on Linux. No shell=true, no eval, no child process on Linux.
No telemetry, no other network hosts; only openrouter.ai. install.sh is 10 lines of cp/mkdir, no curl|sh, no sudo, no rc-file edits.

Prompt-injection surface: whatever text Claude puts in `state` (file contents, diffs, web text) goes to Jev; per brief, injected instructions in state can move answers. SKILL.md mitigates by rule 'signal, not authority; does not grant permissions'. Answers are typed numbers/choices only, so Jev output cannot inject text back into Claude beyond choice keys chosen by the caller.

Skill rule 1 requires asking the user for an explicit yes before sending anything possibly private/credentials, and 'never send secrets'. This is model-enforced only, not deterministic; the existing no-secret-leak.cjs hook does not cover this script's stdin/file content and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in its protected list, and the script reads the key itself so a Bash call `node jev.mjs` would pass the hook.
entries.dataEgress: Exactly the JSON body {model, state, questions} that Claude composes, POSTed over HTTPS to openrouter.ai (then relayed to TypeSafe), plus Bearer key. Content is whatever Claude chooses to put in `state` (could be code, diffs, emails, tickets). No file scanning, no automatic collection, no telemetry. Privacy gate is only a natural-language rule in SKILL.md that asks for user consent before possibly-private text, which conflicts with the goal of frictionless automatic use.
entries.failureMode: Script fails closed to an error object with exit 1 (no fake decision); SKILL.md rule 6 says show the exact error and do not imply Jev decided. 15 s default timeout via AbortSignal.timeout (jev.mjs:24,100), no retry; fallback to the second route only on 404 (:129). Since it is an on-demand skill and not a hook, a failed call cannot block or stall tool execution beyond up to 15 s in one Bash call. Confidence gating (0.6 choice/score; noul 0.35-0.65 uncertain) is advisory text; low confidence means 'Claude decided'.
entries.contextCost: Low. Skill listing entry ~ 420 chars description (~105 tokens) fits well in skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02. Full SKILL.md body (7.9 KB, ~2k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. No MCP tool defs, no hook-injected text. Each use adds the request JSON + result to context.
pros: Genuinely OpenRouter-native: hardcoded typesafe/jev-1.13, both /api/v1/systemone and /api/alpha/decisions, OPENROUTER_API_KEY from env (jev.mjs:19-23,39).
Tiny, auditable, zero-dependency script (141 lines), no argv key exposure, no telemetry, no shell exec on Linux, MIT license; installer is 10 lines of cp.

Reusable as a reference caller: request/answer shape for choice/score/noul with criteria formats is clearly documented in SKILL.md and examples, useful to build a PermissionRequest/Stop hook or a small MCP wrapper.
Sound safety stance: 'signal, not authority', explicit uncertainty thresholds, honest error reporting, no fabricated decisions on failure.
Very low context cost (~105 tokens listing entry) and no impact on latency of normal turns.
cons: Skill-only, model-discretion: not deterministic, no hook, and the description targets support/lead/inbox workflows, so it will not automatically add value in coding; fails the user's core 'automatic' requirement.

Rule 1 forces asking the user before sending possibly private content, which contradicts frictionless automation and, for client code, would fire constantly; enforcement is prose only, not a technical gate.
Immature: created 1 day ago, 4 commits, 2 stars, no tests/CI/releases; benchmark is author's small personal set (~60 items) on business text, not coding decisions.

Route ambiguity: sends the OpenRouter-prefixed model id to /v1/systemone (native schema per brief uses 'jev-1.13'), and falls back to /alpha/decisions only on 404; a 400 from route 1 would surface as a failure even if route 2 works. Unverified since nothing may be run.

Does nothing for the user's permission-automation goal (no PermissionRequest hook, no cookbook recipe); OPENROUTER_API_KEY not in no-secret-leak.cjs list, and the script would read the key from env/file outside that hook's view; secrets dir plaintext file convention duplicates key storage.
Each use costs a Claude turn to author JSON, so latency/cost saving vs. just deciding in-model is marginal for coding.
entries.verdict: Clean, safe, OpenRouter-ready reference script, but it is a business-workflow skill that only triggers at model discretion and asks for consent before sending private text, so it does not deliver automatic Jev use in daily coding. Worth reading as a request-format example (or cherry-picking jev.mjs), not as the integration itself; prefer the OpenRouter PermissionRequest hook cookbook for the automatic behavior.

judge.why: Clean 141-line dependency-free Node script for OpenRouter (Node 24 fine) with a good request-format reference. It targets business workflows, and its consent rule blocks automation.
pros: Tiny, auditable, MIT, no argv key, no exec on Linux
Clear choice/score/noul request examples
cons: Rule 1 makes Claude ask before sending possibly private text, which defeats frictionless use
Sends OpenRouter-prefixed model id to /v1/systemone and falls back only on 404 (unverified)

entries.name: jev-skill (KHAEntertainment)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also npx skills) with one skill, jev-integration. It is a ~14.6KB SKILL.md plus four references (access-paths, frameworks, harness-patterns, calibration-and-ops, ~52KB total). It teaches when and how to integrate Jev: a fit test, access-path choice, framework choice, harness patterns and production rules. It also ships copy-in templates (Python and TS OpenRouter clients, an AI SDK module, and a stdlib-only fail-closed Python PreToolUse Bash gate hook). It has a jev_probe.py smoke-test script and evals/ with skill-fired graders. It has no MCP server, no hooks.json and no auto-installed hook. The plugin manifest declares only the skill. The gate must be copied in by hand.
entries.autoInvocation: The skill auto-triggers only from its description, when the task involves building or debugging Jev, TypeSafe or a hook gate. It has no PreToolUse, UserPromptSubmit or other hook shipped in the plugin, so it will not make Claude Code use Jev automatically in daily coding. The only automatic Jev behavior is the optional Bash gate. That gate is a safety filter (deny or ask only, never allow) and does not reduce prompts in auto or bypass modes.
security: Gate key handling is safe: the key is read from env and sent in an Authorization header via urllib. It is never put in argv or logged (jev_gate.py:164).
Static review found no shell exec, eval, telemetry or installer code in the repo. The gate and probe are stdlib-only urllib. The only subprocess use is the test file, which runs the local gate.

The gate sends the Bash command with a regex redaction pass (jev_gate.py:107-118: private keys, sk-/pk- keys, GitHub, AWS, Slack tokens, JWT, bearer, URL credentials, *_KEY/TOKEN/SECRET=value). It also sends the last user message from the transcript JSONL, up to 1500 chars, and the cwd. Redaction is best-effort. Secrets in file contents heredoc'd into a command, or in prose in the user message, can leak. For client projects this is a real data-egress concern.

Prompt-injection surface: the command string and user text go into Jev state, and an injected instruction could sway the answers. The design mitigates this because the gate never returns allow and has deterministic deny rules first. Jev can only make things stricter.

The gate provides no protection for OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the user's setup. no-secret-leak.cjs must add it to its protected list. The gate's SENSITIVE_PATH only skips its pass rules and does not block reads.
The installer chain (marketplace repo KHAEntertainment/marketplace, npx skills) was not audited. Installing by static copy avoids running it.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine while the skill is only installed. When the gate is wired in, each non-pattern-matched Bash call sends to openrouter.ai: the redacted command (up to 8000 chars), the tool name, cwd, the last user request (up to 1500 chars, redacted) and the fixed question schema, plus the OPENROUTER_API_KEY as a bearer. Calls short-circuited by the deny or pass regexes send nothing. The probe sends a static sample string. There is no telemetry to the author.
entries.failureMode: The gate is fail-closed by design. Timeout, network error, missing key (KeyError on os.environ[key_env]), a bad response or bad stdin all emit ask, or deny with JEV_GATE_ON_ERROR=deny (jev_gate.py:184-201). The HTTP timeout is 4 s per socket operation, not a total deadline, against a 10 s hook timeout (the docstring admits this). A hook that hits its own timeout is discarded and the tool proceeds. For this user that is problematic. With defaultMode auto and bypassPermissions sessions, every OpenRouter outage, an unset key or a slow response causes an interactive ask prompt, and the skill states that ask prompts even in auto mode. In unattended bypass sessions deny mode would hard-block Bash. It is safe but can be disruptive. An allow-capable fail-open variant is not provided.
entries.contextCost: The skill listing entry carries the full description of about 1.0KB (~250 tokens, from SKILL.md:3-15) and counts against skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02. There is no MCP and no hook-injected text. The SKILL.md body (~14.6KB, ~3.6k tokens) loads only when the skill fires, and the references (~52KB, ~13k tokens) load on demand. Idle cost is small. If invoked on a Jev task, the cost is a few k tokens.
pros: Accurate OpenRouter coverage from primary sources: both endpoints (/api/v1/systemone and /api/alpha/decisions), pinned and alias model ids, the docs-URL quirk, and per-path model-id mismatches that cause 404/403/422 (access-paths.md:13-17,90-154, SKILL.md:99-100). It matches the JEV BRIEF.

The gate is well designed as a safety hook. Deterministic deny and pass regexes run before any model call and there is a 3-question Jev call. It never returns allow, so it can only tighten. It self-enforces a deadline with a documented reason (a timed-out hook lets the tool proceed) and handles precedence. OpenRouter is a one-line env switch, JEV_GATE_PROVIDER=openrouter.
Stdlib-only Python with no install step and no third-party dependencies. Static review found no shell exec, no telemetry, and no key in argv. It has offline tests using JEV_GATE_MOCK.

Honest ops guidance: fail-closed for gates vs fail-open for optimizers, pin the version, calibrate thresholds, and a warning that thresholds are placeholders (TODO(calibrate)). It labels unverified claims. The skill has non-trigger evals so it should not fire on unrelated work.
MIT license, small footprint, and the idle context cost is only the description.
cons: It is a knowledge and template skill, not an integration. It does not make Claude Code use Jev automatically in daily coding, which is this user's core goal. It only fires when the user is already building a Jev integration, which contradicts 'never having to prompt use jev'.

The gate is a copy-in template with placeholder, uncalibrated thresholds. Its default provider is TypeSafe, so it needs env wiring, the key in the hook environment, an absolute path in the command (the snippet uses $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR and python3 from PATH, and PATH is overridden here), and adding OPENROUTER_API_KEY to no-secret-leak.cjs protection.

Poor fit for this user's modes. The gate can only deny or ask, never allow, so in auto and bypassPermissions it adds a round trip and extra prompts (fail-closed ask on any error) but removes none. It also sends command text and recent user messages to a third party on client projects, and the only mitigation is regex redaction. The OpenRouter cookbook's PermissionRequest fail-open-to-prompt pattern suits this user better.

Immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, created 2026-09-23, no releases, no CI. It targets an /alpha endpoint with no SLA, and the Jev model itself has documented overconfidence and injection weaknesses. Dependencies on the marketplace repo (KHAEntertainment/marketplace) were not audited.

The 1KB description consumes skill-listing budget (fraction 0.02) for a rarely-needed skill. The gate's 4 s timeout applies per socket operation, not total, so the worst case can approach the 10 s hook limit.
entries.verdict: A well-researched, honest, OpenRouter-correct reference skill, and a decent starting template for a Bash risk gate. But it only helps when the user is building Jev integrations, so it does not deliver automatic Jev use. Its one hook is a stricter-only, fail-closed filter that adds latency and prompts in this user's auto and bypass workflow, and it sends command text to a third party. Useful as a reference to pull ideas from (endpoint facts, fail-closed pattern), not to install as the answer.

judge.why: The best reference for OpenRouter access paths, plus a stdlib fail-closed PreToolUse Bash gate template. The gate can only deny or ask, which is the wrong direction for your goal.
