entries.what: A single documentation-style SKILL.md (about 10 KB) plus plugin.json and marketplace.json. It teaches Claude how to design and write application code that calls TypeSafe System One (Jev), covering the Choice, Noul and Score primitives, composition patterns and live-doc lookup. It contains no MCP server, no hooks, no scripts and no runtime code. It never calls Jev itself, so it cannot make Claude Code use Jev for its own coding decisions.
interface: claude plugin marketplace add typesafe-ai/skills; claude plugin install typesafe@typesafe-ai
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at Claude's discretion when the task is 'add AI decisions to an app'. It does not make Claude Code consult Jev during its own work. It cannot meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically.
security: No executable code: no shell, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in the repo (files: README.md, LICENSE, SKILL.md, two JSON manifests).
No API key handling in the skill. TYPESAFE_API_KEY is only mentioned in the docs page as an env var for experiments.

Prompt-injection surface: SKILL.md instructs Claude to fetch live docs from docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and *.md pages (SKILL.md:26-44). That content is remote and can change, so the vendor's docs effectively steer the agent's behavior. The risk is low, since it is a first-party domain and read-only fetching.
Plugin marketplace installs track the GitHub main branch, so a later release can change the instructions without review. Pin or read the diff on update.
The skill tells Claude to keep credentials server-side in web apps (SKILL.md:149).
entries.dataEgress: The skill itself sends nothing. Claude (via WebFetch or curl) reads public docs pages from docs.typesafe.ai, so the URLs fetched leak only that a doc was requested. No code, prompts or diffs go to Jev or TypeSafe from this skill. Any Jev call happens only in application code that Claude writes and the user runs.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable, because the skill has no runtime dependency on Jev. If docs.typesafe.ai is down, SKILL.md tells Claude to fall back to local docs or SDK types and state the limitation (SKILL.md:41-44). It is effectively fail-open.
entries.contextCost: 0 tools and 0 MCP instructions. At startup only the frontmatter (name plus a roughly 750 char description, about 190 tokens) sits in the skills listing. The full body (about 10 KB, roughly 2.5k tokens) loads only when the skill is invoked or auto-triggered. It injects no hook text.
pros: Official, MIT-licensed, tiny and safe: 12 KB of Markdown/JSON, no executables, no hooks, no MCP, no telemetry. Nothing that can break the existing Bash, Read or Grep hooks.
Near-zero context cost (about 190 tokens of description at startup, about 2.5k tokens only when loaded).

Useful for building Jev features into client apps: correct primitives (Choice, Noul, Score), the pattern of 'ask independent questions in parallel over the same state', and guidance on confidence thresholds (SKILL.md:96-148).
Points Claude at live docs (llms.txt), so guidance stays current without plugin updates.
Popular (2.4k stars in about 5 weeks), maintained by the vendor with a release bot, currently v0.5.7.
cons: It does not call Jev. It is documentation for writing Jev code, so it fails the core requirement of Claude Code invoking Jev automatically for its own decisions.

No OpenRouter awareness. Neither the repo nor the docs page mention OpenRouter, and the docs point to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Claude would default to the direct TypeSafe endpoint unless the user adds an instruction such as 'use OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone'.

The trigger is broad and semantic ('brainstorming what AI could make possible', 'LLM prompt-and-parse step'). It may load unprompted while the user works on unrelated AI features and nudge Claude toward adding Jev to client projects where it is unwanted.
Immature: 2 squashed commits, one human author, no tests or CI visible, and the version is 0.5.x. The main branch is tracked, so instructions can change on plugin update.
Depends on the live docs for the actual API contract, so behavior varies over time and needs network access during sessions.
entries.verdict: Safe and cheap, and worth installing only if you build Jev-powered features in your own or client apps. It is a coding-knowledge skill and not an integration, so it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically'. Pair it with a hook or MCP layer if that is the goal, and add a CLAUDE.md line to prefer the OpenRouter endpoint.

entries.name: aaddrick/building-with-typesafe-jev
entries.what: Unofficial, docs-only Claude Code plugin/skill (also Codex, Antigravity, Muse) that teaches the coding agent HOW TO BUILD applications that call Jev: Choice/Score/Noul primitive selection, question-writing rules, confidence banding, gate/rerank/router patterns, and ~73 KB of prior-art shape files linking 150+ community projects. It contains no runtime: no MCP server, no hooks, no proxy, no code that calls Jev on Claude Code's behalf. Claude Code itself gains no Jev decision-making from it.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion) only, and only when the user's task is BUILDING an app/feature that uses Jev or NL judgments. It does not make Claude Code call Jev for its own decisions (permission gating, commit classification, context routing); SKILL.md itself states Jev 'is not a chat or coding LLM and cannot power a coding agent'.
security: No executable code in the Claude Code install path: plugin has no hooks, no MCP servers, no commands; skill is inert markdown (.claude-plugin/plugin.json and marketplace.json contain only metadata).

Only curl|bash is scripts/install_muse.sh (README for Muse): curl -fsSL codeload.github.com ... | tar -xz, rewrites frontmatter, rm -rf/mv into ~/workspace/skills. Muse-only, not needed for Claude Code, but it is a pipe-to-bash install path advertised in the README.

Key handling guidance is good: SKILL.md:20-24 says never print/echo/log/commit the key, never hardcode api_key=, do not search .env/profiles for it, warns TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs bodies unredacted. It does have the agent run live probes (up to ~10 calls per task) when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is in the shell, so state sent to Jev in probes is whatever the agent chooses.

Prompt-injection surface: skill instructs the agent to fetch https://docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt and .md pages and treat live docs as winning on conflict (SKILL.md line 10), so third-party doc content becomes trusted instructions; minor but real. Prior-art files are 73 KB of links to unvetted community repos.

Supply chain: single maintainer, 4 days old, 1 open issue; marketplace may be set to auto-sync, so a later malicious commit would flow into a global skill. Plugin skill can be pinned by commit SHA to mitigate.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no network calls from the plugin itself.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from the plugin itself. The agent may fetch docs.typesafe.ai pages (outbound GET, no user data). If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set, the agent may issue small live probe calls to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone containing whatever state/questions it designs for the code being built (potentially snippets of the user's project data); it will not do so with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY set. In no case are Claude Code prompts, diffs or tool outputs forwarded to Jev automatically.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable at runtime: no Jev call path exists. If docs.typesafe.ai is unreachable the skill says to read installed SDK types and tell the user. If no key is set it designs from api-reference.md and says so (fail-open, no blocking). No timeouts to configure.
entries.contextCost: 0 tools, 0 MCP instructions, 0 hook-injected text. Always-resident cost is only the skill name+description (~600 chars, about 150 tokens). On trigger, SKILL.md loads ~11.9 KB (about 3k tokens); api-reference.md (11.6 KB, ~2.9k tokens), patterns.md (9.2 KB, ~2.3k) and a prior-art shape file (~6 KB each, ~1.5k) load on demand. Typical triggered turn: 3-8k tokens. Description is broad ('classify, route, triage, filter, extract, score, rank') so it may load on unrelated NL-classification coding tasks and add noise.
pros: Zero risk and zero runtime footprint: no hooks, MCP server, postinstall or network from the plugin, so it cannot conflict with the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus hooks, or caveman plugins.

Genuinely useful when the user (senior dev, client projects) writes code that calls Jev: encodes rules like one snap judgment per question, batch all questions in one call, Score levels as situations, deterministic denylist before Jev, never let a Jev answer alone authorize a side effect. Rules cited in SKILL.md:26-60 are specific and consistent with the Jev brief.

Includes a gates.md shape with a concrete Bash-command gate (DENY regex first, then Noul flags + severity Score, block/review/allow bands) plus a 'Stop hook completion gate' variant: a ready design sketch for the user's own DIY Jev-in-Claude-Code hook. Also references OpenRouter cookbooks 'Gate Agent Tool Calls' and 'Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts' (gates.md:83) as prior art to mine.
Documents OpenRouter usage (base_url https://openrouter.ai/api, model ~typesafe/jev-latest) and Vercel gateway, and pins-to-model-version advice (jev-1.13.0), so generated code can target OpenRouter.

Good hygiene and CI: MIT, plugin validated with claude plugin validate --strict on pinned Claude Code, leaked-key scan, eval harness with isolated containers and a public ledger; code samples were validated against the live API per commit #3.
Cheap idle cost (~150 tokens of description) and installs with two claude plugin commands.
cons: It is not an integration. It never makes Claude Code invoke Jev; it does not meet the core requirement (automatic Jev use inside Claude Code without prompting). It only changes how Claude writes code when the task is already about Jev/NL classification.

API-reference is TypeSafe-direct-centric: default base URL api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, key env TYPESAFE_API_KEY; the live-probe behavior is gated on TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it won't probe using OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and it does not document OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone paths, or OpenRouter key/header conventions beyond one line (api-reference.md:130).

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-26, 8 commits, 1 contributor (aaddrick), no releases, 1 open issue; stars (125) driven by Jev hype. Content may drift from the beta API; it defers to live docs, which are fetched at runtime (untrusted-text-as-authority risk).

Broad trigger description (classify/route/triage/filter/extract/score/rank) can fire on ordinary app work, spending 3-8k tokens on a skill irrelevant to the task; non-Jev tasks may get nudged toward Jev.
Eval claims (0.96 vs 0.65) are self-measured, judged partly by LLMs, on agent-written code without an API key; says nothing about real Jev accuracy or the Theo 'flash router' skepticism.
README advertises curl|bash install (Muse only) and auto-sync marketplace option; single-maintainer auto-updating global skill is a supply-chain consideration for client work (pin a commit if used).
entries.verdict: A well-made, safe, inert knowledge skill for writing code that uses Jev, not a way to have Claude Code use Jev automatically. Worth installing as a cheap companion only if the user builds Jev-backed apps; otherwise it does nothing for the stated goal, which needs a hook or proxy that calls OpenRouter's Jev directly (its gates.md pattern is a good blueprint for that).

entries.name: samtay32/jev-system-architect
entries.what: A single SKILL.md (717 lines, ~19 KB) of architecture guidance. It tells a coding agent how to spot places in a codebase where deterministic code needs bounded semantic judgment, and how to turn them into Choice/Score/Noul questions. It covers fit tests, atomic questions, fan-out, confidence gates, evaluation and a review procedure. It never calls Jev. It contains no code, no API calls, no MCP server, no hooks and no scripts. It defers to TypeSafe's docs and official skill for API details. It is a design-time aid for building apps that use Jev, not a way for Claude Code to consult Jev while coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, chosen at the model's discretion. It fires automatically when Claude judges the task matches, with no user prompt needed. But what it triggers is design advice, not a Jev call. It is not a hook and not a proxy, and it never makes Jev decisions on Claude Code's own behalf.
security: No executable code, so no shell execution, no postinstall and no curl|sh installer.
No API keys are read or handled, so nothing can leak via argv.
No telemetry.
Prompt-injection surface is only the skill text itself. It is static and I read all 717 lines; I found no hidden or agent-directed instructions.
Third-party content loaded into context. It is low risk, but pin or copy a reviewed version rather than symlinking to a live clone.
Its last paragraph (SKILL.md:713-717) tells the agent to 'consult the current official documentation'. That can cause web fetches during use, which is benign.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from this skill. It is static text loaded into Claude's context. It sends no data to Jev, OpenRouter or anyone else. If Claude then fetches TypeSafe docs on the skill's advice, that is an ordinary Claude Code web fetch.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable. There is no Jev call, so there is no timeout, fail-open or fail-closed behaviour. The only failure is the skill not triggering, which is harmless.
entries.contextCost: Resident cost is the frontmatter name plus description, about 500 chars, or roughly 120-150 tokens per session. The full body is 18.9 KB, about 4.7k tokens, and loads only when the skill triggers. It adds no MCP tools and no hooks. Its broad trigger words (classification, routing, ranking, guardrails, prompt-to-JSON) could fire on ordinary LLM-app coding tasks and add about 5k tokens each time.
pros: Zero risk: pure markdown, MIT, no code execution, no keys, no egress. Safe to read statically.
Cheap resident cost, about 120-150 tokens for the description. The body loads only on demand.

Content is good and matches the brief's Choice/Noul/Score model. It gives a fit test, an 'atomic question' rule, fan-out batching, risk-scaled confidence gates, and 'do not use Jev for deterministic or generative work' (SKILL.md:136-164, 194-215).
Useful when the user builds client apps that have LLM-to-JSON parsing, routers or classifiers. It would steer Claude to replace them with typed Jev calls and keep control flow in code.
Provider-neutral and defers to live docs (SKILL.md:29, 594-608), so it will not hardcode stale OpenRouter or TypeSafe fields.
cons: It does not integrate Jev into Claude Code. It never calls Jev, so it cannot give the user's stated goal of Claude Code consulting Jev automatically. It only advises on designing apps that use Jev.
No OpenRouter or TypeSafe endpoint, no env vars, no client, no schema. It tells the reader to go find the official skill and docs for those.
Immature: 3 stars, 0 forks, 5 commits in one day (2026-09-16/17), one author, no releases, no tests or evals. Untested against real agent behaviour.
Ships only a Cursor install path (~/.cursor/skills), with no plugin or marketplace packaging for Claude Code.

Its broad trigger description can fire on unrelated LLM-app tasks and spend about 5k tokens on advice the user did not ask for. Most of the user's daily coding (refactors, debugging, tests) never hits a 'semantic judgment' boundary.

Its 'Default Instruction to the Agent' (SKILL.md:713-717) tells the agent to inspect systems for Jev opportunities. That can nudge Claude to suggest adding a Jev dependency to client projects, which matters for personal versus client work.
The whole thing is 717 lines of prose with heavy repetition, which is more context than a checklist of about 60 lines would need.
entries.verdict: This is a safe, well-written but purely advisory design playbook. It has no Jev runtime, no OpenRouter support and no hooks, so it cannot give the automatic use of Jev the user wants inside Claude Code. It is worth installing only as an optional companion skill, alongside TypeSafe's official skill or an MCP/hook that actually calls Jev, and only if the user builds Jev-backed apps.

entries.name: BenjaminPolge/jev-architect
entries.what: A single Claude Code skill (plus a condensed Codex AGENTS.md mirror) that is a pure design-time prompt. When Claude is designing or auditing an AI feature, it decomposes the feature into steps, applies a gate (closed output, text-only, no generation or reasoning, plus a volume, latency or cost driver), and proposes which steps belong on Jev, an LLM or plain code. It then waits for the developer to approve. It never calls Jev, has no code, no runtime and no dependency, and explicitly does not use Jev for Claude Code's own work. It stays silent for bug fixes and refactors.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). Claude loads it when the task matches 'designing any feature that involves classification, scoring, ranking, routing, yes/no decisions, filtering, moderation, guardrails or triage', or when reviewing a codebase that calls an LLM. It is not deterministic, and it only fires on architecture conversations, not on general coding.
security: Pure markdown; no scripts, hooks, MCP server, install script or postinstall, so no shell execution, telemetry or API key handling in the repo.
No secrets handled, and no key ever appears in argv or process lists.

Only risk is prompt content that steers the model: SKILL.md:156-164 tells the agent to install the typesafe-ai/skills plugin via 'claude plugin marketplace add' after the developer agrees. That is a user-gated third-party plugin install.

The README 'automatic installation' prompt asks the agent to install and self-verify the skill. It is benign but shows the install path is 'paste a prompt into Claude', so prefer a manual cp of the reviewed SKILL.md.
The skill text is small and readable (9 KB), so it is easy to audit; nothing was found to be hostile.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from this repo. It is a static prompt with no network calls. It only causes Claude to write text into the conversation, which already goes to Anthropic. Indirectly it may suggest that the user add Jev calls to their own apps, and that would send state text to Jev, but only after the developer approves.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable. There is no runtime dependency on Jev, so nothing can be slow or down. Worst case is the skill not triggering, or a wrong proposal that the developer declines. The skill itself says to keep a fallback path if the developer adopts Jev (SKILL.md:166).
entries.contextCost: Approximately 110 tokens always resident (skill name plus a 440-char description; 440/4). The SKILL.md body (9,048 bytes, about 2.3k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. Zero tools, zero MCP instructions, zero hook-injected text.
pros: Near-zero cost and risk: one markdown file, about 110 tokens resident, no process, no key, no network, no telemetry (whole repo is 9 KB SKILL.md + docs).
Genuinely automatic: it triggers from the skill description with no 'use jev' prompt (SKILL.md:3).

Well-designed restraint: SKILL.md:94-108 defaults to silence for bug fixes, refactors, image input, decided stacks and low volume, and never swaps a call without approval (SKILL.md:110). This suits daily coding without noise.
Useful on client work when building AI features: it does the 'is this a classifier disguised as an LLM call' analysis, and the audit mode flags closed-output LLM call sites (SKILL.md:23-25).
Apache-2.0, trivially forkable; SKILL.md:183-201 can be edited to point at the OpenRouter endpoint.
Designed to pair with the official typesafe-ai/skills plugin (README.md:213-225), which handles the implementation side.
cons: Does not integrate Jev into Claude Code at all: SKILL.md:11 and README.md:47 say it never calls Jev, so Claude Code's own workflow gets no Jev decisions, which is the user's actual goal.
Only fires on AI-feature architecture discussions; it will rarely trigger in normal daily coding (refactors, bug fixes and so on are explicitly excluded, SKILL.md:106).

Hard-coded to the direct TypeSafe endpoint https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and model 'jev-latest' (SKILL.md:183-188). It has no OpenRouter path and no OpenRouter model IDs (typesafe/jev-1.13, ~typesafe/jev-latest). It would steer the user toward a second provider key, opposite to the OpenRouter-only preference, unless edited.
Heuristic and unmeasured: README.md:200-209 admits the gate is LLM-judged, and the cost and latency claims are vendor-sourced.
Very immature: 3 commits in one day (2026-09-21), one author, 2 stars, no CI, no tests, no releases, and explicitly not affiliated with TypeSafe (README.md:227).

Vendor-promotional bias: it is written to steer architecture toward Jev, and it needs the user to trust that the gate is honest. It is also partly redundant with the official typesafe-ai/skills plugin.
Its 'Jev in 60 seconds' facts (64k tokens per request, endpoint) may drift from the OpenRouter brief (32k context), which risks stale guidance.
entries.verdict: A harmless, tiny, design-time advisory skill, not an integration: it never calls Jev and only nudges architecture proposals toward direct-TypeSafe Jev in AI-feature work. Worth installing as an optional add-on (after editing the endpoint to OpenRouter), but it does not meet the goal of Claude Code invoking Jev automatically for its own tasks.

entries.name: marcodicesare-dev/jev-skill
entries.what: Community (not official TypeSafe) Claude Code/Codex skill that teaches an agent when Jev fits and when not, plus a stdlib-only Python CLI (tools/jev.py, ask/batch/credits) that POSTs {model,state,questions} to a System One endpoint via one of three routes (llmapi default, openrouter, typesafe). Bundles 5 measured question-set recipes, an API reference, and a large field-report (19,367 calls) aimed at building Jev-based pipelines in application code, not at assisting coding.
interface: python3 tools/jev.py batch --states items.jsonl --questions q.json --out answers.jsonl [--workers 16]
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). The description says 'Load when the user asks to use or test Jev, or when a workflow needs semantic classification, routing, scoring, rule checks...' so Claude may load it on such tasks, but it then only gets documentation and a CLI; nothing makes Claude call Jev during ordinary coding. No deterministic hook, no proxy.
security: API key read from env var only (jev.py:28) and sent as Bearer header; never placed in argv or process list. Good.

No shell execution, no eval, no subprocess, no telemetry; CLI only contacts the chosen endpoint (plus api.llmapi.ai/v1/credits for 'credits'). Comment at jev.py:49-51 says exp/tag are not sent or logged.
No curl|sh, no postinstall, install is plain git clone.
State (potentially code/text) is passed on the command line via --state '<json>' (visible in argv/process list to local users) unless a file path is given; load_json accepts a file.
Default route is llmapi.ai, a third-party gateway not otherwise vetted; an agent following SKILL.md example might send data to the typesafe or llmapi routes rather than OpenRouter.
Retries up to 8x on 429/5xx/timeouts with backoff up to 20 s and 30 s timeout per attempt: worst case minutes of blocking.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the agent chooses to put in --state/--questions is POSTed to the selected endpoint (OpenRouter with --via openrouter): arbitrary text/JSON, up to ~32k tokens. Nothing automatic; no hook or proxy captures prompts, diffs or tool output. Author notes Jev is on OpenRouter ZDR list (reference/api.md:82, unverified by me).
entries.failureMode: Not applicable as a hook (none exists). CLI fails open in the sense that a failed call just returns non-zero exit and error JSON to the agent; but retry loop (jev.py:30-42, up to 8 attempts, 30 s timeout each, exponential backoff capped at 20 s) can block a Bash call for several minutes when Jev/OpenRouter is down. Missing key -> sys.exit with message.
entries.contextCost: Very low. One skill: frontmatter description ~700 chars (~180 tokens) always listed in the skills roster. Full SKILL.md body ~7.2k chars (~1.8k tokens) only when the skill is loaded; reference/*.md loaded on demand (api.md ~10k chars, capabilities ~6k). No MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text.
pros: Only candidate here with an explicit, code-level OpenRouter route matching the brief: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY (tools/jev.py:20).
Near-zero context cost (~180 tokens roster entry) and zero latency when unused; no MCP server to run or fail.
Stdlib-only, ~110-line CLI, easy to audit fully; no shell exec, no telemetry, key via env not argv.

Valuable practical knowledge: question shapes, pitfalls (option names reach the model, Noul vs negation not summing to 1, overconfidence by 3-20 points, 1 text per call) and calibration data that would help Claude write correct Jev calls in application code.
Honest about limits (says not to use Jev for writing/explaining; injection flag is not a security boundary), MIT license.
cons: Not an automatic integration: it is documentation plus a manual CLI. Nothing makes Claude Code consult Jev during normal coding; at best the model may load the skill on classification/routing tasks. Fails the user's core requirement.
Aimed at building Jev-powered pipelines (hotel marketing, ad scoring, ticket routing), not at improving an AI coding assistant; none of the 5 recipes address code tasks (recipes/*.json).

Default route is llmapi.ai (third-party gateway, LLMAPI_API_KEY) and the SKILL.md/README quickstart uses --via typesafe; OpenRouter needs explicit --via openrouter, and 'credits' only works for llmapi. An agent following the docs literally will not use OpenRouter.
Does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) that the brief lists, only /api/v1/systemone.
Very young and thin: 1 star, 1 contributor, 11 commits over 2 days, no tests, no CI, no releases; performance claims come from the author's private lab logs not in the repo.
Retry loop (8 attempts, up to 20 s backoff, 30 s timeout) can stall an agent's Bash call for minutes on outage.
--state passed inline in argv would expose content to the local process list; cloned skill directory can change on git pull (unpinned supply chain).
Vendors ~18 MB of PNG/JPG marketing assets and blog-style guides with author promotion (Lumina) into a skills directory, which is noise for a dev tool.
entries.verdict: Useful as a reference and as a tiny OpenRouter-capable CLI, but it is a manually-triggered skill, not an automatic integration, and it addresses app pipelines rather than coding. Reasonable optional companion for writing Jev calls; not the answer to 'Claude Code must use Jev on its own'.

entries.name: Umbylicus/umby-jev-stack
entries.what: A prompt-only "skill tree" of 14 markdown SKILL.md files (each with a questions.json payload) telling an agent to call TypeSafe Jev directly over HTTP (POST https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest) as a cheap classifier. Skills: full-repo code review (six independent Noul questions per file or chunk), diff-gate, secrets, breaking-change, test-gap, agent-safety (screen shell commands before running), prompt-screen, issue-triage, docs-drift, three browser-driving skills, and one Node CLI (Jev Link, site internal-link suggestions). It also ships an unrelated Chrome extension (X post highlighter). It bundles NO MCP server (the README only links the separate NiazMorshed2007/jev-review MCP as optional), no hooks, no .mcp.json. Every skill is manually triggered (README: 'Prompt your agent: Run umby-jev-review on this repo').
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger at best (model discretion): descriptions such as 'Use for a Jev sweep, security/syntax/schema pass, or compiled findings before fixes' could match phrases like 'review this code', but review is heavy and expensive, so it will trigger only when the user asks for a review or a sweep. Nothing is deterministic: no hook, no transparent proxy, nothing runs on edits or commits. Does not meet the user's requirement of using Jev without being told.
security: No network code at all in the 13 SKILL.md skills; the agent improvises curl/fetch with the key from env. curl example puts key in an -H argument, so the key is visible in argv/process list (review/SKILL.md:176-178) if used as written. Better to use a script reading env.
Only real code, link.mjs/lib.mjs, uses fetch with Bearer header in-process (lib.mjs:734-750), 30s AbortController timeout, no key in argv (env read).

Skills say 'Never print the key', 'mask sensitive values in state, logs and reports', 'no secrets in state' - but sending raw source to a third party is the core workflow, so redaction relies on the agent's diligence.

Sends whole file chunks (<=10k chars each) to third-party API; with client projects this is a contractual/NDA concern. Review recommends concurrency = N (e.g. 250 parallel POSTs), which is aggressive and can trigger 429s or cost spikes.
No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in skills. Chrome extension fetches page content and stores key in chrome.storage; irrelevant to Claude Code.

Prompt-injection surface: file content is embedded as Jev 'state' (Jev returns only probabilities, so injection risk from Jev output is low). But agent-safety and prompt-screen ask Claude to trust noul scores as gates; the skills explicitly say a score does not grant authorization.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai: the JEV_API_KEY bearer token, plus state.path, kind, language, imports and up to 10,000 chars of source, diff, shell command text or page text per request, and the question definitions (about 5-17 KB per request from questions.json, the same for every call). For repo-wide review, the full contents of every in-scope source file leave the machine (including .env.example, tests, SQL). Browser skills send page text/controls. Nothing goes to OpenRouter as shipped.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by nature: it is a manual skill, so if Jev is down nothing is blocked. The skills state 'Failed, missing or malformed responses are incomplete work, never clean results' and prescribe exponential backoff on 429/ECONNRESET and splitting on max_tokens_exceeded. No timeout is defined in the SKILL.md workflow. The only coded timeout is 30 s in link.mjs (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, lib.mjs:11), which is far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms. There is no hook, so nothing can stall a Claude Code turn.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tools, 0 server instructions) and no hook-injected text. Claude Code lists all installed skill names+descriptions each session: 14 skills, roughly 300-600 chars each (~1.5-2k tokens total, ~100-150 tokens per skill). When triggered, SKILL.md bodies are 3.3-20.7 KB (review is ~5.2k tokens; whole set 79.6 KB ~20k tokens) and questions.json 1-17 KB (review 14.3 KB ~3.6k tokens). Installing the whole tree therefore costs a few thousand tokens of resident description text for mostly irrelevant skills (browser, link, issue-triage, docs-drift); installing just review/diff-gate is cheaper.
pros: Best-documented prompt/question design for Jev as a code classifier: independent Noul per defect class (never a single Choice), path/kind/language/chunk/imports in state, explicit ignore lists, 10k-char chunk cap, threshold 0.5 with tiering. Reusable questions.json files (review 14.3 KB, diff-gate 16.6 KB, agent-safety 6.5 KB, secrets 7.3 KB) are directly reusable in a custom hook or MCP.

Field-tested lesson in SKILL.md: v1 sweep gave 544 flags of ~1,200 snippets and 543 false positives; v2 tightened questions. Useful calibration data on how noisy Jev is for logic bugs (supports using Jev only as a cheap pre-filter, not a verdict).

umby-jev-agent-safety questions (recursive delete, force-push, DB destroy, prod deploy, secret exfil, privilege escalation, irreversible action) map neatly onto a PreToolUse Bash hook, which suits the user's bypass/auto permission mode.
umby-jev-diff-gate is scoped to git diff, a realistic daily use (pre-commit or pre-PR classification).

No MCP server and no hooks: zero always-on context tokens beyond the skill descriptions, no runtime dependency, no processes to crash, MIT licensed, compatible with Claude Code via plugins add --target claude-code.
Honest about limits: look-only, human decides, evidence must be quoted or 'unlocated'.
cons: Not automatic: every skill is manually invoked ('Prompt your agent: Run umby-jev-review ...'); no hook, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse wiring. Fails the user's core requirement of Claude Code using Jev without being asked.

Hard-wired to TypeSafe direct (api.typesafe.ai, JEV_API_KEY, model jev-latest); zero OpenRouter support anywhere (lib.mjs:16, SKILL.md:104). User wants OpenRouter as provider, so every URL/key/model reference must be edited.

Not an MCP, despite the candidate summary claiming '(+jev-review MCP)': the MCP is only linked as optional (README.md line 'jev-review MCP is optional', review/SKILL.md 'Optional: jev-review MCP'). That repo is a separate project and must be audited separately.

The agent has to hand-write curl/fetch each time with large payloads (questions.json 5-17 KB per request); Claude spends Opus tokens on chunking, pool sizing, the compile table and a mandatory confirm pass, likely costing more than Jev saves. The skill's own history says ~99.8% of v1 flags were false positives.

Repo-wide sweeps send all source code to a third party in up to N concurrent requests (recommended concurrency = N, could be hundreds) - risky for client NDAs and rate limits; curl example exposes the key in argv.

Immature and thin: 1 star, 28 commits over one week (2026-09-19 to 09-26), 2 committers, no CI, no releases/tags, no tests for the skills; 3 of 14 skills are browser/site tools and one is an unrelated Chrome extension, so scope-creepy for a coding tool.
Installing the full tree adds 14 skill descriptions to Claude Code context for mostly irrelevant tasks (browsing, X highlighting, link building).
entries.verdict: Not an MCP and not an automatic integration: it is a set of manually-triggered, TypeSafe-direct prompt skills with no OpenRouter path, so it does not meet the user's goal. Its value is as source material: mine questions.json (especially agent-safety, diff-gate, secrets, review) and the false-positive lessons to build your own PreToolUse/Stop hook that calls OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: @fleeex/jev-orchestrator
entries.what: A Claude Code skill (SKILL.md plus a Node CLI helper) that treats Jev as a cheap decision layer for orchestrating coding workers. Claude writes a compact JSON state and runs `jev-orchestrator decide <strategy|parallel|worker|retry|review|completion|stuck>`. The CLI sends a projection of that state to TypeSafe POST /v1/systemone through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. It applies code-level policy overrides and confidence tiers, then prints a recommendation. It can also launch OpenAI Codex CLI workers in git worktrees, and it logs sessions and estimated cost to JSONL. Its whole purpose is delegate/parallelize/retry/review decisions for Codex workers. It does not do general per-turn coding decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, meaning model discretion. The description says "Use proactively when a task may benefit from delegation...". The README itself admits invocation is 'a suggestion to the model, not a guarantee'. There is no deterministic hook and no transparent proxy. The user must also still install it once.
security: The skill pre-approves exactly one command, its own helper shim (allowed-tools: Bash(${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}/scripts/jev-orchestrator *)). The shim only runs `node <recorded cliEntry>` and never fetches code (src/skill/installer.ts:56-78). That is a good design, but the pre-approved wildcard also covers `codex run`, which launches Codex workers.

API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var first, else from ~/.config/jev-orchestrator/secrets.json (mode 0600). It is passed to the SDK in memory and sent as a Bearer header, not put in argv. The key is stripped from Codex worker environments and redacted from their output (README, src/security/secrets.ts:104-114). Config files reject secret-like keys (schema.ts:112).
Child processes use spawn() with argument arrays and task text goes over stdin (src/util/exec.ts:50). No shell string execution seen. No postinstall script in package.json, only prepublishOnly.

Prompt-injection surface is small, since Jev returns typed probabilities only. The state is built by Claude, and worker summaries and test output (up to 4000 chars) are passed into it. Code-level policy forces irreversible or sensitive-file tasks back to Claude.

Codex workers run in a sandbox (read-only or workspace-write) with no approval-bypass flags. That is separate from Claude Code's own permissions, so with the user's bypass mode a delegated Codex run is only limited by Codex's sandbox.

No telemetry to third parties found. Local JSONL logs go in .jev/sessions/ inside the repo and default to no state recorded (recordState:false). This adds a .jev/ directory to client repos, and src/git/exclude.ts appears to manage git excludes. I did not verify that in detail.
entries.dataEgress: Only the projected state per `decide` call goes to the endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or the override URL) with the question text and rubric. For strategy that is userGoal, currentPlan, repositorySummary (max 2000 chars), task/subtask ids, titles, file paths and a codexAvailable flag. For review, retry and stuck it also includes worker summaries, changedFiles and test or build output truncated to 4000 chars (src/orchestration/state.ts, strategy.ts:50-60). No source files or diffs are sent automatically, but Claude composes the state, so task descriptions, file paths and test output from client projects can leave the machine, and the user's secret-leak hook does not see the CLI's payload. The user prompt goal text is sent. Codex workers separately send task prompts and code to OpenAI (not Jev). Nothing goes to any other host.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. There is a 5 s default timeout (DEFAULT_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=5000, schema.ts:5) and the SDK does 2 retries on 429/5xx/timeouts (client.ts:27,131). After that `decide` exits non-zero with a hint, and SKILL.md says to continue with Claude's own judgment. A missing key gives the exit code EXIT.jevUnavailable. Worst-case added latency on failure is about 15 s or more (three attempts at 5 s plus backoff). Confidence under 0.60 is treated as a fallback tier and ignored. Nothing blocks Claude's tools, because it is a skill-invoked CLI and not a hook.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools and no hooks. The always-on cost is the skill's frontmatter (name, description and when_to_use, about 1.3k chars, roughly 330 tokens) in the skill listing. When invoked, SKILL.md is about 5.1k chars (roughly 1.3k tokens), and the references (decisions.md 5.1k, orchestration.md 4.7k, codex-workers.md 3.6k chars) load only on demand (about 3.3k tokens if all are read). Each decide call returns a small JSON block (a few hundred tokens). Total 330 tokens per session and about 1.5-5k tokens per activation.
pros: Genuinely automatic in the sense the user asked for: a skill with a when_to_use trigger that needs no 'use jev' prompt, and it costs only about 330 tokens of always-on context.

Real Jev code path: uses the official SDK against POST /v1/systemone with typed Choice and Noul questions. src/orchestration/*.ts has worked examples of rubric-based choice options, and the confidence tiers (>=0.85 autonomous, 0.6-0.85 advisory, <0.6 fallback) with hard policy overrides are a sound way to use calibrated probabilities.
Fail-open, 5 s timeout, no network fetch under the pre-approved permission, and a single pre-approved command. Security posture is careful for a v0.1.
Small data footprint: the state projection is field-limited (no code or diffs), state recording is off by default, and there is a cost report ($0.042/M in, output free).
jev.baseUrl and jev.model are configurable, so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs no code change, subject to the response shape matching (not verified).
MIT, has tests and CI on two OSes, and includes a mock engine and demo so it can be evaluated without a key.
cons: Wrong problem for this user. It only decides how to delegate to Codex workers (strategy, parallel, worker, retry, review, stuck). Its value depends on OpenAI Codex CLI plus worktrees, and the user has Opus 5.5 as the main model with no mention of Codex. Without Codex, Jev's only output is a nudge to 'do it yourself', which Claude already knows.
No benchmark and no evidence it improves outcomes. The README's Limitations section says so, and the Jev step adds tool calls and JSON state writing that a frontier model could answer in one thought.
Auto-invocation is best effort: model discretion via skill description, not deterministic. Claude will often skip it, or fire it on multi-file tasks where it adds only overhead.

No OpenRouter support in code: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and https://api.typesafe.ai. OpenRouter works only through the baseUrl and model overrides and an unverified response shape, and the stock `setup` and `doctor` key validation (GET /v1/models) will likely fail against OpenRouter. Storing the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY is confusing.

Very immature: one developer, 6 commits made in one day (2026-09-17), 1 star, 0 forks, npm 0.1.0. A pre-approved Bash wildcard that also launches Codex workers, plus writing .jev/ into client repos, is a lot of surface for questionable benefit.

With the user's bypass/auto mode, Claude-side permission rules that the README calls authoritative are largely inactive, so only Codex's own sandbox limits delegated runs. Client project goals and file lists are sent to a third-party endpoint via a path the secret-leak hook does not inspect.
Bundles heavy machinery unrelated to Jev (worktree manager, Codex adapter, session log). Little reusable for a lean Jev-in-Claude-Code integration beyond the pattern.
entries.verdict: A well-built, security-conscious but very young skill whose entire job is deciding when to hand work to Codex workers. It is a poor match for a Claude-only daily coding flow and gives no OpenRouter support out of the box (only a baseUrl/model override, untested). Worth reading as a reference for wiring Jev's Choice/Noul primitives, but not worth installing for automatic daily use.

entries.name: StevenLi-phoenix/laya-skill
entries.what: Claude Code plugin/skill for System One typed decisions with Laya (open local model: CPU/MPS/CUDA/WebGPU, Jev-compatible server) and hosted Jev via jevpredict.py.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger
pros: Local Laya option avoids sending client data off-machine
Jev-compatible HTTP server allows swapping endpoints
cons: No OpenRouter reference in SKILL.md; TYPESAFE_API_KEY; heavy repo with bundled WebGPU app and 467MB model demo
Laya is a different model with unknown accuracy versus Jev; created today, 1 star

entries.name: PyModel/jev-skill (unofficial Jev design skill)
entries.what: Pure-documentation Claude Code plugin/skill (no MCP server, no hooks, no code that calls Jev at runtime). It teaches the agent how to DESIGN and WRITE code that uses Jev (Choice/Score/Noul, thresholds, 11 implementation shapes) into the user's projects. The SKILL.md description auto-triggers when the task involves classification/routing/gating in code or mentions TypeSafe/Jev/System One. Optionally the agent may probe the live TypeSafe API with TYPESAFE_API_KEY during development. It does NOT make Claude Code itself call Jev for its own decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion): Claude loads it when the task is to write code needing NL judgments or mentions Jev/TypeSafe/System One. It is triggered by what the user's project code needs, NOT by Claude Code's own internal decisions. Does not make Claude Code call Jev.
security: No hooks, no MCP server, no shell execution, no postinstall in the Claude Code plugin; manifests (.claude-plugin/plugin.json, marketplace.json) are plain metadata.
SKILL.md tells the agent not to print/echo/commit TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not to hunt for keys in .env/profile files, keep key server-side; warns TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs request bodies unredacted.
README suggests storing key in ~/.config/typesafe/env and sourcing it from top of ~/.bashrc (key then visible to all shells/agent subprocesses).
Muse installer is curl|bash from raw.githubusercontent main (unpinned) - only for Muse, not required for Claude Code.
Skill instructs the agent to fetch docs.typesafe.ai/llms.txt live and 'live docs win on conflict' - third-party content becomes instruction-like input (prompt-injection surface, low).
Prompt-injection guidance in SKILL.md is good: keep untrusted text in own field, never let a Jev answer alone authorize a side effect, code denylist before Jev.
entries.dataEgress: Plugin itself sends nothing. Only if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set does the agent optionally run small probe calls (about 10 per task) to api.typesafe.ai (or another base_url) containing synthetic/sample state and questions it writes; if it probes with real project data (tickets, logs, code, commands) that content would leave the machine. Agent may also WebFetch docs.typesafe.ai. No automatic egress of prompts, diffs or file contents by the plugin.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable at runtime: nothing sits in Claude Code's loop. If the key is missing the skill says design from api-reference.md and say so; if docs are unreachable read installed SDK types. Effectively fail-open with zero dependency on Jev availability. Generated project code is advised to use SDK RetryPolicy (default 10s HTTP timeout).
entries.contextCost: 1 skill, 0 MCP tools, 0 hooks, 0 hook-injected text. Always-on cost is only the skill listing entry: name+description about 590 chars, roughly 150 tokens. When triggered SKILL.md is about 11.9k chars (about 3k tokens); api-reference.md 11.6k chars (about 2.9k), patterns.md 9.2k (about 2.3k), prior-art INDEX 3.6k (about 0.9k) plus 1-2 shape files of 2-4.6k chars (about 0.5-1.2k each), loaded on demand. A full read is about 66k chars (about 16k tokens) but typical use is 5-8k tokens.
pros: Zero runtime risk: markdown only, no hooks/MCP/postinstall, so it cannot conflict with the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks.
Tiny always-on context cost (about 150 tokens for the description) with progressive disclosure of the reference files.

api-reference.md:130 explicitly documents the OpenRouter route (base_url https://openrouter.ai/api, model ~typesafe/jev-latest), so the user's OpenRouter-key setup is reachable with a one-line base_url change in generated code.

Strong, concrete design guidance (SKILL.md rules 1-11): code denylist before Jev for destructive actions, thresholds in bands, do not carry Noul thresholds to Choice, pin jev-1.13.0, keep untrusted text in its own field, per-command gate design (evals/command-gate).
Description trigger is well scoped and would fire automatically when the user builds classify/route/gate features for client projects, with no 'use jev' prompt needed.
Has CI (checks.yml runs config check + unittest suite) and a published eval (0.96 vs 0.65 no-skill vs 0.77 official skill over 6 tasks x 10 runs, self-reported, LLM-judged) with raw runs committed.
MIT license; works with the official typesafe-ai/skills too (no name conflict).
cons: Does not integrate Jev into Claude Code itself: it only helps write app code that calls Jev. It cannot make Claude Code use Jev for its own coding decisions, which is the user's actual goal.
Auto-trigger only fires for tasks that involve NL-judgment code or Jev/TypeSafe keywords; for ordinary daily coding it never activates, so adds no value there.

Assumes TYPESAFE_API_KEY (SKILL.md:20, README); no OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling; OpenRouter appears only as a one-line gateway note and not the /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone paths from the brief.
Very immature and single-author: 45 commits all on 2026-09-27, one contributor, v0.1.0, 0 stars, 0 forks, repo 3 days old, not endorsed by TypeSafe.
Content is a frozen snapshot of docs (2026-09-25, SDK py 0.7.1 / js 0.6.0) of a beta API, so it can go stale; it defers to live docs, which requires web fetches.
Eval headline numbers are self-reported by the author and graded by LLM judges without an API key, so they measure code-writing style, not real Jev behavior.
Marketplace install tracks mutable main of an unknown author; repo also ships a curl|bash Muse installer (not needed for Claude Code).
entries.verdict: Safe, cheap, well-written documentation skill, useful as an optional add-on when building Jev-powered features in client apps, but it is not an integration of Jev into Claude Code and gives no automatic Jev-in-the-loop behavior. It should not be the answer to the user's request; at best pair it with a real hook/MCP/router integration.

entries.name: BarakChamo/jev-kit
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace "jev", plugin "jev" v0.3.0) that ships three skills (jev-fit, jev-questions, jev-eval) teaching an agent how to WRITE well-formed Jev question maps (state + noul/choice/score questions) for application code, plus two dependency-free Node scripts: jev-run (sends labelled test cases to a Jev endpoint) and jev-audit (offline analysis of results, confidence-threshold fitting). It is authoring/evaluation guidance for developers who build Jev-backed features. It is NOT a runtime integration: it does not route, gate, or decide anything about Claude Code's own work, and it has no MCP server, hooks, or proxy.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion), and only when the task itself is about writing/evaluating Jev questions or choosing between an LLM and Jev for an app feature. It never causes Claude Code to call Jev for its own work.
security: Installing runs nothing: plugin.json declares skills only; no hooks, MCP servers, or postinstall (SECURITY.md).
jev-run sends API key as Bearer header from the environment (never argv); README says it never logs or writes the key. No telemetry found in the script.

jev-run --map/--derive dynamically imports and executes user-supplied JS (also under --check), so a malicious map runs arbitrary code; only relevant if the agent is tricked into running someone else's map.

Skills are instructions that steer the agent's code-writing; a repo update changes agent behavior when installed by name from the default branch (SECURITY.md admits this and offers tag-pinning plus SHA256SUMS). Commits are made by a bot 'jev-kit publisher' from a private repo, so provenance of source diffs is opaque.
Example suites and evals are large recorded data files in the repo (untrusted data, not code the plugin runs).
Author is a third party (Barak Chamo), not TypeSafe; unverified affiliation.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine by merely installing or having the skills loaded (skill text goes to Anthropic as part of normal context only when a skill triggers). Only when the user explicitly runs jev-run does each test case's state and questions go to api.typesafe.ai or ai-gateway.vercel.sh, with the key as bearer. No Claude Code prompts, code, diffs or tool outputs are sent anywhere automatically. jev-audit is offline.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable at runtime, since nothing sits in Claude Code's loop. The skills are passive text (effectively fail-open: if unused, nothing happens). jev-run is a batch CLI: 60s per-request timeout, up to 6 retries with backoff on 429/5xx/timeouts, 401/403 are fatal, stops after --max-failures.
entries.contextCost: No tools, no MCP server instructions, no hook-injected text. Cost is the three skill name+description lines always in the skills listing: about 400+620+640 chars, roughly 450 tokens. Skill bodies load only on trigger (fit about 1.8k tokens, questions about 5.4k plus references, eval about 2.1k). Because the descriptions are keyed to writing/evaluating Jev questions, they will rarely trigger in normal coding.
pros: Well-researched, evidence-backed guidance for Jev question design (16 rules from 57 labelled suites); README claims wrong decisions dropping from 15.6% to 1.1% on a held-out SLA task when agents use the skill. Genuinely useful IF the user builds Jev-backed features in their own projects.

Zero runtime footprint: no hooks, MCP server, install scripts or telemetry (SECURITY.md, plugin.json), so it cannot conflict with the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks, and costs only about 450 tokens of skill listing.
Passive skill triggers on Jev-related tasks with no need to say 'use jev', which matches the no-prompting requirement for the narrow case of authoring Jev code.
Scripts are single-file, dependency-free and readable; API key comes from the environment and is not put on argv; retry/timeout handling is sane; MIT licensed.
Offline jev-audit and --check mode let the user validate maps with no key and no network.
cons: Does not do what the user asked. Nothing here makes Claude Code call Jev automatically for its own decisions (routing, gating, classifying tool calls, triage). It is documentation for developers who ship Jev in applications. The skills trigger only when the conversation is already about writing Jev questions.

No OpenRouter support at all (zero references in the repo). The eval script supports only api.typesafe.ai (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and the Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY). Adding OpenRouter needs a small local patch, and body/response compatibility with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-27, 6 commits, 1 contributor (a publisher bot from a private repo), 0 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases. Rules are 'hypotheses with conditions', two rest on a single measurement, and all accuracy claims are self-reported by the author.
Installing by name tracks the default branch, so future pushes silently change the instructions the agent follows (the author says so in SECURITY.md); on client projects, pin a tag if you install.
Skill bodies are large (jev-questions about 21 KB, about 5k tokens when triggered), a real context hit whenever it does trigger, for a user who only touches Jev occasionally.

Adds a free-form-text dependency on third-party instructions to an agent running in bypass/auto permission mode; low risk since nothing executes, but --map/--derive run arbitrary JS if the agent is told to.
entries.verdict: Not an integration of Jev into Claude Code but a well-built, low-risk authoring-guidance skill pack for people building Jev-backed features; it gives zero automatic Jev usage and has no OpenRouter path out of the box. Install it only as an optional add-on (pinned to a tag) if the user actually writes Jev question maps in their own projects, and pair it with a real runtime integration for the actual goal.

entries.name: dbreunig/building-with-jev-skill
entries.what: Pure-documentation Claude Code plugin/skill (one SKILL.md, about 15 KB) that teaches Claude how to WRITE programs that call Jev (question design, Choice/Score/Noul, state structure, confidence gating, debugging). It never calls Jev itself. It contains no code, hooks, or MCP server. It is a prompt-engineering guide for app developers building on Jev, not a way for Claude Code to consult Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion). It fires only when the task is about writing or improving Jev/TypeSafe code. It does not cause Claude Code to call Jev during ordinary coding.
security: No executable code: no hooks, no scripts, no install scripts, no postinstall, no shell execution, no telemetry, and no network calls in the repo.
No API key handling of any kind.

Prompt-injection surface is minimal: static markdown, and the text is benign guidance. The only risk is that the repo owner could push a malicious SKILL.md update later. Pin a commit or vendor the file (copy to ~/.claude/skills) to avoid that.
The optional 'npx skills add' installer is third-party code from vercel-labs that was not audited. Use the plugin or a manual copy instead.
SKILL.md:94 correctly warns that text in Jev state can steer answers, which is a useful note for anyone building on Jev.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing. The skill has no runtime and sends nothing anywhere. Claude Code itself sends the skill text to Anthropic as ordinary context, as with any skill.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable, since it calls no service. If the skill fails to load, Claude just lacks the guidance. It cannot block any tool call.
entries.contextCost: 0 tools and no MCP instructions. Always-on cost is only the skill name and description (about 300 chars, roughly 75 tokens). Loading the full body when triggered costs about 15,089 chars, roughly 3.8k tokens. No hook-injected text.
pros: Zero risk and zero runtime: 5 static files, no hooks, MCP, scripts or network, so nothing can fail or leak.
Cheap context: about 75 tokens always-on, about 3.8k when loaded.

Substantive, well-organized guidance from a known author (Drew Breunig) drawn from the official docs.typesafe.ai pages. It covers question design, the primitives, speculative fan-out, confidence-gated routing (floors 0.5-0.6, 0.85-0.9 for high-stakes), a symptom-to-fix debugging table, and a warning about injection through state (SKILL.md:94).
Useful whenever the user writes code that calls Jev, for example a custom OpenRouter-based routing or decision hook of their own. It would make Claude write better Jev questions.
Popular for its age (145 stars, 11 forks in 13 days), and its auto-trigger description is narrow enough not to fire on unrelated work.
cons: It does not integrate Jev into Claude Code. It gives Claude no way to call Jev, so it does nothing toward the user's goal of Claude Code consulting Jev automatically.

Its code sample is TypeSafe SDK only (typesafe_sdk, SKILL.md:117). There is no OpenRouter endpoint, no /api/v1/systemone or /api/alpha/decisions example, and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Claude would write SDK code that needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY unless the user tells it otherwise.

Single commit, no license (all rights reserved by default, so unclear reuse or fork rights), no releases, no tests, and no maintenance history. It is pinned to jev-1.13 and will go stale as the model changes.
Guidance is largely a paraphrase of the vendor docs, so the value is convenience, not new capability.
Only helps if the user builds Jev-calling apps. It would sit unused in normal daily coding.
entries.verdict: Safe, cheap, well-written reference skill for authoring Jev questions, but it is not an integration. It cannot make Claude Code call Jev automatically and is TypeSafe-SDK-oriented. Treat it as an optional companion to a real MCP or hook integration (vendor the SKILL.md rather than track the repo), not as the integration itself.

entries.name: grandamenium/jev-anything
entries.what: Independent (non-official) agent skill that walks Claude Code or Codex through designing, planning, scaffolding, testing and tuning a Jev decision layer (noul/choice/score) inside a user's own application code. It ships markdown references, a stdlib-only Python client and a fetch-only TS client that call OpenRouter, blind-labeling and evaluation helpers, and three example scripts. It does not make Claude Code itself call Jev. It is a development-time how-to for building Jev-backed classifiers, routers and guardrails into software.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion), but only for the user-intent phrases 'add jev / jev classifier / put a decision layer in'. It does not fire on ordinary coding, and it cannot make Claude Code consult Jev for its own decisions. It is not a hook or proxy.
security: MIT license; no MCP server, no hooks, no install script, no npm postinstall, no telemetry; install is a plain git clone into ~/.claude/skills (README).
API key read from env (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and sent only as a Bearer header via urllib/fetch, so it is not visible in argv. The client is stdlib only.
No subprocess/os.system/eval/exec found in scaffolding (grep clean).

Prompt-injection surface: Claude follows about 12 KB of imperative instructions from a third-party single-author repo, and the skill tells it to read references and write code. Content is benign on inspection, and the risk is low but non-zero if the repo later changes.
Instructions from a repo that is not vendor-maintained may drift from Jev's live API. The client comments admit the endpoint path 'varies across docs'.
Single commit, 0 forks, 17 stars, no releases and no CI or tests, so there is no review history.
entries.dataEgress: By itself nothing leaves the machine: the skill is passive markdown. Only when Claude scaffolds and the user later runs the generated or bundled client does the `state` string and question spec go to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai if the user picks the direct path). The skill explicitly warns that the state leaves the network and recommends sending only the fields the decision needs.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable at Claude Code runtime, since the skill makes no calls. The bundled client is fail-closed by default (raises RuntimeError on HTTP error or missing key, 30s timeout in Python). The skill instructs Claude to have the user pick fail-open or fail-closed per action for the app being built.
entries.contextCost: Only the skill frontmatter (about 700 chars, roughly 175 tokens) sits in the always-on skill listing. When triggered, SKILL.md adds about 12.5 KB (about 3.1k tokens). Step 0 forces reading 4 reference files (about 23 KB, about 5.8k tokens), so about 9k tokens per invocation, plus more for the plan and evaluation files. No MCP tools, no MCP instructions, no hook-injected text.
pros: Correct, code-verified OpenRouter details: alpha/decisions endpoint, typesafe/jev-1.13 slug, instructions/criteria field names, response shape with usage.cost (scaffolding/jev_client.py:22-24, reference 02).

Useful as a knowledge pack: primitive selection, escape-option pattern for choice, confidence threshold anchors, blind-label evaluation and criteria tuning. It is honest about the fit, privacy and high-stakes limits.
Zero-dependency clients (stdlib and fetch) that can be lifted as-is into a project. The skill is passive, with no runtime footprint, no network and no telemetry.
Low always-on context cost of about 175 tokens, and it triggers only on explicit Jev phrases so it will not pollute unrelated sessions.
Clearly disclaims that it is unofficial and points to TypeSafe's official skill (github.com/typesafe-ai/skills).
cons: Wrong category for the user's goal. It teaches Claude how to build Jev into an app; it does not let Claude Code call Jev during its own coding. It provides no hook, MCP tool or proxy for automatic use.
The trigger needs Jev-related phrasing ('add jev', 'jev classifier'), which is exactly the manual prompting the user wants to avoid.

The workflow is heavy and interactive. It forces an interrogate, educate, plan, sign-off sequence and about 9k tokens of reading. That is a poor fit for bypass or auto mode, and it can stall waiting for answers.

Very immature: created 2026-09-24, one commit, one author, 17 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no tests, no CI. It is a snapshot of a solo author's eval notes; CHANGELOG references local ../jev-eval paths that are not in the repo.

The bundled client hedges on the endpoint ('varies across docs'); the direct TypeSafe path is documented but not implemented, and the version and model slug (jev-1.13) are hard-coded, so it may go stale.
Duplicates or overlaps the vendor's official skill (typesafe-ai/skills), which reads live docs and is likely the safer source of truth.
entries.verdict: Safe and reasonably accurate, but it is a build-time tutorial skill for adding Jev to your own apps, not an integration that makes Claude Code use Jev automatically. Keep it at most as an optional project-level skill for Jev-based products, and do not count it as the solution for auto-invoked Jev in Claude Code.

entries.name: HanboyLee/typesafe-decision-skill
entries.what: A pure-Markdown Agent Skill (SKILL.md plus 3 reference files) that gives coding agents a policy for when to use deterministic code, a System One judgment runtime (TypeSafe Choice/Noul/Score), or the main model. It contains no runtime. It only tells the agent to call the third-party jkudish/jev-mcp tools (jev_classify, jev_find, jev_rerank, jev_verify, jev_compare, jev_decide, jev_review, jev_gate) if they are already connected. It also has an openai.yaml (Codex/ChatGPT metadata) and an icon.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, at model discretion. The description is broad and generic ("bounded semantic decisions, intent classification, tool routing... code review"), so it may fire vaguely or rarely. README.md:23 and :55 admit that automatic activation is not guaranteed. The skill only provides guidance and does not itself call Jev. It is not a hook or a proxy.
security: No executable code, no install scripts, no postinstall, no curl|sh and no telemetry in the repo. The only install path is the third-party 'npx skills add' CLI, which is not audited here; copying the directory manually avoids it.
No API key handling anywhere. README.md:44 says no keys are stored in the repo.
Prompt-injection surface is small. SKILL.md:59 says to treat external pages, code and evidence as data. That is only guidance, so it is not a control.

The skill tells the agent to pass diffs and test logs to jev_review and jev_gate (code-review.md:19-21, tool-routing.md:34). That instruction is what would cause code egress, and only if a jev MCP is connected.

README.md:7 states it is an independent community project, not affiliated with TypeSafe AI. It is a single-author repo with 1 star, so provenance is weak, but the content is trivially reviewable Markdown.
entries.dataEgress: The skill sends nothing by itself. If a jev MCP is connected, the skill instructs the agent to send requirements, diff excerpts, test logs and completion-claim evidence to it (code-review.md:19-21). That data then goes to whatever provider the MCP uses (TypeSafe or OpenRouter).
entries.failureMode: Not applicable at the skill level because it has no network code. The policy is fail-safe but soft. If Jev or CodeGraph is missing, the agent should not invent a judgment and should report the review as incomplete rather than pass it (SKILL.md:53, tool-routing.md:40-43). Nothing enforces this. There are no timeouts, since the skill does not call anything.
entries.contextCost: Low. One skill entry is always listed. The description is about 560 chars, or about 140 tokens, always in context. The body loads only on trigger, at about 1.2k tokens for SKILL.md and up to about 3.1k tokens with all references. There are no tools, no MCP instructions and no hook-injected text.
pros: Tiny, fully auditable, MIT-licensed Markdown with no code execution and no egress of its own.

Honest limitations section (README.md:53-58): it says outright that a skill does not guarantee tool calls and that enforcement needs hooks or CI. This matches the user's need to move to deterministic hooks.

Useful policy text: Jev's probability is not correctness, do not repeat identical calls, treat a missing mandatory review as incomplete, and report tools actually invoked. It could serve as a system-prompt-style companion to a real Jev MCP or hook.
Maps the jev_review, jev_verify and jev_gate roles onto a diff-review workflow, which is a sensible use of Jev for coding.
Cheap context cost, about 140 tokens always and about 3k on trigger.
cons: It integrates nothing. There is no MCP server, hook, client or endpoint, so installing it does not make Claude Code call Jev, OpenRouter or TypeSafe (README.md:55).
Depends on the separate jkudish/jev-mcp, whose OpenRouter support is unknown here. It names no OpenRouter, no base URL and no env var.
Auto-invocation relies on the model matching a generic description. That does not meet the requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told, and it will not fire deterministically.
Immature and unvetted. It has 2 commits in one day, 1 star, no releases, no tests, is a single-author project with an unofficial affiliation claim, and has a Codex/ChatGPT-oriented openai.yaml.
Claude Opus 5.5 already follows most of this generic advice without a skill. The added value is marginal and the description may cause spurious triggers that burn context.
The generic decision-framework wording (FRD requirements, 'System One' orchestration) is not tuned to Claude Code tool semantics such as hooks, subagents or permission modes.
entries.verdict: This is only a policy document. It contains no Jev integration, no OpenRouter path and no deterministic trigger, so it does not meet the goal of automatic use. At most, borrow its guidance text as an optional companion to a real Jev MCP or hook, and do not count it as an integration.
