entries.name: gxinxing/jev-call
entries.what: Tiny 4-file repo: an 88-line stdlib-only Python CLI (jev-call) that POSTs a JSON body (state + typed questions, model injected) from stdin to a System One-style endpoint and prints the raw JSON response; a 30-line SKILL.md that activates only when the user types "jev:" or explicitly asks for Jev; and install.sh that copies both into ~/.local/bin and ~/.agents/skills/jev. Default endpoint is a third-party gateway (tokendance.space), not TypeSafe or OpenRouter. The model (Claude) must hand-author the typed questions every call.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, but the description is deliberately narrow: activates only when the request begins with 'jev:' or the user explicitly asks for Jev (SKILL.md:3, 9). By design it does NOT fire autonomously when Jev would add value. Would need the description rewritten (e.g. 'use proactively for yes/no, pick-one or graded decisions during coding') to become model-discretion; even then it is probabilistic, not deterministic.
security: No shell execution in code; stdlib only; no telemetry; no postinstall; installer is a plain local copy (install.sh:8-10)
API key never in argv: read from env or ~/.config/jev/api-key (jev-call:26-41); good. Key never printed
HTTPS enforced (jev-call:62-63) and redirects disabled (jev-call:18-22) so the bearer cannot be forwarded

BIG RISK: default DEFAULT_ENDPOINT sends the request and bearer key to an unrelated third-party host tokendance.space (jev-call:13) with a non-standard model bocha-jev-v1; if a user sets a real TypeSafe or OpenRouter key without overriding JEV_API_URL, the key is sent to Tokendance
Key precedence: TYPESAFE_API_KEY env wins over the key file, so an unrelated env var would be sent to whatever JEV_API_URL points to

Prompt-injection surface: the skill makes Claude compose the state from repo content; untrusted repo text could steer what is sent, but the output is only probabilities and SKILL.md forbids acting on it alone
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude places in the JSON state and questions fields on each invocation (whatever Claude chooses to include: potentially code snippets, diffs, file contents, error text, commit messages). Sent over HTTPS to JEV_API_URL (default tokendance.space, a third party; OpenRouter if overridden) together with the bearer key. No automatic capture of prompts, files or tool outputs; nothing sent unless Claude runs the skill. README:120 only advises to avoid secrets. Existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook (Bash matcher) would see the heredoc command but not filter semantically.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but non-blocking overall: timeout 60s (jev-call:75, far too long if Jev claims 70-500 ms), HTTP/network error prints message to stderr and exits 1 (jev-call:78-84); no retry, no fallback. SKILL.md:30 tells Claude to explain that the helper is unavailable and not to silently switch endpoints. Because it is a model-invoked Bash call rather than a hook, a failure only costs one failed tool call and Claude carries on; but a hung endpoint can stall a turn up to 60s.
entries.contextCost: Very low: no MCP tools (0 tool defs). One skill description of about 400 chars (approx 100 tokens) always in the skills listing; SKILL.md body (about 2.3k chars, approx 600 tokens) loaded only when triggered. No hook-injected text, no server instructions. Per invocation: Bash heredoc JSON authored by Claude (approx 150-400 output tokens) plus raw JSON response back into context.
pros: Extremely small and fully auditable: 88 lines, stdlib-only Python, no deps, no postinstall, no telemetry (jev-call:1-88)
Good credential hygiene for a POC: key from env/file (not argv), HTTPS-only, redirects refused (jev-call:18-22, 62-63)
Endpoint and model overridable by env (JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL), so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13 needs no code change
Zero context overhead when idle: no MCP tools, one short skill description
Generic pass-through: supports all three primitives (noul/choice/score) without hard-coding a schema, so it is a usable reference for the request shape
MIT licensed, easy to fork/adapt into a purpose-built skill or hook wrapper
cons: Default endpoint is a third-party gateway (tokendance.space) with model bocha-jev-v1, not TypeSafe or OpenRouter; risky default for a key and client-project data (jev-call:13-14)
No OPENROUTER_API_KEY support; OpenRouter key must be smuggled in via the misnamed TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which also collides with a real TypeSafe key if both are used
Trigger is explicit-only ('jev:' prefix) (SKILL.md:9), which directly violates the user's requirement that Claude use Jev automatically without being told
No task-specific intelligence: Claude must invent the questions, criteria and state each time; no coding-oriented presets (e.g. risk of a diff, which file to open, is this test flaky)
install.sh targets ~/.agents/skills, which Claude Code does not read; needs manual copy/symlink to ~/.claude/skills/jev
60s timeout and no retry or fallback; no hook/deterministic path, so it will never gate anything in Claude Code (no PreToolUse/PostToolUse integration)
Pre-release quality: 1 commit, 1 author, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, 4 days old; the response format is never parsed or validated
SKILL.md adds an ask-a-follow-up step (SKILL.md:12) that can interrupt flow in auto/bypass mode
entries.verdict: Safe and readable but only a trivial curl-equivalent wrapper whose skill fires solely on an explicit 'jev:' prefix, so it fails the core requirement of automatic use, and its default endpoint is an unrelated third-party gateway. Useful at most as a 88-line reference for the System One request shape and env-var override pattern; a custom hook/skill written against openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone would be better.

entries.name: jev-audit
entries.what: Independent (not TypeSafe-affiliated) npm CLI plus a SKILL.md that audits a codebase to find LLM call sites that are really decisions and could be replaced by Jev. A zero-dependency regex scanner writes jev-scan.json. The skill then has the agent read each call site, tier it (Replace / Hybrid / Keep LLM / Pure code), estimate savings and write JEV_AUDIT.md. It never calls Jev. It is a one-off migration-planning tool for apps that use LLMs, not a runtime integration of Jev into Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only. Claude loads it when the user talks about auditing or reducing LLM usage or mentions Jev or System One. It never makes Jev calls, never runs as a hook, and does nothing during ordinary coding.
security: Scanner privacy leak: scan.js:46-49 and :105 store line.trim().slice(0,160) for every matching line, and .env* files are scanned (scan.js:75). A line such as OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-live-... therefore lands verbatim in jev-scan.json. That file is written to the cwd and could be committed or read by the agent, which clashes with the user's secret-leak guard.

No network, no exec, no child_process, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry (verified in bin/jev-audit.js and scan.js). Local file writes only: jev-scan.json in the cwd, the skill directory on install, and JEV_AUDIT.md.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill makes the agent read every LLM call site, prompt and system message in the audited repo, and write conclusions into a report. Malicious repo content could steer the report, but the skill grants no new tools.
Report template footer embeds a promotional line (npx jev-audit) that SKILL.md says to keep intact, so client repos would carry vendor-style advertising unless it is removed.

Supply chain: single-maintainer brand-new package (das_vicky), 0 stars, published 2026-09-19. Provenance publishing is configured in CI. The README claims independence from TypeSafe, and the scan-output examples are self-reported.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine from the tool itself (no network code). The skill runs inside Claude Code, so code and snippets it reads go to Anthropic as ordinary session context. Nothing goes to Jev, OpenRouter or TypeSafe.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable, since Jev is never called. If the skill is not triggered, nothing happens. The scanner fails silently on unreadable files (try/catch returns []) and skips files over 2 MB.
entries.contextCost: Only the skill listing: about 700 chars of description (name plus the long trigger sentence), roughly 175 tokens, always present in the skills list. The body (about 6.8 KB) plus two references (about 11.6 KB) load only when triggered, adding roughly 4.5k tokens. There are no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related and honest: the README says it does not call Jev and is independent of TypeSafe, and the code matches that (no network, no exec).
Very low footprint: about 175 tokens of always-on context, zero dependencies, MIT licence, no postinstall, and an OIDC/provenance npm publish workflow.
Useful for the user's client projects that contain OpenAI or Anthropic classification, routing or moderation calls: it gives a cited inventory, tier table and shadow-mode migration plan.
scan.js already recognises openrouter.ai/api endpoints and OPENROUTER_API_KEY as existing LLM calls, and the reference docs have accurate primitives (choice, noul, score) and the batching advice.
cons: Does not integrate Jev into Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hook or proxy, so Claude Code gains no ability to call Jev, which is the user's core requirement.
No OpenRouter support: the reference points to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the OpenRouter Decisions and System One endpoints and typesafe/jev-1.13 model IDs are absent.
Manual, occasional use, and it only fires on audit or cost-cutting phrasing, which is the opposite of the automatic in-flow use requested.
Scanner writes raw matching lines, including .env values, into jev-scan.json (scan.js:75, :105), a secret-leak risk that the user's guard hook might block or flag.
Immature: 4 commits in one day, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, v0.1.0. The savings numbers it produces rest on claimed Jev pricing and latency, which are unverified.
The mandated promotional footer in generated reports is unwanted in client deliverables, and the skill is only relevant to repos that make LLM calls.
entries.verdict: Not the requested integration: it is a static auditing skill that never calls Jev, and it has no OpenRouter path, hook or MCP tool. It is safe and cheap to install as an optional skill for client projects that call LLMs, but it does not deliver automatic Jev use in Claude Code and should not be counted as part of the solution.

entries.name: tiffygk/jev-mode
entries.what: Three Claude Code skills plus a study course about building WITH Jev, not for using Jev as a helper inside Claude Code. jevaluate rates whether other repos use Jev well (LLM-only, no Jev call). jev-lens turns images into a JSON state via blind Claude subagents and optionally checks the state against Jev through uv script jev_check.py (typesafe-sdk, TYPESAFE_API_KEY). jevaluate-harness runs rating rounds and rubric calibration. The repo also has a static study course and CC0 ratings of community Jev projects. Nothing here makes Claude Code call Jev during ordinary coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and the triggers are narrow: 'turn this photo into a Jev state', 'rate this Jev integration', 'jevaluate <url>'. These fire only when the user's request is about building or evaluating Jev projects. Claude will never consult Jev for coding decisions because of this repo, so it does not meet the user's 'automatic use when it adds value' requirement.
security: No hooks, no MCP server, no npm postinstall, no curl|sh installer. Install is a manual folder copy and the skills are prompt text plus Python helper scripts.
API key handled via environment variable only (os.environ['TYPESAFE_API_KEY'] passed to SDK constructor). It is never in argv. The SDK does the actual HTTP.

jevaluate fetches arbitrary third-party repos and READMEs to rate them. That is a prompt-injection surface for the running Claude session (mitigated only by the skill's own instructions). Scripts use gh api and urllib, with no shell=True in the grep hits.
library.py writes to ~/.claude/jevaluate-library and its export step scans for private terms. That is a separate persistent-state directory.
No telemetry found in the scripts read (network calls limited to github.com, api.github.com, raw.githubusercontent.com, and TypeSafe via the SDK).
Third-party dependency typesafe-sdk is resolved by uv at run time from PyPI. This is unpinned supply-chain exposure when jev_check.py is run.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine automatically. jev_check.py, only when the user runs it with --yes and TYPESAFE_API_KEY set, sends the generated JSON state (a textual description of images) and questions to TypeSafe through the SDK. The images and the source code are not sent. jevaluate reads public GitHub repos and sends nothing about the user's own code. The skills themselves run on Claude, so their content goes to Anthropic as usual.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and irrelevant. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY, jev_check.py prints a skip message and exits 3 ('not an error'). The SDK timeout is 120s. No skill sits in any coding path, so a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: Three skills add only name+description lines to the context: about 1,000 chars, roughly 250 tokens. Bodies load only on trigger: jev-lens SKILL.md is 4.9KB, jevaluate 3.2KB, harness 3.7KB, and referenced files (rubric.md 15.7KB, read.md 11KB) load when the skill runs. Zero MCP tools, no MCP instructions, and no hook-injected text.
pros: Small footprint: about 250 tokens of always-on context, no MCP tools, and no hooks, so it cannot slow or break the existing gitnexus/secret-guard setup.
Fail-open: the only live Jev call is optional and skips cleanly (exit 3) without a key.

Useful reference if the user later builds their own Jev integration. jev-lens/jev-rules.md and jevaluate/rubric.md distil TypeSafe's guidance (atomic questions, Choice order rotation, confidence thresholds, treating untrusted text as data). The Choice-rotation averaging in jev_check.py is a sound pattern to copy.

The ratings/ folder (CC0) reviews existing community Jev integrations, including jkudish/jev-mcp, jlowin/vibecheck, qkal/Canny, and valentynkit/jev-belay. It gives independent code-level leads for the other candidates.
Clean install with no postinstall or curl|sh, and the key is read from env only.
cons: Not an integration: it never calls Jev on the user's coding work. It has no MCP server, no hook, and no routing, so Claude Code would not use Jev automatically.
No OpenRouter support anywhere. jev_check.py is hardwired to typesafe-sdk and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the model ID is jev-1.13.0, not typesafe/jev-1.13.
PolyForm Noncommercial license blocks use on the user's client projects and needs a commercial license from the author.

Very young: created 2026-09-28, 30 commits over 2 days by one author, 2 stars, no releases, no CI, and no plugin or marketplace packaging. The commit log shows AI co-authorship, and the repo is self-promotional (a Claude artifact study course).
Skill scope is niche (image decoding and rating other people's repos). Jevaluate would fetch untrusted repos and READMEs, which is an injection surface, and it writes a private library to ~/.claude.
Its heavy workflows are expensive (about 55k tokens of overhead per subagent) and irrelevant to day-to-day edit/debug/test loops.
jev_check.py depends on an unpinned typesafe-sdk pulled by uv at run time.
entries.verdict: Not a candidate for the automatic Jev integration. It is a set of guidance and evaluation skills for people building Jev apps, with no MCP server or hook, no OpenRouter path, and a noncommercial license that excludes the client work. Its only value is as a reading list, especially ratings/ and jev-rules.md, for vetting the real integrations such as jkudish/jev-mcp.

entries.name: microchipgnu/jev-hooks
entries.what: Independent (non-official) TypeScript library, npm jev-hooks 0.2.0, for application developers. It provides React hooks (useChoice/useNoul/useScore) and a synchronous backend run() program model that batch typed Jev judgments and compose them as reactive semantic state. It ships adapters for OpenRouter Decisions, TypeSafe SDK, Cloudflare and Vercel, plus a jev-check TypeScript safety checker CLI and an agent skill that teaches an agent to wire jev-hooks into an application. It is not an MCP server and not a Claude Code hook. It has no Claude Code integration at all.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only. It fires when the user is building an app with the jev-hooks SDK. Jev is never invoked for Claude Code's own decisions.
security: License is UNLICENSED in package.json and GitHub reports no license. Reuse rights are unclear, which matters for client projects.
No postinstall/preinstall scripts. No curl|sh installer. The only runtime deps are @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 and zod.
API key goes in an Authorization Bearer header (src/transport/http.ts:59), not argv. It is read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY or passed via options.
Traces can contain sensitive application data (README says so). Replay/trace are in-memory or user-stored.
The skill is static instructions with no shell execution. `npx skills add` fetches third-party content, so it should be read before install.
No telemetry found in the library. The public demo Worker keeps its own usage counters.
entries.dataEgress: Not applicable to Claude Code as-is, because nothing in Claude Code would call it. If used inside an app, it sends only the state object and questions you pass to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, with the API key as a Bearer header. It has no built-in code, diff or tool-output capture.
entries.failureMode: Library level only. Timeout is 20s by default with 0 retries, and errors throw with a trace. There is no Claude Code fail-open or fail-closed behavior because there is no hook or MCP surface.
entries.contextCost: If the skill is installed, it adds one skill description (about 60 tokens, always loaded) and its body (about 1.2k tokens) plus references (about 3k tokens more) only when triggered. There is no MCP tools or hook-injected text.
pros: Confirms the correct OpenRouter Decisions payload and endpoint (https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, expected response model typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917) in working, tested code (src/transport/http.ts, src/adapters/openrouter.ts). It is a useful reference to copy for a custom hook or MCP wrapper.
Zod request/response validation, response model identity check, timeout, abort and size limits, and usage/cost callbacks, all in the transport.
Includes a MockJudgmentAdapter, replay, and 19 test files, and Choice/Noul/Score answer types that keep the probabilities.
The agent skill is small and well scoped. It is useful only when you build an app that uses Jev semantics.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, or Claude Code plugin. The name 'hooks' means React hooks. It cannot make Claude Code use Jev automatically.
UNLICENSED and no license file. This is risky for client work.
Very new and tiny: created 2026-09-21, 9 commits in 2 days, 1 contributor, 1 star, 0 forks, no GitHub releases, no CI workflows, npm 0.2.0 published 2026-09-21.
Requires Node 24+ and a TypeScript 7 peer, and the design forces programs to be synchronous and side-effect free. That is irrelevant to editing arbitrary repos.
The skill only triggers when the user asks to build with jev-hooks. It adds no value in ordinary daily coding.
The pinned response model id typesafe/jev-1.13-20260917 is hardcoded, so the adapter may break when the model version is bumped unless overridden.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration. It is an app-developer SDK, and its 'hooks' are React hooks. Do not install it for the automatic-Jev goal. Use it only as a verified reference for the OpenRouter Decisions request and response shape if you write your own hook or MCP wrapper, and only install its skill if you actually build apps on jev-hooks.

entries.name: jev-shadow (dreyfus92/jev-shadow)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (v0.1.0, node, zero runtime deps, dist/ committed) that hooks PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure/PermissionDenied for Bash, PowerShell, Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, WebFetch and all mcp__* tools. A local rule table clears routine calls (read-only commands, project scripts, in-project or /tmp edits). Everything else is redacted and clipped, then sent in one POST to the backend's /v1/systemone with a fixed pack of 5 hazard nouls (destructive, exfiltration, remote_code, weakens_security, outside_project) plus a 3-level risk score. Default shadow mode logs verdicts to ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA}/log.jsonl. It joins them by tool_use_id with the auto-mode classifier's PermissionDenied labels and the PostToolUse outcome, and `jev-shadow report` or /jev-shadow:report prints agreement stats. Optional enforce mode adds a sync PreToolUse gate that returns ask/deny (allow prints nothing). Enforce yields to observe-only in auto mode.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic through hooks, with no prompting of Claude needed. Shadow by default and observation only, so it never influences the model. Off until the user runs `jev-shadow mode shadow`. Installs disabled and must be enabled per repo (`claude plugin enable ... --scope local`).
security: Key handling: userConfig sensitive:true (plugin.json). The key reaches the hook process as env CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_JEV_API_KEY, never argv. It is wrapped in an opaque Secret class whose toJSON/toString/inspect print [secret] (jev.ts:129-150) and it is never logged. Not covered by the user's no-secret-leak protected-vars list, and unknown whether the Bash tool env inherits CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_* (unverified).

Config is user-owned (~/.config/jev-shadow/config.json or $JEV_SHADOW_CONFIG). It is never read from the repo, endpoint URLs are constants, and env JEV_SHADOW_MODE can only lower the mode. Invalid or absent config means off. A cloned project cannot redirect egress (config.ts:1-10,71-77).

No shell exec, no child_process, no installer, no postinstall, no telemetry. The only network call is fetch to the backend URL (grep of src/). Zero runtime dependencies (package.json has devDependencies only).

Redaction is a 16-pattern regex table (PEM, URL userinfo, auth headers, sk-/stripe/AKIA/ghp_/glpat/npm_/hf_/slack/JWT, mysql -p, --password flags, KEY=value assignments) applied before clipping, with the order enforced by branded types plus tsc @ts-expect-error tests. Reference values like $TOKEN are kept. It is heuristic: arbitrary secrets, client names, code and business data pass through unredacted.

Prompt-injection surface: the Jev state contains attacker-controllable command, file content and local script text (up to 3 scripts x 4000 chars read from the project). Per the brief, injected instructions can move Jev answers. In shadow mode the effect is only bad data in the log. In enforce mode it could induce a false allow, but allow just falls through to the normal permission flow, so Jev cannot grant permission (render prints nothing for allow).

Enforce-mode fail-open: policy.onError defaults to allow, and a hook timeout always fails open. Rule-table edge: writes whose path startsWith('/tmp/') are treated as routine (rules.ts:310), and I did not verify handling of '/tmp/../' traversal after SENSITIVE_PATHS. Local log stores 200-char redacted excerpts under ~/.claude/plugins/data/jev-shadow-*/log.jsonl.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing until the config file exists (default mode is off). Then, for each non-routine matched tool call, one HTTPS POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone containing: tool name, cwd (redacted, clipped 2000), and for Bash/PowerShell the command (redacted, up to 8000 chars) plus up to 3 referenced in-project script bodies (up to 4000 chars each, files at most 512 KB). For Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit outside the project or on sensitive paths it sends the file path plus a 3000-char content excerpt. For WebFetch it sends the URL and the prompt (1000 chars). For every mcp__* call, including gitnexus and playwright, it sends the server name and JSON-stringified input (up to 4000 chars), because mcp/fetch/other are always_judged (rules.ts:312-315). Read/Grep/Glob are not matched. Also sent: the fixed question pack and the API key in the Authorization header. Routine calls (read-only commands, project tests, in-project or /tmp edits) never leave the machine. Requests go to OpenRouter and on to TypeSafe, a third party, which matters for client projects. In shadow mode it also fires on bypassPermissions sessions, and nothing is compared in those.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe by construction. All hooks exit 0 (ExitCode type makes 2 unrepresentable, cli.ts:47-51). ask() never throws, makes one attempt, and is bounded by a deadline measured from process start (observe 8 s default, capped at 10 s. gate 3 s default, capped at 3.5 s under the hook's 5 s timeout, which a test pins). Errors map to no_key, deadline, firewall (403), http, network or malformed. Shadow: the errors are only logged. Enforce: policy.onError defaults to allow, and a host timeout fails open. Missing, invalid or off config means no egress. Async observers pile up in the background with no host timeout beyond the 10 s cap. The Vercel path has been probed but the OpenRouter path is untested by the repo (no live test).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skills, so no tool-definition tokens and no skillListingBudget usage. The only added text is the /jev-shadow:report command description. Shadow mode injects no additionalContext (observer has no stdout). Enforce mode adds only short deny/ask reason strings (about 30 tokens) when it fires. Effectively 0 tokens/turn in shadow mode.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class backend in code (src/jev.ts:197, config.ts:101), model pinned to typesafe/jev-1.13, no patching needed, and the key is a sensitive plugin option rather than argv or a repo file.

Shadow-first design is verifiably non-invasive. The observer's IO type has no stdout, all exits are 0, config is user-owned and can only be lowered by env, and the kill switch works mid-session (cli.ts:39-51, config.ts:1-10).

Directly produces the evidence needed before trusting Jev: per-hazard agreement with the real auto-mode classifier on the user's own sessions (joins PermissionDenied labels by tool_use_id), with latency and token stats.

Egress hygiene is better than typical: local rule table keeps routine calls off the network, 16-pattern redaction runs before clipping, order enforced by types, plus a leak corpus test and a no-scannable-secrets test.
Zero runtime dependencies, no shell exec, no telemetry, small readable codebase (about 2.4k LOC), CI on Node 20/22/24 with a committed-dist-matches-source check, MIT.

Enforce mode is the one variant that works in bypassPermissions/default/dontAsk sessions, where no classifier exists. It adds a fail-open ask/deny second opinion, consistent with the OpenRouter cookbook's fail-to-prompt posture.
No context cost: no MCP tools or skills, and shadow mode injects nothing.
cons: Measurement tool, not a Jev integration that adds value to the coding loop. The README itself says that for auto-mode users there is nothing to gate yet, only something to measure, and that it is not a replacement for the classifier. It only compares against the classifier when permission_mode is auto, while the user also runs many bypassPermissions sessions, where shadow collects verdicts with no reference label.

Broad egress: every non-routine Bash, every mcp__* call (gitnexus, playwright) and every WebFetch goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe, including up to 3 project script bodies. Regex redaction cannot catch client-confidential code or names, a real concern for client projects.

Enforce mode has weak fit for this user: it stands down in auto, so it only adds latency (up to 3.5 s sync) and ask prompts in bypass sessions, and Jev is overconfident and injectable. Fail-open on timeout and onError=allow.

Very immature: created 2026-09-23, one author, 34 commits, 0 stars, no releases, v0.1, docs directory of rejected design candidates. The repo has 0 OpenRouter-specific tests (only mock-backend tests, roughly 64 test cases, no live check), and /api/v1/systemone is the alpha, no-SLA surface.

Setup friction: installs disabled and needs a per-repo enable, a separate jev_api_key entry (not OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and a manual `jev-shadow mode shadow` config. The /report command depends on `jev-shadow` being on PATH, which is fragile with the user's PATH override in settings env.
A sync node hook spawns on every matched call even in shadow mode (about 50 ms each on top of the gitnexus hooks), and mcp__.* is in the matcher so playwright/gitnexus calls all pay the spawn cost.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered, safe-by-default shadow harness with native OpenRouter support that could generate the calibration evidence to justify trusting Jev. It does not itself make Claude Code use Jev where it adds value, and it sends broad tool-call text (all MCP calls included) to a third party on a brand-new 0-star v0.1 repo. Worth a time-boxed shadow trial on personal projects only, not a daily-driver integration.

entries.name: delexw/claude-code-trace
entries.what: Tauri (Rust + React) desktop/web/TUI viewer for Claude Code JSONL session logs in ~/.claude/projects. Its optional "Analyse efficiency" feature extracts and redacts a per-session summary, posts it to Jev (System One) with about 9 typed noul/score questions, and computes a 0-100 efficiency score, 7 dimension scores and trace-linked findings. It is a post-hoc analytics dashboard for the human, not something Claude Code calls while coding.
interface: No MCP tools, no hooks, no skills, no plugin.json
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted by the human clicking Analyse in a separate GUI/web/TUI app. It has no automatic Claude Code invocation path at all.
security: Jev key is stored in the OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, Linux Secret Service) or read from JEV_API_KEY / JEV_API_KEY_FILE; sent as a Bearer header via reqwest (jev.rs:563), so it never appears in argv
Regex redaction of secrets, bearer tokens and home paths (efficiency/redact.rs) before send, but regex scrubbing is best effort and client code in excerpts may still leak
Per-request user confirmation modal shows the exact payload; Docker/web mode restricts the recommendation provider to local unauthenticated OpenAI-compatible endpoints
Spawns sh, kill, git, ps, osascript, codex and claude as local subprocesses (commands/efficiency.rs:326,335,585; process.rs:24; commands/git.rs), a wider shell surface than a simple viewer
Prompt-injection surface: transcript excerpts are sent to Jev, but the output is only numeric probabilities that are derived arithmetically, so injection can skew scores and cannot cause actions
No telemetry, sentry or posthog found in Cargo.toml or tauri.conf.json; no npm postinstall; Dockerfile and script/redeploy.sh exist, and the README build path is a source build
entries.dataEgress: Only when the user clicks Analyse and confirms: a redacted EfficiencyInput to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Minimized mode sends the first user message (1200 characters), action summaries (500 characters each), tool-call counts and signals, and up to 24 excerpts of user/error messages at 1200 characters each. Full-transcript mode sends every message plus tool_input and tool_result at 5000 characters each. The state is capped at 80k characters. That means user prompts, code fragments, commands and file paths (with the home path scrubbed) leave the machine, which matters for client projects. Nothing leaves without confirmation, and results are cached locally by SHA-256.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to Claude Code, because nothing is in its request path. Inside the app, the feature is inert without a key. It uses a 60 s reqwest timeout (jev.rs:14) with distinct messages for timeout, auth failure and a 400 on oversized state. Errors are shown in the UI and never block anything; it is effectively fail-open.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP server, no hooks, no skills, no injected text. It is a separate process that reads ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl read-only.
pros: Real, working, Jev-specific integration with a clean noul/score usage pattern (specs/14-jev-integration.md) that shows how to use typed questions and derive deterministic metrics from probabilities

Active and well tested: 209+ commits since 2026-03-11 (about 6.5 months), last push 2026-09-30, release v0.18.0 on 2026-09-19, MIT, 374 stars, roughly 943 Rust test attributes plus vitest, pytest and e2e, CI workflows
Privacy-conscious design: redaction, an explicit per-request confirmation modal, the key in the OS keychain, and minimized payload as the default
Documents practical Jev limits from real failures: the 32k-token state limit returns a bare 400 (123k characters rejected, about 100k accepted), which is useful when designing our own payloads
Zero context and latency cost in Claude Code, and safe to run alongside the existing hooks and MCP servers because it is read-only on the JSONL files
Useful as an occasional retrospective on which sessions wasted tokens through thrashing or repeated calls
cons: Does not integrate Jev into Claude Code at all: no hook, MCP tool, skill or plugin, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being prompted
Hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai and jev-latest, with no OpenRouter path or configurable base URL. Using OpenRouter needs a fork and a Rust/Tauri rebuild
Heavy install for little value: Rust 1.88+, webkit2gtk and Tauri toolchain, or Docker, and it spawns several subprocesses
Sends session content (prompts, commands, excerpts) to a third party, which is a concern for client projects, and offers a weaker guarantee than a real secret scrubber since redaction is regex based
Scores are only as valid as Jev's judgement on long agent traces; the model is beta and unverified, with skeptics calling it a router-like model
The maintainer notes it is an independent project and not an official TypeSafe integration, with a solo-dominated contributor base (Yangliu about 111 commits of 209, plus 77 dependabot)
entries.verdict: A genuine, mature Jev consumer, but it is an after-the-fact session dashboard rather than a Claude Code integration. It has no hooks, MCP or skills, is hard-wired to TypeSafe's direct API and needs a Rust rebuild for OpenRouter. It is not a candidate for the automatic-use requirement; treat it only as a reference for noul/score question design and Jev payload limits.

security: API key handling is careful: Secret wrapper redacts repr/f-string, key files and config.toml refused if group/world-readable (settings.py ~95-125, README Credentials section)
--api-key flag exists (cli.py 'api_key' options) so a key passed on argv would be visible in process list; env var/key-file avoid that

Built-in redaction: --redact-preset secrets/pii scrubs fields (password, token, api_key, authorization, cookie...) before data leaves the process (ingest/redact.py), but it is opt-in and key-name based, not content-based
install.sh is a local script (uv tool install), no curl|sh, no sudo, no npm postinstall
No telemetry found in source grep; only network target is the configured base_url via typesafe-sdk

Prompt-injection surface: log contents become Jev state, but Jev returns only typed probabilities (no free text), so injection can at most skew scores; a --fail-on gate could be gamed by attacker-controlled logs
entries.dataEgress: Only what you pass to `jcli analyze`: parsed records (after optional --filter/--select/--redact) plus the question pack text are POSTed as JSON state to base_url/v1/systemone (default api.typesafe.ai). Nothing leaves automatically; there is no background collection. If pointed at Claude Code transcripts (agent.session pack) it would send tool-call logs including file paths, commands and possibly code/secrets unless --redact-preset is used.
entries.failureMode: Not in the Claude Code loop, so nothing to fail. As a standalone CLI: default 10 s per-request timeout (SDK), 2 retries (max_retries default 2, settings.py), concurrency 8; 401/403 aborts (exit 3), 429 after retries exit 4, partial window failures exit 5 with results still emitted; --fail-on exit 6. Fail-closed per invocation, which is fine for CI gates.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill, no injected text. Only cost is if Claude runs it via Bash (a few hundred tokens of table output).
pros: Concrete, readable reference for building Jev requests: shows the state+questions payload shape, the three question types in YAML packs, and --dry-run prints exact request bodies with no key/network
Ships an agent.session pack (activity/progress/read_before_write/repetition) that judges coding-agent tool-call logs - a template for a Claude Code transcript/hook-log monitor built on Jev
Uses the official typesafe-sdk with a Bearer key and overridable TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so OpenRouter routing is plausibly just env vars (base https://openrouter.ai/api, path /v1/systemone)
Good hygiene: private-permission enforcement on key files, secret-wrapping, redact presets, offline test suite, no curl|sh installer
Multiple questions per call amortize cost/latency, consistent with Jev's parallel-evaluation design
cons: Not a Claude Code integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude uses Jev automatically without being told
Batch log-analysis tool for JSON artifacts; does not decide anything inside the coding loop (no permission, routing, or commit-gate decisions)
Immature: 2 commits, 3 stars, created 2026-09-21, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE file despite MIT claim, not published to PyPI
OpenRouter path is only inferred (env override to /api/v1/systemone), never documented or tested by the author; the key must live in a variable named TYPESAFE_API_KEY
Feeding it Claude Code session logs sends tool inputs (paths, commands, code) to a third-party model unless redaction is configured; user has client projects
Adds nothing over calling the typesafe-sdk or OpenRouter decisions/systemone endpoint directly from a small custom hook
entries.verdict: Not a viable Claude Code integration: it is a manual, alpha-stage CLI for scoring JSON/log artifacts with no hook, MCP or skill surface. Useful only as a reference for Jev request shapes and the agent.session pack, which could inspire a custom hook; OpenRouter use would need TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and is unverified.

entries.name: kevnk/jev-claude-statusline
entries.what: Claude Code status-line add-on. A Node hook (hooks/jev-progress.mjs, 328 lines) runs on UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse and Stop. It builds a small state object (task text, last 15 tool summaries, latest assistant message, turn status) and POSTs it to Jev System One with three questions: phase (Score 0-5), done (Noul) and waiting_on_user (Noul). Answers are cached in ~/.claude/cache/jev-progress/<session>.json, and statusline.sh renders a segment such as "45% done - building". It only displays progress. It never changes Claude's behaviour, so it does not use Jev to make any coding decision.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse *, Stop) plus a statusLine command. It runs fully automatically, but its output only reaches the human's status line and never the model.
security: MIT license.

API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or ~/.claude/secrets/typesafe_api_key and sent as a Bearer header via fetch, so it does not appear in argv or the process list (mjs:64-67, :196). The secrets file is not created with restricted permissions by the repo.

No npm dependencies, no postinstall and no curl|sh. Install is a manual cp of two files plus a settings merge. The hook has no child_process or shell execution. statusline.sh only uses jq on local files.
Telemetry: none besides the Jev API call itself.

Data sent: task text (up to 3000 chars), last assistant message (up to 800 chars), and the last 15 tool activities with details. Details are the Bash 'description' field (not the command), file basenames, Grep/Glob patterns, WebFetch URLs, Skill and Agent names, and for other or MCP tools the first string input value truncated to 120 chars (mjs:131-145). That fallback could leak query strings or other MCP arguments.

Prompt-injection surface: transcript content feeds only Jev's typed outputs, and the output is used only for display, so the impact is limited to a wrong progress display. Injected text could not run code.
entries.dataEgress: On the UserPromptSubmit hook nothing leaves the machine. On every PostToolUse (all tools, matcher '*') and on Stop, one HTTPS POST goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone containing: the user's task text (first 3000 chars of the prompt), the last 15 tool summaries (tool name plus a short detail such as a basename, grep pattern, URL, Bash description or the first 120 chars of the first string arg), the latest assistant text (800 chars), and turn status, along with the full question schemas (about 4 KB of static text). File contents, diffs and tool outputs are not sent. The task and assistant text are free text and may contain client code or secrets. For client projects this is a real confidentiality concern, as the README itself warns.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking. PostToolUse and Stop are marked async, so they do not delay Claude. Fetch has an 8s abort timeout (TIMEOUT_MS). Any error is written to the cache as last_error, the status line shows 'jev x', and the hook exits 0. UserPromptSubmit is sync (timeout 5s) but does only local file I/O. A lock file (stale after 20s) skips overlapping PostToolUse evaluations, so a slow Jev means fewer updates, and Stop waits up to 10s. If the key is missing it silently writes last_error and makes no network calls.
entries.contextCost: Zero tokens in Claude's context. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected additionalContext, and the hooks only write to a cache file. The cost is on the Jev side. Each call sends roughly 1.5-3k input tokens, with the static question schema of about 4 KB, and Jev input is priced at about $0.042 per 1M tokens, so it costs a fraction of a cent per turn.
pros: The only candidate here that runs automatically with no prompting, through deterministic hooks, and it is written to be fail-open (async PostToolUse and Stop, 8s abort, exit 0 always).
No dependencies, no postinstall, no shell exec, no MCP tools, and zero context tokens injected into Claude.

Good hook engineering worth copying: lock file, per-pid temp file, stale-lock recovery, superseded-record check, and skipping subagents via agent_id (mjs:311). Its use of typed Score and Noul questions with criteria and examples is a reasonable reference for a Jev integration.
Bash detail uses the description field instead of raw commands, which limits leakage, and the verify script has a check for it (verify-e2e.sh:32).
Cheap at Jev pricing.
cons: It does not improve coding. Jev's output is used only to draw a progress percentage in the status line, and Claude never sees it, so it cannot change tool choices, permissions or completion behavior.

No OpenRouter support. It is hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai and a TYPESAFE_API_KEY (mjs:42, :64), which contradicts the user's wish for OpenRouter-hosted Jev. It also needs a code patch and a check of the response schema.
Takes over the statusLine setting with its own statusline.sh and would replace the user's current status line, and it needs jq.

Fires a network call on every tool call (matcher '*'), sending task text and assistant text to a third party. That is risky for the user's client projects, and the fallback that sends the first string arg of MCP tools (mjs:142) can leak query text.

Immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, created 2026-09-23 (7 days before the audit), no tests in CI (verify scripts are manual and need a real key and transcript), no releases. Accuracy of the progress estimate is unbenchmarked (README says so).
Manual install with no plugin packaging, and the hook assumes the Claude Code transcript format (isSidechain, isMeta, prompt_id), which may break on version changes.
entries.verdict: Skip it for real integration: it is a display-only progress meter tied to TypeSafe's direct API, and it gives Claude Code no Jev decisions. It is only worth reading as a reference for writing a robust async, fail-open Jev hook, and its Score/Noul question definitions can be reused. Treat it as a pattern, not a dependency.

entries.name: killerz3/jevalyzer
entries.what: Standalone Bun CLI (not MCP, hook, or skill) that reads finished agent session logs from disk (Claude Code ~/.claude/projects/*.jsonl, Codex, opencode, Gemini CLI, Antigravity). It scores each exchange with Jev on about 7 (minimal) or 21 (extensive) typed questions, caches results in ~/.jevalyzer (SQLite), and renders an HTML report or TUI with a model leaderboard and preference index. It is an offline, after-the-fact session grader. It has nothing to do with live coding assistance.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. The user or a script runs the CLI manually or via cron. Claude Code never invokes it, and it has no hook, MCP, or skill interface.
security: The API key can be passed with --api-key <key> (src/cli.ts:66), which puts it in argv and the process list. Env vars or ~/.jevalyzer/config.json (chmod 600) are the safer routes.

Whole transcripts are sent by default: prompts, replies, tool calls, and tool output. That includes any secrets or client code that appeared in a session. --redact is opt-in and regex-based (src/core/redact.ts). It catches sk-, ghp_ and similar keys, AKIA keys, JWTs, PEM private keys, emails, and password=/token= patterns, but it misses .env-style values and client code.
No telemetry, according to the README. The only endpoints in the code are the Vercel gateway, api.typesafe.ai, and api.cloudflare.com, all through the SDK.
Prompt-injection surface: transcript content is fed only to Jev, whose output is typed (boolean, choice, score). The tool executes nothing based on that content, so the risk is low.

AGENTS.md tells an agent to install Bun with curl|sh and to clone and bun install a single-author, 2-star repo, which is a supply-chain risk. It also pulls the experimental 'ai' 7.0.105 SDK and @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai. I did not run any of it.
It spawns a process only to open the report (report.ts:450). No postinstall script.
entries.dataEgress: On analyze only: full session transcript text (user prompts, assistant replies, tool calls, tool outputs, possibly reasoning) is sent to the chosen backend (Vercel AI Gateway, api.typesafe.ai, or Cloudflare). This happens in batch, on demand, and never during live coding. ZDR is requested on the gateway by default. scan, report, and tui stay local. Nothing is sent to OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to live sessions, because it is not in the Claude Code loop. As a batch tool it is resilient: it retries, has an adaptive rate limiter that halves the rate on 429s, ends the run cleanly on sustained throttling, and resumes from the content-hash cache. A budget cap (default $5) stops overspend. Claude Code itself is never blocked.
entries.contextCost: Zero. It is not an MCP server, hook, or skill, so it adds no tools, no schemas, no instructions, and no injected text to Claude Code context. (AGENTS.md is only read when someone points an agent at it.)
pros: Useful reference for how Jev is called in practice: 7 or 21 typed boolean/choice/score questions against one shared state, packed under 56k of the 64k context (src/core/budget.ts). Parts of that design could be reused when building a Jev-based hook.
It reads Claude Code's own ~/.claude/projects JSONL, and its adapter (src/adapters/claude-code.ts) is a working parser of the transcript format.
Measured cost is tiny: a 40 MB archive costs about $0.013 at $0.042 per million input tokens.
Good hygiene for its size: MIT license, CI with typecheck and tests, config chmod 600, --dry-run and --redact, budget cap, and content-hash caching.
The Cloudflare adapter (src/core/cloudflare.ts) shows a raw-HTTP custom evaluation model, a template if someone wanted to add OpenRouter.
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code at all: no MCP server, hook, or skill. It cannot make Claude Code use Jev automatically, which is the user's core requirement.
No OpenRouter support anywhere (grep for openrouter finds nothing). It supports Vercel AI Gateway, api.typesafe.ai, and Cloudflare only. The Vercel route also requires a credit card on file.
Retrospective grading only. It scores finished sessions and gives no real-time decisions such as gating tool calls or picking a model, which is where Jev's 70-500 ms latency would matter.
Requires Bun 1.2+ (bun:sqlite), which is not in the user's stack of Node 24, Python, and uv. It is not on npm, so it has to be cloned.
Sends complete transcripts, including client-project code and tool output, to a third party by default. Redaction is opt-in and weak. That is a real concern for client work.

Very young and single-author: 2 stars, 33 commits all in one day range (2026-09-22), no releases. It depends on an experimental AI SDK API (experimental_evaluate) that its own comments say may change in patch releases.
--api-key on the command line exposes the key in the process list.
AGENTS.md encourages an agent to run curl|sh (bun.sh) and install an unvetted repo, which is bad practice.
entries.verdict: Not an integration for Claude Code. It is an offline session-grading CLI with no MCP, hook, or skill surface, no OpenRouter support, and a Bun-only runtime. Skip it for the automatic-Jev goal. At most, read its question bank and Claude Code JSONL adapter as reference when designing your own Jev hook.

entries.name: @typesafe-ai/sdk (official TypeScript SDK)
entries.what: Official zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript/JS client for the TypeSafe API. TypeSafeClient.systemOne({state, questions, model?}) POSTs to {baseURL}/v1/systemone using choice()/noul()/score() question builders, and client.models.list() does GET /v1/models. It gives typed answers, retries, timeouts and logging. It is a library only. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI, so it does nothing inside Claude Code by itself. You would have to write a wrapper (an MCP server or a hook script) around it.
interface: new TypeSafeClient({apiKey?, baseURL?, model?, timeout?, retry?, logLevel?, headers?})
Error classes (TypeSafeError, APIError, APIConnectionError, APITimeoutError, APIUserAbortError)
entries.autoInvocation: Not invocable from Claude Code at all. It is a library that only becomes automatic if you build a deterministic hook (PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit script) or an MCP server around it.
security: No install scripts: grep of package.json found no postinstall or preinstall.
Zero runtime dependencies, so the supply-chain surface is small.
npm 0.6.0 is published with SLSA provenance attestation from GitHub Actions. The publish workflow pins actions by SHA and uses OIDC id-token.

The API key is held in a private field (#apiKey, src/client.ts:236) and sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (:354). It is never put in argv or the URL. If used from an MCP server, pass the key via env, not args.
Default log level is warn. At debug level the SDK logs request and response bodies (client.ts:335-340 area), which would expose state content in logs.
No telemetry found: grep for telemetry and analytics in src gave 0 hits. It sends only X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime and User-Agent headers.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the wrapper puts in the state and questions fields goes to the configured baseURL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if overridden). The SDK reads no files on its own. Data leaving would be exactly what the integrator passes in (prompts, diffs, file contents, tool outputs). With OpenRouter it would pass through OpenRouter and TypeSafe, which matters for client projects under NDA. The header X-TypeSafe-Runtime reveals the runtime name.
entries.failureMode: The SDK does not decide fail-open or fail-closed. It throws APITimeoutError, APIConnectionError or APIError. The defaults are a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries on 408, 429, 5xx and connection errors, with 500 ms backoff up to 5 s, so the worst case is about 30 s or more of blocking (src/retry.ts:5-21). A hook wrapper must set timeout to 1-2 s and maxRetries to 0 and catch every error to fail open. Otherwise a hook would stall Claude Code turns.
entries.contextCost: Zero on its own, since it has no tools, instructions or injected text. Any MCP wrapper built on it would add its own tool definitions (roughly 300-800 tokens for 1-3 tools). A hook wrapper could add zero tokens except the text it chooses to inject.
pros: Official, MIT-licensed, zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, npm provenance attestation: the safest building block for a custom Jev hook or MCP server.

baseURL and key are env-configurable and the path is /v1/systemone, the same path OpenRouter documents, so pointing it at OpenRouter should need only 3 env vars and no fork (src/env.ts, src/client.ts:321).
Typed choice/noul/score builders match Jev's three primitives exactly, so a wrapper is about 50 lines.
Configurable timeout and retry (per client and per call), so a hook can be made fail-open with a short deadline.
Fully typed answers and typed errors. The API key stays out of argv and the URL.
cons: It is only a library. It gives Claude Code no MCP tools, hooks or skills, so it achieves none of the automatic integration goal without custom code.
Young and thin: repo created 2026-09-04, 5 commits, 2 human contributors, npm versions 0.5.7 and 0.6.0 within 3 days. The API may change before 1.0.

No OpenRouter awareness: default model jev-latest lacks the typesafe/ prefix, so it must be overridden. There is no Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) support, and OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified.
Default 10 s timeout with 2 retries is hostile to interactive hooks and must be tuned by the integrator.
The SDK gives no guidance on when Jev adds value for coding. That policy layer (which questions, which triggers) must be written by the user, and Jev is a classifier, not a chat model.
Debug logging would print state bodies, which may include client code.

Vendor-blessed OpenRouter path, but the SDK cannot use /api/alpha/decisions, the endpoint used by OpenRouter's official Claude-Code-relevant cookbook (gate-tool-calls). Both endpoints exist, so this is a minor gap.
Zero Claude Code surface: no hook, MCP server or skill. The SDK does nothing without a wrapper and gives no automatic invocation.

No total-deadline or retry budget, and Retry-After up to 60 s is honored. A PermissionRequest or PreToolUse hook needs an external AbortSignal or hard process timeout, or an outage or 429 storm could stall turns.
models.list() is unusable on OpenRouter (shape mismatch). Any wrapper must not call it in health checks.

Uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY. A wrapper must pass apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY explicitly, or the user has to add a second secret variable. The existing no-secret-leak.cjs hook does not yet protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
Very young: the SDK npm package was created 2026-09-12, and @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai was created 2026-09-16. No pushes for 15 days as of 2026-09-30, and the API is alpha on OpenRouter with no SLA.
State sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe includes any repo content the wrapper passes. This is a data-egress concern for client/NDA projects, and injected instructions in state can move Jev's answers.
entries.verdict: Best foundation if you build your own thin wrapper (a fail-open hook or a tiny MCP server) and point it at OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and model typesafe/jev-latest. But by itself it does nothing inside Claude Code and is not an integration. For a plain hook, raw fetch to OpenRouter would work about as well, since the SDK saves little code.

verification.note: Repo facts re-verified: 259 stars, 34 forks, MIT, not archived, 5 commits, last push 2026-09-15 (v0.6.0), npm 0.5.7 and 0.6.0 plus a bootstrap tag, provenance attestation present, no dependencies and no install scripts. Source-level claims mostly hold: no telemetry, no shell or file access, API key in a private field and sent only as a Bearer header, /v1/systemone at src/client.ts:321. Main audit errors: (1) OpenRouter support is officially documented by OpenRouter for this exact SDK, so it is confirmed, not 'partial/unverified'. (2) The model advice is wrong: the default jev-latest already maps to ~typesafe/jev-latest, and the suggested 'typesafe/jev-latest' is probably not a valid ID. (3) client.models.list() breaks on OpenRouter. (4) Worst-case blocking is understated because Retry-After up to 60 s is honored. (5) Line refs and contributor count are slightly off. The score stays at 5. It is a clean, safe, OpenRouter-ready client library, but it is not a Claude Code integration. It has no hook or MCP surface, so the user must still write and maintain the wrapper and policy, and a dependency-free fetch script matching OpenRouter's cookbook is about as easy. The SDK's real value is typed answers and error classes. If the user builds a fail-open PermissionRequest hook, use apiKey: process.env.OPENROUTER_API_KEY, baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api, model 'jev-1.13' (pinned), timeout about 1500 ms, retry {maxRetries:0}, and a try/catch that falls through to the normal prompt. Nothing was executed or installed; only static reading, gh/npm metadata and OpenRouter docs fetches were used.

judge.why: Cleanest, dependency-free, vendor-blessed client. It is the right base for a self-written hook but has no Claude Code surface at all.
pros: OpenRouter documents this exact SDK: baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api plus OpenRouter key; default model jev-latest maps to ~typesafe/jev-latest server-side, and jev-1.13 pins a version
Typed choice/noul/score builders and distinct error classes (AuthenticationError, RateLimitError, APITimeoutError) so a hook can fail open cleanly
MIT, provenance attestation, no deps, no install scripts, no telemetry, key only sent as Bearer header
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no hook, MCP or skill, so nothing is automatic
No total retry budget and Retry-After up to 60 s is honored; a hook needs maxRetries 0, timeout ~1500 ms and an external AbortSignal
Reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY (pass OPENROUTER_API_KEY explicitly); models.list() breaks on OpenRouter; cannot use /api/alpha/decisions
Adds an npm dependency where plain fetch (as in OpenRouter's cookbook) is about as easy; young package, release mirror

entries.name: kyu1204/oh-my-harness
entries.what: npm CLI (omh / oh-my-harness) that generates a per-project Claude Code guardrail harness (CLAUDE.md, .claude/settings.json hooks, bash hook scripts) from harness.yaml/presets. Jev is an optional layer. (1) `omh init "description"` and `omh modify "request"` call Jev once to choose or edit catalog blocks (Noul per block, Choice for strictness). (2) Rules marked `enforce: true` produce a `semantic-rule-guard` PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Edit|Write|MultiEdit). On every such call it POSTs the tool input to the System One endpoint with one Noul question per rule, and blocks at p>=0.9, asks at 0.6-0.9, and allows below that. (3) An optional `semantic-diff-gate` shells out to the separate `jgrep` tool.
interface: omh sync / diff / doctor / explain / test / uninstall / config / stats / update / catalog list|info / hook add|remove / loop start|run|stop|status|clean
Deterministic hooks (branch-guard, command-guard, path-guard, secret-file-guard, tdd-guard, sql-guard, lint/format/test-on-save, commit gates, stop gates, no-verify/force-push guards)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook. The harness fires semantic-rule-guard automatically on every Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit call in a project where `omh init` has been run and a rule has `enforce: true`. No model discretion and no prompting is needed. The hook only asks Jev a rule-compliance question; it does not provide general decision-making help to Claude. Setup is per project, and it writes .claude/settings.json, harness.yaml and CLAUDE.md into each repo, which is intrusive for client repos.
security: Key visibility: the hook passes the key to curl as `-H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY"` (semantic-rule-guard.ts:69), so the OpenRouter/TypeSafe key is visible in the process list (ps/proc cmdline) for the length of each call.

Key sourcing: the hook falls back to grepping TYPESAFE_API_KEY out of the project's .env via sed (lines 36-38). This is a read of a secrets file, and it will collide with a secret-leak guard that watches .env reads only if that guard matches the hook's own shell, which it should not.

The prompt-injection surface is narrow. Jev returns only probabilities, and rule text comes from harness.yaml. However, attacker-controlled content in the tool call (new_string, content, command) goes into the Jev `state`, and a Noul on it can be gamed, so this is a soft guard. The README states it never relaxes deterministic guards.

Shell execution: the hooks are generated bash scripts, and the rule text is embedded via a quoted heredoc so it is safely quoted. jq is required. The TS `omh` CLI does not exec third-party code besides optional `jgrep`.

No npm postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json scripts are only build, test and prepublishOnly). It is installed with `npm install -g oh-my-harness`, not via curl|sh. Only the file list dist/, presets/ and README is published.

Telemetry: none found (grep for telemetry/analytics only hit an unrelated stats TUI label). The TUI init has a one-time prompt that offers to star the repo via gh (src/cli/github-star.ts), which is opt-in.
entries.dataEgress: For semantic-rule-guard, on every Bash/Edit/Write/MultiEdit call the hook sends to api.typesafe.ai, or to OpenRouter if repointed: tool name, the full Bash command, the Bash description, the file_path, old_string truncated to 2000 characters, and new_string and content each truncated to 4000 characters, plus the enforced rule texts (semantic-rule-guard.ts:52-66). No prompts, no conversation history, no file reads and no tool outputs are sent. Edited code fragments and shell commands, which may contain inline secrets or client code, DO leave the machine on every write. For init/modify, the project description plus the detector facts (languages, package managers, etc.) go to TypeSafe. The request is not sent to Anthropic. There is no telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. There is no key, no curl, a non-200 response, curl failure, or no answers, and in each case the hook logs `skipped` and exits 0 (semantic-rule-guard.ts:39-40,71,74). curl has a hard `-m 10` cap, so the worst case adds 10 s to a single tool call when Jev hangs. The hook script has no set timeout in settings.json, so Claude Code's default hook timeout applies as an outer bound. The TS paths (init/modify) use a 15 s AbortSignal and print a fallback message. A slow or down Jev never blocks the user, but the guard silently disappears in that case.
entries.contextCost: There are no MCP tools or server instructions, so tool-definition cost is 0. The hooks inject text only on block/ask, as a short reason string of roughly 30-60 tokens. The generated CLAUDE.md section from harness rules adds a small managed block per project, roughly a few hundred tokens depending on the rules. The hooks are per-project (.claude/settings.json), not global.
pros: It is the only candidate here that actually wires Jev into Claude Code with a deterministic PreToolUse hook. No 'use jev' prompting is needed, which matches the user's automatic-integration requirement (semantic-rule-guard.ts:11-17).

A sensible use of Jev's strengths: a Noul with calibrated p, block at >=0.9, ask at 0.6-0.9. It emits a real permissionDecision:"ask" for the middle band (lines 88-91). It uses Jev the way the model was designed, with typed questions and no free text.
Robust fail-open: no key, curl failure, non-200 or timeout all allow with a log, and the hard 10 s curl cap. It is additive to the deterministic guards.

It sends only the tool input, truncated (2-4k characters per field), rather than transcripts or file reads. The hook also has a test with a fake local endpoint (OMH_TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT), and an endpoint override already exists in the bash hook.

The repo is active (v0.25.0 released today, 485 commits since March 2026, CI on Node 20/22, 100+ unit test files with recorded Jev fixtures) and MIT licensed, with no postinstall scripts and no telemetry.
The OpenRouter path is nearly free: it needs a base-URL env var plus a one-line model-id patch, since the Bearer auth scheme is the same.
cons: No native OpenRouter support: the model is hardcoded to `jev-latest` (semantic-rule-guard.ts:62; typesafe-chooser.ts:18), and the TS init/modify endpoint is hardcoded with no env override. OpenRouter needs a model id such as `typesafe/jev-latest`, and the OpenRouter System One request and response shape parity is unverified. The key must be supplied under the name TYPESAFE_API_KEY.

The scope is a rule-compliance gate, not a general Claude Code decision helper. It only adds value if the user writes natural-language `enforce: true` rules. It does not route models or pick tools, or triage anything else.

Per-project install: `omh init` writes harness.yaml, .claude/settings.json hooks, scripts and CLAUDE.md into each repo. This is intrusive and may need committing on client projects, and it does not give a global user-level integration. It also merges with existing settings and may interact with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus).

Latency and egress on every mutating call: roughly 0.3-0.8 s per Bash/Edit/Write, and client code fragments (up to 4000 characters per field) and shell commands go to a third-party model on each write. That is a compliance concern for client projects, and the guard can be gamed by adversarial content in the call.
Key handling: the Bearer key is in curl's argv, so it is visible in ps, and it is read from a project .env by sed.

Single-maintainer project (483 of 485 commits) with 17 stars, at v0.25.0 and 6 months old. It bundles a lot of scope (loop engine, TUI, Codex/Pi generators) unrelated to Jev, and it is coupled to the beta Jev API (Jev is early access, so the guard is only as good as p-calibration, since the skeptics' 'flash router' claim is unverified).

Hard deny at p>=0.9 with no allow-once path: a false positive from an overconfident model blocks legitimate Edit/Write/Bash calls, also in the user's bypassPermissions sessions (docs: hooks still run under bypass). The deny reason nudges Claude to rewrite the call, which risks retry loops or work-arounds. The prompt is a single-call yes/no with no repo context ('Answer yes only if the call clearly does what the rule forbids').

Egress has no path or secret filtering (semantic-rule-guard.ts:52-60): Writes/Edits to .env, key files or credentials configs send the new secret content (up to 4000 chars) to a third party. The full Bash command is sent, including inline tokens or `echo $KEY`-style commands and the description field. This contradicts the user's own no-secret-leak posture and is worse than the audit's generic 'client code' concern.

Silent fail-open: curl runs with 2>/dev/null and errors are logged only to omh's JSONL event log (semantic-rule-guard.ts:68-71). The user gets no visible notice when the guard is offline, on OpenRouter's /alpha-tier endpoint with no SLA.
Matcher is Bash|Edit|Write|MultiEdit, so NotebookEdit is not covered. Bash file writes (heredocs, sed -i) are judged only by command text.

Depends on bash, jq, awk and curl, and on omh generating the wrapper: the script uses _log_event, _emit_decision and _OMH_PROJECT_ROOT from a generated logger preamble (src/generators/hooks.ts:~271-395). It cannot be lifted as a standalone global hook without copying that preamble.

The hook is registered as `bash <script>` with no timeout field (hooks.ts:554). The 10 s curl cap is the only bound. Claude Code's PreToolUse default timeout is 600 s (per the docs), not a short outer bound. It runs serially alongside the user's slow gitnexus Bash hook.
Uses a deprecated top-level decision:"block" output for the hard-block path (see corrections).
entries.verdict: The strongest concrete example of automatic, hook-based Jev use in Claude Code, and it is worth stealing the semantic-rule-guard pattern. It is not a drop-in for OpenRouter (hardcoded model and endpoint) and is too intrusive and latency-heavy to adopt wholesale across client repos. The better plan is a small custom global PreToolUse hook that reuses this Noul design and a hardened curl, pointed at OpenRouter.

verification.note: Re-queried now: 17 stars, 2 forks, MIT, not archived, created 2026-03-16, last push 2026-09-30, v0.25.0 published that day, no pre/postinstall scripts. 485 commits, of which 483 are from one author (MINT) and 2 from yhkim. The audit's basic facts all check out. The semantic-rule-guard code matches the description: a fail-open bash PreToolUse hook, one Noul per rule, block at p>=0.9 and ask at p>=0.6, a 10 s curl cap, the key in curl argv, a .env sed fallback, and telemetry-free apart from an opt-in gh star prompt. The main correction is that the hook works on OpenRouter with env vars only (endpoint override plus the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), with no source edit, because OpenRouter maps bare jev-latest itself and its request/response shape matches. I kept the score at 5 even though OpenRouter readiness is better than the audit said. It is still per-project (omh init writes into every repo, including client repos), only a rule gate, sends Write/Edit content unfiltered to a third party on every mutating call, and hard-denies on a model with known overconfidence. It also uses a deprecated decision:\"block\" field. The best use is to copy the Noul-per-rule pattern into a custom global hook with secret/path filtering, ask-only behavior and visible fail-open.  The 'ask' band under bypassPermissions/auto mode is unverified in the docs."

judge.why: Closest to an automatic PreToolUse hook and a good pattern (one Noul per rule, ask at p>=0.6, deny at p>=0.9, fail-open), but per-project, unfiltered egress and a hard deny. Copy the pattern, do not install it.
pros: Real deterministic PreToolUse hook on Bash|Edit|Write|MultiEdit, fail-open on errors, 10 s curl cap
Works on OpenRouter with env vars only; request and response shape verified against OpenRouter docs
Owner-style rules like never add dependencies fit client projects; 485 commits, active, MIT
cons: Hard deny at p>=0.9 with no override, even under bypassPermissions; overconfident model means false positives cause retry loops
Sends full Bash commands and Write/Edit content (up to 4000 chars, including .env or key contents) to a third party with no path or secret filtering
Silent fail-open (curl errors to /dev/null), uses deprecated top-level decision:block, no NotebookEdit, needs its generated logger preamble, per-project omh init
Hook ask behavior in bypass/auto mode is undocumented
