entries.name: onesie (frodi-karlsson/onesie)
entries.what: Go CLI (single static binary) that is a Unix filter over the System One API (Jev). You pipe text in, ask a yes/no, --pick or --rate question, and get a probability/option/level with scriptable exit codes; it also has a batch/stream mode, calibrate, caching, and built-in gates (shell-safety, prompt-injection, personal-data, moderation). It ships a Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json) made of 6 skills (onesie, onesie-gate, onesie-calibrate, onesie-patterns, onesie-setup, onesie-stream) and one SessionStart hook. It has deliberately NO MCP server (README "Why no MCP server"). The plugin teaches Claude how to write correct onesie invocations; it does not by itself route Claude Code's own decisions through Jev.
interface: onesie questions / auth set|status / cache / --print-request / --mock FILE (ONESIE_MOCK)
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description triggers (model discretion) plus one SessionStart hook that only reports status. The descriptions trigger when Claude is WRITING a script/pipeline that needs a judgment ("when a script needs a onesie judgment", "before writing `if onesie`", "before prompting a general model and parsing its reply"); they do not make Claude route its own coding decisions or tool-call approvals through Jev. Nothing is deterministic: there is no PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. To get truly automatic behaviour the user must add their own hook, e.g. a PreToolUse Bash hook calling `onesie -f shell-safety -q --timeout 2 --retries 0 --state "$cmd"` and mapping exit 1 to deny, 7 to ask/permission prompt, others to allow.
security: MIT license (LICENSE, GitHub licenseInfo mit).

API key never in argv: read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY env, or from OS keychain (zalando/go-keyring) or credential file via onesie auth set (internal/cli/auth.go:498-540, internal/creds). No --key flag found. onesie-go redacts headers in debug logs (client.go:388 redactedHeader) and copies http client so Authorization is not leaked on redirect (client.go:77).
However the question text and the state (e.g. the shell command in `onesie -f shell-safety --state 'cmd'`) DO appear in argv/process list and shell history when passed via --state; stdin avoids that.

install.sh (curl|sh from main): well written, set -eu, everything in main(), verifies sha256 vs checksums.txt and, if gh is logged in, `gh attestation verify` build provenance; installs to ~/.local/bin. Still a curl|sh path; alternatives are brew tap or go install (go.mod says go 1.27.1, needs a very new toolchain). I did not run it.
No npm postinstall, no telemetry/analytics code found in Go sources (grep). Only network egress is to the chosen provider plus optional schema URL references.

Prompt-injection surface: text handed to Jev is data classified into typed output (no free text), so the model cannot emit instructions back; risk is limited to a attacker steering the probability (e.g. crafted command hiding intent). The shell-safety gate is a probabilistic classifier, not a sandbox: the README's own worst miss is `echo hello > notes.txt` answered destroys=0.37 (abstain band).
entries.dataEgress: Only what you pass to onesie: stdin / --state / --state-file text plus the question wording and option lists, sent over HTTPS to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai). Nothing is sent automatically by the plugin; the SessionStart hook is fully local (no network, per its own comment). With --cache, responses are stored on local disk (XDG cache, 24h TTL for aliases). If wired into a PreToolUse gate, every Bash command string (which can contain inline secrets, tokens, client hostnames) would go to OpenRouter unless pre-filtered; file contents/diffs only leave if a script pipes them.
entries.failureMode: CLI is fail-closed by exit code contract: any exit other than 0/1/7 means 'no answer' and README's recipe blocks on it (`*) echo 'no answer, blocked'`). Per-attempt HTTP timeout 10s (onesie-go option.go:20), 2 retries (option.go:25), Retry-After honoured up to a cap (--max-retry-after), all overridable via --timeout/--retries. Worst case for a hook using defaults is about 30s+ before failure, so a custom hook should pass --timeout 2 --retries 0 and map non-{0,1,7} to allow. The plugin SessionStart hook is fail-open (always exit 0, 10s timeout) and does no network calls. Because the plugin has no PreToolUse hook, a Jev outage cannot block Claude Code by itself.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 tool definitions. 6 skills: description lines are 251, 330, 402, 295, 328, 298 chars (about 1.9k chars, roughly 500 tokens always in the skill listing); SKILL.md bodies load only on trigger (onesie 13.3k chars, onesie-gate 14k, onesie-stream 15.8k, onesie-calibrate 8.4k, onesie-setup 6.5k, onesie-patterns 5.4k, i.e. roughly 3-4k tokens each when loaded). SessionStart hook injects one line of about 100-300 chars (key status, plus up to 20 saved question names). Very cheap versus an MCP server.
pros: Native, code-verified OpenRouter support: same System One wire protocol at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY (onesie-go provider.go:42-52); one env var switches the provider, no patching needed.
Zero MCP tool-definition cost: 6 skill descriptions (about 500 tokens) and a one-line SessionStart hook; bodies load only when triggered. Explicit design decision against an MCP server.

Ships a ready-made, calibrated gate: `onesie -f shell-safety -q` returns exit 0/1/7 (run / block / ask a human), which maps 1:1 onto a Claude Code PreToolUse hook decision (allow / deny / ask). Also prompt-injection and personal-data gates that could screen tool outputs or fetched web content.
Good security hygiene: key from env/keychain, not argv; redacted debug logs; install.sh verifies sha256 and build provenance; plugin pinned to tag v0.4.3; no telemetry found.
Timeout/retries/cache/mock knobs (--timeout, --retries, ONESIE_CACHE, ONESIE_MOCK, --print-request free dry-run) make it easy to build a fail-open hook and to test it without spending tokens.
Only Jev-specific tool found with a calibration workflow (`onesie calibrate` with --offline --require for CI) which is valuable given skeptic claims that Jev may just be a small-model router.
Well tested for a 9-day-old project (121 test files, CI, releases with attestation, 200 commits).
cons: Not automatic as shipped: the plugin has only skills and a status-only SessionStart hook. Skills trigger only when Claude is writing scripts that need a judgment, not on Claude's own edit/run/review decisions. The user's goal of 'Claude Code uses Jev without being told' needs a custom PreToolUse hook the project does not provide.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 2 stars, 0 forks, 1 human contributor (plus dependabot), v0.4.3, still churning (7 tags in 9 days); pre-1.0 flag/API breakage likely. Repo is a Show HN project.

Requires building/installing a Go binary; go.mod requires Go 1.27.1 for go install, and the README's main path is curl|sh (mitigated by checksum and attestation). User has Node/Python/uv, not necessarily Go.

Shell-safety gate is probabilistic: README's own worst miss is `echo hello > notes.txt` at 0.37; calibrated on only 40 labelled commands, mostly synthetic; would also produce many exit-7 prompts in bypass/auto mode where user wants fewer interruptions. Adds 70-500 ms+ network latency to every Bash call if used as a PreToolUse gate, and sends every command string to OpenRouter.

Commands passed via --state appear in argv/process list; hook must use stdin. Default timeout is 10s with 2 retries so an unconfigured hook can stall ~30s; must set --timeout/--retries itself and map errors to allow.
Overlaps with the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard and permission mode: a Jev gate would be an additional, non-deterministic layer, not a replacement.
Depends on the separate onesie-go SDK (v0.1.0, created 2026-09-29, 0 stars) for all HTTP behaviour, so audit surface is two young repos.

The shipped shell-safety assert includes network < 0.5. Routine dev commands (git push, npm install, curl, gh, ssh, aws) score network 0.94-0.97 and land in exit 7 (ask). In defaultMode auto or bypass this creates constant prompts, the opposite of what this user wants.

The gate is not aimed at the user's actual friction. `rm -rf ./build` is scored 0.60 and blocked, and some dataset labels look wrong (`chmod -R 777 /` labelled destroys=false, scored 0.10). Thresholds are tuned on the same 40 commands, so real-world precision and recall are unknown.

The skills teach Claude to write onesie pipelines. None route Claude Code's own decisions through Jev, so the automatic-use goal is unmet with no custom hook. The skills add always-on listing cost (about 1.9k chars of descriptions) with little daily benefit, since the user's skillListingBudgetFraction is 0.02. Bodies are 5-16 KB each when triggered.

The skills carry `allowed-tools: Bash(onesie:*)`, which pre-approves any onesie invocation while a skill is active. A model-written `onesie --state-file <path>` could send file contents to OpenRouter without a prompt. The user's no-secret-leak hook still inspects Bash, but OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in its protected list.

Every Bash command string goes to OpenRouter (32k context, alpha endpoint, no SLA) if used as a PreToolUse gate. Commands with inline tokens or client hostnames would leave the machine. A regex pre-filter is required for client projects.

Jev's known weaknesses apply directly to this gate: injected text inside a command can shift the score (echo 'rm -rf /' style cases), it is overconfident on unanswerable input, and it is sensitive to label swaps. It must not replace deterministic rules.

In Claude Code, a PreToolUse hook exit code other than 0 or 2 is non-blocking (fail-open), and exit 2 blocks. A wrapper script must translate onesie's exits explicitly (1 to deny, 7 to ask, 2/3/4/5 to allow). Do not pass onesie's exit code through unmapped. The default hook timeout is 600s, so the wrapper must set --timeout and --retries or it can stall for about 30s on outages.
Depends on two young repos, onesie and onesie-go v0.1.0 (0 stars), both created in the last 10 days. The only issue open now (#3) is a flaky macOS-Intel CI failure in the jev package.
entries.verdict: Best building block found for a DIY deterministic Jev integration (OpenRouter-native, shell-safety gate with exit 0/1/7, near-zero context cost, no telemetry), but the plugin itself is only skills and does not make Claude Code use Jev automatically. Use the binary plus your own PreToolUse hook (tight timeout, fail-open, stdin only) rather than relying on the skills, and treat the project as an early-stage, single-maintainer dependency.

verification.note:
Verified and correct in the audit: MIT license, not archived, 2 stars, 0 forks, created 2026-09-20, last push 2026-09-29, latest release v0.4.3, and the marketplace ref pinned to v0.4.3. The six skills exist with the listed description lengths (251/330/402/295/328/298). The SessionStart hook is preflight-only, always exits 0, and has a 10s timeout. OpenRouter support is native and code-verified in the sibling SDK: provider.go:42-52 gives BaseURL https://openrouter.ai/api and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and client.go:22 gives POST /v1/systemone. This matches the brief's /v1/systemone schema with the Bearer key. I found no --key flag, no telemetry in the Go sources, and no exec of external commands outside test tooling. install.sh does verify sha256 and, if gh is available, the attestation. Claude Code details checked against the docs: hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision accepts allow|deny|ask|defer, and exit 2 blocks. The docs do not say whether PreToolUse ask is honored in bypassPermissions, so treat that as unverified. PermissionRequest hooks likely do not fire when permissions are bypassed, so a PreToolUse hook is the right event, as the audit suggests.

I lowered the score from 6 to 5. The plugin does not deliver automatic use, and the skills are mostly irrelevant to daily coding. The only relevant asset, the shell-safety gate, would prompt on nearly every network command and has thin, self-labelled calibration. The project is 10 days old and single-maintainer. It is a decent building block (native OpenRouter, static binary, --print-request dry-run, --mock, tight timeout flags), but the user would have to write and tune the hook and thresholds. I did not execute any code. The claim that it is the category leader was not re-verified against other candidates.

judge.why: Best packaged building block: static Go binary with prebuilt releases, native OpenRouter, dry-run and mock modes, plus a shell-safety gate that could feed a PreToolUse wrapper. But the shipped gate asks on nearly every network command and the skills do not route Claude's decisions.
pros: Native OpenRouter support, checksum-verified installer, --print-request dry run, --mock, tight --timeout/--retries flags
Six skills and a preflight-only SessionStart hook that always exits 0; no telemetry found
Exit codes (1 block, 7 ask) are easy to map in a wrapper
cons: Shell-safety gate is tuned in-sample on 40 self-labelled commands; network<0.5 assert makes git push/npm install/curl score 0.94-0.97 and exit 7 (constant prompts)
Some labels look wrong (chmod -R 777 / labelled safe); calibration claims are thin

Skills teach writing onesie pipelines, not automatic gating, and add listing cost; allowed-tools Bash(onesie:*) pre-approves calls, so a model-written --state-file could ship file contents to OpenRouter
Wrapper must map exit codes explicitly (non-0/2 exits fail open); default model alias jev-latest, so pin typesafe/jev-1.13; repo and SDK are about 10 days old, single maintainer

entries.name: chrishan17/claude-jev-mod
entries.what: A Claude Code "mod" plugin (function-hooks module, not an MCP server or proxy) that registers a single engine.create hook adding a `$.jev.ask({state, questions})` noun to the plugin engine interface. Other plugins' hooks can then call Jev (Choice/Score/Noul) via six providers and read back typed probabilities. By itself it decides nothing and calls nothing: it is a client library with no consumer hooks, no MCP tools, no skills. The candidate summary "router-proxy" is a mislabel; it is a plugin-host SDK.
entries.autoInvocation: Not automatic by itself: it provides the $.jev capability only. Automatic use would require writing (or installing) a separate plugin with deterministic hooks (e.g. tool.call on Bash/Edit) that call $.jev.ask. README's examples (risk score of Bash commands, destructive-command noul) are illustrative, not shipped. So it is a building block toward the user's goal of hook-driven, no-prompt invocation, not the integration itself.
security: API key read from Claude Code process env / settings.json env block via $.env.get; sent only as Authorization Bearer header via host $.http.fetch (register.ts comment 66-67: deliberately does NOT use the session's own OAuth credential). Not in argv, nothing written to disk, no shell execution, no child_process.

No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no npm deps in repo (zero runtime dependencies). Source is ~500 lines and fully readable; supply-chain surface is just the git repo (single author, 1 star, unpinned marketplace add tracks default branch) so a later malicious commit could exfiltrate anything passed to ask or the env keys it reads.

Reads 15 env vars including keys for unrelated providers (Vercel, Cloudflare, LiteLLM, TypeSafe) only via named getters; loader is said to refuse env names a module does not spell literally, which is a useful sandbox property.
Custom endpoints (JEV_ENDPOINT, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, AI_GATEWAY_BASE_URL, CLOUDFLARE_AI_GATEWAY_URL, LITELLM_PROXY_BASE_URL) send the bearer key and state to any URL configured; fine if env is trusted.

Prompt-injection surface belongs to consumers: README admits hook input (file contents, tool results) is untrusted and Jev does not treat state as hostile; question ids are not sent to the model. Jev output is typed probabilities only, so injection can at most flip a decision, not run text.

Depends on undocumented/experimental function-hooks feature; verified string CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, engine.create and plugin-types exist in local claude 2.1.285 binary (grep -c 10/29/18), but feature is flag-gated and behavior could change between releases.
entries.dataEgress: By itself nothing leaves the machine (the mod makes no calls unless another plugin invokes $.jev.ask). When invoked, exactly the `state` and `questions` object the calling hook builds is POSTed as JSON to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with the OpenRouter key, so a hook that passes bash commands, diffs or file contents sends them to OpenRouter and TypeSafe/its upstream. No other data (no prompts, transcript, tool outputs) is collected by the mod.
entries.failureMode: Fail-loud by design: ask() rejects on missing config, non-200, bad body, missing answers (jev-of.ts:37-63). No timeout, retry or fallback is implemented in the mod (timeouts are whatever the host $.http.fetch applies). Whether a failure blocks or passes the tool call is decided by the consuming hook (README: 'failing open is usually right for a guard'). Because there is no consumer shipped, failure of the mod itself has no effect on the session. With no key set, nothing breaks until something calls ask.
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill descriptions, and the mod injects no text into the model context. Only adds the engine.create hook at startup.
pros: Only candidate found so far that hooks into Claude Code's deterministic function-hook engine, which is the right mechanism for 'Claude Code uses Jev without being told': hooks fire on tool.call regardless of model discretion, and $.jev.ask gives calibrated Noul/Score/Choice for gating (destructive command? secret in diff? risk level?).

Real OpenRouter support in code: exact endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and typesafe/jev-1.13 (providers.ts:148-164), and README says OpenRouter is the one path verified against the live endpoint; also supports direct TypeSafe and the ~typesafe/jev-latest via JEV_MODEL override.

Tiny, auditable, zero dependencies, no postinstall, no shell, no telemetry, no MCP tokens, ~500 LOC; uses host $.http.fetch and explicitly does not send the session OAuth credential (register.ts:66-67).

Clean typed contract (types/index.d.ts), good error messages, env re-read per call (key set mid-session works), MIT license, and the required flag string exists in the user's claude 2.1.285 binary (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS, engine.create, plugin-types found).
Good fit alongside the user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse and GitNexus hooks: adds no context cost and coexists as an engine.create layer.
cons: Does not integrate Jev into anything: ships zero consumer hooks, so installing it changes no behavior. User still has to author their own plugin/hook logic (questions, thresholds, state shaping) to get 'automatic' value.

1 star, 1 author, 3 commits, 11 days old, no tests, no CI, one release; correctness of hooks-module loading was not verifiable statically beyond string presence in the binary. Function hooks are flag-gated (CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1) and clearly experimental; could break on Claude Code update (GrowthBook gated 'tengu_plugin_hooks_modules').
Marketplace add tracks the default branch of a personal repo: unpinned supply chain for code that reads API keys from env; for client projects, pin a commit or vendor it.

Provider auto-detect picks TypeSafe before OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is also set, so set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter explicitly. Uses the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint (can change), not the v1/systemone route.

No timeout/retry/circuit breaker in the mod; latency and failure policy fall on each consumer hook. Any synchronous Jev call in a PreToolUse path adds up to 70-500 ms per tool call, and state sent (commands, diffs) goes to OpenRouter/TypeSafe which matters for client code.

Jev is a 32k-context typed classifier, not a coding model: real daily value is limited to guard/routing decisions (risk of command, does diff touch secrets, which subagent/tool to route to), not code generation or review.
entries.verdict: A small, clean, credible OpenRouter-capable client shim for Claude Code's experimental function-hooks engine, and the only route seen that enables deterministic, no-prompt Jev calls, but on its own it does nothing: you must write the consumer hooks (e.g. a Bash risk gate). Best used as a pinned/vendored foundation plus your own hook plugin, not as a finished integration.

entries.name: jev-kit (nikheal25)
entries.what: Thin (~890 lines compiled JS) Node CLI wrapper around @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 that POSTs to /v1/systemone. You pipe or pass state (stdin, --state, --state-file, --state-json, --attach files) plus named --noul/--choice/--score questions, and it prints the official System One JSON to stdout. It is a plain shell tool, with no MCP server, hook or skill shipped. Its README only offers a 'skill blurb' to paste into your own CLAUDE.md or skill. The GitHub repo github.com/nikheal25/jev-kit returns 404 (private, deleted or never public), so only the npm tarball is auditable.
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. No hook, MCP, skill or proxy ships with the package. To make Claude Code use it 'automatically' you must write your own CLAUDE.md rule or SKILL.md with a description trigger (for example 'before finishing a code change, run the jev-kit gate'), and Claude may still skip it. For a deterministic path you would need to add a Stop or PostToolUse hook that calls jev-kit yourself, which the package does not provide.
security: API key: env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or a saved key in ~/.jev-kit/config.json (dir 0700, file 0600, chmod before write; dist/config/credentials.js:73-88). There is no key CLI flag, so the key is never in argv or the process list. Good.

Sensitive-data log: EVERY run appends the full request body (all state, including piped diffs, test output and attached source files), the full response body and the response headers to ~/.jev-kit/logs/jev-kit-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (0600), with 14-day retention (dist/log/write-log.js:50-215). On a client-code machine this is a plaintext copy of code sent to Jev. Disable with JEV_KIT_LOG=off. Response headers are logged unredacted, but the request Authorization header is not captured, because only the body is recorded.

Prompt injection: state comes from untrusted diffs, logs or files and goes into a model that returns only typed probabilities. Injection can skew the numbers but cannot run anything. The help text says never to eval a Choice label. The real risk is that Claude over-trusts a skewed gate.
No shell execution, child_process, telemetry or extra network endpoints in jev-kit's own dist (grep). The only egress is through the SDK, to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL or https://api.typesafe.ai.

set-key on OpenRouter: it validates via models.list() against whatever base URL is set. If it is run without TYPESAFE_BASE_URL set, it would send the OpenRouter key to api.typesafe.ai and fail. Set the env var in the same scope, or skip set-key and use env only.
Single unknown maintainer, repo unavailable, no npm provenance, so supply-chain trust is low. Pin the version and review the tarball. The tarball itself is small and clean.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent pipes or attaches goes to the endpoint in TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (Bearer key in the header), plus the question text. That can include git diffs, test and lint output, and full source files via --attach or --state-file. There is a 32k-token state limit per request. Nothing is sent automatically: egress happens only when Claude runs the command. Locally, the same content is written to the ~/.jev-kit/logs JSONL, which is not sent anywhere. Via OpenRouter, the OpenRouter and TypeSafe data policies apply to client code.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by nature, because it is a plain command Claude runs. On a Jev failure it exits 4 (no key/config) or 5 (E_API) with one stderr line and nothing on stdout, so Claude just gets a failed Bash call and carries on. Timeout is the SDK default of 10 s per attempt with maxRetries 2 (dist/index.mjs:74,518), so the worst case is roughly 30 s plus backoff. The wrapper adds no timeout override, and no flag exposes one. The logFetch wrapper is a passthrough that cannot break the call. There is no hook, so Jev can never block Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: Close to zero standing cost. There are no MCP tools and no hooks. The only injected text is whatever the user adds: the README's 'skill blurb' is about 90 words (~130 tokens) in CLAUDE.md or a SKILL.md description. Claude should run `jev-kit --help` once per session, about 4.5k chars (~1.1k tokens), because the blurb says 'read jev-kit --help first'. The JSON output is about 300-600 chars per call.
pros: Zero standing context cost, because it ships no MCP tools or hooks. Unlike an MCP server, it adds nothing to every turn.

Right primitive fit: pipes diffs, test output or logs straight into Noul/Choice/Score with named answers, so it maps well to gates such as 'unrelated changes?', 'risk category', 'is this file relevant' and skill routing.

OpenRouter-compatible with zero code change: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (dist/index.mjs:58) and posts `${base}/v1/systemone` (line 554), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> plus JEV_KIT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 matches the OpenRouter System One route.
Small and readable: about 890 lines of compiled JS, one dependency (the first-party TypeSafe SDK), no postinstall, no shell exec and no telemetry. Easy to audit or vendor.
Sane key handling: no key flag, so nothing appears in argv or the process list. The saved key file is 0600 in a 0700 dir. Doctor and set-key never write the run log.
Stdout is JSON only, stderr is diagnostics, and stable exit codes 2/3/4/5/70. It is scriptable with jq and safe to wrap in a Stop hook you own.
The README recipes (code-handoff gate, file shortlist by per-file Noul, injection check) match how a senior dev might use a System One model.
cons: Not automatic: nothing triggers it. You need a hand-written CLAUDE.md rule or skill, and Claude will decide when to run it, which contradicts the 'never tell Claude to use jev' requirement unless you add your own hook.

Not OpenRouter-native. It relies on an SDK env var and the unverified assumption that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone body and response match TypeSafe's. doctor and set-key call GET /v1/models, which may behave differently on OpenRouter. Default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID, so you must set JEV_KIT_MODEL.
Unconditional plaintext logging of full request and response bodies (code, diffs, test output) to ~/.jev-kit/logs for 14 days. That is a real leak on client projects unless JEV_KIT_LOG=off is set.

GitHub repo is 404 and there is a single unknown maintainer with no npm provenance. It was created 2026-09-20, ten days old at audit, with 9 versions (0.1.0 to 0.1.30) in 5 days. Tests and CI claims are unverifiable and the package is unstable.

Extra latency and tokens per use: a Node cold start, a Bash round trip and about 1.1k tokens for --help. The SDK timeout is 10 s times 3 attempts, so a slow Jev can stall a Bash call for about 30 s and there is no timeout flag.
32k-token state cap and documented accuracy loss with irrelevant detail. Large diffs must be split by the caller.
Only the System One /v1/systemone route: no Decisions API, no Jev Router, no streaming or batching.
The user's secret-guard PreToolUse hook may block piping sensitive files into it. Jev's usefulness for an Opus-class coding agent is narrow anyway (gates and routing, not code generation).
entries.verdict: A tidy, low-risk, cheap-to-context CLI that could serve as the execution primitive for a self-authored Jev gate (for example a Stop hook or skill) through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter. On its own it is not an integration: it is not automatic, has an unavailable repo, a brand-new solo maintainer, and logs all state to disk by default. If used, pin 0.1.30, set JEV_KIT_LOG=off, and set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_KIT_MODEL, or better, reimplement the ~20-line fetch call yourself.

entries.name: mattn/go-jev
entries.what: Zero-dependency Go SDK (jev.go, 261 lines) plus jev-cli (646 lines) for the TypeSafe Jev System One API. It POSTs {state, model, questions} to a /v1/systemone endpoint and parses typed answers (noul, choice, score) with probabilities and confidence. The CLI has UNIX-pipeline commands: noul, choice, score, grep, ask. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. Claude Code would have to call the binary through Bash, so nothing invokes it automatically.
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is a passive CLI/SDK, so it is only used when invoked (Claude choosing to run it through Bash, or a hook the user writes). It is not usable as-is for the goal of automatic invocation. It could serve as the executable inside a user-authored PreToolUse hook or an MCP wrapper.
security: API key comes only from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and is sent as a Bearer header. jev-cli has no -key flag, so the key never appears in argv or the process list.
Zero third-party dependencies and no go.sum, so the supply-chain surface is one author and the Go stdlib.
No shell execution, no telemetry and no postinstall in the source I read. The only network call is the POST to the configured URL.
A repo-wide grep for exec./os/exec in main.go found nothing.
-url / JEV_API_URL can point anywhere and the Bearer key goes with it. The client does not check that a redirect is same-host, so a poisoned JEV_API_URL would leak the key.
If no key is set, no Authorization header is sent, which is fine for a local tensai server but silently unauthenticated.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the caller pipes into stdin or -s, plus the question text and criteria, sent as JSON to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if repointed, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe). It sends nothing on its own. Code, diffs or tool output leave the machine only if Claude Code (or a hook) pipes them in. Client-project code would go to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe).
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per invocation, and the failure is visible to the caller. Exit status 2 on error and 1 on 'no'. Default timeout is 60 s including retries (jev.go:20), and 429/529 are retried with exponential backoff for up to 3 retries (500 ms, 1 s, 2 s). A slow or down Jev can therefore block the caller for up to about 60 s unless JEV_TIMEOUT is set low (say 2 s). Ambiguity: exit 1 means both 'no' and 'grep found nothing'. A wrapper hook would need its own fail-open logic (timeout 3, ignore non-zero, exit 0).
entries.contextCost: Zero. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook or skill text. Claude would only know about it if the user adds a CLAUDE.md line or a skill, which would cost a few hundred tokens.
pros: Cleanest OpenRouter path of any client: JEV_API_URL, JEV_MODEL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY are all env-configurable with no code change (cmd/jev-cli/main.go:180-196), so the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone endpoint and typesafe/jev-1.13 plug in directly.
Stdlib-only Go, about 900 lines of source. Small enough to audit in minutes, and the audit here found no exec, telemetry or hidden network calls.
The key is read from the environment only, never from argv, so it does not show in ps.

A single static binary with fast startup is a good fit as the executable inside a fail-open PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook. The `noul -q` exit code, `choice` and `ask` (several questions in one request, JSON out) are exactly the hook-friendly primitives.
JEV_TIMEOUT and -timeout allow a hard low timeout, and the 429/529 retry logic is sensible.
Tests plus a 3-OS CI matrix, MIT license, and prebuilt release binaries so Go is not needed on the box.
The typed output (float or an enumerated option) gives no free-text injection channel back into Claude's context.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. It gives Claude Code no automatic invocation, which was the user's main requirement. The user would have to write the hook or wrapper glue themselves.
Default timeout is 60 s with up to 3 retries, which is unsafe for a hook on the tool path unless overridden. Exit codes do not distinguish 'no' from error in every mode, so a wrapper needs care.
No OpenRouter mention anywhere in the repo (grep is empty). OpenRouter parity is inferred from the brief and untested, and OpenRouter's Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) is not supported at all.
The API key must live in a var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY even when it is an OpenRouter key, which is confusing next to a real TypeSafe key.
One week old, v0.0.3, single maintainer, 8 commits, requires Go 1.27 to build from source, and release binaries have no visible signing.
No persistent process or connection reuse, so a TLS handshake on every call adds latency on a per-tool-call hook.
Sending code or diffs to Jev for routing decisions leaks client-project content to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and Jev's own usefulness for coding decisions is unproven.
entries.verdict: go-jev is a clean, auditable, dependency-free client that switches to OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is a passive CLI/SDK and provides no automatic Claude Code integration. Use it at most as the binary behind a self-written fail-open hook (with JEV_TIMEOUT around 2 s), not as the integration itself.

judge.why: Passive Go CLI/SDK from a well-known author; usable from a hook via Bash but nothing automatic and Go is off-stack.
pros: 40 stars, small, scriptable CLI
Well-known maintainer
cons: No integration; you write the hook
OpenRouter path unconfirmed, alpha

entries.name: simota/tenbin
entries.what: A design-time toolkit for TypeSafe System One (Jev), not a runtime helper. It has three parts: a stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript, wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk) with tools to lint, evaluate, batch-evaluate, rerank and walk taxonomies; an Agent Skill (/tenbin, SKILL.md) with a procedure, templates and offline Python scripts; and docs. The intended workflow is that a human asks Claude to design a Jev integration (decompose a judgment into Choice/Score/Noul questions, lint them, measure accuracy per confidence band on labelled data, put thresholds in code), and the resulting application code calls the TypeSafe SDK directly. It does not route Claude Code's own coding decisions through Jev, and it has no hooks.
interface: MCP prompts: tenbin, design_integration, design_questions, decompose_judgment (+1)
Makefile targets: install-claude, register-claude, link-claude, env-file, build-mcp
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. Claude may load the skill on its own when the task looks like classify, route, triage, spam or injection detection, ranking or thresholds. The skill description is keyword-rich, so it will trigger on such requests without the user saying 'jev'. MCP tools are used when Claude decides to. It is never a deterministic hook, and nothing is a transparent proxy. Its trigger is 'the user is building an application feature that needs typed judgments', not 'Claude needs a decision while coding'. Most daily coding sessions will never trigger it. Its own README also says the intended entry is `/tenbin` or 'use the tenbin skill'.
security: API key handling: it is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var. The Makefile registers the server as `claude mcp add tenbin -- sh -c 'set -a; . $HOME/.config/tenbin/env; set +a; exec node .../dist/index.js'`. The key stays out of ~/.claude.json and out of argv, and lives in a chmod 600 env file (Makefile:14, 66-69). This is better than most MCPs, though the wrapper sources the file as shell, so the file is executable code owned by the user.
Alternative documented registration `claude mcp add tenbin -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$TYPESAFE_API_KEY` writes the key into ~/.claude.json (README:~140).
Logging: client.ts:33-38 forces the SDK logger to warn and error only, on stderr, because debug logs would print request bodies unredacted. The README warns never to set TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug.

No shell execution in the server. grep finds no exec, spawn or child_process in tenbin/src, and there is no telemetry code and no postinstall script. The only outbound network calls go through the SDK to api.typesafe.ai.

Prompt-injection surface: the MCP prompts and the skill tell the agent to inspect project files and then generate code (prompts.ts, SKILL.md). Repository contents are handled as data, with an explicit note not to follow them, but the skill still steers the agent to write code with wide edit scope. Jev is also documented as weak against adversarial input.

Supply chain: a single maintainer, 7 commits, a brand-new repo with no releases, and no lockfile audit or CI. @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (created 2026-09-12, MIT) is the only third-party API dependency besides the MCP SDK and zod. A budget guard exists (default 20M tokens, about $0.84 per process, plus a per-call cap of 60k).
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine unless Claude calls tenbin_evaluate, tenbin_evaluate_many, tenbin_rank, tenbin_walk_taxonomy or tenbin_list_models, or runs evaluate.py. What is sent is exactly the state and questions JSON that the agent composed for that call: it can be file contents, tickets, code snippets or candidate lists. It goes to api.typesafe.ai, or to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says, with the Bearer key. Prompts, diffs and tool outputs are not sent automatically. The lint tool, the prompts, the resources and the offline skill scripts send nothing. There are no hooks, so no passive capture of the coding session. This matters for client projects, because the agent chooses which state to send.
entries.failureMode: The server is not on any hot path and has no hooks, so the effect is per tool call. Without a key it starts in offline mode with only lint, prompts and resources (server.ts:24 returns early when the gateway is null). With a key, the SDK does automatic retries with backoff. Errors come back as an isError tool result with guidance (client.ts describeError), so it is effectively fail-open: Claude just gets a tool error and continues. Timeouts are the SDK defaults, and there is a budget, a size cap and a cancellation signal. evaluate.py uses a 60s timeout with retries. A 5xx, 429 or timeout only degrades the current design-time task.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools when a key is set (1 when there is none). Tool descriptions total about 1.7k characters, plus zod schemas for state, questions, options and so on, which I estimate at 2 to 3k tokens for the tool block. That is small compared with Playwright or GitNexus. It also registers 5 MCP prompts and about 8 resources, which are listed but not injected. The `tenbin` prompt, when invoked, injects roughly 15 to 25 KB of guides (about 5k tokens), and the skill body is 12 KB (about 3k tokens) once triggered. The skill description is a 351-char trigger string that sits in the skill listing every session. There are no hooks and no MCP server 'instructions' text.
pros: Real, non-trivial, well-structured code: 7 tools with lint, budget guard, per-call token caps, concurrency pool and error-to-advice mapping (client.ts, tools/*). 68 offline tests with a fake fetch.

The best key handling I have seen among these candidates. The key goes in a chmod 600 env file, the wrapper is registered so the key never lands in argv or ~/.claude.json, and SDK debug logging is forced off (Makefile:14, client.ts:33-38).
A cheap-to-run offline mode: tenbin_lint_questions, the prompts and the guides work with no key and no network, so it can be evaluated with zero spend.
Small context footprint (7 tools, about 2 to 3k tokens) compared with the user's Playwright and GitNexus MCPs.

Genuine value for one job: if the user builds apps that will call Jev, it gives measured Choice/Score/Noul design, calibration on labelled data and cost estimation, and its skill description can auto-trigger for such tasks.
Switching to OpenRouter looks nearly config-only. The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone, which maps to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (unverified against a live call).
MIT licence, a single small dependency set, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec in the server.
cons: It does not do what the user asked for. It uses Jev to help design Jev-powered application code. It does not use Jev to make Claude Code's own decisions such as which file to read, whether a command is safe, or routing, and there are no hooks. Its README states 'Everything runs at design time'.
Auto-invocation is limited to model-discretion skill or tool triggers. On most daily coding tasks it will not fire, and the workflow assumes the user asks for '/tenbin' or 'use the tenbin skill'.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs. It needs an env-var hack (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus the OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY plus an OpenRouter model id). tenbin_list_models will likely break because /v1/models has a different shape, and it is unverified. The hardcoded $0.042 price and 'jev-latest' alias assume TypeSafe direct.

Immature: created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 7 commits from 1 author, 4 stars, no releases, no CI, not on npm, so it has to be built from a git clone and pinned by SHA. The build uses TypeScript ^7.0.2.
Much of the skill and README is in Japanese in places (for example the /tenbin examples), and the skill is a heavy 12 KB SKILL.md plus about 25 KB of guides, which cost context when triggered.

Egress risk on client work: whatever state the agent packs into an evaluate or rank call is sent to a third-party service (TypeSafe or OpenRouter). The tool descriptions actively push the agent to 'put every question that uses this state here, including speculative ones', which encourages broad state.

Prompt and skill text steers the agent toward large generation tasks (design_integration writes SDK code, wiring and tests), which can conflict with the user's existing hooks and workflow if it triggers unexpectedly.
entries.verdict: The most complete Jev tooling I found, with good key hygiene and an offline mode, but it is a design-time toolkit for building Jev-powered apps. It is not an automatic Jev-in-the-loop for Claude Code, and it has no OpenRouter support out of the box (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL might make it work, untested). Keep it as an optional skill or MCP for projects that actually adopt Jev, not as the answer to 'Claude uses Jev automatically'.

judge.why: Skill and MCP that teaches Claude when to classify, route or triage with Jev; model-discretion only.
pros: Claude may load the skill itself when tasks look like classify, triage, spam or ranking
Threshold guidance for typed decisions
cons: Model discretion, not deterministic; OpenRouter path partial
Alpha, 4 stars; adds skill listing cost and MCP surface; unclear coding value

entries.name: @fiale-plus/jev-cli
entries.what: Unofficial Node CLI (bin `jev`) and TS re-export layer over the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. Sends state + typed questions (noul/choice/score) to System One, prints JSON with probabilities, and adds an offline "decision pipeline": bundled packs (verify, screen, route), a fail-closed policy gate with exit codes (0 accept, 2 review, 3 deny, 4 abstain), decision records (state hashed not stored), replay, JSONL batch, doctor, lint. It is not an MCP server and has no hook, skill or plugin manifest. Its CLAUDE.md states "No MCP surface: deliberately out of scope".
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted, or via instructions the user adds. The package ships no hook, skill or MCP, so nothing fires by itself. Claude Code would call `jev` through Bash only if CLAUDE.md or a skill tells it to. A deterministic PreToolUse hook could call `jev decide`, but the user would have to write it. The official typesafe-ai/skills repo (linked from the CLI help) is the more suitable trigger layer.
security: MIT license.
One runtime dependency, the official @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0. No postinstall or preinstall script. `prepare` (npm run build) runs only on git installs or local npm install, not on a registry install.
No child_process, exec, spawn, telemetry or analytics, and no direct fetch in src/ (grep). All network traffic goes through the SDK.

Key handling: env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY is supported, but `--api-key <key>` is also accepted. That would expose the key in argv and the process list, and Claude's transcript, so use the env var only. doctor reports key presence and source, never the value.
SDK logger is forced to stderr (client.ts:48-62). At debug level it may log request details.
Prompt-injection surface: the CLI outputs only numbers and enums, no free text, which limits injection back into Claude. The `screen` pack is documented as advisory, not a security boundary.
entries.dataEgress: ["Whatever the caller passes as --state, --state-file or --stdin, plus the question instructions, goes to the configured base URL (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe as the model host). Nothing is collected automatically.","Claude Code would have to choose and pipe the content itself: code, diffs, file contents or tool output. That matters for client projects.","Records store a sha256 of the state, not the state itself."]
entries.failureMode: Inference commands exit 1 on timeout, transport or API error. The SDK defaults are a 10 s timeout and 2 retries, so a hung call could add about 30 s or more if the caller uses it (override with --timeout/--retries). Whether that blocks Claude depends on the caller, because the CLI is not a hook. Gate and decide are fail-closed (a missing answer abstains, exit 4), which fits approval gates but would block a workflow if wired blindly into a hook. There is no fail-open mode. A hook wrapper would need `|| true` or its own timeout.
entries.contextCost: Zero for tools, since it is not an MCP server. It adds no server instructions and injects no hook text. Cost appears only if the user adds a CLAUDE.md or skill snippet to teach Claude when to call it, roughly 300-800 tokens. Each call also costs a Bash tool call and its output, a few hundred tokens of JSON.
pros: The only candidate here with a working, evidence-based OpenRouter route. The SDK posts to ${baseURL}/v1/systemone with Bearer auth, and OpenRouter documents exactly this env-var swap (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api).
Zero context cost. It is a plain CLI with no MCP tool schemas, which suits a user who already runs gitnexus, playwright and caveman-shrink.
Decision-oriented design: exit codes 0/2/3/4, `decide --format decision` printing one word, and fail-closed gating. This is easy to wrap in a small PreToolUse hook for gating risky actions.
The `route` and `screen` packs (handler routing, prompt-injection screening of untrusted content) are directly relevant to agent workflows.
Thin and auditable. One runtime dependency (the official SDK), no postinstall, no shell exec, no telemetry. Records hash the state instead of storing it.
Hard-coded price estimate of $42 per 1M input tokens matches the brief's ~$0.042 per 1M (the code comment says per Btok, but the value is the same). Each response carries cost.estimated_usd.
cons: No automatic integration. It ships no hook, skill, MCP or plugin. The user's requirement of Claude Code using Jev without being told is unmet unless the user writes their own hook or CLAUDE.md rules.
Very young and single-maintainer: 13 days old, 11 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, v0.2.0, and the maintainer's own 'unofficial' disclaimer. The API surface is churning (0.1.0 to 0.2.0 in 2 days).
`jev models` and `doctor --live` probably break on OpenRouter, because they call GET /v1/models expecting {models:[...]}. I did not verify OpenRouter's response shape.

It is a bare wrapper over the official SDK with no OpenRouter-specific logic, and it does not use the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions). It also does not mention OPENROUTER_API_KEY anywhere. The user must remember the misleading TYPESAFE_* env names.
The `--api-key` flag puts the key in argv. The existing secret-leak guard hook watching Bash would flag this.
Not fail-open. The SDK default is a 10 s timeout with 2 retries, and gate abstains with exit 4. Wired naively into a hook it could stall or block Claude Code.

Weak daily-coding value. Jev answers only typed decision questions (route, verify, noul/choice/score), not code. The best case is gating or routing, and the model quality is unverified (the skeptic claim that it is 'a DeepSeek flash router' remains unresolved).
Sending code, diffs or tool output to a third party (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe) from client projects has data-policy implications.
entries.verdict: A clean, honest CLI that is the most reliable way to reach OpenRouter-hosted Jev through the official SDK, since only two env vars need changing. But it is a building block rather than an integration: it has no hook, skill or MCP, so it cannot deliver 'Claude uses Jev automatically' on its own. Use it as the engine behind a custom hook or skill, pinned to a version, and treat it as alpha software.

entries.name: PerryLink/jevcore (jevcore-mcp)
entries.what: TypeScript monorepo (core `jevcore`, `jevcore-dsh` DeepSeek Harness plugin, `jevcore-mcp` stdio MCP server, CLI). The MCP package exposes 3 model-invoked tools (jev_ask, jev_rank, jev_check) over the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, with an egress contract (per-feature field caps + best-effort secret redaction) and an offline mock provider as default. Primary target is DeepSeek Harness, not Claude Code; the MCP server is a secondary adapter. It is a passive tool server: nothing runs unless Claude decides to call a tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code decides to call jev_ask/jev_rank/jev_check from the tool descriptions ('judgments the rest of the work branches on - routing, classifying, scoring, triaging'). The package ships no Claude Code hook, skill or plugin. To make usage reliable without user prompting, the user would need to add CLAUDE.md guidance or their own hook/skill; expect low and inconsistent call rates since Opus can classify and read evidence itself.
security: No postinstall/install scripts in jevcore-mcp or jevcore (npm view shows only test/build/clean/smoke scripts); no child_process/exec in core or mcp src; no telemetry found in repo code (SDK @typesafe-ai/sdk not audited).

API key is read from env by name at startup (runtime.ts:122), never from argv, never logged per SECURITY.md; SDK log level pinned and 'debug' clamped so request bodies are not logged (live.ts:352-366). Key visible only in ~/.claude.json env block / process environment, not in process args, if configured via --env.

Redaction is best-effort (redact.ts): named sensitive keys plus known secret shapes (sk-, Bearer, AWS/GitHub/Google, JWT, PEM, conn strings). Unrecognised secrets in free text pass through; README states this openly.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results are JSON of numbers/enum labels only, no free text returned from Jev (low). But candidates/evidence strings supplied by Claude are sent verbatim, so untrusted file content Claude passes in reaches a third party.

Single-maintainer project (PerryLink, 40+ sibling DSH plugins, star-farming CTA and directory badges in README) created 2026-09-20 and 10 days old; npx -y would pull whatever is latest unless version-pinned; supply-chain trust is low-medium. Apache-2.0, npm maintainer perrylink. OpenSSF Scorecard workflow present.
Explicit auth-model honesty: startup egress report to stderr; gates hard-off in MCP; tools unrestricted by config (MCP has no config surface to cap fields, runtime.ts:106-111).
entries.dataEgress: On each tool call only: the `state` (jev_ask, capped 16,000 chars, truncated with truncated:true) and question text (cap 4,000, refused if over); jev_rank sends query + all candidates + criterion; jev_check sends claim + evidence. Content is whatever Claude chooses to pass (code snippets, diffs, file text possible). Passed through redaction first (best-effort). Destination with OpenRouter route: https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OpenRouter key (OpenRouter retention/logging applies; in beta). Nothing is sent automatically, no background traffic, no whole-conversation or tool-output interception. Retries can resend the same payload up to 3 times (docs/limits.md). Offline mock is default when no key is present.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open because it is a model-called tool: errors return isError text (server.ts:109-117) and Claude proceeds. But latency bound is long: per-attempt 10s, 2 retries, total budget 40s (config.ts:249-250, classify.ts:311-312, docs/limits.md), and MCP runtime wires no circuit breaker, cache or budget (runtime.ts:154-159 builds JevService with provider/egress only; breaker/cache/budget modules exist in core/resilience but are not used by the MCP entry), so an outage blocks up to ~40s on every call. Startup: if JEV_PROVIDER=live/openrouter with no key, the process exits with error (runtime.ts:123-129, MCP shows failed to connect). Trap: if the key is not delivered and JEV_PROVIDER is unset, it silently runs the MOCK provider that returns hash-derived synthetic answers, with a `warning` field in each result (tools.ts:179-182); Claude might still be misled.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Tool definitions (descriptions + zod schemas rendered to JSON schema) roughly 8k chars of source text in server.ts (about 2,600 chars of question schema plus about 5,300 chars of tool blocks) => roughly 2,000-2,500 tokens after JSON-schema expansion; with Claude Code MCP tool search/deferred tools this is loaded on demand. No MCP `instructions` field set (new McpServer({name,version}) only, server.ts:128). No hooks, so no injected text. Note verbose descriptions (jev_rank description ~1,400 chars of caps arithmetic).
pros: Only candidate here that actually implements OpenRouter routing in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects the openrouter provider and posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (runtime.ts:60-61, openrouter.ts:56,223); no patching needed.
Honest, disclosed egress design: startup stderr report, per-feature caps (16k state / 4k questions), redaction, mock-by-default; no gates or hooks that silently ship tool outputs in MCP mode.
Small surface: 3 tools, no postinstall, no shell exec, key from env not argv, SDK body logging clamped.

Tool descriptions say when NOT to use Jev and demand threshold-application by the caller; jev_check gives a useful supports/contradicts/insufficient distinction; noul 'boundary' support aligns with Jev's docs.
Extensive tests and CI including real stdio smoke test; Apache-2.0; uses TypeSafe's official SDK rather than reimplementing the protocol; Node 24 compatible.
Reaches Jev via model-ID-based System One route so hosted-on-OpenRouter billing works with one key.
cons: Not built for Claude Code: primary target is DeepSeek Harness; no CC hooks/skill/plugin, so 'automatic use without prompting' is not delivered; only description-based model discretion, which Opus 5.5 will rarely need for these tasks.

Repo is 10 days old, single real maintainer (50 commits are a bot-like 'dsh-jev' identity plus PerryLink; 1 GitHub contributor), 0 forks, 0 releases on GitHub, 1 issue; README pushes star CTAs and directory badges; author runs a 40+ plugin farm. Package 0.4.1 was published only on 2026-09-20 while GitHub HEAD is 4 days later. CHANGELOG admits jev_ask returned invalid output on every call in published 0.3.1, and earlier versions had wrong OpenRouter endpoint/model handling: quality churn is high.

Untested against real OpenRouter by me: claims like 'typesafe/jev-latest is rejected by the route' are unverified comments; the openrouter path relies on TypeSafe's SDK with baseURL override and openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone acceptance, and the code does not cover the documented /api/alpha/decisions surface or the '~typesafe/jev-latest' and 'Jev Router' model IDs (regex only allows jev-* or typesafe/jev-*; runtime.ts default 'jev-latest' bare).
Failure latency: 40s worst case per call, no circuit breaker or cache wired into the MCP entry (runtime.ts:154-159).
Silent mock fallback if the key isn't injected (synthetic hash-derived answers with just a warning field); with key + JEV_PROVIDER unset, TypeSafe key takes precedence over OpenRouter.
Redaction cannot catch unrecognised secrets; client projects' code passed by Claude leaves the machine to OpenRouter -> TypeSafe. No user-side field-cap or allow/deny config in MCP.

Low intrinsic value in coding: Jev is a typed classifier, no prose/reasoning; use cases (rank candidates, check claim/evidence) mostly duplicated by Opus itself, at extra turn cost and ~2k tokens of tool definitions.
entries.verdict: A tidy, honestly-documented 3-tool MCP adapter that genuinely supports the OpenRouter route via env var only, but it is a DeepSeek-Harness-first, 10-day-old single-maintainer project with no Claude Code hooks or skill, so it cannot deliver 'automatic' Jev use and adds little over Opus for daily coding. Reasonable as a version-pinned experimental MCP (user scope, OPENROUTER_API_KEY + JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter) only if paired with your own CLAUDE.md/skill/hook trigger.

entries.name: @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai (Vercel AI SDK provider)
entries.what: A small (about 300 LOC of source) Vercel AI SDK provider that exposes TypeSafe System One (Jev) as an experimental "evaluationModel". It works with `experimental_evaluate` from the `ai` package. One POST to `<baseURL>/systemone` sends `{model, state, questions}` and maps choice, score and boolean (noul) answers to typed results with probabilities and confidence. It is a TypeScript library only. It has no MCP server, no hooks, no skill and no CLI, so it does nothing inside Claude Code unless someone writes a hook or MCP server on top of it.
entries.autoInvocation: Not applicable: it is a library, so it only runs when other code calls it. Automatic use inside Claude Code needs a custom deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse or PostToolUse) that calls it. That is the only way to meet the 'without prompting' requirement, because an MCP tool or skill is at the model's discretion.
security: Small surface: 2 runtime deps (@ai-sdk/provider, @ai-sdk/provider-utils), no postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json scripts are build and test only), no shell execution, no telemetry, and no process.env access other than through loadApiKey for TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY.
npm provenance is enabled (SLSA attestation, published by GitHub Actions OIDC via vercel-release-bot).
The API key travels only in an Authorization: Bearer header (no argv exposure). A key set in the environment will be visible in /proc/<pid>/environ.
A User-Agent suffix 'ai-sdk-typesafe-ai/<version>' is added, which is harmless.
Prompt-injection surface: none in the package itself, because it returns numbers and enum choices only. A future hook that feeds the result into Claude context would carry only probabilities.
Repo license is 'Other' per GitHub (Vercel AI's LICENSE), while the npm package declares Apache-2.0.
entries.dataEgress: Everything the caller places in `state` and `questions` is sent to the configured baseURL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai if overridden). The package adds nothing on its own. If a Claude Code hook were built on it, whatever that hook puts in `state` would leave the machine: prompt text, file contents, diffs and tool output. That matters for client projects. The Authorization header carries the API key. No other endpoints are contacted.
entries.failureMode: The library throws APICallError on failure. There is no timeout in the package, only abortSignal passthrough, and core retries 429 and 529 twice. Fail-open or fail-closed is entirely up to the consumer, for example a hook wrapper with its own AbortSignal.timeout that exits 0 on error. The library gives no default protection against a hung request.
entries.contextCost: Zero on its own: no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook text. Any wrapper would add its own cost. A hook that stays silent unless it decides to intervene adds nothing. An MCP wrapper would add about 1 to 3 tools, roughly 500 to 1500 tokens of definitions.
pros: Same Jev OpenRouter schema, trivially pointed at it: base URL override plus apiKey covers openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (evaluation-model.ts:109, provider.ts:27). No fork is needed.
Tiny, readable code (5 source files, 2 runtime deps, no install scripts, npm provenance). It is easy to audit and safe as a building block for a custom hook.
Typed handling of Choice, Score and Noul, with client-side limits (255 options, 10 score levels), rounding metadata, and confidence exposed under providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence.
Backed by Vercel and the AI SDK release process (repo has 27k stars, active pushes on 2026-09-30, unit tests for provider and model, an edge-runtime test config). 12 releases in 2 weeks.
Batches multiple questions against one state in a single request, which suits a hook that asks several gating questions at once.
cons: It is not an integration with Claude Code: it has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI. The user would have to write and maintain the hook or MCP wrapper, which is the actual hard part.

It requires the `ai` package and the `experimental_evaluate` API, which is explicitly experimental and may change. Using it in a hook script adds the ai, zod and provider-utils dependency tree to a tool that only needs one fetch call. A direct `fetch` to /systemone is about 20 lines.

Defaults are wrong for this user: the env var is TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY (the user wants OPENROUTER_API_KEY), the base URL is api.typesafe.ai, and the default model 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter id (it needs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest). Everything must be overridden explicitly.
Only System One /systemone is covered. There is no OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) and no Jev Router model support.
No timeout, no fail-open behavior and no caching in the package. A hung request on a PreToolUse hook could stall every tool call unless the wrapper adds AbortSignal.timeout.
The Vercel AI Gateway claim in the discovery data is not backed by the package or the ai-sdk.dev page.
Sending code, diffs or tool output as `state` in a hook egresses client-project data to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe). Nothing in the package mitigates this.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe and OpenRouter-patchable client library, but it is only a building block. It gives zero automatic Claude Code integration by itself and pulls in an experimental `ai` API for what a plain fetch could do. Rate it as a possible dependency for a custom hook, not as an integration. Prefer a dedicated MCP server or hook that already targets /systemone, or a thin custom fetch-based hook script.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (npm manifest); GitHub reports 'Other' for vercel/ai

entries.name: OpenRouter guide: TypeSafe SDK on OpenRouter (@typesafe-ai/sdk + typesafe-sdk)
entries.what: A documentation page (not a Claude Code integration) explaining that the official TypeSafe SDKs (@typesafe-ai/sdk on npm, typesafe-sdk on PyPI) can be pointed at OpenRouter by setting baseURL=https://openrouter.ai/api and using an OpenRouter key, so client.systemOne({model:'jev-1.13', state, questions}) POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. The SDKs are thin typed HTTP clients (retry, timeout, Zod/pydantic-style typed answers). They ship no MCP server, no hooks, no skills, no CLI. The OpenRouter Jev hub does link a separate cookbook recipe, "Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev", which is the closest thing to a Claude Code integration: a ~150-line Bun/TS PermissionRequest hook that sends Bash commands to POST /api/alpha/decisions with 2 Noul questions (reversible, serves_task; threshold 0.9) after a static RISKY regex list. That recipe uses raw fetch, not the SDK. The SDK is only useful as a building block for custom hooks or MCP tools.
interface: (no MCP tools, no hook events, no SKILL.md, no CLI)
entries.autoInvocation: SDK: none (library). Via the cookbook's PermissionRequest hook: deterministic hook, fully automatic, but ONLY when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog (per the doc: hook 'never sees commands that an allow rule already covers'). In bypassPermissions mode no dialogs occur, so this hook effectively never fires; in 'auto' mode the built-in classifier handles approvals (inference; not verified for PermissionRequest firing there).
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts in JS package.json (checked); no curl|sh installer; MIT; publish via GitHub Actions publish.yml only.

API key sent only as Authorization: Bearer header (js/src/client.ts:354, py transport.py:121), never in argv. Key lives in env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or constructor; a hook process inherits it from Claude Code env, so OPENROUTER_API_KEY must sit in settings.json env or shell profile (visible to every child process). Log level debug prints headers/bodies (client.ts debug logging) - keep at default warn.
SDK sends non-sensitive telemetry-like headers on every call: User-Agent, X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime (client.ts:355-358); no separate telemetry endpoint found in source.

Prompt-injection surface: any state sent to Jev is attacker-influenceable text (file contents, command strings, repo README). Jev returns only numbers, so it cannot be instructed to run tools, but a poisoned state can push probabilities (cookbook itself warns: the static RISKY list, not the threshold, is the security boundary; Jev cannot know a 'cat foo' reads a secret).

Beta model, third-party (TypeSafe) receives content via OpenRouter; OpenRouter data policy for typesafe/jev-1.13 not verified from model page (WebFetch not used); treat client code as sensitive. Existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook should also run before anything is sent.
Cookbook hook idea itself is a permission-bypass risk if misconfigured: an 'allow' from the hook grants the command; deny rules still win per doc.
entries.dataEgress: SDK/Decisions call sends exactly what the integrator puts in 'state' and 'questions' (JSON body, model id). In the cookbook Claude Code hook: the Bash command string, cwd (project path), and optionally tool_input.description (the agent's one-line description; not the user task on Claude Code). No file contents, diffs or transcript by default, but the state is arbitrary so a custom hook could send anything. Traffic goes to openrouter.ai then to TypeSafe as provider. Plus SDK headers (SDK version, runtime).
entries.failureMode: SDK: throws on failure; defaults are 10 s timeout per attempt (retry.ts:5, py constants.py DEFAULT_TIMEOUT=10.0), maxRetries 2 with backoff 0.5-5 s on 408/429/5xx/connection/timeouts (retry.ts:10-22), so worst case roughly 30+ s before throwing; Python retry overall cap 30 s. Fail behavior is decided by the integrator's code. Cookbook hook is fail-open-to-prompt (any error/timeout 8 s returns undefined -> no decision -> normal permission flow; the hook timeout is 15 s). In headless `claude -p` / background subagents, no decision means deny. Cursor's version differs (failClosed flag).
entries.contextCost: SDK itself: zero context (not an MCP server/skill). Cookbook PermissionRequest hook: zero tokens injected (prints nothing unless allowing), so no context cost. A custom MCP wrapper would cost ~1-3 small tools (~300-800 tokens).
pros: Confirms the OpenRouter path is trivial and official: baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key; identical request/response schema to TypeSafe direct (doc + js/src/client.ts:321).
SDKs are clean, MIT, typed, well tested (JS ~120 test cases, dist tests, Python pytest), no install scripts, sane defaults (10 s timeout, 2 retries), Bearer key not in argv.
Gives typed Choice/Noul/Score helpers, which makes writing a robust custom hook or a tiny MCP wrapper easy (answer types inferred).

The linked cookbook provides a real, deterministic Claude Code integration pattern (PermissionRequest hook, static RISKY list first, 0.9 threshold, fail-to-prompt) that needs no model discretion and injects zero context.
Very cheap: ~$0.00002 per decision; free output tokens.
cons: Not an integration: no MCP tools, hooks, skills, or CLI in either SDK repo; the user must write and maintain everything, contradicting 'automatic integration' out of the box.
SDK reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY not OPENROUTER_API_KEY; models.list() is broken against OpenRouter; default base URL is api.typesafe.ai so a missed override sends the OpenRouter key to TypeSafe.

Repos are ~4 weeks old (created 2026-09-04), JS SDK 0.6.0 / Python 0.7.x, beta model; API is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha) and shallow public history (5-6 commits, bot-authored) offers little track record. Skeptic claim that Jev is a small flash router remains unverified.

The only automatic Claude Code use case documented (permission auto-approve) does nothing for this user: bypass mode never prompts, and 'auto' mode already uses a classifier. The hook also adds a network call per prompt and would only ever approve, not improve code quality.

Jev returns probabilities without reasoning and cannot see secrets it is not shown; the cookbook admits the static regex list is the real safety boundary. Sending client-project commands/paths to a third-party provider via OpenRouter is a data-governance issue for client work.

No obvious daily-coding value: Jev is a classifier/router, not a code model; hooks on PreToolUse would add 70-500 ms plus cold start to every Bash/Read/Grep on top of the already-loaded secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
entries.verdict: Useful only as a low-level building block: it proves OpenRouter can host Jev with a base-URL swap, but it is a library, not a Claude Code integration, and the closest documented automatic pattern (PermissionRequest auto-approve hook) is a no-op in this user's bypass/auto workflow. Recommend using raw fetch to /api/alpha/decisions (as in the cookbook) rather than adding an SDK dependency if any custom hook is built.
