entries.name: rhighs/jev-code
entries.what: Experimental coding CLI where Jev, decision-only, selects AST productions grammar-rule by rule; TypeScript SDK with decision sessions, typed routers, and 'decide' CLI mode.
entries.autoInvocation: manual
pros: 'jev-code decide' is a shell-callable Noul/Choice/Score primitive; good SDK reference
Docs, eval tasks, CI
cons: Its own agent, not a Claude Code plugin; stores key in ~/.config; install via curl|sh
No OpenRouter path, no license file

entries.name: AntonioCoppe/jev-harness
entries.what: Unofficial TypeScript library (v0.1.0, not published to npm as far as inspected; clone or install from git) wrapping @typesafe-ai/sdk. DecisionHarness.run() sends state plus choice/score/noul questions to /v1/systemone, aggregates a mean confidence, applies a user-written policy (default minConfidence 0.55, low-confidence result becomes review/escalate/suppress), and supports a shadow mode (returns shadow_noop) and JSONL/OTEL/PostHog decision loggers. It also ships about 40 copy-paste TS recipes (shell-command-gate, pr-risk-gate, done-claim-check, tool-exec-gate and others) and an offline/live eval CLI (jev-eval). It has no MCP server, no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json and no Claude Code integration. The README states it is not a Claude Code /compact replacement. It is a building block for writing your own gate, not a ready-made integration.
interface: Loggers: Console (default), File JSONL, OTEL, PostHog

recipes/* (about 40, e.g. verify-gate/shell-command-gate.ts, pr-risk-gate.ts, done-claim-check.ts, injection-check.ts, tool-call-allowlist.ts, agent-comm-harness/tool-exec-gate.ts, candidate-action-selection/skill-roster-pick.ts)
entries.autoInvocation: None as shipped. It is a library only ("only when prompted" / code you write). It could power a deterministic hook (PreToolUse, Stop) if the user writes a small Node wrapper around it, so it is a possible engine for a hook, not the integration.
security: MIT licensed; both repo and @typesafe-ai/sdk@0.6.0 are MIT
API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or the apiKey option, sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv by the library itself.
No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer in package.json. Only runtime dependency is @typesafe-ai/sdk; playwright, vitepress and tsx are devDependencies only.
Optional PostHog logger sends decision metadata to us.i.posthog.com (or POSTHOG_HOST) only if explicitly configured. It is off by default and excludes state.
The default logger prints decision JSON to stdout. In a hook, stdout is parsed by Claude Code, so it must be disabled with logger:false or redirected to avoid corrupting hook output.

Prompt-injection surface: if used as a gate over untrusted commands or diffs, the classifier input is attacker-controlled. Typed output limits the blast radius, but the recipes' 'allow' verdicts should not be treated as a security boundary.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in `state` and `questions` is sent to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter, which then forwards to TypeSafe). For a Claude Code hook built on the recipes, that would be the full Bash command string, cwd and user goal (shell-command-gate), or diffs and PR text (pr-risk-gate), or the assistant's done-claim and evidence (done-claim-check). Nothing leaves automatically, because the library has no Claude Code wiring. Decision logs, if enabled, contain only ids, action, confidence and usage. The client is a plain fetch and adds no telemetry of its own.
entries.failureMode: Library-level: the SDK uses a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries on connection errors, timeouts, 429 and 5xx (index.mjs:74, 518). run() has no try/catch, so it throws on failure. Fail-open or fail-closed is therefore left entirely to the caller's wrapper. Worst case is about 30 s or more of stall if used naively in a hook, so a tight timeout (about 1-2 s) and retry 0 would have to be set. The recipes default to fail-closed-ish low-confidence handling (shell-command-gate: suppress), which in a PreToolUse hook would block commands, so a fail-open wrapper would be needed. Logger errors are swallowed.
entries.contextCost: Zero as shipped: no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text. A custom hook built on it would inject only what the developer chooses (for example a one-line permissionDecisionReason).
pros: Only about 600 lines of real library code (src/*.ts) that are easy to read and audit, with a clean policy and confidence-gate abstraction

Recipes map directly onto plausible Claude Code hook gates: shell-command-gate.ts (Bash allow/deny/ask with known-safe list and suppress on low confidence), done-claim-check.ts (Stop hook), pr-risk-gate.ts, injection-check.ts, tool-call-allowlist.ts, skill-roster-pick.ts
Shadow mode (mode:'shadow' returns shadow_noop with intendedAction) is a safe way to trial Jev gating in real sessions before enforcing anything
The DecisionBackend interface plus TYPESAFE_BASE_URL make OpenRouter routing a config-level change, with no fork needed
MIT licensed, a light dependency footprint (one runtime dep), no postinstall and no telemetry by default
Eval CLI with JSONL fixtures and --live allows measuring Jev's calibration on your own commands or diffs before trusting it
cons: Not an integration: no MCP server, hook config, skill or plugin manifest, so it fails the user's requirement of automatic use inside Claude Code without writing the glue yourself

No OpenRouter support in code or README (TypeSafe direct only). OpenRouter would need TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model id override, and this is unverified against the live endpoint.

Created 2026-09-18, 57 commits, single author (Antonio Coppe), 16 stars, 1 fork, no releases, no tests or CI (no test script, no .github), and not on npm. Many commits are marketing and research docs, which points to a growth-oriented rather than battle-tested project.
run() throws on network errors and the SDK retries twice with a 10 s timeout. There is no built-in fail-open behaviour, which is dangerous for a blocking PreToolUse hook unless wrapped.
Default logger writes JSON to stdout, which can pollute hook output
Aggregate confidence is a naive mean, and noul confidence is a stand-in (|p-0.5|*2). Gate quality depends on Jev's calibration, which is beta and disputed (Theo's 'flash router' claim).

Recipes such as shell-command-gate duplicate what the existing secret-leak guard and Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier already do, and its README pitch (48.9 s Claude CLI vs 1.3 s Jev) compares different capabilities and is self-reported
Each hook invocation would be a fresh Node process, adding startup and TLS costs on top of the network round trip
Sending shell commands and diffs from client projects to a third-party beta model via OpenRouter and TypeSafe raises client-confidentiality concerns
entries.verdict: This is a decision-gate library and recipe collection, not a Claude Code integration. It has no MCP, hook, skill or plugin, and it supports only TypeSafe directly, though OpenRouter is likely reachable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. It is useful mainly as reference code (shell-command-gate, done-claim-check, shadow mode) if you write your own small fail-open hook, but it is too young and unproven to depend on.

entries.name: jev-recipes (agencyenterprise/jev-recipes)
entries.what: MIT-licensed npm package (jev-recipes 0.9.5, Node >=22.9) of 248 pre-packaged Jev decision "recipes" (route, rerank, gate, grade, diff-hazards, tool-call-gate, etc.) as typed TS functions on top of @typesafe-ai/sdk client.systemOne(). Ships a CLI (list/describe/demo/example/run/evaluate/replay/compare), Vercel AI SDK and LangChain.js adapters (guardTools, routeModelStep, completionCheck, recipeTools), and one Agent Skill (skills/jev-recipes/SKILL.md) that only teaches an agent how to BUILD an app with the library. It is a developer library for app builders, not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, no hooks, no plugin.json/.mcp.json.
interface: jev-recipes/<recipe-id> subpath exports (e.g. diff-hazards, tool-call-gate, model-route)
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. The single skill triggers on the user choosing jev-recipes or asking to build with it, and its body tells the agent to use recipes in application code (npx --no-install jev-recipes list/describe). Nothing here makes Claude Code call Jev on its own. Automatic behavior would require the user to write their own PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook that shells out to `jev-recipes run tool-call-gate|diff-hazards -`.
security: Auth via env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY (Bearer header from SDK); never placed in argv, good. CLI run reads input JSON from a file or stdin so payloads are not in argv either.

package.json has prepack/prepublishOnly scripts but no postinstall/preinstall script found (grep postinstall in sdk package.json empty; repo scripts are dev-only); repo CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts.
No shell execution or curl|sh installer in library source; CLI only reads files/stdin and calls the SDK.

Prompt-injection surface: recipes take untrusted text (diffs, tool calls) as data and return constrained typed outputs, so Jev cannot emit free text into Claude context. But nothing feeds Claude Code with it automatically.
No telemetry found in src/client.ts (logLevel 'off'); the SDK default is set to off by the wrapper.
Very new (created 2026-09-22, 2 contributors, 13 stars, all pre-1.0): supply-chain trust is limited; pin versions.
entries.dataEgress: On `jev-recipes run` or any live recipe call, the JSON input you provide (e.g. a diff, a tool-call description, request text, the policy string) is sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (default) or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/baseURL is set to (OpenRouter if repointed). Nothing is sent automatically from Claude Code; egress is only what a hook or script author chooses to pipe in. The CLI help states 'Live runs send your input to TypeSafe' (cli/index.ts:63). Demo/list/describe/replay are offline.
entries.failureMode: Library level: SDK client timeout 30s (src/client.ts:11), provider or validation errors are thrown; CLI reportError prints to stderr and exits code 1. Adapters fail closed (guardTools blocks and a call with no user message throws, docs/framework-adapters.md). There is no Claude Code hook wrapper, so fail-open/closed behavior inside Claude Code would be whatever a wrapper script the user writes does; the 30s default timeout would be far too long for a hook and would need overriding.
entries.contextCost: Zero as shipped: no MCP tools, no hooks, no injected text. The only Claude context cost is the optional SKILL.md (~3.9 KB, roughly 1k tokens when loaded; description ~50 tokens always listed). Its description gates it to 'when the user chooses jev-recipes', so it will not fire automatically.
pros: Best available source of ready-made, schema-validated Jev prompts and result schemas for coding-relevant decisions: recipes/diff-hazards (secret leaks, destructive commands, debug leftovers, weakened tests, dependency changes), tool-call-gate, action-scope, action-reversibility, model-route, completion-gate. Useful raw material for a custom hook.
CLI `jev-recipes run <recipe> -` reads JSON on stdin and prints JSON, so a hook script in any language can call it without writing SDK code; the API key stays in env, not argv.

Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk; endpoint is POST ${baseURL}/v1/systemone (dist/index.mjs:554), the same path as OpenRouter's System One API, and baseURL/key/model are overridable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL / TYPESAFE_API_KEY / createClient, so repointing to OpenRouter looks trivial.

Serious engineering hygiene for its age: 250 test files, CI with npm ci --ignore-scripts and pack checks, MIT license, offline demo fixtures, evaluation harness with replayable archives, honest caveats about fixtures not measuring accuracy and model aliases drifting.
Adapters (guardTools fail-closed, completionCheck) show a sound design pattern for gating agent tool calls with Jev that could be ported to a Claude Code PreToolUse hook.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no shell exec in library code; low direct supply-chain risk beyond the two deps (@typesafe-ai/sdk, zod).
cons: Does NOT integrate with Claude Code: no MCP server, no hooks.json, no plugin.json/.mcp.json, no marketplace entry. The user's requirement (Claude must use Jev automatically, no prompting) is not met by anything in this repo.
The only skill is explicitly user-triggered and about building apps with the library, so it will never cause Claude Code to consult Jev during ordinary coding.

OpenRouter is not supported or documented anywhere (zero mentions); CLI hard-requires the env var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY (cli/index.ts:118), so using an OpenRouter key means mislabeling it, and the OpenRouter model id (typesafe/jev-1.13) and schema equivalence are unverified by the authors.
Default client timeout is 30 s (src/client.ts:11) and no fail-open wrapper exists; a naive PreToolUse hook would stall or block Claude on Jev slowness unless the user adds timeout/fail-open logic.

Node CLI cold start per invocation would add hundreds of ms on top of the API latency for every hooked tool call; 248 recipes are mostly irrelevant to coding (music, support, RAG), so only ~5-10 recipes matter.
Very young and pre-1.0: created 2026-09-22, 8 days old, 2 authors (essentially one, 83 of 104 commits), 13 stars, v0.9.5 released the same day as this audit; APIs may churn.

Docs describe TypeSafe model 'jev-1.13.0' pinning and warn aliases change behavior, adding maintenance if the user's hook depends on calibrated thresholds (minConfidence) that were tuned on a different model version.
entries.verdict: A well-tested recipe library, not a Claude Code integration: useful only as a source of prompts/schemas (diff-hazards, tool-call-gate, model-route) and as a stdin/stdout CLI that a self-written hook could call. It provides no automatic invocation, no OpenRouter support out of the box (though TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api looks like it would work), and no fail-open handling, so it does not satisfy the goal by itself.

entries.name: AbdelStark/bicameral
entries.what: TypeScript library and Pi coding agent extension: Jev-scored reflexes (tool gate, honest finish, stuck detector) with policy YAML, HUD and /why. Targets the Pi agent, not Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (Pi tool_call events)
pros: Well-structured judgment packs plus policy-as-code and secret redaction before sending state
Useful design reference for gate, finish and stuck reflexes
cons: Hooks are Pi events; no Claude Code adapter
TypeSafe SDK key only, no OpenRouter
Single day of activity, 9 stars

entries.name: docxology/daf-jev
entries.what: Python (httpx) toolkit for the System One /v1/systemone API. It contains a sync/async client, a question builder for noul/choice/score, a concurrent evaluator, confidence and tiered gates, a calibration module, a CLI, a FastMCP stdio server (`daf-jev serve`, 9 tools plus 1 resource) and an agent SKILL.md. It also has a registry of six providers, including openrouter. Much of the repo is research-style extras: a Bayes-net factor elicitation experiment, a manuscript and figures. It is a generic client and toolbox, not a Claude Code coding integration. It has no hooks and no coding-specific questions.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions are generic ("Ask named questions about one state...") and give Claude no coding triggers, so Claude will rarely or never call it unprompted. The SKILL.md description triggers only on daf-jev / System One code work. There is no hook, proxy or deterministic trigger. It does NOT meet the user's "Claude must use it automatically" requirement without extra glue such as a CLAUDE.md rule, or a custom PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook that calls `daf-jev ask`.
security: API key is read from env or a `.env` in the server's CWD (config.py load_dotenv). It is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (client.py:221), and README says it is never returned in tool output. Nothing was found that puts the key in argv on the server side. The `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` route does expose it briefly in argv and stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

The `.env` lookup uses the process CWD, so a `.env` in a client project's directory could be picked up as the source of the key. That is a minor cross-project leak vector, and it conflicts with the user's secret-guard hooks.
No shell execution or subprocess in the server path. The only subprocess use is in manuscript_variables.py, which is a dev script. No curl|sh, postinstall or telemetry found in src (grep).

The MCP tools jev_posteriors_load, jev_reask_plan and jev_docs_verify take arbitrary local file paths and read them (JSON parse). This is a small arbitrary-file-read surface if the model is prompt-injected, and it returns only parsed or validated fields. It is not directly harmful, but it is pointless surface for a coding setup.
Prompt-injection surface: tool output is typed probabilities and labels, with no free text from the model. This is low risk. The `state` argument is whatever Claude sends.
The repo commits a PDF, output files and ~280 files. Single-author, brand-new project (13 days old), version 0.6.0. It is unaudited third-party code that would run with the user's OpenRouter key.
entries.dataEgress: The `state` argument (str or JSON) and the question texts and option descriptions that Claude composes go to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, along with the model name and the OpenRouter key. In practice that means whatever snippets, diffs, file contents or task descriptions Claude decides to put into `state`; nothing is collected automatically. Nothing else leaves the machine, and there is no telemetry. OpenRouter forwards to TypeSafe, so client code could reach third parties. Client-project confidentiality needs care.
entries.failureMode: When Jev is slow or down, `jev_ask` blocks the tool call for up to 60 s per attempt (DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=60.0 in _http.py:60, or JEV_TIMEOUT). There are up to 3 attempts with 0.5-8 s backoff on 429/529 (README config table), which is worst case of about 3 minutes. A failed call returns a tool error, so Claude sees the error and carries on. It is model-discretion, so nothing structurally blocks the session, and this is effectively fail-open. A missing key raises ValueError, which surfaces as a tool error. The circuit breaker in resilience.py is opt-in and is not wired into the MCP server.
entries.contextCost: 9 tools (jev_ask, jev_evaluate, jev_models, jev_composite_score, jev_confidence_gate, jev_tiered_gate, jev_docs_verify, jev_posteriors_load, jev_reask_plan) plus 1 resource. Docstrings sum to about 4.2k chars and signatures about 0.8k chars; with JSON schema overhead I estimate about 6.5k chars, roughly 1.6k tokens. The server INSTRUCTIONS block (~1.0k chars, about 250 tokens) is injected into the system prompt. Total is roughly 1.9k tokens always-on, or about 0.3k tokens if deferred tool loading (ToolSearch) is active. Six of the tools are irrelevant to coding. Hooks inject nothing, since none exist.
pros: Gives a working, source-verified OpenRouter path: providers.py:216-233 targets https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OPENROUTER_MODEL. It has a claimed live OpenRouter run in README/receipts.

The client is a generic, well-typed System One client: strict parsing that tolerates OpenRouter's extra id/provider/usage.cost fields, retries on 429/529, a 60 s timeout, and native or spec-string question building. This is useful as a library and as a CLI (`daf-jev ask`) for writing your own hook.
The local gates (jev_confidence_gate, jev_tiered_gate, jev_composite_score) encode confidence-routing patterns that fit turning Jev probabilities into decisions.
Good engineering hygiene for a young project: MIT licence, CI with a 90% coverage gate, ruff and mypy, 35 unit-test files, tagged releases v0.3.0-v0.6.0.
Server is small (493 lines) and readable, with no shell execution and no telemetry, so it is easy to audit and fork.
Multi-provider registry lets one switch to a local or self-hosted System One (jeff, kev, localjev), which is useful if the client code must stay on the machine.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool with generic descriptions and no coding-specific guidance. Claude will not reach for it without being told, which fails the user's core requirement. There are no hooks, no plugin.json and no .mcp.json.

The MCP server has no default-provider setting: the `provider` argument defaults to `jev` (direct TypeSafe) on every tool. The user must set JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_API_KEY hacks, or Claude must pass provider=openrouter every call, or the fork must be patched (a one-line default change in mcp_server.py).

Default model `jev-latest` may not match the OpenRouter IDs (`typesafe/jev-1.13`, `~typesafe/jev-latest`). It also does not use the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions). It uses only the /api/v1/systemone surface. The bare alias is unverified against OpenRouter.

About 1.9k tokens of always-on context for 9 tools, of which 6 have no coding use (docs_verify, posteriors_load, reask_plan, evaluate, models, composite_score). The Bayes-net posteriors tools read arbitrary local paths.

Not a coding-workflow tool at all: no questions for code review, commit triage, test selection, permission gating or intent routing, and no state-shaping guidance for a repo. Much of the repo is research output (manuscript, PDF, figures, Bayes-net experiments) that adds noise. Single-author (79 of 90 commits), 13 days old, 7 stars, unaudited.
Not published to PyPI and needs a clone plus `uv sync`. The `.env` in CWD is auto-loaded, and the key sits in ~/.claude.json env or gets picked up per-project.
Slow-failure behaviour is unfavorable: a 60 s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn if OpenRouter or TypeSafe is degraded, and the circuit breaker is not wired into the MCP server.
entries.verdict: daf-jev is a real, tested System One client that supports OpenRouter in code. But it is a generic library and toolbox, not a Claude Code integration, and its MCP tools are model-discretion with no coding triggers. It cannot deliver the "automatic, never say use jev" goal. Use it, at most, as a source for the client code and question builders when writing your own thin hook or MCP server (a forked provider default, plus hook-driven calls to `daf-jev ask`), not as the integration itself.

entries.name: jev-harness-router
entries.what: TypeScript library (npm jev-harness-router 1.1.2) that, for each agent turn, makes ONE Jev /v1/systemone call with about 20 Noul/Score/Choice questions (via @typesafe-ai/sdk). Pure code (policy.ts) turns the answers into a model tier, effort level, tool subset and skill suggestion. It has a hard deadline (default 600 ms) with a regex-heuristic fallback, a local cache, and 0 ms shortcuts for acks and "/" commands. An adapter, toQueryOptions(), maps the route onto Claude Agent SDK query() options (model, effort, tools, systemPrompt.append). It is NOT an MCP server, hook, plugin or skill, and it has no Claude Code CLI integration. It is meant for people who build their own harness on the Agent SDK. The catalogue (models, tools, skills) has to be hand-written. The shipped default is the author's own 24-skill catalogue, in Spanish and English.
entries.autoInvocation: None for the Claude Code CLI. It is a library that a custom harness calls before each query(). It is deterministic when embedded in your own Agent SDK program, but it is not a hook, MCP tool, skill or proxy. Getting it into interactive Claude Code would need custom glue. A UserPromptSubmit hook can inject additionalContext, but it cannot change the session model, effort or tool set. A transparent proxy through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is impossible because the user is on subscription/OAuth. Only the skill-suggestion text could be reproduced through a hook.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var, never argv, and sent as a Bearer header. .env is gitignored and .env.example holds a placeholder.
No shell execution, no curl|sh, and no postinstall script in this repo or in @typesafe-ai/sdk. Only prepublishOnly, which runs at publish time.
The SDK redacts headers in debug logs (redactHeaders). The router sets logLevel error.
The message is treated as untrusted input. Tool enablement thresholds are enforced in code, not from the model's answer (README section 3).
No telemetry beyond the TypeSafe API call. Nothing is written to disk except the calibrate script writing .env, and an in-memory cache.

Prompt-injection surface: user text is sent to Jev as state. The output is a typed decision and cannot execute anything. The skill block appended to the system prompt is built from the catalogue, not from the message.
entries.dataEgress: Per routed turn, one POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is repointed. The body is state (latest_user_message truncated to 1200 chars, recent_context truncated to 600 chars of the previous assistant reply, session facts, unavailable_tools) plus the ~20 questions, which embed the catalogue descriptions (about 4,000 input tokens per call by the README's measurement). It does not send file contents, diffs or tool outputs unless the harness puts them into recentContext or openFiles. openFiles is capped at 8 paths and is sent as-is. Client-project prompts and paths would leave the machine for TypeSafe or OpenRouter, so this needs a client-confidentiality check. The two warmup calls send only the string "warmup".
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. The deadline defaults to 600 ms (HARNESS_ROUTER_DEADLINE_MS, calibratable) and is a raced timer (src/jev.ts:~195). There are no retries (maxRetries 0). On a timeout, API error, network error or missing key, the local regex heuristic answers. A late answer still lands in the cache and is not aborted, so as not to break the TLS connection. Fallback rate is 0-16% depending on the day. Fallback quality is worse: under-provisioned tiers go from 7.4% to 31.5%, and skill accuracy from 90.7% to 81.5% by the author's own numbers. A missing key throws MissingKeyError unless MOCK=1.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped, because it registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills. If wired through the Agent SDK it appends a skill-suggestion block to the system prompt each turn, and restricting tools would shrink the tool definitions. Both effects belong to the SDK harness, not to the interactive CLI.
pros: Uses Jev's real strengths (Noul, Score and Choice in one batched call). It reports Jev beating a regex baseline on 181 labelled turns: skill exact 90.0% vs 59.4%, tier too-cheap 3.3% vs 19.9% (README table; self-reported, single labeller).
Well-engineered failure handling: a hard deadline, no retries, a heuristic fallback, and a late answer that still lands in the cache (src/jev.ts).
Cheap: 4,015 input tokens per call, about $0.17 per 1,000 turns (README).
The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer key (sdk index.mjs:513,554,581). Pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api is likely a config-only change.
Includes toQueryOptions() for the Claude Agent SDK, with type-checked options (tests), and 113 offline tests.
MIT, one runtime dependency, no install scripts, no argv secrets. Small and readable (about 4k lines).
Its README findings are useful design lessons for any Jev integration: without recentContext Jev routing is worse than regexes, don't abort on the deadline, and prewarm with two calls.
cons: It does not integrate with interactive Claude Code. It has no MCP server, hooks.json, plugin.json, SKILL.md or settings snippet. It only targets the Agent SDK's query() options, where the harness is your own program. The user's goal is automatic use inside the Claude Code CLI with Opus 5.5 on a subscription.

Interactive Claude Code hooks cannot apply its outputs. The model, effort and tool set cannot be changed per turn from a hook. Only additionalContext text (the skill suggestion) could be reproduced, and even that needs custom glue. The user's OAuth subscription cannot be redirected to a proxy either.

Even where it could work, routing to Haiku or Sonnet would fight the user's wish to use Opus 5.5 as the main model. The value is cost savings, not coding quality. The user is on a subscription, so there is no per-token bill to save.

Sends the user's prompt, the previous assistant reply (600 chars) and up to 8 open file paths to a third party on every turn. That is a confidentiality concern on client projects, and it adds 0.35-1 s of latency per non-shortcut turn.

Fitted to one Spanish/English author's 24 skills and 181 turns, all labelled by that same person. Thresholds, the deadline and the catalogue are not transferable (the README says so). You would have to hand-write a catalogue of your own tools and skills and re-run the eval.
Immature: 12 days old, 3 stars, one author (17 commits, the last on 2026-09-21), no CI, no issues or community. Its only sample of the SDK path is examples/agent-sdk.ts.

OpenRouter is not native. Compatibility rests on the assumption that OpenRouter's systemone response has the same shape as api.typesafe.ai (usage.input_tokens, model, answers). The default model ID jev-1.13.0 differs from OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13, so the env override needs to be set. Unverified.
Restricting tools (the default `restrict` mode) risks stripping Bash, Edit or Write on a misroute.
entries.verdict: A well-built per-turn Jev router for people writing their own Claude Agent SDK harness, and the best reference for how to structure batched Jev calls, deadlines and fallbacks. It is not a drop-in for interactive Claude Code, since it ships no hook, MCP or skill, and a hook cannot change the model, effort or tools per turn. It is worth borrowing ideas from (recentContext, the deadline pattern, and a skill-suggestion hook built on the same questions), not installing.

entries.name: eyenpi/actionreflex
entries.what: Python library (v0.2.0, alpha), NOT a Claude Code hook despite the candidate label. It wraps typesafe-sdk to build a pre-execution "Gate" for agent tool calls: you construct an Action (name, arguments, context) and it sends one Jev System One request containing several policy questions (Noul/Score/Choice). The answers are folded into allow/block/escalate. It ships six built-in policies (destructive_action, intent_mismatch, follows_injected_instructions, contains_pii, scope_of_impact, risk_tier), a @gate.guard decorator, an async gate, and an on_error mode (raise / fail_closed / fail_open). It has no CLI, no MCP server, no hooks.json, no PreToolUse adapter, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md, so it does not plug into Claude Code without you writing a wrapper.
entries.autoInvocation: None as shipped. It is a plain library that only runs when other code calls it. It could become a deterministic PreToolUse hook (the best fit for the user's 'automatic, no prompting' requirement), but the user would have to write and maintain that glue themselves.
security: Key handling: the key comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or an api_key argument, and is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (typesafe-sdk transport.py:121). The SDK logging redacts authorization headers. Nothing is placed in argv.
No shell execution, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, and no telemetry found in the 881 lines of src/actionreflex. The SDK adds only User-Agent and SDK/runtime headers.

The tool arguments and context are sent to the model as state JSON. If a hook fed it tool_results, it would be putting untrusted content into a classifier prompt. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so the injection surface is limited to flipping a verdict, not executing anything.
Supply chain: a single-author, 5-commit, 2-star, 12-day-old repo, installed from git without a pinned SHA, and it depends on a pre-1.0 typesafe-sdk. Pin the commit if you use it.
The SDK is pre-1.0 and pinned to a narrow range (>=0.6,<0.8), so it will break on SDK upgrades.

It is a gate, so a false 'allow' is a security failure. The README admits the default thresholds are untuned, that the weak spot is unintended risks (F1 72.7, specificity 55.4), and that on-task injection hijacks are untested.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever you put in Action.arguments and Action.context is sent as JSON to the configured base URL. That means TypeSafe (api.typesafe.ai) by default, or OpenRouter if you override the base URL. Realistically, for a Claude Code hook that would be the tool name plus the full tool_input (Bash commands, file paths, Edit/Write contents and diffs) and, if you add them, the user request and the recent transcript or tool outputs. The library has no redaction and no allowlist. On client projects this sends code and possibly secrets to a beta third-party model provider (and to OpenRouter if it is routed there). Your existing secret-leak guard hook would have to run before it. Because everything is one request, the payload grows with each policy and each piece of context, and input is billed per token.
entries.failureMode: Configurable via on_error. The default is "raise" (GateUnavailable), which in a hook wrapper would crash the script. Claude Code treats a non-blocking hook error as a non-block, so that behaves as fail-open for the user, but it is accidental rather than designed. "fail_closed" would block every tool call during an outage or rate-limit, which is unacceptable for daily coding. "fail_open" is the sensible mode, but it means no protection when Jev is down. Timeout is None by default (the SDK default applies), so you must set a short timeout, for example timeout=2. There are 2 retries with backoff by default (RetryPolicy), so a slow or down Jev can stall each tool call for several seconds unless you disable retries. All of this is the wrapper author's job.
entries.contextCost: Zero for the library on its own: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill text. A hand-written PreToolUse hook would inject nothing unless it emitted a block or ask reason. Context cost is effectively 0 tokens in the normal case.
pros: It is the only candidate here that uses Jev's real strengths, cheap calibrated yes/no/score answers on every action, and its deterministic gate design matches the user's 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement (a PreToolUse hook needs no model discretion).

OpenRouter routing is nearly free. typesafe-sdk honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (constants.py:6) and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus the OpenRouter key should reach OpenRouter's System One API without a code patch. This is unverified.

Clean, small (881 lines), readable code with no shell exec, no postinstall and no telemetry. MIT licensed. The policies are well-formed Jev questions (Noul/Score/Choice) that can be reused as templates.
One request carries N policies, so adding questions costs input tokens, not round trips. The eval reports $0.19 for 3,584 checks, so cost is negligible.
Published benchmark artifacts (R-Judge, InjecAgent) with committed raw results, and the README is honest about caveats and weaknesses. The on_error fail_open/fail_closed choice is explicit.
Zero MCP tool or context overhead in Claude Code.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration. There is no hook adapter, MCP server, plugin, skill or CLI in the repo, so the candidate label 'hook' is inaccurate. The user would have to write a PreToolUse wrapper (stdin JSON to Action to Gate.check to permissionDecision JSON) and decide the context to pass.

The design targets untrusted agents in production, not a senior developer's own coding agent. The built-in questions (destructive, intent mismatch, injection) overlap with what Claude Code permissions, bypass-mode guards and the existing secret-guard hook already cover, and in bypass/auto mode a Jev 'block' would add friction, not remove it.

False-alarm risk for coding work. Specificity on unintended-risk records was only 55.4 and thresholds are untuned. Normal coding actions like rm -rf node_modules, git reset, migrations and force-push will look 'destructive' and cause noisy escalations. Claude Code has no human review queue, so 'escalate' would have to map to an 'ask' prompt.
Benchmarks are chat/tool-call records (R-Judge, InjecAgent), not Claude Code Bash/Edit traffic, and the author admits on-task hijack injections are untested.
Egress on client projects. Every Bash command, file path and edit body would go to a beta provider with no redaction, and the user has a client-confidentiality concern.

Immature and fragile. It is 12 days old with 5 commits, 1 author and 2 stars, not on PyPI, has no releases, and needs pre-1.0 typesafe-sdk >=0.6,<0.8. Python startup per hook call adds latency, since there is no persistent daemon.
Fail modes need hand-tuning: the default is raise with unbounded timeout and 2 retries, so a slow Jev could stall every tool call unless the wrapper sets a tight timeout and fail_open.
entries.verdict: A well-made but tiny alpha Python library for gating agent actions with Jev. It is not a Claude Code hook or MCP, so nothing works automatically until you write your own PreToolUse glue, and its safety-gate purpose adds little for a developer already running secret-guard and permission modes. It is worth borrowing as a reference for Jev policy design and OpenRouter routing (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), not as the daily integration.

entries.name: @mohan-cao/jev-classifier (with mohan-cao/pi-extensions monorepo)
entries.what: A dependency-free TypeScript transport library for the System One endpoint (POST {endpoint} with {model, state, questions}). It exports callSystemOne (timeout + 429/529 retries), three answer parsers (noul, score, choice), question-spec types, and a TTL cache. Judgment logic lives in sibling packages (jev-classify, jev-phase, jev-verify, jev-trajectory). Those packages are consumed only by pi-jev-response-router, an extension for the Pi coding agent (@earendil-works/pi-coding-agent), not Claude Code. It is a library, not an MCP server, hook or skill.
interface: Pi events before_agent_start and agent_settled (pi-jev-response-router, index.ts:341,416)
entries.autoInvocation: Not applicable to Claude Code. The library is invoked by code. In its native host (Pi) it is a deterministic lifecycle hook (before_agent_start, agent_settled). A Claude Code port would need a hook script written by the user, e.g. UserPromptSubmit and Stop hooks.
security: API key is sent as a Bearer header from an in-memory value and is not in argv; the key is passed by the caller
No postinstall, preinstall, child_process or exec usage in src or package.json; zero runtime dependencies
No telemetry found. The only network call is fetch(config.endpoint) in client.ts:84
Error text includes the first 500 chars of the HTTP response body in JevError (client.ts:107), which could leak upstream details into logs
Endpoint comes from operator env (PI_JEV_ENDPOINT), so there is no request-derived SSRF

Prompt-injection surface: the Pi extension injects a classifier-derived policy section into the system prompt, but the injected text is deterministic and comes from fixed policies. User text is only sent to Jev as state.
entries.dataEgress: The library sends {model, state, questions}. In the Pi extension, state is the user's current prompt plus up to 4 prior history turns (PI_JEV_ROUTER_HISTORY_TURNS). jev-verify additionally sends the full assistant response text alongside the request. A Claude Code adaptation would send prompts and responses (which may include client code) to the endpoint. As written, no file contents or tool outputs leave.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the Pi extension (per the config.ts comment and the changelog note about a swallowed catch). The default timeout is 5s (PI_JEV_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_MS) with 2 retries only on 429/529. Worst case is a hung classifier blocking a prompt for about 5s per attempt. Non-retryable errors throw immediately. The library itself throws, so fail-open is up to the host.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped (no MCP tools, no hooks, no instructions). The Pi extension injects a small policy section into the system prompt, but that code is Pi-specific.
pros: Small, readable, zero-dependency transport (client.ts is about 195 lines) that could be vendored into a custom Claude Code hook
Endpoint, model and timeout are config-driven, so pointing it at OpenRouter is a config change
Sensible fail-open design, short timeout, Retry-After handling and response validation/clamping
Real design lessons from measurement: questions sharing a call perturb each other, so ask one question per call
Apache-2.0 with npm provenance; question specs are plain data and reusable
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration: the only consumer targets the Pi agent harness, and there is no MCP server, hook config, skill or plugin.json
It talks to api.typesafe.ai by default and has no OpenRouter code or docs. The OpenRouter schema match is unverified.
Its policies are tuned on a synthetic eval set, and the verify package's own docs say it is known to be too permissive
Brand new (created 2026-09-21), 0 stars, one author, 32 commits, and a repo README calling it 'slop'
Using it in Claude Code means writing your own hook glue, which would send prompts and responses to a third party for every turn
Its judgments (response shape, phase, verify) steer prompt policy, not coding tool choices, so they add little value for Opus 5.5 daily coding
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration. It is a clean transport library for the Pi harness. Its useful ideas (client.ts, one-question-per-call, fail-open) could be borrowed for a custom UserPromptSubmit hook, but installing it gives you nothing automatic.

entries.name: @ai-sdk/typesafe-ai (vercel/ai packages/typesafe-ai)
entries.what: Vercel AI SDK provider for TypeSafe System One / Jev. It exposes only an experimental evaluationModel (used via experimental_evaluate from the ai package) that POSTs Choice, Score and Boolean (mapped to Noul) questions against a shared state to {baseURL}/systemone. The output is typed answers with probabilities. It is a TypeScript library for app developers. It has no MCP server, hooks, skills or CLI, so it cannot be wired into Claude Code as-is.
entries.autoInvocation: Not applicable: it is a library with no trigger of its own. Automatic use in Claude Code would need extra glue, such as a hook script or MCP wrapper calling it. A deterministic hook is the only truly automatic route, and this package provides none.
security: No postinstall script (package.json scripts are build and test only). No shell execution or telemetry in the 6 KB dist/index.js. Only one network call, to baseURL/systemone.
Key handling: Bearer token in the Authorization header, loaded from TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY via loadApiKey. It is never placed in argv. The user agent is 'ai-sdk-typesafe-ai/<version>'.

Prompt-injection surface is small because the output is typed (choice, probabilities, numbers) with no free text. But the caller-supplied state is sent to a remote model, and a hostile state can bias the decision.

Supply chain: 2 runtime dependencies (@ai-sdk/provider, @ai-sdk/provider-utils), pinned exactly. npm provenance is enabled and the maintainer is vercel-release-bot. The package is 2 weeks old and has had 12 versions in 14 days.
Response schema is validated with zod, and errors go through createJsonErrorResponseHandler.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling code puts in `state` (string or JSON) plus the question instructions and criteria, sent as one POST body to {baseURL}/systemone with model id and bearer token. Nothing is collected automatically. If someone built a Claude Code integration on this, the egress would be whatever code, diffs or tool output that glue code chose to send. That would need a size cap and a secret scrub, and would matter for client-confidential projects.
entries.failureMode: Library behavior only: failures throw APICallError. Core experimental_evaluate retries transient errors (429, 529) up to maxRetries=2 by default. There is no provider-side retry loop (docs/105-typesafe-ai.mdx "Errors and retries"). No default timeout is set, only abortSignal passthrough. Fail-open or fail-closed depends entirely on caller code, and no Claude Code integration exists here.
entries.contextCost: Zero as shipped, because it has no MCP tools, hooks or skills. A custom wrapper (for example a small MCP server built on it) would add its own tool definitions, likely 1 to 3 tools at roughly 300 to 800 tokens.
pros: Confirms the wire format from code: POST {baseURL}/systemone with {model,state,questions}, question types choice/score/noul, and answers with probabilities and confidence (model.ts:108-122, api.ts:8-30). This is a useful spec for writing your own thin Claude Code hook or MCP wrapper.
baseURL is overridable (provider.ts:36), so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 is a one-line change for the /systemone endpoint, if OpenRouter's schema matches.
Small and auditable: about 6 KB of dist, 2 pinned dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, npm provenance, Apache-2.0, maintained by Vercel with an active release cadence.
Sound typed-output handling: limits of 255 choice options and 2 to 10 score levels are enforced client-side, and the two-decimal rounding is declared.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration at all. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or CLI and only plugs into the ai package's experimental_evaluate. The user's automatic-use requirement is unmet.

Reads TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY only (provider.ts:40, model.ts:99). There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY fallback, so you must pass apiKey and baseURL explicitly. The default endpoint is api.typesafe.ai, not OpenRouter.
Covers only the /systemone shape. No use of OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions endpoint or of the Jev Router model, and it is unverified that OpenRouter's /systemone accepts the 'noul' body.

Explicitly experimental: 'Evaluation is experimental' in the README, and the ai package's experimental_evaluate API may change. The package is 14 days old with 12 releases, and only 17 commits touch it, most of them bot releases.
Requires the ai package and zod as runtime dependencies. That is heavy for a hook or MCP script, when a plain fetch of about 30 lines would do.
No timeout, and retries depend on the core, so a slow or down Jev could stall a hook unless the caller sets an abortSignal.
entries.verdict: This is a real Vercel-published Jev SDK provider, but it is an app-developer library and not a Claude Code integration, so it gives no automatic invocation. Its only value here is as a verified reference for the /systemone request and response schema, which a small custom hook or MCP wrapper pointed at OpenRouter could reuse.

entries.name: jev-style (lawrence3699/jev-style, PyPI jev-style)
entries.what: Third-party (chaoliangUNSW / lawrence3699) project that fine-tunes small Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B models to imitate Jev's System One interface and serves them locally via a FastAPI server exposing POST /v1/systemone on 127.0.0.1:8765. It is NOT hosted TypeSafe Jev and never calls OpenRouter. It ships a Claude Code plugin marketplace with two plugins: jev-style (6 skills plus a 5-tool stdio MCP server for decide/noul/choice/score/model_info) and jev-style-guard (a PreToolUse hook that sends every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call to the local model with noul/score safety questions and returns allow/ask/deny, plus regex hard rules). Its own benchmark says hosted Jev scores 86.6% versus 73.6% for its 2B model and about 64% for the default 0.8B.
interface: MCP tool noul(state, question, true_means?, false_means?)
entries.autoInvocation: Two distinct modes. The guard is a deterministic PreToolUse hook that fires on every Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit/Read/WebFetch/mcp__ call, with no user prompting. It is a safety gate, not a productivity feature. The MCP tools and skills are model-discretion: the skill descriptions only trigger when the user is writing classification or routing code or mentions jev-style, so Claude has no reason to call them during ordinary coding.
security: Hook input to the guard is the full tool_input (whole Bash command, whole Write/Edit contents, WebFetch URLs). It goes to the local server, and only to a loopback host unless allow_remote_server is set (guard.py:455). Good default.
Bearer key is read from an env var (api_key_env), never from argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The server compares it with hmac.compare_digest.

The hook command is a shell one-liner (`J=$(command -v jev-style || echo $HOME/.local/bin/jev-style); $J guard || printf ...`). It runs whatever jev-style is first on PATH, so it is a PATH-hijack-style trust point but not unusual.
Guard writes a JSONL log with 300-char previews of every tool call to ~/.local/state/jev-style-guard/guard.jsonl. Client code and secrets fragments can land in that log.

Prompt-injection surface: the model reads attacker-influenced command and file text. The guard drops the Bash `description` field to reduce self-persuasion, and hard regex rules can only tighten verdicts, which is well thought out. A 0.8B classifier is still gameable, and it produces false allows and false asks.
Model weights come from Hugging Face (huggingface_hub, unpinned revision) as safetensors, GGUF or MLX, with a torch and transformers>=5 dependency. Trust in the author's HF repos is required.
entries.dataEgress: With defaults nothing leaves the machine except the one-time Hugging Face weight download. Guard payloads (full tool inputs, including file contents being written and commands) go only to 127.0.0.1:8765. Nothing is sent to TypeSafe, OpenRouter or any telemetry endpoint. If the user switched the URL to OpenRouter with allow_remote_server, every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call, including whole file contents and secrets in commands, would leave the machine, with up to 25.6k tokens per call. That is unacceptable for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe but noisy, in the guard. The server being down, a timeout (timeout_s 8 inside a 20 s hook timeout), a 4xx/5xx, a bad body, a missing CLI or an oversized call all produce on_error=ask (configurable to deny, never allow). With the server down every guarded tool call turns into a permission prompt, which is heavy friction in bypass or auto permission mode. The MCP server's HTTP backend has a 120 s timeout, and a failing tool call just returns an error to the model.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 5 tools with a server-instructions block of about 0.9k chars, and tool defs plus docstrings of about 4.9k chars, so roughly 1.5k tokens always loaded (5.8k chars divided by 4). The 6 skills add short descriptions of about 500-700 chars each, about 0.9k tokens. The guard hook injects no text when it allows (emit_allow=false, so it prints nothing). Ask and deny add a short reason string. Total is roughly 2.5k tokens of static context.
pros: The only candidate that hooks Claude Code deterministically with no user prompting. The PreToolUse guard fires on every Bash/Write/Edit/Read/WebFetch/MCP call, so the 'automatic' requirement is met mechanically.

Fail-safe design. on_error never resolves to allow, and hard regexes are checked in code and can only tighten verdicts. Loopback-only by default, dry_run mode, a JSONL audit log and a disable env var. Careful engineering for a 4-day-old repo.
No data leaves the machine by default, which is good for client projects. The API key is passed by env var, not argv. No telemetry found.
Apache-2.0, an official-looking MCP registry server.json and a clean plugin marketplace layout. Cheap in static context (about 2.5k tokens), and the hook adds nothing when it allows.
The guard's emit_allow=false default means it only adds ask or deny on top of Claude Code's own permission system and never widens it. Useful as a second safety opinion in bypass mode.
cons: It is not TypeSafe Jev and has no OpenRouter or TypeSafe code path. It is a Qwen3.5 0.8B/2B imitation, and by its own README it scores 64% (0.8B, the default) or 73.6% (2B) against hosted Jev's 86.6% on its benchmark. It fails the user's core ask of using OpenRouter-hosted Jev.

The guard does a job the user already covers: a secret-leak PreToolUse hook exists. Adding a probabilistic 0.8B classifier over every tool call yields false asks. In bypass or auto mode a false 'ask' or an outage (default on_error=ask) interrupts the flow, and a false 'allow' gives a misleading sense of safety.

It requires a resident local server with a 0.5-3.8 GB model and torch. On CPU-only Linux the per-call latency is unknown, and it stacks on the existing hooks on Bash/Read. Each hook invocation also spawns a Python process.

Repointing it at OpenRouter would ship whole file contents and commands to a remote API on every tool call. That is a data-egress problem for client work and adds per-call cost and latency, and the design (8 s timeout, request model name hardcoded to jev-style-0.8b-decision-v3, the default model IDs) is not built for it.

The MCP tools and skills are only model-discretion or triggered by classification-code tasks, so they will rarely be used in ordinary daily coding. Nothing here routes or gates coding decisions with Jev automatically apart from the guard.

Immature and single-author. Created 2026-09-25 with 13 commits, 9 stars, 2 contributors (one is a 'jason' account with 10 commits). Tests use only a fake engine. The plugin manifests are at version 0.1.0 while the package is 0.3.0. There is a heavy dependency stack (mcp>=2.0, transformers>=5, torch) and the weights come from the author's personal HF account.
entries.verdict: Not an OpenRouter or hosted Jev integration. It is a local Qwen imitation, and its only genuinely automatic piece is a security guard that duplicates the user's existing secret-leak hook. Skip it for the stated goal. At most, consider the guard idea (not this implementation) as inspiration for a fail-open Jev hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: RevocGG/typesafe-jev-bridge
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node (>=18) localhost bridge (127.0.0.1:8399) that translates OpenAI POST /v1/chat/completions and /v1/responses into TypeSafe's native POST {TYPESAFE_API_BASE}/v1/systemone with body {state, model, questions}, and renders the typed answers back as text. Also ships CLIs: ask-jev.cjs (typed question about file/dir/stdin), audit.cjs (Jev judges every file), autofix.cjs (judge, fix via a separate chat model on a 9Router endpoint, re-judge). It is NOT an MCP server, hook or skill; the only Claude Code integration is pasting a text block into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md telling the model to shell out to ask-jev.cjs. Claude Code cannot use it as a model backend anyway (it speaks Anthropic Messages API, the bridge speaks OpenAI format), and README itself says never route coding to Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion via CLAUDE.md prose only: Claude Code has to decide by itself to run `node .../ask-jev.cjs ...` through Bash. No hook, no MCP tool, no skill, no transparent proxy. Nondeterministic and, since Opus rarely needs a probability oracle for typical coding, it will seldom fire. Also the block hardcodes repo-relative paths (`node typesafe-bridge/ask-jev.cjs` 'from the repo root'), which do not resolve inside the user's other projects; it would need rewriting to absolute paths.
security: Binds 127.0.0.1 only, rejects non-loopback Host (DNS-rebinding guard), rejects any browser Origin unless allow-listed (bridge.js:226, README security model)
No auth by default: any local process of the user can call the bridge and spend the API key unless BRIDGE_TOKEN is set (SECURITY.md admits this)

API key is read from env or typesafe-bridge/.env, sent only as upstream Bearer header, not in argv; setup takes the key via hidden prompt or --key-stdin, so no key in process list. Client tokens are not relayed by default (BRIDGE_ALLOW_KEY_PASSTHROUGH=0)
Regex redaction (lib/redact.cjs) is applied by the CLI by default but bridge-level redaction is OPT-IN (BRIDGE_REDACT=1) so router/agent traffic goes out unredacted by default
Sensitive path denylist (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, .npmrc, .git, *.log) enforced in ask-jev/audit/autofix (lib/sensitive.cjs) but not for content that arrives via HTTP
setup.cjs uses child_process.execSync/spawn (git ls-files, ps, python -m venv, pip install -r requirements.txt) on user machine; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found by grep
entries.dataEgress: Upstream (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_API_BASE points to) receives: the API key as Bearer, the full `state` (flattened chat messages, or file contents with line numbers for --file/audit/autofix; directory listing names for --dir), the question map, and model id. Nothing else; no telemetry. With the CLI, secret-like values are masked first; via the HTTP bridge masking is off unless BRIDGE_REDACT=1. autofix additionally sends flagged files to the 9Router fix model. Truncation limit 200k chars per request (BRIDGE_MAX_STATE_CHARS). Sending client source to a third party (and via OpenRouter, a second party) is a real concern for the user's client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call but not blocking: the bridge/CLI is invoked only when the model runs it, so nothing is blocked if it is down. bridgeFetch retries 429/529/network errors 2x with backoff (max 4s waits, Retry-After capped 10s); upstream timeout 60s default (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS) times up to 3 attempts = worst case ~3 minutes per call; CLI exits 1 with 'cannot reach the bridge' if the bridge process is not running. The bridge must be started manually or via setup --background; no autostart/systemd unit, so after reboot it is silently down and the CLAUDE.md block would make the model hit connection errors.
entries.contextCost: 0 tools and 0 MCP server instructions. The cost is the pasted CLAUDE.md block (~2,000 chars, ~500 tokens) loaded every session, plus the tool-call/result tokens of each ask (small, a few lines). Cheapest of any integration style but only as reliable as the model's willingness to follow the prose.
pros: Genuinely reads/implements the real System One request path: minimal, auditable ~1000-line bridge.js plus small libs, zero dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, no curl|sh (grep of repo)

Decent local security hygiene for a v0.2: loopback-only bind, Host + Origin checks, constant-time BRIDGE_TOKEN, key not relayed from clients, sensitive-path denylist, regex secret redaction in the CLI, offline test suite and CI on Node 18/20/22 x Linux/Windows

TYPESAFE_API_BASE is env-configurable with path /v1/systemone, so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api (-> /api/v1/systemone) is a plausible env-only switch to OpenRouter using OpenRouter key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY

Useful reference for how to phrase typed questions and read probabilities (0.35-0.65 uncertain band, exit code 3 on low confidence, choice/score handling), which can be lifted into a custom hook/skill
Honest about limits: README says Jev is not a chat model, warns against routing code generation to it, labels itself unofficial
cons: Wrong shape for Claude Code: it exposes OpenAI chat/responses, but Claude Code speaks Anthropic Messages to ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL and the user is on OAuth subscription; the 'Claude Code' topic is marketing, the real integration is a CLAUDE.md text block
No automatic invocation: no hook, no MCP, no skill. Relies on Opus choosing to call a CLI, which contradicts the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev without being told)

No OpenRouter support in code (zero 'openrouter' matches); env-only switch is unverified and the model id mapping (bare jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-1.13 or ~typesafe/jev-latest) and the OpenRouter response schema are unconfirmed; the Decisions API is unsupported

Chat-to-typed-question translation is heuristic (regex to guess yes/no vs choice, pickQuestionText scraping JSON spec fields, IS_IT_RE) - the bridge infers a question when none is supplied and README admits a coding prompt gets a meaningless 'yes'
Must be started manually (no service/systemd), no autostart; bridge down means silent failures; unauthenticated by default so any local process can burn the key
Bridge-level redaction is off by default, so agent/router traffic sends raw state (code, diffs) to a third party; highly relevant for client projects under NDA

Immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 15 commits in 2 days, 3 stars, 1 contributor, no commits after v0.2.1; also carries unrelated bloat (autofix with file rewriting, audit, python demo, 9Router-specific tooling) increasing the trust surface
CLAUDE.md snippet hardcodes repo-relative script paths, so it will not work as pasted from other project directories
entries.verdict: Not a fit: it is an OpenAI-format bridge and CLI for 9Router-style setups, not an MCP server, hook or skill, so it gives Claude Code no automatic Jev invocation, and its OpenRouter path is an unverified env-var trick. Worth reading only as a reference for the /v1/systemone request shape and confidence-threshold conventions; build a small dedicated hook or MCP server against openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone instead.

entries.name: jkudish/jev-agent-tools
entries.what: Zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript/Node (>=22) library exporting ask() and resolveTransport(). It picks a carrier (TypeSafe direct, OpenRouter, Cloudflare, Vercel AI Gateway) from env vars, POSTs {state, questions, model}, and strictly validates the reply (answer IDs, probability distributions, choice = argmax, noul in [0,1], usage, model). It returns a typed {ok:false, code} on any problem and never throws. It has no MCP server, hooks, skills, plugin or CLI, so it cannot be wired into Claude Code by itself. It is the shared transport layer for jkudish/jev-mcp (which keeps its own OpenRouter fetch code) and jkudish/jev-browser.
interface: (no MCP tools, hooks, skills or CLI)
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is a library, so nothing invokes it inside Claude Code. Automatic behavior would have to come from a consumer such as jev-mcp (model-discretion MCP tools) or from custom hooks built on top of it.
security: No postinstall scripts and no runtime dependencies, so supply-chain surface is small.
Key is read from env and sent only as Authorization Bearer to the fixed host (openrouter.ai, or api.typesafe.ai/TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). Nothing goes in argv.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is an unvalidated override, so a poisoned env could redirect state and key to another host (typesafe.ts:8).
Errors are fixed strings with status and byte count only; response bodies and credentials are never echoed, and provider names are whitelisted.
No shell execution, no file reads, no telemetry. SECURITY.md states it makes no other network calls.
Outputs are numbers and IDs only and are strictly validated, so the prompt-injection surface on the return path is minimal.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in state and questions goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or api.typesafe.ai, Cloudflare, Vercel depending on env), plus the OpenRouter key. The library itself reads nothing from disk, so egress equals what the consumer (for example jev-mcp) passes. In a Claude Code setup that could be code, diffs and tool output, which is a client-confidentiality concern.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at the library level: any network error, non-2xx, bad JSON or invalid distribution returns {ok:false, code}, and the consumer decides what happens next. The library has no timeout, no retry and no backoff; it only honours the caller's AbortSignal (jev-mcp keeps its own retry and deadline rules instead of using this layer). There is no fallback across providers, since a JEV_PROVIDER that is set but misconfigured errors rather than falling through.
entries.contextCost: Zero: no MCP server, tools, hooks or injected text.
pros: Correct, code-verified OpenRouter support: POST /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and Bearer sk-or- key (openrouter.ts:9-15).
Strict fail-closed validation of Jev output (ID match, distribution sums, choice = argmax, noul range, usage). Useful as a reference or building block for a custom hook script.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, small (about 500 lines of source), MIT, and it never echoes bodies or keys.
Explicit JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter avoids silent fallthrough. Injectable JevTransport makes hermetic testing easy.
Could be the basis for a small home-grown PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit hook script that calls Jev via OpenRouter.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook or skill. It has no Claude Code integration surface and gives no automatic invocation.
Very new and thin: created 2026-09-23, 11 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, 0.1.x, and no OpenRouter live test.
Uses the alpha /api/alpha/decisions endpoint. It drops usage when absent (usage reports 0), so cost tracking is not possible via this path.
No timeout or retry, so a hook built on it must supply its own AbortSignal deadline or risk stalling.
If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is present in env it silently takes precedence over OpenRouter unless JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is set.
Sends X-Title and Referer as jev-browser to OpenRouter.
Its sibling jev-mcp deliberately does not use it for OpenRouter, so it adds little for the MCP path.
entries.verdict: Not an integration for Claude Code. It is a clean, well-validated transport library that correctly targets OpenRouter's Decisions API, useful only as a dependency or reference. Evaluate @jkudish/jev-mcp (the actual MCP consumer) instead and set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter there. For truly automatic use, pair it with a custom hook rather than relying on this package.

entries.name: kierandotai/jev-client
entries.what: Zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript client (Node >=22.18, run via --experimental-strip-types) for Jev. It wraps OpenRouter Decisions API, TypeSafe direct, and Vercel AI Gateway behind a JevClient.decide(state, {noul|choice|score}) call. It adds a mock keyword provider, small helpers (detectUrgency, route, classify, gateToolCall, escalateIfUnsure, severity), and an unauthenticated local HTTP proxy (server/proxy.ts). It is NOT an MCP server, hook, skill, or plugin, and has nothing Claude Code-specific.
interface: helpers.ts: detectUrgency, route, classify, gateToolCall, escalateIfUnsure, severity
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted / not applicable: it is a plain library and proxy with no Claude Code integration surface. Automatic use would need the user to write a PreToolUse hook or MCP server on top.
security: No MCP/hooks/skill/postinstall/install scripts: nothing runs at install (only devDeps typescript and @types/node). No telemetry found.
API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header via fetch (providers.ts:41), not in argv. Keys come from env or constructor.

server/proxy.ts calls server.listen(port) with no host argument (proxy.ts ~line 170), which binds all interfaces, and has no auth, no CORS or size limit, no body cap. Anyone on the LAN or any local webpage can spend the user's OpenRouter key and send arbitrary state through it. Risky when running on client-site networks.
Error messages include up to 500 chars of upstream response body (providers.ts:52). Unlikely to leak the key.
No license file (licenseInfo null), so legally all-rights-reserved; not safe to vendor into client projects.
Jev state is untrusted-data-steerable (README admits adversarial content in state can steer outputs), so gating decisions taken from repo content are injectable.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the caller puts in `state` plus the question text goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (or TypeSafe or Vercel). The library sends nothing by itself; no telemetry. Since it is not wired into Claude Code, nothing leaves until someone writes glue code that decides what (prompts, diffs, file contents) to send. It is subject to OpenRouter's data policy for typesafe/jev-1.13, which matters for client code.
entries.failureMode: Only as robust as the caller. postJson retries 429/500/502/503/504/529 up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff (500ms*2^n plus jitter, honoring Retry-After) (providers.ts:24-66). There is NO default timeout: fetch gets only an optional caller-supplied signal, so a hung connection blocks indefinitely, and worst-case retries add several seconds. Network errors (fetch throwing) are not retried. Errors throw JevError; there is no fail-open behavior. A hook built on this would need its own timeout and try/catch. The 'auto' mode silently falls back to the keyword MOCK provider when no key is set, with only a stderr warning, which would produce fake decisions that look real.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text. It is not registered anywhere. Integration would require new work (roughly 30 lines to write a hook or MCP wrapper).
pros: Correct, minimal reference for the OpenRouter Decisions API wire format: POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with {model, state, questions{type,instructions,criteria}} and Bearer auth (providers.ts:74-80), so it is a useful spec to copy for a self-written hook or MCP server.
Zero runtime deps and no install scripts: static-read auditable in about 45 KB, low supply-chain risk.
Retry/backoff handling for 429/5xx with Retry-After, including a recent 504 fix.
Documents Jev jaggedness (literal reading, no counting/dates) that matters when writing Jev questions for coding gates.
gateToolCall / escalateIfUnsure helpers show the exact pattern for gating a risky tool call by P(yes) and confidence, which maps to a PreToolUse hook design.
cons: Not an integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill, or plugin, so it does not give Claude Code any automatic Jev use. The user's core requirement is unmet.
11 days old, 1 author, 5 commits, 2 stars, no license, no releases, no CI, unpublished to npm: not fit to depend on in client work.
Local proxy binds all interfaces without auth (server.listen with no host): a key-spending open relay if run on a shared network.
No default fetch timeout and no fail-open path, so a naive hook built on it could stall every tool call.
auto provider silently falls back to a keyword mock, and prefers a Vercel gateway key over OpenRouter, both surprising for an OpenRouter-only user.
Uses only the alpha /api/alpha/decisions path (README admits it may move); does not support /api/v1/systemone on OpenRouter.
Helper questions (urgency/ticket triage) are support-desk oriented, with nothing for coding tasks (no diff, commit, test-failure or file-relevance questions).
entries.verdict: A tidy but tiny, unlicensed, 11-day-old TypeScript client that is useful only as a reference for the OpenRouter Decisions payload. It provides no Claude Code integration (no MCP, hooks or skills), so it does not satisfy the automatic-invocation goal; write a small fail-open PreToolUse hook or MCP wrapper yourself instead.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null)

entries.name: chayan-bit/jev-harness
entries.what: Independent (non-official) Python library plus a small CLI that wraps Jev-Frame (chayan-bit's own framework over the typesafe_sdk). It builds four Jev Choice questions (task difficulty, reasoning effort, skill, compaction) from a bounded HostSnapshot that the host must fill in, and returns an advisory-only AdviceReport. It also has a Decisions engine with 7 shadow-judgment families, offline threshold calibration, and a hook renderer that speaks the OpenAI Codex command-hook protocol (PreToolUse, PermissionRequest, PreCompact, PostCompact). It is not an MCP server, a Claude Code plugin or a skill. It does not gather host state itself, so something else must write the snapshot and the report file.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook in principle. The hook is a PreToolUse/PermissionRequest/PreCompact/PostCompact command hook. However, it only reads a pre-written report file. Nothing in the repo refreshes that report automatically. The 'analyze' call is a separate manual or cron step, and the report expires after 5 minutes. It is also targeted at the Codex hook schema. Claude Code has similar PreToolUse JSON, but the code validates Codex-specific fields (turn_id, model, permission_mode, and so on at hooks.py:59-83), and PermissionRequest and PreCompact/PostCompact are not equivalent in Claude Code. So it is not usable as-is.
security: Key is read from an environment variable, never from argv (cli.py:236, providers.py:94), so it does not appear in the process list.
The library has no shell execution: grep of src/ found no subprocess or os.system. Reports are written atomically with mode 0600 (cli.py:50-63).
No MCP server and no prompt-injection surface toward the model, except the additionalContext text the hook emits. The text is built from validated enum options and digests, not free text.

Installs via pip from a git tag, and its dependency jev-frame is also a git URL pin (pyproject.toml). This means no PyPI provenance and a supply-chain trust in one individual's two repos. The transitive typesafe_sdk comes from the Jev-Frame lock.
The hook itself never allows anything and can only deny through a user-supplied exact deny list. This is a good authority design.
SECURITY.md exists with a private vulnerability reporting channel. Actions are SHA-pinned in CI. No telemetry found.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine in hook mode, because the hook is offline. Live 'analyze' sends only the minimized HostSnapshot (at most 16 KiB): task_summary, phase, counts, token usage and the option ids and descriptions the host supplies. This goes to TypeSafe's endpoint through typesafe_sdk, not OpenRouter. The docs explicitly say not to include code, prompts, file contents or commands. The shadow-judgment path sends at most 16 KiB of digest-bound evidence per question, and refuses evidence that matches private-key or API-token patterns. The design is privacy-conservative, but someone must build the snapshot.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for advice. Any provider error, a low confidence below 0.55, or a stale snapshot gives an 'unresolved' report, and the hook then emits {}. The analyze timeout defaults to 8 s and max_attempts is 1, with no retries. Hooks have a 2 s timeout in the generated config. Fail-closed applies only to the user's own deny policy: a malformed policy file or input makes the hook exit 2, which blocks. That is intended, but a corrupt file would block every tool call if matcher '*' is used.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero server instructions. The hook adds a short additionalContext line to PreToolUse only when a fresh report matches the session, and it is empty otherwise. In Claude Code the payload mismatch below would break this in practice.
pros: Well-designed safety model: advice-only, no allow decisions, expiring reports, digest-bound context, and secret-pattern refusal before dispatch.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, and the hook is offline with no network calls.
Real tests (about 1,270 lines of tests across 5 files, run in CI), README snippets executed in CI, lint plus mypy, SHA-pinned actions, release-please and MIT license.
Choice questions like 'which reasoning effort or skill' are a good conceptual fit for Jev's System One.
The API-key handling is clean: env var only, never argv, and reports are written 0600.
Library-level base_url support in Jev-Frame's TypeSafeProvider makes an OpenRouter experiment possible.
cons: Targets Codex, not Claude Code. The hook code validates Codex payload fields and events, and README FAQ and features say Codex. Nothing in the repo mentions Claude Code.
No OpenRouter support: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and the bare 'jev-1.13.0' model, hard-coded in two places, with no base URL option in the CLI.
Not a turnkey integration. There is no snapshot producer and no refresher, so the hook only relays a report file that you must generate. The 5-minute TTL makes this a cron or wrapper build.
Advisory outputs (reasoning effort, difficulty, skill, compaction) cannot be applied by Claude Code hooks. The hook cannot change the model, effort or skill, only add a context line.
Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-25, 16 commits, 1 star, 0 forks, v0.1.1, Development Status Alpha. Author and contributors are the same individual (plus bots).
Installs from git URLs (Jev-Frame is also a 5-day-old personal repo), not PyPI. Two layers of unaudited wrapper sit between the user and Jev.
Would add nothing over a simple custom PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.
entries.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code as delivered. It is a Codex-targeted, TypeSafe-direct-only, alpha Python library that never fetches its own inputs, and it does not support OpenRouter. It is worth reading for its safety patterns (advice-only, TTL, digest binding, budget ledger), but a purpose-built Claude Code hook that calls OpenRouter directly is a better route.
