entries.name: Pasblinn/jev-lab
entries.what: Not a standalone integration. It is a small lab (about 64 KB, POSIX shell scripts plus docs) that wraps and patches gargpratyush/jev-router 0.3.0, a local ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy that asks Jev (choice question) which Claude tier (haiku/sonnet/opus) to use per fresh user turn. jev-lab adds: (a) a 38-line patch to jev-router's proxy.mjs (fixes: skip trailing role=system messages, ignore [SUGGESTION MODE calls, don't apply the cache-rebuild guard on the first turn); (b) a `jev` launcher that runs a pre-session health check against Jev and falls back to plain `claude --settings fallback-settings.json` with alert hooks; (c) a VS Code claudeProcessWrapper; (d) docs on where tokens go and an experimental Jev completion gate (TypeScript, shadow mode, not wired into Claude Code).
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (jev-router via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL) but ONLY when the user launches `jev` / `jev-claude` instead of `claude`, so it is not automatic within a plain `claude` session. It only picks the model tier per turn; it does not make Jev available for decisions such as risk gating, completion checking or context selection (those are roadmap/experiment only).
security: install.sh edits files inside the globally installed jev-router package (src/proxy.mjs) via sed -i and patch; backup to .orig; patch is wiped by any npm reinstall/upgrade, silently reverting to all-Opus routing (docs/01, risk #3)

Trusts a second third-party package (jev-router, 498 stars, created 2026-09-16) that runs a local HTTP proxy between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com and sees every request body plus the Claude OAuth/Authorization headers
API key handling is good in jev-health: piped to curl via --config - so it is not in argv/ps (bin/jev-health:12); key stored in ~/.jev-router.env chmod 600; jev-router passes it via env/SDK
No curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry in the repo itself; no shell injection found, but jev-down-hook interpolates the DOWN reason into an osascript string (macOS only, minor)

Prompt-injection surface: jev-down-hook injects additionalContext instructing the model to announce the failure; content is local and static so low risk. Routing decisions are made from prompt text only, so a crafted prompt or file content in prompt could bias tier choice (downgrade to Haiku for a hard task); docs/06-risks.md admits Haiku gets more things wrong
Not bypass-mode friendly by itself: proxy sits in the middle of all traffic including bypass-permission sessions, no tool-call mediation
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (direct TypeSafe, not OpenRouter): the health ping (constant dummy state) once per session, and, via upstream jev-router, the text of each fresh user prompt (system-reminder blocks stripped), the current model name and the context token count (docs/06-risks.md #4, upstream src/router.mjs state). Code, diffs, file contents and tool outputs are not sent to Jev, but the whole Anthropic request stream (including OAuth headers) transits the local 127.0.0.1 proxy. The user's own prompts may still contain client code or secrets that get sent to TypeSafe. No telemetry in jev-lab.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Startup: jev-health has a 6 s curl max-time; any failure falls back to plain claude with a loud warning (only on Linux the desktop notification is a no-op, the systemMessage still works). Mid-session: upstream jev-router uses a 1.5 s per-attempt timeout, 3 s deadline, 1 retry, and on any error keeps the current model; jev-lab explicitly documents that no alert exists for mid-session outages (docs/02-fallback.md, risk #6). Proxy crash mid-session is a single point of failure (risk #5). Unpatched upstream silently routes everything to Opus.
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero on the normal path: no MCP tools, no skills, no hooks injected when Jev is healthy (README: does not touch ~/.claude/settings.json). Upstream jev-router adds a /jev-explain skill, an injected status line and a 'Jev Router' entry in /model. On the fallback path only: two hooks injecting a roughly 60-token warning per prompt.
pros: Best-documented real-world failure analysis of jev-router: found and patched two silent bugs (SessionStart hook output as a trailing role=system message caused no routing at all; first-turn context guard pinned Opus in projects with large CLAUDE.md). The user has SessionStart hooks (caveman, GitNexus) and likely a large CLAUDE.md, so stock jev-router would silently do nothing for him.
Honest, measured docs: 78% of tokens are in a handful of giant sessions and only about 1% where per-turn routing can act (docs/07); tells the user routing saves little in long sessions.
Good hard-fallback design (health gate, loud warning, never modifies ~/.claude/settings.json, key via stdin not argv).
MIT licensed, tiny and easy to read (about 64 KB); the health gate and the fallback pattern are reusable ideas.
Lab principles are sane: Jev never sole authority on destructive actions, deterministic rules first.
cons: No OpenRouter support anywhere; direct TypeSafe endpoint and TYPESAFE key only. Switching needs an additional patch to upstream jev-router's SDK usage, inside node_modules, which is fragile.

Not automatic in the way the user wants: requires launching `jev` instead of `claude`, and Jev is used only for haiku/sonnet/opus tier routing, not for any other decisions. It runs a local proxy in front of Claude Code, which on an OAuth/subscription login relies on jev-router's pass-through of auth headers; risk of interfering with the main-model choice (user runs Opus 5.5) and with 1M-context window (upstream issue #35 noted).

Tier routing is of low value for this user: he wants Opus for daily work; downgrading turns to Haiku hurts quality (Jev sees only prompt text, not repo) and can invalidate the prompt cache; author's own data says only about 1% of spend is addressable.

Very immature: 1 star, 1 contributor, 6 commits over 2 days, no releases, no CI, no tests for the shipped scripts; badge pins Claude Code 2.1.278 and jev-router 0.3.0 (user runs 2.1.285); patch is against a package version that is moving fast.

macOS-centric (osascript notification, mise shims hardcoded at ~/.local/share/mise/shims/jev-claude); install.sh needs mise; on Linux without mise, health check fails immediately with 'jev-claude shim missing' and always falls back.
Depends on and in-place patches a second young third-party project (jev-router) and adds proxy as single point of failure; no mid-session outage alert.
Sends every prompt text to TypeSafe; problematic for client projects without consent.
The interesting Jev uses (completion gate, failure triage, blast radius) are roadmap or shadow-mode experiments not wired into Claude Code.
entries.verdict: Useful as a source of lessons and ideas (the SessionStart-role=system bug, fallback health gate) rather than something to install: it is a patch-and-wrapper around jev-router, TypeSafe-direct only, requires launching `jev` instead of `claude`, and only does model tier routing, which conflicts with a user who wants Opus for daily coding. Pass on it for the OpenRouter-based, automatic goal; borrow the design notes if evaluating jev-router itself.

entries.name: claude-code-jev-router (aadhar-build)
entries.what: Opt-in per-repo PreToolUse hook that rewrites subagent model via a static subagent_type tier table; v0.1 contains no AI, Jev only as a benchmarked treatment arm via Vercel gateway.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Agent)
pros: Honest, measured README: lookup table baseline, ~25ms, reversible one-command install/uninstall
Ledger and shadow-run infrastructure with tests to compare Jev against the baseline
cons: Not actually Jev in the shipped path; Jev arm uses typesafe-ai/jev via Vercel AI Gateway
Covers only 12-35% of delegations (general-purpose untouched); no savings number yet
Large repo (31k LOC incl. data) for little function

entries.name: alexadark/jev-openrouter-skill
entries.what: Codex skill asking Jev via OpenRouter which model and reasoning effort to use for a described task; returns recommendation only, does not switch model.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (explicit $jev-openrouter invocation)
pros: Uses OpenRouter alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY correctly
Versioned model catalog, includes Opus 5.5 profile
cons: Codex-only (README), catalog is OpenAI-centric; advisory, cannot change Claude Code model
Manual invocation contradicts auto-use goal
1 star, MIT, no tests seen

entries.name: Gamedirection/JevAI-MCP
entries.what: A self-hosted Node/TypeScript MCP server (Streamable HTTP, /mcp on ports 8080 and 3001) plus a React dashboard and SQLite request log. It wraps POST {endpoint}/systemone with 5 opinionated tools (jev_decide, jev_route_task, jev_assess_complexity, jev_should_escalate, jev_choose_strategy) that build choice/score/noul questions for coding-agent routing. It maps confidence to use/guidance/independent, retries, supports backup credentials, and has an optional local/cloud LLM fallback. Agent behavior is steered by server instructions and a shipped jev-routing.md to be pasted into CLAUDE.md. It is meant to run in Docker/K8s as an internal service.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Auto-use relies on SERVER_INSTRUCTIONS plus tool descriptions (and optionally a jev-routing.md pasted into CLAUDE.md). There is no hook, no skill and no proxy, so nothing deterministic ensures Jev is called. Opus will often skip calling a routing tool for tasks it can classify itself. The 'do not call for obvious' language further biases it toward not calling.
security: No auth on /mcp or the dashboard API; README says 'No login. Internal tool only'. Defaults bind 0.0.0.0 (.env.example HOST/MCP_HOST, DEFAULT_SETTINGS mcp.host 0.0.0.0, server.ts bindHost). On a laptop or shared network, any host can call the tools and spend the OpenRouter key.

The settings write API can change jev.endpoint. Cross-origin protection only checks Origin against Host when an Origin header is present (api.ts:57-66), so a non-browser LAN client can repoint the endpoint and capture the Bearer key. There is no DNS-rebinding or Host allow-list on /mcp.

The API key is not visible in argv if supplied via .env or Docker env. If saved via the dashboard, it is stored in SQLite (the README claims 'stored as a hash', but a hash cannot be replayed, so this needs checking in api-key-store.ts). Redaction regexes cover dk-, jv_, apikey_ and sk- patterns (secrets.ts).

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are typed (choice/score/noul), so the injection surface is small. The model composes the state itself, so injected repo text can still influence what gets sent and how it is classified. Then 'strong_yes'/'use' guidance is fed back to the agent.

Optional fallback (JEV_FALLBACK_ENABLED, default false) sends the full state to a configured local or cloud OpenAI-compatible LLM. Off by default. With full storage enabled, state is written to SQLite (truncated to 20k chars).

No postinstall, telemetry or curl|sh found. package.json has an allowScripts entry for esbuild and better-sqlite3 (native build). CI is GitHub Actions and .gitlab-ci.yml. Runs as the node user in Docker. It needs Docker or a build of a monorepo with about 800 KB of source, so there is a large audit surface for a tool that only wraps one HTTP call.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured endpoint (OpenRouter if repointed) with Authorization: Bearer key, X-Request-Id and User-Agent jevai-mcp/1.0.0: whatever `state` Claude composes (free text, object or array, up to 200k chars) plus the question instructions and criteria. There is no automatic collection of files, diffs or tool outputs; egress is limited to what the model chooses to put in state. Locally it stores metadata (caller, project, repository, session_id, sizes, timings) in SQLite by default, and the exact state (first 20k chars) if REQUEST_STATE_STORAGE=full. There is no telemetry to the author. Fallback LLM egress only happens if enabled.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every tool returns {success:false, error:{type:JEV_UNAVAILABLE, retryable}} and the instructions tell the agent to carry on. Defaults are a 10s timeout and 3 retries (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, JEV_RETRIES) with exponential backoff (300ms base, 5s max) and Retry-After support. Worst case is roughly 40s of blocking in a single tool call (4 attempts x 10s plus backoff), which is bad for a 'fast router', though backup credentials trigger only on 401/403/429. If the local MCP server itself is down, Claude Code just shows the MCP as failed and continues. The MCP-layer health returns 200 degraded.
entries.contextCost: 5 tools. By my estimate, descriptions come to roughly 3,000 chars and the zod-derived JSON schemas (state union, questions record with discriminated union, caller and metadata) to roughly 4-6k chars, so about 1.8-2.5k tokens of tool defs when loaded (they are deferred via tool search in current Claude Code, so the name-only cost is small). Server instructions come to about 1,000 chars, roughly 250 tokens. No hooks and no hook-injected text. If you also paste jev-routing.md into CLAUDE.md, that adds about 700 tokens on every turn.
pros: Env-only repointing to OpenRouter: the base URL, model and key are all configurable (client.ts:482, settings.ts:63), and the path is `{endpoint}/systemone`, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone in the brief. No code patch is needed, as long as the schema matches.

It is the only candidate I saw with a real design for coding-agent routing. It ships pre-built question templates, confidence-threshold mapping (use/guidance/independent) and batching guidance, and it fails open with typed errors.

Sound client engineering: retry/backoff with Retry-After, backup credential rotation on 401/403/429, strict zod validation of responses, key redaction, request-size limits, metadata-only storage by default, MIT license, and CI with tests.

The MCP server sets `instructions` and tool descriptions that explicitly say when to call and when not to, which is the closest thing to auto-invocation available without hooks. The Claude integration pack (jev-routing.md, CLAUDE.md snippet) is ready to drop in.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh. The tool surface is small (5 tools) and its typed outputs limit injection risk from Jev to the agent.
Local dashboard with per-call log, latency and cost makes it possible to actually measure whether Jev helps.
cons: It is 4 days old with 5 commits, 0 stars, 0 releases and 2 authors. It was clearly built for the author's own environment (docker-compose comment 'port 8080 is taken by octo-ai-web'; inconsistent defaults between README/settings.ts (defapi, typesafe/jev-1.13) and .env.example/compose (typesafe.ai, jev-1.13.0)).

Massive over-engineering for one HTTP call: a Docker service, SQLite, React dashboard, Helm, K8s and Prometheus metrics for a personal dev laptop. You must run a persistent daemon (with `docker compose up`) before Claude Code starts, or the MCP shows as failed. It is awkward for a stdio/uvx-style workflow, since Claude Code has no supervision of it.

No authentication and binds 0.0.0.0 by default. The unauthenticated settings API can repoint the endpoint (and thus exfiltrate the OpenRouter key) and any LAN host can spend your credits. It is unsuitable on a laptop on client networks without setting HOST=127.0.0.1 and MCP_HOST=127.0.0.1 manually.

Auto-invocation is entirely at model discretion. There is no hook, so 'without ever prompting' is not guaranteed; the instructions themselves tell Opus not to call it when things are obvious, so it will rarely fire. Each call also costs a full tool-call turn.

The value proposition is weak for Opus 5.5 daily coding: routing/classifying tasks, complexity and escalation are things the main model does inside its own reasoning at near-zero marginal cost, so Jev adds latency and tokens rather than saving them. The 'saved tokens' metric is a fixed 1500-token constant.

Worst-case blocking is about 40s per call (10s timeout x 4 attempts + backoff), which is a poor fit for a 70-500 ms router. No OpenRouter support has been verified in tests or docs, only DefAPI and TypeSafe, so schema drift on OpenRouter's /systemone would surface as JEV_INVALID_RESPONSE.
Codebase is roughly 800 KB across a monorepo, so auditing a client-facing tool that handles a paid key is expensive. Fallback mode can send state to arbitrary LLM URLs if misconfigured.
entries.verdict: It is a well-made but heavy, early-stage (4 days old) Docker+dashboard wrapper. It can technically point at OpenRouter through env vars alone. But it is only model-discretion (no hook), is unauthenticated on 0.0.0.0 by default, and its routing/escalation tools duplicate what Opus already does for free. It is worth using only as a reference for question templates or for measuring Jev, not as the daily integration.

entries.name: @barmajja/jclaude
entries.what: Node CLI (commander, zod) from one person (am33ma / Barmajja). Its main purpose is a controller that asks Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter) Choice/Score/Noul questions to pick a Claude model and effort for a task, then launches `claude -p <task> --model X --effort Y` as a subprocess. It also ships a `jclaude hook <event>` subcommand that acts as a Claude Code hook handler. The hook events are user-prompt-submit, pre-tool-use, stop, subagent-stop, post-tool-batch, post-tool-use-failure, permission-request, task-created and task-completed. The repo also has a SQLite/JSON ledger, an offline Jaccard-similarity project memory, a skill catalog, a test selector, and a PKCE login for OpenRouter keys. Its wrapper of `claude` is a zsh function in the source repo. That function is not in the npm tarball and only covers `claude -p`.
interface: jclaude resume / report / memory {list,add,invalidate} / blocker / doctor / auth {login,logout}
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, Stop, etc.), with no model discretion involved. This is the only candidate mechanism here that satisfies 'Claude Code uses it without me prompting'. BUT the npm package ships no hooks.json or settings snippet, so you would hand-write the ~/.claude/settings.json entries (command: node <pkg>/bin/jclaude.mjs hook <event>). The routing purpose (pick model or effort) cannot take effect in an interactive session. README lines 339-343 say hooks cannot swap the model, and the only model-switching path is the zsh `claude -p` wrapper.
security: Not a Jev-trust-boundary tool: hooks send data to OpenRouter unredacted in two paths. The PreToolUse and Stop hooks call JevClient.ask directly with {command} or {response}, bypassing redactRoutingState (hook.js:170-172, ~305). Only the UserPromptSubmit route path applies the regex redactor (decision-contract/redact.js). It covers sk-, ghp_, AKIA, KEY=value and PEM patterns, plus any 40+ char alphanumeric run.

API key is read from .env in JCLAUDE_HOME, the install dir of the package (cli/index.js:277), not from the process env or argv. Nothing appears in the process list. It is written with mode 0600 and never printed. With a global npm install that dir is inside node_modules, and the ledger and state (prompts, commands, permission-event summaries) are written there in plaintext.

No postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry to the author. Deps are only zod, dotenv and commander. Optional central store POSTs hook events (task/permission/stop) to a user-configured AWS endpoint, off by default.

Prompt-injection surface: the UserPromptSubmit advisory injects memory titles, near-duplicate request summaries and cross-project blocker summaries into model context. Those records come from a shared ledger and central store, so poisoned entries would enter context as hook additionalContext (labelled 'advisory').

Shell execution: spawns `claude -p` (run only) and git via execFileSync with an args array, no shell string. Log-reducer spawn is shell-less. The wrapper function shadows `claude` globally in zsh (source repo only).

No license field in package.json or npm metadata (unlicensed by default). Source repo Barmajja/barmajja-aios is not public: gh returns 404, so the only reviewable artifact is the npm tarball with source maps.
entries.dataEgress: The user-prompt-submit hook sends the first 4000 chars of EVERY user prompt (regex-redacted) plus memory evidence and a session/project id to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, as a JSON string in `state` with 4-5 questions. The pre-tool-use hook sends every Bash command (first 2000 chars, NOT redacted). The stop hook sends the last assistant message (first 4000 chars, NOT redacted), so it can carry code, file contents and tool-derived text. task-created sends the task subject (500 chars) and description (2000 chars). All of that goes to OpenRouter and the TypeSafe/Jev provider behind it. It is also stored locally in plaintext under JCLAUDE_HOME/state (ledger, stop-events, permission-events, task-events). The central store is opt-in and would send events to the user's own AWS endpoint. No source files or diffs are sent, except what appears in prompts, commands and assistant messages. The repair loop diff module reads git diffs, but only in `run --repair`.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. Hooks return null on any error, and a missing key means no call is made at all. The JevClient timeout is 8000 ms (config timeoutMs) via AbortController. The CLI has an internal 10 s cap, which is under Claude Code's hook timeout. On a Jev failure, route returns jevError and the prompt hook emits nothing. In `route` a failure resolves to a fallback or review-pause decision. The PreToolUse hook can add an 'ask' prompt for Bash, which in bypass or auto mode may interrupt unattended runs on a false positive. The stop hook is shadow-only and never blocks. In the worst case Jev is slow, so each prompt waits up to 8 s and each Bash call waits up to 8 s before proceeding. Nothing is cached per call.
entries.contextCost: 0 MCP tools and no MCP server instructions, so no per-session tool-definition cost. The cost is hook-injected text. UserPromptSubmit adds a '[jev advisory ...]' block of about 2-8 lines (roughly 60-200 tokens) on EVERY prompt, and more when memory, near-duplicate or blocker lines appear. post-tool-batch and post-tool-use-failure add one line (~40 tokens) only when they match. The advisory content is mostly routing telemetry (profile=haiku/sonnet/opus, effort=) that Claude Code cannot act on in an interactive Opus session, so it is nearly pure noise.
pros: It is the only candidate that uses Claude Code hooks (deterministic UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse and Stop events) to call Jev without you ever mentioning it, so the automatic-invocation requirement is met by design.

Real OpenRouter code path with the wire schema empirically corrected against the live endpoint (state as string, questions keyed by id, Score criteria as level labels, dated model-suffix acceptance). It hits /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 pinned, and the base URL and model are env-overridable. It is a working reference for the request/response shapes.
Uniform fail-open: 8 s abort timeout, errors swallowed, no call when there is no key, and PreToolUse can only 'ask', never 'deny'. A Jev outage will not wedge a session.

Sensible Noul-question design ideas to borrow: destructive-Bash risk (P>=0.6 gives ask), 'looks finished' check on the last message, 'well specified' check on tasks. Also a PKCE headless OpenRouter key flow that avoids pasting keys into sessions.
Small dependency footprint (zod, dotenv, commander), no postinstall, no telemetry to the author, key stored 0600 in .env and not exposed in argv.
cons: The core value (route to haiku/sonnet/opus and effort) is useless for an interactive Opus 5.5 subscription session. The README states hooks cannot swap models, and routing only applies to `claude -p` through a zsh wrapper that is not in the package. The hook output is a passive advisory the model has no reason to act on.

Only the UserPromptSubmit route path redacts secrets. PreToolUse (Bash commands) and Stop (last assistant message) send raw text to OpenRouter and the Jev provider, a real problem for client projects with tokens in commands or env output. Your existing secret-leak guard would not cover these calls.

Latency: one to two extra network round trips per prompt, plus one per Bash call (up to 8 s on timeout), stacked on your GitNexus and secret-guard Bash hooks. Jev's Noul destructive check is much weaker than your deterministic guard and may add false-positive 'ask' prompts, which break bypass and auto mode.

No hook config or settings snippet ships, and the package has no docs (docs/ and shell/ are not in the tarball). The source repo is private, there is no license, and it is a one-maintainer package with 7 releases in about 2 hours on 2026-09-23 and no updates since. It is tightly coupled to Barmajja's projects (config test mappings, skill catalog, AWS central store, Arabic RTL memory examples).

JCLAUDE_HOME is the install dir, so keys, ledger and plaintext prompts/commands land inside node_modules or the global prefix. It also creates a persistent local store of every prompt and permission request, plus an opt-in remote store.

Injects context on every prompt and cross-project 'blockers elsewhere' lines from a shared store, a prompt-injection and context-pollution surface that the user did not ask for. The README itself mislabels the endpoint (/api/v1/systemone) while the code uses /api/alpha/decisions, and the claimed 216 tests could not be verified from the tarball.
Never exercised as an actual Claude Code hook in a real session; per the README the nested-claude path was refused by the permission system.
entries.verdict: Not recommended for adoption as-is. Its model/effort routing does nothing for an interactive Opus subscription session, and its hooks send unredacted Bash commands and assistant messages to OpenRouter with per-call latency. It is worth reading only as a reference for OpenRouter Jev wire format, fail-open hook patterns and Noul question wording, then reimplementing a minimal hook of your own (e.g. one PreToolUse risk check).
entries.license: None declared (no license field in package.json, no LICENSE in tarball)

entries.name: claude-autorouter
entries.what: Local 127.0.0.1 Anthropic-Messages proxy launched via `claude-autorouter claude`, which sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to itself and spawns `claude`. For every /v1/messages request it sends a bounded state excerpt (up to 12,000 chars: latest human task, first task, 1000-char system excerpt, up to 8 recent messages incl. tool results) to Jev /v1/systemone as a single `choice` question (haiku/sonnet/opus), then rewrites the request `model` to the chosen Claude tier and streams the response back. It is a Haiku/Sonnet/Opus cost router, not a general decision tool for Claude Code. Low-confidence (<0.75) picks are bumped to at least Sonnet. It also has an experimental local Ollama (nimble/tev1) evaluator, a status line, and savings estimates.
interface: No MCP tools, no hooks, no skills
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: fully automatic once Claude Code is started through `claude-autorouter claude` (could be aliased as `claude`), with no prompting needed. Plain `claude` launches bypass it entirely, and it does not use the existing hooks. It is not deterministic per tool call but per API request.
security: No dependencies, no install scripts (package.json has no preinstall/postinstall), no curl|sh; only child_process use is spawn('claude') and execFile for version/Ollama checks (bin/autorouter.mjs:133, onboarding.mjs:1)
Keys never passed via argv: setup prompts without echo, env or 0600 JSON config; TYPESAFE_API_KEY and AUTOROUTER_TOKEN stripped from the Claude child env (auth.mjs:53-54)
Proxy binds 127.0.0.1 only (server.mjs:269), requires timing-safe local token, rejects requests with Origin header, fixed upstream allowlist so not an open forward proxy (server.mjs:179-192)

Subscription mode passes Claude Code's OAuth Bearer token through the local proxy to api.anthropic.com untouched (server.mjs:113-116); the token is not cached, but a third-party process sits in the auth path and Anthropic sees a non-first-party base URL
Redirects disabled on the Jev call (redirect:'error'); endpoints must be HTTPS or loopback with no credentials/query (config.mjs:372-379)

Prompt-injection surface: tool results and file contents go into Jev's state; the instructions tell Jev to treat state as data, but a poisoned file could steer tier choice (downgrade to Haiku). Impact limited to model quality, not command execution
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev evaluator (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed) on every inference request: up to 12,000 serialized chars of latest human prompt, first prompt, system-prompt excerpt (up to 1000 chars), up to 8 recent messages (up to 3000 chars each) including tool_result text (file contents, command output, diffs), plus message_count and tool_count. Images, documents, thinking blocks and tool_use inputs omitted. Because client-side secret guards are hooks on tool calls, secrets that appear in tool results or prompts will be included in these excerpts, which matters for client projects. Anthropic still receives the full request as before. Large/multimodal requests also hit Anthropic count_tokens. Local Ollama evaluator keeps classification on-machine (3000 bytes).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, but slow. Jev call has a 1500 ms timeout (AUTOROUTER_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, max 10000) with redirect:error; on timeout/HTTP error/invalid JSON the router returns fallback: Sonnet, or Opus if the client model is Opus, and keeps the pinned/sonnet+ model for continuations (router.mjs:214-223, 297). Requests are never blocked by a Jev outage. Note that the classification is awaited before the request is forwarded, so a slow Jev adds up to 1.5 s to each request. Decisions are cached 5 min by body hash; turn pins for 30 min keep tool continuations on one model.
entries.contextCost: Zero context cost for tools: registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills, injects no text into the model context. Side effects on session config instead: forces ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-haiku-4-5, MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0 (compatible profile), adds a temporary statusLine via --settings (may replace the user's own status line unless AUTOROUTER_STATUSLINE=0), optional CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP.
pros: Truly automatic with no prompt wording: a per-request Jev decision is made by a proxy, not by model discretion, and the design fails open (router.mjs:214-223)
Real Jev usage matches the brief: a `choice` question with per-option criteria and confidence, and a 0.75 confidence threshold that bumps uncertain cases to Sonnet+ (router.mjs:205-208)
Zero context cost: no MCP tool defs, hooks or skill text added, so it does not interact with gitnexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks
Endpoint, model and key are all env/config-overridable (AUTOROUTER_JEV_URL/MODEL, saved config keys), so repointing to OpenRouter is a config change with no code patch

Careful engineering: tool continuations stay on one model, signed thinking/mid-conversation-system/model-specific features preserve the client model, context-size guard with count_tokens, secrets kept out of argv and child env, no deps, no install scripts
Supports a local Ollama evaluator so no code excerpts need to leave the machine, if you accept the measured trade-offs (Nimble 11 s median, Tev1 0.8B 18/24)
cons: Solves a different problem: it downgrades Opus work to Sonnet/Haiku to save money. This user already runs Opus 5.5 as main model on a subscription, where cost savings do not reduce the bill (README itself says savings are API-equivalent only), and quality risk from mis-tiering is real. The Jev value proposition as calibrated decision-maker for other agent choices is not exposed

Compatible profile (default) forces ANTHROPIC_MODEL=haiku and MAX_THINKING_TOKENS=0, disabling client thinking; native profile preserves settings but then most requests hit the 'model_specific_features' preserve branches so little routing happens

Only active when launched as `claude-autorouter claude`; requires wrapping/aliasing claude, and the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL override is inherited by all subprocesses; conflicts with users who set their own base URL/gateway

Sits in the OAuth path: Claude Code subscription Bearer token is forwarded via a local third-party proxy, raising account-policy and supply-chain risk for a 1-day-old, single-maintainer, private-source package

Sends up to 12k chars of prompts and tool results (code, diffs, possibly secrets and client IP) to Jev on every request, including tool-loop steps; this conflicts with the user's secret-leak guard intent and client confidentiality
Adds a serial network hop (70-500 ms claimed, up to 1.5 s on timeout) before every model request, slowing agentic loops that make dozens of calls per task
No OpenRouter support today; schema parity with OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone is unverified, and the key variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY

Very immature: npm created 2026-09-29 with 7 releases in ~1 day (0.2.0 to 0.3.6); GitHub repo is private/404 so no stars, issues, commit history, tests or reviewability; 0.3.6 tarball 404 at audit time
Status line injection may clash with user's existing statusLine; forces ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true on user
entries.verdict: A well-built but narrowly scoped Haiku/Sonnet/Opus cost router that transparently uses Jev via the System One choice API; it is automatic and fail-open, and repointing it to OpenRouter is plausibly a three-variable config change. entries.name: nidhi-singh02/agent-router
entries.what: A Node/TypeScript CLI (`router run "<task>"`) that picks which coding agent (Cursor, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode), model and reasoning effort to use for a task. It filters subscriptions by quota and policy, then asks Jev through the TypeSafe SDK (`systemOne`) to classify the task and rank the remaining candidates. It then launches the chosen agent in a Herdr terminal-multiplexer pane. It is not an MCP server or a hook, and it does not proxy Claude Code's own traffic. It is an external orchestrator that starts agents, and a Claude Code skill (`skills/model-router`) tells an agent to call the CLI.
interface: router status [--usage] / router session [id] [--list] / router accounts / router usage refresh
herdr-plugin.toml panes: route, status, resume, sessions, usage-refresh
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger and only when prompted. The skill fires when the user asks to pick a model, subscription or effort, or when an agent launched by `router` reaches the end of a phase. The launching side requires a Herdr pane (HERDR_ENV=1). It never triggers on ordinary coding, so it does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
security: The README says pre-release. It is 13 days old, 128 commits by 1 person (two git identities), 99 stars, one v0.1.0 release. There is no .github directory, so no CI.

API key handling is good. It supports a macOS Keychain reference (`keychain:NAME`) or an `env:NAME` reference. Config forbids secret values, and launched Herdr commands get an allowlisted environment (docs/privacy.md). The Keychain path is macOS-only.

Client-side guard `assertSafeState` (typesafe-client.ts:29-45) regex-rejects sk-, Bearer, GitHub, Slack, AWS, Google, private-key and URL-with-password strings before any Jev call. It is best-effort and does not catch arbitrary secrets in free text.

It shells out. It runs the `herdr` CLI, git worktree commands, the agent CLIs, and Keychain/official usage CLIs (collectors/verified-command.ts, launch/herdr-client.ts). The pane-text reading and keystroke injection for `/effort` (live-effort) is fragile and UI-coupled.
The build runs `npm ci` and compiles better-sqlite3 natively. Dependencies are few (commander, zod, better-sqlite3, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0).
Optional Cloudflare coordinator and Hermes heartbeat packages are off by default. The README says not to deploy them without approval.
entries.dataEgress: ["Every `router run` sends the task text (free-form user prompt) plus candidateCount and bucketed PR-size enrichment to api.typesafe.ai (docs/privacy.md, README:34-36). Enrichment is bucketed and sends no paths or repo names.","`router effort --session` sends a one-line sub-step (at most 500 characters), the phase, the current effort, and bucketed signals.","No file contents, diffs, tool outputs or conversation are sent.","It does not send Claude Code's own traffic. The agents are launched separately and keep their own subscription auth.","Nothing goes to OpenRouter."]
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for routing. The README says "Routing always calls TypeSafe; there is no fallback". If the call errors, decision-engine.ts returns `typesafe-unavailable`, and only two task families (routine-transformation and metadata) get a deterministic fallback (semantic/fallback.ts:5-24). The router never sits in Claude Code's own request path, so a slow or failed Jev call does not break Claude Code itself. It only blocks a `router run` launch. No custom Jev timeout was found. The SDK has its own timeout and retry policy, and the router uses its defaults.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools and no hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. The only cost is the skill: a SKILL.md of 59 lines (about 1,000 tokens once triggered), with a short description always in the skill list (about 100 tokens). Skill loading is on demand.
pros: The Jev questions are well designed for a real use case. It uses several Jev primitives (Choice for ranking, Score for complexity and consequence, and a confidence policy that asks the user when confidence is below 0.75 on high-consequence tasks). This is useful as a reference for how to call Jev.
Privacy design is thoughtful. Bucketed signals, a local secret-pattern guard, a Keychain reference for keys, and a 0700/0600 state directory.
Large test suite (about 25k lines of TS and tests, vitest, a routing evals JSON) and detailed design docs and specs.
MIT license. The TypeSafe SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so OpenRouter may be reachable with little change.
Includes real Claude Code specifics, such as the CLAUDE_EFFORT variable and Opus 5.5 effort levels.
cons: It does not integrate into Claude Code. It launches Claude Code as one target among four agents inside Herdr. It is not a hook, MCP server or proxy, and it cannot make the user's existing Claude Code session use Jev.
It requires Herdr (HERDR_ENV=1) to launch anything. The user's workflow shows no Herdr.

The only automatic behavior comes from a skill that needs the user to run the router flow first. It is also written around routing between paid subscriptions (Cursor, Codex, OpenCode, Claude), which this single-subscription user does not need.
TypeSafe-direct only, with no OpenRouter code. Switching to OpenRouter is unverified and depends on SDK path and model-ID compatibility. The key resolution is Keychain-first (macOS).
Every run sends the task text to a third party, and routing is fail-closed with no general fallback.
Pre-release and 13 days old: single author, no CI, no security review, v0.1.0.
Heavy build: `npm ci` plus native better-sqlite3 compilation, a SQLite state store, and usage collectors that scrape dashboards.
The SKILL.md tells agents to run `router effort` (keystroke injection into the pane) with no confirmation. That is risky in bypass or auto permission mode.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration. It is a Herdr-based multi-agent launcher that calls Jev via the TypeSafe SDK only. It is useful as a reference for well-formed Jev Choice and Score questions, but not something to install for automatic in-session Jev use with OpenRouter.

entries.name: Bodila51/Jev-chooses-a-LLM (Jev Router for Cursor)
entries.what: A Cursor-specific plugin (rule + 3 subagents + slash commands + stdio MCP server) that sends a task description to TypeSafe System One (Jev) with a Choice question (cost/balanced/intelligence tier), a Score question (complexity) and a Noul question (needs approval), applies a hard policy layer, and tells the parent agent which subagent to delegate to. It also ships a Cursor SDK runner that picks a Cursor model ID. It is not a Claude Code integration: the model tiers are Cursor model IDs (composer-2.5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5), and Claude Code cannot swap models per subagent through this.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool, and only if the Cursor rule text is copied into CLAUDE.md. The tool description says 'Parent agents MUST call this before delegating work'. In Claude Code there is no hook or deterministic trigger, so compliance is best-effort. Unlike Cursor, there is no alwaysApply rule mechanism, so the rule would have to be manually ported.
security: API key is read from env or from a .env in the repo root (mcp/server.ts:6-29, a hand-rolled parser). It is never put in argv. The key is sent only as a Bearer header to the configured baseUrl. Nothing stops baseUrl in config.json from pointing elsewhere.

No curl|sh, no postinstall script, no telemetry phone-home. Local telemetry is written to ./telemetry/events-DATE.jsonl relative to cwd (shared/telemetry.ts). By default it stores only a length and hash digest (logPromptContent=false). With true it stores the first 500 characters of the prompt, after regex secret redaction.
mcp.json uses `npx tsx` at every start, so it needs npm resolution at runtime (tsx is a devDependency and is fetched by npx). Node is spawned with NODE_OPTIONS=--use-system-ca.

Secret redaction patterns exist (shared/redaction.ts), but they are applied only to telemetry. They are NOT applied to the state sent to Jev; the raw task is sent, truncated to 4000 characters (typesafe-client.ts:113).

Prompt-injection surface: the tool result contains an 'instruction' field that tells the parent agent to delegate everything to a subagent. It is script-generated, not attacker-controlled, but the task text is model-supplied and can be steered by injected content in read files, which would bias the tier.

Silent mock fallback: with no TYPESAFE_API_KEY the server uses regex heuristics and returns a 'jev-mock' route without failing. useMock is set to !process.env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY (server.ts:156). It would look like Jev is working when it is not.
entries.dataEgress: The `state` object in every jev_route call goes to api.typesafe.ai (or another baseUrl if configured). It holds task[0:4000] (the raw task text the model passes in), objective, attachment metadata, tool names, and about 12 boolean or flag fields (mcp/typesafe-client.ts:111-132). There are no file contents or diffs unless the model pastes them into `task`. The task text is model-composed, so code or secrets can end up in it, and there is no redaction before sending. Local telemetry files contain digests only by default.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Jev errors, HTTP failures or timeouts (15s default, AbortController at typesafe-client.ts:57) become degradedRouting=true, and the tier falls back to BALANCED (router.ts:62-103). A 15s worst-case stall per route call is a long time for an interactive tool, though it only occurs if Jev hangs. A missing key gives silent mock routing (see security).
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Tool defs (names, descriptions, schemas) are about 3.0k characters, roughly 750 tokens. No MCP server 'instructions'. The Cursor rule (about 1.9k characters, about 480 tokens) is not loaded by Claude Code unless it is copied into CLAUDE.md. Each jev_route result adds roughly 300-500 tokens of JSON. If the 3 subagent files were installed as .claude/agents, that adds a few hundred more tokens. Total is about 1-1.5k tokens fixed plus per-turn results.
pros: Small, readable codebase (about 1.7k lines TS) with a minimal dependency (only @modelcontextprotocol/sdk). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry to third parties, and key handling is env only.

Real use of the System One primitives (Choice, Score, Noul) with a sensible request shape and a clean typed client (typesafe-client.ts). This is a useful reference for building our own OpenRouter Jev call.
Fail-open with a 15s timeout and a BALANCED fallback, and explicit kill switches (enabled:false, /jev-bypass).
Transport is nearly OpenRouter-compatible: the same {model,state,questions} body, so baseUrl and model can be changed via config (providerSupport.openrouterPatchability).
MIT license, with unit tests on the policy and redaction logic.
cons: It is built for Cursor, not Claude Code. The output is 'delegate to subagent X' plus Cursor model IDs (composer-2.5, claude-sonnet-5, claude-opus-5). Claude Code subagents can take a model: frontmatter, but the shipped agents do not set one, and the main model (Opus 5.5) cannot be swapped mid-session by an MCP tool. The real routing benefit lives in the Cursor SDK runner and is unavailable here.

No OpenRouter support: key env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY hardcoded, default URL api.typesafe.ai, zero OpenRouter references. It needs config and env workarounds, and the strict OpenRouter validation of the Score criteria array is unverified.

The routing question ('which Cursor tier is cheapest that still completes the task') is a cost-optimisation gimmick. For a user on Opus 5.5 by subscription there is no per-token saving, so it adds latency and context without value.
Auto-invocation is only via a prompt-level 'MUST call' instruction, which is not deterministic in Claude Code and would fire for every task (an extra tool call and turn each time).
Sends the raw task text to a third-party API without redaction. On client projects this is a data-egress and confidentiality concern, and the silent mock fallback hides a missing key.
Weak maturity: 1 author, 4 commits in 2 days, 3 stars, no releases, no CI, no live-API tests. The regex policy is tuned for email, finance and deploy tasks, not code work.
Config lookup from cwd (config.local.json, config.json) is a possible key-exfiltration vector in untrusted client repos.
entries.verdict: Not suitable for Claude Code. It is a Cursor tier-router with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint whose output (cheap/balanced/expensive Cursor models) cannot change what a Claude Code Opus session does, and it has no deterministic hook. Its only value is as a reference for the System One request shape and fail-open pattern when building a Claude Code hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone directly.
