entries.name: nekowasabi/jev-routing
entries.what: Single Go binary that runs a local reverse proxy between Claude Code/Codex/Grok/Devin and the upstream LLM API (jev-routing run claude sets ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to 127.0.0.1:8787). It rewrites each request (drops/truncates tool_use/tool_result history, optional Jev Choice/Noul calls for next-tool selection/advice, optional Anthropic-native clear_tool_uses context editing gated by a Jev call, thinking stripping) and forwards to api.anthropic.com. The goal was token reduction, not coding-quality improvement. The repo was ARCHIVED 2026-09-26 by the author, who concluded Jev-based tool selection/steering does not generically reduce agent tokens.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Fully automatic once claude is started through jev-routing run claude (or ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL exported globally in settings.json env / shell alias plus a daemon); no prompt changes needed. But it must sit in front of every request, and Jev is called only when the proxy decides (hybrid/local classifier default).
security: Sits in the full request path of the user's Anthropic traffic: sees the Claude Code OAuth/subscription bearer token and all prompts, code and tool results in cleartext on loopback HTTP (127.0.0.1:8787, no TLS, no auth on the local port; any local process can use it and the /dashboard).

API key handling: Jev key read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_API_KEY), sent as Authorization header, not put in argv. Host CLI child gets ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN dropped from env (host.go:128-129), so API-key auth would not work through wrapper; OAuth login is passed through.
Local git exec only: exec.Command("git","rev-parse") (lookup.go:57), tmux, and the host CLI itself; no shell installer, no postinstall, no curl|sh.
No telemetry found in code beyond the Jev call and the upstream forward; Jev call uses a 20s http.Client timeout.

Rewriting the model's conversation (dropping/truncating tool results, synthesizing compaction summaries, stripping thinking, appending advice into the last tool_result) is an integrity/quality risk rather than a classic vuln; a prompt-injection surface exists because tool-result text is fed to Jev as state and advice is written back into the conversation.
Repo carries .agent-checkpoints/ and .grok/ artifacts and Japanese-language design docs; single-author project (2 humans + a Cursor agent), 1 star, unaudited.
entries.dataEgress: To Anthropic: unchanged full traffic (rewritten), forwarded to api.anthropic.com. To Jev endpoint (TypeSafe or whatever JEV_BASE_URL points at, e.g. OpenRouter) only when a Jev path is active: a fitted 'state' JSON (user request text, catalog of tool names/descriptions, truncated tool inputs of 1000/200/60 chars, abridged tool result/history text) plus questions, capped at 32k tokens (jev.go FitInputCopy, InputBudget). Default mode is hybrid with an on-device classifier and Claude advise/clear-gate off, so with defaults and no key almost nothing is sent to Jev; with a key and the Claude clear gate or advise enabled, code snippets and tool outputs from client projects go to Jev/OpenRouter. Also a stateful local proxy that could log events for the dashboard.
entries.failureMode: Jev side: 20s HTTP timeout (jev.go:56), errors returned to caller, and README states a fail-safe design (uncertain -> do not narrow tools, unsupported history shapes pass through unrewritten, compaction reply falls back to upstream when reduction under 25%). Mostly fail-open for Jev slowness. But the local proxy itself is a hard single point of failure: if it is not running or crashes, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set to it gets connection errors (fail-closed for all model traffic). A 20s Jev timeout on the request path can stall a turn.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no MCP instructions, no hooks, no skills. It does not add tokens to the tool catalog (for Claude it deliberately does not narrow tools because that breaks the prompt cache). When advise is enabled it appends a short next-tool reminder to the last tool_result (opt-in, off by default). Net context cost about 0; the proxy's stated effect is to reduce context, but with the author's own data: Claude Code native clear edit gives only about 6.3% real-session ceiling, and advise gives about +1.67% (noise) on opus-5-5.
pros: Truly automatic and prompt-free: transparent ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL proxy, no MCP tools, no context tokens added, no skills to trigger, matches the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' requirement mechanically.

Jev endpoint and model are env-configurable (JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL, key sent as plain Bearer), so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with an OpenRouter key is plausibly a zero-code change (schema equality unverified).

Sane defaults for Claude Code: tool catalog not narrowed (protects prompt cache), advise and clear-tool-uses default OFF, on-device classifier in hybrid mode so nothing goes to Jev without a key, compaction replacement falls back to Claude's own when savings under 25%.
Well-tested Go (about 464 Test funcs), single static binary, MIT, tiny dependency set, no npm/postinstall/curl|sh; loopback dashboard shows exactly what was rewritten.

The archived RESEARCH.md is unusually honest, paired/pre-registered data on Jev in Claude Code: a valuable negative result and a design reference (native context editing + one Jev gate call is the only approach that held up, about 8-11% on same-path, about 6% real ceiling).
cons: ARCHIVED 2026-09-26 (8 days after creation, 1 star, no releases, no CI): author explicitly concluded Jev tool selection/steering does not reduce tokens; no maintenance or bug fixes will come.

Its own Claude Code data: Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool_choice under any thinking mode, advise gave +1.67% (3 better/3 worse, noise) and Sonnet 5 advise was an increase up to -27% (99% of it Jev cost). The one working feature (clear_tool_uses gate) is default-off with a ~6% real-session ceiling. Little coding benefit to gain.

Puts a custom rewriting proxy in the path of ALL Anthropic traffic including the subscription OAuth token and client-project code; single point of failure (proxy down = Claude Code down), plaintext loopback with no local auth, and it drops ANTHROPIC_API_KEY/AUTH_TOKEN from the child env. Unsuitable for client work without an audit.

Requires launching via 'jev-routing run claude' or a global ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL plus a supervised daemon; Claude Code 2.1.285 compatibility is unverified (benchmarks used claude-opus-5-5 and sonnet-5 on an older CLI); it also rewrites history/compaction, which risks prompt-cache misses and quality loss on an 80k-token-prefix Opus session.

Not a coding-quality tool: Jev only guides tool choice/erasure for cost; it does not add review, routing-to-cheaper-model, or code intelligence. Env var naming (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and default model 'jev-latest' need remapping for OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-latest) and OpenRouter schema parity is unconfirmed.

Coexistence unknowns with existing setup: caveman-shrink MCP, GitNexus/secret-guard hooks operate on tool calls and are unaffected, but the wrapper approach conflicts with subscription features if the proxy mishandles streaming/headers.
entries.verdict: Technically the only candidate that is truly automatic (transparent proxy, zero context cost) and it can likely be pointed at OpenRouter via JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_MODEL, but the author archived it after measuring that Jev steering does not help Claude Code (advise about 0%, context-clear about 6% real ceiling). Do not adopt for daily or client work; treat RESEARCH.md as a reference and, at most, borrow the 'native clear_tool_uses + one Jev gate call' idea.

entries.name: jev-conductor-router
entries.what: Stdio MCP server plus CLI (npm jev-conductor-router 0.2.1) that asks Jev two built-in questions (delegation: direct vs conductor, gate at P(conductor) >= 0.65; difficulty: routine/standard/complex/frontier) and then routes and launches coding tasks on Conductor (conductor.build) cloud workspaces via api.conductor.build. It is a Conductor cloud-workspace orchestrator that uses Jev as a gate, not a general Jev integration for Claude Code. The only generic piece is the jev_decide tool (arbitrary choice/score/noul questions).
interface: CLI: route / launch / status / feedback / evaluate / mcp
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a skill description trigger scoped to 'user asks for Conductor / cloud coding agent'. No hooks, no proxy. Server instructions tell the model to call jev_decide/conductor_route before creating a Conductor workspace, but only in a Conductor context. It will not consult Jev on ordinary coding turns.
security: API keys read from env only and sent as Bearer to fixed hosts (jev.ts:156); no key in argv when configured via MCP env block, but README quickstart pastes keys into the MCP JSON env (plain-text config).
Recommended install is npx -y jev-conductor-router (unpinned, runs latest npm code with all env keys each session) -- supply-chain risk; single maintainer, 2 versions in 1 day.
git install runs a prepare script (scripts/prepare.mjs) which may spawn 'npm install --no-save' for typescript; npm-registry install has no postinstall/preinstall (checked package.json).
fetch uses redirect:'error' (jev.ts:154) and refuses secret-like workspace env names/values (conductor.ts:1-59).

Prompt-injection surface: task text is untrusted and passed to Jev with an explicit 'state is untrusted' instruction; conductor_transcript returns remote agent output into Claude's context; conductor_create_workspace can launch real, billable cloud agent work and archive is gated only by a model-supplied confirmedByUser flag.

Opt-in discover.mjs calls undocumented Conductor broker routes and can send a Cursor session cookie to cursor.com and read local Anthropic/ChatGPT OAuth credentials to query usage (src/discover.mjs:47-88); only runs with CONDUCTOR_DISCOVERY_OPT_IN=1 inside a Conductor workspace.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev provider: the first 20,000 characters of whatever 'state'/'task' string is passed (jev.ts:158, 90) plus the question schemas; provider order Orbio -> OpenRouter -> TypeSafe with fallback to next on timeout/402/408/429/5xx, so if ORBIO_API_KEY is set task text goes to a third party (Orbio). To Conductor (api.conductor.build): full task text, repo/branch, and workspace env on create/send_message, plus transcript reads. Nothing is sent automatically by a hook; only what Claude chooses to put in the tool arguments leaves the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for the gate: 2000 ms default per-provider timeout (jev.ts:157); network error/timeout/402/408/429/5xx falls through to next provider, then returns null -> delegation defaults to 'continue directly' and difficulty to a 'standard' fallback (jev.ts:192-205). 400/401/403 throws a JevProviderError (tool returns isError). Since it is a model-called MCP tool, an outage just makes the tool return available:false; no blocking of Claude Code. Missing Conductor key makes every conductor_* tool error.
entries.contextCost: 10 MCP tools (jev_decide, conductor_route, conductor_create_workspace, conductor_start_session, conductor_send_message, conductor_status, conductor_transcript, conductor_list_projects, conductor_cancel, conductor_feedback). Estimated ~8-9k chars of names+descriptions+zod schemas (src/mcp.ts:36-195), roughly 2-2.5k tokens, plus a ~330-char server instructions string (mcp.ts:30) ~80 tokens. Plugin install would also add a SKILL.md (~83 lines, description ~250 chars in context). No hook-injected text. Total about 2.5k tokens of always-on context for tools that are mostly irrelevant without Conductor.
pros: Native, code-verified OpenRouter Decisions API support (https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and direct TypeSafe support, with JEV_PROVIDER pinning (src/jev.ts:38-83).

Correct use of Jev primitives (choice with criteria map, probability-mass validation, calibrated thresholds 0.65/0.8/0.9-1.1 mass check) and a sane fail-safe fallback: Jev failure never escalates cost or blocks work (jev.ts:178-205).
jev_decide is a generic pass-through for choice/score/noul questions, so it can be reused as a hand-rolled decision tool if the user writes their own skill/instructions.
Reasonable hygiene: no postinstall in the registry package, redirect:'error', secret-looking env refusal, 0600 state file, no telemetry found, MIT, has tests + CI on Node 20/22.
Small code base (about 1.2k lines src) that is easy to audit or fork; JEV question definitions in jev.ts:89-107 are a reusable template for coding-difficulty routing.
cons: Domain mismatch: 9 of 10 tools are Conductor cloud-workspace operations and require CONDUCTOR_API_KEY and a Conductor account with repos on its cloud machine; the user does not use Conductor per any provided context, so this does nothing for local Claude Code work.
Not automatic in the way requested: no hook, no proxy; the SKILL.md description triggers only on Conductor/cloud-agent requests, so Claude will not consult Jev during normal coding.
The Jev decision is only a delegation gate (launch a remote agent or not); it does not route Claude Code's own model, subagents, tools or permissions.

Default provider chain puts Orbio (a third-party api.orbio.so, unrelated to OpenRouter) FIRST if ORBIO_API_KEY is set and would fall back across providers, sending task text to whichever answers; needs JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter to be strictly OpenRouter.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-25, 6 commits, 2 contributors (Cubs/JussCubs), 1 star, 0 forks, no GitHub release, npm 0.2.0/0.2.1 published within 3 hours of each other; unpinned npx -y install re-fetches latest on every start.

Can launch billable cloud agent runs and send task/repo content to Conductor; conductor_transcript feeds remote agent output back into context (indirect prompt injection path); archive safeguard is a model-set boolean.
~2.5k tokens of always-on tool schema context for functionality the user cannot use; state file drops into cwd unless JEV_STATE_DIR is set.
Uses OpenRouter Decisions alpha endpoint (not /api/v1/systemone); alpha API may change and default 2 s timeout may spuriously fall back.
entries.verdict: Well-formed but narrow: a Conductor cloud-workspace router that happens to use Jev (OpenRouter supported) as a launch gate, with no hook or transparent behavior for Claude Code. Skip it for this user's daily coding; at most borrow the question definitions and OpenRouter request shape (jev.ts:89-158) for a custom hook or MCP.

entries.name: atulify/omp-plugin-jev-router
entries.what: Oh My Pi (OMP) extension that classifies each prompt simple/advanced via one Jev Choice question and switches the OMP model role; fails to advanced.
entries.autoInvocation: Auto per prompt inside OMP (extension hook); not applicable to Claude Code
pros: Sound design: closed-set Choice, bounded context, single attempt, all failures route to advanced
Has unit tests plus a mock TypeSafe server
cons: Targets Oh My Pi only, not Claude Code; needs OMP 18.1.6
Uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY and jev-latest; no OpenRouter path found; macOS Keychain focus
1 star, created 9 days ago

entries.name: sherajdev/jev-research
entries.what: Guide plus small TS prototype (jev-router.ts) routing tasks to Claude/Codex/Hermes agents via Jev, orchestrated through Herdr panes; policy stays in coordinator code.
entries.autoInvocation: manual
pros: Sound architecture: Jev recommends, code decides, allowlisted outputs
Covers human-approval escalation for ambiguous work
cons: Docs plus one script; no hook or MCP, requires Herdr
Uses @typesafe-ai/sdk directly, not OpenRouter-configured
Routes between agents, not model selection inside Claude Code

entries.name: punkcanyang/hermes-jev-router
entries.what: Hermes Agent plugin: Jev picks model per turn, trim-then-compress context engine, plus a Jev-based tool auto-approve with fail-closed proof scripts.
entries.autoInvocation: plugin hooks inside Hermes (not Claude Code)
pros: Has auto-approve with confidence threshold and fail-closed test matrix (prove_auto_approve.py), a design reference for permission-gate
Trim-before-compress ordering idea
cons: Hermes-only; needs port to Claude Code
TYPESAFE_API_KEY direct only, forbids gateways; 1 star, docs mostly Chinese, install via curl|sh for Hermes

entries.name: peterwanghot/jev-cc-codex-router
entries.what: Single-file Python proxy for Codex (OpenAI Responses API): Jev picks a model tier per new user turn, rewrites the model, escalates on failure, retries flaky upstream errors.
entries.autoInvocation: proxy
pros: Jev API URL configurable (JEV_API_URL), so OpenRouter systemone URL is settable
Clear fallback to baseline model; one Jev call per new turn, reuses tier for tool follow-ups
Zero-dependency single file
cons: Codex/Responses API only; Claude Code subscription/OAuth cannot be pointed at a proxy without ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL
Author says tier prompts are still being tuned; Chinese prompt text; zstd handling
Name says cc but it targets Codex

entries.name: jev-router-mcp (MarcosldcC/Jev_Router)
entries.what: Zed-first ACP router/supervisor with a secondary MCP bin (jev-mcp). The MCP tool jev_delegate takes a coding prompt, asks TypeSafe Jev (System One) two typed questions (noul "too ambiguous?" and choice low/medium/high complexity), then either returns a clarify/confirm instruction to Claude, or picks a downstream model. If it picks "claude" it hands the task back to the calling Claude Code session with a suggestion to run a subagent with model=claude-haiku/sonnet; if it picks Codex, Gemini or DeepSeek it spawns that ACP agent as a child process and auto-approves its tool calls. Jev is used only for prompt classification and an optional Tool Gate (allow/deny/conditional). It is not used for anything a Claude Code user needs, such as memory, retrieval or code decisions.
interface: jev_delegate (MCP tool, inputs prompt and cwd)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no skill and no transparent proxy. Claude Code would call jev_delegate only if the model chooses to based on the tool description, which says to pass the user's request verbatim on the first call. That is unreliable and drifts across sessions, and it is not the deterministic 'always when needed' behavior the user asked for. A CLAUDE.md line telling Claude to call it is not a real solution either, since the user does not want to prompt for it.
security: Repo is 404 on GitHub, single maintainer, single publish 9 days ago. Provenance is weak and the code is not reviewable beyond the npm tarball.

dist/delegation/mcp-child.js: the Tool Gate treats both 'allow' and 'conditional' as auto-approve (allow_once). The comment says there is no live user to ask. 'Conditional' is the risky/destructive bucket, so it is effectively unsupervised.

The Jev-based Tool Gate is only a probabilistic allow/deny. The deterministic block is a title keyword match for database/production/deploy/secret/credential/.env/api_key, which is trivially bypassable.

fs/readTextFile and writeTextFile go through resolvePath(cwd, path). I did not verify it blocks path escapes outside cwd. The child agent can also request terminal/create with an arbitrary command and env: ...process.env. The child inherits the full parent environment, including any keys.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool result text is an imperative 'AÇÃO NECESSÁRIA' block plus a JSON contract that Claude is told to follow. The tool description also tells Claude not to investigate before calling. That is instruction-shaped output injected into the main agent, but it is the author's own text, and the classifier output can steer which model or subagent runs.

API key handling: the key is read from the environment, not argv. Good. The SDK redacts headers in debug logs. No postinstall/preinstall scripts. No curl|sh. No telemetry found in dist. Stdio ownership is safe, and diagnostics go to stderr via log.
entries.dataEgress: To TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed: the entire user prompt as `state` on every jev_delegate call, in the noul/choice call at jev-client.js:36. In the Tool Gate path (only for delegated non-Claude agents): tool kind, tool title and the execution contract. No file contents or diffs go to Jev. To other providers: if Codex, Gemini or DeepSeek is chosen, the prompt, the contract and anything that agent reads through fs/terminal goes to that provider, so client code can leave to a third party the user did not choose. The cwd path is passed as a tool argument, so Claude Code sees it as well.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, locally. classifyTaskWithJev catches any error and returns the regex heuristic plan (jev-client.js:84-87). The SDK default is a 10 s timeout per attempt and 2 retries, so a slow or down Jev can stall a jev_delegate call for up to about 30 s before the fallback. The jev-mcp path has no startup gate. The 'mandatory key' startup exit only applies to the jev-acp bin. If no downstream provider is keyed, Claude is still always enabled (alwaysEnabledProviders: [claude]). A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently gives heuristics only, so the user would get regex 'Jev' with no warning.
entries.contextCost: 2 tools: jev_delegate and jev_status. The jev_delegate description is about 1.9k characters and the input schemas are small, so all tool definitions come to roughly 700 tokens. It has no MCP server instructions and no hook text. But each call injects a 300-1500 token instruction block into context, in Portuguese, and Claude is told to act on it.
pros: Real, working use of the Jev primitives (noul and choice) through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The criteria strings for the ambiguity and complexity questions are sensibly calibrated (jev-client.js:48-52).

OpenRouter repoint is close to trivial on paper. The SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and posts to /v1/systemone with a Bearer token, which matches OpenRouter's System One path shape.
The design is fail-soft: a local regex fallback on any Jev error, and the deterministic security keyword floor is checked before Jev.

It is the only candidate here that actually tries to make Claude Code call Jev from inside a session, and it is aware that Claude Code cannot run it as a backing agent. The Claude branch avoids double billing by handing back to the calling session.
MIT license, no install scripts, key kept out of argv, no telemetry.
cons: The GitHub repo is 404, there is one npm publish and one maintainer, and the age is 9 days. There is no way to audit history, tests or CI, and it could vanish.

The core product is a multi-model router for Zed. For an Opus-5.5-subscription user the useful part is tiny: it mostly suggests spawning a subagent with a cheaper Claude model. The Codex/Gemini/DeepSeek branches need extra paid keys and would send client code to other vendors.

Invocation is model-discretion. Nothing forces Claude to call jev_delegate, so it fails the user's requirement of automatic integration without prompting. And when it is called, the tool text asks Claude to skip its own investigation first, which can make results worse.

It puts Jev in the wrong role. Jev is a calibrated decision primitive and this uses it as a preflight gate on every task. That adds a turn and latency to each request for a marginal gain over Claude's own judgement, and 'ambiguous?' gating can stall work with clarification loops, as the SDK comment at jev-client.js:57-69 admits it hit.

Unsafe defaults: the 'conditional' verdict is auto-approved, child agents inherit the full environment, and the deterministic guard is a keyword match on the title. This is worse than Claude Code's own permission system, which the user already has hooks around. It also conflicts with the client-project secret-leak guard.

Instruction-shaped tool output in Portuguese with 'AÇÃO NECESSÁRIA' that Claude is told to obey, plus ~700 tokens of tool definitions. Worst-case blocking is about 30 s with a silent local fallback, so a missing or broken key looks like it works.
Sends the full user prompt (client project details) to the Jev provider on each call, with no opt-out for sensitive projects.
entries.verdict: Not recommended. It is an early, unauditable single-author Zed router whose MCP path is model-discretion, fires an extra turn on every task and auto-approves its own child agents' risky tool calls. Only its jev-client.js pattern (noul plus choice via the SDK with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter) is worth borrowing for a custom hook.

entries.name: usemilo (Milo routing gateway onboarding CLI)
entries.what: usemilo is a 3-file, single bundled ESM CLI (bin: milo) that rewrites Claude Code / Codex / pi config so the harness's MAIN model traffic goes to a third-party hosted gateway (https://milo-gateway.fly.dev) with model "milo/auto". The gateway uses a small "decision model" (Jev, per its root JSON: decisionBackend "jev") to classify task type and difficulty, picks a tier (fast/mid/frontier) from a roster of cheap OpenRouter models (deepseek-v4-flash, glm-5.3-flash, gpt-5.6-luna, gemini-3.8-flash, etc.), and forwards the request to OpenRouter with the user's OpenRouter key. So Jev is used only as an internal model-tier router; it is not exposed to Claude Code as decisions/tools. For Claude Code it sets env ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=gateway, ANTHROPIC_MODEL=milo/auto, ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="" plus apiKeyHelper reading OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It replaces the Anthropic backend rather than adding Jev alongside Opus.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. After 'milo on', every Claude Code model call is routed automatically without prompting, which satisfies 'no user prompt needed' literally, but it uses Jev as a model-tier router and replaces the main model, not as an extra decision aid Claude Code consults.
security: No postinstall script, no telemetry in the CLI, no curl|sh; CLI only edits config files and spawns the harness (child_process.spawn with stdio inherit) - static read of dist/cli.js.

Key handling in the CLI is decent: OPENROUTER_API_KEY read from env and not written; a prompted key is stored in a 0600 file (mode 384) .milo-openrouter.key in the global ~/.claude dir and read via apiKeyHelper 'sh -c cat <path>'. milo run passes the key via env ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, not argv.

BUT the OpenRouter key is sent as Bearer to an unaudited third-party gateway (milo-gateway.fly.dev) run by an anonymous npm maintainer ([email removed], package created 2026-09-20). The operator can log/keep the key and spend your OpenRouter credit. Gateway has /v1/memory and /v1/preferences endpoints that persist per-key data server-side.

Setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in settings.json makes every prompt, file content, diff, and tool result of the main agent traverse that gateway: full source-code exfiltration surface for client projects (NDA/contract risk).
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY='' plus base URL override overrides subscription/OAuth login behavior; the session stops using the Opus 5.5 subscription.

Hosted service can return arbitrary model output including tool_use blocks; in bypass/auto permission mode a compromised or mis-routed gateway response is effectively remote command execution on the dev machine.
entries.dataEgress: Everything Claude Code sends to its model endpoint: full conversation, system prompt, CLAUDE.md, file contents read, diffs, bash outputs, tool results, plus the OpenRouter API key, all to milo-gateway.fly.dev; then forwarded to whichever cheap OpenRouter model the router selects (DeepSeek, GLM, MiMo, Tencent HY3, etc. per roster). Jev sees the request content for classification. Nothing goes to Anthropic once base URL is overridden.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the whole session: the gateway is the sole model backend (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL). If fly.io gateway is down, slow, or the key is missing, Claude Code cannot run at all (no fallback to Anthropic). No timeouts or fallback logic in the CLI; internal gateway timeouts unknown/unauditable. Mitigation: milo off restores config from .milo-backup.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero hook-injected text, no MCP server instructions. But the model swap is the cost: Opus 5.5 is replaced by whatever cheap model milo/auto routes to; Claude Code warns milo/auto is not in the model catalog; features tied to Anthropic models (prompt caching, extended thinking, exact tool-use semantics, 1M context) may break or degrade.
pros: Truly automatic: a transparent proxy needs no 'use jev' prompt; project-scoped enabling via ./.claude/settings.local.json is reversible (milo off restores .milo-backup) and milo run is a zero-persistence one-shot.
Small and auditable CLI: 3-file tarball, MIT, no dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, spawn-only; key kept out of settings.json (0600 key file / env), not in argv.
OpenRouter-native: uses the user's OPENROUTER_API_KEY and OpenRouter models, and does actually put Jev in a real routing loop (gateway reports decisionBackend jev).
Gateway exposes Anthropic-compatible /v1/messages plus /v1/decisions/:id and x-milo-* headers so routing decisions are inspectable.

Its own skill.md states the sensible design: keep the frontier planner (Opus) and route only sub-task implementation through Milo, which points at the right pattern even though the shipped CLI does the opposite for Claude Code.
cons: Wrong role for Jev here: it replaces the user's main model (Opus 5.5 on subscription) with cheap DeepSeek/GLM/MiMo-class models chosen by a router, degrading quality on client work; Claude Code's own ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL takeover also kills OAuth/subscription usage.
Does NOT call OpenRouter's Jev Decisions API or System One API and does not expose Choice/Noul/Score to Claude Code; no typed-decision value for hooks, permission gating, or task triage.

Sends all prompts, source code, diffs and the OpenRouter key to an anonymous, unaudited hosted gateway (fly.dev) whose source is not accessible (gh 404); unacceptable for client projects; bypass/auto mode magnifies risk of malicious tool_use in responses.
Single point of failure, fail-closed, no fallback; Jev + proxy latency added to every turn.

Very immature: package created 2026-09-20, 5 versions in 2 days, single anonymous maintainer, no public repo, tests or CI, dangling README links; 'milo/auto' unknown to Claude Code catalog; the router's tier policy is a black box (policyVersion v4).
Matches Theo's skeptic framing: it is essentially a DeepSeek-flash-centric router product rather than a Jev integration.
entries.verdict: Not suitable: usemilo swaps Claude Code's entire model backend for an unaudited third-party gateway that routes to cheap models via Jev, rather than giving Claude Code Jev-based typed decisions. Only conceivably useful as a reference for the (hosted-service) routing idea or as a throwaway experiment via 'milo run claude-code' on a personal non-sensitive project with a limited-credit OpenRouter key; do not use on client work.

entries.name: win4r/pi-jev-router
entries.what: A Pi Coding Agent (earendil-works/pi-coding-agent) extension, NOT a Claude Code integration. On each user input (pi.on("input")) it can ask Jev (System One Choice question: quick/general/frontier/unknown) which capability tier a task needs, then deterministic policy code picks one of the user's configured models (health, cost, context, tools, pin/floor gating) and calls pi.setModel. It defaults to shadow mode with Jev networking off. It has slash commands (/route ...) and no MCP server, hooks, or skill.
interface: /route status | init | reload | shadow | auto | off
/route new | brief <text> | floor <tier> | tier <tier> | pin | unpin
/route preview | explain | doctor | stats | cache clear
entries.autoInvocation: "Deterministic Pi input hook, so it is automatic inside Pi. It is not usable in Claude Code at all. Only the design idea (a classify-then-route hook at prompt boundaries) is portable. Claude Code's UserPromptSubmit hook cannot switch the main model mid-session, though it could add context or route subagents."
security: API key comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var only and is sent as a Bearer header. It is not in argv and is not persisted. README suggests a getpass launcher.
fetch uses redirect:'error', a 64KB response cap, a 5s default timeout (bounded 100ms-30s), and a session call/token budget.

The classifier prompt tells the model to treat task text as evidence and not follow embedded instructions. The output is a typed choice, so prompt-injection blast radius is limited to picking the wrong tier.
No shell execution, no postinstall (CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts), and no telemetry. The peer dependency is pi-coding-agent.
Health state is written to .pi/jev-router/health.json with model IDs and timestamps but no prompts. The credential-pattern check is admitted to be non-exhaustive.
entries.dataEgress: "Sent to api.typesafe.ai only when /route jev on is set: task text (the user prompt at a task boundary), the optional briefing (up to 6000 bytes), and flags (image attached, tools required, minimum tier, boundary, prior failure). No full conversation, tool output, system prompt, images, or code files are sent. Prompts can still hold client-confidential text. Jev is off by default."
entries.failureMode: "Fail-open toward the current model. Timeout 5s by default, up to maxAttempts retries (retry-after over 1s aborts), a circuit breaker opens for 30s after 3 failures, and a 401/403 disables the classifier. In shadow mode the current model runs normally. In auto mode it HOLDS the input if no eligible model exists (README), so misconfiguration can block a turn. Not applicable to Claude Code since it cannot load."
entries.contextCost: "For Claude Code: zero (no MCP tools, hooks or skills). In Pi it injects nothing into model context, since it uses input-hook routing and slash commands."
pros: Clean, well-tested reference implementation of a System One Choice call (request shape, 64KB cap, timeout, retry, circuit breaker, budgets, exact cache) in src/classifier.ts. It can be lifted into a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook or a small MCP server.
Conservative design: shadow mode by default, fail-open, no replay of failed turns, only task text sent (not code or tool output), and prompt-injection-aware question wording.
MIT license, CI on 2 OSes, and an honest docs/validation.md that includes a replay of the recorded judgments.
Node 22+ with no runtime dependencies beyond Node built-ins, which matches the user's Node 24.
cons: It targets Pi Coding Agent, not Claude Code. There are no hooks.json, MCP server, skill or plugin manifest, so it cannot be installed or run in Claude Code.

Hard-coded TypeSafe endpoint (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone), TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and model ID 'jev-1.13.0'. There is no OpenRouter path, so it needs source changes and an unverified response shape.
Its purpose is switching between models. That does not fit a Claude Code subscription/OAuth session with a fixed Opus model, and hooks cannot swap the main model.

Very immature: 2 commits, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 12 stars, no releases. The README says production quality and net savings are not established, and the eval is 16 synthetic cases.
It needs manual per-model tier and tool configuration, and the routing gains are unproven for one strong model.
Auto mode can hold an input if no eligible model exists.
entries.verdict: Not usable with Claude Code, because it is a Pi-only extension hard-wired to the TypeSafe direct API. Treat it only as a reference for a Jev Choice-classifier client: the design and classifier.ts are worth borrowing for a custom UserPromptSubmit hook. Do not install it.

entries.name: RyanKung/rotom
entries.what: Rust local gateway (`rotom serve`) exposing OpenAI/Anthropic-compatible endpoints backed by Codex/Grok/Kiro OAuth or a Vercel AI Gateway key, so Claude Code can be pointed at other providers via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. Jev appears only as a passthrough model id (`typesafe-ai/jev`) on a custom `POST /v1/evaluations` route that forwards to Vercel AI Gateway's evaluation-model protocol. It is not a Claude Code integration of Jev: it replaces Claude's model backend and never calls Jev from within a normal Claude session.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy for the model backend only. Jev is never invoked automatically: /v1/evaluations must be called explicitly by a client, and Claude Code does not know the route exists.
security: No MCP, hooks or skills, so no prompt-injection surface into Claude Code from Jev output
Setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to rotom routes ALL Claude Code traffic (code, prompts, tool results) through a third-party local proxy, and this replaces the Anthropic backend
Upstream credentials are stored plaintext-ish in ~/.rotom/auth.json; the README suggests `--api-key local-secret` on argv, which is visible in the process list (ROTOM_API_KEY env is an alternative)
The Codex/Grok/Kiro OAuth reuse is explicitly against upstream ToS risk (LEGAL.md warns that personal OAuth cannot be shared or resold); the project is unofficial
Bundled rusqlite, `cargo install` builds from source (no curl|sh found), no telemetry found in the greps I ran
LGPL-3.0-only license, 6 stars, single main author (110 of 125 commits)
entries.dataEgress: For Jev: only the `state` and `questions` JSON that a client explicitly POSTs to /v1/evaluations goes to ai-gateway.vercel.sh with the Vercel key. Nothing is sent automatically. If used as ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL for Claude Code, the entire conversation, code and tool outputs go to whichever backend provider is chosen (Codex/Grok/Kiro/Vercel) instead of Anthropic.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable for Jev, since nothing calls it automatically. As a Claude Code base-URL proxy it is fail-closed: if rotom is down or unauthenticated, every Claude Code request fails. I found no explicit timeout on the eval route (only a 500 ms daemon probe at main.rs:676).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero hook text, zero skill descriptions. The eval endpoint is not discoverable by Claude at all. Routing the model backend has its own large side effects (Opus 5.5 would be replaced by fallback models; unknown claude-* ids are rewritten to gpt-5.5 by default).
pros: Genuinely supports Jev's typed boolean/choice/score protocol with test coverage (src/src/server/tests/evaluations.rs, evaluation.rs unit tests)
Well-tested, actively maintained Rust codebase (282 tests, CI, releases, v1.5.12)
Reference for the Vercel Gateway evaluation-model wire format (headers plus body), if someone builds a custom Jev client
cons: Vercel AI Gateway only: no OpenRouter (/api/alpha/decisions, /api/v1/systemone) and no TypeSafe direct support, and the wire protocol differs, so patching is hard
It is a model-backend swap for Claude Code, not a Jev integration: no MCP, hook or skill, so Claude never calls Jev automatically
Pointing ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL at it would replace Opus 5.5 with Codex/Grok/Kiro models and reroute all code through a third-party proxy, and the user is on subscription OAuth
Relies on reusing personal OAuth for OpenAI/Grok/Kiro, which the repo's own LEGAL.md flags as ToS-risky
Single-maintainer project with 6 stars, LGPL license, beta maturity
entries.verdict: Not a usable Jev integration for this user: it only proxies Jev through Vercel AI Gateway on a manual /v1/evaluations endpoint, has no OpenRouter path, and offers no automatic Claude Code invocation. Its main use here would be as a wire-format reference, and it should not be installed.

entries.name: @jevrouter/jevrouter (npm only, no GitHub repo)
entries.what: Local Rust daemon (axum, SQLite, launched via a ~1 KB Node shim) that listens on 127.0.0.1:3479 and exposes Anthropic /v1/messages and OpenAI /v1/chat/completions. It asks Jev (Choice over small/medium/large slots) how hard the request is, then forwards to the upstream configured for that slot. It escalates the slot if the upstream fails, and falls back to simple routing if Jev is unavailable. It is a model-tier router, not a coding assistant integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to 127.0.0.1:3479). Fully automatic, with no prompting. But it only works with API-key-style upstream auth and conflicts with the subscription/OAuth login, because the slots need x-api-key plus anthropic-version headers.
security: No public source: GitHub repo jevrouter/jevrouter returns 404 and the org has 0 repos, created 2026-09-19. The package is an opaque 8.6 MB Rust binary that cannot be audited.

Linux binary missing: only @jevrouter/jevrouter-darwin-arm64 exists on npm. -linux-x64, -linux-arm64 (and probably -darwin-x64) return 404, so the launcher hits fail('no binary for linux-x64') on the user's machine.

Publish metadata leaks the author's local path (/Users/tom/code/jevroute/cli/jevrouter-jevrouter-0.1.0.tgz). Single maintainer tomsun28, published 2026-09-20 in one shot. README still says 'Replace OWNER in cli/package.json'.
Launcher uses spawnSync on the resolved binary and JEVROUTER_BIN override. No postinstall script and no dependencies.
API keys are read from env vars named in config (api_key_env), so nothing appears in argv. Slot API keys of the coding provider would transit the proxy.
Binary embeds a Tauri/CORS allowlist (localhost:5173, 1420, tauri://localhost) and an allow_remote option, suggesting a desktop UI. Binding defaults to loopback.
entries.dataEgress: Sends to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone a state built from the request (first_user_message, recent_messages, truncated to max_state_chars) plus the routing question. That includes user prompt text and possibly code and tool results from the conversation. The full request is forwarded to the upstream slot provider. Persisted locally in SQLite. Nothing goes to OpenRouter for Jev. Telemetry is unverified because the binary is closed.
entries.failureMode: Designed fail-open: on Jev timeout or missing key it logs 'jev degraded, falling back to simple routing', and on an upstream failure it escalates to a larger slot ('upstream failed, escalating slot'). The timeout is configurable (timeout_ms). But if the daemon itself is down and ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at it, Claude Code fails closed with connection errors. And on Linux the launcher cannot run at all.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero injected text; it is a transparent proxy. However, it operates on the main-loop model choice, which is a bad fit here.
pros: Truly automatic: transparent proxy needs no prompt or tool-selection by Claude.
Correct conceptual use of Jev Choice (difficulty tiering) with a confidence gate (min_confidence), a cache (cache_ttl_s) and fail-open fallback to simple routing.
Zero context cost in Claude Code (no MCP tools or hook text).
Slot upstreams are configurable (provider_base_url, api_key_env), so coding models could in principle come via OpenRouter.
MIT license declared; tiny dependency-free Node launcher with no postinstall.
cons: Unusable on this Linux machine: the linux-x64 platform package is 404 on npm, so the launcher fails with 'no binary for linux-x64'.
No public source: the GitHub repo is 404, the org has 0 repos, so the 8.6 MB binary can't be audited even where it exists.
Jev endpoint is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai; no OpenRouter support for the Jev call, and no source to patch.
Proxy replaces the main model with a cheaper slot, which conflicts with running Opus as the main model. It also needs an API-key upstream and breaks the subscription/OAuth login (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL).
Routes all traffic, including client code and secrets, through an unaudited local binary, with a plaintext SQLite store of prompts.
Released 2026-09-20, a single 0.1.0 publish, one unknown maintainer, no tests or CI visible, and the README says 'Replace OWNER' (unfinished publish).
entries.verdict: Skip. There is no Linux binary on npm, no public source, no OpenRouter support for Jev, and it works as a model-tier proxy that clashes with Opus and OAuth login. If you want a router, look at the same-idea repos with public source (e.g. BillionsBobby/JevRouter, 301 stars), which are separate candidates and were not audited here.
entries.license: MIT (declared in package.json, no LICENSE file in tarball)

entries.name: jevrouter-ai (Abishek0070/JEV-model-router)
entries.what: A small Node/Fastify gateway (about 1,500 lines of TypeScript, 4 dependencies) that exposes OpenAI-style /v1/chat/completions and a non-streaming Anthropic /v1/messages. For model "auto" it sends the last 6k chars of the conversation to Jev and asks a Choice question, tier = fast | balanced | powerful, plus a Noul "escalate" question. A policy engine and a cost/latency scorer then pick a concrete model from a YAML config (groq-llama, gemini-flash, gpt-mini, claude-haiku, claude-sonnet, gpt-reasoning, mock-echo), and the gateway dispatches to that provider with your own API keys. It is an LLM cost router, not a Claude Code integration. Jev only supplies a coarse tier signal. There is a local regex-heuristic fallback.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy only. Set ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:4000 and every request goes through it. That would be automatic, but it would break Claude Code: with a subscription/OAuth login, Claude Code authenticates to api.anthropic.com, so it will not work through this proxy, and the proxy needs its own ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. It also downgrades Opus 5.5 to whatever the tier map picks. It does not use Jev as a decision aid for Claude's own workflow (hooks/MCP), which is what the user asked for.
security: Keys are read only from env or .env and are sent as Bearer headers. They do not appear in argv. The startup log reports only booleans for configured keys (server.ts:27-46).

Gateway auth is open by default: checkAuth returns true when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty (ingress/auth.ts:7). The server binds 0.0.0.0 (server.ts:313) with CORS origin:true (server.ts:23). On a dev machine this exposes an unauthenticated proxy that spends your upstream provider keys to anyone on the LAN or any web page.
The quota is in-memory only. addSpend records spend but there is no enforcement of the '$1/day' comment.
Gemini's API key is placed in the URL query string (providers/native.ts, generateContent?key=...), which can leak into logs and proxies.

Default jev.order puts jevmodel.org first (config.example.yaml:89). Any key set as JEV_API_KEY is sent as a Bearer token to that non-TypeSafe host as well as api.typesafe.ai (index.ts:19-20). An OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone is not sent there.

Telemetry logs routing metadata via pino, not prompt bodies. However, the exact cache stores full responses in memory keyed by a hash of the prompts. /v1/telemetry/recent is unauthenticated when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty.
entries.dataEgress: Two destinations. (1) To Jev: up to 6,000 chars (jevmodel.ts slices to 8,000) of the concatenated 'role: content' conversation is sent as `state`. In router/pipeline.ts the state is messages.map('role: content').join('\n').slice(0, 6000), so system prompt, user text and pasted code all go out. Jev goes to jevmodel.org, api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai depending on which key is set and the order. (2) To the chosen LLM provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Groq or Ollama), the full messages array with your keys. In a Claude Code setup that would mean sending your entire agent context (files, diffs, tool outputs) to a non-Anthropic model chosen by the router. This matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Jev failures are fail-open. JevRouter.decide (jev/index.ts:41-60) walks the order, skips providers with an open breaker (5 fails then 30 s cooldown), and always falls back to the local regex heuristic. The per-call Jev timeout is 3 s in the example config (800 ms constructor default), so a slow Jev can add up to 3 s per request per failing provider. The order tries jevmodel, typesafe and openrouter in sequence; a missing key throws immediately, so only configured providers cost time. The LLM dispatcher does 2 attempts per model with 100/300 ms backoff and a 30 s timeout, then falls back to the other models in route.allow. If the gateway itself is down, Claude Code would fail closed, because ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL would point at a dead port with no direct path.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks and no skills, so 0 tokens of tool definitions and no injected text. Its effect is on the transport, not the context window: it would replace Claude Code's Anthropic endpoint with an OpenAI/Anthropic-style proxy. This is not a workable path for Claude Code 2.1.x. The gateway's /v1/messages has no streaming (server.ts:269), which Claude Code needs. It drops tool_use/tool_result blocks and ignores the tools array (server.ts:272-276, 278-286), so agentic tool calls break. It returns fixed stop_reason 'end_turn' and does not implement count_tokens, thinking or prompt caching. Model names like claude-opus-5-5 are not in its config.
pros: Genuinely Jev-related: typesafe.ts and jevmodel.ts implement the documented System One Choice + Noul request shape (state, model, questions with criteria) and parse choice, confidence and probabilities (typesafe.ts:37-67). That is a usable reference for a typed Jev client.
Fail-open design with a circuit breaker and a local heuristic fallback (jev/index.ts:41-60). Jev outages would not block traffic by themselves.
Tiny codebase (about 1.5k lines), 4 runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, MIT license. It can be read in about 15 minutes.
Jev is called only for a coarse tier. It never picks a provider, and the policy/scoring stages are deterministic and inspectable (/v1/routing/decision dry run).
OPENROUTER_API_KEY is at least recognised as a Jev provider (openrouter.ai/api/v1 with typesafe/* model), so the design does not lock you to a TypeSafe key.
cons: Wrong tool for the goal. It is an LLM cost router (send easy prompts to cheap models). It does not give Claude Code a Jev decision capability, so it cannot support things like 'should I run tests / is this safe / which files matter'.

It cannot front Claude Code. /v1/messages rejects stream:true with HTTP 400 (server.ts:269), which Claude Code always uses. It also flattens content to text and drops tool_use and tool_result (server.ts:272-276), so the agent loop breaks. It ignores tools, thinking and cache_control.

Subscription/OAuth login does not work through ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to this gateway. It would need a separate Anthropic API key, and routing sends most turns to groq-llama, gemini-flash, gpt-mini or claude-haiku instead of Opus 5.5. That is a large quality regression on client work.

The OpenRouter Jev adapter is a chat/completions hack (openrouter.ts:26-46) using a stale model id typesafe/jev-1 and a JSON-in-prompt contract. It uses neither /api/alpha/decisions nor /api/v1/systemone, so it likely does not work against a typed-decision model, and errors silently drop to the regex fallback (local.ts), which is not Jev at all.
Default order sends conversation state to jevmodel.org first, an unaffiliated third-party endpoint that also receives JEV_API_KEY. No documented relationship to TypeSafe.
Unauthenticated, network-exposed by default: binds 0.0.0.0, CORS origin:true, gateway auth open when GATEWAY_API_KEYS is empty. Dangerous next to client code and provider keys.
Data egress: the full agent context would be relayed to OpenAI, Gemini, Groq or Anthropic, which may violate client confidentiality terms.

Immature: 9 commits over 3 days, single author, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, docs contradict code (.env.example JEV_TYPESAFE_URL is /v1/decisions vs code /v1/systemone). The README claims Claude Code support but the code does not deliver it.
Adds latency on every request with no UI benefit: up to 3 s Jev timeout, no streaming.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this user. It is a 3-day-old, untested LLM cost-routing proxy whose Anthropic ingress cannot stream or carry tool calls, so Claude Code cannot run through it, and its OpenRouter Jev path is a chat-completions shim with a stale model id. Use it only as a reference for the System One Choice/Noul request shape (typesafe.ts:37-67), and build any real Claude Code integration as a hook or MCP server that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.

pros: Native OpenRouter provider (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions via @openrouter/sdk, OPENROUTER_API_KEY auto-detected)
MIT, CI, tests, caching doc, JSON output, published npm 0.2.7

entries.name: systemonemodels.org Claude Code catalog
entries.what: Independent third-party web catalog (last updated 20 Sep 2026) listing Jev integrations for Claude Code in three buckets: MCP servers (jkudish/jev-mcp, rashedInt32/jev-mcp, blakestone-x/jev-mcp, itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp), TypeSafe's official agent skill (typesafe-ai/skills), and community routers/hooks/proxies (jev-model-router, gargpratyush/jev-router, adarshmishra07/jcm-router, tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction, GhalebDweikat/winnow, leepokai/jev-guard, Dicklesworthstone/skillranker, compozy/yoshi, NiazMorshed2007/jev-review, AntonioCoppe/jev-harness). It is not itself installable software, only a discovery index. It states nothing is Anthropic-endorsed and only typesafe-ai/skills is TypeSafe-official.
interface: Hook/proxy tools (winnow, jev-guard, skillranker, fast-jev-compaction, jev-router, jcm-router, yoshi)
entries.autoInvocation: Catalog spans all classes: MCP tools are model-discretion only (Claude must choose to call them, so they do not satisfy the 'never say use jev' requirement without CLAUDE.md nudges); hooks (winnow, jev-guard, skillranker, compaction) are deterministic; jev-router/jcm-router/yoshi are transparent proxies (jcm-router incompatible with OAuth subscription login likely, needs ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL); official skill triggers by description and only when writing Jev-calling code.
security: Catalog is a static third-party site; content fetched was treated as data. No code to run.
Catalog itself flags that 'claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=...' can expose the key in process-list argv (noted from blakestone-x README); prefer env from shell/settings env instead of argv.
itsmostafa recommends curl -fsSL raw.githubusercontent.com/.../install.sh | sh, a curl|sh installer to avoid or review manually.
blakestone-x installs via uvx --from git+https://github.com/blakestone-x/jev-mcp@v0.2.1 (unpinned-by-hash git code, 3 commits, 1 author).

All listed repos were created 2026-08-24 to 2026-09-17 (under 6 weeks old); supply-chain trust is low; several are single-author. Hook tools (jev-guard, winnow, skillranker, yoshi, compaction) see every tool call/result so egress is broad.
Catalog star figures are stale/inconsistent with GitHub (jkudish catalog says 320, GitHub 463; jcm-router catalog 4, GitHub 9), so treat catalog numbers as approximate.
entries.dataEgress: The catalog page itself sends nothing. Egress depends on the chosen tool: MCP servers send only what Claude puts in state/question (model-chosen snippets, diffs, file contents for jev_triage); hooks (winnow, jev-guard, skillranker) send tool inputs/results (file contents, command output) to Jev at TypeSafe or OpenRouter for every matched call; proxies (jcm-router, yoshi) see whole conversation/prompt text. jev-review claims to send focused diffs only. Requests go to api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai; OpenRouter adds a second party.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to the catalog. Per-tool behavior is not covered by the page; the catalog says jev-model-router degrades to a local classifier without a key, jcm-router refuses to start without a TYPESAFE_API_KEY (fail-closed at startup, and as a proxy sits in the Anthropic request path: a serious risk for a subscription/OAuth login). Must be checked per repo.
entries.contextCost: Catalog: zero. Per tool: MCP servers add 1 (evaluate) to 10 (jkudish) tools, roughly 0.5k to 3k tokens of definitions; hooks add small injected text or none; skills add only a description line. Not measured here.
pros: Best single index of the ecosystem: 20+ repos grouped by type, with honest official vs community labeling (only typesafe-ai/skills is TypeSafe-official).

Its OpenRouter claims for itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp were confirmed in source (cmd/evaluate/main.go:152-160) and for jkudish/jev-mcp (src/provider.ts:296-304), so it correctly points to the two MCP servers that work with an OpenRouter-only key.
Reveals the only deterministic (no-prompting) options: hook tools (winnow, jev-guard, skillranker, fast-jev-compaction) and proxies, versus MCP tools which are model-discretion.
Includes useful caveats: argv key exposure, jcm-router's self-reported result that routing the main chat loses money ($106.73 vs $87.19) while subagent routing helps.
Names candidates worth auditing individually: jkudish/jev-mcp (463 stars, 50 commits, OpenRouter), itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp (Go, 121 commits, OpenRouter), winnow, jev-guard, skillranker.
cons: Not an integration, cannot be installed; only a pointer list. Zero direct value for the user's setup beyond discovery.

Secondary source with stale numbers (stars differ from GitHub) and an admitted unconfirmed install command for jev-model-router; the page says 'Most servers need TYPESAFE_API_KEY' which is misleading for the user, since jkudish also supports OpenRouter (verified) and the summary text omits that.
Says rashedInt32 and blakestone-x work only with TYPESAFE key; confirmed in code, so they are not fit for an OpenRouter-only user without patching.

Catalog does not audit hook/proxy tools' provider support, egress or failure modes; hook tools that stream every tool result to a third-party API conflict with client-project confidentiality and the existing secret-guard/gitnexus hooks.

Ecosystem is under six weeks old, mostly single-author, some with 3-10 commits; the catalog offers no security review, and the page's own limits section warns to read READMEs before handing over keys.

Catalog itself acknowledges MCP servers are not deterministic, and Jev is a typed classifier (not a reasoning model), so most listed tools have marginal value for everyday coding beyond triage/pruning.
entries.verdict: Useful only as a discovery index; it is not something to install. Its spot-checked OpenRouter claims hold for jkudish/jev-mcp and itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp (the two MCP servers that work with an OpenRouter-only key); the hook-based tools (winnow, jev-guard, skillranker, fast-jev-compaction) are the only route to automatic invocation and need individual audits.
entries.license: n/a (site); the linked repos checked are all MIT

entries.name: TypeSafe docs: Jev with coding agents (caveat page)
entries.what: Official TypeSafe docs page (no code, no installable artifact). States Jev is not a drop-in LLM for Claude Code/Cursor/opencode/Copilot: no `model: "jev-latest"` switch exists because Jev does not stream text, call tools or edit files. Tells coding-agent users to (a) install the TypeSafe agent skill so the agent writes correct Jev integrations into the apps they build, or (b) use Jev inside their own apps for routing, scoring, guardrails and typed extraction. The page says nothing about MCP, hooks or auto-invocation. The docs' skill_suggestion cookbook does show one relevant pattern: two Jev calls per agent turn pick at most one skill and inject a `<skill_relevance>` line into the system prompt. That is a Jev-as-decision-layer design, not a shipped Claude Code integration.
interface: TypeSafe agent skill (typesafe-ai/skills, MIT, plugin typesafe v0.5.7)
entries.autoInvocation: None for Jev at runtime. The docs page explicitly rejects replacing Claude Code's LLM. The only auto element is the skill's description trigger, which makes Claude write Jev code when building an app. The docs' own advice for the agent-decision use case is that developers write their own code around Jev. That means a self-built deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse) calling OpenRouter Jev, modeled on the skill_suggestion cookbook.
security: Docs page and the skill are static text with no code execution, no hooks, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in the skills repo. Only a plugin marketplace add and install.

The SKILL.md tells the agent to fetch live docs from docs.typesafe.ai. That is a remote-content prompt-injection surface: a later docs compromise could steer Claude's coding behavior. It is low risk but real.
Direct API use needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY as an env var (Bearer header). An OpenRouter path would use OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Neither is in argv unless someone hand-writes curl -H.
docs/models.md: Jev is not trained on customer requests. Zero data retention is available for enterprise customers only, and terms are on /legal, which was not read.
docs/model-jaggedness/jev-1.13.md lists 'adversarial content' as a failure mode. Any Jev gate over untrusted repo or web content can be manipulated and should never be the only security control.
entries.dataEgress: The docs page and skill send nothing. Any Jev decision layer built on the page's advice sends whatever is put in `state` plus the questions to api.typesafe.ai or to OpenRouter and its upstream provider. Text only, up to 32k tokens for state plus the longest question. In a Claude Code hook that would be the user prompt, and possibly diffs, file contents or tool outputs. The design should send a minimal state, such as the prompt plus a skill or tool index, and filter secrets first.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to the docs page. The Python SDK default timeout is 10 s per HTTP operation with retries and backoff, and it honors retry-after on 429. Rate limits are 100K tokens/s and 40 req/s, and the docs warn they change dynamically. Any Claude Code hook built on this must be written fail-open with a short timeout of about 1-2 s, and that has to be implemented by the user. Nothing here provides it.
entries.contextCost: Docs page: 0 tokens. The optional typesafe-ai skill adds one skill entry (about 100 tokens of description in the skill list, roughly 400 chars/4). The 10 KB SKILL.md body, about 2.5k tokens, loads only when the skill triggers, and the skill then fetches docs pages. It adds no MCP tools and no hook text.
pros: It is the authoritative statement, with source, that no `model: jev-latest` swap exists for Claude Code. That kills the transparent-proxy approach and saves the user a dead-end search.

Points to the right architecture for the user's goal: Jev as a typed, calibrated decision layer inside hooks or apps, using confidence gating and intent routing. That is the only way to get the 'automatic' behavior without prompting.

The skill_suggestion cookbook is a working blueprint that fits Claude Code closely: inject `<skill_relevance>` via a UserPromptSubmit hook, with a 0.31 s first call. It reports wrong-skill loads dropping from 16.8% to 7.3% (Haiku 4.5, 488 requests). With the user's many plugin skills this could be useful.
Cheap: $0.042 per 1M input tokens and output is free. Hook-sized states of about 2-5k tokens cost roughly $0.0001-0.0002 per call.
The companion skill is MIT, markdown-only, adds about 100 tokens of context, and has no code to execute, so it is a safe install for when the user actually builds Jev integrations in client projects.
cons: It is documentation, not an integration: nothing here can be installed to make Claude Code use Jev automatically, so the user's core goal is not met by this candidate.

The page and the skill cover only the TypeSafe direct API (api.typesafe.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and never mention OpenRouter. Using OpenRouter means custom code and an untested base URL and model name (typesafe/jev-1.13).

The skill activates only when Claude is building something that fits a Jev use case, so it does not touch Claude Code's own decisions such as skill selection, permission checks or routing. Nothing on it runs at runtime.

Jev 1.13 jaggedness doc: literal reading, weak on numbers and dates, weak with large irrelevant state, adversarial content, and no generation. Hooks over big diffs or repo context are the wrong shape. Good targets are short classification questions.
Beta and rate limits are unstable: the models page says limits change without notice, and the skills repo has 2 commits despite 2.4k stars.

Latency and cost accrue per prompt (about 0.3-1 s if the cookbook pattern is copied). The user already has a busy hook stack (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post, caveman), and each addition adds serial latency and a fail-open burden.
entries.verdict: Not an integration, but the most honest guidance available. It confirms Jev cannot be plugged in as Claude Code's model, so any 'automatic' setup must be a hook-based decision layer the user builds, using the skill_suggestion cookbook as a template with OpenRouter as the endpoint.
