entries.name: claude-x-jev
entries.what: Claude Code skill wrapping OpenRouter's Jev Decisions endpoint. Mostly a CLI (jev.py: ask/route/gate/match/tune/lint/bench/status) driven by 13 slash commands aimed at batch work (email/comment/lead triage, draft verification, entity matching). The only automatic piece is an optional PreToolUse hook that sends each Bash call to Jev with two noul questions (reversible, serves_task) and returns allow, deny or ask. Everything else fires only when the user types /jev-* or uses trigger phrases.
entries.autoInvocation: Only the PreToolUse Bash hook is deterministic and automatic (a permission gate, not a value-add coding helper). The 13 commands are only-when-prompted (slash) or skill-description trigger on phrases like 'classify these', 'score these'; there is no automatic use of Jev for coding decisions (routing, code review triage, test selection, etc.).
security: API key from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env only, sent as Bearer header via urllib (jev.py:145); never in argv, so not visible in the process list. Hook only works if the key is in the env of the Claude Code process itself (shell profile export), meaning every Bash child process inherits it.
No shell=True, subprocess, eval or os.system in jev.py; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall (package.json has no install scripts), no telemetry or analytics found (grep clean).

hook --write (bin/claude-x-jev.js:150) does fs.copyFileSync(settingsPath) unguarded: throws if ~/.claude/settings.json does not exist; it then rewrites settings.json with JSON.stringify (reformats file, drops comments). Backup is kept as settings.json.bak-claude-x-jev.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command text is fed to Jev as state, so an attacker-controlled command string (e.g. from a poisoned repo) can carry text that steers the serves_task/reversible noul answers. Jev returns numbers only, but an 'allow' at >=0.9 skips the human prompt. A regex-free probabilistic model deciding allow on arbitrary shell is a weak control (e.g. 'reversible' definition includes 'only reads or changes files inside cwd', so curl|sh of a local file, or git-tracked destructive edits, may score high).
Hook 'allow' from an alpha 5-day-old single-author project auto-approves commands; the default 0.9 is unvalidated (tune command exists but needs labelled data).

Installer copies files to ~/.claude only; write scope is limited (skill dir, commands dir, settings.json). SKILL.md declares allowed-tools [Read, Write, Edit, Glob, Grep, Bash, WebFetch, AskUserQuestion, Skill, Task], broad but only when the skill is invoked.
entries.dataEgress: For the hook: every gated Bash call sends to openrouter.ai (then TypeSafe, per OpenRouter provider routing) the JSON {tool:'Bash', tool_input: json.dumps(tool_input)[:4000], cwd, task?}. That is the full command line (heredocs, inline tokens/passwords/URLs, file contents written via cat<<EOF) truncated to 4000 chars, plus the absolute project path (jev.py:512-521). No file contents otherwise, no prompts, no diffs, no tool outputs. It runs BEFORE the user's secret-leak guard result is known (hooks run in parallel), so a command containing a secret still goes out. Batch commands (/jev-classify etc.) send whatever fields of the input items the preset lists (up to max_chars each) — explicit user data, dry-run offered. Client-project concern: command text and cwd path leave the machine per call; check OpenRouter data-policy/ZDR for TypeSafe endpoint.
entries.failureMode: Intended fail-open-to-human: no key, network error, bad JSON, non-Bash tool all print nothing and exit 0 (jev.py:500-502, 545-548), leaving normal permission flow. In bypass permissions mode that means fail-open to full auto-execution, i.e. same as today. Weakness: latency, not correctness. decide() retries 4 times with 1/2/4/8s backoff on 429/5xx/network, per-request timeout 20s (gate default, jev.py:667), so a slow or down Jev can stall a Bash call for up to about 115s worst case; the Claude Code hook default timeout (60s for command hooks; hooks.json here sets no timeout) would likely kill it and treat as non-blocking error. No circuit breaker, so every Bash call re-pays the stall during an outage. Also, on 'ask', bypass mode may or may not honour it; in auto mode it forces prompts.
entries.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server, 0 tools. Always-on: skill description 916 chars (~230 tok) + 13 command stub descriptions ~1700 chars (~425 tok) + names, roughly 700 tokens in the skill/command listing every session. SKILL.md body (7.7KB ~1.9k tok) and task files load only on invocation. Hook injects no context text; only a short permissionDecisionReason ('jev: reversible=0.97, serves_task=0.91') shown to the user/tool result.
pros: Correct OpenRouter integration out of the box: hardcoded /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (jev.py:35-52), no patching needed, matches the user's provider choice.
Truly automatic path exists: PreToolUse hook needs no prompting; deterministic, runs on every Bash call, adds zero context tokens and zero tools.

Fail-safe design intent: any error prints nothing and exits 0; key never in argv; stdlib-only Python, no third-party deps, no postinstall, no telemetry; small, readable code (one 30KB script + 11KB installer) that is easy to audit and vendor.

Sound Jev usage patterns worth copying: noul-question tool-gate preset (tool-gate.json), threshold semantics (allow >=0.9, deny <=0.1, else ask), retry/backoff, hook JSON output shape (hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision).
Installer is idempotent, keeps a settings.json backup, preserves user presets on update, offers --project scope.
MIT license; low cost per call (about $0.00004 per gate call at Jev pricing).
cons: Wrong center of gravity for coding: 12 of 13 commands are for inbox/lead/comment triage and batch classification with manual slash invocation. Nothing wires Jev into coding decisions automatically (no code-review triage, test selection, file routing, commit/PR gating beyond Bash).

The one auto feature is a permission gate that duplicates what the user already has: user runs bypass/auto mode with a secret-leak guard hook. Jev 'allow' adds nothing in bypass mode (already allowed), 'ask' would ADD prompts the user does not have today, and 'deny' at <=0.1 is the only real value. The default and shadow settings (JEV_GATE_APPROVE=1.01) make almost every non-obvious Bash call return 'ask', i.e. prompt spam in a workflow that currently has none.

Documentation contradicts code: tasks/gate.md says the hook 'logs every decision to $TMPDIR/jev-gate.log', but the hook only appends stderr on errors (pre-tool-gate.sh:32, jev.py:545); decisions are never logged, so the recommended shadow-mode review of 'what would have been allowed' cannot be done.

Latency and outage exposure: sync call on every Bash, no timeout in the hook config, retries 4x with backoff and 20 s timeouts (up to about 115 s stall), no circuit breaker or cache; competes with GitNexus and secret-guard hooks on Bash matchers.

Sends full Bash command text (up to 4000 chars) and cwd to a third party on every call, in parallel with (not after) the secret-leak guard; unacceptable default for client projects without confirming OpenRouter/TypeSafe data policy.

Only gates Bash by default; Write/Edit/MCP tools require JEV_GATE_TOOLS and env vars (state kept in env, not in the settings entry), and JEV_GATE_TASK is a static env string that cannot know the current task, so serves_task is mostly 'is this routine dev work'.

Immature: 3 commits in one day, 1 author, no CI, no real tests (npm test just parses the file and lints one preset), no releases on GitHub, npm 0.1.1 published 5 days ago; hook --write crashes if settings.json is missing; the marketing benchmark (216 of the author's emails) is self-reported. Promotional content in README (community links).
Depends on OPENROUTER_API_KEY being exported in the environment Claude Code launches from; key then leaks to every child process, and GUI/desktop launches won't see it.
entries.verdict: Not a good fit as a whole: it is an ops/inbox-triage skill whose only automatic feature is a Bash permission gate that is redundant or noisy under bypass/auto mode. Worth mining as a reference implementation (correct OpenRouter endpoint, hook JSON shape, noul tool-gate preset, threshold logic) for a custom, narrowly scoped deny-only hook with a short timeout and no retries, rather than installing it.

entries.name: kinde-starter-kits/jev-agent-authorization (Jev Gatehouse)
entries.what: Not an MCP server and not a Claude Code plugin. It is a Next.js + Convex + Kinde reference web app ("Jev Gatehouse") that puts a server-side guard in front of a demo SaaS workspace API. Agent tool calls reach the guard through Kinde's hosted Secure MCP connection. The guard verifies the Kinde JWT and permissions, then sends non-read calls to Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via the OpenRouter System One endpoint) with 4 Noul questions (matches_intent, destructive, injected, exfiltration), 1 Score (risk) and 1 Choice (verdict_hint: allow/step_up/deny). Policy code turns the signals into allow, step_up or deny. Low-confidence calls go to an LLM judge. Every decision is written to a ledger before the call runs. Held calls need a fresh-sign-in approval page. It includes a 300-case benchmark and an attack playground. It is the best public worked example of Jev typed signals for tool-call authorization on OpenRouter, but it is a design pattern to copy, not something to install into Claude Code.
interface: Kinde Secure MCP connection (hosted by Kinde, config via OpenAPI spec convex/api/openapi.ts)
entries.autoInvocation: Not applicable to Claude Code. Inside its own architecture the guard is a transparent server-side proxy that runs deterministically on every non-read tool call, with no model discretion. That is the property the user wants, but it works at the API layer, not as a Claude Code hook.
security: Not installable into Claude Code, so no direct attack surface on the user's machine. Repo has husky 'prepare' script (dev-only, standard) and no postinstall or curl|sh installer.
MIT license. Single author (sholajegede, 120 of 121 commits), Kinde starter-kit org, CODEOWNERS present.
OPENROUTER_API_KEY is held server-side in Convex env (never in argv), sent as a Bearer header. This is a good pattern.

Prompt-injection design is the main strength. The Jev state marks the user request as verified by the server, marks the agent's stated reason as unverified, and includes recent content the agent read. There is a specific 'injected' Noul question and a fail-closed design (ledger write must succeed before the call runs).
Any local reuse must not send whole files or secrets to OpenRouter. Redaction exists in convex/lib/redact.ts, which I did not review in depth.
Repo benchmark is self-authored (their own 300 cases and labels), so the 0.0% false-allow and 83.7% accuracy figures are unverified vendor-style claims.
entries.dataEgress: In the app: to OpenRouter (then TypeSafe) it sends a JSON 'state' with the tool call (operation, method, arguments), the verified user request text, the agent's stated reason, excerpts of content the agent recently read, and the user's recent call history. To Kinde it sends token verification and permission lookups. To Convex it sends everything, including the ledger. If the pattern were ported locally to Claude Code, the egress would be the tool-call arguments (Bash commands, file paths, edit diffs) plus the user's prompt, unless the user filters it.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design. A Jev error or 3 s timeout gives step_up with reason jev_unavailable (convex/guard/judgment.ts:28). Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY gives step_up (jev_not_configured). An unset judge model holds low-confidence calls (judge_not_configured). Any guard exception gives a 503 and the call does not run (handler.ts handleApiRequest catch). That is right for a production API gate, but a fail-closed local hook would stall the user's Claude Code whenever OpenRouter is down, unless changed to fail-open.
entries.contextCost: None for Claude Code, since nothing is installed. Kinde's MCP would add one tool per OpenAPI operation of the demo workspace API, which is irrelevant to the user's own repos. Zero hook-injected text.
pros: Uses Jev via OpenRouter System One (POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13) with a complete request and response contract in ~100 lines (convex/jev/client.ts), including the questions schema for Noul, Score and Choice, the answers shape, and usage.cost.

Shows the strongest idea for this user: a deterministic gate that treats Jev's calibrated probabilities as inputs to policy code (convex/guard/policy.ts) rather than trusting a single verdict. Their own benchmark reports that the multi-signal approach has less false-allow than a single Jev verdict (0.0% vs 12.4%). The numbers are self-authored, not independent.
Concrete latency and cost data: p50 205 ms and about $0.029 per 1,000 calls for Jev signals, against about 2 s and $0.93 for a Sonnet judge. This is useful for sizing a PreToolUse hook.
Ready-made question set (matches_intent, destructive, injected, exfiltration, risk, verdict_hint) that could be ported almost verbatim into a Claude Code PreToolUse hook.
Sound failure handling patterns: 3 s timeout, explicit reason codes, cascade to a stronger judge only on low confidence.
Decent hygiene for a starter kit: MIT, CI (format, lint, typecheck, test, build), 140 test cases across 20+ test files, CHANGELOG, CODEOWNERS.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook or skill for Claude Code. There is no install path into Claude Code, and it cannot be made automatic without a rewrite.

Requires Kinde (a business account), Convex, and Next.js. It guards a demo SaaS API reached through Kinde's hosted MCP, not the user's local Bash/Edit/Write tools, so it does not protect Claude Code sessions.

The authorization flow depends on server-verified user intent from the in-app console (KINDE_WEB_CLIENT_ID azp check, convex/guard/handler.ts:200-212). An external MCP client such as Claude Code gets intent source 'none', where the client.ts question text says to answer no for matches_intent, so most non-read calls would be held.
Fail-closed step_up on any Jev problem would stall an interactive coding session if ported unchanged.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-23, last push 2026-09-24, 5 stars, 0 forks, no releases, version 0.1.0. Its accuracy figures (83.7% for its own design) come from its own labeled cases and are not independent evidence that Jev is good at judging real Claude Code tool calls.
Adds a verdict per call: latency of about 200 ms is fine for a hook, but every non-read tool call also costs an OpenRouter request and sends command text to a third party.
Doesn't address the user's other Jev use cases (routing, choosing which subagent or model to use, triage, code-review scoring, commit-message classification).
entries.verdict: Not usable as a Claude Code integration, since it is a Kinde+Convex+Next.js web-app demo with no hook, MCP server or skill of its own. It is worth reading as a reference for calling OpenRouter's System One endpoint (convex/jev/client.ts) and for a multi-signal allow/step-up/deny policy, which could be ported to a small local PreToolUse hook that fails open.

entries.name: logicrw/awesome-jev-projects
entries.what: Not an integration. It is a community-run "awesome list" and static React/Vite website. It catalogs 799 GitHub projects that mention or use TypeSafe Jev across 17 categories (src/data/projects.json). It ships a discovery-only Agent Skill ("awesome-jev", SKILL.md, also at skills/awesome-jev/SKILL.md) that tells an agent to fetch the public JSON catalog, llms.txt and llms-full.txt and rank projects by fit. The repo runs 6-hourly GitHub Actions radar jobs plus Issue-based submissions, and takes no PRs. It never calls Jev, OpenRouter or TypeSafe. Its main value for this task is as a curated index of Claude Code x Jev integrations. Many pinned entries are not itself usable as an integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and only when the user or agent is looking for Jev projects. It never invokes Jev decisions during coding. It does not meet the requirement that Claude Code use Jev automatically, because it provides no Jev calls at all.
security: No API keys, no backend and no login. SECURITY.md states the site is static and unauthenticated, with no API-key form.
Repo scripts and workflows are hardened: SHA-pinned Actions, dependency install with --ignore-scripts in read-only jobs, and non-force compare-and-swap publish of a single projects.json entry.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill tells the agent to fetch and read catalog prose that is auto-extracted from third-party READMEs ('readme-extractive' summaries for 479 entries, and 'integration-detected' entries pending human review). It does say to treat that text as untrusted data and not to run submitted repos or snippets, which is good practice.
The skill's 'Install' step uses the third-party 'npx skills add' CLI, which is a supply-chain touchpoint. I did not run it.
Cloudflare Web Analytics beacon on the website only (SECURITY.md). It honors DNT and GPC and does not affect a Claude Code session.

Star and popularity signals are unreliable. tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction shows 7131 stars two weeks after creation. 739 of the 799 catalog repos were created in 2026-09, and 529 have 10 or fewer stars. Catalog inclusion is not a security or quality endorsement (the README and SKILL.md say so themselves).
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves the machine to Jev, TypeSafe or OpenRouter, because this repo makes no Jev calls. If the skill is triggered, the agent does HTTP GETs to logicrw.github.io for the catalog. The requested URL and normal HTTP metadata are visible to GitHub Pages. Code, diffs and prompts are not sent unless the agent puts them in a search query or an Issue submission, and the skill says to ask the user first.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable, since no Jev calls are made. If the GitHub Pages catalog is unreachable, the skill just fails to fetch. It has no hook, so it cannot block or delay tool calls. It is fail-open by construction, but also does nothing automatically.
entries.contextCost: Very low. One skill with roughly a 260-character description, about 65 tokens permanently in the skill list. The 6.6 KB SKILL.md body (about 1.6k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. There are 0 MCP tools, 0 hooks and no server instructions. Fetching projects.json or llms-full.txt for 799 entries would be very large, and llms.txt is the concise version. Those fetches should be delegated to a subagent or filtered with jq or python rather than read whole.
pros: Best available map of the Claude Code x Jev ecosystem. The 799-entry catalog has per-entry category, commit-pinned evidence URLs, verificationStatus and license status, and is machine-readable via projects.json and llms.txt. Use it to shortlist, then audit repos individually.

Honest about its limits. All 799 entries have runtimeVerified=False, and it labels 502 entries 'integration-detected' (README/keyword detected only) versus 232 'source-verified'. It requires compatibility servers to name their real underlying model, which helps with the unverified 'Jev is really a DeepSeek flash router' claim.

Catalog includes concrete auto-invocation candidates for Claude Code. Hook-based: valentynkit/jev-belay (Stop hook), Brainwires/jevwire (MCP plus hooks), muratcakmak/jev-guard and erkamyaman/jev-enforce (guards), 0x7067/claude-jev, jonathanavis96/jev-kit. Transparent proxy or router: gargpratyush/jev-router (472 stars, source-verified, failures keep the current model), ruban-24/switchboard. Context pruning: tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction, winnow, jev-pruner, yoshi. MCP: itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp (330 stars, MIT, source-verified in cmd/evaluate/client.go).

Few OpenRouter-capable Claude Code entries are flagged, which cuts discovery time: chrishan17/claude-jev-mod, Akramovic1/jev-pilot, lazniak/jevskill, ctmx/openrouter-jev-mcp, Protocol-Lattice/harness-router.
Near-zero risk: MIT, a Markdown-only skill, no keys, no shell, tiny context cost. Actively maintained (214 commits in 12 days, updated 6-hourly by bot) and has a security policy.
The AGENTS.md and SKILL.md untrusted-data stance matches how this audit should treat the entries.
cons: It is not an integration. Installing it gives Claude Code no Jev capability, no OpenRouter path and no automatic behavior. It cannot satisfy the no-manual-prompt requirement.
Its skill fires only on 'find Jev projects' style requests, which this user will rarely make once the integration is chosen. Permanent value after selection is roughly zero.

Quality signal is weak. 739 of 799 repos were created in 2026-09, 529 have 10 or fewer stars, and 479 summaries are auto-extracted from READMEs. Only 232 of 799 are source-verified, none is runtime-verified, and 503 have no confirmed license. The 7131 stars on fast-jev-compaction after about 2 weeks looks like inflated or anomalous attention.

Marketing claims in the README ('Sub-100ms', 'Zero Vaporware', 50-100ms) conflict with the brief's 70-500 ms end-to-end and are not measured here. The 1.5-5 s vs 50-100 ms comparison table is unsourced. Do not rely on them.
The catalog is huge (README.md 522 KB, four 470-550 KB READMEs) and full-text projects.json is 799 entries. Reading it naively would burn context, so it needs jq or subagent filtering.
Small maintainer group (2 humans plus a bot). It has a strict no-PR policy, sponsorship slots and analytics, so it is a curated but commercially-flavored directory.
The 'npx skills add' install path adds a third-party CLI dependency for zero benefit here. The skill file can simply be ignored.
entries.verdict: Do not install it as the integration. It is a Jev ecosystem index with a discovery-only skill, no Jev calls and no automatic invocation. Use it once as a research map (the leads above: itsmostafa/typesafe-mcp, gargpratyush/jev-router, valentynkit/jev-belay, chrishan17/claude-jev-mod, Akramovic1/jev-pilot, ctmx/openrouter-jev-mcp), and audit each candidate's source yourself, because no listed entry is runtime-verified.

entries.what: Independent (non-TypeSafe-affiliated) MIT awesome-list and Jekyll site indexing about 240 Jev/TypeSafe resources (78 in the Agent and developer tooling category, 42 client libraries, 50 evaluations). It is a discovery directory, not an integration. It ships one tiny skill (skills/awesome-jev/SKILL.md, 1.8KB) that only tells an agent to fetch the README or resources.json and recommend projects. It contains no Jev calling code, no MCP server and no hooks. Its README does describe the Claude Code-relevant candidates that should be audited separately: jev-use, toolgate, jev-belay, jev-router, Switchboard, jev-pruner, fast-jev-compaction, jev-cli, jev-skill-router, jev-lint, jev-engineering, Oko, Jev MCP (jkudish), Jev MCP (blakestone-x), TypeSafe MCP (itsmostafa), jev-agent-skill and Building with TypeSafe Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and it fires only when the user is selecting Jev resources. It would not fire during ordinary coding, so it does nothing to make Claude Code use Jev automatically.
security: Documentation and static site only. The only runtime code is maintainer scripts (Pillow==12.1.0 is the only pinned dependency) and site JS.
CI checks.yml uses SHA-pinned actions and permissions: contents: read. It runs npx --yes all-contributors-cli@6.26.1 in CI only.

The skill instructs fetching a remote README and JSON at runtime. That content is community-edited and untrusted, so a PR could plant text aimed at agents. The skill does say a listing is not an endorsement, and it says to verify sources and defer to docs.typesafe.ai.
No API keys, telemetry, postinstall or curl|sh in the repo itself.

Each listed project does have its own risk. The README flags several: jev-engineering's published results show blunt injections moved 0 of 30 dangerous commands, but authority framing moved 3 of 30. Jevelry may execute configured run commands without confirmation. jev-pruner, Canny, toolgate and SkillRanker send diffs, command output or session text off-machine.
entries.dataEgress: The repo and its skill send nothing to Jev. The skill only makes read-only WebFetch or gh fetches of the README and resources.json from GitHub or GitHub Pages, which leaks no code. Listed tools egress varies by project: prompts, clipped diffs, Bash output, tool inputs, or code chunks go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter, as stated in each README entry.
entries.failureMode: No runtime dependency on Jev, so nothing can fail. If GitHub or Pages is unreachable, the skill just cannot fetch the list. In the README, fail-open is explicitly described for NeuroLink, jev-belay, jev-lint and Canny (default gate). jev-use and pi-verdict fail closed or escalate on unreachable. These are per-project properties.
entries.contextCost: About 460 tokens for the skill description and body if installed. It adds 0 tools, 0 MCP instructions and 0 hook text. When invoked it fetches a README of about 162KB (about 40k tokens) or resources.json of about 133KB (about 33k tokens), which is heavy unless filtered through jq or grep.
pros: Best single map of the Jev ecosystem for this audit. README.md lists roughly 78 agent/dev tooling entries, including about 15 Claude Code hooks, plugins and MCP servers, each with data-egress caveats. It is the source for finding additional candidates.

Entries are sourced and skeptical. For example, each blurb states what leaves the machine, fail-open behavior, and its own measured results, such as the toolgate 21% ask rate and jev-engineering's injection test results.
Actively maintained: 338 commits in 12 days, pushed 2026-09-28, a release snapshot on 2026-09-21, and 40 contributors.
resources.json is machine-readable, so candidate discovery can be scripted.
MIT license, no secrets, no runtime code, no attack surface beyond fetched text.
README.md:129 confirms the OpenRouter path needs the decisions request shape, not chat completions. That is an important integration caveat.
cons: It is not an integration. It provides no MCP server, hook or automatic behavior, so it cannot satisfy the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told to.
Its only skill fires solely on Jev-resource-selection queries, never during normal coding.
Inclusion is not endorsement. Entries are self-reported by authors and many benchmarks are the authors' own. It is independent and unaffiliated with TypeSafe, so it can lag behind the docs.
README.md is 162KB and resources.json 133KB. Loading them wholesale would burn 30-40k tokens, so use grep or jq.

The listed tools are mostly days old and written by hobbyists, per the 2026-09-17 repo creation. Many are TypeSafe-only, and OpenRouter's request shape differs from chat completions, so each pick needs its own audit.
Privacy: several listed hooks send diffs, Bash output and prompts to a third party, which matters for the user's client projects.
entries.verdict: Useful only as a research index: it does no Jev calls, adds no hooks and nothing invokes it automatically. Do not install its skill. Use resources.json and README lines 341-416 to pick candidates to audit, for example jev-use, toolgate, jev-belay, Switchboard, jev-cli, Oko and jkudish's Jev MCP.

entries.name: kenhuangus/jev-usecases
entries.what: Python library plus click CLI (`jev-usecases list|run|run-all`) with about 40 use-case harnesses that call TypeSafe Jev through the official typesafe-sdk. Each harness builds state plus Choice/Score/Noul questions, applies confidence thresholds in code, and returns an action band (auto/confirm/human/block). It is NOT a skill, MCP server, hook or plugin. It has no SKILL.md, .mcp.json, plugin.json or hooks config, and no Claude Code integration. The discovery label "skill" is wrong; it is a reference cookbook. The most relevant module is `coding_agent_guardrails.py`, a gate for shell/write/edit tool calls. It is only demonstrated on fixtures and is not wired to any hook.
interface: Python: agent_trace, agent_harness, semantic_linting, function_calling, model_routing, llm_guardrails, rag_retrieval, citation_check
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted / not at all: it has no Claude Code integration. Nothing triggers it automatically. It could serve as a design template for a deterministic PreToolUse hook, which would be the only way to get truly automatic invocation.
security: Reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env or a .env file. It uses load_dotenv on the repo root and the CWD (client.py:14-15), so a stray .env in a client project directory would be loaded.
The key is passed in-process to the SDK, not via argv. The optional LLM helper sends the key in x-api-key or Authorization headers (llm.py:107,163), not via argv.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall. grep found none.
No telemetry in the repo code (the SDK was not audited).

The README itself warns that user-controlled text in state can change Jev's answer, which is a prompt-injection surface for a tool-call gate that puts command strings and conversation summaries in state.
The README says thresholds are not ready for unattended production use.
entries.dataEgress: Only when the user's own code calls it: whatever is put in `state`, sent to api.typesafe.ai. For coding_agent_guardrails that is tool name, full command or args, cwd, user goal, conversation summary and protected-path list. As shipped, no Claude Code data leaves the machine, because nothing is wired in. The optional security copilot runners also send incident text to Anthropic or OpenAI.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable as an integration. In the library, get_client raises MissingApiKeyError if the key is missing, and CLI errors exit 1 or 2 (fail-closed for the CLI). The gate function has no try/except or explicit timeout around client.system_one, so an outage would raise an exception. The caller would have to decide fail-open or fail-closed. The LLM helper uses a 60 s timeout.
entries.contextCost: Zero in Claude Code as shipped, since it registers no MCP tools, hooks, skills or instructions. If it were adapted into a hook, the injected text would be only what the hook chooses to print.
pros: Concrete, readable template of how to phrase Jev questions for a coding agent: coding_agent_guardrails.py uses 8 Noul safety conditions, a risk_class Choice (read_only/reversible/irreversible) and a Score severity, combined with thresholds (deny at or below 0.15, allow at or above 0.75) and a deterministic protected-path pre-check. It could be copied into a PreToolUse hook.

Honest about Jev's limits: it cites TypeSafe's jaggedness notes (literal reading, no counting or date comparison, distraction by unneeded state fields, injection via user text) and says code should do exact checks.
Deterministic checks first, Jev second, and the model never executes anything. This is a sound pattern for a gate.
MIT licensed, small codebase (about 900 lines of core plus use cases), easy to audit.
Fixtures for about 40 use cases show working state and question shapes for agent_trace, function_calling, model_routing and semantic_linting, which are the ones relevant to a coding agent.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. Claude Code cannot use it without the user writing the glue, so it does not meet the requirement of automatic use.

Provider support is TypeSafe direct only. No OpenRouter code path, no base_url on the Jev client, and the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone schema is unverified against typesafe-sdk. The user would need to rewrite the client.
Mostly irrelevant domains (SOC, insurance, recruiting, ad tech, financial crime, about 35 of 40 modules) for a developer's daily coding.

Very young and thinly reviewed: 8 commits over 3 days, 2 contributors, 17 stars, no releases, no CI, no PyPI package. Its own README says the runs check typed responses, not correctness, and that the thresholds are not production-ready.

The gate would send full commands, cwd and conversation summaries (which may include client code and paths) to a third party on every call. The README says accuracy drops when state carries extra fields, and the repo sends conversation_summary anyway.

A PreToolUse gate on the user's already busy Bash|Read|Grep chain (secret guard, GitNexus) would add latency per call. The user runs bypass/auto permission mode, so a fail-open gate adds little real safety, and a fail-closed one adds outage friction. The code has no timeout or fallback handling.
Uses load_dotenv() from the CWD, which could load a client project's .env, a hygiene issue for client work.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration at all: a Python cookbook of Jev use-case demos that only supports TypeSafe direct, with no OpenRouter path and no MCP, hook or skill packaging. Worth reading coding_agent_guardrails.py as a template for a self-written fail-open PreToolUse hook, but do not install it.

entries.name: Gitmaxd/agent-seek
entries.what: FastAPI service (MCP Streamable HTTP at /mcp plus REST /v1/search) that runs a You.com web search and then re-ranks the candidates with TypeSafe Jev (Score and Noul questions for answerability, subject match, republisher, prompt-injection risk). It returns a scored URL list and does not write answers. It is a web-search product, not a coding aid, and Jev is used only as a hidden ranking backend.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool (search_web) plus an optional skill description trigger (SKILL.md, 'ranked web search for research or RAG'). No hooks and no transparent proxy. Claude would call it only when it decides to search the web, and it competes with Claude Code's built-in WebSearch/WebFetch.
security: Not a local stdio server: it is a FastAPI HTTP service to self-host, or a hosted MCP at agentseek.dev. The README publishes a shared demo Bearer key (AS_...) and says to paste it into mcp.json headers. Every query goes through a third-party operator, and the key is public and rate-limited to about 5 lifetime searches per IP.

No install scripts and no postinstall. Plain pip install -r requirements.txt (fastapi, uvicorn, httpx, pydantic, dotenv, pytest). No telemetry found in code. Optional Upstash Redis is used for rate limits.

Prompt-injection surface: web results (title, snippet, and page text in deep mode) are returned into the agent context. The repo's own defence is a Jev prompt_injection gate that drops flagged rows. The gate fails 'flagged' when the parse is missing, but subject_match and is_republisher fail open. The repo has no external verification of the gate.
Deep mode fetches arbitrary URLs server-side (packages/core/fetch/page.py), which is an SSRF surface for a self-hosted instance.
Default CORS_ORIGIN=* and a default AGENT_SEEK_API_KEY of dev-agent-seek-key-change-me in .env.example. OAuth state is in-memory.
TYPESAFE_API_KEY is stored in the server .env, not in argv. The client only sends its Bearer key in the MCP headers config.
entries.dataEgress: The search query text (q, at most 500 chars) goes to You.com. Titles, URLs, snippets and (deep mode) fetched page text plus the query go to TypeSafe Jev. When the hosted agentseek.dev is used, the query also goes to the operator, whose privacy page says client IP is stored for the demo quota. Nothing from the code, diffs or repo files leaves the machine unless Claude itself puts code into q. If self-hosted, the operator is you.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on the Jev side. On total Jev failure it returns HTTP 200 with meta.ranking=raw_fallback (You.com order). The Jev client timeout is 8s per call (jev.py:13, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT), and a full cascade makes several calls (Stage A and B, plus page fetches in deep mode). The MCP tool is model-invoked, so if the server is down Claude simply gets a tool error. Rate limiting fails closed (503) if Upstash is configured and down. No Claude Code hooks are involved.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools. The tool definitions are about 1.6k tokens (estimated from the 4 descriptions and schemas in mcp_server.py). The server-level MCP_INSTRUCTIONS string is about 6,000 chars (about 1.5k tokens) and is injected on every session. Total about 3k tokens of standing context. No hook text is injected. Three of the four tools (health, docs, capabilities) add nothing for coding.
pros: Real, working Jev usage (System One Score and Noul questions) with an actual fallback path (raw_fallback) and offline tests (about 30 test files, CI workflow).
MIT license, small readable codebase. JevClient already has base_url and model parameters, so an OpenRouter switch is a small fork edit.
Single-purpose read-only tools, all annotated readOnlyHint. The prompt_injection scoring of web results is a useful defence idea for research with Claude Code.
Doubles as a reference for how to build typed Jev questions (state + questions dict) for ranking, which the user could reuse.
cons: Not a coding tool. It is web search ranking, so it offers little value in daily coding: no code, diff, PR, test-failure or permission-decision use cases.
Jev is hidden behind a server. Claude Code cannot use Jev directly, only through the search_web tool.

No OpenRouter support: hard-coded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev.py:11) and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. Switching needs a fork and a self-hosted server, and the OpenRouter System One schema compatibility is unverified.
Requires two paid upstream keys (You.com and TypeSafe) to self-host, or trusting a stranger's hosted endpoint with a public shared key limited to about 5 searches per IP.
Model-discretion only. Claude Code must decide to call search_web instead of its built-in WebSearch, so it is not truly automatic, and there is no hook to force it.
Costs about 3k tokens of standing context, of which the 3 non-search tools and the 1.5k-token instructions block are mostly waste. Multi-second latency per search.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 2 stars, created 8 days before the audit date, and no pinned dependencies. Deep mode gives a self-hosted server an SSRF surface.
entries.verdict: A fresh, single-author web-search reranker that uses Jev as an internal backend. It does not support OpenRouter and does not help with coding, and the model has to choose to call it. Skip it as the Jev integration for Claude Code; at most read the Jev question design as a reference.

entries.name: jev-tools (PyPI) / Jtools by adiel-hub
entries.what: Python CLI suite (11 commands: jgrep, jsort, jpick, jgate, jwatch, juniq, jhead, jtag, jroute, jmatch, jtools) that pipes text lines/records through Jev Noul/Choice/Score decisions, e.g. `cat log | jgrep "auth failures"` or `jgate "mentions a security incident" && alert`. Written in Python with httpx, ~14k lines total incl. tests. It is a shell-pipeline utility, not an MCP server, hook or skill. It has no Claude Code integration and no mention of Claude Code, agents, MCP or hooks in its docs.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. There is no hook, MCP server or skill. Claude Code would call these CLIs through Bash only if told to (e.g. via CLAUDE.md) or if it discovers them. It cannot meet the user's requirement of automatic, unprompted use without wrapping it in a custom hook, skill or MCP layer.
security: API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header via httpx (client.py:252); no --api-key argv flag found, so the key is not exposed in the process list. Read from env or ~/.config/jev/*.key; jtools doctor warns on world-readable key files.

No curl|sh installer, no postinstall; pure-Python wheel with a single dependency (httpx). Only subprocess use is jwatch --exec (jwatch.py:267), which passes the line as a positional $1 to /bin/sh and refuses quoting spellings that would break that, which is sound handling of untrusted input.
Answer cache at ~/.cache/jev/answers.sqlite stores SHA-256 of (model,state,question) plus answer, not raw text; disable with --no-cache or JEV_NO_CACHE=1.
Sends HTTP-Referer and X-Title (j-tools) headers to OpenRouter, which is attribution only; no telemetry found in src.
Prompt-injection surface: judged text is data going to a typed-decision model, so it can bias a probability but cannot execute anything; the exception is jwatch --exec, which is mitigated as above.
Single-maintainer, 1-star, 2-week-old project: supply-chain trust is low. 78 of 107 commits are authored 'Claude' (AI-generated codebase).
entries.dataEgress: Every record judged (line, paragraph, field, file, or group of candidate lines, around 300 input tokens each) is POSTed to the configured backend (OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions here). SECURITY.md: nothing else leaves the machine. --dry-run shows questions and a redacted state sample first. For client projects this means whatever content the user pipes in (code, logs, diffs) goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default: an API error lets the line pass through unjudged, the run continues, exit code 5 (README.md:247). jgate fails closed, and --strict stops on first error with exit 4. Total deadline via --timeout / JEV_TIMEOUT with jittered-backoff retries and Retry-After handling (client.py:422-513); dollar budget cap via --budget. Only matters if Claude invokes them.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill, no injected text. It only costs context if the user adds a CLAUDE.md instruction describing the commands (~100-300 tokens).
pros: Confirmed native OpenRouter support in code: backends.py:16 and 99-105 target openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model ~typesafe/jev-latest and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it works with the user's chosen provider by setting JEV_API=openrouter.
Well-engineered client: retry with jitter inside a total deadline, Retry-After handling, in-flight dedupe, dollar budget cap, SQLite answer cache keyed by hash, key never in argv.
MIT license, pure Python with one dependency (httpx), no postinstall or curl|sh, 379 tests, CI with mypy strict.

Good reference implementation of the System One wire format: wire.py has request and response shapes for Noul, Choice and Score that could be reused when building a custom Claude Code hook or MCP server.
Practical use cases in Claude's Bash tool: `jgrep` over big logs or test output, `jgate` in scripts, `jtag` or `jroute` for triage.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, and no mention of Claude or agents in its docs, so it fails the requirement of automatic use without prompting.

Solves shell-pipeline text triage, not coding decisions such as permission gating, model routing, or deciding whether to run tests. It competes with grep and ripgrep, which Claude already uses precisely and for free, and it is non-deterministic, costs money and adds 240+ ms per line.
Project is 12 days old, single maintainer, 1 star, one release (v0.1.1), and 78 of 107 commits are authored by Claude; its benchmarks were measured via Vercel, not OpenRouter, and are self-reported.

Privacy for client work: any piped code or log content leaves the machine for OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the user's existing secret-leak hook does not cover this since it is a Bash subprocess sending data outward by design.
Key-selection gotcha: TYPESAFE_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY in env silently takes priority over OPENROUTER_API_KEY unless JEV_API=openrouter is set.
Fail-open default means an outage silently yields unfiltered output. Claude may misread that as 'no match' unless exit code 5 is noticed.
entries.verdict: Real, well-built, OpenRouter-capable Jev CLI, but it is a manual shell-utility toolkit rather than a Claude Code integration. It offers no automatic invocation, and its semantic-grep niche adds little to Claude's daily coding. Use it only as a code reference for the wire format, or as an optional Bash tool documented in CLAUDE.md, not as the primary integration.

entries.name: @leighefford/jev-kit
entries.what: Novelty toolkit of 7 MCP tools (stdio; optional HTTP mode) plus CLI and local web UI that call Jev's System One endpoint: laugh_track (simulated 200-person audience for speeches/jokes), steer_check (per-sentence off-goal/filler/invented-fact check of a draft), semantic_bisect (git bisect judged by Jev; runs a user-supplied shell command in a temp git worktree), physics_interact/physics_sandbox (game-physics judgments), collision_engine (pairwise idea scoring of notes), and jev_ask (raw typed noul/choice/score query). Not a general coding-assistant integration: no hook, no router, no automatic invocation.
interface: CLI: jev-kit serve --http / ui / doctor / laugh / steer / bisect / physics / sandbox / collide
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. Descriptions target speeches, comedy, notes and game physics, so Claude would essentially never call them during coding unless prompted; only semantic_bisect and steer_check are remotely dev-relevant and both are situational. jev_ask has no guidance on when to use it. No hook, no skill, no proxy.
security: No npm postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json; no telemetry found; only network calls go to the configured Jev URL (and Vercel gateway for whisper).

API key: README recommends `claude mcp add ... -e AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=key`, which stores the key in plain text in ~/.claude.json (not in argv of the running server; env only). Web UI saves key to ~/.config/jev-kit/config.json with mode 0600/dir 0700 (src/jev.js:61-67).

semantic_bisect executes an arbitrary model-supplied shell command via `sh -c` (src/tools/semantic-bisect.js:22) in a temp worktree with no sandbox and inherited env (including any API keys); tool description asks the model to confirm with the user, but in bypass/auto permission mode that guard is soft. Prompt-injection from repo content could steer command choice.
collision_engine and laugh_track accept arbitrary filesystem paths (path / audioPath) and read them; audioPath uploads file to Vercel AI Gateway for transcription.
HTTP mode (`serve --http`) uses a random secret path, binds 127.0.0.1 by default; intended for tunnels to ChatGPT, not needed here.
npx -y @leighefford/jev-kit runs unpinned third-party code from a 1-person, 3-day-old package on every launch; supply-chain risk unless pinned by exact version.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model/user passes into a tool call leaves the machine: state text (speech lines, draft text, sources, notes, command output tail up to 8000 chars from semantic_bisect, commit subjects) plus typed question definitions, sent to the configured Jev endpoint (Vercel gateway / TypeSafe / JEV_BASE_URL) with the Bearer key and User-Agent 'jev-kit'. Audio files go to Vercel AI Gateway for whisper. Nothing is sent automatically; no telemetry, no passive code/prompt capture.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft for the session: tool errors come back as isError tool results (src/server.js:29-31); Jev calls retry 429/5xx up to 3 times with 400ms exponential backoff (src/jev.js:185-189). No fetch timeout/AbortSignal is set (grep), so a hung connection could stall a tool call indefinitely. No hooks so it cannot block Claude Code turns; missing key returns a clear error at call time (server still starts).
entries.contextCost: 7 MCP tools (laugh_track, steer_check, semantic_bisect, physics_interact, physics_sandbox, collision_engine, jev_ask). Tool names + descriptions + zod schemas approx 4,500-5,500 chars (~1.2-1.4k tokens) plus ~380 chars server instructions (~100 tokens). No hook-injected text. Roughly 1.3-1.5k tokens of always-loaded (or deferred-searchable) context, mostly wasted on speech/physics tools irrelevant to coding.
pros: Small, readable codebase (~1.3k lines) with a clean minimal Jev client (src/jev.js) whose retry logic, typed-question helpers (noul/choice/score) and answer parsing are directly reusable for a custom Jev MCP/hook.
Has an env-only route to any /v1/systemone base URL (JEV_BASE_URL + JEV_API_KEY + JEV_MODEL), so OpenRouter can probably be pointed at without code changes (src/jev.js:73-84).
jev_ask exposes raw typed Jev queries over MCP, and semantic_bisect is a genuinely dev-relevant idea (judging 'bug tests cannot catch' per commit).
No postinstall scripts, no telemetry, keys only go to the Jev URL; MIT license; offline mocked test suite (~30 tests).
Read-only annotations on most tools; server starts without a key and errors gracefully.
cons: Not built for coding: 4 of 7 tools are entertainment (laugh track, physics, note collisions), so Claude will not use it automatically and the tool defs cost ~1.4k tokens of context for little value.

No OpenRouter support in code or docs; default paths are Vercel AI Gateway or TypeSafe direct; the OpenRouter route relies on an undocumented 'local server' hack that mislabels cost/provider and is untested against OpenRouter's actual schema.
Zero automatic integration: no hooks, skills or CLAUDE.md snippet; user's requirement of automatic use without prompting is not met.
Immature: 3 days old, 1 author, 13 commits, 0 stars, no CI, no releases, version 0.1.0; likely to churn.
semantic_bisect runs arbitrary shell commands from model input with no sandbox and the full inherited env; risky under bypass/auto permission mode and on client repos.
README install command puts the API key in ~/.claude.json plaintext and runs unpinned `npx -y` on every start (supply chain + startup latency).
No fetch timeout, so a hung Jev call can block a tool invocation.
Audio transcription and mic features require a Vercel key regardless of provider; irrelevant here.
entries.verdict: A fun but off-target novelty kit; not a fit for automatic Jev use in daily coding and it has no native OpenRouter support (only a JEV_BASE_URL workaround). Worth mining for its small Jev client and jev_ask/semantic_bisect ideas, not for installing globally.

entries.name: jev-planner
entries.what: Standalone Node CLI (npm jev-planner 0.1.1, MIT) that runs 2+ agent CLIs/chat APIs (codex, claude --print, deepseek, kimi, glm) to draft implementation plans, has Jev (via @typesafe-ai/sdk systemOne) score completeness/feasibility/risk and decide on cross-review and finalizer, then writes one merged plan. It is NOT an MCP server, hook, skill or Claude Code plugin; it only shells out to `claude` as one of its planner agents.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a manual CLI; Claude Code would only run it if the user wrote a custom skill/CLAUDE.md rule telling Claude to call `jev-planner` via Bash. Nothing in the repo (no plugin.json, .mcp.json, hooks, SKILL.md) makes it automatic. llms.txt exists as an agent-readable reference only.
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts; single runtime dependency (@typesafe-ai/sdk).
API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), sent as Bearer header; not in argv. Provider keys are stripped from spawned agent subprocess env (process.ts:45-47, omitEnv).

Spawns `claude --print --permission-mode plan --permission-prompts none --tools Read,Glob,Grep --strict-mcp-config` and `codex exec --sandbox read-only` (providers.ts:86-120): read-only, MCP disabled, reasonable hardening; inherits the rest of process.env incl. ANTHROPIC/OAuth login state.

Prompt-injection surface: repo content (files read by agents, repo snapshot for chat APIs) flows into plan text and into Jev's `state`, but Jev only returns typed choices; plan output is free text to be consumed by the user/Claude, so injected content in repo could bias the plan.
Single maintainer, brand new (created 2026-09-21), 0 stars; releases and CI depend on rxova/shared@main workflows (mutable ref supply-chain risk for the publisher).
No telemetry code found in src; SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers only.
entries.dataEgress: To Jev endpoint: task text, stage text, and the full text of every draft plan (which include repo file names, code snippets and design details the agents produced), per systemOne call. To each planner agent provider: the task plus, for chat APIs (DeepSeek, Kimi, GLM), a bounded snapshot of tracked filenames and top-level project docs; agent CLIs (codex/claude) read the repo locally and send it to OpenAI/Anthropic. Ignored .env files are not read. With Claude Code as one agent this is a second Anthropic session on the same repo. For client projects, DeepSeek/Kimi/GLM would send repo material to Chinese providers unless restricted to --agents claude,codex.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the planner run: it is a batch CLI, no timeouts on Jev beyond SDK defaults (10s request timeout, SDK retries); a Jev error aborts that run (no fallback judge found in jev.ts), while agent calls default to a 600s timeout (cli.ts:88). Since it is not wired into Claude Code, there is no impact on normal Claude Code sessions when Jev is down.
entries.contextCost: Zero if not invoked: no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill, no injected text. If a user creates their own skill/slash command to call it, cost is one short description. The output plan (PLAN.md) can be large and would be pulled into context when read.
pros: Real, working, well-tested Jev integration using all three primitives (choice, score, noul) on real decisions (which plan is stronger, is another review needed, who finalizes) - a good reference for how to phrase Jev questions.

Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with env-based base URL override (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is probably config-only; --judge-model allows typesafe/jev-1.13.
Sensible hardening of the spawned claude: plan mode, Read/Glob/Grep only, --strict-mcp-config, provider keys stripped from child env.
MIT, no postinstall, one runtime dependency, CI + CodeQL, active (83 commits in 9 days).
Useful for occasional big-task planning where two-model cross-review is wanted, and shows cost/latency numbers of a Jev call (~1.2s).
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin; cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
Ships as a heavy batch workflow (spawns codex and nested claude sessions, minutes per run, 2N+1 LLM calls) - costs extra Anthropic/OpenAI quota and does not fit daily edit-loop use.
Requires a second agent (Codex CLI login or DeepSeek/Kimi/GLM key); user has none configured, and sending client repo material to those providers is a data-governance risk.
Still hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming and default model 'jev-latest'; OpenRouter use is untested and doctor's /v1/models probe may fail; OpenRouter Decisions API not used.
Single-maintainer, 9 days old, 0 stars, unpinned reusable-workflow release pipeline; README 'claude25 jev91' benchmark claim not found in repo docs I could grep and is unverified.
Jev is used only as an arbiter of LLM-written plan text (a judgment over long free-text), not on structured app state where System One is strongest; Jev outage aborts the run (no fallback).
entries.verdict: A legitimate but standalone multi-agent planning CLI that uses Jev as judge; it has no Claude Code hook/MCP/skill surface and is manual, slow and quota-hungry, so it does not deliver automatic Jev integration. Useful at most as a reference for Jev question design or an occasional manual planning tool (with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter).

entries.name: sysone
entries.what: Thin open-source client layer (MIT) for a separate, private-source third-party product called "System One Engine" (systemoneengine.com, by Jalil Laaraichi, NOT by TypeSafe or OpenRouter). The npm CLI 'sysone' (a) downloads and runs a SHA-256-pinned closed-source compiled engine runtime and Studio UI locally, (b) provides an SDK client for the engine's own /v1/* HTTP API, and (c) runs a stdio MCP bridge exposing 7 tools (status, patterns, run, decide, logs, tree, dialogue) plus an opt-in 'computer' MCP with 8 Chrome-automation tools. It never talks to Jev or any model provider itself; the engine (or the hosted cloud.systemoneengine.com) makes the Jev call. Recipes are curated 'patterns' (palette-match, citation check, log triage...), not a general coding aid. Jev is reached through Vercel AI Gateway (README), or per SKILL.md newer/self-hosted engines can also use TypeSafe direct or Cloudflare Workers AI.
interface: CLI: sysone app | login | logout | status | target | mcp | computer [doctor]
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus an optional manually-copied passive skill. Nothing deterministic: no hook, no proxy. Claude Code would call the tools only if the model judges a task suits them, and the SKILL.md itself tells the agent to prefer code and to keep planning and synthesis with the reasoning model, which discourages frequent use. Tools are read-only annotated so they auto-approve easily, but the recipes are aimed at palette matching, citation checks, log triage, game dialogue and browser control, not typical coding decisions.
security: API key handling is good in design: the client needs only a scoped consumer token via SYSONE_URL/SYSONE_TOKEN env or a 0600 JSON file (--connection); README explicitly warns against tokens in argv, so no key in the process list if used as documented. Provider key stays in the closed engine.
Client hardening is real: https or loopback-http only, no credentials/path in origin, redirect:'error', 10s timeout, 256KB response cap (src/client.ts:8-18, 60-71).

Launcher downloads a gzip runtime manifest from systemoneengine.com/releases/systemone-runtime-0.5.1.json.gz, verifies a SHA-256 embedded in this package and spawns it with process.execPath (src/launcher.ts:30-34, 157). Trust ends at a closed-source blob from a single-maintainer vendor executed locally with your user rights.
No install/postinstall scripts in package.json; npx execution of an unpinned package is still a supply-chain surface (v0.2-0.7 in 4 days, one maintainer).

Sends X-Sysone-Client-Name/Version and transport headers to the engine on each request (src/client.ts:52-64); opt-in callerModel/reasoningEffort attribution is sent for usage comparison; engine has a 'usage database' and cloud logins, so server-side telemetry/logging is likely but unauditable.
Prompt-injection surface: MCP tool results are JSON of Jev answers; low. Computer companion tools can click/submit forms in Chrome, driven by Jev proposals; high blast radius but opt-in and separate.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the calling model puts into the 'state', 'candidates', log or question fields of sysone_run/decide/logs/tree is POSTed to the engine (local engine, which then forwards to Vercel AI Gateway/TypeSafe/Cloudflare, or to cloud.systemoneengine.com for hosted mode). Nothing is sent automatically (no hook, no proxy); egress is only model-chosen content, which for coding could include code, logs or diffs. Plus client name/version headers and caller model attribution. Cloud mode sends this to a third-party startup (not OpenRouter, not TypeSafe) that stores usage in a database. Problematic for client projects. Computer companion sends page text and accessibility names (not pixels) to the engine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design for the MCP tools: errors return isError with text 'Use the caller's deterministic fallback or reasoning model. Do not retry automatically' (src/mcp-core.ts:158-165). Client timeout 10s per request (src/client.ts:70-73); no retries. Since it is an on-demand MCP tool, Jev being down cannot block Claude Code. Setup failure (no engine / no token) just leaves tools erroring. The local engine must be running separately (npx sysone terminal kept open) or the cloud login valid.
entries.contextCost: 7 MCP tools in the main bridge, about 6.5k chars of descriptions plus zod schemas (RunPatternInput, decide with up to 8 questions x 1600-char instructions, logs, tree, dialogue) = roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens; the separate 'computer' MCP adds 8 more tools (~2-3k tokens) if enabled. No server-level 'instructions' field found (grep). No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. The SKILL.md description (~60 tokens) is the only always-on text if installed.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev (recipes, 'jevlogs', 'jev-tree' heads) and cites TypeSafe docs; Jev-related, unlike many false positives

MIT client with hardened HTTP handling (no redirects, size and time caps, loopback/HTTPS only) and honest, conservative guidance ('keep unknown probability unknown', 'selected ID is not authorization')
Fail-open error messages tell the agent to fall back to deterministic code or reasoning model
No hooks, so cannot slow or interfere with existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks; no per-turn context injection
logs triage and tree (taxonomy selection) are the only marginally coding-adjacent services (e.g. log classification, issue routing)
Hosted free allowance with 'sysone login' avoids running a local server
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: provider is Vercel AI Gateway, (newer engine) TypeSafe direct or Cloudflare; the engine that would need patching is closed source, so OpenRouter is not achievable by a config change, contradicting the user's core requirement

Extra middleman: Claude Code -> sysone bridge -> System One engine (closed, third-party) -> gateway -> Jev; you must trust and run a proprietary binary or send client-project data to cloud.systemoneengine.com
Not automatic: only model-discretion tools; the shipped skill explicitly discourages routine use, and there are no hooks or proxy to make Claude Code use Jev without being asked
Recipe catalog is domain-specific (palette-match, citations, dialogue for a game, browser control); poor match for reading/editing code, permission decisions or commit routing
Needs its own separate running engine and Studio setup with a Vercel key, or cloud account, in addition to no OpenRouter key; extra infrastructure for little value
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 13 commits, single author, 1 star, no CI, versions 0.3 to 0.7 in 4 days; local runtime pinned at 0.5.1 lags the source engine
Data egress of model-chosen code/log content to an unaudited vendor with a usage database, on client projects
Adds 7 tools (about 3k tokens) to context, 15 tools if browser companion enabled, for low expected use
entries.verdict: Real and Jev-related but it is a third-party closed-engine wrapper (Vercel Gateway/TypeSafe/Cloudflare) with no OpenRouter path, no auto-invocation mechanism and recipes aimed at non-coding tasks. Not recommended for this user's OpenRouter-hosted, automatic-in-Claude-Code goal; at most a curiosity for log triage.

entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and the triggers are for design slop review, text humanizing, or plugin audits, not for general coding. security: No network code for Jev at all; agent-plugin-eval scripts (inspect_plugin.py, score.py) import only stdlib argparse/json/os/re/ipaddress/urllib.parse (parse only), no requests/subprocess/os.system found by grep

entries.dataEgress: As shipped: nothing leaves the machine via this repo (no code path calls Jev). If an agent followed the docs and routed to Jev, it would send context_required blobs (plugin manifests, tool definitions, READMEs, design screenshots/CSS, text drafts) as the question context.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design (falls back to inline scoring by the current LLM when no Jev is found), but there are no timeouts or error handling because there is no call. Effectively always runs the fallback.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks, no server instructions. Mostly a general skill dump (23 skills, 19 unrelated) so installing wastes ~5k tokens of listing context; Jev-adjacent commits are a marketing tie-in (Jev badge, 'jev' topic) rather than working code

entries.name: wh000wh000/awesome-jev-live
entries.what: A data-only "awesome list": a Python pipeline (scripts/collect.py, curate.py, render.py, etc.) that queries the GitHub search and code-search APIs, HackerNews and HuggingFace every 2 hours. It renders a README of 823 Jev-related entries (as of 2026-09-30) in 20 languages, each with an evidence grade (official / observed / inferred / unverified). Grade counts are 18 official, 206 observed, 542 inferred and 57 unverified. There is no runtime component, no MCP server, no hook and no skill, so nothing can be installed into Claude Code. Its value is as a discovery index. The "Agent tooling: MCP, hooks, gates and coding agents" category has 251 entries. Claude-Code-relevant leads from data/entries.json: typesafe-ai/skills (official), TypeSafeAI/jev-harness (official), GhalebDweikat/winnow (Claude Code context sieve), tamaratran/fast-jev-compaction (Claude Code compaction plugin), gargpratyush/jev-router (model routing in Claude Code), xafold/jev-router (automatic model and effort switching for Claude Code), Dicklesworthstone/skillranker, jkudish/jev-mcp, burnigtm/jev-mcp, freepik-company/jev-mcp (OpenRouter or TypeSafe), BYK/jev-mcp (eval-first), clouatre-labs/decisions-judge-mcp, King4s/Jev-AI-Skill and tiffygk/jev-mode (Claude Code skills). These are unaudited here and should each be audited on their own.
interface: scripts/*.py (collect, curate, render, translate, build_site, audit...)
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is not an integration. It cannot make Claude Code call Jev automatically, and any automatic behavior has to come from a hook, MCP server or skill in one of the listed projects.
security: Nothing is installed or executed on the user's machine, so the attack surface is limited to reading untrusted text. The README and summaries are aggregated third-party repo descriptions and X/HN quotes (untrusted data).

Grades and star counts are auto-computed and look unreliable. Examples: NandhaKishorM/laya shows 28,888 stars 12 days after creation; browser-use/jev-ultrafast shows 21,481 stars but is graded only 'inferred'; YaoApp/yao (created 2021) is listed. Star numbers, and in places the 'official' label, should not be trusted for ranking without checking against GitHub.
542 of 823 entries are 'inferred' from name or topic only, and 57 are 'unverified'. Some entries are unrelated projects that matched on vocabulary.
scripts/collect.py reads GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN or `gh auth token`. It is the maintainer's tool, so it is not a risk unless you run it.
Two-person repo with mostly automated commits, so there is no review of the content.
entries.dataEgress: None. It is a static repo, and nothing leaves the machine unless the user runs the collector scripts, which call api.github.com and similar public APIs.

entries.name: omni-/ask-jev
entries.what: Windows-only PowerShell UserPromptSubmit hook for OpenAI Codex (not Claude Code). When the user types ':jev' or ':jev ask <question?>', it reads the local Codex rollout JSONL transcript, redacts and truncates it (48 KiB evidence, 64 KiB request), and sends it to TypeSafe /v1/systemone with 13 Noul checks plus one Choice outcome. It shows a probability report through the hook's blocking reason without starting a model turn. It is an explicit, user-typed audit of whether the agent verified its work, at most once per turn. It is not automatic.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. The user must type ':jev'. It is a UserPromptSubmit hook keyed on an exact typed token and does no automatic per-turn or per-tool triggering. The README explicitly says 'no per-turn audits'. This directly contradicts the user's requirement of automatic use.
security: API key is read from the process env or the Windows user env, and sent only as a Bearer header via HttpClient. It is not in argv, and the code redacts configured-key matches from output (lib/Jev.psm1:100, 141).
HTTP redirects are disabled (AllowAutoRedirect=false, lib/Jev.psm1:122). Errors are bounded and sanitized. The response is strictly validated.

Transcript content is treated as untrusted in the policy prompt (lib/Jev.psm1:4). It has no shell execution beyond the PowerShell hook launcher, and no telemetry or curl|sh installer. The worker is killed after 28 s.
Redaction is heuristic. The README says it is not comprehensive secret removal, so code, tool output and secrets in the transcript can reach TypeSafe.
The installer edits hooks.json with a custom JSON text patcher. Codex hook trust is required, and a changed hook needs a new review.
Marker files in the OS temp directory are empty and hashed. Real rollouts and reports are gitignored.
entries.dataEgress: On explicit ':jev' or ':jev ask' only, selected conversation text, user instructions, assistant messages and tool calls/results from the Codex rollout are sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Evidence is capped at 48 KiB and the full request at 64 KiB, after credential redaction (lib/Jev.psm1:42-49, README). Binary/base64 payloads and encrypted reasoning are omitted. Nothing is sent for ordinary prompts or help. Adapted to Claude Code, this would include file contents and diffs seen in tool outputs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for its own command only. On any handled failure (missing key, HTTP error, timeout, malformed response) it blocks the ':jev' command and shows an error, with no retries. It uses a 15 s HTTP timeout and an 8 s internal deadline for transcript work. The supervisor kills the worker at 28 s, and the hook timeout is 40 s. Ordinary prompts are never affected, since they pass through with no network call. If the hook is untrusted or fails to launch, the command simply falls through to the model.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped, because it does not run there. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions and no injected text. In the original Codex design, the blocking report never enters model context, since it costs zero host tokens and is not sent to the model.
pros: Concrete, working design of a Jev use case: an independent typed judge of whether an agent's work was actually verified, using Noul and Choice with strict response validation. The question set in lib/Jev.psm1:11-38 is reusable prompt material.
Sound engineering: redirects disabled, bounded errors, 64 KiB request cap, a policy prompt that treats transcript text as untrusted, no telemetry, and a per-turn atomic once-marker.

Real request/response contract against api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (model jev-1.13.0, usage tokens) is documented in code and verification.md, and is useful as a reference for building a Claude Code hook.
MIT license. It is small (about 1,100 lines of PowerShell) and readable, so porting the question set and validator is feasible.
The hook shows results without a host model turn, so it costs no Claude tokens.
cons: Does not support Claude Code at all. TODO.md lists Claude Code as an unsupported, unverified port, and the README says 'Claude Code and OpenCode are not implemented'.

Windows PowerShell 5.1 only. The installer hardcodes System32/WindowsPowerShell/v1.0/powershell.exe (install.ps1:8), and the env lookup reads the Windows user environment. Linux is unverified and the paths and launcher would not work as-is.
Explicit and manual only (typed ':jev'). Not automatic, which fails the user's core requirement.
TypeSafe direct only. The endpoint is a hardcoded literal at lib/Jev.psm1:130, and it uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The OpenRouter route is not implemented.
Depends on the Codex rollout JSONL format, which the README itself calls 'not a stable Codex API'. Claude Code transcripts have a different format and location.
Immature: a single commit on 2026-09-16, 1 author, 2 stars, no releases and no CI. Tests are Windows-only, and there is no accuracy calibration ('smoke tests, not calibration').
Sends the full conversation, including tool outputs and code, to a beta third-party model. Redaction is explicitly not comprehensive, which matters for client projects.
Audits after the fact, so it does not steer coding decisions during a session. It also adds no value for routing or choosing actions.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this user. It is a Windows-only, manual ':jev' audit hook for Codex with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint. It has no Claude Code support, and no automatic invocation. Only the question set, response validator and request shape are worth borrowing as reference material for a custom Claude Code hook.

entries.name: masa-med-ai/typesafe-screening-mcp
entries.what: Python MCP server (stdio, official mcp>=2 MCPServer + httpx) that screens PubMed / arbitrary title+abstract records against a research question. It runs PubMed E-utilities search/efetch server-side, then sends one Jev System One request per article (Noul 'match', Score 'relevance', plus one Noul per inclusion/exclusion criterion) and applies an include/maybe/exclude rule in plain Python. Purely a biomedical literature-screening tool; it has nothing to do with code, diffs or software work.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus an optional skill description trigger, both tied to literature-screening requests (Japanese-language skill description). No deterministic hook. For ordinary coding work it would never fire, because its tool descriptions mention only PubMed / clinical questions.
security: API key read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env (not argv) - good; README advises against plaintext config
macOS keychain fallback uses subprocess.run(['security', ...]) with fixed args, no shell, no injection; inert on Linux
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh; install is git clone + uv sync (package = false, only mcp>=2 and httpx deps, uv.lock present)
save_full_results_to writes an arbitrary caller-supplied path (opened with 'x' so it never overwrites) - model-controlled file creation, low risk

Prompt-injection surface: article abstracts fetched from PubMed are fed to Jev only, never returned raw to Claude; returned output is only PMID/title/probabilities, though titles are passed through (truncated to 120 chars)
Unpinned dependency mcp>=2 and no CI / signed releases; single anonymous-ish author, 2 stars
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling model passes in: research_question, criteria strings, and per-article title+abstract (abstract up to 12000 chars), sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with the API key; PubMed query terms and PMIDs to eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov. No repository code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs leave the machine unless Claude explicitly pastes them into screen_records, which is not its purpose.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft per item: httpx timeout 60 s, up to 5 attempts with 2**n backoff on transport errors / 429 / 529 / 5xx (worst case ~15+ s of sleeps plus up to 5x60 s waits per article); after retries the article is reported with decision 'error' and the batch continues. Missing API key raises RuntimeError and the tool call fails. Not a hook, so Jev being down never blocks Claude Code itself - only that tool call.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools (search_and_screen, screen_pmids, screen_records) with long docstrings and 8-10 parameters each; server.py docstrings and schemas roughly 5-6k chars, so about 1.3-1.8k tokens of tool definitions (deferred/ToolSearch-loaded in Claude Code, so name-only until used). No server-level 'instructions'. No hooks. The bundled skill adds a ~300-char description to the skills list only if installed. Overall small.
pros: Small, readable, real working example of System One usage: shows the exact request shape {model, state, questions} with Noul and Score primitives, criteria for true/false, and response parsing (answers[id].noul / .score / .confidence / usage.input_tokens) - useful as a schema reference when building our own Jev hook

Good pattern for turning calibrated probabilities into decisions in code (_decide thresholds, sensitivity-first rule), with retry/backoff on 429/529/5xx and per-item failure isolation (server.py:~104-140)
Clean security posture: env var key, no shell exec beyond fixed keychain call, no telemetry, only two deps, MIT license
Keeps bulk data out of Claude's context (returns one line per article) - good context-hygiene design
cons: Domain-specific to PubMed literature screening; zero relevance to code edits, permissions, commit/PR decisions or other coding-time judgements, so Claude would never call it during daily coding
Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai URL (server.py:16), no OpenRouter support or base-URL override; would need a code patch and OPENROUTER_API_KEY handling plus model id change (typesafe/jev-1.13)
Not a hook or proxy: no deterministic automatic integration, which is the user's core requirement
Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, no tests, no CI
Adds three unrelated tools to the tool list and a Japanese-language skill; net negative context/complexity for a coding workflow
Keychain fallback is macOS-only; on Linux only TYPESAFE_API_KEY works
entries.verdict: Genuinely Jev-based but a niche PubMed abstract screener, not a coding integration; do not install. Worth keeping only as a compact reference for the System One request/response schema (state + typed questions -> answers[id].noul/score) when writing our own OpenRouter-backed Jev hook.
