entries.name: ndolinschi/mcpmatch
entries.what: Not an MCP server, hook or skill. It is a private Next.js 15 demo web app (UI in src/app/page.tsx plus one POST route, /api/decide) that takes a typed user goal and picks from a hard-coded catalog of about 40 fake MCP tools. It uses a two-stage Jev Choice: first a category, then a tool within that category. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY it silently falls back to local softmax heuristics and reports mode "demo". It has no Claude Code integration and does not read the user's real installed MCP servers. The README is 6 lines.
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is a standalone web app and never invoked by Claude Code. The user would have to build an MCP or hook wrapper around it.
security: No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh installer.
API key is read from the environment and sent only as a Bearer header, so it is not in argv.
No telemetry found in the source.
Fetch has no timeout or AbortController (src/lib/jev.ts:77).
Error text from the upstream API (first 400 chars) is returned to the client in the 500 body.
/api/decide is unauthenticated, so a deployed instance would be an open proxy to the API key.
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves a Claude Code machine, because it is not wired into Claude Code. If run as a web app, the posted state (goal text, stage, category, catalog_size) plus the questions go to api.typesafe.ai only when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set. Otherwise it is fully local.
entries.failureMode: Missing key fails open to a fake heuristic (mode "demo"), which would give misleading results if mistaken for real Jev output. With a key set, any non-2xx response throws and the route returns 500 (fail-closed). There is no timeout, retry or abort.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook injection. It is not installable into Claude Code at all.
pros: The typed Choice, Score and Noul request and response shapes in src/lib/jev.ts:7-55 are a clean reference for System One payloads: {state, model, questions} in, {model, answers, usage} out.
The two-stage category-then-tool pattern for catalogs above the roughly 255-option Choice limit (src/lib/product.ts:75) is a reasonable idea for routing among many MCP tools.
Tiny and readable, with no dangerous code.
cons: Mislabelled by discovery: it is a Next.js demo app, not an MCP server. There is no MCP SDK dependency in package.json.
The catalog is about 40 hard-coded fake tools (src/lib/product.ts:19), so it never sees the user's real MCP servers.
No OpenRouter support: it uses api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only.
Single commit and single author, created 2026-09-17 with the last push 12 minutes later. No license file, no tests, no CI, no releases, 1 star.
Silent demo fallback returns fake results without a key.

entries.verdict: Not usable for this goal: it is a one-commit Next.js demo with a fake 40-tool catalog, TypeSafe-only, and it has no MCP, hook or skill surface. At most, borrow the two-stage Choice idea and the payload types for a custom OpenRouter-based hook.

entries.name: arnab621/typesafe-jev-plugin
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (2 skills, 2 agents, 1 PostToolUse hook, 2 Python scripts) for batch analytics: the user builds a reusable .sig.json 'solution signature' (state schema plus Choice/Score/Noul questions plus Excel output template), then runs a CSV/Excel/txt dataset row by row through TypeSafe's System One API and exports results to Excel. It is a data-labelling pipeline tool, not a coding-assistant integration. The only hook validates .sig.json files after Write and never calls Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description triggers only, for phrases about building signatures or running datasets through Jev. The hook is deterministic but only reacts to Write of *.sig.json. Nothing triggers during ordinary coding: no code-review, commit, test-triage or routing decision uses Jev.
security: API key can be passed via --api-key on the run-dataset command line (run_dataset.py:291), which puts it in argv and the process list and in the Bash tool transcript. Env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY is the safer path. The skill's Step 1 also asks the user to type the key into chat.
No shell=True. The hook uses subprocess.run with a list argv on a local validator, and the file path comes from the tool event. Low injection risk from the hook.
No install script, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry found. Requires pip install requests openpyxl, which the user does manually.

Prompt-injection surface: run-dataset feeds arbitrary row and document text to Jev, and Jev returns typed output only. The skills run Bash with content from user datasets, so a malicious dataset could steer the calling Claude, but there is no auto-execution path.

No license file (licenseInfo null), so legally it is all rights reserved. plugin.json author says 'KPMG TTI' while the repo owner is an individual (arnab621 / Arnab Dutta): unclear provenance for client work.
Global secret-leak guard hook matching Bash would see the --api-key argument, which is a further reason to avoid that flag.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the user explicitly runs through run-dataset: each dataset row (or document text) mapped into the 'state' object plus the question definitions, POSTed to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Nothing is sent from coding sessions, prompts, diffs or tool outputs. The PostToolUse hook is local only. Note the endpoint is TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to coding turns because there is no automatic call. In batch runs, requests.post timeout=30s per row (typesafe_client.py:45). On HTTPError or any exception the row is recorded as an error and the run continues (run_dataset.py:367-375), so it fails soft per row. There are no retries and no concurrency. The hook never blocks: it always exits 0 and has a 15s timeout.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 tool definitions and no server instructions. Cost is 2 skill descriptions (about 150 tokens combined, from the frontmatter) plus 2 agent descriptions (about 100 tokens), roughly 250-300 tokens always in context. The full SKILL.md bodies (8.4 KB, 3.5 KB, about 3k tokens) load only when invoked. The hook injects text only when a .sig.json is written. Negligible.
pros: Small (about 89 KB), fully readable, no third-party execution beyond requests/openpyxl, no telemetry, no installer script.

Good reference for the System One request shape {model, state, questions} and for how Choice/Score/Noul question definitions are structured. The 6 example signatures are useful templates for designing your own Jev calls.
Fail-soft per row and a low-confidence flag column show a sensible way to consume Jev's calibrated probabilities.
Hook is harmless: it filters on .sig.json and exits 0 otherwise.
cons: Not a coding-workflow integration: it is a CSV/Excel classification batch tool (README: travel reviews, LLM guardrails, VAT). Claude Code would never use Jev automatically for code decisions with it, which fails the user's core requirement.
TypeSafe-direct only. OpenRouter is unsupported, and the advertised TYPESAFE_API_URL override is dead code (never read), so switching needs a code patch.
Very immature: created 2026-09-22, 6 commits, 1 star, 1 fork, 1 real contributor, no releases, no tests, no CI, no license, and the plugin.json author 'KPMG TTI' conflicts with the repo owner.
API key can be passed in argv via --api-key (visible in the process list), and the skill prompts for it in chat.
Sequential unbatched calls, no retries, a 30s timeout, and Python deps (requests, openpyxl) that must be installed by hand.
Pins the model id jev-1.13.0 in all examples and defaults, which does not match OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13.
entries.verdict: Skip it: it is a batch dataset-labelling plugin for TypeSafe's direct API, with no automatic coding-time trigger, no OpenRouter support and no maturity. Only its example signatures and request-shape code are worth borrowing as reference for building a proper Jev hook or MCP tool.

entries.name: victorperr/jev-mcp-elicitation-autopilot
entries.what: A fork of the official MCP Inspector v2.8.0 (Apache-2.0/MIT). The fork adds one commit (e935b22c, 2026-09-29) with a `--elicit jev` flag to the Inspector CLI. When an MCP server sends a form elicitation during a tool call, the CLI answers it itself. Each answer is a Jev call to POST /v1/systemone: choice for accept/decline/cancel and enums, noul for booleans. Answers below a probability threshold cancel the run and exit 9. It supports record/replay for CI. It is a CI test tool for MCP server developers, not a Claude Code integration. It has no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, and Claude Code never runs it.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. A human or CI job has to run the CLI with --elicit jev. Claude Code cannot use it automatically, and it is not a hook, skill or MCP tool.
security: The API key is read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (elicitation-autopilot.ts:166) and sent as a Bearer header (jev-client.ts:61-63). It is not passed in argv, so it does not show in the process list.
No telemetry or shell execution in the added code. It is one fetch call through the existing proxy-aware fetch, with no new dependencies.
Jev responses and server elicitation schemas are treated as untrusted and validated field by field (jev-types.ts:82-89).
Failure detail from the HTTP body is truncated to 500 characters in errors (jev-client.ts:75).
The base URL is overridable by env TYPESAFE_API_URL, so a poisoned env could redirect the key and payload elsewhere.
Very new fork (1 day old, single author). The upstream MCP Inspector base is a large, reputable codebase, but the fork's added code is unaudited.
entries.dataEgress: Only in --elicit jev mode, per elicitation. A single request to api.typesafe.ai carries the policy text, the MCP server's elicitation message, the form schema, and the triggering tool call (name and args). Nothing is sent to OpenRouter. There is no Claude Code data flow at all, because the tool never sees Claude's prompts, code or diffs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed, by design for CI. Timeout is 30 s per attempt (jev-client.ts:67). There are 2 retries with exponential backoff on 429/529 only. A non-OK response or an invalid body throws. Ambiguous answers cancel the elicitation and exit 9. Irrelevant to Claude Code, since it never runs in the Claude loop.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code. It exposes no MCP tools, hooks, skills or server instructions, and injects no text.
pros: Clean, well-tested reference for building Jev requests. The mapping from schema to choice/noul is documented, and jev-types.ts:14-53 gives the wire shape (state, questions with type/instructions/criteria, answers with probabilities/confidence/noul) as a concrete example.
It shows a sound pattern for using Jev's calibrated probabilities: threshold instead of argmax, and abstain-as-cancel (exit 9).
It shows record/replay of Jev answers keyed by a request hash, which could be borrowed for deterministic tests of any Jev hook.

The client is minimal and dependency-free. Retry and backoff on 429/529 are correct. The key comes from env and never argv. The base URL and key are configurable through TYPESAFE_API_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY.
Genuinely useful if the user develops MCP servers with elicitation flows and wants CI coverage of accept/decline branches.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration. It cannot make Claude Code call Jev, either automatically or on request, and it has no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin manifest.
It is a fork of the whole MCP Inspector monorepo (web, TUI and CLI clients) to gain one CLI flag. It is not published to npm and needs a clone and build.
Direct TypeSafe only. The default is api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and there is no OpenRouter support. Its OpenRouter compatibility rests on an unverified schema match.
Immature: 1 day old, 0 stars, one author, no releases. GitHub license detection shows 'Other'. The visible activity is upstream history.
The decision domain is simulating a human answering MCP elicitation forms, which has nothing to do with the user's daily coding decisions.
Claude Code's own MCP client already handles elicitation interactively, and this tool only wraps the Inspector CLI.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration. It is a CI test harness (an MCP Inspector fork) that uses Jev to simulate a user answering MCP elicitation prompts, and it has no hook, skill or MCP surface. Skip it for this goal. At most, borrow its Jev request and response schema and its threshold/abstain pattern as a reference for writing an OpenRouter-based Jev hook.

entries.name: n8mirai/jev2mcp
entries.what: Despite the name and the "router-proxy" label from discovery, it is NOT an MCP server, proxy or Claude Code component. It is a ChatGPT-only Chrome MV3 extension (content script matches https://chatgpt.com/*) plus a local Node HTTP bridge on 127.0.0.1:4328 and a small web companion UI. Before you press Send in ChatGPT it sends your prompt (optionally the last 4 visible messages) plus a hand-configured catalog of tool descriptions to TypeSafe System One as Noul questions (one "needs_tools" plus one per tool). If the probabilities are decisive (<=0.20 or >=0.80) it clicks the matching native ChatGPT "@" picker entries and sends; otherwise it holds the draft. It has no MCP transport, does not discover or connect to MCP servers, and nothing in it references Claude, Claude Code, hooks, or MCP protocol (grep for claude/anthropic/modelcontextprotocol/openrouter returned zero hits). The only reusable idea is the Noul-per-tool routing pattern in src/router.mjs.
interface: npm start / npm test / npm run eval
MCP tools / Claude Code hooks / SKILL.md / plugin.json
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent pre-send interception inside the ChatGPT web page via a browser extension (deterministic, but ChatGPT only). No automatic invocation path in Claude Code.
security: Key read from env var, not argv; not sent to the extension. Launcher optionally calls a ~/.codex/skills/typesafe-ai/scripts/with-key helper (macOS Keychain) or prompts hidden.

Bridge binds 127.0.0.1 only, checks Host and Origin, timing-safe compare of a random per-start token stored at .local/bridge-token (mode 0600), 50KB body cap, max 3 concurrent (src/server.mjs:243-281). Reasonable hygiene.

Bridge sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin for any chrome-extension:// origin matching the id regex (server.mjs:245-249); token still required for /api/route. Any local process is in the trust boundary.
No shell execution besides spawn('open') on macOS when JEV_OPEN=1; no postinstall scripts; no curl|sh; no telemetry found.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompt goes into Jev with an instruction to treat manipulation as data (router.mjs:47); output is only probabilities compared to thresholds, so it cannot execute tools or emit text.
Catalog fields are regex-validated (router.mjs:16-25).
entries.dataEgress: Full submitted prompt text (up to 12,000 chars), optional context (last 4 visible chat messages, up to 6,000 chars, off by default), and the enabled tool names/descriptions go to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Nothing from code files, diffs or tool outputs unless you paste them into a prompt. In its intended use nothing goes to Claude Code contexts at all.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design for its own UI: 20s fetch timeout (router.mjs:148), extension 23s timeout, any HTTP error, timeout, invalid judgment or ambiguity results in the prompt being held for manual review (not silently sent). Not applicable to Claude Code since it is never in that path.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code: 0 MCP tools, 0 hooks, 0 skills, no server instructions, nothing installable into Claude Code.
pros: Clean, well-tested reference for using Noul per candidate tool plus one gate Noul against the /v1/systemone request shape (src/router.mjs:37-64), with sensible thresholds (<=0.20 pass, >=0.80 route, else review) and strict response validation (compose(), router.mjs:66-77).
Conservative security posture for a local bridge (loopback, token, Origin/Host checks, no logging) and MIT license with zero runtime deps.
Request format is identical to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the pattern could be lifted into your own Claude Code hook with a 3-line change.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: it only targets chatgpt.com via a Chrome extension; there is no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin manifest, and it explicitly does not connect to MCP servers (README: 'does not ... connect directly to MCP servers').
Name jev2mcp is misleading; it selects ChatGPT @ picker entries, not MCP tools, and the catalog is static hand-entered text.
Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter support and no env override for base URL or model.
Very young and thin: 4 commits, created 2026-09-22, 0 stars, one contributor identity split in two, no CI running, macOS-centric launcher, self-described experimental; ChatGPT Work unverified.

Its routing pattern is useless for Claude Code's already-good native tool selection (Claude picks MCP tools itself, and deferred ToolSearch handles large tool sets), so even a port would add latency without clear gain.
entries.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code: it is a ChatGPT browser-extension companion, not an MCP server or hook, and it is TypeSafe-direct only. At most, treat src/router.mjs as a code reference for building your own Noul-based hook against OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: jev-acp
entries.what: A standalone Agent Client Protocol (ACP) agent, run over stdio, that wraps the @typesafe-ai/sdk. You use it from an ACP client or IDE such as JetBrains, vscode-acp or acp-ui. It runs a human-driven guided workflow (Choose one, Score against a rubric, Check a statement, plus saved templates). Once the user replies "Run", it calls Jev System One and shows the typed decision, probabilities and confidence. It is a chat-UI front end for humans, not a tool or hook for another coding agent. Claude Code is not an ACP client, so this cannot plug into it.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. A human must select a task in an ACP client, type the input and reply "Run". There is no hook, no model-discretion tool, no skill trigger and no proxy. It is unusable for the goal of automatic invocation in Claude Code.
security: No shell execution and no child_process use in src (grepped). The only file writes are the template store: ~/.jev-acp/templates.json, written atomically via temp file and rename (src/templates.ts:130).

The API key is read from the process environment (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) by the SDK and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv, and the README example passes it through the ACP client's env block. That block is usually a plaintext JSON config file, though.
No telemetry found in jev-acp. The SDK has a console logger at level warn by default. I did not audit the SDK beyond its client and env code.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Only text the human types (or embedded text attachments) is sent to Jev. File links are not fetched. Jev returns typed output with no free text, so nothing can steer Claude Code. Since Claude Code cannot call this agent anyway, the exposure is nil.

npm publishing uses OIDC trusted publishing with provenance (.github/workflows/npm-publish.yml), and the actions are pinned to SHAs. Every push to main auto-publishes a `next` build, which is a supply-chain point if someone tracks @next. A single maintainer plus one co-author control it.

`npx -y` fetches and runs code from npm on every launch. Pin an exact version if it were ever used. The package has no postinstall script (package.json scripts are build, clean, dev, test, typecheck and prepack only).
entries.dataEgress: Only the text the user sends in the ACP chat for the current task (options, question, criteria, state or attached text), packaged as {state, questions, model} and POSTed to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. That URL can be redirected to OpenRouter through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. It does not read repository files, diffs or tool outputs on its own, and it does not send the chat transcript or other tasks' drafts. Templates stay local in ~/.jev-acp.
entries.failureMode: Not applicable to Claude Code, because it is not in the tool loop. Inside an ACP client, errors surface as chat messages and the guided input is kept so the user can retry (README "Session configuration"). Underneath, the SDK uses a 10s timeout and retries with backoff, and cancellation goes through AbortSignal. A slow or down Jev only affects that ACP chat turn.
entries.contextCost: Zero in Claude Code, because nothing loads. It registers no MCP tools, no hooks, no skills and no injected text. It is a stdio ACP agent and Claude Code has no way to connect to it as an agent.
pros: Small, readable, MIT-licensed code. About 2.3k lines of TypeScript with unit tests and a CI matrix on Node 22 and 24. It uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk rather than hand-rolled HTTP.

A correct reference for how the typed System One request looks: POST /v1/systemone with {state, questions:{choice|noul|score}, model} and a Bearer key. Its prompt-to-question parsing in src/parser.ts and src/validation.ts is reusable if someone builds a real MCP server or hook.
OpenRouter switching needs no code change. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL are honored by the SDK.
Low security risk: no shell, no postinstall, no telemetry in the package, and only user-typed text leaves the machine.
cons: Wrong protocol for this user. It is an ACP agent (a chat UI for humans), and Claude Code is neither an ACP client nor able to delegate to one. It cannot be wired into Claude Code via .mcp.json, hooks or skills.

Human-in-the-loop by design: pick a task, type options, reply Run. The README says it will not 'automatically select a task for you' and is not a general assistant. That is the opposite of the automatic use the user wants.

No OpenRouter support in code. It works only through the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL variable, and the default model name `jev-latest` needs a prefix change to `typesafe/jev-latest` for OpenRouter. Both are unverified against OpenRouter's live schema.

Very immature: 4 commits over one day (2026-09-21), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, a two-person team. The npm latest tag is 0.1.0 and the npm README is empty (the discovery entry's 'README empty' refers to the npm page, not GitHub). Pushes to main auto-publish the `next` tag.

Adds nothing beyond what a purpose-built MCP server or hook would do. It wraps the same /v1/systemone call behind a lot of chat-UX scaffolding (templates, pickers, output modes) that is dead weight for a coding agent.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this goal. jev-acp is a human-driven ACP chat agent for JetBrains and VS Code ACP clients, and Claude Code cannot host or call it, let alone invoke it automatically. Its only value is as reference code for the /v1/systemone request shape and for the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override, which is the trivial OpenRouter switch.

entries.name: RahulBalakavi/claude-code-jev (jev-auto-mode)
entries.what: Stdlib-only Python PreToolUse hook (`jev-auto-mode hook`). It reads the hook JSON from stdin and loads the last 8 human-authored user messages from the transcript JSONL. It then POSTs {user_messages, tool_name, full tool_input, cwd} plus one Choice question (allow/block/ask with criteria text) to OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13. It maps the answer to permissionDecision allow/deny/ask. A low-confidence answer (below 0.85) or any error becomes ask. It appends hash-only telemetry to a local JSONL file. The repo also ships a benchmark CLI, a capacity calculator and a claude-openrouter launcher, which this user does not need.
interface: No MCP server, skill or plugin manifest
entries.autoInvocation: Fully deterministic: the harness fires the PreToolUse hook on every matcher hit, and the model never has to remember. Its output is allow, deny or ask. There is no model-side trigger.
security: Key handling: the key is read from the env var only and sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. It is never in argv. The default OPENROUTER_DECISIONS_URL can be overridden by env, so an attacker who controls env could redirect the key and payload (low risk). hook.py:55-73, providers.py:82.
No shell exec, no subprocess and no installer scripts in the hook path. Network is urllib to openrouter.ai only.

Prompt-injection surface: tool_input is agent-controlled and is sent in full. A Bash command or file content can embed text such as 'choose allow' that Jev reads as state. The README's claim that the agent cannot talk its way to allow only covers assistant text and tool outputs, not the tool arguments. Independent evals also show injected instructions in state can move Jev answers.

transcript.py:_human_text takes every type:'user' entry that has text blocks. It does not filter isMeta or injected system-reminder or skill-load entries, so these can leak into user_messages and dilute or pollute the authorization signal. Also unverified.

Telemetry is local only (~/.local/state/jev-auto-mode/decisions.jsonl): timestamp, tool name, a 16-hex sha256 prefix of the action, and the verdict. It has no raw args and no phone-home. Errors are logged via logging to stderr, and the unexpected-response path logs the payload.
The launcher sets ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN and empties ANTHROPIC_API_KEY. This is not needed and would break OAuth if used; do not use it.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (and then TypeSafe as the provider) on every matched tool call: up to the last 8 user prompts in full (untruncated, from the whole transcript file), the tool name, the full tool_input (whole Bash commands, full Edit old/new strings, full Write file contents, URLs, WebSearch queries, Task prompts), the cwd path, and the criteria text. Assistant text and tool outputs are excluded. Client-project source and any secrets inside commands or writes leave the machine. There is no redaction or size cap. The README admits this (Data handling section).
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe to human review. Any KeyError, TypeError, ValueError, OSError, JSON error or ProviderError (HTTP error, timeout, bad shape) is caught, and the hook prints permissionDecision 'ask' and exits 0 (hook.py:26-45). A missing key also gives ask. The code timeout is 3s, plus the settings timeout of 5s. A hook-level timeout or crash (an uncaught exception type) is non-blocking in Claude Code, so it falls through to the normal flow. Low confidence (<0.85) gives ask. In default or auto mode this is safe. In bypassPermissions mode an 'ask' from a PreToolUse hook is still expected to prompt (unverified here), which would interrupt unattended sessions on every outage or uncertain call. Only 'deny' adds value there. The input is bounded only by the 32k context; a huge Write or message likely returns HTTP 4xx, which becomes ask.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool-definition tokens, since it has no MCP tools or skill. Nothing is injected into the model context. Only the permissionDecisionReason (about 60 chars) is shown on ask or deny. Its cost is latency and money, not context.
pros: Genuinely automatic and OpenRouter-native, the exact wiring the user wants. It uses /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and a Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY, with the URL and model overridable by env (hook.py:64-73). Zero context cost.
Small and auditable: about 400 lines of stdlib Python, no runtime dependencies, no shell exec, no telemetry beyond a local hash-only log.

Fail-safe design: every error path becomes ask with exit 0. The user-message-only transcript filter keeps assistant text and tool results out of the prompt. The confidence gate makes allow require at least 0.85 and ask short-circuits.

Includes live measurements (p50 231 ms, p95 459 ms, about $0.00002 per call, 0 dangerous allowed on 18 cases) and an honest README that states the limits, including that it adds a hop to stock auto mode rather than replacing it.
Useful in bypassPermissions sessions: the deny path gives a cheap last line of defense that costs no Claude quota. The Choice-with-criteria request pattern is a reusable template for other Jev hooks.
cons: Immature: one commit, 4 stars, one contributor, no release, alpha Jev endpoint with no SLA. The 18-case synthetic fixture gives 81% exact match, and 17 of the 90 decisions were block escalated to ask. Expect many 'ask' prompts, which is friction in bypassPermissions or auto sessions.

Uses PreToolUse, not PermissionRequest. An 'allow' pre-empts the user's normal permission and auto-mode classifier on every matched call, replacing a stronger classifier with a weaker, overconfident one. It also adds latency to trivial calls because there is no static fast-path or RISKY regex pre-filter, unlike the official cookbook pattern.

Privacy: full commands, file contents and up to 8 user messages go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe for every call, unredacted and untruncated. That is a problem for client projects. Also OPENROUTER_API_KEY must be added to the no-secret-leak protected list.
Tool arguments are an injection channel into the classifier state, and the transcript parser does not exclude meta or system-injected user entries. It re-reads the whole transcript per call.

Only one Choice question with a vague single-prompt policy (no reversible/serves_task Noul decomposition). The example matcher uses the old 'Task' tool name and omits Read, Grep and MCP tools. The launcher and benchmark bloat is irrelevant and the launcher would break OAuth.
entries.verdict: A small, honest and safe-failing OpenRouter-native Jev permission hook that would work automatically, but it is alpha-quality with a single commit and a tiny fixture. It ships as a PreToolUse gate that pre-empts auto mode and sends full commands and code to a third party. Use it as a reference implementation or fork it: put deny/ask-only behavior on a PermissionRequest or narrow-matcher hook with a static pre-filter, redaction and the reversible/serves_task Noul pattern, rather than installing it as-is on client work.

entries.name: RiskAverseTech/toolgate (@riskaverse/toolgate)
entries.what: Claude Code PreToolUse hook (plus optional PostToolUse ledger hooks and an MCP stdio proxy) that acts as a tool-call firewall. Static regex rules run first with no model call. Tool calls to gated tools (Bash, Write, Edit, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit, WebFetch, WebSearch, mcp__*) then go to Jev in one request with about 7 to 11 boolean (Noul) questions: destructive, exfiltration, privilege, secret_exposure, off_task, violates_constraint, unresolved_choice, plus the authorized mitigator. The returned probabilities map to allow, ask or deny via thresholds (deny 0.85, ask 0.55). An action ledger tracks write-then-execute sequences. It is a safety layer, not a coding assistant: it does not use Jev to improve code, routing or review.
interface: toolgate install / doctor / check / audit / init --print
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. A PreToolUse hook with matcher * runs on every tool call without any prompting, plus PostToolUse hooks for the ledger. Claude Code runs it, not the model. This fits the requirement that the user never says 'use jev'. However, the automation is limited to gating tool calls for safety, not coding assistance.
security: MIT license. The package runs no postinstall or preinstall scripts (package.json has only build, test and publish scripts). Runtime dependencies are only ai and yaml.

Key handling: the key is read from env or ~/.toolgate/env. init writes it in plaintext to that file (mode 0600, dir 0700). The key is never in argv (src/cli.ts:65-68, src/backends/openrouter.ts:27-29 uses an Authorization header). It is sent only to the chosen provider.

init edits ~/.claude/settings.json, with a backup. The installed hook command uses absolute paths to node and cli.js. Its built-in static rules ask on edits to ~/.claude/settings* and to the toolgate policy.
Policy is read only from ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml or $TOOLGATE_POLICY, never from the project directory, so a cloned repo cannot reconfigure the firewall (src/policy.ts:220-227).

Prompt-injection surface: tool input and prompt text go into the Jev state as untrusted data. Jev is a typed-output model, so it cannot be told to emit free text, but it is a probabilistic classifier and can be fooled. The authors say so and back it with frozen adversarial sets (19/20, 23/24, 20/24). The reviewers of those sets were other models, and the maintainer ran them.
Redaction of secrets is key-aware and pattern-based. The README calls it a courtesy, not a guarantee.
entries.dataEgress: Only when the model path is used (not for static rules or ungated read-only tools like Read, Grep and Glob), and only to the provider your key selects (OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions, which then routes to TypeSafe). Sent: tool name; tool input (secrets redacted, truncated at 40,000 chars), which includes full Bash commands and the full content of Write and Edit calls, so file contents and diffs the agent writes do leave the machine; cwd; permission mode; the last 3 user prompts from the transcript (redacted; latest up to 6,000 chars, earlier ones up to 3,000 each) plus a session_goal (first substantive request, up to 1,200 chars); ledger session_facts (file paths and booleans, not content). Tool outputs and files that are only read are not sent. For client projects this means client code and prompts pass through OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every Bash, Write and Edit. Use OpenRouter per-key data policies, or set gated_tools narrower or include_task_context: false. A local backend is only on the roadmap.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe by default (fail_mode: ask). On timeout (5 s, one attempt, no retry), HTTP error or missing key, gray-area calls become an ask, and the user sees '[toolgate] NOT gating: ...'. Static deny rules still apply. Internal errors always become an ask. Caveat for this user: in bypassPermissions or dontAsk mode, an ask is converted to deny by default (unattended.ask: deny), so an outage or a borderline call turns into a hard block with the reason fed back to the model. In auto mode an ask shows a dialog. fail_mode: passthrough (fail open) is available but not recommended. The hook timeout is 10 s, so worst-case added latency on an outage is about 5 s per gated call.
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens in the model context. No MCP tools or instructions when used as a hook only (MCP proxy mode is optional and not needed). Allows are silent. Ask and deny emit a short systemMessage and a permissionDecisionReason, about 20-40 tokens, fed back to the model only on deny. No skill or CLAUDE.md injection.
pros: Genuinely automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook with matcher *, so Claude Code invokes it on every gated call and the user never prompts for Jev. This is the only candidate pattern so far with zero model-discretion dependence.
Native OpenRouter Decisions API backend (src/backends/openrouter.ts) with typesafe/jev-1.13. Setting OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone selects it, and there is a test file for it. No patching needed.
Uses Jev for what it is built for: calibrated probabilities on typed Noul questions, not a chat replacement. It is a real, documented use of the Decisions API.
Zero context-token cost. Allows are silent, and the hook adds nothing to CLAUDE.md, tool lists or MCP instructions.
Fail-safe, visible failure handling: 5 s single-attempt timeout, fail_mode ask, and an explicit 'NOT gating' notice. Internal errors become an ask, never a silent allow.

Static rules run first (rm -rf /, curl | sh, edits to ~/.claude/settings*) with no network call. Read-only tools (Read, Grep, Glob) are never gated, so it does not interfere with GitNexus or grep flows.

Layers with the user's setup: the existing secret-leak guard covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, while toolgate adds destructive, exfiltration and off-task judgement on Bash|Write|Edit|WebFetch|mcp__*. It is designed to sit beside Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier as an independent second opinion.
Action ledger catches the write-a-helper-then-run-it pattern that single-call classifiers miss. Frozen sets 7 and 8 show 0 dangerous allows.

Policy is read only from ~/.toolgate/toolgate.yaml, so a cloned client repo cannot weaken the gate. A JSONL audit log with per-axis probabilities and latency stats supports tuning, plus trusted_hosts and trusted_tools for known-good destinations.
Well documented, honest evaluation with per-release changelogs, retracted claims noted, 74 commits in 10 days, and CI plus a package smoke test. MIT license.
cons: It is a safety gate, not a productivity feature. It does not use Jev to make Claude Code write, route, review or plan better. It only adds latency and potential friction, so daily-coding value is defensive.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-18, 2 stars, 1 contributor, 20 npm versions in 10 days, no GitHub releases). Several releases shipped stale dist or missed fixes per CHANGELOG. Evaluations were designed with LLM reviewers and run by the maintainer. No independent adoption evidence.

Its own real-usage data is unfavourable: the first evening had a 40% ask rate (unusable), and the second small log (41 decisions) showed 24% asks. The fix (0.11.0) has not been re-measured on a clean window. Expect nuisance asks.

Interaction with the user's modes: in bypassPermissions or dontAsk (the user's usual), an ask becomes a deny by default, so borderline legitimate work is hard-blocked and the agent has to work around it. Auto mode only shows dialogs. The user would need to tune unattended.ask or thresholds.

Data egress: every gated Bash command, Write/Edit content and the last 3 prompts go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a real concern for client projects and counters the point of gating (the README lists a local backend as the top roadmap item). Redaction is best-effort.

Latency on the hot path: about 0.35-1.2 s added per Bash, Write or Edit call in a long agentic session, in a fresh node process each call; up to about 5 s when Jev or OpenRouter is degraded. Jev is beta and OpenRouter's Decisions endpoint is /api/alpha/.

Duplicates capability the user already has: Claude Code's auto-mode classifier plus the existing secret-leak hook. Marginal added safety is modest, and exfiltration and secret-exposure judgements on the same commands may double-prompt.

OpenRouter path is less exercised than TypeSafe direct: the challenge sets ran on direct TypeSafe, and OpenRouter was only checked with a latency side-by-side and unit tests. The alpha endpoint schema could change. In auto mode the direct key wins if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is also present in the environment.

Overlap with the existing hook chain: matcher * on PreToolUse adds a third hook to Bash calls alongside the secret guard and the GitNexus hook. Hooks run in parallel, and the permission decisions of deny > ask > allow are combined. Fine, but init edits ~/.claude/settings.json, so a manual merge is safer.
Only 2 stars and no evidence that it tolerates a subscription/OAuth Claude Code login plus bypass mode in practice. It is untested here because running third-party code was disallowed.

Outage behaviour in bypassPermissions/dontAsk is inconsistent with the audit: the fail-mode ask is not converted to deny (src/engine.ts:249-251). Claude Code's handling of a hook 'ask' in bypass is undocumented and may be ignored, which would make outages fail-open in the user's bypass sessions.
Any Write/Edit/Bash whose serialized input exceeds 40,000 chars is downgraded to ask, and hard-denied in bypass/dontAsk, so large generated files or big diffs get blocked with no human in the loop.

matcher '*' spawns a fresh node process for every tool call, both Pre and Post (three extra post-event hooks), with ~90 ms of self-reported overhead. Model-path calls run about 0.7-1.2 s synchronously on top of the user's slow gitnexus hooks.

Possible interaction with auto mode (the user's default): a hook 'allow' may short-circuit Anthropic's classifier, so Jev, which the independent evals rate below mid-price LLMs and injection-sensitive, could become the effective gate for gated calls. Unverified, but it needs an empirical check before trusting it.

Client-project egress: full Bash commands, full Write/Edit content (up to 40k chars) and the last 3 user prompts plus session goal go to OpenRouter's /api/alpha endpoint and then to TypeSafe on every gated call. Redaction is regex/key-based and the README itself calls it only a courtesy. This needs an OpenRouter data-policy or ZDR check for client work.

Evaluation evidence is maintainer-run on TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter. The challenge sets were authored and labeled by ChatGPT and frozen by the maintainer, with 19/20, 20/24 and 19/22 headline scores. The documented misses include a Ruby exfiltration ask at 0.84 vs a 0.85 deny line, and npm-script and Bash-side-write gaps in the ledger, so it is not a security boundary. No independent adoption: 2 stars, 0 issues, 1 contributor, 20 npm releases in 10 days, including two retracted stale-dist releases (0.8.0, 0.9.0).

Key precedence hazard: auto mode prefers TYPESAFE_API_KEY over OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and loadEnvFile() imports every var from ~/.toolgate/env, so a stray TYPESAFE key silently bypasses OpenRouter unless backend.provider: openrouter is pinned.
entries.verdict: Best-fit candidate for the requirement of automatic use without prompting. It is a deterministic hook, has native OpenRouter Jev support, costs no context, and fails safe. But it only gives defensive gating, not coding help; it sends code and prompts to a hosted model, and its ask rate and bypass-mode ask-to-deny behaviour need tuning. Install it by hand-merging the hook (init --print), pin provider openrouter, narrow gated_tools to Bash|Write|Edit, and watch the audit log for a week before trusting it.

verification.note: Verified live on 2026-09-30. Repo RiskAverseTech/toolgate: 2 stars, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-18, last push 2026-09-28T22:42Z, 0 open issues. Git shows 74 commits, and npm has 20 versions with latest 0.15.0. The npm package has no install scripts (only build/test/prepublishOnly), and its only dependencies are ai and yaml. Confirmed in source: src/backends/openrouter.ts:13-16 uses OPENROUTER_API_KEY, POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13, sends the key in a Bearer header (not argv), and applies a 5 s AbortController timeout. There are no telemetry calls, and the only shell exec is the doctor self-test plus the optional MCP proxy spawn. Claude Code hooks docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, fetched today) confirm PermissionDenied, PostToolUseFailure and systemMessage exist. A hook 'ask' shows a dialog in auto mode, per the permission-modes docs. Claude Code hook timeouts and non-2 exits are non-blocking, so a hook crash lets the call through. The audit's inventory (provider support, interface, stats, install, latency numbers, pros/cons) is otherwise accurate. Its main errors are the bypass-mode outage claim (an outage gives an ask, not a deny, and whether Claude Code honors an ask in bypass is undocumented), and its missing input-truncation, bypass-deny, per-call spawn and auto-classifier-interaction risks. Score drops from 7 to 6: it is the only truly automatic, OpenRouter-native Jev integration, but it delivers safety gating rather than coding value. It is very immature with single-maintainer evaluations, and it has real friction and failure-mode surprises in the user's bypass workflow. It also sends client code and prompts off-machine on every gated call. Recommend only as an opt-in, narrowed gated_tools trial with unattended.ask: ask, backend.provider: openrouter pinned, and a check of how Claude Code treats a hook ask in bypass mode.

judge.why: The only truly automatic, OpenRouter-native, actively maintained Jev gate that can deny (not only ask) on Bash, Write and Edit in every mode, including bypass. It has shadow-friendly config and a policy file. It is immature and heavier than the minimal option, and it produces friction in bypass.

entries.name: jev-guard (nafiurrahmanniloy)
entries.what: Two stdlib-Python Claude Code hooks. guard.py (PreToolUse, Bash) regex-prefilters commands (commit, push, force-push, PR create/merge, DB write, ssh remote write, paid API); only matches go to Jev in one POST with per-action noul questions ("does the command really do this", "did the user ask or agree", read from the last 3 user messages, the last Claude message and any approved plan in the transcript tail). Below the per-action threshold it emits permissionDecision "ask" and never "allow". For commit, PR create and PR merge it also sends message plus diff (git diff --cached, gh pr diff, capped at 60k chars) with a "diff contains unrelated changes" noul (>=0.5 means ask). Regex-only hard stops deny `git add -A/.` and `git commit -a`. pick_rules.py (UserPromptSubmit) asks Jev one noul per saved memory file (projects/*/memory/*.md) and injects the full text of up to 3 rules scoring >=0.85 as additionalContext. Default mode is "watch" (log only) and must be switched to "enforce" in questions.json.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully deterministic hook, no prompting needed. PreToolUse on Bash fires on every call (cheap regex short-circuit) and calls Jev only for risky commands; UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt if configured. Needs one settings.json edit with absolute python path, a questions.json copy and a key; ships in watch mode so it does nothing visible until "mode":"enforce". It is a PreToolUse hook, not PermissionRequest, so it fires in auto and bypass modes too (unlike the official cookbook pattern).
security: No shell=True. subprocess is used only for git and gh with list args and short timeouts (guard.py:233, 248). The model-supplied command is never executed, only regex-parsed. However git diff/gh pr view run in a folder derived from the command's `cd X &&` / `git -C X` (guard.py:221-228), so the hook reads state from wherever Claude points it.

API key is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header via urllib (guard.py:406-411). It is not on argv and never printed. It is read from os.environ or a chmod-600 .env in the hook dir. Reusing an env var from settings env is cleaner than the .env. The user's no-secret-leak hook does not yet protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so add it.

Redaction is best effort regex (guard.py:57-67): DB URLs, Bearer/Token, *_KEY/*_TOKEN/*_SECRET/*_PASSWORD=, sk-/pk-/rk- (covers sk-or-v1-), GitHub and Slack tokens, JWTs, any 40+ char base64-ish blob. Applied to command, user messages, Claude message, plan, commit description and diff. Code, names and business details are not redacted, so client source diffs leave the machine in plaintext. Secrets in a diff that match no pattern (short passwords, split PEM lines) leak.

Prompt-injection surface: state includes the command text, user messages, claude_last_message and diff, all attacker-influenceable when Claude processed hostile content. Injected text can push 'approved' above threshold (suppress the ask) or push 'unrelated' below 0.5; the brief confirms Jev is steerable by instructions in state. The guard only lowers privilege (ask/deny, never allow), so in default/auto mode the normal permission system still backs it, but in bypassPermissions it is the only gate and is evadable by design: the README itself says a pattern miss (script calling git push internally) escapes it.
Gate is regex on the raw command with heredoc bodies stripped; `bash -c`, scripts and env indirection evade it. Only tool_name Bash is covered.
Local plaintext logs in the hook dir: log.jsonl, replay.jsonl (user messages, redacted), rules_log.jsonl (first 160 chars of every prompt). Git-ignored but persist on disk.
entries.dataEgress: Only for regex-matched risky Bash commands (never ls, tests, etc.) inside `scope` (default the whole home dir, so all personal and client repos unless narrowed). Per Jev call: redacted command (3000 chars), folder relative to ~, git branch, last 3 user messages (600 chars each; an approved plan up to 4000), Claude's last message (800 chars), and for commit/PR create/PR merge the redacted message plus full diff up to 60,000 chars (merge pulls title, body and diff via gh). With pick_rules enabled, EVERY user prompt (1500 chars redacted) plus Claude's previous message (1200 chars) plus a description line for every saved memory file (each becomes a question, up to 220 chars) is sent on every message, in all scoped projects. For client work the picker should be off and the guard scope narrowed to personal repos, or client contracts checked.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-safe toward asking, with holes. Jev unreachable, HTTP error, timeout (3s config), bad JSON, missing key or hook crash gives decision "ask" (on_error "ask") with a visible reason, on risky commands only (guard.py:eval error path, hook() crash handler). Broken config, bad stdin, non-Bash tool or top-level exception exit 0 silently (fail-open, hook() and __main__). Holes: (1) merge path runs gh pr view (10s) plus gh pr diff (15s) sequentially, plus up to 8s git diffs, which can exceed the recommended 15s hook timeout; a Claude Code hook timeout is a non-blocking error, so the command then runs unguarded. (2) Default mode is "watch" so nothing happens until switched to enforce. (3) With defaultMode auto and bypassPermissions sessions, the repo never demonstrates that a hook "ask" still prompts; "deny" (hard stops) is reliable; test this before relying on it. (4) Approval check misses casual yeses: README reports only 54 of 80 clear approvals passing, so expect frequent false asks on commits. (5) Picker: any error means nothing is injected and the prompt proceeds untouched (safe, silent).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skill or tool definitions, so no listing cost and no interaction with skillListingBudgetFraction. Guard emits text only when it asks: a one-line permissionDecisionReason (~40 tokens). Picker (optional) injects a header plus up to 3 memory bodies of up to 1500 chars each, about 1.2k tokens max per prompt, only when a memory scores >=0.85 (README: ~17/25 first-pick relevance). Overlaps in purpose with Claude Code's own auto-memory loading and caveman's per-prompt additionalContext.
pros: Only candidate that judges intent: 'did the user actually say yes to this commit/push/merge' from transcript history (guard.py:135-217 parses user turns, rejections, approved plans, queued commands, skips system reminders and task notices), which static allow rules cannot do; directly relevant to auto and bypass sessions where Claude drifts from 'fix X' to push/merge.
Never emits allow (only ask/deny), so it can only tighten; regex prefilter means most Bash never leaves the machine; ask on any Jev error; crash handler converts to ask rather than silent pass.

Diff-vs-description check catches unrelated changes in commits/PRs before merge; README reports 30/30 planted unrelated changes caught with 0/30 false alarms and a replayed real incident (self-reported).

Thoughtfully engineered: per-action thresholds, per-item enforce switches, watch mode by default with --stats and --replay to tune before enforcing, heredoc-aware command parsing, secret redaction covering sk-or-v1 keys, key via Bearer header not argv.
Stdlib-only Python, about 1000 lines across two files, easy to audit and pin; 47 unit tests with a fake Jev and no build step.
OpenRouter port is a one-line ENDPOINTS entry (guard.py:51-54) because the schema is the /v1/systemone one; the picker reuses guard.load_key so one patch covers both hooks.
cons: Not OpenRouter-ready as shipped: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and Vercel AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY endpoints are hardcoded (guard.py:51-54); needs a local patch and an unverified schema assumption, plus patch-on-update maintenance; tests use a fake endpoint so a schema mismatch would not be caught.

Brand new and unproven: created 2026-09-29, 5 commits in a few hours by one author, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases; all accuracy numbers are self-reported from one developer's history. Approval check let through only 54/80 clear approvals, so it will over-ask on commits.

Heavy data egress: diffs up to 60k chars and conversation text go to a third party with scope '~' by default; the rules picker sends every prompt. Unsuitable for client repos without narrowing scope or disabling the picker; redaction does not cover code or business names.

Weak as the sole gate in bypassPermissions: regex prefilter is evadable, Jev is injection-steerable and overconfident on unanswerable inputs per the brief, and the repo never demonstrates that a hook 'ask' is honored under bypass/auto modes. Merge path can exceed the hook timeout and then fails open.
Hard stops on `git add -A`/`git add .` and `git commit -a` deny outright even without Jev; likely frequent friction for some habits and must be edited in questions.json.

Rules picker overlaps Claude Code auto-memory and caveman context injectors, adds ~0.5 s and an external call to every prompt, and its one-question-per-memory design may hit request-size limits with hundreds of memories (README tested 152).
Another Python process on every Bash call in an already busy hook chain (no-secret-leak fail-closed, gitnexus multi-second); local plaintext logs of prompts and commands accumulate in the hook dir.

TypeSafe direct signups were paused as of Sept 2026 and some Vercel AI Gateway users saw 429s, per the README's own 'why you might not want it'. OpenRouter is therefore likely the only practical path, which makes the local ENDPOINTS patch a requirement. The audit omitted this.
With only an OpenRouter key and no patch, enforce mode prompts on every risky command (commit, push, PR) with a 'could not reach Jev' reason, not just some of them.

Picker request size: build_questions emits one noul question (instructions plus criteria) per memory. I measured about 83k characters (about 20k tokens) for 152 memories. That is close to the 32k-token context limit on OpenRouter and costs input tokens on every prompt (about $0.0009 at $0.042/M). A few hundred memories would exceed the context limit, and any error means nothing is injected.
Picker in the shipped config sends every scoped prompt to Jev in watch mode with no benefit until mode is set to 'on'.

Missing-config case: guard.py load_config falls back to questions.example.json when questions.json is absent, so the guard is active in watch mode from a bare clone, logging (with redacted commands) and sending risky commands to Jev without any deliberate opt-in beyond registering the hook and setting a key.

git diff/gh pr diff subprocess helpers run up to 8s to 15s each. A commit with many `git add` paths can issue up to about 20 extra `git diff --no-index` calls (pending_commit_diff, guard.py:294-308), which stack against the 15s hook timeout. A timeout is non-blocking, so the command runs unguarded (verified in docs: 'A timed-out command hook doesn't block the tool call').
entries.verdict: Best-fitting permission-gate idea in the set: a well-structured, auditable, ask-only hook that uses Jev for genuine intent and diff-vs-message judgement, and it becomes OpenRouter-compatible with a one-line ENDPOINTS patch. But it is a day-old, zero-star, self-benchmarked alpha with heavy diff/prompt egress and unproven behavior under auto/bypass modes, so run it in watch mode first (guard.py only, picker off, scope limited to personal repos, OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the secret-leak list) before enforcing anything.

verification.note: Verified independently. Repo re-queried with gh: 0 stars, 0 forks, MIT, not archived, no release, created 2026-09-29T22:27:57Z, pushed 2026-09-30T00:07:59Z. 5 commits by 1 author. Last commit 2026-09-30 06:07:57 +0600 (4988e65). Interface verified in source: guard.py (hook, --stats, --replay N), pick_rules.py (hook, --try), questions.example.json (8 actions, 2 hard stops, change_check 0.5/60000, rules_picker watch/top_k 3/min 0.85, timeout 3, on_error ask, scope ['~']), 47 test_ defs. No OpenRouter string exists in any .py file. The only mention is a paid_api regex in questions.example.json that matches curl to openrouter.ai. ENDPOINTS at guard.py:51-54 supports only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, as audited. The stdlib-only claim, no shell=True, no telemetry, key sent only as a Bearer header via urllib (guard.py:407-412), and ask/deny-only output (never allow) are all correct. Claude Code semantics, checked against docs: PreToolUse hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision ask/deny is valid. A hook ask escalates even in auto mode. A hook timeout is non-blocking, with a 600s default for command hooks. Matching hooks run in parallel, so the audit's no-serial-stacking claim holds. UserPromptSubmit additionalContext is valid. Behaviour of hook ask under bypassPermissions is not explicitly documented, so it remains untested. Score lowered from 6.5 to 6.0: the OpenRouter patch is doc-verified and trivial, and the failure mode is ask-only, but the project is a one-day-old alpha with self-reported benchmarks and heavy diff/prompt egress with scope ~. The missing-key case spams asks, and the user's frequent bypass sessions give the gate limited assured value. Pin a commit, patch ENDPOINTS with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, run in watch mode first, keep the picker off, and add OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak list. Paths: <scratch path> and pick_rules.py.

judge.why: The only candidate that judges intent: did the user actually ask for this commit, push or merge, plus a diff-vs-message check. Ask-only, regex-gated to risky Bash, and it ships in watch mode. Best fit for the drift problem in auto and bypass sessions.
pros: Regex prefilter, so only commit, push, PR and DB-write commands reach Jev. Never emits allow; the hard stops (git add -A, commit -a) deny without Jev
Reads user turns, rejections and approved plans from the transcript; the diff check reported 30/30 planted unrelated changes caught (self-reported)
Watch mode default plus --stats and --replay for tuning; about 800 stdlib lines and 47 mocked tests
Patch is one line and documented by OpenRouter's own schema

Day-old repo, 0 stars, self-benchmarked; the approval check passed only 54/80 clear approvals at the 85% bar
