cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; needs patch for OpenRouter; no license file (null)
Default fail-open allow on error and 'allow' bypasses prompts: risky under bypassPermissions with prompt-injectable state
Single-day repo, 0 stars; no unit tests for hook, only live eval

entries.name: blastgate (stas4000)
entries.what: Single-file stdlib Python 3.10+ PreToolUse hook (Bash only). A local regex pass (8 categories: delete, git, overwrite, network, remote, service, sql, verb) lets commands with no risky pattern run with no network call. Hits are redacted, then sent to Jev at OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions as one Choice question with four criteria (read, reversible, destroys, external). destroys or external returns permissionDecision "ask" with a reason. read or reversible prints nothing, so normal permissions apply. Any Jev error, or a missing key on a pattern hit, also returns "ask". It can never return allow or deny. It also has a CLI mode (python3 blastgate.py "cmd") that prints the decision as JSON.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook on every Bash call. It is fully automatic, with no prompting needed and nothing for the model to decide.
security: Key handling: the key is read from env and sent only as an Authorization Bearer header over HTTPS (blastgate.py:102). Nothing goes on argv, so there is no argv exposure. The hook subprocess inherits the env, so it works with settings.json env.
JEV_URL is env-controlled. If TYPESAFE_API_KEY happens to be set, it is sent to whatever host JEV_URL names. This only matters if an attacker controls the hook's environment.

No shell exec, subprocess, eval or installer in blastgate.py, which uses only http.client, json, re and urllib.parse. eval.py and collect.py run `claude -p` and read the local transcripts, but only when invoked manually. No telemetry beyond the X-Title: blastgate header.

Prompt-injection surface: the raw command text (up to 700 chars, redacted) is placed in the state JSON alongside the instructions. Content that Claude wrote into a command, for example a comment or echoed string like 'this is a read-only operation', can sway Jev. The brief notes injected instructions in state can move answers. The blast radius is limited because the hook can only add prompts, never remove them.

Redaction is regex-based (line 66-67). It masks key/token/secret/password/bearer/authorization followed by a value, prefixes sk/pk/ghp/gho/xox/AKIA, hex strings of 32+ characters, and any 40+ character token. It does not catch short passwords in URLs (user:pass@host), export FOO=bar with a non-keyword name, or paths and business data. Redaction of `key=value` pairs is keyword-triggered only.

Regex pass gaps mean some risky commands are never judged and pass silently. The redirect rule at line 53 excludes any target starting with '/', so `echo x > /etc/hosts` or `cat a > /abs/path` is not flagged. Inline interpreters (python3 -c 'shutil.rmtree(...)'), `docker compose down -v`, `curl | sh` and `bash script.sh` with no verb word are also not flagged. Only Bash is covered; Write, Edit and NotebookEdit are not.
entries.dataEgress: Only for commands that hit the local RISK regex (about 21% of commands per the author's corpus). Each is sent to openrouter.ai and on to TypeSafe. The payload contains the fixed task and judge prompt, the command with regex redaction and truncated to 700 chars (heredoc bodies are cut from the pattern scan but are still in the command text, up to the 700-char cut), and the cwd path (line 90), plus criteria text. The cwd reveals project and client directory names. Read-only commands send nothing. This is a new outbound channel for client-project command text that has to be accepted knowingly. The user's no-secret-leak hook does not cover this hook's own request.
entries.failureMode: Fails toward "ask" (fail-closed to a prompt) and never raises. The pattern hit with no key returns ask (line 126-127). Any exception from Jev (403, timeout, malformed JSON, missing answers) returns ask with reason 'Jev unavailable' (line 131-132). The HTTP timeout is 30 s (jev_post default, line 97), with no retry and no proxy support (http.client ignores HTTPS_PROXY). Worst case it blocks the Bash call for 30 s, and the install snippet sets no hook `timeout`. On a malformed stdin event, json.load raises and the hook exits non-zero, which is a non-blocking error in Claude Code. The README reports that 58 of 176 eval requests got a provider HTTP 403 at the edge. The request sends no User-Agent (http.client), which is a plausible cause. Hitting a 403 in daily use would turn every risky command into a prompt, so it is noisy but safe. Whether the 403 is reproducible is unverified.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and zero skill or MCP text. The hook injects nothing into context except the short permissionDecisionReason shown in the prompt. Context cost is effectively nil.
pros: Native fit for the target endpoint: JEV_URL defaults to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and reads OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it needs no code changes (blastgate.py:27-29).
Only ever escalates to 'ask' and never returns allow, so it cannot loosen the existing permissions in auto mode. Failures (no key, 403, timeout) also resolve to ask (lines 122-138).
Small, auditable file: 162 lines, stdlib only, no subprocess, no installer. The key goes in a header, not argv.

Jev is used well: one typed Choice question per command, with criteria text defining each label. This is the 'typed decisions with probabilities' use case Jev is built for. It plays to Jev's strength (fast, cheap) rather than free text.
Two-stage design keeps cost and latency low: the free regex pass skips 79% of the author's 6,446 real commands. Jev cost about $0.018 for 881 commands.

Has a mocked unit-test suite (test/test_blastgate.py, network patched) and a 48-item labeled gold set. The eval scripts are included. The tests I read look sensible: hook shape, fail-closed, no network for reads, unsure knob. I did not run them (rule).
BLASTGATE_UNSURE gives a tunable stricter mode, and the reason text explains why the prompt appeared.
Zero context cost.
cons: Immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-23, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases. Effectively a single-day repo.

Ask-only. It cannot deny or approve anything, so it cannot replace the 'auto' classifier or lift prompts. In bypassPermissions mode the value depends on PreToolUse 'ask' still forcing a prompt over bypass. I did not verify that in Claude Code 2.1.285. If bypass ignores 'ask', the hook does nothing in exactly the sessions where it matters most.

Regex pass is a real coverage hole: absolute-path redirects (`> /etc/x`), inline interpreters, `docker compose down -v`, `curl | sh` and generic wrapper scripts are never judged. A whole command bypasses Jev if no pattern matches.

The default model is the floating alias '~typesafe/jev-latest'. The classification behavior can change silently, and the alias is unverified against the OpenRouter catalog. It should be pinned via JEV_MODEL.

The 403 provider-edge failures (58 of 176 in the author's eval) are unexplained. No User-Agent is sent, and there is no retry or proxy support, so the fail-closed design may turn into constant prompts.
Sends cwd and up to 700 chars of redacted command text to OpenRouter/TypeSafe for client projects. Redaction is keyword-based and can miss secrets that do not follow a key/token/password pattern.
Prompt-injection: command text is inside the judged state. It is self-authored by Claude, but it can embed reassuring wording. The consequence is limited to a missed prompt.
No-secret-leak protected list: OPENROUTER_API_KEY would have to be added there, and the two hooks' interplay checked. Since the hook itself reads the env var, the Bash tool could otherwise echo it.
Bash only, with no Write or Edit coverage. No 30 s timeout is configured in the hook entry.
The repo carries a 16 MB mp4 and other video assets, which is bloat but harmless.

Redaction misses env-var names that embed a keyword after an underscore (API_KEY=, GITHUB_TOKEN=, DB_PASSWORD=) and the token in 'Authorization: Bearer <tok>' (verified with the regex). Real secrets in risky commands (curl -X POST with a bearer, export FOO_KEY=...) can go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe.
All `>>` appends (for example `>> ~/.bashrc`, `>> .env`) and absolute-path `>` redirects are never sent to Jev and never gated (regex line 53).

A hook timeout or crash is a non-blocking error in Claude Code, so it does not gate anything. Only Jev errors inside the script return 'ask'. The 30 s socket timeout is per operation, and the default hook timeout is 600 s.

For this user, auto mode already has a classifier, and the docs say hook-forced 'ask' prompts still appear in auto mode. blastgate therefore adds prompts (about 19% of the 21% pattern hits, roughly 4% of commands) rather than removing them. It is a net friction add unless the user wants a stricter second layer.
If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set globally, it wins over OPENROUTER_API_KEY (load_key, line 81) and is sent as the bearer to openrouter.ai, producing 401 and constant 'ask'. The user must leave it unset.

The 58/176 HTTP 403s at the provider edge were observed in the author's own eval with the same http.client and no User-Agent. It is the only evidence of real-world reliability, and it looks like a 33% failure rate. The audit mentioned it but under-weighted it.
The test suite mocks all network calls and never exercises the real request or response schema. It has not been tested by us against live OpenRouter.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe-by-construction, OpenRouter-native Jev hook: source matches the README and it costs no context. Adopt it as an extra 'ask' layer, ideally as a vendored copy with JEV_MODEL pinned and a hook timeout set (10 s). The main caveats are immaturity, regex coverage gaps, and unverified value under bypassPermissions.

verification.note: Re-queried now: 0 stars, 0 forks, not archived, MIT, 1 commit, 1 contributor, no releases, created and pushed 2026-09-23. Source read in full (162 lines). It matches the audit on endpoint (line 27), model alias (line 28), keys (lines 29 and 81), Bearer header (line 102), payload with cwd (line 90), and fail-closed ask on Jev errors (lines 126-132). It has no subprocess, eval or shell exec, no argv keys and no telemetry beyond the X-Title header. Hook output {hookSpecificOutput:{hookEventName,permissionDecision:'ask',permissionDecisionReason}} is valid for Claude Code 2.1.x. The OpenRouter model alias is verified in the live catalog, which the audit had marked unverified. Score is lowered from 7 to 6 because: (1) the redaction and regex-coverage holes are larger than the audit states (API_KEY-style names, Bearer tokens, all >> appends); (2) the user's auto mode already has a classifier and hook-forced asks add prompts; (3) ask-only value under bypassPermissions is still not confirmed by docs; (4) the 1-day-old single-commit repo shows 33% edge 403s in its own eval; (5) a hook timeout or crash fails open (non-blocking). It is still a safe-by-construction, OpenRouter-native, zero-context hook, but not clearly valuable every day. Nothing was executed; regexes were re-implemented in DIR to test behaviour.

judge.why: Smallest and safest Jev hook: 162 stdlib lines, Bash only, ask-only, regex prefilter so about 79% of commands never leave the machine. Best as a vendored copy, but in this user's modes it only adds prompts.
pros: OpenRouter-native with no patching; the alias is verified in the live catalog
Never returns allow or deny, so it cannot loosen or wrongly block anything; Jev errors give ask
Auditable single file with a mocked test suite and a 48-item gold set; zero context cost
Jev cost about $0.018 per 881 commands
cons: 1 commit, 0 stars, one-day-old repo. In its own eval 58 of 176 requests got HTTP 403 (33%; no User-Agent sent), so real-world reliability is unproven

Redaction misses API_KEY, GITHUB_TOKEN and DB_PASSWORD style names and the token after 'Authorization: Bearer'. The regex pass skips all >> appends and absolute-path > redirects, curl|sh and inline interpreters
Ask-only means net extra prompts in auto mode. Value under bypass depends on an undocumented hook-ask behaviour
30 s per-socket timeout with the default 600 s hook timeout. Set timeout ~10; a hook timeout or crash fails open. TYPESAFE_API_KEY, if set, wins and breaks OpenRouter
Sends command text (700 chars) and cwd to OpenRouter and TypeSafe

entries.name: FailproofAI/failproofai
entries.what: Hook policy engine and observability tool for 12 agent harnesses, Claude Code included. About 40 regex or deterministic policies gate tool calls. When ~/.failproofai/jev.json exists and a pack with semantic checks is installed, one Jev request per PreToolUse or PermissionRequest call runs in parallel with the regex policies. Jev can clear a deny only from policies marked "reviewable", and only when it was asked that exact concern. It can also warn or deny on its own. Every Jev question is a Noul (P(yes)) over the redacted call, recent user prompts, the agent's last message, and local facts. Jev is not used at Stop, SubagentStop or PreCompact. Those events only get regex policies and telemetry.
interface: failproofai jev test | status [--json] | models | remove
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic. Every PreToolUse and PermissionRequest call goes through the hook, and Jev is consulted without any model prompting whenever jev.json and a semantic pack are present and a semantic policy applies to the tool class. Fires in bypassPermissions and auto sessions too, since PreToolUse fires regardless of mode. PermissionRequest only fires when a dialog would have appeared, so it is not reached in bypass.
security: Key storage: ~/.failproofai/jev.json at 0600. A file readable or writable by others is refused, and hooks fall back to regex. ~/.failproofai must not be group or world writable, and setup strips those bits. The key is scrubbed from error text. Use --key-stdin. --token leaks the key into argv and shell history, and the docs warn about it.

Config is global-only. A repo-level .failproofai/jev.json is ignored, and the provider, URL and model are never read from env. That blocks a hostile client repo from redirecting Jev. Redirects are never followed (jev-client.ts:475). The URL must be https, or http://localhost in observe mode only.

Prompt-injection posture is deliberate. Hard policy denies are final, and Jev can never make a call more permissive than regex unless it read the whole call and was asked the exact concern. An oversized or cut call (request-cut) or a suspected injection withdraws all clearances but keeps Jev's own deny. A per-policy userCanOverride flag exists. The eval-noted weakness (injected text moving answers) is therefore bounded to clearances of reviewable policies.

Redaction before egress: redact.ts (2937 lines) redacts keys, bearer tokens, KEY= assignments, PEM blocks, URL creds and the process's own secret-named env values, and has an sk-or-v1 OpenRouter key pattern (redact.ts:820). Egress redaction is not a substitute for the no-secret-leak hook.

Third-party code exec: policy packs (JS .mjs bundles downloaded from GitHub) are loaded and run inside the hook process. FailproofAI/jev-policies has 0 stars, no license, pushed 2026-09-24. Pack digests are tracked (pack-manifest and pack-store), but its content was not audited here. The npm package pulls optional platform binaries @failproofai/failproofaid-<os>-<arch>, and the daemon downloader verifies SHA256SUMS.

Root footprint: the recommended `failproofai config` installs a system-scope systemd unit at /etc/systemd/system/failproofaid@<user>.service and runs sudo. The daemon does not see shell env, so the Jev key must live in the file. The hooks-only path (`policies --install`) avoids root.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai, one POST per gated tool call (PreToolUse or PermissionRequest, when a policy with a semantic check applies), under the user's own key and with ZDR-only routing, data_collection deny and no fallback. The body has the tool name and input with secrets redacted, the recent human prompts (harness-injected text stripped), the agent's last message (labelled agent-written), and local facts (path relative to project root, git branch, permission mode). It is capped by MAX_REQUEST_CHARS, and an oversize call is cut and loses its clearances. Separately, opt-out PostHog telemetry carries event metadata (tool_name, policy, decision, jev_outcome, platform, hostname hash), not the payloads. Verdicts with per-question probabilities are logged locally to ~/.failproofai/state/semantic/verdicts.jsonl. Cloud tie-in (Failproof AI Observability) is opt-in via a machine key. With no token, nothing goes to Cloud. For client projects, the client's prompts and command text (redacted) do go to OpenRouter, so it needs a data-handling decision.
entries.failureMode: Jev failures fail open to the regex result for that call. Timeout defaults to 3000 ms (configurable 100-10000), and every failure is a recorded reason (timeout, http-429, out-of-credits, network, model-mismatch, malformed, and others). Client-side rate limit is 5 rps with burst 5. There is no circuit breaker, so a stalled provider costs up to 3 s per gated call until the user lowers timeoutMs (evaluator.ts:54-100 says so). The model must be Jev 1.13.x, otherwise model-mismatch falls back to regex. A hard-policy deny is never overridden. On a machine with the daemon configured, an unreachable daemon or a version skew fails CLOSED and denies tool calls. A broken pack denies the events its policies covered. Without a jev.json, or without a pack containing semantic checks, Jev is inert.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skill. No token cost in context from tool definitions. Hook-injected text appears only when a policy denies or instructs (deny reason or instruct() message), and the Jev guidance for a warning is short. UserPromptSubmit and Stop hooks can add instruct text if policies are installed.
pros: OpenRouter is native and correct: jev-client.ts:202 uses https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with typesafe/jev-1.13, Bearer auth, and provider {zdr:true,data_collection:"deny",allow_fallbacks:false}. `failproofai jev --url https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 --mode observe --key-stdin` is one command, and `jev test` gives a live check.

Very strong safety design for a model that is overconfident and injectable: hard regex denies are final, clearances require the exact concern to have been asked, oversize or suspected injection withdraws clearances, and any Jev failure returns the regex result. A pinned Jev 1.13 family is verified on every answer (model-mismatch), and observe mode records verdicts without changing decisions.
Config hardening is unusually good: global-only jev.json with 0600 and directory checks, no repo or env override of provider or URL, no redirects, key scrubbing, and a masked prompt or --key-stdin.

Covers the hook slots the user lacks (PermissionRequest, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, UserPromptSubmit) for regex policies, and 5k stars with daily commits, 1.0.9 released 2026-09-29, and 407 test files.
Redaction of secrets before egress is extensive (sk-or-v1 pattern included). A local verdicts.jsonl and a dashboard give an audit trail for tuning thresholds.
cons: Jev is not the product's core and is inert by default. It needs a separate external pack (FailproofAI/jev-policies, 0 stars, no license, created weeks ago) plus jev.json. It only sits at PreToolUse and PermissionRequest, so Stop, SubagentStop and PreCompact get only deterministic regex policies, not Jev. Jev use is limited to allow, warn, deny and clear-deny, not a Noul allow-fast-path like the OpenRouter cookbook hook (which grants permission). This tool mainly gates and does not reduce prompts.

Heavy footprint: a Next.js dashboard, a Rust daemon, and about 28 hook entries per Claude Code event in ~/.claude/settings.json. The recommended `failproofai config` needs sudo for a root systemd unit and hooks every detected CLI. The daemon fails closed on outages or version skew, which can deny every tool call. Doing the lighter `policies --install --cli claude --scope user` on the in-process path is the safer route.

Latency stacks on the existing hooks: a node process per event, up to a 3 s Jev wait on gated calls (p50 about 0.5 s), and no circuit breaker if OpenRouter stalls. The gitnexus hook (seconds) and no-secret-leak hook also run on Bash, Read and Grep.

Key handling gaps for this user: FAILPROOFAI_JEV_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY, is the env var, and the daemon ignores shell env, so the key sits in ~/.failproofai/jev.json in plaintext. It needs adding to the no-secret-leak protected list (path plus env var) and the file must remain 0600.

Data egress for client projects: prompts, tool commands and the agent's last message go to OpenRouter on nearly every gated call (ZDR-only, but a third party). It also has opt-out PostHog telemetry with tool_name and policy per call, so set FAILPROOFAI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1 or the config option. Commons Clause license, beta version (1.0.10-beta.0), and the pack executes downloaded JS inside the hook process.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered OpenRouter-native Jev integration found: safe fail-open-to-regex design, hardened key and config handling, and observe mode. It is a large, beta, root-daemon-and-telemetry-heavy product whose Jev layer only refines deny policies through an external new pack. Worth a trial in observe mode via the hooks-only install with telemetry off, but not a lightweight fit for the automatic-Jev-when-it-adds-value goal.

judge.why: Most engineered and hardened, with strong config safety and observe mode, and it is the only one covering the missing Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact and PermissionRequest slots. But Jev is a minor add-on requiring an external policy pack, and the footprint (dashboard, daemon, about 28 hooks, telemetry) is large.
pros: Native OpenRouter with ZDR-only routing; global-only 0600 jev.json; no redirects; the model is pinned to 1.13.x with model-mismatch fallback
Hard regex denies are final; Jev can only clear reviewable policies when asked the exact concern; oversize or injected calls lose clearance; failures give the regex result
Observe mode, a local verdict log and a dashboard; 5k stars, 407 test files, MIT + Commons Clause
cons: Jev is inert without the FailproofAI/jev-policies pack (0 stars, no licence, executes downloaded JS inside the hook); beta version
Recommended `failproofai config` installs a root systemd daemon that fails closed on outage or skew, and hooks every CLI; use `policies --install --cli claude --scope user` instead
About 28 hook entries (a node spawn per event) plus up to 3 s Jev waits and no circuit breaker, stacked on gitnexus
Opt-out PostHog telemetry (set FAILPROOFAI_TELEMETRY_DISABLED=1); the key sits in plaintext in jev.json, so add it to no-secret-leak
Jev usage is limited to refining denies; it does not reduce prompts

entries.name: greghavens/jev-scope-control
entries.what: A single ~2270-line stdlib-only Python script (jev-scope-control) installed as a Claude Code plugin PreToolUse command hook (timeout 15s). It skips read-only tools and provably read-only shell commands in code. For Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, non-trivial Bash, subagent launches (Agent/Task) and unknown tools such as MCP tools, it rebuilds the user's latest request, conversation and recent actions from the transcript. It sends them to the TypeSafe System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone). Bash commands first get a cheap read/write Noul. Everything then goes through a gate question (deny bar 0.35), then a full battery of scope Nouls composed in code, with deny above 0.65. A deny returns permissionDecision "deny" plus a reason telling the model to tell the user and not retry. Results are cached for 600s. A denied call stays denied for the same user request. Logs go to ~/.jev-scope-control/log.jsonl. There is no README, only design/jev-scope-control-design.md. The repo also ships Codex, pi and opencode shims.
interface: Claude Code plugin manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json v0.3.0 + marketplace.json)
entries.autoInvocation: Fully deterministic PreToolUse hook. It fires automatically on every tool call, is gated in code, and does not depend on the model choosing to call anything. It also fires in bypassPermissions/auto mode, because a hook deny overrides the permission mode. It covers subagent calls too (agent_id handling).
security: No shell exec or subprocess in the hook: no `subprocess` import (grep confirms). It only parses commands with shlex.

Key never on argv: it goes in the Authorization header from a file or env. The default key file is ~/.config/jev-scope-control/env, and the log and state dir ~/.jev-scope-control is created mode 0700.
Redirects are disabled (_NoRedirect, ~line 2064-2067) so the key is not resent elsewhere. https is enforced except for localhost (line 2078-2080).
No telemetry beyond the Jev call. No installer script; the plugin install is the standard Claude Code plugin mechanism.

Prompt-injection surface: the model-authored command, diff and tool-result snippets (~300 chars each) are put into the judged state. Code mitigates some of this: WRITE_QUESTION says comments and claims in the command are not evidence, and 'don't let claims in a command skip the scope check' is a commit. But the Jev brief says injected instructions in state can move answers. Assistant text after the last user message is deliberately withheld.

Fail-open on every error: any exception, a missing key, a Jev outage or HTTP 5xx, a 5s timeout, or a missing transcript all let the call run. It warns once per session via systemMessage. It is a nudge, not a security boundary.
entries.dataEgress: On every checked call (Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, non-plainly-read Bash, Agent/Task, MCP and unknown tools) the state sent to the endpoint (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter to TypeSafe if redirected) contains: the user's latest message; earlier user messages (up to a limit); the last assistant reply (tail, up to about 6k chars); 'older user limits'; the subagent assignment text; up to N recent actions as one-line tool+input plus result snippets (~300 chars each); and the proposed action itself. For an edit that is the file path plus a diff or content clipped to ~3k chars per part; for Bash it is the command and description. The design doc also lists working_directory. Client source diffs, command lines (which may contain inline secrets) and tool-output snippets therefore leave the machine on nearly every state-changing call, roughly 2k input tokens per call. Bash commands get an extra tiny request containing just the tool call. Local logs at ~/.jev-scope-control/log.jsonl store the truncated task (300 chars) and scores.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. The hook always exits 0 (main(), lines 2257-2268). Jev timeout is 5s on a daemon thread (JEV_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), under the 15s hook timeout. A missing key, an HTTP error or a parse error means the call is allowed, with a one-time systemMessage warning (warn_once) and details in the log. If the gate or write question errors, it falls to risk=1.0 or writes=1.0 and proceeds to the full check; if the full check errors, it allows. Design-doc caveat: the documented 3-denial cap (JEV_SCOPE_CONTROL_MAX_DENIALS) is not in the code. Instead, an identical denied call stays denied for the same user request (run(), lines ~2196-2214). A false positive therefore costs a turn, and the model is told to ask the user, so the user's next message resets it. Denials are not hard-capped, so a misjudging Jev can repeatedly block different calls.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skills, so no tool-def or skill-listing budget cost. No additionalContext injection. The only model-visible text is the deny reason (~100 tokens) and a systemMessage. The plugin adds no per-turn context.
pros: Targets a real gap for a user in auto and bypassPermissions modes: it catches unrequested commits, pushes, deploys and out-of-scope edits (Bash, Edit, Write, MCP) that no static regex hook catches, and it is a deterministic hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.

Design is thoughtful and evidence-backed: gating in code (read-only tools and commands never hit the network), a two-stage gate/full check with composed decision scores, a 600s result cache, repeat-deny memory, subagent assignment handling, and tuning against 798 real sessions (1.1% denied, 1 known wrong denial). Docs claim 360/360 and 525/525 on labeled cases. Self-reported and not independently verified.

Low blast radius on failure: stdlib-only, fail-open with a one-time warning, no shell exec, key in a header (not argv) with redirects disabled and https enforced. Runs are logged to a 0700 dir. Zero MCP or context cost.
OpenRouter path is nearly free: the request is the exact System One schema, base URL and key are env-configurable, and the endpoint path matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.
Sizeable test suite: 45 hook unit tests with a mock Jev server in test_hook.py, 5 e2e tests, 72 labeled scenario cases plus large probe and scenario JSON, and a real `claude -p` e2e script.
cons: Brand-new alpha: created 2026-09-29 (repo age about 1 day, 15 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no release). It has no README and no LICENSE. The docs and code already drift: the design doc's JEV_SCOPE_CONTROL_MAX_DENIALS cap and the triage's JEV_MODEL override do not exist in the code.

Not OpenRouter-native: the model is hardcoded to "jev-latest" (line 41), not the documented "jev-1.13". OpenRouter may reject it, so a one-line local patch may be needed. The key variable is TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so an OpenRouter key would be stored in a second place (~/.config/jev-scope-control/env), not read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Heavy data egress: user messages, assistant text, diffs and command snippets (possibly client code and secrets inside commands) go to a third party on almost every state-changing call. This is a real problem for client projects. Nothing redacts secrets before sending, and no-secret-leak.cjs does not cover it.

Fail-open with no hard denial cap and tuned thresholds. On an OpenRouter outage or missing key it silently stops checking (one warning per session). Independent evals say calibration is imperfect and injected text in state can sway answers, so it cannot be relied on as a security control. Known wrong denials and near-bar misses are acknowledged in the docs. In bypass mode a wrong denial is a new friction, and an `Agent` launch or unknown MCP call is also gated.

Overlaps with Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier and permissions, and adds per-edit latency (0.2-0.8s per Edit/Write/Bash, more through OpenRouter's alpha endpoint with no SLA) on top of the gitnexus Bash hook.

Depends on the transcript format: it reads transcript_path and waits up to 2s for the call to appear in it, so a Claude Code JSONL format change would silently degrade context, and it would fail open.
entries.verdict: The most relevant and best-engineered candidate for guarding auto and bypass sessions: it fires deterministically and has a real design and test story. But it is a one-day-old, unlicensed, single-author alpha that is TypeSafe-only (hardcoded model "jev-latest", TYPESAFE_API_KEY). It needs a base-URL env plus probably a one-line model patch for OpenRouter, and it sends diffs and transcript text to a third party on every state-changing call, which is a real concern for client work. Trial it on personal projects after pinning a commit, patching the model, and adding OPENROUTER/TYPESAFE keys to the no-secret-leak list.

judge.why: Best-designed scope checker (did the user ask for this edit, commit or subagent?). It targets the real auto and bypass drift problem and actually denies, but it is a one-day-old, unlicensed alpha with heavy egress and fail-open behaviour.
pros: Deterministic PreToolUse, fires in bypass, and denies with a reason telling the model to ask the user
Code-side gating: read-only tools and commands never touch the network; 600 s cache; repeat-deny memory
Tuned on 798 real sessions (1.1% denied, self-reported); 45 mocked unit tests plus e2e; stdlib only, key in a header, redirects disabled, https enforced
Zero context cost
cons: No README and no LICENSE; the design doc drifts from the code (the MAX_DENIALS cap and JEV_MODEL override do not exist)
Fail-open everywhere with only a one-time warning; a Jev outage silently stops checking
Sends user messages, the last assistant reply, diffs and result snippets to a third party on nearly every state-changing call, unredacted
0.3 to 0.8 s per Edit, Write or non-trivial Bash through OpenRouter alpha, stacked on gitnexus; it depends on transcript format and waits up to 2 s
Injection surface in command, diff and result snippets; false denials cost a turn

entries.name: jonathanavis96/jev-kit
entries.what: A monorepo "kit" for TypeSafe Jev + Claude Code. Core is "Airlock": a stdlib-only Python PreToolUse hook registered for every tool (matcher "*"). A local rules table (airlock/rules.py) pre-filters each call in microseconds. Only ambiguous cases (R2 Skill load, R4 long bare shell, R8 sub-agent tier guard, R8 tool-choice/disk-crawl guard, R10 catch-all general-risk) send a redacted typed question to Jev (POST /v1/systemone, model jev-latest, 1.5 s budget) and then allow, warn, deny or rewrite. Pure-code rules cover secret exposure, sudo, destructive commands, commit-secret and Playwright-MCP calls. Also ships: SessionStart health check, warm unix-socket daemon (systemd --user), a Stop-hook wrapper (belay, pinned third-party jev-belay), a 1-tool stdio MCP "browse" (vendored browser-use/jev-ultrafast), and opt-in compaction, review, tuning loop and other extras. Install is a bash script that only prints the settings.json block unless --wire is passed. Not an OpenRouter integration.
interface: PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure hook hooks/airlock_browse_unlock.py (matcher mcp__browse__browse)
Stop hook belay (belay/run.sh wrapping valentynkit/jev-belay at pin 98f39e0)
compaction/, review/, tuning/, docclass/, logtriage/, shim/, filesearch/, monitoring/, claude-update/
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PreToolUse with matcher "*" fires on every tool call without any prompting; SessionStart, PostToolUse/Failure and (opt-in) Stop hooks likewise. No model discretion needed. This is the closest match found to the user's requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically, but Jev acts as a guard/judge on tool calls rather than a general coding helper.
security: API key never placed on argv: urllib Authorization header built in-process (airlock/client.py:39-48), key read from env or a mode-600 file by plain file I/O (airlock/keyfile.py); browse passes it via the subprocess env (browse/server.py:751), not argv.

Redaction (airlock/redact.py) of token-shaped strings before egress, truncation after redaction; a 13-rule redactor in belay. Regex redaction is best-effort, so client code or secrets in unusual formats could still leak in the ambiguous slice.

Everything fails open on error, timeout, budget or missing key, so a guard/deny is advisory rather than a hard security boundary. R11 deliberately ignores the airlock-ok stamp and loop allowance (strict).

install.sh: no sudo, writes only under $HOME per README/header, prints the settings.json block unless --wire; but it git-clones pinned third-party repos (jev-belay, and compaction plugin if enabled), enables systemd --user units (daemon, monitoring, filesearch, claude-update) and the claude-update component runs npm install -g when idle; no curl|sh seen in install.sh grep.

Prompt-injection surface: verdicts come from a model reading tool-call text, and a user_requested question reads recent user prompts (softening only, guarded by a code belt in context.py). Tool results are not sent (except the opt-in compaction plugin, which sends up to about 25k tokens of raw UNREDACTED tool inputs and results per request, per docs/components.md).
No telemetry to a third party by default; optional Uptime-Kuma push (opt-in, status word only). Third-party code pulled in: vendor/jev-ultrafast (browser-use, MIT), valentynkit/jev-belay.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter): for the ambiguous minority of tool calls, a redacted, truncated summary of the call (Bash command text + description + cwd/scope, Skill name/purpose, Agent dispatch description and prompt) plus, for the user_requested softening check, recent user prompts (redacted, truncated). Belay (Stop hook, opt-in) sends task text, final assistant message and check command lines (1,500 + 2,000 char caps, redacted). Tool results, diffs and file contents are not sent by the default guard. Opt-in extras send more: compaction up to about 25k tokens of raw unredacted tool inputs/results per request; browse sends page state and goals to TypeSafe and, with plan=true, to Claude; review sends diffs. No egress for pure-code rules, session check, file search, monitoring. A local log of verdicts is written under ~/.config/airlock.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. client.py DEFAULT_TIMEOUT = 5 s, but enforce.py budget AIRLOCK_BUDGET_MS defaults to 1500 ms (2000 ms on Windows); any exception, malformed answer, budget overrun, missing key or daemon down means ALLOW, logged with error set. Deny/rewrite additionally require confidence >= 0.8 and margin >= 0.4 (0.9/0.5 for rewrite). Default mode is shadow (log only, nothing blocked) until you write "enforce" to ~/.config/airlock/mode. Daemon connect timeout 0.2 s with fallback to a direct HTTPS call. SessionStart check warns once per 6 h when the guard is not judging. Worst case with Jev down is a session with no guard beyond code-only rules, not a stall.
entries.contextCost: Very low for the default hooks: no MCP server, no tool definitions, no skill descriptions. Hooks inject text only when a rule warns or denies (a few lines, e.g. the 2-line tier advice note) and SessionStart is silent when healthy. Optional browse MCP adds 1 tool (description about 1,000 chars plus schema, roughly 400-500 tokens) and the R11 suggestion text when triggered. The repo's own CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md only matter inside the repo checkout.
pros: Only candidate seen that satisfies the hard requirement literally: a PreToolUse matcher-* hook plus SessionStart/Stop hooks run automatically with no 'use jev' prompt.

Respects Jev's actual nature (typed decisions with probabilities, no free text): it asks typed Choice/Noul/Score questions and applies confidence and margin thresholds (>=0.8 / >=0.4) before acting, instead of treating Jev as a chat model.

Safe rollout: default shadow mode logs what enforce would do, python3 -m airlock.report reviews it, kill switch AIRLOCK_DISABLE=1, per-rule rules.json overrides, install.sh --check-only and wire only with --wire, rollback.sh.
Fails open everywhere with a hard 1.5 s budget and a 5 s ceiling; a Jev outage cannot stall the session, and SessionStart warns when the guard silently stopped judging.
Cheap by design: rules table pre-filters most calls locally, only the ambiguous slice reaches Jev, Jev call skipped when a deny is unreachable, 5 percent sampling for tuning.
stdlib-only Python hook, key never on argv, redaction before egress, egress documented per component in docs/components.md (unusually candid, flags compaction as 25k-token unredacted exposure).
Large test suite claimed and present (about 50 test files in tests/, README says 1310 passing) and labelled eval cases for each rule; 64 commits in 11 days, active.
Tier guard (R8) could reduce Opus 5.5 sub-agent spend if the ladder is configured in tiers.json for the user's agent names; belay Stop hook catches overclaimed 'done' messages.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL and model are hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and jev-latest (airlock/client.py:17-18, vendor model.py:283); key only read as TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Using OpenRouter needs a local fork/patch and depends on OpenRouter's /v1/systemone accepting the identical request/response schema (unverified); the user's stated provider requirement is not met out of the box.

Mostly a guard, not a coding accelerator: its value is blocking/warning on risky tool calls and steering cost, not writing or reviewing code better in daily work. Much overlaps with things the user already has: R1 secret guard duplicates the existing PreToolUse secret-leak hook, R9 commit-secret overlaps too.

Direct conflict with existing setup: R11 (strict, no override stamp) denies every Playwright MCP browsing call and points to its own 'browse' tool, which the user's installed playwright MCP would hit unless R11 is turned off via rules.json; R8 grep/disk-crawl steering may interact with the GitNexus Grep|Glob|Bash hooks (a raw-grep steer toward graphify only when graphify-out exists, so likely inert).

Hook on matcher '*' adds a Python process spawn to every single tool call, stacked on the user's two existing hook chains (secret guard, GitNexus pre+post, caveman); mostly milliseconds but cumulative.

Tier guard is built around a custom ladder (scout/workerS/worker/director/fable) and Agent subagent_type names; low value unless the user's agents are configured into it. Rewrite mode silently downgrades sub-agents and is a real risk on client work.

Heavy footprint for a hook: systemd --user daemon, monitoring and filesearch timers, an idle auto-updater that runs npm install -g claude, cloned third-party repos (jev-belay, vendored jev-ultrafast), Windows/WSL/tuning extras. Large surface to audit for client machines; a personal project (about 50 stars, 3 contributor identities, mainly one author, no releases, no CI config in the repo).

Data leaves the machine to a beta third-party API: redacted bash commands, cwd, Agent prompts and recent user prompts. Regex redaction is not a guarantee; on client projects this is a confidentiality question. Fail-open means the guard is not a real security control, and README claims (93 percent pass-through, 0.3 s) are self-reported.

Depends on an unverified vendor product (Jev beta, skeptics say it is a router-like model); calibration thresholds in the kit were tuned against the author's own eval data and workflow, and its installer defaults (belay, auto-updater on, daemon) suit the author's machine.
entries.verdict: The best structural fit for "automatic, no prompting" because it is a deterministic PreToolUse/SessionStart/Stop hook set with shadow mode and fail-open. But it is TypeSafe-direct only (hardcoded URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY), so OpenRouter needs a small unverified fork. It is a guard, not a coding helper, and it clashes with the user's Playwright MCP (R11) and secret hook. I would cherry-pick the pattern (a minimal shadow-mode hook on selected matchers), not install the whole kit on client projects.

entries.name: leepokai/jev-guard
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node (>=20.3) command hook plus Claude Code plugin/marketplace that sends every non-read-only tool call to Jev as typed questions (risk Score 0-3, approval Noul, user_requested Noul, from_untrusted Noul) and every tool result of 200+ chars as injection questions (directed Noul, kind Choice). Policy lives in code (guard.js decide()): deny if risk>=2.5 or from_untrusted>=0.7, ask if risk>=1.5 or approval>=0.75 (unless user_requested>=0.85), else allow. Also sweeps CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, skills, plugins and rules for hidden or malicious instructions, cached by content hash. It is a security guard (an auto-mode classifier clone), not a coding-assistance tool: Jev is not used for routing, code review, test triage or other daily-coding decisions.
interface: CLI jev-guard hook | install claude | key | check | scan | scan-skills | acp
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart, InstructionsLoaded), fully automatic once the plugin is installed and a key is present; no model discretion and no prompting needed. This is the strongest fit for the "Claude must use Jev without being told" requirement, but only for the security-classification use case.
security: No install script and no npm postinstall; zero runtime deps; no telemetry found (grep for postinstall/telemetry/analytics returned nothing); MIT.

Key handling: read from env OPENROUTER_API_KEY or ~/.jev-guard/config.json (0600, dir 0700) by the hook process, so not in the hook's argv. The one-time `jev-guard key sk-or-...` command puts the key in argv/shell history (jev.js:22-31, cli.js:74-86). Key is sent only to the matching provider URL; JEV_BASE_URL gets only its own key (jev.js:19-22).

Per-session memory plaintext at ~/.jev-guard/sessions/*.json (0600): user prompts, tool-call previews, excerpts of flagged content (session.js:89-111). Scan cache stores only sha1 hashes and verdicts.

No shell execution or eval in the hook path; install only edits JSON. Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted tool output goes to Jev as `state`, so an attacker could try to inject the classifier itself (plain data in a typed schema limits the impact, but a false 'clean' is possible). Reason strings echoed to Claude include a truncated command preview, so attacker-controlled text can reach the model.
Guardrail not a sandbox (SECURITY.md); fail-open by default so a bypass by outage or timeout is possible; thresholds calibrated on Jev only.

Bus factor 1: single maintainer (leepokai 23 of 24 commits, npm maintainer kevinleeeee); a hook installed at user scope runs with full trust on every tool call, so supply-chain risk on updates through the plugin marketplace follows main.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (and whatever upstream OpenRouter routes Jev to): (1) for every non-read-only tool call, the agent name, tool name, the FULL tool_input (whole Bash commands, file Write/Edit contents and diffs, MCP arguments), cwd, plus context = last 3 user prompts (700 chars each), the last assistant text, last 6 tool-call previews, and up to 5 flagged excerpts; (2) for every tool result of 200+ chars other than Edit/Write/Glob/Grep, the full result text (up to 60k chars, head and tail kept), which includes Read file contents, Bash stdout, WebFetch pages, MCP output, plus the last user prompt as user_task; (3) at SessionStart and InstructionsLoaded, the full text of CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, skills and rules (one-off, cached by hash). Effectively most code and client data touched in a session leaves the machine. No zeroDataRetention flag is sent on the OpenRouter path (only on the Vercel gateway path, jev.js:68), so retention and ZDR depend on the OpenRouter account and privacy settings. Client-project confidentiality needs a check; the secret-leak guard is not a substitute because secrets in Bash output or Read results are transmitted post hoc.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default: on any exception (no credentials, HTTP error, timeout) hook.js:361-371 writes the error to stderr and returns nothing, so the tool call proceeds. JEV_GUARD_FAIL_CLOSED=1 makes PreToolUse deny when Jev is unreachable (only PreToolUse and Gemini BeforeTool; PostToolUse always fails open). One time budget of 20 s per Jev call (JEV_GUARD_TIMEOUT_MS) with up to 3 attempts on 429/5xx/network errors and 600 ms and 1.2 s backoff (jev.js:57,73-82); the hook timeout is 30 s. With no key set, the hook silently fails open. Fail-closed would be painful with a beta Jev and an outage.
entries.contextCost: Near zero standing cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skill descriptions. Hooks inject text only on events: a systemMessage/additionalContext note at session start or prompt when instruction files are flagged (usually nothing), and a ~350 char reason on a flagged PostToolUse. A deny or ask message is about 250 chars. Clean results inject nothing (allow returns null). Also one extra process spawn per tool event.
pros: Only candidate here that fully satisfies 'automatic, never say use jev': deterministic PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks with matcher .* need no model discretion or prompting.
OpenRouter works from code, not just README: jev.js:5 posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with model jev-1.13 using OPENROUTER_API_KEY; unit tests at guard.test.js:213-246 cover it.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no skill descriptions, nothing injected when calls are clean.

Fits Jev's actual strengths: typed Noul/Score/Choice questions with calibrated probabilities and thresholds in 20 lines of readable policy; no free text parsed. Cost is trivial (~1k tokens x $0.042/M is about $0.00004 per call).

Adds a second-opinion layer on top of the user's bypass or auto mode: catches destructive commands (rm -rf, curl|sh, force push, prod deploys) and prompt injection from web/MCP output, which a secret-leak guard does not cover. Session memory lets a user-asked risky action be allowed instead of nagging.

Small and auditable (about 1000 LOC, no deps, no postinstall, no telemetry, no shell exec); fail-open default means Jev outages do not freeze work; every threshold is env-tunable; JEV_GUARD_SKIP_TOOLS and SKIP_SCAN can trim latency and egress.
Coexists with existing hooks (parallel execution, non-overlapping decisions with the secret guard); JEV_BASE_URL allows a local Kev for offline or sensitive projects.
cons: Not a coding-productivity integration: Jev is used only as a safety classifier, so it gives no help with code review, test triage, routing or planning decisions the user hoped to get from Jev.

Heavy data egress for client projects: all Bash commands, file Write contents, and every Read/Bash/WebFetch/MCP result of 200+ chars (up to 60k chars) plus recent user prompts go to OpenRouter and its Jev upstream; no zeroDataRetention is sent on the OpenRouter path (jev.js:68 only for the Vercel gateway). Likely unacceptable for client code without an OpenRouter ZDR/privacy check or a local Kev via JEV_BASE_URL.
Latency tax on nearly every tool cycle: about 0.6-1.5 s per non-read-only call (pre plus post scan) with a synchronous, blocking hook, and claimed 70-500 ms is not measured on OpenRouter in the repo.

Fails open silently when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is missing, credits run out or the API is down, giving a false sense of protection; fail-closed exists but would block work during a beta-model outage (and PostToolUse is never fail-closed).

Redundant with Claude Code's own auto mode for the user's usual permission modes; in bypass mode, ask-type outputs may not stop actions, and only deny is reliable. False positives are likely: thresholds were calibrated on 21 calls and a few dozen skills by the author, and README admits ask for routine git push or gh pr create (risk 2.0, approval 0.77), which will be noisy for a daily git workflow if the ask is honored.

Version skew: npm 0.3.1 lacks OpenRouter; must track git HEAD (pre-1.0, 24 commits in 12 days, one maintainer with 23 commits, 48 stars, no CI, no releases since 0.3.1). Installing user-scope hooks from an unpinned marketplace main gives that author code execution on every tool call.

OpenRouter default model is pinned to jev-1.13 rather than the ~typesafe/jev-latest alias; the Theo/t3.gg skepticism that Jev may be a small flash router matters more here because classification quality decides deny/ask outcomes and there is no independent evaluation beyond the author's own calibration.

Plaintext session memory (prompts, command previews, injection excerpts) under ~/.jev-guard/sessions on a machine used for client work, and instruction-file sweeps send the user's CLAUDE.md files (loaded via InstructionsLoaded) off-machine.
entries.verdict: The only genuinely automatic, zero-context Jev integration and it really does support OpenRouter (HEAD only, not npm), but it is a security auto-mode classifier rather than a coding aid and it ships most tool inputs and outputs to OpenRouter with a per-call latency cost. Worth trying on personal projects (pinned commit, trimmed via SKIP_SCAN and SKIP_TOOLS, ideally PreToolUse-only), not as a default on client repos without ZDR guarantees.

judge.why: 48 stars and OpenRouter support at HEAD. An auto-mode-style Jev classifier hook; the audit found it ships most tool inputs and outputs to OpenRouter with per-call latency, so it is a personal-projects-only trial at best.
pros: Automatic, zero-context hook with OpenRouter support at HEAD
Most starred dedicated Jev guard; beta
cons: Sends most tool inputs and outputs to OpenRouter on each call, which is unsuitable for client work
Per-call latency; a classifier duplicating Anthropic's auto mode
OpenRouter path is not in the npm release, so pin a commit; details not re-verified by this review

entries.name: bladedevoff/stuntd
entries.what: Local Jev-protocol (/v1/systemone) and OpenAI-compatible proxy that distils typed decisions into a local Laya head; ships an example Claude Code PreToolUse Bash gate (allow/ask/deny).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook (Bash) calling local daemon
pros: examples/devtools includes a concrete Claude Code PreToolUse hook (permissionDecision ask/deny) and flaky-test question
Local answers in ~22-60 ms with fallback to provider, no per-call cost; Apache-2.0, CI, PyPI
README cites Jev via OpenRouter latency (p50 376-389 ms) and $0.042/1M pricing
cons: Needs pip install with torch training, daemon and 50 MB heads; heavy for a hook; example teacher is a rule, not real Jev traffic
Only speaks /v1/systemone to upstream; OpenRouter upstream needs base-URL config, unverified; Anthropic path does not learn
Local head trained on 3000 synthetic rows may be less safe than static regex plus Jev; v0.1

entries.name: Nyarlathoteppppp/pi-heed
entries.what: Pi extension that turns user-stated constraints (EN/ZH) into a scoped replayable policy and checks every side-effecting tool call against it, using Jev via OpenRouter or TypeSafe.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (Pi tool-call interception); not Claude Code
pros: Idea directly transferable: remember 'review only, don't touch' constraints and enforce after compaction
OpenRouter alpha decisions supported; 166 tests, EXPERIMENTS.md and bench/jev-lab.ts with Jev measurements
Once/run/scoped exceptions in policy
cons: Pi-only extension, would need port to UserPromptSubmit+PreToolUse hooks
11 stars, 2 days of commits
Per-call Jev latency on every side-effecting call

entries.name: muratcakmak/jev-guard
entries.what: A Claude Code plugin written as a TypeScript "function hooks" module (hooks/hooks.json = {"modules":["./guard.ts"]}, hooks/guard.ts register(on, options)). It sends noul questions to Jev's System One endpoint and denies or rewrites tool calls from the probabilities. Features: (1) rule guard on Edit/Write/Bash: local regex rules plus Jev-scored semantic rules, one batched request per call, deny at p>=0.7; (2) deploy gate on Bash: deny if "deploys/publishes/merges/sends credential" p>=0.7 and "user asked for exactly this" p<0.5; (3) background mover: known-slow commands get run_in_background, decided by a local regex (Jev's slow score is not used); (4) answer check on turn.complete: 5 noul questions over the final answer, the last 40 tool results and the prompt, then submits one correction prompt; (5) doc router on prompt.submit: off by default; (6) skill gate: denies skills listed in gatedSkillPrefixes when the prompt did not name them (off by default: the prefix list is empty); (7) subagent haiku downgrade: off by default. It also ships a CI twin, scripts/jev-lint.ts, which lints a diff and needs bun.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (function-hook events tool.call, turn.complete, prompt.submit). No prompting needed. This is the only candidate type that satisfies "Claude Code must use it without me saying so", but it works as a guard and not as an assistant that helps with tasks.
security: API key is read from env inside the plugin and sent as a Bearer header through $.http.fetch. It never appears in argv or the process list.
No shell execution in the hook. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry in the repo. Only the configured Jev URL is contacted.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted content (file edits, command text, tool results, the final answer) is embedded in the Jev `state`. Jev returns only typed probabilities, not text, so it cannot inject instructions back. But an attacker string could bias scores and defeat the deploy gate. It is a heuristic guard, not a security boundary.

Secret leakage: whole Bash commands (which may inline tokens) and 12k chars of every guarded Edit/Write body are sent to the third-party endpoint. That collides with the user's existing secret-leak guard philosophy.

Correctness risk: ANSWER_CHECKS asks-on-disk-credential fix text hardcodes the author's private path (~/.config/kai/*.env, guard.ts:179). It would send the model looking for files that do not exist. The author states the plugin was extracted from a private project.
Runs with full plugin capabilities inside the engine ($.http, $.fs.read, $.prompt.submit). The whole thing is about 600 lines and readable in minutes, so it is auditable.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (OpenRouter if JEV_BASE_URL is set): (a) every Bash command in full, plus the user's last prompt (2000 chars); (b) for Edit/Write on files matching the semantic rule regex (default src/**/*.jsx|tsx) the old/new strings or whole file content, truncated to 12k chars; Bash is always sent; (c) at turn end, the user prompt (2000), the final answer (6000) and the last 40 tool calls, each with the input JSON cut to 160 chars and the result cut to 200 chars; (d) optionally the prompt (4000) and note titles for the router, and the Agent prompt (4000). Full file reads and Grep or Read outputs are not sent, except through those truncated tool-result snippets.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. No key, HTTP error, malformed JSON or a thrown error is caught, logged through $.ui.log, and the call proceeds (guard.ts:368-371, 419-421, 477-479). No explicit per-request timeout is set in the plugin. It relies on the engine's hook budget, and the docs say an overrunning hook is "skipped". So a slow Jev stalls each guarded call up to that budget, then passes. Regex rules still work offline. Missing key produces only a debug-log line.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and no MCP instructions. Hooks inject no context by default. The doc router (off) would add up to 3x8000 chars per prompt. When the answer check fires it submits an extra user turn (about 100 tokens plus a full extra Opus response). Deny messages are short.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hook-based, so no reliance on Opus choosing to call a tool.
Drop-in OpenRouter support through JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL. Request and response schema match the OpenRouter System One docs, so no code patch is needed.
Fail-open everywhere and the source is small (618 lines) and readable. Uses noul probabilities with thresholds, which is a sensible use of Jev.
The deploy gate (block unasked push, publish or merge) is directly valuable in bypass or auto permission mode, where nothing else stops those commands.
The answer check catches 'done/passing' claims with no evidence in the turn. Its fix prompts are one-shot, with a nudged flag to prevent loops.
Regex tier runs locally at no cost. Most features are opt-in and off by default. MIT licence, no dependencies.
cons: Depends on an experimental, default-off Claude Code surface (function hooks, CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, 'may change without notice'). Not verified as working on 2.1.285 with a subscription login. Could break on any update.
Immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 7 stars, 8 days old, no CI, no releases, only self-written tests (I did not run any).

Ships an opinionated example rule set that would misfire for this user. The wrong-package-manager regex denies every npm/yarn command (assumes Bun) and the React Native rules do not fit generic projects. The rules must be rewritten before use.

Author-specific leftovers: hardcoded ~/.config/kai/*.env in the credential-fix text, the wrong-package-manager rule, and the declared but unused slowThreshold (the slow mover is regex only). Jev is not actually used for the background mover.

Privacy: every Bash command, edit content and the final answer plus snippets go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Client-project code is a compliance concern, and commands with inline secrets bypass the user's own local secret-guard intent.

Adds a blocking network call to every Bash command and a call at the end of every turn. The answer check can trigger extra Opus turns on false positives (the author already had to make ends-on-promise log-only after a live run pushed the model into unasked work).

The deploy gate is deliberately literal: a general go-ahead is not enough, so the user will be re-asked in bypass mode. It is not a security control and is bypassable through indirect commands. No explicit request timeout. Does not use Jev to help the model code, only to police it.
Coexists untested with the user's other Bash hooks (secret guard, GitNexus), since the function-hook ordering model is separate from command hooks.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed integration that is genuinely automatic and OpenRouter-compatible with a config change (three env vars), but it is a police hook, not a productivity tool. It also rides an experimental, flag-gated Claude Code API, has one commit, and needs its rules rewritten. Best used as a reference or fork for a narrow deploy-gate plus answer-check hook, not installed as-is on client work.

entries.name: clownware/bouncer
entries.what: Claude Code plugin with one PreToolUse hook (Bash|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit). It first applies deterministic hard rules and a fast-path allowlist. It then sends a redacted, structured description of the action plus about 7 noul questions from a user-owned YAML policy to Jev at api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Thresholds turn the answers into allow/ask/deny. Modes are observe (default, emits nothing), guard, full and seatbelt (for bypass sessions: hard rules deny, otherwise silent). It logs to decisions.jsonl and ships /calibrate, /explain, /mode and /status commands plus one SKILL.md.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic. It is a PreToolUse hook on Bash/Edit/Write/NotebookEdit, so it needs no prompting. It ships in observe mode (logs only), so nothing takes effect until the user switches mode. Modes are skipped only for permission modes listed in skip_permission_modes (default plan). The bouncer skill is model-invoked only for explain and tune questions.
security: Hook path has no shell exec of user data. The only child_process use is src/io/reasoning.ts (BOUNCER_REASONING_CMD, spawn shell:true), reached from the `measure` command and not from the hook. That command string comes from the environment.

Key handling is env-only, so no argv exposure (config.ts:153-176). The TypeSafe key is never forwarded to a jev@ URL (config.ts:182-186). The compat and local keys support *_FILE variants. The key is never read from policy YAML, so a cloned repo cannot redirect it.

A repo-level .bouncer.yaml overrides the user policy (config.ts:20-30). A hostile repo can only add prompts or change thresholds. But in mode full it could set thresholds or fast_path to auto-allow, and the docs argue that allow never widens what Claude Code permits. Worth knowing for client repos, since cloning a repo adopts its policy.

Prompt-injection surface: the command text goes into the state. It is structured as JSON fields to reduce impersonation (state.ts:13-17), but the author admits it 'narrows, does not close' the surface and is not a security boundary. Jev is known to be steerable by injected state. The mitigation is that deterministic hard rules run before the model and cannot be argued with.

Redaction: 14 regex shapes (private keys, sk-, ghp_, AKIA, JWT, bearer, url-credentials, assigned-secret) are applied before send and again on log write (redact.ts, log.ts). It is shape matching only, and the source says so. An OPENROUTER_API_KEY value would be caught only by the assigned-secret or sk-or... shape (`sk-or-v1-...` matches the openai-key regex \bsk-... 20+ chars).

CI has a gitleaks scan and action pins by SHA. The installer is the Claude Code plugin marketplace (marketplace.json source ./), with no install scripts. bin/bouncer.cjs is a committed esbuild bundle of about 12.9k lines including the yaml dep, so it is hard to audit and depends on the maintainer's build being honest. The repo is 2 weeks old with one main author, and 91 of 243 commits are by 'Claude'.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on each judged Bash/Edit/Write/NotebookEdit call (not on hard-rule or fast-path hits). It sends a JSON state of tool name, permission mode, cwd-relative and path-labelled facts, the redacted command line (capped at 4096 bytes), file existence, and byte counts for Write and Edit. It also sends about 7 question texts. Write.content, Edit old_string/new_string and NotebookEdit new_source are never sent (state.ts:5-9). Command strings and file paths do leave the machine, including client project names, hostnames and paths, with only regex-shape redaction. Locally it writes decisions.jsonl (redacted state, up to 8 MB x 2) under the plugin data dir or ~/.bouncer.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to the normal Claude Code prompt or flow. Every error path returns no decision (pretooluse.ts header and standDown at 257-296): timeout, bad key, 429 or 5xx, malformed response, an unloadable policy, or a missing policy. A per-session circuit breaker stands down after repeated failures. A partly answered response can never produce allow. A truncated state cannot be approved. on_error: deny is opt-in and is a no-op in observe. Timeouts are the policy timeout_ms (default 800) with at most one retry inside the same deadline, under a 5 s Claude Code hook timeout. With no TypeSafe key set, adapterFor throws an auth error and the hook stands down silently. Hard rules run before the adapter, so seatbelt with no key still gives the deterministic floor. It also wastes a breaker and log write on each judged call.
entries.contextCost: Very low. There is no MCP server and no tool definitions. The hook injects no additionalContext, only a permissionDecisionReason or a rare systemMessage. The one skill description is about 500 chars (about 125 tokens) against the user's 2% skill budget. The four slash-command files add nothing until used. The bin/bouncer.cjs bundle is never loaded into context.
pros: Seatbelt mode is the right shape for this user's frequent bypassPermissions sessions: 19 deterministic hard rules (credential-file reads, git reset --hard, force push, clean -f, stash drop, credential literals on the command line, etc.) deny before any network call (hardrules.ts, default.yaml, evaluate.ts:231). Otherwise it is silent, so it adds no interruptions.

Careful safety engineering: observe by default, no path from error to block (pretooluse.ts:1-6), partial answers cannot allow, truncated state cannot allow, a per-session circuit breaker, and the policy cannot widen Claude Code permissions. The action description is sent instead of file contents or diffs.

Substantial verification for a 2-week-old repo: 34 test files, CI with gitleaks and pinned actions, 10 ADRs, a published calibration table (docs/calibration, 9 runs with committed jsonl), a frozen holdout set and a calibration harness with false-allow gates. The policy is versionable YAML per repo.
No context cost (no MCP, no injected text) and no shell exec in the hook path. Keys are env-only with *_FILE support, and are never forwarded to unrelated hosts.
The wire adapter is already the exact /systemone {model,state,questions} shape, so the fork to OpenRouter is small.
cons: OpenRouter is not supported in the hook. The hook is hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai with model jev-latest and a TypeSafe key (pretooluse.ts:434, jev.ts:19-20). The jev@<url> route exists only in calibrate, so the candidate's 'partial' rating overstates it. Using OpenRouter means forking, editing the TS and rebuilding the 12.9k-line committed bundle. The user would also need a separate TypeSafe key or a patch to use OPENROUTER_API_KEY.
Adds about 0.45-0.55 s (README 437/549 ms) to every judged Bash/Edit/Write, stacked on the gitnexus and no-secret-leak hooks. Bash calls that agents chain almost never hit the fast path (0 of 88).

Sends the redacted command line and file paths to a third party on every judged call. That is a problem for client work, and redaction is regex-shape only. OPENROUTER_API_KEY is still not in the user's no-secret-leak protected list, which is a separate gap.

Duplicates the user's fail-closed no-secret-leak hook. The value of the Jev questions on top of the hard rules is unproven for this user. Calibration is on the author's fixtures and mostly self-written, and Jev is known to be overconfident. It is not a security boundary, and the author says so.

Immature: created 2026-09-18, v0.2.9, 1 star, 2 forks, 2 human contributors plus Claude bot commits, no releases, a bundled artifact, and rapid churn (243 commits in 12 days). Observe mode as the default means no benefit until the user tunes the policy.

In defaultMode 'auto' the hook still runs and its ask/deny may stack with the auto classifier. The docs cover bypass and default modes, and the interaction with auto mode is not documented. Also, `full` (which can remove prompts) is explicitly not yet trusted by the author.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered, fail-safe permission gate that fits the bypassPermissions use case. But the hook cannot talk to OpenRouter: it is hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai, jev-latest and a TypeSafe key, and the jev@ compat route exists only in calibrate. Getting OpenRouter means forking and rebuilding the bundle, and the added latency, the overlap with the existing hooks and the egress of commands to a third party are real costs. Its deterministic seatbelt floor is worth stealing or running keyless, and the Jev layer is secondary.

judge.why: Its seatbelt mode is the right shape for bypass sessions: 19 deterministic hard rules deny before any network call, and it is otherwise silent. The Jev layer is secondary and cannot reach OpenRouter without a fork; steal the hard rules, or run it keyless.
pros: Seatbelt mode: deterministic deny floor for credential reads, force push, reset --hard, clean -f, with no interruptions and no network
Careful safety design: observe by default, partial answers can't allow, a circuit breaker, published calibration table, 34 test files, gitleaks in CI
Sends only a structured action description (never Write/Edit bodies)
cons: Not OpenRouter-capable in the hook; the jev@ compat route exists only in calibrate
0.44 to 0.55 s per judged call; the fast path matched 0 of 88 real calls
Committed 12.9k-line bundle is hard to audit; 2 weeks old, 243 commits (91 by a bot), observe mode by default
Overlaps the user's no-secret-leak hook; its interaction with auto mode is undocumented

entries.name: brunopivetta88/jev-claude (plugin "jev-guard")
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also Codex hook pack) that installs hooks on SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop. Before Bash/Write/Edit/NotebookEdit/WebFetch/Task/mcp__* calls it runs ~35 regex rules ("deterministic floor") and asks Jev 6 Noul questions plus 1 Score question (destructive, secret_exposure, exfiltration, prompt_injection, scope_creep, prod_impact, severity). It merges them with max() and maps the result through thresholds to allow/warn/ask/block. It ships in shadow (log-only) mode. PostToolUse asks 3 questions only on failure or when an action repeats 3 or more times. Stop asks 2 questions (goal_incomplete, unverified_claim) and can force the turn to continue. It is a safety guardrail, not a coding-assist feature. It is not an MCP server and has no skills that call Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. Claude Code runs it on every matching event without any prompting, which is exactly the "automatic" behaviour you asked for. However, it is purely a passive guardrail; Claude never consults Jev for coding decisions.
security: API key is sent as an Authorization: Bearer header from env vars (jev-client.mjs:135, index.mjs:161). It is not put in argv. The hook command line is only node bin/claude-hook.mjs, so no key appears in the process list.

Redaction of outbound payloads (src/redact.mjs:5-13) is regex-based: private keys, AKIA/ASIA, gh*_ tokens, sk-*, xox*, JWTs, KEY=value. It misses arbitrary secrets, DB URLs with passwords and proprietary source code. Each string field is truncated to 4000 chars and objects to 50 keys.

Egress is limited to the configured apiBase, with no telemetry beyond that. But the state dir defaults to '.jev-guard' resolved against the CWD (config.mjs:60, entry.mjs:37) unless CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA is set. In a client repo that could drop .jev-guard/ (session logs, decisions.jsonl, response cache) into the working tree, and it is only gitignored inside this repo.
JEV_GUARD_COLLECT=1 (off by default) writes full redacted tool inputs to disk for training.

A per-project jev-guard.config.json in cwd can override apiBase and provider (config.mjs:106-113). A malicious repo could point the hook's traffic, including your key and code snippets, at an attacker URL. The key is only sent when the URL is chosen via config, since it is attached in the adapter headers.

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs, and on failures tool outputs, are embedded in the Jev state JSON. Jev has no free text output, so the injection risk is mostly bypass of the classifier, and the deterministic floor still stands. With provider openai/anthropic the prompt-injection risk is higher.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured Jev endpoint, per evaluated call: the session goal (your prompt, redacted, max 1500 chars), the proposed tool name and its full tool_input (redacted, max 4000 chars per string field, so Bash commands, Write file content, Edit old/new strings and MCP arguments), the last 8 action summaries (200 chars each), and the cwd path. PostToolUse on failure or repeat also sends the tool result (last_result, sanitised) and the Stop hook sends the goal plus the action summaries. Read, Grep and Glob are never sent. Note the matcher mcp__.* also covers gitnexus and playwright calls (URLs, page content arguments). Whole file contents from Write/Edit leave the machine, so this is a real concern for client code under NDA. The local-only route is provider ollama or jevlab.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default (JEV_GUARD_FAIL_OPEN=1). Jev calls time out at 1500 ms (JEV_GUARD_TIMEOUT_MS), with an abort controller and a HARD_DEADLINE 8 s watchdog that exits 0 (entry.mjs:6-25). Internal exceptions become allow (run.mjs:63-72). A 200 with no parseable answers counts as a failure, not an all-clear. The deterministic floor still applies when Jev is down, and with failOpen=0 the outcome becomes 'ask'. Unparseable input exits 0. It is a well-designed failure path. Caveat: the Stop hook can exit 2 repeatedly to force continuation and I found no stop_hook_active loop guard.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool definitions and no server instructions. Two slash commands and one skill (descriptions about 300 chars, roughly 100 tokens) are added to the listing. The real cost is hook-injected text: in shadow mode, every action that would have warned or blocked injects an additionalContext line of the form 'jev-guard [shadow: would ask]: secret_exposure=0.62 (jev) -> ask...'. That is about 30-60 tokens, and only on non-allow outcomes. Enforce mode adds deny/ask reasons. The status message 'jev-guard: checking action' appears on each hooked call. Small overall.
pros: Fully automatic: five hook events wired through hooks/hooks.json. No prompt like 'use jev' is ever needed.
Well-engineered failure semantics (fail-open, 1.5 s per-request timeout, 8 s watchdog, cache, deterministic floor with Jev only able to raise signals), so a slow Jev cannot wedge Claude Code.

Never emits permissionDecision 'allow', so it cannot widen your permissions or interfere with your existing hooks. It only adds deny/ask/context. It uses Jev's real strengths: typed Noul/Score primitives, calibrated probabilities, no free text.
Shadow mode by default plus a decisions.jsonl audit trail and /jev-status help you tune thresholds. Only the risky tool set is evaluated, so read-only tools cost nothing.
Zero dependencies, Node >=20 only (you have Node 24), and no argv key leak or postinstall. It is fully readable in about 1750 lines.
Multi-provider abstraction lets you run the same hook against a local model (ollama/jevlab) for the sensitive client repos.
cons: OpenRouter is not first-class. The 'openrouter' preset talks to a chat-completions LLM rather than to Jev, and you would need to override JEV_GUARD_API_BASE and JEV_GUARD_MODEL and reuse JEV_GUARD_API_KEY for the OpenRouter key, all on the assumption that OpenRouter's System One schema equals TypeSafe's. That is unverified, and the repo has no test for it.

It only gives you a security guard, not Jev-assisted coding (no routing of tasks, no test-failure triage, no code-review scoring, no next-step decisions). Value beyond safety is low. In your bypass/auto permission mode that safety layer is arguably the most valuable piece, but only in enforce mode. In bypass mode I have not verified that a hook 'ask' still prompts.
Sends Write/Edit file content, Bash commands and MCP args to a third party on every evaluated call. That is a real NDA/client-code concern, and its regex redaction is incomplete.

Overlaps your existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) and the GitNexus hooks. The matcher mcp__.* adds a network call on every gitnexus and playwright MCP call, which are frequent.

Extremely immature: 3 commits over 3 days, one author, 0 stars, no releases, and an unclear maintainer identity (README/marketplace slug bruno-ship-it 404s vs brunopivetta88). The thresholds are guesses, never calibrated on real traffic. Jev is itself beta and Theo's claim that it is a 'flash router' is unverified.
Stop hook exit-2 can trap Claude in a continuation loop (no stop_hook_active guard), and can be a noisy and costly false-positive source ('goal_incomplete' judged from 8 action summaries only).
Default state dir '.jev-guard' resolves against cwd if CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA is missing, which may pollute client repos.
Repo-level jev-guard.config.json can redirect the endpoint, a supply-chain risk when opening untrusted repos.
License is a modified MIT with an attribution request and is not clean for client work.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here that gives truly automatic, hook-driven Jev use in Claude Code, with sound fail-open engineering, but it is a 3-day-old solo guardrail with no OpenRouter-native path and heavy code egress. If you try it, install it pinned and read, run it in shadow mode, route through OpenRouter via env overrides only after you verify the System One schema, and keep it off client repos (or point it at ollama/jevlab) until it has matured.

entries.name: 0xwhrari/jev-agent-switch
entries.what: PreToolUse (*) gate: local redaction and policy, then Jev for ambiguous calls returns pass/review/deny (ask or deny in CC, never allow). Configurable failMode open/closed.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (PreToolUse on all tools)
pros: Local-first: read-only and catastrophic patterns resolved without network; secret redaction before sending
Never returns allow, so cannot weaken permissions; endpoint configurable via env
