Scores drift by up to 0.08 on repeated runs, and the Codex example shows a description phrased as a question dropping serves_task from >0.9 to 0.54, so it is sensitive to the wording of the state.
Data egress to OpenRouter and TypeSafe of every command line, cwd and agent description on client projects (confidentiality/contract risk). Retention policy not verified.
Bun is assumed (user has Node 24, so a port is needed), plus alpha endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) and a beta model, so the API may change. The recipe is about 2 weeks old.
Adds a serialized network round trip before each gated Bash call and one more hook process to an already busy Bash hook chain (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post, caveman).
No Read/Grep/Glob/Edit coverage in the published version, only Bash. Jev cannot judge code quality, so it does not help the actual coding work, only tool gating.
entries.verdict: Useful as a design reference and the only concrete route to automatic, zero-context, deterministic Jev use in Claude Code via a hook, but it is a copy-paste snippet whose stock Claude Code variant (PermissionRequest, fail-open, Bun) does not fit a bypass/auto-mode user. Worth adopting only as a self-written PreToolUse hook (node, fail-closed to ask/deny, Bash-only, after the regex guard) if the user accepts sending commands and paths to OpenRouter/TypeSafe.
entries.license: Docs page under OpenRouter's site terms. No license grant for the snippets was seen. Endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions, an alpha API, and the model is beta.

entries.name: jevexec (Abhishekvrshny)
entries.what: Node (ESM, ink/react for TUI) command guard for Claude Code and Codex. Registers PreToolUse and PermissionRequest hooks (matcher .*). Local regex hard-deny list, then Jev (typed score/noul questions via OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions) for user natural-language guardrails (PreToolUse) and risk/approval/authorization (PermissionRequest). Emits deny/ask/allow, or nothing to defer to the host prompt. Redacted JSONL audit log plus an ink monitor TUI.
interface: No MCP tools, no skills, no plugin.json/marketplace.json
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks on every tool call (PreToolUse) and every permission prompt (PermissionRequest). Fully automatic, no prompting needed. Value depends on the user having authored guardrails. With none, PreToolUse only enforces 6 regex hard-denies.
security: Installer install.sh is designed for curl|bash: git clone into ~/.local/share/jevexec, npm install (runs dependency install scripts), symlink in ~/.local/bin, and edits ~/.claude/settings.json (atomic write, preserves other hooks). Hook command uses an absolute node path (install.sh:221), which is good for this user's PATH override.

src/updater.js auto-updates on every hook run, at most once per 24h: a detached background process runs git fetch and merge --ff-only from the author's main branch into the install dir, and that code then runs as your hook. It is opt-out via JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0 and skipped if the checkout is dirty or off main. It is a live supply-chain channel with no npm install or signature check. Set JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0.

Key handling is decent. It is sent via the Authorization header (not argv). The env file ~/.config/jevexec/env is 600 and rejected otherwise (env.js:306), with symlink refusal in install.sh:41. Only three secret names are loaded. The key sits in plaintext there, and the user's no-secret-leak hook does not protect that path or OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Prompt-injection surface: state includes tool command/path/url fields (safeInput allow-list, 4000 chars each), cwd and user guardrail text. Tool output and file contents are excluded. An attacker-controlled command string can still steer Jev toward 'low risk' and 'authorized'. The local HARD_DENY regexes are trivially bypassable (core.js:6-13) and the READ_ONLY allow-list is narrow. The redact() regex is heuristic.
Local audit.jsonl (600, capped 1 MB, keeps last 500 lines) stores redacted commands and paths, so secrets not matching the redaction patterns could persist locally.
No telemetry beyond the provider call and the git update check. No shell exec except spawnSync bash install.sh (hooks install) and git in the updater.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (or JEV_BASE_URL): per hook call that reaches Jev, host, tool name, selected input fields (command/cmd/script/path/paths/file_path/cwd/url/query/pattern/method/host, each redacted and cut to 4000 chars), cwd, user_intent (only if the host supplies user_prompt), and the full text of all enabled user guardrails. Also the model name. The request is sent as one JSON string and refused if over 32,000 characters. No file contents or tool output. github.com via git for the daily update check unless disabled.
entries.failureMode: Provider failure is fail-open to the normal prompt. Timeout 15s (AbortSignal.timeout, jev.js:86), one retry on 429/5xx under the same 15s budget, hook timeout 20s. Errors become 'unavailable', which produces no output and lets the host decide. The exception is that cli.js:26-29 sets exit code 2 on any thrown error (bad stdin JSON, audit-file write failure such as a full disk or bad permissions in audit() at cli.js:56, unsupported event). Exit 2 from a Claude PreToolUse hook blocks the tool call, so those cases fail closed. A missing node_modules would crash on the static ink import in monitor.js (exit 1, non-blocking). Oversize payloads throw and defer to the host. With guardrails configured, an 'uncertain' Jev answer maps to 'ask' semantics but is emitted as nothing at PreToolUse, so the normal flow decides.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP/tool-definition tokens and no skill listing. No additionalContext injection. The hook only adds a deny or ask reason text when it fires, plus the statusMessage 'jevexec: assessing action' in the UI on every tool call.
pros: OpenRouter is the native default: /api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/jev.js:3-10, 181-186). No patching. Base URL, model and provider are overridable.

Sensible design: typed score/noul questions, thresholds (allow only with risk < 0.35, authorization >= 0.8, no rule conflict), and unavailable/uncertain results defer to the normal prompt instead of allowing (core.js:43-69, adapters.js:174-194). It never returns allow at PreToolUse, so it can't override other hooks' denies.

Good key hygiene: header auth, not argv, 600 env file enforced, redaction of audit entries and error bodies, payload bound with no silent guardrail truncation (jev.js:82-85). Hook command written with absolute node path via shlex.quote (install.sh:221). Installer merges settings non-destructively and has an uninstall.
Zero context cost, purely deterministic invocation, MIT license, 4 mocked test files, and a useful audit log plus monitor for reviewing decisions.
The natural-language guardrail feature (e.g. 'never touch client X repo', 'no pushes to main') is a distinctive capability that pure regex hooks lack, for client-project safety.
cons: The authorization signal cannot work on Claude Code. cli.js:48 reads input.user_prompt, but Claude Code hook stdin carries no user prompt (grep: no transcript reading anywhere). The intent is always undefined, and the question defaults to 'missing intent = not authorized' (jev.js:57). So authorization is expected to stay below 0.8 and PermissionRequest will almost never auto-allow on Claude. That is my inference from Claude's hook input schema, not run-verified. The headline value (safe auto-approval) is therefore largely absent, and PermissionRequest reduces to deny-on-rule-conflict.

Does not fit this user's modes. Defaults are auto and frequent bypassPermissions, where PermissionRequest doesn't fire. Only PreToolUse remains, and it acts only on hand-written guardrails or six easily bypassed regexes. The cookbook pattern (static risky regex then reversible/serves_task Noul questions) is a better fit and lighter.

Repo is 4 days old, 1 author, 20 commits, 0 stars, no releases, package private, alpha /alpha endpoint. Behavior is calibrated only by guessed thresholds ('release calibration remains future work' in docs/architecture.md). Jev overconfidence and injected-instruction weakness apply directly to the allow decision.

Auto-update from the author's main branch inside the hook path (updater.js) plus curl|bash install and npm install is an ongoing supply-chain exposure for a security control on client projects. Must set JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0 and pin a commit.

Robustness gaps: exit code 2 on internal errors blocks tools, and audit failure occurs after assessment and can block. Static ink/react import on every hook adds startup latency. matcher .* means every tool call pays Node startup, and with guardrails a Jev call, next to the gitnexus and no-secret-leak hooks.

hooks/claude.json uses ${PLUGIN_ROOT} with no plugin manifest, so it can't be used as a Claude plugin. The installer writes directly into ~/.claude/settings.json. Key stored in ~/.config/jevexec/env is not covered by the no-secret-leak hook (OPENROUTER_API_KEY still needs adding). A CLI-installed runtime lives outside plugin management.
entries.verdict: Well-structured, OpenRouter-native Jev permission hook with sane fail-to-prompt semantics, but it is 4 days old and its main value (authorization-based auto-allow) likely can't work on Claude Code because there is no user_prompt in hook input. It is also moot under the user's bypassPermissions sessions and adds per-call Node/ink startup, and it carries an auto-update-from-main risk. Better to copy the cookbook PermissionRequest pattern than adopt this, unless the user specifically wants NL guardrails, and then only with JEVEXEC_AUTO_UPDATE=0 and a pinned commit.

entries.name: Barry2llen/agent-jev-approval
entries.what: Small Python package: Codex PermissionRequest hook that applies hard rules, then Jev via official SDK, and only emits ALLOW; otherwise falls back to the native prompt.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (PermissionRequest, Codex only)
pros: Same allow-only, fail-to-user design as the OpenRouter cookbook gate; core ApprovalRequest/Provider/engine is agent-agnostic
Audit log (JEV_AUDIT_LOG) and hard rules run before any provider call
Python package with tests
cons: Only a Codex adapter; Claude Code explicitly out of scope so a PermissionRequest adapter would need writing
Official SDK reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY; OpenRouter only if SDK base_url is overridden
0 stars, MVP; cookbook already covers the same pattern

entries.name: claude-jev-gate (punkcanyang)
entries.what: Python plugin: PermissionRequest hook auto-clicks allow-once on high-confidence Jev approve else defers to human; plus optional local Anthropic-compatible proxy for routing and trim/compress. All off by default.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (PermissionRequest) when enabled
pros: Uses PermissionRequest (the right event; matches the OpenRouter cookbook) with deny/unsure/timeout falling back to human
prove_* scripts and CI, mock-guarded, redaction module, loopback-only authenticated proxy
Three independent default-off switches
cons: Uses typesafe_sdk with TYPESAFE_API_KEY only; no OpenRouter path (needs SDK/base URL patch); Chinese-language docs
Bash matcher scope not clear and no static RISKY regex first; proxy trim/compress rewrites context (risky) and targets DeepSeek/Anthropic upstreams
0 stars, alpha, created 5 days ago; depends on typesafe_sdk on sys.path

entries.name: choiyounggi/jev-gate
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (v0.3.1, installed via marketplace choiyounggi/groundwork) that uses a Jev-compatible System One endpoint (default: LOCAL ollaya server at http://localhost:11435/v1/systemone serving Gemma-4-based winnow:e4b) for three things: (1) PreToolUse Bash gate: hard regex denylist (exit 2 in strict mode), read-only fast path (allow, no model call), then a model layer asking a Choice (risk clear/caution) plus a Noul (destructive) on the command, mapping to allow/ask/exit-2; (2) Stop/SubagentStop gate that blocks a turn once if the last message claims done (p>=0.8) with no verification evidence (p<=0.2); (3) `decide` MCP tool (from the ollaya binary) plus a jev-decide skill telling the agent when to hand classification/ranking/yes-no to the model. It is a safety/guardrail layer, not a productivity assistant. Written for a Korean-speaking macOS user (Korean stop-gate message, Korean docs).
entries.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks (PreToolUse Bash, Stop, SubagentStop, SessionStart): these fire automatically with no prompting, which matches the user's goal of not saying 'use jev'. The decide MCP tool is model-discretion, reinforced by the jev-decide skill description trigger (Korean trigger phrases plus 'three or more items with same criteria'); the author also had to add a line to global CLAUDE.md to make it reliable (hooks/NOTES.md:16), so unprompted use of decide is weak.
security: MIT license; no npm postinstall or package manifest. README.md declares no telemetry; none found in hooks. Logs every decision (full Bash command text, cwd) to ~/.local/state/jev-gate/decisions.jsonl and last-message head to stop-decisions.jsonl, unbounded and world-default perms; could persist secrets typed inline in commands.

scripts/setup-ollaya.sh downloads https://ollaya.dev/install.sh and runs it with sh (curl|sh pattern, script says 'sha256-verified' but that verification is inside the third-party installer); pulls a multi-GB model; starts a background server. Only runs if the user invokes /jev-gate:setup, but the SessionStart hook and setup skill description actively steer the agent toward it. Not executed by me.
Third-party binary 'ollaya' is launched as MCP server by .mcp.json with plugin-provided launcher; unaudited.

Prompt-injection surface: command text and the agent's own last message are fed to the model, mitigated by 'treat as data' instructions and by design where the model can only return allow/ask/block, never widen permissions beyond fast-path/allow; but model 'allow' (clear p>=0.8 and destructive<=0.2) does emit permissionDecision allow, which in normal (non-bypass) mode can auto-approve commands, though README reports the model produced 0 allow in field data because clear confidence maxed at 0.77.

Regex denylist is bypassable by design (README/NOTES admit 18 bypasses found in review, e.g. node -e rmSync); author is candid about this. Fast-path allowlist includes grep/rg/find/sed -n etc. with a global escape-token screen.
Auth: hooks send no credentials at all today; a patch for OpenRouter would put the bearer token on curl's argv (visible in /proc) unless done via -H @file or --config.
entries.dataEgress: With default config nothing leaves the machine (local ollaya on localhost:11435). If pointed to OpenRouter/TypeSafe: every non-fast-path Bash command (up to 3000 chars: first 2000 + last 800), its description field and cwd are sent per call, plus the last 4000 chars of every assistant final message at each Stop/SubagentStop (this can include code, diffs, file paths, client names and any secrets echoed in commands or output summaries). Read-only fast-path commands are not sent. The existing secret-leak guard hook would need to run before this one to be useful; hook ordering is not controlled. Bash commands inline-containing tokens (e.g. curl -H 'Authorization: ...') would be sent to a third party for client projects. Local logs keep the full command text.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere for the model layer: missing jq, curl error or timeout (default 6s Bash, 6s Stop), unparseable JSON, empty fields all exit 0 with a log line and no decision; the model never auto-allows on error. Deterministic denylist stays fail-closed (exit 2) independent of the model and will block matching commands even if Jev is down. Hook timeouts in hooks.json are 10s (Bash) and 15s (Stop), so worst case adds 6s to a non-fast-path Bash call and 6s to every turn end when the endpoint hangs; with an unreachable localhost it fails instantly.
entries.contextCost: Low. One MCP server 'ollaya' with 4 tools (decide, list_models, show_model, pull_model): roughly 600-1000 tokens of definitions (estimate, tool schemas live in the ollaya binary, not readable statically); no server-level instructions in repo. Two skills add descriptions to the skill list: jev-decide (~450 chars) and setup (~400 chars), about 200-250 tokens in total, in Korean. Hooks inject text only on SessionStart when unhealthy (~600-900 chars, about 200 tokens per session) and on block/ask messages. Note the MCP server starts a third-party binary each session and fails with stderr if ollaya is not installed, showing a failed-MCP entry.
pros: Genuinely automatic: hooks fire on every Bash call and every turn end with no user prompting, and the code is fail-open on Jev errors (jev-bash-gate.sh:220-223, 252-253; jev-stop-gate.sh:55-56).

Well-designed pattern for using Jev typed decisions: Choice+Noul question schema, thresholds, deterministic layer first, model can only escalate, full JSONL decision log for tuning (jev-bash-gate.sh:45-51, 206-219). Good reference code for a custom hook against OpenRouter.

Unusually honest engineering: README documents field data from 1,023 Bash decisions and 344 stop decisions, admits model produced 0 useful allows (clear p max 0.77), discloses 18 regex bypasses found in review, and keeps regression tests for them.

Most tests of any candidate here: about 73 pytest cases (test_gate.py 45, test_stop_gate.py 11, test_recommend 7, test_eval 7, test_preflight 3) with a fake TypeSafe-compatible server (tests/conftest.py), so the hooks can be tested without a model.
Env-configurable URL/model/thresholds/timeouts (README table) so pointing at hosted Jev needs little more than an auth header.
Stop-gate 'done claimed without evidence' check is a plausible daily-coding quality feature: 3 blocks in 344 turns, 2 made the agent quote real output.
cons: Does not work with OpenRouter as shipped: no Authorization header is ever sent (curl at jev-bash-gate.sh:220 and jev-stop-gate.sh:55) and no OPENROUTER_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY handling; the whole design is built around a local ollaya server and an ~8 GB Gemma-4 model download, not around hosted Jev. Unverified that OpenRouter's /systemone request/response shape matches.

Thresholds and prompts calibrated only for local winnow:e4b on a 50-item Korean, single-labeler dataset (README limits section); no measurement of typesafe/jev-1.13. Even for winnow the model never produced a confident allow, so the model layer adds only 'ask' friction.

Wrong problem for the user's goal: it is a safety gate, not something that makes Claude Code use Jev where Jev adds value. In bypass/auto mode, model 'ask' just runs the command interactively (README: 41/41) and is denied headless, so the useful path is exit 2 hard blocks, which the user did not ask for and will cause friction on legitimate client work (sudo, curl POST, git push -f, gh release create, crontab, git restore, checkout --).

Overlaps with and adds a second PreToolUse Bash hook next to the user's existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks; with hosted Jev it would send every non-trivial Bash command and every final assistant message to OpenRouter, including possibly client code and inline secrets.
Latency tax: a model call on every Stop/SubagentStop and on non-read-only Bash calls; heredoc denylist false positives (3 of 1,023) and known regex bypasses.

Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-29, 4 commits (all by 1 contributor), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI; hard-coded to author's macOS setup in NOTES.md, Korean-only stop-gate message, Korean skill triggers (jev-decide description is Korean, so English prompts may rarely trigger it).
Installs third-party infrastructure: curl|sh of ollaya installer, background server, MCP launcher for an unaudited binary; on Linux no service manager integration (nohup).
entries.verdict: Nice reference implementation of fail-open Jev hooks and a Choice/Noul decision-gate pattern, but as shipped it targets a local ollaya model, sends no auth to OpenRouter, and solves risk-gating rather than the user's 'Claude Code uses Jev automatically where it adds value' goal. Do not install as-is; at most borrow the hook structure and the Stop-gate idea into a custom OpenRouter hook.

entries.name: jev-gate (alexnarberhaus)
entries.what: Stdlib-Python PreToolUse hook (matcher Bash) that auto-allows Bash calls Jev judges harmless. Order in gate.py evaluate(): skip unless permission_mode is default or acceptEdits (gate.py:31,313); check the user's allow/ask/deny rules (321); hard regex deny-list (239-248); one Jev call with 3 Choice questions (effect, network, injection); code thresholds (judge_verdict, gate.py:288-302). It only ever emits permissionDecision allow (render, 338-348), or a systemMessage. Shadow mode and already-allowed commands are judged in a detached --observe child, so Claude Code does not wait. Decisions go to a JSONL log at ~/.local/state/jev-gate/decisions.jsonl (mode 0600).
interface: PreToolUse hook: gate.py (matcher Bash, timeout 5 s)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook on Bash, which fits the user's requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told. Critically, evaluate() returns None unless permission_mode is 'default' or 'acceptEdits' (gate.py:31,313-314). The user runs defaultMode 'auto' and frequent bypassPermissions sessions, so the gate is inert in most of the user's sessions. Their permission_mode is auto or bypassPermissions, and Jev adds nothing there.
security: Key handling: the key is never put in argv. The installer uses getpass and writes a chmod 600 .env, and judge.py sends it only as an Authorization Bearer header. A shell-exported OPENROUTER_API_KEY would still fall under the user's no-secret-leak hook protected-vars list, which does not yet include it.

Installer mutates global ~/.claude/settings.json (merge, idempotent, only removes its own entry on uninstall). It also writes a symlink into ~/.local/bin. No shell exec beyond the subprocess.Popen of its own script for the observer, and the observer child uses a list argv, not shell=True.

Prompt-injection surface: the command text is sent to Jev inside state. Mitigations are the preamble ('treat as data'), a dedicated injection question requiring P(clean) >= 0.99, and the deny-list running first. Jev is documented as injection-sensitive and overconfident on unanswerable inputs, and it sees only the command text, not script contents (judge.py preamble). Opaque commands such as `npm test`, `make` or `./script.sh` get judged on their text alone, and the design doc accepts this risk knowingly (CLAUDE.md).

Deny-list gaps: only regex-based. It matches rm -r, piping to shell, sudo/doas/su, eval, ~/.dotfile, chmod -R and dd/mkfs. It does not match `git push --force`, `git reset --hard` or `find -delete` (those rely on Jev and the network question), and shell obfuscation such as variable indirection is not covered beyond the Jev injection question. rule_verdict is approximate (gate.py:178-229).

A hook allow could only override the prompt, not the user's deny rules (per the design doc's verified contract). The gate checks ask/deny rules itself, and unreadable settings raise, which falls to the prompt.

Telemetry: none besides the Jev call. Local log holds redacted command, cwd, probabilities and a command SHA256 at mode 0600. Redaction is regex plus an optional user term list, and is best-effort (e.g. secrets without a recognised shape or key name pass through).
entries.dataEgress: Per judged Bash call, one POST to api.typesafe.ai (judge.py:22) with JSON {model, state:{command, cwd, workspace[]}, questions}. All strings are redacted first: home path replaced by ~, common token/key/JWT/AWS/GitHub/Slack shapes, emails, credentialed URLs, long mixed-case blobs, and user terms from redact.txt (judge.py:88-124). Nothing else is sent (no file contents, no transcript). Against OpenRouter, the same would go to OpenRouter (a provider hop), and OpenRouter's own logging or retention policy would apply. Best-effort redaction still leaves client paths, repo names and hostnames visible unless the user lists them in redact.txt.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to the normal prompt, never fail-closed. Missing key, timeout, HTTP error, bad JSON, parse failure, malformed config or any exception ends with no output and exit 0 (gate.py:426-428). The Jev call has a 1.5 s total budget enforced by a thread join (judge.py _post_with_deadline, gate.py:38), inside a 5 s hook timeout. Under bypassPermissions or auto the gate does nothing, so it adds no protection there either.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions and no MCP server or skill. The hook injects nothing into context in shadow mode. In explain and auto modes it may emit one-line systemMessage text such as 'jev-gate: asking: ...' (roughly 30-60 tokens), shown to the user and not the model as far as I can tell.
pros: Deterministic hook with a safe design: allow-only output, code owns the decision, fail-to-prompt everywhere, 1.5 s budget inside a 5 s timeout, and the user's ask/deny rules are honoured (gate.py:326-327).

Good egress hygiene: redaction runs before the send, with a user-defined redact.txt for client names, which suits the client-project use case. The log is chmod 600 and stores a hash plus a redacted command.
Includes an injection question (P(clean) >= 0.99), tiered thresholds, an eval harness with labelled real and adversarial commands plus a cache, and about 125 unit tests.

Stdlib only, small (about 2,000 lines of Python), and readable in an afternoon. Shadow mode with a live watcher lets you measure precision and prompt savings before enabling auto. Background judging keeps the hot path fast.
Needs only about 3 lines patched to move to OpenRouter's /v1/systemone, since the request and response schemas already match.
cons: Skips every permission mode except default and acceptEdits (gate.py:313). The user's defaultMode is auto and they often run bypassPermissions, so the gate would rarely fire. Removing the restriction would turn it into a model-based auto-approver in modes where Claude Code already decides, which the author explicitly refuses to do.

Its purpose is removing prompts, not adding safety or value beyond that. For a user already in auto or bypass mode, Jev's main possible value (a risk second opinion) would need to be reworked to deny or ask, and this code deliberately never does that.
TypeSafe-only: hardcoded endpoint (judge.py:22), TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and model id jev-1.13.0, which may not match OpenRouter's id. It needs a fork and a small patch.

No license, 0 stars, 1 author, 7 commits, created 2 days before the audit and no releases. No track record. The claimed 100% precision was not verified and Jev is documented as overconfident on unanswerable input.

Bash only, with regex deny-list gaps (git push --force, git reset --hard, find -delete and similar rely on Jev). Auto-approving from text alone is risky for opaque commands such as `npm test` or `make`.

Installer edits global settings.json itself. The README's macOS and managed-proxy focus (CA_FALLBACK, /Library/Application Support paths) is not relevant on Linux. Also, the gate hard-codes home-directory assumptions.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered, fail-safe idea, but it is a prompt-remover that deliberately does nothing in auto and bypassPermissions modes, which are this user's normal modes. It is also TypeSafe-only and unlicensed, with 0 stars. Only its redaction module and question wording are worth borrowing (for example into the official PermissionRequest cookbook hook); as a drop-in it adds no daily value for this user.
entries.license: None (GitHub licenseInfo is null and there is no LICENSE file). All rights reserved by default, so reuse or forking has no explicit grant.

entries.name: OpenRouter cookbook: Auto-Approve Coding Agent Permission Prompts with Jev (reference impl: PanAchy/jevvy)
entries.what: Official OpenRouter recipe: a Bun/TS PermissionRequest hook for Claude Code (also Codex, Cursor, OpenCode plugin). A static RISKY regex list runs first. Otherwise it asks Jev two Noul questions ("reversible" and "serves_task") and auto-allows the Bash command only if both score >= 0.9. It abstains, leaving the normal prompt, on any error, timeout or low score. It only reduces permission prompts for Bash commands. It does not add reasoning, code search, routing or review. The installable reference implementation is PanAchy/jevvy (npm @jevvy/permissions v0.5.0, MIT, Claude Code plugin jevvy-permissions@jevvy). It ships its own calibrated four-question policy (harmful, sensitive, untrusted, obscured, all as max-Noul thresholds) and supports providers zen, typesafe, openrouter, vercel, laya and custom.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest, matcher Bash). It fires automatically without any prompt, but ONLY when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog. Per the Claude Code hooks docs (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, fetched via summarizer, so verify locally), PermissionRequest fires in default, plan and acceptEdits modes. It does NOT fire in auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions modes.
security: Recipe: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from process.env in the hook. It is not placed in argv and stays out of ps output. The hook does not run any shell command itself.

Recipe: the RISKY regex list is a heuristic denylist. Bypasses via unusual shell constructs are plausible, and the final gate is an LLM-style probabilistic score. The docs call the scores noisy (0.02-0.05 variance) and tell users to tighten RISKY themselves.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command text and description go into the Jev state. Jev returns typed probabilities only, with no free text and no tool execution, so injection can at worst bias a score. That is still a real risk when it converts a prompt into an automatic allow.

Risk to this user: an auto-allow is a security downgrade whenever a false positive gets through. The Claude Code docs page (fetched via summarizer, so unverified) says a hook 'allow' can override deny rules. The recipe claims it cannot. Check this before trusting it.

Jevvy reads a global config only (~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc). Project repos cannot override it. The key can sit in plaintext JSONC or come from env, and there is a redact helper for error text. Jevvy is a 5-week-old npm package (0.5.0). Installing it runs 3rd-party code with access to the command stream, so pin the version. The workflows pin action SHAs.
No telemetry was seen in the recipe. Jevvy telemetry was not exhaustively audited. Nothing was executed.
entries.dataEgress: Recipe hook sends to openrouter.ai, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe. The payload is the full Bash command string, the absolute project cwd, and (when present) the tool 'description' as the task. Only requests that would otherwise prompt are sent. It does not send file contents, diffs, the conversation or tool outputs. Command strings can still embed inline secrets or client paths. The cwd leaks client project names and paths. Jevvy sends less, only state {action:'shell', resource:<command>}. It does not send cwd or a task. Nothing leaves the machine except for prompt-eligible Bash commands.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to the normal permission prompt, meaning it abstains. Recipe: network errors, non-OK responses, invalid probabilities and an 8 s timeout all return undefined, so no output and the normal prompt shows. It is never fail-closed on Claude Code. The Cursor variant has failClosed true, but the script returns 'ask' on errors. The claude hook timeout of 15 s (recipe) or 10 s (jevvy) caps the worst case. Jevvy adds a 5 s per-request timeout, an in-memory cache and a provider cooldown after auth or credit failures. Missing key gives a one-time SessionStart warning and no auto-approval.
entries.contextCost: Zero. No MCP tools and no skill descriptions (the optional calibrate-permissions skill is separate). The hook only emits JSON or a one-time SessionStart systemMessage warning when misconfigured. The cost is about $0.0000168 per 400-token request.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a deterministic hook and needs no 'use jev' prompt, which matches the user's requirement in its permission mode.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected text.
Fail-open to the normal prompt. It can only remove prompts, never block work. Timeouts are bounded (8 s / 15 s).
Uses OpenRouter directly (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so nothing needs patching. Jevvy also supports openrouter natively.
Cheap: about $0.00002 per decision. Small egress compared with an MCP that sees code.

Jevvy has real engineering: 28 commits, 15+ test files, CI with pinned action SHAs, changesets releases, a calibration corpus (eval/commands.json), MIT license, and a Claude Code plugin (marketplace.json, hooks.json). It skips explicit ask rules and never overrides allow/deny.
Coexists with the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks, because it only touches the PermissionRequest event.
cons: Wrong fit for this user's mode: the user runs bypass or 'auto', and PermissionRequest does not fire in auto, dontAsk or bypassPermissions, so the hook would rarely or never run. It only helps in default, plan or acceptEdits. Worse, it swaps a human prompt for a probabilistic auto-allow, which can be less safe than default mode.
It does not make Claude Code use Jev for coding decisions such as routing, review, test selection, refactor choices or model selection. It is a permission-prompt reducer only.
Only Bash is covered. There is no Edit/Write/MCP gating in the recipe or jevvy hook.
The recipe sends cwd and the description to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe). This matters on client projects. Jevvy sends the command only.
Scores are noisy (0.02-0.05 variance). The recipe's 'reversible' Noul can mis-score commands with side effects outside the repo. The user must maintain their own RISKY list.

The recipe needs Bun and a hand-wired settings.json. Jevvy needs Node >= 22.19 (the user has Node 24), but it is a 5-week-old 0.5.0 package with ~20 stars, one main author (21 of 28 commits) and no proven track record.

Docs conflict on whether a hook 'allow' overrides deny rules (recipe says no, the Claude Code hooks page says yes), and the Claude Code docs page was read through a summarizer, so it is unverified. Needs a local test in default mode.
Key handling: an API key in the hook environment or in ~/.config/jevvy/jevvy.jsonc plaintext. Codex strips *KEY* env vars, though this does not apply to Claude Code.
entries.verdict: This is well built, safe (fail-open, tiny egress, zero context) and OpenRouter-native, but it is a narrow permission-prompt shortcut, not a Jev integration for coding. It also does not fire in the auto or bypass modes this user normally runs. Use it only if the user moves to default or acceptEdits mode and wants fewer Bash prompts, preferably via pinned jevvy with the openrouter provider, not the raw recipe.
entries.license: MIT (jevvy). The recipe is docs code.

entries.name: anpicasso/hermes-jev-approvals
entries.what: A Hermes Agent (NousResearch) model-provider plugin, not a Claude Code hook. It registers a fake OpenAI-style chat client named typesafe-jev. Hermes' smart-approval guardian sends it a <command> block, and the plugin turns that into a Jev Decisions/System One request with 6 typed questions: verdict (Choice), policy_allows, self_advocating, reads_secrets, sends_outbound (Noul) and blast_radius (Score). A deterministic rule chain in jev_policy.py then maps the answers to APPROVE, DENY or ESCALATE. It refuses every other prompt and registers no hooks. It is useful only as a design pattern and reference code for a Claude Code PreToolUse permission gate.
interface: Hermes provider typesafe-jev (kind: model-provider in plugin/plugin.yaml)
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic inside Hermes (transparent: core calls the auxiliary.approval provider whenever a command matches its risky-pattern detector in smart mode). Not usable in Claude Code at all: it cannot be installed there, and the equivalent would be a deterministic PreToolUse hook that you write yourself. That is the fully automatic, no-prompt path the user wants.
security: Good egress hygiene: _validated_base_url enforces https on the default port only, rejects URL credentials, query strings and fragments (__init__.py:373-407)
Cross-origin redirects are blocked so the Authorization header cannot leak (_SameOriginRedirects, :426-446)
Custom hosts never inherit the TypeSafe or OpenRouter key; the key comes only from an explicit key_env (:293-340)

Command redacted before egress via Hermes core redact_sensitive_text(force=True) plus CLI-flag/URL/cookie/curl -u passes, capped at 4000 chars; self-described as best-effort. The redactor depends on Hermes core, so it is not portable as is
API key sent as an Authorization header, not in argv, when it uses urllib in-process
Stdlib only, no third-party dependencies, no postinstall or curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the chosen Jev endpoint
entries.dataEgress: To the configured Jev endpoint (OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions, or api.typesafe.ai): the redacted shell command (max 4000 chars), the description of why it was flagged (max 500), the full operator smart_policy text, the model id and the 6 question definitions. No file contents, diffs, chat history or tool outputs. Locally it writes a JSONL log of redacted commands. If ported to Claude Code, the egress would be Bash commands (and possibly file paths for Read/Edit), which is client code and secrets exposure to OpenRouter and its upstream provider; the redaction must be re-implemented.
entries.failureMode: Fail-to-human (fail-closed for approvals). Any exception, malformed or missing answer, non-2xx or timeout raises, and Hermes core then escalates to the user. There are up to 3 attempts with backoff on 429/529/5xx/network under a 25 s overall deadline (_DEADLINE_S), a default client timeout of 30 s, and the call blocks the agent turn. A missing verdict is read as ESCALATE, but a missing answer to any of the other 5 questions raises. In a Claude Code port you would need to decide between fail-open (fall through to normal permission handling) and ask.
entries.contextCost: None in Claude Code, since it is not a Claude Code component. It registers no MCP tools, injects no hook text and adds no skill. The pattern (a PreToolUse hook that outputs a permissionDecision) would add zero tokens when it allows silently, and only a short reason string on ask or deny.
pros: The only candidate found so far that shows a concrete, working, reasoned use of all three Jev primitives (Choice, Noul, Score) for a real agent-permission decision, with the exact request/response shape against OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions (plugin/__init__.py:895-908)
Confirms OpenRouter Decisions API works with model ~typesafe/jev-latest and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, which removes an integration unknown
jev_policy.py is a clean, pure, golden-tested rule chain (67 lines) that could be lifted straight into a Claude Code PreToolUse hook that returns allow/ask/deny
Fail-safe design: no answer is not a yes, truncated commands never auto-approve, self_advocating prompt-injection question
Strong egress hardening (https-only, same-origin redirects, key isolation, redaction, size cap) is a good checklist for our own hook
Includes offline evaluation tooling and a frozen holdout fixture (24 cases), stdlib-only, MIT licence
Would suit the user's habit of bypass/auto permission mode: a Jev gate could replace blanket bypass with fast typed risk scoring
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: it is a Hermes model-provider plugin (kind: model-provider) that needs Hermes core APIs (agent.redact, provider registry, auth pool); it cannot be installed in Claude Code
No MCP server, no hooks, no skill; nothing to install for our use case, and README explicitly says it registers no hooks

Very young and small: created 2026-09-17, 27 commits, 1 real author (23 anpicasso and 4 Angello Picasso, apparently the same person), 20 stars, 3 forks, v0.3.0 released 2026-09-20; no CI workflow (.github is missing)
Tests are mostly script-style checks, and the plugin/tests files have 0 pytest def test functions (only test_scripts.py has 3), so coverage is unclear. Several are live-network checks
Benchmark claims (8.7x faster, 4.4x fewer prompts, 153 commands) are self-measured on a small corpus and baseline-specific, as the author admits in plugin.yaml

Recall depends on Hermes' upstream regex detector, and the author's own docs show exfil commands such as curl -T ~/.aws/credentials can bypass review (TECHNICAL.md:236-256). A Jev gate is only as good as what you route to it
Sending Bash commands from client projects to OpenRouter and an upstream provider is a data-exposure decision, and the redaction is best-effort
Adds a fail-open vs fail-closed design choice and up to 25 s of retry blocking if ported naively
Solves permission approval only, not code review, routing, classification or other daily coding tasks; low value for a user who mostly runs bypass mode unless they want a safety net
entries.verdict: Not installable in Claude Code (Hermes-only provider plugin), so it scores low as an integration. It is still the best reference implementation found for a single, valuable, hands-off Jev use: a PreToolUse Bash risk gate on OpenRouter /api/alpha/decisions. Steal the question set, jev_policy.py rule chain and hardening list, and write a small ~100-line hook of your own rather than installing this.

pros: Serious engineering: CI, CodeQL, JSONL audit log with hashed commands, benchmark dataset with Jev results and methodology docs
Policy-preserving: allow/deny rules never reach reviewer; failures degrade to manual or deny
cons: Targets OpenCode plugin API; port to a PermissionRequest hook is manual work; no OpenRouter provider (TypeSafe, OpenCode Zen, CommandCode only)
Bun runtime dependency and opencode-specific transcript enrichment

entries.name: kaustav1996/reflex
entries.what: Full coding agent/assistant fork on Pi where Jev checks every tool call, turn and voice transcript and code decides allow/ask/deny; OpenRouter for LLMs and for Jev.
interface: TypeSafe reflex layer inside Pi agent

pros: Uses openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone in code (src/config.ts, onboarding), so OpenRouter-native Jev
Working reference for per-tool-call Jev gate with code-owned policy and visible TYPESAFE trace lines

entries.name: alexj11324/open-jev-approvals
entries.what: Go binary (jev-approve) installed as Claude Code hooks (UserPromptSubmit + PreToolUse, matcher "*"). On every tool call it redacts secrets, sends the tool input plus the current-turn user prompts and a policy doc to TypeSafe System One with 10 typed Choice/Noul questions (risk, authorization, egress, credential probing, destructive effect, etc.), composes a local allow/deny verdict at a 0.70 threshold (exit 2 = block), and audits to SQLite. It is a safety/approval gate that replaces the auto-mode classifier for third-party API setups. It is not a coding-assist, routing or context tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse with matcher "*" fires on every tool call, and UserPromptSubmit on every prompt, with no model discretion. It is automatic, but as a permission gate rather than a coding assistant. Installed per project in <project>/.claude/settings.json, so you would have to repeat it per repo or hand-copy it to ~/.claude/settings.json.
security: Key handling is good: the key is read from a user-level env file (JEV_APPROVALS_ENV_FILE, XDG_CONFIG_HOME/jev-approvals/env, or ~/.config/jev-approvals/env) or the process env. It is never put in argv, so it does not show in ps. A project .env is deliberately ignored (tasks/lessons.md #3).
Endpoint hardening: base URL must be https (loopback http allowed), no embedded credentials, query or fragment, and cross-origin redirects are refused, so the key cannot leak via redirect.

Redaction (internal/sanitize/sanitize.go) is regex-based: private keys, Bearer tokens, AKIA, GitHub, Slack and sk- tokens, and key=value secrets, plus sensitive JSON keys. It is best-effort. Source code, business data and unknown-format secrets are sent unredacted.
No shell execution beyond what the hook does. Pure Go with one dependency (modernc.org/sqlite). No telemetry seen. No curl|sh installer; build is go build.

Prompt-injection surface: tool input and untrusted_instruction_text go to Jev inside the state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection can at most skew the numbers, not run code. Because failure is fail-open, an attacker who can make the call fail (oversized payload, malformed input) gets an allow.
Local SQLite audit DB (~/.local/state/jev-approvals/state.db) stores redacted prompts and tool payloads, which is a new at-rest copy of client-project data.
entries.dataEgress: On every tool call, one HTTPS POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or the configured URL) carrying: harness, hook event, tool name, action kind, the full tool_input after regex redaction (Bash command, Edit/Write file contents and diffs, file paths, MCP arguments), cwd, permission_mode, agent_id, all current-turn user prompt text (redacted), derived facts (target paths, patch ops, executable, payload sizes), lexical hints, the policy document, and 10 question definitions of roughly 3-4 KB. Tool outputs and transcript_path are NOT read. Whole files are not sent unless the model writes them via Write/Edit. Over OpenRouter, this would also pass through OpenRouter and its upstream provider (subject to OpenRouter's data policy). For client projects this means code the model writes and the user's prompts leave the machine on every action.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. HTTP client timeout is 5 s and the whole hook deadline is 8 s (main.go hookDeadline), under the harness hook timeout of 10 s written by the installer. On timeout, HTTP error, invalid response, missing API key, parse error or audit DB failure, the call is allowed and recorded as incomplete (review/service.go:29-52). Only a complete verdict that trips policy, or an authorization change mid-review, denies. Exit 2 is also returned if the verdict cannot be emitted at all. Downside: when Jev is slow, each tool call can stall up to about 5 s before being allowed. A false-positive deny blocks the tool call, and in bypass or auto mode there is no user prompt to override it, so the agent must reason around the block.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions, so no persistent context cost. Hooks inject no text on allow. On deny, a short stderr message ('JEV approval blocked: <reason> (review <id>)') is fed back to Claude. There is a statusMessage in the UI on each call. The vendored typesafe-ai SKILL.md is in the repo but not installed into ~/.claude by the installer.
pros: It is the only candidate here that gives truly automatic, no-prompt invocation: a deterministic PreToolUse hook with matcher "*", so Claude Code never has to be told to use Jev.
It fits Jev's strengths. Typed Choice/Noul questions with calibrated probabilities are exactly what Jev is designed for, and the request shape (state plus questions) matches System One.

Well-engineered security hygiene for a young repo: key only from a user-level env file, never in argv, HTTPS-only with cross-origin redirect refusal, secret redaction before send, and per-session authorization scoping. It also has real tests, CI on two OSes, and an eval harness.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no injected text on allow.

Designed for exactly the case where Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier is unavailable. It is fail-open, so a Jev outage will not stall work, and the changes needed for OpenRouter are small (about two prefix checks plus a base URL).
MIT license, small dependency footprint (one Go module), no telemetry or postinstall scripts.
cons: It is a permission gate, not a coding-productivity feature. For a user on Opus 5.5 with subscription login, Anthropic's own auto-mode classifier already exists, so the value is redundant. In bypass mode the user has deliberately disabled approvals, and this hook would re-add blocking that he opted out of.

No OpenRouter support: TypeSafe direct only. Setting only the base URL and key makes the model-family check ('jev-' prefix) fail against OpenRouter slugs like typesafe/jev-1.13, and because the failure is fail-open, every call is silently allowed. A source patch is needed, and OpenRouter's /v1/systemone schema parity is unverified.

A network round trip on every tool call, including Read, Grep and Glob (matcher "*"). That is +0.2-0.8 s per call when healthy, stacked on the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks, and up to 5-8 s when Jev is slow.

Sends redacted prompts and every tool input (code being written, commands, diffs) to a third party for every action. That is a real concern on client projects, and redaction is regex-based best-effort.

Fail-open with an uncalibrated 0.70 threshold means it is neither a reliable security control nor a proven reduction of prompt friction. The README says the threshold is uncalibrated, and Jev accuracy is unproven (skeptics claim it is a small router model). False-positive denies in bypass mode block the agent with no human override.

Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 17 commits all on that one day, 1 contributor, 4 stars, 0 forks, no releases or prebuilt binaries, requires a Go 1.27 toolchain. Its docs are inconsistent: commit titles say 'fail-closed' while the code is fail-open. Installation is per project, not global, and it also wants its own SQLite audit DB with copies of prompts and tool payloads.
Does not touch any other Jev use case (routing, classification of user intent, code-review scoring, commit triage), so it does nothing for daily coding quality.
entries.verdict: Well-built but narrow: an automatic, fail-open PreToolUse approval gate that duplicates Claude Code's own auto mode and adds a Jev round trip (and a data-egress path) to every tool call. It has no OpenRouter support out of the box, and a naive env-var switch silently turns it into allow-all. Only worth it as a fork-and-patch experiment (relax the jev- prefix check, point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, narrow the matcher to Bash|Write|Edit), not as the main integration.

Includes bench/cases.jsonl for measuring accuracy
Configurable baseUrl

Posts to {baseUrl}/v1/systemone; OpenRouter would need base https://openrouter.ai/api and model rename
