entries.name: nanoDBA/jev-agent-kit
entries.what: Independent Python 3.11+ package (zero runtime deps, ~7.6k LOC in src/jev_kit) that wraps TypeSafe's Jev (System One API) as a cautious "typed judgment" layer for coding agents. Ships a PreToolUse hook for Claude Code (python -m jev_kit.hooks.claude) that asks Jev tool-call-gate Noul questions (destructive? exfiltrates? widens permission?) about each Bash/PowerShell command after heavy egress minimization (command cut to basename, path hashed with HMAC, cmd_* boolean facts computed locally, secret-pattern scan). Also a jev-runtime SKILL.md (prompt guidance, no auto-trigger logic), a CLI (jev-kit), question sets (preflight-route, postflight-verify, stop-or-continue, tool-call-gate), receipts (JSONL), calibration tooling, and a `jev-kit audit` static scanner for skills. By design, hooks start in shadow mode (record only, never change behavior), Jev can never grant/approve, and only tool-call-gate is wired to a host event. The other question sets (routing, verify claims, stop/continue) are NOT wired automatically ("Nothing calls them automatically"). Added value for this user is therefore essentially a second, model-based safety gate on shell commands, and only after per-question calibration with labeled data.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Bash|PowerShell) - fully automatic once registered, no prompting needed. But automatic only for tool-call gating; routing, claim-verification and stop/continue question sets are not wired to any hook (no Stop / UserPromptSubmit / PostToolUse adapter), and the skill has no concrete trigger.
security: API key: env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND (JSON argv run without shell, stdout capped 8 KiB, stderr discarded, deadline-bound); never in argv of the hook, only Authorization header (secrets.py, transport.py). Having both set is a config error. Key command output/text never included in errors.

Transport hardened: fixed HTTPS destination, redirects refused (Authorization not forwarded), env proxies ignored, 1 MiB response cap, TLS default context (transport.py). Note ProxyHandler({}) means corporate proxies unsupported.

Egress minimisation is strong: command reduced to basename, path -> HMAC keyed hash, cmd_* booleans, secret-pattern scan on exact outgoing bytes (egress.py, 790 lines), refuses request on match; source-code fields refused. But the free-text `context` (tool name + Claude's Bash `description`) is plain text and can contain project/client names; live gate requires JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST=agent_context and a JEV_KIT_ATTESTATION JSON file (inventory/DPA attestation) - i.e. heavy compliance ceremony, no telemetry.
Hook runs engine via subprocess `python -m jev_kit.cli` (watchdog.py), no shell; child gets key via inherited env.

Prompt-injection surface small: Jev output is only probabilities validated against a schema; hook can only add friction (ask), never allow. Untrusted description text goes to Jev but cannot cause execution.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found; pure stdlib. CI pins actions by SHA, permissions: contents read. Receipts written to disk (per-user data dir) contain digests/distributions, not raw state.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated Bash/PowerShell tool call, to api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter): JSON with `command` = executable basename only (e.g. "rm"), ~11 cmd_* boolean/null facts, `target` = keyed hash of file path/URL, `context` = "tool=Bash; description=<Claude's description string>" with emails/IPs/phones masked. Never full command line, args, file contents, diffs, tool outputs, transcript, or cwd. Requests matching credential patterns are refused, not sent. Nothing is sent unless JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST includes agent_context and an attestation file exists; otherwise live gate calls are refused before sending (so, out of the box, the hook collects no evidence). ~300-390 input tokens per call.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe by design. Shadow (default): any error/timeout/unparsable event returns {} so Claude proceeds untouched. Enforce: any failure, timeout, uncalibrated question, or non-cleared gate returns permissionDecision "ask" (prompts user), and with the shipped uncalibrated thresholds EVERY checked call including `ls` asks, so enforce is unusable until you calibrate on labeled data. Timeouts: hook self-deadline 8 s (hooks/core.py:34) with a watchdog killing the child process; engine per-call deadline ~10 s with retries/rate budget; recommended Claude hook timeout 30 s. Hook always exits 0. In bypass/auto permission mode, an "ask" decision from a PreToolUse hook still prompts the user, which would break the unattended flow in enforce mode.
entries.contextCost: Near zero tokens injected into the Claude context in hook-only setup: no MCP server (0 tools, no server instructions), hook emits {} or an ask reason string only. If the optional skill is installed, only its name+description enters the listing (~60 tokens); loading it pulls the ~90-line SKILL.md plus references/evidence-contracts.md on demand.
pros: Only candidate here that is a genuinely deterministic, automatic Claude Code integration (PreToolUse hook): no 'use jev' prompting needed, zero context-token cost, no MCP tool bloat.

Very careful security engineering: fixed HTTPS destination, no redirects, key never in argv/body, secret-pattern scanner blocks send, command reduced to basename + local cmd_* facts, path HMAC-hashed, stdlib-only (no supply-chain deps), no telemetry/installer scripts.
Fail-safe semantics: shadow default, hook can never emit allow (only ask), always exit 0, 8 s self-deadline with child kill; cannot break or silently widen permissions.
Honest documentation with measured numbers (latency, cost ~$0.000015/call, variance) and explicit caveats; receipts JSONL give an audit trail for evaluating whether Jev adds value.
Solid test/CI discipline for a young repo (34 test files, mypy strict, SHA-pinned actions, cross-OS matrix); MIT license.
Reusable design ideas (egress allowlist, command_properties parser, question-set + calibration workflow) even if not adopted wholesale.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai (transport.py:86), key env is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, model pinned by regex jev-X.Y.Z that rejects typesafe/jev-1.13 and jev-latest aliases (engine.py:884-890). User wants OpenRouter as provider, so needs a fork of transport + model-pin logic.

Value proposition is narrow for this user: only a Bash tool-call safety gate is wired. The user already has a PreToolUse secret-leak guard and runs in bypass/auto mode; the gate can only ADD friction ('ask'), which is the opposite of what bypass/auto users want, and in enforce mode with shipped uncalibrated thresholds even `ls` prompts. In shadow mode it is pure logging with no user-visible benefit.

No calibrated thresholds ship; calibration requires labeled data from your own commands and per-question/model-version registration - a substantial ongoing workflow before any answer can be acted on. Routing/verify/stop-continue question sets are not auto-invoked at all, so the broader 'Jev when it adds value' goal is not delivered.

Compliance ceremony before any live call: JEV_KIT_SOURCE_ALLOWLIST=agent_context plus an attestation JSON (inventory/DPA) are required, otherwise the live gate is refused and no data is collected. Whether this fits client projects is the user's problem to attest; free-text `description` can still leak client/folder names to a third party.

Latency: author measured ~2.3 s overhead per tool call (Python cold start + child process + key command), with 4-7 s Jev outliers, on every Bash call, stacked on existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus pre/post).

Very immature: created 2026-09-27, 173 commits in ~2 days by one author (largely AI-generated per CLAUDE.md/handoffs), 1 star, no releases, not on PyPI, version 0.1.0; 'wheel install does not ship skill folder' so requires editable install from a clone. Eval labels written by Claude, not independent.
Uses Python subprocess per hook call and ignores env proxies (ProxyHandler({})), which may break behind corporate proxies.
Skill description is generic (no concrete trigger phrases), so model-discretion invocation of Jev would be unreliable; skill is guidance text only.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered, safety-first but pre-alpha hook that only gates Bash commands via TypeSafe's direct API; it lacks OpenRouter support and, for a bypass/auto-mode user, adds ~2 s per call and only friction. Worth mining for ideas (egress minimization, shadow-mode receipts), not worth installing as the Jev integration.

entries.name: @jev-kit/hook-adapters (keiffff/jev-kit monorepo)
entries.what: TypeScript monorepo of 8 packages (Jev contracts, router, eval, semantic-diff, evidence-check, agent-review, hook-adapters, cli) built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. The Claude Code integration is the CLI jev-agent-review --adapter claude-permission, wired as a PermissionRequest hook. It reads the hook JSON from stdin, normalizes it (tool_name, tool_input, last N actual user messages parsed from transcript_path, a standing-policy text, cwd), and asks Jev three Noul questions: policy_compliant, instruction_aligned, high_risk. If thresholds pass (0.7/0.7/<=0.15 in the example) it emits a native allow. Otherwise it emits nothing and Claude's normal permission flow continues. It can never deny. hook-adapters is only the payload converter library. The runnable piece is @jev-kit/cli.
interface: defineContract / JevClient / routeDecision / selectPath / defer / compareDecisionPolicies / evaluateAgentReviewFixtures
No MCP server, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json, no marketplace.json
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PermissionRequest with matcher '*' fires automatically with no prompting and no model discretion. But PermissionRequest fires only when Claude Code is about to show a permission dialog. Under bypassPermissions nothing prompts, so the hook never runs. Under 'auto' mode most actions are decided by the built-in classifier, so the hook fires at most for the escalated ones (unverified whether auto mode invokes PermissionRequest hooks before or after its classifier). It therefore does nothing for a user who mostly runs bypass or auto.
security: No API key in argv. The key is read from the environment by the SDK (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and the CLI takes only --adapter, --config and --status-file paths, so the key is not visible in ps output.

Deterministic secret preflight before any network call (packages/agent-review/src/index.ts:263-291). It matches private-key blocks, Bearer and Authorization headers, AKIA, glpat-, sk-/xai-, AIza, ghp_ tokens, key=value patterns, sensitive JSON key names, and paths such as .env, .npmrc, id_rsa and .git-credentials. On a match it defers with reason 'sensitive-input'. Only tool_input is scanned. userMessages and cwd are also in the request object passed to containsSensitiveValue, but arbitrary secrets in user messages that match no pattern would still be sent. The README itself says it is 'a guard for recognized credentials, not proof'.

No shell execution in runtime code. child_process is used only in scripts/verify-packages.mjs for CI packaging smoke tests. There is no telemetry, no postinstall script in the hook-adapters package.json (checked), and no curl|sh installer.

Prompt-injection surface: the model input is the tool call JSON plus user messages. Jev returns only typed probabilities, no free text, so it cannot be steered into executing instructions. A crafted tool_input could still push scores past the thresholds and cause a false auto-allow. The design has no Jev deny, so a false allow is the only risk. The allow result short-circuits the human permission dialog.
The status file stores only outcome, reason, contract, scores and tool name, not raw input (cli.ts:115-140). It is written atomically via tmp+rename.

Supply chain: a brand-new single-maintainer package (10 days old) with trusted-publishing provenance, plus the also-new @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0. The user would install a global npm binary that runs on every permission request.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden), per permission request: the full tool_input (Bash command, file paths, and for Write/Edit the entire file content or diff strings), tool name, optional description, cwd, requestId (the session_id), the last N (example 4) real user prompts extracted from the transcript, and the standing-policy text, plus the three question strings. Client code has no input-length limit (README). Tool outputs and the rest of the conversation are not sent. On the OpenRouter route this data reaches OpenRouter and the upstream provider under their data policies. That matters for client projects, since Write/Edit payloads can carry proprietary code. Requests containing a recognized credential are never sent.
entries.failureMode: Fail to defer, which is effectively fail-open to Claude's normal permission flow. Any provider error, timeout, missing key, invalid response, sensitive input or missing user context yields no stdout, so Claude Code falls back to its normal permission prompt or classifier (cli.ts:40-43, hook output only when outcome==='allow', integration-design.md failure table). SDK retries are disabled and the SDK timeout is 10 s by default (index.mjs:518), but the example hook timeout is 4 s, so Claude Code kills the hook first. A missed timeout costs at most 4 s of delay before the normal prompt. Bad config or malformed input exits 2. The docs say the invalid-hook case is handled by the hook runtime, and whether exit 2 blocks the tool in Claude Code is unverified. Jev can never produce a deny.
entries.contextCost: Zero tokens added to the Claude Code context. There are no MCP tools, no skill descriptions, no injected additionalContext, and stdout is either empty or a bare allow JSON. The only visible effect is the statusMessage spinner text. No server instructions.
pros: Genuinely automatic once installed: a deterministic PermissionRequest hook needs no 'use jev' prompting. It is a real, clean use of Jev's typed Noul output for a control-flow decision (examples/claude-settings.json).

Very conservative failure model: it can only auto-allow, never deny, and every error path falls back to Claude's normal permission flow (cli.ts:40-43). It adds nothing to the model context (0 tokens).

Sound engineering for a young repo: deterministic secret preflight before network (agent-review/src/index.ts:263-291), strict response validation, retries disabled, atomic status file, contract fingerprints and an offline eval harness (evaluateAgentReviewFixtures) to measure false allows on your own labeled requests.

Built on the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, and the SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. The OpenRouter route is therefore plausibly a config change: `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. Setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and pointing the model at typesafe/jev-1.13 should work.

MIT license, CI on Node 24, provenance-based npm publishing with no stored token, and the user's Node 24 meets the >=22.6 requirement. The repo is also consistent with the OpenRouter cookbook 'coding-agents auto-approve permissions' pattern.
It leaves the existing hooks (secret-leak guard, GitNexus) untouched: they run on PreToolUse and this runs on PermissionRequest. The design explicitly says deterministic hooks stay authoritative.
cons: Wrong hook for this user: PermissionRequest fires only when a permission dialog would appear. In bypass mode it never fires, and in auto mode it covers only the small escalated remainder. It addresses approval fatigue, which this user mostly does not have, and gives no help with routing, code understanding, tool selection or context pruning.

Not OpenRouter-native: it depends on the TypeSafe SDK and its env var names (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). The OpenRouter path works only by aliasing an OpenRouter key into TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and schema compatibility is unverified. The example config model 'jev-latest' would also need renaming to an OpenRouter ID.

Sends complete tool inputs (full file contents on Write/Edit, Bash commands) and recent user prompts to a third-party beta model host on every gated action. That is a real confidentiality concern for client projects. The regex secret guard is heuristic (README concedes it is not proof).

A false allow silently skips the human approval dialog, and the only defense is your own calibration. The shipped fixtures are placeholders, so Jev's actual false-allow rate on real Claude Code traffic is unmeasured. Jev is also a new beta model, and a skeptic-reported 'flash router' claim is unverified.

Very immature: a 10-day-old repo with 1 star, 0 forks, 1 human contributor, 13 commits, 0.1.x versions, and about 37 unit tests that use only mocks, with no live or end-to-end test with Claude Code. Installing a global npm CLI from a one-person package into a workflow that touches client code is a supply-chain risk.

Extra moving parts for little gain: it needs a global npm install, a policy JSON, a status path, and env plumbing so the hook process sees the key. It adds 0.2-0.7 s per gated action. Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier already covers the same niche without a third-party dependency.
hook-adapters alone is only a payload-to-JSON converter. The value sits in @jev-kit/cli and @jev-kit/agent-review, so the candidate name is slightly misleading.
entries.verdict: A tidy, safe-by-design but immature permission auto-approver. It is automatic (deterministic hook), fails back to the normal prompt and costs no context, and it could be pointed at OpenRouter through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. However, PermissionRequest never fires in bypass mode and rarely in auto mode, and it exports full tool inputs, so it delivers little daily-coding value for this user. Treat it as an optional experiment, or as a reference implementation for the OpenRouter cookbook pattern, not a core integration.

entries.name: jev-reactor (KNambiarDJsc/Jev-Reactor, PyPI jev-reactor 0.2.0)
entries.what: Python runtime (Reactor loop, policy toolkit, question packs) plus an MCP gateway, jev-reactor-mcp, that sits in front of OTHER MCP servers listed in a YAML config. For each tools/call to a downstream MCP tool it applies an allowlist, JSON-schema validation, hard rules (permissions, amount limits, duplicates, approval for irreversible tools), then one Jev system_one request (relevant, redundant, task_complete, injection_suspected, next_action, etc.). Only allowed calls are forwarded. Denied calls return isError with a reason. It is a proxy, not a tool provider: it exposes zero tools of its own. It cannot see Claude Code built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Read, Grep) because those are not MCP calls.
interface: MCP tools exposed to the client
jev-reactor CLI (init, run, validate-pack, export-pack, report, replay, etc.)
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy for MCP tools only. Once registered in Claude Code it decides automatically on every call to the allowlisted downstream tools without any user prompt, because Claude Code talks to the gateway as if it were the real server. But this is a gate on other MCP tools, not a way for Claude Code to consult Jev. It does not intercept Bash/Edit/Write/Read/Grep, and it gives Claude no way to ask Jev questions. It would also require removing the original gitnexus/playwright registrations (otherwise the agent just calls the original), and its 'goal' is fixed per gateway in YAML.
security: API key from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, SecretStr, repr=False); never passed via argv. HTTP mode bearer token via --token-env only. No key visible in process list.
Downstream stdio children get a minimal allow-listed environment plus explicitly listed env with ${VAR} expansion; secrets not stored in YAML.
Gateway spawns arbitrary downstream commands from YAML (npx -y ... etc.), so the config is a code-execution surface, but it is user-authored.

Prompt-injection handling is thoughtful: tool descriptions treated as data, heuristic quarantine of instruction-like descriptions, injection_suspected Noul, approval never read from args/_meta, elicitation approvals sealed with request-state and per-call fingerprint. Author openly says heuristics are not proofs and Jev can be swayed.
Best-effort regex redaction (sk-, AIza, key-name masking, also exact TYPESAFE_API_KEY value) before sending to Jev and before persisting; SDK debug logging pinned to INFO to avoid body leaks.
Telemetry: cli.py:1 states no telemetry/phone-home; grep for telemetry/sentry/posthog found none in src.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated tools/call, one request to the Jev provider (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points to, e.g. OpenRouter then OpenRouter/TypeSafe both see it) containing: the configured goal, the proposed tool name, redacted arguments, tool description, tool risk metadata, and capped excerpts of recent tool calls/results (history_max default 50) as fixed state fields. Only MCP downstream tool traffic is affected: for gitnexus/playwright that could include code snippets, file paths, DOM content and page text. Does NOT see Claude Code built-in Read/Edit/Bash/Grep, user prompts or the conversation. Redaction is regex best-effort. Optional local JSONL of decisions (digest of state by default; redacted state only if state: redacted). No other network calls found.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by risk tier, configurable. Default deadline 1.0 s per decision, zero SDK retries, plus asyncio.timeout and a circuit breaker. If Jev is slow/down/errors: write tools go to review, irreversible tools are blocked, read tools get fallback which in enforce mode (default) is NOT run (the model is told the decision service was unavailable); in guard/observe mode fallback lets the call run. Auth errors open the breaker immediately. Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY raises MissingApiKeyError at startup (server fails to build). So with default enforce mode, an OpenRouter or Jev outage stalls all gated MCP tools; recommended to run observe or guard. The MCP server itself failing to start makes the gated downstream tools unavailable to Claude Code entirely.
entries.contextCost: Very low itself: 0 tools of its own; server instructions about 330 chars (about 80 tokens). It re-exposes downstream tools you allowlist, with descriptions truncated to 400 chars each, so cost is roughly that of the allowlisted subset (about 50-150 tokens per tool, e.g. 10 gitnexus tools ~ 1-1.5k tokens) and can be lower than the raw server if you truncate/replace descriptions. Every tool call result gains a small _meta decision block (not shown to the model text unless held back). No hooks, so no injected text. Tool names get prefixed server__tool when >1 downstream, which changes mcp__ names and breaks any existing allow rules/hooks/skills referencing mcp__gitnexus__* (e.g. GitNexus skills and the user's hooks).
pros: Genuinely automatic once wired: transparent MCP proxy, no 'use jev' prompting; decisions happen deterministically in code on every gated call (docs/mcp.md).

Well-engineered safety design for its age: hard rules run before Jev, fail-closed per risk tier, Jev can only make decisions more cautious, approval via sealed MCP elicitation, hostile-description quarantine (SECURITY.md threat table with named tests).
Env-only key handling (no argv exposure), no telemetry, no install scripts, Apache-2.0, strict typing, ~4.3k lines of offline tests, CI with pip-audit.
observe mode lets you log what Jev WOULD have blocked before enforcing; JSONL decision log defaults to digests, not state.

OpenRouter routing looks feasible without code changes because typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 builds URL as base_url + /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, matching OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone; base URL, key and model are all env-overridable.
Zero tools of its own and ~80 tokens of instructions, so no context bloat by itself; description truncation could even shrink downstream tool schemas.
cons: Scope mismatch for daily coding: only gates MCP tools. The user's high-volume, risky actions (Bash, Edit, Write, Read, Grep) are built-in tools and never pass through it; the user's own secret-guard PreToolUse hook already covers those deterministically and for free. The only MCP servers are gitnexus (read-only graph queries), playwright, caveman-shrink, so the gate would judge mostly harmless read calls.
Does not give Claude Code a Jev capability (no Choice/Noul/Score tool for routing, review triage, commit classification, etc.); it is a guardrail, not an integration that 'uses Jev when needed'.

Relevance/redundancy judgments need a fixed per-gateway goal string in YAML, but a coding session changes tasks constantly; 'goal' cannot vary per conversation, so relevance/task_complete signals will be poorly grounded. Docs admit it is unmeasured against live Jev and thresholds are uncalibrated.

Must replace, not add to, existing MCP registrations (else agent bypasses the gate); prefixed tool names change mcp__gitnexus__* to mcp__gateway__gitnexus__* and would break the user's GitNexus skills, hooks and permission allow rules. Also playwright stdio children with allow-listed env only.

Default enforce mode is fail-closed for reads: any OpenRouter/Jev hiccup, 1 s deadline miss, missing key, or schema mismatch blocks gitnexus/playwright calls and can make the agent loop or stall; the redundancy check may wrongly refuse legitimate repeated reads (e.g., re-running a graph query after edits).

Adds a Jev round trip on every gated call, and sends tool arguments plus recent tool result excerpts (code, DOM text from client projects) to a third-party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) with regex-only redaction: client-confidentiality risk. TypeSafe MCA forbids using outputs to train/distill and security testing.

Immature and single-author: 9 commits all on 2026-09-21, 1 star, 0 forks, no GitHub release, alpha classifier, Windows-oriented CI but no live-Jev evidence. Hard-pinned to typesafe-sdk 0.7.x and mcp>=2.2,<3 (very new major); needs Python venv separate from the user's uv workflow (uvx/pipx would work but was not run).

OpenRouter path untested by anyone; TypeSafe direct is the only supported provider, so 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' is unproven and needs a smoke test; the SDK's strict response models may reject OpenRouter's envelope.
entries.verdict: Solid, security-minded but very young MCP guard proxy that is only useful if you want Jev to gate calls to third-party MCP tools; it does not touch Claude Code's built-in Bash/Edit/Read tools nor give Claude a way to consult Jev, so for this user's daily coding it adds latency, data egress and tool-renaming breakage for little benefit. It could be worth a low-risk observe-mode experiment via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, and its ideas (question packs, risk tiers) are more useful as a reference than as the integration itself.

entries.name: fuji-soho/jev-mcp-server
entries.what: Read-only stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript, 7 tools) that acts as an advisory safety gate. jev_check_command and jev_check_test first apply local static deny/review policies (policies/default.json, user and project policy files), then ask Jev a single Noul question ("is this command/test dangerous?") and map the probability to allow (<0.4), review (0.4 to 0.8) or deny (>=0.8), taking the strictest of static and Jev results. It never runs anything itself. It also has a SQLite cache, audit log, human-review and environment-approval workflow, and single-use execution tickets. Jev is reached via Cloudflare Workers AI or the TypeSafe direct API. Not a general coding assistant.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. The README and examples/AGENTS.md rely on the user adding AGENTS.md/JEV_POLICY.md instructions to each project, plus the short server instructions string. There is no hook, no skill and no proxy, so it is not deterministic. Claude Code would only sometimes call jev_check_command before Bash, and would never be forced to. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PreToolUse Bash hook that calls the check, which this repo does not provide.
security: Key handling: the API key is read from a .env file (path via --env-file, so it appears in argv but the key itself does not) and is never put in argv or logs. Sent as an Authorization Bearer header; the README claims keys are kept out of logs, caches and responses.

Secret redaction before egress is regex-based (command-checker.ts:34-36, test-checker.ts:119). It covers KEY=val, --token val, private key blocks and DB URLs, but is not comprehensive. Arbitrary secrets inside testCode or diff can still leave the machine.

Prompt-injection surface: command, testCode and diff are placed in Jev state, and the question instructions tell Jev to treat them as untrusted (cloudflare-jev.ts:22-35). Jev returns only a number, which limits injection impact. The MCP tool outputs are structured and include no free text from the model.

No shell execution, no child_process and no postinstall script in package.json. The only network calls go to api.typesafe.ai or api.cloudflare.com (cloudflare-jev.ts:123), with a 30s timeout and a 1 MiB response cap. No telemetry found.
Writes local state: log/jev.log (mode 0600) and cache/jev.sqlite inside the install directory (audit log, fingerprint cache, tickets). Command text is sanitised to 2000 chars in the audit log.
jev_review_approve and jev_environment_approve are exposed to the same agent, so the 'human approval' can be self-approved by the model, especially in bypass mode. This weakens the design.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai or Cloudflare only (never OpenRouter): for jev_check_command, the redacted command, cwd, environment, target and context. For jev_check_test, the redacted command, full testCode (each test file's contents when testFiles is used, up to a max length), the git diff, framework, context, environment and isolation/runtime evidence (test-checker.ts:119,154-155,297). Nothing is sent unless the model calls a tool, and cache hits skip the network. Whole file contents and diffs from client projects can leave the machine on test checks.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design, but only advisory. Timeout, network error, HTTP error, invalid JSON, invalid shape or missing usage all return decision 'review' with needsHumanReview=true (command-checker.ts:133-135, cloudflare-jev.ts:129-150). Static denies stay deny. The timeout is 30s (REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS = 30000), with no retry and no failover. Because it is an MCP tool and not a hook, nothing blocks the actual Bash call. A 'review' result only affects Claude if the model chooses to respect it. In bypass mode this means a slow or down Jev adds up to 30s of waiting and then a non-binding 'review'.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools registered, all always visible. Tool definitions total about 12KB of registerTool source plus large zod schemas for the test tool (isolation, runtime, runtimeDatabase, configCache, runtimeGuard and execution objects). Estimate about 3.5-5k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas, plus about 100 tokens of server instructions (index.ts:194). Most of this is dead weight for daily coding because the approve/reject/revoke tools are rarely used. No hook-injected text. With Claude Code's deferred tool loading the cost may be lower, but the set is large for two useful tools.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for a good-fit typed decision (Noul P(dangerous)) instead of using it as a chat model. Thresholds 0.4/0.8 map it cleanly to allow/review/deny (command-checker.ts:127).
Static deny rules take precedence over Jev, and API failures degrade to 'review', not 'allow' (fail-closed logic, cloudflare-jev.ts and command-checker.ts:133-135).
Zero shell execution, no postinstall, small dependency set (MCP SDK + zod), MIT license, secret-redaction pass before egress, 0600 log file.
Has tests (7 files, mocked Jev) and the request/response parsing is strict, so the TypeSafe System One wire format is already implemented and could be reused.
Already speaks the System One /v1/systemone schema (same path as OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone), so an OpenRouter branch is a small fork.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint (cloudflare-jev.ts:14) and no base-URL env var. You would have to fork it, or would need a separate TYPESAFE_API_KEY from console.typesafe.ai, which conflicts with the goal of using OpenRouter as the Jev provider.

Not automatic: it is a plain MCP tool that depends on the model or on per-project AGENTS.md text. It does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told. There is no PreToolUse hook. Advice is non-binding, and Claude can ignore 'review' or self-call jev_review_approve.

Very narrow use case (destructive-command and test safety). It does nothing for routing, planning, commit/PR decisions or code triage, and duplicates Claude Code's own permission system and the existing secret-leak guard hook.
Adds 7 tools and roughly 4k tokens of always-present context, most of it for an approval workflow (environment/human review tickets) built around Codex, not Claude Code.
Immature: 4 days old, 11 commits, effectively one author, 0 stars, no release, no CI, no npm package, README covers Codex only. Setup needs clone and build, with .env in the install directory.
Config only via a hand-parsed .env file, not process env. It ignores an exported OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and needs a fixed absolute path in the MCP registration.
For jev_check_test it sends test source and diffs from client projects to a third party, guarded only by regex redaction. That is a real concern for client work.
30s timeout and fail-'review' produce stalls in bypass or auto mode where nothing actually gates the command.
entries.verdict: Well-scoped Jev use (a typed danger probability with a static-deny backstop), but a poor fit for this user. It is TypeSafe/Cloudflare only (no OpenRouter), an advisory model-discretion MCP tool that Claude Code will not reliably call unprompted, immature, and heavy on context for two useful tools. Best treated as reference code for the System One request format and thresholds. Fork it into a PreToolUse Bash hook that calls OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone if a Jev safety gate is wanted.

entries.name: jev-firewall (PyPI, realahsanshah / jev-action-firewall)
entries.what: Python library (not a Claude Code hook or MCP server) that gates an agent framework's tool calls: hard local regex floors, then one Jev System One call (severity Choice, is_irreversible Noul, matches_stated_goal Noul) over redacted tool name, args and one-line goal, mapped to ALLOW/HOLD/DENY via policy.yaml, with fail_mode, approval channels and a JSONL audit log. Adapters exist for LangGraph, LangChain, OpenAI Agents SDK, Google ADK and Semantic Kernel only. There is no Claude Code integration in the source (grep for Claude Code, PreToolUse and settings.json finds nothing). A CLI 'eval' subcommand exists, so a user-written PreToolUse hook wrapper could shell out to it.
interface: CLI: jev-firewall eval <policy> --tool T --args JSON --goal G [--offline]
entries.autoInvocation: None out of the box. It is a library wired into agent frameworks that the user owns the code of, and it cannot hook Claude Code, which is closed. To make it automatic in Claude Code you would write your own deterministic PreToolUse hook (a stdin JSON wrapper) that calls Firewall.evaluate and maps ALLOW/HOLD/DENY to allow/ask/deny. That is a deterministic hook design, but it is custom code, not this project.
security: Key is read from the environment only (OPENROUTER_API_KEY for the openrouter route), never from argv. Keys are kept per route so a TypeSafe key is not sent to a gateway.

Redaction of args before they go to Jev or the audit log (src/jev_firewall/redact.py): sensitive key names, OpenAI, Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Stripe, Slack and Google keys, JWTs, PEM keys, URL credentials, KEY=value secrets, PII. Long strings are truncated. This is regex-based, so misses are possible. Redaction is a useful complement to the user's existing secret-leak hook.

Prompt-injection posture is deliberate: local hard-pattern floors run first and cannot be lowered by Jev, and the rubric tells the model that tool_args are data. The README admits Jev is moved by adversarial text and that hard patterns alone catch only 19 of 50 harmful cases.
Data leaves the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe or its upstream. No telemetry beyond the Jev call. Audit log is local JSONL, append-only.
No postinstall or curl|sh installer; pure-Python wheel built with hatchling. Dependency chain is typesafe-sdk and httpx2 (both new, unaudited here).
The 'eval' CLI takes the tool args as a JSON argv string, so a hook wrapper would expose command text in the process list. Prefer the Python API, or a small stdin-based wrapper.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated call, to the configured route (OpenRouter for this user), so on to TypeSafe: the tool name, the redacted tool arguments (for Bash this means the command text, for Write/Edit the file path and truncated content), and a one-line agent_goal (first user message by default). No conversation history, no tool outputs, no file contents beyond what appears in the tool args. Request is about 680 input tokens (estimated). Redacted args still reveal client project paths and command details. Nothing else is uploaded.
entries.failureMode: Explicit and required in policy.yaml (fail_mode: open|closed, per-tool override). Jev timeout, error, rate limit or malformed reply resolves through fail_mode: closed means DENY, open means ALLOW (hard-pattern floors still apply). timeout_s (example 1.0 s) is enforced three ways (SDK per-request timeout, retry budget, asyncio.timeout) with max_retries 1. For an unattended bypass or auto session, 'closed' would stall Claude on any OpenRouter blip and 'open' would degrade to hard patterns only. HOLD needs an approval channel (CLI prompt, webhook, timeout_deny). None of these map to Claude Code's permission 'ask' without custom glue.
entries.contextCost: Zero for the library or CLI: no MCP tools and no server instructions. A hook only adds text if the wrapper emits a deny reason or additionalContext. Nothing is injected by default.
pros: Native OpenRouter route with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, model ~typesafe/jev-latest and base URL https://openrouter.ai/api (jev/__init__.py:44). Config-only switch, no patching.

Built for exactly the Jev use case: typed Choice/Noul questions on a minimal redacted state, thresholds in code. Good reference for a well-formed rubric (rubric.py) and for the Jev 1.13 guidance on wording.
Disciplined design: explicit fail_mode with no default, hard-pattern floors that Jev cannot lower, per-tool allowlists to skip Jev for reads, secret and PII redaction, JSONL audit.
Apache-2.0, typed, strict mypy, CI on Linux and Windows, about 100 offline tests.

Its policy.yaml, rubric and redaction could be reused as ideas or code for a custom Claude Code PreToolUse hook (a 'risk gate' for Bash) that fits the user's bypass/auto workflow. Python 3.13 and uv are already available.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no hook, MCP server, plugin or skill. Adapters cover only LangGraph, LangChain, OpenAI Agents, Google ADK and Semantic Kernel. Claude Code's own tool loop cannot be wrapped by these. Using it means writing and maintaining your own hook glue.

Solves a different problem than the user asked for. It is a safety gate for the agent's actions, not a way to have Claude use Jev for coding decisions. It only vetoes or escalates, and it adds no coding value.

Unproven with live Jev: accuracy, false-positive rate and end-to-end latency are all 'not measured'. Repeated false HOLDs or DENYs on ordinary Bash and Edit in a coding session are a real risk. Hard patterns catch only 19/50 harmful cases, so the remaining protection depends on Jev, which the README says can be moved by adversarial text.

Fail-mode dilemma for an unattended auto/bypass workflow: closed can block work during an OpenRouter outage, open weakens the gate. HOLD has no clean mapping to Claude Code's 'ask' without extra code.
Adds 70-500 ms network latency per gated call, plus process startup if run per call via CLI. The 'eval' CLI passes tool args in argv, which is visible in the process list.
Sends Bash commands and file paths (redacted only by regexes) from client projects to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a possible client-confidentiality problem.

Very immature: created 2026-09-27, 22 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, alpha, two releases on PyPI. Dependencies (typesafe-sdk 0.7.x, httpx2) are new. It overlaps with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, and Claude Code already has a permission system and its own auto-mode classifier.
entries.verdict: A well-designed but very young (3 days old, alpha, single author) Python guardrail library with a real OpenRouter route for Jev. It cannot be dropped into Claude Code, because it has no hook or MCP layer and only supports other agent frameworks. It gates actions rather than adding coding value, so it is only a reference for a custom PreToolUse risk-gate hook and not a solution to the user's goal.

entries.name: jev-fuse (0xshikhar)
entries.what: Python 3.12+ package (PyPI jev-fuse 0.1.0) that wraps TypeSafe Jev in a local governance layer. It has four parts. (1) A FastAPI gateway (`jevfuse serve`) that proxies POST /v1/systemone with a singleflight coalescer, an LRU+SQLite cache and a SQLite/DuckDB audit log. (2) A Claude Code PreToolUse hook for Bash only (`jevfuse hook pre-tool-use`) that runs a shell-command classifier: AST/tokenizer checks, a deterministic denylist and allowlist, then a Jev "split-noul" fallback. (3) A stdio MCP server (`jevfuse mcp`) with 4 tools. (4) A Claude plugin/marketplace manifest and a SKILL.md. Its real function is a bash-command safety gate. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration for coding assistance.
interface: Hook PreToolUse matcher Bash: `uv run jevfuse hook pre-tool-use`
entries.autoInvocation: Hook for the gate: PreToolUse on Bash is deterministic, but the verdict format is invalid for current Claude Code, so it is ineffective. The plugin manifest ships no hooks file, so the user must hand-add the hook to settings. The MCP tools (fuse_verify, fuse_route, fuse_prune) are model-discretion only; nothing prompts Claude to use them. The SKILL.md description trigger is the only nudge, and it concerns guard and prune.
security: Critical: the hook emits legacy/invented JSON ({"allow": true}, {"deny": ...}, {"ask": ...}; hook/pre_tool_use.py, classifier.py:30-37). Current Claude Code docs require hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision for PreToolUse, and top-level allow/deny/ask are not valid. The docs say exit 0 with no valid decision falls through to normal permission flow. So the ALLOW/DENY/ASK verdicts are most likely silently ignored and the gate is a no-op. The tests only assert the invented shape (tests/test_guard_hook.py:30) and never run against a real Claude Code.

The hook command is `uv run jevfuse hook pre-tool-use` (.claude/settings.json). In any project that is not the jev-fuse checkout, uv cannot spawn `jevfuse`. It exits non-zero, and exit code 2 would block every Bash call. This is an inference from the hook contract and was not tested, because running candidate code was forbidden.

Layer 4 never returns ALLOW: every model verdict below the deadband still returns ASK ('Uncalibrated safety verdict'; classifier.py:~505). Jev adds only DENY signals or nothing. In bypass/auto mode an ASK adds friction and is not a real gate.

The gateway enables CORS allow_origins=['*'] with credentials (server/app.py:52-59). It forwards the caller's Authorization header upstream, and there is no local auth on /v1/decide, /v1/traces or /dashboard. It binds 127.0.0.1 by default, but any browser page could reach it, and traces can contain command text.

API key handling is via env vars only, not argv, unless the user copies the README MCP snippet with the key in the env block of the MCP config. The key is then in plaintext in ~/.claude.json and is visible to any process that can read the environment. classifier.py:460 sends the TYPESAFE_API_KEY as a Bearer header to FUSE_URL, which defaults to localhost.

Persistent state is written to CWD-relative files jevfuse_decisions.db and jevfuse_cache.db (engine.py:103-104) in whichever project directory the process runs from. This pollutes client repos and stores command text and prompts on disk.
entries.dataEgress: Only the Layer-4 fallback contacts Jev. The payload is 'Command to evaluate: <bash command>\nWorking Directory: <cwd>' plus 4 fixed noul questions, sent to the gateway, which forwards to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default). Commands on the allowlist or denylist send nothing. Commands may embed inline secrets or file paths in their text. The MCP tools can send much more: fuse_verify sends arbitrary statement + context (code/logs), and fuse_prune sends up to 1500 chars of each non-user turn (assistant text, tool outputs, code) to Jev. Everything is also stored locally in unencrypted SQLite/DuckDB files in CWD.
entries.failureMode: The design is meant to fail closed toward ASK. The hook wraps errors as ASK, and the classifier returns ASK on non-200 responses, timeouts and connection errors (classifier.py). The client timeout is 2.0s for the hook-to-gateway call. On ConnectError it spins up a full in-process JevFuseEngine (SQLite+DuckDB init) per Bash call, which is slow. The provider-level timeout is 10s with 3 retries and exponential backoff (jev.py:30-31), so a stalled upstream can hold the gateway for up to ~40s. Because the ASK/DENY JSON shape is probably not honored by Claude Code, the practical failure mode is fail-open (the normal permission flow, which is bypass for this user). An exit-2 failure when `uv run` cannot find the script would be fail-closed and would block Bash entirely.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 4 tools (fuse_guard, fuse_prune, fuse_verify, fuse_route). The tool descriptions and schemas total roughly 2,000-2,500 chars, about 500-650 tokens. The MCP server sets no server-level instructions. The optional SKILL.md adds a ~90-word description line to the skill list (~120 tokens) and loads about 1.2k tokens when triggered. The PreToolUse hook injects no text into context, since it prints only JSON or nothing. The plugin install would add the skill, but the repo has no hooks/hooks.json, so the plugin does not install the hook; only the project-level .claude/settings.json in this repo has it.
pros: Genuinely reads the real System One wire: POST /v1/systemone with state/questions/answers, and models Noul/Choice/Score (provider/jev.py:194-214). Base URL and key are env-configurable, so a patched OpenRouter path is close.

Its deterministic Bash guard has useful logic: tokenizer/AST checks, a denylist (rm -rf on root/home, git push --force, dd of=/dev, mkfs, curl|sh) and a read-only allowlist. It is a sensible design for reducing prompts in default permission mode.
Fail-closed intent (ASK on any error) and a 2s client timeout in the hook path.
Apache-2.0, has a test suite (about 85 test functions across 11 files, including golden shell-guard fixtures), and the PyPI package exists.
Singleflight and cache logic would cut duplicate Jev calls if a gateway were ever run.
cons: The Claude Code hook output uses a made-up shape ({"allow": true}) that the current docs say is invalid for PreToolUse. The tests verify only the invented shape, so the flagship integration probably does nothing.

Wrong problem for this user: he runs bypass/auto mode with a secret-leak guard hook already installed. A Bash safety gate adds latency for little benefit, and its model tier never returns ALLOW (always ASK).

Does not use Jev for what Jev is good at in coding (routing, triage, tool selection, relevance). fuse_prune/route/verify are thin wrappers that need Claude to choose to call them, and the tool schema leaks real code and tool outputs to a third party.
No OpenRouter support. The model name is hardcoded to 'jev-latest', and the OpenRouter response schema is unverified. It needs code patching plus a running gateway or in-process engine.

Operationally fragile: `uv run jevfuse` only works inside a checkout or with a global tool install. It creates .db files in the CWD of every client project, uses a wide-open CORS gateway, and pulls in duckdb/fastapi/uvicorn for a 2-second check.

Immature and single-author: 50 commits over about 1 day, 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, the pushed date is 2026-09-24. The README makes unsupported claims (35ms P50, 98% cost savings, 'tamper-evident' logs, a Laya provider that has no code).
Overlaps existing tooling: the user's PreToolUse secret guard already covers the secret-path cases, and it would add a second Bash hook chain alongside GitNexus and caveman.
entries.verdict: Do not adopt. The project is a day-old, single-author proof of concept. Its Claude Code hook emits a decision format that current Claude Code docs say is invalid, and it has no OpenRouter path. Even if fixed, it only gates Bash commands, which adds latency and gives this bypass-mode user little value. At most, borrow its ideas (denylist, deadband, and the noul question design) for a custom hook.

entries.name: omkarghugarkar007/actiongate-jev (ActionGate)
entries.what: Not a Claude Code hook (discovery mislabelled it). It is an agent tool-call authorization platform (TS monorepo, Python SDK, Fastify API, Next.js dashboard). For Claude Code the only relevant piece is scripts/mcp-guard.ts: a stdio MCP proxy that wraps ONE upstream MCP server, and before each tools/call sends the proposed action and the relayed user intent to Jev (6 semantic questions in one request) plus deterministic policy, then consumes a single-use grant before forwarding. It cannot see or gate Claude Code's built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Write, Read), only MCP tools of the server it wraps.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy for MCP tools only: once mcp-guard replaces a server entry in .mcp.json/settings, every tools/call to that server is intercepted deterministically with no prompting. It does not cover Claude Code built-in tools and requires editing/replacing each existing MCP server config (gitnexus, playwright).
security: Sound internal design: grants are HMAC-signed, single-use, bound to canonical action fingerprint; unhandled MCP methods fail closed rather than pass through; _meta stripped before forwarding upstream; prompt-injection instruction in every Jev question says state is data, not instructions.

Explicit self-admission (README): early release, no external security review, dataset labels self-authored; mcp-guard mode is not a boundary against the local machine (policy lives in the same process).

API key passed via env in the MCP config (not argv), good; but Claude Code project cwd .env gets auto-loaded by 'import dotenv/config' in scripts/mcp-guard.ts:1, and the child upstream gets a full copy of process.env (stdio.ts spawn env: {...process.env}).
Spawns an arbitrary upstream command from UPSTREAM_COMMAND with args split on spaces (no quoting), so paths with spaces or quoted args break.
Adopted upstream tools default to REVERSIBLE_WRITE with a generic semantic policy; risk classes are guesses (docs say so).

No telemetry in the guard path (OTLP/webhooks exist only in the API server); no postinstall found in the guard path but a full pnpm workspace install (Next.js, Fastify, drizzle, etc.) pulls a large dependency tree.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter per guarded tools/call: model id plus a minimal state (buildMinimalState in packages/core/src/state-builder.ts) containing the proposed tool name, whitelisted argument fields (target, transaction, order, recipient, record, semanticLabel), the tool's semantic policy statements, and user_intent text (in Claude Code just the placeholder string, since no intent is relayed). Six question definitions. Not the full prompt, repo, diffs, or tool outputs in normal operation, but argument values of the guarded MCP tool leave the machine. Nothing is sent for non-guarded (built-in) tools. Fake provider makes no network calls.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed. If Jev errors, times out, or returns invalid output, decision-engine.ts:53-58 applies failureDecisionForRisk(riskClass, failOpenReadOnly default false), so the call is REVIEW/BLOCK and the tool is not forwarded. Embedded timeout 10 s (sdk-js/src/embedded.ts:99), API server 2 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS). OpenRouter adapter has no retries; TypeSafe adapter retries 429/529 up to 2. A Jev outage therefore breaks every guarded MCP tool, including read-only ones adopted at REVERSIBLE_WRITE. Also each spawn of mcp-guard runs upstream.listTools at startup, so a slow/failed upstream delays MCP connect.
entries.contextCost: Adds no tools of its own; it re-exposes the wrapped server's tools under a new server name. However tools/list emits inputSchema as {type:'object'} only (proxy.ts:100, since PolicyRegistry and StdioMcpUpstream drop upstream inputSchema, stdio.ts:89-92 and 122-131), so Claude sees no parameter schema for the wrapped tools, cutting context but making tools hard or impossible to call correctly. No server instructions. No hook-injected text. Roughly 0 extra tokens beyond the wrapped server's (degraded) tool list.
pros: Real, working OpenRouter Jev integration using the alpha Decisions API with typesafe/jev-1.13, with a live test fixture and a recorded live decision (733 ms, $0.000049); useful as a reference implementation of Choice/Noul/Score request shapes and toWireQuestion translation (openrouter-jev.ts:52-62).
Deterministic + Jev design where the model only supplies evidence and code holds authority; fail-closed on provider errors; single-use grants; honest docs about limits.
Fully config-only stdio integration path with no code (mcp-guard.ts), Apache-2.0, sizeable test suite (~45 test files across TS and Python, CI with Postgres/Redis, CodeQL, e2e).

Useful pattern if the user later wants a policy gate around a risky MCP server (e.g. playwright browser_run_code_unsafe), and the code could be mined for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls the Decisions API.
cons: Wrong tool class for the ask: it is an authorization gateway for agent builders (refund/payment style), not a Claude Code hook, skill, or MCP server; no Claude Code integration exists (no hooks.json, plugin.json, SKILL.md).
Cannot gate built-in Claude Code tools (Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch), which are where the risk is in daily coding; only MCP tools of a single wrapped server, and one guard process per wrapped server.

Claude Code does not relay the actiongate/intent _meta, so every call is judged against the placeholder 'No user intent was relayed', making the semantic alignment questions meaningless (enforce.ts:91-96); with default REVIEW/BLOCK thresholds this likely blocks or reviews many legitimate calls, and REVIEW has no human-review UI in stdio mode.

Wrapped tools lose their input schemas (inputSchema forced to {type:'object'}, proxy.ts:100), so Claude cannot see parameters for gitnexus/playwright tools; also a Jev call per MCP tool call adds ~0.5-1 s and cost, and Jev outage fail-closes all wrapped MCP tools.

Not installable via npx/uvx: must clone the repo and pnpm install a whole monorepo (Next.js, Fastify, Postgres drivers); README says not on npm/PyPI. Pins node>=22, fine with Node 24, but heavy for a hook.

Brand-new and single-author: created 2026-09-19, 34 commits, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, README states no external security review and self-authored eval labels; direct TypeSafe adapter unverified live.

dotenv/config auto-loads the .env of Claude Code's project cwd into the proxy and the whole environment is passed to the upstream child, which is undesirable on client projects; UPSTREAM_ARGS split on spaces is fragile.
Data egress of tool arguments to OpenRouter for every guarded call, on client projects, for marginal benefit.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration: an MCP-proxy authorization gateway for agent products that cannot see built-in tools, gets no user intent from Claude Code, and strips wrapped tools' schemas. Worth reading as a reference for calling the OpenRouter Decisions API and fail-closed handling, but do not install it for daily coding.

entries.name: mywwave/cursor-jev
entries.what: Cursor-only plugin (hooks + stdio MCP + rule + skill, zero npm deps, Node 22.13+) that calls TypeSafe System One (model jev-latest) to gate agent behaviour. Hooks: rewrite/deny Task subagent hops (route by Choice+Noul), deny out-of-scope Write/StrReplace/Delete (scope Noul), split compound prompts, ask before destructive shell, rerank Grep/Glob hits and then DENY any Read outside a top-3 shortlist, and emit a "stop, work is ready" nudge after agent replies. MCP exposes jev_auth, jev_route, jev_judge, jev_ask. State kept in ~/.cursor/cursor-jev.sqlite. Not designed for Claude Code; README says "The plugin is Cursor-only".
interface: MCP resource jev://status; prompts connect-typesafe, route-task
CLI set-key | key | install | uninstall | mcp | hook
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (Cursor events) do the real work with no model involvement; MCP tools plus a skill/rule are model-discretion. Under Claude Code, none of this fires as-is: the hooks are registered in ~/.cursor/hooks.json using Cursor event names (preToolUse/beforeShellExecution/beforeSubmitPrompt/afterAgentResponse) and Cursor response fields (permission, agent_message, updated_input, additional_context). Only the stdio MCP server would load in Claude Code, giving model-discretion tools.
security: Key stored in plaintext ~/.cursor/cursor-jev.env with mode 0600 (src/key.mjs:48-54); key passed via env/envFile, not argv (mcp.json envFile), so not visible in ps. set-key CLI prompts (no --key flag found).

Secret filter is weak: looksSecret (src/session.mjs:3) only matches 'apikey_', 'Bearer <tok>', 'TYPESAFE_API_KEY='. AWS keys, GitHub tokens, private keys, client credentials in Write previews, shell commands or search snippets would be sent to the API.
Write hook sends path + first 1200 chars of new content/old_string to a third party (src/hook.mjs:119-126); on client projects this is source-code egress.

Prompt-injection surface: task text, file snippets and agent responses are fed as Jev state; outputs only feed thresholds, but hook injects fixed strings, not model text, so injection risk is low. However an attacker-controlled repo could steer scope/read gates (deny Reads) via crafted content.

Read gate denies any file not in the reranked top-3 allowlist (src/hook.mjs:210-218) - behavioural risk not security: can block legitimate reads. handleReadGate has no try/catch (unlike other handlers), so a SQLite error crashes the hook.
No telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh; install is a local `node bin/cli.mjs install` that edits ~/.cursor config. install.mjs writes ~/.cursor/hooks.json and mcp.json (would need porting).
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on each gate: full Task prompt (<=12000 chars), user prompt (<=4000 chars, every submit), planned Write/Edit path plus 1200-char content preview, non-routine shell command text (1200 chars) plus user ask, search hit paths plus 180-char snippets (up to 16), Task results (1500 chars) and agent response summaries (1200 chars). File bodies of Reads are not sent. README claims secrets are stripped, but the filter is a 3-pattern regex. Sent to TypeSafe directly, not OpenRouter (would go to OpenRouter after a port).
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: missing key, HTTP error, timeout all return allow/{} (src/hook.mjs try/catch; README 'fail open'). Hook timeout 1.8s, 1 attempt (src/roles.mjs:12-13), Cursor-level hook timeout 5s (hooks/hooks.json). Exceptions: Read gate is uncaught, and once an allowlist exists it fails closed on unlisted paths independent of Jev availability. MCP path uses 15s timeout and 3 attempts with 429/529 retry (client.mjs:5-6, roles.mjs:10).
entries.contextCost: Low for MCP: 4 tools (~1.2k chars descriptions + ~0.8k chars schemas) plus ~330-char server instructions, roughly 600-800 tokens, plus 2 prompts and 1 resource. Bundled SKILL.md (~2 KB, ~500 tokens when triggered) and an always-on rule (2.5 KB, ~650 tokens; Cursor concept, no Claude Code equivalent). Hooks inject text only occasionally (~30-40 tokens like 'Jev routed:... Jev speed: fast...' prefix on Task prompts, stop/scope nudges), but deny messages cost a wasted turn each.
pros: Only candidate seen so far with a full deterministic-hook design for Jev (gates on prompts, writes, shell, search), i.e. the automatic 'no need to say use jev' pattern the user wants - useful as a design reference.
Sensible Jev usage: closed typed questions with thresholds in one reviewable file (src/roles.mjs), code decides, model never generates; matches Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives.
Hooks fail open on timeout/HTTP error/no key, with 1.8s cap and one attempt.
Zero npm deps, MIT, no postinstall/telemetry, key file 0600, key not in argv; small (~137 KB) and easy to audit; 4 test files (~56 tests) using injectable fetcher.
Central client.mjs makes provider swap mechanically small in code terms.
cons: Cursor-only by the author's own statement; hook events, tool names (Task, StrReplace), response schema and ~/.cursor install paths do not match Claude Code (Agent/Edit, hookSpecificOutput/permissionDecision). Would require a rewrite of hook.mjs/install.mjs.
No OpenRouter support: hard-coded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, jev-latest, TYPESAFE_API_KEY; zero mention of OpenRouter.
Brand new and unproven: created 2026-09-20, 4 commits in one afternoon, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, no CI, no issues history; version 0.1.0.

Value proposition (deny Task hops, deny Reads outside top-3, block writes deemed out-of-scope) mostly addresses Cursor cost/latency, and can actively harm a senior dev on bypass/auto mode: false-positive scope denies and Read denies burn turns and derail client work.
Claims of 'almost useless on one-file tweak' and speed gains are unmeasured; no benchmark of Jev gate accuracy (skeptics say Jev may be a small router model).
Heavy per-event egress of code snippets, prompts and shell commands to a beta third-party API with a weak 3-regex secret filter; risky for client projects under NDAs.
Per-event node cold start plus network on every prompt/shell/write/response adds latency stacked on existing PreToolUse hooks; read gate uncaught exception path.
Overlaps and may conflict with the user's GitNexus grep/glob context hook and secret-guard (competing additional_context / deny decisions).
entries.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code or with OpenRouter without a substantial rewrite; treat it as a design reference for hook-driven Jev gating (scope/split/destructive-shell) rather than something to install. The aggressive Read/Write denial and code-snippet egress make a straight port undesirable for client work.

entries.name: BasmaAbouzied0/jev-auto-approve
entries.what: Single-file Python 3 stdlib PreToolUse hook (Bash matcher). For each Bash command it applies a local regex denylist and injection-smell filter, then asks Jev a Noul question ("is this command strictly read-only?") via a POST to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. If P(yes) >= 0.95 it emits permissionDecision "allow". Otherwise it stays silent, so the normal permission prompt appears. It never denies. Its only purpose is to cut permission prompts for read-only commands.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook. It fires automatically on every Bash call with no prompting. However, it exits early unless permission_mode is 'default' or 'acceptEdits' (:81), so it is a no-op in bypass mode and in "auto" mode.
security: The API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent as a Bearer header, so it does not appear in argv. The hook command in settings.json contains no key.
The hook only allows or stays silent, and it never emits deny. The fail-safe direction is good: errors, timeouts, no key, or a low p all fall back to the normal prompt.

Its risk is false approvals. The HARD_NO denylist is incomplete, and the rest is left to Jev. Read-shaped commands that can mutate or exfiltrate are not covered by the regex: find -delete, find -exec (rm is caught, other commands are not), sed -i, awk 'system(...)', xargs, git config, git stash, git fetch/pull/clone (network), git diff --output=, git -c core.pager=..., $(...) and backtick substitution, && and ; chains, tar/unzip -x, make, python -c and node -e. With a plain `python -c` or `xargs`, everything depends on Jev's probability.
Jev is a 32k-context, beta, low-latency classifier, and the skeptic claim that it is a flash router is unverified. The 0.95 threshold was tuned on only 8 negatives.

It also auto-approves reads of sensitive files (cat ~/.ssh/id_rsa, cat .env, printenv). The hook has no sensitive-path awareness. The user's existing secret-leak guard is a separate hook, and the deny-wins ordering there should be tested.

The prompt-injection surface is the command string sent to Jev. The regex filter (# / approve / ignore ...) is a keyword heuristic that is easy to evade with paraphrase, but quoted prose only matters if it reaches a command Jev then rates read-only.
entries.dataEgress: For every Bash command that passes the local gate (single-line, at most 400 chars, no denylist match), the hook sends {command string, cwd path, model} to api.typesafe.ai. This includes any inline args or paths in the command, and it can include secrets if the command embeds them (mitigated only by the denylist and the user's own secret guard). File contents, diffs, prompts and tool outputs are not sent. Non-Bash tools are ignored. Nothing goes to OpenRouter unless patched, and OpenRouter and its upstream provider would then see the same payload.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the sense of "fall back to the normal prompt". The urlopen timeout is 3 s (configurable). The hook's settings.json timeout of 5 s is suggested. Any exception (network, 401, 429, 5xx, bad JSON) is caught (:91) and the hook stays silent. Worst case is 3 s of added latency per gated Bash call while Jev is down, plus a normal prompt. It is never fail-closed and never blocks.
entries.contextCost: Zero context cost. There are no MCP tools and no injected text. The hook only prints a short permissionDecisionReason ('Jev: read-only p=0.97') when it approves, and Claude may or may not see it.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'. Zero context tokens.
Fail-safe direction is right: it never denies, and every error falls back to the normal prompt. The 3 s timeout is bounded.
Small (123 lines), stdlib-only and fully auditable. There is no installer, no telemetry and no dependency supply chain.
It uses Jev for the task it is suited to: a calibrated yes/no on a short string (Noul primitive), with a tunable threshold and a DRY log mode for trialing.
Layered defense: a local denylist runs before any network call, so risky commands never leave the machine.
The request shape (state/questions/noul, /v1/systemone) is the same System One API that OpenRouter exposes, so an OpenRouter port is a ~5-line patch.
cons: Does nothing for this user's setup. Line 81 returns early unless permission_mode is 'default' or 'acceptEdits', and the user usually runs bypass or 'auto', so the hook never calls Jev.
Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It needs a source patch to use OpenRouter (URL, key env and model id), and OpenRouter's exact request and response schema is unverified.
Only one narrow use case: permission prompts for Bash. It does not touch code review, routing, commit or PR decisions or anything else where Jev could add value.

Brand new (created 2026-09-27, 3 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, no release, no CI). Its calibration evidence is 16 commands and self-reported. Denylist gaps (find -delete, sed -i, xargs, git fetch, python -c, && chains, cat of secret files) leave safety resting on a beta model's probability.

Sends each gated command plus its cwd to a third party for a decision that Claude Code's built-in permission rules or allowlist (e.g. Bash(git status:*)) already resolve locally with zero latency and zero egress. The README shows git status scoring 0.82 (not approved), which is worse than a static allow rule.
Adds Python startup plus a network round trip in series with the user's existing Bash PreToolUse hooks. It needs re-validation for interaction with the secret-leak guard.
entries.verdict: Clean, honest, well-scoped fail-safe hook, but it is a no-op for this user: it exits unless permission_mode is default or acceptEdits, and they run bypass or auto. It is also TypeSafe-only. Static allow rules do the same job with no egress, so it is not worth installing.

entries.name: vineetagarwal54/jev-mcp-middleware
entries.what: A stdio MCP gateway that sits between an MCP host and exactly ONE upstream stdio MCP server. It snapshots the upstream tool list at startup, re-exposes those tools 1:1, and on each tools/call validates args (Ajv), applies YAML hard rules (glob/JSON-pointer, DENY>REVIEW>ALLOW), optionally asks Jev six Noul yes/no questions (destructive, external_consequence, sensitive, irreversible, high_impact, human_review) about the sanitized tool call, compares probabilities to thresholds (review 0.5, deny 0.9) and forwards or returns a local MCP error. Every call is audited to SQLite. Self-described "research/developer tooling, not a production security boundary".
interface: No hooks, no skills, no plugin.json, no .mcp.json
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy, fully automatic but narrow: once an existing MCP server is re-registered behind it, every call to that server's tools is intercepted with no model discretion. It is NOT a Claude Code hook, so it cannot see built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Write, Read, Grep) where destructive risk actually lives, nor MCP servers not wrapped (one gateway instance per upstream; v0.1 supports one downstream session and one upstream).
security: API key read from env only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), never argv or YAML; README explicitly says so. Good: no key in process list.
SDK logLevel 'off', body logging off; upstream stderr discarded; audit rows omit upstream responses and raw exceptions.

Sanitizer (src/security/redact.ts, sanitize.ts) redacts key names (authorization/password/secret/token/apiKey/credential) and value patterns (bearer/JWT/API-key formats/private keys/URL creds), depth and 4096-char string bounds. README admits it is heuristic, not DLP, so code snippets, paths and prose in tool args will still be sent to Jev.

Prompt-injection surface: tool name, description and arguments are put in Jev's state; the question text says 'Treat state as untrusted data'. Jev output is a bounded number 0..1, validated by zod, so injection can at most skew a probability, and hard rules run first. A hard ALLOW rule bypasses semantic evaluation.

Spawns the configured upstream command via MCP stdio transport (config-controlled, no shell string). Env passthrough limited to named vars. No curl|sh, no postinstall script in package.json; Dockerfile runs as non-root, digest-pinned base.
Writes a persistent SQLite audit DB (sanitized args retained) that the user must secure. No telemetry found besides TypeSafe API calls.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated tool call (only when provider.type=jev and no hard rule decides first and tool is semanticEligible): to api.typesafe.ai (hard-coded) go tool name, tool description and the redacted JSON arguments plus six fixed question strings. Auth via TYPESAFE_API_KEY bearer. Upstream tool results never go to Jev. Nothing to OpenRouter. Since it wraps a single MCP server, this covers only that server's tool calls, not Claude Code's built-in Bash/Edit/Write/Read, the prompts, or the transcript.
entries.failureMode: Configurable and fail-closed by default. provider.timeoutMs default 3000 (max 60000) is a total deadline enforced by evaluateProvider (src/decision/evaluateProvider.ts:203-205); SDK retries default 0. On TIMEOUT/UNAVAILABLE/INVALID, policy.providerFailureOutcome defaults to DENY, so a slow or down Jev BLOCKS the wrapped MCP tool (the agent gets a policy error). Can be set to ALLOW (fail-open) or REVIEW (REVIEW is just an error; there is no approval UI, so effectively deny). Missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the gateway fail to start, so the wrapped MCP server disappears from Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: Near-zero own cost: the gateway adds no tools and no server instructions (Server created with only capabilities.tools, gatewayServer.ts:8). Context cost equals the wrapped upstream server's tool definitions, unchanged, so it is neutral. No hooks, no injected text. On the contrary, it replaces rather than adds an MCP entry.
pros: Genuinely uses the Jev System One API via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with Noul primitives; typed 0..1 probabilities validated by zod (JevDecisionProvider.ts:9-22), so the integration is architecturally sound and injection-resistant (numeric output only, hard rules first).
Well-engineered failure semantics: hard deadline, explicit providerFailureOutcome (DENY/REVIEW/ALLOW), cancellation never fails open, one audit row per call (router.ts, evaluateProvider.ts).
API key only from env, not argv; sanitizer redacts secrets before egress; audit omits upstream bodies; pinned deps, pinned CI actions, non-root Docker; MIT.
Zero context overhead: adds no tools, no instructions, no hook text.
Good reference implementation of the six-question risk-scoring pattern and threshold policy that could be lifted into a custom PreToolUse hook.
cons: Wrong integration point for this user: it is a proxy for ONE upstream MCP server, not a Claude Code hook. It cannot gate Bash/Edit/Write/Read or any other MCP server, which is where the risky calls happen. The user already has PreToolUse hooks and the existing servers (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) are read-only/browser tools that gain little from a destructive-risk score.

Does not support OpenRouter: hard-coded baseURL https://api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (JevDecisionProvider.ts:28-30); needs a source patch plus a fork, and OpenRouter response-shape compatibility is unverified.
Adds no productivity value (no routing, classification, or code-decision help); it is purely a security/risk gate, and the README itself disclaims it as research tooling and not a security boundary.
Fail-closed default means a Jev outage or slow response blocks the wrapped tool; the missing-key case stops the whole server from starting. REVIEW has no approval UI so it is just a block.

Heavy setup: Node 24 only, native better-sqlite3 build, private package with no release, hand-written YAML per upstream, rewrite of .mcp.json entries, and one gateway process per wrapped server. The catalog snapshot is startup-only (no listChanged), so playwright/gitnexus dynamic tool changes would be missed.

Very immature: 7 commits over 2 days, 2 authors (effectively 1), 0 stars, no releases, no live-Jev test evidence (tests block network; the benchmark is 12 synthetic hand-labelled cases). Persistent SQLite audit of sanitized args on client projects adds a data-retention burden; heuristic redaction can still leak client code/prose to a third party.
Sends tool arguments (potentially client code or paths) to TypeSafe on every gated call, a compliance issue on client projects; sits on the hot path of every call.
entries.verdict: Real, competently written but a 2-day-old proof of concept that wraps a single upstream MCP server with a Jev-based risk gate, so it neither covers Claude Code's built-in tools nor supports OpenRouter without patching. Not recommended for daily coding; at most a design reference for a custom PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

entries.name: ndolinschi/toolgate
entries.what: Not a Claude Code hook despite the candidate label. It is a 283-line Next.js 15 demo web app (single page plus one POST /api/decide route). You paste a planned tool call as JSON. The route sends it to Jev with 5 fixed questions: a Choice for allow/ask_human/deny, a Score for risk, and 3 Noul questions for exfil, irreversible and policy_violation. It returns the answers. With no TYPESAFE_API_KEY it falls back to a regex heuristic that fakes the same answer shape. It has no MCP server, no hook script, no CLI, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a manual web demo with no integration into Claude Code at all: no hook events, no MCP tool, no skill trigger.
security: TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read from the server-side env only (jev.ts:73). It is not in argv, and nothing is logged.
/api/decide has no auth, rate limiting or input size cap. If the dev server is bound beyond localhost, anyone can spend the key.

Untrusted tool-call JSON is passed straight into the Jev state with no sanitization. That is prompt-injection surface, but Jev returns typed probabilities rather than free text, so the impact is limited to manipulating the score.

Fail-open demo fallback: with no key, a regex heuristic silently answers instead (jev.ts:105-115). meta.mode marks it, but nothing enforces it. A gate that silently degrades to regexes is a security smell.
Heuristic deny list is trivially bypassable (product.ts:51). It matches strings like 'rm -rf' and 'sudo', but not variants like find -delete or base64 payloads.
No postinstall scripts and no curl|sh. The dependencies are only next, react and tailwind.
entries.dataEgress: In live mode, the full JSON in `state` (tool name, args, context, goal) plus the question text goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (jev.ts:77-84). In this repo, nothing hooks into Claude Code, so nothing leaves automatically. Only what you paste into the web UI is sent.
entries.failureMode: If the key is present and Jev is down or slow, fetch has no timeout or AbortSignal (jev.ts:77). It hangs until the platform default, and a non-2xx response throws, which becomes a 500 (route.ts:11-13). If the key is missing, it silently uses fake heuristics. For Claude Code there is no fail-open or fail-closed behavior to evaluate, because there is no hook.
entries.contextCost: Zero as shipped. It exposes no MCP tools, injects no hook text, and adds no skill descriptions. If the idea were rebuilt as a PreToolUse hook, the context cost would also be about 0, since hooks add no tokens to the context unless they return additionalContext.
pros: The question design is a sound template for a Jev-backed PreToolUse gate: one Choice (allow/ask_human/deny), one Score for risk, and Noul flags for exfil, irreversibility and policy violation (product.ts:11-45). It maps directly onto Jev's three primitives.
Its permissionDecision-like outputs (allow/ask/deny) match Claude Code's PreToolUse hook decisions, so porting is conceptually easy.
The client is small and readable (jev.ts, about 115 lines) and has no dangerous install steps.
The key is kept in an env var on the server side, not in argv.
cons: The candidate is mislabeled. It is a Next.js demo UI and has no hook, MCP server, skill or plugin, so it cannot be installed into Claude Code.
There is no OpenRouter support. It is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY. That host and request schema are unverified against the OpenRouter docs.
