It has 1 commit, 3 stars, no license, no tests, no CI and a 7-line README, and the last push was 13 days before the audit date. It is a hackathon-style artifact.
The demo fallback silently substitutes regex heuristics when the key is missing. That is fail-open behavior disguised as an answer, which is wrong for a security gate.
No fetch timeout, no retry, no auth or rate limit on /api/decide.

Even as a hook, a per-tool-call gate would be redundant for this user. It would overlap the existing secret-leak PreToolUse hook and the bypass/auto permission modes, and it would add 70-500 ms to every tool call.
entries.verdict: Not a usable integration: it is a standalone Next.js demo of a Jev tool-call gate with no Claude Code hook or MCP surface and no OpenRouter support. At most, copy its 5 question definitions as a design reference for a self-written PreToolUse hook.
entries.license: None (licenseInfo null; all rights reserved by default, so reuse is legally unclear)

entries.name: fast-mcp-gatekeeper
entries.what: A stdio MCP proxy wrapper (not an MCP server itself): you prefix another MCP server's command with `fast-mcp-gatekeeper --`. It intercepts JSON-RPC `tools/call` requests, sends the serialized call to a Jev System One endpoint (noul/score/choice questions) and blocks, redacts or allows the call. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or on ANY error or non-2xx response, it silently falls back to a hard-coded keyword 'simulator' (substring checks such as '../', 'curl ', 'secret'). The README's '<50ms' and demo output are therefore simulator numbers (random 30-50ms), not measured Jev latency.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy: automatic for every tools/call of each MCP server you wrap (deterministic, no model discretion). But it only covers MCP tools, not Claude Code built-ins, and it is not a Claude Code hook.
security: No postinstall scripts, no telemetry, no runtime deps (package.json)
API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not argv (good); but it is sent to a hard-coded, unverified host api.typesafe.ai (src/client.ts:19)

Fail-open by design: empty catch at client.ts:49 and non-ok responses fall through to a keyword simulator; a bad/expired key, timeout or outage silently degrades to substring matching with no warning or log
No fetch timeout/AbortController: a hung Jev request hangs the tool call indefinitely (client.ts:32), i.e. fail-hang rather than fail-open/closed

Simulator is trivially bypassable (e.g. 'curl', 'rm -rf', base64, '$(...)'; does not flag rm -rf, git push --force, etc.) and false-positives on any call containing 'secret', 'password', 'curl ' or 'sk-'
Redaction only handles 'bearer x' and 'sk-...' patterns plus keys named password/secret/token; misses ghp_, AKIA, JWT etc.
entries.dataEgress: With no key: nothing leaves the machine (local simulator). With TYPESAFE_API_KEY set: for every tools/call to the wrapped server, JSON.stringify({name, arguments}) (full tool arguments, e.g. file paths, file contents to write, SQL, shell strings, any embedded secrets) is POSTed to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Not prompts, not conversation, not tool results. It never goes through OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to a keyword simulator on any error or non-2xx (client.ts:41-55), silently and with mode 'simulator' only in an unused field. No timeout on fetch, so a stalled connection blocks the call indefinitely. Proxy crash/child exit calls process.exit. Not a reliable security control.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools of its own. Since it is a transparent proxy, it adds no tool definitions or instructions; the wrapped server's tools/list passes through unchanged. Hooks inject nothing. Effective context cost ~0 tokens, but also zero Claude-visible capability.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a stdio proxy needs no prompt instruction and no model discretion
Zero context cost: adds no tool definitions or hook text to Claude Code
MIT, zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry, key via env not argv; tiny (about 34 KB, easy to audit in minutes)
Correctly frames Jev's primitives (noul/score/choice) as a per-call policy classifier, which is a sensible System One use case
Works with any stdio MCP server, so gitnexus and playwright could in principle be wrapped
cons: The default path is fake: without TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or on any failure) it runs a hard-coded substring matcher while README presents it as Jev-powered, and the '<50ms' demo output (latencyMs 41) is a random 30-50 number from the simulator (client.ts:52)
No OpenRouter support: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY and hard-coded api.typesafe.ai/v1 with no env override for base URL; user wants OpenRouter, and there is no model id sent either
Silent fail-open with swallowed errors (client.ts:49) and no fetch timeout, so it is neither a reliable guard nor a reliably fast one

Guards the wrong surface for Claude Code: user's risky actions are built-in Bash/Edit/Write/Read, which bypass MCP proxies entirely; wrapping gitnexus/playwright/caveman-shrink adds latency and false positives for little gain
Duplicates the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) with a weaker, keyword-based version

Naive simulator false positives on ordinary coding content: any call whose arguments contain 'secret', 'password', 'api_key', 'curl ', '../' or 'sk-' gets redacted or blocked (e.g. playwright fill_form or gitnexus queries on auth code); redaction rewrites arguments and can corrupt a legitimate call
No inspection of tool results, so prompt injection via fetched pages/content is untouched

Brand-new (published 2026-09-20, single version, 0 repo, no public source URL, no CI, 4 shallow tests against the simulator), single unknown maintainer; npx -y unpinned would run it at every session start
README targets Claude Desktop/Cursor/Antigravity; nothing Claude Code-specific (no hook, no .mcp.json, no plugin)
entries.verdict: Skip. It is a thin, unverified wrapper whose default behavior is a keyword-matching simulator dressed up as Jev, with no OpenRouter path, silent fail-open, no timeout, and it only covers third-party MCP tools while missing Claude Code's built-in Bash/Edit/Write. If you want Jev as an automatic guard, write a small PreToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone directly with a timeout and explicit fail-open logging.

entries.name: jevgate (npm)
entries.what: Commercial SaaS wrapper ($9/mo, 500 decisions/mo, 7-day/500 trial) that installs a Claude Code/Codex PermissionRequest hook plus a SessionStart hook. On each permission prompt the hook POSTs the tool call, cwd, permission mode, permission suggestions and the last user prompt (1500 chars) to https://jevgate.dev/api/v1/decide. The server (closed source) asks Jev via Vercel AI Gateway five typed questions and returns allow or nothing (it escalates, so Claude Code prompts as usual). It only helps in modes that would otherwise show a permission prompt. It is a single 503-line zero-dependency JS file (jevgate.js) published by "remotehost". It does not give Claude Code any Jev capability for coding decisions (routing, classification, review).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PermissionRequest matcher '*' plus SessionStart). Fully automatic with no prompting, but ONLY fires when Claude Code would show a permission prompt; README states 'Claude Code only prompts outside auto mode' and the site says 'If you already run in an auto-approve mode, there is no prompt to answer and nothing changes.'
security: Token: stored plaintext in ~/.jevgate/config.json (default umask; writeJson has no mode 0600, jevgate.js:40) or JEVGATE_TOKEN env; `login --token <t>` puts the token in argv (visible in ps) but the default flow does not. It is a jevgate-issued token, not an OpenRouter/TypeSafe key.

No child_process shell execution except spawn of xdg-open/open with the login URL (jevgate.js:464-469); the URL comes from the server response (start.url), so a compromised server could pass an arbitrary URL to the browser opener (no shell, argv form).

No npm postinstall or lifecycle scripts; only a test script; zero dependencies; the tarball has no test/ dir despite the 'node --test test/*.test.mjs' script (files whitelist excludes it), so tests are not inspectable.

`init` mutates the global ~/.claude/settings.json and installs a copy at ~/.jevgate/bin/jevgate.js that runs on every permission prompt; `npx -y jevgate init` executes unpinned latest code from a single-maintainer, 12-day-old package. Anyone with the npm publish token can ship code to every user's hook, and the hook can return allow decisions, so a compromise or malicious server response could auto-approve arbitrary commands.

The server can return decision 'deny' and updatedPermissions via permission_index; the client echoes only Claude's own suggestion (jevgate.js:105-108), but the allow decision itself is entirely server-controlled. Docs claim 'never denies', but the client code implements a deny path (jevgate.js:111-116), so docs and code disagree.

Prompt injection surface: tool_input and the last user prompt are sent as-is to an LLM-backed gate; a crafted command or file content that shapes the task text could bias a p_allow. The gate is a typed classifier with thresholds, which limits but does not remove this. The Jev model is beta.
entries.dataEgress: On every PermissionRequest (only when a permission prompt would show), the full JSON body is sent to https://jevgate.dev (third party 'remotehost' SaaS, then Vercel AI Gateway, then TypeSafe/Jev): harness, hook event, tool_name, the ENTIRE tool_input (Bash command text with any inline secrets; for Write/Edit this includes the full file content or old/new strings, since no truncation is applied; file paths; URLs), cwd, permission_mode, permission_suggestions, and up to 1500 chars of the latest user prompt read from the transcript (jevgate.js:56-65, 281-296). Also the login email. Not sent: whole transcript, repo files unless part of a Write/Edit tool_input, tool outputs. The README/site says 'Nothing else leaves the machine' and 'selected excerpts', but the code sends tool_input unfiltered. For client projects this is client code/commands going to two unvetted intermediaries plus Vercel and TypeSafe. No retention/DPA policy found on the landing page snippet reviewed.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, by design. Client timeout 2500 ms (JEVGATE_TIMEOUT_MS) via AbortController, hook timeout 5 s in settings; any network error, non-2xx, bad JSON, missing token or quota exhaustion returns nothing so Claude Code prompts normally (jevgate.js:83-86). Billing/401 states emit a systemMessage notice once per session/15 min. Worst case cost: up to 2.5 s added before the normal prompt appears.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool definitions, no server instructions. Hook-injected text only: SessionStart additionalContext (~30-60 tokens, only when not signed in/trial over/quota >=80%, at most once per session/15 min) and a systemMessage on decisions when quota is >=80%. Negligible.
pros: Truly automatic: deterministic PermissionRequest hook, no user or model prompting needed, zero context cost (no MCP tools, no instructions).
Fail-open with 2.5 s client timeout and 5 s hook timeout; a Jev outage only reverts to normal Claude Code prompts (jevgate.js:83-86).
Never adds a deny in the documented flow; the conservative gate (risk<=0.35, confidence>=0.85, p_allow>=0.60, excludes install/configure/destructive/external) escalates the ambiguous.
Small, readable, zero-dependency, no lifecycle scripts, MIT; the whole client audited in one pass (503 lines). Local audit log ~/.jevgate/decisions.jsonl with p_allow, risk, latency.
Real Jev integration exists in production form: a proven pattern (typed multi-question call per decision) that could be copied into a self-owned hook that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API directly.
cons: Useless for this user's setup: he runs bypass/auto permission mode, where PermissionRequest never fires (README.md and site say so explicitly). Net effect would be zero decisions and only the SessionStart hook noise.

Not OpenRouter: hard-wired to jevgate.dev SaaS (which uses Vercel AI Gateway); no OPENROUTER_API_KEY path, and the client/server protocol is proprietary and closed source, so it cannot be repointed to OpenRouter (jevgate.js:25,71).

Sends the entire tool_input (including Write/Edit file contents and inline secrets in Bash) plus the latest prompt to a one-person startup, then Vercel, then TypeSafe. That is a poor fit for client projects and undermines the user's own PreToolUse secret-leak guard; the site's 'Nothing else leaves the machine' understates what jevgate.js:56-65 sends.
Paid ($9/mo, 500 decisions/month cap) and trial-limited (7 days/500 decisions); a heavy all-day session burns 500 prompts fast, after which it silently reverts and nags with systemMessages.

Very immature: created 2026-09-18, 6 versions in 24 h, ~51 weekly downloads, 0 dependents, no public source repo, no tarball tests, single maintainer with global settings.json write access and an unpinned npx init; supply-chain risk for a hook that can auto-approve commands.
Docs/code mismatch: README and site say 'never denies' but the client implements deny output (jevgate.js:111-116) if the server returns one; server behavior is unauditable.

Solves only permission-prompt friction, not coding value; Jev's primitives (Choice/Noul/Score) could serve routing/review/test-triage, none of which jevgate exposes. 'Powered by Jev (TypeSafe)' but not affiliated; the ~300 ms figure is self-measured on 12 runs.
entries.verdict: Skip it. It is a real but narrow Jev integration (permission-prompt auto-approver) that does nothing for a user in bypass/auto mode, cannot use OpenRouter, is closed-source SaaS, and ships full tool inputs (including file contents/secrets) to third parties. Only its idea (typed multi-question Jev gate in a fail-open hook) is worth borrowing for a self-built OpenRouter hook.

entries.name: coldteadotai/abide
entries.what: CLI (@coldtea/abide, npm) whose `init` writes four Node hooks into ~/.claude/settings.json (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|apply_patch, Stop). It compiles AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md into a committed .abide/rubric.json by asking the running agent to follow a bundled SKILL.md at SessionStart. After each edit and at turn end it sends the diff plus the rule questions to Jev (one Noul/Choice/Score question per rule). Rules scoring >=0.8 block with a repair request (PostToolUse feedback or Stop decision:block). 0.5-0.8 gives a user-visible note. Also has CLI audit/check/report/replay/calibrate/tune/bench for offline use. Supports Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode.
interface: abide audit / check / report / replay / calibrate / tune / bench / compile / uninstall
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic: PostToolUse on edit tools plus Stop, with no need to prompt "use jev". It does not fire on Bash-only changes at edit time, but Stop catches shell-written files through the git diff. It only does anything when the repo or ~/.claude has instruction files with rules, and rubric compilation is done by the main agent at SessionStart (uses some of the user's model tokens once per instruction change).
security: Key handling is good: read from process env, then .env.local and .env at the repo root, then ~/.abide/.env (credentials.ts:76-92). Never accepted via a CLI flag or argv. `login` uses no-echo raw stdin (secret.ts) and writes with mode 0600 via O_EXCL and refuses symlinks (credentials.ts:132-150). The parser extracts only abide's 3 variable names from .env files. Reading is done inside the abide process, not via an agent tool call, so the no-secret-leak hook is not triggered.

abide does not read OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The OpenRouter key would have to be stored as TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, so the user's protected-vars list should cover that name too, or the key be kept only in ~/.abide/.env.

Installer rewrites the GLOBAL ~/.claude/settings.json in place (settings.ts:71-84). It keeps other hooks via a passthrough schema and removes only entries whose command contains "abide-hook.js". It throws on invalid settings rather than clobbering. It reformats the file as 2-space JSON. Back up before init. Use --project to limit it to one repo.

Shell exec is limited to fixed argv arrays: git (git.ts spawnSync), `node` for the self-test, and `claude -p` with --permission-mode acceptEdits and --allowedTools Bash(node *) Bash(abide *) for compile/tune (claude.ts). Bash(node *) is broad. No shell-string interpolation of untrusted data was seen.

Prompt-injection surface: AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md content is compiled into the rubric and appears in SessionStart additionalContext and repair reasons, so a cloned untrusted repo's .abide/rubric.json would be loaded automatically if the hook is global. Also, injected instructions in the diff can move Jev's answers and suppress a violation, though impact is low because Jev outputs only typed probabilities.

Hook script path depends on the npx cache (packageRoot.ts), so a cache purge breaks the hook silently (fail-open). `npx @coldtea/abide` runs a third-party dependency tree (ink, react, ai) from a 12-day-old org at v0.0.7.
entries.dataEgress: Per check, the Jev POST state is {task, file|files, diff}. `task` is the last user prompt from the transcript or saved prompt, truncated (MAX_TASK_CHARS 600, constants.ts:19; checkRunner.ts:100-104; postToolUse.ts:84). So the README claim that Jev sees only "rule + diff, never the conversation" is slightly inaccurate. The diff is bounded to 24,000 chars (MAX_STATE_CHARS). The questions carry the rule text derived from AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, so instruction content also goes out. Secret-named files and abide-owned paths are skipped (paths.ts isExcludedPath), but secrets hard-coded in ordinary source diffs would be sent. Destination is the base URL (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if repointed, or the Vercel gateway). No abide-owned server and no telemetry found: the only network path is the AI SDK call in jev.ts. Local writes go to .abide/events.jsonl and ~/.abide session state (pruned after 7 days).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. runHook (hookRunner.ts:20-55) sets exitCode 0, installs a hard-deadline timer that emits silent output and process.exit(0), and catches every error. A missing key logs a skip event and lets the edit pass (postToolUse.ts:73-82). Timeout, HTTP error or a wrong model id throws AbideError, which becomes an event and a silent pass (postToolUse.ts:101-111). The real risk is silent uselessness: with a wrong model id or base URL nothing ever checks and the user only learns via `abide report` or .abide/events.jsonl. Blocking is bounded (2 blocks per rule per file per turn, 2 Stop checks per turn), so no infinite loops. A false positive at >=0.8 forces a repair turn (extra Opus tokens). Jev is overconfident on ambiguous input, so expect some noise on subjective rules; `calibrate` exists to tame that.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools and no tool definitions. Hook-injected text only when the rubric is stale or missing: a compile prompt pointing to SKILL.md (13,286 chars, about 3.3k tokens, read on demand). Otherwise zero. Repair messages are a few lines each.
pros: Genuinely automatic and deterministic: PostToolUse on edit tools plus Stop with git-snapshot turn diff (hooks/postToolUse.ts, hooks/stop.ts), matching the goal of Jev being used without asking. Covers files written by shell commands via the Stop diff.

Safe failure modes by construction: every hook path exits 0, has a hard-deadline process.exit (hookRunner.ts:36-39), bounded block counts, secret-file exclusion, and a missing key or network failure lets the edit pass and logs it.

Uses TypeSafe /systemone through the AI SDK provider with a user-overridable baseURL (TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL); the request body matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema. OpenRouter is one constant plus one env var away.

Cheap and light: Jev at $0.042/M input, ~1-1.6k tokens per check, output free. No MCP tools; hook-injected context only on rubric compile. Rubric is a committed readable JSON with per-rule scope globs and banded thresholds (0.8 repair, 0.5-0.8 note).

Real engineering: ~25 test files (~119 cases), replay benchmark of 93 real sessions with published method, calibrate/tune/audit/report tooling, symlink and FIFO defences. Coexists with other hooks (removes only its own entries). MIT, no telemetry found, keys never on argv.
Project-level install (--project) writes only the repo's .claude/settings.json, which suits per-client isolation.
cons: Not OpenRouter-ready: model id hard-coded to "jev-latest" (constants.ts:2) with no env override, while OpenRouter's /systemone reportedly wants "jev-1.13". A wrong id fails silently (fail-open). Needs a fork or dist patch, and the OpenRouter key must be stored as TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY. Nothing in the repo tests OpenRouter.

Sends code to a third party on every edit: changed lines (up to 24k chars), rule text, and the last user prompt (up to 600 chars). README's 'never the conversation' is not exactly true. A concern on client projects. Secrets in ordinary source diffs are not scrubbed.

Synchronous per-edit cost: fresh Node process plus SDK import, ~1s per README, up to 8-20s on timeouts, Stop up to 28s. Stacks with gitnexus and secret-leak hooks on edit tools. Blocks trigger extra Opus repair turns and false positives on subjective rules cost real tokens.

Hook commands point into the npx cache unless installed globally (fragile). init rewrites the global settings.json. Rubric compile relies on the main agent following a SKILL.md, spending the user's tokens, and only works if instruction files exist.

Very young: created 2026-09-18, v0.0.7, 34 commits, essentially 2 authors, no GitHub release or CI directory, alpha OpenRouter endpoint with no SLA. Value depends on having many prose rules in AGENTS.md that linters cannot check; it covers rule compliance only, not general Jev use (no permission gating, no MCP tool).

SECURITY (missed): the base URL is read from the environment, repo-root .env.local, repo-root .env, and ~/.abide/.env, and applies to whichever key is found (credentials.ts:76-92; withBaseURL at ~71). A cloned untrusted repo containing a .env with TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL=https://attacker sends the user's real key (from ~/.abide/.env or env), the diffs and the rule text to the attacker on every edit. The hook is global and needs no prompt. Since the user works on client repos, this is a real key-exfiltration vector. Mitigation: keep the base URL only in the process env or ~/.abide/.env, and never use per-repo .env files.

LATENCY/SIDE EFFECT (missed): UserPromptSubmit runs `git add -A` into a copied scratch index plus `git write-tree` on every prompt (git.ts snapshotTree, ~150-175), with a 5s cap (TURN_START_TIMEOUT_MS). This adds latency to every prompt in big repos. It also writes loose blob objects for every changed or untracked non-ignored, non-secret-named file into the repo's .git/objects, including large binaries. Stop repeats the snapshot (8s cap). The audit only counted per-edit latency.
abide reads .env, .env.local and ~/.abide/.env itself. Only the 3 variable names are extracted, but a client repo's .env is opened by a global hook.

The audit's hook budget line is right, but the Stop hook has no stop_hook_active handling (grep finds none). Loop bounding relies entirely on abide's own session-state counter (MAX_STOP_CHECKS_PER_TURN=2). If that state file is lost or unwritable, the bound is not enforced by the host guard.

Claude Code fit: PostToolUse decision:block only feeds the reason to Claude after the edit has already landed. It cannot undo the edit, and the tool already ran (it works as feedback rather than as a gate). The matcher also omits NotebookEdit, and 'apply_patch' is a Codex tool name, not a Claude Code one.

OpenRouter is a beta /api/v1/systemone with no SLA and a 32k context. The 24k-char diff cap (about 6-8k tokens) fits, but the abide docs and benchmarks were measured only against TypeSafe direct, so OpenRouter latency and error behavior are untested.
entries.verdict: The best-built automatic Jev hook found so far: fail-open, tested, project-scopable, near-zero context cost, and it fires without being asked. Held to 6 because it is TypeSafe-only with a hard-coded "jev-latest" model id (a one-line fork patch is needed for OpenRouter's /systemone), it sends diffs plus the last prompt to a third party on every edit, it adds ~1s synchronous Node latency per edit, and it is a 12-day-old v0.0.7 that rewrites the global settings.json.

verification.note: The main correction is that the OpenRouter blocker is refuted. OpenRouter's System One docs map bare ids `jev-1.13` and `jev-latest` to typesafe/, and the SDK's base URL, path, auth and response shape all line up (verified in the SDK source and the OpenRouter OpenAPI). The route is config-only: TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key>, TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, put in the process env or ~/.abide/.env. I could not run it live, so I mark it 'partial': documented and schema-compatible, but neither abide nor OpenRouter has tested it end to end. Other audit facts hold: fail-open runHook, the hook events and output fields (SessionStart additionalContext, PostToolUse and Stop decision:block, systemMessage) are valid in Claude Code 2.1.x, the bare `node` in the command, the npx-cache path fragility, the 600-char task egress (the README's 'never the conversation' is inaccurate), no telemetry (the only network path is the SDK call), no install scripts (package.json scripts are build and test only), and `claude -p` used only by compile and tune. The audit missed a repo-controlled base-URL override that could exfiltrate the key and diffs from an untrusted clone, and the per-prompt git snapshot cost with its object-store writes. Score moves 6 to 7: the biggest gap (needing a fork) is gone and the fail-open, automatic design is strong. It is capped by the extreme youth (12 days, v0.0.7, 2 contributors, no CI), the .env base-URL hijack risk, per-edit and per-prompt synchronous latency, its narrow fit (rule compliance from AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md only, not general Jev use), and the fact that it is untested on OpenRouter. Safe use: use the env-only base URL, add TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak protected list, install with --project or a stable global path, and back up settings.json first.

judge.why: Best-built automatic Jev hook found. It compiles AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md into a rubric, checks each edit (PostToolUse) and each turn (Stop with a git diff), and blocks at 0.8 or above with a repair request. It fires with no prompting, fails open, has bounded blocks (2 per rule per file, 2 Stop checks per turn), and has almost no standing context cost. The adversarial check refuted the model-id blocker and raised the score from 6 to 7. oh-my-plumb is a near-verbatim fork with extra hosts (Pi, Oh My Pi) and one squashed commit, so it is merged here and scored below upstream.
pros: Automatic and deterministic (PostToolUse on edit tools plus Stop). Covers shell-written files through the turn diff.
Fail-open everywhere (hard-deadline process.exit, every error swallowed). Missing key just logs a skip. Bounded block counts, so no infinite loops.
OpenRouter is env-var only. Request schema matches /api/v1/systemone.
Cheap: about 1-1.6k tokens per check at $0.042/M. No MCP tools. Context is injected only when the rubric is stale.
--project install limits it to one repo (good for per-client isolation). MIT, no telemetry found, key never on argv, about 115 tests, replay and calibrate tooling.
Only touches your rules, so it does not fight the caveman or plannotator hooks.
cons: Silent uselessness on misconfiguration: a wrong URL or model means nothing is ever checked. You must watch `abide report` or .abide/events.jsonl.

Base URL is also read from repo-root .env and .env.local. A cloned untrusted repo could redirect your key, diffs and rule text to an attacker on every edit. Keep the URL in ~/.abide/.env or the process env only, and never use per-repo .env.
Sends up to 24k chars of diff, rule text and the last 600 chars of the prompt to OpenRouter unredacted. This is wrong for client code. README says 'never the conversation', which is inaccurate.
UserPromptSubmit and Stop run git add -A into a scratch index plus write-tree on every prompt. This adds latency and writes loose objects to .git/objects.
Hook commands use bare `node` (your settings env overrides PATH) and point into the npx cache unless installed globally. Both break silently (fail-open).
PostToolUse block is feedback after the edit already landed. Blocks cost extra Opus repair turns. False positives at 0.8 or above on subjective rules are likely.
Rewrites the global ~/.claude/settings.json on init (back it up). The `apply_patch` matcher is a Codex tool name. Only useful if you have many prose rules.
Add TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak protected list.

entries.name: EliaAlberti/jev-rules
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (hooks only, no MCP server, no skills) that gives each project a .claude/jev-rules/*.md rule set (plus optional .claude/jev-map docs). On every UserPromptSubmit it sends the prompt plus one Noul yes/no question per rule/map doc to Jev in a single call, and injects (additionalContext) only rules with P>=0.6, once per session. On PreToolUse for Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit it asks Jev which not-yet-delivered rules apply to the file path (path only) and injects them just before the edit. Optional early-access rules pane (/rules) and a one-line "Jev gave Claude: rule 0.94" message. Purpose is context trimming and rule routing, not code intelligence.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. It fires automatically on UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse for Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit, SessionStart for clear/compact, and PostToolUse for AskUserQuestion. The user never has to say "use jev" and Claude never has to choose to call it. This is exactly the automatic-integration shape the user asked for, but the scope is only rule and context routing.
security: MIT licensed. Zero npm dependencies, no postinstall and no install script. Installed via /plugin marketplace add EliaAlberti/jev-rules, which only clones the repo. Hook code is plain Node ESM using fetch, fs and crypto, with no child_process or shell execution (I did not grep every file, but none of the read files use it).
API key travels only in an Authorization Bearer header (jev.mjs:54). It never appears in argv or the process list.

Key sources: process env, then <project>/.env, then ~/.jev-rules.env (config.mjs:20). Parsing project .env files in client repos is a mild surprise: a repo-supplied .env containing JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY or AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY would be picked up. Only those named keys are used, and the merged env is not written back to process.env.

Prompt-injection surface: the rule files under .claude/jev-rules are injected verbatim as additionalContext. A malicious client repo can therefore plant rule text that Claude reads as trusted instructions. The same is true of CLAUDE.md, but the injection here arrives silently at PreToolUse, right before an edit.

The plugin instructs Claude via additionalContext to ask the pane question (offerInstruction). Accepting rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json env, which turns on the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS flag for ALL plugins. It is opt-in via AskUserQuestion and can be disabled with 'Don't ask again', but a hook that offers to edit global settings is unusual.
No telemetry, but a state file is written to os.tmpdir()/jev-rules (state.mjs:21) and an optional debug log to ~/.jev-rules.log holding an 80-char prompt snippet.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai or Vercel AI Gateway (and to OpenRouter if patched): (1) on every UserPromptSubmit, the full user prompt text (cut to 24,000 chars) plus each rule and map-doc description, and applies/does_not_apply criteria lines. Rule names and bodies stay local because questions are keyed r0, r1... by position (jev.mjs docstring). (2) On the first edit of a file with undelivered rules, the project-relative file path only (basename if outside the project) and the rule descriptions. No file contents, diffs, tool outputs or code are sent (edit.mjs:5-9). The prompt itself may still contain pasted code or client details, and it goes to a third party on every prompt while undelivered rules exist. That matters for client work.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and never blocks. No key, timeout, network error, HTTP error or unparseable reply all lead to every not-yet-delivered rule being injected with a note "Jev was unavailable" (run.mjs:48-55, 99-104). Map docs are only listed, not included. The internal timeout is 2 s by default (configurable 100-8000 ms) and covers both attempts, with one retry on 429/529 after at most 300 ms (jev.mjs:15-21, 162-174). The hook-level timeout is 10 s. Worst case is +2 s on a prompt or on the first edit of a file when Jev is slow. Because rules are delivered once per session, a Jev outage costs tokens rather than correctness.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Injected text per hook call is capped at 9000 chars (about 2250 tokens, run.mjs OUTPUT_BUDGET), and each rule or map doc is delivered at most once per session, resetting after /clear or compaction. It injects nothing if the project has no .claude/jev-rules or .claude/jev-map (run.mjs:247 returns null). It adds a systemMessage line under each prompt, which is visible to the user only, and a one-time AskUserQuestion offer instruction. The design is meant to reduce context versus loading every rule in CLAUDE.md, but the user must first move their conventions into .claude/jev-rules/*.md files.
pros: Truly automatic: pure hooks, no model discretion, no MCP tool definitions, so no context tax for tools.
Uses Jev for what it is actually built for (typed Noul yes/no decisions with probabilities), and it is the only candidate I've seen that does this per prompt and per edit.
Robust fail-open design, verified in code: exit 0 always, 2 s cap, single retry on 429/529, never blocks the prompt or edit (jev.mjs:162-174, jev-rules.mjs).
Small, readable code with no dependencies and no postinstall: about 10 short ESM files, easy to audit and to fork.
Egress is minimal on edits (path only, never contents), and rule names and bodies never leave the machine (questions keyed r0, r1...).
131 offline tests across 8 files (README, CHANGELOG), and the code has a test seam for injecting fetch. It has releases (v0.5.0), a CHANGELOG and an MIT license.
Once-per-session delivery plus a 9000-char budget bound the token cost, and injection resets after /clear and compaction.
Already has a second wire-format backend (Vercel), so OpenRouter is a small additive patch: the typesafe backend already speaks POST /v1/systemone with type noul.

No hook conflicts with the user's existing matchers (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit secret guard overlaps only on NotebookEdit and only in that it never returns a permission decision; GitNexus is Grep|Glob|Bash).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only TYPESAFE_API_KEY/JEV_API_KEY (api.typesafe.ai) or Vercel AI Gateway. The user must fork or patch jev.mjs and config.mjs, and the OpenRouter /systemone schema is not verified to be identical.

Narrow value: it selects among project rules the user writes in .claude/jev-rules/*.md. It gives no code understanding, no routing of tasks or subagents, and no review or risk scoring. A senior developer with a compact CLAUDE.md gets little from it, since a rule set must be big enough to be worth filtering.
Per-project setup: every personal and client repo needs its own rule files with descriptions, so there is adoption friction, and nothing happens where rules are absent.

Sends the full user prompt (up to 24k chars) to a third-party API on every prompt with undelivered rules. Pasted code or client-confidential text would leave the machine, which is a concern on client projects. The user's secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
Edit-time judgment uses the file path only, so it is coarse. A Jev call precedes the first edit of a file, adding 260-520 ms before the write.
Reads project .env for keys and injects repo-controlled rule text as trusted context: a prompt-injection channel in untrusted client repos.

Offers to modify ~/.claude/settings.json to enable an early-access flag that affects all plugins (pane feature). It is optional, but noisy and risky, and it is disabled only by answering 'Don't ask again'.

Immature: created 2026-09-18, 63 stars, 21 commits (visible), 2 authors (both the same person, with Claude as co-author), no CI workflows, and the ecosystem is unproven. Jev itself is in beta with the unverified 'a DeepSeek flash router' skeptic claim.
Marketplace updates overwrite any local OpenRouter patch, so a fork or local marketplace is required.
entries.verdict: Best-shaped candidate for "automatic, no prompting" because it is a pure fail-open hook plugin that uses Jev's Noul primitive, but it only routes project rules and has no OpenRouter backend (a roughly 15-line patch in a fork). Worth adopting only if the user is willing to maintain .claude/jev-rules per project and accepts sending prompts to the Jev provider. Otherwise it is a modest, low-risk add-on rather than a core daily tool.

judge.why: Pure fail-open hook plugin using Noul: on each UserPromptSubmit and file edit it decides which project rules to inject, so rules are not all loaded up front. Modest and low-risk, but only a rule router. Needs per-project .claude/jev-rules upkeep. Audit-only.
pros: Never blocks. No key, timeout or bad reply just injects the not-yet-delivered rules.
Reduces standing rule context. Highest stars among the rule tools.
Simple Noul design.
cons: No OpenRouter backend without a patch.
Sends prompts to the provider on every prompt.
Injected context on each prompt adds to the caveman context and overlaps it.

entries.name: irfndi/oh-my-plumb
entries.what: Near-verbatim fork/rebrand of abide (same README, schema and band.ts) adding Pi/Oh My Pi hosts and a tiered fast-path/guards/micro-eval design; same edit and turn rule checks via Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (PostToolUse + Stop)
pros: Same hook design as abide (fail-open, per-edit rule checks) plus extra hosts (Pi, Oh My Pi) and recorded-payload host tests
MIT, tests and CI pinned against OpenCode versions
cons: Derivative of coldteadotai/abide with a single squashed commit; upstream is more proven (457 stars)
OpenRouter only via TYPESAFE_AI_BASE_URL like upstream; unproven
Provenance unclear for the benchmarks it copies (93-session replay is abide's)

entries.name: harrymunro/decision-first
entries.what: Skill plus optional UserPromptSubmit hook (prompt_hook.py keyword nudge) making the agent try a typed Jev decision before an LLM/regex for bounded judgments, logging every attempt to a lab dir.
entries.autoInvocation: UserPromptSubmit hook nudge (deterministic keyword regex, exit 0 always) plus skill trigger
pros: Closest to the 'auto-use without prompting' goal: hook nudges on classify/triage/rank words, never blocks
Has CI, tests, trigger-eval measurement, changelog, contribution docs
ask.py honors TYPESAFE_API_BASE, so https://openrouter.ai/api works with /v1/systemone
cons: Env names are TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_BASE; OpenRouter needs remapping and unverified model id
Keyword hook adds context on false positives and overlaps caveman UserPromptSubmit
Lab-directory documentation writes add overhead

judge.why: The closest match to 'Claude uses Jev without being told'. A skill plus an optional keyword-regex UserPromptSubmit nudge (exit 0 always) makes the agent try a typed Jev decision before an LLM or regex for bounded judgments. README-level evidence only.
pros: Never blocks. Has CI, tests and trigger-eval measurement.
Nudge is deterministic, so it does not depend on the skill listing budget.
Logs every Jev attempt.
cons: Keyword hook adds context on false positives and overlaps caveman's UserPromptSubmit.
Env names are TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_API_BASE. Model id unverified on OpenRouter.
Jev is no more accurate than Opus for the judgments it nudges toward. Adds a lab-directory write overhead.

entries.name: JevGuard (Jhonnyr97)
entries.what: Claude Code + Codex plugin (TypeScript, bundled to dist/) that enforces project rules with Jev. Rules live in .jevguard/rules.json, each rule being a Jev noul/choice/score question. A single command hook (jevguard-hook) runs on PreToolUse (every tool) and Stop. It batches all applicable rules into one POST {state, model, questions} to {baseUrl}/v1/systemone, compares answers with pass criteria, then denies the tool call (permissionDecision deny) or warns via additionalContext. Four skills (init, rule, pause, resume) generate and manage rules; init, pause and resume have disable-model-invocation.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse and Stop are registered by hooks/hooks.json and fire without any prompting. The user never has to mention Jev. Only setup (key/URL, /jevguard:init per project) is manual.
security: API key is never read from project files. It comes from JEVGUARD_API_KEY or CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_JEV_API_KEY (keychain-backed userConfig, sensitive:true) and goes out only as an Authorization header at client.ts:46. It is not in argv, because the hook is launched as a plain node command.

Committed dist/ bundle is not built from a verified pipeline (no CI), so src and dist can drift. The bundle is 4.3k lines and I did not fully audit it. Only client.ts:42 and the fetch at dist/bin/jevguard-hook.js:4157 were confirmed to match.
Shell use: execSync('git rev-parse --show-toplevel') with a fixed string only (config.ts:37). No user-controlled shell.
No telemetry. The only network call is the fetch to the configured baseUrl.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command, edit content and the last assistant message are sent as 'state' to Jev. Injected text can try to sway the verdict, but Jev returns only typed values, which limits the impact. Rules are checked by a model whose fail-open behaviour means an attacker who crashes or slows the verifier removes enforcement.

Unpinned trust: plugin auto-loads from GitHub main. A 1-star, 1-commit, 1-author repo could push a malicious hook update that runs with hook privileges. The hook runs arbitrary node code on every tool call.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured base URL (OpenRouter after switching): rule text (instructions and criteria) plus the full state of each matching event. For scope bash that is the entire Bash command string, including any inline secrets or tokens. For scope edit it is the full tool_input, meaning entire Write file contents, Edit old_string and new_string, and file paths. For scope response it is the entire last assistant message. Scope 'other' tools (Read, Grep, MCP calls) send their tool_input only when a rule has scope 'all'. File contents returned by Read are not sent (PreToolUse only). Nothing is redacted or truncated (verify.ts and hook.ts), and this includes client project code, so it needs client consent. It also bypasses nothing in the existing secret-leak guard, but that guard only protects reads, not what this hook forwards. Requests to OpenRouter are also seen by OpenRouter and TypeSafe, per their retention policies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on errors: main().catch writes {} to stdout and the reason to stderr, and the exit code is 0 (bin/jevguard-hook.ts:37-40). HTTP errors, 401s, parse errors and answer-type mismatches all allow the call (verify.ts:63). BUT there is no fetch timeout or AbortSignal (grep found none). A hung or slow connection stalls every tool call until Claude Code's own hook timeout kills the process, which is long by default. A killed hook is treated as a non-blocking error, so the call proceeds, but only after that delay. No retry. If the rules file is invalid, the parse error is thrown inside main and swallowed, also fail-open. Pause is done by the flag file .jevguard/paused.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Skills add four descriptions, about 150-250 tokens in total, and init/pause/resume are excluded from model invocation. The hook injects text only when a rule warns (additionalContext) or denies (reason string), which is a few lines. No server 'instructions'. Rule-block reasons and warnings are the only in-context cost, but repeated denial-retry loops can waste turns.
pros: Only candidate here that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: a real PreToolUse/Stop hook backed by Jev, not a tool the model must choose to call.
Uses the exact OpenRouter System One contract; OpenRouter works by changing two env vars plus the model string, with no fork required (client.ts:42, config.ts:23-27).
Batches all rules into a single Jev request and skips the network call entirely when no rule matches the scope (verify.ts:70).
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions.
Fail-open on every error path, so an OpenRouter outage will not brick the session (bin/jevguard-hook.ts:37-40, verify.ts:63).
Key handling is sound: sensitive userConfig in the keychain, never in project files, and the design explicitly keeps it out of argv.
Per-project pause, and per-rule action of block, warn or off; rules are human-readable and diffable in .jevguard/rules.json.
MIT licence, small (about 400 LOC of source), easy to audit and to fork with a timeout added.
cons: Very immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 2 stars, created 2026-09-21, no releases, no CI. Auto-updating a hook from an unpinned GitHub source that runs on every tool call is a supply-chain risk for client work; fork and pin a commit instead.

Exfiltrates full Bash commands, entire Write/Edit contents and the last assistant message to a third party, unredacted. That is a problem for client projects with NDA or code-confidentiality terms. The secret-leak guard does not cover it.
No fetch timeout (no AbortSignal in source). An OpenRouter stall delays every Bash/Edit/Write call until Claude Code's hook timeout, so 'fail-open' is only eventual.
PreToolUse has no matcher, so a node process starts on every tool call including Read/Grep/MCP, even though it exits early when no rule applies.
Adds a network round trip to every Bash/Edit/Write call under bypass or auto mode. The value is a guardrail (rule adherence), not an improvement to coding quality or speed.

Judgment quality is unproven. Rules are passed as prose instructions, Jev has no reasoning, and the thresholds are crude (noul >= 0.5). Expect false-positive denies that make the agent retry, burning tokens. Skeptics call Jev a small-model router.
Stop hook does not check stop_hook_active, so a block on Stop can loop; the default is warn but that warn output shape (hookSpecificOutput additionalContext on Stop) is likely ignored by Claude Code.
README references build-docs/ and a ~/.claude/plans path that are not in the repo, and it says PostToolUse is handled, but the hook is not registered. Small signs of an early draft.
Overlaps with, and adds another blocking hook next to, the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Ordering and combined latency are unknown.
Needs per-project /jevguard:init and rule curation, and /jevguard:rule is model-invocable so the agent can edit its own rules. Silent no-op without a key.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed integration that is actually automatic, and it works with OpenRouter by setting two env vars and jev.model=typesafe/jev-latest, but it is a 1-commit proof of concept that streams your commands and edited code to a third party with no timeout or redaction. Worth using only from a fork pinned to a commit, with a fetch timeout and rules narrowed to bash/edit, and probably only on personal projects.

judge.why: PreToolUse and Stop hooks that verify tool calls and edits against per-project rules, and work with OpenRouter. But it is a one-commit proof of concept with no fetch timeout and no redaction. Audit-only.
pros: Actually automatic (hooks/hooks.json). OpenRouter works by config.
Fail-open on HTTP, parse and type errors.
cons: No fetch timeout, so a hung endpoint can stall every gated call.
Streams commands and edited code to a third party with no redaction.
One commit. Should be forked and pinned, and probably limited to personal projects.

entries.name: @jvsteiner/agent-rules (jvsteiner/agent-rules)
entries.what: Claude Code / Codex / omp plugin that installs 7 hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd), all running one Node script (dist/behavior-hook.js). It sends the user request, the assistant reply, recent tool receipts and code changes to Jev (System One, Choice questions defined in markdown policies) and, on a violation, feeds a correction back to the agent (Stop rewrite, added context or a denied tool call). Also runs 10 legacy regex code rules (ts-no-any, rs-no-unwrap, no-hardcoded-secret and similar). Jev is used as a behavioural judge (premature completion, test-result contradiction, swallowed errors, jargon), not for routing or code generation.
interface: CLI agent-rules (validate, evaluate, compare, inspect, set-mode, status, install-omp)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (7 Claude Code events, registered via hooks/claude.json referenced from .claude-plugin/plugin.json) plus two description-triggered skills. No prompting of 'use jev' is ever needed; it runs on every prompt, tool call and reply once the plugin is installed and the key is in the environment.
security: No install scripts in the published package.json (scripts and dependencies both null); dist bundle has no child_process or spawn; only outbound URL is api.typesafe.ai. Installed hooks 'never download other packages' per README.

API key is read from process.env only (src/jev.js:2) and sent in an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. README states .env is never read by hooks; only the CLI --env-file flag does.

Redaction before egress is a narrow regex (src/runtime.js:12-13, src/review.js:25): sk-..., ghp_/gho_/... tokens and 'Bearer ...' only. AWS keys, private keys, DB URLs, .env contents in tool output or diffs are NOT scrubbed, and would go to the Jev provider. The same weak scrub applies to the local journals.

Local persistence: full-ish request, response, tool inputs/results and code changes (up to 96k chars per item) are written to ~/.local/state/agent-rules/*.json with mode 0600; a data-at-rest copy of client code.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results and code content are placed in Jev's state and questions, but Jev returns only typed choices (no free text), so injection can at worst flip a verdict and trigger or suppress a correction; corrections are authored policy text, not model output. Third-party policy dirs (project .agent-rules/rules) are loaded and can define arbitrary questions and corrections, so a cloned client repo could ship policies that send more data or inject correction text into the agent.
Legacy regex rules emit permissionDecision 'ask' from a hook, which could interrupt bypass/auto mode flows (disable with AGENT_RULES_LEGACY=0).
entries.dataEgress: Per Jev call (src/review.js:233-241 and src/jev.js:9): a JSON body with model, state and questions. State contains, depending on the enabled policies' 'requires/uses': the user's request text, the assistant's final reply, recent tool receipts (tool name, tool_input, tool_response), code changes (file path, new text, old-text context) and constraints, all passed through the narrow secret redactor. Up to 80,000 chars per request, chunked to at most 4 requests (maxReviewRequests). A local 'prefilter' regex skips the call when no candidate matches (test-result-contradiction, premature-completion, cat-* rules have prefilters); unexplained-jargon, swallowed-error and cat-pictures (response) have none, so in practice about one Jev call per Stop event that carries reply text (and code changes for swallowed-error) goes to the endpoint. Destination is api.typesafe.ai today (OpenRouter after patching), which means client code and conversation excerpts leave the machine to TypeSafe and, if patched, to OpenRouter as well. Not sent: .env files, ~/.claude credentials, whole repo.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. review deadline defaults to 2000 ms (config reviewDeadlineMs 100 to 120000), enforced with AbortController plus Promise.race (src/review.js ~270-305); on timeout, HTTP error or bad JSON the findings become 'unavailable' or 'unknown' and no correction or block is issued. Hook timeout in hooks/claude.json is 8 s. A crash in the hook prints only a systemMessage 'review unavailable' (bin/behavior-hook.js:42) and never denies. Missing key: Jev rules abstain, one notice at session start. Journal lock timeout 1.5 s falls back to observe-only. The only fail-closed-ish path is by design: a violation in repair/block mode, or the legacy regex rule 'ask'.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens and no server instructions. Two skills add only their frontmatter descriptions, roughly 90 to 100 tokens total. Hooks inject text only on findings: additionalContext or a Stop-rewrite message limited to the policy's correction (<=1000 chars each, legacy feedback <=8000 chars) and short user-visible systemMessage notices ('Agent Rules (observe): X would have fired'); in normal operation nothing is injected. Corrections consume extra model turns when they fire (max 2 per episode).
pros: The only candidate so far that is truly automatic: pure hooks, no model discretion, matches the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being told.

Uses Jev for what it is built for: typed Choice classifications with per-option probability thresholds (violation min_probability 0.95, winner >= 0.80, unknown abstention), see policies/premature-completion.md. Output is a decision, never free text.

Directly useful for a senior dev: test-result-contradiction is shipped in 'repair' mode (catches 'all tests pass' when a receipt shows failure), and premature-completion and swallowed-error are available in observe mode to calibrate before enforcing.

Fail-open with a 2 s deadline, 8 s hook timeout and bounded corrections (2 per episode); prefilter regexes keep most calls off the network, and commit 'perf: cut Jev input tokens per tool call from about 14,800 to about 600' shows the author is measuring cost.
Zero MCP tool bloat: no tool defs, no server instructions; injected context only on findings.

No postinstall, no runtime dependencies at install time, key via env not argv, MIT licence, decent deterministic test suite and CI on Node 20 and 24; 4 modes (off, observe, repair, block) allow safe rollout, and rules are plain markdown editable per user or per project.
Small codebase (about 1,900 lines in src and bin) that is easy to audit and fork.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/jev.js:2, bin/behavior-hook.js:22); not configurable through config.json. Using OpenRouter needs a code patch in source and dist, i.e. a fork, and the marketplace installs upstream npm, so updates overwrite it. Parity of OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone schema with TypeSafe's is unverified.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-11, 27 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars and 0 forks, 3 npm versions in two days (0.2.17, 0.2.19, 0.2.23). Rapid churn and no external validation.

Data egress is the main risk for client projects: reply text, tool outputs and Edit/Write diffs go to a third-party inference endpoint; redaction covers only sk-, ghp_ and Bearer patterns, so cloud keys and .env-like content in tool output pass through. Also a full local journal of session content in ~/.local/state/agent-rules.

Value is behavioural guardrails, not coding assistance: Jev does not help with routing, code search or decisions about the task itself. Only test-result-contradiction is enforced by default; the rest are observe-only, and the shipped policies include joke rules about cat pictures that will run and cost tokens or add notices.

Accuracy is unproven: evals are tiny, generated-label sets (premature-completion-r2 shows 5 cases, 1 failed, 2 abstentions); README itself says curated cases demonstrate behaviour, not general accuracy. False 'repair' corrections force extra Opus turns.

Overhead: one Node process spawn for every tool call across 7 event types, plus a synchronous Stop-time Jev call up to 2 s; in bypass mode the legacy regex rules can return permissionDecision 'ask', reintroducing prompts (AGENT_RULES_LEGACY=0 turns it off).

Overlaps in spirit with Claude Code's own auto-mode classifier and with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks; project-level .agent-rules policies from a cloned client repo are loaded automatically and could add rules or exfiltrate more state to the provider.
entries.verdict: Best-fit pattern seen so far for automatic Jev use (hook-driven, fail-open, cheap, no context bloat) and worth adopting as a fork, but it cannot use OpenRouter without a two-line endpoint/key patch, is 19 days old with a single maintainer, and ships your replies and diffs to the provider with weak redaction. Run it in observe mode on personal projects first and keep it off client repos until the egress and secret-scrubbing are hardened.

judge.why: Same idea as abide (hook-driven rule review of replies and diffs, 7 events, fail-open, 2 s deadline, observe mode). It has the pattern right but has no OpenRouter support, no stars and weak redaction. Audit-only, not adversarially verified.
pros: Fail-open with a 2000 ms deadline enforced by AbortController.
Observe mode exists. Cheap. No context bloat.
Covers 7 Claude Code events plus two skills.
cons: Needs an endpoint and key patch for OpenRouter.
Ships replies and diffs to the provider with weak redaction.
Zero stars and single maintainer. Abide is more proven.

entries.name: doronp/jevc (jev-compiler)
entries.what: TypeScript CLI/library (npm jev-compiler, bin jevc) that scans CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md style rule files, has the calling agent "lift" decidable rules into a Program JSON (narrow Jev Noul/Choice/Score questions plus a code reducer with thresholds), validates/lints it, and emits gates (SDK module, AI SDK, LangChain, JSON, bouncer/toolgate policy). The Claude Code plugin ships only one skill (/jevc:jevc, no hooks, no MCP). Optional step: the skill copies a sample gate.mjs into a project's .claude/gates/, npm-installs jev-compiler there and registers a per-project PreToolUse Bash hook. At runtime the gate builds state (tool_input plus last 4 user turns from transcript_path), calls Jev via @typesafe-ai/sdk POST /v1/systemone, runs the reducer, and emits allow (silent) / ask / deny.
entries.autoInvocation: Two layers. Setup: only when the user mentions enforcing/gating a rule, the agent ignoring CLAUDE.md, or jevc/Jev (skill description trigger), or via /jevc:jevc; it is authoring-time, not a per-task helper. Enforcement: once a gate is installed in a project's .claude/settings.json it fires automatically and deterministically on every PreToolUse Bash call with no user prompting, which does satisfy 'automatic use' but only for rules you compile, per project, and it must be installed project by project (or hand-moved to user settings with an absolute path and a node_modules-resolvable jev-compiler).
security: Shell exec: no child_process/spawn in src (grep clean). Skill however tells the agent to run `npx -y -p jev-compiler@latest jevc` (unpinned latest third-party code execution) and `curl -fsSL <raw github pinned-commit>/gate.mjs`, and `npm install jev-compiler@0.1.0` into the user project; asks user first before touching the project.

API key handling: read from env only by the SDK (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header; SKILL.md says never write key to files or print it; not in argv. redactErrorBody allowlist scrubs the API error body so echoed state is not leaked into messages (runtime.ts:~212-235, contract.ts).

Prompt-injection surface (a) rule files: jevc ingests CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md that may be attacker-influenced, listed as in-scope in SECURITY.md; the lift step is done by the calling Claude, and the skill relies on Claude to write program.json; citations are NOT verified by `jevc compile program.json` (SKILL.md section 4 says so and has the agent grep quotes manually). (b) Runtime: state sent to Jev contains tool_input and last 4 user turns; Jev is known to be movable by injected instructions in state, so a hostile command or file text quoted in a turn can push an allow verdict. Gate is advisory-quality, not a sandbox (SECURITY.md threat-model note).
Failure-safety of gate: sample gate.mjs exits 1 on import failure (missing jev-compiler), which Claude Code treats as non-blocking, so the gate silently turns off (SKILL.md step 1 states this).

Response-origin check: validateResponse refuses a response whose model is not jev-* unless JEVC_ALLOW_MODEL names it (contract.ts:65-81), protecting against a redirected base URL producing look-alike verdicts.
No telemetry found in src; only outbound is the Jev call. Apache-2.0, SECURITY.md with private reporting, solo maintainer with 7/30-day commitments.
entries.dataEgress: Per gated tool call the gate sends to Jev (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points to, e.g. openrouter.ai/api) the state object: hook_event_name, tool_name, full tool_input (the whole Bash command, which can embed secrets or paths), cwd, up to the last 4 user turns of prose from the transcript, and project_rules text (gate.mjs:62-69), plus the compiled question instructions. Nothing else; no telemetry. Authorization header carries the API key. Observe-mode log (JEVC_MODE=observe) stores only answers, not state. With OpenRouter this data goes to OpenRouter and its provider; no local pre-redaction, so the existing no-secret-leak hook does not cover this egress, and it may not even see OPENROUTER_API_KEY in its protected list.
entries.failureMode: Sample gate fails closed: on any error (missing key, network, timeout, invalid response, non-Jev model) verdict becomes 'ask' (gate.mjs:29, 94-98; JEVC_ON_ERROR=allow flips to allow). Client timeout 5 s with 1 retry (runtime.ts:183-186) so worst case ~10 s hang per call. Caveats for this user: (1) in bypassPermissions/auto mode an 'ask' from a hook may still interrupt sessions, so an OpenRouter outage or missing key stalls every Bash call, or (with ON_ERROR=allow) silently disables the gate; (2) if node cannot import jev-compiler the hook exits 1 = non-blocking = gate off; (3) the ask/deny is a permissionDecision so it is a hard gate for deny. Unlike the OpenRouter cookbook there is no static prefilter, so every Bash call incurs a network round trip unless the user edits the matcher/tool filter.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, no tools, no hooks registered by the plugin: zero tool-definition tokens. One skill; its listing description is 467 chars (~120 tokens) against a 2% listing budget; SKILL.md body 7,824 chars (~1,950 tokens) loads only when triggered. A deny/ask adds only a short permissionDecisionReason string to context. Generated gate adds no per-turn injected text.
pros: Solves a real, specific problem: turns ignored prose rules (e.g. never commit unless asked) into reproducible, unit-testable deterministic gates; verdict is computed in code (runtime.ts runReducer), model only supplies evidence probabilities.

Genuinely careful engineering: strict validators for request, program and response, refusal of NaN/missing answers, redacted API errors, response-model check, fail-closed default (runtime.ts, contract.ts, gate.mjs).

Clean OpenRouter path for transport: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY and hits /v1/systemone with Bearer, so env-only redirect to https://openrouter.ai/api works (sdk dist/index.mjs:56-62,513,554,581).
Strong offline test story: ~916 test cases, 58 recorded fixtures replay with no key, CI on Node 20/22/24; docs, SECURITY.md, CHANGELOG, Apache-2.0.
Zero context cost when idle: skill only, no MCP tools, no plugin hooks; gate output limited to a short reason. Observe mode (JEVC_MODE=observe) lets you dry-run a gate without blocking.
Can read transcript user turns so consent rules ('did the user actually ask to commit?') are answerable, which is exactly the class of rule static regex hooks cannot handle.
cons: Model id mismatch for OpenRouter: jevc hard-pins 'jev-1.13.0' and whitelists only jev-latest/jev-preview/jev-1.13.0 (contract.ts:17-25,134), while OpenRouter systemone uses 'jev-1.13'; needs a patch or a jev-latest test; unverified live.

Not automatic in the sense wanted: it is an authoring toolchain. Each rule needs scan, LLM lift, manual grep citation check, compile, and a per-project npm install plus hand-edited gate.mjs; reducer thresholds are guesses until measured (SKILL.md 'Finish').

Sample gate has no static prefilter, so every Bash call costs a network round trip (~0.2-0.8 s, up to ~10 s on failure) on top of gitnexus and no-secret-leak hooks; fail-closed 'ask' on outage interacts badly with defaultMode auto/bypassPermissions workflows.

Sends full Bash command plus last 4 user turns to OpenRouter unredacted; Jev is known to be steerable by injected state text, so the gate is defence-in-depth not a boundary (SECURITY.md says not a sandbox).

Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-18, 8 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases, 154 commits mostly in two weeks; corpus measured on one day against api.typesafe.ai only, never against OpenRouter; skill uses `npx -y ...@latest` unpinned.

Gate silently off (exit 1, non-blocking) if jev-compiler is not resolvable from the project; requires OPENROUTER_API_KEY to be exposed to hook process (and mapped to TYPESAFE_API_KEY), and it is not in the no-secret-leak protected list yet.

Gate fails open (non-blocking exit 1/127) on import failure, malformed stdin, missing program file, or a bare `node` in the hook command when PATH is overridden in settings env (this user's setup needs an absolute node path); the SKILL emits a bare `node` command.

No truncation of the 4 user turns: large pastes exceed the 45k pre-flight budget (32k on OpenRouter) and turn every Bash call into 'ask'; whole transcript is re-read and parsed synchronously per Bash call.

Sample gate is written for one commit rule (state fields, reason text, tool filter, replay fixture); the agent must hand-rewrite it per rule, and the skill tells the agent to use `npx -y -p jev-compiler@latest` (unpinned) while the gate is pinned to 0.1.0 and a fetched raw-GitHub commit, so scan/compile and gate versions can differ.

Behavior of a hook 'ask' or 'deny' in bypassPermissions mode is not documented by Claude Code; this user's frequent bypass sessions may not be gated by an ask at all, so the main value proposition is unproven for their workflow (auto mode does show hook prompts).

Whole cost model is per-Bash-call network round trip to a /alpha, no-SLA endpoint that has calibration weaknesses (overconfident on unanswerable input, injection-steerable) on a gate used as a deterministic 'rule enforcer'; jevc itself says thresholds are guesses until measured.
Age and bus factor: repo created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 154 commits over only 5 distinct days, single author, 8 stars, 0 forks, 0 issues, no GitHub release; npm 0.1.0 published 2026-09-20.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered candidate for turning CLAUDE.md prose rules into deterministic, tested Jev-backed PreToolUse gates, and its transport is switchable to OpenRouter with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + key, but the hard-pinned jev-1.13.0 model id, per-project manual setup, no prefilter (latency on every Bash call) and fail-closed ask under bypass/auto modes make it a rule-by-rule power tool rather than an automatic daily helper. Use it selectively for one or two high-value rules (e.g. no unrequested commits) after patching the model id and testing live.

verification.note: Re-queried now (2026-09-30): doronp/jevc not archived, Apache-2.0, 8 stars, 0 forks, pushed 2026-09-29, created 2026-09-18, 154 commits, sole contributor, 0 releases, 0 issues; npm jev-compiler 0.1.0 only (published 2026-09-20), deps only @typesafe-ai/sdk ^0.6.0 and yaml, no install/postinstall scripts (verified in npm metadata); SDK 0.6.0 has no install scripts either. Verified from SDK tarball: env TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, default https://api.typesafe.ai, POST /v1/systemone, Bearer auth, SDK default timeout 10s (jevc overrides to 5s, 1 retry). src has no OpenRouter mentions (only fixtures/docs text), no telemetry; only env vars read are JEVC_ALLOW_MODEL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_AI_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Interface items in the audit exist in source (hook output field hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision deny|ask with permissionDecisionReason is valid for PreToolUse; exit 1 non-blocking and exit 2 blocking confirmed in Claude Code hooks docs). Main audit weaknesses: it understates how much the pinned model id blocks OpenRouter use (OpenRouter documents only jev-1.13 / jev-latest / typesafe/jev-1.13) while missing that jev-latest needs no library patch; it overstates fail-closed behavior; it misses the token-budget failure and the bare-node/PATH failure for this user. I did not test live against OpenRouter (no key use allowed), so model-id acceptance and the echoed response model string remain unverified. Score lowered from 6 to 4: it is a per-rule authoring toolchain, not an automatic daily helper; it needs manual per-project setup and gate rewriting; it has no OpenRouter validation, no prefilter, and unproven behavior under this user's bypass/auto workflows. A reasonable use is a single, observe-mode-first commit-consent gate using model 'jev-latest', not a general recommendation.

judge.why: Authoring toolchain that lifts CLAUDE.md rules into tested Jev-backed PreToolUse Bash gates. Best engineering of the set, but per-rule, per-project setup and not an automatic daily helper. The verifier lowered it from 6 to 4.
pros: Verdicts computed in code from Jev probabilities. Strict validators, response-origin check, observe mode, replayable fixtures.
Zero standing context. Can read recent user turns, so consent rules ('did the user ask to commit?') are answerable.
Env-only OpenRouter redirect for transport.
cons: Sample gate fails open on JSON.parse, import failure and bare-node PATH failure (your PATH override), so it can be silently off. Fails closed to 'ask' only inside decide().
Up to 4 whole user turns are sent uncut. A big paste exceeds the 32k OpenRouter context and turns every Bash call into 'ask'. The transcript is re-parsed on each Bash call.
No prefilter, so every Bash call costs a round trip on top of gitnexus. Hook 'ask' behavior in bypassPermissions is undocumented.
Skill uses unpinned `npx -y ...@latest`. Fixtures were recorded on one day against TypeSafe direct only.

entries.name: jev-for-all (emirbartu)
entries.what: Multi-harness Jev wiring (OpenCode plugin is the primary product; Claude Code, Hermes, pi adapters are secondary). The Claude Code adapter (adapters/claude-code, plugin id "system-one") is a hooks-only plugin: on every UserPromptSubmit it asks Jev (via @openrouter/sdk client.alpha.decisions.create, model ~typesafe/jev-latest) which single skill from ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills fits the prompt (1 Choice + 4 Noul gates, optional rerank) and injects that skill body (max 8000 chars) as additionalContext; if Jev confidently says "none" it injects a note and a PreToolUse hook denies the Skill tool until the next prompt. Optional Stop hook (off by default) checks whether a completion claim is backed by a passing check and blocks the stop with a hint. Also ships a browser_task MCP server (needs separate jev-ultrafast checkout + CDP browser). Tool-subset routing is OpenCode-only and cannot be done in Claude Code. The npm package jev-for-all 0.2.1 only ships the OpenCode plugin (files: index.ts, src, spec, bin); the Claude adapter exists only in the git repo.
interface: MCP server browser-task (.mcp.json, uv run python browser-mcp/server.py)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse:Skill, optional Stop) fire on every prompt with no user action, matching the 'never say use jev' requirement, but only for skill routing and the optional completion gate. browser_task is model-discretion MCP tool plus a description-triggered skill. No tool-catalog routing, no coding/decision help for edits, commits, permissions, or model routing.
security: API key read only from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var in the hook (system-one.ts:41); not put in argv by the Claude adapter. The OpenCode installer accepts --key on argv and can write apiKey into opencode.jsonc plaintext (irrelevant for Claude Code).

No shell exec in hooks; browser-mcp spawns `uv run ... jev-runner.py` via subprocess and passes goal via env vars (jev-runner.py header says creds stay in checkout .env, not on cmd line). browser_task drives a real CDP browser with model-chosen clicks and typed values: high prompt-injection and account-action surface.

No npm postinstall, no curl|sh. Marketplace entry uses a symlink to the parent dir (marketplace/system-one -> ..). Hooks import ../../../src/jev and ../../../spec, and .mcp.json uses ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/../browser-mcp, so a plugin install that copies the plugin dir into Claude's cache (rather than --plugin-dir in place) will likely break these relative paths (inferred, unverified).

Prompt-injection: skill bodies from ~/.claude/skills and project .claude/skills are injected as additionalContext; a malicious repo's .claude/skills is auto-scanned and can be injected based on the prompt (project skills are already trusted by Claude Code, but roster text and first 700 chars of bodies also go to a third party). Jev is not an instruction follower, but its answer steers which text is injected.
Local decision/usage log at ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA:-$TMPDIR:-/tmp}/system-one-cc/decisions.jsonl (prompt length, chosen skill, tokens; not prompt text). Falls back to world-readable /tmp.

No telemetry found besides the OpenRouter call itself. Repo is 12 days old, single maintainer plus an AI agent account (67 of 93 commits authored by 'OpenCode Agent'); unreviewed code that runs on every prompt with full env access.
entries.dataEgress: UserPromptSubmit: the full user prompt text (every prompt, including client-project prompts), the roster of skill ids/names/descriptions from ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills, and when rerank runs the first 700 chars of each shortlisted skill body -> openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (then to TypeSafe/whatever provider OpenRouter routes Jev to). Injected skill body stays local. Stop hook (only if SYSTEM_ONE_VERIFY=1): last 2000 chars of transcript incl. text, tool-call names and tool-result bodies plus final assistant message. browser_task: goal, URL and each step's page URL/title/visible text/controls to the policy model. No code files or diffs are sent by default, but prompts routinely contain code/snippets/secrets and the existing secret-leak guard does NOT cover UserPromptSubmit egress.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: no API key, timeout, HTTP error, malformed answer, low confidence, unknown skill id, empty roster, cap of 500 calls/session all print nothing and exit 0 (hooks/system-one.ts main().catch, lib/decide.ts:41). Per-request timeout is 1000 ms (src/jev.ts:48; the 2500 ms default applies only to the OpenCode plugin, index.ts:88), retries disabled, so on slow OpenRouter calls the hook simply skips; hook command timeout 10 s bounds worst case. Caveat: fail-open covers Jev failure but not Jev being wrong: a confident false 'none' blocks the Skill tool for the whole turn/session (state persists until the next prompt overwrites it).
entries.contextCost: Very low static cost: 0 tools from the hooks, 1 MCP tool (browser_task, ~150-300 tokens of description/schema, optional; can be removed by not loading .mcp.json), 1 skill description (~60 tokens), no MCP server instructions. Dynamic cost per prompt: an injected skill body up to 8000 chars (~2000 tokens) when Jev picks a skill (duplicates what Claude would load itself via Skill tool), or a ~20-token 'skills routed externally' note when Jev says none. Roster covers only ~/.claude/skills and project .claude/skills (plugin skills are not scanned).
pros: Only candidate so far with a real, automatic Claude Code integration: hooks fire per prompt without the user ever saying 'use jev' and the code is fail-open with an inert no-key path (hooks/system-one.ts:41, lib/decide.ts).
Uses OpenRouter natively via @openrouter/sdk alpha.decisions with ~typesafe/jev-latest and OPENROUTER_API_KEY, exactly the user's provider; no rewrite needed.

Sensible use of Jev (typed Choice/Noul, cheap wrong-is-harmless hints), spend cap of 500 calls/session, local JSONL usage log, 31 adapter tests plus fixtures/L1 evals, and honest WHERE-JEV-WINS.md listing losses.
Optional Stop verification gate (claim/ran/passed) is a genuinely relevant daily-coding idea for a bypass-mode user, default off, fails open, and reuses shared spec/decisions.json thresholds.
Very small static context footprint (no server instructions, 0-1 MCP tools) and MIT license; cost about $0.0001 per decision.
cons: Value is narrow for this user: skill routing only. Claude Code already auto-triggers skills from descriptions; Jev adds a ~0.6-1 s blocking hop on every prompt to save little. Tool-subset routing, the headline feature, is impossible in Claude Code (README 'Harness ceiling').

Roster blind spot: only scans ~/.claude/skills and <cwd>/.claude/skills, not plugin skills (gitnexus-*, caveman:*, anthropic-skills:*). If Jev answers a confident 'none', PreToolUse denies the Skill tool for the turn, blocking legitimate plugin/marketplace skills the user relies on (roster.ts:199-201, system-one.ts:114-126). Highest-risk behavior for this setup.
Sends every prompt (client-project content included) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every turn, outside the user's secret-leak guard; Stop gate would send transcript tails including tool results.

Immature and fragile install: 12 days old, 6 stars, 2 authors (67/93 commits by an 'OpenCode Agent' account), no releases/tags, no CI, Claude adapter not in the npm package, README paths hard-coded to /home/gerius/..., hooks depend on ../../../src and bun (not in the user's stated toolchain: Node 24 / uv) plus an undocumented `bun install` for @openrouter/sdk; the marketplace symlink/relative-path layout probably breaks under a cached plugin install, so --plugin-dir or a fork would be needed.
Request timeout is 1000 ms in the hook (src/jev.ts:48) so cold OpenRouter calls will often silently no-op; the hook does not pass the 2500 ms used by the OpenCode plugin.
browser_task duplicates the already-installed Playwright MCP, needs an external ~/jev-ultrafast checkout with its own .env, and lets a small policy model drive clicks/typing on real sessions.
Jev is an unverified/beta model (Theo's 'router' claim), and all accuracy numbers here are author-reported on the author's own corpora (64 cases).
entries.verdict: Best-in-class for 'automatic, no prompting' on OpenRouter because it is real hooks-based Claude Code glue, but it only routes skills (plus an optional stop-time verification gate) and its Skill-tool denial can block the user's plugin skills.
