Worth borrowing the pattern (fork the Stop verify gate, fix roster/deny logic, use Node instead of bun), not installing as-is.

judge.why: Real hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse:Skill, optional Stop) for skill routing on OpenRouter. But routing skills is low value at your skill volume, and its Skill-tool denial can block your plugin skills. Borrow the Stop-verify pattern, not the plugin. Audit-only.
pros: OpenRouter native. Fail-open everywhere with a 500-call session cap.
cons: Skill denial logic can block legitimate plugin skills (caveman, gitnexus).
Uses bun. Overlaps native skill selection. Needs a fork to be useful.

entries.name: wellkilo/codex-jev-preflight
entries.what: Fail-open Codex UserPromptSubmit hook (stdlib Python) that asks Jev for task_type, complexity, risk, execution_mode and injects them as advisory context.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit)
pros: Direct blueprint for a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit additionalContext hook: fail-open, output validation to unknown, persistent circuit breaker on exhausted quota
Zero dependencies, 0600 config file, CI and SECURITY.md
cons: Codex-targeted; needs porting hook I/O to Claude Code; TYPESAFE_API_ENDPOINT defaults to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (OpenRouter needs /alpha/decisions schema change)
Adds latency to every prompt for a low-value advisory label; overlaps caveman hook context cost

entries.name: seahsky/kelpie
entries.what: Claude Code plugin with delegation policy skill, four roles and UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse hooks; Jev triage (opt-in) decides whether delegating is worthwhile, keyword fallback otherwise; jev-gate fanout/verify.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook
pros: Jev opt-in requires key AND 'send prompts' consent; keyword fallback without it; benchmark says delegate less
KELPIE_GATE_JEV_URL env override allows pointing at OpenRouter systemone
Hooks for UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse plus jev-gate verify; ~12 tests
cons: Key uses JEV_API_KEY; extra roles/commands/skills add context and prompts the user did not ask for
Adds latency to every prompt (waits for Jev before turn)
Young, 1 star, opinionated workflow

judge.why: Delegation-policy plugin whose UserPromptSubmit hook asks Jev whether to delegate. Opinionated workflow with extra roles and commands you did not ask for, and it waits for Jev before every turn. README-level only.
pros: Jev use is opt-in (key plus consent), with a keyword fallback.
URL override for OpenRouter.
cons: Latency on every prompt.
Adds roles, commands and skills to context.
Young and opinionated.

entries.name: devagrawal09/stanley-code
entries.what: Standalone Node CLI ("stanley") that takes a natural-language request, uses one Jev Choice call to route it to one of 10 deterministic built-in workflows (check diff vs task, review, test gaps, summarize, security/perf/compat review, find relevant code, triage failures, triage review comments), splits the git diff into hunks and asks Jev fixed-choice questions per hunk. Code, not the model, applies thresholds and produces findings/notChecked. Falls back to the Pi coding agent (if installed) for unsupported requests and queues background self-improvement (agent writes new workflows into .stanley/). It is a CLI, not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin; nothing in the repo integrates with Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted / invoked explicitly as a shell command. No hook, MCP tool, skill or proxy in the repo. To be automatic, the user would have to write their own glue (e.g. a Stop or PreToolUse-on-git-commit hook running `stanley "Check these changes..." --json --no-agent --no-persist`, or a CLAUDE.md/skill instruction). That glue is not provided.
security: API key read only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, never from flags or files, so it does not show in argv/process list. SDK logLevel 'off' to avoid logging request bodies.

Best-effort secret redaction (src/adapters/redact.ts) of private keys, AWS/GitHub/Slack tokens, JWTs, bearer, url creds and assigned secrets applied before forwarding/persisting; README calls it best-effort only. Also strips TYPESAFE_API_KEY from git child env (git.ts:31).

Repository workflows in .stanley/workflows/ are loaded via tsx and run as trusted code with user privileges: a malicious client repo containing .stanley/workflows/*.ts gets code execution when stanley is run there. Serious for client projects.

Self-improvement spawns a detached background worker (improvements.ts:288-299) that outlives the CLI and runs the Pi coding agent (with full process env passed through: pi.ts:165-167, env spread) to author code; candidates are staged and require manual promotion.

Pi agent fallback executes an arbitrary coding agent on unsupported requests (pi.ts spawn, shell:false), which in a Claude Code context is a second autonomous agent with its own model provider (would send code to OpenAI/whichever Pi is configured for).
Writes .stanley/runs records to the repo unless --no-persist.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is repointed): the natural-language request, workflow routing metadata, and per-hunk diff text, file path/metadata plus excerpts of repository files (find workflow), test/CI log blocks, review comments; up to 150 hunks per check, 3000 files screened by path, all after regex secret redaction. If the Pi fallback runs, the request and repo context go to Pi's configured LLM provider (e.g. OpenAI via OAuth in their docs). Nothing is sent from Claude Code itself; only what the CLI is asked to inspect.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed but bounded and non-blocking to Claude Code because it is not wired in: each Jev call has a 30s default timeout (executor.ts:108), SDK retries disabled and retries counted in run budgets by the executor; transport failures classified (auth/transient/too_large/rejected) and surface as incomplete/budget_exhausted/unsupported with notChecked; low-confidence routing yields cannot_tell/unsupported rather than a guess. Missing key throws MissingCredentialError. Exit codes 1 and 2 deliberately unused because exit 2 is a blocking signal in agent hooks (output.ts:15), showing the author considered hook use but there is no hook implementation.
entries.contextCost: Zero passive cost: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no skill. Only cost is output tokens when Claude runs the CLI via Bash and reads the report (text + structured data; --json is machine readable). Claude would have to be told (CLAUDE.md line or skill) that the command exists.
pros: Genuine, non-trivial Jev usage: correct use of Choice/Noul/Score-style typed questions with code-side thresholds, so the model never writes free text; matches Jev's System One strengths (bounded classification of hunks).

Useful review-type checks that map to real pre-commit gaps: added test.skip, deleted assertions, weakened expectations, lockfile/CI/config edits, hunks unrelated to the stated task, missing test evidence.

Env-only OpenRouter path: SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone, which is exactly OpenRouter's System One URL; TYPESAFE_MODEL selects typesafe/jev-1.13. No fork needed (schema parity unverified).

Well-engineered: 20k lines with heavy tests, CI on 3 Node versions, pinned action SHAs, explicit budgets, timeouts, honest 'empty findings is not approval' reporting, --no-agent and --no-persist switches, JSON output.
Hook-aware design: avoids exit codes 1/2 (output.ts:15) so it could be wrapped in a hook; no telemetry, no postinstall, no curl|sh.
MIT license; clean read-only-by-default git usage.
cons: Not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it gives no automatic integration with Claude Code at all; violates the user's core requirement unless the user writes their own hook/skill glue.
Not released: not on npm, no GitHub release; must clone, npm ci and build. 10 days old, single author, 22 commits, README says 'Experimental: every request, report, and interface may change'.
Hard-wired to TYPESAFE_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_BASE_URL naming; using OpenRouter means storing an OpenRouter key under a TypeSafe-named variable, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified.

Its own Jev router step duplicates Claude's job: Claude Code already knows whether to review a diff, so Jev-routing a natural-language request adds latency and cost with no benefit; only the diff-analysis workflows are valuable.
Sends diff hunks and file excerpts (post best-effort regex redaction) to a third-party beta model for every run, a concern on client projects; secret scrubber is explicitly not a secret scanner.

Repo-local .stanley/workflows/*.ts are auto-loaded via tsx as trusted code, so running it inside an untrusted client repo is arbitrary code execution; plus detached background improvement worker and optional second coding agent (Pi) with passthrough env, a poor fit for bypass/auto permission mode.
Multi-call design (routing + per-hunk calls, up to 150 hunks) makes runs slow relative to Jev's 70-500 ms claim per call and the hunk-level workflows only run on demand, not per edit.
No MCP means no structured tool schema for Claude; Claude must parse Bash text or --json output.
entries.verdict: A well-built but standalone Jev diff-review CLI, not a Claude Code integration: nothing in it triggers automatically, it is unreleased/alpha, and its Pi-agent fallback plus auto-loaded repo workflows are risky on client repos. Worth mining for ideas (hunk-level Choice/Noul checks like weakened-test detection) or wrapping in a self-written pre-commit hook with --no-agent --no-persist and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter, but not a drop-in answer.

entries.name: jsk4581/jev-blindspot
entries.what: A UserPromptSubmit hook plus a local daemon (127.0.0.1:7461) and browser side panel. For every prompt you type, it sends the prompt, the last 2 exchanges and repo metadata to Jev as one System One call with 6 typed questions: worth_checking (Noul), risk (Score, 5 levels) and 4 knowledge-gap Nouls. If worth_checking is at least 0.65, it spawns a headless `claude -p --model sonnet --effort low` with Read/Grep/Glob in the project directory. That run returns up to 5 "blind spots" for the prompt, shown as cards in the panel. Nothing is injected into Claude's context and the prompt is not modified. It is a human-facing prompt-quality aid, not a way for Claude to consume Jev decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit on every human-typed prompt). It is fully automatic, but the consumer is the human via a browser panel, not Claude. Claude never sees or uses Jev's output.
security: No curl|sh installer and no postinstall script in package.json. There is a single dependency, the official SDK, and no telemetry was seen in the source.
The daemon binds 127.0.0.1 only unless JEV_BIND_EXTRA is set. The panel exposes every prompt, so a LAN bind without JEV_TOKEN leaks all of them. The settings route accepts any allowed host.
Prompt text is put in argv of `claude -p` (brainArgs, src/brain/runner.ts:36), so it is visible in `ps`/procfs to other local users. The API key stays in a 0600 env file and is not in argv.

The Claude brain runs with the user's own settings, hooks and CLAUDE.md. Only the jev-blindspot hook is suppressed (JEV_BLINDSPOT_CHILD=1). The GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks would fire inside every brain run and add side effects and cost. Read/Grep/Glob are allowed and Bash/Edit/Write/WebFetch are disallowed, but the secret-leak guard hook is the only barrier against the brain reading .env or credentials, whose content would go to Anthropic.

The prompt-injection surface is the gate `state` (prompt and history are treated as data, per the comment in state.ts) and repo files read by the brain. The brain output is only rendered in the panel, not fed back to Claude, so the blast radius is small.
The hook edits ~/.claude/settings.json (with a backup) and spawns a detached daemon that persists for up to 30 idle minutes.
entries.dataEgress: To Jev (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter if repointed), per prompt: the prompt (cut at 6000 characters), the last 2 exchanges (user text cut at 500 characters, assistant reply text last 1500 characters), and project metadata (dir name, languages, frameworks, has_tests, has_ci, git branch, is_git_repo). No file contents or diffs are sent unless a reply quoted them. When the gate passes, `claude -p` sends the prompt, the history, the gate flags, the project directory contents it chooses to read, and CLAUDE.md to Anthropic under the user's subscription. Locally, prompts and results are stored in ~/.local/share/jev-blindspot/sessions/*.jsonl for 30 days. Client-project prompts would be sent to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every prompt.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Hook stdin is read for at most 800ms, the POST to the daemon has a 400ms timeout and the hook always exits 0 with no stdout. Gate timeout defaults to 2000ms with retry disabled (JEV_GATE_TIMEOUT_MS). On failure the card shows "gate unavailable" and no analysis runs, unless JEV_GATE_FALLBACK=brain. The brain has a 90s limit. Nothing blocks the prompt, apart from `/blindspot`, which is intentionally blocked.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude's context. It has no MCP tools, no server instructions, and the hook prints nothing to stdout. The only exception is /blindspot, which is blocked and shown to the user. It adds one command file, ~/.claude/commands/blindspot.md, which adds a slash command entry to the list. Extra cost is the separate `claude -p` brain runs, which spend subscription usage on every analyzed prompt and load the user's CLAUDE.md and hooks each time.
pros: Truly automatic: a UserPromptSubmit hook with no 'use jev' prompting, and it fails open (hook exits 0 with a 400ms cap).

It uses Jev's intended primitives well: Noul and Score in a single System One call with 6 typed questions (src/gate/questions.ts), returning probabilities with no free text. The design is a reasonable reference for a Jev gate, with a threshold (JEV_WORTH_MIN) that can be tuned by running `jev-blindspot gate`.
Nothing is injected into Claude's context and the token cost to the main session is zero. The hook is async in effect and never edits or blocks the prompt.

The SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and uses the same /v1/systemone path as OpenRouter's System One API, so repointing to OpenRouter needs only env vars and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13, not a code patch.

Clean, small codebase (about 3.1k lines of TypeScript), MIT, one official dependency, no postinstall or curl|sh, per-repo opt-out via .jev-blindspot-off, and Jev model pinned by default rather than jev-latest.
Its architecture (small typed gate first, expensive model only when the gate says so) is a pattern worth copying for a custom hook.
cons: It does not make Claude Code use Jev. The output is a browser side panel for the human, which conflicts with the user's goal of Claude using Jev when it adds value. It only reviews prompt quality and makes no coding decision for Claude.
It sends every prompt, recent assistant replies and the git branch/dir name to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) on every prompt, including client projects. It is opt-out per repo, not opt-in.

When the gate passes, it spawns a separate `claude -p` Sonnet run that reads the project. That costs subscription usage and load, and loads the user's CLAUDE.md. It also fires the user's GitNexus, caveman and secret-guard hooks inside each brain run (only its own hook is skipped), risking interaction with existing hooks.
Prompt text sits in the argv of the `claude -p` child, visible in the process list.
It needs a person to watch a browser tab. Blindspot cards are easy to ignore, and the value for a senior developer who already knows the work is questionable.

The OpenRouter path is untested and unverified: response schema parity, model ID and the misleading env var name TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The panel's model validator also rejects the slash in 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Very immature: 6 commits, a single author, 20 stars, 8 days old, no CI, no releases, version 0.1.1. It edits ~/.claude/settings.json and also targets Codex, which adds code and surface the user does not need.
Linux and macOS only, and it requires Claude Code 2.1.278 or newer. It relies on flags such as --permission-prompts and --json-schema that could break on updates.
entries.verdict: Not a fit as the integration. It is an automatic UserPromptSubmit hook, but it feeds a human-only side panel, sends every prompt to a third party, and spawns extra Sonnet runs on the subscription, so Claude never uses Jev's decisions. Its only value to this user is as a code reference for building a Jev gate: the six-question Noul/Score set and the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL repoint to OpenRouter.

entries.name: Larkspur-Wang/Jev_steer_or_queue
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (plus a Codex variant) with five hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop, StopFailure) that all run one stdlib-only Python script. When you type a message while Claude is mid-turn, the script calls Jev (Choice timing: steer/queue/interrupt/unclear, plus a Noul explicit_stop) and either lets it through (steer), blocks it and replays it from the Stop hook after the turn (queue), or blocks it and returns continue:false at the next tool boundary (interrupt). Messages sent while idle never reach Jev. It defaults to shadow mode, which only logs. It does not help with code, review or model routing. It only decides how to handle the user's own interjections.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. It runs on every UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and Stop with no user prompting. It only calls Jev when you type while a turn is running.
security: API key is sent in the Authorization header via urllib, not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. Plugin userConfig marks it sensitive (keychain). Alternatively it can sit in plaintext in ~/.jev-steer-or-queue/config.json or in env.
No shell execution, no eval, no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry beyond the Jev call. The script is about 300 lines and easy to audit.
Hook command is python3 on PATH, run for every tool call and prompt. A rogue update to the plugin would be arbitrary code in your hooks, so pin a commit.
Prompt-injection surface: queued user text is re-injected as Stop additionalContext, but it is only the user's own text. Jev output is numeric probabilities, so it cannot inject text.

log.jsonl under ~/.claude/plugins/data/... stores the first 300 chars of every prompt by default (LOG_PROMPTS=true), including client-project text. Session state files store the first 500 chars of the task and the full queued messages, unencrypted.
Blocking on UserPromptSubmit erases the message from the transcript. A misclassified 'queue' or 'interrupt' can silently lose or delay user input, and dropped items are only shown on the next prompt.
entries.dataEgress: Only for mid-turn user messages (not idle ones): new_message (up to 2000 chars) and active_task (first 500 chars of the turn's initial prompt), sent to the TypeSafe endpoint (or OpenRouter if repointed). Nothing else is sent: no transcript, files, diffs or tool output (jev_router.py:137-143). Note the first 500 chars of your prompt can contain client details, and OpenRouter would see them and may log them depending on your data policy settings.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. A missing key, HTTP error, timeout or exception returns an error and the action becomes steer, which is native Claude Code behavior (lines 134-136, 177-180, 230). The default timeout is 2.0 s (JEV_ROUTER_TIMEOUT_S). The hook's own timeout is 10 s for UserPromptSubmit and 5 s for the others. main() wraps everything in try/except and exits 0 (lines 305-308). One caveat is that a silent failure looks like success, since the test notes say only 'jev: null' in the log reveals it. Another is that queued items are lost if the turn ends abnormally.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools, no MCP instructions, so 0 tokens of tool definitions. Hook-injected text appears only when a queued message is replayed from Stop (one short Chinese preamble plus the message, about 50 tokens), or a Chinese systemMessage when dropped items are reported. In shadow mode nothing is injected at all.
pros: Genuinely automatic: hook-based with no model discretion, and zero context or tool-definition cost.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to, a cheap typed classification (Choice plus Noul with calibrated probabilities) with no free text, at 0.4-0.7 s latency.
Safe defaults: shadow mode out of the box, 0.9 confidence thresholds, and fail-open on every error path. Shadow mode lets you audit decisions in log.jsonl for days before enabling it.
Small, dependency-free, readable code (about 300 lines) with no installers or postinstall steps. The API key is in a header, not argv.
OpenRouter repointing is almost config-only: URL, key and model are all env-overridable (jev_router.py:168, :67, :138).
Payload is minimal: only the mid-turn message and a 500-char task snippet, with no code or tool output. Cost is negligible, at about $0.04 per 1M input tokens.
cons: Solves a narrow UX problem (mid-turn interjection timing), not daily coding help. It does not route models, review diffs, or gate tool calls, so its value is small for a senior dev who mostly waits for turns.
The user runs bypass/auto mode and long Opus turns, so mid-turn typing may be occasional. Claude Code's native steering already handles most of these cases.

Active mode can lose or delay input: blocked messages are erased from the transcript, only one queued item replays per Stop, there is an 8-continuation cap, Esc fires no hook so queued items are dropped, and a wrong interrupt call stops work at the next tool boundary. Jev is admitted to be weak on negation and multi-intent messages.
Prompts and criteria are in Chinese and only tested by the author on Chinese and simple English sleep-loop scenarios. English classification quality on real coding messages is unverified.

Registers PreToolUse/PostToolUse with matcher * and spawns python3 on every tool call, adding a small per-call cost next to your secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. Ordering relative to the existing PreToolUse hooks is untested.
Immature: 2 stars, 3 commits, 1 contributor, no tests, no CI, no releases, created a week ago. The repo describes only a manual macOS test on Claude Code 2.1.280, not your 2.1.285 on Linux.
Native TypeSafe API only, and OpenRouter /systemone schema compatibility is unverified. Under a wrong schema it fails open silently, so the plugin would appear installed while doing nothing.
Logs the first 300 chars of every prompt to disk by default, which is a concern on client projects (set LOG_PROMPTS=false).
entries.verdict: A clean, safe-by-default hook that is genuinely automatic, but it only manages mid-turn message timing and is a 1-week-old single-author PoC that talks to TypeSafe direct. Try it in shadow mode via the URL/key/model env overrides if you like, but do not count it as a core Jev integration for daily coding, and do not enable active mode without validating English classification in the logs.

entries.name: jev-prompt-enhancer
entries.what: Single-file Node CLI (cli.mjs, 216 lines) that registers as a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook. For every user prompt it calls Jev (OpenRouter Decisions API) with a noul question ("needs refinement?") plus a choice question (typos, ambiguous, missing_context or none). If P>=0.6 and the problem is not "none", it calls inception/mercury-2 via OpenRouter chat/completions to rewrite the prompt. A second Jev call scores whether the meaning changed (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH). HIGH rejects the rewrite. Otherwise it injects the rewritten prompt as additionalContext ("FYI the user's request could be phrased as..." or, with --auto, "Treat the user's request as..."). It is a prompt-quality tool. It does not use Jev for any coding decision.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), fires on every user prompt with no model discretion. It meets the 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement literally, but only for prompt rewriting.
security: No npm postinstall or install scripts. It has zero dependencies and no shell execution in the CLI itself. The OpenCode plugin it writes uses spawnSync with an argv array, so there is no shell injection.
The API key is read from the env var only and never appears in argv. It is sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS to openrouter.ai only. No telemetry and no other hosts.

--init claude (cli.mjs:139) does s.hooks.UserPromptSubmit = [...], which clobbers any existing UserPromptSubmit hooks. It then rewrites the whole ~/.claude/settings.json with JSON.stringify and makes no backup. This is risky for this user's carefully built global config.

Prompt-injection surface: the model's rewritten text is injected into Claude's context as trusted-looking guidance. With --auto it says 'Treat the user's request as...'. The rewrite comes from Mercury, a small diffusion LLM, and the only guard is a Jev check that scores meaning change. A wrong or drifted rewrite would silently steer Opus. A prompt that contains instructions is also passed to Mercury.
The raw user prompt is interpolated into the Jev and Mercury prompts inside triple-quote delimiters, and a prompt that contains those delimiters can break out of them (low impact).
The README says 'the decision stays yours', but there is no approval UI in hook mode. additionalContext is applied automatically, and the user can only object afterwards in chat.
entries.dataEgress: Every user prompt, in full, goes to openrouter.ai for the Jev call. That includes prompts on client projects and any code, paths or secrets the user pastes. When refined, the prompt is also sent to inception/mercury-2 through OpenRouter (a second provider behind OpenRouter), and then the rewrite goes out again for the fidelity check. It sends only the prompt text (stdin .prompt). It does not send file contents, diffs or tool outputs. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit, so a pasted secret would leave the machine. Data policy for the Mercury/Inception route on OpenRouter is unverified.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in the code: the try/catch prints '{}' and exits 0 (cli.mjs:192-194), and a missing key throws inside the try and is treated the same. There is NO timeout: fetch has no AbortSignal (cli.mjs:32, 49). If OpenRouter or Jev hangs, every prompt submission stalls until the Claude Code hook timeout, which I did not verify and which is generous by default. Add a wrapper such as `timeout 3` or a hook "timeout" setting. HTTP 4xx/5xx from the alpha endpoint (an unstable API) fail open silently, so the tool can quietly do nothing. Also fail-open on a wrong response shape, because ?. chains default to 0 and produce no enhancement.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. The hook injects text only when a refinement fires: about 30-300 tokens of additionalContext per refined prompt ("FYI the user's request could be phrased as: ..."). It injects nothing for clear prompts. Context cost is negligible, but the injected paraphrase duplicates the user's own prompt, which is noise for Opus.
pros: Truly automatic: a real UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.
Already OpenRouter-native: a single OPENROUTER_API_KEY, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13:latest. This matches the user's constraint exactly, with no patching.
Tiny (216 lines), zero dependencies, no postinstall, no telemetry. Fully auditable in minutes. Fail-open on errors.
Good illustration of the Decision primitives (noul, choice and score all used correctly in the request shape), and a cheap gate: clear prompts pass untouched at about $0.00002 per call.
The gate avoids the rewrite step for most prompts, so the added cost per turn is one small Jev call.
cons: Solves a problem this user barely has. A senior dev on Opus 5.5 writing precise English prompts gains almost nothing from typo or vagueness rewriting, and Opus already handles ambiguity or asks.

Weak fit for the goal: Jev is used for prompt hygiene, not for coding decisions (which files to load, whether to run tests, risk of a tool call, context pruning, routing). It does not make Claude Code better at daily coding.
Ships every prompt, including client-project prompts, to OpenRouter and (when refined) to the Inception Mercury model, on every turn. It adds a second vendor and a data-privacy question.
No timeout on fetch, so a slow or down OpenRouter alpha endpoint blocks every message. Fail-open only applies to thrown errors, not to hangs.
--init claude clobbers existing UserPromptSubmit hooks and rewrites settings.json without a backup. It must not be used with this user's existing hook set.

Injected 'refined' text can drift from intent (the README's own limits admit the 0.6 threshold is calibrated on 5 examples). The claimed 'you approve / reject / rework' flow is not implemented in hook mode.
Uses a beta alpha endpoint, and the response field names (answers.*.noul / .choice) were not verified. A schema change would silently disable it because everything fails open.
8 days old, v0.1.0, one maintainer, no source repository, no tests, no CI. The README's evidence is 5 hand-run examples, several in Russian.
The Mercury dependency (inception/mercury-2) means a paid second model and a second failure point.
entries.verdict: Only OpenRouter-native, truly automatic Jev integration in this set, but it uses Jev for the least valuable job (rewriting prompts for a senior dev). It adds latency and sends every prompt to two third-party models. Skip it as a primary integration. If you want its idea, copy the 60-line Jev call into your own hook with a 2-3 s timeout, and point Jev at higher-value decisions instead.

entries.name: jev-skill (fsans)
entries.what: Agent Skill (SKILL.md plus a stdlib-only Python 3 CLI, scripts/jev.py) that wraps Jev judgments for coding agents. Commands are detect-intent, rank, check (security, readability, performance, testability gate), safety, ask (custom noul, choice or score question) and doctor. It calls OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions by default, or the direct TypeSafe API. It adds a 1h disk cache, retry/backoff, and a confidence-to-action policy (auto-apply, confirm, escalate). It also ships an npm installer, jev-skill, that only copies files into ~/.agents/skills or a chosen dir. There is no MCP server, no hook and no proxy. A Claude Code session has to decide to run the CLI through Bash.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at model discretion. Claude Code lists the skill's description and may load SKILL.md when a task looks judgment-shaped. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no MCP tool. Triggering will be inconsistent, because Opus usually just decides such things itself. To make it reliable you would have to add your own hook or CLAUDE.md instruction.
security: API key is never accepted on argv: it is read from the environment or a .env file and sent only in the Authorization header (config.py docstring, client.py:139-146). Nothing sensitive shows up in the process list.

Config loads .env from cwd first, then the skill dir, then ~/.config/jev/.env (config.py:57-61). A project's own .env (client repos) containing OPENROUTER_API_KEY would silently be used, and only known keys are picked up. Env vars win over files. Real env var OPENROUTER_API_KEY beats all files.
No shell execution in the CLI (no subprocess, os.system, eval or exec in scripts/). No telemetry beyond the X-Title: jev-skill header, plus an optional HTTP-Referer, sent to OpenRouter.
npm installer only copies files (skips .env, pyc), has no postinstall and no network access. It defaults to ~/.agents/skills and would not land in Claude Code's dir without --to. Not curl|sh.

Disk cache at ~/.cache/jev-skill stores the full request-derived response as JSON, plus the raw API response. The key is a sha256 of the payload, so code is not stored verbatim in the key. Files are created with default umask, not 0600 (mkstemp gives 0600, then os.replace keeps that).

Prompt-injection surface: the code or prompt goes into Jev's 'state' as structured JSON. The outputs are only numeric probabilities and enum keys, so a hostile repo cannot make Jev emit instructions. The SKILL.md itself tells the agent 'an unsafe verdict always stops the planned action', which lets a false-positive block work.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the agent passes to the CLI leaves the machine, and only when the skill is invoked. detect-intent sends the user prompt text (state.user_request, plus optional context). check and safety send the full code snippet from --code-file (state.code, plus standards). rank sends every candidate's id, label, code and description plus the query. ask sends the question plus arbitrary state. All of it goes to openrouter.ai (which routes to TypeSafe) and is retained by nothing in the skill except the local 1h cache. There is no automatic full-repo, diff or tool-output upload, but for client projects each check or safety call sends client code to two third parties (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe). The secret-leak guard hook would not see the file contents, because they are read by python, not by the Read or Bash tool arguments.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but slow to fail. With no key, doctor prints setup help and exits 1. Errors return {"error":...} with exit 1, and Claude simply continues. Timeout is 30 s per attempt (JEV_TIMEOUT), with 3 retries and exponential backoff on 5xx, 429 (honours Retry-After, up to 30 s) and URLError (client.py:_post_json). The worst case is roughly 30 s x 4 attempts plus about 7 s of sleep, roughly 2 minutes of blocked Bash on an outage. Exit 2 (uncertain) is a soft signal. Tune JEV_TIMEOUT=5 and JEV_RETRIES=1 to bound it. The cache gives a 1h hit for identical payloads. There is no circuit breaker.
entries.contextCost: Small. One skill: about 480 chars of frontmatter description (about 120 tokens) sits permanently in the skills listing. The full SKILL.md is about 4.7 KB (about 1.2k tokens) loaded only when the skill is invoked, plus references/*.md on demand. It adds no MCP tools or server instructions and injects no hook text. Each CLI call costs about 100-300 tokens of JSON output, plus the tool-call overhead.
pros: Native fit for OpenRouter: default backend, default model ~typesafe/jev-latest, endpoint /api/alpha/decisions (config.py:28,104-107). No patching needed and one env var (OPENROUTER_API_KEY) to switch on.
Very low context cost: a single skill with a 480-char description and no MCP tool schemas, unlike an MCP server that adds many tool defs.
Stdlib-only Python and static files: easy to audit (about 1,600 LOC in total), no postinstall, no shell exec, and keys never go on argv.

Sensible handling of Jev semantics: noul certainty is derived as abs(2p-1) because noul has no confidence field, the performance-scale inversion is fixed, and escalate/confirm/auto-apply thresholds exist. That is better than naive use of raw probabilities.
Bounded, typed outputs (enums and numbers only), so the prompt-injection risk from Jev's responses is small. The disk cache also reduces cost for repeated identical checks.
Reasonable test footprint (116 mocked tests) for a v0.1 project. Timeouts and retries are configurable via env.
cons: It is not automatic. It is a skill triggered only at Claude's discretion, so it cannot meet the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told. A SessionStart or PreToolUse hook or a CLAUDE.md rule is still needed.

Its use cases duplicate what Opus 5.5 already does for free inside the turn: intent detection is pointless when the main model reads the prompt itself, and rank, check and safety by a 'System One' model are weaker signals than the main model's own review. Nothing gets cheaper, since each use adds a call.

Sends client code (check, safety, rank) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every use, which is a real problem for client projects. Nothing in the skill gates or redacts (no path or secret filtering), and the existing secret-leak hook cannot see the file contents.

Weak evidence for the 'safety' and 'check' verdicts: the questions are hand-written prompts (builders.py:build_check, build_safety) and Jev is a beta model with no published calibration on security review. The skill tells the agent to STOP on any 'unsafe' verdict, which risks false-positive blocks in bypass/auto mode.

Immature and unproven: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 10 days old, no CI, no releases, and the direct TypeSafe endpoint (api.typesafe.ai/v1/judge) is unverified by the author. The OpenRouter wire format could not be confirmed independently, since the docs pages I tried returned 404.
No use of /api/v1/systemone, only the alpha Decisions endpoint. If OpenRouter changes the alpha API the skill breaks (URL is env-overridable but the payload shape is not).

Worst-case failure blocks Bash for about 2 minutes under defaults (30 s x 3 retries). The cwd .env lookup means a client project's .env could override the OpenRouter key without warning. The npm installer defaults to ~/.agents/skills, not Claude Code's skills dir.
entries.verdict: A tidy, safe-to-read reference wrapper with first-class OpenRouter support and a sound way to interpret Jev's probabilities. But it is only a description-triggered skill, so it does not deliver automatic use, and its judgments mostly duplicate Opus. Use it as a source of code (the interpret/config logic and the payload shapes) for a hook-based integration, not as the integration itself; if installed, copy pinned files, set JEV_TIMEOUT to about 5 and JEV_RETRIES to 1, and avoid it on client code.

entries.name: shaul1991/jev_route
entries.what: UserPromptSubmit advisory plugins for OMP/Claude Code/Codex/Cursor/Hermes: Jev classifies role, work type, depth, specialty; injects advisory context; observe-only bash Tool Risk Gate; JSONL audit log.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook
pros: Advisory only (no model switching), redacts command/paths, skips Jev if secrets suspected
Four parallel Jev questions in one request, 0.6 confidence threshold
Observe-only risk gate is non-blocking
cons: API_URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; macOS installer focus; Korean docs; only 2 tests
Injects extra context every prompt for little concrete value with Opus 5.5
OMP-centric design; observe-only gate does not actually protect

entries.name: Falconiere/toolu
entries.what: Large engineering-discipline marketplace; its plugins/jev plugin ships jev skill + curl/jq jev.sh wrapper (noul/choice/score/ask) and SessionStart+UserPromptSubmit hooks restating a mandate to call Jev before semantic decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger + UserPromptSubmit mandate injection
pros: Only entry that pushes the model to use Jev automatically every prompt via injected mandate, with bats tests including a live test and http mock server
Zero-SDK curl+jq wrapper, batch ask; hooks make no API call and stay silent on trivial confirmations
cons: JEV_URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, default model jev-latest; needs edit of jev.sh for OpenRouter
Per-prompt mandate consumes context and the model may over-call Jev; needs Bun 1.4 for SessionStart hook
Mandatory-use framing makes Jev sole judge of decisions despite known overconfidence; plugin bundled in unrelated 1294-file repo, 1 commit history

judge.why: The only entry that pushes the model to call Jev before every semantic decision via an injected per-prompt mandate. That makes Jev the sole judge despite its known overconfidence, and costs context every prompt. Useful only as a counterexample.
pros: Literally automatic. curl+jq wrapper with bats tests.
cons: Per-prompt mandate wastes context and the model may over-call Jev.
No OpenRouter without editing the script. Needs Bun 1.4 for SessionStart. Single-commit history.

entries.name: Yeachan-Heo/oh-my-claudecode
entries.what: Large Claude Code orchestration plugin; src/hooks/jev adds opt-in shadow-mode Jev judgment points (keyword/skill trigger, task size, intent) logged only, not active.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook, shadow only (ACTIVATED_POINTS empty)
pros: Zero egress by default, 250ms timeout, per-process request cap, excerpt limit 200 chars; degradation contract ADR
Endpoint overridable via OMC_JEV_ENDPOINT so OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone is plausible
cons: Jev points are shadow-mode only, no behavior change today; installing OMC for that would be heavy and overlap caveman/plannotator
Model hardcoded jev-latest and key env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, needing a shim for OpenRouter

entries.name: CrowdLinker/JevPromptCoach
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (v0.3.5) that grades the developer's own prompts against seven "good prompt" habits (named target, success condition, bounded scope, constraints, repro, plan-first, verification) using Jev Noul questions via the TypeSafe SDK POST /v1/systemone. Default mode logs each prompt locally to ~/.claude/jevpromptcoach/prompts.jsonl via a UserPromptSubmit hook with no network. Optional "always" mode scores each prompt inline and prints a systemMessage notice. Slash commands (score, report, config, backfill) are user-invoked only. It coaches the human; it gives Claude Code no decisions or context and does not change how Claude codes.
interface: No MCP server, no skill, no model-callable tools
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook that fires automatically on every prompt. But its output is a coaching notice for the human and a local log; Claude's behavior never depends on Jev. Slash commands are user-only.
security: No postinstall scripts and no curl|sh; dist/ is committed and prebundled (376 KB). The user must trust the committed bundle, which is not reproducible from the marketplace clone alone.
API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or from ~/.claude/jevpromptcoach/.env (0600); it is sent as a Bearer header and is not passed in argv. Error text is scrubbed of the key (jev.ts:50-55).

Redaction is applied to prompts before sending, and to Claude's replies when session context is on: sk-*, ghp_, AKIA, JWT, PEM, Bearer, 16+ hex, and 20+ char random tokens. It is shape-based; word-like passwords with no label survive (README admits this).
Prompt-injection surface is small: slash commands are disable-model-invocation and pass the prompt via a quoted heredoc; Jev returns numbers only, not text.
commands/score.md runs a Bash command carrying the user text, so heredoc quoting matters, but the delimiter is a fixed token.
SECURITY.md exists, telemetry is none, and the only network destination is api.typesafe.ai (or TYPESAFE_BASE_URL).
entries.dataEgress: On-demand default: nothing leaves the machine per prompt; the hook only writes a redacted prompt line to ~/.claude/jevpromptcoach/prompts.jsonl (0600). Sent to api.typesafe.ai (or the base URL you set) only when you run score/report/backfill: redacted prompt text. In always mode, sent on every prompt: the redacted prompt plus up to the last two exchanges of context, meaning the user's earlier prompts and Claude's closing reply text, also redacted (replies can be disabled with JEVPROMPTCOACH_SESSION_REPLIES=0). Never sent: file contents, diffs, tool calls or tool outputs, or project code apart from what the user pasted into prompts or Claude quoted in its closing text. Client-project names and code snippets in prompts and replies could leak under redact mode; metadata_only sends nothing.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. hook.ts:96-99 always exits 0; a missing key, network failure or bad response yields no output. In always mode a hard timer (default 4000 ms, config.alwaysTimeoutMs) resolves null via Promise.race (inline.ts:127-133), so the prompt proceeds with no notice. The SDK is configured with retry maxRetries=2 and 30 s default timeout for commands, but the inline race abandons after 4 s. The hook is also capped at 10 s in hooks.json.
entries.contextCost: Zero tokens of tool definitions (no MCP server, no skills the model can call; 3 slash commands are disable-model-invocation, so their descriptions are not loaded into context). The hook injects no additionalContext. In always mode it emits only a systemMessage, which is shown to the user and is not fed to the model. Effectively 0 context tokens.
pros: It is the only candidate here with a working, automatic Jev hook (UserPromptSubmit) that costs nothing in Claude's context: 0 tool-definition tokens and no additionalContext.
Fail-open by design: it never exits 2, has a hard 4 s inline budget, and a test asserts the wire payload is redacted (test/hook-privacy.test.mjs).

Uses the same POST /v1/systemone Bearer-auth surface as OpenRouter, and the bundled SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so an OpenRouter switch is a small change (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model-id patch).

A good reference implementation of Jev Noul usage: batching seven questions in one call, calibrated thresholds and a labelled eval, all under a bundled, no-install, MIT-licensed dist with no postinstall.
On-demand default keeps data local and is cheap (about $0.06 for 1,000 prompts).
cons: It scores the user's prompt quality, not code, plans or tool calls. Jev never influences what Claude Code does, so it does not meet the goal of Claude Code using Jev when it adds value. It is a personal analytics tool for a senior developer, not a coding aid.
Not OpenRouter-native: the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY, the model id 'jev-latest' is hardcoded (jev.ts:13), and OpenRouter's response schema is unverified. It needs a fork or patch plus a live test.
Always mode adds a blocking network call of up to 4 s to every prompt for a notice that a senior dev will mostly ignore. On-demand mode gets no scores until a command is run.

Always mode sends the redacted prompt plus the last two exchanges of Claude's replies to a third party. On client projects this could leak code snippets or names despite shape-based redaction, which the README concedes.

Very immature: 3 stars, 1 author, 24 commits in 12 days, no releases, no lockfile, and a committed dist/ that has to be trusted. Slash-command surface and behavior are documented against Claude Code 2.1.277 and were not verified on 2.1.285.
The author's own outcome-signal study found the checks do not predict fewer corrections (docs/OUTCOME-SIGNAL.md), so the score's value is unproven.
Adds another UserPromptSubmit hook next to the existing secret guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. That is low risk, but it still spawns Node on every prompt.
entries.verdict: Well-built and safe (fail-open, redacted, no context cost), but it is a prompt-coaching plugin, not a Jev integration that helps Claude Code decide anything, so it does not fit the goal of automatic Jev use inside Claude Code. It is optional and only worth installing on-demand as a curiosity or as a code reference for a hook-plus-/v1/systemone pattern against OpenRouter.

entries.name: wotai-dev/typesafe-jev-tools
entries.what: A single ~18KB bash PreToolUse(Write|Edit) hook (hooks/typesafe-check.sh). Regex gate on the code being written (.ts/.tsx/.js/.py etc.) detects LLM SDK calls (anthropic|openai|messages.create...) or classifier/scorer-named functions (classify*, route*, sentiment*, score*, rank*...). It then injects advisory additionalContext that tells Claude a three-way test (plain code / frontier model / System One = Jev) so Claude decides whether a Jev-style Choice/Score/Noul primitive fits the code being authored. Optional opt-in "judge" (TYPESAFE_CHECK_JUDGE=1 + TYPESAFE_API_KEY) POSTs a ~1500-char snippet to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with 3 questions (2 Noul + 1 Choice) to pick the band. It is a design advisor for code that CALLS a model, not a way for Claude Code itself to use Jev for its own agent decisions. Repo also holds a 149-row Jev vs Haiku 4.5 calibration writeup in the README and an unrelated Minecraft bot subproject (uses @typesafe-ai/sdk).
interface: Gate regex classes A / B_CHOICE / B_SCORE
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Write|Edit), fully automatic, no user prompting. But what it automates is only a nudge telling Claude to consider whether code it is authoring should use a System One model. Claude Code itself never calls Jev for its own decisions (routing, triage, commit classification); the hook is advisory text with a Jev sales-flavoured bias in the decision framing.
security: No shell execution of untrusted input: payload is handled via jq -r and herestrings; snippet passed to jq --arg (safe JSON encoding), key passed via curl -H argument.
API key visible in argv: `curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $key"` puts the key in the process list for up to 4 s (line 173-174), visible to other local users via ps.

Key fallback reads `.claude/typesafe-check.env` and `.env.local` from the project dir with sed (lines 132-134) - it reads a project .env.local file that may hold other secrets, though only the TYPESAFE_API_KEY line is extracted; would also conflict with the user's secret-leak guard on Read/Bash of .env files only if the guard inspects hook subprocesses (it does not).

Prompt-injection surface: the code being written is fed both to Jev (state) and back as advisory text. README acknowledges Jev does not treat data as hostile; author deliberately removed suppression so a code comment cannot silence the advisory. The injected additionalContext text is static apart from band/confidence numbers, so injection into Claude's context via the hook is low.
Judge is OFF by default; explicit opt-in TYPESAFE_CHECK_JUDGE=1 required, README warns that source is sent to a third party.

Writes a log (.claude/typesafe-check.log with file paths, timestamps, verdicts) into every project it runs in, and marker files under $TMPDIR; the repo .gitignore lists .claude/ but the user's projects would need to ignore it themselves, or risk committing file path logs in client repos.
entries.dataEgress: Default (judge off): nothing leaves the machine. With TYPESAFE_CHECK_JUDGE=1: a snippet of up to 1500 chars of the code being written (matched lines +/-3 before, +8 after, up to 8 matches, taken from the Write content / Edit new_string only, not the on-disk file) plus fixed question text and the TypeSafe API key are POSTed to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. At most one call per file per mode per session. No prompts, diffs of unchanged code, tool outputs or file contents beyond that snippet.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by construction. `set -uo pipefail` without -e, curl --max-time 4, every failure (no key, no curl, timeout, non-200, bad JSON) falls back to gate-only advisory; settings command ends `2>/dev/null || true` with hook timeout 10 s. Never emits a deny/block. Worst case adds ~4 s once per file per session, only on flagged authoring writes with judge on.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools, zero MCP instructions, no skill description. Hook injects only when regex fires: ~150-250 tokens for the full three-way advisory (or ~40 tokens brief / preexisting one-liner), once per file per session. Effectively negligible.
pros: Truly automatic: a PreToolUse Write|Edit hook fires with no prompting, matching the user's requirement of no 'use jev' instructions.
Fail-open and bounded: curl --max-time 4, hook timeout 10, `|| true`, never denies; once-per-file-per-session dedupe; judge off by default.
Small, readable, dependency-light (bash+jq+grep+curl); no npm/pip install, no postinstall, easy to audit and fork in 15 minutes.
Author is careful and honest: documents own false positives, has real bug postmortems (SIGPIPE/pipefail, super-linear substitution), and sends only a matched 1500-char snippet.

Contains a concrete, checkable payload for the Jev System One request shape (state + questions with noul/choice, criteria map) at hooks/typesafe-check.sh:159-172 that can be reused as a template for OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

Independent, transparent benchmark (Jev 66.0% acc, ECE 0.121, p50 455 ms vs Haiku 4.5 66.0%, ECE 0.122, p50 631 ms; Jev 50% vs Haiku 42% on commit type) - useful evidence for deciding where Jev is worth calling.
Context cost is negligible.
cons: Wrong purpose for this user's goal: it does not use Jev to help Claude Code do daily coding (file triage, commit type, intent routing, should-I-ask decisions). It only advises when the code Claude is writing contains an LLM call or a classifier-named function; for most edits it is silent.

No OpenRouter support: hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY (hooks/typesafe-check.sh:173,130); needs a patch to route to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with an OPENROUTER_API_KEY and typesafe/jev-1.13, and OpenRouter response shape is unverified against the .answers.<q>.choice parsing.

Advice is biased and heuristic: the gate is a name regex (author admits it is a band-one heuristic wrong in both directions); it will fire on unrelated code (openai/anthropic SDK usage, scoreX helpers) in client projects and inject a 'System One' pitch into a coding agent's context.

Project-scoped install: settings command uses $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks/, so global install (needed for the user's all-projects use) needs edits; it also writes .claude/typesafe-check.log into every client repo, which may be committed by accident.

API key passed in curl argv (visible in ps) and optional key lookup in project .env.local; conflicts in spirit with the user's secret-leak guard, and sends client source snippets to a third party when judge is on (problematic for client projects).
Maturity: 1 star, 1 contributor, 26 commits in 4 days, no releases, no tests for the hook itself; CI covers only the unrelated Minecraft demo.

Sole judge output only tweaks advisory wording; it does not gate or improve any Claude Code action, so measurable value for daily coding is close to zero. Duplicates with the user's existing PreToolUse Write|Edit path would add one more hook process per edit.
entries.verdict: Not what the user wants: it is a small, safe, fail-open advisory hook that nudges Claude when it writes LLM/classifier code, not an integration that makes Claude Code use Jev for its own decisions, and it only supports api.typesafe.ai. Worth mining for the /v1/systemone request template and benchmark data (Jev ~455 ms p50, calibrated, weak on accuracy vs Sonnet), but do not install it as the Jev integration.

entries.name: j1s4nn/jevXagent
entries.what: Local FastAPI proxy (127.0.0.1:9099) meant to sit at ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. For each /v1/messages request it sends the last user message as plain text to a Jev /chat/completions endpoint, then prepends a "SYSTEM EXECUTION CONTEXT" system message containing the raw Jev reply and forwards a rebuilt, stripped-down payload to Anthropic using a stored API key. It does not use the Jev Decisions/System One primitives (Choice/Noul/Score). The "needs_generation" bypass is a substring check for "needs_generation=false" in Jev text, and even then the proxy returns a stub reply rather than skipping generation properly. The 3x faster / 80% cheaper claims are unsubstantiated.
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy (ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:9099). Automatic in principle, no model discretion, but Jev is called on every user message whether or not it adds value, and it must be started manually in a separate terminal.
security: Repo created 2026-09-23, v0.2.0 on 2026-09-24, 13 commits by 1 author, 1 star, 0 forks, no CI workflows, no releases besides one tag. Roughly 250 lines of tests.

Requires a raw Anthropic API key stored in plaintext ~/.jevxagent/config.json (config.py) and sent as x-api-key (proxy.py:136). Incompatible with the user's OAuth/subscription login. adapters/claude_code.py reads settings.json 'apiKey'.
Jev key in plaintext config; sent as Bearer header, not in argv. Inputs typed interactively, so no argv leak.

Prompt-injection surface: raw Jev free-text is placed into a system message unsanitised (context_injection.py:14-39), so a compromised or odd Jev/base_url reply becomes system-level instructions to Opus.
Proxy listens on 127.0.0.1 with no auth on the local port; any local process can use the stored Anthropic key through it.

README claims 'Secure by Default - No credential logging'. Stats JSONL written to cwd by default (stats.py:41), containing per-request metrics. Telemetry to third parties not seen. No curl|sh installer or postinstall (pip install -e . from clone).
entries.dataEgress: The last user message text goes to the Jev endpoint (default api.typesafe.ai/v1, user-configurable) on every turn: the whole message, not only a snippet. Then a rebuilt request goes to api.anthropic.com. Because the payload is rebuilt from Message(role, content: str), other parts are dropped: system prompt, tools, tool_use/tool_result blocks. In practice tool results are not sent to Jev, only the last user-role message text. Claude Code turns with tool_result arrive as user messages with list content, which would fail pydantic validation.
entries.failureMode: Intended fail-open: Jev timeout (0.8s default) or exception yields needs_generation=True and the request passes through (jev_client.py:64-77, proxy.py:87-89). The proxy itself is a single point of failure: if it is not running, Claude Code with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set gets connection refused, so the whole session is fail-closed. Malformed bodies (content as a list of blocks, which Claude Code always sends) raise a 422/500. Non-streaming requests (Claude Code's small-model background calls, title generation, token counting) return an error object. Anthropic upstream errors are streamed through without status handling.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks, no skills, so 0 tool-definition tokens. But the proxy prepends a system message with the raw Jev reply on every request (variable, maybe 50-300 tokens per turn), and it invalidates prompt-cache prefix stability, since a new system message is inserted at position 0 that varies per turn. This wrecks Anthropic prompt caching, which is costly for long Claude Code sessions. The proxy also drops the Claude Code system prompt and tools when rebuilding the payload (proxy.py:142-149), which effectively breaks Claude Code.
pros: MIT license, small (about 700 lines of source), easy to read and audit in 10 minutes
Fail-open intent on Jev timeout or error, with a 0.8s timeout
No hooks, MCP tools or skills, so zero tool-definition context cost and no clash with existing gitnexus/secret-guard hooks
Jev base URL is a config value, so the endpoint can be pointed elsewhere
cons: Does not implement the real Jev API: it sends free text to /chat/completions and greps for 'needs_generation=false', so none of the Choice/Noul/Score typed-probability value is used
No OpenRouter support at all (grep finds zero mentions); porting means rewriting jev_client.py, parsing and injection
Requires a raw Anthropic API key in plaintext config; incompatible with the user's OAuth/subscription login, so it would force pay-per-token billing for Opus 5.5

Would break Claude Code: rebuilds the payload from role/content-as-string only, dropping the system prompt, tools, tool_use/tool_result and cache_control blocks (proxy.py:142-149, models.py:8-10); Claude Code sends list-of-block content, so requests would fail validation; non-streaming returns an error
Injects a variable system message at position 0 each turn, destroying prompt-cache hits
Sends every user message to a third party (Typesafe) on personal and client projects, including client code pasted in prompts
Headline claims (3x faster, 80% cheaper, 'Live Statistics from Production Use') are unsubstantiated: the chart file is missing and statistics/README.md says data has not been generated yet
1-person, 1-week-old repo, 1 star, no CI, README/AI-prompt artefacts (Windows path in instructions_prompt.txt), OpenAI path stubbed, bypass path returns a canned stub
Proxy must be started manually and is a single point of failure for every Claude Code request
Adds a blocking hop on every turn, including tool-loop turns where classification is meaningless
entries.verdict: Do not use. It is a week-old, single-author proof-of-concept that misuses Jev as a text chat model, has no OpenRouter path, needs a raw Anthropic API key, and would break or degrade Claude Code (dropped tools and system prompt, cache invalidation, added latency). Its performance claims are unsupported by anything in the repo.
