entries.name: supercorp-ai/supercov
entries.what: Rust CLI (npm `supercov`, also PyPI, RubyGems, crates.io, Homebrew, go run) that (a) runs your test command in an isolated workspace to compute line/branch/MC/DC coverage for JS/TS, Python, Rust, Ruby, Go, Java, Kotlin, and (b) `supercov quality` / `supercov security` send each source file plus 12 yes/no (Noul) and choice questions to Jev via the System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone) and compute the health scores and security findings itself. It ships a Claude Code plugin (skills + 4 slash commands) that tells the agent to use the CLI on its own when the user asks for tests, coverage, refactoring or a security scan. It is a CLI plus skills, not an MCP server and not a hook. Jev is used only for quality and security scoring; coverage is fully local.
interface: CLI: supercov -- <test cmd>; runs latest [gaps|file|source|assertions]; diff; report; docs <topic>
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion). It fires when the user asks for tests, coverage, refactoring or a security scan, and the skill then tells the agent to run the Jev-backed scan without asking again. It does not fire on ordinary edits, commits or reviews unless the user says so. The slash commands are user-typed only. There is no deterministic hook, so it is not the always-on "Claude Code uses Jev whenever useful" behaviour the user asked for. It could be made deterministic only by adding your own PostToolUse or Stop hook that calls `supercov quality patch`, which you would write and own.
security: MIT license. The repo was created 2026-08-23, so it is about 5 weeks old. It has 141 stars, 5 forks, 604 commits (603 by one author, Domas Bitvinskas, 1 by a contributor), and latest release v2.0.1 published 2026-09-25. Last push was 2026-09-27.

API key is read only from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header via ureq (quality.rs:1332). I found no --api-key CLI flag, so the key does not appear in argv or the process list. The endpoint check rejects plain http except for localhost (quality.rs:148-158), and redirects are disabled (max_redirects(0), :1315), so the key cannot be redirected elsewhere. Response size is capped at 1 MiB and the schema is validated against the request (:1186+).

The plugin is only markdown (skills and commands). There are no hooks, no MCP server, and no shell execution beyond the commands the agent runs. The commands use allowed-tools Bash(npx supercov quality:*) and Bash(npx supercov docs:*). The skill text tells the agent to run scans without asking again when the key is set, which is a consent shortcut. It is not an injection vector, but it does mean code egress happens without a prompt.

npx pulls the supercov package, whose bin/native.js resolves a prebuilt native binary from optionalDependencies (@supercov/cli-linux-x64-gnu etc.). There is no postinstall script, as package.json only has build/test/prepack scripts. Still, `npx supercov` downloads and runs an opaque native Rust binary from npm at 2.0.1, so it is unaudited supply-chain surface. The Homebrew, cargo and go run install paths also exist. Version pinning would be prudent.

The coverage mode executes the user's own test command in an isolated workspace and instruments code. That is a large attack surface (lots of instrumenters and runtimes) if run on untrusted repos, but it is unrelated to the Jev path.
Telemetry: none found. A grep for telemetry/analytics/posthog/sentry found no hits in the source, and SECURITY.md says coverage sends nothing.
entries.dataEgress: Only `supercov quality` and `supercov security` (and `review`, which uses them) send data, and only when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is set. Per SECURITY.md:15 and quality.rs, the request body is the full source file content (or a split slice of it when a request would exceed the 30k token budget, MAX_REQUEST_TOKENS = 30_000, with files over 4 MiB skipped) plus the question set, and the model name (quality.rs:186-201). For `patch` mode it sends the before/after versions of the changed files. It sends no test outputs, prompts or conversation. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with the env override. This means whole-repo source, including client code, goes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. The user should check OpenRouter's ZDR and data-retention policy and the client contracts. `--dry-run` prints the exact requests. A local response cache (`.supercov/`, self-gitignored) makes repeat runs on unchanged files send nothing. Coverage runs send nothing. Cost is about $0.01 per MB of source, so a normal repo costs a few cents per full scan.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice, because it is invoked on demand as a CLI and not in a hook path. On transport failure or timeout it returns an error ("transport failed... retry the command"). The per-request global timeout is 45s (quality.rs:1314), with up to 4 attempts on 429/5xx, backoff capped at 30s and honoring Retry-After. If Retry-After is longer than 30s it errors out immediately. A missing key gives an error message, and the skill tells the agent to fall back to reading the code by hand and say that Supercov did not check it. A failed scan never blocks a tool call. However, a full-repo scan with retries could hang a turn for minutes.
entries.contextCost: Very low at rest. There are no MCP tools and no server instructions. Two skills (about 1.7 KB and 0.9 KB of SKILL.md, of which only name+description sit in the always-loaded listing, about 150-200 tokens total) and 4 slash commands with disable-model-invocation (about 3 KB, loaded only when typed). No hook-injected text. Cost per use is the CLI output the agent reads, which is designed to be short and paginated (`gaps --limit 5`, `--json`).
pros: It is the only candidate I saw with a real, tested OpenRouter path in code: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 hits /api/v1/systemone with a Bearer sk-or- key (quality.rs:136-158, tests/typesafe_base_url.rs, docs/quality.md:41-47). A mock server checks the exact path, header and model, and ~typesafe/jev-latest is tested.

It uses Jev for what it is designed for. Jev returns typed Noul probabilities and the CLI does the arithmetic, so no free text comes back and the results are checkable. The design fits the System One model, and the cost is tiny at about a cent per MB.

Skills auto-trigger from the description, and the skill says to run without re-asking once the key is set. That is close to the "no prompting" wish for the specific case of security-scan, refactor and add-test requests.

Very low context footprint, with no MCP tool schemas and no hook-injected text. There is no telemetry, no postinstall, and no key on argv. Redirects are disabled and https is enforced. The --dry-run flag shows the exact payload before egress.

Content-hash cache, per-model cache keys, and `quality patch` scoped to uncommitted work or branch diff make repeated use cheap. It also gives real local coverage/MC-DC tooling, which is useful independently of Jev and aligns with daily test-writing work.
Actively maintained, with 604 commits in 5 weeks, a large CI workflow set, and 1002 `#[test]` functions counted in the crates.
cons: Not automatic in the sense the user wants. It is a skill triggered only by explicit test, coverage, refactor or security requests, not a hook that runs Jev on every edit, commit or plan. Jev never helps with general routing or decisions in Claude Code, only with this tool's own file scoring.

It ships whole source files, including client code, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every uncached scan, and the skill instructs the agent to do so without asking again once the key is set. With bypass permissions on, this happens silently on client repos. Per-project gating of the env var (direnv) would be needed. The user must check OpenRouter data policy and client contracts.

The user must export a key named TYPESAFE_API_KEY containing an sk-or- OpenRouter key, plus 2 more env vars, before Claude Code starts, and it is set globally unless scoped. The system One path only. A live end-to-end run against OpenRouter was not shown (only a mock).

Young, single-maintainer project (603 of 604 commits by one person, first commit 2026-09-01, 141 stars) with a huge codebase (789 files, 8 languages of instrumenters). The npx binary is an opaque native download. Jev's quality and security judgments are weakly validated: the CHANGELOG itself reports security F1 0.47 (precision 54%, recall 41%), and its own docs say no score threshold has survived calibration.

Answers are only as good as Jev, which the brief says may behave like a routed cheap model. The calibrated catalog targets model jev-1.13.0, and when the model is overridden to typesafe/jev-1.13 the scores may drift, with the cache and diff keyed per model.

The main CLI value (coverage and MC/DC) has nothing to do with Jev. Full-repo scans are slow on a cold cache and cost real minutes and retries on 429, so they are unsuitable for a per-turn hook without wrapping.
entries.verdict: Best-evidenced OpenRouter-compatible Jev consumer found so far. It is a real, tested integration with a tiny context footprint and useful quality, security and coverage output. But it is skill-triggered (only on test, refactor or security requests) rather than an always-on hook, and it exports full source files to OpenRouter without further prompting, so use it as an opt-in per-project add-on (pin the version, scope the env vars with direnv) and not as the main way to get automatic Jev use.

judge.why: Best-evidenced OpenRouter Jev consumer, with a tiny context footprint. It is a skill-triggered CLI for coverage, quality and security scoring, not always-on.
pros: Real OpenRouter path with a mock test for path, header and model
Jev returns Noul probabilities and the code does the arithmetic; cost about a cent per MB
Zero MCP context and no hook latency; 141 stars
cons: Not automatic: fires only when asked for tests, coverage, refactor or a security scan
Ships whole source files to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, and the skill tells the agent to do this silently once the key is set (bypass mode, client repos)
Key must be exported as TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it lands in the process env; no adversarial verification

entries.name: Tech-Byte-Frontier/jevgate (JevGate)
entries.what: Rust CLI code-review gate that parses the repo locally (tree-sitter) into small evidence units (function, file outline, copy pair, test, doc section), asks Jev short typed yes/no questions via POST <root>/v1/systemone, and composes answers in code into review/consider/note findings with location, historical precision and next step. Ships a Claude Code plugin (hooks SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit, Stop; an MCP server `jevgate mcp` with 3 tools; a skill /jevgate:findings) so checks run automatically after each edit and at end of turn, and block the turn (max 3 times) while gate-failing findings exist. Also CI action, git hooks, pre-commit. Needs the separate `jevgate` binary >= 0.27 on PATH.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (the strongest form of automatic): SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse on edit tools, and Stop all run `jevgate hook` with no model discretion or user prompt; the Stop hook can force Claude to keep working. MCP tools and the findings skill are model-discretion but mostly unnecessary because hooks push findings into context.
security: API key sent only as `Authorization: Bearer` header (src/transport/mod.rs:632-646), never in argv; `auth login` reads from hidden prompt or `--with-key` stdin (src/auth/mod.rs:44,83,87, secret.rs); stored in OS keyring or owner-only file; docs claim key never printed or written to reports.

Provider/key mismatch guard: key prefix sk-or-/vck_ refused for the wrong provider; repository cannot choose the host (only env JEVGATE_BASE_URL does), and repo .env is read only for TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so a hostile repo cannot redirect uploads or inject an OpenRouter key.

Hostile-repo scope explicitly in SECURITY.md (path traversal, symlinks, --base revs, .env upload, report.html script injection, serve bound to localhost/no browsers). Private GitHub vulnerability reporting; only latest release supported.

Prompt-injection surface: hook output and finding messages are model-derived text from Jev plus repo text placed in additionalContext/stop-reason; code comments addressing a reviewer are themselves a checked guard. Findings are advisory strings, but Stop-hook block reasons feed straight into Claude, so a poisoned finding could steer edits. Low severity; message templates are code-composed, not free text (Jev returns typed probabilities only).

install.sh is a curl|sh but checks SHA-256 of the release tarball fetched from the same GitHub release (integrity vs. corruption only, not vs. repo compromise); npm launcher has no postinstall script (package.json has none) and downloads the binary on first run, verifying SHA256SUMS. Prefer cargo install --locked to avoid both. Binary is a large closed-loop 98k-line Rust program running with user privileges on every edit; single maintainer.

No telemetry found: grep of src for telemetry/analytics only hits src/units/questions/security (a rule about detecting telemetry in reviewed code). Network calls seen: provider endpoint, key check URLs, npm launcher downloads. Not exhaustively audited.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (typesafe/jev-1.13 via /api/v1/systemone): source of selected units only (individual function bodies, file outlines/member signatures, copy pairs, tests, doc sections, comments with 3 surrounding lines for reviewer-directed text, first 1,200 chars of README prose for one sensitive-data question, callee signatures/callers for follow-ups), plus the question text. Bounded by upload_allow/upload_deny in jevgate.toml, .env and hidden paths never read. Secrets deliberately not judged. With the hook installed at user level (`init --agent claude` default), this applies to EVERY git repo Claude Code edits, including client repos with no jevgate.toml, so client code leaves the machine to OpenRouter/TypeSafe unless you scope with --project or add per-repo upload_deny. No prompts, conversation, tool outputs or diffs as such (though guards send before/after text of rewritten test assertions). Retention per docs (site/src/privacy-and-cost.md, checked 2026-09-28): OpenRouter stores no prompts unless logging enabled and lists the TypeSafe endpoint as ZDR; TypeSafe MCA keeps telemetry/hashes/classifications indefinitely and hosts in US. `jevgate check --dry-run --show-requests` shows exact request bodies offline.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for the agent. The hook always exits 0 (exit 2 would block in Claude Code) and reports problems as a systemMessage/context: missing binary or version <0.27 (the `|| echo systemMessage` wrapper), missing key, HTTP 402, outage, timeout, session lock, non-git dir never block. Timeouts: hook budgets 10s (start), 30s (edit), 50s (Stop), plugin hook timeouts 20/20/40/60s; per-request attempt 20s then retried once; 429/5xx retried up to 6 times (1,2,4,8,8s backoff, up to 30s Retry-After) but never past the hook budget; after a provider failure the hook uses cache-only for 5 minutes then asks again, so an outage costs one delay rather than one per edit. Un-checked end-of-turn is re-checked with the next turn. Fail-closed only in the gate sense: a real gate-failing finding blocks Stop up to 3 times/turn. The MCP tool returns an error, not a pass, on incomplete runs. Risk: OpenRouter serving Jev had ~63% 503 rates on 2026-09-28 (provider.rs:118-126), so intermittent 'could not check' messages and first-check slowness are likely until it stabilizes.
entries.contextCost: Low. MCP server: 3 tools; tool names+descriptions+input schemas approx 3.5k chars (src/mcp/tools.rs lines 8-60) plus server `instructions` approx 2.2k chars (mod.rs:25-3x) is roughly 1.4-1.6k tokens (Claude Code strips outputSchema from the model view per docs). Skill description ~250 chars (~60 tokens) loaded always; body only on trigger. Hooks: SessionStart adds one ~25-token sentence; `init --agent claude` also writes ~/.claude/rules/jevgate.md which loads every session (short). Per-edit findings up to 10 lines / 8,000 chars (~2k tokens worst case, usually 0 when no finding); Stop block reasons similar, max 3 per turn. Using both the plugin's MCP server and hooks is redundant for auto-use; MCP could be dropped to save ~1.5k tokens since hooks do the work.
pros: Only candidate seen so far that is a genuinely automatic, deterministic Claude Code integration: PostToolUse + Stop hooks fire without any 'use jev' prompt, matching the user's core requirement (plugin/hooks/hooks.json).
Native OpenRouter support in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY, https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone, model typesafe/jev-1.13 (src/provider.rs:127-146); works as sole key, no patching.

Uses Jev the way the brief describes it: many tiny typed questions, calibrated probabilities composed in code into a verdict; no reliance on free-text output, which matches Jev's 'not a chat model' nature.

Well engineered fail-open behavior: always exit 0, wrapper echo for missing binary, 5-minute cache-only cool-off after provider failure, bounded timeouts, never treats an outage as a pass (site/src/coding-agents.md).

Cheap: $0.042/M input tokens, answer cache means unchanged code costs nothing; project reports $0.19 for last commits of 118 projects; --dry-run --show-requests gives full egress transparency offline.

Quality-conscious about accuracy: publishes labeled precision per rule/level (function-simplification reviews right 20/23 unseen, 80/93 on 27 more projects), and only fails the gate on rules with >=80% measured precision; honestly reports considers were only ~42-61% right on new projects.
Guardrails against agent gaming (skill forbids editing baseline/toml, allow comments, skipped tests; hook snapshots config at turn start and reports guards).

Solid engineering hygiene for a young project: ~98k lines Rust, extensive CLI integration tests with a mock provider, CI on 3 OSes, clippy -D warnings, cargo-deny, SHA-pinned actions, SHA-256 verified binaries, dual MIT/Apache license.

Coexists with existing hooks: PostToolUse matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit and Stop/UserPromptSubmit do not overlap the user's PreToolUse secret guard or Grep|Glob|Bash GitNexus hooks; `--project` scoping and upload_deny let the user protect client repos.
cons: It is a code-review linter driven by Jev, not a general 'consult Jev for decisions' bridge: Claude cannot ask Jev arbitrary Choice/Noul/Score questions (no tool for the Decisions API, only systemone via fixed rule questions). It gives Claude a second opinion on maintainability, not routing or state-decision value.

Stop-hook blocking can interrupt the flow: up to 3 forced continuation rounds per turn on findings; in a repo with existing findings, code touched by the turn is counted as new, so you must run `jevgate check` + `jevgate baseline` per repo first or Claude will be pushed to refactor legacy functions.

Data egress on client projects: user-level install uploads function-level source of every edited file in every git repo to OpenRouter/TypeSafe (ZDR listed for OpenRouter but TypeSafe MCA retains telemetry/classifications indefinitely; US hosting). Needs per-repo --project scoping or upload_deny for NDA code.

Immaturity: repo created 2026-09-18, 9 stars, 2 forks, 1 human contributor (383/384 commits), 15 releases in ~11 days (0.17 to 0.32), on a beta model; interfaces (thresholds, rule maturity, hook table) are moving fast and the plugin requires binary >=0.27.

Latency and reliability: synchronous PostToolUse hook up to 30-40s; OpenRouter's Jev endpoint showed ~63% 503s on 2026-09-28 per the maintainer's own code comment, and default concurrency is halved to 3, so expect 'JevGate could not check' noise and slow first checks. Skeptic claim that Jev is a cheap router model is untested here; findings' precision (mostly maintainability, 'considers' 42-61%) means a fair number of false-positive nudges.

Requires installing a separate 98k-line native binary (curl|sh, npm launcher that fetches binaries on first run, or cargo build), running with user privileges on every edit; single-maintainer supply-chain risk. Duplicate-run risk if plugin and `init --agent claude` are both used.
Redundant surface: MCP server adds ~1.5k tokens of tools/instructions per session though hooks already do the job; the ~/.claude/rules/jevgate.md written by init also loads each session.
Precision numbers are partly self-labeled by the maintainer or an agent, 9 of 25 unseen projects are the maintainer's own apps, and languages like Kotlin/Swift/Bash are preview-only and never gate.

Writes Git objects into every repo's .git store on each prompt and edit (git hash-object -w of the untracked working tree via a scratch index), including untracked non-ignored files. Also creates a .jevgate/ directory with its own .gitignore in each repo. This is a local side effect on client repos with a user-level install (src/revision/snapshot.rs).

Bare 'jevgate' in the hook command plus the user's overridden PATH: if the binary is not on the hook PATH, four events emit 'could not check' noise and nothing is reviewed. The plugin hooks cannot take an absolute path, so this needs a hand-written hooks block.

OPENROUTER_API_KEY must be in the environment Claude Code launches hooks with (or saved via 'jevgate auth login', which takes precedence). Putting it in Claude's env exposes it to Bash/printenv in bypassPermissions sessions, and it is not yet in no-secret-leak's protected list. Using 'auth login' (keyring or owner-only file) avoids this.

OpenRouter path is ~1 day old in the maintainer's code (0.30.0, 2026-09-28) and was seen with 50-63% 503s the same day. Retries run up to 6 attempts and 23s+ of pauses, so edits can stall up to the 30-40s hook budget, and outages skip review and degrade to cache-only for 5 minutes.
A repo-local .env containing TYPESAFE_API_KEY takes precedence over the user's OpenRouter key, silently routing that repo's code to whatever account the key belongs to (client repos could hit this).

Hooks are not registered for SubagentStop, so Stop-time gating covers only the main agent's turn (PostToolUse edit checks do still fire for subagent edits). Turn snapshots also include edits made by parallel agents or people in the same checkout, so findings can be misattributed.
Repo history was force-pushed (issue #2 mentions main force-pushed for 0.13.0) and the only third-party OpenRouter request is still open: low community validation, 9 stars.

Unscoped 'jevgate' on npm is an unrelated package (v0.2.2 by remotehostai). A mistyped 'npm i -g jevgate' installs the wrong thing; the correct one is @tech-byte-frontier/jevgate or 'cargo install jevgate' (crates.io owner tauanbinato matches the repo).
entries.verdict: Best-fit candidate for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: deterministic hooks plus native OpenRouter support make it work today with just OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and it fails open. Adopt it as a per-project (not user-global) quality gate, after baselining and with upload_deny for client repos, but understand it is a code-review linter, not a general Jev decision tool, and it is 12 days old with one maintainer.

verification.note: Verified from source (v0.32.0, HEAD 9a42f11 on 2026-09-29) and live gh/npm/crates.io queries. Confirmed: OPENROUTER service in src/provider.rs:127-146 (OPENROUTER_API_KEY, https://openrouter.ai/api, typesafe/jev-1.13), POST {root}/v1/systemone at provider.rs:216-217, Bearer header at transport/mod.rs:632-646 (no key in argv), and the 63% 503 comment at provider.rs:118-126. Also confirmed: 3 MCP tools (jevgate_check, jevgate_findings, jevgate_rules) and hooks SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse (Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit) and Stop in plugin/hooks/hooks.json with timeouts 20/20/40/60. Repo metadata is right: 9 stars, 2 forks, Apache-2.0 per GitHub (MIT OR Apache-2.0 in plugin.json), not archived, last push 2026-09-29. Claude Code correctness holds: the hook emits {decision:block, reason} on Stop (agents.rs:251) and handles stop_hook_active (agents.rs:175); PostToolUse and SessionStart use hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (agents.rs:254); systemMessage is valid; the hook always exits 0 and the '|| echo' wrapper covers a missing binary. I lowered the score from 7 to 6: it is the best automatic-hook fit, but it is immature (single maintainer, 12 days old, force-pushed main), risky for client code under a user-global install, and its OpenRouter path was flaky when tested. Even scoped with --project and upload_deny, it is not a 7. I did not run any code. judge.why: The only member with native OpenRouter support and a genuinely automatic full hook loop (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|NotebookEdit, Stop). It is a maintainability reviewer, not a general Jev decision layer.
pros: Deterministic hooks: no 'use jev' needed; hook always exits 0 and emits valid Claude Code JSON (decision:block on Stop with a stop_hook_active guard, additionalContext elsewhere); verified against v0.32.0 source
Fail-open on outage (degrades to cache-only for 5 min); key sent as Bearer, never in argv; 3 MCP tools available
Apache-2.0/MIT, tests and CI present, active maintenance
cons: Writes Git objects into every repo's .git on each prompt and edit (hash-object -w of the untracked working tree), plus a .jevgate/ dir, on client repos
Plugin hooks use bare 'jevgate'; with your overridden PATH it prints 'could not check' noise on every event, and hooks.json cannot take an absolute path without hand-written hooks
Retries up to 6 attempts and 23s+ pauses can stall an edit for 30-40s; the OpenRouter path is about 1 day old
Full edited files go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe; a repo-local .env TYPESAFE_API_KEY silently overrides your OpenRouter key; Stop gating skips subagents; an unrelated 'jevgate' package exists on npm

entries.name: ckorhonen/jev-lint
entries.what: Fuzzy linter for coding agents. A Claude Code/Codex PostToolUse (or PreToolUse with --pre) hook takes the code each Write/Edit/MultiEdit adds, gates ~170 built-in rules (TS/React, Swift, Kotlin, Rust, Python, Ruby, Bazel; security, tests, performance packs) plus repo rules in .jev-lint/ by regex, and sends the remaining rules as Jev "noul" (yes/no) questions in ONE POST /v1/systemone call. Findings with p>=0.8 ("fix these") or 0.5-0.8 ("double-check") are injected back into the agent as additionalContext (or deny in --pre mode). Also a Stop/SubagentStop re-check hook, a local findings log, and 5 skills for setup, rule generation, and a learning loop.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: runs on every Write/Edit/MultiEdit with no model discretion and no user prompt (PostToolUse, optional PreToolUse, Stop/SubagentStop). Skills are only for setup/rule authoring.
security: No curl|sh, no postinstall, no runtime deps; MIT license; .gitleaks.toml present.
API key is sent only in Authorization header from inside the process (never in argv); key file refused if mode has group/other bits (jev.ts:37); macOS Keychain lookup only on darwin.
installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json and ~/.codex/hooks.json (with .bak files) and symlinks skills into ~/.claude/skills: it modifies global config, run dry-run first.
Hook command line is JEV_LINT_MODEL=... bun <path>/src/hook.ts: no secrets in argv.

Sends code to a third party on every matching edit; no secret redaction before send. Existing secret-leak guard does not cover PostToolUse Write content going to the network, and a Write of a file containing secrets (.env is not a matched extension, but .ts/.py with hard-coded keys is) would be transmitted.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the model returns only numbers; injected text is static per-rule 'fix' strings from rules/*.json or repo .jev-lint/*.rules.json (repo-controlled rules in a cloned client repo could inject arbitrary fix text into the agent context, and per-repo config can change thresholds).
entries.dataEgress: The added code of every Write/Edit/MultiEdit to files with a supported extension inside the working repo (Write = entire file content; Edit = new_string only; MultiEdit = joined new_strings), plus absolute file_path, language, and the rule question texts, sent to /v1/systemone (TypeSafe today; with a patch, OpenRouter and then TypeSafe's Jev backend). Files >24k chars are skipped; files outside cwd (/tmp, scratchpad) skipped (hook.ts isInsideRepo). Stop re-check re-reads flagged files from disk (up to 8, 24k chars each) and sends them. Not sent: prompts, conversation, tool outputs, diffs of removed code, Bash commands, files never edited. Client-project code goes to third parties by default, so needs per-repo opt-out or a project-scoped install.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: any exception, timeout (JEV_LINT_TIMEOUT_MS default 8000; hook timeout 15 s in settings), 4xx/5xx or missing key exits 0 silently (hook.ts:135-139, retries default 0). No key means it silently does nothing (only the installer/smoke test warns). In --pre mode a slow/down Jev adds up to ~8 s before each write but never blocks; false alarms can deny an edit at most twice per rule+file per session. Rewake/async mode removes latency at the cost of interrupting the agent later.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. Hooks inject text only when a rule fires (a few lines per finding plus a trailing sentence, ~50-300 tokens per flagged edit). The 5 skills, if linked into ~/.claude/skills, add ~5 descriptions of ~400-600 chars each (~600-700 tokens permanent), and their bodies (4-10 KB each) load only on trigger. The skill descriptions can be left unlinked (omit --skills) for zero baseline cost.
pros: Only candidate found that is truly automatic: a deterministic hook fires on every Write/Edit with zero prompting, exactly the user's requirement.
Uses Jev for what it is built for: yes/no calibrated probabilities over many rules in one cheap call; no free text, no chat replacement; thresholds (0.8/0.5) map directly to Noul output.
Zero MCP tools and no server instructions, so no permanent context tax; hook text only appears when a rule fires.
Fails open with bounded timeouts, so a slow or down Jev can't wedge Claude Code; async rewake mode avoids blocking entirely.
Regex 'when' gate cuts model calls to ~1/3 of rules; 24k char cap; skips files outside repo; MAX_FILES=8.
Per-repo control via .jev-lint/config.json (disable, skipPaths, thresholds) and --project install, useful to keep client repos out.
Small readable codebase (~2.4k lines TS, no runtime deps), MIT, tests present; core client jev.ts is 84 lines so OpenRouter patch is tiny.
Coexists with existing hooks: it only registers PostToolUse Write|Edit|MultiEdit (+Stop), disjoint from the secret-guard and GitNexus matchers.
cons: No OpenRouter support out of the box: non-typesafe.ai hosts get the literal key 'local' (jev.ts:62) and the key resolver ignores OPENROUTER_API_KEY; needs a fork/patch in jev.ts and daemon.ts, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified (docs 404 for me).
Model IDs differ (jev-1.13.0 in code vs typesafe/jev-1.13 on OpenRouter), and the installer hardcodes MODEL and writes hook command lines that must be edited.
Sends every edited file's content to a third party by default with no redaction; risky for client projects unless installed per-project or with an allow/deny list.
Requires bun, which the user's stack (Node 24, uv) doesn't include; the hook is a per-edit process spawn.

Brand new (created 2026-09-26, 30 commits in 2 days, 1 contributor, 5 stars, no releases, no CI) and results are self-reported; Jev itself is beta and Theo-style skepticism about the model is unresolved.

Quality is a linter for style/practice rules, not general coding assistance; opinionated 170-rule defaults (e.g. no magic numbers, restating comments) may be noisy for a senior dev, and each flag makes Opus spend extra turns (+$0.04/+10 s per task per author).

Installer rewrites global ~/.claude/settings.json and symlinks skills; the user's settings already carry several hooks, so merge needs review. Repo-provided .jev-lint/ rules in cloned client repos are trusted input that reaches agent context.
Fails silently when the key is missing or the endpoint rejects it, so a misconfigured OpenRouter setup will look installed but never lint anything unless JEV_LINT_DEBUG is set.

Egress has no secret redaction: any Write of a .ts/.py/etc with a hard-coded key or client code goes to a third party; existing no-secret-leak.cjs does not cover this path; OPENROUTER_API_KEY is also not protected there yet
Coverage gap: Bash-based file writes, NotebookEdit and out-of-repo files are never linted, so behavior is inconsistent under bypassPermissions
Injects an instruction telling the agent not to mention the check to the user (opaque behaviour, possible confusion when Opus makes unexplained extra edits)
Author-measured cost of use: +~10 s and +$0.04 (Opus tokens) per task from fix loops, dwarfing the ~$0.00015 Jev cost

Daemon spawns a detached long-lived bun process and does keepwarm GETs to the base URL every 45 s while active; daemon identity ignores any OpenRouter key so a patched fork must also fix daemonClient.ts
Stop/SubagentStop hooks have 20 s timeout and re-read flagged files from disk and send them again to the third party
Requires bun, not in the user's stack; a missing or broken bun means the hook silently no-ops
OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone and /alpha docs could not be confirmed (404), so request/response parity for the patched client is untested; endpoint is alpha with no SLA
Findings log ~/.local/state/jev-lint/findings.jsonl keeps code excerpts of client code in plaintext
entries.verdict: Best-fit pattern for the user's goal (deterministic, invisible, fail-open PostToolUse hook, zero MCP context), but it is a TypeSafe-only alpha tool: to run on OpenRouter you must patch about 5 lines in jev.ts/daemon.ts and confirm the /api/v1/systemone schema with one real call. Use it (forked, pinned, project-scoped, ideally with a redaction/allowlist step) rather than installing it globally as-is.

verification.note: Re-queried: 5 stars, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-26, last push 2026-09-27T23:01Z, 30 commits, 1 open issue. Core facts in the audit (jev.ts:23-24,62,69, hook.ts fail-open, key never in argv, key file mode check, no postinstall, no curl|sh, 24k cap, isInsideRepo skip, absolute-path hook commands) all verified against source. Hook output fields (PostToolUse additionalContext/decision:block, PreToolUse permissionDecision deny + additionalContext, asyncRewake with exit 2) are valid Claude Code 2.1.x constructs; the design is fail-open. Score lowered from 7 to 6: it is a TypeSafe-only alpha tool needing a multi-file patch (jev.ts, daemon.ts, daemonClient.ts, installer model id), needs bun, has unverified OpenRouter schema/model-id parity, sends client code with no redaction by default, has partial edit coverage (no Bash writes), and is a 4-day-old single-author repo. Still the best fit pattern for invisible automatic use, so 6 (useful idea, notable gaps) rather than lower; recommend only as a pinned, forked, project-scoped trial with a redaction/allowlist step and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the secret-guard list.

judge.why: Best hook design (invisible PostToolUse lint with fail-open), but TypeSafe-only and needs bun and a fork.
pros: Deterministic PostToolUse hook on Write|Edit|MultiEdit; fail-open on any error or 8s timeout; key never in argv
Absolute-path hook commands from the installer; skips files outside the repo and over 24k chars
Warm daemon keeps latency low
cons: OpenRouter needs a fork: the isTypeSafe gate and daemon identity only know TYPESAFE_API_KEY; model id 'jev-1.13.0'/'jev-latest' unconfirmed on OpenRouter
Requires bun; a missing bun means the hook silently no-ops; the installer rewrites settings.json

No secret redaction on egress; tells the agent 'don't mention this check to the user'; Bash-based writes and NotebookEdit are not covered; Stop/SubagentStop 20s timeout; findings log keeps client code excerpts in plaintext

entries.name: 7hemas7er/jev-hooks
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also its own marketplace) that calls a Jev-compatible POST /v1/systemone backend (TypeSafe Jev, or self-hosted rizzo-flow) with typed noul/choice/score questions. (1) Commit reviewer: a PreToolUse hook on Bash (if Bash(git *)) intercepts git commit, builds the staged diff, runs regex detectors (live keys, private keys, prompt-injection phrases, bidi chars, CI files) that set lane floors, splits the diff into ~2000-token chunks, asks 7 questions per chunk plus 5 global ones, and config/policy.json turns the probabilities into a lane: BLOCK (deny), SECURITY REVIEW (ask), NITS (notes plus escalation to Claude), MERGE (status line). (2) Opt-in effort router: a function hook (hooks/register.ts) classifies each typed prompt with 7 questions and lowers per-turn effort, never above the session's. (3) Skills /jev-review and /jev-status, a jev-review CLI, a guard on Edit/Write of .jev-hooks/, a PostToolUse commit log, and a GitHub Action.
interface: PreToolUse hook Bash (if Bash(git *)) -> run-node.sh commit
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: the commit reviewer fires automatically on every git commit Claude runs through Bash (PreToolUse, matcher Bash, if Bash(git *)), with no prompting needed; the guard fires on Edit/Write of .jev-hooks/. The effort router is an opt-in function hook on every typed prompt (needs an env flag and an account beta). The /jev-review skill is description-triggered and on demand. It never covers commits made in the user's own terminal.
security: Single author (7hemas7er), 0 stars, 0 forks, repo created 2026-09-27, 65 commits in 3 days; v0.10.0 on 2026-09-30; no GitHub release, no topics. Self-declared 'public preview'.

Runs unsandboxed command hooks (outside Claude's sandbox) on every Bash tool call matching git *; the trust boundary is a young single-maintainer repo. Installed by /plugin from GitHub main; updates only when version is raised and user runs /plugin update.

No dependencies (package.json has none), no npm postinstall, no curl|sh installer; Node >=22.18 type-stripping runs the .ts directly. run-node.sh only probes for node binaries in nvm/fnm/volta/asdf/mise/n/brew paths.

API key: sensitive plugin option kept out of settings.json and delivered to hooks via CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY env of the hook process only; key only in Authorization header, never in URL/logs; never in argv (CLI takes key from env or key file, never a flag). Key is sent only to the URL of its own layer (TYPESAFE_API_KEY never goes to a LAN host). Key file warns if group/world-readable.

Client uses fetch redirect:'error' (no key or body follows redirects), 4 MiB response cap, https required except loopback/RFC1918/Tailscale/.local hosts. Hand-written strict URL parser to prevent host-confusion tricks.

Git hardening: spawnSync without shell, fsmonitor/hooks/external diff/textconv/pager disabled, minimal env without keys, temp index copy, symlinks not followed. Hostile .jev-hooks/ project rules can only tighten, not loosen.
entries.dataEgress: Commit reviewer (default on once review_url is set): the staged diff (chunked, ~2000 tokens each, plus file list, commit title/description for the 5 global questions) is POSTed to the backend on every git commit Claude runs. For non-local backends it is first redacted: detector-recognized secrets and their repeats replaced by random same-shape values, PEM blocks replaced whole, sensitive files (.env, .pem, credentials) sent as path only, guardrail mask map applied if present (nothing sent if the map is invalid). Secrets no regex recognizes still leave (docs/backends.md says to prefer local rizzo for private repos). Full source code in the diff therefore goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe: relevant for client projects under NDA. Effort router (off by default): every typed prompt (redacted) is sent to the backend. Nothing else (no file reads, tool outputs, or transcripts) leaves. A floor of BLOCK skips the backend call entirely.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, visibly: backend down/slow/misconfigured lets the commit proceed with a one-line notice once per session per error kind; deterministic regex floors still apply offline (private keys, live AWS/Stripe/GitHub/Slack tokens -> BLOCK even with backend off). Missing Node >=22.18 also fails open with a systemMessage. Timeouts: hook timeout 180 s in hooks.json, policy total budget (config/policy.json:69-76) with 60 s per-request timeout_ms and a 1 s margin before deadline; timeouts are never retried. Router timeout 1.5 s then turn proceeds unchanged, with a 30 s busy backoff. Risk: with a slow remote backend a commit can wait up to tens of seconds before the fail-open path.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero MCP server instructions. Two skills (jev-review, jev-status) add two short skill descriptions to the listing (~150 tokens total). Hooks inject text only on git commit: a one-line status for MERGE, or a compact data block (check ids, probabilities, files/line ranges) for NITS/escalation, roughly a few hundred tokens; the /jev-review skill returns the same block. Router notices are not sent to the model.
pros: Only candidate seen that is genuinely automatic in Claude Code: a deterministic PreToolUse hook on git commit needs no user prompt and no model discretion, exactly the user's requirement.

Works with OpenRouter by configuration alone: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key, because backend.ts appends /v1/systemone and OpenRouter documents its System One API as TypeSafe-SDK-compatible (bare jev-latest mapped to typesafe/).
Uses Jev the way it is designed: closed noul/choice/score questions, probabilities to thresholds in editable JSON (config/checks.json, policy.json), verdict computed by code rather than free text.
Fail-open with deterministic floors (private keys, live tokens) that hold even with the backend down or unset; no risk of blocking the user's workflow.

Careful security engineering: key as sensitive plugin option not in settings.json or argv, no redirects, https-only for non-local hosts, redaction before remote send, hardened git, no diff lines fed back to Claude, no dependencies or postinstall.
Zero MCP tools and near-zero context cost; complements (does not collide with) the existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks, since it hooks git commit/Skill/Edit only.
~900 offline tests (18.8k lines under tests/), CI on Node 22.18 and 24 with pinned action SHAs, manifest validation, weekly Claude Code compat job; honest docs on limitations.
cons: Very narrow use: only reviews commits (and optionally routes effort). Does not help with code search, context, refactoring or planning, so it adds little to 'daily coding' beyond a pre-commit second opinion.

Thresholds and calibration were fitted on rizzo-flow (Spark-X2.5-4B) and a small synthetic bench, not on real Jev; docs/backends.md admits the 'jev' profile trusts TypeSafe's calibration claim unverified. README itself says treat verdicts as a second opinion, not a gate. Real false-positive/negative rates on the user's diffs are unknown.

Zero OpenRouter support in code or docs; OpenRouter compatibility rests on OpenRouter's docs, and was not tested here. /jev-status uses GET /v1/models, which OpenRouter answers in a different shape, so the status skill likely errors.

Full staged diffs of personal and client repos go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every commit; redaction is regex-only, so unrecognized secrets and proprietary code leave the machine. Problematic for client/NDA work unless scoped per project or disabled there.

Brand new and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-27, 65 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, no release; it is unsandboxed code in the hook path, updated straight from GitHub main. Would need a pinned commit and a review before trust.

Effort router needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, an early-access API that may break between Claude Code releases, and a per-turn-control beta the user's OAuth subscription may not have; without it every effort change flushes the prompt cache. Should stay off.
Redundant in part with existing setup: the PreToolUse secret-leak guard and Anthropic's security-guidance plugin already cover credential leaks on commit; docs warn that both run on git commit.
In bypass/auto permission mode the SECURITY REVIEW 'ask' still interrupts (docs say it asks even in auto mode); adds seconds of latency per commit on a remote backend.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and the only truly automatic (hook-driven) Jev integration seen for Claude Code, and it should work with OpenRouter by setting review_url=https://openrouter.ai/api and an OpenRouter key. Its scope is only a pre-commit second opinion with thresholds not measured on Jev, and it sends full diffs off-machine and is a 3-day-old solo project, so pin a commit, read it, keep the router off, and enable it only on personal repos first.

judge.why: Narrow but the safest hook design: a PreToolUse hook on `git commit` only, so no per-edit latency. It redacts secrets before sending and fails open.
pros: Fires only on `git commit` (if Bash(git *) filter), so about 1-3 s per commit and nothing on other Bash calls
Regex detectors set lane floors deterministically; secrets are redacted before non-local egress; lanes BLOCK/ASK/NITS/MERGE come from editable JSON
Fail-open with a visible notice; about 900 offline tests; SHA-pinned CI
cons: Thresholds fitted on a local 4B model and a synthetic bench, not on real Jev; README calls it a second opinion, not a gate
Only commit review (the opt-in effort router adds up to 1.5s per prompt; keep it off); full diffs still leave the machine
Not adversarially verified; 0 stars, solo author, 3 days old

entries.name: @lakeday/perch
entries.what: Node CLI (npm @lakeday/perch 0.3.5, MIT) that does semantic code linting: it parses a git repo with tree-sitter, sends each method or file plus rule questions to a System One (Jev) endpoint as typed Choice/Noul/Score questions, and reports probability-ranked findings (perch scan, check, issues, close, rules, doctor). It ships a Claude Code skill (perch setup claude-code writes .claude/skills/perch/SKILL.md) that the model loads by its description. It is not an MCP server and installs no hooks. Perch is a real consumer of the System One API, which is the strongest real-world Jev usage found, but it is a linter product, not a general routing or decision layer.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model-discretion). The description says 'verify code changes in flight, scan a branch or diff, check one method right after editing, confirm a fix landed before opening a PR'. Claude Code loads the skill on its own judgement, and then Claude runs the perch CLI via Bash. There is no deterministic hook. The perch author observed for Cursor that description matching is unreliable and worked around it with alwaysApply: true (src/setup.js:38-46). Claude Code has no such option, so triggering will be probabilistic. To make it automatic and reliable you would add your own PostToolUse hook on Edit|Write or a pre-PR/Stop hook that runs perch check, and that is not shipped.
security: No MCP server and no hooks, so no new tool surface or PreToolUse interaction. The only agent-facing artifact is a markdown skill.
API key is read from env (PERCH_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv. doctor prints only the key length and never its value (src/checks.js:37).
Shell execution is limited to git via execFile/spawn with an argument array and '-c core.hooksPath=/dev/null' (src/git.js:12,67). There is no shell string and no curl|sh installer.

The published package has a 'prepare' script (node build.mjs), but it does not run for a registry install and build.mjs is not in 'files'. No postinstall. The tree-sitter pack downloads parsers from GitHub releases at first use, a runtime network fetch of native or wasm code from a third party.

Prompt-injection surface: the Jev output is typed and probabilistic, with no free text, so findings cannot carry instructions. The skill does tell the model to read the code before changing it and never to rewrite working code to satisfy a probability. Rule files under .perch/rules are repo content, so a hostile repo can define rules, but they only become model questions.

Default credential path (no PERCH_BASE_URL) is Perch Cloud, a separate third-party SaaS at dash.perchscan.com. It also receives repository name and scan results (/v1/scans/start|append|finish). Avoid it, or set PERCH_BASE_URL.
entries.dataEgress: In direct mode (PERCH_BASE_URL set) the following goes to the configured endpoint (OpenRouter, then TypeSafe): for each method or file, the request body is {model, state:{path, name, line, source: full method or file source, plus 'seen' context such as callees, callers and neighbours}, questions:{rule text and criteria}} (src/units.js:319, src/systemone.js:34). That is real source code, up to 24k tokens of state per request, across many requests per scan. Only methods changed or tracked in git HEAD are read, using git cat-file at the committed HEAD, but 'check' reads files from disk. Diffs, conversation text and tool outputs are not sent, and neither are .env files, unless they are committed and in scope. Results are cached locally in .perch/. With the Cloud default, the same content plus organizationId, repositoryId and the git remote name goes to dash.perchscan.com. For client projects, OpenRouter (and TypeSafe behind it) sees client source code, so check the client's policy. OpenRouter's logging and data-collection settings are a separate control.
entries.failureMode: Not in the critical path of Claude Code: perch is a separate CLI that only runs when the model or the user invokes it. The client retries network errors and HTTP 429/5xx up to 4 attempts with exponential backoff, starting at 2 s and honouring Retry-After (src/systemone.js:38-52). 401/402/403 abort the whole run at once with an AuthenticationError. The direct-mode fetch has NO per-request timeout (AbortSignal.timeout only in the Cloud paths, cloud-auth.js:17,76,163), so a hung TCP connection can stall a scan. Errors exit 1, and findings exit 3, which the skill tells the agent to read as a result and not a crash. In practice it fails open with respect to Claude Code, since the agent just sees an error from a Bash call. It is not a gate unless it is wired into CI or hooks, and the user would need to add that.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. The skill adds only its name and description (about 90 words, roughly 130 tokens) to the always-loaded listing. The full skill.md (188 lines, roughly 1.9k tokens) loads only when the description triggers. There are no hooks and no injected text per turn. It is the cheapest option in context terms. The per-project .claude/skills copy means it only appears in repos where perch setup was run, unless the file is copied to ~/.claude/skills.
pros: Truly uses Jev for a coding job (bug and semantic-rule detection with calibrated probabilities), which is the most direct 'Jev inside coding workflow' example found, and it matches Jev's typed-decision design (Choice/Noul/Score) rather than misusing it as a chat model.

OpenRouter works by configuration alone: PERCH_BASE_URL and PERCH_API_KEY are honoured (src/cloud-client.js:110,121), and OpenRouter documents /api/v1/systemone as TypeSafe-SDK compatible with bare model IDs mapped to typesafe/. This has not been tested end to end.

Very cheap on context: no MCP tools, no hooks, about 130 tokens of always-on skill description, and a small footprint that will not interfere with the existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks.

Not in the critical path: an outage cannot block Claude Code. Retries with backoff are built in, and 402/401 abort the run cleanly with a clear message. Exit-code semantics (3 = findings, not a failure) are documented for agents.
Incremental and cached: unchanged methods are skipped, --since origin/main scopes to a branch, and check works on uncommitted code, so post-edit checks are about $0.0002 and quick.

Active and reasonably engineered for its age: 137 commits (130 by one author) in 14 days, 316 stars, 34 test files, CI with lint, typecheck, tests, CodeQL and release-please, MIT license, and a clean source tree with an execFile array and a hardened git call (core.hooksPath=/dev/null).
Rules are user-definable (perch.yaml), so client-specific conventions can be encoded as semantic lints and reused.
cons: Auto-invocation is only probabilistic. It is a skill triggered by description and is not a hook, and the author's own note in src/setup.js says description matching can miss ('fix this bug' does not read as semantic linting). Achieving 'always used when needed' needs a self-built PostToolUse or Stop hook, which is not provided.

Sends real source code (full methods plus callers and neighbours, up to 24k tokens per request, many requests) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. That is a client-confidentiality decision for client projects, and there is no local-only mode. The default path without PERCH_BASE_URL sends it to a third-party SaaS (Perch Cloud) as well.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-16, 11 releases in 8 days, 0.x API, pre-1.0 CLI flags will churn. It was published by one npm account, and the dependency chain includes a runtime parser download from GitHub releases. Treat it as beta.

No per-request timeout in direct mode (src/systemone.js uses bare fetch), and a whole-repo scan means hundreds of requests, so cost and time can surprise. It is opt-in per scan, and the skill warns against scanning everything.

Only a linter or reviewer, not a general decision or routing layer. It does not cover the broader ideas for Jev in Claude Code (tool choice, routing, permission classification, commit triage), and its quality depends on Jev's bug-detection model, whose claims (the Theo skepticism) are unverified. Finding noise is possible: the docs explain how rules can answer 'in the sixties' about everything.

Bug/finding quality for your stack is unverified. Tree-sitter language coverage and first-run parser download add friction, and it needs a git repo with at least one commit (scan reads HEAD, not the worktree, except for check).

OpenRouter compatibility (usage and charge fields, the 128-option Choice limit, 24k state) is inferred from docs only. Perch's message strings and limits mention Perch Cloud's bug model, so a quirk on OpenRouter is plausible.

Not automatic: model-discretion skill only, plus per-repo file. `perch setup claude-code` writes .claude/skills/perch/SKILL.md into each working tree (dirties client repos unless gitignored) and the author himself concedes description matching is unreliable (setup.js:35-46); Claude Code has no alwaysApply equivalent, so it does not meet the user's 'never have to prompt' requirement without a self-built hook.

The published 0.3.5 has no Cloud mode, no rolling-pool concurrency and no parser-download retries; the audit's described behavior (and 0.4.0's Cloud key-as-token path) will change on the next release (PR #156 open), so the recommended env config may behave differently after an upgrade.

Misconfiguration leaks the OpenRouter key: after 0.4.0, PERCH_API_KEY without PERCH_BASE_URL sends the key to dash.perchscan.com; in 0.3.5 it goes to api.typesafe.ai. PERCH_BASE_URL is required, must be the full URL https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (not the /api base), and OPENROUTER_API_KEY itself is not read (must be re-exported as PERCH_API_KEY, and it is not in the user's secret-guard list).

Prompt-injection/evasion: code under scan is untrusted state fed to Jev, and per the Jev evals injected instructions in state can move answers (e.g., a comment can suppress a finding), so a clean perch scan on hostile or client code is weak evidence; repo-defined rules (perch.yaml, .perch/rules) also shape the questions and any rule text surfaced in output goes back into the agent's context.

Bare fetch with no timeout in direct mode (systemone.js:34, also in 0.3.5), so a stalled connection blocks the tool call; 32-way concurrency at HEAD can also trip OpenRouter/TypeSafe 429s on the alpha endpoint (no SLA), which it handles by retrying 4 times with 2/4/8 s backoff.

Runtime dependency on GitHub releases for tree-sitter parsers (native/wasm code fetched at first use) plus ~4 MB unpacked bundle; scan reads git HEAD not the worktree, so uncommitted edits are only covered by `check`, and known open bug #218 means check findings on uncommitted code cannot be closed/deduped.
entries.verdict: The best-fitting Jev tool for actual daily coding found so far: a cheap, non-invasive skill and CLI that works with OpenRouter through two env vars and costs almost nothing in context. However, auto-invocation is only description-triggered, and for real automation you would need to add a small PostToolUse or pre-PR hook yourself. Use it as a complement (post-edit or pre-PR semantic lint) rather than as the whole integration, and only on repos where sending source to OpenRouter is acceptable.

verification.note: Repo stats and most source citations check out (systemone.js endpoint/headers/retry/no timeout, tokens.js limits, setup.js alwaysApply rationale, execFile-array git, .perch/.gitignore, key never in argv). Main faults: (1) audit conflates unreleased HEAD with published npm 0.3.5, which has no Perch Cloud and no rolling pool; Cloud arrives with open release PR #156; (2) misses the concrete key-egress trap (PERCH_API_KEY set without PERCH_BASE_URL sends the OpenRouter key to dash.perchscan.com after 0.4.0, or to api.typesafe.ai on 0.3.5); (3) understates the 32k OpenRouter context (confirmed via models API) vs Perch's 60k request budget; (4) misses issue #63 and PR #173 showing OpenRouter is not officially supported or tested and that a future OPENROUTER_API_KEY path would use a non-Jev chat model; (5) cost display will read 'price unknown' because OpenRouter's model id is prefixed typesafe/. OpenRouter compatibility is plausible by doc and code reading (request/response shapes match OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone) but unverified end to end; I did not run anything. Perch is a manually invoked semantic linter, not a general decision layer, and cannot deliver the user's 'automatic' requirement without a custom hook, and it ships client source to OpenRouter/TypeSafe. A useful complementary tool, but best category-leader claim holds only in the narrow 'real Jev consumer' sense; 5.5 rather than 6.5. Files: <scratch path> (spec.md, pkg/package/dist/cli.mjs).

entries.name: patdown (@patdown/claude)
entries.what: Fuzzy-lint CLI plus Claude Code plugin. Rules are markdown files (AGENTS.PATDOWN.md, optionally with rule packs). For every Write/Edit, a PreToolUse hook rebuilds the proposed file, then asks Jev one yes/no (noul) question per matching rule about the whole file. If P(yes) is above 0.85 it returns permissionDecision deny with the rule text. The same rules also lint a tree in the CLI and in a GitHub Action.
interface: PreToolUse hook Write|Edit (packages/patdown-claude/hooks/hooks.json, timeout 120s, internal deadline 90s)
entries.autoInvocation: Fully deterministic. The hook fires on every Write and Edit in any project with an AGENTS.PATDOWN.md, with no prompt needed. It works under bypassPermissions because PreToolUse denies still apply. This fits 'automatic', but it enforces per-repo written rules rather than using Jev for general judgment. The model never decides to invoke it, other than the optional run-patdown skill, which is model-invoked from its description.
security: License is 0BSD (LICENSE, package.json). GitHub reports it as 'other'.

Repo created 2026-09-18, last push 2026-09-24, 82 commits, 3 authors (about 62 tyler-dot-earth, 19 Tyler Nieman, 1 Mr Jev), v0.11.0 after 17 tagged releases in 3 days. Very young and fast-moving, with 15 stars and 2 forks. The plugin docs say 'Claude Code was not available when the first cut was written; validate with claude plugin validate' (docs/claude.md).
46 test files exist in the repo (the triage said 55). The Claude hook has only proposed-file.test.mjs. judge-write-edit.mjs has no visible test file, so the hook entrypoint itself is untested here.

API key is read from the env var via Effect Config.Redacted (typesafe-judge.ts:184) and never passed in argv. Error output is limited to machine identifiers, not response bodies (typesafe-judge.ts:79-181).

The hook uses no shell exec. It runs plain node, does process.chdir(cwd), and dynamically imports 'patdown', '@patdown/rules', 'effect' and '@effect/platform-node' resolved from the project's node_modules (judge-write-edit.mjs:102-134). It therefore runs whatever code the project's node_modules contains, which is a supply-chain and untrusted-repo execution surface. The docs also recommend pnpm add -D patdown in each project.

Prompt-injection surface: the whole proposed file content is sent as Jev state, and injected instructions there can move the answer, per the Jev brief. Because the decision is only a deny, injection can suppress a block but cannot cause code execution.
entries.dataEgress: For each Write or Edit, and for each rule whose globs match the file, one request goes to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/v1/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default, openrouter.ai/api if configured). It contains the FULL proposed file contents as `state`, the rule body as the question instructions, and the model name. The API key goes in the auth header. Files matching the .env, pem, id_rsa and credentials exclusion globs are skipped. For client projects this means every edited source file is sent to OpenRouter, and then to TypeSafe. That needs client consent and an NDA check. There is no local allowlist or opt-out except deleting AGENTS.PATDOWN.md, and the size cap is the model's token limit, not a patdown setting.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed. Any judge error (network, 401, 429, 5xx, max_tokens_exceeded, invalid response, the 90s internal timeout, or a missing package) is written as permissionDecision deny with 'patdown judge failed (not converted to a pass)' (judge-write-edit.mjs:229, timeout at 136-152). Only a missing AGENTS.PATDOWN.md is a quiet allow with a stderr line (judge-write-edit.mjs:224). Serious edge case: if `patdown` or `@patdown/rules` is not installed in the project, isMissingModuleMessage matches, the error is not the missing-rules message, and the hook DENIES every Write and Edit with an install hint (judge-write-edit.mjs:87-133, 208-229). A globally enabled plugin would therefore block edits in every project that lacks the devDependency, including client repos. Files whose diff exceeds about 97 KB (docs/jev-input-limits.md, HTTP 400 max_tokens_exceeded) are blocked, not skipped. Write and Edit are matched, but MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and Bash writes are not.
entries.contextCost: Near zero for tools: no MCP server. The plugin adds one skill (run-patdown, description about 190 chars, roughly 50 tokens) which uses a little of the 2 percent skill listing budget. Hooks inject no additionalContext. On a deny, the rule text is returned to the model (a few hundred tokens per violation). The context cost is in the rule denials, not in listings.
pros: Real deterministic automation: a PreToolUse Write|Edit hook fires with no prompting and still applies in auto and bypassPermissions modes, which is the closest of these candidates to the user's 'never say use jev' goal.

OpenRouter path needs no code change. The default TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + '/v1' + '/systemone' (typesafe-judge.ts:206-215; the test asserts /v1/systemone with the noul body) means setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus jev-1.13 should hit OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.

Good hygiene: the API key stays in env (Redacted), never argv. Provider error prose is never echoed. .env, pem and credential files are excluded. Path-escape checks exist. Yes/no cutoff (0.85) is configurable per rule.

Per-repo rules in AGENTS.PATDOWN.md and shipped packs (typescript, effect, anti-slop) suit client-specific conventions. The CLI `ask --stdin` is a handy general Jev primitive, for example on a git diff.

Also usable in CI through the composite GitHub Action. Zero MCP context cost. Licensed 0BSD. Active: 17 releases in 6 days, 46 test files, documented Jev input limits (docs/jev-input-limits.md) with real measurements.
cons: Very young (created 2026-09-18) and unproven. The plugin was written without Claude Code available ('validate before relying on it', docs/claude.md). The hook script has no test of its own, only proposed-file.test.mjs.

Fail-closed and dangerous when installed globally: in any project without `patdown` and `@patdown/rules` in node_modules, every Write and Edit is denied (judge-write-edit.mjs:87-133, 208-229). It requires pnpm add -D patdown in each project, which is invasive for client repos.

Sends full file contents of every edited file to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, a real confidentiality issue for client projects. Whole files are judged, not diffs, so large files hit the ~97 KB / 32k-token limit and are then blocked.

Latency and reliability tax on every edit: Node cold start plus Effect import plus a Jev call per matching rule, with a 90 s worst-case stall. Jev is /alpha with no SLA and is overconfident on unanswerable input, which gives false blocks and false passes and frustrates flow.

Only enforces user-written lint-style rules. It does not use Jev for Bash permission decisions, task routing or review, so it covers only part of the 'use Jev whenever it adds value' goal. Only Write|Edit are covered (no MultiEdit, NotebookEdit or Bash writes). Needs the TYPESAFE_API_KEY alias, so it cannot read OPENROUTER_API_KEY directly.
Depends on unreleased-style Effect 4.0.0-rc.116 and Node >=22.22.2 (Node 24 is fine). The package name @effect/ai-typesafe was not inspected, so its endpoint path and auth header are unconfirmed.
Repo metadata is thin: no topics and license shown as 'other' on GitHub, although the file is 0BSD.
entries.verdict: The most complete and best-documented deterministic Jev hook, and it is OpenRouter-ready through TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_API_KEY (the OpenRouter key) and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL=jev-1.13. It only enforces written per-repo style rules. It also fails closed, denying every Write and Edit in any project without patdown installed and on any Jev error or oversized file, and it sends whole files to a third party. Use it only per-project, opt-in, in personal repos that already contain AGENTS.PATDOWN.md and the patdown devDependency. It is a poor fit as a global auto-on hook, especially for client work.

judge.why: Cleanest per-repo rules design (AGENTS.PATDOWN.md, PreToolUse Write|Edit deny), but fail-closed and risky as a global install.
pros: Deterministic PreToolUse hook that applies under bypassPermissions; zero MCP context; key not in argv; excludes .env/pem/credentials
Also a CLI and GitHub Action; per-rule thresholds (0.85); `patdown ask` is a handy general Jev CLI
cons: Fail-closed: any Jev error, timeout (90s) or oversized file (~97KB) denies the edit, and a project without patdown installed denies every Write/Edit
Full file sent per matching rule; Node cold start plus Effect import on each edit (0.5-1.5s); the hook entrypoint has no test of its own
Runs code from the project's node_modules; docs admit it was written without Claude Code available

entries.name: doeixd/jev-pref
entries.what: Node CLI (npx jev-pref, MIT) that acts as a semantic "AI linter" over git diffs. The user defines checks in jev-pref.json (Noul conditions and Choice classifications, e.g. "does this change introduce shared mutable state?"). `review` collects the working, staged, PR or arbitrary diff, splits it per hunk or per file, sends state and questions to Jev via the `advocaat` SDK in one batched call, then maps P and confidence to approve/advisory/fix_now with exit codes 0/1/2. Also has `setup` and `sync` (agent-facing protocol text), `tune` (calibrates thresholds on labeled evals), `doctor`, `examples`, plus a GitHub Action for PR review. It is not an MCP server and not a hook. It ships one thin skill (skills/jev-pref/SKILL.md) that only says to run `npx jev-pref setup`. The integration intended for Claude Code is a paragraph the agent writes into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md telling itself to run `npx jev-pref review --hunks` after substantial implementation work.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only, via instructions in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (the "After a substantial bout of implementation work, run npx jev-pref review --hunks" snippet) plus a discovery-only skill trigger. There is no shipped Claude Code hook, MCP server or proxy. Automatic in the sense the user wants (never say "use jev") only works if the snippet exists in each project's CLAUDE.md (or the user's global ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md) and the model follows it, which is probabilistic. Deterministic automation would require the user to add a Claude Code Stop or PostToolUse hook that runs `jev-pref review --json` themselves, which the repo does not provide (it offers a git pre-commit example only).
security: API key is env-only by design (config.js:6-8, 308). It is never accepted via flags or files, so it does not appear in argv or the process list. That is good.

Data is sent to whatever JEV_BASE_URL points at (config.js:87). The config layers also accept baseUrl from jev-pref.json and jev-pref.local.json, and from a fenced ```jev-prefs block inside CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md (config.js:3, 116-140). A malicious or untrusted repo could therefore redirect diffs to another host. It could not steal the key from a file, but the Bearer key from the env would be sent to that host. This matters on client projects.

Repo-controlled command execution: `agent.command` in jev-pref.json (or the fenced block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) is run with execFile whenever the outcome matches agent.on (agent.js:55, config.js:389-403). No shell is used, but any cloned repo's config can run an arbitrary binary with the full diff on stdin. Never run this in untrusted repos.

Prompt-injection surface: diff and file contents go to Jev, which has no free text output and returns only probabilities, so injection can bias verdicts but cannot cause text-based hijack. However the `setup` and `sync` output is instruction text the agent obeys, and it is generated from repo content (AGENTS.md etc.). That is a mild surface.
No postinstall scripts. Runtime dependency is a single 260-line SDK (advocaat), which I read in full. It only does fetch to baseURL, with no telemetry and no filesystem or exec use.
No telemetry found in jev-pref src (no calls other than the Jev request, plus local git and `gh pr view`).
entries.dataEgress: Per Jev call the payload (review.js:395-430, git.js:133-204) contains: the config prefs (ids, questions, labels, guidance), git status, diff --stat, the branch name and scope, and the diff text. That text is the full tracked diff, split per hunk or file and capped at 20,000 chars per request (30k-token Jev input limit). Untracked files that are not gitignored (git ls-files --others --exclude-standard) are also read and sent in full, up to 100 files and 20k chars each. A `.env` that is not ignored, or scratch files, would be sent. Binary files are skipped. `--staged`, `--pr` and `--diff` scopes send the corresponding diffs. Nothing is sent from Claude Code conversation, prompts or tool outputs, only git state. Destination: api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if JEV_BASE_URL is set, in which case OpenRouter and TypeSafe both see client code. Supports a zeroDataRetention flag for the Vercel gateway only. Pricing is about $0.042/M input tokens, so a review costs fractions of a cent, but per-hunk mode can make up to 10 calls (maxHunks) per review.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by contract for the CLI: exit code 2 on config, infra or timeout failure, and the docs state that 'exit 2 is never approval'. Timeouts are 60 s per call (AbortSignal.timeout, jev.js:52), and 429/529 are retried up to 5 times with backoff 500ms doubling, capped at 30s (jev.js:26-28, 62-66). Worst-case stall is therefore roughly minutes per call. Other HTTP errors fail immediately. Because it is not a hook, nothing blocks Claude Code on its own: the agent just sees a failed command and, per the recommended CLAUDE.md snippet, treats it as 'not approval', and there is a 3-loop limit. If wired as a hook, fail-open versus fail-closed depends on the user's wrapper script, and the default `jev-pref review` exit codes would block in a Stop hook if used naively.
entries.contextCost: Near zero tools: 0 MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. Skill description is about 35 tokens, always listed. The CLAUDE.md snippet the agent writes is about 150-250 tokens permanently in context for that repo. `npx jev-pref setup` prints a very large protocol once during setup (setup.js is 517 lines, so roughly 5-8k tokens, one-time). Each `review` prints a short verdict, about 100-800 tokens depending on findings. No hook-injected text.
pros: Actually uses Jev's real primitives (Noul, Choice, and batched questions) for a well-scoped, well-fitting job: classifying diffs against project-defined semantic rules. This is what a System One model is good at, unlike chat-style uses.

Provider indirection is nearly complete in code: JEV_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL, JEV_API_KEY are all honored (config.js:86-88; jev.js:49-50), and the SDK posts to {base}/v1/systemone, the exact OpenRouter route, so pointing it at OpenRouter is likely env-only.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, tiny skill, one CLAUDE.md paragraph. Works with the user's existing hooks and MCP without conflict.
Sane security defaults for keys: env-only, never in argv; execFile without shell; no telemetry; one small dependency I read in full.

Machine-readable interface: --json output plus stable 0/1/2 exit codes, --dry-run to preview what would be sent, --raw for numbers, and `tune` to calibrate thresholds on labeled diffs. This is easy to wrap in a hook.
Cheap: about $0.042/M input tokens on OpenRouter, so a review of a 20k-char diff is a fraction of a cent.
Bounded input handling: 20k-char per-request budget, hunk/file splitting, and a pre-flight check against the 30k token limit, so calls do not fail on big diffs.
MIT licensed, has tests and passing CI, and a clearly documented boundary of what Jev should and should not judge (docs/principles.md).
cons: Not automatic. There is no hook, MCP server or proxy. Invocation relies on Claude following a CLAUDE.md sentence, so it is model-discretion and can be skipped, which conflicts with the user's stated 'Claude Code must use it when needed' goal unless the user writes their own Stop/PostToolUse hook wrapper.

OpenRouter support is undocumented and unverified: the string 'openrouter' appears nowhere in the repo, the README/`doctor`/`setup` all steer to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and `doctor` only recognizes JEV_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY and VERCEL_OIDC_TOKEN (doctor.js:34-39). It would need a live test with `JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api`.

It is a diff linter, not general assistance: value only appears where the user has authored good semantic rules (jev-pref.json) per project. On client projects that means writing and maintaining checks and modifying their repo or CLAUDE.md, which some clients will not want.

Data egress: full diffs plus non-ignored untracked files (up to 100 files, 20k chars each) leave the machine to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. That is a compliance question for client code, and there is no local secret redaction; even the secrets suite works by sending the diff to the model.

Repo-controlled behavior: baseUrl and agent.command can be set by files inside the reviewed repo (jev-pref.json, jev-pref.local.json, or a fenced block in CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md), giving a repo the ability to redirect the diff and the Bearer key or execute a binary. Unsafe to run automatically in untrusted client repos.

Very young and single-author: 12 days old, 46 commits in 2 days, 1 contributor, 11 stars, no pushes since 2026-09-18, tests mostly don't exercise the live client, and the tool is pinned to the 0.0.x SDK. High breaking-change risk in a beta-model ecosystem.
`npx` unpinned means running whatever is newest on npm each time (supply-chain exposure, plus multi-second cold-start latency). Pin the version or vendor it if used.

Calibration is unproven: the Jev model is beta and skeptics claim it resembles a small router model. Semantic-lint verdicts (P>=0.7 gating) may be noisy, and the tool's own docs admit thresholds need calibration on labeled diffs.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here that puts Jev to a job it suits (typed Noul/Choice judgments about code changes), and it is probably switchable to OpenRouter via JEV_BASE_URL plus JEV_MODEL plus JEV_API_KEY, though I did not test that live. It is not automatic on its own: the intended integration is a CLAUDE.md instruction, so the user would need to add a Stop/PostToolUse hook wrapper for deterministic use, and should pin the version and avoid running it in untrusted client repos because repo config can set the endpoint and execute a command.
