entries.name: TheBous/jev-flash-review (mirror of lucvalse/jev-flash-review)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also Codex/Cursor/OpenCode manifests) shipping one local stdio MCP tool, review_diff, plus 3 skills (review-pr, review-free, review-loop). The agent supplies a unified diff plus title/description/taskContext. The engine chunks the diff and asks the TypeSafe System One API about about 447 built-in rules across 19 JSON files. Each rule is a Choice question (YES/NO/N/A) sent in batches of 80 rules per call, per diff chunk, in parallel. Then a second Choice picks the evidence hunk, a third confirms it, and a fourth rates impact. Output is JSON with the full rule matrix, confirmed violations and a summary with a blockers count. It is a rule-based code-review gate, not a general decision helper. A Cloudflare Worker remote variant and a CLI (npm run review -- PR) also exist.
interface: MCP tool review_diff(diff, title?, description?, taskContext?)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion via skill description triggers only. There are no hooks, no proxy and no server instructions. review-loop's description ('Use when implementing a nontrivial change and the project's rule engine should gate it') is the only broad trigger. review-pr and review-free fire when the user asks for reviews. Whether Claude picks review-loop unprompted in daily work is not deterministic and cannot be relied on. Getting deterministic behavior would need a user-written Stop or PreToolUse hook or a CLAUDE.md rule, which the plugin does not provide.
security: API key is read from env by the SDK and sent only as a Bearer header over TLS. It is never placed in argv, and the stdio server takes no key arguments, so it is not visible in the process list. The SDK redacts the authorization header in debug logs (index.mjs:285-287).

No shell execution inside the engine (it never reads the repo or runs git). The skills do instruct the agent to run gh/git commands. `gh pr diff` for client PRs pulls the diff into the agent's context and out to the API.
No telemetry in the repo. The SDK sends User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers to the configured base URL.

Supply chain: private package with no published npm release. Building needs npm install of a large dev tree (wrangler, release-it, commitlint, husky with a `prepare` script, esbuild allowScripts). No curl|sh installer.

Prompt-injection surface: diff text and taskContext go into the typed-question state. Jev outputs only typed probabilities, so it cannot emit instructions. The tool result contains the rule question text and locations, all from static rules, so the injection risk to Claude is low. The bigger risk is a review-loop skill that pressures the agent to obey the engine's verdicts, including the 'rationalizations' table.
Remote Worker: a single static bearer token; POST-only; the Worker holds TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Not needed for local use.
entries.dataEgress: On every review_diff call, the full diff (all added and removed lines, chunked), title, description and taskContext are sent to the configured Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden). The same content is re-sent in each of the parallel calls: roughly 6 rule batches per chunk (447 rules / 80 per call), then the evidence, confirm and impact calls. Rule text is sent every time. Nothing is read from disk by the engine. The agent decides what goes in the diff, and the README asks the user to never send secrets, .env files or lockfiles. For client projects, this means client source diffs go to TypeSafe and, via OpenRouter, to OpenRouter as well. This is a privacy and contract risk. The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard only matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it does not inspect this MCP call.
entries.failureMode: There is no hook, so nothing blocks the session. Per-attempt timeout is 60 s (judge.ts:13) with the SDK default of 2 retries, so a hung API can stall one tool call for about 3 minutes plus backoff. Failures are all-or-nothing: engine.ts uses Promise.all and throws on any judge error or missing answer (engine.ts:38-43, 119), which the MCP SDK returns as an isError result. Effectively fail-open for Claude Code, since the session continues. The skills, however, say STOP and never do a manual review when the tool is missing, so Claude will halt the review workflow rather than degrade. The fan-out of parallel calls (chunks x 6 batches, plus evidence, confirm and impact) risks 429s or rate limits on OpenRouter. There is no client-side concurrency cap.
entries.contextCost: Low static cost, high per-call cost. Static: 1 MCP tool. The description is about 540 chars and the schema has 4 fields with descriptions (about 900 chars), so roughly 350-400 tokens. No server-level 'instructions'. The 3 skills add about 3 short descriptions (about 60 tokens each) to the skill list. Loading a skill body costs about 400-800 tokens. No hooks and no injected text. Dynamic: the tool returns JSON.stringify of the entire matrix, `results` for all 447 rules plus `violations`. Each entry carries rule_id, the question text, severity, answer, probability, confidence, evidence and impact, roughly 60-100 tokens each. That is an estimated 25-45k tokens returned into the main context per call (my estimate from the code; not run). review-loop repeats this every iteration, so it can burn 100k+ tokens quickly. A subagent would be needed to contain it.
pros: Genuinely integrates Jev's Choice primitive through the SDK: ('select instead of generate' evidence location, confidence gating at 0.55, confirm pass). This is the closest real example of Jev as a typed decision engine rather than a chat model.

Provider is configurable with zero code changes via the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL / TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL env vars (index.mjs:56-61), so OpenRouter routing is plausible: base https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model ID like typesafe/jev-1.13.
Only one MCP tool, so the always-on context cost is small (about 400 tokens) and there are no hooks to slow down your existing Grep|Glob|Bash hooks.
Engine never reads the repo, key never goes through argv, and the SDK redacts auth headers; the architecture is clean (Judge port, tests for engine and diff, CI running tsc and npm test).
Includes a Claude Code marketplace plus plugin manifest, skills and slash commands, so nothing needs writing to try it. Also has a Worker option if you want the key kept off the laptop.
cons: Wrong shape for the goal: it is an explicit code-review gate, not a background helper. Claude only calls it if the skill description matches or you ask; there is no hook, so 'automatic whenever useful' is not met.

Likely broken on a plain /plugin install: .mcp.json runs dist/server.js, but dist/ is gitignored and not in the repo. You must npm install and npm run bundle in the plugin cache (executes third-party build scripts, incl. husky prepare), and re-run after every update.

Heavy result payload: the tool returns the full 447-rule matrix as JSON, an estimated 25-45k tokens per call into Opus's context, and review-loop re-runs it each iteration. This is a big cost for daily use.

Sends whole diffs plus taskContext to TypeSafe/OpenRouter several times over per review. For client projects this is a data-handling and NDA problem, and your secret-guard hook does not cover MCP tool calls.

Very immature and low-trust: 1 star, 1 author (lucvalse), 37 commits over 2 days, last push 2026-09-19, no release, no LICENSE file (plugin.json claims MIT). The repo is owned by TheBous while the docs point to lucvalse, so the provenance is confusing.

Rule set is opinionated and huge (447 rules over 19 files, a mix of security, ai-generated-code and others). Expect noise for personal projects and a rule-tuning burden. The confidence thresholds (0.55, 0.1 margin) are admitted guesses ('tune from field data, not theory').

Failure handling is all-or-nothing (Promise.all), with 60 s x 3 attempts and no concurrency cap, so a Jev hiccup or OpenRouter 429 can hang or fail a whole review. The skills forbid falling back to manual review, so Claude stalls instead of degrading.
The Worker variant hardcodes the TypeSafe key path and has no base URL passthrough, so OpenRouter would need a patch there.
entries.verdict: A real, sensibly built Jev integration, but a niche rule-based review gate rather than an always-on assistant. It is opt-in by skill description, ships unbuilt, dumps a huge JSON into context, and sends full diffs out. Worth trying only as an optional pre-merge review on personal repos (with OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). Do not treat it as the main automatic Jev integration, and keep client code out of it.
entries.license: Ambiguous: GitHub reports no license (licenseInfo null) and there is no LICENSE file in the repo root. plugin.json and .claude-plugin/plugin.json declare MIT. The vendored .agents/skills/typesafe-ai has its own LICENSE.

entries.name: jev-debtgate
entries.what: Tech-debt gate for agents and CI. Local code (git diff plus ast-grep AST pass) collects metrics, sends a compact "state" (stats, file list, static-analysis findings, up to 12,000 chars of raw diff) plus fixed Jev typed question packs (choice/noul/score) to the TypeSafe System One endpoint, then a local policy turns per-option probabilities into allow/review/block, a confidence floor and a suggested model tier. Exposes 3 MCP tools over stdio, a CLI (diff/gate/file/init/doctor), a GitHub Action, and an agent skill pack written for Cursor (.cursor/skills).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool (tool descriptions tell Claude to call before finishing a refactor / when tests turn green) plus an optional skill description trigger (only if SKILL.md is manually copied to ~/.claude/skills, since init targets .cursor/). No hooks are shipped; nothing is deterministic. Could be made deterministic by the user adding a Stop/PostToolUse hook that runs the CLI 'jev-debtgate diff --json --fail-open', but that is DIY.
security: API key read from env var TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (or a cwd .env parsed by hand in src/env.ts:61-84); placed in Authorization header, not argv. If configured through .mcp.json env block it stays out of process argv (README pattern uses npx -y jev-debtgate mcp, key in env). Note the .mcp.json.example ships a literal empty key field, tempting people to paste the key into a project file.

src/env.ts loadDotEnv() reads .env from the project cwd on every requireApiKey()/MCP start and injects ALL vars into the MCP process env (not sent anywhere, but reads project secrets file into a third-party process); real key lookups fall back to a repo .env, which mixes per-client keys.
TYPESAFE_URL env var redirects the Bearer key to any URL (src/jev.ts:20), acceptable since env is user-controlled.

Shell execution is limited to execFileSync('git', argsArray) with no shell (src/collect/git.ts:23), no injection via strings; but base ref arg comes from the model and is passed as a git arg (could be option-like, low risk).
No telemetry code found; only network call is the single fetch in src/jev.ts:29.

No postinstall; package has a 'prepare' script (tsc build only) that runs on git installs, not on registry install; npm tarball ships prebuilt dist/. Deps include native @ast-grep/napi + 12 lang grammars (large native supply chain surface) and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk, zod.
entries.dataEgress: On each tool call: the git diff against base truncated to 12,000 chars (src/collect/git.ts:140-154 diff_excerpt: truncate(diff,12000)), git --stat truncated to 4,000 chars, the list of changed files with add/remove counts, static-analysis findings (skipped tests, empty catches, SQL concat, type escapes, timeouts with code snippets), repo basename, base ref. For debt_assess_file: file path, LOC, function names/sizes, import buckets, sibling counts, 90-day churn (README claims 'the full repository is not uploaded'). Sent to api.typesafe.ai by default or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_URL is redirected. Includes any secrets present in changed lines because the diff is not scrubbed; the user's PreToolUse secret guard does not cover MCP tool egress. Client-project code leaves the machine, which needs contract clearance.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by default at the tool level, but harmless: with failOpen false (default, src/config.ts:36-39; MCP reads it from .debtgate.json or DEBTGATE_FAIL_OPEN env) any Jev error throws (src/assess.ts:25) and the MCP tool returns an error to Claude, which can simply continue. With DEBTGATE_FAIL_OPEN=1 it returns verdict review with confidence_floor 0 and fail_open:true (assess.ts:26-37). HTTP behavior in src/jev.ts: retries only 429/529, up to 4 attempts with 400/800/1600/3200 ms backoff (~6 s of sleeps) ; NO fetch timeout or AbortSignal, so a hung connection would stall the tool call until the undici default (~5 min headers timeout) or Claude Code MCP tool timeout. Other non-2xx errors throw immediately; no retry on network errors. Empty diff short-circuits with allow without calling Jev.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Names + descriptions + input schemas (zod with cwd/base/collect_only/file describe strings) about 1,500-1,800 chars, roughly 400-450 tokens. No server 'instructions' field (src/mcp.ts:126-129 only name/version). No hooks. Optional SKILL.md adds about 60-80 tokens of description in the always-loaded list, body 1.4k chars only when triggered. Tool results are pretty-printed JSON (JSON.stringify(data,null,2)) of full report incl. all answers with probabilities, metrics and reasons, maybe 1-3k tokens per call. Very light overall.
pros: Genuinely uses the Jev typed primitives (choice/noul/score) with well-designed fixed question packs in src/packs.ts (direction, debt_kind, is_workaround, severity, safe_to_auto_merge, model_tier, needs_human): an actual Jev use case, unlike a generic wrapper.
Policy operates on calibrated probabilities and a confidence floor, not argmax (src/policy.ts, 255-line policy.test.ts), which fits how Jev is meant to be used.

Most work is local and deterministic (git + ast-grep AST metrics); the empty diff short-circuits without any API call, so cost is near zero (about $0.042/M input tokens, roughly 3-5k tokens per call).
Small, readable code (about 1.2k lines of src), MIT, fail-open mode, shadow mode, collect_only flag to dry-run without egress.
Speaks the exact OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone request/response shape (checked against OpenRouter's OpenAPI), so OpenRouter works by env vars TYPESAFE_URL + key only.
Very small context footprint: 3 tools, about 450 tokens, no server instructions, no hooks.
The 'workaround gate' (timeout bumped, test skipped, empty catch, sleep added to turn tests green) targets a real agent failure mode.
cons: Narrow purpose: only technical-debt review of diffs/files. It does not help with the bulk of daily coding decisions (routing, triage, permission decisions, commit/PR classification), so it is a niche add-on, not the integration backbone.

Not automatic: relies on Claude honoring tool descriptions; no hook; the skill is installed to .cursor/skills by init, not for Claude Code. User explicitly wants no manual prompting, so this only partially meets the requirement unless wrapped in a custom Stop hook.
Ships no OpenRouter support or docs: default hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and key variable is TYPESAFE_API_KEY; must repurpose env vars (works per spec but untested).
Sends up to 12k chars of raw diff to a third party on every call, unscrubbed; problematic for client repos and the user's secret-leak-guard doesn't cover MCP egress.
No fetch timeout/AbortSignal (src/jev.ts:29), no retry on network errors; a stalled request can block the tool call for minutes. Backoff sleeps up to ~6 s on 429.

Immature: 5 commits in one day (2026-09-21), 1 contributor, 1 star, no GitHub release, no CI workflow in the repo, only a 0.3.0 npm publish; the default `npx -y` unpinned install executes new versions from a solo author with native deps.
Reads project .env files into its process (src/env.ts), mixing client secrets into a third-party process.

Advisory value depends on Jev quality, which is unproven on code-quality judgments (skeptics call Jev a router-like model); the question packs are the author's own opinions with no eval data in the repo.
Unit tests cover policy/config/collect only; no test of jev.ts HTTP path or MCP protocol (mcp-smoke.mjs script exists but is not part of npm test).
entries.verdict: A tidy, well-scoped PoC that really uses Jev's typed primitives, and it can run against OpenRouter through env vars alone, but it is a narrow tech-debt reviewer that fires only at model discretion and ships raw diff excerpts off-machine. Worth trying at most as an opt-in extra on personal repos (pinned version, DEBTGATE_FAIL_OPEN=1), not as the core auto-integration.

entries.name: @itsoltech/jev-code-review
entries.what: A pull-request reviewer built on Jev, shipped as a GitHub Action (dist/index.js) and an npm CLI (`jev-review`, dist/cli.js). Each rule in a YAML config is one narrow Choice, Noul or Score question. Every changed hunk is sent to Jev as a numbered-line state. Plain code, not the model, turns the probabilities into findings, a composite score and a verdict. Comments come from templates and are never generated. The CLI reviews the local branch, staged changes, a stdin diff or a GitHub PR, and prints text, markdown, json or SARIF. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill.
interface: Presets jev:recommended, security, correctness, code-slop, maintainability, tests, and others
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or wired by the user. The package has no hooks, MCP server or skill of its own. Automatic use would need a custom PreToolUse hook matching `git commit` / `gh pr create` that runs `jev-review --staged --format json`, which the README hints at with 'for a pre-commit hook' but does not ship.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or .env, never from argv, so it does not show in the process list; CLI has no --api-key flag.
Auto-reads .env in cwd when TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset (src/cli/main.ts:144), which is a mild surprise in client repos.
SDK log level is forced to 'warn' so request bodies (the diff) are not logged even with TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug (jevPort.ts).
Config is loaded from the PR base commit, so a PR cannot relax its own rules. A built-in jev:base prompt-injection guard is included.
Comments are template-generated, so diff text cannot inject free-form output into PR comments. Jev returns typed probabilities, so the model-output injection surface is small.
The package.json postinstall script and telemetry: I found none in package.json; no analytics or sentry strings in dist/cli.js.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points at): the review-rule question text, the PR title and description (or oldest commit subject and commit messages), the config's project_notes, and the numbered diff lines of each changed hunk with file paths. Diffs only, not whole files, and not Claude Code prompts, transcripts or tool outputs. With --pr it also calls the GitHub API using gh's token. Excluded and binary files are skipped. Client code diffs would go to the Jev provider, and to OpenRouter and its upstream if routed there.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default. policy.on_error defaults to 'neutral' (src/config/schema.ts:266), so Jev or GitHub failures give a neutral result. Setting on_error: fail makes exit code 1. SDK per-request timeout is set from budget.request_timeout_seconds (default 30 s), with retries on 408, 429 and 5xx (maxRetries 3 in jevPort.ts, backoff 500 ms to 5 s, Retry-After honoured up to 60 s). Timed-out or too-large requests are split in two. The run has a 600 s budget (run_timeout_seconds) and a token budget; skipped work is reported in the summary. A CLI wrapper would still need its own hook timeout.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-schema tokens, because it is a CLI. No hooks or server instructions. Cost appears only if you add a hook or skill; the JSON or text output (findings list) would then be injected into context, plausibly 200 to 2000 tokens per review depending on findings. A skill description would add about 50 to 100 tokens.
pros: Real, working Jev integration: the SDK call is `client.systemOne` on POST /v1/systemone with typed Noul/Choice/Score questions (src/jev/jevPort.ts, dist/cli.js:29332). It is the most complete example found of using Jev the way it was designed.
Code-side policy, thresholds and needs_human_band: findings are deterministic, calibrated by the code, and comments are templated, so there is no hallucinated review text.
OpenRouter can very likely be used with no code change, via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and a Bearer key, since the SDK reads the base URL from env and OpenRouter serves /v1/systemone under /api.
CLI mode gives a natural Claude Code hook target: --staged, --diff - and --format json/sarif, with clear exit codes (0, 1, 2) and no writes without --post.
API key stays out of argv and logs; SDK debug logging (which would log the diff) is force-disabled.
Fail-open by default (on_error neutral), so an outage does not block commits. Good retry, backoff, splitting and budget handling.
Zero context cost, with no MCP tool definitions or server instructions.
MIT licence, CI-checked builds, semantic-release with OIDC npm publishing, and substantial calibration datasets under eval/ that show the rules were actually measured.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin.json. Automatic use needs custom glue, and this is a rule-based PR linter rather than a general coding aid.
Very young and tiny: created 2026-09-23, 13 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 4 npm versions in 1 day, all from one author; the API is likely to change.

TypeSafe-first: OpenRouter is not mentioned anywhere in the source, docs or defaults. The default model is jev-latest, the README uses jev-1.13.0, and OpenRouter wants typesafe/jev-1.13; the env-var trick is untested.
Env var naming is misleading: an OpenRouter key must be put in TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It also auto-loads .env from the current directory.
It sends client diffs, PR text and file paths to a beta third-party model via OpenRouter; there is no consent or allowlist layer, and the secret-leak guard hook does not cover this path.
Latency is batch-like (per-hunk requests, seconds to minutes), so it only fits commit or PR-time checks and not the interactive loop.

The value is mostly in GitHub Action / PR-review use; for a local Claude Code session it overlaps with Claude's own code-review, which is stronger on free-form reasoning, so Jev adds a cheap second opinion at best.
The committed dist/cli.js is a 2.2 MB bundle; npx runs it unreviewed, and I did not run it (static audit only).
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration, but the best-engineered real-world Jev consumer found: a CLI reviewer that could sit behind a custom pre-commit or pre-PR hook and probably works on OpenRouter with only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY set. It is too young and PR-review-specific to be the core integration, so use it at most as an optional commit-time gate after testing the OpenRouter route.

entries.name: Indosaram/typesafe-judge
entries.what: Rust CLI (choice, noul, score, diff, eval) returning raw Jev wire JSON, with a git-diff gate for pre-commit/CI (exit 0/1) and a typesafe-ai agent skill/plugin.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger / manual CLI or git hook
pros: Diff gate gives a scriptable pre-commit/CI check with exit codes
Single Rust binary usable by any agent through Bash, no MCP context cost
Retry with backoff on 429/529
cons: DEFAULT_API_URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, no OpenRouter path visible
Requires cargo build; no license, no tests dir, 1 star, single-day repo
Not automatic: agent must decide to call it

entries.name: russfranky/jev-crawlers
entries.what: Unix-pipe bug-discovery tools (seed, expand, judge, verify, report, crawl): follow leads through callers/config and judge each node with Jev typed verdicts; jev-verify checks cited file:line grounding.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CLI; could be wrapped as skill/MCP)
pros: Usable on any repo from Bash; grounded verifier fails closed on fabricated citations
Costed and labeled evals with recorded results; redaction and never reads .env
cons: Uses Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY) rather than OpenRouter; requires porting lib/jev.mjs
Not automatic; 1 star, 6 days old, precision unproven

entries.name: @amtec-advisory/repo-audit
entries.what: npm CLI (repo-audit) that sends changed code hunks plus plain-English rule questions to Jev (Noul/Choice/Score) and converts scores into lint-like findings, a Read-first risk ranking and a behavior search (find). "repo-audit live init" writes a PostToolUse hook (matcher Edit|Write|MultiEdit|apply_patch) into ~/.claude/settings.json that re-reviews each agent edit and returns decision:block with findings to Claude, plus SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks that start a detached background file watcher. Also ships an Agent Skill, a Claude Code stop-hook example and a GitHub Action.
interface: repo-audit live hook / live ensure / live status
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit|apply_patch fires automatically after every Claude edit with no prompting; SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit hooks keep a background watcher alive. This is the only candidate style that satisfies 'automatic without asking'. Optional skill is description-triggered.
security: API key stored owner-only via `auth login` hidden prompt; explicitly never accepted via argv (bin.js auth help text) so no process-list leak

No postinstall script in package.json; no curl|sh installer; but `repo-audit init` optionally runs `npx skills add Amtec-Advisory/repo-audit --skill repo-audit-cli -y` (bin.js:3480,3715) fetching remote code/skill from an unverifiable repo
Modifies ~/.claude/settings.json (user-global) to add PostToolUse, SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit hooks; reversible by rerunning setup, but coexists with the user's secret-guard/GitNexus hooks
Spawns a detached background watcher process per git worktree (bin.js:3810-3822), idles out after 30 minutes; spawns git, gh, claude/codex CLIs

Optional REPO_AUDIT_REPORT_URL POSTs repo slug, rule ids and levels (not code) with the user's GITHUB_TOKEN/GH_TOKEN or `gh auth token` as Bearer to that URL (bin.js:3747-3762); opt-in env var only, but a token-forwarding path to be aware of

Depends on ai/@ai-sdk/gateway/@vercel/oidc, so pulls Vercel AI Gateway auth paths; single npm maintainer (benjisaddik), org account created recently, source repo not public so dist cannot be diffed against source
entries.dataEgress: Selected source: changed hunks (diff windows up to about 6000 chars, request cap 80k chars, 8k-token reference files) plus rule questions and sibling/reference file content go to the provider (Vercel AI Gateway or api.typesafe.ai) on every agent edit, and again for the background watcher on any editor/script edit. That is real client code leaving the machine on each file save. README states this ('Selected source and questions go to your provider'). Vercel gateway path offers zeroDataRetention flag; direct TypeSafe path has none. Nothing goes to OpenRouter. Optional report URL gets only rule ids/levels plus a GitHub token.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design for hooks: live hook wraps everything in try/catch and returns nothing on error (bin.js:4235-4248); runLiveCheck child spawn has a 30s timeout and returns null on error/status 2/no stdout; hook timeout 30s in settings, SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit ensure hooks 5s. If a check is incomplete (provider failure, budget) it returns null and does not block. Direct client: 45s abort, 3 attempts with exponential backoff on 429/5xx; gateway client: 240s abort, 5 retries (worst case far exceeds the 30s hook timeout, which kills it). Slow Jev therefore costs up to 30s per edit before failing open.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. Hook-injected text only when a finding fires: decision:block reason with formatLiveReason (rule ids, locations, scores), likely a few hundred tokens per hit, and a block causes Claude to take an extra turn. Optional repo-audit-cli skill adds one skill description line (about 50-100 tokens). Very light on context.
pros: Only candidate here that is a real deterministic hook: PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit fires without the user ever saying 'use jev', exactly the requested automatic behavior
Fail-open everywhere in the live path (try/catch, 30s hook timeout, null on incomplete), so an outage will not wedge Claude Code
Uses Jev for what it is good at: typed yes/no and scored questions about a diff (swallowed errors, weakened tests, stale async) with thresholds, not free-text
Zero MCP tools and no server instructions, so context cost is near zero until a finding fires
Key never accepted via argv, stored owner-only; no postinstall or curl|sh; MIT; has `--dry-run` style preview and a `doctor` command; PR mode reads policy from base commit
Can run with either Vercel AI Gateway (zeroDataRetention) or TypeSafe direct, with retry/backoff and a run budget (maxHunks, maxRequests, timeoutSeconds)
cons: No OpenRouter support at all (zero references); providers are Vercel AI Gateway or api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone only, base URL hardcoded and not env-overridable, so the user's stated OpenRouter-hosted Jev goal is not met without patching bundled dist or a rewriting proxy

Source repo is not public (github.com/Amtec-Advisory/repo-audit returns 404 for gh and API; org shows only pdf-inspector), 0 visible commits/CI/tests, single npm maintainer, 9 days old (first publish 2026-09-21): cannot audit source, only minified dist; skill and example hook files referenced by README are not in the tarball

Ships changed client code to a third party on every agent edit and again via a file watcher for non-agent edits: a real client-confidentiality issue on client projects, and the watcher runs for any edit in the worktree

Installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json and adds a hook to every session (SessionStart and UserPromptSubmit spawn node each prompt) alongside the user's existing secret guard and GitNexus hooks; also `init` runs `npx skills add Amtec-Advisory/repo-audit -y`

decision:block after each edit forces Claude into extra turns on any finding, which with a screener of unknown precision (README admits 'not an accuracy benchmark' and Theo-style skepticism about Jev) can create noisy loops; adds 1-5 s and up to 30 s synchronous latency per edit
Live hook shells out `check` in a subprocess per edit, so per-edit cost is Node startup + git + several Jev calls; heavy in bypass/auto mode with rapid multi-file edits
Optional REPORT_URL forwards a GitHub token from env or `gh auth token`; low risk since opt-in, but a token-forwarding path exists
entries.verdict: Architecturally the right shape (deterministic PostToolUse hook, fail-open, zero context cost) and the only one of its kind, but it cannot use OpenRouter, has no public source, is days old, and streams client code to a third party on every edit. Treat it as a design reference or a personal-projects-only experiment via TypeSafe direct; do not adopt for client work, and prefer a small in-house hook that POSTs a Jev Noul/Choice question to OpenRouter.

entries.name: mizchi/jev-lint
entries.what: Node 24 CLI (npm jev-lint 0.7.0), a natural-language linter. ast-grep matchers pick code (functions, comments, tests, catch blocks, shell scripts, AGENTS.md, commit diffs). About 100 shipped rules each ask Jev one sentence as a score, noul or choice question, and matches above a per-rule cutoff are printed as findings. It also ships as a Claude Code plugin with 1 skill plus 4 slash commands (/jev-lint:review, commits, prose, new-rule), and it can write optional git pre-commit and pre-push hooks. It has no MCP server and no Claude Code hooks. Claude uses it only when the skill description matches or the user runs a slash command. It is a whole-file or diff review tool, not something that helps while Claude writes code.
interface: skill jev-lint (skills/jev-lint/SKILL.md, description about 700 chars, body about 10.5 KB)
entries.autoInvocation: Skill-description trigger only. It fires when the user or code mentions jev-lint or .jev-lint.yaml, and, per the description, on 'any request to check code for something a conventional linter cannot decide'. It is NOT triggered by Claude editing code. The slash commands are manual. The only deterministic automatic path is the git pre-commit or pre-push hook, which fires when any tool (including Claude's Bash git commit) commits. That is a git hook, not a Claude Code hook, and it would cover Claude-made commits.
security: API key is read only from env (src/jev.ts:36) and sent in an Authorization header (src/jev.ts:361-366), so it is never in argv. A literal apiKey in the config file is a hard error (config.ts:160).

Runs `npx -y jev-lint` (unpinned fetch of the latest npm version) in the slash commands and in the git hooks docs. That is a supply-chain surface on every hook run. The author's own hook uses the checked-out CLI instead.
No postinstall or preinstall scripts in package.json. No telemetry found in src/ (grep). Shell execution is limited to execFile of git and ast-grep with argument arrays, with no shell string.
The verdict cache .jev-lint/baseline.json is trusted input, and the docs say so: anything that can edit it can silence a rule.

Prompt-injection surface: the code, comments and commit messages being judged are sent to the model, and it returns only numbers. So a comment cannot inject text into Claude from Jev. The slash commands do make Claude read the findings and open code, which is normal.

The `baseUrl` config key can redirect all source to another host. A malicious repo .jev-lint.yaml could set baseUrl to exfiltrate code to an attacker host whenever the user's key env var is present; the key is sent as a Bearer token to that host. This matters for client repos (check with --base-url and the config before running).
entries.dataEgress: Full source text of each judged file (state.source, enclosing_code, symbols, imports, module identity), related test excerpts, the git diff and stat plus commit message for commits mode, the full AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md text, and rule-declared context documents. Each request goes to the configured base URL (default api.typesafe.ai) as {model,state,questions}. Nothing is sent from Claude's own prompts, tool outputs or conversation, because it is not a proxy. It sends whole files, so `check src` on a client repo ships the entire codebase to a third party. Suppression comments (jev-lint-ignore-file) skip sending. There is no built-in secret redaction, and .env files could be sent if included in files:.
entries.failureMode: The CLI is fail-open for hooks. It retries 5xx or network errors 4 times with backoff, uses a 60 s per-request timeout (src/jev.ts timeoutMs=60_000) and retries 429 separately. On failure it exits 3 (requests failed), and the shipped git hooks deliberately let exit 3 through, and also exit 0 when no key is set. In the slash commands, Claude just reports the failure. The whole-run wall time can be long: about 5 s for 2,300 subjects with 32 in flight, per docs/cost.md. Because it is not in Claude's tool loop, a Jev outage never blocks Claude.
entries.contextCost: Very low. There is no MCP server, so 0 tool definitions. The skill adds about 700 chars of description (roughly 175 tokens) to the always-on skill list. The body is about 10.5 KB, roughly 2.6k tokens, and loads only when triggered. The plugin also registers 4 slash commands with a short description each (about 100 tokens in total). No hook-injected text.
pros: Uses Jev exactly as designed: typed score/noul questions with calibrated cutoffs, so it exercises the primitive well and Jev's cheap latency ($0.042/M input; a full 2.3k-subject self-lint cost $0.09).

Base URL and model are already overridable via env or config (src/jev.ts:269-270, config.ts:236-246), so pointing at OpenRouter's /v1/systemone should need only TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_LINT_MODEL and apiKeyEnv, with no fork.
Ships a real Claude Code plugin (plugin.json and marketplace.json valid) with a skill and slash commands, so install is two /plugin commands.

The git pre-commit hook is the one truly automatic path: it triggers on Claude's own `git commit` without any prompt to Claude, reviews staged lines only (a fraction of a cent) and judges the staged diff against the repo's AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md.

Careful failure design: hooks fail open (skip on no key, tolerate exit 3), never block by default (no shipped rule has severity error), verdict cache and --retry to tame noise, and --dry-run prices a run without any request.
Key never in argv or config file; no postinstall or telemetry; CI uses SHA-pinned actions and a keyless replay test; 36 test files; MIT.
Catches real AI-coding failure modes that tsc/eslint miss: stale comments, names that overclaim, tests that do not test what they claim, and a diff violating CLAUDE.md.
cons: Not an automatic in-session integration. No MCP tool and no Claude Code hooks (PostToolUse/Stop) ship, so Claude will not call Jev while coding. The skill only triggers when jev-lint is mentioned or the user asks to 'check code for something a linter cannot decide', which contradicts the requirement to never prompt.

It is a batch reviewer of whole files and diffs, not a decision-helper Claude can consult mid-task (routing, classification, yes/no gates). Only a fraction of Jev's Choice/Noul/Score value is exposed, and only through fixed rules.
Author-measured precision is about 80% (one finding in five wrong) and scores near cutoffs move by hundredths between runs. A noisy reviewer in an all-day bypass-mode workflow adds triage work.

Sends whole source files and diffs (and CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md) to a third party; on client projects this is a real confidentiality question, and no redaction exists. A hostile repo .jev-lint.yaml can set baseUrl to redirect code and the Bearer key.
Slash commands and docs use `npx -y jev-lint` (unpinned latest) and Node 24 with an ast-grep binary; every run resolves a fresh package, a supply-chain and startup-latency cost.
OpenRouter path is undocumented and untested by the author (no 'openrouter' in src). Model id 'jev-latest' must be overridden. The response schema match is unverified from code.
Very new (11 days old, 209/237 commits by one author, releases page stale at v0.2.1 vs 0.7.0). API and rules are churning (threshold migration, rules by language in a week).
Rules are code-quality oriented (naming, comments, tests, prose, shell), useful in review but only a small slice of daily coding.
entries.verdict: A well-built, low-context Jev linter that could be pointed at OpenRouter with three env settings. But it is not an automatic Claude Code integration: it is a skill plus manual slash commands, and only a git pre-commit hook fires on its own. Use it at most as an optional commit-time reviewer on personal repos, and weigh the code-egress risk before enabling it on client projects. It does not meet the goal of Claude using Jev by itself when useful.

entries.name: mizchi/jev-test-filter
entries.what: Node 24 CLI (npm bin jev-test-filter, v0.1.3) plus a Claude Code plugin (skill and /filter-tests command). It reads the git diff, discovers tests with ast-grep (vitest, jest, node:test, bun, Playwright, cargo, go), and sends the whole diff as one Jev "state" with one Score question per test to POST {base}/v1/systemone. It gates the returned scores (cutoff 2.0, unsure band, touched tests always selected) and emits or execs the runner's own filter args. Any failure falls back to running everything.
interface: CLI jev-test-filter [--base REF|--staged] [--format vitest|jest|node|bun|playwright|rust|go] [--exec -- CMD...] [--json] [--dry-run] [--cutoff N] [--unsure-below N] [--unsure-margin N] [--context FILE] [--replay FILE] [--verify-snapshots]
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger only: Claude loads SKILL.md when the description matches ('only run affected tests', 'which tests does this PR need') or the user runs /filter-tests. There are no hooks and no proxy, so nothing runs deterministically. Without a wrapper (e.g. a PreToolUse hook rewriting `vitest run`, which the repo does not provide), Claude will not use it on its own for every test run. The skill also does not install the CLI. Claude would call `npx jev-test-filter`, which downloads and runs npm code at runtime.
security: No MCP server, no hooks, and no postinstall or curl|sh installers. package.json has only build, typecheck, test and prepack scripts.
API key comes from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and goes only in the Authorization: Bearer header (src/jev.ts:382). Not in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
Third-party code is spawned only through execFile/spawn with argv arrays (git, cargo, go, and the user's --exec command). No shell is involved, so there is little command-injection surface.

The full unified git diff is sent to a third party, including any secrets or client code in the changed lines. The runtime code has no redaction. secretlint appears only as a devDependency and pre-push hook for the repo itself, and test code has an onRequest leak assertion (src/jev.ts:105). This matters for client projects.

Prompt-injection surface: diff text is sent to Jev, but Jev returns only typed scores, so injected text in a diff cannot drive tool calls. It could at worst sway the scores and deselect a test. Test names and files are also embedded in questions.
Writes .jev-test-filter/*.json into the repo (untracked noise unless gitignored). Records contain test names and answers, not the diff.
entries.dataEgress: The whole `git diff` (working tree vs HEAD, or vs --base), capped at 96k chars (src/state.ts), plus `git diff --stat` and the changed file list. Each test's file path, title path and line range go into the questions (src/questions.ts). Test bodies and unchanged files are not sent, but any file whose lines are in the diff is sent with context. The destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL says (OpenRouter if you set it, so OpenRouter also sees it). Nothing leaves the machine unless the tool is invoked. Chat prompts and other tool outputs never leave.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: no API key, a Jev error, a missing answer, no tests found, or a diff too large all fall back to "run everything", with the reason on stderr and in the result (src/run.ts:186-232, 257-266). Request timeout is 60 s (src/jev.ts:286), with 4 retries for network/5xx using exponential backoff up to 20 s, and up to 8 retries on 429. A worst-case outage could therefore stall for minutes before falling back, but the fallback is safe. The one fail-closed case is exit 1 on a repo with more than one framework and no --format. Selection is nondeterministic near the cutoff. The truncated-diff guard forces a full run when less than 50% is selected.
entries.contextCost: Tiny: no MCP tools and no hook-injected text. The plugin adds one skill whose frontmatter description is about 1,000 chars (about 250 tokens), plus /filter-tests (about 60 tokens of description). The SKILL.md body (about 6 KB, about 1.5k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's real strength: a typed Score primitive, one state plus N questions in one round trip, with per-test calibrated confidence. It is the most idiomatic Jev use case found (src/questions.ts).
Endpoint and key are env-configurable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_TEST_FILTER_MODEL), so pointing at OpenRouter needs no code change, if OpenRouter's System One schema matches.

Robust fail-open: every error runs the full suite. A wrong selection is the only real risk, and the tool guards against it (touched tests always chosen, unsure band, dynamic titles always chosen, truncated-diff guard).
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, one skill description of about 250 tokens. No hook overhead on the existing Bash/Grep hooks.
Does not use a shell (spawn/execFile with argv) and passes the key in a header, not argv. No postinstall scripts and no telemetry.
Broad runner support (vitest, jest, node, bun, Playwright, cargo, go) and offline --replay for tuning without paying again.
MIT license, readable code, a substantial test suite.
cons: Not automatic. Autonomy is only through a skill description, at the model's discretion. Claude will normally just run `npm test`. There is no hook that rewrites test commands, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic use without prompting.

Narrow use case: test selection only. It does not help with general coding, review, routing or planning. Its value depends on slow suites (Playwright, integration tests); for fast unit suites the author himself says the overhead can exceed the saving.

Sends the full working-tree diff to Jev or OpenRouter with no redaction. That conflicts with client-project confidentiality and the user's secret-leak-guard posture. The user's PreToolUse guard would not see this network egress, since it happens inside the CLI.

TypeSafe-only in code and docs. The SKILL.md and /filter-tests command insist on TYPESAFE_API_KEY, and the command stops if it is unset. OpenRouter use would be a hack (a TYPESAFE_* var holding an OpenRouter key), and the schema match with /api/v1/systemone was not confirmed.
Very young and single-author (58 of 59 commits by mizchi, created 2026-09-21, v0.1.3). It has no CI, no releases and 31 stars. It is alpha quality and the behaviour will churn with Jev's beta API.
Selection is nondeterministic near the cutoff, and a wrong deselection can hide a regression. The skill itself says never to use it as a merge gate.

Requires Node >=24, npx downloads at runtime, and it writes .jev-test-filter/ record files into each repo. The CLI needs installing separately from the plugin, which creates an unpinned supply-chain hop.
Retry and timeout budget (60 s timeout, 4 retries, 8 rate-limit retries) means a Jev outage can delay the fallback by minutes.
entries.verdict: A well-built, honest Jev consumer that is fail-open and cheap in context. But it is a narrow, manually-triggered test-selection tool, not an automatic Claude Code integration. It is TypeSafe-direct, so OpenRouter would work only via a base-URL/key env override that I could not verify against OpenRouter's schema. It is worth an optional per-project install for repos with slow Playwright or integration suites, not as the primary Jev integration.

entries.name: ibrahemid/git-jev-stage
entries.what: Node CLI (`git jev-stage "<sentence>"`) plus a Claude Code plugin/skill that classifies each unstaged git hunk as include/exclude/mixed for a plain-language description, using one Jev `choice` question per hunk via TypeSafe's System One endpoint, then stages the selected hunks atomically (temp index, index.lock, stale-snapshot check). It only stages; it never commits or edits working files. Also exports a small library (planSelection/applySelection/TypeSafeJevProvider).
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model-discretion): Claude loads the skill when the user asks to commit/stage part of the working tree. It is not a deterministic hook, and it does not fire during ordinary coding, only on partial-staging requests; with a broad 'commit everything' request Claude will just use git add/commit.
security: API key handled via env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), sent as Bearer header by the SDK; not passed in argv, so not visible in the process list (only the staging sentence is in argv).

Risk: src/cli/loadEnv.ts:59-77 auto-loads the nearest `.env` between cwd and repo root into process.env for any variable not already set. A cloned client/untrusted repo could ship a .env setting TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (jevClient.ts:120) to redirect the user's globally-set API key plus hunk text to an attacker host. Same pattern lets a repo .env supply its own key. No allowlist or warning.

No curl|sh installer, no postinstall script in this package or in @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (its package.json scripts have only build/check/docs entries). package.json has an `allowScripts` entry for esbuild (dev only).
Shell execution is limited to git via src/git/runGit.ts with fixed flags; no user-supplied strings interpolated into a shell (not fully audited line by line).
SDK is configured with logLevel 'off' (jevClient.ts:49), and error messages omit response bodies; no telemetry in the tool itself. SDK sends User-Agent/X-TypeSafe-SDK/X-TypeSafe-Runtime headers.

Prompt-injection surface: hunk text (untrusted code/comments) goes into the Jev question, but Jev returns only a typed choice validated against a fixed label set (validateChoiceAnswer), so injection can at worst flip include/exclude for a hunk; low-confidence falls back to 'mixed' and unstaged. Plan is verifiable via `git diff --cached` before commit.
entries.dataEgress: Per README 'What leaves the machine' and code: the staging sentence, optional exclusion sentence, changed file paths, hunk headers and full hunk text (added/removed lines with 6 lines of context, plus neighboring same-file hunks as context) for all unstaged tracked changes are POSTed to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or to TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). No tool outputs, no whole files, no conversation. Untracked files excluded. With OpenRouter, the same payload would go to openrouter.ai and be subject to its provider/logging policy. For client projects this means proprietary diff content leaves the machine on every invocation.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the classification level but not silent: a missing key with --yes/--json exits 1 (MissingApiKeyError); interactive without key asks per hunk; missing/invalid/low-confidence/too-large answers become 'mixed' and are left unstaged (policy.ts). Request errors throw ProviderError. SDK timeout is 60 s with 2 retries (jevClient.ts:23-24), so worst case is minutes of blocking on a slow endpoint (Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms). Requests are windowed and run 4 concurrently (windowing.ts DEFAULT_CONCURRENCY=4). Nothing is staged if the snapshot goes stale (exit 3). Never blocks other Claude Code tools since it only runs when the skill invokes it.
entries.contextCost: Near zero. No MCP server (0 tools, no server instructions) and no hooks. Only the skill listing entry: name + description (~290 chars, roughly 70 tokens) is always in context; the SKILL.md body (~3.3k chars, roughly 800 tokens) loads only when the skill triggers.
pros: Genuine, well-fitted use of Jev's Choice primitive: per-hunk include/exclude/mixed with calibrated probabilities and a confidence threshold, so uncertain hunks are left unstaged rather than guessed.
Ships as a real Claude Code plugin+skill with a description trigger, so Claude can pick it up automatically when the user says 'commit just the auth fix' without naming Jev.
Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no hooks, no proxy; ~70 tokens of always-on listing.

Uses the System One endpoint, and the SDK path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key is a plausible zero-code switch apart from the model id.
Provider abstraction (JevProvider interface, baseURL/model constructor options) makes an OpenRouter wrapper via the library trivial.
Safe engineering: atomic index update with lock and stale-snapshot check, never commits, never touches working files, --dry-run and --json modes, fail-soft to 'mixed'.
Unusually thorough tests and fixtures and a CI matrix for a 12-day-old repo; MIT license; tiny dependency footprint (one first-party SDK).
No prompt-injection amplification: Jev output is a validated enum plus probabilities.
cons: Narrow scope: it only helps with selective hunk staging, an occasional task, not daily coding flow; Claude already stages via git add -p or explicit file lists.

Model id blocker for OpenRouter: hard-coded 'jev-latest' is always sent (jevClient.ts:22,84) and overrides TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL; the CLI has no model flag/env, so OpenRouter's 'typesafe/jev-latest' needs a patch or the library API.
README and SKILL.md only document TYPESAFE_API_KEY from a waitlist key; no OpenRouter support or docs, and OpenRouter response compatibility is untested.
Sends full diff hunks (proprietary client code) to a third party on every call; problematic for client projects without approval.
`.env` auto-loading from the repo tree (loadEnv.ts) lets an untrusted repo redirect key and diff via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.
Skill only triggers on explicit partial-commit phrasing; it is not a deterministic hook, so 'automatic' integration is limited to that niche and Claude may not choose it over plain git.
Immature: 1 contributor, 2 stars, 22 commits, v0.1.1 from 2026-09-18, and no history of external use; Jev itself is beta and skeptics doubt it is more than a small router model.
Skill pre-allows `git commit *`/`git add *`, and --yes stages without review, so a wrong include silently lands in the index (mitigated by the confidence threshold and Claude's diff --cached check).
Requires global npm install of a 12-day-old package on PATH (plus Node 22+), extra supply-chain surface.
entries.verdict: A well-built, legitimately Jev-based skill for one niche job (stage only the hunks matching a sentence), auto-triggered by the skill description with negligible context cost, but it is a narrow, alpha, single-author tool that only speaks TYPESAFE_* today. OpenRouter works only with a small patch or library wrapper (base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus model typesafe/jev-latest); use it as an optional add-on for personal repos, not as the core Jev integration, and avoid it on client code without approval to send diffs out.

entries.name: kestrel-review
entries.what: Open-source (community, explicitly not affiliated with TypeSafe) code-review CLI `kestrel` (npm kestrel-review 0.4.3). A deterministic pipeline reads the git diff, matches builtin rule packs (TS/JS, Python, Java, Go, Rust, C#), compiles each rule into typed Jev Choice/Noul/Score questions, sends redacted diff hunks to Jev, bands the probabilities into report/uncertain/drop, and emits line-anchored findings (terminal, JSON, SARIF, Markdown, PR gate). Ships a SKILL.md and two slash commands (/kestrel review, explain) for Claude Code that just shell out to the CLI; Claude writes the prose. It is a code-review-on-diff tool, not a generic Jev decision layer.
interface: kestrel eval / view / github post / gitlab post
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger (model discretion): fires when the user asks to review code/changes/commit/branch or 'is this safe to merge'. It will NOT fire on ordinary edit/coding turns, and no hook or proxy exists to force it. Slash commands are manual. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PostToolUse/Stop hook that runs `kestrel review --staged`.
security: API key never in argv: read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or credentials file (0600 on POSIX), hidden-prompt input via kestrel auth set (src/auth/prompt.ts); status shows last 4 chars only

src/security/redact.ts redacts private keys, AWS/GitHub/Slack/OpenAI keys, connection strings and password/token assignments from hunks before sending; path denylist (.netrc, .aws/credentials, .git-credentials...). Regex-based, so not exhaustive (no OpenRouter sk-or- pattern seen, though sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{20,} may partly match; hyphenated keys likely not)
No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json; no curl|sh installer found; deps include tree-sitter native packages (prebuilds) and @typesafe-ai/sdk

Executes git and, unless --untrusted, may run static tools (src/git/exec.ts, doctor); SKILL.md tells Claude to run `npx -y kestrel-review` on command-not-found, i.e. fetches and runs latest npm code from a 1-day-old single-maintainer package (supply-chain risk)

Prompt-injection surface: diff content goes to Jev, which returns only typed probabilities (low injection impact); optional --llm narrator / --explore / llm-shim send diff-derived text to a generic LLM endpoint (off by default)
OpenTelemetry only if --otel or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT set, said to omit source; no default telemetry seen
entries.dataEgress: Redacted diff hunks plus enclosing function/class context and rule question text go to the configured Jev endpoint (TypeSafe api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter only if base URL overridden). Not whole repos, but real client source lines in diffs leave the machine; `--preview --show-payload` shows the payload. Local cache in .kestrel/cache (in the project dir). Optional narrator/explore/llm-shim send to whatever llm.baseURL is (default api.openai.com/v1) - off by default. No telemetry by default.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the review itself: missing key exits 3 in non-interactive/CI; provider errors exit 3; HTTP provider retries 3x with 200ms*2^n backoff on 429/529/network; default timeout 10s per request (jev.timeoutMs), concurrency 8, rate limiter, cache 30d. For Claude Code the failure is soft: it just returns an error to the skill run and Claude continues; nothing blocks tool calls because there are no hooks. Interactive first run without key silently prompts then falls back to mock (results flagged non-AI).
entries.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server, zero tools. Skill: description ~450 chars always in context (~120 tokens); SKILL.md body 3.7 KB (~950 tokens) loaded only when triggered; the two slash commands ~0.8 KB total. No hook-injected text. Cost is in the JSON report Claude must read fully (SKILL.md forbids head/tail), which can be large per review.
pros: Only candidate here that is a real, working Jev consumer with a concrete use case: pre-commit style review of diffs with calibrated probabilities, using Choice/Noul/Score (README, src/pipeline/questions.ts)
Near-zero context cost: no MCP tools, ~120-token skill description, no hook text, so it does not compound with gitnexus/playwright tool-def overhead

OpenRouter path is achievable by config alone: http provider posts to `${baseURL}/v1/systemone` (src/jev/http.ts), which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with baseURL=https://openrouter.ai/api and model override
Key handling is sane: env or 0600 file, never argv, hidden prompt, redaction of common secrets before egress, `--preview --show-payload` to audit outgoing data
Fail-closed with clear exit codes and mock/replay modes; CI with pinned action SHAs; Apache-2.0; no postinstall scripts; agent-audience JSON output designed for Claude to consume
Team-defined `checks` in .kestrel.yml compile into Noul questions, so client-specific rules can be encoded per project
cons: Project is 1 day old (created 2026-09-29, 10 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 0 forks) and 0.4.x released within a day; APIs and behavior will churn; no independent usage or validation

Not affiliated with TypeSafe and Jev's review quality is unproven (skeptics say it is a small router model); calibration numbers in repo are mock, real calibration needs a paid key (docs/07-calibrate)

No OpenRouter support in code; key env var hard-coded to TYPESAFE_API_KEY (credentials.ts:26); OpenRouter request/response schema parity is assumed not verified; default model id 'jev-1.13.0' differs from OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13

Not automatic: model-discretion skill triggered only by review phrasing; no hook. You would need to author your own PostToolUse/Stop hook around `kestrel review --staged` to get 'use it without me asking', which is not provided
Redirects real client diffs to a third party (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe) with regex-only redaction; client NDA exposure needs per-project opt-in
SKILL.md falls back to `npx -y kestrel-review` (unpinned remote code execution from a brand-new single-maintainer package) and writes to shared /tmp/kestrel.json

Overlaps with Claude Opus itself, which already reviews well; value is a cheap second-opinion gate, not a Jev-in-the-loop for Claude's own decisions; findings are template text from rules, coverage limited to shipped rule packs
entries.verdict: A legitimate but very young, community-made Jev-based diff reviewer that could be pointed at OpenRouter with a base-URL override and is cheap on context, yet it is only a manually or phrase-triggered review skill, not an automatic Jev integration. Treat it as an optional pinned CLI (installed globally, not via npx) behind your own commit/Stop hook rather than the core solution.

entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger / manual
pros: Bundled SKILL.md so Claude Code can run it on request; docs/JEV_PROTOCOL.md shows request design
Parallel scanning, cost.rs, retries, HTML/CSV export, taxonomy
cons: Endpoint hardcoded in src/jev.rs to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; needs code change for OpenRouter
Requires Rust build; retrospective repository mining, not per-turn value
Sends diffs of client repos to Jev

entries.name: DanRWilloughby/snifftest
entries.what: Prose linter for Markdown/text: local countable rules free, optional Jev judgment rules; Claude Code plugin (/snifftest), pre-commit hook, GitHub Action, SECURITY.md and consent flow.
entries.autoInvocation: manual + git pre-commit
pros: Proper .claude-plugin manifest, skill, pre-commit hook, GitHub Action, CI, tarball allowlist, gitleaks
Local-first with explicit consent before sending text; benchmarks vs Claude models via OpenRouter
cons: Prose/docs only, not code review; low daily value for coding
Jev call uses TYPESAFE_API_KEY/api.typesafe.ai; OpenRouter key only used by bench
Manual invocation, not automatic

entries.name: jev-spec (nozomi-koborinai)
entries.what: Independent (unaffiliated) npm CLI + two Agent Skills. It checks source code against Markdown spec requirements: per target it sends spec text plus all matched code files in ONE Jev System One request with noul/choice/score rubrics, then compares the returned probabilities against thresholds in jev-spec.config.ts and exits 0 (pass), 1 (drift) or 2 (setup/runtime error, fail-closed). It is a CI/pre-commit spec-drift linter, not an MCP server, hook or router. The two skills (jev-spec-init, jev-spec-fix) only teach the agent how to install/configure the CLI and to work through a failing check.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model-discretion). jev-spec-init fires when the user talks about spec checks, setup or CI gating; jev-spec-fix when a jev-spec check fails. Neither makes Claude Code call Jev on its own during ordinary coding. The CLI itself runs only if the project has a jev-spec.config.ts and something (git pre-commit hook, CI, or the agent following the skill) invokes it. No deterministic hook, no MCP tool, no proxy is shipped.
security: API key is read from env/config and sent only as Authorization Bearer header via the SDK (not argv), so it does not appear in the process list; SDK redacts headers in debug logs (redactHeaders).
Custom base URL is blocked unless client.allowCustomBaseUrl===true (jev-evaluator.ts:106), a good guard against key redirection, but the guard is itself set in a config file that is executed as code.

jev-spec.config.ts/js is loaded via jiti and EXECUTED in every run including --dry-run (README states this). Any repo you open with a hostile config gets code exec when the tool runs; for client projects it only matters if config is untrusted. The jev-spec-init skill also tells the agent to run npm install and npx.

Child processes use execFile without a shell (git ls-files, git show :path), revision ranges pass --end-of-options (src/context/git-diff.ts, docs/specs/security.md REQ-GIT-01/03). Path root-jail, symlink not followed, .env/.git/*.pem/*.key/SSH keys excluded by filename only.
No redaction of file contents: README and jev-spec-init SKILL.md say all matched files are sent as-is; a hard-coded secret in a matched file goes to the API.

Prompt-injection surface: spec and code are wrapped in <specification_context>/<untrusted_source_code> tags plus an ignore-embedded-instructions preamble (src/evaluator/prompt-security.ts); the README calls this 'a mitigation, not a guarantee'. Since Jev emits only numbers, injection can only skew probabilities, not exfiltrate.
entries.dataEgress: On a live check (not dry-run/mock): for each in-scope target, the full text of the Markdown spec (tables replaced with '[table omitted]'), the full contents of every file matched by codePaths (up to 500 files, 2 MiB each, 120,000 chars total per target), the rubric questions/options, and the model name go in one JSON POST to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or the custom base URL such as OpenRouter). With OpenRouter this means code goes to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. No git diffs are sent (--staged/--diff only select targets; the whole target is sent), and Claude Code prompts/tool outputs are not involved. Nothing is sent for untouched targets in --staged mode. No redaction.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design (docs/specs/fail-closed.md): any error yields exit 2, unreadable/NaN answers fail assertions, oversize targets abort the run before anything is sent, missing API key aborts unless --mock/--dry-run. Default SDK timeout is 10 s (jev-evaluator.ts:218 timeoutMs ?? 10_000) with SDK maxRetries 2 and backoff (sdk index.mjs:74), so a slow or down Jev could stall a hook for tens of seconds, then return 2 and block a commit. Claude Code would only be blocked if you wire it into a pre-commit or Claude Code hook yourself and treat 2 as blocking.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. Two skills add only their name+description to the always-on listing: about 402 + 508 chars, roughly 230 tokens total. Full SKILL.md bodies load only when triggered: jev-spec-init 20,429 bytes (about 5k tokens) and jev-spec-fix 10,427 bytes (about 2.6k tokens). No hook-injected text.
pros: Real, working, well-tested Jev consumer using the correct System One primitives (noul/choice/score) with per-target thresholds and deterministic exit codes; genuinely fits Jev's typed-decision design rather than pretending it is a chat model.

Talks to the same /v1/systemone path with a Bearer key (SDK index.mjs:554,581), and the base URL, key and model are all overridable, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api is a config-only change (allowCustomBaseUrl:true, model 'typesafe/jev-1.13').
Cheap and fast for a commit gate: one request per touched target, --staged/--diff skip untouched targets and need no key, --dry-run validates offline.

Strong safety posture for its size: fail-closed exit codes, execFile without shell, root-jail and symlink checks, custom-URL opt-in guard, npm provenance, no postinstall, no telemetry, ~195 tests plus self-spec probes.
Tiny always-on context footprint (~230 tokens for both skill descriptions), no MCP tool schemas.

Skills are cleanly written and could help the agent set up and fix spec gates in spec-driven projects; the pre-commit use case can be wired outside Claude Code (git hook) so it is deterministic and not dependent on model discretion.
cons: Not an integration of Jev INTO Claude Code: no MCP server, hook, plugin manifest or router. It gives Claude Code no automatic Jev usage during coding; automatic behaviour requires you to write a git pre-commit or Claude Code PreToolUse/Stop hook yourself.

Only useful in repos that have Markdown specs with requirement IDs and a hand-written jev-spec.config.ts (rubrics per requirement, tuned thresholds). Most personal and client projects have no such specs, so utility for daily coding is narrow; the jev-spec-init workflow is heavy (20 KB skill, threshold tuning against the live model).

OpenRouter support is only by inference: no OpenRouter code path, docs or tests, key must go into a TYPESAFE_*-named variable or config apiKey, and the response schema on OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified against what mapAnswers expects (answer.noul, probabilities, legend).

Sends entire matched source files unredacted to a third party (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe if routed that way); for client projects this is a confidentiality/contract issue, and the default 10 s timeout with 2 retries could make a hook hang before failing closed.
Executes jev-spec.config.ts via jiti on every run, including dry-run, so cloning an untrusted client repo and running the tool executes its code.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-20, 6 npm versions in 9 days, 11 stars, 54 of 115 commits by 'Cursor Agent'), explicitly unaffiliated with TypeSafe; accuracy claims (29/29 probes) come from its own author, and its own README lists Jev accuracy limits (large targets, non-English, tables not sent, literal question phrasing needed).
Probabilities are non-deterministic-ish gating signals: false positives will block commits and false negatives give a false sense of safety; pre-commit gating on a beta model adds friction.
entries.verdict: A solid, safe, honest spec-drift linter that genuinely uses Jev, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with a config-only change, but it is a niche CI/pre-commit tool rather than a Claude Code integration and will not make Claude use Jev automatically. Worth adopting only for spec-driven repos, wired as a git pre-commit hook; do not count it as the answer to the automatic-integration goal.

entries.name: HexyeDEV/JevPR
entries.what: Self-hosted GitHub App (FastAPI, Celery, Postgres, Redis) that routes PR review effort (LOW/NORMAL/SPECIAL) with Jev and can approve or request reviewers per YAML policy.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (GitHub webhook)
pros: Clean provider boundary (providers/jev.py has configurable base_url/api_key)
Policy-as-YAML mapping decisions to actions
cons: Heavy infra (DB, Redis, webhooks) for a personal workflow; not a Claude Code tool
Auto-approve of PRs on Jev output is risky given overconfidence

entries.name: raihankhan-rk/diffjury
entries.what: Next.js web app: paste a public PR URL, one Jev systemOne call returns risk scores, review depth, security/design need, and verdict; uses @typesafe-ai/sdk.
entries.autoInvocation: manual
pros: Good 9-question template (risk, blast_radius, missing_tests, verdict) reusable for review prompts
Trims large PRs to fit 32k context
cons: Web UI only, no MCP/CLI/hook; public PRs only
TYPESAFE_API_KEY with SDK jev-latest; no OpenRouter

entries.name: git-jev (crates.io)
entries.what: Rust git extension: pre-commit/pre-push hook sends staged diff to Jev for secret, injection and destructive-payload probabilities; blocks on thresholds.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic git hook (not a Claude Code hook)
pros: Single small static binary, blocking ureq, 8s timeout
Installer chains existing git hooks; pre-push too
MIT, has CI/release workflows
cons: Hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; not switchable to OpenRouter without patching (TypeSafe signups reportedly closed)
Fail-closed on API error blocks commits; single main.rs, README claims (80ms, hallucination screening) unverified, marketing-style README
Diff-only state with no message/context; overlaps jev-commit and existing no-secret-leak hook

entries.name: fallow-verdict
entries.what: Node CLI (npm fallow-verdict 0.1.0) that runs the Fallow JS/TS SAST scanner, then sends each security finding (metadata plus numbered source excerpts) to Jev's System One endpoint as fixed Noul/Choice/Score questions. Deterministic policy code turns the probabilities into survivor, dismissed or needs-human-review verdicts and writes a Markdown/JSON report. It also ships 4 SKILL.md skills (security-triage, review, similar-code, rules) for coding assistants. It is a narrow SAST triage batch tool, not a general Jev integration for Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion), and only for phrases such as pre-PR review, security triage, similar-code. The skills explicitly require running --dry-run and getting a user 'yes' on cost before every real run, and forbid use in hooks ('No skill runs fallow-verdict in a hook', 'Never run in a hook that fires on each commit or each assistant turn'). So it is not automatic in the user's sense, and by design cannot be made silent without rewriting the skills.
security: API key read from env var named by engine.apiKeyEnv, sent as Bearer header (not in argv); redacted from error bodies (jev.ts replaceAll(apiKey,'[REDACTED]')); never written to state
State files in .fallow-verdict/ written mode 0600 but contain scanner evidence that may include source literals/credentials; init gitignores the dir
Evidence collector refuses paths outside project root incl. via symlinks

Prompt-injection: engine has no tools and only returns probabilities; policy requires multiple agreeing answers plus a canary question and 'hostile text' flag for dismissal; finding_id never taken from response
JS/TS config files execute code locally (docs advise JSON config for untrusted repos)
No postinstall script, no curl|sh installer, no telemetry (README); spawns local fallow binary and git rev-parse only
entries.dataEgress: One HTTPS POST per judged candidate to {baseUrl}/systemone (default api.typesafe.ai) containing model, the question set, and a packet: Fallow finding metadata (id, kind, category, CWE, severity, sink callee, trace locations, flags) plus numbered source windows (default radius 20 lines, up to ~28k state tokens) around sink, source, trace hops and controls. Project-relative paths. Real code excerpts of client projects leave the machine to Jev/OpenRouter. Nothing is sent for scan/report/status/eval/--dry-run. packet.blind withholds category/CWE only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-loud, run-level: 10s default request timeout, up to 3 attempts with jittered backoff on 429/5xx/timeout (honors Retry-After up to 60s), pacing to 1000 req/min, circuit breaker opens after 5 consecutive failures or immediately on 401/403/402. Candidates that cannot be judged are left pending and the run exits 2 (incomplete). This is a standalone CLI so it never blocks Claude Code turns unless the agent invokes it; there is no hook, so no fail-open/closed hook semantics.
entries.contextCost: Near zero unless used: no MCP server, no tools, no hooks, no injected text. The 4 skills only add name+description entries to the skill list (~4 descriptions, roughly 150-200 tokens each, ~700 tokens total) and only if the user copies them into .claude/skills. Full SKILL.md bodies load only when triggered. The JSON output the agent parses adds per-run tokens.
pros: Best-engineered real Jev consumer found: strict zod validation of Noul/Choice/Score responses, versioned model pin (jev-1.13.0) to avoid alias drift, pacing, retry/backoff, circuit breaker, cost caps (--max-cost-usd) and --dry-run cost estimate

Demonstrates the right usage pattern for Jev: fixed typed questions plus deterministic policy code that treats probabilities as inputs, with a human-review bucket for uncertainty and hostile-text canary
Base URL, key env var and model are all config (engine.baseUrl/apiKeyEnv/model), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone needs no code change
Skills are shipped in the package and are honest and conservative: dry-run first, --fail-on off, never in hooks, config/close left to user
check command gives a per-file edit-loop re-judge with clear exit codes (0/1/3), usable after edits
Extensive tests and CI on Node 22/24, SHA-pinned actions, no postinstall, no telemetry, sends nothing on dry-run
Zero context cost when not triggered; no new MCP tools polluting the tool list
Useful pattern to copy: the question catalog and decide.ts policy are a worked example for building own Jev hook (e.g. 'is this diff risky' Noul)
cons: Scope is narrow: only JS/TS security findings from Fallow (plus preview review and similar-code kinds). Does nothing for routing, permission decisions, commit/PR gating or general coding decisions

Not automatic: skills require asking the user for a yes on cost before each real run, contradicting the user's requirement that Claude Code uses it without being told; removing that gate means editing shipped skills that 'change with the CLI'
Requires Fallow (separate optional peer dep) and works only for JS/TS repos; useless for Python or other client projects
Sends source excerpts of every finding to a third party; client-project code egress needs client consent and OpenRouter/TypeSafe retention terms check

Default is TypeSafe direct (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and the model name is 'jev-1.13.0'; OpenRouter uses 'typesafe/jev-1.13', and OpenRouter's /systemone request/response schema equality was not verified (docs fetch 404)
Immature: v0.1.0, 1 contributor, 2 stars, 25 commits in 9 days, README calls it a preview; evaluation only on fixtures and NodeGoat, and safe fixed-origin fetches still needed human review
Skill install is manual copy or symlink from node_modules; no plugin/marketplace packaging yet (roadmap)
Requires npm install --save-dev in each project, modifying package.json of client repos; state dir holds source literals
Findings are only as good as Fallow's candidates: a vulnerability Fallow misses never reaches Jev
Probabilistic verdicts: README warns Jev can misread protections or misleading comments, so 'dismissed' can hide real vulns
entries.verdict: A well-built but narrow, alpha-stage SAST triage CLI for JS/TS that can be pointed at OpenRouter through config, but it is not an automatic Claude Code integration and by design asks the user for approval before spending. Worth cherry-picking for security review on JS/TS projects and as a reference implementation for a custom Jev client, not as the daily-driver Jev integration.

pros: Abstain-by-threshold design, marketplace Action, tests, real 200-530 ms output
HUSH_ENDPOINT and HUSH_MODEL env overrides make OpenRouter switch easy

Fits only when user maintains repos with many issues

entries.name: @diffpal/lintpal (LintPal)
entries.what: Go CLI (npm wrapper @diffpal/lintpal -> per-platform binary) that checks git diffs against Markdown rules in .lintpal/rules/**/*.md. For each rule it sends bounded changed-source context plus rule text to a Decisions endpoint (Jev Noul yes/no questions), applies per-rule probability thresholds and a severity gate, and emits findings v5 JSON/Markdown, optionally as GitHub PR review comments. The candidate summary's "jevlint binaries" is wrong: the binary is `lintpal`. It is a CI/PR linter, not an MCP server, hook, skill or Claude Code plugin. Nothing in the repo targets Claude Code (grep for claude/mcp/hook finds only ADK/architecture docs).
entries.autoInvocation: only when prompted (no Claude Code integration at all). It is a CLI meant for CI. Automatic use would require the user to write their own Claude Code hook (e.g. PreToolUse on `git commit` or a Stop hook running `lintpal lint --uncommitted --provider openrouter`).
security: Token never accepted as CLI flag value (env var only), so no key in argv/process list
Presets bind the key to a fixed destination; custom URL/path/token-env overrides rejected for presets; redirects not followed; custom cannot name a preset key variable
Report and metrics output is scanned for the credential value and fails/suppresses on match
Reads worktree-root .env automatically unless --no-env-file (values not exported to process env)

No postinstall script; npm wrapper only execFileSync's the platform binary; binaries come from separate optionalDependencies packages (21 MB unpacked), supply chain rests on one maintainer (metalagman)
