Rule packs importable from GitHub (pinned tag) are prompt-like text sent to the model but the model returns only typed probabilities, so injection can only flip a finding, not run tools
entries.dataEgress: Changed lines of the diff plus bounded surrounding source context (request budget default 24 KB, max 30 KB per request, 1 MiB provider request cap; source blob up to 2 MiB) and the rule Markdown text go to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and onward to TypeSafe/Jev), once per applicable rule/batch. With --uncommitted this includes untracked files. Nothing else (no prompts, no chat, no tool outputs). The user's client-project code would leave the machine to OpenRouter on every run, which the docs flag as something to clear per repository.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the tool but only affects its own process: per-attempt timeout 15 s, up to 3 attempts, retry on 429/529/5xx with Retry-After capped at 2 s (transport.go:25-27, 142), whole-run timeout default 2 m (max 10 m). On failure it prints a fixed error category and no partial report. Oversized or canceled runs fail without a report. Because it is not wired into Claude Code, it can only block the session if the user adds a hook that treats non-zero exit (10 = findings, others = error) as blocking.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-definition tokens, no server instructions, no hook-injected text, no skill. Only cost is whatever the user adds (e.g. a hook printing Markdown findings to Claude on stdout/stderr).
pros: Genuinely Jev-based and the only candidate here with first-class OpenRouter support in code: --provider openrouter, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, /api/alpha/decisions, default model typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.go:37-39, options.go:99-102)
Uses Jev exactly as designed: typed Noul yes/no questions with probability thresholds per rule, no free-text parsing, deterministic severity gate
--uncommitted mode reviews the working tree, so a user-written pre-commit or Stop hook could give an automatic 'do my changes violate our written rules' check
Strong hardening for a 1-week-old project: key from env only, fixed destination per preset, no redirects, output credential guard, bounded sizes, retries with caps, no telemetry, no postinstall, MIT
Rules are plain Markdown in the repo, versionable, and per-client-project, which fits mixed personal and client work
Zero context cost in Claude Code because nothing is registered
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin; the user's requirement of automatic use with no prompting is not met out of the box

Purpose is PR policy linting against explicit written rules, not general daily coding decisions (routing, permission classification, next-action choice) where Jev's Choice/Score might help Claude Code
Ships nothing for the user: they must author rules (or import lintpal-rules packs) and write their own hook glue and exit-code handling
Sends diff and source context of every run (including client code, untracked files) to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; docs require per-repo clearance, a real concern for client projects

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-23, 42 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 10 npm releases in 7 days, platform binaries in separate packages; live precision/latency/cost never validated (docs admit eval uses fake probabilities)
Uses the alpha Decisions endpoint, which may change; v0.x CLI/report schema (findings v5) churn is likely
Per-run latency and cost scale with rules x changed files, unsuitable for per-tool-call hooks; candidate metadata 'jevlint' is inaccurate
entries.verdict: Real, well-built, OpenRouter-capable Jev consumer, but it is a PR/CI rule linter with no Claude Code surface, so it does not deliver automatic in-session Jev use. Optionally wrap `lintpal lint --uncommitted --provider openrouter` in a commit-time hook for repos where you can approve code egress, but do not treat it as the Jev integration.

entries.name: jev-affected
entries.what: CLI and library (npm jev-affected 0.3.0) that takes a git diff, sends it plus your natural-language "when:" conditions to Jev as Noul questions via the @typesafe-ai/sdk, and turns P(true) into a run/skip plan for your own shell task commands (tests, build, codegen). It is a CI/test-selection tool, not an MCP server or Claude Code plugin. It ships a passive SKILL.md for agents. The README says no MCP server is planned.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, and even that is not wired up: nothing is installed into ~/.claude/skills automatically (the README says to point an agent at or copy the directory). It would fire only when the repo has jev-affected.yml or the user asks which tests a change affects, and the model decides whether to follow it. There is no deterministic hook, no MCP tool and no proxy. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PostToolUse/Stop hook that runs `jev-affected plan --working-tree`.
security: API key read only from process env (src/config.ts:101); YAML keys named apiKey/api_key are rejected (config.ts:89). The key is never put in argv; the SDK sends it as a Bearer header. SDK logging is off (logLevel 'off'), retries are 0.

Sensitive-file guard: default exclude globs for .env*, *.pem, *.key, *credentials*, *secret*, *token* (config.ts:16-23); when such a file is in the diff, all tasks RUN and no semantic request is sent (git.ts:~198). It cannot catch secrets embedded in ordinary source files, which the SECURITY.md admits. Overall this is better than a naive diff uploader.

Runs configured task commands with shell:true, so it is only as safe as the repo's jev-affected.yml. This is a code-execution vector on a cloned untrusted repo if the agent runs `jev-affected run`. The SKILL.md says to treat the commands as repository code.

Prompt-injection surface is small. The diff is sent to Jev, which returns only probabilities, so there is no free-text output for an agent to obey. The main risk is a poisoned skip decision, which is fail-open toward RUN for low P only if the model is wrong.

No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh, no telemetry (README Privacy; nothing in the code). Dependencies: @typesafe-ai/sdk, picomatch, yaml, zod. The SDK is TypeSafe's own package and was not audited beyond baseURL/auth. A repo-controlled TYPESAFE_BASE_URL env var could redirect diffs, so the README warns to inspect it.

Release workflow uses npm provenance-style permissions (id-token: write), gated on the repo variable ENABLE_RELEASES. SECURITY.md has no private reporting channel set up yet ('Once the public repository is configured').
entries.dataEgress: On plan/why/run (and eval --live) it sends to the Jev endpoint the sanitized git state: base and head SHAs, the list of changed files (paths plus status) and the unified diff text, capped at analysis.maxDiffBytes (default 100000 bytes). It also sends your configured natural-language task conditions. Prompts, tool outputs and the full repo are not sent; only the diff. Files matching secret globs make it skip the request entirely. `inspect` and `cache` are local, and `doctor` only hits the models list. Client code diffs would go to the provider (OpenRouter or TypeSafe), which matters for client-confidentiality.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open toward RUN, which is the safe direction. A missing key, timeout (default analysis.timeoutMs 10000, SDK timeout, retries 0), provider error, invalid probability or missing model version all mean every semantic candidate task runs, with a warning (planner.ts catch block, README Safety). Policy keys can only be 'run'. Worst-case added delay is 10 s per plan call. With OpenRouter the model-regex check would make this fallback fire permanently, silently disabling the benefit.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. The only Claude Code context cost is the SKILL.md description (about 60 tokens always loaded) plus the roughly 500-token body when it triggers. It installs no hooks. Real cost appears only if the skill fires: the agent runs the CLI, and `plan --json` output is small.
pros: Uses Jev for what it is suited to: typed Noul yes/no probabilities on a diff, with no free text and a fail-open RUN policy and hard thresholds. It is a real, concrete use of a System One model.

Good security hygiene for a v0.3: env-only key, YAML key rejection, secret-file globs that suppress the request, `inspect` to preview egress, no telemetry, no postinstall, small codebase (about 1,600 lines) that is easy to audit.
Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, which honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and hits /v1/systemone with a Bearer key, so pointing it at OpenRouter's System One surface is close to a config change.
Zero context tax: no MCP tools, no hooks, one small skill.
Tests (core, cli, provider), a CI matrix on 3 OSes and Node 20/22, a live-eval methodology with a zero-false-skip gate. MIT.
cons: It is not an integration into Claude Code. It has no MCP server or hook, and the README explicitly says none is planned. Automatic use inside Claude Code would need your own hook glue.

Solves test and CI task selection, not general coding assistance. For a developer who already runs the test suite via Claude, the saving is wall-clock test time, and it needs a per-repo jev-affected.yml with hand-written conditions and trusted commands.

OpenRouter is not supported out of the box. The model-version regex /^jev-\d+\.\d+\.\d+$/ (planner.ts) would reject OpenRouter ids like typesafe/jev-1.13, which forces every task to RUN. You would need a fork, and TYPESAFE_API_KEY would have to hold your OpenRouter key (confusing, and it risks sending the key to the wrong host if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is unset).
The skill's `run` executes shell commands from the repo config. On client repos or freshly cloned untrusted ones that is an execution risk under bypass permissions.

Very immature: created 2026-09-20 (10 days old), 8 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 3 npm versions in about an hour. The 'Public Beta' claim rests on 7 synthetic-fixture live evals with a 50% unnecessary-run rate. The README itself says offline eval verifies plumbing, not accuracy.
Sends client diffs (up to 100 KB) to a third party on every plan. Secret filtering is filename-based only.
Alias jev-latest disables the cache, so it makes a network call every time; the default 10 s timeout could stall a Stop or PostToolUse hook.
entries.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-safe Jev use case for CI/test selection. It is not a Claude Code integration and cannot run automatically, and it is not OpenRouter-ready without a small fork. It is worth borrowing as an example pattern (diff -> Noul -> thresholded action) but not as your daily-coding Jev integration.

entries.name: sable-inc/jev-linter-action
entries.what: GitHub Action: semantic CI checks over repo files using user-defined yes/no questions; passes if each expected answer meets a probability threshold; per-file or bundle mode.
entries.autoInvocation: CI workflow
pros: Well-tested (9 test files), thresholds per question, honest limits documented
Checked-in bundle, no install step
cons: CI only, hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone
Prompt-file oriented, not daily coding in Claude Code

entries.name: @rikalabs/proof
entries.what: Bun/TypeScript (Effect) tool that judges diff hunks against plain-English rules using Jev Noul/Choice/Score calls. It has three parts. (1) CLI 'proof review' (git diff, changed lines only) and 'proof lint' (walks the repo, 50-line windows, 20 parallel Jev calls, optional .proof/cache.json) driven by a proof.rules.ts file. (2) A GitHub composite action that posts inline PR comments. (3) A stdio MCP server, 'proof mcp', that exposes a single tool, proof_check. There is also an Amp-only plugin (jev and judge tools plus a SKILL.md) that does not apply to Claude Code. It is a PR/code-review linter, not a general Jev decision gateway.
interface: Amp plugin (.amp/plugins/proof: jev, judge, skill proof:jev)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Nothing forces Claude to call proof_check. Its description ('Check one diff hunk against one plain-english rule') gives Claude no cue to call it during normal edits, and it needs an inline rule statement each time. The repo ships no hooks.json, no Claude Code plugin or marketplace manifest, and no Claude skill (the SKILL.md is Amp-only). To make it automatic, you would have to write your own PostToolUse/Stop hook that shells out to 'bunx @rikalabs/proof review' (the CLI, not the MCP), or add CLAUDE.md instructions.
security: No postinstall, preinstall or install scripts in package.json or on npm (only lint/test/check/start scripts).

Requires Bun >= 1.2 (engines), and the bin is a raw TypeScript file (./src/cli.ts). It is run as 'bunx @rikalabs/proof mcp', which fetches and executes the package each start unless pinned, so a supply-chain surface on every launch. Pin the version.

API key: read via Config.Redacted from env and sent only as 'Authorization: Bearer' to TYPESAFE_API_URL. It is not put in argv when passed through the .mcp.json 'env' block. The README's Claude Code example puts the literal key in .mcp.json, which is a risk if committed.
The endpoint is fully controllable by the TYPESAFE_API_URL env var, so the key and diffs go wherever it points. Fine if it points to OpenRouter.

Prompt-injection surface: the diff and rule text are interpolated into the Jev question. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so an injected diff can at most skew a number. README: 'probabilistic findings never authorize actions'. The Claude-side risk is small.
No shell execution in the MCP path. cli.ts uses Bun.spawn for git diff in review/lint only. GITHUB_TOKEN is used only for PR comments.
entries.dataEgress: For proof_check: the 'statement', the 'file' path and the full 'diff' hunk supplied by Claude are serialised into the System One request body and POSTed to TYPESAFE_API_URL/systemone with the Bearer key (default api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if overridden). That means code from the diff, file paths and the rule text. It sends nothing else, with no filesystem access, no tool outputs and no whole files (lint mode sends 50-line file windows). There is no redaction, and Claude decides what to pass. No telemetry to Rika Labs was found. .proof/cache.json is local and written only by lint, and it is disabled by default in MCP.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed as a tool error in MCP. Jev outage or malformed output returns a string tool error ('Jev evaluation failed (provider unavailable or invalid output)') and never a clean zero. Claude simply sees an error and continues, so nothing blocks. The CLI fails on outage (README: 'Jev outages... fail the CLI'), so a pre-push hook would block pushes. No retries, no provider fallback. No explicit timeout was found in the MCP path (the 30 s Effect.timeout in Amp.ts:74 is Amp-only), so a hung request depends on the HTTP client and MCP client timeout. The old commit message 'cli fails open on Jev outage' has since been superseded.
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (proof_check). About 700 chars of name, description and schema, so roughly 175-250 tokens, which is negligible. No server 'instructions' field was found in Toolkit.ts, and no hooks inject text.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's typed primitives (Noul/Choice/Score) and returns calibrated probabilities. It is a real Jev consumer, not a wrapper on chat completions.

The hardcoded TYPESAFE_API_URL/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_MODEL config points at POST {base}/systemone (protocol.ts:15, index.ts:21-24). OpenRouter exposes /api/v1/systemone, so an env-only switch to OpenRouter is plausible with no fork.
Tiny footprint: 1 MCP tool at about 200 tokens, no hook text injection, no postinstall, MIT.
Honest safety model: errors are never reported as a clean pass, findings are advisory, the diff is treated as data, and the typed output limits the injection blast radius.
The CLI 'review' command, which judges only changed lines against a versioned proof.rules.ts, is a sensible fit for a pre-push or Stop-hook gate that would enforce team conventions no linter can.
The stdio MCP is a clean, dependency-light Effect implementation with exact-pinned dependencies and 9 test files (about 1,150 lines).
cons: Not automatic: a single opt-in model-discretion tool with no cue to fire. It fails the user's requirement of 'Claude Code must use it when needed' without extra hook glue that this project does not provide.

Narrow scope: only 'does this hunk violate this English rule'. It is not a general router or decision layer for Claude Code (no routing, no command classification, no permission or next-step decisions).
Needs Bun and an unpinned 'bunx' launch on every MCP start; an npm package whose bin is raw .ts. There is a supply-chain and cold-start cost, and no Node-only path is documented.

Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 27 commits in 3 days by one author, 0 stars, 0 forks, 0 releases, no CI (.github absent), version 0.5.2 and pre-1.0. It depends on rc-tagged Effect 4 and a single-author rc fork of the TypeSafe client. The README admits live Judge inference is unverified.

OpenRouter compatibility is untested. There is no OpenRouter mention, and the strict response decoding may break on any schema difference. The client is bound to the TypeSafe rc schema and may not match the OpenRouter /systemone or alpha Decisions API.
Egress of source diffs with no redaction (the README itself warns), and the guard hook won't catch Claude-supplied MCP args. No explicit timeout in the MCP path.
No Claude Code integration assets (no plugin.json, hooks, .mcp.json in repo). The included opencode.json has a hard-coded /Users/dallenpyrah path, showing the repo is a personal working checkout.
entries.verdict: A real but narrow Jev consumer for rule-based diff review. The proof_check MCP is a single opt-in tool that Claude won't reliably call unprompted, and the repo has no Claude Code hooks or skills. Its useful part is the 'proof review' CLI, which could be wired to a Stop/pre-push hook, with OpenRouter reachable through TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api/v1 (untested). Too young (3 days, single author, rc dependencies) to adopt now. Watch it or borrow its Noul-per-hunk pattern.

entries.name: jev-review-gate (RomanXSad)
entries.what: GitHub Action gating protected jobs on Jev answers about the diff (rule pack in YAML; secret paths blocked locally). Also has Cursor postToolUse/stop hook samples.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CI); Cursor stop hook sample
pros: Deterministic secret-path rules never upload files
Editable rule packs; Cursor Stop-style hook example portable to CC Stop
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and model jev-latest, TYPESAFE_API_KEY only
Only 1 test, 0 stars, created 2026-09-29
CI focus, not local coding

entries.name: jgrep-action (kyu1204)
entries.what: Composite GitHub Action wrapping jgrep: fail PRs when an English rule matches the diff, or output test files a diff can affect. Accepts api-key or openrouter-api-key.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CI)
pros: OpenRouter key accepted directly
Test selection mode maps to test-impact analysis
cons: CI-only; 4 files, thin wrapper over external jgrep tool
Not callable inside Claude Code sessions

entries.name: devagrawal09/jev-review
entries.what: Standalone Node 24 CLI plus local dashboard (127.0.0.1:4317) that reviews a git diff or a whole JS/TS codebase using many narrow TypeSafe Jev calls. The pipeline is a Noul risk matrix per file over 5 dimensions, then Choice/Score file profiles, Choice evidence-hunk selection, Score severity and Choice owner routing. Orchestration, thresholds and ranking live in code. Output is a JSON report saved under reviews/ and viewed in the dashboard. It is NOT an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, and has no Claude Code integration. It is a private:true reference/demo app; the README calls it an experiment.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. Claude Code cannot discover or call it automatically. It could only run if you wrote your own hook or skill that shells out to `npm run review:changes`.
security: No hard-coded secrets. The key is read by the SDK from the env var, and the SDK sends it as a Bearer header, so it is not in argv. The scripts use node --env-file=.env, which keeps it out of the command line.
No shell injection. Git calls use execFileSync with an args array and `-C cwd` (src/adapters/git.ts, repository-files.ts), and there is no shell.

Dashboard binds to 127.0.0.1, allows GET/HEAD only, serves a fixed allowlist of 3 assets, and sends CSP and nosniff headers. The report JSON is served unauthenticated on loopback, and any local process or browser tab could read it.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted diff and source text is passed as `state` to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities and choices, no free text, so the injection blast radius is limited to skewed scores. The code does not act on model output beyond ranking.
package-lock is committed. The only runtime dependency is the official SDK, which has no postinstall.
No telemetry in the repo. The SDK's logging is not verified beyond a log-level setting.
entries.dataEgress: Full file contents (codebase mode, chunked into regions via sourceRegions/SCREEN_REGION_LINES) and full unified diffs with 3 lines of context (changes mode) of every JS/TS file in scope, plus changed test files. This is sent to the configured base URL, api.typesafe.ai by default or OpenRouter if overridden, on every run. Untracked files are included. Only .js/.ts/.jsx/.tsx/.mjs/.cjs files are sent. .env is not sent unless the file is git-tracked and matches SOURCE_FILE, and it does not, but nothing scans for secrets embedded in source. A whole-codebase scan sends the entire source tree, which is a real client-confidentiality issue. Nothing else leaves the machine.
entries.failureMode: Not connected to Claude Code at all, so nothing to fail-open or closed there. Standalone, it is fail-closed per run. A Jev error during screening throws `Screening <file> failed` (workflow.ts) and aborts the whole review. The save command exits 1 and leaves the previous report unchanged. Profile and locate calls have no try/catch either. The SDK gives 10s per attempt with 2 retries and backoff. Concurrency is 3 and follow-ups are capped at 8. A codebase scan makes about 1 call per source region, plus 5 profiles and up to 8 follow-ups, so it takes minutes on a big repo.
entries.contextCost: Zero as shipped: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no hooks, no skill. If run through Bash, the JSON report is large (per-file matrix plus findings) and would need to be truncated or summarised.
pros: Best available worked example of Jev's real intended pattern: code owns the workflow, and Jev answers many small typed Noul/Choice/Score questions with calibrated probabilities. It can be copied into a Claude Code hook or skill design.

Its code shows concrete prompt/criteria design for a diff-risk gate: per-dimension Noul questions with true/false definitions and examples, thresholds (SCREEN_THRESHOLD 0.7, ROUTE_SEVERITY 1.5, BLOCKING_SEVERITY 2, MIN_LOCATION_CONFIDENCE 0.55), and a Choice over hunk ids with a noMatch fallback (src/domain/config.ts, src/review/judgments.ts).

The SDK it uses reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL and posts to /v1/systemone (sdk index.mjs:513-554). That matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone path, so pointing it at OpenRouter with an OpenRouter key looks env-only.
Safe code hygiene: execFileSync with arg arrays, no shell, loopback-only dashboard with a fixed asset allowlist, MIT license, one small dependency, no postinstall.
643 stars and 42 forks in 2 weeks, so it is a visible reference from an ecosystem author (Dev Agrawal).
cons: Not an integration at all. It has no MCP server, hook, skill, plugin.json or .mcp.json, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told.
Overlaps and duplicates what Opus 5.5 already does with /code-review. Jev returns only probabilities, so there is no explanation or fix, and the README admits findings are review prompts, not proof.
JS/TS only (SOURCE_FILE regex /\.(?:[cm]?[jt]sx?)$/). It ignores Python and other languages, which is a poor match for a user on Node and Python projects.

Sends full diffs and whole-source contents of the repo to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe). That is a client-confidentiality risk for the user's client projects, and there is no redaction or allowlist.
Fail-closed batch design: any single Jev failure aborts the run. Sequential stages with a 10s timeout and 2 retries make it slow for interactive use.

Very immature: 5 commits by 1 author on one day (2026-09-16/17), no tests, no CI, no releases, and private:true, so it is not installable as a package. Star count reflects hype around Jev's launch, not maturity.
Requires a Node 24 clone plus npm install, and a separate .env file for the key. It needs an SDK env override to reach OpenRouter, which is undocumented and untested here.
The dashboard is a manual side workflow outside Claude Code's terminal loop, and adds nothing for headless or agent use.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration: it is a standalone demo review CLI and dashboard, so it cannot give the user automatic Jev use. Treat it as a design reference for building a Jev-backed PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook or skill (thresholded Noul/Choice gates, with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL pointed at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone), not as something to install.

entries.name: taste-lint
entries.what: npm CLI (taste-lint 0.5.0) that lints copy, typography, motion, SEO and (with --profile code) engineering smells (N+1, dead code, weak tests) in Markdown/MDX/TSX/CSS/source. About 200 rules: mechanical regex/AST checks that need no key, plus "Jev questions" sent as Noul (boolean) requests whose probabilities are banded into act/review. It is a build/CI-time linter for prose and UI, not a Claude Code integration and not a general-purpose Jev tool. It ships a SKILL.md that tells an agent how to run the CLI, and `init --agent` appends guidance to AGENTS.md.
interface: taste-lint eval / tune / extract / rules check / schema
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted, or when the agent reads the skill description and matches phrases like "lint the copy" or "scan for N+1". No hook and no MCP. In effect the user would have to ask, or would have to add an npm script or lefthook step by hand.
security: Key sent as Authorization: Bearer header only, never in argv; read from env AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY (jev.ts:118-134, 181-186). An optional --api-key style option exists only via the library API
Responses validated fail-closed and never logged (jev.ts:42-98); errors are category plus HTTP status only
No postinstall or preinstall scripts in package.json; npm package published with provenance attestation
Spawns git and a local Chromium (src/lib/spawn.ts, --url); the linted repo is untrusted input but is parsed, not executed
Prompt injection surface is small: Jev returns only probabilities, so lint content cannot steer an agent except via the SKILL.md/AGENTS.md text
Pre-1.0 and a single maintainer: supply-chain trust is limited, and 10 days old
entries.dataEgress: With a key set, code and text from the linted files leaves the machine. Each unit (a text string, JSX element, or with --profile code a source excerpt up to about 6000 tokens, otherwise capped at about 1500) plus context keys and the rule question is POSTed to the provider (Vercel AI Gateway or api.typesafe.ai) at src/map/jev.ts:167-186. With --dry-run or no key, nothing is sent. Answers are cached locally in results/. It never sends Claude prompts or tool outputs, because it is not attached to the Claude Code session at all. On client projects, --profile code would ship client source to a third party.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for a CLI run: 10s timeout per request (jev.ts:165), 3 retries with exponential backoff and Retry-After capped at 30s, then a thrown ProviderError that ends the run. Invalid responses also throw. It is not a hook, so it cannot block Claude Code. The mechanical checks work offline and act-band mechanical findings fail the run.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero hook text. The optional SKILL.md adds a description of roughly 200 tokens of always-loaded skill listing, and about 1.5k tokens when invoked. The AGENTS.md block from init --agent is about 100 tokens.
pros: Real, working, well-tested Jev consumer: 40 test files, CI, provenance-signed npm releases, MIT, and it exercises Noul at scale, so it is a useful reference for batching, caching, retry/timeout and fail-closed response validation (src/map/jev.ts)
No-key --dry-run mode gives about 28 blocking mechanical checks for UI copy and typography with no data egress
--profile code catches N+1 queries, unbounded reads, swallowed errors, secrets in logs, tests asserting only mocks; outputs SARIF and JSON, and --since limits to changed lines
Caches Jev answers under results/, so reruns over unchanged files cost nothing and the price is cents
The direct-transport body matches OpenRouter's System One shape, so patching the base URL is plausible
Ships a SKILL.md, so an agent can operate it once told to
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code: no MCP server, no hooks, no plugin manifest. The only agent surface is a SKILL.md triggered by phrases like 'run taste-lint', which is exactly the 'user must prompt' pattern this user wants to avoid

No OpenRouter support: only Vercel AI Gateway (documented path) and api.typesafe.ai; no OPENROUTER_API_KEY and no --base-url CLI flag, so using OpenRouter needs a fork or a wrapper over the library API
Jev is used as a lint backend for prose/UI rules (all Noul), not as a decision engine for coding-agent choices such as routing, permission checks or when-to-run-tests
Most of the pack is review-only: 28 blocking checks and 177 that only report, and the README admits they are 'pattern ports nobody has yet watched on a real codebase', so noise is likely
--profile code sends source excerpts to a third party, which is a problem for client repos; it is off by default without a key but the Jev path needs one
Only 10 days old, single maintainer (47 of 66 commits, plus bot and Claude), 7 stars, alpha; Node >=24.11 required (user has Node 24, so fine)
Focus is web front-end copy, and the user's daily coding is general, so relevance is narrow
entries.verdict: Real and well-built, but it is a prose/UI-copy linter that happens to call Jev, not a Claude Code integration: no MCP, no hooks, no OpenRouter, and it only runs when asked. Use it as a reference implementation for calling Jev (retry, cache, validation) or as an optional --dry-run npm script for front-end projects, not as the automatic Jev layer.

entries.name: @blazejkustra/softlint
entries.what: GitHub Action (plus a small CLI, `softlint`) that reviews PR diffs against plain-English rules in softlint.json. It splits the diff into hunks, asks Jev one Noul (yes/no) question per (hunk x rule), then a Choice question to pick the offending added line. It emits GitHub warning annotations for findings at or above a threshold (default 0.8). Real Jev use: Noul + Choice via the System One endpoint. Not an MCP server, hook or skill.
interface: GitHub Action blazejkustra/softlint@v1 (action.yml, runs dist/index.js on node24)
No MCP tools, no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It runs automatically on GitHub pull_request events in CI, which is outside Claude Code. Inside Claude Code it would have to be called by hand or through a user-written wrapper, for example a PreToolUse hook on `git push` or `gh pr create` that pipes `git diff` into the CLI.
security: API key: CLI takes it from the JEV_API_KEY env var, not argv, so it does not show in the process list. It is sent as a Bearer header over HTTPS. The SDK redacts authorization headers in logs (cli.js:2059).

No shell execution, no postinstall or install scripts (package.json scripts are build/test/eval only), no curl|sh, and no telemetry beyond SDK headers (User-Agent, X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime).

Prompt-injection surface: diff content and rule text are interpolated into Jev questions. Jev returns only typed probabilities and a choice, so injection can at most skew a score or suppress a finding. It cannot run actions.
Fork PRs do not get secrets on pull_request. The README warns about pull_request_target.
The npm tarball contains only a minified bundle and no source. Source is on GitHub, but a review of dist against src was not done.
Maintainer is a single individual and the package is 11 days old, so supply-chain trust is low.
entries.dataEgress: The unified diff of the PR (or of stdin/--diff in the CLI), split into hunks. Each hunk is truncated to 6,000 chars, with up to about 60k chars per request. It also sends the file path per hunk, the rule text, and the added lines (for the locate step). Lockfiles, dist/ and binaries are skipped. Data goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or wherever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points (OpenRouter if set). Nothing else: no prompts, no tool outputs, no full files. The rules file is read locally. The GitHub token is used only to read the PR diff from the GitHub API.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed but not a hook. The SDK retries up to 5 times with a 60s timeout per request. On persistent failure the Action calls core.setFailed, and the CLI has an unhandled top-level await rejection with a nonzero exit. The CLI exits 1 when there are findings and 2 when the key is missing. There is no Claude Code hook, so nothing could block a tool call. If wrapped in a hook, the wrapper would have to enforce its own short timeout and fail-open.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code as shipped: no MCP tools (0 tokens of tool definitions), no server instructions, no hook-injected text, no skill description.
pros: Genuine, well-structured Jev usage: batches up to 200 Noul questions per request, and a Choice question to locate the offending line (src/jev.ts:19-105). It is a good reference for Jev's Noul/Choice primitives.

The SDK path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API path, and the base URL is env-overridable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), so pointing at https://openrouter.ai/api is plausible with no code change.
Cheap: about $0.001 per PR according to the README, and it computes its own cost (jev.ts:110-125).
A usable CLI (`git diff | softlint`) with exit codes, which could back a pre-push or pre-PR hook that checks plain-English team rules on client projects.
Clean and tiny source (about 420 lines), MIT license, 36 offline tests, no install scripts, and the key is passed by env var, not argv.
Egress is limited to diff hunks and rule text, which is a small and understandable surface.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration at all: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. The candidate summary's `other` kind is right, and it is really a CI tool.
Nothing runs automatically inside Claude Code, which fails the user's core requirement. Even a wrapper hook would have to be written from scratch.
It is a PR-level diff reviewer, so it does not help with per-edit or per-tool-call decisions during daily coding. Value only appears at review time.
Very immature: repo created 2026-09-19, version 0.0.1, 10 commits, 1 contributor, 6 stars, no GitHub release, and the `npx github:` install path is unpinned.
The CLI hard-codes the model `jev-latest` with no flag, and the OpenRouter ID is `~typesafe/jev-latest`. OpenRouter compatibility of the request/response payload is unverified.
Reads only JEV_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY, and has no provider abstraction.
The npm tarball ships only a bundled dist with no src, so auditing means cloning GitHub.
The accuracy claims (11/11) come from the author's own curated examples, which is weak evidence for real codebases. Findings are sent to a third party, which needs client consent on client projects.
entries.verdict: A legitimate small Jev consumer (Noul/Choice over PR diffs), but it is a GitHub Action and CLI, not a Claude Code integration. It offers no automatic invocation, MCP, hook or skill. Use it at most as a reference or as the engine behind a custom pre-push or pre-PR hook, not as the integration.

entries.name: jev-action (cachix)
entries.what: Generic GitHub Action running typed Jev requests (labels, questions, request-file) with assert expressions; installs pinned model-clis/jev CLI; PR label triage.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CI)
pros: Flexible assert expressions on answers
From Cachix, pinned CLI release
cons: Depends on external model-clis/jev CLI; provider routing not visible here
CI-only, one test file

entries.name: @drkmttr/adhere
entries.what: A CLI linter (Bun-compiled binary, npm launcher) that checks a repo against natural-language rules in .adhere/rules/*/RULE.md (Must/Never code examples). Each source file is sent to Jev via the System One API as Noul/Choice questions; rules whose P(violation) exceeds a threshold (default 0.8) are reported with a located section. Results are cached in .adhere/cache/. It is a linter for a repo, not a Claude Code integration: it ships no MCP server and no hooks. It ships 3 skills (adhere, adhere-setup, adhere-fix) that teach an agent to run the CLI and fix findings. Written by TypeSafe-adjacent author (Cooper Maruyama, darkmatter), README says "powered by Typesafe".
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (adhere skill: 'Use when writing or editing adhere rules...'; adhere-fix: 'Use when adhere, or CI running it, reports errors...'). Claude will only use it in repos that already have .adhere/ rules. No hook or MCP tool; nothing fires on ordinary coding. It could be wired as a PostToolUse/Stop hook by the user, but that is not provided.
security: API key: read from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or ~/.config/adhere/credentials.json written via tmp file mode 0600 + rename (Credentials.ts:94-110); sent as Bearer header, never in argv. Held as Redacted.
Sends file contents to api.typesafe.ai on every judged file (README:45); no local-only mode. Client repo source leaves the machine to a third party; comments are blanked first but code is not.

Prompt-injection surface is small for Claude Code itself (Jev returns only typed numbers), but the bundled adhere-fix skill tells the agent to run `adhere lint --yes` unattended and 'never ask before a run ... never stop to report its cost', and README recommends piping it into `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` / `codex exec --yolo`. README itself warns fork PRs can steer the agent to exfiltrate secrets.

RULE.ts rules (and appendState hooks) are executable TypeScript run under Bun on every lint; `adhere install org/repo` copies rules from arbitrary GitHub repos incl. RULE.ts that then run on lint (install.ts, README) - arbitrary code execution vector from installed shared rules.
Shells out to git clone --depth 1 for install/list; no telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics in src empty). Retries transient errors 3x with exponential backoff; 30s timeout per request.
Native prebuilt binary distributed via optional npm deps: supply-chain trust in the @drkmttr scope; package 8 days old with 20 versions in a week.
entries.dataEgress: Full text of every source file judged (comments blanked), split into ~30-line numbered sections as `state.code`, plus rule descriptions and Must/Never example code, sent to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Custom RULE.ts appendState hooks can add arbitrary extra file content (e.g. schemas). Nothing from Claude Code prompts, tool outputs or conversations is sent - only repo files when adhere lint runs. Results cached locally in .adhere/cache/ (meant to be committed).
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the CLI: JevUnavailable refuses the whole run with a non-zero exit (Jev.http.ts:65,149); per-request timeout 30s, 3 retries with exponential backoff from 500 ms; a 400 max_tokens_exceeded skips the file; a Cloudflare 403 block page is reported as JevBlocked. Not a hook, so it can never block a Claude Code tool call unless the user wires it into one; all-cached runs need no network or key.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no server instructions, no hook-injected text. Only cost is 3 skills: their descriptions sit in the skills listing (~150-250 tokens total; the 'adhere' description is ~90 words); SKILL.md bodies (adhere ~2.7k tokens, adhere-fix longer) load only on invocation. Nothing installed into ~/.claude automatically - `adhere skill <name>` merely prints them.
pros: Real, non-trivial, purpose-built Jev consumer: uses Noul and Choice primitives correctly (Jev.http.ts NoulAnswers/ChoiceAnswers/LocateAnswers), a good reference for how to frame typed questions with numbered code sections and thresholds.

Active and fairly well tested for its age: 194 commits by mainly one author, 20 npm versions in 8 days, ~4.1k lines of tests, CI on every PR, MIT licensed, and an eval/ directory with measured studies (e.g. only 1 of 20 findings real on one rule, which the skill honestly discloses).
Content-keyed judgment cache (.adhere/cache/) that can be committed means repeated runs and CI pay nothing and need no key or network - cheap at ~$0.042/M input tokens.

Ships Claude Code-compatible skills (adhere, adhere-setup, adhere-fix) with descriptions that trigger on relevant tasks, at negligible context cost; adds no MCP tools, hooks, or context injection, so it will not collide with the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks.
API key handling is careful (env or 0600 file, Redacted, not in argv), no telemetry found, no postinstall script.
cons: Hard-codes https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (Jev.http.ts:46) and only reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY: no OpenRouter support at all, no base-URL override, so it cannot satisfy the 'OpenRouter-hosted Jev' requirement without forking and rebuilding the Bun binary.

Not an automatic Claude Code integration: no MCP server, no hook. It only activates via skill description in repos that already have .adhere/ rules; it does not use Jev to help Claude decide anything during normal coding (routing, gating, classifying tool calls).

It is a repo-wide linter, the wrong shape for interactive daily coding: whole files are uploaded to a third party and full runs cost many requests and seconds-to-minutes; the docs say typical false-positive rate is high for some rules and the fix skill says to verify every finding.
Sends full client source code to api.typesafe.ai (README:45) - a data-egress and contract concern for client projects, with no local/offline judging mode.

Risky agent guidance: adhere-fix says to run unattended, ignore cost, and README promotes `claude -p --dangerously-skip-permissions` piping; RULE.ts from `adhere install` executes arbitrary code on lint. On the user's bypass-permission setup this widens the attack surface.

Very young and single-author (152 of 194 commits from one person, 2 stars, repo created 2026-09-22, Effect 4 release candidates and TypeScript 7 pinned); requires a native binary from optional npm dependencies.
entries.verdict: A well-built but narrow Jev-powered repo linter that only talks to api.typesafe.ai directly; it is not an MCP/hook integration and cannot use OpenRouter without a fork. Skip it for the automatic OpenRouter-Jev goal; at most use it as a design reference for Noul/Choice question framing, or later as an opt-in CI linter on personal repos.

entries.name: jev-review-action (fatwang2)
entries.what: GitHub Action for configurable submission review and PR classification with Jev only, no text model; catalog and policy driven.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CI)
pros: No-LLM classification with policy/catalog config
Tests and dependabot, SECURITY.md
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY
CI/PR-triage focused, not for local Claude Code

entries.name: @dakdevs/lintrules
entries.what: A Rust CLI (shipped on npm as prebuilt native binaries, plus a GitHub Action) that lints a repo against Markdown rules in .lintrules/. Each rule has YAML front matter (title, globs, optional applies-to). For every matching file it sends the rule body and the numbered file source to Jev as Noul yes/no questions ("does the file violate the rule?", "does this rule need cross-file context?"). It turns the returned P(yes) into violation, pass or inconclusive using thresholds (violation 0.8, pass 0.2, inapplicable 0.1). It prints file:line findings or JSON and exits non-zero on failure. With --base it reports only findings on changed files and lines. It is a CI/pre-commit style code linter. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or Claude Code plugin.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or wired up by the user. It has no Claude Code integration. Automatic use would require the user's own hook, for example a PostToolUse/Stop hook or a git pre-commit hook that runs `lintrules --base HEAD --format json`. It would run deterministically but coarsely. It cannot make Claude Code decide 'use Jev when it adds value'.
security: No postinstall or install scripts; the README states none are needed, and package.json only has prepublishOnly. scripts/install-cli.sh is used only by the GitHub Action and runs npm install --ignore-scripts.

The npm tarball contains about 8-9 MB opaque prebuilt binaries per platform. I cannot verify they match the GitHub source. The package has a registry signature, but I did not confirm provenance attestation. Two npm versions were published within 16 minutes (1.0.0, 1.0.1). package.json in the repo is already 1.0.2, so the registry is behind the repo.

API keys are read from env vars and sent as a bearer header (crates/lintrules-provider/src/lib.rs:79). They are not passed in argv, so they do not show in the process list. The wrapper passes process.env through to the binary.

Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted file contents and rule text go into the state sent to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities and no free text, so an injection can only flip a verdict, not run tools. Outputs are used only as yes/no gates.
Local writes: .lintrules/.cache.json, which stores full provider responses keyed by a sha256 of the request. Nothing is executed from repo content.
No telemetry found in the source I read. I did not grep the whole tree for it. Single maintainer, 1 star, 11 days old, so supply-chain trust is low.
entries.dataEgress: Full source of every file matching a rule's globs is sent to the provider, line-numbered, together with the rule text (scan.rs:200, 254-256, 292). In cross-file mode all matched files go in one request, up to max_context_chars=100000 (about 25k tokens). It respects .gitignore, so untracked secrets in ignored files are excluded. Committed .env or config files matched by a glob such as '**/**' would be sent. Nothing is sent from Claude Code's prompts, tool outputs or conversation, since the tool is not connected to Claude Code. With --base, only changed files are checked, but the whole file is still sent. Traffic goes to the chosen provider (TypeSafe, Vercel AI Gateway or Cloudflare), never to OpenRouter. For client projects this means whole-file source leaves the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design: provider errors, invalid JSON, HTTP non-2xx, inconclusive probabilities (between the pass and violation thresholds) and oversized context all count as check failure (README: 'failed provider calls all fail the check'). The HTTP client timeout is 45 s with no retries (crates/lintrules-core/src/provider.rs:70; post() in lintrules-provider/src/lib.rs:72-90). That suits CI, but in an interactive hook a Jev outage would block or noisily fail every edit unless the hook wrapper swallows the exit code. The cache reduces repeat calls and skips caching for inconclusive answers.
entries.contextCost: Zero for MCP or skill tokens: no MCP server, no tool definitions, no instructions, no hook-injected text unless the user writes a hook. If wrapped in a hook or Bash call, its stdout (file:line findings) is the only cost. That output is short and structured, and --format json is available.
pros: Real, MIT-licensed, typed Rust code that uses Jev for what it is suited to: Noul yes/no verdicts with calibrated probabilities and thresholds (scan.rs, config.rs). It is not a chat-model wrapper.

A well-scoped use case: natural-language project conventions ('forms show inline validation errors') checked semantically. Static linters cannot do this, so it could run as a post-edit or pre-commit gate.
Sensible design: --base reports only introduced findings, a result cache skips repeat calls, honest 'no silent truncation' behaviour, and an inconclusive band instead of guessing.
No install scripts. API keys are not in argv. Jev's typed output limits the prompt-injection impact.
Adding a provider is a documented, small Rust change, and the TypeSafe adapter body shape is a near match for OpenRouter's System One API.
Cheap to run: at about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, a 100k-char file scan costs a fraction of a cent.
cons: No OpenRouter support: three hardcoded providers (TypeSafe, Vercel, Cloudflare) with no base-URL override. Using OpenRouter needs a Rust fork and local build, and the user said OpenRouter is the desired provider and no other key exists yet.

Not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. It cannot make Claude Code call Jev on its own, so it fails the user's core requirement of automatic, model-decided use. At best the user hand-writes a hook.
Whole-file egress: it sends full file source to a third party gateway. That is a risk on client projects, where it is unsafe unless globs are narrowed and secrets are gitignored.
Fail-closed with a 45 s timeout and no retry, and per-file calls with up to 4-way concurrency. That is too slow and brittle to run per edit. It suits CI, not an interactive loop.

Very immature: 11 days old, 1 star, single maintainer, 24 commits, all on 2026-09-18/19. The npm tarball is a 42 MB bundle of opaque binaries that cannot be verified against source, and it lags the repo (1.0.1 vs 1.0.2).
Value depends on the user writing and maintaining a .lintrules/ rule set in each project; it does nothing for general coding assistance or Claude's own decisions.
It duplicates something Claude can already do by reading the rule and the code, at higher latency, and Jev is unproven (a possible DeepSeek-flash router, per the brief).
entries.verdict: A legitimate but narrow Jev-based semantic linter aimed at CI and PR checks. It has no OpenRouter provider (hardcoded TypeSafe, Vercel and Cloudflare) and no Claude Code hook, MCP or skill surface, so it cannot deliver the requested automatic, model-decided Jev use. Treat it as an optional pre-commit or CI gate at most, and only after forking to add an OpenRouter adapter.

entries.name: jev-entropy-gate
entries.what: Standalone Node CLI (jevg) for large code migrations. It finds candidate sites with a regex or ast-grep rule from a YAML file. It sends each site (file, line, snippet plus context lines, task text) to Jev's System One API with one Choice question (rewrite_class: deterministic, judgment or manual) and one Noul question (can_safely_automate). It computes normalized Shannon entropy from the Choice probabilities and buckets each site as auto, assisted or manual. `apply` rewrites the auto sites with the rule's own replacement string or AST fix, with no model involved. `record` and `calibrate` refit thresholds from human feedback. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a plain CLI with no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin manifest. Claude Code would call it only if the user or a custom skill told it to run `jevg` via Bash. This fails the requirement of automatic use with no user prompting.
security: API key is read from the JEV_API_KEY env var only and sent as a Bearer header. It is not passed in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
No telemetry found. The only network call is fetch to api.typesafe.ai.
No postinstall or preinstall script in package.json. Runtime dependency is a single pinned native module, @ast-grep/napi 0.45.3.
The only child_process use is Windows ACL verification in src/apply/windows-acl.ts, which does not run on Linux.

Prompt-injection surface: repo snippets and comments go into Jev's `state`. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so text injection cannot steer output beyond skewing the numbers. A hostile repo could still make a risky site score as auto.
Write risk: `apply --write` rewrites files in the target repo. The transaction code has safety checks, but a wrong 'auto' verdict silently changes client code.
entries.dataEgress: Per candidate site, JSON to api.typesafe.ai: relative file path, line number, matched text, a code snippet with `context` lines (default 3) on each side, the rule's task text, and the question definitions. Whole files are not sent, only snippets around matches. Nothing is sent unless the user runs scan or apply, and there is no background egress.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the CLI. src/jev/client.ts:32-33 sets a 30s timeout and 2 retries with backoff (250ms doubling, Retry-After capped at 5s) on 429, 529 and 5xx. After that it throws JevApiError and the command aborts. It has no interaction with Claude Code, so if Claude ran it via Bash, a Jev outage would surface as a failed command and nothing else would break.
entries.contextCost: Zero. It has no MCP tools, no hooks, no skill and no server instructions, so it adds no tool definitions or injected text. Adding it to Claude Code would need the user to write a skill or CLAUDE.md note, which would cost a few hundred tokens.
pros: It is a real Jev integration. It uses the Choice and Noul primitives properly and derives normalized entropy from the Choice probabilities (src/entropy.ts, src/classify.ts:53-81). That makes it a concrete example of using Jev calibration for a decision.
Small egress footprint: snippets with context lines rather than whole files. The key is only in an env var and a Bearer header, with no telemetry and no install scripts.
Reasonable engineering for a young repo: 16 test files, a 6-OS CI matrix with SHA-pinned actions, a transactional apply with a dry-run default, an incremental cache and a calibration loop.
The Jev call is a single small HTTP client (src/jev/client.ts), so the request and response schema is easy to lift as a reference for our own Jev integration.
MIT license, and the CLI is unlikely to break other Claude Code tooling because it doesn't touch ~/.claude.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. Nothing lets Claude Code call it automatically, so it directly fails the user's 'no prompting, must trigger itself' requirement.
It solves one narrow batch problem: bulk migrations such as fetch to apiClient or console to logger, each needing a hand-written YAML rule. This user's daily coding rarely matches that use.

Not OpenRouter-compatible. The endpoint api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and model jev-latest are hardcoded (client.ts:3-4) and only JEV_API_KEY is read. Using OpenRouter would need a fork or a patch to the bundle, and OpenRouter's /systemone schema parity is unverified.
Sends client code snippets to a third-party API. Through the direct TypeSafe endpoint that is a data-handling decision for client projects.

Alpha and single-maintainer: 0 stars, 1 contributor, created 2026-09-21, 2 npm versions. The thresholds (entropy about 0.65, Noul veto) come from the author's own 'real-run entropy ladder' rather than an independent evaluation, so a confident wrong 'auto' can silently rewrite code under `apply --write`.
Chinese-language strings and rule files (task text, band labels) and a Chinese-first CLI, which is friction for client-facing use and for Claude's prompts.
Installing it means a global npm install of a native-module package from an unknown publisher.
entries.verdict: A genuine but narrow Jev demo: a batch migration triage CLI with no MCP, hook or skill surface, so it can never fire on its own inside Claude Code. It is also hardcoded to TypeSafe's direct API. Don't adopt it for the OpenRouter-based auto-integration. At most, read client.ts and schema.ts as a reference for the System One request format.

entries.name: jevtriage
entries.what: GitHub composite Action plus small Python CLI (pip jevtriage 0.1.0) that fetches a PR's title/body/diff, asks Jev one System One Choice question (ready / needs_review / risky) through typesafe-sdk, and exits 0/1/2 with a confidence gate (ready needs confidence >= 0.8). It is a CI PR-merge gate. It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or Claude Code plugin.
entries.autoInvocation: Not applicable to Claude Code. It runs only in a GitHub Actions workflow on pull_request events, or when the CLI is run by hand.
security: TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read from the environment, never from argv, so it does not appear in the process list. The GitHub token is passed via env and sent as a Bearer header only to the GitHub API.

action.yml pins actions/setup-python by SHA. PR title and body are passed via env vars and not interpolated into the shell script, which avoids script injection. The Action installs jevtriage==0.1.0 from PyPI at run time, which is a supply-chain dependency on a single-maintainer package.
PR title and body go to Jev as untrusted text. There is a prompt-injection surface, but Jev returns only a typed label with probabilities, so the impact is limited to a manipulated verdict.

No shell execution, telemetry or postinstall found in src (grep showed only urllib GitHub calls). The README example uses permissions pull-requests: write and issues: write, which are needed only for labels.
A 'ready' verdict is advisory and comes from a beta model, so it should not replace human review.
entries.dataEgress: In CI only: the PR title, the body (capped at 8k chars), the unified diff (capped at 32k chars by default), the file list and stats go to TypeSafe (or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points to). Nothing runs on the developer machine unless the CLI is run by hand. Nothing is read from Claude Code sessions.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design. Missing key, unpinned model, API error, unusable response or identity mismatch all exit 2 with {"error":...}. Low confidence gives exit 1. There is no explicit Jev call timeout in this repo (the 30s timeout in github.py:59 covers GitHub only); timeouts are left to typesafe-sdk defaults, which I did not verify. This suits a CI gate but would be wrong for an interactive assistant.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code. It adds no tools, MCP instructions or hook text.
pros: It is a real, well-structured reference for building a Jev Choice question. The question is 3 criteria with instructions, and the gate reads ChoiceAnswer.confidence and probabilities (questions.py, gate.py, client.py). It shows the typesafe-sdk system_one(state, questions, model) call shape.
Model pinning rejects floating aliases and checks that response.model matches the request (pinning.py, client.py:70). This is a sensible practice for a beta model.
Fail-closed exit codes suit a CI merge gate.
MIT license. The API key comes from env only. The Action pins setup-python by SHA and avoids shell injection from PR text.
It has offline replay fixtures and tests that use a mocked client.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it cannot make Claude Code call Jev automatically. It has no Claude Code integration at all.
It supports only TYPESAFE_API_KEY through typesafe-sdk. No OpenRouter code path exists (grep for 'openrouter' in src is empty), which is the provider the user wants.
It is very new and small: created 2026-09-20, 4 commits by 1 author, 1 star, alpha status. There is a single release, v0.1.0, and the last push was 2026-09-21.
The scope is one fixed PR-triage question in CI. It does not fit editing, commit or tool-call decisions.
Fail-closed behaviour and the lack of a Jev call timeout are wrong for an interactive tool.
Its PR diff egress (up to 32k chars) to a third party matters for client repos if used in CI.
entries.verdict: Not a Claude Code integration. It is a single-purpose CI action for PR triage on the direct TypeSafe API, with no OpenRouter path. Skip it for daily coding. At most, use it as a code reference for the Choice question shape and for confidence gating, and consider it separately as a GitHub CI check.

entries.name: iso-jevdit
entries.what: Standalone npm CLI (not an MCP server, hook or skill) that chunks a codebase, sends each chunk plus typed Choice questions to Jev via the OpenRouter Decisions API, and writes an ISO 27001 Annex A audit report (Markdown + JSON) from a bundled knowledge base. Only 3 of ~36 planned checks exist. It is a batch compliance scanner, not a Claude Code integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted (manual CLI run, or a Claude Code Bash call the user explicitly asks for). Nothing triggers it automatically.
security: No MCP server, no hooks, no postinstall script. The npm package has only runtime deps ignore, picocolors and zod.
Single network target is openrouter.ai, via fetch. No telemetry found in src (grep). The only child_process use is execFile in src/util/git.ts and src/util/fs.ts, which are local git and ACL helpers.

API key is stored in plaintext ~/.isojevdit/credentials.json (restricted to the current user). --key=<key> puts the key in argv and shell history. SECURITY.md:74 documents this, and stdin '--key -' is offered. OPENROUTER_API_KEY env is also supported.
Report has a redactSecrets option (src/report/redact.ts). Source code is sent as-is to OpenRouter and then to TypeSafe (SECURITY.md:50 'Your source code leaves your machine, by design').
Prompt-injection surface: the code chunk is placed inside the Jev state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injected text cannot execute or produce prose.
Not audited by anyone else. Zero stars, one maintainer, a repo created 2026-09-20.
entries.dataEgress: On a full audit, every eligible source file, chunked to about 32k tokens, is sent as state.files[{path,start_line,content}] plus optional project_context and the question specs. It goes to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and onward to TypeSafe. Secret redaction is optional (redactSecrets). Only the OpenRouter key check GET /api/v1/key is a separate call. Nothing else is sent.
entries.failureMode: It is a standalone CLI, so it has no effect on Claude Code sessions. Internally, requests time out after 60s, retry up to 4 times (429 waits at least 10s), and a 401/403/404 aborts the run with an error exit. Not applicable to fail-open or fail-closed behaviour inside Claude Code.
entries.contextCost: 0 tokens. There are no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text. The repo ships its own CLAUDE.md and .claude/PLAN.md for contributors, and these are not installed by npm (the package 'files' list excludes them).
pros: Clean, working reference for the OpenRouter Decisions API wire format: POST /api/alpha/decisions with {model,state,questions}, a choice question with a criteria map, and reading .answers. See src/providers/openrouter.ts and src/jev/request.ts.

Uses the ~typesafe/jev-latest alias, with pricing of $0.042 per 1M input and $0 output, and a 32k context budget with a 0.9 safety factor. This is useful as a source of well-formed Jev prompt patterns (question, focus, violation/compliant/not_applicable criteria with examples).
Zero context cost, no hooks, no postinstall, MIT licence, a small dependency set and a real unit test suite.
Documents Jev-specific pitfalls: it is not a chat model, it never returns prose, and it cannot give line numbers.
cons: It is not a Claude Code integration. It has no MCP server, hook or skill, so it cannot give the automatic use the user wants.
Batch audit of a whole repo for ISO 27001. This is not a daily-coding loop, and it takes minutes per run.
Only 3 of ~36 checks are implemented (SQL injection, crypto and one organizational check), and localization and caching are not built. Findings are only approximate chunk ranges.
Sends the user's full source code, including client code, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (a data-egress and NDA concern). Redaction is optional.
Very young and unproven: 8 commits over one day, one maintainer, 0 stars, no CI and no releases.

Plaintext credentials file, and the --key argv leak path if used carelessly. It does not use the OPENROUTER_API_KEY convention as a first-class path in the code (apiKeyEnv is only wired through config).

Its answers are Jev probabilities over 'violation' and 'compliant' with no explanation. A compliance verdict from an unverified beta model, described as a router-like model by skeptics, may not be audit-grade.
entries.verdict: Not useful for automatic Claude Code integration. It is a niche ISO 27001 batch-audit CLI, not an MCP server, hook or skill, and it sends whole repos off-machine. Its only value is as a small, readable reference for the correct OpenRouter Decisions API request and response shape when building a real Jev hook or MCP server.

entries.name: jev-intent-review
entries.what: A Rust-only PR intent reviewer, shipped as a CLI (jev-intent-review) and a GitHub Action. It reads a requirement from a spec, issue or PR body. It then builds candidate call sites (changed functions, callers one hop out, callees, siblings) using tree-sitter, and asks Jev fixed Choice questions about each. The report sorts calls into worth checking, not settled, read as holding, and not required. It is not an MCP server, hook or skill. The README says maintenance stopped on 2026-09-29 after it lost its own sealed evals: against a frontier model it found fewer known defects (-0.47, 2 wins and 15 losses over 17 repos), and it detected 0 of 17 past defects.
interface: No MCP tools, no hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. It is a CLI or a CI Action, with no hook, MCP or skill trigger. Automatic use in Claude Code would need custom glue.
security: No shell execution: grep for child_process, execFile and spawn in src/ returned nothing relevant.
API keys are read from env vars only, never argv, so they do not appear in the process list.
Each key is sent only to its own fixed host URL (client.ts:365-371). A URL with userinfo is rejected, and http is allowed only for loopback (client.ts:220-223).
src/evidence/redact.ts redacts by content and excludes sensitive paths (.env, *.pem, id_rsa*, .npmrc, tfstate, ...) before anything is sent.
The Action runs npm ci --ignore-scripts and refuses pull_request_target.
CI actions are pinned by SHA.
entries.dataEgress: Per judgment, a redacted state containing the requirement text plus code evidence goes to the chosen Jev host. The evidence is function bodies, callers, callees and diff excerpts from a Rust repo, with secrets redacted by pattern. --candidates-only sends nothing. Nothing goes to Anthropic or to OpenRouter. The optional JEV_TRACE_FILE keeps a local copy of the request state.
entries.failureMode: Fail-loud in a CLI run. It uses a 30s per-request timeout (client.ts:379, AbortSignal.timeout at :467) and retries with Retry-After or backoff, including on 529. It has a run-wide deadline and a request and byte budget, and errors are typed (timeout, network, budget, bad_response). It has no interaction with Claude Code, so there is nothing to fail open or closed inside the session.
entries.contextCost: Zero: it registers no MCP tools, hooks or skills. Only if the user wrapped it themselves would the cost be one Bash call's output.
pros: It is real, well-engineered Jev client code. It has strict response validation (readChoice checks probabilities in [0,1] and choice membership), typed errors, a retry and budget layer, and it records the Jev model version returned.
Its own README documents that typesafe/jev on Cloudflare is the measured path, which is useful as calibration data. It also records that 'jev-latest' on TypeSafe may be a different version.

Its measurements are an honest negative result for Jev-as-PR-reviewer: it found fewer defects than a single frontier-model request, with 2 wins and 15 losses, and 0 of 17 past defects. That is useful evidence against relying on Jev for code review.
The redaction and sensitive-path exclusion design is careful, and the fixed-URL key binding is a good pattern to copy.
Dual licensed MIT OR Apache-2.0, with about 69 test files and CI on Node 22 and 24.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook or skill, so it cannot integrate with Claude Code automatically.
Maintenance stopped on 2026-09-29 and the npm release stays at v0.1.1. It is 11 days old with 0 stars, 0 forks and 1 contributor.
It is Rust-only, with two question types. The user's stack is unknown but is likely mostly non-Rust.
There is no OpenRouter support. Only Cloudflare, TypeSafe direct and Vercel are wired. TypeSafe and Vercel were never verified live, and a custom JEV_API_URL expects the Workers AI form.
It fails its own evals against a frontier model, so it adds little beyond what Opus 5.5 already does for PR review.
It is batch and slow, with many requests per PR. It sends code evidence off-machine to a third party, which matters for client projects.
The repo is still worth mining as a reference for Jev request and response shapes, but it should not be installed.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this goal: it is a stopped, Rust-only PR-review CLI and Action with no Claude Code integration and no OpenRouter path. Its own sealed evaluation shows it losing to a single frontier-model call (2 wins and 15 losses). Treat it as a reference and cautionary data point only.

entries.name: jev-bouncer (alsoleg89/jev-guard, repo renamed from jev-guard)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (single-file stdlib Python bouncer.py, v0.5.0, MIT). PreToolUse hook judges Bash, Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit and mcp__* calls by sending a redacted state and typed Choice/Noul questions to the Jev /systemone API, then returns allow, deny or nothing. Hard-coded tripwire regexes can never be auto-allowed. A built-in read-only allowlist skips the API entirely. WebFetch and WebSearch get deterministic URL exfiltration tripwires only, with no API call. PostToolUse runs an injection sentinel on web, search, MCP and network-y Bash output and adds an additionalContext warning, or blocks with inject_action=block. It also writes a local audit log and cache under ~/.jev-bouncer and has report, calibrate and suggest commands. It also reads the Makefile target, npm script or script file a command names and judges that too. Defaults to mode=dry (log only, nothing enforced).
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic: harness-run hooks on PreToolUse and PostToolUse, no model decision or prompting needed. It matches the requirement of never having to say 'use jev'. Defaults to mode=dry, so it does nothing user-visible until JEV_BOUNCER_MODE is set to guard or on.
security: Key handling: the bearer goes in an HTTP header from urllib (bouncer.py:506-509), so no argv exposure. The key comes from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or a plaintext ~/.jev-bouncer/key file (README suggests chmod 600). The plugin does not read OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

No shell exec of user data. The only subprocess/os.system matches in a grep for exec calls were none in the API path. Nothing is eval'd. The hook only reads files: it reads Makefile, package.json and script files up to 64 KB, refuses '..' paths and escaping symlinks, and sends a ~1500-char excerpt to the API.

Redaction: token-shaped values (ghp_, sk-, AKIA, JWT, Bearer, token=) are redacted before the API call, the log and stderr (bouncer.py:279). It is pattern-based and misses short or oddly encoded secrets, which SECURITY.md admits.

Prompt-injection surface: attacker-controlled command text, file excerpts and tool output go into the Jev 'state' as data. Jev is independently reported to be steerable by injected instructions in state, and SECURITY.md says identical input varies by about +/-0.03. Mitigations: tripwire regexes that can never be auto-allowed, hard-stop deny, allow only if p(danger)<0.10 and all risks<0.40. Untrusted repos' .jev-bouncer.json can only tighten (policy, policy_file, hold_patterns only).

Allow semantics: in mode=on an allow decision resolves in the permission layer and skips Claude's auto-mode classifier for that call. Per the README, Claude Code deny rules and explicit ask rules still win. mode=guard enforces deny only and never widens permissions.
No telemetry beyond the configured API URL. Local log ~/.jev-bouncer/log.jsonl (0600, redacted commands truncated to 500 chars, rotated at 20 MB) and cache dir (0700, 6 h TTL) hold command text.
entries.dataEgress: Once a key is configured, even in the default dry mode, the following go to the configured URL (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter after config) on every unlisted call: the Bash command (redacted, up to 8000 chars), the cwd absolute path, the agent's Bash description (300 chars), a plain-language policy from .jev-bouncer.md if present, and a referenced-script excerpt (~1500 chars from Makefile, package.json or script files). Edits send the file path and content or diff. MCP calls send the tool name and input JSON. PostToolUse scans send up to 8000 chars of tool output (head plus 2000-char tail) from WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP, and Bash after network commands. That includes the outputs of gitnexus and playwright MCP calls, which may contain client source code. Results are also cached locally. With no key, nothing leaves the machine. Web tools never trigger API calls. Client-project code and paths therefore go to TypeSafe or OpenRouter, and OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe. A per-project opt-out is not built in; it would need JEV_BOUNCER_MODE/scan/edits/mcp=off via env or config.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default (bouncer.py:26, 1358-1363). No key, network error, HTTP error, timeout or malformed response makes the hook print nothing to stdout and the normal Claude permission flow applies. JEV_BOUNCER_FAIL=ask forces a prompt on error, in on/guard modes only. Per-call API timeout is 8 s (cfg timeout, no retry) inside a 15 s hook timeout, so a hung API adds up to 8 s per non-allowlisted call, and it stacks with gitnexus hooks. Missing Python means the hook is skipped (run.cmd exit 0). Missing key means judge is None for edits and MCP calls. Local tripwires plus allowlist still work without a key. Because fail is open, an outage silently removes the deny protection; it never wrongly allows.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions (no MCP server, no skills), and 5 slash commands whose descriptions are short (about 350-700 chars of frontmatter across 5 files, roughly 300 tokens if listed). No SessionStart or UserPromptSubmit injection. Hook-injected text appears only on a flagged injection (about 250 chars of additionalContext plus classifierContext) or a deny reason line. Effectively negligible.
pros: Real automatic integration: harness-level hooks on Bash, edits, MCP and web, no prompting; plugin manifest, marketplace.json, hooks.json and 5 commands all present and consistent (plugin.json, hooks/hooks.json).

Safe failure design: fail-open with optional fail=ask; hard tripwires that no model score can override (bouncer.py decide(), HARD_STOP); repo-local config can only tighten; mode=dry default and mode=guard (deny only, never widens permissions) fit a user running auto and bypassPermissions.

Directly comparable to the OpenRouter cookbook pattern but more thorough: local read-only allowlist skips the API (README: 51/77 routine commands with no call), 60-plus read-only shapes, reads what make/npm/script targets actually run, WebFetch/WebSearch exfil tripwires with no API call, redaction before egress and logging.

Switching to OpenRouter is configuration-only: JEV_BOUNCER_URL and JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL are honored (bouncer.py:46, 86) and the request body {model,state,questions} matches TypeSafe's /systemone schema that OpenRouter proxies. Only the key variable name is off (TYPESAFE_API_KEY).

Zero context cost: no MCP tools, no skill listing pressure, no injected text unless something is flagged. Stdlib-only Python with no deps, no installer scripts, no telemetry; key sent in a header, not argv.

Good audit tooling: log, report, calibrate, suggest, JEV thresholds tunable on own history; SECURITY.md is candid about limits; CI matrix on ubuntu and macos (Python 3.9, 3.12, 3.13); test_bouncer.py is about 80 KB of offline assertions with a fake HTTP server; eval.py with a published corpus and raw probabilities in docs/eval.json.
MIT license, latest tagged release v0.5.0, actively iterated (20 commits, single author).
cons: Very young and unproven: created 2026-09-19, 1 star, 0 forks, 20 commits by one author within about a day, no external users or review. The whole 81 KB bouncer.py would need a personal audit before trusting it to run on every tool call (only key paths were read here).

OpenRouter path untested by the author: default host and model are TypeSafe-only ('jev-1.13.0' vs OpenRouter 'jev-1.13'); it reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY, not OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key has to be placed under a misleading name or in ~/.jev-bouncer/key. It does not use /api/alpha/decisions. No test covers the OpenRouter response envelope, and OpenRouter's alpha endpoint has no SLA, with fail-open meaning silent loss of protection.

Heavy data egress by default in scope: after configuring a key, even dry mode sends command text, cwd, edit contents and MCP inputs, plus up to 8000 chars of MCP/web/Bash output on PostToolUse, to a third party (then TypeSafe via OpenRouter). This is a client-confidentiality problem for the client projects unless scoped off, and there is no per-project kill switch besides env or config.

Latency: author measured p50 770 ms and p95 888 ms per unlisted call, and a PostToolUse scan on top for MCP, web and network Bash. It fires on every mcp__* call (gitnexus, playwright), each with an 8 s timeout budget and no retry. The 200 ms OpenRouter figure is unverified.

Fit for this user is partial. In bypassPermissions there are no prompts to save, so only deny/tripwire and injection warnings add value, and in auto mode a Jev allow skips Claude's classifier for that call. The allow path therefore weakens one safety layer for a model whose calibration is documented as imperfect and injectable. The recommendation is guard mode only, not on.

Eval is author-labelled on a small corpus (268 commands, 32 edits, 30 MCP calls, 34 results), the shipped thresholds were tuned on the same corpus, and OpenAI-compatible backend numbers are unmeasured. Results are non-deterministic (+/-0.03). The plugin says it is not a security boundary.

Overlaps and can conflict with the user's stack: existing no-secret-leak.cjs hook fails closed, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not on its protected list. The key would be visible in the environment of every hook process. It duplicates part of the OpenRouter cookbook's PermissionRequest pattern, which is lighter (a Bash-only hook that falls back to a prompt).

CI has never run successfully: all 10 GitHub Actions runs failed because the account is billing-locked. The 80 KB test suite is unverified externally, and I did not run it either (static review only).

Tripwire hits are 'defer' only. For this user (auto plus frequent bypassPermissions) the only enforcement is Jev deny at p>=0.95 with a hard-stop risk, or the WebFetch/WebSearch shape rules. The value in bypass mode is much thinner than the audit implies.
