Web-tier deterministic denies are hard blocks with no prompt, even in bypass: localhost:3000, raw IPs, non-standard ports and .local hosts are all denied. This gives false-positive risk for dev servers.

No circuit breaker or outage backoff: each non-allowlisted PreToolUse and each PostToolUse scan can add 8 s during an outage. Edits and MCP calls have no local fast path, so every Write/Edit costs a network round trip once a key is set.
Logging of redacted Bash commands happens for every Bash call even without a key (PostToolUse 'ran' rows), and each Bash call spawns Python twice (Pre and Post).
With backend=openai, OPENAI_API_KEY from the environment is sent as Bearer to the configured openai_url; the default is localhost, but a misconfigured URL would leak that key.
run.cmd depends on python3 being on the PATH the hook process sees. The user's overridden PATH could make the plugin silently inert.
classifierContext is not a documented Claude Code hook field, so that advertised auto-mode integration is unverified and likely a no-op.

OpenRouter's Jev endpoints are alpha and have no SLA, and Jev's own docs flag injection sensitivity. Nothing in the plugin sets OpenRouter provider options such as zdr, so client code egress cannot be constrained through the plugin.
entries.verdict: The best-built Jev integration for Claude Code: fully automatic hooks, tripwires that models cannot override, fail-open behavior, a local audit log, zero context cost, and OpenRouter reachable by setting JEV_BOUNCER_URL and JEV_BOUNCER_MODEL. Its costs are that it is 11 days old with 1 star, the OpenRouter path is untested, it sends command, edit and MCP output text off-machine, and each unlisted call adds a network round trip. Use it only after auditing bouncer.py, in mode=guard (never on) and with scan/edits/mcp scoped down for client projects.

verification.note: Re-verified live. The repo has 1 star, 0 forks, 0 open issues, MIT, not archived, and the latest release is v0.5.0. There are 20 commits by one author. The last commit is 2026-09-20 04:58Z (07:58 +03:00), and the repo was created 2026-09-19. The repo renamed from jev-guard to jev-bouncer. Most audit claims hold. bouncer.py has no subprocess, eval or telemetry. The bearer key goes in an HTTP header. Only the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or ~/.jev-bouncer/key is read. The URL is read only from the JEV_BOUNCER_URL env var, so a cloned repo cannot redirect it. The repo's .jev-bouncer.json can only tighten. All five commands exist, the hooks.json matchers are as stated, and mode defaults to dry. The 51/77 and 770/888 ms figures match docs/eval.md and the README. The Cursor and Gemini adapters have never been run in those agents, per the CHANGELOG. OpenRouter compatibility is real, because /api/v1/systemone and its schema match the code. It is config-only but still not first-class: the OpenRouter key must go in TYPESAFE_API_KEY or the key file, the default model must be overridden, and it is untested by the author. I lowered the score from 7 to 6. There is no CI evidence at all, since the billing lock meant the tests never passed in CI. The tripwires do not deny, so they give little protection for a bypassPermissions user. The plugin is 10 days old (a single 10-hour burst of commits) and unreviewed. Egress of client code (edits, MCP outputs, Bash commands) to a third-party alpha API is on by default once a key is set. The recommendation stands: only in mode=guard, with edits, mcp and scan scoped down for client projects, after reading bouncer.py. Do not use mode=on. I did not execute any third-party code or tests. The clone is at <scratch path>

judge.why: Best-built automatic hook integration: stdlib-only Python, no MCP tools or skills (near-zero context cost), local read-only allowlist and tripwires skip the API, web tier is deterministic, redaction before egress, audit log with report, calibrate and suggest commands. Ships in mode=dry, so it is safe to try. Use mode=guard only (deny only, never widens permissions), never mode=on.
pros: Fully automatic PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks, no prompting needed; zero tool-definition or SessionStart context cost
Fail-open with optional FAIL=ask; hard-stop rules a Jev score cannot override; repo-local config can only tighten; URL is env-only so a cloned repo cannot redirect it
Local allowlist skips the API for about 51/77 routine commands; 6h response cache; dry-run log and calibrate replay support the shadow-mode rollout the evidence recommends
OpenRouter endpoint and schema verified against OpenRouter's own docs; no subprocess, eval or telemetry found; key sent in a header, not argv
cons: CI has never run: all 10 Actions runs failed with 0 steps (billing lock), so the 80 KB test suite is unverified externally; 1 star, 20 commits in about a day
Tripwires only defer and never deny, so in bypassPermissions they add nothing; only Jev deny at p>=0.95 with a hard-stop risk, or the WebFetch/WebSearch rules, bind
Web tier hard-denies localhost, raw IPs, non-80/443 ports and .local hosts even in bypass: false-positive risk for dev servers and playwright-adjacent work
No circuit breaker: an outage costs up to 8 s per non-allowlisted Pre call and per Post scan; edits and MCP calls have no local fast path, so every edit and MCP call pays a network round trip

Once a key is set, command text, edit contents, MCP inputs and up to 8000 chars of MCP/web output go to a third party (client-code risk); the OpenRouter key would sit under the name TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which no-secret-leak.cjs does not protect
run.cmd resolves python3 on the hook PATH; the user's overridden PATH can make it silently inert; classifierContext output is not a documented Claude Code field

entries.name: ursuciprian/reflex (@ursuciprian/reflex)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also Codex, opencode, pi) that is a deterministic-hooks pre-execution risk gate for shell commands, plus a prompt-injection guard on tool results. Rules, a read-only list and a fast lane settle roughly half of commands locally with no API call (the README cites 51% on one engineer's week). Commands the rules leave open go, when the Jev engine is enabled, to Jev as one request with six typed questions (mutates, blast, env, exfil, on_task, injection). A local policy.json then turns the answers into pass, ask or deny. It also ships a small advisory MCP server (5 read-only tools) and a skill. Jev is optional; the default engine is local.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks, with no user prompting. PreToolUse fires on Bash, Task, Agent, Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit and every mcp__ tool. PostToolUse guard fires on WebFetch, WebSearch, Read, Bash and mcp__ tools. UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt. The MCP tools and the skill are additionally model-discretion. This is the only fully automatic Claude Code path among the candidates I would expect for OpenRouter-Jev, but what it automates is risk-gating of shell commands, not general coding decisions.
security: Age: repo created 2026-09-24, npm first published 2026-09-25, 6 days old on 2026-09-30. 302 commits by ONE author (Ciprian Ursu), no other contributors, 3 stars, 0 forks. The GitHub release is titled v0.16.0 but tagged v0.15.0 (npm is at 0.16.0). Very high churn: 85 commits on 2026-09-29 alone, and 'fix(gate): tamper check ...' bypass fixes on the day of audit.
MIT license. No npm postinstall/preinstall script (package.json scripts are test/eval only). package.json declares no runtime dependencies, and I saw none in the manifest.

Key handling is careful: the key travels in the Authorization header, never in argv (install.mjs and hook commands take only flags like --mode). keyRouteError pins the OpenRouter key to https://openrouter.ai. fetch uses redirect:'error'. Errors log the HTTP status only, and the key is scrubbed from error text (providers.mjs:166-190). The plugin key is a sensitive userConfig option kept in system secure storage.

Fail-closed design: hook.mjs and failsafe.mjs exit 2 or answer ask if the script fails to load. In enforce mode, Jev errors, timeouts or malformed answers give the policy fallback (ask), never a pass. The default never emits allow, so a wrong Jev answer can only add a prompt.

Installers: README offers `curl -fsSL .../install.sh | bash` and `npx @ursuciprian/reflex setup`. Neither is needed for the plugin route (/plugin marketplace add ursuciprian/reflex). install.sh runs `npm install --global` into ~/.local/share/reflex. `reflex setup` edits ~/.claude/settings.json (hooks plus permissions.ask rules) and writes ~/.config/reflex/config.json. The plugin route changes no settings.

Prompt-injection surface: the guard ingests web pages and MCP results and sends them to a hosted model (Jev), which adds an attacker-influenced-input path into the judge. The 'injection' question exists for this. Mitigations: typed outputs only, and the model cannot emit shell. The README admits the guard is a heuristic filter and the rules are pattern matching, not a shell parser ('treat as a strong filter'). The SECURITY policy lists the known bypasses (scripts changed between check and run, nesting deeper than 2 levels, >256KB).
entries.dataEgress: With engine=jev, ONLY for commands the rules, read-only list and fast lane do not settle: the redacted command; the cwd path; environment names (AWS profile, region, kube context, terraform workspace, git branch); the agent's last message and last 5 commands (redacted and truncated); and the first 16 KB of a local script the command runs (make recipe, npm script), never .env or credentials files. The injection guard additionally sends, per inspected result of WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP tools, network-command Bash output, or a Read of a file outside the project, up to 8 chunks x 3000 chars redacted, the tool name, a redacted origin and the last 1000 chars of the user's prompt (docs/GUIDE.md:1493-1497). Conditional instructions send the first 4000 chars of the prompt only when a fragment is undecided. Redaction is a regex list (AWS/GitHub/Slack/OpenAI tokens, bearer headers, *SECRET/TOKEN/PASSWORD=, JWTs, private keys), which the GUIDE itself calls 'not DLP'. Via OpenRouter, the data goes to OpenRouter AND is passed on to TypeSafe, so two processors' terms apply; the GUIDE tells users to check both before rollout. That matters for client projects. With engine=local (the default) nothing leaves the machine. Logs stay local in ~/.local/state/reflex/.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed in enforce mode. One deadline (REFLEX_TIMEOUT_MS, default 3000 ms) covers all retry attempts of a Jev call. 408, 409, 429 and 5xx are retried, at most 3 attempts with jittered backoff, only if the wait still ends before the deadline. Network errors are not retried. A timeout, an HTTP error or a malformed reply gives the policy fallback `ask`, so a human is prompted, never a silent pass. Rules, the read-only list and the fast lane keep working locally. An internal error gives ask in enforce mode and pass in shadow mode. The Claude Code hook timeouts are 10s (PreToolUse) and 15s (guard PostToolUse), and Claude Code's own handling then applies. Consequence for this user: an OpenRouter outage in enforce mode turns into more permission prompts on uncertain commands, which is annoying in bypass mode. A missing key in the plugin does not error; the engine silently degrades to local (plugin.mjs default).
entries.contextCost: MCP server: 5 tools. Names, descriptions and schemas total about 4.8 KB in the source lines 28-70, so roughly 1.2-1.5k tokens, plus the server instructions (about 100 tokens) telling the model to call reflex_check before shell commands. That instruction is redundant with the enforcing hook, and it makes the model spend extra turns calling reflex_check (each call runs the gate again, so possibly a second Jev call). The skill description adds about 60 tokens. Hooks inject text ONLY on findings: PostToolUse additionalContext on an injection warn/block, and UserPromptSubmit additionalContext when a conditional instruction fragment matches. Otherwise pass is silent. About 4 hook entries fire on Bash calls (PreToolUse, PostToolUse gate, PostToolUse guard, PermissionRequest), each a fresh `node` process. The plugin is a large code bundle (gate.mjs is ~228 KB) but it costs no context.
pros: Truly automatic: the plugin registers PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest and UserPromptSubmit hooks (hooks/hooks.json), so Claude Code invokes it with no 'use jev' prompt. That is exactly the auto-invocation requirement.

OpenRouter is first-class in code, not just docs: providers.mjs:26-29 targets openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13, a host-pinned key, and attribution headers. It also has mock tests for the request shape and the retry/timeout paths.
Well-built failure semantics: a single 3 s deadline across retries, ask on any Jev error in enforce mode, malformed answers treated as unavailable, and hook.mjs/failsafe.mjs exit 2 on load failure.

Uses Jev for what its typed Choice/Noul/Score outputs suit (calibrated probabilities from a policy.json, not free text), so it is a genuine System One use case. Default never emits allow, so Jev can only add prompts.

Cheap: about 1k input tokens per uncovered command, roughly $0.04/M, and the author's replay estimates about $0.47 per week of 13,743 commands. The rules layer cuts about half of calls before they reach the API.

Safe rollout path: the plugin starts keyless in shadow mode, and `reflex replay claude --since 7d` reads your existing transcripts with nothing executed, so you can see what it would have flagged before sending anything to OpenRouter.
Stands down if the same hooks are also in settings.json, so no double-judging. It coexists with your other hooks: Claude Code runs hooks in parallel, and Reflex only tightens (ask/deny).
Key hygiene: sensitive plugin option, never in argv, and no telemetry found.
cons: Its value is command-risk gating, not 'Jev makes coding better'. For a senior dev on personal + client repos with no prod/terraform/kubectl focus, most commands are read-only or ordinary build/test, so Jev calls will be rare and the benefit modest. The project is aimed at infra teams (terraform, kubectl, freezes, SOC2 audit).

Duplicates existing safeguards: overlaps with your PreToolUse secret-leak guard (both see Bash|Mcp), and with Claude Code's own auto mode and permission classifier. In bypass mode, whether a hook 'ask' still prompts is not verified by me. If it does, an uncertain command in bypass mode now produces prompts you deliberately turned off; if it does not, the gate is moot.

In plugin mode the key MUST be entered through the /plugin Configure dialog. An exported OPENROUTER_API_KEY is deliberately ignored and scrubbed (plugin.mjs). Without the key the plugin silently runs local-only, so it is easy to think Jev is active when it is not; `reflex doctor`/status is needed to confirm.

Client-code exposure: with jev, command text, cwd paths, the agent's last message and 5 previous commands, 16 KB of script bodies, and up to 24 KB (8 x 3000 chars) of every web/MCP/out-of-project-Read result go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. Redaction is regex-only ('not DLP'). That may breach client confidentiality terms, so the guard would need to stay local-engine for client repos.

6 days old, single author, 3 stars, 302 commits (85 in one day), a live bypass-fix stream, and a release tag that does not match the version. Docs and code disagree on scope: README says only shell tools are gated while the hook matcher includes Edit/Write/MCP. Expect breaking changes.

Per-call overhead: about 4 hook processes per Bash call plus PreToolUse on Edit/Write and every mcp__ call. The MCP server adds about 1.3-1.5k tokens per session, and its instruction ('call reflex_check before running a shell command') is redundant with the hook and can add extra model turns and duplicate Jev calls.

Not verified against OpenRouter live: all published accuracy numbers (171/171 tool gate, 97%/100% injection) are for TypeSafe-direct jev-1.13.0. The OpenRouter route is tested only against a mock. Jev on OpenRouter is beta on the /alpha/ endpoint, so a path change would break it (OpenRouter returns HTTP errors, which mean ask). Pinned to minor jev-1.13 (no 'latest' alias).
entries.verdict: The only real candidate that fully automatically wires OpenRouter-hosted Jev into Claude Code (deterministic hooks, first-class openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions support, fail-closed, cheap). But it is a week-old, single-author, infra-safety gate rather than a general coding aid, it duplicates your secret-guard and permission modes, and it ships up to ~24 KB of tool results and command context per event to OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Try it in plugin shadow mode plus `reflex replay` on personal projects first, with the local engine for client repos.

judge.why: The only candidate audited as natively OpenRouter-hosted Jev: deterministic hooks, rule and read-only fast lane settles about half of commands locally, PostToolUse injection guard, fail-closed in enforce mode with a single 3 s deadline across retries. It is a gate and does not add coding value. Not verified adversarially.
pros: Native OpenRouter Decisions endpoint support, so no key renaming or patching
Deterministic hook plugin with a rule fast lane, a 3 s single-deadline retry budget and prompt-injection screening of tool results
Cheap per call, since about half of commands never leave the machine
cons: Fail-closed in enforce mode means a Jev or OpenRouter alpha outage or false alarm can block work in bypass sessions
Week-old, 3 stars, single author; duplicates the secret guard and permission modes
Sends command text and tool output off-machine; no adversarial verification of its claims here

entries.name: agent-chaperone
entries.what: A "calibrated firewall" for agent tool calls. It is both an MCP stdio/HTTP proxy that wraps other MCP servers and a Claude Code plugin whose PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure hooks screen Claude Code's own built-in tools (Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch, Read, Grep, NotebookEdit). Each screen combines deterministic rules (allow/deny lists, secret regexes, shell rules) with a small battery of typed Jev questions: destructive, exfiltration, severity, instructs_reader (prompt injection), secret_in_args, plus optional off_task and policy_violation. Thresholds live in a YAML policy. Modes are shadow (default, blocks nothing, logs only), enforce and strict. Held calls return permissionDecision "ask" and can be released with `agent-chaperone approve <id>`. Withheld results are replaced through updatedToolOutput. It also keeps a local digest of MCP tool lists to detect rug-pulls.
interface: agent-chaperone log [--follow] | show <id> | approve <id> | trust <server> | report | replay [--policy] | task "..."
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure matchers fire on every matching built-in tool call with no model discretion and no user prompting. For MCP tools, the proxy is transparent only after the MCP config is rewritten with `wrap`. The screens are automatic, but they are a security gate. They do not give Claude decision-making help, and Claude never calls Jev itself.
security: Key handling: src/backends/typesafe.ts:6-8 says the package never reads the key. The SDK takes it from TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so there is nothing in argv or the process list. SDK logLevel is pinned to 'off' (typesafe.ts:224) because debug logging would print request bodies. src/proxy/upstream.ts:27 strips TYPESAFE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY and AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY from the environment of wrapped MCP servers.

Response bodies from the backend are never copied into failure messages or the audit log (typesafe.ts:8-14, 118-160), which limits injection back through the log. Zod validation and size guards at entry points; SECURITY.md says no eval or shell interpolation of content.

Supply chain: the plugin's first hook call runs `npm install agent-chaperone@<version>` at runtime (scripts/plugin-hook-lib.mjs:111-140, plugin-hook.mjs) with its own npm cache. There is no curl|sh and no postinstall script. It is still a runtime fetch from npm of a 3-week-old, 2-maintainer package, and its transitive deps run on every tool call.
No telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics returned nothing). The only network calls are to the configured model backend and npm on first install.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is sent to Jev as data. README admits adaptive attacks will get through, the model does not treat input as hostile by default, it is not a sandbox, and 8-13 of 68 benign 'discusses injection' items are false positives. A fail-open screen is a second opinion, not a control.
Audit log stores arguments and results locally unless AGENT_CHAPERONE_STORE_CONTENT=0 is set. Secret patterns are redacted before send and before write, which is regex-based and best-effort.
entries.dataEgress: Every screened Claude Code tool call leaves the machine to the configured backend (api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai if repointed): for pre hooks the Bash command, Edit/Write file paths and content, WebFetch URL and prompt; for post hooks the full Bash stdout/stderr, Read file contents, Grep matches and WebFetch results (long results are screened by first and last chunks). This is source code and command output from personal AND client projects. Secret-shaped strings are regex-redacted first. Results the allow/deny lists settle never reach the model. Per-server `screen_calls/screen_results: false` opt-outs exist in the policy file. With `agent-chaperone task` or the suggested UserPromptSubmit hook, the user's prompt is also sent with every call. With the OpenRouter chat path, content goes to openrouter.ai and then to openai/gpt-4o-mini. Nothing else is sent, and there is no telemetry.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in shadow and enforce, and fail-closed only in strict mode (SECURITY.md, src/screening/gate.ts and src/hooks/run.ts failure handling). SDK per-attempt timeout is 10s and 2 retries with a 30s total budget (typesafe.ts:36-40). The OpenAI-compatible path has a 20s timeout (openai.ts:32). A dead or slow Jev therefore stalls each Bash/Read/Grep call for up to 30s before failing open. A missing key means rules-only and every judgment records that no model was asked. An unreadable policy file makes the pre hook return 'ask' (main.ts:660-678), which prompts on every screened call, so a broken policy is loud. An npm install failure lets calls through and is not retried for 10 minutes. Session-scoped caching avoids repeat asks for identical state.
entries.contextCost: Very low. It exposes no MCP tools, so tool-definition cost is 0 in plugin mode (the proxy adds none of its own either). The plugin adds one skill; the description is short, about 100-150 tokens (SKILL.md not sized precisely). Hooks inject nothing when a call passes. Injected text appears only for held/withheld/annotated calls (a notice of about 50-100 tokens) or a policy-load failure. Setting a task via UserPromptSubmit adds nothing to context. It does add an audit log on disk.
pros: Only candidate here that is truly automatic: plugin hooks fire on every Bash/Edit/Write/WebFetch/Read/Grep call with zero prompting, which is exactly the 'Claude Code uses it without me asking' requirement.

Uses Jev for what its typed, calibrated probabilities suit: yes/no and ordinal judgments (destructive? exfiltration? does this tool output instruct the AI?). Published benchmark on jev-1.13: AUC 0.976 on InjecAgent, 0.993 on hand-labeled tool calls, 1,947 requests for $0.062 total, so per-call cost is negligible.

Direct Jev code path: uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk /v1/systemone. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL are read by the SDK, so repointing to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is likely env-only (needs a live test).
Safe rollout: default 'shadow' mode blocks nothing and logs what it would have done; `report` and `replay` let the user tune thresholds from their own traffic before enforcing.
Context-cheap: no MCP tool defs; nothing injected on pass. Coexists with existing hooks (matchers overlap on Bash but it never auto-approves, and the README/ADR describe coexistence with ECC).

Fixes a real gap for a bypass/auto-permission user: content-aware second opinion on rm -rf, force-push, curl-with-secrets and prompt-injected WebFetch/Read/Grep results, which permission prompts cannot see.

Careful engineering: fail-open launcher that never crashes a call, response-body text never copied into the log, redaction before send, SDK debug logging pinned off, the plugin's matchers tested against docs, 42 test files, CI, and an honest 'what it is not' section and known false positives.
cons: Sends the full stdout of Bash, Read file contents and Grep matches, plus Write/Edit content, to a third-party API on every screened call. That is client source code on client projects, and regex redaction is the only protection. This is a real confidentiality and NDA problem unless the client work is excluded through policy.

OpenRouter is not a first-class provider. The tool's own OPENROUTER_API_KEY path calls chat completions on openai/gpt-4o-mini with uncalibrated probabilities, not Jev, and the README says so. Getting Jev via OpenRouter depends on the untested TYPESAFE_BASE_URL trick, and the model-ID mapping (typesafe/jev-1.13 vs SDK 'jev-latest') is unconfirmed. If you set OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone you silently get GPT-4o-mini.

Per-call latency of roughly 0.3-0.7s on every Bash/Read/Grep (twice, pre and post), with a worst case of 30s per call if Jev is slow. Over a full day of agent work this is noticeable, and it stacks with the existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.

It is a guardrail, not a coding accelerator. It does not use Jev to route, pick files, decide next steps or review diffs, so it does not deliver the 'Jev adds value to coding' idea beyond safety. Because the user runs bypass/auto mode, enforce-mode 'ask' prompts would reintroduce interruptions.

Immature and low-adoption: created 2026-09-18, 21 stars, 2 real contributors, v0.3.3, API churn likely. The plugin does a runtime `npm install` on first use. Unmeasured questions (off_task, policy_violation, description_steers) are not benchmarked. Author-run benchmark only: 8-13 false positives out of 68 benign security-doc samples, and recall of 0.805 for InjecAgent at threshold 0.5. It is not a sandbox and adaptive attacks pass through.
Duplicates part of the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and adds a second 'ask' source on overlapping matchers. The plugin hook wrapper spawns Node per call.
Shadow mode's default value is only diagnostic: until the user reads the logs and switches to enforce, it protects nothing. Enforce needs tuning.

Default shadow mode still ships all screened Bash output, file contents and Edit/Write bodies to the backend on every call while blocking nothing, so there is egress from install day with zero protection until the user tunes and switches to enforce.
No per-project or per-path opt-out for built-in tools (only the global 'built-in' pseudo-server), so client repos cannot be excluded without per-project env or policy-file swapping.

To use Jev the OpenRouter key must be placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the environment Claude Code launches with. That env is inherited by Bash tool commands, and the user's no-secret-leak hook does not protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The tool strips the key only for wrapped MCP servers (src/proxy/upstream.ts:27), not for Bash.

Setting OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone (which the user may add for other Jev work) silently selects openai/gpt-4o-mini via chat completions, sending code to OpenAI through OpenRouter with uncalibrated scores. This is only a stderr/startup warning, and hooks are non-interactive.

Runtime dependency chain at first hook call: `npm install agent-chaperone@<ver>` into the plugin data dir (scripts/plugin-hook-lib.mjs:111-125, no --ignore-scripts, though the package itself has no postinstall). A failed install is retried only every 10 minutes and screening is silently absent in the meantime. Single npm maintainer (sepehrsafari) on the package.

Pre and post hooks together mean Bash, Read and Grep pay a Node spawn plus a Jev round trip twice per call. The worst case is a 30s total budget per call if Jev or OpenRouter (an /alpha endpoint with no SLA) is slow, and hooks.json sets no explicit timeout, so Claude Code's 600s default command-hook timeout is the outer limit.

Behavior of PreToolUse permissionDecision 'ask' under bypassPermissions and 'auto' is not documented. The Claude Code hooks docs are silent, so for this user's bypass sessions the enforce-mode hold may be ignored or degrade, and only 'deny' is certain to bind. Unverified either way.
Only 21 stars, 2 contributors, created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), v0.3.3 released 2026-09-23. The 'Design-partner note' issue (#86) shows a rapidly moving scope.
entries.verdict: The strongest genuine, automatic, Jev-based Claude Code integration found so far: a deterministic hook plugin with an honest shadow-first design that uses Jev for calibrated safety judgments. It is not an OpenRouter-native tool, though: the OpenRouter route in code is an uncalibrated GPT-4o-mini fallback, and using real Jev via OpenRouter means an untested TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override. Its egress of all Bash output and file contents is a real cost on client projects, and it adds safety rather than coding help. Try it in shadow mode on personal projects first, and exclude client repos via policy.

verification.note: Re-queried now: 21 stars, not archived, Apache-2.0, created 2026-09-18, last commit 2026-09-23 (release 0.3.3), npm 0.3.3 with a single npm maintainer, no postinstall script (checked with gh api and npm view). Hooks are valid in Claude Code 2.1.x per the official docs: PostToolUse updatedToolOutput applies to all tools, PostToolUseFailure exists, PowerShell is a matcher, and matching hooks run in parallel. The Monitor matcher is not documented, though the plugin's hooks.json uses it. The interface and question battery listed in the audit exist in source, and I found no telemetry. The audit's core reading is accurate: OpenRouter in code is a chat-completions fallback on openai/gpt-4o-mini, marked uncalibrated. The real Jev-via-OpenRouter route is TYPESAFE_BASE_URL only, so partial support stands. The main audit error is the model id: it should be 'jev-1.13' for /api/v1/systemone, not 'typesafe/jev-1.13'. The rest of my corrections are smaller. Enforce mode is partly fail-closed for rule-flagged dangerous calls. Shadow mode still egresses everything. Client-repo exclusion is not possible for built-in tools. The repo's docs/design.md wrongly claims a Decisions-endpoint path. I lowered the score from 6 to 5. It is a safety guardrail, not a coding aid. Egress of all Bash output and file contents to a third party begins immediately in shadow mode. OpenRouter-Jev is untested and the audit's suggested config was partly wrong. Latency is doubled on Bash, Read and Grep. It cannot exclude client projects. The repo is 12 days old. It is the best genuinely automatic hook integration seen, but not at the 7+ level. Not verified: live OpenRouter body parity, and whether 'ask' binds in bypassPermissions.

judge.why: Most engineered and most-starred hook plugin (45 vitest files, an honest shadow-first design, also an MCP proxy). But shadow mode already ships every screened call and result off-machine while blocking nothing, built-in tools cannot be excluded per project, and setting OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone silently sends code to gpt-4o-mini.
pros: Shadow default plus enforce and strict modes; enforce still holds rule-flagged calls when the model is unreachable
Screens Bash, Read, Grep, Edit, Write, WebFetch and MCP results with PostToolUse updatedToolOutput
Real tests, Apache-2.0, no postinstall, no telemetry found
cons: Shadow mode egresses all Bash output, file contents and edit bodies from day one with zero protection
No per-project or per-path opt-out for built-in tools; pre and post hooks double the Jev round trips on Bash, Read and Grep; runtime npm install into the plugin data dir on first call
Docs claim a Decisions-endpoint path that does not exist in code; behavior of a hook ask under bypass is undocumented; own AUC benchmark is self-run

entries.name: claude-jev (dr-dimitru/claude-jev-plugin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (no MCP server) that wires TypeSafe System One (Jev by default) into hooks. PreToolUse on Bash|Write|Edit asks 4 typed questions in one request (destructive? exfiltration? beyond requested scope? impact score) and warns (shadow mode, default) or returns permissionDecision "ask" (enforce mode). PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure on Bash checks output for leaked secrets (replaces output via updatedToolOutput on success) and classifies failures into fixed local advice. UserPromptSubmit stores a bounded copy of the user prompt as context for the gate. Also ships a `claude-jev` CLI (check/ask/status/...) and two skills (jev, and user-only decide).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse Bash|Write|Edit, PostToolUse Bash, PostToolUseFailure Bash) - fully automatic, no prompting or model discretion needed. This matches the user's 'Claude Code must use it automatically' requirement, but only as a passive guardrail/classifier, not as a decision engine Claude consults for design choices (the /decide skill is user-invoked only; the /jev skill just documents a manual CLI).
security: API key sent only as Bearer to a validated endpoint: HTTPS or loopback HTTP, no embedded credentials (src/client.ts:188-210); key is never in argv (read from env or file); registered keys are redacted from errors (src/client.ts:23-48)
Project-level config (.claude/claude-jev.json) cannot set model, endpoint, timeoutMs, retries, apiKey or apiKeyFile, blocking repo-controlled key exfiltration - important for client repos
Plaintext apiKey in JSON is rejected; apiKeyFile relative path resolves under ~/.claude
No child_process/spawn/exec in src or bin (grep found none), no postinstall, zero runtime deps, no lockfile by design; no telemetry other than the TypeSafe/configured endpoint calls
Plugin never returns permissionDecision allow from model confidence; only warn/ask (or deny in headless with blockWithoutUI:true) so it cannot weaken existing permission rules

Prompt-injection surface: command text and file content sent to Jev are untrusted but Jev returns only typed probabilities (no free text) and advice strings are fixed local text, so injection can at worst flip a verdict; it cannot inject instructions into Claude
entries.dataEgress: To the configured endpoint (default api.typesafe.ai; would be openrouter.ai if reconfigured): for every Bash/Write/Edit PreToolUse call: cwd (absolute path), tool name, tool_input truncated (Bash command / Write-Edit content and file_path, arguments capped at 400 chars each), plus the user's latest prompt (first 1200 chars) as user_request. For PostToolUse(Failure) on Bash: cwd, command (400 chars), is_error, and output first 2000 chars - on success only when local prefilter (secret regexes, high-entropy tokens, secret-reading commands like env/.env/credentials) matches, unless successCheck:"always". Total serialized state capped at 8000 chars. Not sent: transcript, session id, API key, full files. On OpenRouter this also passes through OpenRouter's logging/provider policies. Client projects' paths, code snippets, commit-worthy content and prompts leave the machine - contractual concern for client work.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: missing key, bad config, timeout, network error, 429/529, malformed response, cache lock timeout, state failure and hook timeout never block; no-verdict is not cached as clear. One 15 s total deadline per request (includes retries, default 2 retries with backoff; honors Retry-After only if it fits). Claude hook timeout 20 s (prompt hook 5 s), so a degraded endpoint can stall each Bash/Write/Edit call up to ~15-20 s before proceeding. In enforce mode with unknown prompt host it asks; in dontAsk/bypassPermissions modes gate.blockWithoutUI false = fail open, true = deny. Default mode is shadow (warn only).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions. Hooks inject text only on flagged actions (short warning strings) and on failed Bash commands (fixed one-line advice per failure_class) - roughly tens of tokens per event, none on clean calls. Skills add two short descriptions to the skill list (jev ~20 tokens; decide has disable-model-invocation so it is not in model context) - total baseline cost about 30-50 tokens. Very cheap in context terms.
pros: Only candidate so far that is truly automatic: registers deterministic hooks, no 'use jev' prompting ever needed (hooks/hooks.json)

Well-engineered for safety: fail-open everywhere, 15 s deadline, never emits 'allow', shadow mode default, strict response validation, project config cannot redirect endpoint or key (protects client repos)
Zero runtime deps, no MCP server, no child_process, no postinstall, no lockfile - small audit surface (~26 KB client.ts, all readable); BSD-3-Clause
Endpoint and model are configurable, so OpenRouter is a config-only switch on paper; local key file avoids env/argv exposure
Serious test suite plus CI on Node 22/24 and published, reproducible benchmark data comparing hosted Jev vs Kev vs Laya
Near-zero context cost (no tool schemas, ~30-50 tokens baseline)
Complements bypass/auto permission mode: adds a semantic 'ask' safety net (enforce mode) exactly where the user has permission prompts off
Uses Jev for what it is designed for (typed Noul/Score/Choice decisions, no free text), and advice is fixed local text so no prompt-injection channel back into Claude
cons: Adds ~0.5 s synchronous latency to every Bash/Write/Edit call (repo's own benchmark: median 471 ms hosted); noticeable across all-day use, worse via extra OpenRouter hop

Sends cwd, command text, Write/Edit content (400 chars) and the user's prompt (1200 chars) to a third party on every tool call - problematic for client projects; no per-project exclusion beyond per-project gate.enabled:false

Does not natively support OpenRouter: docs/code only mention TypeSafe; OpenRouter wire compatibility of /api/v1/systemone (response shape, echoed model id) is unverified and the strict validator would fail closed-to-no-verdict (silently fail-open) on any drift; '~typesafe/jev-latest' likely trips the model-family check

Value is marginal for this user: already has a PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and permission modes bypass/auto mean shadow mode only prints warnings; hosted Jev missed 1 of 9 dangerous commands and false-alarmed 1 of 13 (rm of a report file)
Fail-open + 15-20 s worst-case stall per call if endpoint is degraded (3 attempts inside the 15 s budget), on a beta service
Secret-leak output check sends the secret itself to the remote service when the prefilter matches

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-20, 2 stars, 1 contributor, no releases/tags, plugin distributed through a separate personal marketplace repo); committed dist/ JS is what runs, so it must be re-verified on each update
Only Bash/Write/Edit are covered; Read/Grep/other tools and MCP calls are not judged; does not give Claude a Jev consult tool for design/triage decisions
Overlaps hook ordering with the user's existing Bash PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus) - all run per Bash call, compounding latency
Enforce-mode ask is disabled in bypassPermissions (user's frequent mode); only blockWithoutUI:true gives a hard deny with no prompt, which could block work on false alarms
Hooks call bare `node` in exec form; user's overridden PATH may make all hooks silently inert

Write/Edit content and Bash commands (possibly containing secrets) are sent to OpenRouter before any local secret check; prefilter for outputs is broad, so routine output containing 'token:' or 'password=' is sent remotely
Prompts and verdict cache persisted on disk under ~/.cache/claude-jev (0600, time-based retention)
Project .claude/claude-jev.json from a cloned client repo can disable the gate or change thresholds/tools/mode
No OpenRouter code, docs or tests; every claim of OpenRouter working rests on OpenRouter docs plus config generality, not on a live call
Benchmark is tiny (9 dangerous / 13 routine, 3 runs), self-run by the author, and missed chmod -R 777 /
Shadow mode (default) only prints a systemMessage to the user, not to Claude; it gives no Claude-side consultation, so Claude does not actually 'use' Jev for decisions

entries.verdict: Best-in-class for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement and the safest engineering seen (fail-open, no allow, project config cannot redirect the key), and it should work with OpenRouter via a global-config endpoint/model/apiKeyFile change, but only as a guardrail: ~0.5 s on every Bash/Write/Edit and code/prompt egress make it a poor always-on default for client work. Install pinned from a reviewed clone, start in shadow mode with OpenRouter config, enable globally only for personal projects (or for enforce mode where bypass permissions are used), and verify the OpenRouter response schema with one real call first.

entries.name: BasmaAbouzied0/jev-secret-guard
entries.what: Single-file Python 3 PreToolUse hook (144 lines, stdlib only) for Write|Edit|Bash. It scans outgoing content (Write content, Edit new_string, Bash command) with 8 local regexes for known key formats (GitHub, AWS, Anthropic, OpenAI, Stripe live, Slack, Google, PEM private key), and denies on a hit with no API call. For other high-entropy tokens (>=20 chars, entropy >=3.8, has digit and letter, not a placeholder, hash or path) it sends a MASKED version (first 3 chars, length, charset, plus up to 300 chars of the surrounding line) to Jev as a Noul question ("is this a real credential?"). It denies at p>=0.80, asks at p>=0.30, and does nothing below that. It asks the user if there is no key or Jev errors or times out.
interface: Env JEV_SECRET_BLOCK / JEV_SECRET_ASK / JEV_SECRET_TIMEOUT / JEV_MODEL / TYPESAFE_API_KEY
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: it fires on every Write, Edit and Bash tool call with no model discretion, so it is the kind of automatic integration the user wants. The Jev call happens only for calls with an entropy candidate.
security: API key sent as a Bearer header via urllib, not via argv, so it does not show in the process list.

Key read only from env; no telemetry; no shell execution; no eval. The only network call is the Jev request (README says the secret value is masked, and the code confirms it: masked_context replaces the token with the mask at line 77).

Masking caveat: only the flagged token is masked. Up to 300 chars of the surrounding line are sent in clear, so other secrets or code on that line leak. Each candidate's line is sent, and only tokens matching the entropy heuristic are masked. Multiple candidates on one line each get a separate call where the other tokens remain unmasked.

Prompt-injection surface: the untrusted line text goes into Jev's state. Jev returns a typed probability only, so the blast radius is small, but an attacker-controlled file line could try to lower p. Known-format regexes stay deterministic regardless.

Coverage gaps (verified in code): matcher is Write|Edit|Bash only, so MultiEdit and NotebookEdit are not covered. Edit checks new_string only. There is no check on Read or Grep output (secrets flowing into context), which the user's existing guard covers.

Regex weaknesses: the OpenAI pattern, and the PLACEHOLDER check, skip any token containing 'test', 'example', 'your' or 'fake' (line 35), so a real key containing 'test' passes (e.g. sk_live_...test...). Only the first 5 candidates are checked (line 111).
entries.dataEgress: Only for unknown-format high-entropy tokens on Write, Edit or Bash: JSON {model, state.text, questions} to api.typesafe.ai (as written) with text being up to 300 chars of the line containing the token, with the token replaced by 'abc…MASKED(N chars, charset ...)'. Nothing else is sent: no whole files, no diffs, no tool outputs, no prompts. Known-format hits and placeholders never leave the machine. If pointed at OpenRouter, that same payload goes to OpenRouter (and on to TypeSafe). The line remainder is not masked (see security), so client code around a token can leave the machine, which matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-toward-human, with one fail-open hole. Jev error, timeout (3 s urlopen timeout) or a missing key returns 'ask' rather than allow (lines 113-118). But the hook timeout in the README is 5 s, and up to 5 candidates are checked serially at 3 s each (up to 15 s). If the hook is killed at 5 s Claude Code treats it as a non-blocking error and proceeds, i.e. fail-open for the slow case. The stdin JSON parse failure also returns 0 silently. In bypass/auto permission mode it is unverified whether 'ask' from a hook still prompts (documented hook behavior says ask forces a prompt, but auto mode may auto-resolve it); it would be worth testing before relying on it.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP/tool definitions. Zero tokens injected when clean. On deny or ask, only a short reason string (~30 tokens) is shown to Claude or the user. No server instructions.
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic PreToolUse hook, no prompting needed, matching the user's requirement.
Jev is used for what it is designed for (a typed Noul probability on a narrow question), not as a chat replacement, with calibrated thresholds you can tune (JEV_SECRET_BLOCK/ASK).
Zero context cost, no MCP, stdlib-only Python, 144 lines: easy to audit, vendor and patch (matches the user's Python 3.13 setup).
Privacy-conscious design: known formats are handled locally, and the token itself is masked before it is sent. Key in a header, not argv.
OpenRouter switch is a trivial patch (same schema, URL + model id + key), since the code hardcodes only API_URL.
Covers Write/Edit content, which the user's existing guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not, so it complements rather than replaces it.
cons: No OpenRouter support out of the box (hardcoded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY); needs a local fork/patch and an unverified OpenRouter response-shape assumption.
Heavily overlaps the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard on Bash; the unique value is Jev judging unknown-format secrets in Write/Edit, a narrow benefit.
Serial 3 s timeouts x up to 5 candidates exceed the recommended 5 s hook timeout, which turns the slow path into a fail-open (hook killed, tool proceeds).

Heuristic false positives/negatives: skipping any token containing 'test/your/example/fake' can let real keys through; base64/hash-like strings in real code cause 'ask' prompts that interrupt bypass/auto workflows.
Sends 300 chars of surrounding unmasked line context to a third party (OpenRouter and TypeSafe) on client projects; other sensitive content on that line is not masked.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, 3 days old, no CI, no releases, and the accuracy claims come from just 12 samples (6 secrets, 6 harmless).
Does not cover MultiEdit, and checks only Edit's new_string; no scanning of Read/Grep results.
entries.verdict: A well-scoped, tiny, auditable hook that uses Jev the right way (typed Noul probability, masked input, fail-toward-human) and is genuinely automatic, but it is a 3-day-old single-author PoC that needs a 3-line patch for OpenRouter and duplicates most of the user's existing secret guard. Worth vendoring as a reference or as a Write/Edit complement (with a fixed timeout budget and the matcher extended to MultiEdit), not as a headline Jev integration.

judge.why: Tiny and fully auditable, and the right shape (local key-format regex first, then a masked Jev Noul, error returns ask). It mostly duplicates the user's own no-secret-leak.cjs, and only helps as a Write/Edit complement or as reference code.
pros: 144 lines, easy to read fully; fails toward a human (ask), not allow
Uses Jev the right way: masked input, typed Noul
cons: Duplicates the existing secret guard; 0 stars, poc; a 3 s urlopen timeout inside a 5 s hook leaves a fail-open hole
Needs patching for OpenRouter

entries.name: hookgate
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also Codex CLI) with three zero-dependency Node hook handlers that ask TypeSafe Jev typed questions. (1) PreToolUse on Bash: Choice{allow,ask,deny} plus Noul "destroys data/state outside repo?" gives ask/deny; a confident allow passes through by default. (2) Stop: Noul "does the final message claim completion that git status does not support?" can block a stop once per prompt, behind a local regex prefilter (EN+IT). (3) PostToolUse on WebFetch|WebSearch|Read|Bash, off by default: Noul prompt-injection screen adding additionalContext. Also audit log, per-session cache, rule-promotion suggestions, doctor, report. Ships in audit mode by default (0.0.3): judges and logs but never blocks until mode=enforce is set in ~/.hookgate.json.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: PreToolUse(Bash), PostToolUse(WebFetch|WebSearch|Read|Bash), Stop, registered via plugin hooks/hooks.json. Fully automatic, no prompting, no model discretion. Only effect-producing after mode=enforce.
security: No MCP server, no shell execution of user input; only execFileSync('git', ['status','--porcelain','--branch']) with 1.5 s timeout (handlers.mjs:15). No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, zero runtime dependencies, no telemetry found (grep).

API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY, sent as Bearer header via fetch; never placed in argv (hook command is `hookgate.mjs pre-tool-use`, payload via stdin). Not visible in process list. Key must be exported to the Claude Code process env.

Redaction before egress (redact.mjs:4-34): private keys, sk-/rk-/pk- keys, GitHub/AWS/Slack/Google tokens, Bearer/Basic, JWTs, KEY/TOKEN/SECRET=value assignments, --password/--token flags, URL passwords, 40+ hex. Regex-based, so novel secret formats and secrets in file contents (injection gate on Read) can slip through.
Repo-level config hardening: a cloned repo can only tighten, cannot set failClosed/model/timeout/mode=audit (config.mjs:40-93). Good against malicious-repo config, a thoughtful design.

Prompt-injection surface: the Bash command and (optionally) tool output are fed into a Jev question as state. Injected text in a command could try to sway a classifier; the defense is that a confident allow only passes through and never widens permissions. Being fed untrusted content to a small classifier is a bypass surface, so it is a narrowing heuristic, not a security boundary.
Audit log ~/.hookgate/decisions.jsonl (or CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA) stores verdicts and a command prefix, not full command; session cache files store answers keyed by hash. Local only.
entries.dataEgress: One HTTPS POST per uncached decision to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT). Command gate (all Bash calls): redacted shell command (up to 12k chars), its description, last two segments of cwd, permission_mode. Stop gate (only when local prefilter sees a completion claim, ~2/3 of stops by their own measurement): agent final message (max ~7.2k chars) + stop_reason + first 60 lines of git status --porcelain (file names/branch), redacted. Injection gate (off by default): redacted tool output of WebFetch/WebSearch/Read/Bash up to 12k chars, which would include file contents and web pages. Never transcript or session id. For client projects: file paths, branch names, command contents (paths, hostnames, table names) leave the machine to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if routed there, which adds a second party). Per-session cache dedups identical commands, though their measurement puts real repeat rate at about 0%.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design (README, hooks.json description, hookgate.mjs:14-17). No key, timeout, HTTP error, malformed JSON, exception -> exit 0 with empty stdout, so Claude Code's normal permission flow applies. Fetch timeout 2000 ms default (config.mjs:17, range 100-10000), hook timeout 5 s in hooks.json; note Claude Code's own hook timeout kills the process if exceeded (non-blocking error). failClosed:true only in enforce mode makes command gate 'ask' on outage (user-level config/env only). Slow Jev costs up to 2 s per Bash call before falling open. Bad answer shape -> decision null -> pass. Stop gate: stop_hook_active guard plus one-block-per-prompt marker prevents loops.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool-definition cost (no MCP tools, no skills). Hooks inject text only when acting: ask/deny reason (~150-250 chars) on flagged commands, Stop block reason (~300 chars) when it blocks, rule-promotion systemMessage after 3 confident verdicts on the same prefix, and additionalContext (~250 chars) if injection gate enabled and positive. In audit mode (default) nothing is injected except promotion messages. Statusline text shows 'hookgate: judging the command' during each Bash call.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: hooks fire on every Bash call and every Stop with no prompt from the user, exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' requirement, and zero context/tool-schema cost.

Genuine, well-chosen Jev use case: calibrated Choice/Noul for a small binary/ternary decision where a full LLM hook would cost seconds (their measured type:prompt judge on opus: 3.5 s p50, $0.129 per decision).
Fail-open everywhere with hard timeouts (jev.mjs:22, hooks.json timeout 5), no key -> silent no-op; will not wedge a bypass-mode session on a Jev outage.
Ships in audit mode: you can run it for days, run `hookgate report` for false-positive rates on YOUR real commands before enabling enforce. Safe rollout path.
Endpoint and model are overridable (HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT, HOOKGATE_MODEL), so pointing at OpenRouter is likely env-only; key var needs aliasing.

Careful security engineering: redaction before egress, repo config can only tighten, command >12k chars asked rather than partially judged, no postinstall, zero deps, small readable ~1000-line code base I read fully.
The Stop 'unverified completion' gate is a novel, useful idea for Opus-driven long sessions (catches 'all tests pass' with dirty tree), and Italian/English lexicon suits this user.
cons: Solves safety gating, not coding productivity: it never routes work, retrieves context, or improves code; value is only in preventing destructive commands and false 'done' claims.

Largely redundant/overlapping with the user's existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard, and in bypass/auto permission mode the user has chosen not to be prompted: an 'ask' output would re-introduce prompts (possibly annoying) while only 'deny' is effective. Confident 'allow' does nothing by design.

Adds latency to EVERY Bash call (~60 ms Node spawn + Jev RTT, up to 2 s timeout), plus a Stop-time call on ~2/3 of turns, with Claude Code running hundreds of Bash calls/day; real-Jev latency and accuracy are unmeasured by the author.

Accuracy is unproven: README says benchmark not run, defaults to audit, and author's rule is 'under ~90% agreement it ships ask-only'. Skeptic claim that Jev is a small router model makes false positives on odd but legit commands (chained pipes, scripts) a risk; their own data says 94% of real commands are chains/pipes/scripts.

Data egress for client projects: every Bash command (redacted by regex only), cwd tail, git status file names and final assistant messages go to a third party (TypeSafe, and OpenRouter if routed). Injection gate would send file contents. Could breach client NDAs.

Very immature: 8 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0.0.3, no real-Jev tests, README claims about Codex verified live but nothing about Claude Code 2.1.285 with `args` array in hooks.json (untested by me; verify the plugin hook format is accepted).
Hard-coded TYPESAFE_API_KEY name (no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support) and OpenRouter wire compatibility with /api/v1/systemone unverified; model id format differs (jev-latest vs typesafe/jev-latest).
Stop gate can block finishing and cost extra agent turns (Opus tokens) on false positives; one block per prompt limits damage.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here that actually fires automatically inside Claude Code hooks, with sane fail-open design and a safe audit-first rollout, but it is a safety/verification gate rather than a coding accelerator, unbenchmarked on real Jev, adds latency to every Bash call, and sends command data off-machine. Worth trying in audit mode via HOOKGATE_ENDPOINT/TYPESAFE_API_KEY aliasing to OpenRouter (pin a commit, review with `hookgate report`), not something to enforce blindly on client repos.
