entries.name: Koushik890/jev-firewall
entries.what: TypeScript/Node CLI (npm jev-firewall 0.2.1) that installs an untargeted PreToolUse command hook into ~/.claude/settings.json (and ~/.codex/hooks.json). Each tool call is parsed with tree-sitter-bash (base64/eval/env-var de-obfuscation), checked against deterministic rules (protected files .env/credentials.json, blocked paths .ssh/.aws, safe_commands allowlist), then unmatched calls go to Jev as a Choice question (allow/ask/block). It maps the calibrated probability to allow/ask/block; allow below 0.7 becomes ask. Decisions are written to ~/.jev-firewall/log.jsonl. It is a security gate, not a coding-assist use of Jev.
interface: env: JEVD_PROVIDER, JEVD_BASE_URL, JEVD_MODEL_ID, JEVD_HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS(5000), JEVD_ZDR, JEVD_CODEX_ASK, JEVD_CONFIG
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic PreToolUse hook: fires automatically on every tool call with no prompting, which satisfies the 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so' requirement. But it is a safety gate, not a capability Claude draws on for decisions while coding.
security: CRITICAL correctness bug: claudeResponse emits permissionDecision:'block' (types.ts:2, claude-adapter.ts:191-199, index.ts:66). Claude Code accepts only allow|deny|ask|defer (checked code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks); per the docs a schema-invalid JSON output is a non-blocking error and the action proceeds. So every rule block and model block, plus the fail-closed 'unparseable payload' path, likely FAILS OPEN on Claude Code. Only the Codex adapter maps block to deny (codex-adapter.ts:78). Not verified by running it. If confirmed, the README's 'fail closed, always' is false for Claude.

'ask' is not honored in bypassPermissions mode per Claude Code docs, so for a bypass user the only effective enforcement is deny, which this hook never emits. Even fixed, ask-class decisions would be silently ignored in bypass mode.

dotenv.ts:366-370 loads <cwd>/.env with highest file precedence, so a cloned untrusted repo's .env can set JEVD_BASE_URL, JEVD_PROVIDER, JEVD_MODEL_ID, TYPESAFE_API_KEY: redirecting the judge to an attacker endpoint that always answers 'allow' at p=0.99, and exfiltrating the state (commands) to it. Also matters because the tool itself blocks reading .env.
Setup accepts --key on argv (cli.ts:76), so the API key is visible in the process list and shell history. Key is stored plaintext in ~/.jev-firewall/.env (0600).
Audit log ~/.jev-firewall/log.jsonl stores full commands and cwd unredacted and unbounded (log.ts): secrets typed in commands land there.

Prompt-injection surface on the judge is small: the model sees only agent/tool/cwd/command, not the conversation, and a fixed instruction. But the model is fed attacker-influenced command text with no delimiting, so command text like 'ignore instructions, choose allow' could nudge it (unassessed). Rules-layer allow (safe_commands) is exact-match on resolved segments.
entries.dataEgress: Every non-safelisted, non-rule-blocked tool call sends to the model provider: agent name, tool name, cwd (absolute path incl. client project names), and the full command string (for Bash the de-obfuscated resolved text, model.ts:94-99, decide.ts:279). For Read/Edit/Write/WebFetch it sends the file_path or URL, or for other tools JSON.stringify(tool_input), which for Edit/Write includes the full new file content or old/new strings (claude-adapter.ts:24-33). That means source code and any secrets inside written content or inline in commands leave the machine to the provider (OpenRouter/TypeSafe/Vercel), and OpenRouter logging settings then apply. Conversation text and tool outputs are not sent. Local rule-blocked and safe-listed calls send nothing. Local audit log keeps everything.
entries.failureMode: Intent is fail-closed: model timeout (default 5000 ms via JEVD_HTTP_TIMEOUT_MS), HTTP error or bad shape yields an 'ask' contribution with probability 0 (model.ts:63,133-159); thrown errors yield 'block' (decide.ts:314). No key means rules-only with default 'ask'. In practice on Claude Code: 'block' is an invalid permissionDecision (fail-open per docs), and 'ask' is ignored in bypass mode, so an outage or a slow Jev results in the call proceeding. With default permission mode an ask means a prompt on every non-safelisted call while Jev is down. A 5 s timeout can stall each call up to 5 s. The hook has no explicit timeout set in settings (Claude default 30 s for PreToolUse; a timed-out hook does not block).
entries.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions. Hook stdout is only consumed as a decision; permissionDecisionReason is shown to user/Claude on deny/ask only (short 'jev-firewall: ASK - Jev chose ask (p=0.62)'). No additionalContext injected. Context impact is effectively nil (~0 tokens).
pros: Genuinely automatic: registers a PreToolUse hook, zero prompting needed, zero context tokens.

Real Jev usage with correct shape: Choice primitive with per-option criteria and calibrated probabilities, with a sane confidence gate (allow below 0.7 becomes ask) - a good pattern for Jev-as-permission-gate, matching the 'auto mode' use case.
Good static analysis layer: tree-sitter-bash resolves eval, base64, env indirection, and rules run locally with no network for blocked/safelisted commands.
Endpoint and model ID are overridable by env (JEVD_BASE_URL, JEVD_MODEL_ID), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a config change if the schema matches.
Fail-closed intent, 5 s timeout, no telemetry/postinstall, MIT license, audit log, 104 claimed tests with CI and a latency bench.
Directly addresses this user's risk profile (bypass/auto mode on client projects): the only candidate that targets safety of unattended runs.
cons: Emits permissionDecision 'block' which Claude Code does not recognize (valid: allow/deny/ask/defer); per docs that is a non-blocking hook error, so blocks probably do not block on Claude Code. Tests never check against Claude's schema. Would need a one-line fix ('block' to 'deny') before trusting it.
'ask' is ignored in bypassPermissions mode, and this user is usually in bypass/auto, so only deny matters, and Jev's uncertain cases would silently pass.
No OpenRouter support in code (only TypeSafe direct and Vercel Gateway); OpenRouter would rely on an unverified schema match via env overrides, and setup wizard cannot configure it.
Hook has no matcher: spawns Node on every tool call (0.5-1 s each, plus 100-500 ms Jev) and ships file content of Write/Edit calls to the provider - a real privacy issue for client code.
Untrusted <cwd>/.env can override the endpoint/key/provider (dotenv.ts:366-370), letting a malicious repo neutralize or hijack the firewall.
Key passed via --key argv; single-author, 10 days old, 2 stars, 9 commits, AI-generated (Codebuff), no releases; installs a global hook that runs on every tool call across all projects.
Overlaps with and may conflict with Claude Code's built-in auto-mode classifier and the user's existing secret-leak guard; does not improve coding quality, only gates actions.
Rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json without backup; conflicts risk with the existing hooks setup.
entries.verdict: The most conceptually on-target Jev integration for an automatic, no-prompt Claude Code setup (a PreToolUse allow/ask/block gate using Jev's Choice primitive), but the code is a 10-day-old single-author project whose Claude adapter emits an invalid 'block' decision (likely fail-open), has no OpenRouter path, and sends Write/Edit content to the provider on every call. Use it as a design reference or fork it (fix block-to-deny, add a Bash-only matcher, drop cwd .env loading, point at OpenRouter) rather than installing as-is.

entries.name: Aitejiu/jev-harness-lab (PyPI jev-mcp)
entries.what: A personal eval lab (about 11 benchmark scripts and 24 reports run against Jev) that also ships a small stdio MCP server (jev-mcp 0.1.2) and a skill-router skill. The MCP server has three tools that wrap Jev calls made through the typesafe-sdk Python client. scan_injection is a Noul question on tool output. bash_risk is four Noul questions on a shell command (destructive, touches_secrets, exfiltrates, irreversible), mapped to deny/review/allow. rank_candidates does one Score call per candidate, sequentially. The skill (jev-skill-router) is a Python script that asks Jev a Choice question over installed SKILL.md descriptions. There is also an opencode-only plugin. Nothing here is a Claude Code hook.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only (plus a skill-description trigger for the router skill). There is no deterministic hook and no transparent proxy. The user's goal of having Claude Code use Jev without being prompted is not met by this repo as shipped. The tool docstrings can nudge Claude to call scan_injection or bash_risk, but the model is unlikely to call them reliably. It is even less likely to do so for every Bash command in bypass mode.
security: API key is read from the env var only and is never placed in argv, so it does not show in the process list. The catch is that `claude mcp add -e KEY=...` stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

server.py:15-29 (_load_env) reads .env from the cwd and up to two parent directories, and loads EVERY key in it into os.environ (setdefault) whenever TYPESAFE_API_KEY is unset. In a client project that has a .env, this pulls that project's secrets into the MCP process environment. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY explicitly in the MCP config avoids the read.

Supply chain: a 6-commit repo from a single anonymous author, 2 stars, created 11 days ago. Both README install commands (`uvx jev-mcp`, `uvx --from git+...`) run unpinned latest code. Dependencies are `>=`.

Prompt-injection surface: scan_injection and bash_risk take attacker-influenced text as `state` for a decision model. That is a classifier, not a chat model, so the output is bounded to probabilities. However, an attacker who controls the command or tool_output can craft content to lower the score, and a guard that fails to detect an attack is the failure that matters.

The tool design is structurally weak as a guard. The model has to choose to call scan_injection AFTER the untrusted text is already in its context, and then re-emit the whole text as a tool argument. That defeats the purpose and costs output tokens. bash_risk is the same: it is advisory only, so it is not a gate.
skill_router.py (root) silently sets HTTPS_PROXY/HTTP_PROXY to 127.0.0.1:7897 if that port is open. That is harmless for most users but is a surprising side effect. It is not used by the MCP server.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured base URL only (OpenRouter or api.typesafe.ai). bash_risk sends the full shell command plus the optional `context` string. scan_injection sends tool_name and the entire tool_output with no truncation or redaction, which can include code, file contents and secrets that appear in tool results. rank_candidates sends the query and up to 10 candidate passages, which are code or files. Nothing is sent unless the model calls a tool. Because the model chooses the arguments, whatever it decides to pass is what leaves the machine. There is no secret redaction, and the existing secret-leak hook would not see the MCP arguments unless its matcher covers mcp__jev__*. With OpenRouter as the provider, this data also passes through OpenRouter's and TypeSafe's logging policies, which matters for client projects.
entries.failureMode: There is no try/except anywhere in server.py, so an SDK exception (timeout, 429, 5xx, missing key) surfaces as an MCP tool error to the model. The SDK default is a 10 s timeout with up to 2 retries (SDK constants.py:22, retry.py:52), so a slow or down Jev can stall a tool call for about 30 s or more. With a missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY, `TypeSafeClient()` is built at import time (server.py:34), so the server most likely crashes at startup and shows as a failed MCP server. Because the tools are advisory and model-called, a failure is effectively fail-open: the model carries on and nothing is blocked. That is not a security guarantee. The server does not fail closed, and it has no configurable timeout.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Tool names + descriptions + schemas come to roughly 1.6-2.0k chars, or about 450-550 tokens, estimated from the docstrings and the parameter schemas. The server `instructions` string is about 230 chars, roughly 60 tokens. Total resident cost is about 0.5-0.6k tokens per session. The optional skill adds one description of about 800 chars, roughly 200 tokens. No hook-injected text, because there are no hooks.
pros: Cheap to try and OpenRouter-compatible by configuration. The SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, and the SDK path /v1/systemone plus base https://openrouter.ai/api gives exactly OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (SDK constants.py:6-15, _core/constants.py:5).

The Noul/Score prompts in server.py:79-143 are the most useful artifact. They are a well-worked four-dimension shell-risk rubric (destructive, secrets, exfiltration, irreversible) with true/false/not_for criteria and tuned thresholds. They could be lifted into a PreToolUse Bash hook, which is the deterministic integration this user actually wants. They fit a user who often runs in bypass or auto mode.

Real measured evidence exists (eval/results/*.jsonl are committed): InjecAgent P/R 100% at threshold 0.10 with 0% benign false positives, bash-gate danger catch 100% and benign pass 98.2% (README benchmark table, n=130 self-built), P50 0.3 s. A rare case of a Jev integration with data behind it, though vendor-adjacent and self-reported.
Tiny code (191-line server) and static reading found no shell exec, no postinstall, and no telemetry. Small enough to audit and vendor.
Low resident context cost of about 0.5k tokens for 3 tools.
cons: Not automatic. It ships only MCP tools and a skill, with no hooks (no hooks.json, no plugin.json). Claude Code will call scan_injection or bash_risk only if the model chooses to, which fails the user's core requirement. It cannot act as a gate in bypass mode.

scan_injection is the wrong shape for Claude Code. The text is already in context before the model can call it, and the model has to copy the whole output back as an argument, which costs tokens and can exceed the 32k Jev context. It would need to be a PostToolUse hook, not an MCP tool.

rank_candidates is not useful for coding. It scores at most 10 short passages, one sequential HTTP call each, and returns only indices. Claude Code already has Grep and GitNexus for code retrieval, so it adds nothing there.

The skill router is aimed at opencode and targets a 501-skill catalog. The user's skills list is about 40 with good descriptions already in the system prompt, so a Jev pre-selection step would save little and add a network hop. The router script also has the surprising HTTPS_PROXY auto-set behaviour.

The .env auto-loading (server.py:15-29) can pull an unrelated client project's .env into the process. There is no timeout config, no error handling, and the client is constructed at import, so a bad key crashes the server at startup.

Very immature and unaudited: 6 commits over 2 days, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no tests, no CI, no root LICENSE file. The README recommends unpinned `git+` execution. The repo is also mostly Chinese-language docs.
Data egress goes through a third-party classifier (via OpenRouter, then TypeSafe) and includes commands, tool outputs and code with no redaction, which is a concern on client projects.
The OpenRouter path is unverified end to end. The response schema was not confirmed to match the SDK's parser.
entries.verdict: Not worth installing as-is for automatic use. It is only model-discretion MCP tools, with no hook, so Claude Code will not use it on its own, and scan_injection is structurally the wrong tool shape. It is worth mining for the bash_risk rubric and thresholds (server.py:79-143), which could go into a PreToolUse hook, and it does show that an OpenRouter switch is config-only via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL.
entries.license: MIT declared in pyproject.toml and in skills/jev-skill-router/LICENSE. There is no root LICENSE file, and GitHub reports licenseInfo null.

entries.name: is-malicious
entries.what: npm CLI (is-malicious 0.1.1) plus a skills.sh agent skill that scans a repo for covert or data-stealing code. It walks eligible text files, packs them into chunks and sends full file contents to Jev's System One endpoint. Each request asks all check categories as Noul questions, plus a Score for overall risk and Choices for category, hot file and reason. Suspicious chunks get a second pass over line windows. It prints findings with file, line range, category, probability and confidence. Exit codes are 0 clean, 1 high finding, 2 error or skipped chunk. It is a one-shot security vetting tool for unfamiliar code, not a coding-assistance helper.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, model-discretion. The description says to use it 'immediately after git clone' and before install or run, so Claude Code will load it on its own after a clone. It is not a deterministic hook. A PostToolUse hook on Bash matching `git clone|gh repo clone` could make it deterministic. Nothing about it is Jev-as-decision-maker for normal coding.
security: Key handling is sound. The key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var only. It never goes in argv or the process list, and it is sent as a Bearer header to the configured base URL.
--base-url and TYPESAFE_BASE_URL let all file contents and the key go to any http(s) host, including plain http. Fine for OpenRouter, but a poisoned env var would exfiltrate the code.

The skill pushes `npx --yes is-malicious` on every run. That fetches and executes the latest npm version unpinned. Each scan is a supply-chain trust decision on a 2-maintainer, 5-day-old package (npm maintainer luantak, one account).
No npm postinstall script (package.json has only build, prepack, scan, test). No curl|sh. The only shell in the skill is run.sh, which is benign and uses exec.

No telemetry in the candidate code; the SDK's own telemetry was not verified beyond the endpoints found. Discovery skips .env and .env.* files, lockfiles and binaries. Commit 'fail closed and protect sensitive configs' shows credential-like JSON is filtered. Other secrets embedded in source files are still uploaded, and that filtering is best-effort.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted repo code is put into the Jev state. Jev returns only typed probabilities, which limits injection impact, but a hostile repo can still try to bias scores toward clean. The skill also tells the agent that high findings mean 'stop', so a crafted repo could cause a denial of work.
entries.dataEgress: Full contents of every eligible text file: source, config, build and CI files. Files are chunked, with extra blank lines collapsed, so the whole repo is uploaded, up to 400 KB per file. .env files, lockfiles, binaries, gitignored files and dist/lib/build output are excluded. Also sent: review rules, check prompts and line-window text on the second pass. Sent to api.typesafe.ai, or to whatever base URL is configured (OpenRouter, in the user's setup). Nothing else leaves the machine. This is a heavy upload for CLIENT projects, and it needs client consent and NDA review.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed for the scan. The SDK retries twice (maxRetries 2) with a 60s per-request timeout. Any chunk that cannot be scanned is listed as skipped and the CLI exits 2. The skill instructs the agent to say so and 'not invent a result'. It is not in the coding critical path: it is a standalone command, so a Jev outage cannot block edits or tool calls. Only the pre-install vet is affected. A missing key makes run.sh exit 2 immediately.
entries.contextCost: Small. One skill: the frontmatter description (~400 chars, about 100 tokens) is always in context. The SKILL.md body (~3.3k chars, about 800 tokens) loads only when the skill fires. No MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook-injected text. Report output (a few hundred to a few thousand tokens) lands in context only when a scan runs.
pros: Genuine, working Jev integration that uses all three primitives (noul, choice, score) in a sensible way, so it is a good reference for how to build typed-question prompts (src/jev.ts).

Auto-trigger is real and needs no user prompt. The SKILL.md description fires after git clone or gh repo clone and before npm install. This is a legitimate use case for a senior dev who pulls in unfamiliar repos.

OpenRouter works with no code change: base URL https://openrouter.ai/api plus a --model override. The SDK POSTs /v1/systemone with a Bearer header, which is the same surface OpenRouter exposes. The author added the base-url support explicitly (commit #5, 2026-09-23).
The key stays in env, never in argv. No postinstall. MIT licensed. Excludes .env, lockfiles and gitignored files. Cost is cheap: about $0.042 per 1M input tokens, and the report prints token usage.
--diff-from lets you vet only changed files. The exit-code contract (0/1/2) is clean, and the skill fails closed and says so instead of inventing results.
Has 13 test files, and the fail-closed and sensitive-config commits show some hardening.
cons: Wrong problem for daily coding. It only fires on git clone or on an explicit 'is this repo safe' question, so it adds nothing to editing, review, refactor or debugging turns. It does not use Jev to improve Claude Code's own decisions.
Uploads the ENTIRE repo contents to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter). Unsuitable for client projects without consent, and of little use on the user's own code.
Model-discretion skill only, not a hook. Trigger reliability depends on Claude noticing the clone. In bypass or auto mode Claude may skip it, or may run npm install first.

Needs manual patching for OpenRouter. The key must go in a misnamed TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL must be set, and run.sh has no --model passthrough. The documented TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL is not implemented, so the default 'jev-latest' would probably fail on OpenRouter, where the id is typesafe/jev-1.13. That means editing run.sh or calling the CLI directly.

Runs unpinned `npx --yes is-malicious`, executing third-party code from a 5-day-old, 2-maintainer, 2-release package with 33 stars, on the machine that holds the user's secrets. This is the same risk the tool claims to mitigate. Pin the version, or vendor it.

Immature and unreliable as a security control. No CI, beta model, and skeptics say Jev behaves like a small router model. Heuristic probabilities give both false negatives (a clean report gives false comfort) and false positives (the skill says 'stop, do not install' on high findings). The README concedes that a clean report is not proof.
Untrusted-repo content is fed to the model, which is a prompt-injection or score-biasing surface.
The instruction to stop on findings can interrupt legitimate workflows, and hidden cost accrues on large monorepos (400 KB files, 12-way concurrency, second passes).
entries.verdict: A real, cheap, OpenRouter-compatible (via base-url and model overrides) Jev skill with a genuine auto-trigger, but it only solves pre-install malware vetting after git clone. It does nothing for everyday coding, and it uploads whole repos and runs unpinned npx code. Treat it as an optional, pinned, niche add-on for unfamiliar third-party repos, not a core Jev integration, and never point it at client code without consent.

entries.name: win4r/jev-security-scan
entries.what: Not an MCP server: a Claude Code/Codex Agent Skill (SKILL.md + stdlib-only Python 3.10 CLI) that audits a LOCAL Skill/MCP project for prompt injection, credential theft, exfiltration, supply-chain, persistence etc. Runs regex static checks, then in jev mode sends redacted 12k-char source chunks to TypeSafe's System One API (Noul triage questions per category, then a verify pass with Choice window/context questions) and applies heuristic thresholds. Only useful for vetting third-party skills/MCPs before install, not for general coding.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only (model discretion): Claude may load it when the user asks to review/vet a skill or MCP for malicious behavior or before installing one. The Chinese description and narrow scope mean it will rarely trigger, and SKILL.md wants an explicit user request to authorize sending source to TypeSafe. Not a hook, not proactive.
security: Security-conscious design: never executes target code, refuses symlinks/FIFOs/protected secret files, output files 0600 and no overwrite, python -I -B isolation, redirects blocked (jev_client.py:11-14), response size cap 2MB, strict response validation
API key read from env or getpass, never argv (good; no process-list leak); passed only as Bearer header
Best-effort secret redaction only (scan.py:40-140); README/SKILL.md admit it does not anonymize proprietary source
Prompt-injection surface: it deliberately ingests untrusted third-party skill text; mitigated with a BOUNDARY prompt and SKILL.md 'treat as data', but the results feed Claude's report
No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry other than the TypeSafe calls; single 1-commit repo, no release, no signed tags, so supply-chain trust is only 'read it yourself' (small, 1200 lines)
Author is an individual (win4r), 11 stars, unaudited
entries.dataEgress: Only in jev mode: redacted source snippets (12k-char chunks, up to 400 files/8MB, up to 80 HTTP attempts) of the scanned Skill/MCP target plus relative filenames, to api.typesafe.ai. Not the user's own project, prompts, diffs or tool outputs unless the user points it at their own code. Local mode makes zero network calls. Normal OS proxy settings still apply.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open/soft at the tool level: it is a manual CLI, not in any request path, so Jev downtime cannot block Claude Code. Inside the scan: 45s timeout, one retry on 429/5xx after 2s, 401/403/redirect disables client; failures recorded as errors and reported as coverage gaps (exit 3), falling back to static findings; unverified triage hits become 'verification_unavailable' review findings.
entries.contextCost: Very low: no MCP tools, no hooks. One skill whose frontmatter description (~200 chars, in Chinese) sits in the skill listing (~60 tokens); the 4.5KB SKILL.md body (~1.1k tokens) loads only when the skill triggers. Nothing injected per turn.
pros: Genuine, well-engineered Jev use of both Noul and Choice primitives with a two-pass triage/verify design and strict schema validation (jev_client.py:22-52), a good reference implementation of the System One request shape {model,state,questions}
Very safe to install: stdlib-only, ~1200 lines, no hooks, no MCP server, no context bloat, key never in argv, redirects blocked, 29 offline tests + pinned CI

Real value for this user specifically: he installs third-party MCP servers/skills/plugins (gitnexus, caveman, playwright) and works on client projects, so vetting them is a legitimate security task; local mode is fully offline and free
Honest calibration language and coverage reporting (skipped files, failures, exit 3), no overclaiming
MIT, easy to fork; OpenRouter port is a few lines if the OpenRouter /v1/systemone envelope matches
cons: Not an MCP server and not for coding: it audits other people's skills/MCPs, so it adds no Jev value to daily edit/debug/refactor work
Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai with TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter support at all, contradicting the user's requirement, and needs a local fork with unverified response-schema compatibility

Cannot be automatic: it is an occasional, explicit-consent, manual scan; SKILL.md tells Claude to explain the source transfer and the Chinese description makes auto-triggering unlikely; no PreToolUse/install hook to vet MCPs on add

Immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 11 stars, no releases, 11 days old; only 4 self-authored synthetic specimens as validation, no accuracy data; author's own docs say two Jev passes are not independent verification
Sends source to a third party (redaction best-effort), a concern for client-owned code; Jev-specific gain over the static regex checks is unproven (Jev sometimes only downranks or reconfirms)
Fixed 45s timeout with sequential calls; large targets can consume up to 80 calls and unknown billing
entries.verdict: A tidy, safe, single-purpose Jev skill for vetting third-party Skills/MCPs, not a coding integration and not an MCP server; it is TypeSafe-only (hardcoded endpoint) and manual, so it fails the automatic and OpenRouter requirements. Worth a look only as a reference client or an optional forked pre-install audit tool, not as the core Jev integration.

entries.name: caiovicentino/jev-shield
entries.what: Semantic security layer built on Jev (model 'typesafe-ai/jev' via Vercel AI Gateway, using the Vercel `ai` SDK's experimental_evaluate). Ships four pieces in one repo. (1) A stdio MCP firewall proxy (`jev-shield wrap -- <cmd>`) that screens tools/list descriptions for poisoning, tool calls for exfiltration/destructive/injection/credential hazards, and tool results for injection/secrets, with taint tracking and JSONL audit. (2) A CLI `jev-shield verify` (JSON on stdin, typed verdict on stdout). (3) A Claude Code skill (SKILL.md) that tells the model to call the CLI before risky actions. (4) An opt-in Claude Code PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook, plus an opencode plugin. It is a security guardrail, not a coding-assist integration. It uses Jev Choice/Noul/Score-style questions (boolean and score) over tool-call and tool-output state.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. (a) The opt-in PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks are deterministic and fully automatic: no user prompting, and they cover all Bash, Edit, Write, WebFetch, WebSearch and mcp__* calls. (b) The skill is a description-triggered skill for risky actions only, and it is cooperative and unreliable. (c) The MCP proxy is transparent per wrapped server, but Claude Code's .mcp.json must be edited to wrap each server. Only (a) satisfies the requirement 'Claude Code must use it when needed' with no prompting, and only for security screening, not general decision-making.
security: MIT licensed, no telemetry code of its own. All screened data goes to Vercel AI Gateway and then to TypeSafe/Jev.
No curl|sh and no npm postinstall script (package.json has only demo/eval/install-* scripts). install.sh is local-only and uses sed with the repo path.

The hook has a fallback to `npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield verify` when LOCAL_SRC is empty (hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs:23). That would be an unpinned run of GitHub HEAD code on every tool call. With install-hooks the path is rewritten to the local checkout, so it is only a risk if the hook is copied by hand.

The SKILL.md tells the model to run `npx -y jev-shield verify` and falls back to `npx -y github:caiovicentino/jev-shield`. That is an unpinned, mutable dependency executed by the agent. The unscoped npm name `jev-shield` is not shown to be owned by the author, so it is a typosquat or dependency-confusion risk.

install-hooks.mjs rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json wholesale (JSON.parse then JSON.stringify). This would silently drop comments or unusual formatting, and it edits user config without a backup. It also stacks with existing hooks: PreToolUse Bash and mcp__.* would run alongside the user's secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.

verify-cli.mjs:198-202 loads a .env file from the repo root into process.env. That is benign, but it is a secrets file read outside the user's control. The API key is in the environment, not in argv, so it is not visible in `ps`.
entries.dataEgress: Everything screened goes to Vercel AI Gateway and then to the Jev provider. PreToolUse sends the full tool_input JSON (ev.tool_input) with no truncation for calls: entire Bash commands (which can contain inline secrets), full Write/Edit/MultiEdit content and diffs (i.e. source code, including client code), WebFetch/WebSearch URLs and queries, and all mcp__* arguments. PostToolUse sends the first 8000 and last 4000 characters of every Bash, WebFetch, WebSearch, Grep and mcp__* result (file contents, command output, search hits). The MCP proxy mode sends the full tools/list schemas plus up to 12k characters of each result. The prompts and chat are not sent. On the user's setup this covers personal and client code, and Vercel becomes an additional data processor, a contractual issue for client work. Vercel's data retention is not documented in this repo.
entries.failureMode: The hook and CLI fail open by default, but the user experience of that is poor. If verification errors (no key, network down, Vercel outage, or a 30 s timeout on execFileSync), then in PreToolUse the hook does not silently pass. It emits permissionDecision 'ask' with 'verification unavailable' (hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs:84-90). In a session without AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, every Bash/Write/Edit/MCP call would therefore raise a confirmation prompt, which also undermines the user's bypass mode. In PostToolUse, failure means exit 0 (pass). JEV_FAIL_MODE=closed makes it exit 2, which blocks. The timeout is 30 s per call with the local checkout, or 60 s via the npx fallback, and it is synchronous, so an outage or hang stalls the agent for up to 30 s per tool call. The MCP proxy's verifyCall catch block fails open as 'annotate' (verify.mjs:180); with fail_mode closed it blocks.
entries.contextCost: Near zero context by default. The hooks add no tool definitions, and the MCP proxy adds no tools of its own, only wraps the ones you give it. The only context cost is the skill description, roughly 100 tokens (SKILL.md:3, about 430 chars). If the skill body is invoked, it adds about 1.1k tokens (4.4 KB). Hook text is injected only on a flag: a deny/ask reason (short) or a PostToolUse block reason (about 60 tokens). Flagged MCP tool descriptions get an appended warning line.
pros: The only candidate found so far with a fully deterministic, no-prompt Claude Code integration of Jev: the PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks in hooks/claude-code/jev-shield.mjs need no 'use jev' from the user, which matches the automatic-integration requirement.

Makes real use of Jev's calibrated probabilities as a typed decision engine (boolean and score questions batched in one call, policy thresholds review 0.35 / action 0.7 / severity_block 2.0 in config/policies.json). This is a legitimate System One use case rather than a chat replacement.
Has a working opt-out (uninstall-hooks.mjs, JEV_HOOK_OFF=1) and a documented kill switch. Cost is tiny (about $0.00002 to $0.00003 per check, 4.2e-8 USD per input token in verify.mjs:7).

Ships an eval harness (eval/run.mjs, about 23 KB) and a candid report with documented limitations (truncation bypass, over-blocking of .env to internal recipients, PII in support tickets) instead of only marketing numbers.

The prompt-injection screen of PostToolUse results (WebFetch, WebSearch, MCP output) is genuinely useful for a client-work setup that runs in bypass or auto permission mode, where nothing else checks fetched content.

MIT license, no telemetry code, no install-time code execution beyond the explicit install scripts. The code is small (about 135 KB total, of which 46 KB is the lockfile) and quick to audit in full; I read all of the runtime code.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the only provider is the Vercel AI Gateway (verify.mjs:1, policies.json:2, AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY everywhere). The user must create a Vercel account and key, or fork and rewrite runEval against openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, which contradicts the OpenRouter-hosted Jev requirement.

Wrong job for daily coding: it is a security gate that adds a verdict only on risk, not a decision helper that improves coding (no routing, triage, or 'does this test need to run' style use). It helps with injection defense but does not make Claude Code faster or better at coding.

Heavy per-call overhead: two hook events, each spawning node plus the `ai` SDK and a network round trip, adding about 1 to 3 s to every Bash/Edit/Write/MCP call, on top of the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks. That is a large cumulative cost for all-day agentic sessions.

Broad data egress to a third party: every Bash command, full file write/edit content and 12k characters of every tool result go to Vercel and TypeSafe. Unacceptable by default for client projects under NDA, and it works against the user's own secret-leak guard hook, which exists to keep secrets off the network.

Fail-open is actually fail-to-prompt: when the key is missing or the gateway is down, the PreToolUse hook returns permissionDecision 'ask' for every call (jev-shield.mjs:86-89). In the user's bypass or auto mode this creates constant prompts, or is ignored, so the result is either friction or silent no-op. There is no local timeout shorter than 30 s.

False-positive risk in normal dev work: its own report shows `.env` or customer exports to internal recipients, and PII, scored payload_sensitivity 0.92-0.93 and blocked. A coding agent routinely touches .env, migrations, curl calls and git push --force, so 'annotate' becomes 'ask' and 'block' becomes deny, which would collide with the user's workflow.

Immature: 8 commits over one day (2026-09-16 to 2026-09-17), single contributor, 4 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, no unit tests (only a self-run eval against the live API), and nothing since 2026-09-17. README explicitly says it is not a security boundary.

Installer hazards: install-hooks.mjs rewrites the user's ~/.claude/settings.json without backup, the hook has an unpinned `npx github:` fallback, and the skill recommends `npx -y jev-shield` (unverified unscoped npm name). audit.jsonl in the repo dir logs command and output previews in plaintext.

Its own truncation is a known bypass (injection past 12k or after the 8000+4000 hook window is missed), so the security value is partial. Also, the hook classifies Bash as a generic 'shell_exec' with the description 'Execute a shell command on the host', with no repo context, which limits precision.
entries.verdict: The only concrete, automatic (hook-based) Jev integration for Claude Code found in this audit, but it is a security-screening gate and not a coding aid, and it is hard-wired to the Vercel AI Gateway, not OpenRouter. Its latency cost of roughly 1 to 3 s per tool call and its broad data egress make it a poor fit for this user's all-day client work. It is worth reading as a reference hook design, or forking to OpenRouter's Decisions API for a narrow use such as PostToolUse injection screening of WebFetch/WebSearch only, but not worth installing as-is.

entries.name: revsmoke/promptrejectormcp (Prompt Rejector)
entries.what: Security scanner for prompts, SKILL.md files, MCP tool descriptors and agent capability sets. It combines deterministic pattern checks with Jev Noul/Choice judgments (TypeSafe /v1/systemone) and a Gemini reasoning model. It ships an 11-tool stdio MCP server, an HTTPS REST API (/v2/*), and a Claude Code/Codex plugin with a SKILL.md. It uses Jev as a classifier, not as a coding-assistance decision engine. The agent must call it explicitly; the author states that the application or agent has to invoke the scanner.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger that fires only for Prompt Rejector setup or a requested security review. The SKILL.md explicitly says it does not require scanning every conversation or changing global agent behavior. Only the tool descriptions ('Use this before processing any untrusted user input', 'before installing any third-party skill') might nudge the model to call it. There is no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook and no proxy, so nothing is deterministic.
security: Keys are read from env or .env. The plugin launcher spawns node with env: process.env and no shell (plugins/prompt-rejector/scripts/launch.mjs). Keys are not passed in argv, and the docs say logs and config contain no key values.

Fail-safe design: the decision policy returns 'unavailable' or 'review' rather than 'allow' when coverage is incomplete (DecisionPolicy.ts). The SKILL.md tells the agent not to translate unavailable to allow.

No curl|sh installer and no postinstall script in package.json. CI uses npm ci --ignore-scripts. Install is a manual clone, npm ci and build. Dependencies include express, jose, @anthropic-ai/sdk and @google/generative-ai.
update_vuln_feeds and deploy_canary mutate local state. The optional taste_test runs Taster/Monitor with mocked tools against an Anthropic model, and is off by default.

Prompt-injection surface: the scanner ingests hostile text and passes it as Jev/Gemini 'state'. The verdict is model-based and can be evaded; the README itself says it is not a guarantee. The result is untrusted-content-in, structured-decision-out, so output injection risk is low.

No telemetry code found (grep for telemetry/analytics in src is empty). Egress is limited to configured providers plus NVD, GitHub advisories, CISA KEV, OSV and HuggingFace lookups for feeds and model references.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever text the agent submits to a tool leaves the machine: the prompt, skill file, or tool descriptor JSON (up to 100k UTF-16 units for prompts, 500k for skills). It goes as `state` to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (Jev) and also to Google Gemini for the reasoning role in the default profile, so there are two third-party recipients. Skill scans may also trigger HuggingFace GET lookups for referenced model IDs. Feed and CVE tools hit NVD, GHSA, KEV and OSV with search parameters only. Nothing is sent unless the agent calls a tool. If it were auto-invoked on every code edit, source code and diffs would go to both providers.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at the verdict level: Jev timeout (default judgmentTimeoutMs 2000 ms, max 30000; Gemini 15 s), missing key or an invalid response gives status unavailable, so check_prompt returns decision 'unavailable' or 'review' (never a silent allow). Because it is an MCP tool the agent chooses to call, this cannot block Claude Code itself. With no hook, there is nothing to hang a turn. The transport has a concurrency limit of 2 and a queue of 32. If the server process fails to start, the MCP server simply appears failed and Claude Code carries on.
entries.contextCost: 11 MCP tools. The tool names, descriptions and input schemas in src/mcp/mcpServer.ts lines 85-255 total about 9.2k characters, roughly 2.3k tokens, which is deferrable through Claude Code's tool search. There are no MCP server 'instructions' (grep found none). The plugin adds one SKILL.md whose description is about 400 characters, roughly 100 tokens, always in the skills listing. No hook-injected text.
pros: Real, non-trivial Jev integration: a native, strictly validated /v1/systemone adapter using Noul and Choice, with probability-sum checks, model pinning and batched questions (TypeSafeAdapter.ts).
Fail-closed decision policy that never turns an unavailable or incomplete result into allow (DecisionPolicy.ts), with a 2 s Jev timeout.
Ships a Claude Code plugin/marketplace with a launcher that uses no shell and no npm, and has no postinstall script or curl|sh installer.
Useful niche for this user: vetting third-party MCP servers, skills and plugins before installing them. That fits this evaluation task, where skills and MCPs are being adopted.
Offline replay tests and committed live-smoke evaluations make the Jev claims checkable without spending credits.
Small context footprint (about 2.3k tokens for 11 tools, no server instructions, no hooks).
cons: Hard-codes api.typesafe.ai; there is no OpenRouter support, base-URL override or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. It needs a fork patch (URL, key env, model-ID regex, resolved-model check, strict envelope schema) and OpenRouter's response shape is unverified.

The default profile requires a second provider (GEMINI_API_KEY) for the reasoning role. Prompt and skill decisions cannot reach 'allow' on Jev alone, so a second vendor also receives the scanned text.

Not automatic: no hooks. It never runs unless the model decides to call a tool or the user asks, which fails the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' goal. Building a hook around it would mean wiring PreToolUse to a local HTTPS API yourself.
Scope mismatch: it is a security classifier for untrusted text, not a coding aid. Nothing here uses Jev for routing, code review or commit decisions.
Multi-second latency per scan (Gemini leg) and a paid call on both providers per check; scanning every prompt or diff would leak client code to two vendors.
Heavy setup: source checkout, npm ci and build, .env, optional mkcert TLS for the REST API. It is not on npx.
Immature and single-maintainer: 2 stars, 3 forks, about 8 months old, mostly AI-authored commits, v1.2.0 released 2026-09-21. Sprawling docs (PLAN, SPEC, RESEARCH_*) for a small user base.
Detection quality is only vendor-evidenced (a synthetic recorded example); the README disclaims guarantees.
entries.verdict: A genuine, well-engineered Jev consumer, but it is a manual prompt/skill/MCP-descriptor security scanner rather than an automatic daily-coding integration. It is hard-wired to api.typesafe.ai, needs Gemini too, and has no hooks. It is worth keeping as an optional, occasional vetting tool for third-party skills and MCP servers after patching or accepting direct TypeSafe billing. It is not the answer to 'Jev via OpenRouter, automatically'.

entries.name: xienda/dsh-jev-verify
entries.what: DeepSeek Harness plugin: jev_decision, jev_verify, jev_guard_status tools; opt-in auto-guard (regex blacklist then Jev risk noul, loop guard); live benchmark of 27 labeled questions.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic pre-execute hook (DSH) + model-discretion tools
pros: Deterministic blacklist first, then Jev risk noul; fail-open with warning; same shape as the OpenRouter cookbook gate
jev_verify measures accuracy/latency/calibration against the live API (96.3% on 27 cases, own report)
baseURL is a settings field so re-pointing is feasible
cons: DSH plugin format, not Claude Code; needs a port
Benchmark of 27 cases is small and self-reported
Fail-open guard would deny/allow on overconfident Jev

entries.name: jevcoreagent
entries.what: Local Node/TypeScript stdio MCP server plus CLI (jevcore / jev-guard) that acts as a risk and safety gate for coding agents, not as a general coding helper. It composes a deterministic regex hard-policy (secrets, rm -rf, force push, DB migrations, auth, payments, CI privilege, web3) with one batched TypeSafe System One call (@typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0: Choice for task domain, Score for 4-level risk, several Noul questions for risk factors and security review). It returns a typed decision (execute / plan_first / approval_required / block). The Claude Code adapter is only templates: an optional PreToolUse Bash hook that runs the deterministic `jev-guard check` (no Jev call), and an advisory CLAUDE.md telling the model when to call the MCP tools. Built Cursor-first; the runtime dir is ~/.cursor/jev-coding-guard/.
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. (a) MCP tools are model-discretion, steered by an advisory CLAUDE.md that you would have to merge yourself (no automatic install into ~/.claude). Claude may skip or ignore them, and the README itself says the hook is the hard gate and the CLAUDE.md is advisory. (b) The optional PreToolUse Bash hook is deterministic and automatic but does not call Jev, only regex policy. Jev is therefore not on any deterministic path. There is no UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse or Stop hook and no skill.
security: API key: read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var by the SDK. The MCP config example uses env `${TYPESAFE_API_KEY}` expansion, and `claude mcp add --env KEY=...` would place the key in the argv and process list, which is the documented pattern. The key is stored in ~/.claude.json in plaintext unless the env-expansion form is used. Docs say the server never exposes the key.
No postinstall/preinstall scripts. package.json scripts are build/test/tools only. No curl|sh installers. The npm tarball contains dist, src and adapters (237 files).

Shell execution: the server itself runs none. context-router.ts runs `git` via spawnSync to list candidate paths in the cwd, and setup.ts runs `node --check` (doctor). The PreToolUse hook spawns node with the command on stdin, not on argv.
Telemetry: none to third parties. Opt-in local SQLite (JEV_GUARD_LOCAL_EVIDENCE=1) with de-identified metadata, off by default. The only network egress is the TypeSafe/SDK call.

Prompt-injection surface: tool inputs (userTask, diffSummary, repositoryContext) come from the model and go into the Jev state, so injected text can skew the classification. Hard-policy regexes run first and can only escalate. Output is typed, but the CLAUDE.md tells the model to print 'agent.headline/plan' text verbatim, which is a small model-echo surface.

Hard policy is regex-based, so it is evadable, and it is prone to false positives (any 'auth', 'token', 'DELETE FROM', 'migration', 'deploy' mention triggers approval_required or block). Secret redaction is also regex-based.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL host): a Bearer key plus JSON state {task, touchedFiles[], mentionsProduction, context} and the question definitions. The task, command, diffSummary and testSummary strings are model-authored and pass through redactSecrets (regex) first (policy.ts:881-896, engine.ts:245). Preflight `block` rules (secret paths, rm -rf and similar) send nothing. Not sent: raw file contents or full diffs, unless Claude puts them in diffSummary or repositoryContext. File paths of touched files are sent. Fan-out (default on) can make a second call, and context rerank (default on) can make an extra call with candidate path identifiers. For client projects, task descriptions and repo paths still leave the machine via OpenRouter to TypeSafe, and OpenRouter logs metadata.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe, not fail-open. The MCP provider timeout is 25 s (15 s for the rerank) and the SDK also retries. On provider failure or invalid output, the engine falls back deterministically: ordinary tasks become plan_first, elevated-risk ones become approval_required, and block comes only from hard policy. Under CLAUDE.md, plan_first means show a plan and wait, and 'do not continue with high-risk actions while the assessment is unavailable'. A slow or down Jev therefore stalls or nags the workflow instead of silently passing. An MCP tool error is reported to the model as isError. The PreToolUse hook fails closed (deny) on a missing binary or errors. It calls no network, timeout 15 s inside a 30 s hook limit.
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (jev_assess_task, jev_assess_command, jev_review_diff, jev_guard_report). The estimate for tool names, descriptions and input schemas is about 1.2-2k tokens (12+ .describe fields, batchItems and batchStrategy options), plus outputSchemas if the client includes them. There are no MCP 'instructions' (capabilities: {tools:{}} only). The advisory CLAUDE.md adds about 700 tokens on every session if merged into ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. Every assess result includes an `agent` Contract block (headline, plan, choices, actions) that the CLAUDE.md asks Claude to print verbatim, adding hundreds of tokens per call. The hook injects only a short reason string on ask or deny.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's typed primitives (Choice, Score, Noul) in one batched systemOne call, and code owns the workflow. That matches the intended use of System One, with a real question pack in src/question-packs.ts.

The Jev call goes through the official @typesafe-ai/sdk with a configurable TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. The path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone, so the switch is plausible with env changes plus one model-id patch.
Hard-policy runs first, offline and deterministic. Blocking rules make zero model calls, and the model can never override a block. Secrets are regex-redacted before egress.
Fail-safe design: provider errors and invalid risk scores degrade to plan_first, never clamp or fabricate. Fail-closed hook.

Ships an explicit Claude Code adapter (MCP config, PreToolUse hook, CLAUDE.md, dry-run installer) that never touches ~/.claude.json, and a Jev-independent `jevcore check` CLI usable as a secret and destructive-command guard.
About 60 test files with a fake provider, Apache-2.0, no install scripts, opt-in local-only telemetry. Read-only tool annotations.
Local evidence and report tool could later show how often Jev changed the mode.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for daily coding: it gates risk (approve, plan, block), it does not help write, find or review code. It gives Claude no code-quality signal, only a domain label and a risk number.
Not automatic in the way you want. Jev is only reached if Opus chooses to call an MCP tool following an advisory CLAUDE.md. The one deterministic piece (the Bash hook) does not use Jev at all.

Conflicts with your bypass/auto permission workflow. The policy returns approval_required for any auth, migration, deploy, payments, npm publish, CI secrets or terraform work, and the hook maps that to `ask`. It also stacks a fourth Bash hook next to your secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks. Regex rules produce false positives on ordinary client work.

OpenRouter is not supported out of the box: no OpenRouter code, the model is hardcoded to bare 'jev-latest' (provider.ts:228) and the MCP entrypoint does not pass a model. It needs a patch or fork and an untested compatibility check of the request/response shape.

Cursor-first codebase: the runtime dir is ~/.cursor/jev-coding-guard, docs use `zsh -lc`, the Write hook uses Cursor's protocol. The Claude Code parts are templates that the user must wire up by hand.

Very immature: repo and npm package created 2026-09-22, 4 commits in one day, 1 star, one anonymous maintainer, no CI, 0.1.x alpha. Not vetted for a client-project dependency that receives your task text and API key.
Sends task descriptions, file paths and context summaries of client projects to TypeSafe via OpenRouter, with no way to keep it fully local other than skipping Jev.

Latency and context tax on invoked turns: an extra tool call plus a mandatory verbatim 'JEVCore:' print block per assessment, and a fail-safe fallback that downgrades to plan_first when Jev is slow or down.
Its own README says 'IDE/CI integration beyond that is still future work', and the Jev value claims (latency, calibration) are not backed by published results.
entries.verdict: Real Jev integration (Choice/Score/Noul via the official SDK) but it is a risk-gate/approval layer, not a coding accelerator, and the Claude Code side is advisory templates plus a hook that does not call Jev. It is a day-old, single-maintainer, Cursor-first alpha with no OpenRouter model support and it clashes with bypass-mode workflows. Worth mining for its question-pack and policy ideas, or using the Jev-independent `jevcore check` idea, but not something to install as the daily driver.

entries.name: kierandotai/jev-scout
entries.what: Node MCP stdio server that replaces Claude Code's WebSearch/WebFetch with guarded_search, guarded_fetch and research_report. It wraps SearXNG, Brave or DuckDuckGo, makes one Jev call per search result (relevance, credibility, worth_fetching) and one per fetched page (answered, content_class, steering_risk), and annotates or gates the results. It writes a JSONL ledger under ~/.jev-scout and serves a local SSE dashboard. It is a web-research observability tool, not a coding-assistance tool.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. There are no hooks and no skill. The README states 'coverage is voluntary by design'. Claude can still use the built-in WebSearch/WebFetch instead. The only way to force use is `permissions.deny: ["WebSearch","WebFetch"]`, and that removes the native tools entirely.
security: Keys are read from process.env inside jev-client (server-mcp.ts:690 comment) and are never put in argv. The .env file is the recommended place.

SSRF guard on guarded_fetch: blocks loopback, RFC1918, link-local/metadata, CGNAT and IPv6 mapped ranges, and re-validates each redirect hop. The DNS-rebinding window is documented as residual and is not closed.

Prompt-injection handling: untrusted titles, snippets and page excerpts are wrapped in delimiters with a 'data not instructions' clause (judge.ts ~46-51). steering_risk is advisory only, and fetched text is still returned to Claude in full.
Adds a new web-fetch path with only partial protection. It gives the model an unguarded-content channel unless the built-in WebFetch is denied.
Dashboard binds 127.0.0.1 on an ephemeral port and rejects any Host header other than 127.0.0.1:<port> (dashboard.ts:197).
Writes a persistent JSONL ledger to ~/.jev-scout/ledger-YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (ledger.ts:87). The payload holds queries, goals and URLs. Page bodies are hashed, not stored.
entries.dataEgress: Search queries go to SearXNG (self-hosted), Brave or DuckDuckGo. Fetched URLs are requested directly by Node. To Jev, via OpenRouter, it sends only a whitelist: goal, query, result title, snippet, domain, or a pre-truncated page excerpt for the fetch judgment (README 'Noisy state is filtered'; judge.ts ~244). It does not send source code, diffs or Claude's transcript, unless the model puts code in the search `goal` or `query` strings. The OpenRouter bearer key goes in the Authorization header. Locally, a ledger of queries and URLs is written to ~/.jev-scout.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. A Jev error or timeout delivers the result unscored (`scored:false`), and the budget reservation is refunded (pipeline.ts ~230, catch block). An exhausted budget passes results through with budget_exhausted:true. The per-call timeout is 30 s (DEFAULT_JUDGE_TIMEOUT_MS at pipeline.ts:147). jev-client retries on RETRY_STATUSES with backoff, MAX_ATTEMPTS attempts. Judging is sequential (`for` loop with await, pipeline.ts ~253), so with 8 results and a slow Jev a single search could take up to 8 x 30 s. Session caps are 300 calls and $0.05. If the search backend chain fails, guarded_search returns a backend_chain_failed error. The DDG fallback is often blocked.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools (guarded_search, guarded_fetch, research_report), with zod input and output schemas for each. The descriptions run to about 400-700 chars each and bake in the mode and thresholds. Estimate about 1.5-2.5k tokens for tool definitions, from chars/4. No MCP `instructions` block and no hooks, so no per-turn injection. Each guarded_search response adds annotation JSON for 8 results (scores, confidence, reasons), which is likely 1-3k tokens per search on top of the results.
pros: Real, working Jev integration with OpenRouter as a first-class provider: OpenRouterProvider posts to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 (jev-client src/providers.ts:74-85).
Fail-open design (pipeline.ts catch block), per-process budget caps (300 calls / $0.05) and an unscored badge mean it cannot block or silently bill you much.
Solid engineering for a PoC: SSRF-guarded fetcher, 13 test files, an injection-aware rubric and a versioned rubric with drift harness.
Cheap: about $0.0001 per judgment, and the cache skips repeats.
steering_risk on fetched pages is a useful prompt-injection tripwire when Claude reads untrusted docs or web pages.
No hooks or context injection, so it will not conflict with your existing PreToolUse secret-guard, GitNexus or caveman hooks.
cons: Solves web-research source scoring, not coding decisions. It does not do code-path routing, permission gating, commit classification or test triage, so it adds no value for most of a day of coding.
Not automatic. Claude may keep using the built-in WebSearch/WebFetch. Forcing use means denying those tools, which replaces well-tuned native search with a SearXNG or DDG setup you must run.

Heavy setup: a docker SearXNG container with a settings.yml edit, two sibling repos to clone and build (jev-client is a file: dependency, unpublished), and an env-loading gotcha because `claude mcp add` does not read .env.
No license (licenseInfo null), 0 stars, 1 contributor, 11 days old, no releases and no CI. That is a risk for client projects.
Env trap: if AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY or VERCEL_AI_GATEWAY_KEY is set anywhere, jev-client 'auto' prefers the Vercel gateway over OpenRouter. Pin JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter.
Sequential per-result Jev calls can add seconds per search, and the zero-config DDG backend is often blocked.
Adds 3 tools (about 1.5-2.5k tokens) to every session, permanently, for occasional use.
Accuracy claims (88% relevance, 96% credibility) come from a 25-item self-labeled set run through a different provider.
Writes a persistent query and URL ledger under ~/.jev-scout, which matters for client work.
entries.verdict: A competent but narrow proof of concept. It works with OpenRouter-hosted Jev, but it only scores web search results and pages, which is a small part of daily coding. It is model-discretion rather than automatic, and it has no license. I would skip it as a core integration. At most, use it as a reference for jev-client's OpenRouter request shape when building a hook-based Jev integration.
entries.license: None (GitHub reports licenseInfo null; no LICENSE file). Legally all rights reserved, which matters for use on client projects.

entries.name: @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails (repo codebam/jev-guardrails)
entries.what: Monorepo by a single author. (1) @codebam/jev-guardrails: a TypeScript library that asks Jev typed guardrail questions (screenInput, assessAction, screenObservation, verifyClaim) and maps the probabilities to allow/review/block; it has transports for TypeSafe direct, OpenRouter Decisions, and a hosted service. (2) @codebam/eval-jev-guardrails (the audited npm package): an `eval-jev` CLI plus OpenCode, Hermes Agent and DeepSeek Harness pre-tool-call hook installers. These hooks only talk to a paid third-party proxy, https://eval.seanbehan.ca (Cloudflare Worker + D1 + Stripe, prepaid credits), not to OpenRouter. (3) @codebam/dsh-jev-guardrails: a DeepSeek Harness plugin. (4) apps/eval-site: the Worker source for the proxy. There is no Claude Code integration anywhere in the repo, and the word "claude" appears nowhere in it.
interface: Library API: createGuardrails().screenInput / assessAction / screenObservation / screenOutput / verifyClaim
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook in OpenCode/Hermes/dsh (tool.execute.before, pre_tool_call, tools/pre-execute). For Claude Code it is NOT available out of the box. A PreToolUse command hook (deterministic, fires every tool call, model never prompted) could be built on the library, but that is custom work.
security: Key handling: the eval_ key is stored in ~/.config/eval-jev/config.json with mode 600 and dir 700 (config.ts:152-154). It is sent as a Bearer header, not in argv. The OpenRouter transport also uses a Bearer header (openrouter.ts:157).

Egress trust: with the audited hook package, every tool call goes to a single individual's hosted service. Its D1 schema has an evaluations table with request_hash, verdict_json, tokens and cost, and a global cache keyed by request hash. Full request state may or may not be logged, and the hook cannot verify that. The operator holds the OpenRouter key and can read all traffic.

No client-side redaction in the hook package: grep for redact finds nothing in eval-jev-guardrails/src. Only the library has redact.ts (best-effort patterns for AWS, GitHub, sk-, JWT, bearer and private keys). The hosted hooks send raw tool arguments, including Write contents, Bash commands and inline secrets.
The threat model doc admits the agent can edit the plugin or key, and that fail-open is not a safety guarantee (docs/threat-model.md).

Prompt injection: the block reason is returned to the model as text. The verdict text comes from the remote service, which is a low-risk injection channel if the service is compromised. Jev itself returns typed output.
Shell execution: the CLI runs only xdg-open/open (cli.ts:287-290). No postinstall or preinstall scripts (only prepublishOnly). No curl|sh installer.
entries.dataEgress: The audited hook package sends, for each guarded tool call, {side:'action', state:{tool, arguments (full tool input: Bash commands, Write/Edit contents, file paths, URLs), workspace (cwd path)}, sessionID/callID} to https://eval.seanbehan.ca/v1/evaluate. It is not redacted client-side. The Worker then forwards it to OpenRouter Decisions with its own key. The library route with provider 'openrouter' would send a redacted state directly from your machine to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with your key, which is better. Tool results and prompts are not sent by the OpenCode/Hermes hooks (only actions), unless you use the library's screenObservation or screenInput.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default (hook.ts:15, DEFAULT_FAIL_MODE='open'). EVAL_FAIL_MODE can be open, review or closed. The client timeout is 5000 ms by default (client.ts:232-238, EVAL_TIMEOUT_MS). A `review` verdict is denied by default, which risks false-positive blocks. The library has retries: 2 retries with backoff, up to 5 s, which adds delay before failing. With the worst-case timeout of 5 s per tool call, an outage could stall every call before it falls open.
entries.contextCost: Nothing in Claude Code today: the package ships no MCP server, skill or Claude Code hook. A custom hook built on the library would add 0 tool definitions and 0 context tokens, except when it blocks; the reason text (~50-80 tokens) is fed back to the model. Any Claude Code hook that emitted extra additionalContext would add tokens.
pros: Shows a working pattern: a deterministic pre-tool-call hook that asks Jev a typed Choice/Score question and maps its probabilities to allow/review/block with a fail-mode setting. That is the kind of automatic, prompt-free integration the user wants (a Claude Code PreToolUse hook could reuse the decision table in hook.ts).

The library @codebam/jev-guardrails has a real OpenRouter Decisions transport (openrouter.ts) using the ~typesafe/jev-latest model, with retries, an OPENROUTER_API_KEY env var and the correct endpoint /api/alpha/decisions. It is the only candidate I saw that implements the Decisions API with the right schema.
The library has a best-effort secret redactor (redact.ts) that runs before state is sent, and a cache (cache.ts) that reduces repeat calls and cost.
Configurable: fail-open/review/closed, review allow/deny, and tool skip and allow lists (EVAL_SKIP_TOOLS / EVAL_GUARD_TOOLS) are useful for tuning the hook to skip Read/Grep.
MIT license, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh installer, an honest threat-model doc, and a test suite included in the repo.
cons: No Claude Code support at all: the hooks are for OpenCode, Hermes and DeepSeek Harness. Zero occurrences of 'claude' in the repo. There is no stdin/stdout PreToolUse adapter, no hooks.json snippet and no settings.json installer.

The packaged hooks route via the author's paid proxy eval.seanbehan.ca (prepaid Stripe credits, EVAL_API_KEY), not OpenRouter. That conflicts with the user's stated wish to use OpenRouter-hosted Jev, and it sends raw tool arguments (client code, commands, possible secrets) from client projects to an unknown individual's server. That is a serious client-confidentiality problem.
No client-side redaction in the hook package, unlike the library.

Only guards (a safety classifier for tool calls). It gives no other Jev value in daily coding: it does not route work, pick tools, triage or rank. With Opus 5.5 in auto/bypass mode it duplicates the existing secret-leak guard and Claude Code's own permission classifier.

Fail-open default with a 5 s timeout and retries, and `review` denied by default: a slow Jev stalls every tool call, and false positives will block legitimate calls like rm -rf node_modules or curl|bash in scripts.

Immature: 10 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 15 commits, no CI, no releases, and a version string mismatch. It is a commercial side product that could disappear or change pricing; it needs a paid key before the first call.
Adds one network hop per tool call on top of the existing three global PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).
entries.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code as shipped and not OpenRouter-native: the eval-jev hooks target OpenCode, Hermes and dsh and route all tool-call data through the author's paid proxy. The only reusable part is the @codebam/jev-guardrails library (OpenRouter Decisions transport plus redaction), which someone could wrap in a custom PreToolUse hook for a narrow safety-check use. Treat it as a reference implementation, not an install.

entries.name: 24601/rh-guard
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + skill + hooks) that guards against reward-hacking by agents (editing tests/graders/hidden evals, hooks, oversight files). It needs a locally running Next.js "sidecar" (npm run dev on 127.0.0.1:43147). The sidecar runs regex/structural detectors first, then makes one Jev System One call per hook event (about 14 Noul questions plus 1 Choice plus 1 Score) to score risk. In enforce mode it returns deny or steer text to Claude Code. It is an eval-integrity gate for agent evals and benchmarks, not a general coding assistant. It gives no code review, routing, or other help.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse on Bash|Edit|Write|StrReplace, Stop). It fires automatically with no user prompting, but it is a gate/scorer only and adds no capability. The skill is description-triggered and rarely relevant.
security: MIT license. Repo created 2026-09-17, so it is 13 days old. Latest commit 2026-09-28. 153 commits from 2 authors (Basit Mustafa 124, 'Cursor Agent' 29). 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases. package.json is private:true, so it is not published to npm.

Installing it means git clone + npm install of a Next 16 / React 19 / shadcn app (about 390 KB package-lock). That is a large dependency surface for a hook, and npm install can run dependency postinstall scripts. package.json itself has no postinstall.
API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, .env.local) in the sidecar process and sent as a Bearer header via fetch. It is not put in argv. The hook script itself carries no secret.

The sidecar listens on an unauthenticated localhost HTTP port (43147). It is bound to 127.0.0.1 in the npm scripts. Any local process can POST to it and spend the Jev key, and can read scoring responses.
claude-hook.sh runs curl --data-binary @- with input from stdin, so payloads stay out of argv. No shell execution of untrusted input was found in hooks/*.sh. hooks/run.ts uses JSON.parse only.

The tool_input and prompt sent to Jev are untrusted data placed in Jev's 'state'. The answers are typed probabilities and cannot inject free text. Deny and steer messages to Claude are fixed constants (AGENT_DENY / AGENT_STEER), so there is no free-text injection path back into Claude.
entries.dataEgress: To the local sidecar, on every matched event: the entire raw Claude hook JSON (prompt text, Bash commands, Edit/Write tool input including file contents and patches). To api.typesafe.ai (or the overridden OpenRouter endpoint) on each non-structural-deny event: a packed 'state' JSON with tool_name, the parsed command, target paths, a diff summary (patch clipped), the user prompt (clipped to 4000 chars, 800 if the state is over 12000 chars), the artifact role, and about 16 question definitions. That is code and command content from personal and client projects leaving the machine via UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse (src/lib/risk/jev.ts:97-147, 316-338). Structural denies skip the Jev call. The secret-leak guard is not integrated: secrets pasted in prompts or in Bash commands are sent as-is.
entries.failureMode: Mixed, and worse than the docs suggest. Jev call: 1200 ms AbortController timeout (jev.ts:77). On timeout, HTTP error or missing key, collectNeural falls back to lexical scoring, so Jev failure is fail-open to regex only. Sidecar: the UserPromptSubmit and Stop HTTP hooks are fail-open (Claude Code ignores non-2xx and timeouts). The PreToolUse command hook claude-hook.sh is deliberately FAIL-CLOSED. If the sidecar is not running or is slow (curl --max-time 8), it prints a deny and exits 2, which blocks every Bash/Edit/Write/StrReplace call. The plugin does not start the sidecar, so a fresh session, a reboot or a crashed 'next dev' would stop all editing and shell work until the user runs 'npm run dev' by hand. Any handler exception in the route also returns a fail-closed deny (route.ts:29-41). Default mode is enforce, so false positives on words like 'grader' or 'hidden test' could block real work.
entries.contextCost: Low from tools. There is no MCP server and 0 tool definitions. The skill's frontmatter description is about 400 chars (roughly 100 tokens) and lists eval-design topics only, so it rarely triggers in daily coding. The hooks inject text only when the verdict is not ok: fixed AGENT_STEER / AGENT_STOP strings of a few hundred chars. If the skill did trigger it would load a 1.2 MB SKILL.md (roughly 300k tokens), which does not fit in the context window. That is a real risk if the description matches.
pros: Real Jev integration in code (jev.ts): it uses all three primitives (Noul x14, Choice, Score) in a single System One call. It is a working reference for the request/response shape, with typed parsing and validation of answers (parseSystemOneResult).
Endpoint, model and key are all env-configurable (TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT / TYPESAFE_MODEL / TYPESAFE_API_KEY). Pointing it at OpenRouter should be a config change if the schema matches.

Fully deterministic automatic invocation via hooks, with no need to prompt Claude. A structural regex layer denies before any network call, and Jev is only a soft signal on top of it. Has shadow and review modes for a safe rollout.

Real test suite and CI, MIT license, and a Claude Code plugin manifest that installs with two commands. Claude only sees fixed opaque deny/steer strings, so Jev output cannot inject free text into the model.
cons: Wrong problem for the user: it targets reward hacking (agents tampering with graders, hidden tests, hooks) in agent evals. It gives a daily coder no routing, review, permission triage or commit gating value, and mostly false-positive risk.

Fail-closed PreToolUse hook depends on a manually started Next.js dev server. If it is down, all Bash/Edit/Write calls are denied. That conflicts with the user's bypass/auto workflow and with the existing hook stack (secret guard, GitNexus).
Heavy footprint for a hook: git clone + npm install of Next 16/React 19/shadcn, a resident dev server, and an unauthenticated localhost port that spends the API key for any local process.
Every user prompt, Bash command and edit diff from personal and client projects goes to Jev, with no redaction. There is also a UserPromptSubmit hook on every prompt.
Native OpenRouter support is missing in code (TypeSafe direct only). The OpenRouter route relies on an unverified schema match and on stuffing the OpenRouter key into a TYPESAFE_API_KEY variable.
Very young (13 days, 3 stars, 2 authors, one of them a bot), hourly auto-generated 1 MB README / 1.2 MB SKILL.md, no releases. The SKILL.md would blow the context window if the skill triggered.
Latency: 0.3-1.5 s added per prompt and per tool call, in a Next dev server on the hot path.
entries.verdict: Not recommended for daily coding. It is a niche reward-hacking/eval-integrity gate whose fail-closed hook needs a manually run Next.js sidecar, and it sends prompts and diffs to Jev with no redaction. Its only real value here is as reference code for the System One request shape and for typed-answer parsing (jev.ts), which can be lifted, not installed.
