entries.name: jev-sudo
entries.what: A standalone Node CLI wrapper (jev-sudo <command>) that sends a shell command to a "Jev System One" endpoint (noul isDestructive, score riskLevel, choice actionPolicy) and then blocks, prompts, or execSync-runs the command. It is not a Claude Code hook, MCP server or skill. Without TYPESAFE_API_KEY, or on any fetch failure or non-2xx response, it silently falls back to a hard-coded keyword-matching "simulator" (rm -rf, drop table, git push --force, etc.) that fakes 35-60ms latency and reports "Jev System 1" in the output.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted or manually prefixed. It ships no hook config, MCP server or skill. It would need a custom PreToolUse Bash hook that calls it, and that hook would parse the JSON output, since the CLI itself exits 0 in --check mode regardless of policy (cli.ts:265-267).
security: No postinstall, no runtime deps, no telemetry, no curl|sh. Tarball has 23 files and about 34 KB, all readable.
Sends the full command string, cwd, USER and SHELL to api.typesafe.ai in the live path (guardian.ts:142-147). Bearer key is read from an env var, not argv, so it is not exposed in the process list.

Silent fail-open to a naive substring matcher when the API is unreachable or returns an error (client.ts:43-46). The output still says 'Jev System 1' (model label 'jev-system1-sim' appears only in JSON), so the user can believe Jev vetted a command when a keyword list did. This misrepresents the protection.

The simulator is trivially bypassed. Only literal substrings are matched, so 'rm -r -f /', 'find / -delete', 'shred', 'git push -f origin' without spaces, encoded or base64 payloads, and 'rm -rf $HOME' variants may get 'allow' (e.g. 'rm -rf ~' matches 'rm -rf' but not the '/' catastrophic branch). Any command not in the list is 'allow' with 0.96 confidence.

The command is passed as a joined string to execSync (shell), so quoting and argv boundaries are lost. Wrapper args like -f are stripped from the wrapped command, corrupting commands such as 'git push -f' (the -f is treated as the tool's own force flag and removed, changing behavior).

Not a hook, so it does not intercept anything by itself. It only guards commands the user or agent explicitly prefixes with jev-sudo. The interactive y/N prompt needs a TTY and would hang or fail under Claude Code's Bash tool.
entries.dataEgress: Live mode only (requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY): the command string, cwd, username and shell go to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. Nothing else (no code, diffs or file contents). In simulator mode nothing leaves the machine. Nothing goes to OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open to the keyword simulator on any exception or non-OK response. There is no fetch timeout (no AbortSignal), so a hung connection blocks the command indefinitely. A malformed 200 response falls back to defaults: isDestructive 0.05, riskLevel 'low', policy 'allow' (guardian.ts:174-179), which is also fail-open.
entries.contextCost: Zero if used as a plain CLI, since it adds no MCP tools, no skills and no hook text. It also adds no automatic behavior. To make it automatic you would have to write your own PreToolUse hook wrapper around `jev-sudo --eval "$cmd" --json`.
pros: Tiny, fully readable codebase (about 400 lines of TS, no runtime deps, no postinstall, MIT), so it is easy to audit and to fork.

The Noul/Score/Choice bundle in one call (guardian.ts:149-172) is a sensible illustration of how a Jev decision gate for risky shell commands could be shaped. It could be borrowed as a template for a custom PreToolUse Bash hook that calls OpenRouter.
Has --eval --json output that a hook could parse.
Command-risk gating is a legitimate Jev use case (a low-latency typed decision) that complements the existing secret-leak guard.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no hook, MCP or skill, so it cannot be automatic without custom glue.

No OpenRouter support. It targets api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with a request schema that does not match the OpenRouter System One or Decisions APIs as described, and the base URL is not configurable by env.

Default and fallback mode is a hard-coded keyword matcher that prints 'Jev System 1' and invents 35-60 ms latency (client.ts:49). This is misleading for a safety tool, and the tests only cover that fake path.
Silent fail-open with no timeout. Any 200 response missing fields defaults to 'allow'.
Interactive y/N prompt and execSync of a re-joined string break in Claude Code's non-TTY Bash tool. It also strips -f from wrapped commands.
Effectively no adoption or vetting: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 162 weekly downloads, and it does not exercise the real API in tests. Its superiority over a plain deny-list hook is unproven.
Redundant with Claude Code's own permission modes, and in bypass mode a guard has value only if implemented as a hook, which this is not.
entries.verdict: Skip it: a single-commit CLI wrapper, not a Claude Code integration, with no OpenRouter support. Its default path is a fake keyword matcher labelled Jev, and it fails open with no timeout. The only thing worth keeping is the idea of a Jev Noul/Score/Choice gate for risky Bash commands, which should be built as a small custom PreToolUse hook against OpenRouter with a strict timeout and an explicit fail-open or fail-closed policy.

entries.name: connectedGraph/claude-jev-warden
entries.what: A single-purpose PreToolUse hook (Node ESM, .claude/hooks/warden.js) that fires on Write|Edit|MultiEdit. If the target file ends in .svg or the content contains "<svg", it sends the first 4500 characters to OpenRouter's Decisions API (typesafe/jev-1.13) with a hardcoded "Dynamic Animated SVG: Monkey riding a bicycle" rubric (one noul and two choice questions). If verdict is not approve_dynamic_exquisite or P(yes) is below 0.8, it exits 2 with feedback so Claude rewrites the file. It also ships a CLI, bin/jev-audit.js, that scores an SVG file the same way. It is a demo or benchmark for an SVG art-director gate, not a general coding integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PreToolUse on Write|Edit|MultiEdit). It is automatic, but its only trigger is SVG content. There is no reachable code path for a general coding decision.
security: API key is read from the environment or a .env file, never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list. .env is in .gitignore.

Hardcoded author-specific fallback paths: 'C:/Users/18086/.workspace/git-workspace/jev-browser/.env' and ../../../jev-browser/.env (warden.js:14-15, jev-audit.js:14-15). It also loads .env from process.cwd() (warden.js:12), so on client projects it would load whatever .env sits in the cwd into process.env (secrets stay in that process, but this is sloppy and conflicts with the user's secret-leak guard philosophy).
Writes warden.log next to the .claude directory (warden.js:6,28) with tool names, scores and file paths. It does not log content. The log file is gitignored.
No shell exec, no eval, no telemetry, no curl|sh, no postinstall.

Prompt-injection surface: file content is sent to Jev as state, but Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection can at most flip the gate verdict. The reject feedback text is static and embeds only the enum key of the deficiency.
Wrong branding headers: HTTP-Referer https://github.com/jkudish/jev-browser and X-Title jev-art-director are attributed to another project on the OpenRouter dashboard.
entries.dataEgress: For each Write/Edit/MultiEdit whose target is .svg or whose content contains '<svg': the file path plus the first 4500 chars of content or new_string go to openrouter.ai (and on to TypeSafe). Non-SVG edits send nothing. For a typical user there is almost no egress, because the hook does nothing for ordinary code. Note that MultiEdit puts edits in tool_input.edits, and the code reads only content and new_string, so MultiEdit content is never inspected. It fails silently for MultiEdit.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open. A missing API key, a thrown fetch error or a non-JSON stdin all exit 0. A non-2xx HTTP response falls through the if(response.ok) block to the APPROVED_TOOL log and exit 0. There is NO fetch timeout or AbortController, so a hung OpenRouter connection would block the Write/Edit until Claude Code's hook timeout (60s by default) and stall the turn. Only a valid low-score response fails closed (exit 2). Missing fields default to values that REJECT: noul falls back to 0.5, so the write is blocked and Claude gets a misleading rejection. Since that only happens on SVG writes, the blast radius is small.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools and no MCP instructions. Nothing is injected on approval, except stderr text on exit 0, which is not shown to the model. On reject, about 350 tokens of feedback, all about monkey and bicycle SVG animation. Practically zero for normal coding.
pros: It is the only candidate found that is automatic (a hook, no user prompting) and uses OpenRouter, so it shows the hook plus Decisions API pattern working end to end. Its request/response parsing is a usable reference: state and questions payload, noul and choice types with a criteria map, answers.<key>.noul / .choice / .confidence (warden.js:90-145).
Sound gate design to copy: PreToolUse, exit 2 with stderr feedback to force a rewrite, missing key means bypass, fetch errors mean allow.
Small and readable: 189 lines, zero dependencies, MIT, no postinstall, no shell exec, key never in argv.
The SVG scores in README/compare.html give a rough reading on Jev's behaviour, though they are the author's own and unverified.
cons: The rubric is hardcoded to 'Monkey riding a bicycle' animated SVGs (warden.js:76-121). Any SVG Claude writes in a real project (icons, logos) would be judged against monkey/bicycle criteria and likely rejected, producing wrong feedback. This is actively harmful if installed globally.
Not general-purpose: no code-quality, test, security, commit or routing decisions. Non-SVG operations are unconditionally approved (warden.js:183-185).
No fetch timeout, so a slow or hung OpenRouter call stalls the Write/Edit for up to Claude Code's hook timeout.
Non-2xx responses (401, 429, 5xx) silently pass, and a missing field defaults to a false rejection (noul 0.5).
MultiEdit inputs are never read (uses content and new_string only, not edits[]), so the matcher advertises coverage it does not deliver.
Hardcoded Windows path of the author (C:/Users/18086/...) and a cwd .env auto-load; also uses another project's HTTP-Referer.
Project-scoped install only (relative command path). Not packaged as a plugin, npm package or marketplace entry, with no tests or CI, 2 commits, 1 star, created 11 days before audit.
The README claims of 'IQ multiplier' and benchmark scores are single-run, unaudited, and mix Jev with unrelated models (Doubao, DeepSeek). Treat them as marketing, not evidence.
Uses the alpha Decisions API path (/api/alpha/decisions) and covers only the noul and choice primitives.
entries.verdict: Do not install: it is an SVG-only demo gate hardcoded to a monkey-on-a-bicycle rubric, so it adds nothing to daily coding and would misjudge any real SVG. It is still worth reading as a minimal working reference for a PreToolUse plus OpenRouter Decisions API hook, whose pattern (exit 2 on low P(yes), fail-open, add a timeout) can be reused in a custom hook.

entries.name: Akramovic1/jev-pilot (jev-pilot Claude Code plugin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin built on Claude Code's early-access "function hooks" (TypeScript hook module, no MCP server). Before every user prompt it POSTs the prompt, the last 4 messages (max 2000 chars, text plus tool names only), and some counters to Jev at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone. It then uses the typed answers to (a) set the main conversation's reasoning effort per turn (low..xhigh, raised to max after 2 failed tool calls), (b) pick the model (haiku/sonnet/opus) and effort of each spawned subagent, (c) pick one skill and attach its SKILL.md to the prompt while hiding Claude Code's own skill listing, (d) attach advice blocks (strategy direct/delegate/parallel/graph, ask-first for vague requests, failing-test-first for bugs, design pack). It also has an optional "crew" layer: a local 127.0.0.1 proxy (jev-router) that sends jev-<slot> model requests to OpenRouter and Codex/OpenCode CLI reviewers, an animated terminal pet, and a decision ledger/report. Jev is used only as a routing classifier; it never writes code or text.
interface: hooks tool.call, turn.start/complete, session.start/end/compact, skill.prompt, command.run, ui.render
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks: fully automatic without any prompt mention. Runs on prompt.submit, turn.step and agent.spawn events, so it fires on every prompt and every subagent spawn regardless of what the user or model says. This is the only integration style in this audit that meets the 'Claude Code must use it by itself' requirement, but it applies Jev only to routing decisions (effort/model/skill/strategy), not as a tool Claude can consult about the code.
security: API key: declared sensitive:true userConfig in plugin.json; install.sh passes it as 'claude plugin install ... --config openrouterApiKey=<key>' (install.sh ~line 260-262), so the key is briefly visible in argv/ps during install; a safer path is to install by hand or set it via Claude Code's own prompt. In clone mode the key is written in plaintext to ~/.claude/settings.json pluginConfigs (with backup). The key is sent only as Authorization Bearer to openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai / ai-gateway.vercel.sh if those keys are chosen); it is never put on argv by the plugin at runtime.

Advertised install is curl|bash of a 13 KB install.sh from a 1-week-old single-author repo; it runs claude CLI, python3/node JSON edits, creates a symlink in ~/.local/bin. Read it before running; no sudo, no postinstall scripts, no npm deps.

Function hooks run arbitrary TS inside Claude Code with the plugin's $ API (http, fs, process.run, env, store, session.messages, agent.register). Observed uses are benign: process.run only for 'codex login status', 'opencode --version/auth list/models', 'codex debug models'; fs writes under ~/.claude/jev-pilot/ and skill-override files; fetches only to openrouter.ai, api.typesafe.ai, ai-gateway.vercel.sh, and raw.githubusercontent.com/VoltAgent/awesome-design-md (the design pack tells Claude to fetch DESIGN.md files from there, a small prompt-injection surface). No telemetry endpoints found (grep of all URLs in hooks/, router/, bin/, install.sh).

jev-router (only when started by claude-jev): listens on 127.0.0.1:8799, requests must carry a 32-hex secret path from ~/.claude/jev-pilot/router-secret (chmod 600), browser requests with Origin are refused; nohup+setsid supervisor loop keeps it alive after the terminal closes; it sits in the path of ALL Anthropic traffic including the user's OAuth bearer token (streams unchanged, key never crosses over per code comments). Adds a persistent local daemon and a single point of failure; can be disabled with JEV_ROUTER=off.

Prompt-injection surface: injects extra context blocks into user prompts (strategy/quality/design advice, full SKILL.md of the Jev-picked skill, a session note telling Claude not to pin subagent models). A skill wrongly picked because of a manipulated prompt could load the wrong SKILL.md, but Jev output is a constrained typed choice, so it cannot inject free text itself.

/jev-pilot:setup (opt-in, asks first) rewrites skill overrides to hide every skill from the model, with a backup and a restore command; if a user runs it and later uninstalls without restore, skills stay hidden (README warns).
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (and then TypeSafe/Jev host) on every prompt: the full user prompt text (any pasted code, stack traces, client names or secrets in it), up to 4 prior messages / 2000 chars including assistant prose and tool NAMES (never tool inputs or outputs, per hooks/context.ts header), counters (prompt length, files mentioned, has_code_or_error, tool-kind counts), the name plus description of EVERY skill and command available (about 300 chars of each SKILL.md opening; excerptChars default 300), custom-agent info, and file-name-derived platform hints (cdk.json, vercel.json, Dockerfile). Per subagent spawn: the entire subagent prompt/brief, description and agentType (briefs can contain code and file contents). Not sent: file contents read by tools, diffs, tool outputs, the OAuth token. Optional and off by default: Codex/OpenCode reviewers (own CLIs, own accounts) and custom OpenRouter model slots, which would send whole task context to those models. OpenRouter logs/prompt-retention settings and provider routing for Jev apply; client-project prompts leave the machine on every turn, so check client contracts and the OpenRouter data policy.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. askJev (jev-model-router.ts:127-165) races the fetch against io.sleep(timeoutMs) (default 1500 ms, installer sets 1500); on timeout, non-2xx, network error or unparsable answer the decision is null and the turn/subagent proceeds unchanged (effort and model left as Claude Code chose), with a routine note in the pet/log. Missing key falls back to Claude Code's built-in $.model.classify classifier. The router proxy also falls back to Sonnet on Anthropic if a custom slot fails. Weak spot: prompt.submit is awaited, so a slow Jev costs up to 1.5 s before every prompt and up to 1.5 s per subagent spawn; there is no circuit breaker seen, so an outage repeats the wait each time. Also fail-open in the negative sense if the hooks module is not enabled: silently does nothing until CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-definition tokens. Per-prompt injected text: a session note on the first prompt and after compaction listing what jev-pilot controls, plus conditional blocks (strategy advice, quality advice, design pack, step-back notes, full SKILL.md of the picked skill, which can be thousands of tokens). With hideListing=true (default) it REMOVES Claude Code's skill listing from context, which can save tokens for a user with many skills, but takes skill discovery away from the model and depends on Jev's pick. Under claude-jev, sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true (deferred tool schemas) because a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL otherwise inlines every tool schema. Transcript lines only if display is transcript/both (default is the pet UI, which only draws in the interactive terminal).
pros: Only candidate that is truly automatic: deterministic hooks on prompt.submit/turn.step/agent.spawn, no need to ever say 'use jev' (hooks/jev-pilot.ts registers all modules).

OpenRouter is first-class: hooks/model-router.policy.ts:209-253 posts TypeSafe-shaped {model,state,questions} to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with ~typesafe/jev-latest by default and pinnable typesafe/jev-1.13; it exactly matches the brief's System One surface, and per-answer confidence is used for thresholds (raise at 0.3, lower at 0.6).

Uses Jev for what it is built for (typed choices with calibrated probabilities), not as a chat model: Choice for effort/tier/strategy/skill, Noul for risky/underspecified/bugfix/design, so the design fits the primitives.
Fail-open with a 1500 ms hard timeout and built-in classifier fallback; a Jev or OpenRouter outage degrades to stock Claude Code behavior (jev-model-router.ts:127-165).

Data minimisation is considered: tool inputs/outputs are never sent (hooks/context.ts), subagent briefs are sent without conversation, context capped at 4 messages / 2000 chars, all configurable via contextMessages/contextChars.

Every part has a live kill switch (/jev effort|subagents|skills|strategy|quality|design|pet off, /jev all off) and plugin.json exposes ~50 options, so the risky parts can be disabled while keeping effort and subagent-model routing.

Hooks are separate function-hook modules, not settings.json hooks, so they should not collide with the existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus pre/post hooks or caveman hooks; installed 2.1.285 binary does contain the CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS gate the plugin needs.

Reasonable engineering hygiene for a 1-week-old repo: about 320 test cases in 15 files, CI, CHANGELOG with measured numbers, a decision ledger and /jev-pilot:report to check whether it pays off, MIT license, no telemetry endpoints found.
Sensible defaults for Opus 5.5: starts at xhigh at most, needs 0.6 confidence to downgrade, raises effort on repeated failures, and keeps an explicitly named subagent model.
Works with a subscription/OAuth login per README (effort changes keep the cache), and does not need ANTHROPIC_API_KEY.
cons: Depends on Claude Code 'function hooks', which the installed 2.1.285 binary itself labels early access ('hooks modules are not turned on for installed plugins ... set CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1'); API can change any release and it would silently stop working; needs the env var in settings.json (plain claude) or the claude-jev wrapper.

Very immature: created 2026-09-23, 36 commits in 7 days by a single author, 6 stars, 1 fork, plugin.json 0.12.0 ahead of latest release tag 0.11.0, about 12 releases in a week. Benchmarks (76 labelled prompts, 40 briefs, jev-bench 8/8) are self-run and unverified.

Every prompt and every subagent brief goes to OpenRouter/Jev, including client-project text; skill names and descriptions plus 300-char SKILL.md excerpts of all your skills (dougthepug, empat, gitnexus etc.) also leave the machine. There is no per-project exclusion switch, so client work needs a contract/policy check or a per-project disable.
Blocking latency: awaited request before every prompt (claimed 0.5 s, up to 1.5 s timeout) and again per subagent spawn; no circuit breaker, so an OpenRouter incident costs 1.5 s repeatedly.

The value is mostly cost/effort routing; on a subscription (Opus 5.5, OAuth) the savings show as quota rather than money, and jev-pilot's own changelog concedes Opus 5.5 did the right thing with or without its advice on the quality tasks (9-vague, 10-transfer), with only 11% cheaper. Jev never sees the repo, so it cannot improve code quality directly.

Invasive by default: hideListing=true removes Claude Code's skill listing and replaces it with a Jev-picked SKILL.md injected into the prompt; wrong or missed picks mean the model cannot discover skills itself, and it interacts with the existing skill-heavy setup (gitnexus-*, caveman, design skills). Also injects advice blocks into prompts that change Claude's behavior (ask-first, failing-test-first, subagent strategies) without an explicit user choice.

Adds a session note telling Claude not to set subagent models or create agent types to pin them, which conflicts with custom workflows the user or CLAUDE.md may define, and overrides subagent model choices except explicitly named ones.

claude-jev launcher starts a persistent detached local proxy on 127.0.0.1:8799 and repoints ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL through it, putting the OAuth traffic through third-party code and a daemon (secret-path protected, but a new failure/attack surface); needs JEV_ROUTER=off, or use plain claude with the env var instead. Also sets ENABLE_TOOL_SEARCH=true globally for the session.

Install path is curl|bash and puts the key on argv (claude plugin install --config openrouterApiKey=...), visible to other local users in ps for the duration; clone mode stores the key plaintext in ~/.claude/settings.json.

Scope creep: pet UI, Codex/OpenCode reviewers, custom OpenRouter model slots, design pack, tuning ledger. Large surface (8.4k lines of hooks) to audit for a router that only needs ~3 hooks; the user can disable most, but must review them.

Only uses /api/v1/systemone, not the Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions); it cannot be extended to arbitrary decisions in the user's own workflow without editing the plugin. It also cannot provide a 'consult Jev on X' tool, so it is not a general Jev integration.

Unverified claim that Jev behaves like a DeepSeek-flash router (per skeptics) means the routing quality rests entirely on the author's threshold tuning; user-side ledger review is required to trust it.

Defaults override the user's own settings: routeMainEffort=true and routeSubagentModel=true by default, so effort and subagent model change on every prompt without opt-in. That is a bigger behaviour change for a defaultMode 'auto' / bypassPermissions user than the audit conveys.

Function hooks are early access and gated. The 2.1.285 binary says: 'hooks modules are not turned on for installed plugins ... (early access ...)'. Without CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1, or if the API changes, the plugin silently does nothing. The binary also has guard rules around plugin agent.spawn hooks, so behaviour under auto or bypass modes is untested.

Timeout is a race, not an abort, and there is no circuit breaker or backoff (jev-model-router.ts:146-157). During an OpenRouter incident (no SLA, /alpha-tier) every prompt and subagent spawn pays up to 1.5 s. The timeout also self-tunes from the ledger (line 330).

Startup subprocess and network side effects even in the default 'standard' mode: 'codex login status', 'opencode --version', 'opencode auth list' (15 s timeouts, background) and a GET to openrouter.ai/api/v1/models for crew checks.

Does not fit the actual need to let Claude consult Jev on code decisions (approve or deny a Bash command, pick an option). It routes Claude Code's own effort, model and skill only. The OpenRouter cookbook PermissionRequest pattern is not provided, so it only partly answers the goal.

Model id risk: the default '~typesafe/jev-latest' alias tracks the newest Jev, so routing behaviour can change without notice. Pinning needs a manual openrouterModel setting, and the pin id format for the /v1/systemone route is unverified.
In clone mode, pluginConfigs in ~/.claude/settings.json holds the OpenRouter key in plaintext. That file is readable by Read/Grep, and the user's no-secret-leak hook does not protect it by default.
entries.verdict: The only real candidate that gives automatic, no-prompting Jev use in Claude Code (deterministic function hooks) and it supports OpenRouter's /v1/systemone natively with a fail-open 1.5 s timeout. It is a one-week-old, single-author, early-access-API plugin that sends every prompt and subagent brief to OpenRouter and hides your skill listing by default, so if you try it, pin a reviewed commit, install by hand with the env var in settings.json (skip the curl|bash and claude-jev proxy), and disable skill-hiding, design pack and crew features, keeping only effort and subagent-model routing.

verification.note: Core claims verified in source: the OpenRouter endpoint POST https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (hooks/model-router.policy.ts:209-253) with a Bearer key from userConfig openrouterApiKey and the {model,state,questions} body. The Claude Code 2.1.285 binary contains the function-hooks gate string and prompt.submit, turn.step, agent.spawn, prompt.attachment and skill_listing. Fail-open with a 1500 ms race is confirmed (jev-model-router.ts:127-165). Repo facts re-queried: 6 stars, 1 fork, not archived, 36 commits, one author, created 2026-09-23. Errors found were mostly minor (27 releases not 12, about 282 tests not 320, about 7.4k hook lines not 8.4k, model-id discrepancy against the brief). The score goes from 6.5 to 5.5 for two reasons. The main behaviours (main effort routing, subagent model override, skill-listing hiding) are on by default and override the user's own settings. The plugin depends on an early-access API and is one week old, with a single author and self-run benchmarks. It is still the only candidate that runs automatically. It suits a cautious trial only: install by hand, pin a reviewed commit (e61f801), skip curl|bash and the claude-jev proxy, and set hideListing=false, designPack=false and routeMainEffort=false at first. I did not exercise the live systemone route with a key, so the accepted model ids are unverified.

Depends on early-access function hooks (needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1); can silently do nothing after an update, and behaviour under auto/bypass is untested

entries.name: jev-skill-scout
entries.what: Claude Code plugin built on the early-access "function hooks" (mods) API. On every typed prompt (session.start builds a skill roster; prompt.submit judges) it calls TypeSafe System One twice: (1) one Choice over all installed skill descriptions plus a __none__ option, and three gate Nouls; (2) if the gate passes, a second Choice/Noul pass over the top 3 skills with the first 700 chars of each SKILL.md. If a winner has fit >= 0.3, it appends a `<skill_relevance>` line to the prompt context telling Claude to load that skill with the Skill tool. It also ships an offline audit CLI (`npx jev-skill-scout audit`) that replays ~/.claude/projects transcripts through the same judgment, and a `doctor` command for skill descriptions. This is the closest thing found to "Jev used automatically, no user prompting" as it is a deterministic hook, but the scope is only skill selection.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: function-hook on session.start and prompt.submit fires on every typed prompt with no model discretion and no user phrase needed. Requires CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1. It only nudges Claude to load an existing skill; Claude still decides.
security: No shell/exec, no spawn, no postinstall, no curl|sh; package.json has no scripts beyond audit/test and no dependencies. Plugin declares 'Runs: nothing. No shell' and calls only $.clock, $.env.get, $.fs.{exists,list,read}, $.http.fetch, $.session.cwd, $.store, $.ui (README 'What it can reach'; reach level L3 network).

API key: read via $.env.get or plugin userConfig marked sensitive (plugin.json), sent only as Bearer header (scout.js:130); not in argv for the hook. CLI accepts --key on argv (cli.mjs:24,133), which would show in the process list; env var avoids it.
Sees every typed prompt (raw text), so the data-egress surface is broad even though code is small.

Prompt-injection surface is limited: Jev returns typed probabilities, worst case a wrong or missing skill hint; the injected line tells the model to ignore it if it does not fit (scout.js:199-201). However skill names/descriptions from installed third-party plugin SKILL.md files are placed into the Jev request and the winner name is interpolated into the context line unescaped; a hostile skill name could inject text into the model context (low risk, requires malicious installed skill).
No telemetry beyond the TypeSafe call; audit writes only to --out dir.
Depends on Claude Code function-hooks early-access API which 'may change between releases without notice'; validated on 2.1.278 while user runs 2.1.285, untested there.
entries.dataEgress: On every typed prompt of >=12 chars (not starting '/'), to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone: the full prompt text (cut to 4000 chars, scout.js:49), a 400-char recent_context field (currently passed '' by the hook), all installed skill names plus descriptions (400 chars each), and on the 2nd call the first 700 chars of the top 3 SKILL.md bodies. Not sent: source files, diffs, tool outputs, assistant replies. Still, prompts on client projects routinely contain code snippets, paths, error text and business details, so every client prompt leaves the machine to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter plus provider if patched). The audit CLI sends all historical human prompts from ~/.claude/projects (21.4M input tokens in the author's run) after a cost confirmation.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Per-call abort plus Promise.race timeout, default 4000 ms (register.ts:68-83, scout.js:122-143); on timeout, HTTP error, exception, no key, empty roster or short prompt the original prompt proceeds untouched and is entered exactly once (register.ts:105-109). Cost of a slow Jev is added latency up to ~4 s per prompt before the model starts (status line shows 'no answer in N ms'). No retries by default (retries=0). Disabled with no key.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-schema tokens, no MCP server instructions. Only per-prompt injection when a skill is picked: a ~55-token `<skill_relevance>` block (about 200 chars) appended as context. Nothing injected on 'no skill' turns. Adds nothing to the static prefix so prompt caching is unaffected. Plugin has no skills/agents/commands of its own.
pros: Truly automatic: prompt.submit hook fires on every typed prompt; meets the 'never say use jev' requirement without model discretion or MCP tool descriptions.
Near-zero context cost: no tools, ~55 tokens only on turns where a skill is picked; does not touch the static prefix so caching holds.
Fail-open with hard 4 s timeout and 'enter prompt exactly once' guard (register.ts:105); will not block work if Jev/OpenRouter is down.
Shadow mode (`shadow`/JEV_SKILL_SCOUT_SHADOW=1) lets the user watch picks in the status line before allowing injection, and the audit can measure obedience before/after.
Real Jev use-case that matches its design (typed Choice/Noul decisions over an app state) and follows TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook; thresholds configurable via plugin settings.
Small, readable, dependency-free, no shell execution, no postinstall, MIT; static review is easy (~1.7k LOC total).

User has many skills (gitnexus-*, caveman, design skills), so skill-miss reduction is a plausible daily win; audit gives evidence on the user's own transcripts before committing (about $0.9 for 3k prompts).
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only (scout.js:7, register.ts:48); no OpenRouter support, so the user's chosen provider needs a fork/patch, and the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified.

Depends on Claude Code function hooks, an early-access API that may change without notice and needs CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1; validated on 2.1.278, user on 2.1.285, so may silently stop working after an update (README: builds without it ignore the modules key).
Narrow scope: only nudges skill loading. Does not offer Jev for code decisions (permission auto-approval, routing, review risk scoring, commit type, etc.) which is where most daily value might be.
Sends every typed prompt (client project text included) to a third party; a NDA/client concern, plus the audit uploads entire prompt history.

Adds blocking latency (two sequential calls, ~0.5-3 s) to every typed prompt for a benefit the author's own data says is ~50% precise (15/30 hand-labelled misses right) and the 'miss rate' metric is Jev-judged, not ground truth.
Cannot suggest Claude Code's bundled skills (code-review, simplify, etc.) since they are not on disk (README Limits), and only affects typed prompts, not subagent/tool loops.
Immature: 0 stars, 1 contributor, ~11 days old, no CI, no releases; overlaps with typesafe-mod and skillranker which do the same thing, so it is one of three competing implementations.
Uses Opus 5.5 main model, which loads skills well already; the cookbook gain (16.8% to 7.3% wrong-skill loads) was measured on Haiku, so benefit for this user is uncertain.
entries.verdict: Best-in-class proof that Jev can run automatically inside Claude Code (deterministic prompt.submit hook, fail-open, near-zero context cost), but it is skill-suggestion only, hardwired to api.typesafe.ai, and rides an early-access flag. Worth trying in shadow mode with a small OpenRouter fork (swap ENDPOINT/key/model) and running its audit first; do not rely on it as the sole Jev integration.
