security: API key: TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env, or plaintext in ~/.config/skillpick/config.json (mode 600, chmod set in cli.ts). `skillpick set-key <key>` puts the key in argv and shell history. The hook itself passes no secrets in argv.
No shell execution of prompt content: the hook only reads stdin JSON and the skill files, and calls fetch through the SDK.

Prompt-injection surface is small: the output is only a skill name that must be one of the roster keys (Jev returns a choice from the supplied options), inside a fixed template. But SKILL.md files in cloned client repos (project .claude/skills, .agents/skills) are read and their descriptions and 700-char body excerpts are sent to the API, so an untrusted repo can shape ranking or exfiltrate its own text only to Jev.
install rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json (idempotent, leaves other hooks alone per README). Hooks run in parallel with the user's existing UserPromptSubmit hooks, if any.

No telemetry in skillpick code. TypeSafe states it does not train on requests, per the README. With OpenRouter as gateway, OpenRouter and TypeSafe's provider policies would both apply and are unverified here.

Supply chain: one dependency (the official SDK), a bun.lock, no postinstall, a 1-person 11-day-old repo. Read-only audit of the source found nothing malicious. The install-for-me agent prompt in the README makes an agent clone and run third-party code, so do it by hand.
entries.dataEgress: Per submitted prompt (unless it starts with '/' or is under 12 chars): the full user prompt text, plus the name and description of every SKILL.md found in the cwd and in the home skill dirs (call 1). Call 2 adds the full description and the first 700 chars of the body of the top 3 skills. It runs about 18k input tokens per prompt on a 140-skill roster. No code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs or assistant messages are sent, only the current prompt with no conversation history, so follow-ups like 'yes do it' under 12 chars are skipped. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter (and its upstream provider) if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is set. Client-project prompts can contain confidential specifics, so this needs a per-project SKILLPICK_DISABLED=1.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open, but it blocks first. Any thrown error is caught and only written to stderr, exit 0 (src/cli.ts:106-110), and no key or empty roster returns silently. The SDK timeout is 15 s per request with 2 retries and backoff (SDK maxRetries: 2), against a 15 s hook timeout. A hung Jev can therefore stall every prompt for up to about 15 s until Claude Code kills the hook, and the hook then adds nothing. There is no circuit breaker and no cache. Bun stdin read has no guard. Gating decisions are also silent, since a failed call injects nothing rather than 'none relevant'.
entries.contextCost: 0 MCP tools and no server instructions. The hook injects a fixed block per prompt (about 40-55 tokens when a skill is picked, about 20 for 'No installed skill appears relevant'). That accumulates across a long session, roughly 5k tokens per 100 prompts, and it defeats no prompt caching because it sits at the end. The roster in the system prompt is untouched. Nothing else is added.
pros: It is truly automatic: a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never says 'use jev', and it writes to settings.json idempotently with uninstall and a SKILLPICK_DISABLED=1 kill switch.

It is the only candidate here that is a real, working Jev application with a documented measurement: 93.3% correct on covered requests, and the same pick on 3 repeat runs (24/24). Its design follows TypeSafe's official skill-suggestion cookbook.
OpenRouter looks trivial to swap in: the official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to {base}/v1/systemone, so base=https://openrouter.ai/api needs zero code changes.
Fail-open by design: it never blocks a prompt on an error, and it uses stdin rather than argv for prompt data.
Small footprint: no MCP tools, no server instructions, about 20-55 tokens injected per prompt, one official dependency, no postinstall, MIT.
Useful for this user only if their roster is big: they have gitnexus-* (about 9), caveman (about 8), design and other skills, so it may reduce wrong skill loads.
cons: It solves a narrow problem: picking which skill to load. Claude Code already lists skill descriptions natively and Opus 5.5 loads them well, so the marginal gain is unproven for this user, and the author's own benchmark shows 24% needless suggestions and confident wrong picks that can mislead (cookbook: 37 fixed, 7 broken).
Blocking latency on every prompt: p50 0.8 s, p95 1.8 s. A slow OpenRouter call can stall up to 15 s with 2 retries, and there is no caching or circuit breaker.

Data egress on client projects: every prompt plus skill descriptions and body excerpts go to a third party (and through OpenRouter). Client confidentiality needs a per-project disable, and nothing automates that.
Requires Bun, which the user does not list (Node 24 only), and depends on an absolute bun path baked into settings.json, which breaks if the clone moves ('STALE').

OpenRouter is unsupported in the documented config: the key variable is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model default is 'jev-latest' (the OpenRouter id is typesafe/jev-1.13), the schema equivalence with OpenRouter's /systemone is unverified, and the config-file key has no baseURL. The author has never tested OpenRouter.
Immature: 1 author, 5 commits, 11 days old, 2 stars, no CI, no releases, tests cover only roster parsing and hook formatting, and the benchmark was self-run on one machine (skills the author owns).
Adds a plaintext key file, and set-key puts the key in argv/shell history. Small rosters (<8 skills) make the nearest skill win even when nothing fits.
It does not touch the higher-value Jev uses (permission decisions, risk gating, routing subagents, review triage) that this user wants.
entries.verdict: A working, honest, low-context and fail-open Jev hook, and the only one of its kind found here, but it only nudges skill selection, which Claude Code already does well natively. Its cost is 1-2 s of blocking per prompt plus egress of every prompt, and the project is 11 days old with no OpenRouter test. Worth trying with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api on personal projects, not as a core piece of the daily setup or on client repos.

judge.why: Follows TypeSafe's cookbook and has a documented measurement, but the blocking latency and retries are risky.
pros: Idempotent settings.json install with uninstall and a SKILLPICK_DISABLED=1 kill switch
Own benchmark: 93.3% correct on covered requests, 24/24 repeat-stable
Env-only OpenRouter switch is plausible
cons: Bun/TypeScript; SDK timeout 15 s with 2 retries can stall a prompt; p50 0.8 s, p95 1.8 s
24% needless suggestions and confident wrong picks in its own data
Sends every prompt plus skill descriptions and body excerpts off-machine; no per-project disable

entries.name: le0u0/jev-skill-selector
entries.what: Claude Code/Codex plugin: bash select_skill.sh sends task plus installed skill names/descriptions to Jev choice and returns a matching skill or none; catalog builder, on/off toggle, tests.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger (model discretion); no hook
pros: Directly targets skill selection with unit tests using mock curl and a recorded report
Only names/descriptions sent, not skill bodies; on/off toggle
Endpoint configurable, likely switchable to OpenRouter
cons: Own report: 13/17 correct (76.5%), false pick on a non-skill task, ~1.75 s latency
Needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no license; model must call the skill so not truly automatic
Skill listing already handled by Claude Code; large catalogs may exceed 32k context

entries.name: vinilana/jev-gateway (jev-claude launcher)
entries.what: Local Hono/Node HTTP proxy (127.0.0.1:8789 for Claude) that sits between Claude Code and api.anthropic.com via ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL. On each POST /v1/messages carrying tools it flattens system prompt plus conversation into a Jev "state" and asks Jev one Choice question (which tool, including no_tool_needed) plus a Noul (needs tool?). It also asks speculative arg questions for closed-set params. If Jev is confident (default >= 0.7) it either forces tool_choice, answers directly with a synthesized tool_use, or (for Claude Code, since thinking is on and prompts are cached) appends a hint as a text block styled as a system-reminder to the last user message. Otherwise the request is forwarded unchanged. It is not a hook or MCP server. It does not cover subagent or plan-time reasoning, only the next-tool pick. Bench results are mixed (see verdict).
interface: x-jev-gateway: off header; env JEV_ROUTING, JEV_MIN_CONFIDENCE(0.7), JEV_TIMEOUT_MS(4000), JEV_DIRECT_CALLS, JEV_ON_NONE, JEV_DEBUG_DUMP_DIR
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent proxy. Once ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL points at the local gateway (via jev-claude wrapper, shell alias, or env in ~/.claude/settings.json) every /v1/messages call is routed automatically with no user prompting. However the daemon is not auto-started by Claude Code: it is started only by the jev-claude launcher (or `jev-claude --start`). Truly automatic use needs a wrapper alias for claude or a SessionStart hook plus systemd user unit, otherwise ECONNREFUSED. It steers next-tool choice only. It does not give Claude Code any new capability, and Claude may ignore the hint.
security: API key: entered via hidden prompt, stored in ~/.jev-gateway/.env with mode 0600 and dir 0700 (bin/setup.mjs:38-40). Sent only as a Bearer header to the provider URL, not in argv. The daemon inherits the env from launcher (process.env), so OPENROUTER_API_KEY is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ, not in argv.

Your Anthropic OAuth bearer token from Claude Code transits the local proxy on every request (forwarded untouched, src/upstream.ts:311-316). It is bound to 127.0.0.1 by default (config.ts:69), with no auth on the local port unless ROUTER_API_KEY is set; any local process/user can hit it, and the daemon persists after sessions close.

Prompt-injection surface: hint mode injects a <\system-reminder> block into the last user message that Claude treats as harness text (messages.ts:490-502; open issue #40). Tool names are sanitised to /^[\p{L}\p{N}_.:/-]{1,128}$/ (decide.ts:55) so an MCP tool name cannot break out. Jev picks only a tool name from the client's own roster, so it is a steering nudge, not arbitrary text. In forced/direct mode the gateway can synthesise tool_use calls with Jev-chosen enum/boolean args, bypassing model reasoning. Direct is disabled when thinking is on (decide.ts:197), so with Opus 5.5 it stays hint mode.

No postinstall/preinstall scripts, no telemetry found (grep). Only runtime deps hono and @hono/node-server. Published to npm via trusted publishing (no token), GitHub Actions pinned by SHA in ci.yml. Single maintainer (Vinicius Lana, 54 of 74 commits), brand-new 12-day-old package and a 265-star, 36-fork repo. No curl|sh installer. Opt-in JEV_DEBUG_DUMP_DIR writes full conversations to disk (headers redacted).
Detached daemon spawn and xdg-open of the dashboard are the only process execution. No shell strings.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev provider (OpenRouter if configured) on every request that has tools, which is nearly every Claude Code turn: system prompt truncated to 4000 chars, the newest conversation turns up to 60k chars total and each message/tool_call args/tool_result clipped to 4k chars (state.ts, messages.ts:429-465), i.e. user prompts, assistant text, Bash commands and tool outputs including file contents read, plus every tool name and description (up to 1024 chars each, 48k budget) and questions (questions.ts). A second shortlist call is made when tools > 120. Issue #24 measured a median of ~34.5k input tokens per call (max 49k). Images and thinking blocks are stripped and become a placeholder. The full unmodified request also flows to api.anthropic.com as before. OpenRouter sees code and secrets that show up in tool results. The existing PreToolUse secret guard does not protect this path, since it runs before tool output enters the conversation but not on the proxy. The response contains only probabilities. Local logs at ~/.jev-gateway/claude.log store metadata, not prompts. Cost is roughly $0.042 per 1M input tokens, so ~34k tokens per turn is about $0.0015 per turn (my estimate from the brief pricing).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design and tested (test/failopen.test.ts). Jev timeout is 4000 ms (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS) with one 100 ms retry on 408/429/5xx/network error (jev.ts:200-257), so the worst case before falling back is about 8.1 s of added delay per request (a slow but not dead Jev is the risk). Any Jev error, unexpected answer, low confidence, unparseable body, adapter exception or 400/422 from the upstream on a rewritten request leads to the original bytes being forwarded (app.ts:214-234). Missing key stops the launcher and exits 1 when non-TTY. If the daemon is not running, plain claude with ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL set in settings.json would get ECONNREFUSED with no fallback, so it is fail-closed at the transport level unless the launcher or a hook keeps it alive. A daemon started with a different upstream refuses to start.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-definition tokens, no MCP instructions, no hooks. Only added tokens are the hint block on hint turns (about 50 tokens, roughly 200 chars, appended after the cache breakpoint at messages.ts:497, so the prompt cache prefix stays intact). Because it changes the last user message, the hint is replayed as part of history on later turns. Issue #37 reports Claude Code showing "Compacting conversation..." immediately when routed through the gateway on a 250-tool profile. The reporter found the same with routing off, and later evidence points to a 429 rate-limit from upstream rather than a gateway bug, so it is unresolved and worth testing.
pros: Only candidate that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: transparent proxy, zero context cost, no MCP tools or hooks, so it does not clash with the existing gitnexus/playwright/caveman/secret-guard setup.

OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (providers.json:105-111, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, typesafe/jev-1.13) and issue #24 shows it live with Claude Code; setting JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is all that is needed.

Designed around Claude Code constraints: hint mode when thinking or cache_control is present, never direct-answers when thinking is on (decide.ts:197), hint is appended after the cached prefix, and it keeps the OAuth login (only ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL is set, ~/.claude untouched).

Robust fail-open engineering with tests: 20 test files covering failopen, router, messages, and CI on Node 22.15 and 24 with SHA-pinned actions, plus a dry-run /router/decide, routing on/off toggle and a dashboard for A/B token comparison.

Small, readable codebase (about 3.2k lines TS, 2 runtime deps), MIT, no postinstall/telemetry, npm trusted publishing, key stored 0600. Easy to audit and to fork/patch (e.g. add a confidence-based or timeout tweak).
cons: Value for Opus 5.5 is unproven and possibly negative: the project's own benchmark shows Opus 5 in Claude Code +22% output tokens and +83% time on the feature task and only marginal gains on bugfix. Only Fable 5.1 clearly improved, and the README itself says expect better tool picks, not lower cost or latency.

Adds real latency on the critical path on every tool-bearing turn: issue #24 measured 1.3 s median (up to 3.9 s) with ~34k input tokens per Jev call, 88% of results thrown away as low confidence. Worst-case fail-open delay is about 8 s (4 s timeout x2 attempts).

Data egress is broad: conversation text, bash commands, file contents from tool results and full tool descriptions go to OpenRouter on nearly every turn, which matters for client projects and bypasses the local secret-leak guard's intent. Would need a per-project opt-out (x-jev-gateway: off header or a scoped env) for client repos.

Not integrated as a Claude Code plugin/hook: requires a background daemon that only the jev-claude wrapper starts, and a settings.json ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL with no daemon means every request fails (ECONNREFUSED). Needs your own systemd user service or launcher alias, and the OAuth bearer transits an unauthenticated localhost port.

Immature and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18 (12 days old), 74 commits, 54 by one author, 0.5.0, open issues include #37 (Claude Code compacts/disconnects on large tool roster, unresolved), #40 (hint disguised as a harness <\system-reminder>, a prompt-injection-style trust channel), and #24 (cost of roster re-send). OpenRouter endpoint is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha) and the README admits OpenRouter path was tested only with mocks in the README. The advertised 250-tool MCP roster triggers a two-stage (shortlist then decide) call.

Setting ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL to any non-first-party host makes Claude Code clamp its context window to the 200k class. Issue #53 (closed, documentation only) and #37 comment: effectiveWindow=180000 vs 980000 direct, early autocompact, 40k CLAUDE.md limit warning, reproduced on Claude Code 2.1.283. The gateway cannot fix this. It is a major loss for a user on Opus 5.5 with a 1M window and was missed by the audit.

Claude Code docs list a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL as a configuration without MCP tool search (it falls back to WaitForMcpServers). The user's gitnexus and playwright tool schemas would then be loaded upfront every turn, adding context cost. Confirmed via a WebFetch summary of code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp, so treat it as medium confidence.

Direct mode still exists for non-thinking requests. decide.ts:197 only blocks direct when thinking is on, and JEV_DIRECT_CALLS defaults to true. For any request without thinking (e.g. Haiku subagent or background calls, or a session with thinking disabled) whose chosen tool has only closed-set params, the gateway can answer with a synthesized tool_use and skip the model entirely. Issue #39 shows this bug class was hit once (sessions stuck when thinking was on). Audit said 'stays hint mode with Opus 5.5', which is only true while thinking stays enabled. Set JEV_DIRECT_CALLS=false.

The tool_use block for a hint-steered request is still chosen by Jev with only about 12% of turns yielding a hint in the only live sample, and 56% low confidence. Most calls buy nothing but add roughly 1.3 s median latency to every tool-bearing turn.

OpenRouter dependence: /api/alpha/decisions is an alpha endpoint with no SLA, and the OpenRouter public docs do not list it (WebFetch of the API overview found no mention). Real-key verification exists only as issue #24 (one user's log). The README itself says the OpenRouter path has not been run with real keys.

A rule to add for the existing no-secret-leak hook: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in the protected list, and the gateway stores the key in ~/.jev-gateway/.env and keeps it in the daemon's /proc environ. Every routed turn also sends the last ~60k chars of conversation (tool results and file contents clipped to 4k each) plus the system prompt (4k chars) to OpenRouter, in bypassPermissions client-project sessions where the guard hook never sees this path.

The daemon inherits the launcher's full environment except UPSTREAM_API_KEY and ROUTER_API_KEY, and it has no local auth by default on 127.0.0.1:8789 (ROUTER_API_KEY optional). Any local process can use it, and the OAuth bearer transits it.

Open issue #40: the hint is deliberately dressed as a harness <\system-reminder>, a trust channel the model weights above user text. It could silently stop working, or become a source of derailed turns that look like harness output.
Provider auto-selection picks TypeSafe first if TYPESAFE_API_KEY is also set, so JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter must be exported explicitly for the daemon.
entries.verdict: Technically the best fit for 'automatic, never say use jev' since it is a transparent local proxy with OpenRouter support, fail-open behaviour and zero context cost, but its own benchmarks and issue #24 show it is slower and no cheaper for Opus 5 in Claude Code (hint-only, 1.3 s per turn, 88% discarded), so treat it as an opt-in experiment behind a wrapper with routing off for client repos, not a default. Measure with `jev-claude --routing off/on` and the dashboard before adopting.

verification.note: Verified against a fresh clone (HEAD 38f2923, v0.5.0) and gh/npm queries. Confirmed correct: OpenRouter is a native provider (src/providers.json:10-17, POST to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, Bearer auth, http-referer and x-title headers at src/jev.ts:95-105). JEV_PROVIDER selection, fail-open (decide.ts, app.ts:214-234), the 4 s timeout and single 100 ms retry, the launcher setting only ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL, MIT licence, no install scripts, and no telemetry all hold. The npm package is jev-gateway (the scoped name 404s). The audit is right that it is the only candidate that meets 'automatic', but the score drops from 5 to 4 for this user. The audit missed the client-side side effects of a custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL: the context window clamps from 1M to about 200k, and MCP tool search is unavailable. It also overstated the low-confidence share, claimed the hint is replayed in history (it is not), and cited line numbers that do not exist. It understated the direct-mode exposure on non-thinking requests. Combined with 1.3 s median added latency, a project benchmark that is negative for Opus on the feature task, broad code egress to OpenRouter in client projects, an alpha endpoint, a 12-day-old single-maintainer project, and a fail-closed transport if the daemon dies, it is an opt-in experiment behind a wrapper (jev-claude, JEV_DIRECT_CALLS=false, routing off for client repos). It should not be set globally in settings.json.

judge.why: Genuinely automatic proxy for tool hints, but the ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL side effects are severe for a 1M-context Opus user.
pros: Native OpenRouter and fail-open on Jev errors, with a 4 s timeout and one retry
Readable ~2.5k lines of TypeScript; ~3.6k lines of tests; no telemetry
Only candidate here that reaches every request without hooks
cons: A custom ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL clamps Claude Code's context window to the ~200k class (180k vs 980k), triggers early autocompact and disables MCP tool search
Its own benchmark is negative on a feature task for Opus (+22% output, +61% input, +83% time); only ~12% of turns yield a hint and 56% are low confidence
Fail-closed transport if the daemon dies; no local auth on 127.0.0.1:8789; sends ~60k chars of conversation plus system prompt to OpenRouter (bypass-mode client sessions unguarded)
Direct mode can synthesize tool_use without the model on non-thinking requests (set JEV_DIRECT_CALLS=false)

entries.name: bestagentkits/jev-skillful (Skillful, @mrgoonie/skillful CLI)
entries.what: Zero-dependency Node/TypeScript CLI that installs a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook (also Codex, Pi, OMP). On every prompt it scans local skills, agents, commands and MCP entries (~/.claude/skills, plugins, agents, commands, ~/.claude.json, .mcp.json), builds a BM25 shortlist of about 15, and sends ONE System One request to TypeSafe. The request has one choice question over the shortlist plus 'none', and one noul question per candidate. It injects at most one primary and two runner-up capability names (max 480 chars) via hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext. It is a capability router, not a coding-decision engine. It also has local telemetry, an HTML dashboard and an A/B benchmark harness.
interface: No MCP tools, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: a UserPromptSubmit command hook that runs on every user prompt with no model discretion and no need to say 'use jev'. That matches the user's automatic-integration requirement. Scope limit: it only fires on user prompts. It does not see tool calls, plans, diffs or subagent decisions.
security: No runtime dependencies and no postinstall/preinstall scripts, so the npm supply-chain surface is small. The release workflow uses npm trusted publishing (OIDC) with provenance.

API key is read only from the environment: never a CLI flag (so it is not in argv or `ps`), never a config file (config/resolve.ts:39 rejects key fields), and client.ts:4-8 states it is never put in an error message. Sent only as an Authorization Bearer header.

Install modifies the shared ~/.claude/settings.json (timestamped backup, atomic write, idempotent, remove-only-own-entries). If the JSON is unparseable it writes nothing. It also silently installs into Codex, Pi and OMP configs if those are present, unless --runtime claude-code is passed.

Prompt-injection surface: the injected text contains the skill or MCP name and a 140-180 char description taken from SKILL.md frontmatter (render.ts:73), i.e. attacker-influenced content from any installed plugin or project-local .claude/skills or .mcp.json flows into model context. It is capped at 480 chars and prefixed '[skillful]', so the risk is low but not zero.

The live request has NO secret redaction. redact.ts is only used for `export-case`. MCP entries are described as 'MCP server (transport): <url or command>' (collect.ts:107-112). A URL containing a token or query key, or a project .mcp.json in a client repo, would be sent to the provider if that server makes the shortlist. The prompt is truncated to 1000 chars (thresholds.ts:51) but is otherwise sent raw, so a pasted secret would leak. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover UserPromptSubmit.

Local files: ~/.cache/skillful/routes.json (stores a prompt hash, not the prompt) and ~/.local/state/skillful/events.jsonl (0600, hash and char count only). No telemetry leaves the machine and there is no update check (docs/telemetry.md).
entries.dataEgress: Per prompt, on a cache miss, to the configured base URL (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter with SKILLFUL_BASE_URL): (1) the user's prompt text, truncated to 1000 chars (route.ts:194-197), unless SKILLFUL_UPLOAD_PROMPT=false, which sends '(prompt withheld...)' and lets Jev choose only from the locally chosen shortlist; (2) about 15 candidate capabilities from the local catalog: id, kind, name and a description of up to 200 chars. The id embeds runtime and scope; MCP descriptions carry the server URL or command string. Never sent: file contents, diffs, tool outputs, the conversation transcript, sourcePath, MCP args or env. With OpenRouter the same payload also transits OpenRouter, and OpenRouter's docs list optional session_id, user and trace fields that skillful does not set. Because the prompt goes to a third party on client projects, that is a confidentiality decision.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design, and this is the strongest part of the code. The hook has a 2000 ms total budget (SKILLFUL_BUDGET_MS, thresholds.ts:50), a 1800 ms per-attempt HTTP timeout, and up to 2 retries with backoff only on 429 and 529, all bounded by an AbortSignal (client.ts, route.ts:206-221). A top-level catch in runner.ts:227 guarantees a return, exit 0 and nothing on stderr. Caveat: on every degraded path (timeout, 401, 5xx, network, malformed, missing key) it injects one line into context: '[skillful] Could not resolve a capability suggestion... run: npx @mrgoonie/skillful' (degrade.ts:131). With no key configured, or with the key or endpoint wrong, every single prompt gets that noise line and a wasted scan. The prompt is never blocked. A skipped or none decision injects nothing.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens and no server instructions. Hook-injected text is at most 480 chars, about 120 tokens, only when a capability is chosen with sufficient probability (noneThreshold 0.4, minWinnerProbability 0.25). Most trivial or local-edit prompts inject nothing by design. On any degraded path it injects a 150-char (about 40 token) reminder every prompt. Net context cost is very low, but the user's CLAUDE.md-style skill list is already in Claude Code's context, so the benefit is also low.
pros: Truly automatic: a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, with no prompting needed and no MCP tools to bloat context.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, code is small and readable, and the fail-open design is genuinely careful (top-level catch, exit 0, budget-bounded aborts, retries only on 429/529).

Key handling is disciplined: env-only, never argv, never logged. Install is idempotent with backups and only removes its own hook entries, so it is safe next to the existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
Provider switch to OpenRouter is a pure config change (SKILLFUL_BASE_URL + SKILLFUL_MODEL + key in TYPESAFE_API_KEY), because the wire schema matches OpenRouter's System One API.

Honest about its limits: README publishes recall 0.60 holdout / 0.82 dev, says the outcome benchmark was never run, and makes no unproven claims. Good use of Choice with a 'none' option and per-candidate Noul, which is a proper fit for Jev's primitives.
Has privacy knobs (SKILLFUL_UPLOAD_PROMPT=false, SKILLFUL_DISABLE=1) and local-only telemetry.
cons: Solves a marginal problem for this user: Claude Code already lists installed skills and agents with descriptions in context. There is no evidence that a hint improves task outcomes (benchmark never run), and holdout recall is only 0.60 against its own 0.90 target, so it will often miss or suggest the wrong capability.

Not published on npm (E404) and has no releases, so the advertised `npx @mrgoonie/skillful install` fails today. It needs a clone and build, with the hook pinned to an absolute checkout path. Very young (13 days), 15 commits, one author, 5 stars, and its own docs admit Claude Code's OAuth session was untested for the bench.

Adds synchronous latency to EVERY prompt, up to a 2 s budget (README cold route 1446 ms), on top of Node startup and a catalog scan across a large plugin tree. That is a poor trade for a daily-driver workflow.

Sends the raw prompt (up to 1000 chars) plus catalog names and MCP URL/command strings to a third party with no secret redaction on the live path (redact.ts is export-case only). That is risky for client projects, and the existing secret guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit. The upload can be disabled but then the model sees no task text.

Key variable is hard-coded as TYPESAFE_API_KEY (runner.ts:147), so OpenRouter use needs an alias, and there is no first-class OpenRouter support or test. noul criteria omitted might 422 on OpenRouter (unverified). Env must reach the hook via settings.json env (plaintext key) or a wrapper.

Degraded/no-key state injects a nag line into context on every prompt, which is the opposite of unobtrusive. Only routes to skills, MCP servers, agents and commands. It does not use Jev for other coding decisions (permission risk, commit/PR gating, test selection, code-review triage), which is where a fast typed-decision model would add real value.
entries.verdict: Well-engineered, safe-to-fail hook that gives the automatic no-prompting integration the user wants and can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars. But it is unpublished, unproven on outcomes (recall 0.60 holdout), adds up to about 1.5 s to every prompt, sends prompts to a third party unredacted, and only routes skills and MCPs, which Claude Code already lists. Treat it as an optional experiment or as a reference implementation of Jev-in-a-hook (Choice plus Noul with a 'none' option), not as the daily driver.

judge.why: Most carefully fail-open hook and easiest env-only OpenRouter switch. Poor recall and per-prompt cost keep it low.
pros: Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall; env-only key handling, never argv or logs
2000 ms total budget, exit 0 on everything; idempotent install with backups that removes only its own entries
BM25 shortlist over skills, agents, commands and MCP entries
cons: Holdout recall 0.60 against its own 0.90 target; no evidence that a hint improves outcomes
npx install fails (E404); hook pinned to an absolute checkout path
Up to 2 s synchronous latency on every prompt plus Node startup and a plugin-tree scan

entries.name: n23eos/jev-skills
entries.what: Seven opt-in advisory skills (skill picker, model chooser, test prioritizer, bug/plan/context decisions) with a uv-installed jev-skills CLI; fail-open, automatic mode off by default; supports Claude and Codex.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger / manual (automatic decisions off by default)
pros: Careful safety posture: --private flag, sanitization guidance, SECURITY.md, docs/evaluation.md, CI
Broad set of decision skills including test prioritizer and skill catalog picker
cons: README itself says benefits unproven; automatic use disabled and needs explicit agent instruction
TypeSafe-only key/endpoint, no OpenRouter mention
Installs a uv tool from git; model-discretion invocation is weak for the always-automatic goal

entries.name: holstered
entries.what: A single Rust binary (`holstered`) that runs as a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook, and also for Codex, Gemini CLI, Hermes and Cline through the polyhook crate. On each prompt it scans SKILL.md files under ~/.claude/skills, ~/.codex/skills, ~/.agents/skills, ~/.gemini/skills and ~/.hermes/skills. It shortlists the top 20 by BM25 over name and description, then sends the shortlist to Jev as one Choice question (skills plus a "none" option). If Jev picks a skill, that SKILL.md body (capped at 8,000 bytes, shared across picks) is injected as additionalContext. Up to 2 runner-up skills are injected when their probability is at least 0.2. On none, error, timeout or missing key it injects nothing and passes the prompt through. Its role is skill routing, not general Jev decision support such as gating tool calls, picking models or triaging.
interface: UserPromptSubmit hook: `holstered` (no args, reads hook JSON on stdin)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), with no model discretion. It runs on every prompt without the user saying anything. The hook itself is deterministic, and Jev is called inside it.
security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from the environment only and sent as a Bearer header via ureq (src/jev/ask.rs:64-66). It is not in argv, so it does not show up in the process list. Error strings carry only the status or transport failure, not headers (ask.rs:61-62).

There is no telemetry, no shell execution, no postinstall script (npm view shows no scripts) and no curl|sh installer. The hook only reads local files and makes one HTTPS POST. The Go shim downloads a release binary and verifies SHA256SUMS. The npm packages use provenance.
HOLSTERED_JEV_URL is an unrestricted override, so anyone who can set the env can redirect prompts and the key to another host. That only matters if the environment is already compromised.

Prompt-injection surface: the chosen SKILL.md bodies (up to 8KB) are injected verbatim into context with 'Follow it for this task'. Any file in ~/.claude/skills or the other scanned roots, including third-party skills, is therefore trusted. The skill descriptions (the criteria sent to Jev) are attacker-influenced text only if a malicious skill is installed. Jev's output is a constrained choice, and unknown names are dropped (pick.rs:50), so the model cannot inject free text.
Skills are walked with follow_links(true) up to depth 5, so symlinks in skill dirs are followed, and any SKILL.md with a description is read.

Supply chain: a single maintainer, 4 stars, project less than a week old (created 2026-09-25, npm 1.2.0 published 2026-09-26). The hook is a binary that runs on every prompt with access to the key, so it needs review or a pinned version. A Rust build from source (cargo install --locked) would be safer than a prebuilt npm binary, which I did not inspect.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions on every submitted prompt (skipped only if the prompt is empty, no skill has a BM25 match, or the key is unset): the user prompt clipped to its first 500 and last 1,500 characters (src/prompt.rs:122-133, so up to 2,000 chars; CONFIGURATION.md wrongly says first 2,000), the name and description of up to 20 shortlisted skills, and the API key. It sends no file contents, diffs, tool outputs or conversation history. Pasted logs or code in the prompt do go out, so for client projects any pasted secrets or proprietary code in the prompt reach OpenRouter and TypeSafe. OpenRouter's data policy applies. Setting HOLSTERED_KEV_URL to a local Kev keeps everything on the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Any read error, missing key, HTTP error, timeout or unparsable answer leaves the prompt untouched (src/main.rs:33-39, src/select.rs:104-106 prints the error to stderr, tests/timeout.rs and tests/fallback.rs). The default timeout is 8s (HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS), well under Claude Code's default hook timeout, which the docs put at 60s. A slow Jev delays every prompt by up to 8s before it gives up. It retries nothing and has no circuit breaker, so a Jev outage costs 8s of latency per prompt. Lowering HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS to about 2000 is advisable.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so there are no tool definitions and no server instructions. The hook injects text only when Jev picks a skill: up to 8,000 bytes (about 2k tokens) total, plus about 30 tokens of header, and up to 2 runner-ups share that budget. It is often zero on chit-chat prompts. Because a hook re-injects on every matching prompt, a long session can accumulate several skill bodies, since the same skill is not deduplicated across turns.
pros: Fully automatic: a UserPromptSubmit hook fires on every prompt with no 'use jev' wording, which is exactly the requested integration model, and it coexists with the existing PreToolUse and GitNexus hooks.
Native OpenRouter support with the right endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions) and model (~typesafe/jev-latest), using only OPENROUTER_API_KEY. No code patching is needed.
Fail-open by design (empty response on any error, timeout or missing key), it never blocks a prompt, and its tests cover timeout and fallback.
Zero context cost when it declines, no MCP tool definitions, and injection is capped at 8KB. Runtime is a static Rust binary, so there is no Node or Python startup and no postinstall script.

Uses Jev for what it is designed for: a typed Choice with probabilities, with a pick threshold and runner-up threshold you can tune. The README reports 29/32 correct picks and 6/6 correct abstentions on its own 38-prompt set, with a 915 ms median.
Small, readable codebase (about 700 lines of source) that is easy to audit or fork. MIT, npm provenance, CI with clippy and fmt.
cons: Solves a narrow problem: routing prompts to local SKILL.md files. It only helps if you keep many custom skills under ~/.claude/skills. It does not scan project-level .claude/skills or plugin-provided skills, because roots.rs:155-161 only looks in $HOME dirs, so the plugin and skills available in this environment are largely ignored unless HOLSTERED_SKILLS_DIRS is set. Claude Code already auto-triggers skills from their descriptions, so the marginal value is modest.

Sends every prompt (up to 2,000 chars, including pasted logs or code) plus skill descriptions to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. This is a real concern on client projects, and there is no redaction or per-project opt-out except unsetting the key. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
Adds about 1s of blocking latency to every prompt, up to 8s during a Jev outage, with no circuit breaker. Jev is in beta and the OpenRouter endpoint is 'alpha', so the URL and schema may change.

Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-25, 48 commits, 4 stars, 1 contributor, 3 npm versions in 3 days). There is no independent evidence beyond its own small eval, and I did not run any of it. Installing an unreviewed prebuilt binary that handles your API key on every prompt needs some care.

Documentation inconsistency (CONFIGURATION.md says the first 2,000 chars are sent; the code sends head 500 plus tail 1,500). Skill bodies are injected verbatim with 'Follow it', so any third-party skill becomes trusted instructions.

It does not use Jev for other daily-coding decisions such as permission or tool-call gating, model routing, or task triage. The 'Jev' part is limited to one Choice call. It also needs OPENROUTER_API_KEY in the environment Claude Code starts from, which is not configured yet.

Plugin hooks.json runs bare `holstered`. The user's settings env overrides PATH and requires absolute paths, so the npm global bin (or ~/.cargo/bin) is likely not found. That gives exit 127, a non-blocking error, and a silently dead hook. The fix is a user-level settings.json hook with an absolute path to the binary (or the wrapper), not the plugin.

OPENROUTER_API_KEY must be in the environment of the process that starts the hook. The audit's suggestion of the settings.json env block also exposes the key to every Bash tool call and to Claude itself. The existing no-secret-leak hook does not list OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so it would not stop `echo $OPENROUTER_API_KEY`. A tiny wrapper script that reads the key from a 0600 file and execs holstered would keep it out of the session env. The protected-vars list should be updated either way.

Low marginal value for THIS user: ~/.claude/skills holds only 13 skills (dougthepug-design, empat-design, find-skills and 10 gitnexus-*, plus a 'synced' entry), and ~/.agents/skills holds 4. The plugin skills (caveman:*, anthropic-skills:*, etc.) live outside the scanned $HOME roots (roots.rs:14-23). Claude Code already sees these 13 skills in its own listing (skillListingBudgetFraction 0.02), so routing them via a paid, ~1s-per-prompt network call gains little.

Stateless: nothing dedups across turns (no session state in src/). The same SKILL.md body (up to 8,000 bytes) is re-injected on every matching prompt, with a forced 'Follow it for this task' directive that overrides Claude's own judgement about whether to load the skill. Under the 10,000-char per-hook additionalContext cap (Claude Code docs), 8,000 bytes plus headers just fits, but three picks lose most of each body to truncation.

Every prompt's skill-shortlist descriptions (local skill names and descriptions) are sent out as well as the prompt text. The user prompt (which may carry injected instructions from pasted content) is also the Jev state, so a poisoned paste could steer which local skill gets force-injected. The blast radius is limited to installed skills.

polyhook caller detection is env-first (POLYHOOK_CALLER, CLAUDE_CODE_VERSION, ..., GEMINI_PROJECT_DIR) before JSON heuristics. A stray GEMINI_PROJECT_DIR or CURSOR_SESSION_ID in the environment would make it emit the wrong output format for Claude Code, and the failure is silent. The chain is polyhook 0.2.0 -> polyhook-core 0.2.0, a second young single-author dependency that is also a supply-chain hop.

Floating model alias `~typesafe/jev-latest` (not pinned to jev-1.13) means routing behaviour can change silently. The /alpha endpoint has no SLA. Every prompt pays a ~1s median network call, and up to 8s on an outage with no circuit breaker.
Skill discovery does a full WalkDir with follow_links(true), reading every SKILL.md on each prompt. This is cheap with 13 skills, but it is unbounded work with symlinks.
entries.verdict: The best fit found so far for 'automatic, no prompting': a deterministic, fail-open hook that already targets the OpenRouter Jev Decisions API correctly. Its scope is only skill routing over ~/.claude/skills, and it sends every prompt to OpenRouter, so it is worth using only if you keep a large personal skill library; audit or build it from source, set a shorter timeout (about 2s), and avoid it on sensitive client repos.

verification.note: Verified from source: Jev via OpenRouter is native. It POSTs to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model ~typesafe/jev-latest (a real OpenRouter alias). The request is one `choice` question over the BM25 top-20 skills plus `none`, and the answer is read from answers.skill.choice/probabilities. Claude Code correctness is confirmed: polyhook-core emits hookSpecificOutput{hookEventName:"UserPromptSubmit", additionalContext}, and `{}` for approve, which is valid for UserPromptSubmit. All error, timeout and missing-key paths exit 0 with no output (main.rs:33-39), and any other exit code is non-blocking per the Claude Code docs, so it fails open. There is no shell exec, no telemetry, no install scripts and no key in argv, and the npm package has only optionalDependencies; the audit's security claims hold. The audit's substance is largely right, but it has wrong line references throughout, a wrong 'no Node at runtime' claim for the npm route, a stale 60s timeout claim, stale eval numbers, and it missed the PATH and key-exposure problems in this specific environment. I lowered the score from 6 to 4. The integration model is right (automatic and fail-open), but the value to this user is narrow: only 13 personal skills are scanned, plugin skills are ignored, and Claude already lists them. Each prompt sends its text and skill descriptions to OpenRouter and TypeSafe and adds ~1s. The project is 5 days old with a single maintainer and 4 stars. A hardened setup would use a built-from-source binary, an absolute-path user hook, a key-file wrapper, HOLSTERED_TIMEOUT_MS around 2000, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY added to the secret-leak guard. Even then it stays a skill router, not general Jev decision support. Clone used: <scratch path> (HEAD 5c29a03 = latest v1.4.0). Extracted polyhook, polyhook-core and the npm tarball are under <scratch path>

judge.why: Cleanest, safest skill hook with native OpenRouter and a fail-open path in source. Low value for a 13-skill setup.
pros: Verified: no telemetry, no shell exec, exit 0 with no output on every error path; BM25 top-20 plus none as one Choice
Correct UserPromptSubmit output format for Claude Code
Hardened build path exists: build from source, absolute-path user hook, key-file wrapper, timeout ~2000 ms
cons: Plugin hooks.json runs bare `holstered`; with your overridden PATH this fails with exit 127 and is silently dead (use a user-level hook with an absolute path)
Scans only $HOME skill roots (13 skills); plugin skills are ignored, so the marginal value is small
Forces a 'Follow it for this task' directive and re-injects up to 8,000 bytes of SKILL.md every matching prompt; floating alias; ~1 s per prompt
npm route adds Node startup per prompt; OPENROUTER_API_KEY needs adding to the secret guard

entries.name: onlyjq04/jev-agent-hooks
entries.what: Node hook bundle (no deps, ~1.4k lines) that uses Jev (System One) in two hook points. (1) UserPromptSubmit skill suggester: on every non-slash prompt it builds a roster of the user's skills (~/.claude/skills, project .claude/skills, enabled plugins), makes up to two Jev calls (Choice over roster plus 3 gate Nouls, then Choice over top 3 with 700-char SKILL.md excerpts plus a 'fits' Noul each) and, if fit >= 0.7, injects one additionalContext line 'Relevant to the current request: X. Ignore if it does not fit'. (2) PreToolUse on Agent: a Jev gate asks Noul 'is this agent suited to the task' and Choice 'which model tier (haiku/sonnet/opus/fable)' and denies once per session/agent/tier if Jev disagrees. Also ships a rule-based subagent-model-gate (denies Agent/Workflow calls without an explicit model alias), a SubagentStop gate (blocks empty final messages), a `jev` CLI wrapper, a jev-decide skill (model-discretion: rank candidates, act-or-ask, verify-before-claiming-done), a subagent-model policy skill, and 4 preset agents (mech/bulk/deep/oracle). Also targets Codex, pi, Grok Build.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse Agent, SubagentStop): run without user prompting on every event, but their effect is advisory (one-line ignorable suggestion) or a one-time deny. Plus jev-decide skill: skill-description trigger, Claude's discretion to shell out to `jev` CLI via Bash. So it satisfies 'automatic' in a limited way, but the automatic Jev uses are skill routing and subagent model routing, not code decisions.
security: API key is read from env only and sent as an Authorization header via fetch; never appears in argv/process list. Good.

No telemetry to third parties; only api.typesafe.ai is contacted. Local JSONL logs in ~/.claude/logs include the first 200 chars of every prompt (jev-skill-suggest.jsonl) and the subagent task description; jev-cli log omits state.

install.sh is local-only (no curl|sh, no postinstall). BUT link() does `rm -rf` on any real directory at the destination (e.g. an existing ~/.claude/skills/jev-decide or ~/.claude/agents/<name>, and ~/.agents/skills/<name>) and it links every skills/* dir and agents/*.md into your dirs; the README instructs cloning and running it. Review before running; destinations are fixed from $HOME.

Injected additionalContext is a fixed template with only the skill name interpolated from the local roster; low prompt-injection surface. Roster contents (third-party plugin SKILL.md text) are sent to Jev as criteria, so a malicious skill could bias the pick but only to another local skill.
alreadyDenied() writes a JSON state file at os.tmpdir()/jev-agent-gate-denied.json (predictable shared path in /tmp, read-modify-write without locking; low-risk on a single-user box).
Hooks run with bypass-mode user privileges; code is small and readable (read all of jev-lib, jev-skill-suggest, jev-agent-gate in full).
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (TypeSafe direct; would be openrouter.ai if patched, adding OpenRouter as a second processor): (a) every user prompt, truncated to 6000 chars; (b) the last assistant text message from the transcript, last 1500 chars; (c) descriptions (250 chars each) of ALL installed skills/plugin skills on the first call, and 700-char SKILL.md body excerpts of the top 3 on the second; (d) for each Agent dispatch: the subagent prompt (up to 8000 chars), description, agent name/description, which routinely contains code snippets, file paths and task details. README itself warns not to put secrets in agent prompts. No file contents or diffs are sent directly, but prompts and subagent prompts on client projects can contain client code/IP. There is no secret redaction, and the existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover this path because it runs inside the hook process, not via a Bash/Read tool call.
entries.failureMode: Jev-dependent hooks fail open: skill-suggest wraps main in .catch(() => {}) and returns silently without key/CLAUDECODE (jev-skill-suggest.mjs:165-183); agent-gate catches Jev errors and allows (jev-agent-gate.mjs ~line 124-128). Per-request timeout 4 s (jev-lib.mjs:11), two sequential requests for skill suggest, hook timeout 10 s in settings snippet, so worst case a prompt is delayed ~8 s before proceeding without suggestion. Agent-gate is fail-open but can deny (once per session/agent/tier; identical resubmission passes). NOT fail-open: subagent-model-gate.mjs is a pure rule gate that denies any Agent call lacking an explicit haiku|sonnet|opus|fable alias and preset mismatches, with Chinese denial text; independent of Jev availability, it changes Claude Code behavior for every subagent spawn. Can be disabled with CLAUDE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_GATE=off.
entries.contextCost: Very low. No MCP server: 0 tools, 0 server instructions. Always-loaded skill listings: jev-decide description ~430 chars (~110 tokens), claude-subagent-model description ~120 chars (~30 tokens) plus 4 agent descriptions (~470-1230 bytes each incl. Chinese, ~250 tokens total in Agent tool listing). Per-turn hook injection: one ~45-token line only when best fit >= 0.7 (README: ~3 of 34 turns, so rare). Full jev-decide body (~1k tokens) loads only when invoked; claude-subagent-model body is 10 KB (~2.5k tokens) if the model loads it.
pros: Genuinely automatic: UserPromptSubmit and PreToolUse hooks fire with no user phrasing, matching the 'never say use jev' requirement; hooks return additionalContext / permission decisions per the real hook protocol.
Fail-open on every Jev path (try/catch, AbortSignal 4 s, missing key => no-op), so a Jev/OpenRouter outage will not block Claude Code.
Tiny, readable, dependency-free code; all Jev traffic funnels through one function (hooks/jev-lib.mjs:6), so retargeting to OpenRouter is a ~4-line edit.

Uses Jev for what a calibrated classifier suits (pick a skill from a roster, tier fit), following TypeSafe's own skill-suggestion cookbook; has shadow mode (JEV_SKILL_SUGGEST=shadow, JEV_AGENT_GATE=shadow) to log without acting, which is the safe way to trial it.
Honest README: reports its own weak results (gate barely separates, near-duplicate skills split probability, misfires on short phrasing) and raised threshold to 0.7 from real data.
Low context cost (no MCP tools, ~100-400 tokens of always-on listings, injection only on ~10% of turns); API key not in argv; MIT license.
jev-decide skill gives a model-discretion path for act-or-ask and verify-before-done checks, closest thing in this repo to Jev helping actual coding decisions.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only (https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, model 'jev-latest' at jev-lib.mjs:6-10); zero OpenRouter support, so it needs a fork/patch, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified from source.

Value is narrow for this user: skill-suggest only helps when you have a large skill roster, and the author's own data show it is marginal (3 suggestions in 34 turns, near-duplicate skills confuse it, 'correct' labels are just what the agent loaded). Claude Code already auto-selects skills from descriptions; the hook adds 1-3 s blocking latency to EVERY prompt for a rarely-shown hint.

Sends every prompt (6000 chars), last assistant reply (1500 chars), and full subagent prompts (8000 chars, often containing client code) to a third party; no redaction; risky on client projects and duplicates exposure if routed via OpenRouter.

Bundled subagent policy is the author's personal workflow and is intrusive: rule gate hard-denies any Agent/Workflow call without an explicit haiku|sonnet|opus|fable alias, references a 'fable' tier and Chinese-language deny messages/agent prompts, and would fight the user's Opus 5.5 setup and existing workflow scripts; the Jev tier-gate can also veto subagent dispatches (a wrong answer costs a retry turn).
Overlaps/conflicts with existing hooks: adds a second UserPromptSubmit hook and Agent PreToolUse hooks next to the caveman and gitnexus hooks; roster scan reads all enabled-plugin skills each prompt.
install.sh does `rm -rf` on real directories at link destinations and symlinks skills/agents into ~/.claude and ~/.agents; must be reviewed/adapted rather than run blindly.
Very immature: created 2026-09-20, 10 commits over 4 days, 2 stars, 1 fork, no tests, no CI, no releases, single-user evaluation; latency and accuracy claims are not reproducible.
Does not use Jev where it would help daily coding most (commit/PR classification, risk gating of destructive Bash, test triage, retrieval reranking); those would need to be built on top.
entries.verdict: Useful as a reference implementation of the correct hook shape (UserPromptSubmit additionalContext plus PreToolUse gate, fail-open, shadow mode) and a one-function patch point for OpenRouter, but not worth installing as-is: TypeSafe-only, marginal skill-suggest value at 1-3 s per prompt, unredacted prompt egress, and an opinionated Chinese-language subagent-model policy that would fight this setup. Cherry-pick jev-lib.mjs plus jev-skill-suggest.mjs in shadow mode (or the jev-decide skill) with the URL/key patched to OpenRouter, and skip the model gate, agents and install.sh.

entries.name: abgregs/jev-skill-router
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (and own marketplace) with two hooks. UserPromptSubmit reads ~/.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md (name+description only), sends the prompt + last ~2000 chars of transcript + every skill as one Jev Noul each (sharded 250/request, parallel) to TypeSafe systemOne, thresholds probabilities (invoke >=0.85, suggest 0.80-0.85, cap 6), and injects 'Skill routing verdict ... do not select skills yourself: Invoke: ...' as additionalContext. A PreToolUse matcher=Skill gate denies Skill calls not on the approved list (fail-open on missing/stale state). Defaults to a keyword mock judge with no network; real Jev only if .skillrouter.json has {"judge":"jev"} plus a key. Skill routing only, not general coding decisions. Also ships CLI (route, doctor, install claude) and a static demo site.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit + PreToolUse on Skill) once plugin is installed; fully automatic, no prompting. Real Jev is off by default and needs a per-project .skillrouter.json {"judge":"jev"} (or ~/.skillrouter.json for global) plus key in env.
security: MIT license; package.json private:true, not on npm; install via /plugin marketplace add abgregs/jev-skill-router (plugin.json, marketplace.json read).

Executes committed prebuilt bundles dist/hooks/*.mjs (SDK + gray-matter bundled, thousands of lines) on EVERY prompt and every Skill call: the source-vs-bundle match is unverified and a later push to the repo silently changes code that runs with your privileges; pin a commit/fork if adopted.

API key from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY or .env.local (process.loadEnvFile, cwd and package dir); never on argv; sent as Bearer header only. Reads .env.local from the project cwd, which for client repos may contain unrelated variables (loaded into hook process env only).

No telemetry/postinstall/curl|sh found (grep). No shell execution in hooks. Writes turn state incl. full prompt in world-readable-by-default /tmp/jev-skill-router/turn-<session>.json (plaintext prompt persists up to 24h).

Prompt-injection surface: additionalContext is generated from skill ids only (no user text echoed), but skill names/descriptions from ~/.claude/skills are sent to Jev and used verbatim in Noul instructions; low risk. The gate is a policy layer and can deny legitimate Skill calls when the judge returns an empty verdict (README admits this regime).
Only 16 commits over ~9 days, single author, 0 stars, no releases, no unit tests (only inspect/bench scripts), CI only deploys demo pages.
entries.dataEgress: With judge=jev (opt-in; default is mock with zero network): on every user prompt, sent to the Jev endpoint: full prompt text, last ~2000 chars of recent user+assistant text turns from the transcript, and name+description of every skill in ~/.claude/skills (repeated per shard; one Noul per skill). openFiles/projectRules fields exist but the Claude Code hook does not populate them. No file contents, diffs, or tool outputs are sent. Prompts on client projects therefore leave the machine on every turn (to TypeSafe, or OpenRouter if repointed).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: any exception in the UserPromptSubmit hook -> exit 0 silently (hooks/user-prompt-submit.ts:132-135); gate allows on missing/stale state or error (pre-tool-use-gate.ts:84). But the hook has no internal timeout ("Claude Code's own hook timeout is the bound", :11-12) and hooks.json sets no timeout; the SDK default is 10s per attempt with 2 retries (408/429/5xx) and backoff, so a slow/down Jev can stall each prompt for roughly 30s+ before failing open. Missing key with judge=jev throws -> silent no-op. Real gap: a fully empty verdict makes the gate deny agent-chosen skills not named in the prompt (README documents this), which is fail-closed for skills.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no server instructions, no tool schemas. Hook injects only when verdict non-empty: ~300-500 chars (~75-125 tokens) per turn plus a short user-visible systemMessage; silent on conversational turns. Side effect: instructs model 'do not select skills yourself', and obedient models load every invoked skill (~2k tokens each, up to 6 = ~12k tokens/turn by README's own estimate).
pros: The only candidate seen here that is a truly automatic, hook-based Jev integration: user never types 'use jev'; runs on every prompt (hooks/hooks.json) with fail-open behavior.

Uses Jev for what it is designed for: many independent Noul yes/no judgments sharded across parallel requests; measured 132-306 ms for 51 skills; good reference implementation of toState()/noul() usage and the currentRequest vs earlierConversationBackground framing lesson.
No MCP tools and near-zero context cost when no skill matches (~100 tokens injected); no argv key exposure; no telemetry or postinstall; MIT.
Safe trial path: defaults to free mock judge (no network), config-gated real Jev, clean uninstall, per-project exclude/alwaysAllow/threshold knobs.
SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and Bearer auth, so pointing it at https://openrouter.ai/api with an OpenRouter key is plausible with zero code changes (needs a live test).
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: only skill selection. Opus 5.5 already picks skills reasonably; benchmark evidence is Sonnet on bare Claude Code, n=3 per cell, 61% vs 33% hit rate, and author admits cost/turn deltas unsupported and junk counts confounded.

Only routes ~/.claude/skills (user-prompt-submit.ts:71); skills delivered by plugins (caveman, gitnexus-*, etc.) are never on verdicts, so the gate can deny them unless named or in alwaysAllow; with an empty verdict the gate blocks the agent's own correct skill choices (README documents this failure).

Sends every prompt plus recent transcript and the whole skill catalog to a third party on every turn, including client-project prompts; plaintext prompt also cached in /tmp/jev-skill-router/turn-*.json for 24h.
No internal timeout: SDK 10 s x 3 attempts can stall each prompt ~30 s when Jev/OpenRouter is degraded (jev is beta); adds 0.5-3 s to every prompt when healthy.

Recall-biased default (0.85) makes obedient frontier models load up to 6 skills (~12k tokens) per turn; injected text tells the model not to choose skills itself, conflicting with user's existing hook/plugin stack behavior.

Immature: created 2026-09-21, 16 commits in 9 days, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests or releases; runs unaudited committed dist bundles (supply-chain risk if repo updates); OpenRouter path untested by the author; response-shape compatibility unverified.
Does not use Choice/Score or general code decisions (e.g. should-I-run-tests, is-this-secret, risk gating) that would benefit daily coding.
entries.verdict: A well-engineered but narrow proof-of-concept: automatic, fail-open hooks that use Jev Noul fan-out for skill routing, and the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL should let it run against OpenRouter. It adds latency, sends every prompt off-machine, misses plugin-provided skills, and can block skills via its gate, so for Opus 5.5 daily coding it is at most a pattern to copy, or a ungated (UserPromptSubmit-only) experiment from a pinned fork.

entries.name: @maromocooo/skill-dispatch (skilldispatch)
entries.what: Node/TypeScript CLI (skilldispatch) that registers user-level Claude Code (and Codex) UserPromptSubmit hooks. On each prompt it discovers the native skill catalog (local, plugin, synced skills), sends the RAW prompt plus each skill's name/description/agent/scope to Jev as one Noul question per skill (via @typesafe-ai/sdk client.systemOne), applies a threshold policy (0.75, max 4 skills) and either only logs a trace (shadow, default) or, in opt-in advisory mode, injects a 'consider invoking these skills with the native Skill tool' additionalContext listing skill names (max 4096 bytes). Also adds PreToolUse/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure observers that record native Skill invocations locally, plus trace analytics and an eval harness. It is a skill router/observability tool, not a general coding-decision integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt with no user action (fully automatic once installed). But Jev's output only nudges Claude toward skills via advisory context; Claude retains discretion, and shadow (default) does nothing visible to the agent.
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json; only prepack build. No curl|sh installer.

API key read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env (never argv); hook command argv contains only node path + cliPath + 'hook claude' (src/registration/command.ts:42). validateApiKey enforces printable ASCII. Errors sanitized (JevRequestError carries no cause/request/credentials, client.ts:21-27); SDK logLevel 'off'.

Prompt-injection surface is narrow: skill descriptions are sent to Jev as data; advisory output only includes safe native skill identifiers (no descriptions/bodies/probabilities) capped at 4096 bytes (src/hooks/advisory.ts:12-16,58-77); Claude still decides whether to call the Skill tool.

Fetch uses redirect:'error' (client.ts:39). Global hooks ignore project-level skilldispatch config unless hook.trustProjectConfig true; even then project cannot choose provider/mode (docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md).
Local files: HMAC-hashed prompts by default (raw storage opt-in), 0600/0700 permissions, symlink/hardlink checks. No telemetry/cloud upload of traces per README and code grep.

Hook installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json (user scope) - low risk but it modifies global config alongside user's existing PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus hooks; adds PreToolUse/PostToolUse observers on Skill tool (matching only Skill presumably) with its own matchers.
entries.dataEgress: On every UserPromptSubmit: the full RAW user prompt text plus, for each candidate skill (up to 48 per chunk, chunked, concurrency 2), name, description, agent ('claude-code'), scope are POSTed to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe direct) with Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/providers/jev/questions.ts:14-17,26-31; client.ts:59-82). Not sent: skill bodies, file paths, cwd, code, diffs, file contents, tool outputs (README 'Privacy and security'; docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md). The prompt is repeated in every chunk request. Traces stay local. With a patched OpenRouter path, OpenRouter would also see the same payload. Client projects: raw prompts (which may include pasted code/secrets/client names) leave the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: hook wrapped in try/catch (src/hooks/runtime.ts:37-43,108-110) returns nothing on parse/setup/provider/timeout/storage errors. Defaults: request timeout 1800 ms, overall routing budget 2500 ms, retries 0 (options.ts:22-23, README), hook registration timeout 5 s. Missing key produces a doctor warning and routing fails open (no silent mock fallback). In default shadow mode the hook is registered async so Jev slowness/outage never blocks the turn; in advisory mode a slow Jev delays prompt by up to ~2.5 s and on timeout injects nothing (partial/degraded results not injected: runtime.ts:117-120).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, zero tool-definition tokens, no server instructions. Shadow mode injects nothing. Advisory mode injects at most 4096 bytes (about 1000 tokens max, typically about 100-150 tokens: ~330-char intro/conclusion boilerplate plus up to 4 '- skill-name' lines) as UserPromptSubmit additionalContext only when at least one skill clears the 0.75 threshold.
pros: Truly automatic: UserPromptSubmit hook, no need to tell Claude to 'use jev'; install command is idempotent and edits user settings while preserving existing hooks (src/registration/document.ts, manage.ts).

Genuine Jev usage via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 systemOne with Noul primitives (the right primitive for 'does skill apply', calibrated P(yes)); Jev is a good fit for cheap yes/no relevance gating (~$0.042/1M input tokens).

Careful engineering: fail-open on everything, 1.8s/2.5s timeouts, async shadow default, no shell in hook command (exec-form argv), no postinstall, sanitized errors, sane privacy defaults (HMAC prompts, 0600 files), pinned CI action SHAs, ~397 tests, Node 20+24 CI.
Zero context cost in shadow mode and small bounded injection (<=4096 B) in advisory mode; no MCP tools bloating context.

Built-in observability (recommended vs injected vs actually-invoked Skill calls, eval harness with recall/precision gates) lets you measure whether Jev routing actually helps before enabling advisory.
MIT license; code is small and readable so a fork adding OpenRouter is feasible.
cons: No OpenRouter support: baseURL hardcoded to https://api.typesafe.ai (src/providers/jev/client.ts:61), only TYPESAFE_API_KEY is read, and the model regex rejects OpenRouter IDs containing '/' (options.ts:8). User wants OpenRouter-hosted Jev, so a local fork/patch (3 small edits + local build) is required; OpenRouter response compatibility with the SDK is unverified.

Narrow use case: only routes to Claude skills. It does not use Jev for other coding decisions (permission/risk gating, whether to run tests, which files, plan vs act). Value depends on how many skills the user has; with a handful of skills benefit is marginal, and native Claude skill selection via descriptions already exists. Tool-call-level decisions, where Jev could add most value, are out of scope.

Sends the raw prompt to an external service on every prompt, repeated per 48-skill chunk; for client projects this is a real confidentiality issue and the existing secret guard (PreToolUse) does not filter UserPromptSubmit prompts. README itself warns sensitive prompts should not be routed.

Advisory mode is synchronous (extra 100-500 ms+ Node spawn and full catalog rescan each prompt, up to 2.5 s); shadow mode, the default, injects nothing so Claude never benefits automatically until user opts in and reinstalls.

Extremely immature: repo and npm created 2026-09-23 (one week old), 2 commits, single author, 0 stars/forks, 0.1.0; README states no measured Jev accuracy and 'no superiority over native Claude routing is claimed'; labels in benchmark are AI-assisted drafts; single 'smoke test' anecdote.
Only recommends; Claude may ignore it, and the observed-invocation evidence is positive-only, so measured benefit is hard to prove.

Installs seven+ hook registrations into global ~/.claude/settings.json (UserPromptSubmit plus Pre/PostToolUse/PostToolUseFailure observers), adding a Node process spawn on each Skill tool call; more moving parts alongside gitnexus/caveman/secret-guard hooks. Bypass/auto permission mode does not affect it but debugging hook interplay costs time.
Depends on TypeSafe SDK 0.6.0 workaround for an Undici tee crash on Node 20/22 (client.ts:29-51); user is on Node 24 so likely irrelevant but indicates SDK fragility.
entries.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context-cost UserPromptSubmit hook that really calls Jev, but it only does skill recommendation, is one week old, hardcodes api.typesafe.ai (needs a small fork to reach OpenRouter), and ships raw prompts out on every turn. Worth reading as a reference implementation or running in shadow mode after patching, not a core daily-coding integration.

entries.name: ydmw74/jev-skill-router
entries.what: Stdio MCP skill_select implementing TypeSafe cookbook: one Choice over all skills plus Noul gates, then top-3 rerank; suggests at most one skill. Built for Hermes.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Cookbook-backed: wrong skill loads 16.8% to 7.3% on Hermes catalog; 375 loc, easy to audit/adapt
Uses Decisions API (cookbook style), likely close to OpenRouter alpha
cons: Hermes-targeted, needs adaptation to Claude Code skill roster and a UserPromptSubmit hook to be automatic
No tests; 0 stars; agent must call the tool itself

entries.name: MuskanPaliwal/skill-picker
entries.what: Python CLI (stdin request + skills dir -> JSON ranking of skills by Jev fit probability, 2 calls ~1.9s); agent turns output into a question. Not a hook itself; hook configs in repo are Entire scaffolding.
entries.autoInvocation: manual (CLI; would need own UserPromptSubmit hook)
pros: Read-only JSON output, never invokes skills; reports status unavailable and fails open without a key
Has pytest tests (router, evaluate, catalog, api_key) and TYPESAFE_API_KEY_COMMAND helper for key retrieval
cons: Endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone; no base URL override, needs code edit for OpenRouter
No Claude Code hook/skill wiring shipped; user would have to add a UserPromptSubmit hook and 2 calls (~2s) per prompt
Created one week ago, 0 stars

entries.name: Dicklesworthstone/skillranker (sr)
entries.what: Standalone Rust CLI (binary `sr`, ~150k LOC) that, on each Claude Code UserPromptSubmit, reads the session transcript plus the visible skill roster, asks Jev two typed questions (a wide Choice over up to 254 skills plus "none", then a rerank with Choice/Noul fit checks on a shortlist), and injects at most one "Suggested skill for the next step: X" line as additionalContext. Advisory only; abstains silently. Also ships eval/replay/ledger/feedback tooling.
interface: sr feedback / snooze / stats / ledger / budget / observe
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: UserPromptSubmit with an empty matcher, so it fires on every user prompt with no user or model action. It is advisory: Claude may ignore the suggested skill. It fires only on user prompts, not on mid-turn tool calls or subagent steps.
security: API key is read from the environment only (TYPESAFE_API_KEY), so it does not appear in argv. The key is origin-scoped: it refuses to emit the Authorization header to any other origin (src/jev/endpoint.rs:13, :413-426).
Redirects are hard failures, ambient HTTP(S)_PROXY variables are not trusted, and HTTP is allowed only for loopback and never with a credential. unsafe_code is forbidden (Cargo.toml).
Networking needs explicit opt-in (network.enabled in trusted user config), and a project-level file cannot enable it. Credential presence alone does not enable it.
Outgoing context is redacted, but the README admits it cannot catch all confidential prose. Dry-run and disclosure receipts let you inspect the payload.

Hook installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json (preview first, backup, lock, digest check). It also drops a usage skill and shell completions via install.sh, which is a curl|bash installer with SHA256 verification. The fallback source build pulls git-pinned dependencies.

Prompt-injection surface: skill bodies and descriptions from the roster, and transcript and tool output, go into the Jev request. Jev returns typed decisions, not free text. The injected output is a locally validated skill ID within a 1,024-character cap, so the injection risk is low.
entries.dataEgress: On each user prompt, and only if network is enabled, the standard profile sends the newest prompt, recent conversation history, recent tool calls and results, project signals such as dirty paths, plus every candidate skill's description and body excerpts (up to 254 candidates and a 96 KiB request) to the provider. Everything is redacted first. Minimal profile and --no-tools reduce this. Without a code diff step, file contents appear only where tool results are in the recent transcript. Because the destination would be a patched OpenRouter endpoint, this content of client-project sessions would transit OpenRouter and TypeSafe. Local state: SQLite ledger and response cache (at most 10 minutes) under ~/.local/share/sr.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. The hook never blocks: errors give empty stdout, a sanitized stderr line, and exit 0. Internal deadline is 3000 ms from process entry with 200 ms reserved for cleanup; the installed harness timeout is 4 s. Per-invocation budget is 2 logical requests and 4 HTTP attempts, with retry and Retry-After honored inside the deadline. Stale or late responses are not published. A circuit breaker and shared attempt allowance are optional. The worst case is a UserPromptSubmit that takes up to about 3-4 s before Claude starts.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. The hook injects at most one short line per prompt (typically 20-40 tokens, 1,024-character cap), and injects nothing on abstention or failure. The installed usage skill adds one skill description to the skill list. That is the lowest context cost of any Jev integration, but it also gives the smallest benefit.
pros: The only candidate seen so far that is truly automatic and deterministic: a UserPromptSubmit hook, so the user never has to say 'use jev'.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to (typed Choice and Noul with calibrated probabilities and a 'none' abstention), following TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook.
Very small context cost: no MCP tools, at most one injected line, silent on abstain.
Strongly fail-open with a 3 s deadline, a 4 s harness timeout, bounded retries and a circuit breaker, so it cannot wedge Claude Code.
Careful key handling: env-only key, origin-scoped bearer, no redirects, no proxy trust, network opt-in, redaction and dry-run disclosure receipts.
Hook installer is safe: previews, backs up, and merges without touching the existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks. It is also cleanly uninstallable.
Substantial engineering: 731 commits in 13 days, 152 test files, replay and eval tooling, and a written design plan.
Already handles Claude Code specifics: transcript parsing, skill roster with override and shadow resolution, and explicit 'don't use skill X' handling.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the code accepts only a root origin plus /v1/systemone, or Cloudflare. Using OpenRouter needs a source patch and a fork to maintain (moderate effort).

It only picks skills. The user's stated goal was to use Jev where it adds value in daily coding. It provides no code-level decisions such as risk of an edit, whether a command is safe, or which file to read. Value depends on having a large skill library; with a handful of skills it gains little.
Adds a synchronous network round trip (two sequential Jev calls, unmeasured p50 about 0.6 s, up to 3 s) before every prompt.
Sends conversation history, tool results and skill bodies from all projects, including client work, to a third party. Redaction is best-effort, and the flow would add OpenRouter to the data path.

Very new and alpha: created 2026-09-17, no release, no visible CI, one dominant author, main is moving daily, and CHANGELOG Unreleased lists many correctness fixes (for example large-roster live ranking was failing). The dependency stack (asupersync, frankensearch, git-pinned) is niche.
Non-standard license with an Anthropic/OpenAI rider whose terms (execute, benchmark, 'on behalf of') are ambiguous for a Claude Code user on client work.
Installer is curl|bash (with checksum), and there is no prebuilt release, so a source build needs Rust 1.95 and Git and pulls git dependencies.

Requires TYPESAFE_API_KEY (or a patched equivalent) to be exported into the environment Claude Code is launched from, which is awkward for a GUI or launcher and for subscription/OAuth users who have no such key setup.
The hook fires only on UserPromptSubmit, so it never helps during long autonomous runs in bypass or auto mode, where most of the tool calls happen.
entries.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context UserPromptSubmit hook that is genuinely automatic, but it only recommends skills, is TypeSafe-direct or Cloudflare only (an OpenRouter patch is needed), is very young, and adds a network round trip to every prompt. Treat it as a reference design for a hook-based Jev integration, not something to install as is.

judge.why: Fail-open and deterministic, but a very large codebase for a one-line hint, and OpenRouter is not supported.
pros: Deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, 3 s internal deadline, exit 0 on errors
