Wide Choice over up to 254 skills with none abstention plus rerank; silent on abstain
At most one injected line
cons: OpenRouter path rejected by design; needs a patch and maintained fork
~150k LOC is hard to audit for a hook that sees every prompt and transcript
Two sequential Jev calls (~0.6 s p50, up to 3 s); only helps with a large skill library

entries.name: kunchenguid/firstmate
entries.what: Agent distro (AGENTS.md, skills, bash scripts) to orchestrate a crew of coding agents in worktrees; optional fm-dispatch-resolve.sh uses Jev to match briefs to dispatch rules, plus a jev-mem guard.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger / script invoked by first-mate agent; optional
pros: Very active, well-documented, supports Claude harness; Jev use is optional and localised to shell scripts
Dispatch resolver has 5 s timeout and 0.6 confidence floor with fallback to agent reasoning
cons: Jev is a minor optional piece; adopting the whole distro is a large workflow change
Endpoint fixed to api.typesafe.ai and jev-latest; no OpenRouter switch (script edit needed)
Multi-agent crew model overlaps with your own setup and is not needed for Jev

entries.name: Devin-AXIS/jev-dsh-decision
entries.what: Jev decision engine plugin for DeepSeek Harness and iPolloWork: recommend tools/skills/agents, score outputs, batch up to 64 questions; exposes jev_evaluate/jev_status/jev_check_connection.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion tool in DSH/iPolloWork; manual skill
pros: Clean shared core (service/jev.mjs, dsh.mjs) with tests; generic evaluate(state, questions) tool plus jev-decision SKILL.md
Explicit design rule: Jev recommends, host agent executes
cons: Targets DSH/iPolloWork plugin systems, not Claude Code MCP/hooks; docs in Chinese
Uses api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only
Skill says use when user requests Jev - not automatic

entries.name: JevRouter (BillionsBobby/JevRouter)
entries.what: Node/TypeScript CLI + SDK + stdio MCP server ("jevrouter" npm-style package, installed via npx github:) that asks Jev one typed Choice question ("which tool/model/subagent should handle this?") over a caller-supplied candidate list, then applies local policy (permissions, risk, confirmation, confidence gate) and writes a JSON receipt to .jevrouter/decisions. It is decision-only: it never executes the selected capability. For Claude Code it installs, per project, a /jevrouter Skill, a CLAUDE.md rule block telling the agent to route "meaningful capability choices", a route.mjs helper, and optionally a .mcp.json entry exposing jev_route and jev_capabilities. Also has plan (multi-step), discover, evaluate (Choice/Score/Noul), a local dashboard, and an HTTP serve mode.
interface: Skill /jevrouter (skills/jevrouter/SKILL.md, description: "Use Jev to choose the next tool, model, or subagent when a task has competing capability choices, the user asks for routing, or the next step is uncertain")
CLI serve / serve-mcp / dashboard / decision show
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: CLAUDE.md rule plus skill-description trigger (and optional MCP tool with server instructions). No hook, no transparent proxy. Whether Claude routes at all depends on Opus following the prompt text; the README concedes explicit /jevrouter invocation for the first task. Decision is never enforced or used to change the main model, spawn agents or gate tools ('does not switch the host underlying model', SKILL.md).
security: API key handling is good: read from env only, never written to files or argv (credentials.ts:6-20, secret entered via raw-mode TTY prompt; agent-setup.ts:88 writes "${OPENROUTER_API_KEY}" placeholder into .mcp.json). Caveat: docs/cookbook/05-mcp-adapter.md shows a literal key in .mcp.json env, which would land in a client repo if copied.
HTTPS enforced for custom endpoints, cleartext only on loopback (provider.ts:77-94, tested in endpoint-security.test.ts).

No postinstall script, but package.json has a prepare script (tsc build) that runs on git install; quickstart is npx --yes github:... straight from the default branch of a 1-week-old, unpinned repo (supply-chain risk; pin a commit SHA if used). No curl|sh installer found.
No telemetry in src; the only extra outbound call is the Cloudflare playground function for their website. Dashboard binds 127.0.0.1 and is read-only.
discover --mcp spawns every configured MCP server (executes commands from the config) and discover --cli runs `<cmd> --help`; not part of the default agent setup path but a shell-exec surface.

Setup writes into the project tree (CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills, .mcp.json, .gitignore, .jevrouter/) with backup-and-append and refusal to follow symlinks (agent-setup.ts:187-206). Safe for the user's files but pollutes client repos with files that embed an absolute path to the installed dist/cli.js (agent-setup.ts:109), which points into the ephemeral npx cache and goes stale.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai (or api.typesafe.ai): whatever Claude puts into the route call, i.e. a task summary/request string, optional context object, and the candidate list (tool names, descriptions, input schemas) as JSON state plus the choice criteria. Content is authored by the model at call time (via the Bash heredoc or MCP arguments), so it can include file paths, snippets or client details if the model decides to include them; the tool does not itself read source files, diffs or tool outputs. Sent with Authorization: Bearer key and referrer headers identifying 'JevRouter'. Local: full request and raw response persisted to .jevrouter/decisions/*.json per project. No other network destinations found in src.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by construction (advisory). Provider timeout (20s OpenRouter / 15s direct), HTTP or auth error is caught and returned as status no_decision with fallback.type provider_error (router.ts:328-330, 430-436); CLI exit code 1 or 2; Claude simply carries on per SKILL.md ('explain the fallback and gather better inputs'). Nothing blocks tool use because nothing is a hook. Worst case is a 20 s wait plus a wasted turn. Missing key throws 'Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY' (runtime.ts:26). CLI runs with the cache disabled, so no offline fallback unless the SDK cache flag is set.
entries.contextCost: Skill mode (default): skill listing entry about 230 chars description (~60 tokens) always loaded; CLAUDE.md block about 690 chars (~170 tokens) always loaded per project; SKILL.md body ~3.2k chars (~800 tokens) when invoked, plus each route call costs output tokens for the model to hand-write candidate JSON (100-500+ tokens) and a JSON result echoed back (decision includes raw_jev, candidate list, probabilities; often 1-3k tokens). MCP mode (--with-mcp): 2 tools, ~1.5k chars of names+descriptions+schemas (~400 tokens) plus server instructions ~470 chars (~120 tokens); jev_route result is pretty-printed JSON both as text and structuredContent (duplicate payload). No hooks, so nothing injected per tool call.
pros: Native OpenRouter support against the correct endpoint (POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, ~typesafe/jev-latest) with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, so the user's chosen provider works without patching (provider.ts:156, runtime.ts:28).
Only real Claude Code integration of the three routing ideas found here that ships an end-to-end Skill + CLAUDE.md + optional MCP installer, with doctor --live connectivity check.

Careful engineering: keys never in argv/disk, HTTPS-only endpoints, symlink refusal, backup-then-append of CLAUDE.md, decision-only with policy gates, append-only receipts, ~89 tests and CI, MIT, single small dependency, ~3k lines readable in an hour.
Fail-open advisory design: provider error just yields no_decision, cannot break a coding session.

Exposes all three primitives via evaluate()/questions (Choice, Score, Noul) and a reusable SDK, so pieces (provider.ts, buildQuestions) are a good reference for a custom hook that asks Jev Noul/Score questions.
Own benchmark is honest that it measures next-tool prediction, not task completion (README), with Jev beating DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on cost and first-5 hits.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: it routes among tools/models/subagents, but in Claude Code Opus already picks tools in the same forward pass; a Jev call to pick a tool costs an extra turn and tokens for a benchmark accuracy of 38-44% position-wise hits versus an unbenchmarked Opus baseline. Nothing enforces or consumes the result; Opus can ignore it.

Not truly automatic: relies on the model reading a CLAUDE.md sentence and a skill description and deciding to route. No PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hook, so the 'never prompt use jev' requirement is only probabilistically met, and the README recommends invoking /jevrouter explicitly first.

Model must hand-author the candidate JSON each call (no automatic enumeration of Claude Code's real tool list), burning output tokens and risking wrong or invented candidates; the skill itself warns against reusing example catalogs.

Per-project install writes CLAUDE.md, .claude/skills/jevrouter, .mcp.json (with --with-mcp), .jevrouter/ and a .gitignore edit into every repo, including client repos, and helper scripts embed an absolute path to an ephemeral npx-cache dist/cli.js that goes stale (agent-setup.ts:109). There is no user-global (~/.claude) install path.
Data egress of task text and tool descriptions to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on client work, chosen by the model at runtime, plus plaintext receipts per project.

One-week-old, alpha (v0.1.0, no releases, no npm publish), installed with npx from the default branch of GitHub with a build step on install; 301 stars mostly hype-driven; author-run benchmark on 10 tasks only; alpha Decisions endpoint may change.
Extra Bash/MCP round trip on every routing decision adds seconds plus 1-3k tokens of pretty-printed JSON result (with raw_jev) to context; MCP result duplicates payload in text and structuredContent.

Interacts awkwardly with existing hooks: its Bash-invoked CLI call would pass through the user's PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus Bash hooks each time, adding further latency, and in bypass/auto mode nothing distinguishes it from any other command.
entries.verdict: Well-built, OpenRouter-native and safe (fail-open, decision-only), but it is a prompt-driven advisory router for a decision Opus already makes, so it adds latency, tokens and per-project repo clutter for little proven gain and does not deliver deterministic automatic use. Worth reading as a reference for provider.ts and the primitives, not worth installing as the daily Jev integration; a small custom global hook calling Noul/Score/Choice on specific gates is the better route.

judge.why: Well engineered and OpenRouter-native, but not automatic: it depends on the model choosing to call a skill or MCP tool.
pros: Native OpenRouter support with a doctor --live check
Keys never in argv or on disk; decision-only with policy gates and append-only receipts
Readable, tests and CI
cons: Relies on a CLAUDE.md sentence and model discretion, so the 'never say use jev' goal is not met
The model must hand-author the candidate list each call, burning output tokens; the result is advisory and can be ignored
Extra turn to route a tool that Opus picks in the same pass; benchmark 38-44%; name collides with TypeSafe's jev-router product

entries.name: win4r/jev-skill-suggester
entries.what: A Codex-oriented skill plus stdlib-only Python CLI (scripts/suggest.py) that scans local SKILL.md directories (default ~/.codex/skills and ~/.agents/skills), then uses Jev Choice and Noul questions in a two-stage pipeline (batched roster ranking, then detailed check of up to 12 candidates) to suggest at most one installed skill, or none/uncertain. It only outputs a JSON report. It does not execute skills, change settings, or register hooks. The README explicitly says it adds no automatic hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, at model discretion. It has no hook and the docs say 'no automatic hooks'. Claude Code would load it only if the description matches the situation, which is a narrow case: choosing between many skills. The SKILL.md body also says not to run it on every message. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or getpass, and is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header (jev_client.py:92). It never appears in argv. SKILL.md forbids putting keys in command arguments.
Endpoint is hardcoded and redirects are refused (NoRedirect), so credentials cannot be bounced to another host.
No shell execution, subprocess or os.system in the scripts (grep found none). It uses stdlib urllib only, has no dependencies, no install script, no postinstall and no telemetry.
Invoked as python3 -I -B (isolated mode). Reads are bounded: no FIFOs, no final symlinks, 160 KB per entry, 256 skills.
Heuristic credential detection blocks transmission of skills whose text looks like secrets; the docs admit it does not catch every secret. Task text and paths inside prose are not anonymized.

Prompt-injection surface: untrusted SKILL.md descriptions and body excerpts go into Jev state. Impact is limited because the output is only a typed distribution and nothing is executed. The design doc says it is not a security certification.
entries.dataEgress: Only in Jev mode: the task text (up to 12,000 bytes), plus every eligible skill's name, description and content hash. In the detail stage it also sends bounded SKILL.md body excerpts (about 6 KB each, at most 12 candidates). Filesystem paths are omitted. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai; nothing goes to OpenRouter. Code, diffs and tool outputs are not sent unless the caller pastes them into --task. Local mode makes no network calls.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the tool. Any API error or timeout raises ScanError, and the status becomes 'incomplete' with exit code 3. There is one 2-second retry on 429/5xx and a 45 s timeout per attempt, so worst-case latency is about 90 s per call across up to 12 attempts. Auth failures disable the client. Since nothing is wired into Claude Code as a hook, a failure only affects the model's explicit invocation, and the model just proceeds without a suggestion.
entries.contextCost: Very low. There is one skill, and the frontmatter description is about 150 Chinese characters, roughly 100-150 tokens, always loaded. The SKILL.md body (54 lines, about 1.5k tokens) loads only when the skill is triggered. No MCP tools and no hook-injected text.
pros: Clean, well-validated reference implementation of a real Jev use case (Choice plus Noul, two-stage skill routing), mirroring TypeSafe's own skill_suggestion cookbook.
Strong hygiene: stdlib-only, no subprocess, hardcoded endpoint, no redirects, key via env or getpass, bounded reads, strict response schema validation, 24 h cache with 0600 mode.
Explicit user consent model: it separates local (offline) mode from Jev mode, and --require gives a deterministic path for a skill the user named.
Documented failure semantics and call budget (12 attempts, timeouts, exit codes), and a 25-test offline suite plus a CI matrix (py3.10/3.13, macOS).
Very small context footprint, MIT license, and the code is a useful template for a custom hook that reuses the same request builders and validator.
strict validate_response, and a jev_client.py that already speaks /v1/systemone, would carry over to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone if the envelope is identical.
cons: TypeSafe-direct only. No OpenRouter path, and the design doc says 'no custom endpoint'; it needs a fork to change the URL, key env var and model ID, plus verification that OpenRouter's envelope matches.

Not automatic: there is no hook, and the docs explicitly forbid running it on every message. Claude Code would trigger it only via a description match. That conflicts with the user's goal of Jev firing without being asked.

Built for Codex (~/.codex/skills, ~/.agents/skills, agents/openai.yaml). Claude Code skills live in ~/.claude/skills and plugin caches, which need explicit --root/--skill-file flags. Claude Code already lists skill names and descriptions natively, so the value is marginal unless the user has hundreds of skills.
Unnecessary latency and cost on simple tasks (the design doc admits this), plus a Bash invocation and a permission prompt outside bypass mode.
Sends the task text and skill descriptions and excerpts to a third party (TypeSafe), which matters for client projects.

Weak provenance: a single commit, one author, created 2026-09-19 (11 days old), no releases, no issues history. 33 stars are mostly novelty. Its performance is unvalidated (the docs say so), and the docs and README are largely in Chinese.
Solves a narrow problem (skill routing) and does not touch the broader Jev uses: gating tool calls, risk scoring, code-review triage, permission decisions.
entries.verdict: A careful, safe reference implementation of Jev skill routing, but it is TypeSafe-only, Codex-oriented, description-triggered rather than hook-driven, and narrow in scope. It does not meet the goal of automatic OpenRouter-hosted Jev in Claude Code. Use it as a code template or pattern for a custom hook, not as the integration.

entries.name: DECRUX9812/typesafe-skill-router
entries.what: Opt-in Hermes Agent plugin: pre_llm_call asks Jev (jev-latest) which single skill from the roster fits and appends a short skill_relevance line to the user message. Fails open.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (Hermes), would be UserPromptSubmit in CC
pros: Exactly the skill-routing pattern (roster -> Choice/Noul -> one-line hint), with cache and offline tests
Stdlib only, CI, MIT; fail-open on every error path
cons: Hermes plugin API only (plugin.yaml, pre_llm_call); needs rewrite as Claude UserPromptSubmit hook
TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_BASE_URL; no OpenRouter key handling
Would need skill roster discovery from ~/.claude/skills; extra Jev call per prompt

entries.name: ShivamPansuriya/jev-skill-gate
entries.what: Node CLI (zero deps) that registers a Claude Code SessionStart hook (optionally UserPromptSubmit). At session start it discovers all installed skills, builds a project-signal state (stack, top-level dirs, branch, last 12 commit subjects, deps, 1200-char README excerpt), sends one Jev request with one noul question per skill ("is this skill relevant"), then writes skillOverrides (name-only / user-invocable-only) into .claude/settings.local.json to shrink the skill manifest. Falls back to a local TF-IDF scorer with no key. It is a context-trimming tool, not a general Jev decision integration: Jev is not used to gate tool calls, route models or make coding decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (SessionStart, optional UserPromptSubmit). Fully automatic after one-time install, no prompting needed. But Jev is used only for skill-manifest relevance, not for any general coding decision.
security: API key: env var wins; config --api-key stores in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate.json mode 0600, but passing it as a CLI arg exposes it in argv/ps and shell history during that one command (bin/jev-skill-gate.mjs:299). Hook itself reads key from env/file, not argv.
Sends Authorization: Bearer key over HTTPS via node:https (http.mjs) to the configured baseUrl; a repointed baseUrl (or plain http) would leak the key, but that is user-controlled.

User provider plugins in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate/providers/*.mjs are dynamically import()ed and executed on every hook run (providers/index.mjs:53): arbitrary code by design, only from user's own dir.

Self-update (update.mjs) downloads main-branch tarball from codeload.github.com and then executes the fetched code with --check/--help: unpinned auto-updating of code that runs in a SessionStart hook on every session = supply-chain risk if author account is compromised. install.sh is a documented curl|bash of raw.githubusercontent main.
No npm postinstall, no telemetry beyond the scoring call; stats ledger local in ~/.claude/jev-skill-gate/stats.json.

Prompt-injection surface: skill descriptions (from third-party plugins) go into Jev as claim parameters, but Jev returns only probabilities, so injection can only bias which skills show, not execute anything. UserPromptSubmit mode injects skill name+description text into the model context (additionalContext) from local skill files only.
entries.dataEgress: SessionStart mode (once per session, or when cache misses): to the Jev endpoint, the full name+description of every discoverable skill (user, project and plugin skills, including any private/client-specific ones) plus project state: project directory basename, detected stack labels, top-level directory names (max 25), git branch, last 12 commit subjects, up to 40 dependency names from package.json, and first 1200 chars of README (signals.mjs:52-106). No source code, diffs or tool outputs. Client repo names, commit subjects and README text do leave the machine, which matters for client projects under NDA. UserPromptSubmit mode additionally sends the user's prompt (first 4000 chars) on every prompt with no cache (signals.mjs:113, gate.mjs useCache:false). Cache key includes state JSON (branch and recent commit subjects), so each new commit changes the key and forces a fresh paid call (cache.mjs:24-26), despite the 7-day TTL.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Provider error/timeout falls back to local TF-IDF (gate.mjs:221-228); scores that don't separate or thin state leave every skill visible (gate.mjs:49-69); unscored skills stay visible; hook errors are caught and session continues ungated (bin ~L251). Caveat: per-request timeoutMs 20000 with maxRetries 4 and exponential backoff (config.mjs:81-82, runner.mjs:44-69) can exceed the hook's 30s timeout when Jev is slow or 429ing, in which case Claude Code kills the hook and session start is delayed up to 30s before proceeding ungated. Free-tier 429s were documented by the author.
entries.contextCost: Adds nothing: no MCP tools, no server instructions, no always-on text. Net negative context: claims 12,750 -> ~3,185 tokens on a 217-skill install (author's own estimate, /context showed 9.9k baseline, so real saving ~7k). User's real saving depends on skill count; with the user's skills (gitnexus x9, design skills, caveman etc., roughly 50-60 listed) saving is likely 1-3k tokens, small versus Opus context. UserPromptSubmit mode injects up to 5 skill descriptions per prompt (about 300 tokens) when triggered.
pros: Genuinely automatic (SessionStart hook, no 'use jev' prompt) and the only candidate seen so far that has a real measured Jev use case with cost figures (~$0.0007/session at $0.042/M).
Very well-engineered safety: fail-open at every level, never writes 'off', atomic writes, exact restore, preserves user-set overrides, unscored skills stay visible.

Zero dependencies, readable ~4.5k lines of Node, MIT, provider abstraction with base URL + model override so OpenRouter can be added with one small provider file or config (typesafe provider + baseUrl https://openrouter.ai/api/v1, model typesafe/jev-1.13).

Uses Jev exactly as designed (typed noul questions, calibrated probabilities, single parallel pass over 200+ options) and honestly reports a committed eval, a local no-key fallback and its own limits (README 'Known limits of this evidence').
Composes with the user's existing hooks: only adds a SessionStart entry, merges into settings.json, does not touch PreToolUse (secret guard, GitNexus) matchers.
cons: No OpenRouter support in code (zero 'openrouter' matches); env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY/AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY only, so it needs aliasing or a custom provider, and OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified.

Solves a narrow, small problem: trims skill descriptions (~10k tokens on a 217-skill library; the user has far fewer, and Opus context and prompt caching already absorb the cost). Does nothing for code decisions, routing, permission approval, or task classification, which is what the user meant by integrating Jev.

Sends skill catalogue plus repo name, branch, last 12 commit subjects, dependency names and README excerpt of every project (including client repos) to a third party on each cache miss; UserPromptSubmit mode sends the user's prompt every turn. Poor fit for client/NDA work without care.
Cache key includes recent commit subjects and branch, so in an actively committed repo the 7-day cache misses often, adding a blocking network call to session start.
Retry budget (20s x 5 attempts with backoff) exceeds the 30s hook timeout: a slow or rate-limited Jev can stall session start ~30s before failing open.

Evidence is thin: 4 of 20 eval cases ran against real Jev (429 free-tier), 1 contributor, 12 commits, 8 stars, 13 days old, no CI, stale test badge; verified only against Claude Code 2.1.274 and relies on skillOverrides/reloadSkills semantics that may change.

Self-update pulls and executes unpinned main-branch code inside a hook that runs every session; writes .claude/settings.local.json into every project including client repos; hiding skills is silent so a miss costs quality unnoticed.

Hidden skills reduce auto-discovery of the user's own skills (gitnexus-*, design systems) in projects where the state signal is weak or the vocabulary doesn't match; the 0.15 nameOnly threshold survives one labeled skill by 'exactly zero' margin per README.
entries.verdict: Well-built, safe, genuinely automatic hook, but it only uses Jev to trim skill descriptions, which yields a small saving for a user with a modest skill set while shipping repo metadata (commit subjects, README, branch) off-machine, and it has no native OpenRouter support. Treat as an optional, low-priority experiment (with provider=fallback or a patched OpenRouter provider), not the core Jev integration.

entries.name: eran-broder/jev-skills
entries.what: Claude Code (and Codex) plugin that moves skills out of the model's always-on skill listing into ~/.jev-skills/library. On UserPromptSubmit and after Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/WebFetch/WebSearch tool results, a Node hook sends the prompt, the last 3 assistant turns and the tool output to Jev as one "noul" (yes/no) question per skill. Skills with P>=0.6 (max 3, once per session) have their SKILL.md body injected as additionalContext. It is a skill router only: it does not help with code review, model routing or other coding decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, SessionStart, PostCompact) with no model discretion. The user never has to say 'use jev'. This is the automatic pattern the user wants, but the only thing it decides is which skill to inject.
security: plugin.json declares typesafe_api_key as sensitive userConfig, which Claude Code stores in its credential store and passes to the hook as an env var. This is the better path. Inside the hook the key is only in the environment, not in argv.
`jev-skills setup <key>` puts the key in argv, visible in the process list and shell history, and writes it in plaintext to ~/.jev-skills/config.json with no chmod (cli.ts:29, config.ts:114-118).
Each request carries the Authorization Bearer header to the hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint. There is no TLS pinning or host override. Retries go up to 3 attempts on 429/502/503/529.
No shell execution in the hook path, no eval, no postinstall script and no curl|sh installer. package.json has only dev scripts. The only child_process use is scripts/test.ts (dev).
No telemetry beyond Jev calls. The local log ~/.jev-skills/log.jsonl records event names, skill names and probabilities, not prompt text.

Prompt-injection surface: tool output (web pages, files) is sent to Jev as state. Adversarial content can raise a skill's probability, but the injected text only comes from your own local SKILL.md files, so the impact is low. The injected header says 'Follow their instructions', so a malicious skill dropped into the library gets full trust.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on every non-empty prompt, and on every PostToolUse of Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/WebFetch/WebSearch with output of 200 chars or more (observeToolResults defaults to true). Payload (state.ts): the user prompt clipped to 6000 chars, the last 3 assistant text blocks plus tool names, the basename of the project directory, and for tool results the tool name, the full tool_input (Bash commands, file paths, grep patterns, URLs) and the tool_response clipped to about 3000 chars. That is file contents, command output and possibly secrets or client code. It also sends every skill's name and description, once per question. Diffs are not sent as a separate item, but they appear whenever a Bash git diff or Read result goes through. In practice this is a near-continuous stream of client-project content to a third party. If pointed at OpenRouter, it would go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe under their data policies. Injected skill bodies stay local.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. main().catch logs the error to log.jsonl and exits with no output (hook.ts:206), so the prompt is never blocked. A missing key throws MissingApiKeyError and is also swallowed. The per-request timeout is 6000 ms (configurable), with up to 3 attempts on 429/502/503/529 and backoff of 300 ms x 2^n or Retry-After. A network error or timeout is not retried and throws, which fails open. The worst case is a slow hook: the hook timeout is 15 s, and a degraded Jev could add several seconds to each prompt and each Read/Bash/Grep call, because the hook is synchronous. There is no circuit breaker or negative cache. Errors are silent (logged only), so a wrong OpenRouter response schema would leave the plugin quietly doing nothing.
entries.contextCost: 0 MCP tools, no MCP server and no server instructions. Always-on cost is 0 tokens from the plugin, and it also removes skill listings once skills are migrated (README claims about 1,350 tokens per 13 skills). Hook-injected text: a one-line header plus up to 3 full SKILL.md bodies, capped at 24,000 chars (about 6k tokens) per call and once per skill per session, plus a one-line systemMessage 'jev-skills loaded: ...'. Nothing is injected when no skill scores at or above 0.6. Gain for you is modest: your listed skills (about 30 descriptions, roughly 3-4k tokens) are already a small share of the context. Plugin-provided skills (caveman, gitnexus) are not moved by migrate, which only handles ~/.claude/skills.
pros: Truly automatic: hook-based (hooks/hooks.json), no prompting, and it fails open (hook.ts:206) so it cannot block work.
Zero MCP tools and zero always-on tokens, unlike an MCP server.
Correct use of Jev's strength: many parallel yes/no questions that come back as calibrated probabilities. The threshold, cap and once-per-session dedup are sensible (select.ts, session.ts).
Small, readable TypeScript (about 1,000 lines), MIT license, no postinstall, no shell exec, no runtime dependencies. The key is a sensitive plugin option that is not written to settings.
Exact-form hooks (command + args) and CI on ubuntu and windows with a stale-dist check. Useful reference implementation for a custom Jev hook.
Endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so a fork is a small change.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai (client.ts:3) with no override, and the key is TypeSafe-only. You would need a fork and a dist rebuild, and the response-schema match with OpenRouter is unverified. This contradicts the requirement that OpenRouter be the provider.

Data egress is large: prompts, assistant text and the full tool_input plus about 3k chars of every Read/Bash/Grep/Glob/Web tool output are sent to a third party on nearly every step. That is a serious concern for client projects and bypasses your secret-leak guard's intent. You would have to set observeToolResults=false to reduce it, which removes the mid-task value.

Narrow value: it only routes skills. It does nothing for permission decisions, model routing, review triage or other coding decisions. Your skills are few and mostly small, so the token saving is a few thousand tokens per session at best. Plugin skills are not covered by migrate.

Latency tax: a synchronous network call on every prompt and on every Read/Bash/Grep result (about 0.3-0.5 s each, up to 15 s if Jev is degraded), on top of your existing GitNexus and secret-guard hooks that fire on the same tools.

Requires moving skills out of ~/.claude/skills into ~/.jev-skills/library. This breaks the /skill and Skill tool discovery you use today and makes skill invocation depend on a beta model's probabilities (a miss means the skill silently never appears).

Very immature: 7 days old, 4 commits, 1 contributor, 6 stars, no releases. Tests cover only pure helpers, with no client or hook tests. Committed 20k-line bundle. The Theo/t3.gg skepticism about Jev's quality is unverified, but false negatives here would be invisible.
Fail-open errors are silent (log only), so a misconfiguration or API schema drift looks like 'works, injects nothing'. `setup <key>` leaves the key in argv and in a plaintext config.json.
entries.verdict: Best-in-class example of an automatic, deterministic Jev hook for Claude Code, but it solves a small problem (skill-listing tokens) at the price of continuously sending client code and tool output to a third party, with a hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint. Not recommended for daily use. Worth reading as a template if you build your own hook, and only if you fork it to OpenRouter and turn off tool-result observation.

entries.name: deyna256/langchain-skill-router
entries.what: Drop-in LangChain deepagents SkillsMiddleware: per turn a judge (Jev adapter) picks which SKILL.md to load; claims 113k->25.8k tokens on 236 skills, 90% vs 88% accuracy.
entries.autoInvocation: proxy/middleware per turn (LangChain only)
pros: Concrete benchmark of per-turn skill routing (token cut, accuracy held)
Pluggable judge protocol with confident-pick vs top-3 candidate fallback plus find_skill
CI, typed Python, PyPI
cons: LangChain deepagents only; not usable inside Claude Code
Jev adapter uses typesafe_sdk (TypeSafe base URL), no OpenRouter path seen
Design pattern is the value, not the code, for this user

entries.name: VishiATChoudhary/toolJev
entries.what: Python MCP gateway (FastMCP) that sits in front of your other MCP servers and replaces their tool lists with just two tools: search(query) and execute(code, session). search does BM25 + bge-base embedding recall, then one Jev call to rerank and score fit. execute runs agent-written Python in a Pydantic Monty sandbox where upstream tools are mcp.<server>.<tool>() and jev.choice/noul/score/ask/map do bulk typed decisions. Aimed at 100s of tools and bulk per-item triage, not at general coding assistance.
interface: MCP tool execute(code: str, session: str|None)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no skill, no proxy. Claude Code decides whether to call search/execute; it only replaces upstream tools if you route them through it. Does not make Claude Code call Jev on its own for coding decisions.
security: No API key in argv: key read from env by the SDK; SDK logging redacts Authorization headers (logging.py:45).

Upstream server secrets (e.g. GITHUB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN) live in plaintext in tooljev.toml env/headers tables; you would have to duplicate every upstream (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) into this file and they would be spawned as children of tooljev.

README states 'The sandbox is not authorization': agent-written Python can call any allowed upstream tool, including destructive ones (playwright run_code_unsafe, gh tokens), with no per-call approval prompt per tool; Claude Code's normal per-tool permission/hook gates (secret-leak guard PreToolUse on Bash|Read|Grep, GitNexus hooks) would not see the inner mcp.* calls, only the single execute call. In bypass/auto mode this is a large hole.
Monty sandbox has no filesystem/network/env access per README/sandbox.py:9; bounded by CPU/mem/call caps. Sandbox escape risk is that of a young third-party interpreter (pydantic-monty).

Persistent unredacted JSONL trace of every search query, every executed code string and every host-call args/results at ~/.tooljev/traces/YYYY-MM-DD.jsonl (trace.py:11-18, server.py:57,64), on by default with no rotation; would accumulate client code/secrets returned by tools.
Prompt-injection surface: upstream tool results flow into sandbox variables and Jev state; Jev returns only typed probabilities so it cannot inject text, but agent-written code acts on them.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint only: search query text plus the top-15 candidate tool names/descriptions (search.py) and, in execute, whatever state you pass to jev.* (tool results such as ticket bodies, file/issue text, arbitrary JSON) along with question instructions. Not sent automatically: Claude Code prompts, repo files, diffs, unless the agent's code passes them to jev. Local disk: full traces of queries, code and tool call args/results to ~/.tooljev/traces. Embeddings (bge-base) run locally. Upstream servers see calls as normal.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call: HostedJev.decide retries 429/529 via SDK (max_retries=3) plus 4 attempts with 1s/2s/4s backoff on 5xx/timeout, client timeout 30s (decider.py:43-68), then raises DecisionError. In search this makes the search tool error (no visible fallback to retrieval-only found in decider.py; search.py not exhaustively audited for try/except); in execute it surfaces as an exception in agent code. Worst case a single call can block roughly 30s x 4 plus 7s backoff. Because all upstream tools are hidden behind tooljev, if the gateway process or an upstream fails to start, the tools vanish from Claude Code entirely.
entries.contextCost: Tiny: 2 tools (search, execute). execute description is PRELUDE_DOC about 2.3k chars (~600 tokens) plus schema; search doc ~350 chars; server INSTRUCTIONS ~500 chars (~125 tokens). Total roughly 800-1000 tokens. No hooks inject text. But adopting it would mean hiding the existing gitnexus, playwright and caveman-shrink servers behind the gateway, changing their tool naming (mcp__gitnexus__* no longer native) and breaking skills/hooks that reference them.
pros: Genuine, working Jev integration with real benchmarks (MCPToolBench++, LiveMCPBench, When2Call, 400-ticket triage): 98.8% accuracy for $0.063 vs $0.332 with Haiku (README:20-30, bench/RESULTS.md).
Very small context footprint (2 tools, ~1k tokens) and pays off at scale: with 612 tools it cut input tokens 77% and cost 28% vs Claude Code's native tool search.
Clean decider abstraction (decider.py) so backend swap is a small change; SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and model config, so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is plausibly env-only.
Honest README: states when not to use it (<100 tools, latency-sensitive), documents negative results and that sandbox is not authorization.
MIT, CI on 3.11/3.12, ~44 offline tests with fake decider, sandbox resource limits, per-server allow-lists, confidence-gated hand-back to the LLM.
cons: Wrong problem for this user: solves large-tool-catalog overload and bulk triage; user has only 3 MCP servers (~50 tools) where README says direct calling is more accurate and cheaper (87 tools: 0.94 vs 0.89).

Not automatic Jev usage in Claude Code: model-discretion tool, and to benefit you must proxy gitnexus/playwright/caveman-shrink through it, breaking native mcp__gitnexus__* names, GitNexus PreToolUse/PostToolUse hooks and gitnexus-* skills that match those tools.

Bypasses existing safety: inner mcp.* calls run inside one execute call, so the secret-leak guard hook and Claude Code per-tool permissions do not see them; risky in bypass/auto mode with playwright browser_run_code_unsafe.
Adds latency and turns: search then execute (2 extra turns), README's agent bench 34 s vs 18 s.
Plaintext unredacted local traces of all code and tool results in ~/.tooljev/traces by default; upstream secrets copied into a TOML.

Very immature: created 2026-09-28 (2 days old), 8 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, no release, not on PyPI, alpha classifier; benchmarks use mock upstreams and 1-2 reps of 36 tasks (89% vs 81% is 3 tasks, author's own caveat).

Heavy optional deps (torch, sentence-transformers) for dense recall; OpenRouter response-schema compatibility with typesafe-sdk untested; if Jev fails, search errors with no clear fallback and tools disappear.
Does nothing for the user's actual daily coding decisions (which file to edit, whether to run tests, permission classification).
entries.verdict: A well-built but narrowly scoped Code Mode gateway for hundreds of MCP tools or bulk triage; not a coding-workflow Jev integration and not automatic. For a 3-server setup with permission hooks it adds latency and bypasses guards, so skip it, though its decider.py plus the SDK base_url/env pattern is a useful reference for pointing typesafe-sdk at OpenRouter.

entries.name: lomeshdutta/skill-router
entries.what: Python CLI (skill-router 0.2.0) plus a Claude Code SessionStart hook. The hook injects an instruction telling Claude to establish a one-sentence session goal and run `skill-router intent set "<goal>"`. That command lists all installed skills (project, user, plugins, built-ins) and calls Jev's System One endpoint once, with 3-4 questions in parallel: needs_skill (Noul), task_kind (Choice), installed_skill (Choice over every skill, plus a "none" option) and skills_sh_topic (Choice). It prints one of three outcomes: load skill X, search skills.sh via find-skills, or no skill needed. It only does skill routing. It is not a general coding-decision layer. An opt-in per-prompt UserPromptSubmit hook exists but is off by default. A mock keyword mode runs when no key is set.
entries.autoInvocation: Hybrid. The SessionStart hook is a deterministic hook, but it only injects text. The actual Jev call happens only if Claude obeys the instruction and runs `skill-router intent set` via Bash, so it is model-discretion. In a session where the first message already states a goal, Claude infers one; otherwise Claude asks the user 'What are you trying to get done this session?', which is a user prompt the user wanted to avoid. Later task pivots need the user to type /intent, so nothing is automatic after the first call. The opt-in UserPromptSubmit hook is fully deterministic but noisy.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var or a .env in the project root or ~/.config/skill-router/.env (router.py:34-51). It is sent as an HTTPS Bearer header by the SDK and is not put in argv. A test asserts the key never reaches the decision log.

Prompt-injection surface: hook output is instruction text injected into Claude's context. Installed skill names and descriptions from third-party plugins are sent to Jev as data. Claude is told to relay the output and to 'load skill X' from Jev's choice, and the SKILL.md forbids installing anything without a yes. The outcome-B text lists skills.sh search results (package names) as optional installs.

Shell execution: subprocess `git rev-parse` (context.py, 1.5 s timeout) and `npx -y skills find <query>` (skills_sh.py:299). The `npx -y` runs a remote, unpinned npm package (skills) at hook time, only in outcome B. It uses a scrubbed env {DISABLE_TELEMETRY, PATH}. The query is built from the user prompt or goal and passed as an argv element, with no shell.
No curl|sh and no npm postinstall. Install is git clone + uv sync + writing the hook into settings (`install-hook --write` edits ~/.claude/settings.json).
No telemetry of its own. Local writes go to ~/.cache/skill-router/ (decisions.jsonl stores the first 160 chars of prompts in per-prompt mode, plus cwd and goal).
Single maintainer, 12 days old, 3 stars, and depends on an early typesafe-sdk 0.6.0. The invariant script checks hosts in src/ only, not payloads.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or whatever TYPESAFE_BASE_URL points at, e.g. OpenRouter). Per SECURITY.md and context.py:160-184, the payload is: the session goal (or, in per-prompt mode, the prompt plus up to 3 earlier user messages at 400 chars each), the project directory name (not the full path), file counts by extension (top 8, depth <=2), which marker files exist, the git branch name, the first 500 characters of the project's CLAUDE.md (or .claude/CLAUDE.md), and the name and description of EVERY installed skill (about 9,100 input tokens per call at ~130 skills). It does not send source code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs. It does send the CLAUDE.md head and the goal text, which for client projects may include confidential project descriptions. To skills.sh via npx, only a search query built from the goal. There is no per-project opt-out except the SKILL_ROUTER_DISABLE=1 env var.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Hooks are wrapped in catch-alls and return 0 (hook.py:388, cli.py session-start). `intent set` catches all exceptions and prints 'Could not get a routing decision... proceeding without a suggestion' (cli.py:~120). SDK timeout is 8 s with max_retries=1 (router.py:29,145), so the worst case is about 16-17 s of blocked Claude tool execution inside the `intent set` Bash call. The SessionStart hook itself never calls Jev, so session start is not delayed. Without a key it silently falls back to a keyword mock, labelled 'mock', which gives low-quality picks. A misconfigured OpenRouter base URL, model or schema mismatch would surface as an error string and no suggestion.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so no tool-definition tokens. The SessionStart hook injects about 720 characters (~180 tokens) of instruction each session. Each `intent set` result adds ~100-200 tokens. Reading the injected instruction and running the extra Bash call costs one turn. The optional /intent skill adds a ~60-token description to the skill list. In per-prompt mode, ~100-250 tokens per prompt.
pros: Real, working Jev integration in code. It uses System One with Noul plus Choice over up to 255 options, which is exactly the primitive Jev is designed for (router.py:133-167, questions.py). It is a real example of the kind of decision Jev is good at.

OpenRouter switch needs no code change. The SDK it depends on reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, and uses path /v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone surface (verified in the SDK source, not yet tested end to end).

Fail-open everywhere, with an 8 s SDK timeout, catch-alls on hooks and a SKILL_ROUTER_DISABLE kill switch. The failures found by independent reviewers were fixed with regression tests. It has CI, an invariant script and an eval harness with reported accuracy.
Cheap: about $0.0004 per call (~9k input tokens at $0.042/1M). A once-per-session call means negligible spend and context (~180 tokens).
Small codebase (about 1.5k lines of Python), MIT, no install script, no postinstall, no telemetry, and the code is easy to audit and fork.
Useful for a user with many skills and plugins (caveman, gitnexus-* and others), where a semantic pick can surface a relevant skill Opus would otherwise not load.
cons: Narrow scope: it routes skills only and does not touch daily coding decisions (which file, which tool, whether to run tests, risk gating). Opus 5.5 already sees the skill list and descriptions in-context and can pick skills itself. The marginal value is small.

Not truly automatic for this user. The Jev call happens only if Claude follows an injected instruction to run a Bash command. If the first message has no clear goal, Claude asks the user a question first, and later pivots need a manual /intent. This contradicts the 'never prompt' requirement.

Once per session, based on a one-sentence goal, so it cannot react to what happens mid-session. The per-prompt mode that would is opt-in and was judged noisy by the author (repeated skill-creator suggestions).

Privacy risk on client projects: it sends the first 500 chars of CLAUDE.md, directory name, git branch, extension counts and all installed skill names and descriptions (~9k tokens) to the Jev provider on every call. There is no per-project allowlist, only a global env kill switch.

Immature: 12 days old, 19 commits, 1 contributor, 3 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, alpha classifier. It depends on typesafe-sdk 0.6.0 (Sept 2026). The eval set is small (19 cases) and was tuned on the author's machine, and the independent reviewer saw ~5 s latency.

Installation is clumsy. It needs a git clone with a local venv and writes an absolute path to a .venv/bin into ~/.claude/settings.json. The bundled /intent skill runs `uv run skill-router` from the repo root, so it breaks in other project directories. `npx -y skills find` pulls unpinned remote code in outcome B.

OpenRouter path is untested. If the OpenRouter response schema differs from TypeSafe's (e.g. the model name prefix, wrapper fields), typesafe_sdk parsing would fail and the tool would silently degrade to 'no suggestion'. Also, with the key missing, it silently falls back to a keyword mock.
entries.verdict: A tidy, honest, well-tested proof of concept for Jev-based skill routing that could be pointed at OpenRouter by setting three env vars, but it is narrow, alpha, and not truly automatic: it relies on Claude choosing to run a Bash command once per session and may ask the user a question. It also leaks CLAUDE.md excerpts and the full skill catalogue to the provider. Treat it as a reference implementation of the Jev System One call pattern, not as the main integration.

entries.name: himomohi/jev-skill-router
entries.what: Local Python (stdlib+httpx+PyYAML) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, skill_router, plus an optional Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook. It indexes a directory of trusted SKILL.md files and calls TypeSafe's System One API (Choice to rank skill descriptions, then Noul+Score to verify shortlisted excerpts) to decide which skill body to inject into the main model's context. Purpose is to keep a large skill catalog out of Claude's context; it is not a general coding-decision helper.
interface: CLI: setup / auth / serve / config-snippet / route / plan / doctor [--live] / park / restore / benchmark / hook
entries.autoInvocation: Two modes. (a) Default: model-discretion MCP tool, nudged by the server instructions and a bridge skill; not deterministic, and Claude Code lazily lists MCP tools so it can be skipped. (b) Optional --hook: deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook that routes on every submitted prompt, but only ever selects SKILL.md files, so it automatically 'uses Jev' for skill selection only, not for any coding decision.
security: API key sent only as Bearer header to a fixed HTTPS host, redirects not followed (jev.py:160). Key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or a supported OS keychain; no plaintext file fallback (config.py:91-111). Key never appears in argv.

No shell execution in the server; MCP is stdio only, read-only tool. Only subprocess use is setup calling 'claude mcp add' with a fixed argument list (integrations.py:136). Install.py runs pip in a venv (network installs from PyPI), no curl|sh, no npm postinstall.

Setup mutates user state: writes ~/.claude.json via claude CLI, writes a skill into ~/.claude/skills, and with --hook merges a UserPromptSubmit entry into ~/.claude/settings.json (with backup). park --apply moves your skill folders to a vault (interferes with existing skills and plugins).

Prompt-injection surface: skill text is sent to Jev as evidence and then returned verbatim to the main model as instructions; SECURITY.md concedes this is not a sandbox and that injection defense is incomplete. Only trusted skill roots are safe. Path reads block traversal and symlinks.

Hook path is worse for secrets: every raw user prompt (up to 64KB read) goes off-machine to the provider, and there is no redaction (SECURITY.md admits it cannot reliably detect secrets). This bypasses the intent of the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, which does not cover UserPromptSubmit.
No telemetry uploader; in-memory cache only. Single-author repo, 9 days old, no independent audit.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai only (not OpenRouter as shipped): the focused task text (with the hook, the entire raw user prompt on every turn; with the MCP tool, whatever task/context the model chooses to pass), all skill names and descriptions in the catalog (batched, up to 24KB per request), and up to 900-char excerpts of shortlisted skill bodies (SECURITY.md: excerpts may include interior and final portions). Does not send code files, diffs, tool outputs or the full conversation unless Claude places them in the task/context fields. Local skill files are read but only descriptions and excerpts leave the machine.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking. The hook catches RouterError and prints an additionalContext line saying routing is unavailable and to continue under ordinary rules (cli.py:138-146), exit 0. MCP returns isError text. Bounds: 15 s per HTTP request, 45 s per route deadline, 32-request cap, 2 retries on 429/5xx with capped backoff (max 8 s, honors Retry-After), no retries on network errors (jev.py:246-250). The hook is registered with timeout 120 s (integrations.py:152), so a slow or down Jev can stall each prompt for up to 45 s before the turn proceeds. No fallback to another model or keyword routing in live mode (by design).
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool. Tool name+description (~300 chars) + inputSchema (7 properties, ~1,100 chars) + annotations, about 1,500 chars, roughly 400 tokens. Server 'instructions' BOOTSTRAP ~480 chars (~120 tokens). Bridge SKILL.md adds a ~80-token description to the skill list. Total about 600 tokens fixed. The project's own benchmark (README) says this is a net loss for small catalogs (-27% at 5 skills) and only pays off at 50+ skills. With the hook, each prompt gets an injected additionalContext of either the selected skill JSON (up to 12,000 chars = about 3k tokens, max_output_chars) or a ~150-char status line every turn.
pros: Genuinely uses the System One primitives the way Jev is meant to be used (Choice for ranking at router.py:42, Noul plus Score for verification at router.py:51-52) and enforces confidence and fit gates (min_fit 0.65, min_confidence 0.5), so it is a real, non-toy Jev integration with typed decisions and strict response validation (jev.py:29-55).
Ships an actual deterministic auto-invoke path for Claude Code (UserPromptSubmit hook), so no 'use jev' prompting is needed; fails open with clear status text.
Careful engineering: request/time budgets, cancellation, byte caps, no redirects, keychain-only key storage, SHA-pinned CI on 4 OS targets, 2.5k lines of tests, backups before editing client configs.
MIT licensed, small readable code (about 1.5k lines), no telemetry, no shell tool exposed.
The endpoint, key var and model are three isolated constants, so an OpenRouter fork is a small diff (jev.py:15, config.py:34, config.py:92).
cons: Wrong problem for this user: it only decides which SKILL.md to load, so it adds nothing for daily coding decisions (test triage, permission or risk gating, routing, code review verdicts). Value exists only if the user has 50+ skills; at small catalogs it costs more context than native progressive disclosure (README's own table, -27% at 5 skills).

No OpenRouter support as shipped: hardcoded api.typesafe.ai endpoint and TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, contradicting the user's requirement for an OpenRouter-hosted Jev. Needs a fork, and the OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone schema equivalence is unverified.

Hook mode sends every raw prompt (possibly containing client code, paths or secrets) to a third party with no redaction, on personal AND client projects, and runs before the user's PreToolUse secret guard could act; plus 2+ Jev calls and a Python process launch on every single turn.

Never validated live: author states Jev accuracy, latency, cost and real model task success are unmeasured; the 3-star, 9-day-old, single-author project has no field use. Jev's claimed accuracy here rests on a possibly-router-like model (Theo's claim) and is untested.

Invasive setup: park moves existing skill folders out of discovery paths, writes ~/.claude.json, ~/.claude/settings.json and a bridge skill, and pip-installs a private venv; conflicts with the user's plugin-managed skills (caveman, gitnexus), which park does not manage. Native skills stay visible unless removed, negating the context savings.
Injects selected skill text (which may carry prompt injection) as additionalContext each turn; 45 s route deadline with 120 s hook timeout can noticeably stall interactive typing when Jev is slow.
entries.verdict: A well-built but narrow tool: it uses Jev solely to pick SKILL.md files, needs an OpenRouter fork (hardcoded TypeSafe endpoint and key), and its hook ships every prompt to a third party and adds Jev latency each turn. Only worth considering as a reference implementation of Choice/Noul/Score usage, or if the user later accumulates a very large skill library; not recommended for this user's daily coding.

entries.name: TypeSafe cookbook: Skill suggestion (docs.typesafe.ai/cookbooks/skill_suggestion)
entries.what: Official TypeSafe recipe (Python, not an installable tool) that picks at most one skill per agent turn from Nous Research's Hermes 182-skill roster. Request 1 is one system_one call: a Choice over all 182 skills (option criteria = the 60-char index description) plus 3 Noul gate questions ("is an action wanted rather than explanation?"); if the mean gate is under 0.30 nothing is suggested. Request 2 re-ranks the top 3 with full descriptions plus about 700 chars of each SKILL.md and adds a per-candidate "fits" Noul; if the best fits value is under 0.30 nothing is suggested. The winner is injected as a <skill_relevance> block appended after the cached system prompt. Reported result over 488 requests against claude-haiku-4-5 (jev-1.12, run 2026-07-31): wrong-skill loads fell from 16.8% to 7.3% and needless loads from 9.8% to 4.0%. The floor with the correct answer handed over was 2.5% and 1.2%. Requests were LLM-written and self-described as easier than real user prompts. The recipe is a blueprint for a Claude Code UserPromptSubmit skill-router hook, but it ships no Claude Code hook.
interface: Claude Code hook / MCP tool / skill
entries.autoInvocation: Recipe only, so nothing runs automatically as shipped. A port as a UserPromptSubmit hook would be fully deterministic and automatic, needing no user prompting. The recipe's own design is a per-turn pre-processor whose output is appended to the system prompt.
security: No installable artifact. Copying the recipe adds pip deps: typesafe-sdk, cooksafe, anthropic, matplotlib, ipython. I did not vet them.
API key would be read from an env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY or an OpenRouter key). It would not appear in argv if used from a hook, as long as it is read from env.

Prompt-injection surface: the user prompt and SKILL.md excerpts are passed as state to Jev. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injected text cannot produce free-text instructions. The only text that reaches Claude is a skill name chosen from a fixed roster, so injection risk is low.
If turned into a hook, the hook itself must be written and audited by the user. Nothing here executes shell commands or telemetry.
Docs pages carry text aimed at AI agents (the 'install the TypeSafe skill' prompt in the quickstart). I treated it as data and did not act on it.
entries.dataEgress: In the recipe as written: the full user prompt goes to TypeSafe on every turn (and the last request only, not history). Also sent: the whole skill roster (182 names plus 60-char descriptions, about 16k chars) in request 1, and for the top 3 candidates the full descriptions plus about 700 chars of each SKILL.md in request 2. Ported to Claude Code this would send every prompt, which may contain client code or secrets, to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, plus the names and descriptions of installed skills. It sends no file contents or tool outputs unless the author adds them. Pairs poorly with client projects under NDA.
entries.failureMode: The recipe has no failure handling. The client timeout is 120 s, there is no retry, and the code has no try/except. A port to Claude Code would need its own fail-open wrapper with a short timeout (for example 1 to 2 s) that exits 0 with no injection. Failure of the advisory hint is harmless if fail-open. Fail-closed would block prompts, which is unacceptable.
entries.contextCost: If ported to a UserPromptSubmit hook: zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. It injects about 40 tokens per turn (one <skill_relevance> line, roughly 150 chars) or a short 'no skill relevant' line. Claude Code would still list its own skills, so this adds a hint and does not remove tokens. The context saving the cookbook advertises (a truncated roster) does not apply, because Claude Code already truncates skill descriptions and has no 182-skill index to trim.
pros: Official TypeSafe recipe with a fully specified, working design (thresholds 0.30/0.30, shortlist of 3, 700-char excerpts). It gives the exact confidence-gated two-stage pattern to build a real Claude Code hook.

Fits the user's requirement of automatic use: a UserPromptSubmit hook would be deterministic, so the user never says 'use jev'. Output is only a skill name from a fixed roster, so Jev cannot inject free text.
Cheap and fast per the demo: about 0.1 to 0.3 s per request, and both stages are single calls. At about $0.042/M input tokens, roughly 5k tokens per prompt costs about $0.0002 per turn.
Honest evaluation: reports a floor (2.5% and 1.2%) and admits the requests are easier than real ones. Measured error reduction was more than half (16.8% to 7.3% wrong loads).

The claimed benefits are relevant for a user with many installed skills (dougthepug-design, empat-design, gitnexus-*, caveman, anthropic-skills:* and so on), where wrong or missed skill triggers are a real annoyance.
cons: Not an integration. There is no hook, MCP server, plugin or installer, and the user would have to write, test and maintain the hook, roster extraction and thresholds themselves.

Measured on a different agent: Hermes, claude-haiku-4-5 via the Anthropic API, and a forced skill_view tool. Claude Code with Opus 5.5 already selects skills from full descriptions in its own system prompt, so the 16.8% baseline error rate likely overstates the headroom. No evidence is given for Claude Code.
Only helps skill selection, which is a small part of daily coding. It does nothing for code edits, search, planning or permission decisions, so the value per turn is small.
Sends every prompt and the skill roster off-machine on each turn. That is a concern for client projects, and the provider list is OpenRouter plus TypeSafe with a beta model.

Evaluation set is LLM-written (Sonnet 5), 'easier than real user prompts', with a Mastodon-to-X false positive showing the recipe can suggest a wrong skill for near-miss requests. Suggesting a wrong skill can mislead an agent that is told to 'ignore if it does not fit'.
Adds a 0.25 to 0.5 s serial delay before every prompt, and up to 2 s if a port uses a timeout. Needs a fail-open wrapper because the recipe has none.

Uses the TypeSafe Python SDK and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. OpenRouter support is inferred, not shown, so the recipe needs porting and testing against /api/v1/systemone. Requires Python plus pip deps, or a reimplementation as a Node or curl hook.
entries.verdict: Useful only as a design blueprint for a custom UserPromptSubmit skill-router hook, not as something to install: there is no shipped Claude Code integration, and the measured gains come from a much weaker agent (Haiku on Hermes' 60-char index) than Opus 5.5 in Claude Code. If built, it must be fail-open, use a short timeout and go through OpenRouter, and it would send every prompt off-machine for a marginal skill-selection gain.
entries.license: Recipe code license not stated on the page. The roster data comes from NousResearch/hermes-agent (MIT). Depends on the cooksafe and typesafe-sdk packages, which I did not inspect.

entries.name: jev-skill-router
entries.what: Single-file Node CLI (cli.mjs, 258 lines, zero dependencies) that sends one OpenRouter Jev Decisions request per user request (state = request + catalog of up to 60 local SKILL.md name/description pairs; questions = complexity score, use_skill choice, confidence score) and prints JSON telling the agent which skill to load. Also has a skill supply-chain scanner (Jev choice questions for prompt injection and dangerous commands on the first 6 KB of each SKILL.md) and a GitHub SKILL.md installer. Despite the "skill" label it is NOT a SKILL.md or plugin. It is a CLI, and it only reaches the model if the user pastes a rule into CLAUDE.md telling Claude to run it.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only. The mechanism is a pasted CLAUDE.md instruction ('Before answering any non-trivial request, run jev-skill-router ...'), which depends on Claude choosing to comply on every turn and deciding what counts as 'non-trivial'. There is no hook, no MCP tool, no SKILL.md trigger and no proxy. A CLI is not a deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, though a 5-line hook wrapper around this CLI or its API call could be made deterministic.
security: API key read from env only (cli.mjs:87), never in argv, which is good. The user request text IS passed as argv, so it is visible in ps and process lists (one more leak surface next to the secret-leak guard hook).
No timeout or AbortController on fetch (cli.mjs:89). The fail-open catch only handles errors, so a hanging connection stalls the Bash tool call until the tool timeout.
No postinstall or install scripts. The package is clean and only uses fs, path, os, fetch. No child_process, no eval, no telemetry beyond the OpenRouter call and, for --install, GitHub.

--install pulls unpinned SKILL.md content (ref HEAD) from arbitrary GitHub repos and writes it under ~/.jev-skill-router/library. That directory is not a Claude Code skill dir, so nothing is auto-loaded, but discoverSkills() reads it and the catalog is fed to Jev, so a hostile skill description is a prompt-injection surface into the router. It only affects a choice among names, low blast radius.

The security audit is a probabilistic classifier on the first 6 KB of a skill (cli.mjs:131). Content past 6 KB is unscanned, and Jev is a typed-decision model, not a code-audit tool. It gives false assurance (TRUSTED) and README marks API errors as UNKNOWN but does not block. Treat it as a heuristic.

The router output is instructions fed back to Claude ('Load the X skill and follow it'). The skill name is chosen from the local catalog, so it cannot inject free text, but any attacker who controls a SKILL.md name or description can steer the routing.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai only (plus api.github.com and raw.githubusercontent.com for --install). Routing call sends: (a) the request string Claude passes on the command line, truncated to 4000 chars (cli.mjs:239), which is whatever Claude paraphrases and could contain client project detail; and (b) name plus first 140 chars of description for the 60 skills with the LONGEST descriptions from ~/.claude/skills, ~/.codex/skills, ~/.opencode/skills, ~/.jev-skill-router/library and ./skills (cli.mjs:234-237). Nothing is sent about code, diffs or file contents unless Claude pastes them into the request. --scan sends the first 6 KB body of every discovered SKILL.md. Note the plugin skills dir is skipped (walkMd excludes 'plugins', cli.mjs:47), so the user's caveman, gitnexus and other plugin or project skills are likely not in the catalog.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on missing key, HTTP errors and JSON errors: prints {use_skill:false,...} and exits 0 (cli.mjs:256-258). There is NO fetch timeout and NO retry, so a slow or hanging OpenRouter stalls the Bash call until the tool-level timeout (default 2 min). It is also fail-open at the agent level in the sense that nothing enforces the rule: if Claude skips the CLAUDE.md instruction, routing simply does not happen.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool-definition cost: no MCP server, no tools, no server instructions. Only the pasted CLAUDE.md rule (about 70 tokens, recurring every session). Per user request, if Claude obeys, there is one extra Bash tool_use plus a JSON result of about 80 to 120 tokens, roughly 200 tokens of transcript per turn, accumulating over a long session. No hook-injected text.
pros: Correct Jev usage: exact Decisions endpoint and model from the brief (cli.mjs:24-25), OpenRouter key only, and a sensible use of typed Choice/Score primitives, with cheap cost per call.
Tiny and auditable: 258 lines, zero dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, no child_process or eval. The whole thing can be read in 5 minutes, so vendoring or forking is easy.
Fail-open on API errors and a missing key (cli.mjs:256-258) so it never blocks Claude.
Zero context cost from tool definitions, since there is no MCP server.
Reusable pieces: the request shape (state + questions with choice/score, cli.mjs:238-245) and the skill-audit prompts are a good reference for writing a proper UserPromptSubmit hook.
cons: Solves a problem Claude Code already handles natively: Claude Code lists skills with descriptions in context and triggers them itself. This user has about 40 skills, which is cheap in context, so routing adds latency and a network hop for little value.

Not automatic: it requires a pasted CLAUDE.md rule and Claude's compliance every turn. That contradicts the requirement 'Claude Code must use it without me prompting'. Also there is no --init that writes the file, it only prints.

Discovery misses the user's real skills: it scans ~/.claude/skills but explicitly skips any dir named 'plugins' (cli.mjs:47), so plugin-provided skills (caveman, gitnexus, etc.) are invisible. Project-level .claude/skills is not scanned, only ./skills.

Catalog is cut to the 60 skills with the LONGEST descriptions (cli.mjs:234-235), not the most relevant ones, so short-described skills are silently unroutable. Descriptions are truncated to 140 chars, which throws away trigger phrases.
No fetch timeout (cli.mjs:89): a slow OpenRouter call stalls a Bash tool call up to the tool timeout on every turn.
Request text appears in argv (ps-visible) and 60 skill names plus the user prompt go to a third party on client projects; there is no opt-out or redaction.
Adds a full extra model turn (about 1.5 to 4 s and about 200 tokens) to every non-trivial prompt, which is bad for an all-day workflow; in bypass mode the user might not even notice it.
Immature and unverified: 3 versions in 15 minutes, no repo, no tests, no CI, single anonymous maintainer, README claims are unverifiable. The pinned jev-1.13 model, not jev-latest.

Only covers skill routing and skill auditing. It does nothing for real coding decisions (which file, whether to run tests, risk gating, permission decisions, model or subagent routing), where Jev's calibrated probabilities are actually useful.
Security scanner is a heuristic on the first 6 KB of a skill and is likely to give false TRUSTED verdicts; the 'UNKNOWN' state does not block anything.
entries.verdict: A small, honest, correctly wired OpenRouter-Jev CLI, but it is a poc that only auto-runs via a pasted CLAUDE.md rule, misses plugin skills, and duplicates Claude Code's built-in skill triggering. Not worth installing; at most use it as a reference for the Decisions request shape and vendor a UserPromptSubmit-hook version with a timeout if skill routing is ever wanted.

entries.name: Jev-router (Jamesjiwei19981027)
entries.what: Cross-agent (Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Antigravity) shared runtime: Jev-decided capability routing (advice only) and save-token-jev compaction. On Claude Code it is only a jevrouter skill plus a CLAUDE.md routing rule. Not the typesafe/jev-router product.
entries.autoInvocation: skill trigger plus CLAUDE.md rule (model discretion)
pros: Route is advice only, Agent's own permission flow untouched; falls back to normal behavior when Jev unavailable
JEV_BASE_URL/JEV_API_URL configurable, so OpenRouter could be pointed at
Reads key from a protected file with error redaction
cons: Windows-first: README says tested only on Windows 11, macOS/Linux untested; Claude Code has no compaction or hook integration
Claude Code path relies on the model choosing to call a skill, so automatic use is unreliable
0 stars, early, name collides with TypeSafe's jev-router and BillionsBobby/JevRouter, confusing

entries.name: kitze/skillbox
entries.what: Self-hosted (Docker + Bun + Hono + PostgreSQL + React UI) versioned skills library exposed to agents over HTTP MCP and a Node stdio bridge (cli/skillbox.mjs). Jev is used in exactly one place: the recommend_skills MCP tool, which sends the task text plus all authorized skill descriptions to Jev as Score questions (one per skill, 0-4 scale) and returns skills scoring >=3. It is a skill-picker, not a general code-decision layer. It is not a plain "skill"; it is a server app whose bootstrap SKILL.md tells agents to call search_skills at the start of each task. The Jev key is entered in the Skillbox web UI and stored server-side, not read from the environment.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger plus model-discretion MCP tool. The bootstrap SKILL.md description says 'ALWAYS browse the Skills Library at the start of a task', which prompts Claude to call search_skills; recommend_skills is explicitly additive and optional ('still call unqueried search_skills once'). Jev is not invoked by any deterministic hook and is never used for coding decisions.
security: Jev key stored server-side, AES-256-GCM in Postgres, key derived from SKILLBOX_ADMIN_TOKEN (SECURITY.md); never returned by API. Key never appears in argv on the client.
Client token passed via SKILLBOX_TOKEN env or 0600 config file (cli/skillbox.mjs:15-28); CLI prints args (task text) only in argv, no secrets.
Outbound fetch uses redirect:'error', bounded response size (128 KB) and never logs provider bodies (recommendations.ts:145,:190-205).

Prompt-injection surface is real: the whole design is that the agent loads user-managed skill bodies from a server and follows them (bootstrap SKILL.md: 'follow applicable guidance'). A compromised or poisoned skill library equals instructions injected into Claude Code. Jev rubric explicitly treats descriptions as untrusted (evaluationRequest).

No shell exec of skill code in the server (README: never executes uploaded skill code); CLI fetch validates paths, hashes and checksums. install-client.py rewrites Claude/Codex/Cursor configs (backups made) and should be reviewed before use.

No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall; setup requires Docker. Web UI is single-owner admin-token auth; need TLS reverse proxy for remote use. Pulling images and running a Postgres stack is a sizeable attack surface for a personal tool.
entries.dataEgress: Claude Code -> your Skillbox server: task strings passed to recommend_skills/search_skills (<=2000 chars), model/harness identity headers (X-Skillbox-Model), and skill-use reports. Skillbox server -> OpenRouter (https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions): the task text and every authorized skill's id + description (chunks of <=32 skills). No code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent to Jev by design, though the task text is whatever the model writes as the task, which could contain client project detail. Results cached 5 minutes in server memory.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. recommend_skills falls back to deterministic lexical search with an explicit fallbackReason (timeout, rate_limited, unavailable, authentication_failed, invalid_response, catalog_limit, busy) and noMatch=null. Deadline 8000 ms (DEADLINE_MS), rate cooldown from Retry-After, max 10 model calls/min per scope, max 2 concurrent, one failed OpenRouter batch fails the whole request to fallback (recommendations.ts:10-14, :335-398). If the Skillbox server itself is down, the MCP tools error and the bootstrap skill says to report it.
entries.contextCost: 5 base MCP tools (search_skills, recommend_skills, load_skill, read_skill_file, report_skill_use) plus up to 4 write tools (upsert_skill, propose_skill_update, list_skill_proposals, archive_skill) depending on permissions; est. roughly 1.5-2.5k tokens of tool definitions (recommend_skills description alone is about 620 chars). The bootstrap skill adds a short description (about 60 tokens) always and about 700 tokens when triggered. search_skills at every task start injects the full skill index (up to 220 chars per skill, so 200 skills is about 11k tokens), which grows with library size. No hook-injected text.
pros: OpenRouter Jev works out of the box in code: POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13, Score primitive, parsed answers[skill_i].score, usage.cost aggregated (recommendations.ts:138-166, :222). It is a working, tested reference for the Decisions API Score request/response shape.
Careful failure handling: 8 s deadline, fail-open to lexical search, rate limit cooldown, batch limits, cache, no partial ranking, redirect:'error', bounded response size.
Key is encrypted server-side and never enters Claude Code's env, argv or context.
Uses Jev for what a calibrated scorer suits (rank N candidates against a task) with an injection-resistant rubric.
MIT, clear SECURITY.md, ~74 tests, mocked-provider tests for OpenRouter batching.
Bootstrap skill gives genuinely automatic behavior for the skill-discovery step without the user prompting.
cons: Jev only ranks skills in a library the user would have to build and host; it adds no Jev value for code edits, tool routing, permission decisions, or commit/PR choices, which is what the user wants.
Heavy infrastructure for a personal setup: Docker Compose + PostgreSQL + Bun server + admin UI, versus the user's existing Node/uvx-only tooling.
Jev call is behind an optional recommend_skills tool the model must choose to call; the mandated flow is search_skills, which does not use Jev, so Jev is often skipped. Not deterministic.

Key entered through the web UI and no env var support (no OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so it cannot be wired into Claude Code settings or hooks; the candidate's TYPESAFE_API_KEY evidence is wrong for the code.
Sends task text and all skill descriptions to OpenRouter on each cache miss; client-project task text leaves the machine (via your server).
Every task start pays for search_skills output in context that grows with library size, and installs a ALWAYS-trigger skill that will fire on all tasks including trivial ones.
Skill bodies are remote instructions followed by the agent, a prompt-injection channel that conflicts with the user's secret-guard hooks and client-work confidentiality.
Very young and single-author: repo created 2026-09-17, 11 commits, 1 contributor (3 identities), no releases, no CI, version 0.1.0; stars are likely hype-driven.
Adds nothing to existing setup that Claude Code's built-in Skills and skill descriptions do not already do locally at zero latency.
entries.verdict: Real and Jev-integrated (OpenRouter Decisions API supported natively, fail-open), but Jev is confined to ranking skills in a self-hosted library, which is a poor match for automatic Jev use inside daily Claude Code coding. Worth reading as a reference for the Score request shape; do not install it as the integration.

entries.name: TheoOliveira/pi-jev
entries.what: A Pi coding agent (pi.dev, not Claude Code) extension. It uses the @typesafe-ai/sdk client to call Jev System One.
