It registers 3 model-callable tools: jev_find_tools (activate inactive tools by Noul probability), jev_find_skill (rank SKILL.md files) and jev_evaluate (generic Choice/Noul/Score). It also has opt-in hooks for per-prompt auto-routing, auto model selection, a tool-call guard, compaction, and agent orchestration. A separate jev-gate CLI checks a git diff or stdin against acceptance criteria and exits 0/1/2. The runtime is TypeScript against Pi's ExtensionAPI (pi.on, pi.registerFlag, pi.setActiveTools). It is not an MCP server and has no Claude Code hook, plugin or skill manifest.
interface: /jev status | help | skills | test | enable | disable | auto | auto-model | tool-guard | compact | agents | auto-agents
entries.autoInvocation: Inside Pi: opt-in hooks (--jev-auto, tool-guard, compact), which are deterministic hook events, plus model-discretion tools (jev_find_tools, jev_find_skill, jev_evaluate). For Claude Code: none. It ships no .claude-plugin, no hooks.json, no MCP server and no SKILL.md. Only the jev-gate CLI can be called from a Claude Code hook, and that needs custom wiring.
security: MIT license. The repo has only a SECURITY.md that gives a private email for reports.

Key handling: TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env or a plaintext file ~/.pi/agent/secrets/typesafe_api_key. The key is sent only as a Bearer header by the SDK. It is never put in argv by this code, but the jev-gate criteria and its diff do pass through argv/stdin.

Shell execution: gate.ts:76-82 runs execSync('git diff HEAD') and 'git diff --cached' with fixed strings, so there is no injection from user input. bin/jev-gate.js spawnSync's node with tsx and the runner path, and it forwards process.argv.
No postinstall script in package.json and no curl|sh installer. It depends at runtime on the tsx and @typesafe-ai/sdk npm packages. It is published with npm --provenance via CI (publish.yml).
No telemetry in the code. The SDK sends X-TypeSafe-SDK and X-TypeSafe-Runtime headers.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompts, tool descriptions and skill descriptions are interpolated into Jev question strings (auto.ts, router.ts). Jev returns only typed probabilities, not free text, so the injection blast radius is limited to wrong activation or skill suggestions. The tool-guard is a probabilistic block/allow on hallucination, not a security control.
entries.dataEgress: The user prompt goes to Jev in auto mode (auto.ts state:{task: prompt, tools, available_skills}), with candidate tool names and descriptions and skill names and descriptions. jev_evaluate sends whatever state the model supplies, which can include diffs or file contents. With tool-guard on, every tool name and its full input parameters leave the machine (file paths, Bash commands, edit contents), and the error content of failed tools is sent too. The gate CLI sends the full git diff HEAD, a file, or stdin. Compaction sends tool-history entries. All of this goes to api.typesafe.ai by default, or to whatever PI_JEV_BASE_URL says. There is no redaction layer. The client-project code and secret-leak concerns are real if tool-guard or the gate CLI are used. Auto mode alone leaks only the prompt text and tool metadata.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open for auto-routing. AutoJev.route() catches every error and returns skip('error'), so the turn continues untouched (auto.ts). ToolRouter.findAndActivate falls back to activating nothing. The tool-guard checks are wrapped in try/catch, and I did not read the catch branch, so I am assuming it allows the call. The gate CLI is fail-closed by default (exit 2) and fail-open only with --fail-open. Timeouts are the SDK defaults: 10 s per request (index.mjs:519, timeout ?? 1e4) plus a retry policy. That means a slow Jev can stall a Pi turn for up to about 10 s times the retries, since auto mode awaits the call in before_agent_start. There is no custom short timeout in pi-jev.
entries.contextCost: Not applicable to Claude Code, because it cannot be loaded there. In Pi it adds 3 tools. The description and schema text in src/tools.ts is about 6.8 KB including code, so the tool definitions are roughly 0.6-0.8k tokens. Auto mode injects a short 'jev-auto' message only when skills match. There are no MCP server instructions.
pros: The gate check is real. jev-gate turns a diff or command output plus natural-language criteria into P(pass) with clean exit codes (bin/jev-gate-runner.ts, src/gate.ts). It is host-agnostic and could be called from a Claude Code Stop hook or CI as a cheap second opinion.

Base URL and key are env-configurable (PI_JEV_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, src/jev.ts:15-24). The SDK posts to {base}/v1/systemone, so https://openrouter.ai/api plus an OpenRouter key maps to the documented System One endpoint with no code change.
Correct primitive usage: Noul for tool and skill relevance, batched into one call per prompt, with a threshold constant (0.65). Auto mode is fail-open and never throws.
Opt-in and cost-honest design: the README lists which features spend Jev requests. It has typecheck, 12 test files, CI and npm provenance publishing, and MIT license.
Ideas transfer: the tool-guard and 'ask Jev Noul questions in a hook' patterns are useful design references for building a Claude Code hook.
cons: Wrong host. It is a Pi extension (ExtensionAPI: pi.on, pi.registerFlag, pi.setActiveTools, package.json 'pi' key). It cannot be loaded into Claude Code. It has no MCP server, no hooks.json, no plugin.json and no SKILL.md. The 'tool routing' value (dynamically activating tools) has no Claude Code equivalent, because Claude Code's tool set is not switched at runtime by hooks.

Not OpenRouter-native. There is no OpenRouter string in the code, the model default is 'jev-latest' rather than typesafe/jev-1.13, and the README says TYPESAFE_API_KEY from console.typesafe.ai. OpenRouter works only through the undocumented-in-repo env override and would need a live test.
Very young and single-maintainer: 19 commits in 8 days, 1 contributor, v0.6.0, 58 stars. Behaviour of Jev-based routing is unproven, and Theo's 'flash-router' skepticism applies.

Automatic features are opt-in and, in Pi, cost one Jev request per prompt or per tool call. Tool-guard sends every tool input to a third party, which conflicts with the user's client projects and the existing secret-leak guard. There is no redaction.

The 10 s default SDK timeout with retries, awaited in before_agent_start, can stall a turn when Jev is slow. The README's 'fails closed safely' claim is contradicted by the code, where auto mode fails open.
The Node/tsx runtime is heavy for a hook. jev-gate spawns node with tsx on every call, adding cold-start latency, and would need npm install of the peer/dev tree to run.
entries.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code as shipped. It is a Pi-specific extension with no MCP, hook or plugin surface. Only the jev-gate CLI and the design patterns (batched Noul relevance questions, diff-vs-criteria gate) are reusable. It is worth borrowing the ideas, not installing the package, and any Claude Code hook should call OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone directly.

entries.name: safzanpirani/pi-jev-skill-picker
entries.what: A Pi coding agent (Earendil Works pi-coding-agent) extension, not a Claude Code skill despite the "skill" label. It hooks Pi's before_agent_start event to delete the generated <skills> catalog from the system prompt. It registers two tools: skill_search and skill_load. skill_search sends one Jev Score question per enabled skill (levels: unrelated / adjacent / directly applicable), with the task text in shared state. It loads the full SKILL.md of the top N skills (default 3, minimum score 1.6 out of 2). skill_load reads skills by name from disk and never calls Jev. If Jev fails or there is no key, it falls back to lexical keyword matching. The value is saving about 19k tokens per request on a 137-skill catalog.
entries.autoInvocation: In Pi, the catalog strip is deterministic through the event hook. Skill selection is model-discretion: promptGuidelines tell the model to call skill_search before substantive work. Not applicable to Claude Code, as it has no extension API for this.
security: API key sent as Bearer header only, never on argv. It is read from the env or a JSON config file (README recommends chmod 0600), and the code does not check the file's permissions.
No shell execution, no postinstall script, no curl|sh, and no telemetry in the source. package.json has only devDependencies, and the published files are extensions/README/LICENSE.

The only network call is a POST to the configured endpoint. PI_SKILL_JEV_ENDPOINT is fully overridable, so anyone who can set env vars could redirect skill descriptions and the task text to another host.

Prompt-injection surface: skill_search returns full SKILL.md bodies as tool results that the agent is told to follow. Skill content is trusted local data, but a malicious skill or a description crafted to score highly would get its instructions injected. The score is a probability-weighted position, not a safety filter.
Small codebase (about 830 lines of source) that is easy to audit. Single maintainer, 8 commits, and 37 stars in 10 days, so it has no track record.
entries.dataEgress: The task string the agent writes (its own summary of what it is about to do, including named tools, services, and files) plus the name and description of every enabled skill, each truncated to 1200 chars. This goes to api.typesafe.ai in one request per 50 skills, and a 137-skill catalog is about 38.6k Jev input tokens per call. No source code, diffs, file contents, or tool outputs are sent unless the agent puts them in the task text. Skill bodies are read locally and never sent.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. There are up to 3 attempts per shard with exponential backoff (250ms, then 500ms) and Retry-After honored on 429/5xx. Each attempt has a 20s timeout (worst case is over 60s per shard). If every shard fails, or there is no key, it falls back to lexical matching that returns skill metadata and paths. If only some shards fail, it uses the partial ranking and says so. A skill_search error never blocks the agent (skill-jev.ts:196-236).
entries.contextCost: In Pi it is net-negative, saving about 19k tokens per request by stripping the catalog. The cost is two tool definitions of roughly 500-800 tokens (long descriptions plus promptGuidelines injected into the system prompt), plus the full SKILL.md bodies returned per search. For Claude Code the impact is not applicable, because it cannot run there. Claude Code already lists skills with only a one-line description each, and that list is not removable through hooks.
pros: Concrete, working reference for the Jev System One Score request and response shape: {model, state, questions:{id:{type:'score',instructions,criteria[]}}} returns answers[id].score and .confidence (jev.ts:194-205, 208-231). Useful to copy when writing your own hook or MCP.
Endpoint and model are env-overridable (PI_SKILL_JEV_ENDPOINT, PI_SKILL_JEV_MODEL), so pointing it at OpenRouter is a config change, not a code change.
Well-engineered failure handling: fail-open, retry on 429/5xx, Retry-After, lexical fallback, and partial-shard tolerance. The core logic is unit-tested with a stubbed fetch.
Clean security posture: no shell, no postinstall, no telemetry, key never on argv, MIT license, 830 lines that are easy to read.
The idea of ranking skills per task with a cheap calibrated classifier is sound. It gives about $0.0016 per call at Jev pricing and is a good pattern to port.
cons: It is a Pi agent extension. It uses Pi's ExtensionAPI (pi.on('before_agent_start'), pi.registerTool) and cannot be installed or loaded in Claude Code. Nothing is usable without a rewrite.

The main saving depends on stripping the skills catalog from the system prompt. Claude Code hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse) cannot remove or rewrite the built-in skill listing, so the core benefit does not port.

The Claude Code equivalent would be a UserPromptSubmit hook that ranks skills and injects additionalContext. That would add Jev latency to every prompt and duplicate Claude Code's own skill matching, and the user's list is only about 30 skills.
Its key handling is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only. It works with OpenRouter only by putting an OpenRouter key in a misnamed variable, and OpenRouter /systemone schema equivalence is unverified.
Very early: 8 commits, one author, no CI, no releases, 10 days old, and version 0.1.0. The default 20s timeout with 3 retries can stall a turn for a minute in the worst case.
It solves skill selection only. It does not address the user's other Jev use cases in Claude Code, such as permission decisions, routing, or triage.
entries.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code: it is a Pi-only extension whose key benefit (stripping the skill catalog from the system prompt) has no Claude Code hook. Treat it as a reference for the Jev Score request format and the fail-open pattern, not as an integration. Do not install it.

entries.name: GodsBoy/jev-agent-skill-router
entries.what: Python 3.11 stdlib-only library and CLI (jev-router route/evaluate/report/validate-results) that routes a natural-language request to one skill out of a catalogue of (name, description) pairs. It batches the catalogue (8 per batch, 4 parallel workers), calls Jev Choice on each batch, keeps the top 2 per batch, and repeats until a final Choice plus Noul calls (needs_specialist, needs_review, fit_N) can run. Python thresholds then produce route, no_skill or review. It is a research demo for the Hermes Agent skill catalogue (443 skills). It is not a Claude Code integration and does not load or execute skills. The name "router-proxy" in the discovery record is wrong. It is a client library, not a proxy.
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is only run when explicitly invoked from the CLI or imported as a library. It has no hook, MCP, skill or proxy surface, so Claude Code would never call it automatically without new glue code.
security: API key is read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY environment variable only. There is no CLI key flag, so the key never appears in argv or the process list. Dotenv files are not read (transport.py:41-46, README).
Key is validated as printable ASCII, and __repr__ omits it (transport.py:44,49).

HTTPS to a fixed host, with redirects disabled via a _NoRedirect handler (transport.py:18-28). This prevents the Bearer token leaking on a redirect. Response size is capped at 2 MB and the timeout is 30 s.
No subprocess, eval or exec in the runtime. There is no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh installer. The tests use subprocess only for git ls-files.

Prompt-injection surface: user request text and skill descriptions are sent inside the question text. The policy strings tell Jev to treat them as data (policy.py:11-45). The output is typed and only ever selects among the given options, so injection can at worst mis-route. The library executes nothing.
Error handling collapses exceptions to short codes (raise ... from None), so response bodies and key material are not leaked in errors.
entries.dataEgress: Each API call sends the full request string (up to 16,000 chars), plus the names and descriptions (up to 2,000 chars each) of the skills in that batch, to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. The payload is state.request plus the question text and options. For a catalogue of N skills, every skill description is sent at least once per route (batching then a final round). The library itself never reads code, diffs, files or tool outputs. Anything it sends is only what the caller passes as the request. Nothing goes to OpenRouter, since the endpoint is hardcoded to TypeSafe. The client does not retain raw response bodies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-safe at library level, with no retries. A single call has a 30 s default timeout (HttpTransport timeout=30.0, transport.py:32). Any HTTP, connection or invalid-response error becomes an error code, and route() returns outcome "review" with reason "api_error" (router.py:114-131). The CLI exits with 2. There is no automatic retry, and no fallback to the lexical baseline unless the caller adds one. Without a hook wrapper, nothing blocks Claude Code, because there is no integration. Observed: one of 72 cases in the final run hit invalid_response, and the initial pinned model jev-1.12 returned HTTP 400 for all 12 cases.
entries.contextCost: Zero for Claude Code today, because it registers no MCP tools, no MCP instructions, no hooks and no skills. If someone wrapped it as a UserPromptSubmit hook, the injected text would be small (a JSON decision or a short hint). Approximate cost of the repo itself as installed context: 0 tokens.
pros: Clean, dependency-free reference implementation of Jev Choice and Noul calls, with the exact System One request and response schema (transport.py:52-77, parse_response). It is useful as a template for a custom hook or MCP wrapper.
Careful security hygiene: key only from env, redirects disabled, response capped at 2 MB, HTTPS-only, no shell execution, no telemetry, no install scripts.
Strict validation of Jev output (probabilities sum to about 1, choice equals argmax, exact key sets), which guards against malformed responses.

Real, published measurements against a lexical baseline on synthetic data (68/72 vs 51/72). Its honest disclosure of limitations is credible. It also empirically shows that jev-1.12 returned HTTP 400 and that jev-latest resolved to jev-1.13.0.
Fail-safe abstention design: on API error it returns review instead of guessing.
About 101 offline tests with CI and strict mypy.
cons: Not a Claude Code integration: no MCP server, hook, SKILL.md, plugin manifest or .mcp.json. The auto-invocation requirement is completely unmet.

TypeSafe-direct only. The endpoint is hardcoded (transport.py:12), the env var is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and the model regex jev-* rejects OpenRouter ids (policy.py). The user wants OpenRouter, so this would need a fork.

Solves a different problem: selecting one of hundreds of Hermes-style skills. The user's Claude Code setup has a handful of skills and MCP servers, and Claude Code already matches skills by description. A 1.3 s multi-call router in front of that adds latency with little value.
Slow and chatty by design: about 4 API calls per request and a 1.3 s median, which is noticeable if run per prompt.

Very young and single-author: 4 commits, all on 2026-09-16, no releases, no PyPI package, 24 stars. Exploratory results with reused test data, and the author states that they do not establish production accuracy or calibration.
25% of outcomes are 'review' (abstain), and 3 of 72 were unnecessary reviews. A hook built on this would often punt back to Claude anyway.
Sends the user's full prompt and all skill descriptions off-machine on every route, a concern for client projects.
entries.verdict: Not usable as an automatic Claude Code integration: it is a Hermes-oriented skill-routing benchmark library with no MCP, hook or skill surface, and it only speaks to api.typesafe.ai. Its main value is as a small, well-validated reference for the System One request and response schema and for the abstention thresholding pattern. If the user builds a custom hook, borrowing transport.py (swap the endpoint to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone) is worthwhile, but adopting the repo itself is not.

entries.name: Protocol-Lattice/harness-router
entries.what: Python tool-selection router that uses Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter Decisions API) as a Choice classifier over the host harness's tool catalog. It ships 4 pieces: (a) Claude Code project hooks (SessionStart tool discovery, UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse precompute of a 'next tool', PreToolUse deny+re-plan if Claude picks a different tool at confidence >= 0.85), (b) an MCP server with route and route_mcts tools, (c) a skill that tells the model to call it rarely, (d) a CLI/daemon (unix socket in /tmp). It does not route models or generate code. It only picks between tools Claude already has.
interface: MCP tool route(goal, tools[], observation?, last_action?)
MCP tool route_mcts(root_state, states[], transitions[], simulations<=4096, max_depth<=8, use_jev_prior)
CLI har / harness-router route, route-mcts; harness-router-mcp
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PostToolUse, PreToolUse, SessionStart). It really is automatic with no user prompting. It is not model-discretion: MCP and skill are optional extras (skill description says rarely/only-when-asked). Caveat: it automates a decision the user does not need, choosing among Claude's own tools, not code-review or classification decisions.
security: No curl|sh, but the recommended installer is `curl ... main/scripts/install_hook.py | python3 -`: unpinned code from the main branch executes and writes hook scripts that then run on every prompt/tool call (supply-chain surface). It has a symlink refusal and .bak backups, and is project-scoped.
Also installs from `git+https://github.com/...@main` (unpinned); the package is not on PyPI.
API key is read from env only and sent as a Bearer header via httpx, not argv. Good hygiene: the code asserts the key is not in the payload and redacts it from error text (provider.py).

Sensitive data is NOT redacted: only the API key is filtered. Tool output (PostToolUse tool_response[:4000], clipped to ~512 chars per field by RoutingConfig.state_field_limit) and user prompts go to OpenRouter. A Read of .env or command output containing secrets can leak in that snippet.

Hook state written to the project dir: .harness-router/sessions/*.decision.json and .decisions.jsonl contain goal and observation in plaintext and are appended without rotation. The installer adds .gitignore entries, but hooks/ and .claude/hooks are committed unless the user avoids that.
Daemon spawns a detached Python process listening on /tmp/harness-router-<uid>.sock, with no auth beyond filesystem permissions; the socket path is in shared /tmp.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, on UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse (and via MCP route): the user's prompt text (goal, first 1600 chars, clipped to ~512 chars in the router state), the last tool's output text (first 4000 chars from the hook, clipped to ~512 chars by the router), last tool name, and the name plus description (about 96 chars each) of every candidate tool including all MCP tools. File contents and command output that appear in tool responses leak in the snippet; the diff or whole repo is not sent wholesale. This also applies to client projects. OpenRouter/TypeSafe then see the client-code fragments. Secrets are not scrubbed except the API key itself.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: every hook wraps errors and prints nothing or {}. Timeouts are 4 s per Jev call (hook timeout 5 s); MCP tool 2 s; missing key returns fallback. Provider errors become fallback, and an unavailable daemon falls back to a subprocess CLI call. Worst case per event is roughly 4-5 s stall on UserPromptSubmit or PostToolUse if OpenRouter hangs (synchronous hooks). Also fails open if the catalog is missing. However, when the router works but is wrong, PreToolUse actively DENIES Claude's tool call (fail-closed for that call, one retry), which is the bigger risk in practice.
entries.contextCost: MCP server: 2 tools (route, route_mcts) plus server instructions (~300 chars). route_mcts has a large nested schema (MCTSState, MCTSTransition, RouteCandidate), so estimated ~700-900 tokens of tool defs in total; only ~50 tokens if the MCP is omitted and hooks used. Skill: ~60 tokens of description in the always-loaded listing. Hooks inject additionalContext on every user prompt and every PostToolUse ('Harness Router selected X as the next tool (confidence ...). Use that tool...', ~40-60 tokens each), i.e. roughly 50 tokens x every tool call, and SessionStart injects the catalog path. Deny messages add a whole extra model turn (re-plan), the costly part.
pros: Truly automatic through deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit / PreToolUse / PostToolUse), which matches the 'never say use jev' requirement in mechanism.
OpenRouter-native out of the box: correct Decisions API URL, typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY. No patching needed (config.py, provider.py).
Careful engineering on failure: fail-open everywhere, short timeouts, redirect at most once per state, never emits permissionDecision allow, refuses to put API key in payload and redacts errors.
Decent test surface for an alpha (13 test files incl. provider, MCP server, installers) and an honest BENCHMARK.md that publishes a negative result.
Claude hook code is small, readable stdlib Python (about 130 lines per hook), so it is easy to audit or fork.
Discovers the live tool catalog including MCP tools from Claude itself rather than a hard-coded list, so GitNexus/playwright tools would be in scope.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for this user: it routes between tools Opus 5.5 already picks correctly; Jev adds a second opinion over 'Read vs Grep vs Bash', not a real decision (review triage, risk scoring, commit classification) where calibrated probabilities pay off.

Own benchmark (BENCHMARK.md) shows the integration doubled tokens (+105.9% main-model, +109.8% full system) and doubled wall-clock (115.8 s -> 228.9 s); 54/58 routings fell back. The Claude-hook variant is unbenchmarked.

PreToolUse deny+re-plan on a stale prompt-time precompute (30 s TTL, threshold 0.85): a decision made from the user's prompt is compared against whatever tool Claude proposes later, so correct calls can be denied, costing a model turn. In bypass/auto mode this adds friction with no safety benefit.
Data egress on every prompt and every tool result for personal AND client projects: prompt text plus 512-4000 chars of tool output go to OpenRouter with no secret/PII scrubbing except the API key.

Synchronous hook per prompt and per tool call (fresh python3 process + up to 4 s network) adds ~0.5-1 s per tool call on top of existing GitNexus, secret-guard and caveman hooks; hook ordering/interaction with GitNexus additionalContext is untested.
SessionStart spawns `claude mcp serve` and `claude --print` to enumerate tools on every start/resume/compact, which respawns the user's gitnexus and playwright MCP servers.

Installer is project-scoped and hard-wired to $CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR/.claude/hooks and $ROOT/hooks/pre_decision.py, and commits scripts into client repos; a user-global install requires manual rewrite. README says PreToolUse calls the router MCP, but the shipped pre_tool_use.py only reads the precomputed decision file (docs and code diverge).
Very young and thin: created 2026-09-25, 2 contributors, 19 stars, no releases, not on PyPI, unpinned `main` installs, no test CI, alpha per its own README. Installs via curl | python3 from main.
route_mcts is impractical for Claude (needs a model-authored simulated state graph) and its large schema costs ~500+ tokens for no daily value.
entries.verdict: Real, OpenRouter-native and genuinely automatic via hooks, but it uses Jev for the least valuable job (second-guessing Claude's tool choice) and the authors' own benchmark shows about 2x tokens and time; it also sends prompts and tool output of client projects to OpenRouter on every step. Do not install as-is. At most mine its provider.py (about 200 lines) as a reference for the Decisions API request/response schema.

entries.name: jackbarunz/jev-tool-router
entries.what: Node MCP stdio proxy (jev_router) that sits in front of OTHER MCP servers. Instead of exposing hundreds of external tool schemas, it exposes ~10 routing tools. find_tool sends the agent's plain-language capability request plus downstream tool names/descriptions (truncated to 240 chars) to Jev via Vercel AI SDK experimental_evaluate as a Choice with a none_of_the_above option; if P>=0.90 it returns that one tool and its full schema, otherwise a BM25 shortlist. It can proxy calls (call_tool / call_readonly_tool) and has an extra evaluate_work_with_jev tool that scores work (boolean/score/choice questions). Built and documented for Codex (setup script rewrites ~/.codex/config.toml and AGENTS.md); not built for Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a Codex AGENTS.md instruction ("call find_tool first"). No hooks. In Claude Code you would have to add equivalent CLAUDE.md text; the model would still choose whether to call it. Not a deterministic hook and not a transparent proxy. Only the tool-routing function is automatic-ish once downstream MCPs are hidden; evaluate_work_with_jev is only triggered by user phrasing.
security: API key read from env AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY only; never written to config; not passed in argv (good). Setup script refuses literal env values / credential-like args in downstream servers.

Downstream MCP servers are spawned as child processes from router.config.json (arbitrary commands, npx -y some-mcp-server in template) - normal for a proxy but adds a supply-chain surface; mcp-remote pinned to 0.14.2 in generated wrappers.

Proxy call_tool bypasses Claude Code's per-MCP-server permission naming: every downstream call becomes mcp__jev_router__call_tool, so allow/deny rules and hooks matching specific tool names (e.g. secret-leak guard, gitnexus matchers) stop seeing the real tool. In bypass/auto mode this hides what is being run.
Prompt-injection surface: downstream tool descriptions are fed to Jev and returned to the agent; a malicious MCP description could steer routing. Upstream error bodies are bounded/redacted.
Not sandboxed; no postinstall scripts in package.json; no curl|sh; no telemetry code found (no fetch() in src or scripts). Only outbound call is via AI SDK to the Vercel gateway.
Unofficial single-author repo, 8 stars, no CI, no releases: low review and supply-chain assurance. Skill installer (npx skills add) runs third-party tooling.
entries.dataEgress: Per find_tool: the agent's capability request string, optional task context (up to ~6k estimated tokens), and every routed downstream tool name plus description (truncated to 240 chars) go to Vercel AI Gateway then TypeSafe Jev. Full tool schemas and downstream tool results are not sent. For evaluate_work_with_jev: goal, requirements, work text and evidence supplied by the agent (can include code/diffs) go to Jev. No file reading by the router itself, no telemetry. Not sent to OpenRouter in the current code. Data also transits Vercel.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft on find_tool: Jev error or P<0.90 returns a compact BM25 shortlist plus guidance, not the full inventory (router-core.mjs ~582-640; commit 2e03611). Downstream connect timeout 15s and tool timeout 60s defaults (config.mjs:62-63) via withTimeout; unhealthy sessions evicted and rebuilt; mutating calls not replayed. But there is NO timeout visible on the Jev evaluate() call itself (only downstream calls use withTimeout), so a hung gateway could stall find_tool. Server hard-fails at startup (throw) if AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY is missing (server.mjs:21-23), so in Claude Code the whole jev_router MCP would fail to connect and any tools moved behind it would be unreachable. evaluate_work_with_jev has no try/catch fallback seen; errors surface as tool errors.
entries.contextCost: 10 tools registered (find_tool, get_tool_schema, search_tools, list_servers, list_tools, list_all_tools, call_readonly_tool, call_tool, evaluate_work_with_jev, router_status). Tool definitions in server.mjs total ~14.5k chars including code, so names+descriptions+schemas are approx 2.5-3.5k tokens (estimate). No MCP server-level instructions; the intended AGENTS.md routing instructions are Codex-specific. Net effect for this user: their MCP surface is small (gitnexus ~17 tools, playwright ~25 tools, both well-scoped and deferred/tool-searched by Claude Code 2.x), so router saves little and Claude Code already has native MCP tool search (deferred tool loading), which makes this router largely redundant there.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev for a sensible System One task: a confidence-gated Choice with an explicit none_of_the_above and a 0.90 threshold, with deterministic BM25 fallback.

Careful engineering: pessimistic token preflight against Jev's documented 32k/64k limits, tournament routing for >254 tools, bounded fallbacks, no replay of mutating calls (README, policy.mjs 383 lines).
Good secret hygiene: key only via env, refuses literal env/credential-like args when migrating, backs up configs before mutation.
MIT licensed, small readable codebase (~2.4k lines src), 5 test files including a mock MCP.
evaluate_work_with_jev shows a useful Jev pattern (P(complete), P(needs revision), quality score) that could be reused as a Stop-hook style review if reimplemented against OpenRouter.
README notes related work fast-jev-compaction (tamaratran), a separate candidate worth auditing.
cons: Built for Codex, not Claude Code: setup script edits ~/.codex/config.toml and AGENTS.md; nothing for ~/.claude.json, .mcp.json, hooks, or CLAUDE.md. Would need manual wiring.

No OpenRouter support: only Vercel AI Gateway (AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY, model 'typesafe-ai/jev'). Switching needs replacing the AI SDK experimental_evaluate calls with OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone code (moderate work, fork maintenance).

Solves a problem this user mostly does not have: Claude Code already defers/searches MCP tools, and the user has only three small MCP servers. Routing adds an extra turn per tool use and hides real tool names from permission rules and existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus matchers).
Not automatic in Claude Code sense: relies on the model choosing to call find_tool; no hook-level guarantee.
Startup hard-fails without AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY; no visible timeout on the Jev call itself.
Very immature and tiny: created 2026-09-20, 5 commits over 2 days, 1 author, 8 stars, no CI, no releases, private package not on npm.
evaluate_work_with_jev description is triggered by the Italian phrase 'valuta con Jev', i.e. user-prompted, and sends work text/code to a third-party gateway.
entries.verdict: Well-crafted Jev-based MCP tool router, but Codex-specific, Vercel-Gateway-only, and solving context bloat that Claude Code's native MCP tool search and this user's small MCP set already handle; it would also mask tool names from existing hooks. Not recommended for this setup; at most mine the confidence-gated Choice pattern and the evaluate rubric for a custom OpenRouter-based hook.

entries.name: shimo4228/jev-skill-router
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (Python 3.10+, stdlib only) with one UserPromptSubmit hook. On each prompt it sends the prompt plus the whole installed-skill roster (user, plugin, project skills; full descriptions) to TypeSafe System One in two steps (wide ranking + yes/no gate, then top-3 with full SKILL.md bodies and per-candidate fit). It logs a JSONL decision row and, only in opt-in inject mode, adds a one-line additionalContext pointer naming at most one skill. Default is shadow mode (log only). The README itself concludes it is unlikely to help a strong model, and the author removed it after one week (5% of suggestions followed by use of that skill; 13 of 20 sampled unused ones off-target).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: UserPromptSubmit fires on every prompt with no user or model action needed. But it only does skill-suggestion routing, not general-purpose Jev decisions.
security: API key: env var, plugin sensitive userConfig (keychain, exported as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY env, not argv), or key file; Bearer header only, never in argv or process list (hooks.json args contain only the script path)
Host pinned to api.typesafe.ai over https; redirects refused (_RefuseRedirects) to avoid leaking key; HTTP error bodies discarded (jev_client.py:189-191)
No shell execution; the only subprocess is Popen(sys.executable, this file) with fixed argv for shadow mode (route.py:125-145), detached via start_new_session
Log file created 0600, symlink refused; prompt text not logged (only hash/length)

Prompt-injection surface: only a skill name from the local roster is injected inside a fixed template, and the README says untrusted strings were sanitised; project SKILL.md read only if it resolves inside the repo, but that content is sent off-machine
No secret scrubbing of prompts; no telemetry beyond calls to TypeSafe; no curl|sh or postinstall; README admits no independent human audit (LLM-reviewed only)
entries.dataEgress: Per routed prompt to api.typesafe.ai (not OpenRouter): full prompt text (up to 4000 chars; longer and '/' prompts skipped), name plus whole description of every roster skill (user, enabled-plugin, project; 50-60 skills ~ 10k input tokens), and for the top-3 candidates the entire SKILL.md body (incl. private project skills; symlinks in user/plugin skills followed). Conversation history, tool outputs, code, diffs and file contents are not sent, except indirectly via SKILL.md symlink targets. Secrets pasted in prompts are sent as typed. Local decisions.jsonl stores hash/length not text.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: every failure (no key, timeout, API/HTTP error, oversize, redirect) exits 0 with one log line. Shadow mode detaches a child (30s budget) so turns are never delayed. Inject mode blocks the prompt up to a 3.0s wall-clock budget across requests (hook timeout 5s); over-budget results are discarded. No retries. Without a key it silently does nothing.
entries.contextCost: Near zero. No MCP tools, no MCP server instructions. Hook injects nothing in shadow mode and ~30 tokens (one <skill_relevance> line) per prompt in inject mode when a skill clears the gate. Plugin ships one SKILL.md whose ~110-token description enters the skill listing (roughly 150 tokens total). Note the cookbook approach does not reduce Claude's skill-listing tokens.
pros: True automatic invocation: UserPromptSubmit hook fires every prompt, no 'use jev' needed (hooks/hooks.json)
Well-engineered safety: fail-open everywhere, shadow-first default, detached child so zero turn latency, 0600 log, host pinning, redirect refusal, key kept out of argv (jev_client.py:50-145)
Stdlib-only Python, no postinstall/curl|sh, small auditable codebase (~1400 lines runtime), offline tests, SHA-pinned CI
Unusually honest README with measured evidence: 28/539 suggestions followed (~5%), 13/20 unused off-target, author removed it (README, evals/README.md)
Useful as a reference implementation of a UserPromptSubmit + additionalContext Jev integration and of a shadow-log eval method (evals/shadow_join.py) that can be reused for other Jev hooks
Negligible context cost (~30 tokens/prompt in inject mode)
cons: No OpenRouter support: host hard-pinned to api.typesafe.ai and key read only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it cannot work with the user's OpenRouter-only setup without forking and weakening/editing the pinned-host control (jev_client.py:34,123-145)

Narrow scope: only skill suggestion. Does not use Jev for permission gating, task routing, model/effort selection, commit/PR decisions, or code-review triage, which is where added value for this user would be

Weak value for Opus 5.5: Claude already sees all skill descriptions; the author's own data shows ~5% follow-through and mostly off-target suggestions, and he removed it (README 'A week in shadow mode...')

Large egress for a per-prompt hook: whole roster plus full SKILL.md bodies of top-3, including private client project skills, sent to a third party each prompt; no scrubbing of secrets in prompts; problematic for client projects
Inject mode adds 0.7-1.6 s blocking latency per prompt and 10-25k input tokens per turn (cheap at ~$0.042/M but noisy); thresholds uncalibrated and tuned on English roster while measured on Japanese
Very young (9 days, 11 commits, 1 contributor, 7 stars, no releases), hardcoded model 'jev-1.13.0' not the OpenRouter ID typesafe/jev-1.13; LLM-reviewed only, no human audit
Shadow mode (default) produces no user-visible benefit; benefit only emerges after opt-in to inject, which the author does not recommend
entries.verdict: Well-built but narrowly scoped and self-declared unhelpful (author removed it; ~5% follow-through), and it cannot use OpenRouter without a fork that changes its host-pinning security control. Not recommended for daily use; worth reading only as a hook-pattern and shadow-eval reference for building your own OpenRouter-based Jev hook.

entries.name: maker-KK/todo-jev
entries.what: Python CLI experiment classifying a request into 3 tiers (local rule/skill/big model) and matching among 20 bundled skill profiles; aside/jev/SKILL.md is a keyword heuristic AGENTS.md hook (Korean).
entries.autoInvocation: manual (AGENTS.md hook instruction, not a CC hook)
pros: Skill-selection idea with apply/exclude conditions matches skill-tool-router need
Offline fallback and benchmark_80 eval data included
cons: Hardcoded api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, no base URL config; execution handlers are stubs
Korean-only skill, keyword heuristic, 4 stars, single-day commit history

entries.name: redreamality/jev-skill-selection
entries.what: Python stdlib-only UserPromptSubmit hook (plus Codex/Hermes/OpenCode adapters) that scans SKILL.md files in ./.claude/skills and ~/.claude/skills. On each user prompt it decides which skills to keep or drop, either by local Jaccard keyword overlap (default) or by one Jev Noul question per skill via POST {base}/v1/systemone. In Claude Code 'hard' mode it writes skillOverrides ("off" for drops, "on" for keeps) into the project's .claude/settings.local.json. Optional 'soft' mode returns additionalContext. Goal: shrink skill-listing context, not code-related decisions.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), fully automatic with no prompting. It only gates the skill list, though. It does not give Claude a general Jev decision capability for coding.
security: API key is read from env and sent as a Bearer header, never in argv, so there is no process-list leak (jev_client.py:90,128).

Hard mode mutates files on every prompt: it rewrites <cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json in client and personal projects, and merges 'on' for kept skills, so it can clobber the user's own skillOverrides. Writes are non-atomic-safe only via tmp+replace, and unparseable JSON is silently replaced with {} (common.py:257-285), which can wipe a user's settings.local.json (permissions, env).

Prompt-injection surface is low: Jev returns numeric probabilities and there is no free text back into context in hard mode. SKILL.md bodies (400-char excerpts) are sent to Jev, but the output is only used for thresholding.
No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall. Uses stdlib urllib only.
TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is env-overridable, so a poisoned env could redirect the prompts.
JEV_E2E_LOG, if set, appends the first 500 chars of every prompt to a file.
entries.dataEgress: In jev mode only, per user prompt, to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter after patching): the full user prompt text (state={'message': prompt}), plus for each candidate skill (up to 32 after local prefilter) its name, description and a 400-char body excerpt. It sends no code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs, since it only fires on UserPromptSubmit. In the default local mode nothing leaves the machine.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but slow. hook.py:25-29 catches any exception, logs to stderr and exits 0, so the prompt proceeds. There is no local fallback when the Jev call fails, so no filtering happens that turn. The HTTP timeout is 30 s (models.py:52), matching the 30 s hook timeout in the example settings, so a hung API can block every prompt for up to 30 s. There is no retry or circuit breaker.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and zero tool-definition tokens. Hard mode injects no text (empty hookSpecificOutput). Soft/both modes inject up to ~9000 chars (~2.2k tokens) per prompt. Net effect is a potential reduction, since dropped skills are hidden. The skill listing is only ~100 tokens per skill, so savings are modest unless the user has hundreds of skills.
pros: It is a real, automatic, deterministic hook that needs no 'use jev' prompt, and it uses Jev's Noul primitive as intended (one yes/no per skill).
Stdlib-only Python with no dependencies, MIT licensed, and no telemetry or installers. The code is small (about 60 KB of source) and easy to audit or fork.

Endpoint, key and base URL are env-driven, so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13) provided the schema matches.
The default local mode works offline with no key. Jev mode has a local prefilter (top 32) to bound the payload.
Fail-open exception handling at hook.py:25-29 means a broken hook will not block the user.
cons: It solves a narrow problem (trimming the skill list) that Claude Code already handles with progressive disclosure (about 100 tokens per skill), so the gain is small. Its own README demo saves about 1 KB of characters.
It never asks Jev to make coding decisions (model routing, risk gating, permission decisions, test selection), so it does not deliver the user's goal of Jev being used when it adds value.

It mutates <cwd>/.claude/settings.local.json on every prompt in client projects, and overwrites unparseable files with {} (common.py:257-285). This can wipe permissions or env and creates config churn. It also forces 'on' for kept skills, overriding user preferences.

The hard filter takes effect after prompt submit, so a settings reload may lag by one turn. It only sees ~/.claude/skills and ./.claude/skills, so plugin and marketplace skills (caveman, gitnexus) are not covered.
Jev mode sends every user prompt to a third party, which is a concern for client projects. It has a 30 s timeout with no local fallback and adds a blocking round trip per prompt.
It has no OpenRouter support in code (only the TypeSafe env names), and the OpenRouter schema is unverified. Model-id mapping (jev-1.13.0 vs typesafe/jev-1.13) is not handled.

It is very immature: 1 commit, 1 author, 2 stars, created 2026-09-21, no CI, no releases, and not on PyPI. The example settings use a non-portable ${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR} path. The author is inconsistent (the repo owner is redreamality; pyproject URLs point to i3u8).
entries.verdict: Skip it as the main integration. It is a genuine but tiny hook that only prunes the skill list, it mutates project settings files on every prompt, and Jev mode ships every prompt off-box for negligible savings. It is worth borrowing only as a reference for the UserPromptSubmit-to-System One call pattern (Noul per option over env-configurable base URL) when building a custom OpenRouter hook.

entries.name: micic-mihajlo/jev-tool-runner
entries.what: Codex-CLI-specific integration of TypeSafe Jev as a tool selector. Main feature (router-cli.ts + router-server.ts) launches a loopback OpenAI-Responses-API proxy and starts `codex` with a temporary custom model_provider pointing at it. Before each coding-model request, Jev (Choice primitive via @typesafe-ai/sdk systemOne) picks one of up to 8 "offered" native read-file calls for files explicitly named in the user message, or hands off. Selected call is synthesised as a fake Responses tool_call so Codex executes it and the OpenAI request is skipped. Also contains a legacy MCP server (single tool run_tools, Jev-driven read-only investigation loop over an internal workspace with rg/read/run_command) and legacy Codex lifecycle hooks (SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop) that pre-inject Jev-gathered evidence. Coverage is intentionally narrow: only numbered reads of explicitly named relative files; no search planning, test selection or arbitrary commands. Upstream is hard-locked to api.openai.com / chatgpt.com, so it cannot front Anthropic/Claude Code traffic.
interface: Codex hooks via scripts/codex-integration.mjs install (hooks.ts, hook-cli.ts)
entries.autoInvocation: Native router: transparent proxy (deterministic, automatic) but Codex/OpenAI Responses API only, cannot sit in front of Claude Code. Legacy hooks: deterministic lifecycle hooks (UserPromptSubmit/Stop) but in Codex hook format and installed into Codex config by scripts/codex-integration.mjs. MCP run_tools: model-discretion tool invocation only; the model decides after it has already reasoned, which the README itself says cannot remove reasoning. Nothing in the repo targets Claude Code (grep 'claude': no hits).
security: No curl|sh installer, no postinstall script in package.json; deps are few and reputable.

API key handling: read from a --key-file via process.loadEnvFile (router-cli.ts:19, hook-cli.ts:22), not argv; router-cli.ts:18 deletes TYPESAFE_* from the child Codex env; redact() (config.ts:25-32) strips the key, apikey_*, sk-*, Bearer tokens before sending to Jev. Key not visible in ps.

Router: binds 127.0.0.1 only, random 32-byte token in x-jev-router-key header checked with timingSafeEqual (router-server.ts:18-22,58); token however is passed inside `-c model_providers.jev_router.http_headers=...` argv to codex (router-cli.ts:27-28), so visible in the process list to local users (loopback-only, low impact).
Upstream allow-list enforced (official OpenAI hosts only, no redirects, router-server.ts:50-52,105); forwards OpenAI auth headers only to those hosts.

Shell execution: runProcess uses spawn shell:false with allow-listed argv from config, scrubbed env (process.ts:48-51); legacy hooks use workspace snapshots and lock dirs. Reasonable hardening for a POC.

Prompt-injection surface: legacy MCP/hook feed repo file contents and command outputs to Jev (which only returns a choice among fixed options) and inject evidence back into the coding model, labelled 'untrusted data' (hooks.ts:136). Jev output is validated against candidate set (jev.ts:73-77) so it cannot invent actions.
entries.dataEgress: Native router mode: to TypeSafe only redacted goal text (first 2400 chars of the user's latest message), offer descriptions (e.g. 'Read src/access.mjs lines 1-160'), and completion IDs; no source output (docs/DAILY-USE.md, tool-selector.ts:72). Legacy MCP/hooks mode: goal (<=4000 chars), plus up to 8 recent observations (up to 8000 chars each, 22,000 total) of file contents / command outputs, workspace file count (jev.ts:36-55); hooks.ts:88 says 'Source/output are sent to TypeSafe'. Redaction is regex-based only (apikey_, sk-, Bearer, the TYPESAFE key), so other secrets in files (e.g. .env values, private keys, AWS keys) can egress to TypeSafe/OpenRouter in legacy mode; problematic for client code. Full conversation goes to OpenAI upstream in Codex router mode (irrelevant for Claude Code).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Router: Jev call has 5s SDK timeout, 0 retries, 6s AbortSignal; on any error or timeout falls back to normal upstream model request (router-server.ts:82,90-93; tool-selector.ts:64). Legacy runner: 15s timeout with 1 retry (jev.ts:22-23); hooks catch all errors and emit only a systemMessage 'Jev hook unavailable' (hook-cli.ts:25-27); on degraded state PreToolUse dedupe is disabled (hooks.ts:145). Stop hook can block up to 2 times to force verification. MCP run_tools returns isError result with status error/time_limit.
entries.contextCost: MCP mode: 1 tool (run_tools) ~ 250-400 tokens total (name+description+schema; description embeds configured command ids/argv, mcp.ts:47) plus ~110-token server instructions string (mcp.ts:42). Legacy hooks: SessionStart injects ~150 tokens (hooks.ts:88) and UserPromptSubmit injects up to 18,000 chars (~4,500 tokens) of JSON evidence per prompt (hooks.ts:133,136), a large recurring cost that may duplicate what Claude would read anyway. Native router mode: zero added context (transparent proxy), but Codex-only.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev's Choice primitive with sensible validation: candidate-set check, probabilities check, fail-open fallbacks (jev.ts:72-77, router-server.ts:90-93).
Clean, defensive engineering for a POC: loopback-only, token-authenticated proxy, strict upstream allow-list, spawn shell:false with scrubbed env, redaction, atomic 0600 state files, SHA-pinned CI.
Honest README: states narrow coverage and that legacy benchmarks do not prove savings; live-smoke harness asserts Jev actually selected a call.
SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, so pointing the Jev call at OpenRouter (/api/v1/systemone) is env-only with no code change, if schema parity holds.
Legacy hook code (hooks.ts) is a useful reference for a deterministic UserPromptSubmit/PreToolUse/Stop pattern with Jev fail-open handling that could be re-implemented for Claude Code.
cons: Built for Codex CLI, not Claude Code: the only truly automatic mechanism (model-provider proxy) speaks OpenAI Responses API and rejects non-OpenAI upstreams (router-server.ts:50-52); would not work with a Claude subscription/OAuth session.
Native router only offers numbered reads of files explicitly named in the prompt; README admits no search planning, test selection, or command routing: near-zero value for real daily work with Opus.

Legacy hooks are wired to Codex hook schema and Codex installer (codex-integration.mjs); UserPromptSubmit runs an investigation loop on every prompt and injects up to ~4.5k tokens, with up to 15 s blocking latency, overlapping the user's existing GitNexus graph-context hook and duplicating what Claude's own Read/Grep would do.

MCP run_tools is model-discretion: Claude must decide to call it, contradicting the requirement of no 'use jev' prompting; and it duplicates Claude Code's native Read/Grep/Bash with a slower, less capable investigator.
No OpenRouter awareness or docs; model slug default jev-1.13.0 differs from OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13, needing manual env in a key file; OpenRouter schema parity unverified.
Legacy mode sends file contents/command outputs (up to 22 KB per decision) to a third party with only regex redaction: risky for client projects.
Immature and unlicensed: 3 commits in one day, 1 contributor, 2 stars, no releases, not on npm, private:true, no LICENSE (cannot legally reuse/fork).
TypeSafe cookbook-style demo of Jev as a router; Jev's Choice replaces only a trivial decision (which of <=8 file reads), so it offers negligible cost or latency benefit against Opus 5.5.
entries.verdict: A tidy but narrow, unlicensed, Codex-only proof of concept; its automatic path is an OpenAI Responses proxy that cannot front Claude Code, and its Claude-compatible parts (a single model-discretion MCP tool, Codex-format hooks) are not automatic or useful for you. Worth reading only as a design reference for a fail-open hook that calls Jev via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api.
entries.license: None (GitHub licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file); all rights reserved by default

entries.name: chy4pro/jev-in-mcp
entries.what: Stdio MCP relay/gateway (TypeScript, 858 LOC). Sits between Claude Code and your real MCP servers: it connects to them as a client (config in ~/.config/jev-in-mcp/config.json), re-exports every downstream tool as <server>__<tool>, adds <server>__use_jev(goal) per server plus one global use_jev(goal) and jev_status. use_jev runs a loop (via jev-dev-kit runLoop): each step POSTs a Choice decision to Jev (candidates = that server's tools, plus enum/boolean params as extra choices), executes the chosen tool on the downstream server, and repeats up to max_steps (default 20). String/number params that Jev cannot choose are written by the calling Claude model via MCP sampling or a needs_input/session round trip. It is NOT a hook or a code-aware tool: it only routes tool calls among MCP servers.
interface: use_jev(goal, servers?, max_steps?, pause_after?, session?, input?)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill, or proxy. Claude decides whether to call use_jev based solely on the tool description ('Use it for multi-step tasks whose every value is in the goal'). Since Claude has direct access to the same tools (pass-through) and is a stronger planner, it will rarely prefer use_jev; this does not meet the 'used automatically when useful, without asking' requirement and gives no deterministic trigger. It also would not intercept built-in tools (Read/Edit/Bash/Grep), only MCP tools.
security: MIT license. No hooks, no shell execution of user input by the relay itself; exec only in setup.ts:144 to xdg-open a fixed localhost URL.

API key: read from JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/OPENROUTER_API_KEY env or ~/.config/jev-in-mcp/credentials.json (mode 0600, dir 0700; config.ts:87-90). Key is sent only as Bearer header (jev.ts:11), never argv. Setup page is plain HTTP on 127.0.0.1 random port with no CSRF/Origin check (a malicious local web page could POST and switch provider/model, but cannot read the key); form values are reflected unescaped (setup.ts model value attribute) minor self-XSS.

'import' copies every server's env and headers (GITHUB_TOKEN etc.) from ~/.claude.json, including all per-project sections, into a second plaintext file config.json (mode 0600) - secrets duplicated at rest; the importer reads ~/.claude.json wholesale.

Bypass surface: replacing your MCP servers with the relay moves them behind a gateway. Downstream tools run with the relay's process env (downstream.ts:20 merges process.env). use_jev lets a 300 ms classifier auto-execute tool calls; the only guard is per-tool deny lists (delete_repository etc. must be listed by hand); Claude Code permission prompts see only 'use_jev', not the underlying tool, so hooks/permissions keyed to mcp__gitnexus__* or mcp__playwright__* would not apply to calls made inside use_jev.

Prompt-injection: downstream tool results (first 800 chars) are fed back into Jev state and drive next tool choices, and result text is returned to Claude; Jev can only pick among listed tools, but a poisoned web page/file could steer which tools run in the loop.

Dependency jev-dev-kit pulled from a GitHub tag (github:chy4pro/jev-dev-kit#v0.4.0), 'prepare' script builds on install (arbitrary build-time code from a 1-star repo). Not on npm (404), so 'npx -y jev-in-mcp' in README does not work today; install requires npm install -g github:... . No telemetry found.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (or the endpoint override) on every use_jev step: the goal text, the server/tool names and descriptions (candidate sentences), plus the last calls with arguments and results truncated to result_chars=800 each (relay.ts:210, 238; encode() actually sends all recorded calls of the run, results 800 chars each). Tool results can contain file contents, page snapshots, code, and secrets that pass through the downstream servers. Nothing is sent when Claude calls the passed-through <server>__<tool> tools directly. With sampling, values are written by the Claude model (already Anthropic). HTTP-Referer/X-Title identify the app to OpenRouter.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the Claude level in the sense that Claude can still call the pass-through tools directly, but weak handling inside: jev.ts:17-30 retries 429/503/529 up to 3 times with 0.8/1.6/3.2 s backoff, other errors throw; there is NO fetch timeout or AbortSignal anywhere (grep found none), so a hung connection would hang the use_jev call until Claude Code's MCP tool timeout. If no key is set, use_jev returns an explanatory error (relay.ts:165) and pass-through still works. A downstream server that fails to connect is recorded and skipped (downstream.ts:30-32), but the relay is now a single point of failure for ALL migrated MCP servers: if it crashes at startup (e.g. missing dist/jev-dev-kit build), gitnexus, playwright, etc. all disappear.
entries.contextCost: Tool count = N downstream tools (all re-exposed under longer names, so no savings and they add a 'mcp__jev__server__' prefix) + one <server>__use_jev per server + global use_jev + jev_status. For gitnexus (~17) + playwright (~26) + caveman-shrink: about 45 passthrough tools (roughly equal to today's token cost, plus a few tokens each for longer names and '[server]' prefixes) plus about 5 new tools. Each use_jev description is ~330 chars plus a list of all usable tool names (playwright's would be ~500+ chars) and a ~700 char JSON schema, so roughly 200-300 tokens each: about 1.0-1.5k extra tokens total. No server 'instructions' field, no hook-injected text. Claude Code tool-search deferral would hide them anyway, but the value is negative: it also prevents the built-in per-server deferral grouping.
pros: Genuine OpenRouter support in code: default endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13, accepts OPENROUTER_API_KEY (src/jev.ts:10, config.ts:44,80); endpoint is overridable so it can follow /api/v1/systemone if needed.
Small, readable codebase (858 LOC), MIT, key stored 0600 and not in argv; setup page keeps key out of chat.

Sensible design for a niche: Jev only chooses among enumerated tools/enums, the calling model writes free-text values, deny/allow lists and per-tool description overrides exist, max_steps cap, stuck/repeat detection via the kit.
Handles sampling and a needs_input/session fallback; skips servers that fail to connect.
Author documents a live 6/6 run on OpenRouter (and Vercel gateway) with Jev per-step latency ~300 ms.
cons: Solves the wrong problem for daily coding: it automates chains of MCP tool calls (filesystem, github, browser) that Claude already does better; Claude Code's core work uses built-in Read/Edit/Bash/Grep which the relay cannot see. Only evidence is a 6-task filesystem demo; 'Other servers have not been tried yet' (README).
Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool with no hook; Claude has the raw tools too and will rarely pick use_jev. Fails the user's key requirement.

Invasive install: you must replace gitnexus/playwright/caveman-shrink entries with a single 'jev' server, changing every tool name to mcp__jev__<server>__<tool>. This breaks existing hooks/matchers, skills (gitnexus-* skills reference mcp__gitnexus__*), permission allowlists, and makes the relay a single point of failure for all MCP servers.

Security regression: use_jev executes downstream tools autonomously inside one opaque call; permission prompts and PreToolUse hooks (secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit; GitNexus hooks) never see the inner calls (e.g. playwright browser_run_code_unsafe is a candidate unless denied). Tool results (page/file contents) are sent to OpenRouter.

Immature: created 2026-09-20, 9 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 0 forks, no CI (.github absent), 3 test files, v0.1.1, not on npm (npm view 404, so README's 'npx -y jev-in-mcp' fails), depends on a 1-star github-only package jev-dev-kit#v0.4.0 built at install ('prepare').

No fetch timeout/AbortSignal; retries only on 429/503/529; worst case hangs until Claude Code's MCP timeout. Setup page has no CSRF protection; import duplicates all secrets into a second plaintext file.

Jev's Choice primitive over dozens of Playwright/GitNexus tools degrades with candidate-set size (DESIGN.md admits this), yielding a global two-stage workaround; browser and graph tools require object/array params that Jev cannot express and are excluded from use_jev (candidates.ts unsupportedReason).
Context: +5 tools with long descriptions and full duplicate re-export of ~45 existing tools, with no saving.
entries.verdict: A well-scoped proof of concept that really does talk to OpenRouter Jev, but it is an MCP-to-MCP tool-routing gateway, not a coding assistant: it is model-discretion only, requires replacing your existing MCP servers with a single relay (breaking hooks, skills and tool names, and hiding inner calls from your permission/secret-guard hooks), and is one-star, one-week-old, unpublished on npm. Do not adopt it for daily Claude Code use; at most study it as a reference for how to format Choice requests against /api/alpha/decisions.

entries.name: nekowasabi/jev-routing-mcp
entries.what: Dependency-free Node HTTP MCP server (127.0.0.1:8787) that routes tool selection via System One; on-device heuristic without key, TypeSafe jev-latest with key. Has skill and Claude example.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: No dependencies, includes skills/jev-routing/SKILL.md and examples/claude-code.sh
Graceful offline fallback without a key
cons: Endpoint hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, no base URL override
Manual server start on HTTP, key passed as Bearer header; two tests; niche tool-dispatch concept

entries.name: maxkulish/jevroute
entries.what: Planned Rust UserPromptSubmit hook that asks Jev which installed skill fits and injects one confidence-gated (>=0.9) hint line. Repo currently only has a PRD; no code.
interface: planned: Rust CLI as UserPromptSubmit hook (jevroute eval)
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit), not yet implemented
pros: PRD reports 53/55 and 46/50 with zero wrong picks at 0.9 threshold, p50 ~297 ms
Design keeps Claude's own skill listing and only adds a hint; silent on doubt or error
cons: Repo contains only docs/prd; no binary, no license, no README
Targets a Mac Keychain single user; no OpenRouter path documented
0 stars, created yesterday

entries.name: tool-prune
entries.what: Tiny JS/Python library (not an MCP server, hook, or plugin). Given a query and a tool catalog, it returns the best-matching tool(s) with probabilities, and can prune a large tool list to the top-K before the list goes to an LLM. It has two engines: an offline TurboQuant vector search, which is the default, and a cloud call to TypeSafe System One (Jev) that uses a Choice question over the tool descriptions plus a Noul 'requires_generation' question. It also has dispatch(), which runs a handler directly when confidence is at least 0.85. It has no Claude Code integration at all.
entries.autoInvocation: None. It is a library that a developer imports into their own agent code. There is no hook, MCP server, skill or proxy, so it cannot be invoked automatically by Claude Code. Claude Code would need a custom wrapper, and the model plans and selects its own tools, so tool routing is not something Claude Code lets an external component do.
security: No postinstall or preinstall scripts (js/package.json), and no curl|sh installer. The npm tarball is 6 files, and its lib/ is identical to the repo's js/lib.
The API key comes from TYPESAFE_API_KEY or options and goes in an Authorization header, so it does not appear in argv.
The library does not read .env. Only the bench script bench/run.mjs:11-16 does, and it regex-parses TYPESAFE_API_KEY out of a .env file. That is bench code and is not shipped in the npm package.
No telemetry found in the library code.
The optional dependency turboquant-search is loaded by dynamic import, which adds a supply-chain surface if it is installed.
There is no timeout or AbortController on fetch. A hung request hangs the caller.
entries.dataEgress: Only with the typesafe engine (an API key is set): the whole `state` object (the raw query string, or whatever object the caller passes, e.g. {intent: prompt}) and the full criteria map (every tool name and description), sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. With no key, everything runs offline and nothing leaves the machine. Any Claude Code wrapper would have to send the user prompt and the tool catalog, and possibly code context, to a third party.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the library. A non-2xx response throws 'tool-prune API error', and network errors propagate. There is no timeout, no retry, and no automatic fallback to the offline engine. The engine is chosen only by whether a key is present, so a failing cloud call does not degrade to turboquant. A wrapper would have to add try/catch and a timeout.
entries.contextCost: The library adds 0 tools and 0 tokens to Claude Code, because it is not wired in. Its only relevance to context is as a technique: pruning MCP tool schemas before they reach the LLM. Claude Code's MCP tool search and deferred tools already do this natively. The user's setup (gitnexus, playwright, caveman-shrink) has roughly 60 tools that are already deferred.
pros: MIT, zero required dependencies, no install scripts. The published npm tarball matches the repo source (I diffed lib/).

It shows a concrete Jev request shape: choice with a criteria map, plus a noul question, posted to /v1/systemone with Bearer auth. That is a useful reference for writing an OpenRouter System One client (js/lib/router.js:77-101).
A sensible offline fallback engine, and the calibrated 'confidence >= threshold' dispatch idea is reasonable as a design.
Small and easy to audit (334 lines of router code).
cons: It is not an integration. There is no MCP server, hook, skill or plugin, so it gives Claude Code no automatic behavior.

It solves a problem Claude Code does not have. Claude Code chooses tools itself, and its native deferred tool search already handles large MCP catalogs. An external router cannot intercept or restrict the tool list per turn.
It talks only to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with TYPESAFE_API_KEY. There is no OpenRouter support, and the model default 'jev-latest' is not an OpenRouter ID.
Fail-closed and no timeout: the cloud call has no fallback to the offline engine and no AbortController.
Very immature: created 2026-09-17, 15 commits, 1 contributor, 7 stars, no releases, CI only deploys the docs site, and the PyPI version lags npm.
The headline benchmarks (100% top-1, 97.5% end-to-end) are self-reported, run on BFCL and synthetic catalogs, and I did not verify them. The Python package is at 0.2.0 against JS 0.3.0.
Sending the user's prompts and tool catalog to a third party would be a data-egress problem on client projects, in exchange for no clear gain.
entries.verdict: Not usable for the goal. It is a tool-routing library for people building their own agents, with no Claude Code integration and no OpenRouter support. Skip it, but keep js/lib/router.js:77-129 as a reference for the Jev choice/noul request and response shape when building a custom OpenRouter-based hook.

entries.name: daniel-farina/nitro
entries.what: A fork of xAI's Grok Build CLI (Rust, Apache-2.0, upstream 1.0.38), renamed 'nitro'. On the first model step of each turn it makes one Jev call, with one Noul per tool asking whether the request needs that tool. Tools below a 0.30 probability are dropped from the chat model's tool list for that turn, except six core workspace tools. It is a standalone replacement agent for Grok, not a Claude Code integration. Only about 1000 lines of Rust (crate xai-grok-typesafe plus a hook in xai-grok-shell) are Jev-specific.
interface: env: TYPESAFE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY+TYPESAFE_PROVIDER=openrouter, TYPESAFE_ENDPOINT, GROK_TYPESAFE=off, TYPESAFE_DISABLED, TYPESAFE_REASK, NITRO_DUMP_REQUESTS
entries.autoInvocation: Transparent, deterministic, inside its own agent loop. It is not usable from Claude Code, which has no hook to filter its tool list per turn. Claude Code sends its tool definitions itself, and a hook cannot remove them from the request.
security: The API key is stored plaintext in $GROK_HOME/typesafe.json with mode 0600 (config.rs:130). It is sent as a bearer header, not in argv, when set through the TUI. The env var route is also fine.
No shell execution or prompt-injection surface in the Jev crate. Jev output is only probabilities, and its only effect is dropping tools.
A failed or garbage answer results in passthrough, so a hostile response cannot add tools.
Building a 4200-file vendored Grok Build is a large supply-chain surface. Nothing in the Jev part is suspicious.
The repo is 1 commit from a new account (created 2026-09-20).
entries.dataEgress: Per turn, to TypeSafe or OpenRouter: latest_user_request truncated to 6000 chars, previous_assistant_reply truncated to 1500 chars, and the tool names and descriptions (router.rs:122-124, 165). No file contents, diffs or tool outputs go to Jev. The X-Title header is 'Grok Build'. Everything else goes to xAI as normal for Grok Build.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. There is a 4 s hard timeout (client.rs:15). On any error, timeout, or missing answer the full tool list is used (router.rs, README). Core tools are never dropped, and the list is never emptied.
entries.contextCost: None for Claude Code, because it does not run in it. In Grok, it cuts tool schemas from about 11K to 2.9K tokens per request.
pros: Concrete, working reference of a Jev use: one batched request of Noul questions per turn (one Noul per tool) against the OpenRouter Decisions API, with a 0.30 floor and fail-open. It is the best documented example of a Jev request/response shape (model, state, questions to answers).
research.md documents a useful finding: re-deciding tool lists on every step breaks the prompt cache and cost 70% more. The lesson is to decide once per turn and freeze the result.
Explicit OpenRouter support (Decisions API, typesafe/jev-latest, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so the client code shows exactly which endpoint and body OpenRouter expects.
Small data egress: only the user request (6000 chars) plus a 1500-char assistant reply and the tool descriptions.
Fail-open with a 4 s timeout and a core-tool floor.
cons: It is a fork of xAI's Grok Build CLI and does not integrate with Claude Code in any way. It is a different agent with a different model (grok-4.6).
Claude Code cannot filter its own tool list from a hook. The technique does not transfer, and the Opus subscription/OAuth path has no per-request tool narrowing.
The 22-40% saving is measured only on Grok with xAI pricing, on 2 tiny greenfield tasks (calculator, todo app) with 2 runs per cell. It is not evidence for Claude Code on real repos.
Immature: 1 commit, 5 stars, no CI, no releases, no root LICENSE file, and the whole Grok Build source is vendored. It is not maintainable as a fork.
No MCP server, hook, or skill is provided, so there is nothing to install into Claude Code.
Claude Code with MCP servers already defers tool schemas (ToolSearch), so the saving would be much smaller in this user's setup.
entries.verdict: Not usable in Claude Code. It is a Grok Build fork with a Jev tool-narrowing step, not an MCP server, hook, or skill. Keep it only as a reference for the OpenRouter Decisions request shape and the once-per-turn, fail-open pattern.
entries.license: Apache-2.0 (code vendored from xai-org/grok-build, plus the added crate declaring Apache-2.0). GitHub reports no license; there is no LICENSE file at the repo root, only grok-build/LICENSE.

entries.name: abhishekashokvkumar/jev-mcp-dispatcher
entries.what: Despite the candidate label "mcp-server", this is NOT an MCP server. It is a standalone Python CLI/REPL (jev_mcp_dispatcher.py, 751 lines) that acts as an MCP CLIENT: it spawns a stdio MCP server (default: a bundled song-player demo, overridable via MCP_SERVER_COMMAND), lists its tools, then routes a typed-in natural-language command to a tool using Jev Choice/Noul primitives (tool pick, per-word yes/no highlighting for argument extraction, enum Choice, compound-command splitting) and calls the tool. It is a proof of concept demonstrating Jev-only tool dispatch, and has no Claude Code integration (no hooks, no skill, no plugin, no .mcp.json).
interface: No MCP tools, hooks or skills exposed
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted, and not even then: it is a separate program a human runs in a terminal. It is not a hook, skill, MCP tool or proxy, so Claude Code cannot invoke it automatically.
security: API key is read from env or .env (python-dotenv, .gitignore covers .env); it is never put in argv. Auth handling is inside the SDK, which I did not audit.
Runs the MCP_SERVER_COMMAND string as a subprocess (shlex.split, no shell). That is expected for an MCP client but means the env var is a command-execution vector.

README's known gaps include no confidence gating, and booleans silently default to False. If it were wired to a real tool server, mis-dispatch could run wrong or destructive tools with wrong arguments.
Nothing here is a prompt-injection surface for Claude Code, since it is never in Claude's loop.
No postinstall, curl|sh installer or telemetry in this repo. It does no logging beyond the console Tracer, which prints all questions and answers to stdout.
No license, single anonymous-ish author, 12 days old, 4 stars: low supply-chain trust.
entries.dataEgress: Every user command string, plus each individual word of it (one Noul question per word), is sent as Jev 'state' to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, together with all downstream tool names and descriptions. It has no hook into Claude Code, so it would send nothing from Claude sessions unless the user types commands into its own REPL.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the script. The SDK default timeout is 10s (typesafe_sdk constants.py:22) and there is no retry logic (README). In REPL mode exceptions print 'Error:' and continue; in scripted mode they propagate. Irrelevant to Claude Code, since it is not in its execution path.
entries.contextCost: Zero if used as-is, because Claude Code never loads it. It exposes no MCP tools, no server instructions and no hook text. (If someone rewrote it as an MCP server, it would still be one tool at most.)
pros: Useful reference implementation of how to build with the System One API: batching Choice, Noul and Choice-1..5 questions in one system_one() call (jev_mcp_dispatcher.py:~304-345), and the per-word Noul span-extraction trick.

Shows the SDK is a thin httpx client that reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and hits /v1/systemone, so pointing it at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone by env var alone looks feasible. That is useful evidence for other integrations.
The README is honest about its limits, including a clear caveats list, with pinned dependencies and .env gitignored.
Confirms Jev-only tool routing is a plausible design pattern, which could inspire a UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook that classifies intent.
cons: It is not an MCP server, hook, skill or plugin. The discovery label 'mcp-server' is wrong. It is an MCP client and CLI demo, and nothing in it can be registered in Claude Code.
Cannot fulfil the user's core requirement (Claude Code uses Jev automatically without being told). It has no integration surface and does not sit in Claude Code's loop.

Solves a problem Claude Code does not have: Opus already does tool selection and argument extraction natively, with far better accuracy than per-word yes/no highlighting. Its own README admits the design cannot handle pronouns, computed values, optional parameters, nested types, or paraphrase.
Proof-of-concept quality: 8 commits, one contributor, no tests, no CI, no license, no release, one day of activity (created and last pushed 2026-09-18), 4 stars.
OpenRouter is not supported in code. Only the SDK's TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override might make it work, and model naming and auth were not verified.
Downstream-tool dispatch with no confidence gating and silent boolean-False defaults would be unsafe to point at real developer tools.
entries.verdict: Not usable for this goal. It is a 751-line Python demo CLI that dispatches typed English commands to a stdio MCP server via Jev, not an MCP server, hook or skill, and it has no Claude Code entry point, no license and no tests. Treat it only as a reference for the System One request shape and for the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/OpenRouter endpoint idea.
entries.license: None (licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file). Default all-rights-reserved, so reuse or adaptation is legally unclear.

entries.name: greghavens/jev-no-bullshit
