entries.what: Stop hook (Python stdlib script, 1901 lines, plus an early-access Claude Code hook module hooks/jev.tsx) that reads the session transcript, splits the final assistant summary into sentences, and sends the summary, the user request, recent tool calls and results, and per-sentence and per-action Noul questions to Jev's /v1/systemone endpoint. The questions cover unverified claims (5 sub-questions), weasel words (2), empty rhetoric and paltering (per action). Scores above thresholds (0.65 for unverified, 0.7 for the rest) send the assistant back once per request with a quoted note. Supports Claude Code, Codex, pi and opencode. Every check is logged to ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl.
interface: No MCP server, no skills, no slash commands
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook: it fires after every assistant turn end with a non-empty last_assistant_message and needs no prompting. It does not fire on SubagentStop, so subagent summaries are not checked, but the parent's summary that relays them is. It runs in interactive sessions and bypassPermissions sessions alike.
security: Key handling: the key is read by the script from ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env (parsed, never sourced; a line with 'export' is refused). It is sent only as an Authorization Bearer header via urllib, so it is never in argv. Nothing is passed on the command line except the script path. The file is not permission-checked by the script; 0600 is only advised in the README.
https-only guard on TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (http allowed only for localhost/127.0.0.1/::1). Redirects are disabled (_NoRedirect, line 1540), so the bearer token is not forwarded on a 3xx.

Standard library only: no pip or npm dependencies, no shell exec, no subprocess, no os.system in the script. The TSX module calls $.process.run(['python3', script]) with an argv array, not a shell string.

No telemetry beyond the Jev call. No install scripts. The plugin is installed via claude plugin marketplace add from a 1-author, week-old repo, so pinning a commit or reading the script is the real supply-chain control.

Prompt-injection surface: the state sent to Jev contains attacker-controllable tool output (file contents, web pages, command output). An injected string could lower the flag scores, so the verifier can be evaded. That only fails to flag. An attacker cannot cause tool execution through this hook. A false positive makes the assistant re-summarise once, and the note is built from the model's own quoted sentences and truncated action labels.

No secret redaction anywhere in the script: no matches for redact or secret. Tool inputs (300 chars) and results (2,000 chars plus up to 1,000 chars of evidence lines plus up to 3,000 chars of outline) go to the API as-is. A secret in Bash output would be uploaded. The existing no-secret-leak hook helps by blocking many reads, but not everything.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or the TYPESAFE_BASE_URL host, i.e. OpenRouter then TypeSafe) on every Stop where a last_assistant_message exists: the full final summary (clipped to 30k chars and split into sentences), the user's task text, tool calls of the current turn (input clipped to about 300 chars, with up to about 300 chars of evidence from the middle), their results (about 2,000 chars each plus up to 1,000 chars of matched lines and up to 3,000 chars of line-start outline; clipping scales up to fit a 16k-token actions budget), up to 10 earlier actions in full and older ones as one-liners (up to 6k tokens), and the last 2 conversation messages (2,000 chars each) plus older ones as one-liners (up to 8k tokens). The total is capped near 32k state tokens. Content includes client code snippets, paths and command output, with no redaction. Locally, the script writes ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl and state/*.json. On OpenRouter the request also passes through OpenRouter's infrastructure and its data policy.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. main() catches all exceptions and returns an 'unchecked' systemMessage (line 1891). API/HTTP/timeout errors are logged and the turn ends normally. A missing key produces a warning, and the module pins it on the status line. Jev timeout is 10 s (JEV_TIMEOUT_SECONDS), enforced with a daemon thread and a deadline. The hook timeout is 30 s, and the transcript wait is up to 3 s. The auto-retry with a smaller budget on HTTP 400 max_tokens_exceeded shares the same 10 s deadline. Redirects are capped at 1 per request (JEV_NO_BULLSHIT_MAX_REDIRECTS), and each sentence is called out once. It cannot trap the model in a loop. Caveat: if the model name 'jev-latest' is rejected by OpenRouter, every turn shows an 'unchecked' warning (noisy but harmless). In Claude Code the module path needs the early-access plugin hook modules. Without them it falls back to a classic Stop block that shows a 'Stop hook error' row.
entries.contextCost: Zero standing context: no MCP tools, no skills, no injected system text. Tokens are spent only when a summary is flagged: the note is about 100-300 tokens, and the assistant then produces a revised summary (Opus output tokens plus one more turn). Default cap is one send-back per request. Jev-side cost is about 5-15k input tokens per check for typical turns (about 32k worst case, 64k with questions), roughly $0.0002-$0.0015 per check at $0.042/M. Trivial pure-chat replies with no sentences or actions are skipped.
pros: Fills the missing Stop-verifier gap with a deterministic hook: no 'use jev' prompting, and it works in auto and bypassPermissions sessions, where unsupervised false 'tests pass' claims are most costly (jev-no-bullshit:1740-1901, hooks/hooks.json).

Fail-open design that is actually implemented: the outer try/except (line 1891), a 10 s deadline in a daemon thread, no-redirect opener, and a cap of 1 send-back per request with per-sentence callout dedupe. It cannot loop or wedge a session.

Endpoint shape already matches OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api gives https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (lines 39, 1551-1557) with the {state, model, questions} body and Noul answers parsed as the System One schema.

Thoughtful engineering against Jev's limits: token estimation against the 32k/64k limits, retry on max_tokens_exceeded with a smaller budget, threshold tuning from replays of real checks (docs/statistical-decision.md), and a 'repeat callouts' limiter.
Key kept in a separate ~/.config file read directly by the script, so it is not in settings env or argv. Only https (localhost excepted), and redirects are refused.

Stdlib-only Python, so no dependency supply chain. Real test surface: about 118 test functions across 7 Python test files plus hooks/jev.test.tsx, and a CI matrix on Python 3.10 and 3.13 that also runs e2e tests against the pinned claude 2.1.281 CLI. The README states it was tested with Claude Code 2.1.281, close to the user's 2.1.285.
Very low money cost per check (about $0.001) and zero standing context cost (no MCP tools or skills).
cons: Model name hardcoded as 'jev-latest' (line 36), with no env override. OpenRouter documents 'jev-1.13', so out of the box against OpenRouter the check may return 4xx on every turn (fail-open, so a warning each turn). It needs a source patch or a maintained copy or fork. Plugin updates would overwrite the patch.

No OpenRouter mention anywhere in the repo, so OpenRouter behaviour (rate limits on /v1/systemone, alpha endpoint stability, 32k context, no SLA) is untested. The script's tuned thresholds are calibrated on api.typesafe.ai's 'jev-latest', which may differ from jev-1.13 (the eval brief notes calibration is imperfect).

Sends task text, code snippets and command output from every turn to a third party (TypeSafe via OpenRouter) with no redaction, and it is on by default for all projects. For client projects this is a real confidentiality and NDA concern. The user would need a per-project disable (project-scoped enabledPlugins or a path guard in a wrapper). Full summaries are also logged at rest in ~/.jev-no-bullshit/log.jsonl with no rotation.

The Claude Code send-back UX relies on the early-access hook-module API (hooks/jev.tsx, hooks/claude-code.json, $.prompt.submit). It is fragile across Claude Code versions (only 2.1.281 verified). The fallback is a 'Stop hook error' row using Stop block feedback.

False positives cost a full extra Opus turn (tokens plus wait time) and the verifier can be evaded by injected content in tool outputs. Evals show calibration is imperfect, so the utility is a probabilistic nudge, not a guarantee. It cannot check claims that are unverifiable from the transcript, such as work done in other sessions. Subagent (SubagentStop) work is not checked directly.

Immature: created 2026-09-23, 40 commits in about a week (33 by the author, 7 by Claude), 1 human contributor, 3 stars, 0 forks, no releases, and no license (licenseInfo null), so legally all rights are reserved and use or modification of the code is not formally permitted, which matters for client work. Version 0.4.0.

Latency of up to about 13 s worst case per turn end (3 s transcript wait plus 10 s API deadline), and the Jev call on a large payload may be slower than the p50 of 200 ms on OpenRouter's alpha endpoint.

The user's other hooks (gitnexus, caveman) are unaffected, but the OpenRouter key would sit in a second place. The existing no-secret-leak hook's protected list should also cover it, and reading ~/.config/jev-no-bullshit/env with Read may be blocked or need an allowance.

On by default for every project once the plugin is enabled: every Stop sends the summary, task text, tool inputs and results, and conversation snippets to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. There is no per-project allowlist or redaction in the script, so confidential client repos need project-scoped disabling of the plugin.

There is no LICENSE file and licenseInfo is null. Re-verified with gh: created 2026-09-23, pushed 2026-09-29T20:03Z, 3 stars, 0 forks, no release, not archived. For a version-pinned copy in client work this is a legal gap, not just an immaturity signal.

'jev-latest' floats: OpenRouter aliases it to the newest Jev release, so thresholds (0.65/0.7) tuned by the author may drift silently when a new Jev ships. There is no env override to pin jev-1.13 short of editing a copy.
When the key is missing or an error occurs, log() writes the full summary to log.jsonl, so the plaintext log fills even with no successful checks. The log has no rotation.

Hook modules (hooks/jev.tsx, early access) are gated: README says they stay off for third-party providers, nonessential-traffic-disabled or unrolled-out accounts, and CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 forces them. Without modules, the plain Stop block shows a 'Stop hook error' row on each flag. The user's OAuth login likely qualifies, but this is unverified.
entries.verdict: Best-fitting candidate for an automatic Stop-time honesty check: deterministic, fail-open, cheap, zero standing context, and its /v1/systemone request shape is OpenRouter-compatible via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Before it is usable, the hardcoded model 'jev-latest' must be changed to 'jev-1.13' in a pinned copy or fork. The lack of a license, the unredacted egress of client code, and the week-old, early-access hook-module dependency mean it should be run from a pinned local copy and disabled for confidential client repos, not adopted as-is.
entries.license: None (GitHub licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file)

verification.note: Re-verified from source and OpenRouter docs. Stars 3, forks 0, no license, not archived, last push 2026-09-29, 40 commits (33 human, 7 Claude), version 0.4.0, and the Stop hook plus hook-module files all exist as described. Key handling is correct: it is read from a file or env and sent as a Bearer header via urllib. There is no subprocess, shell or os.system call and no redaction. I kept the score at 7. The integration is easier than the audit said, which raises it. The Claude Code Stop-hook fields (decision:block, reason, systemMessage, stop_hook_active, last_assistant_message, transcript_path) are standard and consistent with the code.

Verification corrected the audit: no source patch is needed for OpenRouter. Best combination of automatic firing, fail-open engineering, real tests and OpenRouter readiness, but held back by no license and unredacted default-on egress.
