entries.name: qkal/Canny (canny-warden)
entries.what: Supervision layer for Claude Code and Codex CLI built purely from hooks (zero runtime deps, plain Node ESM, compiled dist committed). Keeps an append-only ledger of edits and commands under ~/.canny/sessions. A deterministic Stop hook blocks the agent from finishing when code files changed but no test/build/lint check has passed since the last edit. Pattern checks deny secret-shaped strings on write, ask on test removal or skips, and rewrite `npm test | tail` to run with pipefail. Jev is used only as an optional advisor through the Noul (yes/no) primitive. (1) After each edit, one Noul per project rule (bullets extracted from CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md, up to 24) asks whether the diff breaks it; a p>=0.9 yes becomes an additionalContext note. (2) At Stop, when unverified edits exist, one Noul asks whether the final message claims the work is done; p<=0.1 can only relax the block. Jev never blocks anything itself. Answers are cached by content hash on disk and logged so `canny replay` is offline and deterministic.
interface: hook: PreToolUse (matcher = edit and shell tools)
canny remove / trust / status / sessions / replay / hook
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (SessionStart, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop) run on every relevant event with no model discretion and no need for the user to say 'use jev'. This is the strongest fit for the 'automatic, never prompted' requirement. However, Jev's role inside the hooks is narrow: two fixed Noul questions, and the Jev call only happens when rules exist or the Stop is unverified.
security: API key handling: read from an env var and sent in the Authorization header only (src/jev.ts:88-96). It is never in argv or the process list, and the hook command line holds only the node path plus `hook --agent claude`.

No telemetry and no other network calls. fetch appears only in src/jev.ts. The only child process is `git check-ignore` with a 2s timeout (src/checks.ts:178). No postinstall, no curl|sh, no npm dependency chain. The install is a git clone that runs the committed compiled dist/, so the supply-chain risk is trusting the author's repo and pulling main.

The README install is 'paste a prompt into your agent', which is a prompt-injection-shaped habit. Clone and init manually, and review dist/ at a pinned commit. dist is committed and CI verifies it matches src, but that is only as strong as the repo owner.

Local plaintext storage. ~/.canny/sessions ledgers hold full command lines, and the README admits a secret on a command line lands in the ledger. ~/.canny/jev/<hash>.json caches the full request body, meaning clipped diffs up to 4000 chars per side plus the agent's final message, in plaintext at mode 0600 (dir 0700). Client code therefore persists on disk.

The hook rewrites Bash commands (updatedInput) and can deny or ask. This is a large behavioural surface layered on the user's existing PreToolUse hooks, with unknown ordering and merge semantics when multiple hooks return updatedInput or decisions.
The .canny.json trust model is a speed bump. The loosening fields are inert until `canny trust`, keyed by content hash, but the README concedes that an agent with shell access can run trust itself.
entries.dataEgress: With a key set: (a) after every Edit, Write, or shell-written file, for each changed file not matching config ignore, the state {rules[] (up to 24 bullets extracted from CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or .claude/CLAUDE.md), change:{file relative path, added text clipped to 4000 chars, removed text clipped to 4000 chars}} plus one question per rule goes to the endpoint, which would be OpenRouter, which forwards to TypeSafe. (b) At Stop, only when code was edited and no check has passed, the agent's final assistant message goes as {message}. Not sent: prompts, whole files, Read or Grep outputs, or tool results (src/hook.ts:194-232). Without a key, nothing leaves the machine. Requests are skipped when no rules are found (`if (!rules) return allow`), when the file matches ignore, or when allow:['rules'] is set, but those fields need `canny trust`. This is real client code egress to a third party for the rule check. It can be constrained by allow:['rules'], which leaves only the Stop message, or by adding `ignore` regexes for client repos.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on all Jev failures. There is no key, or an HTTP non-2xx, a timeout (AbortSignal.timeout of 3000ms by default, configurable via CANNY_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS), or a network error. Each returns null (src/jev.ts:89,102,112-122), the error is logged to the ledger, and the deterministic rules stand alone. A crash anywhere in the hook is caught, logged to ~/.canny/errors.log, and answers `{}`, so Canny cannot block the user (src/cli.ts:86-98). The hook timeouts are 10s for PreToolUse and 15s for PostToolUse and Stop. The deterministic Stop block is by design fail-closed when there are unverified code edits, and it is capped by Claude Code at 8 consecutive blocks and relaxes on a repeated Stop unless strict is set. That block does not depend on Jev.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so no tool-definition or server-instruction tokens. Five hook events are registered. Always injected: the SessionStart note, about 60-80 words or ~100 tokens per session. Conditional injections: a rule-violation note per broken rule (~50-150 tokens, only when Jev p>=0.9), a repeat-failure note, a pipefail-rewrite additionalContext line (~30 tokens each time the agent pipes a check into tail), and the Stop block reason (~80 tokens, plus one extra turn when the agent has not run checks). Overall it is very low context cost and never bloats the tool list.
pros: It is the only candidate here that gives truly automatic Jev use with zero prompting: registered hooks fire on every edit and Stop, and Jev is called without model discretion (src/install.ts:58-62, src/hook.ts:185-233).

Jev is used in the 'right' System One way: narrow atomic Noul questions, thresholds at 0.9 and 0.1 that are wider than the ~0.05 drift, and a content-hash cache so identical inputs give identical answers (src/jev.ts:11-13,39-41,77-87). It can never block on Jev alone.

OpenRouter switch is config-only: request and response shape match OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone OpenAPI example (state, model, questions with type noul, and answers[id].noul). Only the key variable name is hard-coded to TYPESAFE_API_KEY, which can be set in the Claude env block.

Fail-open everywhere on the Jev path (3s timeout, errors logged, null answers), and a hook crash returns {} so it cannot brick the session (src/cli.ts:86-98). Jev-down means the deterministic guard still works.

Actually useful for daily coding regardless of Jev: a done-gate that catches 'Done' with no test run, test-skip and removal guard, and a pipefail rewrite for `| tail`. Fits Opus in auto or bypass mode, where nobody watches every step.
Zero runtime dependencies, no telemetry, no postinstall, one fetch call site, and a small readable codebase (about 2,000 lines of TS) that is easy to audit and fork.

Testing above its age: 12 test files, coverage gates, CodeQL, dist-drift check in CI, real Claude Code and Codex payload fixtures. It also honestly reports that its own bench showed no outcome change and only avoided overhead.

Per-project .canny.json (verify, ignore, rules, allow:['rules']) lets you turn off code egress for client repos while keeping the deterministic gates. It also has an SessionStart hook that tells the agent the rule up front, which avoids wasted blocked turns.
cons: Jev is a minor, optional part. All blocking is deterministic and works without any key, so Canny does not deliver 'Jev deeply integrated into Claude Code'. It adds a rule-violation note and one relax-only claims_done check.

It sends real code diffs (up to 4000 chars per side per file per edit) and the final message to OpenRouter and TypeSafe on every edit, and caches them in plaintext under ~/.canny/jev. That is a serious concern for client projects, so you would need allow:['rules'] or ignore lists, which themselves need `canny trust` per repo.

The rule check fires up to 24 Noul questions per edited file, derived from heuristically extracted bullets in CLAUDE.md. Your global CLAUDE.md has many instruction-like bullets, so quality and hit rate are uncertain and there is no evidence of value. The README says the effect on agent quality is unmeasured, and Jev is unverified in this role.

Stacks a lot of hooks on top of yours. It registers PreToolUse and PostToolUse on the edit and shell tools, which overlaps with the existing secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) and GitNexus (Grep|Glob|Bash pre and post), and it rewrites Bash commands through updatedInput. Interaction and ordering with other updatedInput or additionalContext hooks is untested, so there is a real chance of conflict.

The Stop-block can add extra turns and tokens on Opus 5.5 subscription usage, and its ledger heuristics (regex-based shell parsing) can misjudge. The README itself lists commands it does not see (xargs rm, python -c writes) and its 'ask' decisions may behave differently in bypass or auto permission mode (not verified).

The OpenRouter key must be stuffed into TYPESAFE_API_KEY because the variable name is hard-coded. There is no OPENROUTER_API_KEY support, no live-endpoint test, and the README explicitly notes the Jev half is built against docs and mocks.

Young and single-author: 23 commits over 19 days, 106 stars, not on npm, and installed by a 'paste this prompt to your agent' flow with `git pull --ff-only` updates from main. That is a supply-chain and stability risk unless pinned to a commit.
Latency is added on every edit and shell tool call: two Node process spawns (~80ms) plus up to a 3s Jev wait per edit when OpenRouter is slow, and the wait is not bounded per turn.
Claude Code 2.1.285 was not verified against it. Fixtures come from an unspecified older Claude Code version and the bench used 2.1.278.
entries.verdict: Canny is the only audited option that uses Jev truly automatically, through deterministic hooks with fail-open behaviour, and it is config-only to point at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (URL, model and the key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY). But Jev only adds a small advisory layer to a mostly non-Jev done-gate, and every edit's diff leaves the machine and is cached in plaintext, which is risky for client repos. Adopt it as a pinned, per-project or personal-project guard with allow:['rules'] for client work, and watch for hook conflicts with your existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks.

judge.why: Most mature and most-starred hook suite (MIT, 12 Vitest files, committed dist verified by CI). Its deterministic Stop gate blocks when code changed and no check passed since the last edit, and Jev only adds a rule-violation note and a claims_done relax-only check. Safest design (Jev can never block alone) but Jev is a minor part and per-edit diff egress is heavy.
pros: Deterministic done-gate works without any key; Jev is advisory only, with 0.9/0.1 thresholds and a content-hash cache
Fail-open Jev path with a 3 s timeout; a hook crash returns {} so it cannot wedge a session
Zero deps, no telemetry, key only in the Authorization header; can be installed globally
Install is by git clone plus init --global, with a committed dist that you can pin and review
cons: Runs PreToolUse and PostToolUse on every edit or shell call (about 80 ms of Node overhead per call, plus up to 3 s awaiting Jev), stacking on your gitnexus hooks
Sends per-edit diffs (up to 4000 chars per side) to OpenRouter and caches them in plaintext under ~/.canny/jev, which is unsuitable for client repos without allow:['rules'] plus 'canny trust'
Up to 24 Noul questions per edited file from bullets extracted out of CLAUDE.md; your global CLAUDE.md is instruction-heavy, so the hit rate is uncertain
Effect on agent quality is unmeasured by the author; the README install is 'paste this prompt into your agent'; modifies ~/.claude/settings.json

entries.name: VladyslavHontar/clear-head
entries.what: Claude Code Stop hook (single Python stdlib script, 484 lines). At the end of each substantial turn that used tools, it reads the session transcript, splits the final answer into sentences, uses Jev Choice/Noul primitives to classify which are factual claims about the codebase, retrieves keyword-matched tool-output lines as evidence, then asks Jev if each claim is supported/contradicted/not addressed. It blocks the turn (decision:block) with a list of [CONTRADICTED]/[UNSUPPORTED]/[STALE]/[RELAYED]/[UNVERIFIED] claims so Claude must verify or downgrade them. It is a hallucination/claim-verification guard, not a general decision router.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: registered as a Stop hook in settings.json, runs automatically at the end of every turn (that produced an answer and used tools). No prompting needed. Fully matches the user's 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement, but it fires at end-of-turn, not for choosing options mid-work.
security: API key stored plaintext in ~/.claude/hooks/jev/.env (umask 077, mode 600) or env; sent only as Authorization Bearer header via urllib, so it is NOT in argv/process list (stop_verify.py:73-81). Installer read -rsp avoids echo.

No MCP server, no shell execution of model-derived strings, no eval; only stdlib urllib. Hook output is a block reason built from claims (model text), so it is a small prompt-injection-into-self surface but not exploitable for RCE.
Transcript evidence lines (tool outputs, possibly hostile file content) are put into the judge state; a poisoned file could try to manipulate Jev verdicts (low impact: only affects blocks).

install.sh is run locally from a clone (not curl|sh); the --kev path git clones a third-party repo and runs 'uv sync' (executes build/install of Kev deps) and downloads ~8 GB weights; not needed for the OpenRouter route.

No npm/pip postinstall; no telemetry beyond the chosen judge endpoint. Local log.jsonl and sent.jsonl are written next to the script and grow unbounded, containing code excerpts (secrets in tool outputs would persist in sent.jsonl).

Interaction with the user's existing secret-leak guard: this hook reads tool outputs from the transcript including any secrets that were Read/printed and ships excerpts to a third party; the guard on PreToolUse does not cover this egress.
entries.dataEgress: Per turn, to api.typesafe.ai (or OpenRouter if patched): (1) up to 60 sentences of the assistant's final answer plus the first 12,000 chars of the full answer (pass 1, stop_verify.py ~L330); (2) per factual claim, up to 12 keyword-matched tool-output lines / 1,200 chars (LINES_PER_CLAIM, CHARS_PER_CLAIM at :37), i.e. excerpts of file contents, grep results, command output; (3) up to 120 commands/paths used (READS_CAP) unless the WAF rejects, then omitted; (4) up to 3,000 chars of doc comments from files read (DOC_CHARS). Not sent: user prompt in general (only user-message numbers are used locally), whole files. Everything sent is mirrored to sent.jsonl (L373). For client projects this is code leaving the machine to a third party; the README itself warns about this. Zero Data Retention terms on OpenRouter/TypeSafe are unverified.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open: any exception is logged and swallowed (stop_verify.py:477-482) unless JEV_FAIL_CLOSED is set; per-request timeout 30s (jev) / 50s (kev), hook-level timeout 60s (180s for kev) so the harness kills it and proceeds. Exception: local Kev backend down blocks once (BackendDown). Observed real-world failure: Cloudflare WAF 403s silently disabled checks until a User-Agent fix and a retry-without-commands fallback were added, i.e. silent degradation is a known risk. False positives can block the turn and force Claude to do an extra round (one extra turn maximum thanks to stop_hook_active guard).
entries.contextCost: Zero tool/MCP definitions and no server instructions. A Stop hook adds no per-turn prompt tokens except when it blocks: the reason text (~100-400 tokens plus the listed claims) is injected and triggers an additional Claude turn (extra Opus tokens for verification reads and rewrite). Silent when passing.
pros: Only candidate found so far that is a real deterministic Stop hook: fires automatically on every turn, satisfying 'Claude Code must use it without me asking'.

Good fit for the Jev use case: uses Choice and Noul primitives with calibrated probabilities and thresholds (JEV_CONTRA, JEV_FIRM, JEV_FACT) instead of free text, playing to Jev's strengths as a cheap judge (about $0.042/M input tokens).
Zero context cost in the normal path, no MCP tool definitions; pure Python stdlib, no dependencies, no postinstall; easy to audit (484 lines).
Provider swap to OpenRouter is a few lines because the code already targets the System One /v1/systemone wire contract with a pluggable BACKENDS dict.

Thoughtful engineering born from real dogfooding: STALE rule for outside-world status, RELAYED for subagent claims, numeric claims not found in output, evidence floor to avoid blocking derivations, loop guard via stop_hook_active, per-tool-call-id evidence tagging, and it logs every payload to sent.jsonl for auditing.
Fail-open by default with 30s timeout and 60s hook timeout, so a slow or down Jev/OpenRouter will not wedge the session; JEV_HOOK=off per-shell kill switch (useful for client work).
Has offline unit tests (test_stop_verify.py) and a replay harness with measured agreement numbers, unusual for a 12-day-old repo; MIT license.
cons: Hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY; needs a small patch (base URL, key var, model id typesafe/jev-1.13) to use OpenRouter, and the OpenRouter response envelope compatibility is unverified.

Sends excerpts of code, tool outputs, doc comments and the assistant's answer to a third party on every qualifying turn; problematic for client projects and it bypasses the user's PreToolUse secret guard since secrets already in tool output would be shipped and stored in sent.jsonl.

Purpose is narrow: catches unsupported claims in final answers; it does not help with routing, permission decisions, tool selection or code choices. Value depends on how often Opus 5.5 makes false codebase claims.

Keyword-based retriever (not semantic), so false positives/negatives; the README admits that true claims not read this session are flagged, and blocks force extra Claude turns that cost Opus tokens and interrupt flow, especially annoying in auto/bypass mode.

Immature: 2 stars, 1 fork, single author (two git identities), 23 commits in 6 days (2026-09-18 to 09-24), no CI, no releases; hand-tuned thresholds that need per-project tuning; the WAF/User-Agent breakage shows brittleness of the direct API and it silently stopped checking before being noticed.

Relies on Jev being good at entailment judgments, an unproven use of a beta model; skeptics claim Jev is just a small router; the author's own Kev comparison shows judges disagree heavily (Kev agrees with Jev only 12% on contradicted).
Stop hook does not check claims made in the turn that answers a block (stop_hook_active exemption), nor Claude's mid-turn decisions; log.jsonl/sent.jsonl grow unbounded with code excerpts.
Would co-exist with the user's existing Stop/PreToolUse hooks but adds another Python process per turn; no OpenRouter attribution headers.
entries.verdict: The best fit found for 'automatic, no prompting': a small, auditable, deterministic Stop hook that uses Jev's Noul/Choice properly and fails open. With a ~5-line patch to point at openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and OPENROUTER_API_KEY it is viable, but treat it as an opt-in claim-checker (disable with JEV_HOOK=off for client repos) because it ships code excerpts off-machine and its value is narrow.

judge.why: Small (484-line stdlib Python) claim-checker: classifies final-answer sentences as factual claims with Choice/Noul, pulls keyword-matched tool-output lines as evidence, and blocks unsupported claims once. Best conceptual fit to 'false claim about the codebase', with thoughtful rules for stale and relayed claims. Needs a patch and ships code excerpts every turn.
pros: Uses Choice and Noul as designed, with thresholds (JEV_CONTRA, JEV_FIRM, JEV_FACT); easy to audit
Fail-open with a stop_hook_active guard (at most one extra turn); JEV_HOOK=off switch per repo
Dogfooded: fixes for the WAF 403 silent-failure case, and STALE and RELAYED rules
MIT; about 24 offline tests
cons: Needs a 5-line patch for OpenRouter; response envelope compatibility unverified; no CI
Ships up to 12 tool-output lines per claim plus doc comments to the API and mirrors all of it to sent.jsonl, bypassing your secret guard
Keyword retriever gives false positives on true claims not read in the session; 1-3 s at turn end from 2-3 sequential calls
Known silent-degradation risk (WAF 403 disabled checks until fixed); narrow purpose

entries.name: stop-rules (haystackeditor)
entries.what: Per-repo Stop hook for Claude Code (and 13 other agents). On turn end it diffs the working tree against a stored baseline, cuts changes into git-diff hunks (or tree-sitter functions), attaches 25 context lines, and asks Jev one Noul question per hunk per rule from .stop-rules.md (up to 4 pieces per call). POSTs {state, model, questions} to /v1/systemone and reads answers[id].noul. Hunks at or above a bar (default 0.6) go back to the agent via exit 2 on stderr; asyncRewake wakes the agent in the background. A loop guard hands off to the user after 3 rounds. Optional OpenAI gpt-6-luna judge. Single committed 399KB bundled bin/stop-rules.mjs (11k lines), no npm install.
entries.autoInvocation: Fully automatic and deterministic: Stop hook fires on every turn end in any repo where init was run; asyncRewake runs it in the background and only re-engages the agent on exit 2. Independent of permission mode (auto/bypassPermissions do not affect it). Per-repo, not global: each repo needs init + .stop-rules.md, and the hook path uses CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR, so a user-level settings install would need manual adaptation.
security: Key handling is good: key via env, key file, or stdin login (0600); never argv; redact() strips the key from error text (jev.ts). Only child process is git via execFile (git.ts), no shell strings.

Installer writes into the repo (.claude/settings.json, .stop-rules/ 390KB bundle, .stop-rules.md, other agent configs) and tells you to commit them; init is run by you, but a committed hook means anyone cloning runs a 400KB minified-ish bundle as a Stop hook. Review before use on client repos.

Bundle is committed and can only be checked via scripts/bin.mjs --check (byte-for-byte rebuild); I did not rebuild. Bundle contains a comment path from the author's Mac scratchpad (line 4145) - cosmetic.

Prompt-injection surface: code hunks are sent as Jev state, so injected text in changed files can push scores down (Jev brief) and silently suppress violations; feedback text returned to the agent contains rule text and line quotes only.

Adds OPENROUTER key exposure: key must be in hook env or a file; the existing no-secret-leak hook does not protect OPENROUTER_API_KEY yet. No telemetry found (grep for telemetry/analytics empty); only calls the Jev/OpenAI/team endpoint.
entries.dataEgress: Every turn end: the added/changed hunks since last check (git diff vs baseline, including untracked non-ignored files), plus 25 unchanged lines above and below each change, plus your rule text, to the configured endpoint (OpenRouter -> TypeSafe). Lockfiles, .min, .map, .csv, .log, svg and data-only files are skipped (src/diff.ts:28-65) but there is no .env/secret-file filter; an untracked, non-gitignored .env or hardcoded key in a changed hunk would leave the machine. Answer cache (per piece) reduces repeat sends; state and cache live in the git dir, not the worktree. Client-project code goes to a third party on every turn.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open and non-blocking. Cannot-run (network, 401, 402, 429 exhausted, 5xx, busy) returns exit 1 with a reason, which Claude shows as a hook error but does not block; baseline is held so the next turn retries the same change (holdsBaseline in jev.ts). Retries: 3 attempts with 1-16 s backoff, per-request timeout 90 s (jev.ts fetchOnce), hook timeout 120 s. Halves and resends on max_tokens_exceeded (relevant to the 32k OpenRouter context). Loop guard: 3 violation rounds then handoff to user (check.ts:53). Main risk is false positives waking the agent up to 3 times per change.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool defs (no MCP, no skill). Hook text only enters context on violations: stderr report with hunk, rule, score, and quoted line, typically a few hundred tokens per violation. A wake-up also costs a full extra agent turn (main-model tokens) per violation round, up to 3 rounds.
pros: Fills a real gap: user has no Stop hook, and this is a genuine automatic quality gate that needs no 'use jev' prompt and works under auto/bypassPermissions

OpenRouter works config-only: request/response schema in src/jev.ts matches OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone; STOP_RULES_JEV_ENDPOINT is taken verbatim and TYPESAFE_API_KEY_FILE avoids putting the key in env
Non-blocking and resilient: asyncRewake, 90 s request timeout, 3 retries with backoff, halving on max_tokens_exceeded, baseline held on failure, loop guard after 3 rounds
Good key hygiene (stdin login, 0600 file, redaction, no argv) and no telemetry found; only git via execFile
Cheap: Jev ~$0.042/M input, per-piece answer cache, lockfiles/generated files skipped; extensive docs/TUNING.md with measured runs and author-published false-positive analysis
cons: Not global: init writes per-repo files (.claude/settings.json, .stop-rules/ bundle, .stop-rules.md) and asks you to commit them, which is intrusive on client repos; a personal user-level setup requires hand-wiring and per-repo rules
Sends changed hunks plus 25 context lines to OpenRouter/TypeSafe every turn; no secret-file filter for untracked .env; confidentiality concern for client projects
Days old (created 2026-09-19, 55 commits by 1 author, 0 stars, no release), no test files in repo (only build/verify scripts), 11k-line bundled file to trust

Quality depends on hand-written rules and uncalibrated Jev (author's own TUNING shows scores wobbling 0.45-0.80 on same code, single-hunk context); false positives cost extra main-model turns, up to 3 rounds

Untested against OpenRouter by author; key must be provisioned via settings env, and user's no-secret-leak hook lacks OPENROUTER_API_KEY; triage claim about STOP_RULES_ENDPOINT was wrong (team-mode variable)
entries.verdict: A real, well-engineered automatic Stop-hook gate that can be pointed at OpenRouter Jev with three env vars (STOP_RULES_JEV_ENDPOINT full URL, STOP_RULES_JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13, TYPESAFE_API_KEY_FILE), fail-open and background. Held to 6 by per-repo commit-heavy install, per-turn code egress on client work, uncalibrated Jev with agent-loop false-positive risk, and a days-old untested single-author codebase; best trialed on one personal repo first.

judge.why: Per-repo Stop hook that diffs the working tree against a baseline, asks one Noul per hunk per rule from .stop-rules.md, and wakes the agent via asyncRewake and exit 2 for hunks at or above 0.6. This is the best-engineered code-quality gate (background, cached, retries, halving on max_tokens_exceeded), but per-repo, commit-heavy and the most egress-heavy design.
pros: asyncRewake means the turn is not blocked; only violations re-engage the agent
Config-only OpenRouter path; key via stdin login (0600) or key file, redacted from errors; no telemetry
Retries with backoff, 90 s request timeout, baseline held on failure, loop guard after 3 rounds; per-piece answer cache
Skips lockfiles, minified and generated files; TUNING.md publishes the author's own false-positive analysis
cons: Not global: init writes .claude/settings.json, a 390 KB bundled .stop-rules/stop-rules.mjs and .stop-rules.md into each repo and asks you to commit them, which is intrusive on client repos
Sends changed hunks plus 25 context lines each side every turn, with no filter for an untracked, non-gitignored .env
Created 2026-09-19, 1 author, 0 stars, no tests in repo, an 11k-line bundle to trust; not adversarially verified
Scores wobble (0.45-0.80 on the same code); false positives wake the agent up to 3 times per change

entries.name: valentynkit/jev-belay
entries.what: Claude Code plugin with one Stop hook (node belay.mjs, zero dependencies). At the end of each turn it reads the local transcript slice since the last user prompt and uses regex belts to detect (a) file edits and (b) a passing test/build/lint runner. Only if files changed and no check passed afterwards does it make one Jev System One call (4 questions: claims_done, claims_verified, verification_applies, outcome). If Jev says the closing message is an unverified "done", it exits 2 with a reason on stderr, so Claude keeps working and runs the tests. It fails open on every error. Also ships shadow mode, a decision log, a TUI (watch/stats/last/doctor) and two skills (why, doctor).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook, fired by the harness on every turn end with no model discretion and no need for the user to say anything. Jev is consulted automatically, but only on turns where files changed and no passing check followed (author measured 17.7% of stops).
security: API key sent only as Authorization Bearer header via fetch (belay.mjs:503); not in argv or process list. Plugin userConfig marks it sensitive (Keychain). Manual setup puts it plaintext in settings.json env block.
Zero npm dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh installer, no child_process/exec/spawn in belay.mjs (grep found none); static-only audit, I did not run anything.

Outbound payload is redacted before sending (belay.mjs:52-76 SECRET_RULES: private keys, Authorization/bearer, api_key/password/token=..., URL creds, sk-, ghp_, npm_, AKIA, xox, AIza, JWT), home dir rewritten to ~. Regex redaction is best-effort, so secrets pasted in prose prompts could still slip through.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompt and final assistant message go into Jev state; Jev returns only typed probabilities (no free text), so output cannot inject instructions. The nudge text is fixed template plus the failed check command string from the transcript.
Writes only under ~/.claude/belay (sessions/*.json always; decisions.jsonl only if log=on, 5 MB rotate). Decision log stores task and final_message text locally.
No telemetry beyond the Jev call. Endpoint overridable via JEV_BASE_URL (whoever controls that env controls where prompts go).
entries.dataEgress: Per gated stop only: user task text (first 1500 chars of the last prompt, redacted), the assistant's closing message (last 2000 chars, redacted), file_changes count, and a list of check commands with passed/failed (e.g. "npm test -> passed"). No diffs, file contents, tool outputs or paths beyond ~ (belay.mjs buildState 465-478; README 'What leaves your machine'). Model and question definitions are also sent. Stops with no edits or with a passing check make no network call. Client-work risk: the user's prompts and Claude's summaries can contain client names, code identifiers, and business detail, and they would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe on ~18% of turns (author's corpus). Redaction is regex only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. No key, unparseable payload, no readable transcript, gate says nothing to check, network error, HTTP error, garbage answer, or any uncaught exception all lead to exit 0 (belay.mjs main() catch, runHook returns). Retries up to 3 attempts with 600ms*2^n backoff on 429/5xx inside one shared budget, default 20000 ms (JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS), under the hook timeout of 25 s. So a hung Jev/OpenRouter can stall the end of a turn for up to about 20 s before failing open. stdin read timeout 10 s. Loop protection: stop_hook_active, one block per prompt, 60 s cooldown, max 3 blocks per session, host cap of 8. Recommend lowering JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS to about 5000 for OpenRouter.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no MCP server instructions, no tool-definition tokens. Two skills (why, doctor) add only two short description lines to the skill listing (about 30 tokens). The hook injects text into context only on a block: about 90 tokens (the nudge, roughly 350 chars) at most 3 times per session. Silent otherwise (exit 0 with no output unless shadow mode or DEBUG).
pros: Truly automatic: a Stop hook, so the user never prompts for Jev; matches the requirement exactly.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to (typed noul/choice decisions with calibrated probabilities, no free text), with code owning thresholds and evidence, so Jev is not asked to reason.
Same wire format as OpenRouter's System One API (POST {base}/v1/systemone, Bearer, {model,state,questions}), so OpenRouter works by three env vars, no fork needed.
Very cheap and low overhead: about $0.00005 per gated stop, no network on ~82% of stops, zero context tokens from tool definitions.
Fail-open by design with loop caps (1 per prompt, 60 s cooldown, 3 per session); a wrong call costs one extra test run.
Zero dependencies, no exec/spawn, no postinstall, readable 800-line single file; 13 test files run offline against a fake Jev, CI matrix Node 20/22.

Shadow mode plus decision log and stats let the user trial it for a week with no behavioral change; complements rather than collides with the existing PreToolUse secret guard and GitNexus hooks (different event).
Egress is narrow and documented (prompt, closing message, counts), with redaction before send, better than any tool that ships diffs or file contents.
Useful for the user's Opus 5.5 in bypass/auto mode, where nobody watches each turn and false 'tests pass' claims are the main risk.
cons: Very new (created 2026-09-18, 12 days old, 37 commits in 3 days, single author, 20 stars, 2 forks, 0.2.0), so it is likely to churn.
Only ONE use case (unverified-done gating); it does not give Claude general access to Jev for routing, classification or other decisions. It is a narrow win, not 'Jev integrated in Claude Code'.

OpenRouter path is not implemented or tested by the author: default is api.typesafe.ai, model pin jev-1.13.0 must be overridden to typesafe/jev-1.13, and the key env var is named TYPESAFE_API_KEY (an OpenRouter key goes in a misnamed variable). The README AUROC 0.976 was measured on a TypeSafe direct call on n=100 with 12 positives and proxy labels from Sonnet (wide CI 0.915-1.0).

Sends the user's prompt and Claude's closing message off machine on ~18% of turns; for client projects this is a confidentiality issue and redaction is regex-only. Could be mitigated by a per-project disable, but the hook has no per-repo allowlist (only the global key/plugin toggle).
Misses read-only turns (no edits, so no check) and custom test scripts unless the check regex is set; only one of four thresholds is empirically swept.
Hung endpoint can hold the end of a turn up to ~20 s (default budget) before failing open; needs JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS tuning.

The plugin's install instructions use the plugin marketplace, which pulls third-party code executed on every Stop; with bypass permissions on, pin a commit SHA or vendor and read it. I did not run it.

Redundant with the user's own habit or a plain command hook running tests; the value depends on whether Opus 5.5 actually falsely claims done (unknown), and only about 8% of turns get blocked in the author's corpus.
Beta model with skeptic claims that Jev is a router in disguise; the hook's value rests on Jev calibration being real, which only the author's small corpus supports.

Open issue #1 (pytest -q failure counted as pass) is a silent false negative for a Python/uv user: verified-looking runs suppress the Jev call entirely. More generally, the 'check-pass' default when the runner's summary format is unrecognised and no is_error flag is present means any unsupported runner output is treated as a pass.

On OpenRouter, the default model jev-1.13.0 and the audit's suggested typesafe/jev-1.13 are both probably rejected. Failures are swallowed by the fail-open design, so a misconfigured setup looks healthy but never blocks. Run `belay.mjs doctor --live` or shadow mode with JEV_BELAY_DEBUG=1 to confirm it works.

JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL are not plugin userConfig fields (only key, threshold, log, shadow, check are). The OpenRouter setup therefore needs an env block in settings.json, and the OpenRouter key would sit in plaintext under the misnamed TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The user's no-secret-leak hook protects neither that name nor OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Evidence quality: the AUROC 0.976 was measured on n=100 with 12 positives, with proxy labels, on the direct TypeSafe route. Nothing validates behaviour through OpenRouter or on this user's Opus 5.5 outputs.

Single-author repo 10 days idle with unanswered bug reports; 800-line hook runs on every Stop with full user privileges. In bypassPermissions sessions, pin a commit SHA or vendor the file after reading it. The plugin marketplace install tracks the repo head.
Only Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit count as changes. Turns where Claude edits through Bash (sed, patch, codegen) are never checked.
entries.verdict: Best-fit auto-invoked Jev integration seen so far for daily coding: a deterministic, fail-open, dependency-free Stop hook that already speaks the OpenRouter System One wire format, so it works with OPENROUTER_API_KEY through JEV_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 and a lowered timeout. It is a narrow single-purpose guard from a 12-day-old solo repo, so run it in shadow mode first, pin a commit, and disable it on confidential client repos.

verification.note: The source-level claims hold up. There is no exec/spawn, no postinstall and no telemetry, and the only network call is to base/v1/systemone. Every error path exits 0. Egress is task (1500 chars) plus final_message (2000 chars) plus counts, redacted by regex. The Stop hook with exit 2 and stderr is valid in Claude Code 2.1.x, runs in auto and bypassPermissions modes, and receives last_assistant_message. Timeouts are non-blocking, and belay's 25s hook timeout with a 20s budget is sound. The stats also check out: 20 stars, 2 forks, MIT, not archived, 37 commits over 3 days, one contributor. The audit's central OpenRouter recipe is partly wrong, though. /v1/systemone on OpenRouter wants the bare model id jev-1.13, not typesafe/jev-1.13, and the recipe was never tested. A wrong model id would be swallowed by the fail-open design, so the hook would look installed but never block. The audit also missed three open issues, including a pytest -q false negative that matters for this user. It also said there was no per-repo opt-out, but enabledPlugins in project settings provides one. I lowered the score from 6.5 to 5.5 because it is a narrow single-purpose guard with an unvalidated OpenRouter path. It would only reach 7 or above if the OpenRouter path were confirmed to work and the pytest -q bug fixed. Recommendation: shadow mode first, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13, and a shorter JEV_BELAY_TIMEOUT_MS.

judge.why: Zero-dependency Node Stop hook that calls Jev only when files were edited and no passing test/build/lint ran afterwards. That gating gives the narrowest egress in the category (task 1500 chars and final message 2000 chars, regex-redacted). Verification cut the score: 3 unanswered open issues, including a pytest -q false negative that hits your Python stack, an unvalidated OpenRouter path, and a repo idle for 10 days.
pros: Only calls Jev when it matters (edits, no passing check); read-only turns cost nothing
No exec/spawn, no postinstall, no telemetry; every error path exits 0; MIT, 20 stars, 37 commits
Wire format matches OpenRouter for the Noul half (the choice-answer shape is undocumented)
Per-project opt-out via enabledPlugins; shadow mode and doctor --live to confirm it works
cons: Issue #1: a failing 'pytest -q' is classified check-pass, so Jev is never asked (silent false negative for uv/pytest users); unrecognised runner output is treated as a pass
OpenRouter model id must be set by hand, and a wrong id looks healthy but never blocks
Bash edits (sed, heredocs, codegen) never count as mutations; only Write, Edit, MultiEdit and NotebookEdit

JEV_BASE_URL and JEV_MODEL are not plugin userConfig fields, so the key sits in settings env under the name TYPESAFE_API_KEY, unprotected by your secret hook; AUROC 0.976 was measured on n=100 with 12 positives

entries.name: noplan-inc/limpet
entries.what: Claude Code (and Codex) plugin that installs a Stop hook (single stdlib-only Python file, limpet.py, ~600 lines). When the agent is about to stop, it sends the last 3 messages, this turn's tool-call one-liners and the final message to Jev, asking one yes/no (Noul) question per plain-language rule in ~/.limpet/rules.md ("Is the agent violating this rule? Rule: ..."). If a rule's P(violation) exceeds a per-rule threshold (LIMPET_BLOCK), the hook exits 2 with a stderr line and the agent is sent back to work once. Default is shadow mode (log only, never block). Also ships `suggest` and `calibrate` CLI commands that mine your past transcripts to propose rules and thresholds.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic Stop hook: fires on every agent stop with no prompting and no model discretion. This is exactly the 'Claude Code must use it when needed' shape, but it only covers the single decision point 'is the agent stopping too early'.
security: Key handling is good: plugin userConfig marks keys sensitive (secure storage), `key set` uses getpass/keychain so the key never appears in argv; the hook reads the key from env/keychain and sends it in an Authorization header via urllib (no key in process list at runtime). Only `claude plugin install --config typesafe_api_key=...` puts it in argv once.

LIMPET_KEY_CMD is executed with shell=True (limpet.py ~139) with an 8 s timeout; only sourced from env/plugin config/~/.limpet/env, so not remotely injectable, but ~/.limpet/env is plain text and any writer to it can set it.
Keychain lookup spawns `secret-tool lookup` on every stop (2 s timeout); on headless Linux without a Secret Service this is a no-op after timeout.

Prompt-injection surface: assistant/user text and tool-call strings (up to 200 chars each) are interpolated into the Jev state as data, and Jev only returns probabilities (no free text), so injected text can at worst flip a probability and cause a false block/pass. The stderr block message is limpet-authored plus rule text and percentages, not model output.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no telemetry other than the Jev call; stdlib only so no supply-chain deps. But the plugin is fetched live from a 1-contributor, 2-week-old GitHub repo and runs on every stop, so pin a commit or vendor the file. CI workflow pullfrog.yml references many provider secrets but is workflow_dispatch only (repo-side, does not affect users).

Local log ~/.limpet/log.jsonl stores session_id, cwd, transcript_path and first 500 chars of every final assistant message in plain text (retained indefinitely, not rotated). For client projects this leaves client-derived text on disk outside the project.
entries.dataEgress: Per stop, to the chosen provider only (api.typesafe.ai or Vercel gateway; OpenRouter after patching): up to 3 previous messages (each truncated to 2000 chars, newest first, user and assistant text), the final assistant message (2000 chars), and up to 40 one-line tool-call summaries from the current turn ("Bash: <command up to 200 chars> -> ok/error", or file_path/pattern/url first string arg), plus the rule texts. File contents, diffs and tool outputs are not sent, but Bash commands and prompts/assistant prose can contain client names, paths, hostnames and inline secrets in command strings. The user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard does not cover this channel. suggest/calibrate additionally send stop/reply pairs from all projects over the last N days.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. main() returns 0 on missing key, API error, timeout, malformed answers (probabilities None are ignored) and any top-level exception (limpet.py 331-360, 600-605); urllib timeout is 20 s, hook timeout 30 s, keychain 2 s and key cmd 8 s inside that budget. Worst case Jev hangs: the agent stop is delayed up to ~20 s, then proceeds. Default with no LIMPET_BLOCK is shadow mode (never blocks). Push-back is capped at once per stop chain via stop_hook_active. Errors are only recorded to the log unless LIMPET_DEBUG=1.
entries.contextCost: Zero tools, zero MCP instructions, zero tokens on normal turns. Only when it blocks does it inject one stderr line (~40-80 tokens: 'limpet: this response may violate: "<rule>" (91%). If it does, follow the rule and keep working. If it does not, say why in one line, then stop.') which forces at least one extra assistant turn (real cost is the follow-up turn's tokens, and a possible spurious 'no, this is fine' reply on false positives, which the README says are ~5% by design).
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a Stop hook with no prompt changes, matching the user's 'never say use jev' requirement; verified in hooks/hooks.json and limpet.py main().
Uses Jev for what it is actually good at (typed probability judgments, no free text) with cost ~ $0.0001 per stop, i.e. a few cents per heavy day; one call carries all rules in parallel.
Fail-open on every error path and shadow mode by default, so it cannot wedge a client-project session; push-back capped once per stop via stop_hook_active.
Zero context cost on normal turns (no MCP tools, no injected text) and no conflict with the user's existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
Small, auditable single stdlib Python file (~600 lines, MIT), no deps, no postinstall; keychain-based key storage via secret-tool works on Linux.
Existing 'typesafe' provider already speaks the System One request shape, so retargeting to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is a ~10-line patch.
calibrate gives honest, data-driven thresholds and reports AUROC per rule, which is a rare, credible way to evaluate whether Jev helps at all.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: only api.typesafe.ai and Vercel AI Gateway (limpet.py:35-38); user would need a TypeSafe key or a fork/patch, and I could not verify OpenRouter's exact response field for Noul.

Modest measured effectiveness by the author's own numbers: AUROC 0.50-0.64, catches only 5-12% of bad stops at 5% false positives ('a cheap nudge, not a wall'), and labels are noisy. Opus 5.5 with a strong system prompt may stop early less often than the author's mixed agents, so benefit for this user is unproven.

Solves only one problem (early stopping / handoff); it does not give Claude Code Jev-based routing, permission decisions, tool selection or code-review scoring, which is what the user's broader integration goal implies.

Sends conversation excerpts and Bash command lines (including possible client names/paths/inline secrets) to a third party on every stop; the user's secret guard does not cover this and it is a compliance question for client projects. Local log also stores 500 chars of each final message plus cwd/transcript path in plaintext.

Very immature: 1 contributor, 13 commits all on one day (2026-09-17), 5 stars, no releases/tags, 13 days old, only ~5 test functions (no API-call tests). Plugin installs float on the default branch of a personal repo, so supply-chain pin is manual.

Exit-2 Stop blocking forces an extra full Opus turn on each hit (and false positives force a pointless 'it's fine' reply), which costs subscription usage and can annoy in bypass/auto mode where the user already wants uninterrupted runs.

Default rules are tuned to the author's habits (e.g. 'Don't hand work to human', 'give time estimate') and some rules like 'Don't say done without running tests' show AUROC 0.50 (no signal); requires the calibrate step before it is worth turning blocking on.
suggest/calibrate read every project's transcripts on the machine (including client projects) and send them to the provider, an unsafe default for a mixed personal/client workstation.
entries.verdict: The only real, deterministic auto-invoked Jev integration in Claude Code I found here: a safe, fail-open Stop hook that costs nothing in context. But its value is a narrow anti-early-stop nudge with weak measured lift, it lacks OpenRouter support (needs a ~10-line fork), and it ships conversation and Bash-command excerpts off-machine, so run it in shadow mode from a pinned, patched local copy rather than installing the marketplace plugin as-is.

judge.why: Cleanest anti-early-stop nudge: one stdlib Python Stop hook, shadow mode by default, plain-language rules in ~/.limpet/rules.md, one Noul per rule. Honest about weak lift (AUROC 0.50-0.64). Needs a fork for OpenRouter and covers only a narrow problem.
pros: Shadow by default (never blocks until LIMPET_BLOCK is set), fail-open on every path, one push-back per stop
Small and auditable (about 600 lines, MIT, no deps); no diffs or tool output sent
Keys held in plugin sensitive storage or keychain; about $0.0001 per stop
cons: No OpenRouter support, so a fork is needed
Own numbers: catches only 5-12% of bad stops at 5% false positives, so expected benefit is small on Opus 5.5
Sends prompts, assistant prose and Bash command lines (client names, paths, possible inline secrets), which your PreToolUse secret guard does not see
LIMPET_KEY_CMD runs with shell=True; per-stop secret-tool spawn (2 s timeout); suggest/calibrate send cross-project history

entries.name: muse0509/jev-preflight
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (Go binary, invoked via bash wrapper) with two hooks. UserPromptSubmit takes a private git snapshot of the working tree. At Stop it diffs against that baseline, filters and best-effort redacts the diff, then makes one POST to TypeSafe's System One API with 8 fixed Noul questions (behavior regression, auth boundary, input validation, data integrity, error handling, compatibility, lifecycle, regression tests). If any P(yes) is at or above 0.85 (uncalibrated), it returns hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext asking Claude to investigate once more, at most once per prompt. Modes are assist, report and off. It is fully deterministic and needs no prompting.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook. UserPromptSubmit and Stop fire on every turn with no user prompting and no model discretion. Once enabled it is fully automatic. It ships defaultEnabled false and needs an explicit `claude plugin enable`.
security: API key goes only in the Authorization: Bearer header. It is read from the env or a sensitive plugin option, never from argv, and diagnostics use fixed error classes only (client.go:43-48).
The endpoint is fixed and the client refuses redirects (client.go:65). There are no retries. Responses are capped at 64 KiB and strictly validated.

Best-effort regex redaction (internal/redact/redact.go, 8 rules for PEM keys, auth/cookie headers, *password/secret/token/api_key assignments, AWS keys, Bearer, sk-/ghp_/xox tokens, JWT). It is explicitly not DLP. Business logic, file names and unknown secrets go out. Snapshots of the working tree, including untracked files, are held unredacted in a private git object store on disk until cleanup, with a 24 h fallback TTL after crashes.

Prompt-injection surface is low. Only the diff is sent and only fixed-format numbers come back. The injected additionalContext is templated from the axis IDs, probabilities and quoted file paths, with no model free text. A malicious file name is strconv.Quote'd.

The wrapper is a small bash script that execs a prebuilt binary. There is no curl|sh, no postinstall and no telemetry. The marketplace pins the release-zip SHA-256, but the binaries are opaque unless you build them yourself. Single unknown maintainer, no signed release, 1 star.
Repo config cannot change the endpoint, which avoids a malicious repo redirecting the diff. It can set mode off or add excludes only.
entries.dataEgress: The redacted unified diff of the turn's changes, plus the changed-file list, sent to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (US-hosted) at every Stop that has a non-empty diff. Diff context lines and removed lines carry surrounding old code. Eight fixed question texts and model=jev-latest go with it. The user prompt, transcript and tool outputs are not sent. Git-classified binary files send path and status only. Tracked files matching .gitignore are still eligible. Default excludes cover lockfiles, build/vendor dirs, minified files and docs/media. The cap is 64 KiB of state, and an oversized diff skips evaluation entirely. The key leaves only in the auth header. Client repos would send code to TypeSafe unless excluded via .jev-preflight.json or mode off.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. A missing key, network error, timeout, non-200, invalid response, oversized diff, bad config, missing binary or unsupported platform all exit 0 and let Claude finish. The API call has a 2000 ms default timeout (configurable to 60 s) inside an 80 s runner deadline and a 90 s hook timeout. It makes at most one request per Stop, with no retry. A non-blocking systemMessage notice is shown once per session and error class. One risk: the persist-before-call design means an interrupted evaluation is not retried, so that turn is simply unchecked.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool definitions (no MCP, no skill), so idle context cost is 0 tokens. Hooks inject text only when triggered. That is roughly 150-250 tokens of additionalContext (up to 3 axis lines plus the file list plus a fixed paragraph) on the minority of turns at or above the 0.85 threshold, and one extra Claude investigation round on those turns (real token cost, not Jev cost). A report-mode systemMessage is about 40 tokens. Otherwise nothing is injected.
pros: It is the only candidate here that meets the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement by design: deterministic Stop hook, turn-scoped diff, at most one continuation per prompt (runner.go, protocol.go).

It matches Jev's actual design of typed Noul probabilities. It sends 8 calibrated yes/no questions and gets back numbers, with no free text to hallucinate or inject, and this is a natural cheap pre-merge risk screen for Opus.
Fail-open with tight bounds: 2 s timeout, single request, no retry, no redirect, 64 KiB response cap, and empty or read-only turns make zero calls.
Zero idle context cost (no MCP tools, no skill descriptions), and the additionalContext is templated and short.

Careful engineering: strict config parsing, a repo config that cannot redirect the endpoint, key never in argv, path/lock/TTL cleanup, a real Go test suite (about 108 tests) and cross-OS CI, a pinned-SHA archive marketplace, and honest docs (threshold 'uncalibrated', redaction 'not DLP').
The endpoint path /v1/systemone matches OpenRouter's System One API, so an OpenRouter port is a small patch.
MIT, and small enough (about 2.3k non-test Go lines) to audit fully and fork.
Per-repo .jev-preflight.json lets you set mode off or exclude paths on client projects.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the endpoint is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai and it needs TYPESAFE_API_KEY. That contradicts the user's stated goal of an OpenRouter-hosted Jev, and it needs a fork plus Go build plus local plugin hosting to fix.

Model is the bare `jev-latest`, not OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-latest or ~typesafe/jev-latest, so the model string must change too. I could not verify that OpenRouter's request and response schema is identical to TypeSafe's (the docs URL returned 404).

Sends source diffs (with surrounding context and removed lines) of personal and client repos to a third-party US service on every code-changing turn, with only regex redaction. Client work needs per-repo mode off or exclusions, or explicit consent.

Very immature: 3 commits over 2 days (2026-09-18 to 2026-09-20), 1 contributor, 1 star, prerelease v0.1.0, 'independent, not affiliated', the README says CI was pending when it was finalized, verified on synthetic code only, and no real-world signal quality.

The 0.85 threshold is explicitly uncalibrated. The 8 fixed generic questions on a diff-only view, with no repo context, may produce false-positive or always-low scores, and each positive triggers an extra Opus investigation round (cost and time). The skeptic claim that Jev is a small router model is relevant to how well it judges code risk.

UserPromptSubmit does a synchronous git snapshot of the whole working tree, including untracked files, on every prompt. Unredacted copies sit in a private git object store, which is heavy on big repos or repos with large untracked assets.
Binary releases are prebuilt and opaque, from a single unknown maintainer with no signing. Safe use means building from source yourself.
In bypass/auto permission mode the Stop feedback only nudges. It is not a gate, and there is no MCP tool for on-demand or in-loop use of Jev (for example for planning or routing).
It covers only one Jev use case (turn-end diff risk). Other Jev-fitting uses (task routing, confirmation classification) are not addressed.
entries.verdict: The best-engineered and only truly automatic Jev-in-Claude-Code integration so far: a deterministic Stop-hook risk gate, fail-open, with zero idle context cost. But it is TypeSafe-direct only, so it needs a small fork (endpoint, key env var, model ID) to use OpenRouter, and it is a 3-commit, 2-day-old one-maintainer beta that ships client source diffs off-machine. Use it as a template or fork rather than installing it as-is, and enable it only on personal repos.

judge.why: Best-engineered of the diff-gate designs (Go, about 108 tests, cross-OS CI, 2 s timeout, no retry, at most one continuation per prompt), asking 8 risk Noul questions about the turn's diff. Ships defaultEnabled false. Not usable with OpenRouter without a Go fork, and it uploads source diffs.
pros: Fail-open with tight bounds; zero API calls for read-only turns; zero idle context cost
Repo config cannot redirect the endpoint; client refuses redirects; strict response validation
Real test suite; the injection surface is low because only a diff goes out and only numbers come back
cons: No OpenRouter path without patching the Go source and hosting your own plugin build
3 commits over 2 days, 1 star, prerelease v0.1.0, one maintainer
Redacted diffs plus context and removed lines leave the machine every code-changing turn; unredacted snapshots sit in a private git store for up to 24 h after crashes
UserPromptSubmit takes a synchronous working-tree snapshot on every prompt, slow on big repos

entries.name: rashedInt32/jev-gates
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (pure Node ESM, zero deps) with nine Jev-judged "gates" implemented as hooks. As of v0.9.0 only the claims gate is on and only the Stop hook is wired. After each turn it sends the last prompt, final reply and this turn's tool calls and outputs to Jev. Jev says whether each reply sentence claims an action or result, and whether the turn's tool output supports it. Unsupported claims block the stop (exit 2, reason on stderr) once, so Claude corrects itself or actually runs the check. Opt-in gates (done, proof, rules, scope, intent, prompt check, bash guard, commit guard) need env flags and, for most, hand-wired hooks.
interface: Stop hook: hooks/stop-gate.mjs (wired in hooks/hooks.json, timeout 20s, status message "Jev: checking the reply")
UserPromptSubmit hook: hooks/intent-guard.mjs (NOT wired; manual settings.json entry)
Env config JEV_GATES=active|shadow|off, JEV_GATES_CLAIMS=off, JEV_GATES_TIMEOUT_MS, thresholds
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: a Stop event fires on every turn with no model discretion, so it is fully automatic and needs no prompting. Only the Stop hook is wired by the plugin. Other gates need hand-edited settings.json hooks.
security: Key is read from env or a 0600 file, never argv (lib/jev.mjs:81-91), so it does not appear in the process list. It is sent per request over a private Unix socket to the broker, which holds no key (lib/broker.mjs:76-79) and refuses a different baseUrl (line 178).

Regex secret redaction (lib/redact.mjs) is applied to everything sent and logged: PEM keys, URL passwords, Bearer/Basic, key=value pairs for api key/token/password names, and sk-, ghp_, AKIA, AIza, glpat, npm_ and JWT shapes. Best effort only. Source code, business data and unlabeled secrets pass through.

Data dir ~/.claude/jev-gates is chmod 0700 and files 0600. It keeps decisions.log, cache, last-*.json and proof/*.json, which hold redacted excerpts of prompts, replies, tool outputs and diffs persistently on disk. The broker socket and process are user-scoped.

No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev API. Zero npm dependencies. package.json is private with only a test script. Install is via the /plugin marketplace, which runs plugin files as the user.
Shell execution: only execFileSync("git", args) in lib/git.mjs, and spawn(process.execPath, [broker]) detached. The rest is static parsing of commands.

Prompt-injection surface: user prompt, reply and tool outputs are labelled as untrusted data in the questions. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection can at worst flip a gate decision. Every gate only escalates and never approves.
entries.dataEgress: With the default claims gate, each Stop sends to the Jev endpoint (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter then TypeSafe): the last user prompt (up to 8k chars), the final assistant reply (up to 12k chars), this turn's tool calls and their outputs (Bash commands and output, file reads and edits, subagent reports), and the last three earlier assistant replies. The total cap is 48k chars (JEV_GATES_MAX_CHARS). Redaction removes the recognizable secret shapes. With JEV_GATES_PROOF=on it also sends git diff excerpts against HEAD. Client source code, file contents and command output leave the machine on every turn that used tools. Only the first 100 chars of decisions are logged locally. With OpenRouter, the request goes through OpenRouter and then TypeSafe, so check OpenRouter's data policy and the per-provider ZDR settings. Client NDAs may forbid this.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. Missing key, HTTP error, malformed answer, timeout (8 s default, JEV_GATES_TIMEOUT_MS), oversized state (>48k chars), no tool activity recorded, or any thrown error all mean exit 0 with no output, so Claude stops normally (stop-gate.mjs:52-55, 92-95, 244-246; lib/jev.mjs header). Hook timeout is 20 s in hooks.json. Worst case is about 8 s of added wait per turn when Jev hangs. A block is issued once only, because stop_hook_active short-circuits the second stop (stop-gate.mjs:34-37). A false positive costs one extra Opus turn of tokens. Broker failure falls back to a direct call.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools, no MCP instructions, no tool defs. Nothing is injected on normal turns. Only when a claim is blocked does a short stderr message (about 100-300 tokens) get fed back to Claude. Opt-in UserPromptSubmit gates would inject a one-line note per flagged prompt. Effectively free for context.
pros: Truly automatic. It is a plugin-shipped Stop hook (hooks/hooks.json), so the user never says "use jev".
Makes sound use of Jev's strength (calibrated Noul probabilities, no prose). Fail-open, escalation-only design with thresholds, shadow mode and a decision log.
Works with OpenRouter by config alone: JEV_GATES_BASE_URL plus JEV_API_KEY, because OpenRouter's System One endpoint mirrors TypeSafe's wire format. No fork needed.
Zero context cost, zero dependencies, no argv key exposure, 0600 files, secret redaction. Small, readable code (about 3k lines).
Reasonable test suite (about 120 test cases across 13 files against a local stand-in API). The author already cut noisy gates after a week of real use (v0.9.0), which shows honest calibration.
Complements the user's existing setup: the secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks are PreToolUse/other events, so the Stop hook does not overlap with them.
Addresses a real pain point: Opus claiming "tests pass" without running anything.
cons: Sends prompts, replies and full tool outputs (code, command output) to a third party on every turn. On client projects this is a real confidentiality and NDA issue. Regex redaction is best-effort, and it adds a hop through OpenRouter.
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18, 24 commits, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, and it has already changed defaults once (0.9.0 breaking). Expect churn.
Not tested against OpenRouter by the author, and the docs mention only api.typesafe.ai. The full base-URL path must be set by hand, and a shape mismatch would just silently fail open.
Stop-hook latency of about 0.5-1.3 s per turn (measured by the author, slower than Jev's claimed 70-500 ms). The first call in a session pays for a cold connection and broker spawn.

The claims gate judges sentence by sentence and has documented false positives and blind spots (long outputs truncated, restated results, lagging transcript). It can trigger an extra Opus turn. The 'wrong' costs are small but nonzero.
Narrow value: it catches unsupported 'I ran X' claims only. The other eight gates are opt-in, need manual hook wiring, and by the author's own account mostly interrupted without catching anything.
It runs a persistent detached background Node process (broker) plus a growing decisions log and last-*.json files holding redacted excerpts on disk.
Bypass/auto permission mode: a Stop-hook block still works, but PreToolUse 'ask' gates lose their force in bypass mode. Only the Stop gate is relevant, which is the one with value.
Silent-inactivity risk on this user's PATH: the shipped hook uses bare `node` and the user's settings override PATH (see corrections). The plugin can look installed and never run.

Input amplification: for each reply sentence (up to 16) the gate sends two Noul questions whose instruction text is about 1.0k and 2.3k chars (hooks/stop-gate.mjs:132,140). That is up to about 53k chars (~13k tokens) of question text on top of the state, and the 48k-char cap in JEV_GATES_MAX_CHARS covers the state only. Worst-case requests approach OpenRouter's 32k context. An oversized request would be rejected and silently fail open, so the longest and most valuable turns may go unchecked. Cost stays trivial at $0.042 per 1M tokens, and this is unverified as to the actual rejection behaviour.

Untested against OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone (only api.typesafe.ai). A shape mismatch, an unknown 'jev-latest' alias or a 4xx would produce zero gating with no visible signal except decisions.log, which is only written for some paths (HTTP errors are thrown and swallowed by main().catch at stop-gate.mjs:244 without logging).

Large egress that the user's client work cannot tolerate: last prompt (8k), final reply (12k), up to 20k chars of tool calls and outputs (Read/Grep/Bash results, i.e. client source and command output) and 3 prior replies go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe every tool-using turn. Redaction is regex-only. Check OpenRouter data-policy and ZDR for the TypeSafe provider before enabling on client repos.

A prompt-injected tool output (web page, repo file) can steer Jev's evidence score. The worst outcome in the Stop gate is a spurious block, which is bounded by stop_hook_active, or a missed block. It cannot approve any action.

Independent Jev evals cited in the brief show overconfidence on unanswerable inputs. The claims gate depends on thresholds calibrated by one author on about 73 replayed turns plus a few one-run sessions. The README itself reports that most blocks in early real use were the gate's own blind spots (15 of 73 blocked at 0.7.4 and 5 at 0.8.0). Expect false-positive extra turns.
Unrequested detached background Node process (broker) with a 1h idle exit plus a Unix socket under ~/.claude/jev-gates. The user's key travels over that socket on each request.
entries.verdict: The best automatic, zero-prompt Jev integration found so far: a deterministic Stop hook that uses Jev the way it is meant to be used, fails open, costs no context, and can be pointed at OpenRouter with two env vars. It is too young to trust blindly, and it ships full tool outputs to a third party each turn. Run it in JEV_GATES=shadow on personal projects first, and keep it off on NDA client repos.

verification.note: The audit's core facts check out. Repo metadata was re-queried today and matches: 0 stars, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-18, last push 2026-09-29, 24 commits, one contributor, no releases, no CI. In lib/jev.mjs the base URL is a full path taken verbatim from JEV_GATES_BASE_URL (lines 23, 187). The key comes from env or file and is never put in argv. Only a Stop hook is wired. It is fail-open: every error path returns silently, and the block is exit 2 with stderr, guarded by stop_hook_active (stop-gate.mjs:34, 240-241). That is valid Claude Code Stop-hook behaviour, and last_assistant_message and transcript_path are real Stop payload fields. Broker key handling matches the audit (per-request over a 0600 socket, refuses a different baseUrl). The score is lowered from 6.5 to 5.5, mainly for four reasons. (1) The bare `node` in hooks.json collides with the user's overridden PATH, which the audit did not consider. (2) OpenRouter is only claimed, never exercised, by the author. (3) Every tool-using turn ships redacted client code and command output to a third party, and that egress is the reason it must stay off NDA client repos. (4) The audit overstated the on-disk data footprint and mislocated why the key belongs in settings env. Value is real but narrow: it catches unsupported 'I ran X' claims, and the author's own logs say Claude rarely lies. For this user it is a reasonable shadow-mode experiment on personal projects only, after fixing the node path and adding the key to the no-secret-leak protected list. I did not execute any candidate code. I re-read source and re-queried gh, the OpenRouter typesafe-sdk doc and docs.typesafe.ai/api.md. The Jev API docs do not state a context limit and the OpenRouter doc does not either, so the 32k figure is from the brief only.

judge.why: Claims gate (only Stop wired in v0.9.0): checks whether each reply sentence claims an action that the turn's tool outputs support, with JEV_GATES=shadow mode and a broker for the key. Verification found the shipped hook uses bare 'node', which collides with your overridden PATH so it would silently never run, plus large egress and a 32k-context risk.
pros: Zero deps, MIT, fail-open everywhere, block guarded by stop_hook_active; shadow mode built in
Key kept out of argv; the broker holds it over a 0600 socket
Catches unsupported 'I ran X' claims, the class of error that matters most in unsupervised bypass sessions
About 119 tests
cons: hooks.json uses bare 'node'; with your settings PATH override the hook exits 127 on every Stop and does nothing (wire it by hand with an absolute node path)

Sends last prompt (8k), reply (12k), up to 20k chars of tool calls and outputs and prior replies each tool-using turn; per-sentence question text can approach 13k tokens, so long turns may be rejected by the 32k context and silently unchecked
0 stars, no CI, 1 open issue, no releases; OpenRouter untested; broker is an unrequested detached background process
The author's own logs show most early blocks were the gate's own blind spots (15 of 73 turns blocked at 0.7.4)
