entries.name: Parth1811/JevFlow (jevflow plugin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (Python stdlib, hooks-only, no MCP server) that makes Claude plan multi-step work as a phased "flow" (.jevflow/flow.json) with shell checks. On every Stop it runs the checks, sends a curated state to Jev (System One choice/noul/score questions: which phase, phase done, stuck, off-goal, claims-done, progress) and a pure-code policy decides allow-stop / block-with-next-step / advance phase. Also offers optional gates (Bash risk gate, WebFetch injection screen, subagent/task completion checks), a live web viewer, a statusline and a supervisor that relaunches claude --resume.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for the enforcement side (Stop/PostToolUse/SessionStart run with no user prompt), but the entry point is model-discretion plus heuristic nudges: without `jevflow auto on` Claude is merely told (SessionStart hint / UserPromptSubmit additionalContext) that it may run `jevflow start`; with auto on, task-like prompts create a draft flow deterministically and Stop blocks until Claude writes a valid plan. The Jev call itself is fully automatic once a flow is active; it is a Stop-time judge, not a general-purpose decision helper for coding steps.
security: API key: read only from plugin userConfig (sensitive, stored in credential store, passed as CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_JEV_API_KEY to hooks) or JEV_API_KEY env; sent only in the Authorization header, not argv (jev_client.py:70,173); redacted from error bodies and repr (:80,:133). Key is scrubbed from env of flow checks (project.py _check_env) and notify commands. README admits the agent runs as the same user and could still read env.

Checks are arbitrary shell commands (shell=True, project.py:349) taken from flow.json, which the LLM itself writes; the Stop hook executes them outside Claude's permission prompts. With auto-planning the prompt goal becomes flow content. A prompt-injected agent could plant a malicious check that later runs in a hook; README: 'Not a sandbox... review flow changes like code'.
notify.command also runs with shell=True from flow.json (notify.py:75).
Prompt-injection surface: Jev sees Claude's last-message tail and check output, but 'Jev informs, code decides' policy and checks outrank the model; injection screen gate is optional and off.

No curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall, no third-party dependencies (stdlib only), no telemetry found. Only network call is urllib to the Jev endpoint (jev_client.py:130). SessionStart hook creates a symlink in ~/.local/bin (cli_install.py) - a side effect on the user's machine.
Live viewer binds 127.0.0.1 read-only. MIT license, single author, 7 stars, no CI directory, no releases, and loop/state.json leaks the author's local path (harmless).
entries.dataEgress: Only to the configured Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai today) on Stop and optional gates: goal (verbatim user prompt in auto mode), phase names + done_when, check exit codes and output tails (can contain code, test output, secrets printed by tests), last 4k chars of Claude's last message, changed file names with line counts from git (no contents unless privacy.send_diff=true), last 5 decisions. Optional gates additionally send Bash command lines (best-effort regex redaction) and WebFetch results. Nothing is sent when no key is set or in a project without .jevflow (except no-op hooks). Client-side, per-session budget max_jev_calls default 200.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Launcher hooks/jevflow prints {} and exits 0 on any crash and maps only the deliberate code 42 to exit 2; handle() catches all exceptions and returns {}. Jev errors, missing key or malformed answers give a degraded 'checks only' path that never blocks without evidence (docs/REFERENCE.md conditions degraded_*). Client timeout 15s, up to 3 retries with backoff (max 8s) => worst case roughly 1 minute per Jev call inside the Stop hook (hook timeout 600s); gate calls use shorter timeout/retries. Hard caps: max 6 blocks per session, 7 consecutive-block cap below Claude Code's 8, draft plan blocks at most 3 times, then archived as abandoned. Exception: a Stop with a failing user check does block (intended behaviour) and a corrupt flow.json yields a systemMessage disabling it for that stop.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tool defs). One skill: description ~330 chars (~80 tokens) always listed, body ~1.1k tokens loaded on trigger. Five slash commands add small listing entries. Hook-injected text: no-flow projects get a ~600 char SessionStart hint (~150 tokens) per session; every task-like prompt (>=8 words) gets a ~600 char nudge (~150 tokens) in projects with .jevflow but no active flow; active flows inject goal + phase table at SessionStart and a one-line [jevflow] message per phase change, plus block-reason text on each blocked Stop. Claude must also author flow.json phases, which costs output tokens per task.
pros: Genuinely automatic: no 'use jev' prompt needed; hooks fire on their own, and `jevflow auto on --project .` makes every task-like prompt start a tracked flow (README 'Many flows'; auto.py:1-20).

One of the few Jev integrations that actually exploits Choice/Noul/Score primitives with calibrated probabilities as a typed decision (judge.py:227-256: current_phase choice, stuck/off_goal/claims_done nouls, progress score) instead of using it as a chat model.

Sound safety design: 'Jev informs, code decides', checks always outrank Jev, fail-open launcher (hooks/jevflow), degraded checks-only mode, block budgets under Claude Code's 8-block cap, per-flow max_jev_calls=200, key redaction.

Zero dependencies (stdlib Python; user has 3.13), no MCP server so zero tool-schema context cost, no postinstall or curl|sh; small readable code (~5.8k lines) with 356 claimed tests incl. hook fixtures.
Directly addresses a real daily pain (Opus declaring 'done' with red tests, drift after compaction), and re-injects goal after compaction.
Small OpenRouter patch: only jev_client.py:24-25 (plus key) needs to change since the key is a generic Bearer token.
cons: No OpenRouter support: URL and model are hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai and jev-latest (jev_client.py:24-25), no env override. User must fork/patch, and plugin updates would overwrite a patch; OpenRouter request schema equivalence is unverified.
Very immature: created 2026-09-24, 45 commits in 4 days by one author, 7 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, README says 'Status: MVP'; 356-test badge is self-reported and I did not run them.

Heavyweight workflow imposition: makes Claude write phased plans with shell checks for every 'real task', blocking Stop up to 6 times per session; for a senior dev on Opus 5.5 this can be friction, extra tokens and false-positive blocks, especially in bypass/auto mode where unattended loops may burn turns.

Only judges at Stop time; it does not help with mid-task decisions (which file, risk of an edit, when to run tests). Jev's value here is largely a verifier over Claude's last message tail, and the checks (deterministic shell commands) do most of the work; Jev is only used to confirm.

Spawns a Python process on every PostToolUse '*' and Bash PreToolUse for every tool call, stacking on top of the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks (added latency, hook-ordering interactions). Stop hook may also conflict with caveman/other Stop hooks.

Security tradeoffs for client work: flow.json checks and notify commands run via shell=True inside hooks, outside Claude's permission layer; data egress includes test output tails and Claude message tails to an external API (not okay for confidential client code without consent); SessionStart writes a symlink into ~/.local/bin; the SessionStart hint and per-prompt nudge inject text into context in every project.
Auto-planning uses a crude word-count/question heuristic (auto.py looks_like_task), so behaviour is unpredictable; .jevflow/ directories dirty client repos unless gitignored.
entries.verdict: The only candidate here that fires automatically (Stop/SessionStart hooks) and really uses Jev's typed probabilities, with a careful fail-open design, but it targets a task-completion-verifier workflow rather than general coding help and has no OpenRouter support (hard-coded api.typesafe.ai), so it needs a small fork. Treat as an opt-in per-project experiment (auto mode on, pre_tool gate off) rather than a global default, given its youth, hook stacking and the data it sends externally.

entries.name: erkamyaman/jev-enforce
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (npm jev-enforce 1.1.1) with two command hooks: a Stop hook checks Claude's final reply, and a PostToolUse hook (Edit|Write|MultiEdit) checks the newly written text. Both are checked against rules extracted from CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .claude/rules. Rules are classified once (Jev Choice, cached in ~/.cache/jev-enforce/scopes.json) as reply, code, both or none. Each check sends one batched System One request with one Noul question per rule ("Does the text break this rule?"). If P >= 0.7, the hook returns decision:"block" with the quoted rules, so Claude rewrites or fixes in the same turn. It fires at most once per turn (stop_hook_active guard). It is a CLAUDE.md compliance linter using Jev as a cheap judge. It does not add Jev-based routing or decisions to the agent's own work.
interface: hook PostToolUse Edit|Write|MultiEdit (cli.js hook post-edit, timeout 30s)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (Stop and PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit). Fully automatic with no prompting, which matches the user's requirement in form. But the only Jev use is a CLAUDE.md compliance judge, not a general decision aid for Claude Code.
security: No runtime dependencies, no postinstall scripts, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the Jev call. Only network destination is api.typesafe.ai (src/jev.ts:1).
API key is read from env (hook.ts:211) and sent as a Bearer header, never put in argv. The recommended setup puts it in plaintext in ~/.claude/settings.json.

Non-secret-aware egress: any Write/Edit content is sent, including .env or credentials files, since only CLAUDE/AGENTS/rules files are excluded (hook.ts:181). This bypasses the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard, which only covers Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit.

Prompt-injection surface: the checked text (reply or file content) is placed in Jev state next to the rule questions. Jev returns only typed probabilities, so the injection blast radius is limited to a false negative or false positive. The block reason quotes only rule text from the user's own CLAUDE.md, not model output.

Filesystem writes: ~/.cache/jev-enforce/scopes.json (rule classification cache) and pending/<session>.json (end mode, contains edited text in plaintext), or the CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA dir. The session_id is sanitized (hook.ts:188).

Plugin executes committed dist/src/*.js, which is only verified in CI by check-dist. Anyone installing trusts the repo owner; a single-maintainer, 9-day-old repo with auto-updating plugin marketplace is a supply-chain risk for client work.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai on every Stop and every Edit/Write/MultiEdit: the full last assistant message (up to 60k chars, head+tail truncated, check.ts:65-78), and the newly written text of each edit, meaning the code content Claude just wrote (new_string or content) plus the file path. Rule text extracted from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, project CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md and .claude/rules, once for classification and then again in every question. It does not send the user prompt, tool outputs, or the existing file contents around an edit. For client projects this means client code and the user's global CLAUDE.md go to a third party (TypeSafe direct, or OpenRouter plus its upstream provider if patched). README states this too ("Your reply text, edits and rules go to TypeSafe's API").
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. With no key or JEV_ENFORCE_OFF=1 the hook returns null. Any thrown error is caught in cli.js:40-45, written to stderr and exits 0 with no output, so Claude proceeds unblocked. Timeout is 15s per fetch (jev.ts:26) with up to 2 retries on 429/529 (400ms then 800ms backoff), while the hook is hard-killed at 30s by hooks.json; a killed hook is a non-blocking error. Worst case a slow Jev stalls each edit or turn end for up to 15-30s. There is no circuit breaker: if Jev is down, every edit pays the timeout. The first call in a new project also does a classification pass. The one-block-per-turn guard and stop_hook_active mean it cannot loop.
entries.contextCost: Zero tool or MCP definitions, no server instructions, no skills, so a baseline cost of 0 tokens. Hook text is injected only on a violation: a reason of about 100-300 chars (about 25-75 tokens) quoting the broken rules, plus a systemMessage to the UI. The Stop block forces an additional assistant turn.
pros: Truly automatic: two deterministic hooks, no prompting, zero context-token overhead (no tools, no skills), with the block message shown only on a violation.
Small, readable, dependency-free code (about 450 lines of src). Static audit is easy, and there is no postinstall or shell exec.
Fail-open by design (cli.js:40-45): missing key, network error or bad JSON never breaks a session.

Well-chosen Jev use: one batched Noul request per check with one question per rule matches Jev's typed-decision strength. Cost is about $0.0027 per 59-case benchmark run, and the input is cheap at $0.042/M tokens.
Honest, reproducible benchmark (93% precision and recall at 0.7) and a README section on limits. Rule scope classification is cached, and it respects CLAUDE.md precedence, including AGENTS.md.
Fits the user, who already keeps a long ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md of rules. It adds enforcement that a plain CLAUDE.md lacks, and the CLI `check` can run in CI. MIT licensed.
The endpoint is one hardcoded URL and one body shape, so a fork that points at OpenRouter is a small diff.
cons: Does not support OpenRouter: TYPESAFE_API_KEY and api.typesafe.ai only, model 'jev-latest'. The url option exists in createAsk but is never wired to env, so OpenRouter needs a forked and rebuilt committed dist. OpenRouter's request and response schema equivalence is unverified.

Sends every edit's new code and every assistant reply to a third party, including for client projects and including .env or secret writes (not excluded). It sidesteps the existing PreToolUse secret guard, which does not cover Write/Edit content.
Synchronous latency on every edit (about 0.35s p50, more if degraded) with no circuit breaker. Worst case 15-30s stalls when Jev is slow or down. Retries are only on 429/529.

Only judges style and rules that fit in one snippet. It cannot see the surrounding file or repo state (README: 'never add a dependency' scored 0.56, editing an old migration scored 0.06). About 7% false positives, so needless Opus rewrite loops. The fix is not re-checked.

Narrow value for a senior dev who already has caveman/GitNexus/secret hooks: it enforces prose and style bullets, and most of this user's CLAUDE.md is workflow rules (classified 'none'). Linters and tests already cover code rules better. It does nothing for routing, planning, permission or tool-choice decisions, which is where Jev would add real value.

Very immature: 9 days old, 9 stars, 1 open issue, 2 contributors, 25 commits, release tags v1.0.0 to v1.1.1 in 4 days, no PR CI, sole maintainer. Supply-chain trust risk for client work. Committed dist/ must be trusted.
Plaintext API key in settings.json, and pending edits stored in plaintext in ~/.cache in end mode.
entries.verdict: Clean, small, fail-open hook plugin that is genuinely automatic, but it is a CLAUDE.md compliance checker rather than a general Jev integration, and it is hardwired to TypeSafe's direct API. Using OpenRouter needs a fork (about 5 lines plus rebuild, schema parity unconfirmed), and it ships all written code and replies to a third party. That last point is a real problem for client work. It is optional and low priority, best run in `end` mode after a patch, and only on personal projects.

entries.name: Nanako0129/stingray
entries.what: Claude Code (and Codex) Stop hook, one bash script (hooks/stingray.sh, 646 lines) using jq, curl and perl. When a turn ends, it redacts the last assistant message and POSTs it to TypeSafe System One (model jev-1.13.0) with Noul questions from questions.json. Questions: no_action, broken_promise, watch_claim, watch_mismatch and wrong_language. If a score is at least tau (0.5), it exits 2 with a fixed nudge on stderr, so Claude keeps working. The nudge covers a turn that did nothing, an announced action never carried out, a promise to watch CI with nothing running, or a reply in the wrong language. The hook is off by default and needs env switches (STINGRAY, STINGRAY_SHADOW, STINGRAY_SHAPE3, STINGRAY_LANG). It is a follow-through guardrail, not a general Jev integration.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook: registered on the Stop event, so it fires automatically at the end of every turn with no prompting, once installed and a switch is set. It does not use Jev to help with coding decisions, only to police Claude's own turn endings.
security: API key appears in curl argv: hooks/stingray.sh:562 uses -H "Authorization: Bearer $KEY", so the key is visible in ps and /proc/<pid>/cmdline for the duration of each call (up to 6s). The README says nothing about this. It matters on a shared machine.

Key is read from ~/.config/typesafe/api_key or TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The README prefers the file because env vars leak to child processes. Setting TYPESAFE_API_KEY in the settings.json env block, as the README suggests for the switches, exposes it to every tool subprocess.

Outbound guard: STINGRAY_ENDPOINT must be https or loopback (:552-557). The request body is scanned for sk-, gh*_, github_pat_, AKIA and PEM patterns before sending (:~529), and a match cancels the request. It is a good defensive design, but a regex denylist.

Redaction (perl, hooks/stingray.sh:~395-450) strips fenced code, inline code, URLs, block quotes and any line containing a path or filename. It masks SHAs, issue numbers and project names derived from cwd and the git remote. The README states plainly that redaction does not achieve zero private content and that the substance of the work survives.

Prompt-injection surface: Claude's own final message goes to Jev, and the nudge sent back is a fixed paragraph, not model or Jev generated. The Jev result is only a numeric score, so injection can at worst cause a spurious block (limited to 3 per session) or suppress one. Cron prompts and background task descriptions are also sent.
Shell execution: none beyond the script itself. No eval, no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry other than the call to api.typesafe.ai. The state dir holds decisions.jsonl and counters.
entries.dataEgress: Only when a key is set and a switch is on: one POST per turn (that has a non-empty last message) to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (or STINGRAY_ENDPOINT). Payload: the last assistant message after redaction (code, paths, URLs, quotes and SHAs removed), truncated to the last 2400 bytes; the tool NAMES used this turn (no arguments); for each background task its status and description; for each cron its prompt; the name of a pending handoff session; and the language name for shape 4. User prompts, tool arguments, file contents, diffs and command lines are not sent. Redaction leaves the substance of the work readable, which the README admits. Nothing goes to OpenRouter today.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on every path (README section "Friction only ever goes up"): no key, no jq, no questions.json, secret pattern in payload, network error, non-200, malformed JSON, score outside [0,1], loop guards (stop_hook_active plus MAX_BLOCKS=3 per session). curl --max-time defaults to 6s (:561). The author measured 6.15s for a hung endpoint against a 10s hook timeout, so at worst the turn end is delayed about 6s and never blocked. It cannot make Claude do less, but the check silently does not run when Jev is down, and there is only a stderr note.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP or tool definitions and no server instructions. The hook injects no text on a normal turn. On a block it injects a fixed stderr nudge of about 100-150 tokens, and the model is then forced through one extra turn (extra Opus cost). If the OpenRouter response does not match the parser, the hook fails open and prints a short "(stingray: unavailable ...)" line to stderr.
pros: Truly automatic and deterministic: a Stop hook, so Jev runs without any prompt from the user. It also adds no tool definitions and no context cost at all.

Real, sensible Jev use of the Noul primitive (P(yes) with a threshold), with an offline mutation suite and a fixture-based calibration harness. Unusually honest README, with precision/recall/FPR published and limits listed.

Fail-open everywhere, with a per-session cap of 3 blocks and a double loop guard, so it cannot trap a session. It is off by default, and STINGRAY_SHADOW=1 gives log-only records in decisions.jsonl for a safe trial.
Single readable bash file (646 lines), MIT, no npm or pip install, no telemetry. A SHA-pinned CI on Linux and macOS. The dependencies (bash, jq, curl, perl) are already present on this Linux machine.

STINGRAY_ENDPOINT and STINGRAY_JEV_MODEL overrides make an OpenRouter switch a config change if the request and response shapes match. It targets a real annoyance: Opus stopping with 'I'll now do X' or 'I'll watch CI' and nothing done.
cons: Wrong provider out of the box: only api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. OpenRouter needs the untested override (endpoint, model ID typesafe/jev-1.13, OpenRouter key placed in TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and possible jq path edits. The 8-day-old repo has never been tested with OpenRouter.

Narrow scope: it only judges Claude's own turn endings. It gives no Jev help for routing, choosing between options, or coding decisions, so it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev whenever it adds value'. It covers one use case.

Prompts are calibrated on Traditional Chinese: questions.json criteria are in Traditional Chinese, and the README says English criteria have zero live measurements. The 81.8% precision comes from the maintainer's own Chinese transcripts. For an English-speaking user, accuracy is unknown, and recall was only 14.1% in the maintainer's own data.

Sends every turn's redacted final message (last 2400 bytes) to a third party that publishes no retention limit. Redaction leaves the substance of the work readable by the author's own admission. This is a compliance risk on client projects, and it happens on every turn even in shadow mode.

API key passed on the curl command line (visible in ps). Adds about 0.7-1s at each turn end, and a false positive costs a whole extra Opus turn. There is a 'watch' shape that assumes the background_tasks payload and SendMessage transcript formats of a specific Claude Code version (2.1.278 measured, transcript format 2026-09-26). It may break on 2.1.285.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-20, 5 stars, 1 fork, 88 commits by essentially one person. Mutable install from GitHub, and the model is pinned to jev-1.13.0, while OpenRouter naming and behavior differ.
entries.verdict: A well-engineered, fail-open, zero-context Stop hook that really does run Jev automatically, but it only polices half-finished turns, is tuned on Traditional Chinese, targets TypeSafe direct (OpenRouter needs an untested env override), and ships every turn's redacted message to a third party. Worth a shadow-mode trial on personal projects only, not a core Jev integration.

entries.name: olivdx/jev-mcp
entries.what: Python (FastMCP, stdio) MCP server plus CLI "jev-mcp" that acts as a "done gate" for coding agents. The agent itself writes a summary and test result into decide(goal, extra, tests); the server redacts goal/tests, sends it via typesafe-sdk system_one() to Jev with 7 fixed questions (5 Noul: goal_addressed, goal_ambiguous, tests_blocking, incomplete_work, scope_creep; 1 Score: risk_regression; 1 Choice: next_action), then local policy code (thresholds, profiles default/strict/ci) maps the probabilities to fix / ask / done. Built for Cursor, and it never collects git diffs itself (git is an empty placeholder).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. No hooks, no SKILL.md, no plugin.json, no CLAUDE.md snippet; the README workflow ("agent runs tests, writes extra, calls decide, obey verdict") assumes the agent is told to call it (Cursor rules). The tool docstring alone does not say "call at end of every task", so Claude Code will call it rarely unless you add a CLAUDE.md line or a Stop hook running `jev-mcp gate`. That would go against the user's 'no prompting' requirement unless wired via hook/CLAUDE.md, which you must add yourself.
security: API key never in argv when using env/file: key resolved from TYPESAFE_API_KEY env or ~/.jev-mcp/credentials.yaml (0600, dir 0700) - credentials.py:14-40. BUT `jev-mcp key add <API_KEY>` puts the key in argv/shell history (one-time only).

Redaction is partial: redact_text (util/redact.py) covers PEM keys, Bearer, sk-*, gh*_, AKIA, KEY/TOKEN/SECRET=value patterns, but state_builder.py:76-77 sets state['extra']=extra with NO redaction (a test even asserts 'secrets in extra are not double redacted', test_state_builder.py:29); only goal and tests stdout/stderr are redacted. Agent-written summary and log tail in extra go to Jev raw.

No shell execution in the running server: the shipped code does not collect git or run tests (state_builder 'we do not collect diffs'); util/proc.py and collectors/runner.py exist (arg-vector subprocess) but are not wired into decide (dead code, docs claim otherwise in old specs).

Prompt-injection surface: input is agent-authored text, output is a typed verdict; a compromised or lazy agent can write a flattering summary and get 'done' (gate is self-attested, not verified against the real diff).

No install hooks (poetry, no postinstall). No curl|sh. No telemetry in code beyond local logging via trace() to logger. HTTP transport unauthenticated but localhost-only and optional (stdio by default).

Supply chain: single anonymous-ish author (Olivier Taylor / 1hoodlabs), 0 stars, 11 commits in 9 days, no LICENSE file, unpublished PyPI name. Depends on typesafe-sdk 0.7.x (official typesafe-ai repo) and mcp>=1.6.
entries.dataEgress: Per decide call: state = {goal (redacted), git: empty placeholders, tests {command, exit_code, timed_out, stdout, stderr (redacted)}, extra (agent summary/plan/verification, NOT redacted)} plus question instructions, POSTed to /v1/systemone at TYPESAFE_BASE_URL (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if overridden - OpenRouter then also sees it and routes to TypeSafe). No source files, diffs or repo scans are read by the server itself; only what Claude chooses to write in extra/tests leaves the machine. Key verification (key add / health probe) calls GET /v1/models. Local logs record state_bytes size, action, confidence, project_root, not payloads.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed inside the tool, but effectively advisory to Claude Code: on missing key, 401, 429, timeout (default request_timeout_s=60, max_retries=2 in config.py JevConfig) or connection error, decide raises RuntimeError('[code] message') and Claude sees a tool error; nothing blocks the session because MCP tools are model-discretion. Worst case a hung Jev costs up to about 60s x (1+2 retries) on that call. The CLI gate returns exit 3 on tool error; if wired as a blocking hook it would fail-closed unless the hook script maps 3 to allow.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools (decide, health, describe). Estimated about 350-600 tokens total: FastMCP auto-schema for decide has 6 params (goal, tests: dict|None, project_root, profile, extra: dict|None) plus a 3-line docstring (~700 chars), health ~250 chars, describe ~200 chars, roughly 1.6-2k chars / 4. No server-level instructions field. No hook-injected text (no hooks shipped). Cheap, but health/describe are noise tools for Claude.
pros: Only candidate so far with real typed-decision design: uses all three Jev primitives (Noul/Score/Choice) with calibrated probabilities and keeps the action logic in deterministic local policy code (decision/policy.py, 25 tests) rather than letting Jev choose.

OpenRouter switch is config only: typesafe-sdk 0.7.2 honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone with Bearer auth (transport.py:121, config.py:61), so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus JEV_MCP_JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 targets OpenRouter's System One API without editing code.
Small, readable, well-tested for its age (about 150 tests, CI on Linux+Windows, lint), stdio transport, tiny context footprint (3 tools, no server instructions, no hook output).
Headless `jev-mcp gate` with exit codes 0/1/2/3 can be wrapped in a Claude Code Stop hook to make the check deterministic instead of model-discretion.
Explicit security posture: no shell interpolation, key 0600, key never via MCP tool, localhost-only http, key masking.
cons: Self-attested gate: it judges what Claude WRITES about its own work (extra.summary), not the diff or test output. It does not run tests or read git (git is an empty placeholder), so it adds little independent signal for Opus 5.5; garbage-in gives 'done'.

Not automatic in Claude Code: no hook, skill or plugin manifest, Cursor-only docs; Claude will rarely call decide unprompted. Getting auto-invocation needs your own Stop hook or CLAUDE.md rule, and a Stop hook that emits fix/ask can loop Opus with extra turns.
Adds real per-task cost: Claude must generate the summary/verification JSON and take an extra tool turn; value is marginal for a senior dev on subscription Opus.
extra is sent unredacted to Jev/OpenRouter (state_builder.py:76-77), a leak risk on client projects; redaction regexes are narrow (no JWT, DB URLs, .env style unless KEY=value).

Unpublished and unlicensed in practice: PyPI name mcp-jev-mcp 404s so README install fails; no LICENSE file; 0 stars, 1 contributor, 11 commits in 9 days, v0.2.0 with policy and question set ids already churned to v3.

entries.verdict: A clean, small proof-of-concept for a "should I stop?" gate that can be pointed at OpenRouter with three env vars, but it is Cursor-oriented, self-attested (Claude grades its own summary), unpublished on PyPI and offers no automatic Claude Code invocation. entries.name: shiftynick/jev-axi
entries.what: Node CLI (npm jev-axi 0.7.2, wraps @typesafe-ai/sdk) exposing Jev as shell commands (pick/rate/check/ask/rank/filter/find/diff/files/triage/guard/progress/commit/recipe). Its autonomous parts are real Claude Code hooks installed by `jev-axi setup`: a PreToolUse safety hook (matcher Bash|Write|Edit|MultiEdit; routine calls decided locally, others sent redacted to Jev for destructive/exfiltration/remote-code/weakens-security/outside-project scores), Stop + PostToolUse supervision hooks (is the job done, is the agent stuck), SessionStart context hooks, git pre-commit/commit-msg/pre-push hooks, and a GitHub Action. Also ships two SKILL.md files. No MCP server.
interface: hook stop / post-tool-use (Stop timeout 20s, PostToolUse timeout 15s, no matcher)
recipe, cache, usage, stats, models, config
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse safety, PostToolUse and Stop supervision, git hooks) fire automatically with no prompting; the skills and the CLI commands (triage/diff/files/guard) are model-discretion only. The author's own benchmark (docs/skills-do-not-get-used.md) found 0 of 22 free-choice runs loaded the skill, even with a SessionStart hook or custom subagent, so only the hook layer is truly automatic.
security: No postinstall/preinstall in package.json; no curl|sh installer; the GitHub Action does run npx -y jev-axi@version in CI (action/run.mjs:46).

API key from env, .env/.env.local walk-up (config.ts:120-133) or config file; passed to the SDK as Bearer header, not put in argv (setup/hook commands take no key in argv, but `config set apiKey <key>` and README suggest argv entry at setup time). SECURITY.md: key never written to ledger or cache.

Hook redacts secrets from commands before sending (safety.ts:30-90 redactSecrets); sends contents of any local script the command executes (up to MAX_SCRIPT_CHARS) and a content excerpt of Write/Edit outside project.

Supervise hooks send up to 20,000 chars of diff, 12,000 chars of tool output, prompts (first/latest) and last 30 tool events; credential files (.env, *.pem, .npmrc) excluded, but only pattern-based redaction protects client code and proprietary content.

Prompt-injection surface is mitigated by design: Jev returns only typed probabilities, never text, so injected content cannot steer the hook's output beyond scores; hook only denies/asks, never auto-approves. guard is explicitly a probabilistic aid (SECURITY.md).
Local audit logs: ~/.config/jev-axi/stats/{safety,supervise,usage}.jsonl and response cache contain decisions/metadata (cache keyed by hash of state).
entries.dataEgress: Safety hook: for non-routine Bash/Write/Edit calls only, the redacted command string, contents of any local script it runs, and a redacted content excerpt for out-of-project edits go to the Jev endpoint. Supervise hooks: every turn end with repo changes sends first/latest prompt from transcript, up to 20k chars of git diff and 12k chars of recent tool output; every 10 tool calls sends the last 30 tool-call summaries. Manual commands send whatever files/logs/diffs you pipe. Routine read-only commands, project tests/builds and in-project edits stay local. With the OpenRouter base-URL trick the traffic goes to OpenRouter (and its upstream), not api.typesafe.ai; the only other outbound call is the npm version check.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open with one fail-closed default. Hook API timeout 6s (HOOK_TIMEOUT_MS, hook.ts:45), stop 10s, maxRetries 0; settings hook timeouts 15s/20s. Missing key, timeouts, network errors: fall through to normal permission flow (source=error, decision allow). HTTP 403 (API firewall rejection) is denied by default (--on-error auto, hook.ts:86,128), which could block legitimate calls, especially if OpenRouter returns 403 for a key/credit/region/moderation problem; set --on-error allow to avoid. Supervise hooks stay silent on any error. Git hooks skip quietly if unreachable. Manual CLI uses a 60s client timeout (client.ts) and a 24h response cache.
entries.contextCost: Hooks: zero tokens when silent; PostToolUse injects a short additionalContext note only when concern is flagged; SessionStart hooks (jev-axi setup hooks, optional) inject a jev-axi status/command summary each session. No MCP tools, so 0 tool-definition tokens. Two skills add only their name+description to the listing (roughly 100-150 tokens each, descriptions are about 500 chars); full SKILL.md bodies (~7.3KB, ~1.8k tokens, and ~7.6KB) load only if invoked. Deny/ask reasons are short strings.
pros: Only candidate reviewed so far that is genuinely automatic: real PreToolUse/Stop/PostToolUse hooks, so Claude Code never has to be told to use Jev (hook.ts:16-30, 210-264).
Fast local pre-filter means routine calls (read-only, project tests/builds, in-project edits) never touch the network, cutting cost, latency and egress; only risky-looking calls reach Jev.

Never auto-approves and only returns deny/ask or silence, so it composes with the bypass/auto permission mode as an extra brake without weakening existing guards; redacts secrets before sending and skips .env/*.pem/.npmrc.
OpenRouter reuse is plausible with zero code change: the SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and posts to /v1/systemone, which matches OpenRouter's System One path.
Honest author: benchmark shows Jev did not lower agent cost and the skill goes unused; ships warn-only defaults and advises running supervise warn-only before --block.
MIT, idempotent installer with --remove, no postinstall, no telemetry beyond an opt-out npm version check, sensible tests and cross-OS CI, local audit logs of every decision.
Extra useful commands for manual use: triage of failing logs, diff review before commit, guard for fetched web content (relevant to playwright use).
cons: Not OpenRouter-native: TYPESAFE_API_KEY naming, default model jev-latest vs OpenRouter typesafe/jev-1.13, error hints point to api.typesafe.ai; OpenRouter compatibility is inferred from source and untested.
Very young and thin: repo created 2026-09-16, 26 stars, 68 commits, one main author; fast-moving API (0.7.x) and pinned to a beta model.

Jev is a classifier, not a reasoner; the author's own benchmark found no reliable cost or file-read savings and that the skill was never used, so for daily coding the value is mostly the safety net, not productivity.

Safety hook is redundant or overlapping for this user: already has a secret-leak PreToolUse guard and runs in bypass/auto mode where the author's ask/deny semantics would interrupt flow; adds another Node spawn on Bash alongside GitNexus hooks.
Default 403-means-deny policy fails closed and could block legitimate calls if OpenRouter returns 403 for credits/key/region issues, and the reason text tells the agent to hand it to the user.

Data egress on client projects: supervise sends prompts, up to 20k chars of diff and 12k chars of tool output per turn to a third-party (OpenRouter and upstream); redaction is pattern-based only, a compliance concern for client code.
PostToolUse hook has no matcher, so a Node process spawns on every tool call of every session even when it does nothing; Stop hook can add up to 10s at turn end.
Supervise verdicts are admittedly uncalibrated (README) and reading the job from the transcript relies on an unguaranteed format; --block can send the agent back to finished work.
Skeptic caveat on Jev quality (router-like behavior) applies to every judgment it makes; no independent validation beyond the author's 44-case safety set.
entries.verdict: Best automatic-integration candidate found so far because it ships real PreToolUse/Stop/PostToolUse hooks with local fast-path, redaction and fail-open behavior, and it can plausibly be pointed at OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api (untested). Its value is a cheap safety/supervision layer rather than coding productivity, so install it only user-level PreToolUse with --on-error allow (skip supervise on client repos) after a manual curl test against OpenRouter.

entries.name: jevctl (Nasrallah-AL/jev-cli)
entries.what: MIT TypeScript npm CLI (`jevctl`, binary `jev`) wrapping TypeSafe Jev with commands verify, screen (prompt-injection and substance check), find, classify, extract, rerank, match, route, ask, compact, batch, plus auth/config/models/update. A Claude Code marketplace plugin (plugin/, name `jev`) adds one skill (SKILL.md, allowed-tools Bash(jev:*)), 8 slash commands (/jev:verify, screen, route, find, extract, compact, classify, ask) and an early-access function-hook module (fast-jev.ts) that replaces Claude Code's compaction summary with Jev-guided verbatim truncation. There is no MCP server. The plugin does not talk to any API itself; the skill and commands make Claude run the `jev` CLI through Bash.
entries.autoInvocation: Partial and model-discretionary. The skill's description makes Claude likely to run `jev screen`, `verify` and `find` when the task matches, but nothing is deterministic. There is no PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PermissionRequest or UserPromptSubmit hook, so untrusted WebFetch and Bash output is never screened automatically. Slash commands are user-invoked. The only deterministic behaviors are the two function hooks (session.compact, turn.complete), which need CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 and a TYPESAFE key, so with OpenRouter only they would need patching. To meet the 'automatic without prompting' goal, the user would still write their own hooks (for example a PostToolUse WebFetch screen using `jev screen --fail-on block`, or the cookbook PermissionRequest gate) that call this CLI. That is feasible because of the stable exit codes.
security: Key handling: keys come from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), OS keychain or a 0600 credentials file (src/credentials.ts:49-58). `jev auth login` reads the key from a masked prompt or --key-stdin. There is no --api-key flag, so the key is not exposed in argv. Config and status print keys masked. The keychain backends shell out via execFileSync (credentials.ts run()); the plan's Linux Secret Service path was not fully audited.

Shell exec: only execFileSync with argument arrays (credentials.ts, commands/update.ts). No shell string interpolation was seen in src. `jev update` runs `npm install -g jevctl@latest`. src/versionCheck.ts and cli.ts:168-180 run `npm view jevctl version` via execFileSync on ordinary commands, at most once a day, cached in the config dir. That is a hidden network call and subprocess. It is suppressed by JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1 or -q.

Telemetry: none found in src (grep for telemetry and analytics came back empty). The only extra egress is the daily npm update check. HTTP-Referer https://github.com/Nasrallah-AL/jev-cli and X-Title jevctl are sent to OpenRouter (provider.ts:233-234), which is harmless attribution.

Prompt-injection surface: the skill (SKILL.md) tells Claude to run `curl -s $url | jev screen` and act on the JSON. The screen model is the Jev model, which independent evals say can be moved by injected instructions inside the state, and is overconfident on unanswerable inputs. `pass` therefore gives false comfort. /jev:screen allows Bash(curl:*) and WebFetch. Fetched content is written to temp files and passed as @file, which is safe from argv injection. The skill's 'block' guidance is good behavior, but it relies on model discretion.

Trust chain: the plugin adds the skill allow-list Bash(jev:*) and Bash(npx jevctl:*). `npx jevctl` fetches and runs npm code at call time, so it is a supply-chain and auto-approval risk if used as the fallback. Prefer a global install pinned to a version. The hook (early-access function hooks) runs plugin TypeScript inside the Claude Code engine with $.http.fetch, $.env.get and $.settings.read access. It can read the whole settings env, but the code only reads TYPESAFE_API_KEY (fast-jev.ts:245-252). Third-party plugin code runs in-process, so pin the version and review it.

Compaction hook risk: it sends the full transcript (tool inputs and outputs, up to maxStateTokens 25000) to the provider (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if patched). That includes any secret or client data that appeared in tool output. It also alters the conversation by truncating tool results to 300 chars and dropping calls. There is a fallback, but a wrong 'not needed' decision silently loses context.
entries.dataEgress: CLI: exactly the state and questions of each call go to the provider. With OpenRouter that is POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with body {model:'typesafe/jev-1.13', state, questions} and Bearer OPENROUTER_API_KEY. State is whatever text you pass: claims, evidence, fetched pages, file contents for find (up to 250 files at 2000 chars each), and so on. --dry-run prints the exact request first. Also a daily `npm view jevctl version` call to the npm registry (suppress with JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1). Compaction hook: the fitted conversation history (tool call inputs and results, up to about 25k estimated tokens per request, several requests, concurrency 4) goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone with the TYPESAFE key. It is not wired to OpenRouter. No other telemetry found.
entries.failureMode: CLI: fail-closed in the sense of a non-zero exit. Errors give exit 1 (network, config, malformed response). A judgment match gives exit 2 (default --fail-on: verify contradicted, screen block). validateAnswers (provider.ts:120-150) rejects missing or mistyped answers so a proxy failure cannot masquerade as a pass. The default timeout is 30 s per attempt (config.ts:49), and the TypeSafe transport retries twice. Nothing blocks Claude Code, because the CLI is invoked by the model through Bash. If the CLI is missing, the skill says to tell the user. Hook: fail-open to the built-in summary on missing key, HTTP or parse errors, budget overflow or a low reduction ratio (fast-jev.ts session.compact try/catch and next(event)). The turn.complete handler swallows errors and skips auto-compact. The risk is not failure but a successful yet wrong compaction (a lossy truncation replaces the summary). Note that the auto-compact trigger at 60% context is more aggressive than Claude Code's own default.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so no tool-definition overhead. The skill listing entry costs its description (about 1.3 KB, roughly 330 tokens) against the user's 2% skill listing budget. The 8 slash commands add about 8 KB of files in total, and their one-line descriptions are listed. When the skill is invoked, SKILL.md (13,253 chars, about 3.3k tokens) is loaded once into context. Each /jev:* command adds about 250-320 tokens. The hook injects no text into context. Compaction shows a toast and UI log only. Every jev call adds JSON output tokens unless --pluck is used.
pros: The CLI supports OpenRouter today with no patching: src/provider.ts:223-232 POSTs to /api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and the OPENROUTER_API_KEY bearer. Setting JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter suffices, and it also handles the 'jev-latest' to 'jev-1.13' mapping that OpenRouter needs.

Broadest single surface for Jev: screen (injection plus substance), verify, find, classify, extract, rerank, route, batch, all with --json, --pluck and stable exit codes (0/1/2) that are usable as gates in the user's own hooks. That fits the OpenRouter cookbook fail-open pattern.

Careful engineering: validateAnswers rejects malformed proxy responses so a failure cannot count as 'probability 0'. --dry-run shows the exact outgoing payload. There is a stderr notice when a stray OPENROUTER_API_KEY silently triggers a third-party hop. Keys are never accepted on argv, and keychain or a 0600 file is used. Uses execFileSync with arrays, not shell strings.

Real test and CI investment for a 12-day-old project: about 200 vitest cases across commands, provider, config, output and the hook (test/plugin/hook.test.ts), CI on Node 20/22/24, biome, `claude plugin validate`, a drift check for the vendored hook, CHANGELOG, SECURITY.md, docs per command. MIT with NOTICE. Published on npm (0.2.3) and matching GitHub releases.

Zero MCP overhead and small always-on context: only a skill description entry, no tool schemas. SKILL.md gives sound guidance (check exists_verdict before trusting the top hit, treat `unclear` and `review` as a human decision, never ask the user to paste keys into chat). Works for personal and client projects when scoped, since --dry-run lets the data sent be inspected.

Compaction hook has sensible safeguards (falls back to the built-in summary on error or when reduction is under 25%, keeps recent messages and all user/assistant text, a concurrency cap, a toast with counts) and is a genuine novel use of Jev for context pruning.
cons: The only deterministic automation is the compaction hook, and it is TypeSafe-only: fast-jev.ts:189 and 245-252 require TYPESAFE_API_KEY, the URL is hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (request.ts:6), the default model is 'jev-latest' (not valid on OpenRouter), and there is no baseUrl or provider option. The user would need a local fork, and updates would overwrite it.

The hook depends on the early-access CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 feature; the type reference was generated on Claude Code 2.1.274 (user has 2.1.285). Replacing Claude Code's summary with lossy truncation, and auto-compacting at 60% context, is risky on client work and untested against this user's setup. Full transcripts (including any secrets in tool output) would leave the machine. Not recommended to enable.

Auto-invocation relies on the model choosing to run `jev` (skill description and Bash). There is no PreToolUse, PostToolUse or PermissionRequest hook shipped, so untrusted web fetches are not screened deterministically and the user's 'never have to prompt use jev' goal is only weakly met. The user would need to write their own hooks around `jev screen` / `jev ask`.

Requires a global `npm install -g jevctl` (the skill falls back to `npx jevctl`, which fetches unpinned code at run time and is pre-approved via allowed-tools Bash(npx jevctl:*)), plus a Node CLI cold start on every call. Its hidden daily `npm view` subprocess on normal commands needs JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1.

Jev screen has documented weaknesses (injected instructions in state can move answers, overconfidence), so a `pass` is not a guarantee. The skill instructs Claude to trust `block/review/pass` outcomes without warning about this.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-18, 23 stars, 3 forks, 0.2.x with pre-1.0 breaking-change warnings, marketplace plugin.json at 0.2.0 vs npm 0.2.3, the OpenRouter route uses the /alpha endpoint, and the OpenRouter key must start with sk-or- or is ignored silently in auto. The OPENROUTER_API_KEY is also not in the user's no-secret-leak protected-vars list yet.
entries.verdict: Solid, well-tested Jev CLI that already works with OpenRouter and gives stable exit codes for gating (screen, verify, ask), which is the best building block found for the user's own PermissionRequest/PostToolUse hooks. As a plugin it is only partly automatic (the skill is model-discretionary, and the deterministic compaction hook is TypeSafe-only, experimental and risky for client work), so use the CLI (pinned global install, JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1) and skip the compaction hook.

judge.why: Best building block rather than a turnkey suite: a tested Jev CLI with stable exit codes (0/1/2), --dry-run and --pluck that you can call from your own hooks. As a plugin it is not automatic, and the compaction hook is TypeSafe-only and risky.
pros: Works with OpenRouter today without patching; screen, verify, find, classify, ask, batch, all with --json
Careful engineering: response validation rejects malformed proxy replies, --dry-run shows the outgoing payload, no key on argv, execFileSync arrays, no telemetry, about 200 tests, CI on Node 20/22/24
No MCP tool cost; skill descriptions cost about 330 tokens of the 2% listing budget
Exit codes are usable as fail-open gates in a self-written PermissionRequest or PostToolUse hook
cons: Auto-invocation depends on Claude choosing to run `jev`. No Pre/Post/PermissionRequest hook is shipped, so the 'never prompt me' goal is only weakly met
Compaction hook needs the early-access function-hooks flag and TYPESAFE_API_KEY, hardcodes api.typesafe.ai, sends full transcripts and replaces the summary with lossy truncation. Do not enable it
Skill pre-approves Bash(npx jevctl:*), which fetches unpinned npm code; use a pinned global install. Hidden daily `npm view` call (set JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1)
Skill tells Claude to trust `curl | jev screen` pass results, but Jev is injection-sensitive; 12 days old, single maintainer, /alpha endpoint

entries.name: Brainwires/jevwire (npm jevwire, Claude Code plugin "jev")
entries.what: Third-party (Brainwires, single author Josh Guyette) Claude Code plugin plus MCP server plus library built on TypeSafe's System One /v1/systemone endpoint. It has 7 MCP tools (jev_rank, jev_pick, jev_verify, jev_evaluate, jev_gate_action, jev_next_step, jev_list_models), and a large hook suite that runs without the user or model asking. The hooks: a PreToolUse gate on Bash/Write/Edit/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit/Agent/Task/mcp__*; a semantic lint of edits; a git-commit diff scope and staged-secret check; a PostToolUse prompt-injection screen on WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__*; a Stop-hook check that the final message is not unfinished and that its claims match git diff HEAD; and UserPromptSubmit bookkeeping. Hot-path hooks are type:"http" posts to a loopback daemon on 127.0.0.1:10522. It is a guardrail and verifier, not a coding accelerator.
interface: Hook PostToolUse and PostToolUseFailure (Approval / async ledger)
Slash commands /jev:on, off, status, why, calibrate, daemon
entries.autoInvocation: Mostly deterministic hooks, which is what the user asked for. PreToolUse/PostToolUse/Stop/UserPromptSubmit fire automatically with no prompting and are gated by a deterministic prefilter (no model call on read-only or in-project ordinary calls). The 7 MCP tools plus the jev-decisions skill are model-discretion (description trigger) and Opus may rarely choose them. So the automatic part is guardrail work (risk notes, injection screen, stop check, lint, commit scope), not acceleration of coding tasks such as ranking files. Hook types are 'http' and 'command', and both run for all of the user's Bash/Edit/MCP calls in addition to the existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks.
security: No curl|sh installer, no postinstall script, and no telemetry found. The only child_process use is src/hooks/daemon/control.ts spawning its own daemon, and the Stop claim check runs git via execFile with an argv array and GIT_EXTERNAL_DIFF/GIT_PAGER stripped (SECURITY.md). The committed bundles (hook.mjs, mcp.mjs at 40k lines) are not auditable line by line, but CI checks they match the source.

The API key is sent to a local HTTP daemon on a fixed port. Every http hook sends Authorization: Bearer $CLAUDE_PLUGIN_OPTION_API_KEY and X-Jev-Env-Key: $TYPESAFE_API_KEY to http://127.0.0.1:10522 (hooks.json). SECURITY.md itself lists the residual risk that another local user who binds 10522 first receives the key and the hook payloads, and says multi-user hosts are unsupported. That is fine on a single-user box.

The daemon authenticates with a sha256 timingSafeEqual key comparison. But a hook post with no matching key is still served if its body names a known session id (SECURITY.md), and a keyless daemon runs unauthenticated. /v1/health is unauthenticated and leaks no secret. The key is never logged, and redact() in server.ts masks it in errors.

The key does not appear in argv. The MCP server receives it via env (JEV_PLUGIN_API_KEY), which is visible to the same UID via /proc/<pid>/environ. The bare-MCP install form `claude mcp add ... -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=sk-...` stores the key in plaintext in ~/.claude.json.

Jev is explicitly not injection-hardened (SECURITY.md). Text in a fetched page or file that argues for its own approval can shift the probabilities, and the plugin is advisory only. It can never emit permissionDecision allow, and Claude itself can bypass a tripwire by re-issuing the call with '# jev:intended <reason>'. It does not deliver security enforcement. Under bypassPermissions, ask_on_trip does nothing, so the only effect is that Claude sees a deny or note.

Its notes and tripwires inject text into Claude's context that is shaped by untrusted content (tool inputs and results). The README says the wording is deliberately declarative to avoid tripping Claude's injection defenses. That adds noise and gives the user's existing GitNexus, caveman and secret-guard hooks a new interaction surface.
entries.dataEgress: Sent to the configured Jev endpoint (TypeSafe by default; OpenRouter if repointed), per SECURITY.md and the source. (1) PreToolUse: the tool name plus a redacted excerpt of the arguments, capped at 4,000 chars (Bash commands, file paths, Write/Edit content excerpts, and MCP tool inputs), together with the last 3 user prompts (2,000 chars each) and the captured Agent/Task subagent prompt. The gate is skipped for read-only and allowlisted calls (prefilter). (2) Edit lint: the edit content, the current file for a Write, and up to 12 rule lines extracted from CLAUDE.md. (3) git commit: the staged diff (git diff --cached). (4) PostToolUse screen: the whole WebFetch/WebSearch/mcp__* result in 16,000-char chunks, up to about 128k chars, which covers all GitNexus, Playwright and other MCP outputs. (5) Stop: the final message (tail 6,000 chars) plus the git diff HEAD and the extracted claim sentences. (6) Explicit MCP calls: file contents when jev_rank paths/glob or jev_verify evidence_path are used (up to 512 KB per file). Redaction is regex-based. Nothing is sent to any third party other than the Jev endpoint, and no telemetry was found. Through OpenRouter, that traffic also goes to OpenRouter and its upstream provider under OpenRouter's data policy. For client projects this is a real confidentiality concern: diffs, code excerpts and MCP outputs leave the machine on every judged call.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Every hook exits 0 with empty output on any error, and the http hooks are ignored if the daemon is down or the connection is refused. The hook Jev timeout is 1,500 ms with 0 retries (src/hooks/config.ts:99-104), under a 5 s Claude Code hook timeout. The MCP server uses a 30 s deadline with up to 3 retries and jittered backoff (429/5xx/network only), so an explicit tool call can stall up to 30 s. A missing key means the judgment hooks are inactive; only the deterministic regex checks (rm -rf ~, force-push main and similar) still run. A retired or wrong model id (for example jev-1.13.0 on OpenRouter) or a schema mismatch fails silently as error records in the log, so there is no visible breakage, and no protection either. The one fail-closed-like behavior is the Stop block, at most once per prompt; false positives have happened (0.6.3 fixed a case where the check blocked its own author). Port 10522 in use means the hooks are inactive for the session, with a warning.
entries.contextCost: MCP: 7 tools. By source, description plus zod schemas total roughly 25-35k chars, so about 6-9k tokens of tool definitions loaded every session. The rank tool's description and schema are the biggest, and the whole rank.ts file is 26 KB. This is an estimate: I did not run the server, and 2.3-26 KB per tool file includes code. The plugin manifest passes 13 env vars. No MCP server 'instructions' text was found. The skill jev-decisions adds one description line (about 100 tokens), with the body loaded only on trigger. Hook-injected text: notes are capped at 5 per prompt, deduped for 30 min, and described as rare in advisory mode, with the sample messages 40-80 tokens each. Tripwires and stop blocks are a few lines plus an extra Claude turn to re-issue the call. Six slash commands are also registered. Each judged hook also registers a statusMessage that flashes in the UI.
pros: It is the only candidate found that delivers what the user literally asked for: automatic use via hooks, with no 'use jev' prompt. The PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Stop and SessionStart hooks in plugin/hooks/hooks.json fire on their own, and a deterministic prefilter keeps most calls at about 3 ms and $0.

The base URL is an env var (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, config.ts:109 and hooks/config.ts:252). OpenRouter's documented path /api/v1/systemone matches the client's hard-coded /v1/systemone when the base is https://openrouter.ai/api, so the switch is likely config-only. The body {state, model, questions} is plain.
Careful engineering against Jev's limits: it never asks Jev to count or reason, uses regex gates plus Noul questions, and pins the model version to avoid probability drift (config.ts:33-40).
Fail-open everywhere, with a 1.5 s hook timeout, 0 retries, a memo and a loopback daemon that keeps the TLS connection warm. Cost is negligible: about $0.064 for a heavy day.

The Stop verify catches a real class of Claude errors: claiming tests pass when the ledger says they failed, and claiming files that do not exist (git diff HEAD check). Commit checks (staged-secret tripwire, pr_scope, message vs diff) fit daily work.

Never prompts the user and is compatible with bypass mode: notes go to Claude and denies are answerable by Claude, and it never returns allow, so it cannot override the user's permission rules. Kill switches are simple: JEV_HOOKS_DISABLE=1, gate=off, /jev:off.
MIT license, dependency-free hook bundle, no postinstall, no telemetry found, extensive tests and CI, transparent SECURITY.md, and it honestly admits it is advisory.
cons: The default target is TypeSafe direct. Nothing in the code knows OpenRouter, and I could not verify that OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone envelope matches; the OpenRouter docs URLs I tried returned 404. A mismatch means parseEvaluateResponse throws and every hook silently fail-opens. The model id also has to be changed to typesafe/jev-1.13, and the hooks.json header X-Jev-Env-Key is hard-wired to $TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so the OpenRouter key must be exported under that name.

Data egress is large and broad for client work: Bash commands, edit contents, staged diffs, git diff HEAD, the final message, prompts, and the whole output of WebFetch and every MCP tool (GitNexus, Playwright) go to a third party (and via OpenRouter, to a further one). Redaction is a regex 'net, not a guarantee'. This may conflict with client NDAs.

The value is guardrails, not coding acceleration. Under bypass/auto permission mode the user has chosen no gating, and this adds a classifier whose output goes only to Claude, which can override with '# jev:intended'. It is not a security boundary, and Jev is not injection-hardened (SECURITY.md). It overlaps the user's existing secret-leak guard and adds another PreToolUse layer on the same Bash calls as GitNexus and the secret guard.

Synchronous PreToolUse hooks add about 0.2-1.2 s to judged calls (p95 1.17 s), plus a Jev call on Stop, on top of the 3 ms prefilter cost. OpenRouter's extra hop is unmeasured. False positives and extra Claude turns are possible (0.6.3 fixed a Stop check that falsely blocked its own author twice; SECURITY.md notes trips add turns).

Context and complexity cost: 7 MCP tools (about 6-9k tokens estimated) that Opus will rarely call, 6 slash commands, 13 plugin env vars, and a resident daemon on a fixed port 10522 with the API key sent in headers. The port-squat risk is documented, and a port conflict silently disables the hooks.

Immature: created 2026-09-17, 32 commits, one contributor, 22 stars, no GitHub release, six 0.x releases in four days. It comes from a third party that could ship breaking changes or malicious code via the marketplace, and Jev itself is a beta model that Theo-style critics call a flash-router. Bundles are 40k-line minified-style artifacts that are hard to audit.

Some hooks are noisy by design (routing, lint, commit note) and the user cannot easily tell whether fail-open silence means 'fine' or 'broken'. /jev:status is the only visibility, with no OpenRouter smoke check.
entries.verdict: This is the best fit found for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement, because it does everything through deterministic hooks with prefilters, fail-open behavior and negligible cost, and OpenRouter is probably reachable with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a model id change. But it is a young single-author guardrail plugin (not a productivity booster) that sends diffs, commands and all MCP output to a third party. Pilot it on personal projects only, after verifying the OpenRouter schema with one manual call, and consider disabling screen_results and lint for client repos.

entries.name: @garygentry/system1 (decide CLI + System 1 plugin)
entries.what: Third-party monorepo (not TypeSafe official) shipping (a) the `decide` Node CLI (npm @garygentry/system1) that sends closed judgements (noul/choice/score) about files, diffs, logs or piped text to typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions, with per-repo egress consent, secret scrubbing, spend caps, thresholds and replayable fixtures; and (b) a Claude Code/Codex/Pi plugin "system1" with an `ask` skill (model-invocable, tells the agent when to call decide), a UserPromptSubmit routing-hint hook, and an opt-in Stop-hook "done-check" guard that judges the session diff against TASK.md / .system1/done.md criteria and blocks the stop once if a criterion is clearly unmet. No MCP server; integration is CLI + skill + hooks.
interface: CLI decide doctor / ping / config egress / guard enable|disable|status / spec list|check / route / scout(opportunities)
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. (1) Skill-description trigger: the `ask` skill is model-invocable, so Claude loads it on its own when it is about to grind through many items, but the author's own evidence says unaided Claude reaches for it only ~66% of positives. (2) Deterministic-ish hint hook: UserPromptSubmit regex nudges Claude (91% of positives on the author's blind set, no false triggers), still model-discretion whether to comply. (3) Deterministic hook: Stop done-check runs by itself every stop once enabled per repo, no model choice involved. No transparent interception of every Claude tool call or Opus reasoning. It does not use Jev for PreToolUse gating (destructive-command spec exists in cookbook but is a recipe you must wire yourself).
security: API key read from OPENROUTER_API_KEY env or ~/.config/system1/credentials (never argv, per README/wiring.ts); sent only as Bearer to the endpoint; doctor/never prints key; does not read project .env

Per-repo egress consent required for live calls (.system1/config.yaml); agent-run `config egress allow` and `guard enable` are refused without user-only flags (--confirm/--i-consent) - but in bypass mode an agent could still be told to run them, so consent is a soft barrier

Always-on scrubber (egress/scrub.ts) redacts sk-or-, sk-ant-, GitHub, AWS, Slack, Stripe, JWT, private keys, url creds and NAME=value secrets; secret-shaped files excluded; out-of-repo content withheld unless --allow-outside; oversize refused not truncated. Explicitly 'a safety net, not a guarantee'

Shells out only to git via execFile (guard/git.ts, sources/read.ts), no shell strings; no telemetry/analytics found in grep; no postinstall in the published package (only devDependency onlyBuiltDependencies esbuild)
Plugin shim may run `npx --yes @garygentry/system1@0.5.1` (downloads from npm) when the CLI is absent - not in hooks (SYSTEM1_NO_NPX=1); SYSTEM1_CLI env can point exec at arbitrary node file

Prompt-injection surface: file/diff/log content is sent to Jev, but Jev returns only typed probabilities, so injection cannot yield free text; the risk is manipulated verdicts (e.g. a repo file saying 'not destructive') and the done-check block message is authored by the tool, not the model
entries.dataEgress: Only in repos with egress consent: the text being judged (file contents, diff hunks, piped logs/output, criteria bullets, files named by criteria, evidence files, untracked new files for done-check), after secret-file exclusion and string scrubbing, to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and onward to TypeSafe's Jev via OpenRouter). Prompts are NOT sent: the UserPromptSubmit hook is local regex only. HTTP-Referer/X-Title headers identify the tool. For client projects this means client code goes to OpenRouter+TypeSafe once consent is granted per repo; consent is per repo, so client repos can simply stay un-consented.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Per-attempt timeout 5 s, up to 3 attempts with 400 ms exponential backoff on 408/429/5xx/529 (transport/openrouter.ts:9-55), so worst case roughly 15 s plus backoff for a manual decide call. Hooks always exit 0 with `|| '{}'` fallbacks; UserPromptSubmit timeout 10 s; Stop hook timeout 60 s but done-check latencyMs default 5000 then 'not checked: ...' note and the stop goes through; missing key/spend cap/provider error also fall through with a visible reason. Missing CLI in the plugin-only install silently skips the check (documented). Replay miss is an error, not invented answer. The agent never gets a fake decision.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, so zero tool-schema tokens. Skill descriptions always in context: ask ~1021 chars, design ~474 chars; guard/scout/setup are disable-model-invocation (they only list names, not descriptions, or are hidden) - approx 400-500 tokens total, plus SKILL.md bodies (ask 7.4 KB ~1.9k tokens) only when loaded. UserPromptSubmit hook injects a one-line hint only on matching prompts (rare by design). Stop hook injects a one-line status per stop when done-check is enabled (e.g. 'System 1 done-check: 2 of 3 criteria met') and a blocking reason when it blocks. Large decide outputs are summarised (--format brief) so raw items do not pass through context.
pros: Native OpenRouter: endpoint https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and OPENROUTER_API_KEY are the defaults (transport/openrouter.ts:5, wiring.ts:40); no patching, matches the user's provider choice

Only candidate I inspected that delivers automatic use without a prompt from the user: model-invocable ask skill + UserPromptSubmit routing hook + opt-in Stop-hook done-check that runs deterministically
Zero MCP tools, so no tool-definition context tax and no extra long-running server process; skills add about 500 tokens
Fail-open everywhere: hooks exit 0 with {} fallback, 5 s per-attempt timeout, done-check 5 s latency cap, 'not checked' notes so a skipped check is never shown as a pass

Serious egress hygiene: per-repo consent (agent cannot grant it), secret-file exclusion, 20+ secret regex scrubber that includes sk-or/sk-ant keys, out-of-repo content withheld, oversize refused, spend guard ($0.05/200 calls, $0.01 per session for done-check), live vs replay labelled
Cost is trivial (about $0.00004 per 700-token item; ~$0.00004-0.00005 per done-check) and outputs are typed, so injected repo text cannot make Jev emit free-form instructions
Coexists with the user's hooks: the Stop and SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit events do not overlap the existing PreToolUse secret guard or GitNexus Grep/Glob/Bash hooks
Honest, measured docs: docs/evaluation.md and calibration.md state Brier 0.028, routing 66% to 91%, and list what is NOT measured (choice, score, other languages)
Spec + fixture system lets useful judgements become offline-replayable tests in CI (decide spec check), good for the user's client projects
Per-repo enablement means client repos can be left un-consented so no client code leaves the machine
cons: Very new and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-22, 91 commits in 8 days, 1 human contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub release, README says 'only its author has used it' and 'Outside users: None yet'; 9 npm versions in 8 days signals API churn (README badge even still says 0.4.0)
Jev itself is a beta alpha endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions): any OpenRouter schema change breaks it; the author states no fallback to another model by design

Jev only pays off on batch or closed-judgement work; for typical daily coding (edit, debug, refactor) the ask skill rarely fires, so value is mostly done-check and occasional log/CI triage; the README itself lists 'not for everything'

Auto-invocation is not fully automatic: the skill and hint rely on Opus choosing to call decide (66% unaided, 91% with hook on the author's own tests); the only deterministic piece is the Stop done-check, which needs TASK.md/.system1/done.md criteria that the user must write and keep updated

done-check false-block risk: when Claude stops to ask a question, it blocked in 9 of 12 measured cases (docs/guard.md); blocks once only, but adds friction; Stop hook plus SessionStart hook run on every session even when dormant (~55 ms)
Requires a global npm install plus the plugin; plugin-only install can silently skip checks after an update because hooks use SYSTEM1_NO_NPX and the npx cache may lack the new version

Consent barrier is only advisory in bypass/auto permission mode: nothing but the tool's refusal logic stops an agent from running the user-only flags if told to, and the user must still run `decide config egress allow` in every repo where they want it
Sends real code/diffs to OpenRouter and TypeSafe once consent is granted: needs client contract review for client projects; scrubber is regex-based ('a safety net, not a guarantee')
Not a PreToolUse gate: it does not intercept dangerous Bash commands or secret reads automatically; the destructive-command spec is a cookbook recipe the user must wire into a hook themselves

Calibration validated only on yes/no over two TypeScript repos with an AI labeller; choice/score/other languages unmeasured, so treat probabilities as rankings; skeptic claim that Jev is a flash-class router remains untested here
Bundled CLI executes unreviewed third-party JS on every prompt and stop (hooks run node with local file reads); I did static review only and did not run it

Repo-controlled trust boundary (missed security issue): a committed .system1/config.yaml can set egress.consent.granted=true, enable the done-check guard, and set `endpoint` to any http(s) URL. Every `decide` call then sends the user's OPENROUTER_API_KEY as a Bearer header, plus scrubbed repo content, to that URL. Any cloned third-party or client repo becomes a key-exfiltration and consent-bypass vector. This is worse in defaultMode auto and bypassPermissions sessions, and the Stop hook can trigger it with no agent action. Mitigations for this user: never install the plugin globally without an env-level SYSTEM1_ENDPOINT pin (env beats both files, load.ts:~176), or use a low-limit dedicated OpenRouter key, and review .system1/config.yaml in any freshly cloned repo before starting a session.

OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in the user's no-secret-leak protected-vars list. The key must reach hook and Bash processes through the settings env or the ~/.config/system1/credentials file. That means an extra secret in the environment of every Claude Bash call, so update the guard first.

Auto-invocation does not cover Claude's autonomous decisions: the UserPromptSubmit hint is a local regex over the user's own prompt. It steers only when the user words a batch or judgement request, and Opus can still ignore it (66% unaided, 91% with the hint on the author's own blind set).

done-check has a low-friction failure mode but real friction in practice: it blocks a stop when Claude stops to ask a question in 9 of 12 measured cases (docs/guard.md). It needs curated criteria files in each repo, and writes .system1/ state (guard/state.json, config, ledger) into the working tree, so client repos need a .gitignore decision.

Data leaves via OpenRouter to TypeSafe (alpha endpoint, no SLA) and the scrubber is 15 regexes with self-described 'safety net, not a guarantee'. Any client contract that forbids third-party code transfer applies once consent is granted.

Very young project: created 2026-09-22, 9 npm versions in 8 days, 0 stars, no GitHub release, a single human author who is the only user. Alpha-endpoint churn or author abandonment is likely to break it, and the plugin pins to the exact npm version 0.5.1.
entries.verdict: Best-fitting integration found for this user: OpenRouter-native, no MCP context cost, fail-open, and the only one with real auto-invocation (ask skill + prompt-hint hook + opt-in Stop done-check). Adopt it as the primary layer but only per-repo with egress consent (skip client repos initially), pin the version, expect Jev to matter mainly for batch triage and done-check rather than everyday edits, and treat it as an early-stage single-author tool.

It does not use /api/v1/systemone. Fail-open: 5 s per attempt, 3 attempts, always exit 0. The Stop hook returns {decision:'block',reason} and honours stop_hook_active. No MCP tools or extra skill-list entries (ask skill only, guard/setup/design/scout are disable-model-invocation)
