Depends on CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1 experimental hooks module and CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE=50; shims override built-in /code-review and /review
Bundles opinionated TDD guard, ponytail and caveman dependencies; router tier mapping tuned for other models

entries.name: @muthuishere/jevx
entries.what: A Go CLI (jevx, stdlib only, closed to 1 author) plus an installed Agent Skill (SKILL.md) and an optional set of Claude Code hook "plugins". The CLI posts {model,state,questions} to any System One URL and prints verdicts (yes/no/unsure, pick key, score level) with exit codes 0 yes, 1 no, 3 unsure, 4 error. Commands: is, pick, filter, rank, ask (batch, saved questions), judge, question, context, defaults, cache, plugin, hook, profile, stats, install/uninstall. `jevx install` copies the skill to ~/.claude/skills, ~/.agents/skills (and ~/.codex/skills), and writes one `jevx hook run EVENT` entry per plugin event into ~/.claude/settings.json (with a .bak file). Shipped plugins (all disabled, shadow mode first): stop-judge (Stop), bash-guard (PreToolUse:Bash), injection-screen (PostToolUse:WebFetch|WebSearch), route (UserPromptSubmit, tells Claude to delegate simple requests to a haiku sub-agent). There is no MCP server. Default endpoint is TypeSafe direct (https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone, model jev-latest, key TYPESAFE_API_KEY); custom endpoints are added as profiles.
interface: jevx question / context / defaults / cache / stats / profile
entries.autoInvocation: Two mechanisms. (1) Skill description trigger: model-discretion, Claude loads the skill when it judges the task is classify/triage/filter/rank/'ask the user A or B'/'before handing back a turn', then runs `jevx ...` via Bash. Most daily coding (edit, debug, refactor) rarely matches, so it will fire only occasionally, and Opus 5.5 may decide to just reason itself. (2) Deterministic hooks (Stop, PreToolUse:Bash, PostToolUse:WebFetch, UserPromptSubmit) that run without any prompting, but ship disabled and need `jevx plugin enable X` + `mode X act`; this is the only truly automatic path. No transparent proxy / router.
security: No API key in argv: keys are referenced as $VAR in profile headers and expanded from env only at request time (core/core.go:604-614); profile list prints the literal. Good.
No telemetry or update check per docs/reference/privacy.md; only network call is the configured System One URL (core.go:673-678, http.Client with per-request timeout).

Folder plugins load from the nearest .jevx/plugins.json walking up from cwd with NO trust prompt (core/core.go:351-368 LocalDir, core/plugin.go LocalPlugins/AllPlugins); a plugin may carry `exec` (runExec -> `sh -c <command>`, plugin.go ~runExec) and `enabled:true, mode:act`. A cloned client/third-party repo shipping .jevx/plugins.json therefore gets arbitrary shell execution on every matching hook event once jevx hook entries are installed (they are, globally, by `jevx install`). Same for .jevx/questions.json changing question wording. Real supply-chain/prompt-injection-adjacent risk on client repos; user runs bypass mode.

Installers: npm postinstall downloads a binary from GitHub Releases and runs `jevx install` (npm/install.js) with NO checksum/signature verification (release publishes checksums.txt but neither install.js nor install.sh checks it); install.sh is curl|sh. Binary is unsigned, fetched over HTTPS from the author's repo; a compromised release = code exec. postinstall exits 0 on failure. The npm package itself has provenance (OIDC trusted publishing in release.yml) but the binary trust is separate.

`jevx install` rewrites ~/.claude/settings.json (writes .bak-jevx-<ts> backup, validates JSON, atomic rename; core.go:1071-1090) and adds hook entries for Stop, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit with no tool matcher (filtering is inside the binary), timeout 20s. Touches the user's global hook setup alongside the secret-guard/GitNexus/caveman hooks.

Redaction exists (core.go:799-815: private keys, xox, AKIA, AIza, JWT, bearer, KEY=value) and is applied by cut() for hook states (plugin StateOf) but README/privacy docs say 'Redaction is your job today' for skill-driven --in/stdin content: whatever Claude pipes into jevx is sent verbatim.
entries.dataEgress: To the configured endpoint (OpenRouter if you add the profile): the question text, the full input Claude passes (stdin, --in, each line of --lines/--states files, so log lines, ticket text, file excerpts, diffs, anything Claude chooses to pipe in; unredacted), merged `## Jev` sections from ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, ~/.codex/AGENTS.md, ~/.agents/AGENTS.md, ~/AGENTS.md and the nearest folder AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, plus --context text. Note: only the ## Jev section is read, not the whole CLAUDE.md. For plugins (if enabled): PreToolUse = tool name + tool_input JSON cut to 3000 chars + cwd (every Bash command, or file content for Write/Edit if you add such a plugin); PostToolUse = tool_input 1500 + tool_response 3000 chars; UserPromptSubmit = user prompt cut to 3000 chars; Stop = last request + agent text + last 25 action summaries in ~1600 chars. Hook states pass through Redact(); skill-driven input does not. Request also carries model name and the Authorization header. Local-only: answer cache (~/.cache/jevx, hash-named, stores answers not inputs), content-free ledger (~/.local/share/jevx/calls.jsonl), verdicts.jsonl (state up to 2000 chars). No other outbound calls.
entries.failureMode: Fails open for hooks and closed for the CLI. Plugin Run() returns Decision{allow} on any error, including missing key, network, invalid reply (core/plugin.go Run fail()). Per-request timeout default 60s with 3 tries on 429/5xx/network with 0.5s*try^2 backoff (core.go:106,648-655), but the installed hook entry has timeout 20 s in settings.json, so in act mode a hung Jev can stall a tool call up to 20 s before Claude Code abandons the hook (non-blocking error). Shadow mode is detached (only ~50ms added) and cannot delay the agent. CLI (skill path): exit 4 on any error, never read as 'no'; strict reply validation (exact question ids, probabilities in [0,1] summing to ~1, choice must be an offered key; core.go:693-728). Missing key: exit 4 with help text naming TYPESAFE_API_KEY (would confuse an OpenRouter-only user unless the profile is default).
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so zero tool-schema cost. Skill: name+description always in the skill listing (~700 chars, ~180 tokens); full SKILL.md (~13.7KB, ~3.4k tokens) loaded only when the description matches, scenarios.md (~10KB, ~2.6k tokens) on demand. Hooks: no injected text unless a plugin fires; route plugin injects ~50 tokens as additionalContext on simple prompts; warn/context decisions add a one-line reason. Each jevx CLI call adds its stdout (small table/lines) to context.
pros: Only candidate reviewed here that is both an auto-triggering skill AND a deterministic hook layer in one install, with zero MCP tool-definition context cost (no tools list; only ~180 tokens of skill description permanently).

OpenRouter switch is genuinely trivial from code: profiles take any URL/headers with $VAR expansion, and the request body {model,state,questions} matches OpenRouter's documented /api/v1/systemone schema; one `jevx profile add` + `profile use`.

Fail-open hooks with shadow-first rollout: plugins start disabled, then shadow (detached, logs only, ~50ms), and only `mode act` can deny/ask; `plugin test`, `plugin log` let the user calibrate on their own sessions before trusting it.
Honest verdict semantics: unsure band and exit code 3, errors exit 4 and are never 'no', strict fail-closed response validation, retries on 429/5xx.

Keys never in argv or config file (env $VAR expanded at request time); content-free ledger, no telemetry, local answer cache makes repeated identical calls free; installer backs up settings.json and removes only its own hook entries on uninstall.

Read-only per-repo context via the `## Jev` section of existing CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md means no extra config files to maintain; folder .jevx/questions.json lets calibrated questions be committed per repo.
MIT, Go stdlib only (no third-party deps to audit), small readable codebase (~2.5k lines of Go); npm publish uses OIDC provenance.
cons: Very new and single-author: repo created 2026-09-27 (3 days before audit), 37 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, 1 fork, npm 0.10.0 to 0.11.0 in two days, INPROGRESS.md documents constant churn (renamed jevcli to jevx mid-flight). Its own docs say 'MCP: none, keychain: none, eval: none'.

Thin test/CI coverage: 9 Go test functions across 6 files; the only workflows are release.yml (build + publish, no `go test` step) and pages.yml. Nothing verifies the hook/settings.json rewriter beyond a few unit tests.

Undisclosed-by-default RCE surface for client work: .jevx/plugins.json in any repo (walked up from cwd, no trust prompt) can define an enabled `exec` plugin that runs `sh -c` on hook events; `jevx install` registers those hooks globally. Cloning a client repo or a third-party repo that ships .jevx/ is enough. Combined with bypass permission mode this is worse than the average skill.

No checksum/signature verification of the downloaded binary in npm postinstall or install.sh despite checksums.txt being published; npm postinstall also auto-runs `jevx install`, which edits ~/.claude/settings.json (global hooks with no matcher, so a process spawn on every tool call/prompt/stop even while disabled). Conflicts with the 'do not modify settings' comfort level and with the existing hook stack (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).

The value for daily coding is unproven and small: skill tasks are batch classification (log lines, ticket triage) that a coding session rarely needs; Opus 5.5 will usually just reason. The author's own notes cite negative evidence that Jev second-guessing a strong model lost accuracy (194 to 173 of 200) and that Stop-judge claims need an eval first. Thresholds (0.35/0.65, destroys 0.8) are uncalibrated defaults; 'act' mode risks false denies on legit commands, and bash-guard duplicates the user's existing secret-leak guard (and Claude Code's own permission system).

Data egress on client projects: skill-driven input is sent verbatim to OpenRouter with no redaction (docs: 'Redaction is your job today'); enabled plugins send every Bash command (3000 chars), prompts (3000 chars) and web tool results to the third party. Privacy-sensitive for client code.

Latency and cost in act mode: +0.4-0.7 s inline on every Bash call (bash-guard) or every prompt (route), hook timeout 20s so a slow Jev can stall up to 20 s; route plugin costs one paid call per prompt. Beyond negligible token price, the latency compounds in long agentic sessions.

Default and error messages are TypeSafe-centric (TYPESAFE_API_KEY help text); OpenRouter needs manual profile setup and model naming (typesafe/jev-1.13 vs jev-latest, which OpenRouter says it doesn't serve as an alias per the jev-mcp docs) and is untested by the author. Uses /v1/systemone, not the Decisions API.
entries.verdict: A clever, clean-code skill+hook layer that is the closest thing to 'Claude Code just uses Jev' without an MCP tool tax, and switching to OpenRouter is a one-line profile. But it is 3 days old with one author, has an unvetted .jevx/plugins.json exec path and unverified binary downloads, and its real auto-invocation (hooks) needs opt-in per plugin; treat as an experiment: install skills only (JEVX_NO_HOOK=1, and do not let npm postinstall touch settings), pin an OpenRouter profile, and try shadow mode before considering act.

entries.name: jeveloper (pur4v)
entries.what: All-in-one Claude Code plugin: Jev consulted before first action each turn, gates every tool call, verifies outputs, Stop 'warden' judges completion, plus path/tree/search/fanout commands and stats.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse *, PostToolUse *, Stop)
pros: OpenRouter first-class (/api/alpha/decisions, ~typesafe/jev-latest, OPENROUTER_API_KEY, wins over TypeSafe key); CI workflow, CHANGELOG, SECURITY.md
Hooks fail open on keyless, timeout (5s) or below threshold; metered stats command
Covers many roles (gate, verify, stop, fanout) in one install
cons: Hooks on every tool call in Pre and Post plus Stop: heavy latency and cost, README admits 'heavy by design'
Blocks the first action of each turn until Jev is consulted; driver mode offloading decisions to Jev is speculative and savings unbenchmarked
Overlaps and would conflict with existing gitnexus/no-secret-leak hooks; keyless mode silently mocks; 1 star, 8 days old

entries.name: jev-cli (Gilbert09)
entries.what: TypeScript Claude Code (and Codex) plugin that wraps Jev in hooks. guard is a PreToolUse gate on Bash/Write/Edit that scores destructiveness with Score/Noul questions and returns allow, ask or deny. screen is a PostToolUse check for prompt injection in WebFetch/Read/Bash output, with modes warn, block or quarantine. done is a Stop hook that catches unsupported completion claims. rank is an MCP semantic-grep tool. guard and screen are on by default; done and rank are off. It calls Jev through @typesafe-ai/sdk POST /v1/systemone and caches answers on disk for 30 minutes.
interface: PreToolUse hook: jev guard (matcher Bash|Write|Edit, timeout 10s)
PostToolUse hook: jev screen (matcher WebFetch|Read|Bash, timeout 10s)
MCP tool: rank (stdio server 'jev' via bin/jev.mjs mcp)
Config: ~/.jev/config.json or JEV_CONFIG_PATH; env JEV_MODEL, JEV_SCREEN_MODE, JEV_DEBUG, JEV_FORCE_ENABLED, JEV_CACHE_DIR, JEV_STATE_DIR, JEV_CODEX_ASK
entries.autoInvocation: Fully deterministic for guard (every Bash/Write/Edit), screen (every WebFetch/Read/Bash) and done (every Stop, a no-op while disabled). This matches the requirement 'never having to prompt use jev'. rank is model-discretion MCP and was called 0 times in 18 benchmark sessions, so it is not effective. The tool description is well written, but does not help.
security: No LICENSE file: gh licenseInfo is null. package.json and plugin.json declare MIT, and marketplace.json lists MIT, so the intent is clear but there is no legal grant in the repo.

No telemetry. The only network egress is the SDK call to baseURL. No fetch, exec or spawn appears in runtime code. The single spawnSync (src/install.ts:151) runs jev's own binary with a fixed payload in `jev install`.

The API key is never in argv. It comes from an environment variable, a plugin userConfig field (sensitive: true) or ~/.jev/config.json in plaintext. The hook command lines contain no secrets. The sdk sends it as an Authorization Bearer header.

Prompt-injection surface: the state sent to Jev contains untrusted command text, file content and web content. Jev's own evals say injected instructions in state can move answers. The guard input is agent-generated, so a compromised model could word a command to look benign. Per the Jev brief, calibration is imperfect. The guard also lets a benign-looking 'allow' skip nothing, since hooks only add gating, but a false allow while bypassPermissions is on has no other backstop.

When screen warns, the hook writes additionalContext into the model's context, and that text includes origin and a content excerpt. The excerpt is attacker-controlled, so this is a small secondary injection channel (screen/decide.ts:127; not deeply audited).

Redaction (src/core/redact.ts:10-28) covers sk-ant-, sk-, ghp_, xox, AKIA, PEM blocks, JWTs and KEY=value assignments. It would catch sk-or-v1-... OpenRouter keys through the sk-[A-Za-z0-9]{16,} pattern only if there are no hyphens after 'sk-or'. The hyphen is not in the class, so 'sk-or-v1-…' would NOT match that generic pattern, though the *_API_KEY=value pattern would. Redaction is regex best-effort and the README calls it 'not a guarantee'.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter, and from there to TypeSafe, if the base URL is redirected. Sent per event: (1) guard, on EVERY Bash/Write/Edit call: the command text (max 4 KB), cwd, repo root, description, and for Write/Edit the file path plus up to 4 KB of new content or old/new string. (2) screen, on EVERY WebFetch/Read/Bash result of 24 bytes or more: up to 40 KB of the output or file content, plus the origin URL, path or command. In practice this is a large share of everything the agent reads and every command output in a client repo. (3) done, only if enabled: the last assistant message plus a transcript summary. (4) rank, only if enabled: candidate paths and file snippets. Everything is regex-redacted for credential shapes first; excludeGlobs suppress only .env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa* and .git/**. Source code, client business logic, DB query output and logs are NOT excluded and will leave the machine. Via OpenRouter the payload also passes through a second third party. Not suitable for client projects under NDA or DPA without explicit sign-off.
entries.failureMode: guard fails CLOSED to 'ask' on timeout (1500 ms per request, watchdog 3000 ms), a missing key, an API or malformed error, an unparseable payload, or a Write/Edit without a file_path (jev.ts, guard/handler.ts:134, cli.ts:35-43). It always exits 0 with JSON, so it never uses exit-2 blocking. Since guard fires on every Bash/Write/Edit, an OpenRouter outage, a 429 on the /alpha endpoint with no SLA, or a missing key turns into a permission prompt on every tool call. The guard ignores permission_mode (only typed at types.ts:13, never read), so it still runs in bypassPermissions and auto. Whether Claude Code honors a hook 'ask' under bypassPermissions is not verified here, but the risk is either constant prompts or a silent override. screen, done and rank fail OPEN and silent. done intervenes at most once per turn. The SDK has maxRetries 2 by default but is bounded by the AbortSignal and the timeout. Node 24 cold start is added on top of each call.
entries.contextCost: Low, and mostly deterministic: one MCP tool (rank), with a description of about 2.4k chars (questions.ts:139-160+) plus a schema of about 1k chars, so roughly 700-900 tokens, only if MCP tools are loaded rather than deferred. The tool is useless while rank.enabled=false, so it is wasted context, and the plugin has no way to drop it short of removing .mcp.json. No SKILL.md, no MCP instructions field and no SessionStart/UserPromptSubmit injection. Hook-injected text appears only on a screen detection (a short warning, possibly quarantined content) and on a done block (a reason). Zero cost on ordinary turns.
pros: OpenRouter is reachable with configuration only: the SDK honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and appends /v1/systemone (sdk dist/index.mjs:58,513,554), and src/core/jev.ts:25 passes only apiKey. Set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, the OpenRouter key as TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13. This corrects the README-level 'no' triage.

The only candidate with real end-to-end evidence: 1,176 Claude Code sessions, guard +29 pts and screen +33 pts on haiku (p<0.001), with raw JSONL in bench/results. It honestly reports done and rank as null and ships them disabled. It also documents its own benchmark artefacts and bugs.

Safe failure design: the wire contract is exit 0 plus JSON only, there is a per-hook watchdog, guard fails closed and screen fails open, and done intervenes once per turn. Unit tests cover the decision logic (about 260 test cases in 9 files across guard, screen, done, rank, hook, redact and cache), plus a 157-case live fixture suite and scripts/smoke.sh for wire contracts.
Compiled dist is committed, so the plugin works with `/plugin install jev` and no build. Config is per-capability, so you can run screen only, or guard only.

screen closes a gap the current setup does not cover: PostToolUse prompt-injection screening of fetched content and file reads, with an excludeGlobs list and a quarantine mode that replaces the tool output. The team's existing hooks are all pre-execution or regex-based.
Thoughtful decision logic: separate thresholds measured over multiple runs, probability mass and tail checks rather than a bare argmax, and a Codex output mapping pinned by tests.
cons: The benchmark applies to haiku and sonnet only. Sonnet shows -3 pts (p=0.388, no measurable benefit) and Opus is never tested. The user's main model is Opus 5.5, which likely has even less headroom, so most of the measured benefit probably does not apply, while the latency and egress costs do.

guard fires on every Bash/Write/Edit, ignores permission_mode, and fails closed to 'ask' on ANY timeout or API error. With an /alpha OpenRouter endpoint with no SLA, a p95 of 600 ms against a 1.5 s cap, and frequent bypassPermissions sessions, this creates either constant interruptions or unclear behaviour. The plugin has no way to disable itself in bypass mode.

Broad data egress: screen ships up to 40 KB of every Read, WebFetch and Bash output to a third party, and guard ships Write/Edit content. Only .env, .pem, .key, id_rsa and .git are excluded. The README also says guard sends 'not file contents', which contradicts guard/handler.ts:104-111. This is a real problem for client projects.

Overlaps and stacks on existing hooks: no-secret-leak (which fails closed), gitnexus (seconds) and existing permission classifiers. Three to four synchronous hooks per Bash call compound latency. The regex redactor does not clearly cover OpenRouter 'sk-or-v1-...' keys, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY would additionally need adding to the no-secret-leak protected list if it is stored as an env var.

No LICENSE file (licenseInfo null) despite MIT metadata. One author, 6 commits over 2 days, 1 star, no release, no external users or issues. The dist bundle is committed, so the audited src may not equal what runs (not verified; the bundle was not built or run here).

rank MCP is dead weight (~700-900 tokens of tool definition, 0 adoption in the author's own benchmark, disabled by default). done is disabled by default and hooks a no-op node spawn at every Stop. Neither the OpenRouter response schema nor jev-1.13 compatibility with these question rubrics has been verified; question wording was tuned against jev-latest on TypeSafe's API.

Jev's independent evals (overconfidence on unanswerable inputs, injections in state moving answers) apply directly: the guard judges attacker-influenced text, and a false 'allow' under bypassPermissions has no second line.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered Jev integration seen, with an evidence-backed benchmark and fail-safe hooks, and it switches to OpenRouter with env vars only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL=jev-1.13). For this user the benchmark benefit does not transfer (haiku-only, no gain on sonnet, Opus untested), guard fail-closed on every tool call under bypassPermissions plus the /alpha endpoint is a friction risk, and screen sends up to 40 KB of every read and command output off-machine, which is a problem for client projects. If tried at all, run a screen-only install on personal repos (guard disabled) after adding OPENROUTER_API_KEY to the no-secret-leak list, and treat it as an experiment.
entries.license: None in repo (no LICENSE file; gh licenseInfo null). package.json, plugin.json and marketplace.json declare MIT.

judge.why: Best-engineered hooks and the only real benchmark (1,176 sessions), but the benefit does not transfer to an Opus main model, guard fails closed on every tool call and screen ships up to 40 KB of every read off-machine.
pros: Deterministic guard (PreToolUse), screen (PostToolUse injection check, with quarantine mode) and done (Stop); per-capability enable and timeouts; screen-only install is possible
Guard measured +29 pts and screen +33 pts on haiku (p<0.001), with raw JSONL; done and rank honestly reported as null and shipped disabled
Wire contract is exit 0 plus JSON with watchdogs; about 260 unit tests, a 157-case live fixture suite, compiled dist committed
cons: Benchmark covers haiku and sonnet only; Sonnet shows -3 pts (no gain) and Opus was never tested
Guard runs on every Bash/Write/Edit, ignores permission_mode and fails closed to 'ask' on any timeout or API error. With the /alpha endpoint and a 1.5 s cap, that means constant prompts on any outage

Egress: screen sends up to 40 KB of every WebFetch/Read/Bash result, and guard sends Write/Edit content, which the README understates. Not suitable for client repos; the regex redactor likely misses sk-or-v1- keys
No LICENSE, 1 star, 2 days of history; rank MCP is dead weight (0 adoptions in 18 sessions); question wording was tuned on jev-latest at TypeSafe

entries.name: weiping/jev-claude-code
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace jev-engineering, plugin jev v0.2.1) that wires TypeSafe Jev into deterministic hooks. Python hooks call Jev via typesafe-sdk with typed Choice/Noul/Score questions and keep all thresholds in code/config: (1) PreToolUse(Bash) permission gate: hard deny regexes, readonly allowlist, else Jev decides allow/ask/deny plus egress and network-requested checks; (2) PostToolUse(Bash) output ladder: chunks output of 80+ lines and shows each chunk in full, excerpt or hidden, saving the original for recall; (3) UserPromptSubmit: conditionally loads project guidance files and suggests project tools per rules.json/tools.json; (4) PreToolUse(Agent) router: downgrades mechanical subagent work to haiku, blocks sensitive work on cheap models, denies duplicate subgoals; (5) skills /jev:init, /jev:stats, /jev:snapshot, /jev:recall plus cheap-worker and readonly-reviewer agents. Defaults to shadow mode (calls Jev and logs, changes nothing) until mode=enforce.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse/PostToolUse on Bash and Agent, UserPromptSubmit, SessionStart); the user never has to say 'use jev'. Skills /jev:recall is also description-triggered. Ships in shadow mode: nothing changes behavior until mode=enforce.
security: API key read from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY by SDK and sent as Bearer header; never in argv. Repo's own .claude/jev/config.json adds a deny rule for echoing the key.

Fixed pip install of pinned typesafe-sdk==0.7.1 at first SessionStart via setup.sh (runs pip install in a venv; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall); transitive deps are unpinned (httpx2>=2, pydantic, tenacity) - supply-chain surface.

Hook input passes untrusted text (commands, script contents, command output, subagent prompts) into a model only for typed classification; no free text returned, so prompt injection can only flip a probability, but a crafted command/output could bias allow/hide decisions. Deny regexes run before Jev.

Permission gate returns permissionDecision 'allow' in enforce mode when Jev confidence >= 0.85: this can auto-approve commands and bypass the user's normal prompt; an attacker-influenced command could be judged benign. Deny-regex list is weak (bypassable by obfuscation, e.g. variable indirection).

Output ladder can hide up to all chunks of long Bash output from the model (only if no error detected at 0.5), a correctness risk not a security one; original saved unencrypted under .claude/jev/state/outputs (gitignored via auto .gitignore) and may contain secrets.
Local logs .claude/jev/logs/decisions.jsonl record full commands and answers, incl. anything secret in commands.
entries.dataEgress: Sent to TypeSafe (or OpenRouter if repointed) on every non-trivial event: (a) each Bash command not matching the readonly allowlist or a deny regex: command string, cwd, repo_root, the latest user prompt (last_prompt.txt) and the first 4000 chars of any script file it runs (python/bash/node/sh/ruby X); (b) every Bash output of 80+ lines: up to 3000 chars per 25-line chunk (up to 60 chunks, so up to ~180 KB of tool output) plus the command and user prompt; (c) every user prompt in projects with rules/tools.json: full prompt text and list of up to 200 changed file names (git diff --name-only, untracked); (d) every Agent dispatch: up to 6000 chars of subagent description+prompt, and up to 50 prior subgoal texts (300 chars each). Not sent: full file contents via Read/Edit, diffs, and the main model context. Note the secret-leak deny patterns only cover .ssh and .env in the command string; secrets echoed in command output (env dumps, logs) would go to the provider.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open (no decision, exit 0). guard() in jevlib.py:332-342 swallows all exceptions; permission_gate/output_ladder/agent_router catch Jev exceptions, log, and emit nothing, falling back to Claude Code's normal permission flow / unmodified output. Client timeout is 4s per attempt with 1 retry and 8s total budget (jevlib.py:316-319, default.json timeout_s 8), hook timeouts 15-20s. So a slow/down Jev costs up to ~8s per Bash call before falling back; no circuit breaker, so every Bash call pays this while Jev is down. Also silent until venv install finishes (run-hook.sh) and if TYPESAFE_API_KEY missing, SDK raises and hook fails open. Caveat: fail-open on the gate means outage = default permissions, which is safe.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no MCP server instructions. Skills: 4 skill descriptions (init, stats, snapshot, recall; recall description ~250 chars) plus 2 agent descriptions, roughly 300-500 tokens total in the system prompt. Hooks inject no text in shadow mode; in enforce mode UserPromptSubmit injects up to 9000 chars (~2.2k tokens) of guidance per prompt only where rules.json matches, and the output ladder shrinks Bash output (net negative context, plus a footer of ~200 chars per trimmed output). Denial/reason messages add small text.
pros: Truly automatic: all behavior is hook-driven (hooks.json:1-28), matching the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev without being asked, with zero MCP tools and near-zero standing context cost.

Right primitive-to-task fit: uses Choice/Noul/Score for classification decisions (permission risk, output relevance, model tier, sensitivity, dedupe) with thresholds in config, which is exactly what a probability-only model is suited for.
Fail-open everywhere: guard() and per-hook try/except emit nothing on Jev failure (jevlib.py:332-342; permission_gate.py:76-80), so an outage or beta breakage cannot brick Claude Code.
Shadow mode by default plus /jev:stats lets the user log Jev decisions for a week against real work before enabling enforce, a sane rollout for a beta model.

Only reads the SDK-level knobs: TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and configurable model make OpenRouter repointing a config-only change (SDK constants.py:6, transport.py:134) - no source edits or fork needed if OpenRouter's schema matches.
Subagent router (haiku downgrade, sensitivity gating, duplicate-subgoal denial) and output ladder target real cost/context savings for a heavy Opus 5.5 subagent user.
Reasonable engineering hygiene for a 3-day-old repo: ruff + shellcheck + unit + e2e CI, MIT license, no postinstall/curl|sh, output originals recoverable via recall.py.
cons: Project is 3 days old, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 8 commits, single-author unreviewed hooks running on every Bash call; plugin update pulls new executable code automatically.

Hardcoded to the TypeSafe SDK (typesafe-sdk==0.7.1); no OpenRouter code or docs. Works with OpenRouter only if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL + model name override behave identically; untested by the author and unverified by me. Model default 'jev-1.13.0' is a TypeSafe name, OpenRouter uses 'typesafe/jev-1.13'.

Weak value for this user: the permission gate is redundant in bypass/auto permission mode (user is not prompted anyway), and its 'allow' output can only bypass prompts, while its 'deny/ask' would newly interrupt bypass-mode sessions and break unattended agent runs.

Adds a blocking network call plus Python venv startup on every non-allowlisted Bash command; overlaps and stacks with existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard and GitNexus Bash hooks (ordering/updatedInput/permissionDecision conflicts possible).

Large data egress for a client-work user: commands, script contents, up to ~180 KB of raw command output, subagent prompts and every user prompt go to a third party (OpenRouter and then TypeSafe). Client code/secrets in output would be transmitted; only .ssh/.env command-string regexes protect it. Needs NDA/client-policy review.

Output ladder is risky: can hide relevant lines from Opus based on a beta model judgment (no-error case only); a 'router-like' model (Theo claim) deciding what the coding agent sees could silently degrade quality.

Operational sharp edges documented in GOTCHAS.md: silent no-op until venv installs (first session does nothing), stale .installing lock blocks forever, no circuit breaker so outage costs up to 8s per Bash call, Python 3.10+ checked silently.

Python subagent-router downgrade assumes the user uses cheap haiku subagents; with Opus main and OAuth subscription the cost saving is not billed per token, so the 'cheaper' benefit mostly doesn't apply; prompt_context needs per-project /jev:init and rules.json curation to do anything.
entries.verdict: Best-in-class example of how to integrate Jev automatically (hooks, typed questions, fail-open, shadow mode), and it is repointable to OpenRouter via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model override, but it is a 3-day-old single-author alpha whose main features (permission gate, model downgrade) add little in bypass mode on a subscription, with heavy data egress. Worth installing only in shadow mode as a measurement tool, or forking/borrowing its hook patterns rather than enforcing it on client projects.

entries.name: skylence-org/claudecode-jev-marketplace
entries.what: Claude Code marketplace with two plugins. "core" is an opinionated Claude Code baseline (fork of core-claude 0.9.8). It bundles a regex judge-hook rules engine, writing-guard, statusline and CLAUDE.md guidelines, plus a POSIX-sh `jev` helper (curl + jq) that calls TypeSafe's System One API. Two hooks use Jev. jev-intent-gate (PreToolUse) asks two Nouls, "was this pinned dependency version backed by a registry or lockfile lookup" and "does this edit raise a version", and blocks with exit 2 if the version looks recalled from memory. jev-research-nudge (Stop) asks one Noul, "did the last assistant turn hedge a checkable fact", and blocks the first stop once to ask for verification. "herdr-agent-org" is a multi-agent org for the Herdr multiplexer. It uses Jev for a tier gauge on dispatch and a review-gate check at accept, and needs herdr >= 0.7 plus HERDR_ENV=1. The repo also carries herdr-plugins (a Rust relay daemon, waker, aw-context). The Jev surface is narrow: two rare-event gates, not a general coding assistant.
interface: plugin herdr-agent-org: tier-gauge, review-gate-check, dispatch-worker, 7 role skills, 4 session hooks, .mcp.json relay
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks. Once the plugin is enabled, the PreToolUse jev-intent-gate and the Stop jev-research-nudge fire automatically, with no user prompt and no model discretion, and hooks.json registers them from the plugin. Both are gated by a regex before Jev is called, so Jev is actually invoked only on dependency pins or manifest edits, and on stops with hedged prose. This is the closest of any candidate to the user's "Claude Code must use it when needed" requirement. The use cases are narrow, however.
security: API key handling is good. The key goes only in an Authorization header via curl; no key appears in argv. It is read from env, a chmod-600 file (with a perms warning) or the macOS Keychain (scripts/jev:71-92, :218).

The cache dir is mkdir -m 700 and only trusted if it is owned by the user and is not a symlink (scripts/jev:206-215). The audit log stores answers plus a checksum of the state, not the state itself (:22-24).
There is no curl|sh installer, no npm postinstall and no telemetry. It is pure sh + jq + curl. Install is via /plugin marketplace, ref main (a moving target, not pinned to a SHA).

The /core:setup skill is invasive. It sets bypassPermissions, disables adaptive thinking, auto-memory and org-memory, sets disableWorkflows, edits ~/.bashrc, appends to ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, and deletes other hook entries by regex (judge-hook.sh, writing-guard.sh, research-nudge.sh). It also installs its own judge-hook that fires on every tool call. This would collide with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks and conflicts with their CLAUDE.md conventions. It is avoidable by installing only the two Jev hooks by hand.

Prompt-injection surface: transcript content (user messages, commands, assistant text) is sent to Jev as DATA in a typed-answer model, so injection can at most flip a probability. It fails open, so injection cannot cause a lockout. It could steer a block/no-block decision. No shell execution of untrusted data was seen in the Jev hooks; the tool input is passed through jq --argjson.
The regexes are a safety net, not a security boundary. The repo says so in judge-rules.json `_caveats`.
entries.dataEgress: Per README "What leaves the box" and the code. jev-intent-gate sends the tool_input (the full Bash command or the Edit/Write content and path, which can include file contents being written to package.json/composer.json), the last 3 user messages (each truncated to 1500 chars) and the last 12 shell commands (400 chars each). It sends these only after a regex pre-match on a pinned dependency install or a package.json/composer.json edit. jev-research-nudge sends the last assistant turn (up to 12000 chars). It sends it only when that turn contains a hedge word (might, may, probably, likely and so on), which is common in prose. The herdr tier gauge sends the lane brief. The review gate sends file paths, commit subjects and the --stat summary; the diff is sent only if JEV_SEND_DIFF=1. All of it goes to api.typesafe.ai today (or the OpenRouter host after patching). This is client-project data leaving the machine. JEV_DISABLE=1 per repo turns it off. The existing secret-leak guard does not cover these hooks; user messages or commands containing secrets would be sent.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere. With no key, JEV_DISABLE=1, a timeout, a non-2xx status, an unparseable reply or missing jq/curl, `jev` prints nothing and exits 0, and the hooks allow (scripts/jev header :15-19, :186-189, :203-204, :228-238). Timeout is JEV_TIMEOUT, default 5 s (curl -m), applied to the whole request. A worst case of 5 s is added only on a slow or down Jev at a matching event. Caller bugs (unknown set or invalid state) exit 2, which for a hook means block, but the bundled hooks pass fixed sets. The hooks themselves fail open on missing jq or transcript. The only new blocking behavior is exit 2 when Jev answers below its thresholds.
entries.contextCost: Very low. There are no MCP tools in the core plugin. The Herdr plugin adds a relay MCP (http://127.0.0.1:7431/mcp) that will not connect unless the Herdr daemon runs. core adds 5 skill descriptions (setup, doctor, session-handoff, uninstall-claude, purge-claude-user-scope). The setup description alone is about 1.2k chars, so roughly 600-900 tokens in total for the skills list. herdr-agent-org adds 7 more skills, which the user does not need. No MCP server "instructions". Hooks inject text only on a block, as a one-line templated reason of about 100 tokens. However, /core:setup appends a full guidelines block (Advisor, Decisive Thinking, Coding, Review Mindset, Writing) to the user's global CLAUDE.md, which is a permanent per-turn context cost and would override the user's own conventions.
pros: The only candidate seen that is truly automatic, through deterministic hooks (plugins/core/hooks/hooks.json), with no user prompting and no reliance on model discretion.

Careful integration design. Jev is used only at rare event boundaries behind regex gates. Every call fails open with a 5 s cap. There is a request-checksum cache, an audit log of answers (jev-audit.jsonl) and a stub mode for tests (scripts/jev header).

Reusable pattern. scripts/jev is a small POSIX sh + curl + jq client. Base URL and model are env-overridable (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MODEL), and questions and thresholds are externalized in jev-questions.json with a per-box overlay. It is easy to retarget to OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone.
The key is never in argv and can live in a chmod-600 file, which fits the user's security posture. No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry.

Solves a real Claude Code failure mode. Version pins recalled from memory are caught before they land, and the intent gate is deterministic-first (a lookup-regex short-circuit skips Jev when `npm view` was run). Its comments note that judge-hook's `claude -p` escalate path is inert on OAuth logins, which matches the user's login type.
Test scaffolding exists. There is jev.test.sh (stub-driven), judge-hook.test.sh (about 40 KB) and a GitHub Actions matrix on ubuntu and macOS.
cons: No OpenRouter support at all. The repo has zero mentions of openrouter, and it uses TypeSafe direct with a TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The OpenRouter patch needs TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, an OpenRouter key in place of the TypeSafe key, and JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13. It relies on OpenRouter's System One schema matching TypeSafe's ({state, model, questions} in, .answers out), which is unverified. `jev doctor` would break (it calls /v1/models).

The Jev use cases are tiny and niche. Two Nouls decide a dependency-pin check that a plain regex plus the lookup short-circuit mostly handles. One Noul decides a hedged-fact nudge. Neither adds much to a senior dev's daily flow, and the hedge Stop hook can be false-positive noise, forcing an extra Opus turn (hedge grep matches 'may', 'likely' and 'might' constantly, which triggers Jev on many turns).

/core:setup is heavy-handed and conflicts with this user's environment. It forces bypassPermissions, disables adaptive thinking and both memory systems, disables workflows, writes ~/.bashrc, appends a large block to the global CLAUDE.md and strips hook entries by regex. It also adds a second judge-hook PreToolUse rules engine on every tool call beside the user's existing secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks. To use it safely the user would have to cherry-pick the two Jev hooks and skip the setup skill. The plugin also asserts it 'replaces core-claude' (a plugin the user may not have), and the hooks.json ships judge-hook unconditionally, so installing the plugin alone gives the extra hook.

Immature and single-author. It was created 2026-09-19 (11 days old), has 14 commits, 1 contributor (Jonas Vanderhaegen), 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, no license file (GitHub licenseInfo null; only plugin.json says MIT) and the plugin version is 0.2.4. It installs from ref main, so any push lands in the user's hook chain unreviewed.

Data egress of client code and conversation. The last 3 user messages, the last 12 shell commands, manifest edit contents and the last assistant turn (up to 12 KB) are sent to a beta third-party endpoint. This is unsuitable for confidential client projects without a per-repo JEV_DISABLE=1, and it is outside the existing secret-leak guard's coverage.

Half of the marketplace (herdr-agent-org, org-relay, org-waker, aw-context) is irrelevant unless the user runs the Herdr multiplexer. It adds 7 skills and a local MCP entry that will just fail to connect.

Thresholds (0.6, 0.7) are uncalibrated 'starting points' from vendor cookbooks, not measured. A false-positive block at PreToolUse under bypass mode interrupts flow. The model is pinned to jev-1.13.0 with a 5 s timeout, and the README measured 1.1-1.5 s, well above the claimed 70-500 ms.
entries.verdict: It is the best reference for automatic, deterministic Jev use inside Claude Code: fail-open hooks behind regex gates, and a clean env-configurable `jev` shell client. Do not install the plugin as shipped. /core:setup would override the user's permission mode, memory and thinking settings and add a competing judge-hook, and there is no OpenRouter code. Instead lift scripts/jev and the two hooks (jev-intent-gate, jev-research-nudge) into a personal plugin, point them at OpenRouter's System One endpoint with typesafe/jev-1.13 after a real schema check, and accept that the payoff is narrow.
