entries.name: yusupsupriyadi/jev-skill (jev plugin for Claude Code)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (also cross-agent skills) with 3 hooks and 5 skills. A UserPromptSubmit hook sends the prompt plus names and descriptions (truncated to 200 chars) of every installed skill, command and subagent to Jev as a 'choice' tournament (chunks of 200 options, then a run-off, plus a triage noul/score call). It injects a "[jev] Suggested skill / close second / suggested subagent / workflow size" block into Claude's context. A Stop hook judges each turn that changed files or ran commands. It sends the final message, changed paths, shell commands run and by default a git diff (12k char cap, untracked files included). Findings (unverified claim, needs tests, secret, risk, reviewer) are parked on disk and replayed at the top of the NEXT prompt. Everything is advisory and fail-open.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit + Stop + SessionStart) via plugin hooks.json, with no user prompting needed. Only after a key is present; skills (/jev:*) are extra and manual. This directly meets the 'Claude Code must use it without me saying so' requirement, although the value is limited to advisory hints (skill suggestion, post-turn nag), not delegating actual work.
security: API key handling is good: config store written with mode 0o600 plus chmod (lib/setup.mjs:50-53); setup skill pipes the key via stdin (--key -) so it is not in argv; env var wins over store; a key is only sent to its own provider; key is verified before it is saved.

But /jev:setup asks the user to PASTE the key into the chat, so it enters the Anthropic conversation context and transcript; env var OPENROUTER_API_KEY avoids this and is the better path for this user.
Plugin option mirroring copies /plugin-entered keys into the plaintext config.json (0600) on every session start.

No curl|sh, no postinstall, zero runtime dependencies for the plugin. The installer (cli/) has 2 npm deps and runs spawnSync('claude ...', {shell:true}) with fixed args; the plugin route needs none of it.
Hooks only shell out to git (spawnSync with arg array, 5s timeout, path filtered to inside cwd). No eval, no user-controlled shell strings.

Prompt-injection surface: output is templated from numeric answers and skill ids/descriptions taken from local skill files (200-char cap) and injected into context as additionalContext. Model output is typed so Jev cannot inject prose, but a malicious third-party skill description is echoed into context (low risk). Injected text says 'not an instruction'.
entries.dataEgress: Per prompt (routing): full user prompt text, project hint (cwd basename, git_repo flag, detected languages), and id + first 200 chars of description of EVERY installed skill/command/agent (about 27k tokens for 537 entries per the README; 3 to N parallel calls). Per turn (judge, Stop hook): Claude's final message (up to 4000 chars), list of changed file paths (max 40), every Bash command the turn ran (with failed flag; commands can embed secrets or client paths), and by default the git diff of changed files (12k chars) including untracked files up to 64KB each (new .env-like files are not excluded by name, only by .gitignore). All of it goes to openrouter.ai (and OpenRouter's upstream provider TypeSafe). For client projects this is source-code egress to two third parties unless send_diff=false / judge_enabled=false. There is no per-repo allowlist or secret redaction; the plugin's own secret-check runs in the model, not before sending.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open everywhere: runHook swallows all errors and exits 0 (hook-io.mjs:84-94); no blocking decision is ever emitted. No key means completely idle. Per-call timeout defaults 2500 ms (judge min 4000 ms) via AbortController; failed chunks are dropped via Promise.allSettled; failed triage defaults to 'is task'. Hook timeouts (8s route, 15s Stop) are in hooks.json. Worst case the user waits about 2.5 s (parallel calls) + 2.5 s (sequential run-off) ~5 s before the prompt goes through with no suggestion. Stop hook is synchronous at end of turn (up to 4+ s). Bad keys or no credit (402) just silently yield no suggestion, so it can rot unnoticed unless /jev:doctor is run.
entries.contextCost: Static: 5 skill entries (name + description each ~250-400 chars, ~400-500 tokens total in the skills listing), zero MCP tools, zero MCP server instructions. Dynamic: UserPromptSubmit injects ~120-200 tokens ([jev] pick + description + close second + subagent + size + disclaimer) only when a suggestion clears the threshold (relevance>=0.5), plus 50-100 tokens of judgment recall at the next prompt when findings exist. Negligible compared with other MCPs. Note the important side effect: suggestions on every task prompt add a small nudge that may conflict with the user's existing hooks (GitNexus) or skills. The 27k-token figure is what is sent to Jev, not to Claude.
pros: Only candidate found that gives truly automatic, deterministic Jev use in Claude Code via hooks (UserPromptSubmit + Stop), with no 'use jev' prompting, matching the user's core requirement.

Native OpenRouter support with correct alpha endpoint (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions) and ~typesafe/jev-latest slug, auto-selected when OPENROUTER_API_KEY is set; also TypeSafe direct as fallback; JEV_API_URL/JEV_MODEL overrides in case the alpha path moves (providers.mjs, config.mjs:80-130).
Strictly fail-open and advisory: every hook error is swallowed, exit 0, never blocks a tool call (hook-io.mjs:84-94), so it cannot break the bypass/auto workflow; idle with no key.
Zero MCP tools and near-zero static context cost (5 short skill descriptions); dynamic injection ~150 tokens and only when confident.

Sensible design for Jev's strengths: typed choice/noul/score questions, tournament for >255 options, gate on 1-P(none), judge compares claim vs commands actually run (the 'claimed done, ran nothing' check) - a genuine use of a calibrated classifier.
Key hygiene: 0600 store, stdin-based key entry, key verified before save, env var precedence; granular kill switches (JEV_ROUTE, JEV_JUDGE, JEV_SEND_DIFF, JEV_ROUTE_EXCLUDE, JEV_TIMEOUT_MS).
Clean small codebase (~2.3k lines incl. skills), readable, no dependencies, MIT, good test coverage of hook path with mock server.
cons: Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-22, 18 commits in 2 days, 1 star, 0 forks, no releases, no CI, version 0.4.0 labelled by author's README as only verified on Windows; expect breakage.

Value is modest: with this user's small catalog (a few dozen skills: gitnexus-*, caveman, dougthepug, etc.) skill routing adds little; the README itself says it is not worth it for a handful of skills. Claude already sees skill descriptions.

Data egress is heavy for client work: whole prompts, all skill descriptions, Claude's final messages, every shell command run and a git diff (incl. untracked new files) go to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every turn by default (send_diff=true). Needs send_diff=false or per-project disabling for client repos; no secret redaction, no repo allowlist.
Latency tax: 1.5-4 s (README) synchronous on every task prompt plus up to ~4 s on the Stop hook each file-touching turn; run-off call is sequential. Noticeable in a daily workflow.

Judgment verdict only surfaces on the NEXT prompt (Stop hook cannot inject), so 'unverified claim' warnings arrive late and may be stale; threshold heuristics (0.7/0.4/score>=2) are untested against real-world false-positive rates; Jev has no reasoning trace so findings are just labels.

Silent failure mode: expired credit (402), rate-limit or alpha API path changes result in no output at all, so the integration can die unnoticed; /jev:setup asks user to paste key into chat (enters transcript) unless env var is used.

Overlap and interaction risk with existing hooks (GitNexus graph-context pre/post hooks, caveman hooks): another UserPromptSubmit additionalContext injector and a Stop hook adding latency; the suggested-skill hint may fight with the user's own skill conventions.

Depends on the alpha OpenRouter Decisions API and on Jev quality (skeptic claim it is a flash router unverified); uses 3-N parallel requests per prompt which multiplies rate-limit exposure. Tests were not run and live behaviour not verified here.

Route hook reads input.user_prompt but Claude Code sends `prompt` (docs, live capture in claude-code#77167, user's own caveman hook), so skill/subagent routing silently never runs; remaining value is only the Stop judge.
Hooks use bare `node` on PATH in exec form. The user's settings override PATH, so this may silently fail; a wrapper command with an absolute node path would be needed.
Floating alias ~typesafe/jev-latest is the default model, and the fallback model is never used in hooks, so alias drift or removal gives silent total failure. Pin typesafe/jev-1.13 via JEV_MODEL.

Stop-hook egress bypasses the user's no-secret-leak protections: Bash commands (400 chars each), Claude's final message and diffs go to a third party unredacted. OPENROUTER_API_KEY is not in the user's protected-vars list, and plugin key mirroring into config.json adds another plaintext copy.
No activity since 2026-09-23, with 0 issues, 0 forks and 1 star, so there is no external validation and no maintainer response history.
Judge findings arrive one prompt late and are not shown to the user (Stop hook prints nothing), so they only add context noise in bypassPermissions sessions where nothing is reviewing anyway.
entries.verdict: Best-fit integration found for the 'automatic, no prompting' requirement: hook-based, native OpenRouter, fail-open, negligible context cost. But it is a 2-day-old single-author alpha whose benefit is small with a small skill catalog, adds seconds of latency per turn and ships prompts/diffs to third parties by default. Install with OPENROUTER_API_KEY in env, set JEV_SEND_DIFF=false (or judge_enabled=false) and consider judge-only, and verify with /jev:doctor before relying on it for client projects.

verification.note: Verified from source (not executed): OpenRouter support is real and correct. providers.mjs:19-27 has POST https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, model ~typesafe/jev-latest or typesafe/jev-1.13, and env OPENROUTER_API_KEY; jev-client.mjs:92-108 sends {model,state,questions} with a Bearer header; the slugs and endpoint match the OpenRouter Jev docs. Most audit facts hold: fail-open runHook (hook-io.mjs:84-94), Stop timeout floor of 4000 ms (judge.mjs:176), send_diff default true, untracked-file egress limited by .gitignore, 0600 store, no install scripts. The audit missed one critical defect. The route hook (the main feature for this user's 'use it automatically' goal) reads `user_prompt`, but real Claude Code 2.1.x sends `prompt`, so routing is dead and its mock-payload tests hide it. Confidence is medium because I could not run the plugin; the evidence is the current hooks docs, a live payload capture in claude-code#77167, and the user's own working caveman hook. Score drops from 6.5 to 4.5: the Stop judge still works but is late, advisory, adds up to ~4 s per file-touching turn and sends code and commands to third parties. It becomes viable (about 6) if the one-line field fix lands (`input.prompt ?? input.user_prompt`), node is invoked by absolute path, and JEV_SEND_DIFF=false plus a pinned model are set. Not recommended as-is.

judge.why: Verification found its headline feature dead: the route hook reads input.user_prompt, but Claude Code sends `prompt`, so skill and subagent routing silently never runs. Only the Stop judge works, and it is late and advisory.
pros: OpenRouter support is real and correct; fail-open hooks; 0600 key store; no install scripts
The Stop judge still works and could become useful after a one-line fix (`input.prompt ?? input.user_prompt`)
cons: Routing is inert on real payloads, and the mock-payload tests hide the bug
Bare `node` in exec-form hooks under your PATH override; floating ~typesafe/jev-latest default with an unused fallbackModel
Stop judge sends Bash commands and diffs (tracked-file diffs included) unredacted to a third party and adds up to about 4 s per file-touching turn; no activity since 2026-09-23

entries.name: Project1Dev/Jev-MCP (jev-control-plane)
entries.what: Python stdlib-only MCP server (17 tools) plus a 7-event Claude Code hook suite (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SessionEnd) and status line. The hooks send small bounded decisions to typesafe/jev-1.13 on the OpenRouter Decisions API: task class, worker model, subagent tier and count, verification level, whether Bash output should be trimmed, which file or function a task will touch, whether to /clear or /compact, and progress checkpoints. It then enforces some of the results through hook outputs. It can deny or rewrite Agent calls, replace large Bash output with a trimmed version, block Stop once when tests are missing, and (in tmux only) paste /model and /clear into the pane. It is a router and gate for the agent, not a code-quality helper.
interface: MCP jev-route / jev-select / jev-dispatch / jev-checkpoint / jev-event / jev-complete / jev-outcome
MCP jev-completion-check / jev-guard / jev-review / jev-context / jev-context-budget / jev-loop-guard / jev-select-environment / jev-models / jev-bypass / jev-audit
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks for 7 events, so Claude Code runs Jev without the user or the model asking. This is the only candidate style that satisfies 'no prompting'. The MCP tools are model-discretion and are not needed. Hooks activate automatically after `./install.sh --hooks`.
security: Key handling is decent. The key is read from env or ~/.claude/jev/.env (mode 600) and sent only in the Authorization header. It is never in argv (jev/client.py, jev/config.py). Errors are redacted (client._redact), and policy.redact_text scrubs prompt text and secret-shaped strings before egress.
No curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry found. The only outbound hosts are openrouter.ai (Decisions API and the /api/v1/models feed).

HIGH RISK: the hooks can alter agent behaviour. They deny Agent calls (scripts/setup_claude_code.py registers PreToolUse for Agent|Task; claude_code.py:1908), rewrite the subagent model via updatedInput, and replace Bash tool output via updatedToolOutput (claude_code.py:1261). They also block Stop once (claude_code.py:2275-2300). The tests are mocked only, and the code base is 2 days old.

HIGH RISK: jev/autoclear.py spawns a detached process that runs `tmux paste-buffer` and `send-keys` into $TMUX_PANE to type /model and /clear plus the user's held-back prompt. It also edits ~/.claude/settings.json to restore the default model (autoclear.py:242-250). This is on by default inside tmux and is disabled with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0 or JEV_AUTOMODEL=0. A wrong or manipulated Jev answer could clear the conversation or switch the model. /clear needs at least 0.8 confidence.

The prompt-injection surface is moderate. The Jev response is a constrained choice validated against a shortlist and confidence floors, so injected text cannot produce free text. Tool output content is not sent to Jev, but the command string and the size and shape of the output are. Prompts, subagent briefs and repo text can still bias the classification.

scripts/setup_claude_code.py rewrites the user's global ~/.claude/settings.json (backup written). It adds 7 hook groups and a statusLine. It uses `python3 <path>` and a fixed timeout of 10-30 s per hook.
entries.dataEgress: To openrouter.ai only. (1) Task text: the user prompt, secret-redacted and capped at 2000 chars (claude_code.py:274-279, TASK_TEXT_CAP), plus prompt size, intent and risk tags. Also up to 700 chars of Claude's last reply for follow-up prompts (_last_reply). (2) Subagent briefs: description plus prompt, capped at 1500 chars, plus 400 chars of parent task (agent_tier). (3) Bash trim: the command (redacted, 400 chars), the output size, line count and error-like line count, plus 600 chars of task. Output content is NOT sent (claude_code.py:1213-1220). (4) Location chain (locate.py): file paths and one-line summaries (docstring, first comment, top-level names) for up to 400 files, plus 12-line code snippets (160 chars per line) of candidate functions or files for the beam step (EVIDENCE_LINES = 12). So client repo structure and small code fragments leave the machine. (5) Checkpoint evidence counters (files changed, tests run and failed, repeats). Whole files, diffs and tool outputs are not sent in the hook path. The MCP tools jev-review and jev-context can send model-supplied diffs or text if Claude calls them. Retention is per OpenRouter and TypeSafe policy, which I did not check. Client work in the 12-line snippets and file-path lists is a real exposure to consider.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open. jev-cc-hook always exits 0 and catches BaseException (scripts/jev-cc-hook). Handlers record an error and let the tool call proceed (claude_code.py docstring). HOOK_JEV_TIMEOUT defaults to 20 s (JEV_HOOK_TIMEOUT), and the hooks have 10-30 s timeouts in settings. The route call runs in a background process. The prompt waits at most 4 s (autoclear.WAIT, locate.MAX_WAIT = 4.0). apply_pending_route waits for the job at the first Agent/Task call or Stop, up to about JOB_TIMEOUT*2+5 s, then falls back to a default route (job_timeout). A missing key marks the task bypassed with a warning. JEV_OFFLINE=1 or JEV_HOOKS=0 disables it. Two things are not fail-open: the Stop hook blocks once by deterministic rule (not a Jev outage), and the subagent cap denies only on a real Jev 'no'. The default retries count is 0, so one transient error simply skips that decision.
entries.contextCost: The MCP server exposes 17 tools. Tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 20.4k chars in jev/server.py lines 44-515, roughly 5.1k tokens. It sets no server-level `instructions` field. Hooks inject at most one short `[jev] ...` line per task (route_context, for example "run the tests for changed code after your last edit"), plus occasional checkpoint, location ("likely file X") and context-advice lines. Notes shown to the user use systemMessage and cost nothing. The design deliberately keeps injected text small, so I estimate less than 300 tokens per task. Trimming Bash output can reduce context. With hooks alone (no MCP registration), the token cost is near zero. The MCP server is optional and could be skipped.
pros: Only candidate seen that is truly automatic: 7 command hooks fire without any 'use jev' prompt (scripts/setup_claude_code.py EVENTS).

Native OpenRouter: defaults to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (jev/config.py:13-17). JEV_ENDPOINT and JEV_MODEL are overridable, so ~typesafe/jev-latest works.
Uses Jev the way it is designed: typed Choice questions with probabilities, validated against shortlists and confidence floors, with deterministic fallbacks (decide_route, _pick, confident()).
Fail-open hooks with bounded timeouts, a 4 s max prompt wait, background route jobs, and kill switches: JEV_OFFLINE=1, JEV_HOOKS=0, #nojev in a prompt, JEV_TRIM=0, JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0.

Egress is designed to be small and redacted: capped prompt text, and Bash output content not sent for trimming. Zero-dependency Python with no install-time code fetch. Uninstall is supported (`install.sh --uninstall`).
Cheap: about $0.00005 per route call per the code comments. Useful for subagent-tier downgrades, Bash trimming of 12k+ char logs, and stop-gate tests on code changes.
Has an audit log and TUI dashboard to measure whether Jev actually saves anything.
cons: Very young and unproven. Created 2026-09-29, 4 commits, 2 authors, 0 stars, no releases, and the last commit dropped OpenCode support and reworked the install layout. Expect breakage.

Optimised for saving subscription tokens by routing to cheaper models, which conflicts with a user running Opus 5.5 as the main model. It routes workers and subagents to Sonnet/Haiku tiers and can paste /model and /clear into tmux. That trades output quality for cost and changes behaviour silently.

Invasive hooks. It denies or rewrites Agent/Task calls, replaces Bash output with a trimmed version, blocks Stop once, and edits ~/.claude/settings.json. These stack with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman) which also touch the same tool matchers, so conflicting updatedInput or updatedToolOutput results are possible.

Autopilot (autoclear.py) drives tmux with paste-buffer and send-keys and rewrites the default model in settings.json. It is on by default inside tmux and is risky in bypass or auto permission modes. It must be disabled with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0.

Sends prompt text (2000 chars), the last reply (700 chars), subagent briefs, and a file-path and summary index plus 12-line code snippets to a third party (OpenRouter, TypeSafe). That may be a problem for client projects.

Assumes the user has a Claude Code subscription pool and a `claude` CLI (Sonnet worker, Opus reviewer defaults). It does not use the TypeSafe direct API or the /api/v1/systemone endpoint, only the alpha Decisions API, which may change.

Benefit for an Opus-main, senior-dev workflow is modest: the routing, trimming and location hints save tokens, not correctness. Jev's ability to classify tasks better than a heuristic is unproven (skeptics' router claim). The repo is 19k lines for a job that mostly could be done by 2 or 3 hooks.
The MCP server adds about 5k tokens of tool schemas if registered and not deferred, and the tools are redundant when hooks are installed. Install it with hooks only.
Tests are mocked only; no measured latency or quality data was verified.
entries.verdict: The only reviewed candidate that is truly automatic and OpenRouter-native, but it is a brand-new cost-router that rewrites subagents, trims Bash output, blocks Stop and can drive tmux, so it fits an Opus-first, hook-heavy setup poorly. If trying it, install hooks only with JEV_AUTOCLEAR=0, JEV_AUTOMODEL=0 and a low-spend key, and skip the MCP server, or cherry-pick its ideas (Bash trim, subagent tier, stop gate).

entries.name: @ismaelsoilet/jev-harness
entries.what: Tri-runtime (Python/TS/Rust, same logic) "System 1.5" gate toolkit for coding agents: CLI + stdio MCP server + git pre-commit hook + optional Claude Code plugin/skill. Six gates: test-failure triage, abort/doom-loop check, model-tier routing, completion verification, reasoning-effort modulation (produces provider params for GPT/DeepSeek/etc., not applicable to Claude Code), nudge/continue. Deterministic regex heuristics run first and offline (default, no key). With a key it calls Jev System One (Choice/Noul/Score questions) for ambiguous cases and falls back to the offline engine on any failure. It is a wrapper that sends only the test-failure log or step text to Jev; it does not intercept Claude Code itself.
interface: CLI abort-check, route, verify, reasoning-effort, nudge-gate
CLI status, doctor, metrics, export foreman, replay
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger in the Claude Code plugin (skill triggers on test failure / about to declare done / repeating failed approach). No deterministic hook: the repo ships no hooks.json, no PostToolUse/PreToolUse/Stop config for Claude Code. Its own guide advises pasting a CLAUDE.md protocol block, i.e. the user must instruct Claude. This fails the user's requirement of guaranteed automatic use unless the user writes their own PostToolUse(Bash) hook that pipes failed test output to `jev-harness test-gate` (the CLI exit-code contract makes that feasible) and a Stop hook around `verify`.
security: API key sent as Bearer header only; never placed in argv when supplied via OPENROUTER_API_KEY env (MCP server has no key flag). CLI --api-key style flags not verified; the MCP path is env-only.

Credential discovery reads .env files walking up 4 parent dirs from cwd (client.ts:397-421) plus .jev.json api_key and ~/.config/jev/credentials.env and ~/.commandcode/auth.json. It parses only key names it knows, but it does open client-project .env files, which conflicts with a secret-leak guard philosophy; also a hostile repo's .jev.json/.env can silently choose the provider/key (repo-controlled config can redirect which key is used, and .jev.json can set model).
Request body: redactSecrets() strips API keys, JWTs, GitHub/AWS tokens, DB URLs, private keys before sending (client.ts:145,464); shape-based only, README admits it is not DLP.
Error text is scrubbed of the key (client.ts:541,645).

Prompt-injection: input logs treated as data, gates escalate on text that addresses the judge (gates.ts:65-76) and adversarial tests exist; outputs are typed enums, so the model output cannot inject free text. BUT skip_llm=true returns an action_recommendation string like 'pip install X' / 'npm install -D X' derived from the log; docs tell Claude to execute it immediately without deliberation, which is a real supply-chain/typosquat and injection vector when logs come from untrusted code (agent auto-installs a package named in an attacker-controlled error message).

No postinstall script (package.json scripts only build/test); zero runtime dependencies; MIT; npm Sigstore provenance badge. Recommended MCP command is `npx -y` unpinned, so every session pulls whatever the latest publish of a 1-maintainer, 9-day-old package is (18 versions in 9 days).
entries.dataEgress: Offline default: nothing leaves the machine. Live (OPENROUTER_API_KEY present): HTTPS POST to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions containing model, the typed questions, and the state = redacted failure log (head 2,000 + tail 4,000 chars per README privacy matrix) or, for other gates, the proposed step / attempts summary / task description / criteria+evidence text / nudge transcript tail, all as supplied by Claude in the tool call. Payload cap MAX_STATE_CHARS about 32k tokens. OpenRouter then forwards to TypeSafe (provider.only=['typesafe'], no fallbacks). Not sent automatically: source files or diffs, unless Claude passes them as evidence to jev_verify_completion. Because the model chooses what to put in tool args, egress is model-discretion, not bounded by a hook.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by default (failOpen=true, client.ts:279): 401/403 -> immediate fallback to offline simulation with stderr warning and degraded_reason auth_N; 429/5xx/timeout/network/malformed -> retry up to maxRetries=3 with exponential backoff (500 ms base, cap 5 s, honors Retry-After up to 30 s) then offline fallback. Per-attempt timeout 15 s (timeoutMs default). Worst case on a hung endpoint about 45 s plus about 1.5 s backoff for a single tool call, during which Claude Code blocks on the MCP call. Responses carry is_mock / degraded_reason so the model can see it degraded. Never blocks Claude permanently; the offline heuristic answer is returned. No circuit breaker across calls, so each call re-pays the timeout during an outage.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. TOOLS_MANIFEST (mcp.ts lines 20-180) about 8.9 KB of names, long descriptions (Use when / Do NOT use when / Returns), and schemas, roughly 2.2k tokens (chars/4), always resident (or deferred behind ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.1.x, which lowers baseline cost). No MCP server `instructions` field (initialize returns only capabilities.tools). No hook-injected text. If the recommended CLAUDE.md snippet (about 5 lines) is added, minor. Outputs duplicate every field in snake_case and camelCase (skip_llm/skipLlm, is_mock/isMock, etc., mcp.ts result mapping), inflating each tool result.
pros: Real, working OpenRouter support against the correct Decisions endpoint (client.ts:22, :301, :502 with provider.only=['typesafe']), default model typesafe/jev-1.13, OPENROUTER_API_KEY env; no patching needed.
Offline-first and fail-open: works with zero key, zero network, never leaves Claude stuck; degraded_reason and is_mock make degradation visible to the model.
Zero runtime dependencies, no postinstall, MIT, secrets redaction before egress, key scrubbed from errors, local state at 0600.
Ships a Claude Code plugin (plugin.json, .mcp.json, SKILL.md) with a sensible trigger description, and CLI exit-code contract (0/1/2) that is easy to wrap in your own PostToolUse hook.
Real test suite, tri-runtime parity tests, CI matrix, calibration replay harness with ECE, npm provenance; unusually rigorous for a 9-day-old repo.
Uses Jev the way it is designed (typed Choice/Noul/Score questions, probabilities, uncertainty/entropy thresholds) rather than as a chat replacement.
cons: Not automatic: MCP tools plus a skill rely on Opus deciding to call them; no hooks.json shipped; docs recommend editing CLAUDE.md to tell Claude to use it, which is exactly what the user wants to avoid.

Value proposition is mismatched to this user: goal is saving frontier tokens on missing-package/flaky errors, but Opus 5.5 on a subscription resolves 'ModuleNotFoundError' in one turn anyway; the tool call round trip can cost more than it saves. Most gates (route tiers, reasoning-effort provider params for GPT/DeepSeek/Qwen) cannot be applied to Claude Code's own model.

Overwhelmingly offline regex heuristics; Jev is only consulted for ambiguous cases, and the published accuracy numbers come from engine=mock, so they do not validate Jev; effort and nudge gates measured 0.625 accuracy.

skip_llm=true plus 'execute the recommended command without deliberating' guidance creates an auto-install path driven by log text (typosquat/injection risk), risky on client projects in bypass/auto permission mode.

Credential resolver reads .env from cwd and 3 parent dirs, .jev.json (repo-controlled) and other providers' keys with fixed precedence (TYPESAFE > CMD > VERCEL > OPENCODE > OPENROUTER), so it may reads client .env files and pick the wrong provider; conflicts with a secret-leak guard mindset.
Unpinned `npx -y` in recommended MCP config from a single-maintainer, 10-star, 9-day-old package with 18 releases; supply-chain and cold-start latency exposure.
Fail-open path can stall a call up to about 45 s during outages (15 s timeout x 3 attempts) with no cross-call circuit breaker.
Tool payloads duplicate every field in snake_case and camelCase; 6 tool descriptions about 2.2k tokens resident.

README contains marketing claims (80-90% token savings, up to $5 saved) that are estimates, and doc/emoji volume plus AGENTS/openspec scaffolding suggest heavily LLM-generated repo; Foreman/CommandCode/OpenCode-specific features are irrelevant to Claude Code.
entries.verdict: Best-engineered of the Jev wrappers on OpenRouter support, offline fallback and tests, but it is a model-discretion MCP/skill toolkit aimed at saving tokens on other vendors' frontier models, not an automatic Claude Code integration. Useful only as a source of a `test-gate` CLI you might call from your own PostToolUse hook; do not adopt as the primary integration.

entries.name: decisionkit-core (DecisionKit)
entries.what: Installer + library (npm decisionkit-cli / decisionkit-core 0.1.2) that wires Jev-backed typed decisions into coding agents. For Claude Code, `npx decisionkit-cli init --agent claude` writes per-repo PreToolUse, PostToolUse and UserPromptSubmit command hooks into `.claude/settings.json`, adds a `decisionkit_locate` stdio MCP server to `.mcp.json`, and npm-installs decisionkit-core into `<repo>/.decisionkit/hooks`. Tiers: (1) Guardrail: Jev Noul/Score on each tool call, and it denies calls it rates destructive. (2) S0 context: on each user prompt it runs a local grep/rg sweep, sends candidate cards to Jev, and injects a digest as additionalContext. (3) Read triage: advisory note that a read is likely irrelevant. (4) Critic: note on empty tool results. Every decision is logged to `.decisionkit/receipts.jsonl`. This is the only candidate found so far that gets automatic, prompt-free Jev use in Claude Code through deterministic hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (PreToolUse, PostToolUse, UserPromptSubmit) that fire without any user prompting. This is what the user wants. The only model-discretion piece is the decisionkit_locate MCP tool.
security: API key handling is good: the key comes from process env or the cwd `.env` and is sent only as an `Authorization: Bearer` header over fetch (providers.ts:209-213). It is never put in argv, so it is not visible in the process list.
Hook commands are `node "${CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR}/.decisionkit/hooks/hook.mjs" pre|post|prompt` (init.ts:371-372). Nothing is passed on the command line.

init runs `npm install` in `.decisionkit/hooks` (init.ts:397), pulling decisionkit-core from npm at install time. Its transitive dependency @typesafe-ai/sdk is a supply-chain surface. Hooks execute that node_modules code on every tool call, so a compromised release would run with the user's privileges and see all tool inputs. I found no postinstall script in the repo's package.json files, but I did not audit the SDK.

The installer edits `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json` inside the client repo, and it creates `.decisionkit/` (node_modules, receipts.jsonl) there. I found no gitignore handling in init.ts, so this risks committing hook config and receipts into client repos.
Receipts in `.decisionkit/receipts.jsonl` can include command previews (120 characters) and S0 paths. That file may leak into git.

Prompt-injection surface: the S0 digest and critic/triage notes are injected into model context as additionalContext. The digest contains file excerpts from the repo, so hostile repo content could be echoed to the model with tool-like authority. The guardrail deny is driven by Jev probabilities, which are non-deterministic and could be manipulated by content in the tool input.
entries.dataEgress: Everything below goes to openrouter.ai (or TypeSafe) as JSON `state`. (a) Guardrail: `{tool, input: <full tool_input>}` for EVERY non-read-only-bash tool call (host-hook.ts:175-178, decisionkit.ts:193-194). That includes full Edit/Write/MultiEdit contents (new_string, file content), non-allowlisted bash commands (which may embed secrets, tokens and DB URLs), Read/Grep/Glob arguments, and mcp__* tool arguments. (b) S0: the full user prompt (up to 4000 chars), the cwd, and candidate file cards (relative paths, matched line excerpts of about 60 chars, export outlines, digest summary) via decisionkit.ts:455-500. (c) Read triage: file path plus the worktree path (decisionkit.ts:291, not file content). (d) Critic, on empty results only: tool, tool_input, empty result preview. (e) MCP locate: task text plus candidate file names. No wholesale file contents are sent for reads, but Write/Edit payloads and prompts are sent. For client projects this is a real code and IP egress to a third-party model provider on every edit, and it is not gated by any per-repo opt-in besides installing the hooks per repo.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. There is no key, timeout, HTTP error, or JSON parse failure that blocks the agent: runHostHookStdin swallows all errors and exits 0 with no output (host-hook.ts:228-250), and no-key gives a permanent fail-open (decisionkit.ts:103-108). Per-attempt hard timeout is 2000ms (decisionkit.ts:31) with one retry for 408/422/429/5xx and network errors (150ms backoff; a timeout abort is not retried). Worst case per hook is roughly 2s, or about 4.2s with a transient error plus retry, and a guardrail miss lets the tool call through. The installed Claude hooks set no `timeout` field (only the Codex hooks do, init.ts:469-471), so they rely on Claude Code's default hook timeout. Because each hook is a fresh process, the verdict caches do not apply on the Claude path. Blocks are stochastic: a false-positive deny on a legitimate rm/git reset/migration in bypass mode would stall the agent.
entries.contextCost: Low from MCP: 1 tool (decisionkit_locate, about 60 tokens of definition) and the MCP server sends no `instructions` field (mcp.ts:82-91). Hook-injected text costs more. S0 injects a digest of about 1.2k chars (about 300 tokens; the README measured 1245 chars) plus a trailer on most prompts. The guardrail deny message is about 60 tokens per block. Triage/critic notes are short. The two installed skills add a small description footprint (2 skills). Net context is likely modest, but the digest can steer Opus toward the wrong files. The README's token savings compare against pi baselines, not Claude Code.
pros: Only candidate found that gives fully automatic, hook-driven Jev use in Claude Code, with no need to say 'use jev'. It targets the official hook surfaces (PreToolUse deny, UserPromptSubmit additionalContext).

OpenRouter is a real first-class transport in code: `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` alone selects `POST openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions` with `typesafe/jev-1.13`, and DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER pins it. No patching is needed.
Fail-open everywhere, with a 2s hard timeout and one bounded retry. It cannot brick a session, and kill switches exist (DECISIONKIT_ENABLE=0, DECISIONKIT_S0=0).
Static read-only bash allowlist and non-empty-result critic fast path avoid Jev calls on the most common cases (tax-fastpath.ts). The API key is never in argv.
A guardrail tier is attractive in bypass/auto mode, since a probabilistic 'is this destructive' gate adds a safety net on rm/DROP/force-push, and receipts give an auditable log.
Uses the Jev primitives correctly (Noul, Score, Choice), and pack wording is data-driven with a per-host Claude pack.
MIT licence, npm provenance and signatures on 0.1.2, CI matrix on Node 20/22, and about 60 unit tests.
cons: Extremely young: repo created 2026-09-21, 8 commits, 1 author, 3 stars, 0 forks, no GitHub releases, 0.1.x on npm. The README says BETA and calls the Jev API alpha. There is no field data on Claude Code, and all benchmarks are pi with cheap models.

PreToolUse has no matcher, so nearly every tool call, not just Bash/Edit/Write, incurs a fresh node process plus a Jev round trip. There is no cross-invocation cache (each hook is its own process). That is a lot of serial latency in an all-day session.

Data egress is broad: full Edit/Write/MultiEdit contents and all non-allowlisted bash commands (possibly with secrets), plus prompts and match excerpts, go to OpenRouter and the Jev provider on client projects. It conflicts with the user's own PreToolUse secret-leak guard philosophy, and the hooks would run in parallel with it, so the secret guard cannot pre-filter what Jev sees. A client NDA would probably forbid it.

The Claude Read-triage tier is effectively broken: host-hook.ts:187-190 passes taskContext=worktree (the cwd path) as the 'task', so a per-Read Jev call judges relevance with no real task. It costs latency and can steer Opus away from files it needs.

Guardrail duplicates or fights existing protections and is stochastic (thresholds on Jev probabilities). False-positive denies interrupt work; false negatives give false safety. Blocks tell the model to stop and ask the user, which can stall autonomous bypass-mode runs.

S0 digest duplicates what Opus 5.5 with Claude Code's own Explore/Grep, plus the user's GitNexus graph hook, already do. It adds 3+ serial Jev calls (about 3.5s) to every prompt and can inject a wrong file pick. The overlap with gitnexus and its hooks is likely.

The installer is per repo and invasive: it edits `.claude/settings.json` and `.mcp.json`, creates `.decisionkit/` with node_modules, runs `npm install`, adds skills, and does not gitignore. It is a poor fit for client repos; global/user-level install is not supported by init.ts, so you would hand-write a user-level settings entry.
Installed Claude hooks have no `timeout` set, and the retry doubles worst-case latency.
The decisionkit_locate MCP tool adds a redundant, model-discretion search tool alongside Grep/Glob/gitnexus, and the two calibrate/bench skills are noise.
Uses only the alpha /decisions endpoint on OpenRouter, a moving target.
entries.verdict: The only OpenRouter-capable, hook-driven, prompt-free Jev integration for Claude Code, and its fail-open design is sound. But it is a 9-day-old single-author alpha whose broad, matcher-less hooks send full edit and command payloads to a third party and add serial latency on every tool call, and it duplicates GitNexus and the user's own guards. Do not run `init` as-is on client repos. At most, hand-cherry-pick a narrow user-level PreToolUse guardrail (matcher `Bash`, with a timeout of about 3s) on personal projects, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and DECISIONKIT_PROVIDER=openrouter, and disable S0 and triage.

entries.name: qualixar/jev-decision-layer
entries.what: Third-party (Varun Pratap Bhardwaj / Qualixar; not official TypeSafe) Claude Code plugin bundling a Python stdio MCP server (qualixar-jev, 20 tools), 3 skills, 7 slash commands and 2 hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit). It wraps Jev calls (Choice/Score/Noul-style typed questions) with a local broker daemon (unix socket), per-workspace consent enrolment via a browser wizard, a best-effort secret screen, an act/verify/ignore gate (always capped to verify in 1.0.10) and local receipts. Supports Codex, Claude Code, VS Code, Hermes, Antigravity. In Claude Code the hooks do NOT call Jev: they only inject a fixed advisory sentence telling the model that jev_route / jev_typed_decide / jev_recipe_try exist. Jev is only called when Opus decides to call an MCP tool.
interface: MCP legacy: jev_health, jev_policy_status, jev_policy_check, jev_catalog, jev_describe, jev_run_fixture, jev_evaluate
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools nudged by hooks. The hooks (SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit) are deterministic but only inject a static advisory string; they do not route or call Jev. Whether Jev is ever used depends on Opus choosing to call jev_route/jev_recipe_try/etc., plus skill-description triggers. Nothing is called transparently. Also requires per-workspace enrolment through a browser wizard, so it will not be active in new client repos until /jev-setup is run there.
security: Stdlib-only Python, no npm postinstall, no curl|sh installer; install is via claude plugin marketplace (git clone of repo), so all code runs as the user once hooks/MCP are enabled

API key never in argv: sent as Bearer header over pinned HTTPS host (jev_auto/providers.py:36); Linux secret-tool gets key via stdin only (credential_store.py header); legacy .env/key files require 0600, owner match, single-link, no symlink ancestors (jevkit/providers.py _safe_regular_file)
Setup wizard is a loopback HTTP server on 127.0.0.1 with strict CSP, 600 s expiry, launched by fixed packaged script with filtered env (mcp.py _open_setup); key entry is never in chat

Hooks are advisory-only: always exit 0, never emit permissionDecision, PreToolUse deliberately not registered (claude_hook.py:1-25); no interference with existing secret-leak/GitNexus PreToolUse hooks
Secret screen (require_clean on payload and response) is explicitly best-effort, not DLP (README); a diff or reduced text may still leak proprietary code

Prompt-injection surface: tool descriptions/hints are static; provider responses are schema-validated (protocol.validate_response) and capped at 1 MB; results are typed probabilities, no free text, and gate caps to 'verify'
entries.dataEgress: Nothing leaves on hooks (they only print fixed text). Egress happens only when the model calls an MCP tool, and only to api.typesafe.ai or openrouter.ai (per config): JSON {model, state, questions}. Depending on tool this is: task text plus candidate ids/descriptions (jev_route), arbitrary state object (jev_typed_decide), a diff up to 16,000 chars (jev_review_diff), source text up to 20,000 chars and the extraction (jev_verify), up to 100,000 chars of text (jev_reduce), passages (jev_rerank), recipe input objects (jev_recipe_try). data_classification (public / internal-minimized / restricted) is model-supplied per call and checked against the workspace's reviewed scope; secret screen is best-effort. Prompts as a whole and full tool outputs are not sent automatically. Local receipts and state stored under user state dir (7-day retention default).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open in practice. Hooks: any exception, oversized input, missing cwd, or unenrolled workspace produce no output and exit 0 (claude_hook.py:111-127); launcher exits non-zero silently if no Python 3.11+ at the four hard-coded paths (non-blocking hook error). MCP: provider timeout default 12 s (settings.py:20, configurable 1-30 s), non-200 -> PROVIDER_HTTP_xxx, transport failure -> PROVIDER_TRANSPORT_FAILURE_NO_RETRY (never retried, since call may be billed); tool returns isError text and the model proceeds without Jev. No fallback to another provider (Jev-only never silently falls back to Laya). A stuck call can add up to ~12 s to a turn, and a broker BROKER_VERSION_MISMATCH/START failure surfaces as tool error.
entries.contextCost: Tool count 20 in one MCP server (7 legacy in jevkit/mcp_server.py + 13 in jev_auto/mcp.py). Estimated tool defs approx 3,000-4,000 tokens (about 12-16k chars: long descriptions, jev_evaluate case_id enum of 20 ids, many object/array schemas), reducible if Claude Code defers MCP tools via tool search. Server instructions ~45 tokens. Plus 3 skill descriptions (~150 tokens) and 7 command descriptions (~200 tokens) in the listing. Hook-injected text: SessionStart hint ~80 tokens once; UserPromptSubmit hint ~45 tokens on every prompt (only in enrolled workspaces), accumulating in transcript. Skill bodies (2.7-4.7 KB) only load when triggered. Tool results are compact JSON.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class, code-verified provider: hard-coded https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13 and OPENROUTER_API_KEY (jevkit/providers.py:43-49); no patching needed
Safe, well-behaved Claude Code hooks: exit 0 always, no permission decisions, no PreToolUse, so no clash with the user's secret-leak guard and GitNexus hooks

Real security engineering: key sent only in Authorization header, 0600/owner/symlink checks on key files, secret-tool via stdin, pinned host with profile hash cross-check, 1 MB response cap, no retry on ambiguous failure
Good egress controls for client work: per-workspace enrolment, data_classification tiers, daily request limits, local receipts, offline selftest (114 fixtures) that needs no key
Only network destination is the chosen provider; no telemetry found; MIT; stdlib-only Python, no postinstall/curl|sh
Broad, ready-made decision surface (route, review_diff, test-selection and patch-review recipes, verify, rerank, reduce) that maps to real coding decisions
CI matrix includes ubuntu with a disposable Secret Service test and high per-module coverage floors
cons: Not really automatic: the Claude hooks only inject a 'consider jev_route' sentence; Jev is called only if Opus chooses to, which contradicts the user's goal of Claude Code using Jev without being told (claude_hook.py:40-54). The README's prompt-time file/skill suggestion is a Codex hook path (hooks.py / jev_hook.py), not Claude

Every jev_* call costs an extra Opus tool round trip; for closed choices Opus already answers in-context faster than a tool call, so net latency and token effect is likely negative (README itself admits 'no token, cost, or task-time saving has been measured')

Context tax: 20 tools (~3-4k tokens of defs), 7 commands, 3 skills, plus a hint injected on every prompt; 7 legacy tools (jev_health, jev_policy_*, jev_catalog, jev_describe, jev_run_fixture) are pure noise for daily coding
Every shipped recipe is SPECIFICATION_NOT_MODEL_EVALUATED, so the gate never returns 'act' (max 'verify'); authors state the repo has no labeled provider evaluation; thresholds are demo values

Very immature: created 2026-09-25, 2 stars, 1 contributor, 47 commits in 4 days, releases 1.0.8 to 1.0.10 in 2 days (GitHub latest release tag v1.0.8 while README/plugin says 1.0.10), heavy churn = breaking-change risk; independent, not official TypeSafe
Linux is explicitly 'experimental and unverified'; macOS is the only supported platform. The README says a native Claude Code MCP tool turn and hook firing under a live session have not been verified

Setup friction: per-workspace browser wizard for every personal and client repo; Linux wizard needs libsecret secret-tool + D-Bus keyring (or hand-crafted legacy env-var config); launcher only probes 4 fixed python3 paths and ignores uv/PATH/Python 3.13 in ~/.local

Model-controlled egress: the model picks what goes in state/diff/text and self-declares data_classification; a diff (16k chars) or reduce text (100k chars) from a client repo can go to a third-party provider; secret screen is best-effort
Pins jev-1.13 IDs; cannot use ~typesafe/jev-latest or the Jev Router, and there is no configurable base URL
Adds a persistent local broker daemon and unix socket per workspace
entries.verdict: Best-engineered and the only candidate that truly supports OpenRouter Jev out of the box, but for Claude Code it is not automatic (hooks just nudge Opus to call 20 heavy MCP tools) and it is a 5-day-old single-author alpha with unverified Linux/Claude paths. Worth a scoped trial (route/review_diff only, public or minimized workspaces), not a default global install.

entries.name: notque/vexjoy-agent
entries.what: A very large personal Claude Code toolkit (86 agents, 62 SKILL.md skills, ~100 hooks, 265+ Python files incl. tests) whose headline feature is /d, a Jev-powered router. When the user types "/d <request>", a UserPromptSubmit hook runs scripts/jev-route.py, which sends {request, detected languages/frameworks} to Jev (Choice/Noul questions over an agent/skill manifest) and injects JEV_RESULT into context. Then the model must run jev-intent-align.py to get an "intent alignment" receipt before dispatching to an agent/skill/pipeline. It also ships an optional jev-auto-compact function-hook plugin (Jev judges which tool calls to prune at ~60% context), plus Jev-based browser/design/review helper scripts and teaching skills (building-with-jev, grill-jev). Jev is a routing/classification layer for the toolkit's own /d pipeline, not a general coding assistant.
entries.autoInvocation: Mostly only when prompted. The only Jev entry point on the prompt path is the explicit '/d' command (regex ^\s*/d\b in jev-route-injector-userprompt.py); a normal prompt never touches Jev. The skill description ('Jev request router...') does not make Claude choose it on its own. The one genuinely automatic Jev use is the jev-auto-compact function-hook plugin (turn.complete at >=60% context), which is a deterministic hook but needs the experimental function-hooks runtime, TypeSafe key, and only affects compaction, not coding decisions.
security: License MIT. 426 stars, 48 forks, no GitHub releases (latestRelease null), created 2026-03-18, last push 2026-09-30 (very active). Effectively a single-maintainer project: git shortlog of the 200-commit shallow clone shows 197 commits by notque; 3 other contributors with 2-3 commits each.

Key handling is careful: API key sent only as an Authorization header via stdlib urllib, never in argv; the Vercel bridge gets a minimal env allowlist (jev_vercel.py:33-49, NODE_OPTIONS deliberately excluded); error receipts never include request bodies (jev_vercel_gateway.mjs safeErrorReceipt).

scripts/jev_redact.py and plugins/jev-auto-compact/hooks/redact.mjs strip secrets before anything goes to Jev (states 'nothing goes to api.typesafe.ai with a secret in it'). Tested (redact.test.mjs). This is a redaction layer, not a guarantee against leaking client code or names.
Reads the key from ~/.env via python-dotenv (jev_transport.py:22-23), from the process env, or from Claude settings env (jev-auto-compact.mjs:732-733).

install.sh is not curl|sh (run locally after clone) and uses npm ci --ignore-scripts, but it is invasive: it takes over ~/.claude by default (TAKEOVER=true: 'trash and replace' unowned entries at desired paths), symlinks about 86 agents / 62 skills / ~100 hooks, merges 70+ hook registrations across 10 events into settings.json, and runs chmod 600 on history.jsonl. Conflicts with the user's existing PreToolUse guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks are likely; --no-takeover and --dry-run exist.

Prompt-injection surface: hooks inject the JEV_RESULT JSON and many other advisory strings into model context; the pretool-prompt-injection-scanner.py and posttool-bash-injection-scan.py hooks exist. Also runs Python subprocess with list-argv (no shell) for the route script.
entries.dataEgress: For /d: the user's request text (after redaction) plus a 'project' field (detected languages/frameworks/datastores from marker files in cwd) plus the routing questions with the agent/skill manifest descriptions (jev-route.py:614-643). The intent-alignment call also sends the model's proposed-intent restatement. Not file contents or diffs in the /d path. For the optional auto-compact plugin: message text and tool inputs and tool results (truncated to head/tail snippets, redacted) from the live transcript, i.e. real code and command output, are sent to api.typesafe.ai every time it compacts. Browser/design/compact scripts send page text or evidence packs. Everything goes to TypeSafe direct or Vercel AI Gateway, never OpenRouter, in the shipped code. Nothing else leaves the machine except the toolkit's unrelated integrations (Reddit, WordPress, GitHub) which are opt-in.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open throughout. The UserPromptSubmit hook returns nothing on any error, timeout or non-zero exit and falls back to SKILL.md Phase 1 running the script itself; 4s per attempt, up to 3 retries on 429/529 with jittered exponential backoff capped at 5s, 24s hook budget inside a 26s host timeout. jev_router_common has a circuit breaker on 401/402 (persisted across processes for JEV_BREAKER_TTL_S) and a SQLite response cache (JEV_CACHE_TTL_S default 120s). README says 'if npm unavailable, /d falls back to /do'. Auto-compact falls back to the built-in summarizer on missing key or low reduction, and returns skip for self-triggered compactions. Worst case is added latency of up to about 24s on a /d turn when Jev is down.
entries.contextCost: Very high if installed as designed. Installer registers 86 agents and 62 skills (each with a name and description in the system prompt, roughly 20-40k characters of listings, i.e. an estimated 6-12k tokens; skills/meta/d/SKILL.md alone is 15 KB, about 3.8k tokens, when loaded), plus about 70 hooks across SessionStart (16), UserPromptSubmit (7), PreToolUse (18), PostToolUse (16), Stop, SubagentStart/Stop etc. Several hooks inject text on every session or prompt (session-context, afk-mode, retro-knowledge-injector, rules-distill-injector, pending-advisory-injector) and /d additionally injects the JEV_RESULT JSON and mandates further scripted steps. No MCP server, so zero tool-schema cost. Cherry-picking only the /d skill plus the one hook would cost about 1-4k tokens.
pros: Real, working Jev integration with production hardening: retry/backoff on 429/529, circuit breaker on 401/402, SQLite response cache, request-size splitting against Jev's documented limits (jev_limits.py), secret redaction before egress (jev_redact.py, redact.mjs), cost/latency stats scripts.

Direct-path wire format ({state, model, questions} with Bearer auth to /v1/systemone) is the same as OpenRouter's documented System One API, so an OpenRouter switch is a small patch of about 3 constants, not a rewrite.
Fail-open design: hook never blocks a prompt, so a Jev outage costs latency, not correctness.
Good reference material: skills/meta/building-with-jev and jev-production-lessons.md document Choice/Noul/Score usage, calibration and decision cards, useful for writing our own hooks.

jev-auto-compact is the one piece that fires automatically and deterministically (function hooks at 60% context) and applies Jev to a real Claude Code problem, pruning tool calls verbatim instead of LLM-summarizing.
MIT, very active, decent tests and CI; keys kept out of argv and the Vercel bridge gets a minimal env.
cons: Not automatic for the user's goal: Jev is only invoked when the user types /d (jev-route-injector-userprompt.py DETECT_PATTERN = ^\s*/d\b). Ordinary prompts, edits and Bash calls never call Jev, which is exactly what the user said they do not want.
No OpenRouter support at all (grep finds zero 'openrouter'); only api.typesafe.ai direct or Vercel AI Gateway. URL is a hardcoded constant; key env var checked in about 10 scripts.

Jev is used as a router over this toolkit's own 86 agents/62 skills. Without that agent ecosystem, /d has nothing to route to, and Opus 5.5 with plain Claude Code already delegates fine, so the value for a senior dev is low and unmeasured (repo's own what-didnt-work.md records routing reversals).

Installer takes over ~/.claude (trashes unowned entries by default) and registers about 70 hooks across 10 events; high collision risk with the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks, and heavy per-session context injection.
Bus factor of one (197 of 204 commits by a single author), no tagged releases, fast churn (204 commits in 3 months), opinionated persona/voice/Reddit/WordPress content unrelated to daily coding.

Auto-compact plugin sends redacted transcript content (tool inputs and results, including client code fragments) to TypeSafe on every compaction, and depends on the experimental function-hooks runtime and a hardcoded TypeSafe URL; concern for client projects.
The intent-alignment step relies on the model obediently running another script after /d, so it is only partly deterministic; adds up to two Jev calls plus Python and Node startup per /d turn.
Subscription/OAuth main model is unaffected, but /d dispatch relies on the Task/Agent flow of the toolkit's own agent files, so it does not integrate with plain Claude Code sessions.
entries.verdict: A serious, well-engineered Jev consumer, but Jev is wired to an explicit /d command inside a huge opinionated toolkit and only to TypeSafe or Vercel, so it fails the user's core requirement (automatic use, OpenRouter). Do not install it; mine it for patterns (redaction, breaker/cache, size splitting, the auto-compact function-hook idea) and consider the jev-auto-compact idea only after re-pointing its URL to OpenRouter.

entries.name: @aitofy/jev-awesome-skills
entries.what: A small (about 870 lines of TypeScript) Node CLI named `jev` plus 8 SKILL.md files (policy, gate, route, guard, verify, triage, review, act). Each skill tells Claude to build a System One request (state plus choice/noul/score questions, with presets from `jev questions <usecase>`), run `jev --file request.json`, and apply one fixed policy. Stop if harm.score >= 1.5. Proceed if the pick probability >= 0.9 and determined.noul >= 0.9. Otherwise ask. The CLI redacts secret-shaped strings from state before sending. On a missing key or transport error it returns source:"fallback" (fail-open). It is not an MCP server and has no hooks. Claude only runs it through Bash, when a skill description matches or the user asks.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger only, i.e. model discretion. Claude reads the descriptions and decides to load a skill, then decides to run the CLI. That fits 'do not have to say use jev' only loosely and is not deterministic. There are no hooks, so nothing fires at PreToolUse. The skill text itself says to skip Jev when a file or command already answers the question, and for a known-dangerous command to ask the user without Jev. In practice the model will rarely invoke it, and jev-guard/jev-verify depend on the model remembering to self-check. It also needs a global `jev` binary and the key exported in the Claude Code environment.
security: API key is read only from env TYPESAFE_API_KEY (src/judge.ts:13-20) and never goes in argv. The error path scrubs the key from the message (judge.ts:106-108). The key is not visible in the process list.

State redaction (src/redact.ts): drops the value of any object key matching api-key/token/secret/password/authorization/credential, and regex-scrubs sk-*, jv_live_*, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=... and 'Bearer ...' strings. It is best-effort only: free-text secrets of other shapes (AWS, GitHub ghp_, private keys, DB URLs) pass through, so it is weaker than the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard.

No exec, no child_process, no eval. Runtime is only fetch to one hardcoded host. There is no postinstall. `prepare` runs tsc only on git or local install, not on npm tarball install. No curl|sh installer.
No telemetry (README and SECURITY.md say so; grep finds no other network call).

Prompt-injection surface: the model-facing policy lives in SKILL.md. The command and diff text that Claude places in `state` is untrusted, but Jev returns only probabilities, so the injection impact is limited. The bigger risk is over-trust: the skill tells Claude to skip asking the user when Jev says 'proceed'. A probabilistic classifier could therefore weaken an ask/confirm step.
The package is a 2-day-old single-author npm package with a scoped name and no provenance. Pin the version and read the dist before use.
entries.dataEgress: Only what Claude writes into the `state` JSON, and only when Claude decides to invoke the CLI. Typically that is the exact shell command, cwd and task (guard), a claim plus test receipts (verify), a diff or diff summary (review), or the user request plus skill names (route). If Claude puts a full diff or file contents in state, that leaves the machine, redacted only by the secret-key and regex scrubber. It goes to api.typesafe.ai today, and it would go to openrouter.ai after patching, where it is then subject to OpenRouter's provider routing and logging. Nothing else is collected. There is no automatic capture, and no hook sends tool outputs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design for missing key, HTTP or network exception, or non-Jev body (judge.ts:30-43, 66-70). The result is source:"fallback" and Claude is told to decide on its own or ask. There is NO timeout or AbortSignal on fetch (judge.ts:55). A hung TypeSafe or OpenRouter connection would block the Bash call until the Bash tool timeout (default 2 min). readBody swallows non-JSON and HTTP errors into {status}, which then becomes 'not_jev_answers' fallback. Fail-open on the guard skill means the 'safety' check silently vanishes when Jev is down (the skill says to ask the user before anything hard to undo).
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no hook text. The 8 SKILL.md files total about 11.3 KB (about 2.8k tokens) if all are read. Claude Code injects only name+description at startup: about 8 descriptions of roughly 300-450 chars each, which is about 3.2 KB or about 800 tokens of always-on skill listing. The full body of a skill (about 300 tokens each, the policy one about 800) loads only on trigger. Cheap. Each use also costs a Bash call plus the JSON it prints.
pros: Very light footprint: 0 MCP tools, no hooks, about 800 tokens of always-on skill descriptions, no interference with the existing PreToolUse hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman).
Small, readable code (866 lines TS, no runtime deps, no exec, one hardcoded host). It is easy to audit and to patch in about 5 lines for OpenRouter.
Sensible, codified policy: numeric cutoffs (0.9/0.9/1.5, stop wins) are shared by code (src/branch.ts) and skill text. It never invents a probability on failure. Explicit fail-open contract.
Redacts secret-shaped keys and tokens from state before the body is built. The key is read from env only, not argv, and scrubbed from errors.
Good use-case fit for the Jev primitives (choice, noul, score): guard, verify and gate are closed decisions. Ships request templates and offline fixtures so the wiring can be dry-run without a key.
MIT, no telemetry, CI on Node 20 and 22, and tests cover the request and response contract.
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint (src/defaults.ts:114) and key var (src/judge.ts:13) are hardcoded to TYPESAFE. The user wants OpenRouter as the provider, so a fork or patch is mandatory, and the OpenRouter response envelope is unverified against parse.ts.

Not automatic: it relies on the model choosing to load a skill and run a Bash CLI. There is no hook, so the guard and verify checks are not deterministic. This misses the user's core goal of Claude Code using Jev without being prompted.

Adds a full extra LLM round trip (Opus writes the request JSON, runs Bash, reads the result) for each Jev call, which is likely slower and costlier than the 70-500 ms Jev call itself. It is a poor fit for high-frequency decisions.
No fetch timeout and no retry. A stalled connection blocks until the Bash tool timeout. The fail-open guard silently removes safety when Jev is down.

Redaction is a narrow regex list (sk-, jv_live_, Bearer, TYPESAFE_API_KEY=) and misses AWS, GitHub, JWT and private keys, so client-project secrets in diffs or commands could leak to a third party. It duplicates but is weaker than the user's own secret guard.

Policy asks Claude to skip user confirmation when Jev says proceed at >=0.9. That is risky in bypass or auto mode and rests on an unvalidated, beta, 'possibly a flash router' model. Nothing has been benchmarked, and the README itself says the linked projects are not endorsed.

Immature and thin: 6 commits over 1 day, 1 author, 2 stars, alpha 0.1.1, no release tags or provenance. `jev` must be installed globally and put on PATH by hand, since the skills give no path or npx form.

Overlaps with existing tooling: gate/route/triage/review/act duplicate what Claude already does natively or via GitNexus. Only guard and verify add a distinct 'second opinion' value, and that is better done as a deterministic hook.
entries.verdict: A clean, tiny, well-scoped reference client and skill catalog, but it is a skill (model-discretion Bash CLI), not an automatic integration, and it is hardwired to api.typesafe.ai. Use it at most as a source of question presets and policy cutoffs (jev-guard and jev-verify) for a custom OpenRouter-based PreToolUse/Stop hook. Don't install it as the daily integration.

entries.name: damian87x/jev-claude-orchestrator
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (skill /conductor-max + 4 subagent definitions + 2 hooks + stdlib-Python CLI jevo.py) implementing a "madmax" orchestrator: the main model plans up to ~50 tiny slices, slice-worker subagents (haiku/sonnet/opus, in git worktrees) implement them, and Jev (System One, /v1/systemone) answers typed questions for triage (tier/risk/needs_human/shared_surface), QA (does gate evidence meet acceptance), staged diff review, worker health (stuck/off-track) and a watchdog. Policy/thresholds/vetoes are in code and fail closed. The hooks only act on subagents whose agent_type contains "slice-worker" and whose prompt starts with "JEV-SLICE: <id>"; for the main session and ordinary work they are no-ops.
interface: jevo.py triage / check / review / qa / gate / health / watch / report
entries.autoInvocation: Mixed. Hooks (SubagentStop, PostToolUse) are deterministic once installed but self-filter to slice-worker subagents, so they never fire in the user's normal coding. The skill is model-discretion by description ('large goal that decomposes into many small independently testable changes'), and the whole flow only engages when the main model chooses to run /conductor-max and dispatch workers with the JEV-SLICE marker. It is not an automatic Jev integration for daily coding.
security: No MCP server; stdlib-only Python; no postinstall or curl|sh installer; no telemetry found (grep). npm package publishes the same files.

API key sent as Authorization Bearer header via urllib (not in argv, so not visible in ps); key never logged or written to ledger (jevlib.py:1-4, 183-188). Lookup order includes walking up parent dirs for any .env and reading TYPESAFE_API_KEY (jevlib.py:53-65), and ~/.pi/agent/secrets/typesafe_api_key.
NoRedirect opener refuses 3xx so key cannot be redirected to another host (jevlib.py:25-32); fallback never receives the key.

run_gate() executes the slice's gate string with shell=True (jevo.py:118) inside the hook; gate is written by the conductor model, and workers cannot edit slice files by design, but a prompt-injected conductor could run arbitrary commands. Runs with user permissions; timeout 600s.

Prompt-injection surface: worker tool output, diffs and gate tails go to Jev as 'trusted state' (README admits worker output could argue with it); mitigated by code vetoes (allowlist, secret regex on added lines, failure counts) and by never letting Jev approval merge/push. Returned steer text is injected into worker context.
Plugin hooks are global-scope once installed but self-filter on agent_type; parses transcript file (first 20 lines) for JEV-SLICE marker.
entries.dataEgress: Only in slice-worker flows: acceptance criteria, gate stdout/stderr tails (~1.5 KB+), the full git diff of the slice (up to 60k chars, untracked files included via git diff --no-index), and every 8th tool call a summary of last 12 worker actions (tool name, target command/path up to 160 chars, first 200 chars of result) go to BASE/v1/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if switched, which then also passes to OpenRouter and TypeSafe). Not sent: main-session prompts, code outside slice diffs, non-worker tool calls. README warns explicitly: do not use on code you cannot send to a third party (relevant to client projects). Secret-pattern veto on added diff lines runs before sending only in the review stage.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design for approval: any Jev error, timeout (30s default), malformed answer, HTTP error => escalate (mark slice for conductor), never approve; up to 3 retries on 429 honoring Retry-After (bounded by timeout). Health check and PostToolUse hook are fail-open no-ops (never block a tool, exit 0 on any exception). Fallback servers opt-in and cannot approve. SubagentStop hook timeout is 900s, so a bad network could stall worker stops for a long time (30s timeout x calls plus 600s gate). Outside slice-worker flows nothing can block.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tool defs). Always-on: skill name+description ~640 chars (~160 tokens) plus 4 agent descriptions (~250 chars each, ~250 tokens total) listed in the Task/agent list. Skill body 9 KB (~2.3k tokens) and jev-questions.json 5 KB (~1.2k tokens) load only when /conductor-max is invoked. Hooks inject nothing except the occasional steer inside slice workers (a short string every 8 calls when Jev flags stuck/off-track).
pros: Real, working use of Jev decisions inside Claude Code hooks: SubagentStop can block a worker from stopping (exit 2) based on gate + Jev QA + staged review, and PostToolUse injects steering via additionalContext (hooks/subagent_stop.py, post_tool_use.py).
Uses exactly the /v1/systemone endpoint and Bearer auth that OpenRouter exposes; only base URL + key + model id need changing (env vars TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, JEV_MODEL), no code edits.

Careful engineering: fail-closed policy in stages.py, vetoes before Jev, strict response validation (jevlib.malformed), redirect refusal, 429 handling, key not logged, stdlib-only, no installer scripts.

Has ~1050 lines of unit tests (6 test files) including regression tests from live runs; README includes measured Jev accuracy per stage (QA 96.3%, health 95.3%, triage 46.3%, review 9.5%), which is honest and useful evidence about where Jev is and isn't reliable.
Concrete, reusable ideas: typed triage/QA/health question sets in skills/conductor-max/references/jev-questions.json that can be lifted into a custom lightweight hook.
MIT license, tiny footprint (no MCP tool token tax, ~400 tokens always-on).
cons: Wrong shape for the user's goal: it is a parallel-subagent orchestrator that only engages inside /conductor-max slice workflows; no Jev help during ordinary daily coding, which the user explicitly wants automatic.

Author's own measurement shows Jev triage 46.3% and review 9.5% agreement with frontier majority (README table), so two of the four judgment stages are weak; system is 'starting guesses, not calibrated', v0.2 label vs 0.4.1 manifest (npm shows 0.4.0, manifest 0.4.1).
Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-22, 19 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars/forks, no CI, no GitHub releases; hooks run arbitrary gate commands with shell=True.

PostToolUse hook has no matcher, so a python3 process spawns on every tool call in every session even though it is a no-op outside slice workers; user already has several hooks (secret guard, GitNexus) adding latency.
Sends full diffs and gate output to a third party (TypeSafe, plus OpenRouter if routed there): risky for client projects (README says so itself).

OpenRouter compatibility is untested by author (no OPENROUTER references; env var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY would carry an OpenRouter key; model id must be changed to typesafe/jev-1.13); a schema mismatch would silently degrade to escalate on every call.

Costs and complexity of madmax orchestration (up to 50 subagent slices, worktrees, opus/sonnet/haiku workers) are heavy for a subscription user and overlap with Claude Code's native subagents; requires disciplined slice packets (JEV-SLICE marker) that the main model must be told to produce.
entries.verdict: Well-built but narrow: a slice-conductor for large parallel refactors, not an always-on Jev layer for daily coding, and its hooks are inert outside /conductor-max slice workers. Worth mining for its typed question sets, hook exit-2 gate pattern and OpenRouter-compatible /v1/systemone call (config-only switch), but not worth installing as the main integration.

entries.name: daraujo85/jev-claude-engine
entries.what: Node ESM (zero-dependency) toolkit that wires TypeSafe Jev "System One" into Claude Code through 4 deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit skill router, PreToolUse Write/Edit rule/regression guard that can block with exit 2, PostToolUse test-coverage nagger, PreCompact instruction injector), 6-7 explicit skills (discover, explore, review, plan-evaluator, anti-regression, browser-test), a `jev` CLI, a localhost telemetry dashboard, and an OpenCode plugin. Uses Choice/Noul/Score primitives through a small JevClient (fetch, 1.5-2.5 s timeout, fail-open).
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PreCompact) run without any prompting, the closest match so far to the user's 'automatic, never say use jev' requirement. The skills (/jev-review, /jev-explore, etc.) are only description-triggered or explicit slash use.
security: CRITICAL: scripts/install-hooks.js:16 hardcodes a live-looking API key (apikey_2222c29a...bc63) committed to the public repo (also appears in README.md); it is written into ~/.claude/settings.json env as TYPESAFE_API_KEY and JEV_API_KEY (install-hooks.js:35-36), so running the installer as-is makes every hook send the user's code to Diego's TypeSafe account and requests appear under a leaked shared key. Treat key as burned; never run installer unmodified.

install-hooks.js:15 hardcodes PROJECT_DIR=/Users/diegoaraujo/Documents/projects/jev-claude-engine (macOS path); hooks registered in settings.json would point to a nonexistent path on this Linux box until edited.

Installer edits ~/.claude/settings.json in place: writes a .bak, but silently deletes any PostToolUse hook whose command contains 'boltcontext' (install-hooks.js:42-49), appends to UserPromptSubmit[0], and rewrites the whole file with JSON.stringify.

API key resolution reads ~/.claude/settings.json env (providers.js:6-17) and stores plaintext keys in settings.env, so the key is exposed to every child process Claude spawns (including Bash tool env); key is sent in Authorization header, not argv (good).

Prompt-injection surface: skill-picker injects additionalContext derived from a remote model's choice string (one of the criteria keys, low risk); guard output is numeric. Rule text from CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules and skill descriptions from disk are trusted input.

Shell exec: skills/jev-discover/discover.js:24,40 interpolate the user query into execSync(`graphify query "..."`) with only double-quote escaping (shell injection via $(...) or backticks); jev-review/guard use fixed git commands; dashboard.js:979 exec(`open ${url}`) (macOS only, localhost url).
entries.dataEgress: On every user prompt (skill-picker): the complete prompt text plus up to 50 skill IDs and 100-char descriptions. On every Write/Edit (rule-guard): file path, up to 4000 chars of the proposed new content/new_string, and project rules text from CLAUDE.md/.cursorrules-style files. On edits to auth/billing/etc. files (test-verifier): path, test filenames, first 2500 chars of tool_input JSON. On PreCompact: session id and utilisation only. Skills on demand: git diff, candidate file paths/snippets. Destination is whatever provider resolves (api.typesafe.ai by default when any TYPESAFE/JEV key or settings.json key is present; openrouter.ai only if JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter or no other key). Also local copies of 280-char previews into .jev/telemetry.jsonl in every project and ~/.jev. Client/proprietary code goes to third parties with no allowlist/redaction and no coordination with the user's secret-leak guard.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design: fetch aborts after 1500 ms (2500 ms when a TypeSafe key resolved, providers.js:77), returns a fallback object with empty answers, and every hook does main().catch(()=>process.exit(0)); missing key just yields a 401 -> fallback. Caveats: (1) no per-hook timeout in the installed settings.json entries, so worst case each prompt / each edit waits up to 1.5-2.5 s plus node cold start when Jev is slow; (2) when Jev IS up the PreToolUse guard is effectively fail-closed on false positives (exit 2 hard-blocks the edit at p>=0.8) and it only sees the snippet, so blocks on legit edits are likely and would stall bypass/auto-mode autonomous runs.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, zero tool defs, no server instructions. Cost is hook-injected text: skill-picker adds ~40 tokens ('[JEV ROUTER: Invocar skill ...]') plus a systemMessage on each routed prompt; test-verifier ~80 tokens on control-file edits; compaction hook ~100 tokens. Installing 4-6 skills adds ~150-300 tokens to the skill listing. Net context cost is low; the claimed 'saves 90 skills x 350 tokens' does not hold because Claude Code still lists all skills and the picker only appends a hint.
pros: Only candidate so far that gives truly AUTOMATIC integration: hooks fire on UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse and PreCompact with no 'use jev' prompt, exactly the user's requirement.

Correct mental model for Jev: only Choice/Noul/Score typed questions, small state payloads, answers treated as probabilities with thresholds (0.8 block, 0.5 route); fail-open everywhere with AbortController timeout.

OpenRouter already a first-class provider option in code (providers.js:33-38, OPENROUTER_API_KEY), so a fork needs mostly model id + schema verification; ~2.5k LOC excluding dashboard, zero dependencies, no postinstall, readable, per-hook enable/threshold config (jev-config.js).
Good hook ideas worth cherry-picking: per-hook config toggles, control-file test-coverage nag, diff pre-filter for review, per-feature latency/cost telemetry; MIT licensed.
cons: Committed live-looking API key in install-hooks.js:16 and README plus installer that writes it into ~/.claude/settings.json: unacceptable for client work; would route code to someone else's account.
