Installer is author/macOS-specific (PROJECT_DIR=/Users/diegoaraujo/...) and destructively rewrites global settings.json, deleting another tool's hook (boltcontext); it does not account for the user's existing secret-guard, GitNexus and caveman hooks and its PreToolUse Write|Edit hook would run in parallel with them.

Not truly OpenRouter-ready: sends model 'jev-latest' not 'typesafe/jev-latest'; request/response schema (state, questions, answers.*.noul/probability) unverified against OpenRouter System One / Decisions API and no live-API tests; OpenRouter only wins if JEV_PROVIDER is set explicitly, otherwise any TYPESAFE/JEV key or settings.json key silently wins and sends data to api.typesafe.ai (unverified host).

Dubious value per hook: rule-guard judges a 4000-char new_string with no view of the existing file or callers yet hard-blocks (exit 2) at p>=0.8, so false-positive stalls in bypass/auto mode; skill-picker adds 150-600 ms to EVERY prompt for a false 'saves 90 skills' claim; PreCompact custom_instructions JSON contract likely ignored; all 'tokens/latency saved' numbers are hardcoded constants, not measurements.

Privacy/leakage: whole prompt and code snippets leave the machine on every prompt/edit with no redaction or allowlist; writes .jev/telemetry.jsonl (with prompt previews) into every project incl. client repos; dashboard binds all interfaces without host restriction; discover.js shell-interpolates prompts into execSync.

Extremely immature and single-author: created 2026-09-29, 31 commits in 2 days, 0 stars/forks, no CI, mock-only tests; prompts hardcoded in Portuguese (may skew results on English code); depends on external tools (graphify, grepai, browser-harness) the user lacks; version mismatch (v0.4.0 release vs package.json 1.0.0).
entries.verdict: Best conceptual match for 'automatic, no prompting' because it is hook-based, but it is a 2-day-old POC with a leaked hardcoded API key, a destructive macOS-specific installer, an unverified OpenRouter schema (wrong model id), and hooks (hard-blocking guard, per-prompt router) that add latency and leak code for questionable benefit. Do not install; at most fork and cherry-pick the client/hook skeletons after fixing model id, key handling and guard scope.

entries.name: Ajasra/jev-hooks
entries.what: Python (stdlib-only core) hook runtime, "jev-harness-runtime" v0.1.0, that calls Jev (System One) from lifecycle hooks. It has adapters ONLY for Google Antigravity and OpenAI Codex, not Claude Code. Features: Safety Gate (regex critical-command denylist plus Jev noul questions "routine?" and "destructive?" on Bash commands), Speculative pre-flight (git status injection), Dynamic Skill Router and Knowledge-Item matcher (Jev `choice` over .agents/skills and .agents/knowledge), Output Verifier and Semantic Lint (Jev noul over diffs). Also a SQLite rule/telemetry store, an optional MCP server with 8 tools, and a CLI (hook, doctor, authorize, stats, lint, verify, mcp).
interface: jev hook --harness antigravity|codex (stdin JSON -> stdout JSON)
MCP tools (jev mcp, requires mcp>=2 extra)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hooks (UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse and others), which is exactly the automatic, no-prompting model wanted. BUT the shipped configs target Antigravity (.agents/hooks.json, Windows `cmd /c` paths) and Codex (.codex/hooks.json with command_windows only). There is no Claude Code settings snippet and no `claude` adapter. Claude Code would need a new adapter plus a settings.json hooks block.
security: API key sent as a Bearer header via urllib (client.py:64), so it is not visible in argv or the process list.

Key loading walks .agents/.env, ./.env (the project .env) and ~/.gemini/config/.env and copies every KEY=VALUE it finds into os.environ (client.py:15-30). Any project's .env is parsed on every hook run. It stays in-process but is a needless read of client secrets.

The Safety Gate sends the raw Bash command to OpenRouter unredacted (safety.py, client.evaluate with clean_command(operation.command)). Commands containing inline tokens, curl -H 'Authorization', DB URLs and similar leave the machine. redact() is applied only to verification, semantic-lint and telemetry paths, not to the safety call.

Prompt-injection surface: skill and knowledge items are injected into the model context from repo files (.agents/skills, .agents/knowledge), and a repo-local jev.json can set skill_roots and knowledge_roots (PROJECT_ALLOWED, paths.py:14-19). A hostile cloned repo can therefore feed content into the agent context. Trust-sensitive keys (data_root, rules_db, policy_floor) are correctly rejected from project config.
The hook reads the transcript file (transcript_path) and parses recent prompts and errors from it (adapters/base.py:extract_turn_context), so user prompt text is sent to OpenRouter.
Local SQLite store at ~/.local/share/jev/jev.sqlite3 records events. Result data and errors are redacted, but the store still holds decision history and one-use allow rules.
entries.dataEgress: Only to openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone (or api.typesafe.ai). Per event: (1) UserPromptSubmit sends the user's prompt (redacted, capped 1500 chars), an assembled envelope of up to 4000 chars (project goal, session objective, active file path, git branch, first 600 chars of git status, last error, prior context) and skill/knowledge catalog names plus descriptions. (2) PreToolUse sends the raw, unredacted Bash command string and tool name for every Bash call that passes the regex denylist and has no matching stored rule. (3) Verification and lint send code snippets and diff hunks, redacted with a secret regex, up to 8-12k chars. It does not send whole files or tool outputs by default. Note that the prompt and every shell command from client projects go to a third party.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open, with a timeout too tight for Jev. Default semantic timeout is 0.25s (paths.py:105) and the hook deadline is 0.30s (adapters/base.py:142). Jev's claimed latency is 70-500 ms plus network and a Python cold start, so a large share of calls will time out. On any client exception the safety gate returns ALLOW ('semantic_unavailable', safety.py end) and the router features silently abstain. The regex denylist still runs offline. Fail-closed cases: a malformed PreToolUse event or an unparsable operation returns deny (cli.py:39-42, runtime.py:_safety), and the Codex adapter maps needs_confirmation to a hard deny. Under Claude Code bypass/auto mode there is no interactive approve path, so a false-positive semantic 'destructive' (>=0.5) would block the command outright. Only the `jev authorize` CLI can whitelist it.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools are needed for the hook path (zero tool-definition tokens). The optional MCP server adds 8 tools, roughly 500-800 tokens with short one-line descriptions. Hooks inject up to context_budget=12000 chars (about 3k tokens) on UserPromptSubmit, but only when a feature fires: git status up to 3000 chars, a skill body, a knowledge item. On Codex a telemetry HTML comment footer is appended. With no .agents/skills or .agents/knowledge in the user's projects, nearly nothing is injected; the skill and knowledge features are useless for Claude Code layouts.
pros: Uses the hook model the user wants: fully automatic, deterministic, no 'use jev' prompting (registry.py FEATURES, .codex/hooks.json).
OpenRouter is first-class in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY selects https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone and typesafe/jev-1.13 (client.py:46-62), and the request shape matches TypeSafe's System One API.

The Codex adapter's stdin/stdout JSON is very close to Claude Code's hook protocol (hook_event_name, session_id, cwd, tool_name, tool_input, transcript_path, hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision/additionalContext). A `claude` adapter is probably a ~60-line copy of adapters/codex.py plus a `--harness claude` choice.

Good architecture in places: stdlib-only core, ports and adapters, a deterministic regex floor that runs even when Jev is down, trusted vs project config separation (paths.py), one-use authorization with a digest, and unit tests with a fake client.
Uses Jev for what it is suited to: typed noul and choice micro-decisions (destructive?, needs git?, which skill?), never free text, matching the System One design.
Stdlib-only core and no npm postinstall or curl|sh means low supply-chain risk; a pip -e install of a single-author repo is easy to read and audit.
cons: No Claude Code support at all. `--harness` accepts only antigravity|codex (cli.py:81,101), and the adapters directory has only those two. Reading it is a reference implementation, not an integration.
Windows-first docs and hook configs (cmd /c, mklink, %USERPROFILE%, command_windows). The user is on Linux.

Overlaps the user's existing tools, and its value is thin for this user. The regex safety gate duplicates their existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard and Claude Code permission rules. Speculative git status duplicates the GitNexus hook. The skill and knowledge routers read .agents/skills, not ~/.claude/skills, and Claude Code already does skill selection natively.

The timeout budget (0.25s semantic, 0.30s deadline) is below Jev's claimed 70-500 ms end-to-end once the cold Python start is counted. Most semantic calls will silently fall back to allow, so the 'safety' value is mostly the regex list.

Raw Bash commands go unredacted to OpenRouter (safety.py) on every non-denylisted Bash call. That is a real client-confidentiality exposure for a bypass-mode user with client projects; only the semantic-lint and verification paths redact.
In bypass/auto mode, the Codex mapping of needs_confirmation to hard deny has no human-in-the-loop path. Jev false positives block work, and the escape hatch is a separate CLI command.
Project .env files are parsed into the hook's environment on every run (client.py:15-30).

Immature: 5 days old, 1 author, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, no LICENSE file (README claims MIT), version 0.1.0. RFC-heavy docs (26 proposals, about 300KB) versus about 44 tests. Some hooks (jev_output_pruner) still default to the direct TypeSafe endpoint and Antigravity behavior.
Uses the older /api/v1/systemone surface, not the newer /api/alpha/decisions surface. It sends the whole 'state' as a prompt string or dict with no typed schema.
entries.verdict: Not usable for Claude Code as shipped: it has only Antigravity and Codex adapters, Windows-oriented configs, and a 0.25s timeout that will mostly fail open. It is worth reading as a design reference for a Claude Code hook (a few noul questions on Bash and UserPromptSubmit, OpenRouter /systemone, a deterministic fallback), but a small purpose-built hook is safer than adopting this repo (unredacted commands leave the machine, no license, 5 days old).
entries.license: None in repo (no LICENSE file; GitHub licenseInfo null) even though README claims MIT and links ./LICENSE

entries.name: JEV_Claude_plugin (klukacin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin with Bash risk gate, prompt triage, subagent model router (Agent call rewritten to haiku/sonnet), Stop claim check and MCP tools. Author disabled it after 6 days: hooks cost more time than saved.
entries.autoInvocation: deterministic hooks; MCP tools model-discretion (never called unprompted per author)
pros: Uniquely valuable field data: ~18,000 logged decisions; Bash gate 126 min added latency and prevented nothing; MCP tools never called unprompted; docs/findings.md is evidence for what NOT to build
Subagent model router idea (Agent tool rewrite haiku/sonnet, high-stakes stays on session model) saved an estimated $70-110 in six days at API prices
145 passing tests, claude plugin validate passes
cons: Abandoned by its author on 2026-09-26; README headline 'FAILED AFTER RESEARCH AND TESTING'; would add latency for no benefit
TypeSafe-only (api.typesafe.ai, TYPESAFE_API_KEY, jev-latest), no OpenRouter; installer writes env.TYPESAFE_API_KEY into settings.json
Model router matters little for a user on subscription/OAuth with Opus (savings are API-price figures) and quality trade-off; committed bin/jev-mcp binary unverifiable

entries.name: yonatangross/orchestkit
entries.what: OrchestKit is a very large Claude Code plugin (107 skills, 36 agents, about 170 hook entries across ~30 hook events) that has two opt-in, env-flagged Jev seams inside its hooks. (1) Session-category classifier: on the first prompt of a session it asks Jev for one typed Choice over 8 work categories (branch name plus first 600 chars of the prompt), used to color/label the session. (2) Route judgment (ORK_ROUTE_JEV=shadow|steer): every build-shaped UserPromptSubmit prompt is sent to Jev as a Choice over 19 route classes plus 4 side judgments (worktree, browser, mutation risk, operator); in steer mode a one-line reminder such as "route: dev_fix -> /ork:fix-issue (conf 0.83)" is injected as prompt context. A third Python lane (skills/expect/scripts/jev_shadow.py) is a shadow classifier for the /ork:expect browser-testing skill. Jev is used purely as a hidden, deterministic-hook classifier; it is not a general coding tool and the value only exists if you adopt the entire OrchestKit skill catalog (route classes map to /ork:* skills).
interface: Plugin skills catalog (107 skills, 36 agents, no MCP server, no .mcp.json)
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (UserPromptSubmit and session-identity hooks fire automatically, no model discretion), but the Jev part is dormant until env vars are set, and its only effect is a routing hint (steer) or session color/log (shadow/jev category). It never decides tool use or code changes on its own.
security: MIT license (LICENSE, GitHub licenseInfo).

Key handling: read from env ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY only; never logged (comments 'Error text only, never the request'). Sync steer path spawns `node -e <script>` and passes key and endpoint via the child's env and body via stdin, explicitly not on argv (route-judgment.ts:~515-570); child env is scrubbed to PATH plus these vars. Good practice; no key in the process list.

Egress guard on route seam: redacts secrets, emails, phone numbers, 9-digit ids, op:// refs and clients/<dir> names, rescans the serialized request in raw and JSON-decoded form, and refuses the call if anything survives (fail closed on egress). The session-category seam is weaker: raw git branch plus first 600 chars of the first prompt with only whitespace normalisation, no redaction (README itself says its egress posture differs from the expect/route lane).

Prompt-injection surface: Jev output is a closed enum/probabilities parsed against a fixed set (parseWorkCategory / parseRouteIntent), so a malicious reply cannot inject free text into Claude's context; the injected nudge is built from a static class-to-executor table.

The plugin as a whole is a huge attack/behavior surface: ~170 hook entries incl. PreToolUse x20, PostToolUse x28, PermissionRequest x4, Stop x12, SessionStart x21, plus a bundled minified dist (plugins/ork/hooks/dist/*.mjs) that a reviewer must trust; it would be stacked on the user's existing secret-guard and GitNexus hooks with unknown ordering/interaction. It also has PermissionRequest and PermissionDenied hooks that could interfere with the user's bypass/auto permission mode.

Telemetry: README states no analytics ping, no crash reporter; optional telemetry sinks only fire if user sets ORCHESTKIT_HOOK_URL / ORK_HQ_TELEMETRY_URL. Dockerfile and postinstall not observed as required for plugin install (no postinstall in package.json grep).
entries.dataEgress: Default: nothing (both Jev lanes are off unless ORK_SESSION_CATEGORY_PROVIDER=jev|shadow or ORK_ROUTE_JEV=shadow|steer AND ORK_TYPESAFE_API_KEY are set). When on: (a) category lane sends git branch name plus the first 600 chars of the session's first prompt, un-redacted, to api.typesafe.ai; (b) route lane sends, for every build-shaped prompt, the first 1,500 chars of the prompt after redaction (secrets, emails, phones, ids, op://, clients/ dir names replaced by tokens) plus the repository basename (max 40 chars) and an opening_turn flag. No code, diffs, file contents or tool outputs are sent. (c) expect lane sends goal, last verify result, page elements and candidates. Everything goes to api.typesafe.ai by default (a third-party processor); it would go to openrouter.ai only if the endpoint is patched. Client-project caveat: the category lane's lack of redaction and the redactor's Israeli-phone-specific and clients/-directory-specific patterns mean prompts on client projects can still contain client identifiers.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open on routing: no key, timeout (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS / ORK_ROUTE_JEV_TIMEOUT_MS default 3000 ms), non-2xx, malformed body, confidence below floor (0.5 route, 0.8 category), or daily token budget (2M) exhausted -> existing path runs untouched (decided_by=table/haiku); 402/429 trips the seam off for 24 h. Fail-closed only on egress-scan hits (call refused, nothing sent). Costs when slow: category lane makes the first prompt of a session wait 1.1-1.7 s cold, up to 3 s; steer mode blocks the synchronous UserPromptSubmit handler on a spawned node child for up to 3 s (+1 s child timeout margin) per build-shaped prompt. Shadow-route mode keeps the hook process alive until the call settles.
entries.contextCost: No MCP server, so 0 MCP tools and no server 'instructions'. The cost is the plugin itself: 107 skills whose frontmatter descriptions total about 34.7k chars (~8.7k tokens) always loaded in the skill list, plus 36 agent descriptions (extra, not measured), plus plugin CLAUDE.md. Hooks inject context: the route steer adds one short line (~20-30 tokens) per build-shaped prompt; the once-per-session executor reminder is a one-liner; many other OrchestKit hooks inject additional prompt context (not audited in full). Net: roughly 10k+ tokens of standing context for the catalog, alongside the user's existing skills, for a Jev feature that contributes a ~25-token nudge.
pros: Genuinely wires Jev into Claude Code via deterministic UserPromptSubmit hook, so no 'use jev' prompt is ever needed; a real, working reference for the classify-the-prompt use case.

Well-engineered failure semantics: everything fails open with 3 s timeout, daily token budget, 24 h circuit-breaker on 402/429, and egress fail-closed with a two-pass redaction scan (route-judgment.ts:235-300).
Key never hits argv: sync path passes key via child env and body via stdin (route-judgment.ts ~515-570). Jev replies are parsed against closed enums, so no prompt-injection channel from the model.
Route seam endpoint is env-overridable (ORK_ROUTE_JEV_ENDPOINT), so OpenRouter is a small patch away; request format is standard System One (state/model/questions).

Active project: 286 stars, MIT, commits daily through 2026-09-29, releases (v9.8.1 on 2026-09-29), CI workflows, dedicated Jev tests (tests/unit/test-jev-*.mjs, executor-route-nudge-jev.test.ts, mock_jev.py fixtures) and held-out eval numbers documented (93.5% at >=0.8 confidence).
Pins model jev-1.13.0 for reproducibility and logs one auditable line per prompt plus jsonl records (labels and sha256 only).
cons: Does not support OpenRouter as shipped: zero 'openrouter' in the repo; category seam has hardcoded endpoint and model (session-category-provider.ts:53,56); route model 'jev-1.13.0' is not env-overridable and OpenRouter wants 'typesafe/jev-1.13'; requires forking/patching source and the bundled dist, and the patch must be redone on each of the near-daily releases.

Not a general Jev integration: the only Jev use is classifying prompts into OrchestKit's own /ork:* route classes and session colors. Without adopting the whole toolkit (107 skills, 36 agents) it is useless; it offers no decision primitives (Noul/Score) for coding tasks like risk-gating edits, test selection, or commit/PR triage.

Enormous blast radius for a small benefit: ~170 hook entries incl. PermissionRequest, PermissionDenied, PreToolUse x20 and Stop x12 would be layered on the user's existing secret-leak guard, GitNexus hooks and caveman plugin, with likely conflicts, overlapping context injection and a bypass/auto permission-mode interaction; ~8.7k tokens of skill descriptions added to every session.

Jev's value here is tiny: a 20-token routing hint that the main model (Opus) can already derive; the README's own comment says steer mode 'the model still reads the /ork:auto table and says whether it agrees'.

Latency: category lane blocks first prompt 1.1-1.7 s cold; steer blocks each build-shaped prompt by up to 3 s via a new node process, contradicting the 70-500 ms claim (they measured cold-start and TLS overhead of a fresh process).

Privacy on client work: category lane sends un-redacted first prompt and branch to a third party; route redactor patterns are tailored to the author (Israeli phone numbers, clients/ directory names), not the user's environment.

Route classes and the 'executor reminder' logic are specific to author's telemetry ('think skills 141x vs executor skills 6x'), i.e. an opinionated workflow; the Jev features are marked opt-in/shadow/experimental with issue references (#4233), so they can change or vanish.
Single dominant author (125 of 200 sampled commits, remainder bots); large surface (299 MB clone) and rapid churn make auditing the bundled dist impractical.
entries.verdict: A well-engineered but narrow, TypeSafe-direct-only Jev classifier embedded in a huge opinionated plugin; it proves the hook pattern (UserPromptSubmit + fail-open + redaction) is viable but is not worth installing for this user, and OpenRouter needs a source patch. Best used as a design reference for a small custom hook rather than as a dependency.

entries.name: King4s/Jev-AI-Skill
entries.what: Python skill plus stdio MCP server (jev-loop, 9 tools) that uses Jev via the TypeSafe direct API. It has a build/review Loop (loop_*), four stateless Gate tools (triage, verdict, decide, pick) meant to run before spending a large-model turn, and CLI helpers (route.py, git_decide.py, find_code.py, --watch). It is aimed at agent-orchestration cost saving (cron and event triage, review rounds, owner questions), not at the interactive coding decisions a Claude Code user makes all day. There are no hooks; use depends on the model following SKILL.md and the MCP server instructions.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools plus a skill-description trigger. The server "instructions" and SKILL.md tell Claude to call gate_triage, gate_verdict and gate_decide 'every time, before reasoning' in those moments. The skill description is name-driven (jev, jev-loop, kør loopen, byg med jev), so it fires mostly when the user says those words, which conflicts with the "never say use jev" requirement. There is no deterministic hook, so triggering depends on model compliance. The Gate moments (cron and poll events, review rounds, owner questions) are rare in an interactive session.
security: API key is read from env or ~/.config/jev-loop/typesafe_api_key and sent as a Bearer header. It is never put in argv, and the install script only passes the key as an env reference for Hermes (install.sh:64-72). No key in the process list.

Loop executes `shell=True` commands taken from the goal JSON (jev_mcp.py:109), with a 300 s default timeout. This is arbitrary code execution driven by a model-written goal file. The README admits it, and bypass mode makes it riskier.

Gate/Loop inputs are model-composed strings from Claude, so hostile repo content that reaches those strings could influence a decision. Decisions are probabilistic and low-stakes for triage, but the skill tells the agent to skip work on 'ignore' or 'known'.

The --http mode has no authentication (README and the serve_http docstring). If it is bound to 0.0.0.0, the /jev endpoint would be an open proxy that spends the key, and /mcp would let anyone start loops that run shell checks on that host. The default host is 127.0.0.1.
The MCP server is registered at user scope with an absolute path to the venv and script. Runtime pip deps (mcp>=2.2, requests) are unpinned and there is no hash pinning.
No telemetry found in the code. Run state and a decision tape are written to runs/*.jsonl next to the script, or under ~/.local/state/jev-loop/runs.
entries.dataEgress: Sent to api.typesafe.ai only, over HTTPS (TypeSafe, not OpenRouter), and only when a Jev tool is called. The payload is {model, state, questions}, where state is what Claude composes. gate_* sends up to 40 events (each clipped to about 600 characters), findings, evidence tails, option labels and descriptions, and question text. loop_* sends the goal, acceptance criteria, a limited project file list, check outputs (last 2000 characters per check) and short turn notes. route.py sends the task, context and skill descriptions. git_decide.py sends repo facts (branch, commit subjects, counts). find_code.py is the biggest one: up to 2000 chunks of 2400 characters of raw source from the repo go to TypeSafe, which is unsuitable for client code. Full files and diffs are not sent by the hooks or MCP tools, because there are no hooks and nothing observes the session automatically.
entries.failureMode: The MCP tools return {"error": ...} through safe() when Jev fails (jev_mcp.py:~650). SKILL.md says to 'do the work the expensive way' and never treat an error as ignore, which means fail-open to normal Claude work by instruction, not by mechanism. Jev HTTP calls use a 60 s timeout with up to 4 retries and exponential sleep on 429/529 (jev_mcp.py:86-100). Worst case is several minutes blocked inside one tool call. The upstream forwarding path has a 90 s timeout and retries 4 times on connection errors. With no API key, RuntimeError is returned as an error dict. The --gate and --watch CLIs exit 2 with error JSON.
entries.contextCost: Server: 9 tools. Tool defs (names, docstrings, schemas) come to roughly 4.6 KB of source, so about 1.2-1.8k tokens once schemas are added. The server "instructions" string is about 600 characters, or about 150 tokens. The skill adds its name and description to the listing (about 520 characters, about 130 tokens), and the 22 KB SKILL.md (about 5.5k tokens) loads whenever the skill triggers. No hooks, so nothing is injected per tool call. Total idle cost is about 1.5-2k tokens, which is moderate; 9 tools for a mostly irrelevant workflow is poor value.
pros: Real, inspected code with 8 test files, CI on Linux and Windows, an MIT license, and releases. It is more than a README skill.

Gate design is sensible for Jev's strengths: short structured state in, calibrated probabilities out. The instructions for each question type are well framed (noul and choice primitives in jev_mcp.py:493-620).
Fail-safe wording: on an error, do the work the normal way. Errors return as dicts and do not crash the server.
Key handling is clean: env or a chmod 600 file, no argv exposure, no telemetry, and no npm postinstall. The installer never pipes to sh.
gate_decide and gate_pick could plausibly reduce 'should I ask the user?' interruptions, useful in auto mode.
JEV_UPSTREAM forwarding is a ready-made seam for a translating proxy to OpenRouter.
git_decide.py's hard blocks (no direct push to main, identity and private-pattern blocks) are a useful guard, though only if actually called.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the only endpoint is api.typesafe.ai and the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY. The base URL is hardcoded in 3 files, with no env override. It cannot be used with an OpenRouter key without patching.

The hooks Claude Code would need for automatic use do not exist. Triggering relies on the model reading a 22 KB SKILL.md and 9 tool descriptions. The skill description is keyword-driven ('jev', 'byg med jev', 'kør loopen'), which is the opposite of the user's wish to never say 'use jev'.

The problem it targets is agent-fleet cost (cron jobs, notifications, chat-room events, Hermes, Codex) and not interactive coding in Claude Code. In a normal Claude Code session the Gate moments barely occur. Its author's own audit says the biggest token sinks were scheduled jobs and echoed exit codes.

Loop is a whole competing orchestration protocol (start, decide, execute, record_turn, review) that overlaps with and fights Claude Code's own agent loop and plan mode. It also runs shell checks from the goal file with shell=True, which is risky under bypass permissions.
find_code.py ships raw source excerpts (up to 4.8 MB in 2000 chunks of 2400 characters) to a third party. That is unacceptable for client projects, and it is uncached and slow.

The project is 6 days old, with 30 commits on a single day. It is essentially one author with AI agents (5 commits by 'Hermes Agent'), has 3 stars and 0 forks, and is unproven. Docs and the skill are partly in Danish. mcp>=2.2 with the mcp.server.mcpserver import is a fresh, unpinned dependency.
Adds 9 tools plus a 22 KB skill to context for capabilities that are mostly irrelevant, on top of gitnexus, playwright and caveman.
--http mode has no authentication, and the shared-server setup expects a tailnet. Failure retries can stall a tool call for minutes.
entries.verdict: Well-built for its niche, but the niche is not yours. It gates agent-fleet turns (cron, notifications, review rounds), it is TypeSafe-direct only (no OpenRouter), and its auto-trigger is a name-driven skill plus model-discretion MCP tools instead of hooks. Use it as a reference for Gate question design (noul/choice framing), not as your daily integration. If you did adopt it, install only the Gate tools behind an OpenRouter-translating JEV_UPSTREAM proxy, and skip Loop and find_code.py.

entries.name: AkashPriyadarshii/jev-superpowers
entries.what: Fork/re-skin of obra/superpowers (20 skills: 14 original superpowers skills plus 6 jev-* variants) with Claude Code plugin hooks (SessionStart context injection, PreToolUse Bash git-commit gate, Stop gate). The repo contains NO Jev API client code: every Jev call is delegated to separate third-party CLIs (jev-axi, jev-scout, git-jev, jev-guard, supercov, limpet) that the model is told, in markdown, to run. It is essentially a prompt/workflow wrapper around other people's tools.
entries.autoInvocation: Hybrid. Deterministic hooks: SessionStart context injection (always), PreToolUse on Bash matching git commit/push (runs `git jev check`), Stop hook on every turn end. Jev usage itself is skill-description/prompt driven (model-discretion): the injected 'MUST INVOKE' router pushes Claude to run jev-axi/jev-scout/jev-guard via Bash, so real Jev calls depend on the model obeying instructions and on 6 external CLIs being installed. No transparent proxy, no MCP.
security: No network code in repo itself; no curl|sh, no npm postinstall, no telemetry in the repo (grep clean). install.sh only cp -r skills into ~/.agents/skills.
API key: repo never reads/forwards the key; it is a plain env var consumed by external CLIs (their argv/process-list behavior not audited; env vars are not in argv by default).

hooks/pre-commit parses the hook JSON with a fragile grep on the first '"command"' field: matches any command containing 'git'...'commit'/'push' anywhere (e.g. echo, grep 'git commit' logs) -> false-positive blocks; also may miss multi-line/escaped commands. No injection risk since it uses [ ] case matching only.

hooks/stop runs `bash ./scripts/test.sh` from the CURRENT PROJECT dir if present: executes arbitrary project-supplied script on every turn end (risk on untrusted/client repos), and `limpet check` if installed.

Prompt-injection surface: session-start hook injects an <EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT> block instructing the model it MUST invoke skills; skills instruct running external binaries on repo content (stack traces, diffs) piped to a cloud service; jev output treated as authority.

Supply chain: skills require installing 6 third-party tools from different authors (cargo/npm global installs: jev-axi, jev-guard, supercov, jev-scout, git-jev, limpet) - each unaudited here and each an additional trust boundary.
entries.dataEgress: The repo itself sends nothing. Through the external CLIs it instructs Claude to run: architectural question text + context (jev-axi pick --text), full build/test output and stack traces plus diff snippets (jev-axi triage/check), the staged git diff (git jev check, per README/site: 'Git staged diff (240 lines)'), shell commands (jev-guard), dependency search queries (jev-scout, also queries crates.io/GitHub). On the TYPESAFE endpoint (api.typesafe.ai) by default, so client source/diffs would leave the machine to TypeSafe; nothing goes via OpenRouter as shipped. Stop hook runs local commands only.
entries.failureMode: Mixed and mostly FAIL-CLOSED by design. pre-commit hook: missing git-jev, non-zero status or no '[PASS]' in output => exit 2 blocks every git commit/push (and any Bash command whose text contains git..commit/push). There is no timeout in any hook script and hooks.json sets none. Stop hook: uncommitted changes => exit 2 every turn, i.e. Claude is forced to commit/stash before it may stop (loop risk/auto-commits, conflicts with users who do not want commits). Skills tell the model to STOP and never degrade silently when the key/tool/registry is missing (docs/CONFIDENCE.md 'Missing tool / key / offline: STOP'). Jev slow/down therefore blocks commits and stalls the session. run-hook.cmd on Windows fails open (exit 0) when bash is absent.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools. SessionStart injects ~2.2k chars of SKILL.md plus wrapper text = ~650 tokens on every startup/clear/compact (it also claims 'EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT'). Plugin skill listing: 20 skills with descriptions (~150-300 chars each, ~1.2k tokens total). Loading a skill body costs 0.5-8k tokens (jev-* skills 2k chars each; inherited subagent-driven-development is 32KB ~8k tokens, writing-skills 26KB ~6.5k tokens). Hooks add latency and stderr text on block.
pros: Only candidate here that actually wires Claude Code lifecycle hooks (SessionStart/PreToolUse/Stop) so behavior is automatic rather than requiring a prompt; git commit/push gate on the staged diff is a genuinely sensible Jev use case (Noul/Choice on diff risk).
MIT license, static-only content (markdown + short bash), no build step, no postinstall or curl|sh: easy to read fully in 10 minutes, low direct supply-chain risk from the repo itself.
docs/CONFIDENCE.md gives a clear act/confirm/stop threshold policy, and the idea of pairing Jev's calibrated probabilities with human-approval gates is a good pattern to borrow.
Supports a local TYPESAFE_BASE_URL override convention (could be pointed at a compatible endpoint) and includes an offline mock server.
cons: No Jev/OpenRouter code at all: zero references to openrouter.ai, /api/alpha/decisions or /api/v1/systemone; everything depends on 6 unaudited third-party CLIs that each need TYPESAFE_API_KEY, so it cannot use the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev without patching every downstream tool.

Stop hook exits 2 whenever the working tree is dirty and runs ./scripts/test.sh of whatever project you are in: forces commits/loops on every turn, breaks normal exploratory or client-repo workflows, and executes project scripts each turn. Combined with bypass/auto mode this is disruptive and risky.
PreToolUse commit gate is fail-closed and fragile: without git-jev installed all `git commit`/`git push` (and any Bash text containing both words) are blocked; grep-based JSON parsing; no timeouts.

Bulk: bundles the entire upstream superpowers skill set (20 skills, ~150KB) duplicating jev-* variants, injects an EXTREMELY_IMPORTANT MUST-invoke block every session start/compact, and mandates the workflow (brainstorm gate, human approval) that conflicts with existing GitNexus/caveman setup and a senior user's fast loop; jev-scout is Rust/crates-centric.

Immature and inconsistent: created 2026-09-18, 52 commits by a single author mostly CSS/site fixes, no releases, STATE.md says MVP in progress, marketplace.json is upstream's stale metadata, install.sh copies to ~/.agents/skills (not Claude Code's plugin path), CI is only a frontmatter/grep test (24 checks, no real hook behavior against Jev), README 'benchmarks' are unverified design targets.

Data egress of diffs/test output/stack traces from client projects to TypeSafe cloud via external CLIs (not OpenRouter), a compliance concern; skills also treat Jev output as authority though Jev is a beta typed-decision model, not a code reviewer (supercov 'quality' and 'hallucinated package' claims are unverified).
entries.verdict: Not recommended to install as-is: it is a superpowers fork whose Jev usage is entirely outsourced to unaudited CLIs bound to TYPESAFE_API_KEY (no OpenRouter path), and its Stop/commit hooks are fail-closed and intrusive. Worth mining only for the idea of a small PreToolUse git-commit diff gate plus the confidence-threshold policy, reimplemented against OpenRouter's Decisions API in your own hook.

entries.name: utk2103/jev-studio
entries.what: Python package (PyPI jev-studio 0.2.1) bundling three things. (1) A `jev` CLI (stdlib urllib, ~4k LOC) that wraps TypeSafe Jev/System One with commands verify, screen (prompt-injection check), classify, extract, match, route, ask, find, rerank, compact (shrink agent transcripts), batch. (2) A `jev-studio` MCP server (FastMCP, stdio) that exposes one prompt `jev` and one tool `jev_instructions`. Both only return a hard-coded placeholder string per mode (`Jev — full mode. Standard ruleset.`); the MCP server never calls Jev or any API. (3) A Claude Code/Codex plugin (`prompt-studio@jev-studio`) with SessionStart/SubagentStart hooks that inject the same placeholder string, a UserPromptSubmit hook that tracks `/jev lite|full|ultra|off`, and two slash commands. The README describes 'MCP tools for Choice/Noul/Score' but no such tools exist in server.py. The real Jev functionality lives only in the CLI, which Claude would have to call through Bash on its own initiative (nothing in the plugin tells it to).
interface: CLI jev classify / extract / match / route
CLI jev models / auth / config / update / version
entries.autoInvocation: Nothing that uses Jev is automatic. The SessionStart/SubagentStart hooks are deterministic, but the injected text is the placeholder 'Jev — full mode. Standard ruleset.', which does not tell Claude when or how to call Jev, so it changes no behaviour. The MCP tool jev_instructions is model-discretion and merely returns that placeholder. The useful CLI (screen, verify, classify, compact) runs only if Claude decides to shell out to `jev`, or if the user wires their own hook, and this repo ships no such hook or skill.
security: MCP server and hooks make no network calls and execute no shell commands; hooks are stdlib-only Python that print static text. Attack surface of that part is tiny.
Flag-file handling is careful (lstat/O_NOFOLLOW, 64-byte cap, 0600, tmp+replace), _jev_common.py:70-127.

CLI keys: read from env or OS keychain. On Linux, `secret-tool store` receives the secret via stdin, not argv (credentials.py:129). On macOS `security add-generic-password ... -w secret` (credentials.py:110) puts the key in argv, but that does not affect this Linux user. Fallback is a 0600 file.
CLI uses an SSL default context and a timeout on every request. `jev --dry-run` prints the request without sending it.
Daily PyPI update-check phones home to pypi.org (cached 24h at ~/.config/jev/update-check.json, disable with JEV_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1). No other telemetry found.

Auto provider selection silently prefers TYPESAFE_API_KEY and falls back to OPENROUTER_API_KEY or Cloudflare. It prints a stderr notice for third-party hops (provider.py:26-46). Set `-P openrouter` or JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter to pin it.
entries.dataEgress: MCP server and hooks: nothing leaves the machine. CLI only, when invoked: the `state` (whatever text/files/stdin the caller passes, such as code, diffs, tool output or transcripts for compact) plus the typed questions go as JSON to the chosen provider (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions, api.typesafe.ai, or api.cloudflare.com). The Authorization key, HTTP-Referer https://github.com/utk2103/jev-Studio and X-Title jev-studio headers go with it. Also a GET to pypi.org/pypi/jev-studio/json once a day. The CLI does not send anything unless someone runs a jev command.
entries.failureMode: Hooks: fail-open. Timeout 5s, exceptions swallowed (jev_activate.py:28-30), python3/python fallback via sh. Worst case the placeholder text is not injected. MCP server: no external dependency, and it fails only if `mcp` 2.x gets installed (fixed by the <2 pin). CLI: fail-closed per call. Errors exit 1 (transport, timeout, HTTP>=400, malformed answers); a tripped judgment exits 2 with --fail-on. Timeout is configurable via --timeout or JEV_TIMEOUT_MS (default not verified). There are no retries in provider.py, and nothing degrades gracefully because nothing calls it automatically.
entries.contextCost: Small, because the plugin does almost nothing. MCP server: 1 tool (jev_instructions, description ~105 chars plus a one-string schema) and 1 prompt, about 80-120 tokens of tool definitions. No server `instructions` field. Hooks inject ~35 chars (about 10 tokens) at SessionStart and at each SubagentStart. The UserPromptSubmit hook adds text only when the user types /jev. Total under 150 tokens. The context spent buys no functionality.
pros: The `jev` CLI does support OpenRouter (Decisions API, sk-or- key, typesafe/jev-1.13), so an OpenRouter-only setup works with `-P openrouter` or JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter and needs no patching.

The CLI offers directly useful judgments for a coding agent: `jev screen` (prompt-injection check on fetched web text or tool output), `jev verify`, `jev classify`, `jev route` and `jev compact` (transcript pruning). It is a good reference for what Jev primitives look like in practice.
The MCP/hook parts are almost zero-risk: no network, no shell execution, silent-fail hooks, tiny context footprint (<150 tokens).

Reasonable hygiene for a young project: MIT licence, CI, trusted-publisher PyPI release, `mcp<2` pin after a real bug report (#11), Linux keychain via secret-tool with the key on stdin, `--dry-run`, and a stderr notice on third-party provider hops.
Usable as a manual toolbox: `jev screen --fail-on block,review` in a pipe or a CI gate is a real workflow.
cons: The MCP server is a stub. Its only tool returns 'Jev — full mode. Standard ruleset.' (instructions.py:11-15). The README's 'MCP tools for Choice/Noul/Score' claim is false, and the module docstring itself says 'Extend ... with the real Jev ruleset'. Adding it gives Claude Code zero Jev capability.
The SessionStart/SubagentStart hooks inject the same placeholder, so they do nothing except cost a Python process launch per session, subagent and prompt.

No automatic invocation of real Jev. Claude must decide to run `jev ...` through Bash, and nothing here (no SKILL.md, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook) says when. This fails the user's central requirement, which is that Claude uses Jev without being told.

The plugin format is partly wrong for Claude Code: the commands are .toml (Gemini/Codex style, not Claude .md), and the README's install name `prompt-studio@jev-studio` does not match the manifest name `jev-studio`.

The CLI is Python and has to be installed globally, and it shells out through Bash. That collides with the user's existing hooks: the secret-leak guard matcher covers Bash, so every `jev` call is scanned, and the GitNexus hook fires on Bash. Context and permission-prompt friction follow.

Weak provenance: one maintainer, 36 commits in 11 days, 17 stars, 3 placeholder-only tests, and the CLI is a port of the third-party Nasrallah-AL/jev-cli. The CLI is untested. Version drift (pyproject 0.2.0 vs release 0.2.1) suggests a manual process.

The OpenRouter path is pinned to jev-1.13 (not ~typesafe/jev-latest), uses only the alpha Decisions endpoint, has no retries, and `-P auto` prefers TYPESAFE_API_KEY over OpenRouter if both are set, so the user must set JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter explicitly.

If the ruleset text is ever filled in upstream, it is auto-updating untrusted text injected into every session and subagent (supply-chain and prompt-injection channel via pip and marketplace updates).
entries.verdict: Not a real Claude Code integration of Jev. The MCP server and hooks only serve a placeholder string and make no Jev calls. The genuinely useful part is the separate `jev` CLI, which supports OpenRouter but is never invoked automatically. Skip the MCP/plugin; the CLI is at best a reference for building your own PreToolUse/PostToolUse hook that calls OpenRouter's Decisions API.

entries.name: 47vigen/catherd
entries.what: A Bun/TypeScript Claude Code plugin (skill + slash commands + 26-tool stdio MCP server) that orchestrates multi-agent autopilot builds: Claude plans/verifies, Codex/opencode/Cursor/Grok/Antigravity/headless-Claude workers write code. Jev is used only internally as a small classifier: 3 typed question sets (route-v2: work kind + difficulty for a lane; finding: design vs code defect; same-defect: yes/no) posted to TypeSafe's /systemone to choose which worker model/effort rung to use. It is not a general-purpose Jev integration for Claude Code sessions.
entries.autoInvocation: Only when prompted. Skill description says to use it only when the user asks for catherd/orchestration ('Not for a plain request that merely mentions an architect, a verifier, a review...'); /catherd command is explicit. MCP tools are exposed to the model but are run-protocol tools that need a run started via the skill. Jev itself is never called on ordinary coding turns; it is invisible plumbing inside catherd's route tool.
security: Jev key sent as Authorization: Bearer header, never in argv; stored 0600 in ~/.config/catherd/credentials.json or env TYPESAFE_API_KEY; key registered with log redactor; catherd strips TYPESAFE_API_KEY from env of spawned worker processes (SECURITY.md)
Log redaction of KEY/TOKEN/SECRET env values and key-shaped strings; run folders 0600/700 but hold briefs that can quote code

Workers are spawned CLIs (Codex, opencode, claude, etc.) with your logins; access levels are advisory for Claude workers ('Claude's Bash tool can still write'); preflight runs lane-authored shell commands (allowlisted env, 120 s timeout) - an untrusted-input surface driven by LLM-written lane files
Plugin launcher uses bunx to fetch catherd-cli@1.2.1 from npm at runtime if no global install matches (supply-chain surface); no postinstall scripts in package.json
Docs recommend several curl|bash installers for worker CLIs (opencode, cursor, grok, antigravity) though catherd itself does not run them
Background sync fetches public model sources (models.dev, OpenRouter models list, LiteLLM, Arena, Vectara, Epoch AI) every 12h; no telemetry found in grep of src; Artificial Analysis key optional
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone only: for route-v2, a state of {title, owns[], fast_check, body} derived from the lane file with fenced code replaced by '[code omitted]', secrets scrubbed (scrubSecrets), body capped (capBody); for finding/same-defect, reviewer finding text plus lane text (state passed to verdict()). So planning prose and finding text leave the machine, not raw code or diffs by design. Also unauthenticated GETs of public model catalogs. Worker CLIs separately send whatever they see to their own vendors (Codex/OpenAI, etc.). Local jev.jsonl stores only a state hash, not the state.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. jev-client.ts retryingFetch: 10 s per attempt, 2 retries with 500 ms doubling backoff and Retry-After (capped 10 s), 25 s total deadline. No key, HTTP error, timeout or unparsable reply returns answers=null and routing falls back to the lane file's Kind/Difficulty, else the profile default rung (routing-service.ts route()); jev.use='off' skips the call. Worst-case added stall on a Jev outage is about 25 s per route call, plus route waits up to 5 s on model-discovery refresh. Answers are cached per run by request key (same model/state/questions).
entries.contextCost: 26 MCP tools always loaded while plugin is enabled (9 run, 5 lane, 3 dispatch, 4 protocol, 5 setup); several descriptions are long paragraphs (route's is several hundred chars). Estimated ~6-9k tokens of tool definitions (registration files are 32.9 KB total incl. code; descriptions+zod schemas roughly 24-28 KB / 4). No server 'instructions' field found in server.ts. SKILL.md is 54 KB (~13.5k tokens) but loads only when the skill triggers on /catherd; skill description itself is short. No hooks, so no injected per-turn text. Sits next to gitnexus/playwright, adding to the user's tool-count budget for zero benefit in normal coding.
pros: Genuine, non-fake Jev integration in code: real /systemone client with retries, timeouts, Retry-After, request-key caching, reply validation, drift detection against pinned model jev-1.13.0

Good reference for Jev question-set design: catalog/jev.json shows Choice questions with criteria, confidence rules ('rule' thresholds), fail-open default answers, and an audit log (jev.jsonl with hashes, not state)
Fail-open everywhere: Jev down or key missing never blocks work; jev.use can be turned off
Key hygiene is above average: Bearer header, 0600 file, log redaction, key stripped from child envs, code fences and secrets scrubbed before egress
Well tested for a young repo: 172 test files, CI on two OSes, changesets, architecture tests, live-test gate
MIT licensed, no hooks or postinstall, no telemetry found
cons: Not an automatic Jev-in-Claude-Code integration: Jev only picks worker model rungs inside an explicit /catherd autopilot run; it does nothing for normal edits, commits, permission decisions or tool routing
Requires explicit /catherd invocation, contradicting the user's 'never say use jev' requirement

Direct TypeSafe only: JEV_BASE hardcoded to https://api.typesafe.ai/v1 (jev-client.ts:5), key only from TYPESAFE_API_KEY/credentials.json; no OPENROUTER_API_KEY, no base-URL override, model id jev-1.13.0 not OpenRouter's typesafe/jev-1.13; needs a fork to use OpenRouter
Runs on Bun, not Node/uv; extra runtime plus at least one worker CLI (default profile needs Codex/OpenAI login) that the user does not have configured
Heavy footprint: 26 always-on MCP tools (~6-9k tokens) and a 54 KB skill, for a workflow orchestrating other vendors' agents, duplicating Claude Code subagents
Bypass-mode risk: spawns detached Codex/opencode/etc. workers with the user's logins and advisory-only sandboxing on client repos; lane planning text and reviewer findings are sent to a third party

Very new and single-author (6 stars, created 2026-09-24, 654 commits in 6 days, ~73% authored by 'Claude' co-author commits, 0 forks); runtime bunx fetch of an npm package at launch; docs pipe curl|bash for worker installs

Heavy interaction risk with user's existing hooks: workers 'load your Claude Code hooks, skills and plugins' (Cursor/Grok read ~/.claude) so secret-guard and GitNexus hooks would run in foreign agents
entries.verdict: Not a fit: catherd uses Jev only as a hidden model-router for its own multi-vendor autopilot, fires only on explicit /catherd, hardcodes the direct TypeSafe endpoint (no OpenRouter), and costs ~26 tools plus a Bun runtime. Worth reading only as a reference for a well-built fail-open /systemone client and typed question sets (catalog/jev.json).

entries.name: SantiagoPrada2005/jev-mcp-tool
entries.what: A remote MCP server meant to be deployed as your own Cloudflare Worker with a Durable Object for sessions. It exposes 4 tools (guardrail_gatekeeper, context_pruner, stop_condition_eval, speculative_eval). Each tool wraps one or more Jev noul/choice/score questions. It first calls Cloudflare Workers AI 'typesafe/jev' via the env.AI binding, and only if that throws does it fall back to OpenRouter POST /api/alpha/decisions with model typesafe/jev-1.13. The tools are aimed at RAG and agent-safety use cases, not coding. Claude Code cannot connect to it directly. It needs the mcp-remote npx bridge or a native HTTP MCP entry pointing at a Worker URL.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The tools' Spanish 'Invoca esta herramienta cuando...' descriptions are the only automatic-trigger mechanism. An optional system-prompt paste (AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md) makes it more insistent. There is no deterministic hook, no proxy and no plugin. The 4 tools do not fit coding events (edit, commit, test), so Claude will rarely or inconsistently pick them without prompting.
security: Secret leak: the committed .mcp.json:6 and :19 contain a real-looking bearer token, 'jev_mcp_...', for the author's live Worker (jev-mcp-server.santiagopradamoreno.workers.dev). Anyone can use it. It is a bad-hygiene signal and it means the author's public deployment is not private. Do not reuse it.
Never point Claude Code at that public URL. The author's Worker would see everything you send it, including client code.

The README config puts the token in argv via mcp-remote '--header Authorization: Bearer ...', so it is visible in ps output. The mcp-remote bridge is also an unpinned 'npx -y' that fetches and executes third-party code on every start.

Auth is a single shared static token with a non-constant-time compare (src/index.ts:46). The token is also accepted as a ?token= or ?auth= query param (line 43), which leaks into logs and URLs. CORS is Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *.

The guardrail_gatekeeper prompt-injection detector is a thin classifier, not a defense. Its output is untrusted model text that decides ALLOW or QUARANTINE, and the instructions in AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md are a prompt-injection surface of their own if pasted into a system prompt.
Cloudflare observability is enabled (wrangler.jsonc), so Worker logs are retained. console.log records model and timing only (jev.service.ts:99), not payloads. No telemetry beyond Cloudflare's.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in tool arguments is sent over HTTPS to the deployed Worker, and then to Cloudflare Workers AI or to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions. That means untrusted_text, RAG chunks, the artifact (full code, diffs or plans for stop_condition_eval) and arbitrary state for speculative_eval. Nothing leaves automatically. The model chooses what to send. Because it is a hosted intermediary, you get an extra party: whoever runs the Worker (you, if self-deployed) plus Cloudflare. Your OPENROUTER_API_KEY lives in Worker secrets on Cloudflare. It does NOT go through the OpenRouter key on your machine, so this is not a 'local OpenRouter-key integration'.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open, but only because it is a model-discretion tool. On errors the DO returns isError:true from tools/call (session.do.ts:222-236) and Claude just continues. There is no explicit timeout or AbortController on the OpenRouter fetch (jev.service.ts:72), so a hung upstream relies on Worker limits. There is no retry. If Workers AI 'typesafe/jev' returns without answers, it hard-fails with no fallback (line 60). If the Worker or mcp-remote bridge is down, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools vanish, as with caveman-shrink. There is no hook, so nothing can block the session.
entries.contextCost: 4 tools. Estimated about 1.5-2.2k tokens of tool names, descriptions and schemas (around 6-9k chars of the ~250 lines in src/tools/index.ts plus the long Spanish descriptions). Claude Code defers MCP tool schemas, which reduces the cost. No server 'instructions' field found. No hooks, so nothing is injected per turn. If the user pastes AGENT_INSTRUCTIONS.md into CLAUDE.md, add roughly 600-700 tokens of 'MUST delegate' directives on every session, which is not recommended.
pros: Genuinely wraps Jev's typed noul/choice/score primitives and hits the correct OpenRouter endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions, model typesafe/jev-1.13) with the right body shape, jev.service.ts:72-85.
speculative_eval is a clean generic passthrough (arbitrary state plus typed questions in one hop) that could be adapted as a building block.
The design of stop_condition_eval (rubric-based completion gate) is conceptually the closest to something useful in a coding agent.
Streamable HTTP plus SSE, session DO, bearer auth, and health endpoint are present, with mock-based Vitest coverage of all four tools and the fallback path.
MIT declared and a small codebase (about 900 lines of src), so it is easy to audit in full.
cons: Requires you to deploy and operate your own Cloudflare Worker with Durable Objects. That is a heavy and unnecessary hop compared with calling openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions directly from a local hook or stdio MCP.
OpenRouter is only a fallback behind an unverified Workers AI model 'typesafe/jev' (jev.service.ts:23). Your OPENROUTER_API_KEY sits as a Cloudflare secret, not locally.
A real bearer token for the author's live Worker is committed in .mcp.json:6/:19. The author's own security posture is weak, and the public URL must never be used.
Tool set is for RAG and agent perimeter security (guardrail, context pruner). No coding-specific tools: no diff/commit risk, test triage, permission gating, or file routing.

Entirely model-discretion auto-invocation. No hooks, so it cannot deterministically fire on PreToolUse, Stop or similar events. It would not satisfy 'Claude Code must use it when needed without my prompt'.
Claude Code needs the unpinned mcp-remote bridge (npx -y) with the token in argv, or native http transport with a static header. There is no stdio option.
No timeout on outbound fetch, no retries, no CI, no release, no LICENSE file (GitHub license null), 1 contributor, 9 commits over one day (2026-09-23), 0 stars. Effectively a weekend PoC.
Sends full artifacts (code, diffs) to third-party infrastructure when stop_condition_eval is used, a problem for client projects.
entries.verdict: Not recommended for adoption. It is a one-day-old, single-author PoC that needs a self-hosted Cloudflare Worker, uses OpenRouter only as a fallback, has RAG/guardrail tools that do not match coding, and offers only model-discretion invocation. Its only reusable value is as a reference for the /api/alpha/decisions request shape (src/services/jev.service.ts:72-85), which a small local hook or stdio MCP could call directly.
entries.license: MIT declared in package.json, but no LICENSE file and GitHub reports licenseInfo null

entries.name: cyrusasco/typesafe-mcp (typesafe-dispatch plugin)
entries.what: A personal ZCode-first (also Claude Code/Codex) plugin that wraps the direct TypeSafe System One API in a zero-dependency Node stdio MCP server (5 tools) plus a large "typesafe-dispatch" skill (~21 KB) and hooks. The pipeline: gate, ts_feasible, one batched Jev call (Battery #1) to choose workflow, executor, risk and difficulty, ts_decide thresholds, then dispatch to subagents (GLM/ZCode, DeepSeek, Qwen, codex-cli). Also has a subagent PreToolUse "on_spec" guard, a post-work review-comment script, a skill-suggestion tool over ~/.zcode/skills, and a JSONL ledger. It is a multi-agent dispatch router built around one author's ZCode setup, not a general coding-assistant Jev integration.
interface: CLI scripts/cli.mjs, guard-spec.mjs, subgoal.mjs, api-exec.mjs, review-comment.mjs, progress-page.mjs
entries.autoInvocation: Partial and heavy-handed. UserPromptSubmit hook (deterministic keyword regex) injects instructions telling the model to run the skill and the whole pipeline, and the model then decides whether to call MCP tools (model discretion). PreToolUse hook is deterministic but only acts on ZCode sess_subagent* sessions. Not a transparent proxy. Jev is not called silently by code on the main session's tool path; it is only called when Claude chooses to follow the injected instructions.
security: API key is read from env, .env or ~/.claude/settings.json and sent as a Bearer header via fetch. It is not in argv and is never logged per the code, which is a good practice.
Hardcoded endpoint https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (no override), so a forked-in OpenRouter URL is the only way to route elsewhere.

Egress redaction is 4 regexes (sk- keys, key/token/secret/password=..., Bearer, AWS AKIA/ASIA) applied to string values only. Weak against JWTs, PEM blocks, DB URLs, GitHub PATs and client code or data. The guard hook sends the proposed Bash command or Edit/Write input (first 500-600 chars) to the API.

Prompt-injection surface: the UserPromptSubmit hook injects a long imperative instruction block into context on many prompts. The skill tells the agent to push specs, run background dispatch and loop on judge every 15-30s. It also causes the agent to embed raw Jev JSON in subagent prompts.

Shell execution: the MCP server itself does not exec (no execSync/spawn other than the launcher spawning server.mjs). scripts/api-exec.mjs and review-comment.mjs call DeepSeek/Qwen APIs (with a user-private Qwen tunnel) and may shell out to codex-cli. These scripts are invoked by the agent via Bash.
No postinstall, no curl|sh, no telemetry beyond the TypeSafe calls. Writes state to ledger/, dedupe-cache.json (persists Jev results), skills-index.json in the data dir, and ~/.zcode/typesafe-state/.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (not OpenRouter): whatever `state` and `questions` the calling LLM composes for ts_ask, i.e. task text, cwd, file lists, executor registry, user prompt summaries, and for the guard the proposed Bash command or Edit/Write input (500-600 chars). ts_suggest_skill sends the whole local skill catalog (names and descriptions) plus SKILL.md excerpts. Secrets are only redacted by 4 regexes. The state is capped by the 32k Jev context. The ledger stores hashes and counts, not content. Additional egress in scripts (review-comment.mjs and api-exec.mjs) sends diffs and specs to DeepSeek or Qwen or codex-cli, which is unrelated to Jev and a serious client-code concern for this user.
entries.failureMode: Mostly fail-open with degradation. No key, daily cap (200k tokens), or breaker open (3 consecutive failures, 5 min cooldown) return {mode:"degraded",reason} without calling the API. Per-request timeout is 5000 ms (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS), with 429/529 retried up to 2 times with backoff, so worst case is roughly 5 s per attempt before the tool returns degraded. The guard hook fails open on degraded or missing data. The destructive regex check is fail-closed by design. Risks: the launcher retries the server up to 3 times on early exit; a dropped MCP server leaves the session toolless (the author documented this). In the shipped plugin layout, plugin/hooks/subagent-guard.mjs imports `../plugin/server.mjs`, which resolves to plugin/plugin/server.mjs and does not exist; this looks like a broken import that crashes the hook with a non-blocking error on every Bash/Edit/Write (unverified, static reading only).
entries.contextCost: Roughly 5 MCP tools (ts_ping, ts_ask, ts_decide, ts_safety, ts_feasible) plus ts_suggest_skill = 6 tools; the tool names, descriptions and schemas are about 6-7 KB of text, or about 1.6-2k tokens always loaded (ts_ask, ts_decide, ts_feasible and ts_suggest_skill descriptions are long). No MCP server `instructions` field. The skill adds a frontmatter description of about 1 KB (about 250 tokens) always visible, and a 20.9 KB (about 5-6k tokens) SKILL.md body once triggered. The UserPromptSubmit hook injects about 1.1 KB of dense Cantonese/English text (about 600-900 tokens) on every prompt matching a very broad regex (build, implement, create, install, refactor, migrate, upgrade...), which is common in daily coding. Estimated baseline 2-2.5k tokens, plus 6-7k more whenever the pipeline triggers.
pros: Genuinely automatic trigger path exists for Claude Code: plugin/hooks/hooks.json registers UserPromptSubmit plus PreToolUse and plugin/.mcp.json auto-wires the MCP server, so no 'use jev' prompting is needed (though it works by nudging, not by hard integration).

Sound engineering primitives worth borrowing: deterministic ts_decide thresholds (choice >=0.75 auto, noul deadband 0.35-0.65), 5 s timeout, 3-failure circuit breaker with 5 min cooldown, daily token cap, no-key degraded mode, 45 s same-payload dedupe, JSONL ledger with hashes only.
Zero npm dependencies, no postinstall, no curl|sh installer, MIT license, Bearer key never logged or in argv. It is static-readable (about 45 KB server) and easy to audit or fork.
Shows real, dated pilot evidence (ledger audits, token counts such as 833 tokens per Battery #1 call) that Jev works as a routing/guard judge in practice.

Server is a thin JSON-RPC stdio wrapper; the ts_ask primitive (state plus choice/noul/score questions) is generic and reusable, and swapping to OpenRouter needs about a 3-line change (URL, key var, model id).
cons: No OpenRouter support at all: URL hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai (server.mjs:48), key only TYPESAFE_API_KEY, no openrouter string anywhere. Requires a fork, and OpenRouter's System One schema equivalence is unverified.

Designed for ZCode with GLM/DeepSeek/Qwen executors (executors.json, ~/.zcode paths, sess_subagent id prefix, Cantonese prompts). Claude Code's Opus/Sonnet/Haiku subagents are not in the registry, so the routing answers are meaningless for this user's setup.

Its purpose is a multi-agent dispatch orchestrator that adds a heavy ritual (gate, feasible, ask, decide, subgoal dedupe, guard push, background judge polling, review-comment) to every build-shaped prompt. That is the opposite of low-friction daily coding and burns Opus turns and tokens.

Hook regex is very broad (create|install|implement|refactor|upgrade...) and injects about 1.1 KB of Cantonese imperative text on many ordinary prompts. It also mandates spawning background subagents and sending diffs/specs to DeepSeek/Qwen/codex-cli, which is a client-confidentiality hazard on client projects.

Likely-broken shipped hook: plugin/hooks/subagent-guard.mjs imports ../plugin/server.mjs, a path that does not exist inside the plugin layout, and it only acts on ZCode sess_subagent sessions anyway, so on Claude Code it is dead weight that still spawns Node on every Bash/Edit/Write and conflicts with the user's existing PreToolUse hooks.

Very immature: created 2026-09-19, 17 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, only a hand-run smoke script (scripts/smoke.mjs, 23 checks). Version strings disagree (server VERSION 1.1.0 vs plugin 1.8.0), and a private tunnel URL was committed and force-push purged in the history.
Egress redaction is 4 regexes, and ts_suggest_skill sends the local skill catalog to the API. It uses only the direct TypeSafe endpoint, so it cannot satisfy 'OpenRouter as Jev provider'.

Jev's own semantics do not fit the wrapper: skeptics call it a small-model router, and here it is used as a router for tasks Claude Opus could simply decide, so cost and latency benefit is unproven for a single-main-model subscription user.
entries.verdict: Not suitable to install: it is a ZCode multi-agent dispatch harness with hardcoded api.typesafe.ai (no OpenRouter), a broad Cantonese prompt-injecting hook, and a likely-broken guard hook under the plugin layout. Mine it for ideas (thresholds, breaker, dedupe, degraded mode, ts_ask schema) but build or fork a small OpenRouter-based wrapper instead.

entries.name: jev-stack (aleksvega umbrella installer)
entries.what: Not a skill or integration itself. It is a 134-line zero-dependency Node CLI (npx jev-stack) that only git-clones five separate third-party repos (fast-jev-compaction, jev-ultrafast, jev-prompt-enhancer, jev-skill-router, cdp-browser-launcher) into the current directory, and runs "npm install -g --prefix <dir>" inside two of them (fast-jev-compaction, jev-prompt-enhancer). It ships an AGENT_PROMPT.md that asks an agent to walk the user through the same installs. It has no MCP server, no hooks, no SKILL.md and no plugin manifest, and it wires nothing into Claude Code. The payload repos are the real tools. The most Claude-Code-relevant one is jev-prompt-enhancer, whose "--install" writes a UserPromptSubmit hook that can rewrite every user prompt. The npm keywords list "claude" and "codex".
interface: payload: fast-jev-compaction hooks/fast-jev.ts plus jev-compact, jev-gate, jev-qa, jev-find CLIs
entries.autoInvocation: None for jev-stack itself (only when the user runs it or pastes AGENT_PROMPT.md). The only automatic mechanism in the stack is the payload jev-prompt-enhancer UserPromptSubmit hook, which is deterministic per prompt but needs a separate manual install step. The other CLIs (jev-compact, jev-gate, jev-qa, jev-find) are invoked manually or via git hooks, not automatically by Claude Code.
security: Installer uses execSync with shell:true and string-interpolated commands (bin/jev-stack.js:65,78,81). Repo URLs are hardcoded and the target dir comes from JEV_STACK_DIR or cwd, so the injection surface is limited but real if the path has quotes.

Runs 'npm install -g --prefix <dir>' inside freshly cloned unpinned third-party repos (bin/jev-stack.js:81), so it executes their lifecycle scripts and dependencies with no pinning, no commit SHAs and no checksum. HEAD of five personal repos with 0-1 stars is trusted blindly, a supply-chain risk.
git clone --depth 1 of the default branch with no ref pinning. The author can change behavior at any time without an npm release.
Payload jev-prompt-enhancer rewrites every user prompt via a UserPromptSubmit hook and sends it to two OpenRouter models. That is a prompt-integrity and confidentiality risk on client projects.
Payload jev-gate is described as a 'pre-push guardrail' that decides on model output. The README says deterministic checks take priority, but that was not verified.
AGENT_PROMPT.md is a prompt-injection-style installer script. It tells the agent to clone and smoke test repos, though it does say not to ask for secrets.
entries.dataEgress: jev-stack itself sends nothing. It only clones from github.com. Payload egress, from sampled files: jev-gate.py POSTs to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (presumably diff or push content, unverified). jev-prompt-enhancer sends the full user prompt to Jev and to inception/mercury-2 on OpenRouter for rewriting. The compaction tool sends session context to Jev, which is code and conversation content, so file contents and tool outputs are at risk. There is no local-only mode. Everything goes to OpenRouter and its upstream providers.
entries.failureMode: jev-stack itself has none, because it is a one-shot installer. Payload jev-prompt-enhancer states it is fail-open, returning the original prompt on error (cli.mjs header). jev-gate.py uses a 60 s urlopen timeout (jev-gate.py:57), and a slow API would stall a push. Fail-open or fail-closed for jev-gate was not determined.
entries.contextCost: jev-stack: 0 tokens. It is not an MCP server, skill or hook. Payloads: fast-jev-compaction ships a SKILL.md (size not measured). jev-prompt-enhancer adds no tool schemas but replaces the prompt text per turn. The scripts are CLI tools that Claude would have to call through Bash, which adds definition cost only if the user writes skills or CLAUDE.md instructions for them.
pros: Everything is already OpenRouter-native: the payloads use https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-1.13, matching the user's provider choice (jev-gate.py:15,51; cli.mjs:19-21).
Zero-dependency installer that is short (134 lines) and fully readable, with no postinstall and no telemetry in the installer.
The jev-prompt-enhancer payload does have a real Claude Code UserPromptSubmit hook design (updatedPrompt / block), and its fail-open stated behavior fits the 'automatic' goal.
States the sensible rule that deterministic checks (tsc, builds, secret scans) are never replaced by a Jev decision.
cons: It is only an installer that git-clones other repos into cwd. It adds no MCP tool, hook, skill or plugin to Claude Code by itself, so it delivers no automatic integration.

The automatic piece (prompt enhancer) rewrites the user's prompt and then asks for approval. That is the opposite of a silent, zero-friction integration, and it feeds every prompt (including client code and secrets) to two extra models.
Very immature: 2 commits, 1 author, 0 stars, created 2026-09-22, no tests, no CI, no releases, no LICENSE file. The payload repos are equally new, with 0-1 stars.
Supply-chain risk: unpinned HEAD clones plus 'npm install -g --prefix' run lifecycle scripts from personal repos on a machine that holds client code.

Uses Jev for tasks it is not designed for (compaction, code QA, NL file search, browser steps) with claims like '~100x cheaper' and 'same reliability' that are unbenchmarked in the repo. Jev is a typed decision model, not a free-text summarizer, so the compaction claim is doubtful.

Does not overlap with the user's needs: a Claude Code user with Opus already has /compact and GitNexus. The pre-push guard duplicates the existing secret-leak hook. The browser agent duplicates Playwright MCP.
README/AGENT_PROMPT are marketing-heavy; the AGENT_PROMPT asks an agent to run installs, an unnecessary prompt-injection-shaped path.
The payload fast-jev-compaction hooks.json is only {modules:['./fast-jev.ts']}, which is not a Claude Code hook schema, so Claude Code integration of that tool is unclear.
entries.verdict: Skip it. jev-stack is a 134-line clone-and-npm-install-g wrapper for unpinned, week-old personal repos, and it integrates nothing into Claude Code itself. If any part of the stack is worth a look, it is the jev-prompt-enhancer UserPromptSubmit hook as a standalone (audit it separately), but its prompt-rewriting and approval flow is unlikely to suit a bypass-mode, client-work workflow.
entries.license: MIT (package.json:license and npm metadata). GitHub licenseInfo is null because there is no LICENSE file in the repo.

entries.name: UditAkhourii/quicksilver
entries.what: Claude Code skill (SKILL.md plus one zero-dependency Node script, qs.mjs) that lets Claude offload bulk judgment work to Jev. Claude runs `node qs.mjs filter|classify|rank|find|ask ...` through Bash. The script reads files, dirs, logs or JSONL, sends each item (or packed batches with --fast) to POST {API}/v1/systemone using noul, choice and score questions, and prints a compact shortlist. The output marks borderline items with `?` and ends with a token-savings footer. The idea is that Jev rules out items so Claude never reads them.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion skill trigger via the SKILL.md description. It is not deterministic, because there is no hook or proxy. The README claims 'Claude uses the skill on its own', but with Opus 5.5 and existing habits (Grep/Glob, GitNexus graph hooks, subagents) it may frequently not fire, or may pick grep or GitNexus instead. The description is well written, with explicit 'use BEFORE reading many files/logs' triggers and clear skip conditions. Reliability could be raised by a one-line reminder in ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md, or by a UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook nudge, but that is extra work the repo does not provide.
security: Key handling: read from the JEV_API_KEY or TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var, or ~/.quicksilver/config.json written with 0600 plus chmod (qs.mjs:36-40, 548). It is sent only as an HTTPS Bearer header via fetch, so it never appears in the process list during normal use. Exception: `qs setup <KEY>` and `install --key KEY` put the key in argv and shell history. The SKILL.md even tells Claude to run `qs setup <KEY>` if the user pastes the key in chat, which puts it in the transcript and argv. With env vars from settings.json this path is avoided.
No telemetry. The only network calls go to API (default api.typesafe.ai) and GET /v1/models. Local stats are written to ~/.quicksilver/stats.json (counts only).

No curl|sh, no postinstall script, and no npm dependencies. `npx github:UditAkhourii/quicksilver` runs unpinned code from a 2-commit, 5-day-old repo on main, and the recommended install fetches whatever is on main. Safer: clone, read, then copy the skill dir by hand, or pin a commit SHA.
Only child process is `git ls-files` via execFileSync with an argument array, so no shell injection. Writes are limited to config, stats and the optional --save FILE.

Secret guard: SECRET_RE (qs.mjs:19) skips .env*, *.pem/.key/.p12/.crt, id_rsa*, .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, credentials.json and secrets.*, and .gitignore is respected inside git repos. Hardcoded secrets inside ordinary source files, config.yaml, docker-compose, CI files and logs are still uploaded. The --no-secrets-guard flag exists. The directory walk fallback ignores dot-dirs, but files given explicitly, stdin and --items bypass path checks (paths still go through the regex, stdin does not).

Prompt-injection surface: file and log text is sent to Jev, which only returns typed probabilities, so the injection blast radius is limited to skewed verdicts (a file can trick a filter into hiding or surfacing itself). Output printed back to Claude is only ids, numbers and clipped line text (the log/line text is attacker-controlled and is read by Claude). The skill itself instructs Claude to treat results as a shortlist.
entries.dataEgress: The content of every file, line or item you point it at leaves the machine. This is full file text up to 60k chars per item (--max-chars), with files up to 2 MB read, sent as `state.content` plus the file's relative path as `state.source`, together with the question text. Destination is api.typesafe.ai by default, or openrouter.ai/api if QUICKSILVER_API_BASE is set. This covers source code, logs, tickets and contracts. Excluded: .env, keys, certs, credential-like filenames, .gitignored files, lockfiles, minified files, binaries. Not excluded: hardcoded secrets inside normal source or log files. Nothing is sent unless Claude runs qs. Claude's own prompts and transcript are not sent. For client projects there is a real NDA and data-processing question, and with OpenRouter the content also passes through OpenRouter's provider routing.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level, because qs is just a Bash command. Nothing blocks Claude if Jev is slow or down, and Claude reads the files itself. The exit codes are: 3 for a missing or rejected key (401 or 403), 4 for a bad request (400 or 422), and 5 for exhausted retries. Each request has a 60 s AbortSignal timeout (qs.mjs:93). It retries up to 5 times with exponential backoff (500 ms x 2^n, honoring Retry-After) on network errors and 408, 409, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504 and 529. A dead endpoint therefore costs around 5 minutes wall clock per request, with 16 concurrent requests, before qs dies. One failed request aborts the whole run (die exits the process), so there is no partial result. If Claude hits an error it can just fall back, but nothing enforces that. The skill does say to rephrase or lower the threshold when nothing matches.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools, no hooks and no injected hook text, so zero tool-definition tokens. Always-on cost is the skill name plus description in the skill listing, about 1,050 chars, or roughly 260 tokens. When Claude triggers it, the full SKILL.md body loads: about 163 lines and roughly 6.5k chars, or about 1.7k tokens. Each run adds a short output of about 1 to 4k tokens (id lists, footer). qs.mjs itself is not read into context (it is only executed). Per-turn cost with the skill idle is negligible.
