pros: Only candidate here that is a working, end-to-end Jev integration built around Claude Code, and it works purely from source-verified schema: the noul/choice/score request bodies in qs.mjs:327, 367, 414 and 443 match the System One shape (state + questions -> answers/usage) that OpenRouter's Jev page documents.

OpenRouter switch is config-only, with no patching: QUICKSILVER_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_API_KEY=<OpenRouter key> and QUICKSILVER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13 in the settings.json env block. The code appends /v1/systemone, giving exactly the documented /api/v1/systemone.
Zero deps, about 590 lines of readable Node, and no postinstall, no curl|sh and no telemetry. It was easy to audit end to end, and needs Node >= 18 (user has 24, so globs work).

Skill design is right for this user: no MCP server and no hooks, so it adds about 260 tokens of always-on context, no per-turn latency, and cannot break or slow normal tool calls. It does not collide with the existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks.

Good ergonomics for an LLM caller: compact output, repeated log lines collapsed into ranges, a `?` borderline band that tells Claude to double-check, per-item requests by default (they measured packing hurting accuracy 100% -> 76%), and honest guidance on when not to use it (grep for exact matches, tiny inputs, generation).
Sensible safety defaults: secret-file name regex, .gitignore respect, 2 MB cap, and the 60k-char truncation marker `~`.

Useful jobs for daily coding: repo-wide 'which files handle X' funnels, log triage, bulk ticket/test-failure labelling, and needle-in-large-file search. The benchmark reports 100% F1/hit@k on several of these with 77-96% fewer Claude tokens, at a median Jev cost of about $0.004 per task.
MIT licensed; the skill can be copied and pinned locally so it can be maintained by the user.
cons: The benchmark is self-reported by the author on 12 tasks with a Claude subagent as baseline, and the repo has 2 commits, 1 contributor, no tests, no CI and no releases (created 2026-09-25, 5 days before the audit). It also shows failures: BGL log triage F1 23% vs 54%, commit classification 76% vs 83%, and security shortlist 89% vs 100%.

Automatic invocation is only a skill-description trigger. It is model-discretion, and with the user's Grep/Glob/GitNexus habits it may often not fire. There is no hook or enforcement, so the 'never prompt Claude to use Jev' goal is met only probabilistically.

Data egress is the whole content of files, up to 60k chars each, to a third party (TypeSafe, or OpenRouter plus its provider). The guard is filename-regex only, so hardcoded secrets in ordinary source, YAML or logs still go out. This is a real problem on client projects under NDA, and the user's secret-leak hook does not inspect what qs uploads.

Not natively OpenRouter: the default model 'jev-latest' and the default base URL are TypeSafe-direct. Config-only fix, but I could not test that OpenRouter's response envelope matches exactly, and `status` only tests reachability via /v1/models.

The scope of value is narrow. It saves Claude tokens on bulk reading, but the user is on a subscription (OAuth) where the savings are usage-limit headroom rather than dollars. Opus with Grep/GitNexus is already strong at file discovery, and the results are only a shortlist, so Claude still has to read survivors and check the `?` items.

Failure handling is blunt: up to 5 retries with 60 s timeouts (about 5 minutes worst case), and any single failed request kills the whole run with no partial output. Jev is beta, so 429 and 529 are likely on large scans at 16 concurrency.

Install path risk: `npx github:UditAkhourii/quicksilver` executes unpinned main from a brand-new single-author repo. The `setup <KEY>` path puts the key in argv and Claude's transcript if used as the skill suggests.
Wall-clock is no better than Claude on huge scans (their own benchmark: 56 s vs 64 s, 39 s vs 39 s), and cost scales with content size (lodash find $0.21, log scan $0.04).

`qs status`/`qs setup` on OpenRouter return 'ready' for any key because GET /api/v1/models is unauthenticated, so the skill's mandatory first step gives false assurance. A dead or wrong key shows only on the first real call.

Key handling mismatch: qs ignores OPENROUTER_API_KEY. Putting a duplicate JEV_API_KEY in the settings.json env block exposes it to all Bash/child processes, and that name is not in the user's no-secret-leak protected list. Safer options are an exported var in a shell profile, or ~/.quicksilver/config.json (0600) written with a hidden-prompt `setup` run in the user's own terminal, keeping in mind that `status`/`setup` cannot validate the key on OpenRouter.

Secret-guard gaps are larger than the audit lists. No match for .git-credentials, .pgpass, *.tfstate/*.tfvars, service-account JSONs, .docker/config.json, kubeconfig, *.env, wp-config.php, or ~/.claude/.credentials.json and ~/.claude.json. `find` has no per-file size cap beyond 2 MB and sends whole files. For client/NDA repos this is a real leak path that the existing no-secret-leak hook does not cover, because it does not inspect what qs uploads.

No allow rule or `allowed-tools` frontmatter: every `node .../qs.mjs` call is a Bash call that needs approval. In defaultMode 'auto' the permission classifier may prompt or block a script that uploads file contents to an external host (untested here). That undermines the 'automatic, never prompt' goal unless the user adds a Bash allow rule for the exact qs.mjs path.

Unpinned floating alias: the default model 'jev-latest' maps to ~typesafe/jev-latest on OpenRouter, so behaviour and calibration can change silently. Pin 'jev-1.13' for reproducibility. Independent evals also report overconfidence on unanswerable inputs and injection sensitivity, and the author's own bench shows weak spots (BGL F1 23% vs 54%, commits 76% vs 83%, security 89% vs 100%).

Bash timeout interaction: default 2-minute tool timeout versus a 6.5 min worst-case retry loop and output only at the very end. Large scans (3k lines took 64 s; the default --limit is 5000 items) need an explicit timeout or run_in_background.

Docs drift inside the repo: SKILL.md says 8 parallel while code uses 16, and plugin.json version is 0.1.0 while package.json is 0.2.0. There is no CI, tests, releases or issues, 2 commits and 1 contributor, and the package is not on npm (404), so the only install paths are the unpinned GitHub npx or a clone.
entries.verdict: Best-fit, lowest-overhead Jev integration found so far for Claude Code. It is a lean skill with no hooks and no MCP tool-schema cost, and OpenRouter works through three env vars. The catch is that auto-triggering is probabilistic, it uploads full file contents to a third party with only a filename-based secret guard, and the project is 5 days old with self-reported benchmarks. Use it on personal projects after auditing/pinning a local copy, and treat it as opt-in per repo for client work.

verification.note: Re-queried now: 90 stars, 4 forks, MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-25, 2 commits (2026-09-25), 1 contributor, 0 releases, 0 issues, no tests or CI, not on npm. All of these match the audit. I read all 590 lines of qs.mjs, SKILL.md, bin/quicksilver.mjs and the install scripts. There is no OpenRouter string in the repo, but OpenRouter support is real via QUICKSILVER_API_BASE=https://openrouter.ai/api plus a key in JEV_API_KEY. OpenRouter's docs say its /api/v1/systemone implements TypeSafe's request/response shapes, and qs.mjs uses exactly that shape (state, questions, and answers.*.noul/choice/probabilities/confidence/score/legend, usage.input_tokens). I could not make a live authenticated call, so the OpenRouter response envelope is doc-verified, not tested. The audit's biggest error was claiming the default model 'jev-latest' is invalid on OpenRouter; it is mapped to ~typesafe/jev-latest, so the model env var is optional (pin jev-1.13 anyway). The largest missed gaps are that status/setup cannot validate a key on OpenRouter (the public /models endpoint returns 200 for a fake key), the key must be duplicated under JEV_API_KEY with the protected-vars gap, `find` sends whole files uncapped, and the secret regex misses many secret filenames including the user's own ~/.claude credential files. Auto-invocation is still only model-discretion via a 764-char description. The score stays at 6.5: it is the lowest-overhead, hook-free and MCP-free option, with good ergonomics and honest guidance, but it is a 5-day-old, single-author, untested alpha with an unreliable key check on OpenRouter and a weak egress guard. Recommend a locally pinned copy, model jev-1.13, a Bash allow rule for the exact qs.mjs path, and adding the key env name to the secret-leak hook before use on client repos.

judge.why: Lowest-overhead option: a skill plus one zero-dependency Node script (filter, classify, rank, find, ask) with no MCP server and no hook. The OpenRouter switch is config-only. It fits the one place Jev adds value, bulk relevance triage over many files or lines, at very low cost. It is still model-discretion only, and its safety guards are weak.
pros: No MCP schema or hook latency; the skill listing entry is about 190 tokens and the body about 2.2k tokens only when triggered
Reads OpenRouter's /v1/systemone shape natively; one env var switches the endpoint
Honest author guidance; bench cost under $0.25 per large run
Single readable 590-line script, easy to audit and pin locally
cons: qs status and setup report ready for ANY key on OpenRouter because GET /v1/models is unauthenticated
Key must be duplicated under JEV_API_KEY, and that name is not in the no-secret-leak list
Secret-path regex misses *.env, .git-credentials, .pgpass, tfstate, service-account JSON, kubeconfig and ~/.claude credentials; find uploads whole files uncapped
No allow rule, so each qs.mjs call is a Bash call that auto mode may prompt or block
Worst-case retry loop about 6.5 minutes versus the 2-minute Bash timeout; docs say 8 parallel but code uses 16
Auto-invocation is description-trigger only

entries.name: buchmark/claude-jev
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json) that bundles a stdio MCP server (committed, esbuild-bundled dist/server.js, TypeScript source, uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk) exposing 5 Jev tools, a "jev" SKILL.md with a description-based trigger, and 4 slash commands. Four tools are presets (review findings, hypothesis ranking, option picking, file-relevance filtering) with question texts and verdict thresholds hardcoded in code; jev_ask is a generic escape hatch. The server reads source snippets from disk itself (line ranges), so code does not pass through Claude's context, and sends them plus typed questions to Jev.
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only, via two soft channels: (1) MCP tool descriptions that say 'Run it on your own candidate findings before presenting a review', 'Use it right after a broad grep, glob...' etc. (src/adapters/tools/*.ts); (2) the jev skill whose description triggers on code review, false positives, why is this failing, which approach is safer, is this reachable, which files matter. There are NO hooks, no CLAUDE.md snippet, no deterministic trigger. The four slash commands are manual. With Opus 5.5 in bypass/auto mode it will sometimes call them during reviews/debugging/planning, but nothing guarantees it, and the skill itself says 'not for every step'. To make it more automatic the user would need to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a small hook/SessionStart reminder.
security: No shell execution, no postinstall, no curl|sh; install is a committed prebuilt bundle. Downside: dist/server.js (1.4 MB, bundled MCP SDK + TypeSafe SDK + zod) is an unreviewable blob that must match src; README itself warns it must be rebuilt and committed manually, so it can drift from source.

API key handling: plugin option marked sensitive (README says macOS Keychain; on Linux this likely falls back to plaintext credentials storage - unverified). Key is passed via env (JEV_API_KEY / TYPESAFE_API_KEY), not argv, so not visible in the process list arguments. SDK logger at debug level logs headers/bodies (dist/server.js ~38000) but default log level is not debug.

Filesystem guard in src/infrastructure/fs-source-reader.ts:14-32: hard denylist for .env*, .git, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .gcloud, .npmrc, .netrc, credentials*, secrets.*, *.pem/*.key/etc; realpath + containment check against client MCP roots; 4 MB ceiling; binary refusal. It is filename-based only: secrets hardcoded inside ordinary source files (config.ts, settings.py, terraform.tfvars, docker-compose.yml with passwords) are still sent. Complements but does not replace the user's PreToolUse secret-leak guard, which will NOT fire on MCP tool calls (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so files read by the MCP server bypass that hook.

Prompt-injection surface: source content is sent to Jev as data and Jev returns only numbers, so injection can at worst skew a probability (README admits this). Jev's numbers then feed Claude, but output is compact text of numbers/labels, not free text. Verdict labels come from fixed code thresholds. Low risk of instruction injection into Claude; moderate risk of manipulated verdicts (a malicious comment could make a real finding get dropped).

Model-supplied `path` arguments: Claude (or injected content) can request any in-root file, so untrusted repo content that steers Claude could cause exfiltration of any non-denylisted in-root file to the Jev provider. Bounded to session roots.

No telemetry in plugin code; SDK sends User-Agent and X-TypeSafe-SDK/Runtime headers. Single author, 7 stars, brand-new: supply-chain trust rests on one unknown GitHub account (owner name 'oxdev' in manifests vs GitHub user buchmark).
entries.dataEgress: With source reading on (default true): file contents of the line ranges / files named in each tool call (up to 64 KB per source, 20 sources per call, default; up to 1 MB / 200 via options), plus the task text, finding claims/failure descriptions, hypothesis text, option summaries, and question text, go to the configured endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default; would be openrouter.ai and then OpenRouter's upstream if patched via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL). The full state is re-sent with every request of a fan-out (up to 8 requests per call). Only what Claude explicitly puts in a tool call leaves the machine; nothing is sent automatically on prompts, diffs or tool outputs unless Claude calls a tool. Set JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false to send only text passed in the call. Relevant for client projects: client code goes to a third party (TypeSafe/OpenRouter), and OpenRouter data-retention/logging policy applies.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level: errors are caught in src/adapters/respond.ts:15-21 and returned as isError text (missing key, budget, forbidden path, HTTP error, MalformedAnswerError), so Claude just sees an error and proceeds. Missing key does not crash the server; it errors on first call with an explanatory message (typesafe-jev.ts:6-13, 133). SDK defaults (dist/server.js 37955, 37599): 10 s request timeout, maxRetries 2 with 0.5-5 s backoff and Retry-After up to 60 s on 408/429/5xx, so a worst case for a slow/down endpoint is roughly 30+ s blocking per tool call (requests in a fan-out run in parallel). Being an MCP tool, not a hook, it never blocks tool execution or prompts; Claude can ignore failure. If server process fails to start, only the tools disappear.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools. Estimated tool defs: 5 descriptions of roughly 500-700 chars each (about 3k chars) plus zod-derived JSON schemas with .describe() text for sources, questions (nested discriminated union), findings, hypotheses, options, candidates (about 6-8k chars) - approx 2.5k-3.5k tokens total in the tool list (deferred/ToolSearch in Claude Code 2.x may reduce this to names only until needed). Skill: description frontmatter ~800 chars (~200 tokens) always listed; the full SKILL.md (~4.5 KB, ~1.1k tokens) loads only when triggered. 4 slash commands add ~4 short one-line descriptions. No MCP server 'instructions' field is set (server.ts:14 constructs McpServer with only name/version). No hook-injected text. Per-call output is a compact block of numbers.
pros: Purpose-built for Claude Code and Jev: presets for the exact moments Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives fit (review finding triage, hypothesis ranking, option choice, grep-hit filtering), with prompt text and thresholds kept in reviewable code (src/domain/catalog/*).
Best auto-invocation story among plugin-style options: both skill description triggers AND tool descriptions steer Claude to call it during review/debug/plan without the user saying 'use jev'.
Server reads files itself from line ranges, so source never enters Claude's context, and the filter tool triages grep hits cheaply.
Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so wire format tracks TypeSafe's real API; SDK already honors TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, making OpenRouter (/api + /v1/systemone) a config-level switch rather than a fork.

Decent engineering hygiene for a week-old repo: hexagonal layout, strict TS, 72 offline tests, budget planner that refuses instead of truncating (src/domain/budget.ts), explicit fail-safe error responses, MIT, single-file committed bundle with no postinstall.

Sensible egress controls: hard secret-file denylist, realpath containment against client roots, size caps, JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING kill-switch for client repos, per-call request cap (JEV_MAX_REQUESTS).
Non-blocking design: no hooks means no interference with the user's existing PreToolUse secret guard, GitNexus hooks or caveman hooks, and no added latency when Jev is unused.
Honest README about limits (kept a planted false positive at 0.57; Jev weaknesses), and skill rule that Jev output is never authorization for destructive actions.
cons: Not OpenRouter-native: hardcoded to TypeSafe direct by default; OpenRouter requires undocumented env override TYPESAFE_BASE_URL plus a model ID (typesafe/jev-1.13) that plugin.json's enum-restricted JEV_MODEL option does not list, and schema parity with OpenRouter's System One API is unverified.

Auto-invocation is only model-discretion: no hook, so use will be inconsistent; it depends on Claude choosing to assemble structured findings first. The added workflow (Claude writes candidates, Jev filters) costs extra Claude tokens/turns on top of Jev's cost.

Value is unproven and skeptical: Jev is a beta model, filter quality is modest (the README's own demo kept a planted false positive), and the calibration claim is a property of aggregates. Gating review findings on it can drop real bugs (an injected comment or a bad prior can lower `real`).

Bypasses the user's secret-leak PreToolUse guard (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit does not cover MCP tools); only a filename denylist protects hardcoded secrets in source files. Client code leaves the machine to TypeSafe/OpenRouter and upstream, a compliance question for client projects (mitigable with JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false, which weakens the main benefit).

Brand-new, single-author (8 commits all on 2026-09-18, 7 stars, no releases, no CI); committed 1.4 MB dist bundle must be manually rebuilt so it can drift from src; plugin is 'private: true' with mismatched owner name (oxdev vs buchmark).
Context tax of about 3k tokens for 5 tools plus skill description on every session, for capabilities that only cover four narrow scenarios.
Retry/timeout defaults (10 s x up to 3 attempts) mean a degraded endpoint can stall a tool call for tens of seconds; not configurable through plugin options.

README says the sensitive API key goes to the macOS Keychain; on this Linux machine the storage behavior is unclear, so the safer path is an env var, which leaves the key in plaintext shell profile/settings.

Budget constants assume TypeSafe direct (64k total, 32k state+question) while OpenRouter serves a 32k context; default fan-out packing may produce requests OpenRouter rejects, with no config knob for the token limits
--check self-test cannot work on OpenRouter because models.list is unsupported there and check() calls it first

SKILL.md and all tool guidance are triggered by model discretion only; on a Opus 5.5 auto/bypass workflow there is no guarantee any Jev call happens, and there is no PermissionRequest/PreToolUse integration, so it does not deliver the cookbook-style deterministic gating

Plugin forwards only JEV_* env; TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY must be set in the user's environment or settings.json env (which also exposes the OpenRouter key to every Bash subprocess and should be added to the no-secret-leak protected list). Plugin command is bare 'node', which depends on PATH that the user's settings env overrides

Reader guard is filename-based; MCP tool calls bypass the user's PreToolUse no-secret-leak hook (matcher Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so an injected or mistaken path argument for any non-denylisted file in root (terraform.tfvars, docker-compose.yml, .docker/config.json, .kube/config, *.tfstate are not in FORBIDDEN) is sent to OpenRouter/upstream

Jev answers can be steered by injected instructions in the sent source, so verdict thresholds that drop findings (keep/keep_low/drop) can suppress real bugs; this is a review-quality risk not just an egress risk
Active fork of scope: a feat/opencode-support branch exists, showing the maintainer is spreading effort; main has no releases or tags to pin
entries.verdict: The most complete and best-designed Jev integration for Claude Code found so far (skill plus tools plus presets, sane guards, offline tests), and the closest to 'Claude uses it on its own'. But it is TypeSafe-direct with an untested OpenRouter path via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and the model enum, auto-use is only soft (no hook), and it is a week-old single-author project, so pilot it on personal repos with source reading toggled per client project.

verification.note: Verified by static reading and gh/web only (nothing run). Core audit is largely accurate: 5 tools (jev_review_findings, jev_rank_hypotheses, jev_pick_option, jev_filter_relevance, jev_ask), jev skill, 4 slash commands, 7 stars, MIT, not archived, 8 commits on 2026-09-18 on main, no hooks, fail-open MCP errors via respond.ts, SDK timeout 10 s and maxRetries 2, no baseURL in code but SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL. Corrections: OpenRouter switching is officially documented (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api + OpenRouter key as TYPESAFE_API_KEY; bare model IDs incl. default jev-latest are mapped by OpenRouter), so the audit's model-enum obstacle is mostly wrong; but two OpenRouter-specific gaps were missed: --check breaks because models.list is unsupported, and hardcoded 64k/32k budgets vs OpenRouter's 32k context. Audit's config.ts line numbers (190-191) do not exist. A second branch (feat/opencode-support) explains the 09-21 push. Score lowered 6.5 -> 6.0: OpenRouter path is easier than the audit says, but auto-use remains soft (fails the user's core requirement), the plugin is alpha single-author with no releases/CI, egress bypasses the secret-leak hook, and the size budgets are not OpenRouter-tuned. Best used as a personal-repo pilot, ideally paired with a CLAUDE.md rule or SessionStart nudge, and JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false on client repos. Unverified: Claude Code passing parent env to plugin MCP child and Linux storage of the sensitive option.

judge.why: Claude Code plugin with a bundled stdio MCP (jev_review_findings, jev_rank_hypotheses, jev_pick_option, jev_filter_relevance, jev_ask), a skill and 4 slash commands. The server reads files itself, so source stays out of Claude's context. The OpenRouter path is officially documented and low effort.
pros: Official-SDK based, so schema parity with OpenRouter is by design
Server-side file reading saves context
Fail-open MCP errors; SDK timeout 10 s with 2 retries
JEV_ALLOW_SOURCE_READING=false available for client repos
cons: Model-discretion only, with no hook or CLAUDE.md nudge shipped
Budget constants assume TypeSafe direct (64k total, 32k state) but OpenRouter is 32k, so requests can be rejected
--check breaks on OpenRouter because models.list is unsupported

entries.name: bojansandhaus/jev-decisions-hermes

entries.name: PyModel/jev-judge-mcp (jev-judge-mcp on PyPI, MCP server name "jev")
entries.what: Python (3.12+, stdio, POSIX only) MCP server that wraps TypeSafe Jev as 11 typed judgment tools (verify, screen, find, classify, decide, rerank, compare, extract, review, gate, score). Every tool call sends the caller-supplied evidence and a bounded question to a Jev provider. Local policy code turns the returned probabilities into auto, review or escalate. It also ships CLI subcommands (setup, install, doctor, judge, gate, calibrate), two opt-in Claude Code PreToolUse command hooks (hook gate, completion-hook), and two skills served as MCP resources/prompts (jev-mcp routing, jev API cookbook). The repo is a Python rewrite of a TypeScript reference server, created 2026-09-23 and about a week old.
interface: jev-skill://jev-mcp/SKILL.md and jev-skill://jev/SKILL.md (MCP resources and prompts)
jev-judge-mcp hook gate (opt-in PreToolUse command hook)
jev-judge-mcp setup | install | doctor | judge <tool> | gate | calibrate
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools. Guidance arrives through the server instructions (instructions.py: 'jev_gate is the recommended final judgment before claiming done... unless tests... already settle completion'; jev_screen before reading external text; jev_verify for other agents' reports), an optional CLAUDE.md rule block (docs/agent-rules.md) and MCP-served skills. There is no deterministic trigger by default, and install does not enable hooks. Deterministic triggering exists only via two opt-in PreToolUse hooks: hook gate (Bash|Write|Edit, all actions) and completion-hook (git push / gh pr create / gh pr merge, but it needs pre-made claims and tests files from env vars, so it is awkward to run automatically). The repo's own bench shows that when the agent is left to choose, it called Jev on 0 of 150 tasks (Pi/DeepSeek), and one Pi pair never called it at all. Claude Code's selection behavior with these instructions is only measured on a tiny study.
security: API key handling is careful. Keys come from env only, plus an optional 0600 key file in a 0700 dir (keyfile.py, fsutil). Every SecretStr setting is redacted from logs and error text (ADR-0008/0017, settings.py:250-276). Provider URL, model and key can never be set by tool arguments (ADR-0008), which closes an SSRF and key-exfiltration route.

Key is passed via env reference (${VAR}), never argv. setup refuses a key on the command line (setup.py). The one exception is the Claude Desktop --desktop-key flag, which writes the key in plaintext to that app's config, but that is not relevant to Claude Code.

No curl|sh, no postinstall (PyPI wheel via uvx). subprocess use is limited to: a fixed-argv git diff for the gate CLI (cli.py:150,207), a sandboxed regex worker for jev_extract (extract/worker.py:229), and the installer's verify/launch --version checks. Regexes run in a worker pool with stdlib re (ADR-0004/0018), so ReDoS is contained.

No telemetry phone-home. Telemetry is local spans/metrics. Prompt payload capture is off unless JEV_MCP_TELEMETRY_PAYLOADS is set (SECURITY.md). The response cache is off by default. If enabled it writes judged state to ~/.cache/jev-mcp at mode 0600.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool arguments are model-authored and can contain attacker text from fetched pages. The repo itself admits that jev-1.13 does not treat state as hostile and that injected instructions can move an answer (skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md, verify anti-injection ADR-0068). The jev_screen tool is itself a Jev judgment, so it is not a hard security boundary.

Supply chain: a single maintainer (elkaix, 203 of 210 commits, remainder bot) and an account about a week old. Hard version caps on mcp and typesafe-sdk because it uses their private internals (pyproject.toml comments). Pin ==0.7.0 and review before bumping.
entries.dataEgress: MCP tools: only the arguments the model puts into a tool call go to the provider (openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions). That is evidence text, diffs, test logs, candidate lists and fetched pages, plus the question and options. Jev never sees the wider conversation. Nothing is sent automatically for a turn you did not trigger. OpenRouter therefore receives whatever the agent chooses to pass, which can be client code, since jev_gate, jev_review and jev_verify take raw diffs and logs. The verify and screen tools have no size cap. Headers sent: Bearer key, HTTP-Referer = the GitHub repo URL, X-Title jev-mcp. Optional hook gate: sends cwd, permission mode, tool name, and the full Bash command or Write/Edit input (through redact_action pattern redaction, hook.py:170-192) to the provider on EVERY watched tool call, so Write/Edit file contents leave the machine per edit. No other network destinations found in the code (grep of URLs).
entries.failureMode: MCP tools fail closed and visibly. A missing key returns an error in the tool result, an invalid provider answer becomes invalid_response, and an unknown confidence never reaches auto (policy). Claude then falls back to normal checks, as the agent rules tell it to. Timeouts: each attempt has a 30 s timeout, up to 3 attempts with backoff, inside a 90 s budget (retry.py, README operator notes). Over stdio there is no whole-call deadline (ADR-0021 stdio-attempt-deadline), so a call can stall Claude for up to about 90 s in the worst case; cancellation is propagated. hook gate: missing credentials or bad stdin are fail-open (silent), but a provider error or timeout gives ask with a 30 s hook timeout, and JEV_HOOK_REQUIRED=1 makes missing credentials ask too. completion-hook: fail-open on provider errors, silent on non-push commands.
entries.contextCost: 11 tools. The repo's frozen snapshot of the 10 original tool definitions is 18,353 JSON chars (about 4.6k tokens); jev_score adds roughly 0.6-0.8k, so about 5.2-5.5k tokens if tool schemas are loaded eagerly. Claude Code's tool search defers MCP schemas, so the steady-state cost is 11 tool names plus the server 'instructions' string. That string is about 1.5k chars (about 375 tokens), built in instructions.py, and includes the on-demand policy text. The optional hooks inject no text into context (they emit only a permission JSON). The jev-mcp skill is an MCP resource/prompt, so it costs nothing unless read. The recommended CLAUDE.md rule block adds about 700 tokens if the user pastes it in.
pros: OpenRouter is a first-class provider in code (providers/openrouter.py:18, resolver.py:138), using the alpha Decisions API with slug typesafe/jev-1.13. Only OPENROUTER_API_KEY=sk-or-... plus JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter is needed, and no TypeSafe account is required.

The most complete and best-documented Jev integration found. It covers 11 tools that map onto real coding steps (done-claim gate, patch review, injection screen, docs-vs-code drift, candidate rerank), plus a policy layer that fails closed (unknown confidence never returns auto).

Strong secret hygiene for a week-old project: env-only credentials, redaction derived from the settings schema, no per-call provider override (SSRF closed), key file 0600, no telemetry phone-home, no curl|sh or postinstall.

Unusually honest evidence: the README itself reports the agent was slower with Jev (Claude Code +4.6 s, 6/9 solved both ways) and that automatic use left Jev uncalled on 150/150. It says to skip Jev when tests, types or lint already settle the answer. This matches a senior dev's 'add value or stay out of the way' need.

Provides real deterministic hook hooks (hook gate, completion-hook) that can only deny or ask (never allow), so they can add a safety net on top of the user's existing hooks. The hooks live in separate opt-in JSON fragments (docs/harness/*.hooks.json) that can be merged by hand, and they do not break the existing secret-guard or GitNexus hooks since PreToolUse hooks compose.
Large test suite and CI (unit, property, parity against a frozen TS reference, security, load), pinned dependency bounds, and a version-pinnable uvx launch (==0.7.0).
cons: Automatic use is not really delivered by the MCP alone. The model decides whether to call the tools, and the server's own studies show it often does not (0/150 on Pi). To make Claude Code use it reliably the user must add CLAUDE.md rules and/or hooks, and the repo has no plugin manifest or Claude Code SKILL.md, so it is not a one-step 'automatic' integration.

Its own numbers argue against heavy use in daily coding: slower with Jev on every solved pair, no accuracy gain measured, 140k vs 36k tokens per solved task in the 2026-09-27 study, and no certified operating points (docs/EVIDENCE.md). The policy thresholds are inherited parity defaults, not calibrated on Jev.

The opt-in hook gate would send every Bash command and every Write/Edit body (after pattern redaction) to OpenRouter and add roughly 0.5-1.5 s per call, all day, on client projects. It turns provider errors into 'ask', which in an unattended bypass/auto session may block or interrupt.

Client-code egress: jev_gate/review/verify take raw diffs and logs, and jev_verify/jev_screen have no size cap. On client projects, model-chosen tool calls can ship proprietary code to a third party (OpenRouter plus TypeSafe). The user needs a per-project disable or a permissions deny rule.
completion-hook is hard to use automatically: it needs JEV_COMPLETION_CLAIMS and JEV_COMPLETION_TESTS files that something must produce before every push.

Setup tooling assumes a TypeSafe key: setup verifies against TypeSafe, and install writes ${TYPESAFE_API_KEY} references (install/launch.py:25,186). The OpenRouter route needs a hand-written MCP entry, and an unset ${VAR} reference can break server start.

Young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-23, 29 stars, 3 forks, 7 releases in 7 days, 203 of 210 commits from one author), with private-API dependence on the mcp SDK (bounded to >=2.2,<2.3). It uses only the alpha Decisions endpoint, pins 'jev-latest' to jev-1.13 in code, and POSIX only.

Injection weakness is acknowledged: jev-1.13 does not treat state as hostile, so jev_screen is a soft filter. The Jev model may also be a cheap router (unverified skeptic claim), and this repo's quality numbers (89/92 on the JevBench subset) are self-run and small-n.
entries.verdict: The best-engineered and only OpenRouter-native Jev MCP found, and the most sensible base for a Claude Code integration: register it by hand with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_PROVIDER=openrouter, and pin the version. It only gives model-discretion, not guaranteed, automatic use. Its own benchmarks show Jev makes the agent slower with no measured accuracy gain, so limit the automatic part to the tools plus a short CLAUDE.md rule (jev_gate before done/PR when tests do not settle it, jev_screen for fetched web text), and skip the per-action hook gate on client work.

judge.why: Best-engineered and best-tested option, with 11 coding-shaped tools (gate, review, screen, compare, find and others) and the only shipped PreToolUse gate hooks. It is still not an auto-use integration: the MCP tools go uncalled, and the hooks are deny/ask-only and fail to ask.
pros: Native OpenRouter path with no patching
Strong hygiene: key never in argv, 0600 key file, log redaction, no telemetry
Its own docs are honest that agents were slower with Jev
Completion hook targets git push and PR create/merge only
cons: Hook gate never emits allow and fails to ask on any provider error, unsure answer or over-32k payload, which creates prompts in auto and bypass sessions
Sends full Write/Edit contents and every Bash command off-machine with pattern-only redaction; adds Python cold start to every Bash/Write/Edit call
Own bench: 0 of 150 unprompted calls, +4.6 to +10 s per use, no accuracy gain
Six days old, MCP SDK private internals pinned tight, POSIX only, and uvx runs PyPI code
Adds an 11-tool surface of about 5k tokens if not deferred

entries.name: @bmccarn/tracecheck
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server plus CLI plus one Claude/Codex skill that uses Jev (System One typed decisions) as an independent verifier for code-review claims. The agent forms a defect hypothesis and selects source excerpts; tracecheck_verify asks Jev if the concern is supported and returns support, impact, uncertainty and a missing-evidence category. It also offers tracecheck_assess (19 quality dimensions on caller-supplied diff/files) and a Git-based preview/review path that collects change packets and sends them to Jev. It never edits or executes the reviewed code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion only: an MCP tool set plus a description-triggered skill ('Verify suspected code defects with Jev after an implementation checkpoint, during a code review, or after a repair'). No hooks, no proxy. Claude may pick it up unprompted when reviewing or finishing an implementation, but firing is non-deterministic and the skill workflow is heavy (agent must write hypothesis, collect excerpts, then call verify). Hard automatic triggering would require adding your own Stop/PostToolUse hook, which the project does not ship. The package also has no default-on behavior.
security: No postinstall/preinstall scripts in package.json (only prepack/prepublishOnly, which do not run on consumer install). Runtime is a single 2.2 MB esbuild bundle dist/plugin.mjs committed to the repo; CI checks bundle matches fresh build (ci.yml 'node scripts/build.mjs --check'), but the bundle is hard to audit by eye.

API key read only from env (JEV_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/OPENROUTER_API_KEY), sent in an Authorization header, never in argv. No .env autoload, no key persistence (README:412). Plugin .mcp.json has no env block, so the server inherits the shell environment Claude Code was started from.

TYPESAFE_BASE_URL must be HTTPS unless loopback and cannot contain credentials/query/fragment (src/jev.ts:92-103) - prevents key exfil to plain HTTP, but an attacker who controls env could still point it at any HTTPS host.

Outbound secret screening on every string sent (src/safety.ts assertSafeOutbound: private keys, AWS/GitHub/OpenAI/Slack/Google/Stripe/npm tokens, key=value assignments, URL passwords); it fails closed with an error naming the field, and the collector skips files with credentials, symlinks and binaries. Best-effort per its own comment, not DLP.

File reads hardened: O_NOFOLLOW, realpath inside root, TOCTOU identity check, 256 KB per file cap (safety.ts readSource). Git invoked via execFile/spawn with --literal-pathspecs, --no-ext-diff, --no-textconv and SAFE_CONFIGURATION; README:501-505 documents that a hostile checkout's .git/config can still name commands for git (only relevant for untrusted repos, e.g. client code you did not author).
Response handling bounded (512 KB cap, zod validation, probability sum check); error bodies not surfaced because they may echo source.
entries.dataEgress: On tracecheck_verify: hypothesis text, contract, up to 12 source excerpts (max 60 KB) and the target quote, chosen by Claude. On tracecheck_assess: task, diff, files (path+content) and repositoryContext supplied by Claude. On tracecheck_review: collected changed files, their base versions, related callers/tests/dependencies (~60k chars per packet in the author's example, 180 KB request cap, 32k-token model context). Sent to openrouter.ai (which forwards to TypeSafe) with the user's OpenRouter key. Failing the local secret-pattern screen blocks the request. Nothing else leaves the machine; the project has no backend and no telemetry. For client projects this means client source is sent to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (two processors) whenever a tool fires.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open from Claude's perspective (advisory tool): errors come back as MCP tool errors and Claude continues without a verdict; nothing blocks edits or commits. Per-request timeout 45 s default (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, max 1 h) including retries; up to 3 attempts on network errors and 429/5xx/529 with backoff 500 ms*2^n; honors Retry-After only up to 10 s, otherwise errors out. Overall deadlines: verify VERIFY_TIMEOUT_MS, assess 90 s, review 300 s. Incomplete reviews are reported as 'Review incomplete for packet' limitations and not cached. Local secret-screen hit or >180 KB request fails closed (no send). If no key is set the server still starts; preview works, live tools error with a setup message. In the worst case a tool call stalls Claude for the timeout duration (tens of seconds).
entries.contextCost: 4 MCP tools (tracecheck_verify, _assess, _preview, _review). Descriptions are long (~350-500 chars each, ~1.7k chars total) and input schemas are big (verify: evidence array of 5-field objects, target, missingContext; review/preview share a scope object with base/includeUntracked/task/repositoryContext/collection plus long describe() strings; assess: task/diff/files/repositoryContext/scope/previousEvaluation with nested metrics record). Estimate roughly 3,000-4,500 tokens of tool definitions loaded per session (about 12-18k chars / 4), unless Claude Code defers MCP tools behind ToolSearch, in which case only names are resident. Server sets no 'instructions' text (createServer passes only name/version, src/mcp.ts:117). Skill adds only name+description (~330 chars, ~80 tokens) to context until triggered; body is 3.5 KB plus a references/tool-usage.md loaded on first call. No hooks, so no per-call injected text. Tool results are JSON reports (can be several KB each, and assess returns 19 metrics).
pros: Genuine OpenRouter support in code: OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone routes to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with no patching (src/jev.ts:36-37,63-67), and it strips OpenRouter's relayed max_tokens_exceeded error correctly (jev.ts:172-176).

Uses Jev for what it is good at: typed, calibrated yes/no and scored judgments as a second opinion on a specific hypothesis, not free-text generation; response schema (choice/noul/score with probabilities summing to 1) is strictly validated against the question set.

Most security-conscious candidate profile: outbound secret screening that fails closed, symlink/TOCTOU-safe reads, HTTPS-only base URL, key only in env and header, bounded responses, no telemetry, no install scripts.
Advisory and read-only (readOnlyHint, never edits or runs code), so nothing can break the working tree; fail-open when Jev is slow or down.
Only 4 tools and no hooks, so it does not conflict with existing GitNexus/secret-guard PreToolUse hooks and adds zero per-turn latency.

Real engineering rigor for its age: 19 test files, CI on Node 22/24, pinned action SHAs, bundle-drift check, calibration and accuracy docs with honest negative results (recall 7/12 full-file, 0/12 false positives on clean variants).
Ships a Claude plugin manifest (.claude-plugin/plugin.json, marketplace.json pinned to v0.4.0, .mcp.json using ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}) so install is a plugin add rather than hand-editing.
Local preview shows request count and bytes before any code is sent, and maxRequests budget caps spend/egress.
cons: Automatic use is weak: relies on Claude choosing to invoke the skill/tools; the workflow requires the agent to author a hypothesis plus evidence packet, so it will fire rarely and inconsistently unless you add a custom hook or CLAUDE.md rule. Does not meet 'must use Jev when needed' on its own.

Narrow use case (code review/defect verification only); does nothing for routing, permission decisions, commit/PR classification, or other System One primitives users may want daily. Most of Jev's Choice/Noul/Score value is not exposed as generic tools.

Measured accuracy is modest: 58% recall counting abstentions (5/24 abstentions), a full-repo review returned inconclusive on 18 of 19 dimensions (docs/accuracy.md); the benchmark used a private repo so it cannot be reproduced, and author admits injection resistance is not established.

Very young and single-maintainer: created 2026-09-17, 2 stars, 1 fork, 1 contributor, 183 commits in 13 days, v0.4.0 only; README itself says native Claude UI install was not exercised end to end (docs/integrations.md:93).
Tool schema/definitions are large (~3-4.5k tokens) for a rarely-used feature, unless MCP tool search defers them.

Client-code egress: every call ships source to OpenRouter plus TypeSafe with the same key; the regex screen is best-effort and is not a substitute for client NDAs. Needs a per-project allow/deny decision.
Uses the System One /v1/systemone API, not the newer Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions); could lag if OpenRouter changes the alpha surface.
Default model 'jev-latest' floats, so results are not reproducible unless JEV_MODEL is pinned; a stray TYPESAFE_API_KEY in env silently overrides OpenRouter.
2.2 MB minified bundle is what actually runs; auditing requires rebuilding from src, and it is fetched via npx/plugin from a single npm publisher.
entries.verdict: Best-built and safest Jev integration for code review, with real OpenRouter support and no hook or latency cost, but it is a narrow advisory review tool that Claude invokes at its own discretion, not a broad automatic Jev layer. Worth installing pinned at v0.4.0 (with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and JEV_MODEL pinned) as one component, but to get true automation you must add your own hook or rule, and think twice before enabling it on client repos.

judge.why: Narrow, careful verifier for code-review claims. It has a local secret screen, a 180 KB cap, fail-closed on screen hits and a real OpenRouter path. Its skill workflow is heavy and firing is non-deterministic.
pros: Native OpenRouter support with pinnable v0.4.0
Advisory only; never edits or runs code
Local secret-pattern screen; bounded deadlines
Reported review p50 about 194 ms
cons: Model-discretion only; heavy agent workflow (write hypothesis, collect excerpts, call verify)
Sends diffs and excerpts to OpenRouter; risky on client repos
Multi-packet review can take minutes
2 stars, no independent review

entries.name: fast-facts/jev-mcp
entries.what: Small Go stdio MCP server (about 2.9k lines incl. tests, single dependency: modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk v1.8.0) that wraps TypeSafe's System One endpoint (POST {base}/v1/systemone). It exposes 7 tools. Each is a prebuilt "recipe" of Noul/Choice questions plus local threshold policy: jev_verify (claims vs evidence), jev_screen (prompt-injection/substance/relevance gate for untrusted text), jev_find (rank candidates), jev_pick (choose one or none), jev_extract (pick a verbatim span), jev_classify (batch classify items), jev_ask (raw noul/choice/score escape hatch). Thresholds live in the server (internal/policy), and Jev only returns probabilities.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill or proxy. Claude will call jev_* only if it judges the tool descriptions relevant. The descriptions are generic ("Rank candidates...", "Judge fetched or external text...") and are not written to trigger in a coding workflow. Meeting "never say use jev" would need extra glue, such as a CLAUDE.md rule, a skill, or a PostToolUse/PreToolUse hook that calls the tools. Nothing here provides that. The only naturally auto-triggerable tool is jev_screen after WebFetch, but it needs explicit steering.
security: MIT license (LICENSE present).

API key comes from the environment (config.go:21) and is sent only as a Bearer header (client.go:288), so it is not in argv if configured via .mcp.json env. The README example does show putting the key inline in the client config JSON.

No shell execution, no file access and no telemetry found in internal/ or cmd/. The only outbound network call is client.go:290 to baseURL+/v1/systemone. TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is arbitrary and unvalidated (an env override, so low risk).

Response body capped at 1 MiB (client.go:295). Error bodies are truncated to 200 chars and returned to the model (client.go:339-347), which is a minor injection or leak surface only if the endpoint is malicious.

Prompt-injection surface: user query/purpose strings are string-concatenated into Jev question text (e.g. pick.go:124, screen.go:386). Output is only numeric or ID-constrained (choice validated against the id set via policy.AcceptPick), so tool output cannot carry attacker prose. jev_screen is a classifier that could be evaded, and it is not a security boundary.

Install path is `go run github.com/fast-facts/jev-mcp/cmd/jev-mcp@latest`. This compiles unpinned, mutable latest code from a 0-star personal repo on every cold start, a supply-chain risk. Pin a tag or commit and build a binary after reading the code.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the model passes in a tool call goes to api.typesafe.ai, or to openrouter.ai if repointed. That is candidate texts (up to 250 items, each truncated to 2000 chars, so code snippets, file paths, error text), claims and evidence, text to screen (fetched web pages), classify items, and the query/purpose strings. Nothing is collected automatically: no diffs, tool outputs or prompts are captured unless Claude chooses to pass them as arguments. The server has no hooks or proxy, so it sees nothing else. Under OpenRouter, provider logging and retention settings would apply to those payloads. That matters for client code, so review the data policy before pointing it at client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the workflow level. Failures return an MCP tool error to Claude, which can just continue, and nothing blocks the session. A missing TYPESAFE_API_KEY makes the process exit with log.Fatal at startup (main.go:15), so the MCP server shows as failed to connect, and Claude Code continues without it. HTTP client timeout is 30s per attempt (client.go:230). Up to 3 attempts (maxAttempts=3) on network errors and on 408/429/500/502/503/529, with backoff of 1s and 2s or Retry-After. Worst case is about 93s of blocking on a hung endpoint, which is far above the claimed 70-500ms. There is no circuit breaker and no configurable timeout. A dead or slow Jev stalls whichever turn calls it, but only when Claude decides to call.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools. Descriptions total about 2.1k chars, and the JSON schemas from struct tags (38 jsonschema annotations, nested Candidate/Class/Item objects, plus `any`-typed fields) probably add another 4-5k chars. Estimate about 6-7k chars, or about 1.5-2k tokens of tool definitions (chars/4), cheaper if Claude Code's MCP tool search defers them. The server sets no MCP "instructions" field (server.go:19 passes nil options). No hooks, so zero injected text per turn. Per-call output is small numeric JSON, though jev_find echoes candidate text back in top hits.
pros: Cleanest technical fit for OpenRouter of the Jev MCPs. Base URL and model are env-configurable and the path is /v1/systemone, so TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-latest should work with zero code changes (unverified end to end).
Small, readable and auditable: about 1.5k non-test lines, one dependency (go-sdk), no shell exec, no file access, no telemetry. The 250-item and 2000-char caps are enforced (candidates.go).

Recipes encode sensible policy locally (none options, an exists Noul guarding against a confident wrong top hit, thresholds and auto/review split, ID-set validation of Jev's choice). This is better than a bare passthrough.
jev_screen (prompt-injection gate on fetched content) and jev_pick/jev_find (which file or which error among N) map onto real coding-agent needs and cost about $0.04 per 1M input tokens.

Failures are tool errors, not session blockers, and the response body is capped. Unit tests cover client, policy and each tool, there is a CI build/test on PRs, and live tests are skipped without a key.
Stdio server that adds no per-turn hook latency and does not disturb existing GitNexus, secret-guard or caveman hooks.
cons: Very young and unproven. Created 2026-09-18, 5 commits in the clone (3 by one author, 2 by renovate), 2 contributors, 0 stars, 0 forks, no description or topics, v1.0.1 published 2026-09-29. The tool set could change quickly.

Not automatic. It is just 7 MCP tools relying on Claude's discretion, with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, no server instructions, and descriptions written for generic agents. It won't meet the goal of Claude using it without prompting unless extra glue is added.

OpenRouter is not officially supported. The docs and AGENTS.md say "TypeSafe key only / No other LLM provider", the env var names are TypeSafe-specific, and the response-schema match with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone is unverified. The default model id "jev-latest" would 404 there without an override.

Runtime is awkward. Go must be installed, there are no release binaries, and the documented `go run ...@latest` compiles unpinned code at every cold start, which suits neither a client-project machine nor fast MCP startup. Building a pinned binary is the safe route.
Weak failure bounds. The 30s timeout and 3 retries are hard-coded, so a slow Jev can stall a turn for about 93s, against the claimed 70-500ms.

Limited daily value for an Opus 5.5 workflow. Candidates and results still flow through Claude's context, so there are no token savings. The tools are useful mainly for ranking or classification of shortlists and for a screen gate, and Opus does these well by itself. jev_screen is probabilistic and shouldn't be treated as an injection defense.

Data egress. Code snippets and fetched pages pass to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter) whenever the tools are used, which is a concern on client projects and would need a review of the OpenRouter data policy.
Uncapped Retry-After sleep (client.go:78-84,144-153) makes worst-case stall unbounded, and timeout/retries are not configurable.

jev_screen has no input-size cap or truncation; large fetched pages will exceed OpenRouter's 32k context and error out, and screening requires Claude to echo the whole page as output tokens after having already read it.

Go is not in the user's listed toolchain (Node, Python, uv, gh); go.mod requires go 1.27.1 (very new), with no release binaries (v1.0.1 and v1.0.0 have 0 assets), so an extra toolchain must be installed and a pinned build maintained.

The recommended `claude mcp add -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY` writes the OpenRouter key into ~/.claude.json in plaintext and into argv; the no-secret-leak hook does not yet list OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

Does not implement the official OpenRouter cookbook pattern (PermissionRequest hook on Bash, Noul reversible/serves_task, fail-open to prompt), which is the concrete automatic, high-value integration for this user (auto-approve in defaultMode auto). It contains no hooks at all.
Under bypassPermissions sessions a model-discretion advisory tool gates nothing; results are advisory only.
Reported server Version constant is "0.1.0" (internal/mcp/server.go) while released tag is v1.0.1, and a semantic-release cron publishes tags daily from master, so 'latest' churn is likely.
Tool text (candidates, claims, evidence, screened pages) that Claude passes is sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; API errors (first 200 chars of upstream body) are returned into Claude's context.
entries.verdict: Best-built and most OpenRouter-friendly Jev MCP audited (env-configurable base URL, model and path, tiny auditable code, sensible recipes), but immature (about 12 days old, 2 contributors, 0 stars) and it only provides model-discretion tools, so automatic use needs extra steering such as a CLAUDE.md rule or skill. Use it pinned and built locally, pointed at OpenRouter after a smoke test, mainly for a jev_screen/jev_pick pattern rather than as a general integration.

verification.note: Re-queried now (2026-09-30): fast-facts/jev-mcp has 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 open issue (Renovate dashboard), MIT, not archived, created 2026-09-18, last push 2026-09-29, v1.0.0 and v1.0.1 with 0 assets, 5 commits (3 human, 2 renovate). Confirmed: exactly 7 tools registered (jev_ask/verify/screen/find/pick/extract/classify); POST {base}/v1/systemone with Bearer key; env vars TYPESAFE_API_KEY, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, JEV_MCP_MODEL; no os/exec, file access or telemetry (only net call is client.go:100/106); 1 MiB body cap and 200-char error trim; 30s timeout x 3 attempts; zero hits for 'openrouter' in the repo. OpenRouter compatibility is real but unofficial for this repo: OpenRouter's docs (guides/community/typesafe-sdk.md and the systemone API reference) confirm base URL https://openrouter.ai/api, the /v1/systemone path, Bearer OpenRouter key, TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/TYPESAFE_API_KEY env vars, matching request/response shapes, and that bare `jev-latest` is auto-mapped to typesafe/jev-latest, so the audit's 'model id would 404' claim is wrong (a positive correction). Negative corrections: many cited line numbers are invalid (client.go has 164 lines), file/line counts are off, worst-case stall is unbounded via uncapped Retry-After, jev_screen cannot truly pre-screen (Claude sees the page first; no size cap vs a 32k context), and the suggested install command leaks the key into argv and ~/.claude.json. Core verdict stands: a tidy, small OpenRouter-ready but model-discretion-only MCP from a 12-day-old 0-star repo that does not deliver 'automatic' use or the cookbook PermissionRequest pattern. Score 5.5: best MCP-shaped Jev candidate, but automation gap, Go toolchain, immaturity and stall risks keep it in the 5-6 band. Static reading only; nothing was installed or run.

judge.why: Small, tidy Go stdio MCP with 7 tools (ask, verify, screen, find, pick, extract, classify), a 1 MiB body cap and no file or exec access. It is technically clean, but model-discretion only, and the Go toolchain is an extra.
pros: Small attack surface: no os/exec, no file access, no telemetry
Only network call is one POST to /v1/systemone
Bounded response size and error trimming
cons: Uncapped Retry-After sleep means an unbounded stall
jev_screen has no input cap, so pages over 32k fail; Claude has already read the page before screening it
Needs Go 1.27.1 and has no release binaries
The suggested claude mcp add -e KEY=$OPENROUTER_API_KEY puts the key in argv and plaintext ~/.claude.json
No hooks, so no automatic use and no cookbook gating

entries.name: kbhuw/jev-sift
entries.what: MCP tool 'classify' screening up to 50 files, URLs or text items against a query or 1-8 typed questions, returning compact relevance probabilities so the agent reads selectively.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP
pros: Real context saver: content goes straight to Jev, only probabilities return; concurrency 8, per-item errors, truncation flags
Small (575 loc), tests present, skill included, most-starred candidate (48)
cons: Hardcoded https://api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and jev-latest; needs code edit or fork for OpenRouter (dist/server.mjs bundled)
Sends file contents and fetches URLs (SSRF/leak surface, reads local paths); no hook for auto-use, depends on model discretion

Only probabilities return to Claude
Per-item errors and concurrency 8
