entries.name: claude-jev-funnel (jev-funnel plugin)
entries.what: Claude Code plugin with one skill (jev) plus a zero-dependency Python 3.9+ CLI (skills/jev/scripts/jev.py, about 2500 lines). The CLI has commands ask, batch, rank, eval, doctor and usage. It sends batches of items with typed noul/choice/score questions to Jev and bands the answers into confident and uncertain groups (the "funnel"). Confident answers are handled in code; only the uncertain band goes to Claude or a human. The skill has two modes: A) judge many items during a session, B) help write Jev integrations in apps (Kotlin, Swift, Python references). It is NOT an MCP server and ships no hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Skill description trigger, at model discretion. It fires on bulk classify/score/rank/triage tasks, or on mentions of Jev, TypeSafe or noul. It is not deterministic. The README suggests adding a CLAUDE.md rule (Closed-set bulk judgments over ~20+ items go to the jev skill before any cheap LLM subagent) to make the routing explicit.
security: OPENROUTER_API_KEY is read from the environment only and sent in the Authorization header, so it is not in argv or the process list (jev.py build_headers).
Redirects are refused (NoRedirect handler) so the bearer token is never resent elsewhere; response size is capped at 8 MB.

Outgoing state, questions and criteria are scanned for secret patterns (OpenRouter, Anthropic, AWS, GitHub, Google and Slack tokens, private-key blocks) and refused on a match. --lenient does not relax this. This is a partial substitute for the user's own secret-guard hook.
No shell execution, no subprocess, no os.system in jev.py (grep found none). No curl|sh, no postinstall, no telemetry code found.

Local artifacts: usage ledger at ~/.config/jev/usage.jsonl and sqlite answer cache at ~/.cache/jev/cache.sqlite. The cache stores item payloads, so client code may persist on disk. Ledger can be disabled with JEV_NO_LEDGER=1 and the cache dir is set with JEV_CACHE_DIR.

Prompt-injection surface: none in the plugin itself (no hooks and no MCP). Jev returns numbers only, so returned data cannot inject text. The skill runs jev.py via Bash, which is trivial to do in bypass mode.
entries.dataEgress: Only when the skill runs: the state (item text such as log lines, diffs, file contents or review text) and the typed questions are POSTed to openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (default), plus the API key in the Authorization header. Nothing is sent on session start or on ordinary prompts, and nothing is sent automatically for arbitrary tool output. OpenRouter's data policy applies. Client code could be sent if Claude chooses to triage client files or diffs, so the user has to steer that. Local ledger and sqlite cache keep copies of the payloads on disk.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by nature. It is a skill run on demand, not a gate, so Claude Code is never blocked when Jev is down. jev.py has a 30 s per-attempt timeout and up to 5 attempts with backoff on 408/429/5xx/529 (worst case several minutes for one call). It honors Retry-After up to 60 s and gives typed errors for 402 (no credit), 403 and 404 (the alpha endpoint may change). When it fails, Claude can fall back to judging the items itself.
entries.contextCost: No MCP tools (0 tool definitions). Passive cost is one skill entry: name plus a description of about 1000 characters, roughly 250 tokens in the skill listing every turn. When triggered, SKILL.md (about 23 KB, roughly 5.8k tokens) loads, and Claude may also read references/*.md (question-design.md is about 32 KB, api.md about 20 KB, roughly 5-8k tokens each). No hook-injected text and no server instructions.
pros: Uses OpenRouter's /api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY by default (jev.py:65-70), so it works with the user's chosen provider with zero patching; TypeSafe direct is a flag away.

Truly automatic invocation with no user prompt: the skill description triggers on bulk classify/triage tasks, and the README offers a CLAUDE.md snippet to make routing explicit. This is the only kind of automatic integration the candidate offers, and it adds no hook latency to ordinary turns.
Very low always-on context cost: no MCP tool schemas, only about 250 tokens for the skill description, versus thousands for an MCP server.

Codes real Jev pitfalls: keyed rather than positional item references (the docs quote 29/320 wrong positionally, 0/320 keyed), a required no-match option on every choice, per-type calibration bands (noul ECE 0.012, choice 0.086, score 0.254), 32k context enforcement, and a dry-run cost estimate.

Sound engineering hygiene: stdlib only, no subprocess or shell, no redirects, 8 MB response cap, an outgoing secret scanner, a resumable batch with sqlite cache, a usage ledger showing real usage.cost, about 205 tests, CI on 3 Python versions, and Apache-2.0.

Honest 'When not to use it' section: it says a Jev skill router inside Claude Code adds little, and that file-relevance screening on a manageable codebase showed no effect in a 390k-line benchmark. It also says single judgments should be left to Claude.
cons: Its use case is bulk (about 20+ items) closed-set judgments such as triaging logs, lint warnings, review comments or PR diffs. Typical daily coding (edit, debug, refactor, run tests) rarely triggers it, so it will mostly sit idle. This is not a general Jev integration for coding decisions.
Model-discretion skill trigger, not deterministic. Opus may skip it or judge items itself; there is no hook that forces routing, and the bypass/auto permission mode does not change that.
Not an MCP server and no hooks, so it cannot intercept tool calls or gate actions with Jev (for example a risk score on a Bash command). Only a separate hook or MCP tool could do that.

Data egress risk on client projects: when triggered it POSTs file, diff or log content to OpenRouter and keeps the payloads in ~/.cache/jev/cache.sqlite and a usage ledger on disk. The regex secret scan is not a substitute for the user's own PreToolUse secret guard, which does not cover this Bash-invoked script's payloads.

Very young and single-author: created 2026-09-24, 10 commits, 2 stars, 1 contributor, three releases in two days, no external adoption or issue history. Its code is executed by Claude via Bash, so it needs a read-through or SHA pin. The upstream /alpha/ endpoint may change.

Retry policy of 5 attempts with a 30 s timeout could stall a turn for minutes when OpenRouter is degraded; there is no fail-fast option seen in the code. Skepticism about Jev's real quality (Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim) is unaddressed here, and the vendor-favouring benchmark citations (Greenberg A/B) are not independently verified.

Loading the full SKILL.md (about 5.8k tokens) plus references when triggered is heavy for a single small classification, and the skill mixes in app-building content (Kotlin/Swift) that this user will not need.
entries.verdict: The best-built and lowest-overhead option for an OpenRouter-hosted Jev with automatic skill triggering, but it only fires on bulk closed-set triage, so it barely touches everyday coding. Treat it as a cheap, optional add-on (pin the commit SHA, read jev.py first, set JEV_NO_LEDGER and JEV_CACHE_DIR, and put the CLAUDE.md routing rule in place) rather than the core of the Jev integration.

judge.why: Plugin with a skill and a zero-dependency 2,500-line Python CLI that bands answers into confident and uncertain groups, so Claude only sees the uncertain remainder. Good design for bulk triage, but it fires only on 20+ item closed-set jobs.
pros: OpenRouter by default; no hooks; zero overhead on ordinary turns
Confident/uncertain funnel is the right pattern
Bench: 500 items in 3.9 s for about $0.006
cons: Barely touches everyday coding
Local ledger and SQLite cache keep copies of payloads on disk
Retry loop can run several minutes
Description-trigger only; needs a CLAUDE.md routing rule

entries.name: paulrobello/jev-mcp-server
entries.what: Bun/TypeScript stdio MCP server (plus an ask-jev SKILL.md) that exposes six Jev tools: server-side code reads files or runs a gated command, sends them as state to Jev, and returns only typed answers (noul/choice/score) so the file content never enters Claude's context. It is a vendored port of paulrobello/ten-levels-of-jev levels 6 and 8-10 for Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus a skill-description trigger. The tool descriptions actively nudge Claude ('Prefer this over reasoning out a classification, risk score, or yes/no with confidence yourself', index.ts:148-149) and the skill description lists triage/classify/score triggers, but there is no deterministic hook, so Claude will only sometimes reach for it. Nothing forces use, and grep/Read/gitnexus will usually win for daily coding tasks.
security: API key: sent as Bearer header from process.env (client.ts:140, 16), never in argv unless the user passes it via 'claude mcp add -e', which then lives in plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The relay key is read from ~/.config/jev/key or JEV_OPENROUTER_KEY (jev.ts:20-28).
fetch uses redirect:'error' (client.ts:19) and a 30 s total timeout, so redirect-based key leaks are blocked.

ask_jev's `command` param executes an arbitrary shell string via child_process.exec (index.ts:64-92) with the user's env (including OPENROUTER_API_KEY and any other secrets) and a 60 s timeout. The only guard is an LLM gate: Jev classifies the command as read_only/reversible/irreversible and blocks only when irreversible confidence >= 0.6 or destructive_intent >= 0.7 (level06/bash-gate.ts:39-68). 'reversible' commands (edits, installs, curl|sh, git commit, writes, network exfiltration) pass. Yet the tool is annotated readOnlyHint:true (index.ts:116-121), so a client or the user's auto/bypass mode may auto-approve it. This effectively adds a permission-bypass side door around the user's Bash hooks (the secret-leak PreToolUse guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, not mcp__jev__*), so it would also see .env files by path.

File reading has no secret filter: readFileState accepts absolute paths and any relative path including ../ (level08/read-state.ts:29-46); SKIP_DIRS is only node_modules, .git, .sessions, dist, build, coverage, .pi (level09/prune.ts:10-18). No exclusion of .env, .npmrc, keys, or ~/.ssh. Files go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe. The user's secret-leak guard would not be triggered because the read happens inside the MCP process.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents are sent to Jev as state; Jev returns only typed values (no free text), so injection can only skew probabilities (e.g., make a malicious file look 'safe' or make the gate say read_only for a destructive command in a command string that Claude itself supplies). Return values are validated strictly (client.ts:158-223), which is good.

Telemetry: none to third parties. Every call writes a JEV_EVENT JSON line to stderr including answers and the source (jev.ts:77-79), which Claude Code may capture into MCP logs; the file content is not logged.
entries.dataEgress: Whole file content (up to about (32k-4k)*4 = 112k chars per file per call, ask_jev_files up to 255 files/call, one HTTP request each), file paths, cwd, question text, command strings and captured stdout/stderr (up to 200k chars each) go to the configured endpoint: by default a localhost relay (cc-router, not publicly available), or, with OPENROUTER_API_KEY, https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions and downstream TypeSafe. Egress happens on every tool call, not just once. No secret filtering. Conversation history and Claude's prompts do not leave, except whatever Claude writes into `state`/questions.
entries.failureMode: Per-call fail-open for the agent: on error the tool returns isError text and Claude carries on (index.ts:58-61). Client retries 429/502/503/529 up to 3 attempts with 500 ms exponential backoff, capped 8 s delay, 30 s total deadline (client.ts:31-33, 205-241), so a hung provider can stall a tool call for up to 30 s (5 s for the command gate via withGuardTimeout, jev.ts:84-97; gate then fails CLOSED and refuses the command). Missing OPENROUTER_API_KEY without a relay means ECONNREFUSED to 127.0.0.1:8792 on every call (no silent mock, by design). Because it is model-discretion, a broken server just means Claude does the work itself.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools, roughly 7-8k chars of names, descriptions and JSON schemas in src/index.ts, so about 1.8-2.2k tokens (QUESTION_SCHEMA is repeated inside ask_jev_files' description). No MCP server 'instructions' field (McpServer constructed with name/version only, index.ts:114). No hooks, so zero injected text per turn. The optional skill adds one description line (about 150 tokens) always loaded, and the SKILL.md body (about 900 tokens) when triggered. Tool results are small structured JSON (per-file answers), which is the real context-saving point.
pros: Only candidate here that actually ships tools tailored to coding-agent use: judging files (bool/choice/score) and picking which file to open, with the content never entering Claude's context, i.e. genuine context savings on directory triage (index.ts:195-236).

Direct OpenRouter path is implemented in code with the alpha Decisions endpoint and ~typesafe/jev-latest alias (client.ts:19-25), so setting only OPENROUTER_API_KEY makes it work with no patching; OpenRouter is the only live provider, matching the user's requirement.

Strict response validation (envelope, usage, probabilities sum to 1, declared choice keys, score legend) fails loudly on contract drift (client.ts:158-223); redirect:'error', timeout, bounded retries.

Automatic-ish invocation: tool descriptions and the ask-jev SKILL.md description carry triggers, so Claude can use it without 'use jev' being typed; low fixed context cost (about 2k tokens, no hooks, no per-turn injection).
Clean, small, readable codebase (about 3.4k lines, mostly vendored), MIT, no install scripts; offline mock for testing with JEV_BACKEND=mock.
Reports cost (usage.cost) in every result and logs JEV_EVENT to stderr, useful for checking spend and whether Jev is actually being called.
cons: Brand new: 1 commit, 1 contributor, 0 stars, created 2026-09-29 (one day old), no releases, no CI; the whole thing is a personal port of the author's demo repo ten-levels-of-jev, and src/jev/ is vendored 'do not edit'.

Defaults are wrong for this user: with no env it points to the author's private http://127.0.0.1:8792 cc-router relay (jev.ts:18, 40-44; cc-router repo does not resolve on GitHub), README install command hardcodes /Users/probello paths, and it requires Bun.
Does NOT use the /v1/systemone endpoint the README and brief mention; the direct path is /api/alpha/decisions (alpha, may change). Never verified against live OpenRouter in this audit.

Serious security gap: ask_jev `command` runs arbitrary shell via exec gated only by a probabilistic Jev classifier that lets 'reversible' commands (writes, installs, network) through, while the tool is marked readOnlyHint:true, so with the user's bypass/auto permission mode it bypasses the permission prompt and the existing Bash secret-guard hook, and the child inherits OPENROUTER_API_KEY.

No secret filtering on file reads: .env, keys and absolute/parent paths are allowed and their full contents are sent to OpenRouter/TypeSafe on every call, which is a real problem on client projects with NDA code. The user's secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tools.

Not deterministic: relies on Claude's discretion, and Claude's own Grep/Read/gitnexus is usually better for coding; Jev is a probability classifier with no reasoning, so for the daily loop the value is limited to triage-style questions (which of 200 files touches billing, risk score), not edits, tests or debugging.

Unproven quality of Jev on code judgments; an LLM-router-like model (Theo's claim) may give miscalibrated probabilities, and the tools return numbers Claude may over-trust. Fan-out of up to 255 parallel calls per tool call can hit rate limits and burn credits.
Tiny test suite (about 7 cases, mock only), no live test; no automatic update path (git pull, and re-vendoring upstream by hand).
entries.verdict: The most relevant Jev-for-Claude-Code MCP found: it supports OpenRouter directly (via /api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY) and gives model-discretion triage tools, but it is a day-old single-commit proof of concept with author-specific defaults and a serious side door (LLM-gated shell exec plus unfiltered file reads sent off-machine). Usable only after review: run it with the command param and secret-path reads restricted (or fork to drop `command`, add .env/key excludes and a deny in permissions), and treat it as an optional triage helper, not a deterministic integration.

judge.why: Six tools that read files server-side and return only typed answers, which saves context. It has a serious side door: an LLM-gated shell command path plus unfiltered file reads.
pros: Native OpenRouter use
File contents never enter Claude's context
Tool descriptions nudge use
cons: Command execution gated by Jev, and the gate fails closed
No secret filtering on file reads; author-specific defaults
Up to 255 parallel requests per call
One-day-old proof of concept

entries.name: thedv91/jev-mcp (npm: jev-agent-mcp)
entries.what: Stdio MCP server (Node/TS, npm jev-agent-mcp 0.1.0) exposing 5 tools that wrap TypeSafe's Jev via the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (POST {base}/v1/systemone, Bearer auth): generic judge (Choice/Noul/Score), rank_candidates, verify_claim (exact-quote match then a Choice per claim), and two multi-request review pipelines (review_changes for diffs, review_files for source) that run five Noul screens per file plus follow-up Choice/Score requests. Adds threshold logic (certainty high/medium/low, noul uncertain band, needs_escalation). Ships a SKILL.md telling the agent when to call which tool (before declaring done, before hard-to-undo actions, when reviewing).
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by tool descriptions ("WHEN TO USE ... at a decision point") and by an optional description-triggered skill (SKILL.md: before declaring work done, before hard-to-undo actions, when asked to review). Nothing deterministic: no hook, no proxy, so Claude Code may rarely or inconsistently call it, and it will not fire without the model choosing to. Could be made more automatic only by adding your own Stop/PreToolUse hook or CLAUDE.md rules on top.
security: No npm lifecycle install scripts (only prepack -> tsc); no curl|sh installer; no child_process/exec/spawn/fetch/fs in src (grep clean); server code only calls SDK systemOne. Tool annotations readOnlyHint/openWorldHint set.
API key read only from env by SDK; sent as Bearer header, not in argv if passed via `env` block. But `claude mcp add -e 'X=${VAR}'` keeps key out of config. Not visible in process list argv.

Single maintainer (thedv91 / npm publisher nopbongdem, different identity than GitHub author 'Harry'), repo 9 days old, 0 stars: supply-chain risk when run via `npx -y` in a bypass-permissions setup; pin version and audit the tarball.
Transitive trust in @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (official, MIT, 3 versions, created 2026-09-12) and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk.
TYPESAFE_LOG_LEVEL=debug logs request bodies (includes code/diffs) to stderr; default is quiet.

Prompt-injection surface: tool outputs are numbers/ids only (no generated prose), but review findings echo file paths/lines and claim text supplied by the caller; low risk. Agent-supplied state is untrusted code sent to a model that may mis-rank.
entries.dataEgress: Only what the calling agent puts in tool arguments is sent, to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (api.typesafe.ai by default; OpenRouter if base overridden): judge state/questions, verify_claim claims plus raw evidence (test output, diffs, logs), rank_candidates candidate text, review_changes/review_files full unified diffs or full file contents (up to 100 files each, truncated by truncateMiddle), and many fan-out requests per review. The server reads no files and runs no commands itself, so nothing leaves unless Claude decides to pass it. SKILL.md says to exclude lockfiles/vendored/secret-bearing content, but nothing enforces it: the existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard does NOT cover MCP tool arguments (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit). Client project code could go to a third-party model; needs a per-project policy.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at tool level, not a hook. Missing key: server starts, each call returns isError text (src/typesafe.ts:21-22, 37-49). SDK defaults: 10 s timeout per request (index.mjs:518), maxRetries 2 with 0.5-5 s backoff, so a single judge call can block ~30 s+ when Jev is down/slow; review tools fan out (CONCURRENCY=3, up to dozens of requests) so can take minutes; failed requests reported in failed_requests and review carries on (types.ts:53), all-fail returns an error. The agent, not the server, decides what to do; SKILL says a tool error is never approval. No circuit breaker and no configurable timeout via env (timeout not exposed).
entries.contextCost: 5 tools always loaded (no deferred/tool-search assumption). Descriptions are about 8.4k chars (judge 2165, rank 1944, verify 1653, review_changes 1328, review_files 1297) plus large input schemas with long .describe() strings and output schemas; estimated ~4-6k tokens in tool definitions (chars/4 estimate, roughly 2.1k tokens descriptions plus schema overhead). McpServer created with no `instructions`, so no server-instructions block. No hooks, so no per-turn injected text. Optional SKILL.md adds ~5.9k chars (~1.5k tokens) only when loaded; its ~500 char description sits in the skill listing.
pros: Only candidate so far that is genuinely Jev-shaped: wraps the real /v1/systemone endpoint through TypeSafe's official SDK (src/typesafe.ts, SDK index.mjs:554), covering all three primitives via a generic judge tool.

OpenRouter switch is config-only: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/TYPESAFE_API_KEY/TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL from env and posts to /v1/systemone with Bearer, which maps to https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone with an OpenRouter key.
Good agent-facing design: descriptions state when to use and how to read probabilities, with calibrated-threshold handling (needs_escalation, noul band) and explicit 'error is not approval' guidance.

verify_claim (do the tests pass / is bug fixed evidence check) and judge as a pre-action gate map directly onto real daily-coding decision points; string-match fabricated-quote check costs no model call.
No install scripts, no shell/file/network code beyond the SDK, small readable codebase (~170 KB incl. lock/README), MIT.
Low context footprint versus many MCPs (5 tools, no server instructions, no hooks), and no added latency when unused.
cons: Not automatic: pure model-discretion tools plus an optional skill; Claude Code will not reliably call it, contradicting the requirement of automatic use without prompting. Needs extra hooks/CLAUDE.md to enforce.
OpenRouter is not a supported provider in code or docs; compatibility with OpenRouter's System One schema and the model id typesafe/jev-1.13 is untested and unverified.
Extremely immature: 9 days old, 2 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, no CI, no releases, single npm version; 'jev-agent-mcp' publisher identity differs from GitHub author.

Sends full diffs and file contents of personal and client repos to a third-party model; nothing enforces exclusions and the existing secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool args; client-confidentiality risk.

Review pipelines are heavy fan-out (5 screens per file plus follow-ups, minutes for large diffs) and cost/latency grow with change size; review quality depends on an unproven, possibly router-like model (skeptic claim unverified) and default thresholds are admittedly uncalibrated.
10 s timeout x 3 attempts with no exposed knob and no circuit breaker: a Jev outage can stall a turn ~30 s per call; `npx -y` cold start adds session startup risk.
Jev returns no reasoning or free text, so its value over Opus 5.5 own judgment for coding is unproven; ~4-6k tokens of always-on tool definitions for tools the model may seldom use.
entries.verdict: The most complete Jev MCP found so far and one config change (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/API_KEY) away from OpenRouter, but it is alpha, untested, model-discretion only, and sends whole diffs off-machine, so it satisfies neither the auto-invocation requirement nor client-safety by itself. Use it only as the tool layer, pinned and audited, paired with a deterministic hook or CLAUDE.md rule (e.g. Stop-hook gate on verify_claim) if Jev is to be used automatically.

entries.name: eaisdevelopment/jevmcp
entries.what: Claude Code and Codex plugin: one MCP server (uv script) with spec-drift, CI-failure triage and code-audit-against-CLAUDE.md-rules tools plus three skills; Jev screens, agent investigates flagged items.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP with skill triggers
pros: Real task-specific tools with label semantics (DRIFT/CHANGE/BREAKS/review/??/ok/not checked) that never treat unknown as pass; preview_* tools estimate cost before calling
Release 1.7.6 with changelog, PRIVACY and SECURITY docs, smoke and spec-drift CI workflows; code-audit checks code against approved CLAUDE.md rules; CI triage uses gh
Standard Claude plugin manifest with user_config for key; measured cost $0.0013 for a 131-requirement spec check
cons: TypeSafe endpoint only (api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone) with TYPESAFE_API_KEY; no OpenRouter/baseUrl option, requires editing jevkit.py
Ten MCP tool schemas plus three skills add context overhead every session; needs spec map/rule map setup before value; single-author 0 stars

judge.why: Most complete task-specific plugin (spec drift, CI failure triage via gh, code audit against CLAUDE.md rules) with cost preview tools and clean unknown-is-not-pass semantics. Needs spec-map and rule-map setup and has 10 tool schemas plus 3 skills of overhead.
pros: Label semantics that never treat unknown as pass
preview_* tools estimate cost first
Changelog, PRIVACY and SECURITY docs, CI workflows
cons: TypeSafe-only; needs a fork for OpenRouter
Ten tool schemas plus three skills add session context
Setup work before any value; single author, 0 stars
Model-discretion triggers only

entries.name: chungsubeen0/jevmcp (jev-mcp)
entries.what: Local Python MCP server (stdio by default, optional Streamable HTTP) that exposes 7 tools where the frontier model hands over a structured "state" (failure output, diff summary, requirements, findings, candidates) and gets back Jev "noul" probabilities mapped to labels and a "user_decision" advisory. It only uses the Noul primitive (no Choice or Score). It adds validation, input truncation, a SQLite cache, local telemetry and secret redaction. It never edits code. Calls go to POST {base_url}/v1/systemone.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, made "automatic" only by tool descriptions ("Use before broad reasoning when scope is unclear") plus a CLAUDE.md block the user must paste in. There is no hook, no skill, no proxy. Claude Code will not reliably call it after every failing test, since the descriptions are hedged ("Use selectively", "Do not call for trivial decisions"). The README's recommended shadow mode adds an "advisory: treat as telemetry" line to results, so the outputs are explicitly non-binding. A deterministic PostToolUse hook could not call it without writing new code. It also cannot cover Jev's typical uses (routing, gating hooks) since only Noul-on-coding-artifacts is implemented.
security: API key is read from environment only (config.py:220); project YAML cannot set api_key, base_url or telemetry.store_content (config.py:176-177), which blocks a malicious cloned repo from redirecting the key. The key is not in argv, but a .mcp.json 'env' entry can carry it, and the README warns that some clients do not expand ${VAR}.

HTTPS-only base URL, host allowlist (default api.typesafe.ai only), follow_redirects=False (typesafe.py:27-41, 66-69). Error and log redaction of api keys and tokens (errors.sanitize_message, telemetry/privacy.py SecretLogFilter).
No shell execution: grep for subprocess/os.system/eval/exec in src and scripts found nothing. No file-read or shell tools exposed, and no code-writing tools.

Prompt-injection surface: state sent to Jev is untrusted repo and test output. The README concedes Jev can be biased by injected text, but Jev returns only floats and the server never returns APPROVED/SAFE labels. Impact is limited to skewed advice for Claude. Injection through the MCP tool result into Claude is low, since responses are structured JSON.
HTTP transport is opt-in, needs a Bearer token, binds to 127.0.0.1 by default, and non-loopback bind needs an extra env flag. stdio is the default, so no listening port is opened.
SQLite cache and telemetry in ~/.local/share/jev-mcp with 0600/0700 permissions. It stores hashes, not content, unless store_content is enabled in user config. There is no remote telemetry.
entries.dataEgress: To api.typesafe.ai (or openrouter.ai after re-pointing), and via OpenRouter on to TypeSafe: the normalized `state` JSON, which is whatever Claude puts in the tool arguments. Depending on the tool this is: the task goal and requirement text; command, exit code and up to ~50k chars of failure output; diff_summary (up to ~25k chars); changed file paths; previous failure summary; findings; candidate file snippets (up to 8k chars each, 25 candidates); and free-form state in jev_judge. The hard cap is max_state_chars = 100,000 (config.py:89). Also sent: the question instructions, the model id and the Bearer key. The MCP has no file-read or shell access, so it only sends what Claude chooses to put in. There is no secret scrubbing of state before sending; redaction applies to logs, errors and telemetry only. Nothing goes to the maintainer, and there is no remote telemetry. Locally it writes hashed telemetry and a cache. For client projects, this means client code excerpts and test output go to OpenRouter and TypeSafe (a beta service with 0 promise of data-handling terms verified here).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. Errors come back as structured JSON (PROVIDER_TIMEOUT, PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE, RATE_LIMITED, INVALID_PROVIDER_RESPONSE, INTERNAL_ERROR with a retryable flag) instead of raising, and Claude continues (tools/_common.py:safe_run; README says "No fabricated probabilities"). Startup never contacts TypeSafe. Defaults: timeout 30 s (bounds 1-120), max_retries 1 for 408/425/429/5xx/529 and timeouts with a 0.2 s sleep (typesafe.py:16, 109-135). Worst case on a hung provider is roughly 60 s of blocked tool call, and 401/403 fails immediately with a "check TYPESAFE_API_KEY" message. The timeout is far above the claimed 70-500 ms, so lowering it to about 3-5 s is advisable. Missing key gives an immediate PROVIDER_UNAVAILABLE.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools (jev_triage_failure, jev_compare_attempts, jev_check_completion, jev_rank_context, jev_classify_findings, jev_assess_risk, jev_judge). Descriptions total about 2.1k chars (250-390 each; ~530 tokens). Pydantic-generated input schemas with nested models ($defs for TaskInput, FailureEvent, Attempt, Finding, ContextCandidate, ClientMeta and others; models.py is 3.2k chars of source) add an estimated 8-11k chars, so the total is roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens of tool definitions (estimated statically, not measured). No MCP server `instructions` (FastMCP("jev-mcp") is created without them, server.py:50). No hook-injected text, since there are no hooks. The suggested CLAUDE.example.md adds about 1.7k chars (~430 tokens) each session. With deferred MCP tool loading, the definitions only cost a name-list line until fetched. Each tool result adds JSON with meta, signals and user_decision (probably a few hundred tokens).
pros: Same wire schema as OpenRouter System One (state + questions{type:noul,instructions}, answers[id].noul): jev-mcp typesafe.py:72-79,137-157 vs OpenRouter docs. OpenRouter use needs only 4 env vars (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, TYPESAFE_ALLOWED_HOSTS=openrouter.ai, key, model typesafe/jev-1.13), no code changes in the likely case.

Best-engineered Jev integration seen so far for coding: injection-aware (project YAML cannot redirect the key, host allowlist, no redirects), fail-open structured errors, bounded timeouts/retries, input truncation with warnings, local hashed-only telemetry, 0600 files.
Read-only by design: no shell, file or write tools, so a compromised Jev response cannot cause actions; responses can't say APPROVED/SAFE_TO_MERGE.

Real test discipline for an early repo: about 33 test files, contract/schema snapshots, adversarial and secret-leak tests, golden corpus, CI with nightly live tests, plus a client-specific Claude Code config and profile (interactive).
MIT licence, stdio by default (no open port), lazy startup with no network on init, doctor script for offline checks, Python/uv-friendly.
Use cases are on point for Claude Code: failure triage, stuck detection across attempts, requirement coverage, risk flagging.
cons: Immature and single-author: 5 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, 0 forks, no releases, not on PyPI, created 2026-09-17 and last pushed 2026-09-18 (about 12 days stale on 2026-09-30). Commits are Cursor-co-authored. No published eval results: eval-results/ has only a README and GATES.md states accuracy numbers are unset, so claimed usefulness and savings are unverified.

Not automatic. Invocation depends on Claude's discretion plus a pasted CLAUDE.md block, and the docs themselves say to call Jev 'less often' in Claude Code. There is no hook to trigger it deterministically after a failing test.

Claude has to serialise the state into tool arguments. Writing failure output and diff summaries as Opus output tokens can cost more than the ~$0.042/M-input Jev call saves, and it adds seconds per call. The design is aimed at cutting Opus reasoning, but the plumbing may erase that.

It maps every question onto Noul via generic prose instructions. Only 1 of about 23 questions defines criteria (true/false), while OpenRouter's docs list criteria as required on noul questions, so calls may 400 on OpenRouter until patched. This is untested.

Default model alias 'jev-latest' and default host api.typesafe.ai are TypeSafe-specific. OpenRouter needs TYPESAFE_* env var names to be reused for an OpenRouter key (confusing but harmless), and a mismatch of model id will produce HTTP 4xx.

Heavy tool surface for uncertain value: 7 tools with nested schemas cost roughly 2.5-3.5k tokens of context, and with the CLAUDE.md block about 3-4k. Rejects planning/architecture/debugging questions by design, so it does not help the most valuable Opus work.

Sends failure output, diffs and file snippets (up to 100k chars per call) to OpenRouter and TypeSafe with no pre-send secret scrubbing (redaction covers logs/errors only). Sensitive for client projects, and it conflicts in spirit with the user's secret-leak guard hook.

Timeout default 30 s with one retry means a stalled provider can block a tool call for up to about 60 s. Jev is beta and Theo-style skepticism (router-like behaviour) is unresolved, and the outputs are probabilities that the README itself says are not gates.
Only Noul is used, with no Choice or Score. It cannot express routing or gating decisions (for example 'which of N options'), which is Jev's other main strength.
entries.verdict: The most careful and best-tested Jev MCP for coding agents, and repointing it to OpenRouter is a config-only change (plus possibly default criteria). However, it is a 1-day-old single-author PoC with no published accuracy data, invocation is model-discretion rather than automatic, and the token cost of Claude serialising state into tool calls may cancel any savings. Worth trying as an opt-in, shadow-mode experiment pinned to a reviewed commit, not as the primary automatic integration.

entries.name: ccai40359-wq/jev-triage
entries.what: Python CLI/library plus a Claude Code PostToolUse(Bash) hook. When a test command (pytest, vitest, jest, go test, cargo test, npm test, etc.) fails, it parses the output, applies about 16 regex rules locally (ModuleNotFoundError, KeyError env var, EADDRINUSE, timeout...), and only for ambiguous failures makes one Jev call (a Choice question RETRY/FIX_CODE/FIX_ENV plus a Noul flakiness question) to TypeSafe. It then prints a short verdict and advice line. It also keeps a local cost/latency ledger with a stats command.
entries.autoInvocation: Deterministic hook (PostToolUse on the Bash tool), so it needs no prompting. However, there is a likely integration bug that I did not verify by running it (third-party code is not to be run). Per my knowledge of Claude Code hook semantics: (1) plain stdout from a PostToolUse hook on exit 0 is shown in the transcript/verbose view and is not added to the model's context; only JSON with hookSpecificOutput.additionalContext (or UserPromptSubmit/SessionStart stdout) reaches the model. hooks.py:_emit() writes plain text at lines 89-93 and 168-170, and a grep for additionalContext or hookSpecificOutput finds no match anywhere in the repo. (2) A failing Bash command (non-zero exit) is generally reported as a tool error, which fires PostToolUseFailure rather than PostToolUse. The installed matcher is registered only under PostToolUse, and extract_output() reads tool_response/tool_result keys that the failure payload may not contain. Both points need a live check in Claude Code 2.1.285 before relying on it. Treat 'the model sees the verdict automatically' as unproven.
security: API key is read only from the environment and sent in an Authorization: Bearer header via http.client, so it does not appear in argv or the process list.

Hard-coded host allowlist (api.typesafe.ai) with a DNS check that rejects private, loopback and link-local addresses. It does not follow redirects and refuses non-https. This is a reasonable SSRF defense but blocks OpenRouter until patched.

Secret redaction before egress: 9 regexes cover GitHub tokens, sk- keys, api_key/password/token=, bearer tokens, DB URLs, JWTs and AKIA keys. It is best-effort and pattern-based, so client-specific secrets can leak. The test-output text can also contain PII or proprietary code snippets from assertions.

The prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns typed probabilities, not free text. The hook prints only fixed advice strings plus a root-cause reason from local rules, so injected text in logs cannot easily steer Claude. The 'likely root cause' line is rule-derived, not model text.

No shell execution, no telemetry, no postinstall and no curl|sh. The only file writes are ~/.jev-triage/ledger.jsonl (no raw log text) and ~/.claude/settings.json on --install. --install modifies the user's global settings, which is acceptable but should be done by hand here.
Single anonymous author with an unknown identity. The account and repo are 9 days old and have 1 star. Supply-chain trust is low, but the code is about 2.2k lines of readable stdlib Python.
entries.dataEgress: The only external call is the Jev request, and only for failures the local rules cannot resolve. It sends the parsed failure fields (test name, error type, location, message, stage, summary line) and a compacted log excerpt of up to 9000 characters, with the first and last parts of the log and every failure block, after regex secret redaction. The API key goes in the Authorization header. Nothing else leaves the machine: no repo files, diffs or non-test command output. It is limited to test commands that fail.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. run_hook() catches BaseException and always returns 0. Jev call timeout is 8 s (hook timeout 15 s in settings), with a single retry after 0.35 s on 429, 5xx and TLS errors, so the worst case is roughly 16 s or more. A timeout, a bad key, a missing key or a network error yields a degraded verdict and prints nothing. There is a design flaw: the retry can add to blocking time on the hook's synchronous path, and Claude waits for the hook to finish.
entries.contextCost: Zero MCP tools and no server instructions, so no per-session token cost. It is a hook only, and text is injected only when a test command fails: about 3-4 lines (about 60-100 tokens). Caveat: see autoInvocation. If Claude Code does not feed PostToolUse plain stdout to the model, the injected cost is 0 and so is the benefit.
pros: Truly automatic trigger model: a deterministic PostToolUse hook restricted to failing test commands (12 runner regexes), so the user never has to prompt 'use jev'. Zero MCP tools means zero standing context cost.

Sensible, cheap architecture: local parser and rule layer resolve 7 of 16 real logs (44%) with no network call, and Jev is only called for ambiguous failures, so cost and latency stay low ($0.000334 for 16 logs per the ledger).
Fail-open discipline is real: BaseException is caught, the exit code is always 0, and tests cover the hook and security paths (111 offline tests; 7 test files, about 1.5k lines).

Honest README: it discloses measured Jev latency of 0.8-2.5 s against the advertised 70-500 ms, admits the 16-log eval was written by the prompt author, and records the earlier 76.9% score. This is useful independent evidence for the latency and calibration skepticism.
Good egress hygiene: secret redaction before sending, SSRF and redirect protection, a 9000-character cap, no raw logs in the ledger, and no key in argv.
It matches a legitimate System One use case (a typed 3-way Choice plus a Noul), so it doubles as a working reference for building a request payload.
cons: No OpenRouter support: the host allowlist is hard-coded to api.typesafe.ai (triage.py:36, 109-120), the key is TYPESAFE_API_KEY only, and the model is jev-latest. It must be forked and patched, and the OpenRouter schema compatibility is unverified. This conflicts with the user's stated requirement to use OpenRouter.

The value proposition is narrow: it only helps after a test failure. The rules already do the obvious cases, and Claude Opus 5.5 reading the same traceback usually classifies it correctly without a second-hand hint. Jev adds 1-6 s of hook wait on a failing run in exchange for a hint the main model rarely needs.

Probable delivery bug: plain stdout from a PostToolUse hook is likely not injected into the model's context, and a non-zero Bash exit likely triggers PostToolUseFailure instead. Nothing in the repo uses additionalContext or PostToolUseFailure, so the advertised 'agent sees it as context' behaviour is unverified and may be a silent no-op on Claude Code 2.1.x.

Quality signal: 2 commits, 1 contributor, 1 star, no CI, no release, no PyPI package, 9 days old, described as Alpha. Only a self-reported 16-log evaluation, which the author admits is not field accuracy. Jest is not covered by a real fixture.

Risk of wrong-direction advice: the hook says 'do not re-run the suite unchanged' on FIX_CODE and FIX_ENV. Rule false positives (for example 'timed out' or 'permission denied' matching assertion text) could mislead a model into skipping a valid retry.

--install edits ~/.claude/settings.json, which the user manages with existing hooks (secret guard, GitNexus, caveman). It is safer to add the entry manually. It also requires a global pip install that puts a jev-triage binary on PATH.

Leaks part of client test output (assertion text, stack traces, paths) to a third party, only partly mitigated by regex redaction. This matters for the client projects; on the OpenRouter route, prompt logging and retention policy would need checking.
entries.verdict: A small, carefully written and honestly documented test-failure triage hook, and it is the only candidate here that gets automatic invocation from a deterministic hook rather than model discretion. But it is TypeSafe-only (needs a fork for OpenRouter), the payoff is marginal for an Opus-class main model, and the hook likely fails to inject its output into Claude's context on current Claude Code. It is worth borrowing as a design pattern (rules first, Jev for the ambiguous remainder, fail-open) rather than installing as-is.

judge.why: The only candidate with deterministic auto-invocation as a PostToolUse(Bash) hook on failing test runs. It applies about 16 local regex rules first and calls Jev for the ambiguous 56%, fail-open. Worth borrowing as a pattern, not installing: its plain-stdout output probably never reaches the model, and the payoff for Opus 5.5 is marginal.
pros: Rules first, Jev only for the ambiguous remainder
Fail-open with always exit 0
Sends only failing test output, secret-redacted, up to 9000 chars
cons: Prints plain text rather than additionalContext JSON, so Claude likely never sees it
Median 1.1 s on Jev-resolved failures, worst case about 16 s, stacked on the gitnexus Bash hook
TypeSafe-only; 1 star; unverified by running

entries.name: bytesjev (PlanningChecker)
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (npm bytesjev 0.2.1) exposing one tool, PlanningChecker. Claude sends the verbatim user request, its plan items (change + rationale) and optional repo_context. The server makes one Jev System One call per plan item, in parallel, with 4-6 yes/no (noul) questions each: necessary, requested, convention, safety, speculative, droppable. Deterministic TS thresholds then turn the probabilities into keep / simplify / review per item. It is advisory only. It also ships a SKILL.md that tells Claude when to call it (after planning, before the first edit), an optional localhost dashboard (port 4310) and a status line. It is an anti-overengineering plan checker, not a general Jev bridge.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion, steered by a skill description trigger. Nothing is deterministic (no hooks). The MCP tool description says 'Call it once after you have a plan and before you edit any file', and the SKILL.md description says 'Use after you have formed a plan for a non-trivial user request'. In a Claude Code session that is bypass or auto mode with little formal planning, Claude may often skip it or make it inconsistently. The skill also requires the verbatim user request, so it is skipped when that cannot be recovered. It could be made near-deterministic only by adding your own hook or CLAUDE.md rule, e.g. a PreToolUse/ExitPlanMode nudge.
security: MIT license. Deps are minimal: zod, @typesafe-ai/sdk 0.6.0 (official, MIT), @modelcontextprotocol/sdk. No postinstall or preinstall in package.json (checked the npm tarball). No curl|sh.

API key in argv: `setup` runs `claude mcp add ... -e TYPESAFE_API_KEY=<key>` via spawnSync (src/cli.ts:80), which puts the key in the argv of a child process, visible in `ps` briefly. `--key X` is also accepted (cli.ts:50). The key is then stored plaintext in ~/.claude.json. The server never logs the key (log lines omit it). Env-var registration avoids the argv exposure.

Reads `.env` from the package dir AND process.cwd() (src/config.ts:194-211) and sets ANY unset [A-Z0-9_] variable, including TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. A malicious or client repo with a crafted .env could redirect Jev traffic (request, plan, repo_context) to an attacker host, since the server is launched from the project cwd. Set the vars explicitly in the MCP registration to reduce the risk (existing env wins).

Prompt-injection surface: tool output is deterministic TS strings. Reasons and evidence are sentences from Claude's own submitted text, chosen by word overlap, plus fixed templates. Jev returns only numbers, so there is no free-text channel from the remote model. The residual risk is a poisoned plan item, which is Claude's own input.

`setup` modifies ~/.claude/settings.json (adds a statusLine only when none exists) and writes ~/.claude/skills/bytesjev. This user already has hooks, so it would probably skip the statusLine; do not run `setup` blindly.

The dashboard (`viz`) is an unauthenticated HTTP server on port 4310 with no CORS handling. It holds the history of request and plan text in memory. The MCP server POSTs every call's full state to VIZ_URL (default http://localhost:4310) on each call, with a 5s timeout, and disables itself after the first failure. Localhost only, but any local process can read it. It is optional.
entries.dataEgress: Each call sends to Jev (api.typesafe.ai, or OpenRouter if base URL is redirected) one request per plan item. The state JSON contains the verbatim user request (cap 4000 chars), repo_context (cap 8000 chars, which Claude composes from what it observed, so it may include file names, paths and code conventions), the item's change and rationale (1000 chars each), and the other items' change text (src/jev/primitives/necessity.ts:500-506). For N items the full request and context are therefore sent N times. No file contents, diffs or tool outputs are sent unless Claude puts them in repo_context. The skill says not to include secrets, but there is no scrubber, so it relies on model compliance; the secret-leak hook does not cover MCP tool payloads. A second local egress goes to http://localhost:4310, the same data to the dashboard, if it is running. Client-confidential requests and paths would go to a third party (TypeSafe or OpenRouter), which needs a policy decision for client projects.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open at the tool level. checkPlan (src/mcp/planning-checker.ts:354-384) catches all Jev errors and returns status 'unavailable' with a category (no_api_key, timeout, network, auth, rate_limit, server_error, unknown), an empty results array and a limitation saying 'proceed without the check'. The skill also says to proceed silently and retry at most once. A missing key gives an immediate 'unavailable' with no network call. The per-call timeout is 20s (BYTESJEV_TIMEOUT_MS, src/mcp/index.ts:227), and the SDK's own retry with backoff sits inside it, so worst-case stall is about 20s per check. Not fail-closed, and it never blocks edits. The relay to the dashboard has a 5s timeout and self-disables. Outside the fail-open path, a malformed Jev answer (e.g. an OpenRouter shape mismatch, `a.necessary!.noul` on undefined) would throw inside assessNecessity, but that is inside the try/catch and would surface as 'unknown'.
entries.contextCost: Low. One MCP tool. The description is about 1.17k chars, and the input schema (user_request, repo_context, plan_items with id/change/rationale plus describes) and the output schema add roughly 1.5k chars. That is about 650-800 tokens in the tool definition, or fewer if Claude Code defers MCP tools. The server sets no `instructions`. The skill adds a frontmatter description of about 400 chars (~100 tokens) always loaded, and a 4.2k-char SKILL.md body (~1k tokens) loaded only when it triggers. No hooks, so no per-call injected text. The status line and dashboard cost no context. Each invocation costs output tokens for Claude to write the plan items (and repo_context), roughly 300-1500 tokens, plus the ~1k-token result back into context.
pros: It is a real, coherent Jev use case that fits the primitive well: many independent yes/no (noul) questions per item, with the thresholding done in deterministic TS rather than by a chat model (src/jev/primitives/necessity.ts, planning-checker.ts:242-320). It is a faithful demonstration of Jev as a 'System One' decision layer.
Only one tool and about 700 tokens of tool definition. The design is advisory, never edits, and fails open (planning-checker.ts:365-380), so an outage cannot block coding.
Automatic-ish integration: a shipped SKILL.md with a strong trigger phrase plus a self-describing tool description, so the user never types 'use jev'.

Lets it work with OpenRouter with no code change. The official SDK honours TYPESAFE_BASE_URL, and its path /v1/systemone matches the OpenRouter System One API once the base is https://openrouter.ai/api (sdk index.mjs:513, 554).
Output is safe from injection because Jev returns only numbers and the reasons are quoted from Claude's own text. Input caps (25 items, 4k/8k chars) and truncation are reported in `limitations`.
Has an offline test suite with a fake Jev (about 34 test cases across 5 files, test/*.ts), and a small readable codebase (~1.3k lines of TS) that is easy to audit or fork. MIT license.
Cheap: about $0.04/M input tokens, so a 6-item plan of about 2k tokens each is roughly $0.0005 per check.
cons: Narrow value for this user. It only critiques plans for overengineering. It does not cover code review, test selection, risk scoring, routing or permission decisions. Opus 5.5 already plans well, and the 'droppable'/'necessary' judgments come from a model that sees only 4k chars of request and 8k of self-reported context, so the signal is only as good as what Claude chooses to write. The README itself says 'false positives are expected'.

Not deterministic: it relies on Claude choosing to call it. There are no hooks, and in bypass/auto mode there is often no explicit plan step, so triggering will be inconsistent. The skill explicitly excludes trivial requests.

No OpenRouter support out of the box. The `setup` command is TypeSafe-key-only and stores the key in argv/~/.claude.json. You must register the MCP by hand with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and a typesafe/jev-1.13 model id. OpenRouter compatibility of request and response shapes is not verified by the project (no OpenRouter tests).

Egress and privacy: sends the user request and Claude-composed repo_context, once per plan item, to a third party. Sensitive for client projects. There is no secret scrubbing beyond a prompt instruction.

Very immature: repo created 2026-09-27, 8 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars/forks/issues, no releases or tags, no CI (.github missing), 3 npm versions in one day. npm 0.2.1 lags git HEAD (0.3.0 in source). Unpinned `npx -y bytesjev` is a supply-chain risk.
The .env loader reads the cwd's .env and can set TYPESAFE_BASE_URL/API_KEY from any repo you open, which is awkward for client repos (possible traffic redirection or a stray key).

Extra cost on the Claude side: Claude must write out structured plan items and repo_context, which adds tokens and a turn to every non-trivial task. The token cost probably exceeds the benefit unless the tool catches overengineering often.

Adds a dashboard and status-line machinery (unauthenticated localhost HTTP server, files in ~/.claude) that the user does not need and that `setup` may try to install; also a per-call POST of full state to localhost:4310.
entries.verdict: A tidy, honest, fail-open proof-of-concept that is the right shape for Jev, but it addresses a narrow problem (plan overengineering) and triggers only when Claude decides to call it. It is very young (2 days old, 1 author), so at most treat it as an optional add-on. If used, pin the version and register it manually with TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api and a typesafe/jev-1.13 model id, not via `setup`, and avoid it on confidential client repos. It is not a primary integration.

entries.name: diegozhou114-cloud/jev-agent-quality
entries.what: Stdio MCP server exposing one read-only tool jev_review (task + diff -> scores, confidence, weak spots) plus a SKILL.md that tells the agent when to call it automatically after meaningful changes.
entries.autoInvocation: model-discretion MCP with skill trigger policy
pros: Risk-based trigger policy in SKILL.md (skip formatting, docs, one-liners) and iteration rules (previousEvaluation, stop when score-chasing) gives automatic use without prompting
Has unit tests (client, mcp, input, transform); zero-install committed dist; single small tool means low context cost
cons: Endpoint constant JEV_API_ENDPOINT hardcoded to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone and key named JEV_API_KEY; no base URL override so OpenRouter requires a source edit
Model discretion only; committed dist/ is unaudited build output; 0 stars, single-day project

entries.name: NiazMorshed2007/jev-review
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (Node, TS bundled to dist/server.js) exposing one tool, jev_review. The coding agent sends task, diff, files and repositoryContext. The server builds 57 typed questions (19 quality metrics x [Noul applicable, Score 1-10, Choice weakness]) and POSTs them with the state to TypeSafe's /v1/systemone using model jev-latest. It maps the Score/Noul/Choice answers to per-metric 1-10 scores, confidence, up to 5 rubric-derived priorities, and deltas versus previousEvaluation. A bundled SKILL.md plus MCP server instructions tell the agent to run an iterative implement, score, improve, rescore loop on every nontrivial task. It is a quality-score feedback loop and does not provide Jev as a general decision router.
interface: Install: npx plugins add NiazMorshed2007/jev-review --target claude-code
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool plus skill-description trigger, reinforced by strongly worded server instructions ('For every nontrivial coding task, call jev_review...'). It is not deterministic. There is no hook, so Claude Code will not always call it, and in a session with many other instructions and tools it may be skipped or over-used. It does not require the user to say 'use jev', but nothing guarantees it will fire.
security: API key is read from env JEV_API_KEY and used only in the Authorization header (client.ts:62-65). It is not in argv unless the user puts it there. Manual `claude mcp add` without --env keeps it out of the process list.
No shell execution, no postinstall (package is private, no scripts run at install), no telemetry, no other network endpoints found in src or by grepping dist (only api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone).
Error handling does not echo response bodies (client.ts:105-128), only mapped messages, so the key does not leak in errors.

Supply-chain: the committed dist/server.js is 1.39 MB, bundled with the MCP SDK and zod. It cannot be fully audited by reading and is not built by CI. Only the JEV constants were confirmed to match src. Running it means running an unaudited bundle.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool takes agent-chosen diff and files, and Jev returns only typed numbers, so response injection is minimal (fixed rubric strings from metrics.ts). The main risk is the reverse, an injected agent exfiltrating file contents via the files[] argument to a third party. Only the model decides what to send.

The user's existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit, so it does NOT cover mcp__jev-review__jev_review inputs. Secrets already in context (from Read) could be forwarded without a check. Only SKILL.md's advice 'Never send secrets' applies.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the agent puts in task, diff, files[].content and repositoryContext leaves the machine as JSON to api.typesafe.ai in the unmodified version (or to OpenRouter, then TypeSafe, if patched). That is source code, diffs and requirement text, and the SKILL loop calls it repeatedly (baseline, then after each improvement), so the same code is sent many times per task. Also sent: 57 static question definitions (about 20 KB, roughly 5k tokens) per call. previousEvaluation is compared locally and not sent. No automatic repo reads, telemetry or other endpoints. Client-project code goes to TypeSafe/OpenRouter under their retention terms, which conflicts with typical client NDAs unless approved.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open. Errors are caught in the tool handler and returned as isError text (mcp/server.ts:50-56), so Claude continues without a score. Client timeout is 30 s per attempt (client.ts:51), with 2 retries on 429/529/5xx and backoff up to 5 s (client.ts:52,80-83,144-153). A worst-case hang can therefore be about 90 s+ of blocked agent turn. A missing JEV_API_KEY gives an error only at first call (the server still starts and lists the tool). There is no circuit breaker, so the agent may retry the tool on later turns.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool, jev_review. Tool description is about 900 chars (about 225 tokens). Input schema includes the nested previousEvaluation with 19 metric objects (the schema may be $ref'd or inlined; inlined would be much larger), estimated 1.5-3k tokens. Server instructions are about 1.1k chars (about 280 tokens), always injected. The skill description is about 450 chars (about 110 tokens) in the skill list. Total estimated roughly 2-3.5k tokens of standing context, moderate for a single tool. Hooks add no text. Every tool call adds the returned Evaluation JSON, which is large (19 metrics with fields, about 1-2k tokens), plus the diff/files the model must write into the call as output tokens on Opus, which is the real recurring cost.
pros: Truly automatic in the sense the user wants: server instructions and the skill description tell Claude to call it on nontrivial tasks without being asked (src/mcp/server.ts:9-19, SKILL.md). No hooks needed, so it does not collide with the existing GitNexus/secret-guard hooks.

Uses Jev in the way it is designed: only typed Score/Noul/Choice primitives, no free text, and it says explicitly that Jev cannot explain root causes (README 'How it works'). Honest about limitations.

Small, readable codebase (about 1.3k lines of TS excluding tests). client.ts is easy to audit and shows a single outbound endpoint, no telemetry, and key only in the Authorization header. Fail-open with mapped errors.
OpenRouter port is small: endpoint, model and env constants (client.ts:13-14, environment.ts:4) since OpenRouter /api/v1/systemone uses the same {model,state,questions} body.
MIT, 231 stars and 20 forks in 13 days suggest community interest and some eyeballs on it. Cost per call is negligible ($0.042/1M input, output free).
cons: No OpenRouter support: endpoint, model and key var are hardcoded to TypeSafe direct, so the user's stated goal needs a fork/patch plus editing or rebuilding a 1.39 MB committed bundle, and the patch has to be maintained.

Very young and single-author: 4 commits all on 2026-09-17, 1 contributor, no releases, no CI, about 13 unit tests with fakes only, and no evidence the live OpenRouter or TypeSafe schema was tested beyond the author's own runs.

Value is doubtful for daily coding: it returns 1-10 scalars on 19 dimensions from a model with no reasoning, and priorities/reasons are canned rubric text (transform.ts:39-43, metrics.ts), so the agent must still diagnose everything itself. The score is unvalidated as a predictor of code quality, and the skeptic 'cheap router model' claim is unaddressed.

Token and time burn: the SKILL demands a loop of score, inspect, improve, rescore ('A single baseline call is not completion'), which on Opus 5.5 means the model re-emitting diffs/files as tool arguments several times per task, plus about 1-2k tokens of JSON per result. This is likely to exceed the savings from a $0.042/M scoring model many times over.

Code egress with no guard: diffs and full file contents go to a third party under the model's own choice. The user's secret-leak hook does not match MCP tool names, and client-project code would be sent to TypeSafe/OpenRouter. There is no allowlist, redaction or size limit (README: 'does not impose an additional character... limit').

Auto-invocation is only advisory prose; behavior will be inconsistent, and a bypass/auto-permission session would let it fire on every task without a check. There are 57 questions per call that add payload and latency for every review.
Recommended install path (`npx plugins add`) adds another unaudited third-party installer; the bundle is not reproducibly built.
entries.verdict: A tidy, auditable single-tool MCP that auto-nudges Claude toward a Jev score loop, but it is TypeSafe-only (needs a fork to use OpenRouter), 13 days old with one author, and its output is canned scores rather than actionable review. It burns Opus tokens and ships client code out with no guard, so use it only as a patched, optional experiment and not as the core Jev integration.

entries.name: NicolasRisso/JevMCP
entries.what: Python (mcp>=2.2, httpx) stdio MCP server exposing one tool, jev_ask. The agent passes typed questions (noul/choice/score) plus file paths, globs, dirs or inline texts. The server reads the files locally, chunks them (60k chars), POSTs one request per file with all questions to Jev (OpenRouter Decisions endpoint or TypeSafe direct), and returns compact confidence-scored answers plus an unsure list. Goal: fan-out classification of many files without loading them into Claude's context. Note the candidate summary says "has hooks": that is wrong. The only hook is a git pre-push test runner; there are no Claude Code hooks.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no Claude Code hooks, no skill, no CLAUDE.md snippet and no plugin manifest (repo ships CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md for its own development only). Claude calls jev_ask only if the tool description convinces it, so it will be used rarely and unpredictably. Getting reliable automatic use requires you to add a CLAUDE.md rule or a skill, or a UserPromptSubmit or PreToolUse hook nudging use on bulk file scans. Note that Claude's own Grep already covers most "which files mention X" cases cheaply.
security: API key is read from the process environment and sent as a Bearer header (client.py:160). The installer explicitly never puts keys in argv or on the command line (cli.py:169-177), so keys are not in the process list. The key must be exported in the shell profile (README suggests ~/.bashrc), which leaks it to every child process.

Server reads ARBITRARY local paths/globs/dirs the agent supplies, with no root confinement, allowlist or secret-file denylist (sources.py:34-49 uses glob/open directly). It can read .env, ~/.ssh, credentials, and uploads the contents to OpenRouter. Your existing PreToolUse secret-leak guard matches Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit and would NOT cover mcp__jev__jev_ask, so this bypasses that protection. Mitigate with a matcher on mcp__jev__.*.
Only guard is JEV_MAX_ITEMS=500 (server.py:142). Binary files are skipped by a NUL-byte sniff.

Prompt-injection surface: file contents go to Jev and Jev's answers come back to Claude. docs/limitations.md admits Jev trusts instructions hidden in text. Answers are typed numbers or enum values (no free text), so injection can flip an answer but cannot inject instructions into Claude's context. Choice values echo criteria keys that Claude itself supplied.

No shell execution besides subprocess.call of the `claude` CLI in install/uninstall, with a fixed argv (cli.py:36). No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh. README's install is git clone plus pip install -e into a venv, i.e. running unaudited code from an editable checkout; a later `git pull` changes the code with no review. Zero stars, single author, 8 days old.

No telemetry found (grep for telemetry and other network calls; only the configured Jev endpoints are used). httpx INFO logging is suppressed (server.py:25). Error strings include the first 300 chars of a response body (client.py:174), which is low risk.
entries.dataEgress: To OpenRouter (and via it TypeSafe): the full text of every file/chunk the agent points at (up to 60k chars per request, up to 500 items per call), plus the question instructions and criteria, plus the model name. The API key goes in an Authorization header. Nothing else: no prompts, conversation, diffs or tool outputs unless Claude passes them via `texts`. Files are sent in whole, including secrets if Claude names them. OpenRouter data policies apply to client code, so check for client contract restrictions. Response usage reports input_tokens only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft at the tool level, not a hook, so Claude is never blocked. httpx timeout is 30s per request (client.py:127). Retries on network errors and on 429/502/503/529 with 1s, 2s, 4s backoff, up to 4 attempts (about 7s of waiting, worst case about 2 minutes total per item with timeouts). 401/402/403 mark the provider dead and 400/413/422 fail immediately. Per-item failures come back as {"error":...}; if all items fail with the same error the call raises one ToolError (server.py:65-68). Missing key gives ConfigError only at call time, not at server startup, so a misconfigured server still loads its tool definition and wastes context every turn. With JEV_FALLBACK plus both keys it switches providers after 2 attempts. No circuit breaker across calls.
entries.contextCost: 1 tool. Description is 503 chars and the hand-written schema is 425 chars in compact JSON, so about 930 chars, or roughly 250-300 tokens per session including the tool name (the README says about 1 KB). It is a deferred tool in Claude Code, so it may only cost the name until loaded via ToolSearch. No MCP server "instructions" field found. No hook-injected text. Results are a few chars per answer.
pros: Native OpenRouter support: with only OPENROUTER_API_KEY set it uses https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with typesafe/jev-1.13 (config.py:15-19), matching your provider choice with no patching.

Tiny footprint: one tool, about 930 chars (roughly 250-300 tokens) of definition, hand-trimmed schema, structured_output=False to avoid duplicate results (server.py:119,149). This is the leanest possible way to expose Jev.

Well matched to Jev's real strengths: batches all questions per file into one request, fans out concurrently, and passes on uncertainty via [value, conf, top2] and an unsure list so Claude re-checks only doubtful items (compact.py, server.py:60-61).
Sensible resilience: retries with backoff, per-item errors, dead-key detection, optional cross-provider fallback (client.py); the tool never blocks a Claude turn beyond its own call.
Key never in argv: installer omits keys and the server reads env (cli.py:169-177); `jev-mcp check` gives a cheap connectivity test.
Honest docs on limits (counting, dates, injection) in docs/limitations.md; MIT license; small readable codebase (about 600 lines) that is easy to audit or fork.
cons: It is NOT automatic. Pure model-discretion MCP tool with no hooks, skill or CLAUDE.md snippet, which fails your core requirement of Claude using Jev without being told. The 'has hooks' claim in discovery is false (only a git pre-push test hook).

Reads arbitrary paths with no confinement or secret denylist and uploads whole files to a third party. Your secret-leak guard (Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit) does not cover mcp__jev__jev_ask, so it creates a hole for client projects; you would need to extend the hook matcher.

Use case is narrow: bulk classification of many files. Typical Claude Code work (edit, debug, refactor) rarely needs 'which of these 300 files...' and Grep/GitNexus already handle it locally, free and exact. Jev cannot count, do arithmetic or reason, and is easily fooled by injected text.

Very immature: 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor, 16 commits all on 2026-09-22 (8 days old), version 0.1.0, no releases, no CI (no .github), no lockfile, README says API may change. Tests exist (6 files, 40 test functions) but were not run per the rules.
Depends on the OpenRouter alpha Decisions endpoint (/api/alpha/decisions), which may change or break without notice; does not use the more stable /api/v1/systemone.

Install path is git clone plus pip install -e (editable, unpinned mcp>=2.2), not a published PyPI/uvx package; needs the key exported in shell profile, and misconfiguration only surfaces at call time.
Chunk results are not aggregated (docs/limitations.md open items), so large files return path#N entries that Claude must merge by hand; character-based chunking rather than token-based.
Added latency and cost are small but every call moves client code to OpenRouter and TypeSafe, a compliance question for client projects.
entries.verdict: The cleanest and cheapest Jev MCP wrapper, with genuine OpenRouter support and a very small context cost, but it is an opt-in model-discretion tool: nothing makes Claude Code use it automatically, and it has an unrestricted file-upload path that bypasses your secret guard. Treat it as a reference implementation to fork or wrap behind hooks and a path denylist, not something to install as is for daily work.

entries.name: kindintelligence/jev-rust-review
entries.what: Claude Code plugin (marketplace + plugin.json + .mcp.json + skill + subagent) for Rust-only code review. A Rust MCP server (rmcp, stdio) reads the git diff itself, runs cargo clippy / cargo-semver-checks, splits the diff into units, and sends typed Jev questions (up to 42 core plus framework questions per unit) to POST {api_url}/v1/systemone for triage, then again to verify Claude's candidate findings (supported/refuted/insufficient_context, severity score, category). Claude does the reasoning and the fixes; Jev only routes and gives a second opinion.
interface: MCP tool evaluate_rust_changes(repo_path?, scope?, dry_run?, profiles?, max_units?)
MCP tool verify_rust_findings(findings[1..20], repo_path?, scope?, dry_run?)
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion, two paths: (1) skill description trigger 'Use when asked to review Rust code or Rust changes' so it fires only if the user asks for a Rust review, not on every edit or commit; (2) the three MCP tools with server instructions, which Claude could call unprompted but nothing forces it. No hooks (no PostToolUse on Edit, no pre-commit/Stop hook), no proxy. So it does not meet 'Claude uses Jev automatically when it adds value' beyond Rust review requests; it is Rust-specific and review-triggered.
security: API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY / JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_KEY), never argv; .mcp.json passes it via env from plugin userConfig (sensitive:true, keychain). Client uses bearer_auth; no key in process list. Config test asserts the secret is not Debug-printed (config.rs ~196).
Redirects disabled (jev.rs redirect Policy::none) so a 307/308 cannot re-post key and code elsewhere; endpoint must be https unless loopback (endpoint_error).

src/redact.rs skips secret-named files (.env*, *.pem, *.key, id_rsa*, .npmrc, *credential*, *secret*) and regex-redacts token shapes (AWS, GitHub, GitLab, Slack, Stripe, Google, sk-, JWT, private keys) before sending; heuristic, not a guarantee, and does not match OpenRouter sk-or-v1 explicitly except via generic sk- rule (sk_token needs 20+ chars of [A-Za-z0-9_-], which sk-or-v1-... satisfies).

Shell execution: server spawns git and cargo via tokio Command with argument vectors, no shell, no stdin (cargo_tools.rs ~372-410, clippy.toml disallows other spawns). BUT cargo clippy/check executes the repository's build.rs and proc macros: running on an untrusted/client repo is arbitrary code execution by design; the skill tells Claude to ask first in untrusted repos and offers --no-cargo, and JEV_RUST_REVIEW_CARGO=0 disables. With bypass/auto permission mode, that asking is weak.

launch.sh: curl/wget only from https GitHub releases (--proto =https, tlsv1.2), verified against SHA256SUMS from the same release (same trust origin as the binary, so protects against corruption/tamper of the asset, not a compromised repo owner); falls back to cargo build --release --locked of the plugin's own source. No curl|sh, no npm postinstall. Dependency surface is a normal Rust crate tree (Cargo.lock committed, #![forbid(unsafe_code)]).

Prompt-injection surface: diff text goes into Jev state and Claude's context; DESIGN.md/eval include a prompt_injection fixture (3/3 found). Jev outputs are typed numbers, so Jev cannot inject text back; Claude reads only structured fields plus the diff.
entries.dataEgress: On evaluate_rust_changes and verify_rust_findings: JSON {model, state, questions} with changed Rust code hunks plus enclosing items (units up to 6000 tokens, up to 400k tokens and 60 units per evaluation), file paths/line ranges, project facts (edition, MSRV, runtime), and for verification the claimed lines plus definitions of items named in the claim from elsewhere in the repo, after secret-file skipping and regex token redaction. Sent directly (no proxy, no telemetry) to {JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_URL}/v1/systemone (TypeSafe by default; would be OpenRouter, an additional third party that sees code, if repointed). Not sent: whole repo, non-Rust files, Claude's conversation, tool outputs from other tools. cargo_diagnostics sends nothing off-machine. GitHub releases download only at first launch. Dry-run mode returns request bodies without sending. Client-project code leaving to Jev/OpenRouter is a contractual concern for client repos.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. No key or unauthorized/insecure endpoint: status jev_unavailable, skill falls back to a Claude-only review with a banner (verify tool still does tool_reported dedup without a key). Per-request timeout 30 s (JEV_RUST_REVIEW_TIMEOUT_SECS), connect timeout 10 s, up to 3 retries (max 10) with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After capped at 30 s, on 408/429/529/5xx/network; other 4xx are non-retried errors; per-unit failures give status partial. So a dead Jev can stall a review for minutes worst-case (30 s x 4 attempts + backoff per request, concurrency 4) but never blocks Claude Code itself. cargo runs are bounded by a 600 s timeout, which can be long. First-run: MCP server fails the 30 s startup window while building (documented) and needs a manual /mcp reconnect.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools; tool descriptions total roughly 3.8k chars (grep of description strings = 3,780 chars) plus JSON schemas for scope/findings inputs, so approx 1.3-1.8k tokens always resident (if MCP tool search/deferred loading is active it drops to names only). Server instructions string about 600 chars (~150 tokens). Skill: name+description in the always-loaded listing (~450 chars, ~110 tokens); SKILL.md body is 16 KB (~4k tokens) loaded only when invoked, plus per-dimension reference files (16 dimensions + 3 frameworks) loaded only when flagged; agent rust-reviewer.md 5 KB. No hooks, so nothing injected on ordinary tool calls. A review's tool results (flagged lists, facts) add more per invocation. Total resident cost is about 2k tokens, all for a Rust-only feature.
pros: Best-engineered Jev integration of its kind: uses Jev exactly as its brief says (typed Noul/Choice/Score questions in bulk, no prose), with two concrete uses (cheap triage, verification gate) and Claude keeping the reasoning; DESIGN.md documents Jev's weak spots and works around them.
Jev cost is negligible ($0.013 for 60 eval runs, jev.rs ~$0.042/M tokens) and calls are fast, so the Jev part is not the bottleneck.

Endpoint path is /v1/systemone and URL/model/key are env-configurable (config.rs:112-117), so pointing at OpenRouter's https://openrouter.ai/api/v1/systemone is a 3-env-var change, no fork needed, provided OpenRouter's schema matches.

Safety hygiene above typical: no shell, argv vectors, redirects disabled, https enforced, secret-file skipping and token redaction, dry-run mode that shows exact outgoing payloads, checksum-verified downloads, forbid(unsafe_code).
Fail-open with a clear banner, and tool_reported dedup works without any key, so it degrades gracefully to a Claude-only review.
Real test suite and CI (wiremock HTTP tests, 33 recorded fixtures, install/tamper tests, macOS+Linux, MSRV), MIT license, no telemetry, no hooks that could slow or break every tool call.
Low always-on context cost (~2k tokens) and it does not interfere with the existing PreToolUse/GitNexus/caveman hooks.
cons: Rust-only: every question, lint, and reference is Rust (clippy, cargo-semver-checks, syn). Useless for non-Rust personal/client work; no evidence the user's daily stack is Rust.
