Not automatic: triggers only when the user asks for a Rust review (skill description) or when Claude elects to call the MCP tools. No hook fires on edits, commits or Stop, which fails the user's core requirement of Claude using Jev by itself when needed.

Marginal value on its own benchmark: author's eval shows Claude alone 45/48 vs Claude+Jev 47/48, and the one hard fixture (symlink_check_then_delete) went 0/3 to 2/3, at +$1 Claude cost per 60 runs. Self-run and self-built fixtures; no independent validation.
Alpha and tiny: 33 commits over 3 days by one author, 2 stars, v0.1.0, explicitly 'in active development' with interfaces/thresholds that may change; not affiliated with TypeSafe or Anthropic.

No OpenRouter support tested or documented; whether OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone accepts the identical body, model id typesafe/jev-1.13, and returns the same answer shape is unverified. Key env naming is confusing (OpenRouter key goes in the 'typesafe_api_key' userConfig or JEV_RUST_REVIEW_API_KEY; TYPESAFE_API_KEY overrides).

Source-build friction: no prebuilt binaries yet, needs Rust toolchain, first launch takes 65-75 s and exceeds the 30 s MCP startup timeout, so the server shows failed until manual /mcp reconnect. Ships and runs an unaudited compiled binary with your key.

cargo clippy runs the target repo's build.rs and proc macros; on client repos with bypass/auto permission mode the 'ask first if untrusted' guidance is effectively unenforced, so it is arbitrary code execution from the reviewed repo. Must use --no-cargo or JEV_RUST_REVIEW_CARGO=0.
Sends client source code (hunks plus related item definitions) to a third-party model API (TypeSafe or OpenRouter); redaction is regex-based best effort. Relevant for client NDAs.
Review latency and clippy build cost can be significant (up to 600 s cargo cap), and it competes with the user's own cargo build lock unless an extra target dir (an extra full build) is configured.
entries.verdict: High-quality but narrow reference implementation of Jev for Rust PR/diff review only; patchable to OpenRouter via env vars, but it is a review-on-request skill, not an automatic, language-agnostic Jev integration, and it is v0.1 from a one-person repo. Worth borrowing as a design pattern (triage plus verify gate, dry-run, redaction) or installing only if the user does substantial Rust work and pins the tag.

entries.name: pedroknigge/mcp_jev
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) wrapping the official @typesafe-ai/sdk. Exposes 5 tools: a catalog of 13 hand-written "packs" (review_diff, code_audit, command_risk, verify_gap, boundary_check, model_router, skill_router, i18n_copy, etc.) plus a generic run_questions tool for custom Choice/Noul/Score calls. It also ships a CLI (doctor, dogfood, smoke, scan, urlcheck, hosts write, config set-key) and a very large SKILL.md (about 51 KB) meant to teach agents when to call it. There are no hooks, so it never intercepts tool calls. Everything is model-discretion or skill-triggered.
interface: CLI: doctor / dogfood / smoke / scan <path> / urlcheck --base URL / hosts print|write / config set-key|status|path
entries.autoInvocation: Model discretion only. Two mechanisms: (a) the MCP tool descriptions, which are generic and steer the model to use them only for typed judgments; (b) the skill description trigger, which fires on keywords like 'Jev', 'PR audit', 'review diff', 'code audit', 'model router'. Since the user does not want to type "jev", and ordinary coding prompts rarely contain those words, this will fire rarely and unpredictably. There is no deterministic hook, no PreToolUse/PostToolUse integration and no transparent proxy. Making it automatic would need a CLAUDE.md rule or hooks written by the user.
security: MIT license. Not published to npm (README says so; npm view mcp_jev returns 404), so the install path is git clone + scripts/install.sh, which runs npm install && npm run build. That pulls transitive deps and the package.json 'prepare' script (tsc) at install time. Nothing is pinned by a signed release.

API key handling is mostly decent: stored in ~/.mcp_jev/.env at chmod 600 with the dir at 700 (user-config.ts:72-97), host mcp.json stays keyless, and ping and errors never echo the key. Weaknesses: install.sh passes $TYPESAFE_API_KEY on argv to 'config set-key' (visible in ps briefly), the 'config set-key <key>' argv form is supported (cli.ts:305), and the generated wrapper does `source ~/.mcp_jev/.env` (executes it as shell), so anything written there runs.

hosts write modifies ~/.claude.json and ~/.claude/settings.json by read-modify-write with a non-atomic writeFileSync (hosts.ts:255-278). This is risky on a live ~/.claude.json that holds OAuth and project state. Do the registration manually or with `claude mcp add` instead.
Key precedence quirk: the stored ~/.mcp_jev/.env key overrides the process env key (user-config.ts:118-125), so an OPENROUTER key exported in the environment can be silently ignored.

Prompt-injection surface: the tool outputs are typed JSON (probabilities), which is small. But run_questions/run_pack take free-form 'instructions' and state built by the model, so untrusted repo content flowing into state can steer Jev's answers. No shell execution in the server tools. urlcheck makes HTTP requests to user-supplied bases only when invoked from the CLI.
No telemetry found in src. Outbound calls go only to the configured TypeSafe base URL. There is no fetch( in src; the network client is the SDK.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev endpoint (api.typesafe.ai by default, or OpenRouter if TYPESAFE_BASE_URL is overridden): exactly the `state` JSON plus the typed questions that the model builds for each run_pack/run_questions call. The model chooses what goes into state. The pack schemas ask for diff summaries, file lists, commands, claims and evidence names, and code_audit accepts an `excerpt` of file text (src/scan.ts:522-533 slices raw file content to MAX_EXCERPT_CHARS). The CLI 'scan' command reads files up to 1 MB, skips .env files and applies .gitignore (scan.ts:238,414), and sends path, signals and optional excerpts to code_audit. Nothing is sent automatically: no hook or proxy reads prompts, tool outputs or files. On client projects, egress happens only when the model decides to call the tools. The existing secret-leak PreToolUse guard will not see the MCP call's payload (its matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit), so state could carry secrets that pass unchecked.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open relative to Claude Code: a slow or down Jev only makes that MCP tool call return isError JSON (server.ts:21-27), and the model carries on. Timeout is a hard-coded 20 s (config.ts:9, DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_MS, no env override). The SDK also has retry maxRetries: 2 by default (sdk dist/index.mjs:74). A dead endpoint can therefore stall a turn for roughly 20-60 s per call before the error comes back. A missing key returns a friendly error, not a crash. If the MCP server fails to start, Claude Code just shows it as failed and nothing else breaks.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools: list_packs, describe_pack, run_pack, run_questions, ping. Tool names+descriptions+schemas are about 3,000 chars (server.ts:36-129), roughly 750 tokens. The server sets no `instructions` field. The skill adds its frontmatter description (about 1,300 chars, roughly 330 tokens) to every session's skill list. When triggered, the SKILL.md body is about 51 KB (roughly 13k tokens), and it points to a 54 KB pack-catalog.md (roughly 13k more tokens) if read. Every use starts with list_packs (a catalog of 13 packs) and, when unfamiliar, describe_pack (full JSON schema): a further 2-5k tokens per use. No hook-injected text. Baseline about 1k tokens; a real use costs 5-30k tokens, which is heavy.
pros: Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk, so the wire format is TypeSafe's own. The SDK POSTs /v1/systemone with a Bearer token, which lines up with OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone once TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api is set. OpenRouter therefore works via env vars only, with no fork.
The tool surface is small: 5 tools, about 750 tokens of definitions, no server instructions, no hook text. That is cheap to keep loaded.
Typed run_questions is a general Choice/Noul/Score escape hatch, so it does not lock the user into the 13 packs.

Reasonable engineering hygiene for its age: MIT, 26 test files, CI, typed inputs validated with zod, strict validation of Choice/Noul/Score shapes (custom-questions.ts), key stored chmod 600 and never echoed.

Packs that map to coding decisions (review_diff, command_risk, verify_gap, boundary_check, code_audit, skill_router, model_router) could serve as building blocks for a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy later, and the pack question definitions are a useful reference for writing your own.
Nothing runs unless invoked; there is no telemetry and no background process.
cons: No automatic integration. It ships no hooks, no PreToolUse or UserPromptSubmit wiring and no proxy. It only fires when the model reads the tool descriptions or the skill triggers, and the skill's triggers are keywords like 'Jev', 'TypeSafe' and 'PR audit'. That directly fails the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev without being told.

Explicit OpenRouter support is absent: 'openrouter' appears nowhere in the source, docs or scripts. It relies on the undocumented-here TYPESAFE_BASE_URL trick plus a manual JEV_MODEL slug (the default 'jev-latest' is a TypeSafe ID, not an OpenRouter one). The OpenRouter payload compatibility is unverified. The installer and doctor also insist on a TypeSafe console key.

The workflow is token-heavy for a 'fast decision' tool: list_packs, then describe_pack, then run_pack, with a 51 KB SKILL.md and a 54 KB pack catalog to load. The main model (Opus) must hand-build state JSON, so a call adds seconds of Opus latency and thousands of tokens, which cancels Jev's 70-500 ms advantage.

The 13 packs are speculative, agent-authored guesses at judgment tasks (the repo's own docs say 'invent questions' and 'dogfood'), with no evidence that Jev outperforms a plain Opus judgment on review or command risk. The `command_risk` pack states it is not an allowlist, so it cannot replace a real guard.
Sends model-chosen code/diff/command summaries to a third party on client projects, and the user's secret-leak guard does not cover MCP tool payloads.

Very new and immature: 11 days old, 1 star, single maintainer with Cursor-agent commits, releases v0.0.x, and an install path (clone, npm install, build, wrapper that sources .env) with no signed artefacts. `hosts write` rewrites ~/.claude.json non-atomically, so registering by hand is safer.
Hard-coded 20 s timeout with SDK retries (2), and no env override, so a slow endpoint can block a turn for up to about a minute.
Stored-key-over-env precedence (user-config.ts:118) makes swapping providers error-prone.
entries.verdict: Cleanly written, small MCP wrapper around the official SDK, and it can be pointed at OpenRouter with env vars alone (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13). But it is a passive toolbox with no hooks, and its skill triggers on keywords, so it will not deliver the "Claude uses Jev automatically" goal. It also carries heavy skill and catalog token costs for every real use. Treat it as a reference or a fallback tool, not the primary integration. Automatic behaviour would need a custom hook or CLAUDE.md policy built on top.

entries.name: minhgv/jev-mcp
entries.what: Repository-blind, read-only stdio MCP server (Node/TS, 9 tools, 8 question-pack resources) wrapping @typesafe-ai/sdk. The calling agent must pass task/observation/diff/claims as tool arguments; the server sends them to Jev as state plus typed Noul/Choice/Score questions, then maps confidences to auto|review|escalate with deterministic TypeScript policy. Also ships a git-collector CLI (context, ci-shadow, doctor, eval) that builds redacted diff bundles for a host/CI adapter. No hooks, no plugin.json, no marketplace.json, no .mcp.json; only a SKILL.md, an AGENTS.md pointer, and Cursor/Codex config examples.
interface: CLI: jev-mcp doctor | eval | context | ci-shadow
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There are no hooks, no plugin manifest, no proxy. The only steering is the tools' descriptions plus an optional SKILL.md (description-triggered; Claude Code skill in skills/jev-mcp/SKILL.md must be copied to ~/.claude/skills) and an AGENTS.md pointer, so Claude may or may not call jev_* on its own; there is no deterministic trigger. Making it automatic would need the user to add a CLAUDE.md rule and/or write their own Stop/PostToolUse hooks that call `node dist/index.js eval|context` (that CLI path is usable from a hook, which is the most valuable reusable part).
security: API key is read from env (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) and sent as Bearer header; never in argv when set via `claude mcp add --env` in config, but docs/install.md and examples/codex.config.toml also show `codex mcp add jev --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=ts_...` (key in argv/shell history) and hardcoded keys in JSON config; use an env reference instead.
SDK logger is off (logLevel 'off') and custom logger writes to stderr, so no stdout corruption or key logging observed; SDK redacts headers in debug logs.
No telemetry beyond SDK headers (User-Agent, X-TypeSafe-SDK, X-TypeSafe-Runtime).
No shell execution in the MCP server itself; only src/collector.ts uses execFileSync('git', args) in the CLI collector path (array args, no shell). Server code does no fs reads of the repo.

Redaction (collector.ts:36-49) is regex based (PEM, Bearer, AKIA, JWT, xox, sk-/pk-/key-, ts_/gh*_, keyword=value) and applies only to the collector CLI path; direct MCP tool calls from Claude pass whatever the model puts in the arguments unredacted, so it is not a barrier for Claude Code usage. The user's existing secret-leak hook does not cover mcp__ tool args (matcher is Bash|Read|Grep|NotebookEdit).
No curl|sh installer or npm postinstall. scripts/checkout-d-drive.ps1 is Windows-only and irrelevant.
entries.dataEgress: Whatever the model puts in tool arguments is POSTed to the configured base URL (default https://api.typesafe.ai; would be openrouter.ai and then routed by OpenRouter to TypeSafe): task text, observation (test output, diffs, blockers), full diffs up to 200-300k chars for jev_review (truncated to about 32k tokens by limits.ts fitState), requirement/claim text, and text under screening. State is truncated to a 32k-token budget. Nothing is read from disk by the MCP server itself. For client projects this means client code diffs and test output leave the machine to TypeSafe/OpenRouter on every call; redaction only happens if the CLI collector is used, not on MCP tool calls.
entries.failureMode: Effectively fail-open for Claude Code. It is an on-demand MCP tool, not a hook or proxy. On timeout (SDK default 10 s, 2 retries with backoff, so worst case around 30 s plus backoff blocking one tool call), 4xx/5xx, or missing key, the tool handler catches the error and returns an MCP error result (server.ts toolError) that Claude can ignore. Missing key throws JevConfigError. Within tool results, malformed Jev output fails closed to 'review'/'escalate' actions and missing or truncated evidence forces 'review' (advisory only; nothing blocks Claude Code). No circuit breaker or configurable timeout env var (timeout is hard-coded to the SDK default, since typesafe.ts passes no timeout).
entries.contextCost: 9 tools. Descriptions total roughly 2,000 chars. Input JSON schemas (zod converted): flat tools about 300-700 chars each (about 3.3k chars for the flat ones by my regex count), but jev_review is a union of a legacy flat schema and the v2 changeContext schema (manifest, sections, verification records, provenance, risk signals, with many nested fields), likely 4-6k chars, and jev_assess_change_risk / jev_check_requirement probably reuse the context schema too. Estimate about 3-5k tokens of always-loaded tool definitions (fewer if Claude Code defers MCP tools via ToolSearch as in this session). No MCP server 'instructions' field observed. No hook-injected text. Resources add small listing overhead. Per-call cost is much higher than definitions: the model must emit the diff or observation as output tokens in the arguments (thousands of tokens), which on Opus is expensive and slow, partly defeating the 'cheap decision' purpose.
pros: Best-documented tool surface among Jev MCPs found: 9 typed recipes (coding_loop, review, change_risk, requirement, verify, screen, rank, issue, evaluate) with real Choice/Score/Noul question packs in src/packs/*.ts, deterministic policy thresholds (JEV_MCP_AUTO_ACCEPT 0.8 / REVIEW_AT 0.5 / BLOCK_AT 0.75) in TypeScript.

Base URL is env-overridable and the SDK path /v1/systemone equals OpenRouter's System One path, so pointing it at OpenRouter looks config-only (TYPESAFE_BASE_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, JEV_MCP_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13).
MIT, small readable TypeScript, no postinstall, no curl|sh, no shell exec in the server, stderr-only logging, readOnlyHint annotations on every tool.
Failures are contained: errors become MCP tool errors, and Jev output that is malformed or evidence that is missing degrades to review/escalate, never a false auto-pass.

Ships a CLI (`eval`, `context`, `ci-shadow`) that can be invoked from a Claude Code hook without MCP, and a git collector with regex secret redaction, useful building blocks for a deterministic Stop-hook diff gate.
jev_screen (prompt-injection probability on fetched text) is a concept that fits Claude Code's WebFetch/Playwright use on client projects.
cons: Not automatic for Claude Code: pure model-discretion tools, no hooks/plugin/marketplace. User's requirement (no prompting) is unmet unless they add their own CLAUDE.md rules and hooks. README and configs target OpenCode, OMP, Cursor, Codex; Claude Code is mentioned only in one line of docs/install.md.

Repository-blind by design: Claude must serialize diffs, test output and claims into tool arguments, costing Opus output tokens and time for every call. The tool that fetches nothing cannot save tokens vs. just reasoning, and the 'cheap routing' premise (jev_coding_loop model_tier) is meaningless for a Claude Code session pinned to Opus 5.5 with no router to act on the result.

Leaks diffs/test output of client projects to TypeSafe/OpenRouter on each call, with no redaction on the MCP path (redaction only in the CLI collector) and existing secret-leak hook does not match mcp__ tool calls.

Extremely young and thin: created 2026-09-17, last commit 2026-09-18, 7 commits, 1 star, 0 forks, no releases, no npm package, tests are mock-only (src/mock.ts) so real Jev behavior is unvalidated; README admits cost savings are unmeasured and CI gate is shadow-only. The v1 review input is already deprecated and slated for removal.

OpenRouter support is inferred, not implemented: key must live in a var named TYPESAFE_API_KEY, `doctor`'s GET /v1/models call likely mismatches, default model 'jev-latest' must be overridden, and Claude can pass a per-call `model` arg. Response-schema parity with OpenRouter is unverified.

Heavy, over-engineered contract for jev_review v2 (200-300k char diffs, manifest, sha256 subject digest, provenance, trusted-adapter allowlist) that a model cannot sensibly populate by hand; realistic usage requires the separate `context` CLI adapter, i.e., extra glue.

Tool-definition footprint of roughly 3-5k tokens for 9 tools, most of which (classify_issue, rank, requirement, evaluate) are rarely useful in day-to-day single-developer coding; hard-coded 10 s timeout x 3 attempts can stall a turn during an outage.
entries.verdict: A tidy but very early, client-agnostic MCP wrapper that is worth mining (question packs, thresholds, git collector CLI) and could reach OpenRouter with two env vars, but it does not deliver automatic Claude Code integration and forces the model to hand-feed diffs as tool args. Not recommended as the primary integration; at most use its CLI from your own Stop or PreToolUse hook after verifying OpenRouter response parity.

entries.name: MorenoLand/Moreno.Jev
entries.what: Single-file (293 lines) Python stdio MCP server (FastMCP, mcp==1.26.0) plus a Codex/Pi-style Agent Skill. It wraps TypeSafe's direct System One endpoint with six code-oriented tools. Each tool packs the caller-supplied code, diff, log or report into 'state' and sends a fixed set of Noul/Choice/Score questions to Jev. Nothing is read from disk by the server, so Claude has to paste the content into the tool call. Written for Codex and Pi. The README never mentions Claude Code.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools only. The bundled skill is explicitly opt-in ('when the user asks for Jev review'; 'only when the user requests Jev or invokes this skill'), and the README's suggested AGENTS.md text is likewise 'when I ask for Jev review'. There are no hooks, no proxy and no deterministic trigger. To get automatic use you would have to write your own CLAUDE.md or skill-description rules (for example 'after each diff call jev_review_diff') and change the skill wording. Even then it is only as reliable as Claude's compliance, and nothing in the repo gives Claude Code a reason to reach for it.
security: API key comes from the process environment (jev_mcp.py:77), not argv, so it is not visible in the process list. The README says to forward it via env_vars/inheritEnv rather than writing it to config.
Bearer key is sent only to the hard-coded host api.typesafe.ai over https. Redirects are blocked (_NoRedirectHandler, lines 21-23), so the key cannot leak through a redirect.
Hard caps: request 512 KB (lines 14, 85-89), response 1 MB (line 95), 45 s timeout (line 16). Error messages are scrubbed to a status code only.
No shell execution, no file access, no telemetry, no logging of bodies. Code inspection confirms the README's 'does not read repository files or persist prompts' claim.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Output is a dict of numeric probabilities and enums, not free text. Real risk is upstream: Claude pastes content into the args, so whatever Claude submits (including secrets that appear in code or logs) goes to a third party. The existing secret-leak guard hook does not cover MCP tool args.

Supply chain is small: one PyPI dependency (mcp==1.26.0, pinned and locked) and a single 293-line file that is easy to audit. The repo is 3 days old with one author, so there are no external reviews and the maintainer could push changes. Pin a commit SHA if used.
entries.dataEgress: Everything Claude passes as tool args goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone (TypeSafe direct, not OpenRouter): full code snippets, diffs, test or build logs, bug reports, hypotheses, context strings, and language/command strings, up to 512 KB per call, plus the Bearer TYPESAFE_API_KEY. Nothing is sent automatically, since the server reads no files. The volume is whatever the model chooses to paste. For client projects this means client source code leaves the machine to a beta third-party API. If retargeted to OpenRouter, it would go to OpenRouter and then TypeSafe.
entries.failureMode: Fail-soft, not a hard block. There is no hook or proxy in the path. On timeout (45 s), HTTP error, invalid JSON or a missing key, the tool raises RuntimeError and MCP returns an isError result. Claude sees a short message and carries on. There is no retry, no circuit breaker and no fallback. The 45 s ceiling is far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms, so an outage would stall a single tool call for up to 45 s. The server never blocks edits or commands.
entries.contextCost: 6 MCP tools. Estimated ~800-1,000 tokens always loaded (about 3.5k chars of names, docstrings and JSON schemas: 5 tools with 2-5 string params each, and jev_evaluate with free-form Any/dict). Some of this could sit behind deferred tool loading. No server-level 'instructions'. The skill adds ~30 tokens of frontmatter only if installed; its ~1.4k-char body loads only when triggered. No hooks, so no text is injected per turn. Each call also costs its argument tokens (the code or diff Claude must re-emit into the tool call, which can be thousands of output tokens) and a small dict result (~100-200 tokens).
pros: Tiny, fully readable: one 293-line file, one pinned dependency, MIT license. A full audit takes minutes and forking it for OpenRouter is a ~4-line change.
Good security hygiene for a POC: key from env (not argv), redirects refused, 512 KB/1 MB/45 s limits, sanitized errors, no file reads, no telemetry.

Question design fits Jev's primitives properly. Categories are enums, severity uses Score scales, and there are separate 'evidence_sufficient' and 'needs_human_review' Noul checks. Good templates for hooks or a custom MCP: review_diff, check_hypothesis, and test-output classification map to real daily coding moments.
Includes jev_evaluate as a generic escape hatch for custom Choice/Score/Noul questions.
Non-blocking failure mode: errors are just tool errors, and it cannot break Claude Code sessions.
Low steady-state context cost (~1k tokens for 6 tools) and no per-turn hook injection.
cons: Not automatic: the skill and README explicitly gate use on the user asking for Jev, which contradicts the user's main requirement. Nothing pushes Claude Code to call it, and it has no hooks.
No OpenRouter support. Hard-coded api.typesafe.ai and TYPESAFE_API_KEY. It needs a fork or patch before it matches the user's OpenRouter-hosted setup, and OpenRouter schema parity is unverified.
Claude Code is not a target: only Codex and Pi are documented. It should work as a generic stdio server, but nothing has been tested there.
Very immature: repo created 2026-09-27 (3 days old), 3 commits, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no releases, no tests, no CI, no real-world usage. The 45 s timeout is far above the claimed Jev latency.

The model must paste code or diffs into args. This costs Opus output tokens and adds seconds of latency per call, and leaks whatever it pastes (client code, secrets in logs) to a third party. The secret-guard hook does not inspect MCP args.

Heavy on the review-quality question: Jev returns only probabilities with no reasoning, and Theo's 'DeepSeek flash router' claim is unverified. A 'has_concrete_bug' probability from a small model on a pasted diff is a weak signal versus Opus's own review. Duplicates part of the existing /code-review and gitnexus detect_changes.
Install is a manual git clone plus uv sync into a .venv (no uvx or PyPI package). This makes updates and reproducibility manual, and the path is machine-specific.
entries.verdict: A clean, safe, well-written 3-day-old proof of concept, but it is opt-in by design, TypeSafe-direct only, and untested with Claude Code, so it fails the 'automatic, OpenRouter' requirement as shipped. Its best use is as reference code for the question templates and the hardened request client (no redirects, size caps, env-only key) in a custom OpenRouter-based hook or MCP. As a drop-in install it scores low.

entries.name: koosbcom/jev-delegate
entries.what: Local stdio MCP server (Node/TypeScript) plus a SKILL.md, packaged for both Codex and Claude Code (.claude-plugin/plugin.json bundles skill + MCP). Exposes two tools. search_and_rank runs ripgrep inside the workspace root, dedups and filters hits, then asks Jev (typesafe/jev-1.13 via OpenRouter Decisions API) one Noul question per candidate ("does it satisfy the relevance criterion") and returns hits ranked by P(yes). classify_items assigns caller-supplied labels (2-20, plus reserved other/insufficient_context) to up to 200 English text items using Jev Choice questions. On any Jev failure it returns a bounded raw fallback. Narrow scope: not a router, not a general delegate. Despite the name it cannot delegate coding work.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion. The tool descriptions say "Use automatically when raw search would exceed 20 candidates or about 4K tokens" and the skill description triggers on search hits >20 candidates, but Claude must first think of the pattern set and relevance criterion BEFORE searching, and Claude Code's native Grep/Glob and the existing GitNexus hook are the default reflex; the model rarely knows the hit count in advance, so triggering will be inconsistent. No deterministic hook, no proxy, no way to intercept Grep results. Not truly automatic in the sense the user wants.
security: API key read from env only (config.ts:24), sent only as Bearer header to openrouter.ai; not in argv or process list (no CLI args carry it). .mcp.json/plugin.json pass no key; note plugin.json mcpServers has no env block so child inherits the parent env.

Privacy filters are heuristic: denied path parts (.git, .env*, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, credentials, secrets, id_rsa, id_ed25519) and extensions (.pem .key .p12 .pfx .jks .keystore) in src/privacy.ts:1-30; 7 secret regexes (sk-/AKIA/ghp_/xox/bearer/key=value>=12 chars/PEM) applied to snippets and to criterion/patterns. Misses many secret formats (e.g. Stripe sk_live_ with underscore prefix partially, JWTs, connection strings with passwords, .npmrc, service-account JSON, .netrc); path-denylist does not cover .npmrc, .pypirc, .netrc, kubeconfig, *.tfstate. README itself warns filters are heuristic. Client-project code snippets leave the machine.

rg spawned via child_process.spawn with args array (no shell) and patterns passed as -e values (search.ts:55,79), so no shell injection or flag injection; globs rejected if absolute or containing '..'; realpath + ensureInsideRoot check. rg respects .gitignore (default) so ignored files excluded. Symlink targets not followed by default.

Prompt-injection surface: repo text (snippets) goes into Jev state, but Jev returns only typed probabilities, so an injected snippet can at most bias a relevance score (could hide/promote a hit); output to Claude is JSON with snippets from the repo (normal untrusted-file-content risk, same as Grep).

Telemetry is local only: metadata JSONL (tool, latency, counts, model, cost, fallback_reason; no content) at ~/.codex/state/jev-delegate/usage.jsonl even under Claude Code (config.ts:38-40, dir mode 0700, file 0600); disable with JEV_DELEGATE_TELEMETRY=off. No network telemetry. Odd Codex path for a Claude Code user.

No postinstall scripts, no curl|sh; installer is manual git clone + npm ci (runs third-party dep tree incl. typescript 7.0.2 / vitest 5.0.1 pins; package-lock present). Uncommon version pins would need review before npm ci.
entries.dataEgress: Only to https://openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions (and then to whichever upstream provider OpenRouter routes Jev to, typically TypeSafe). Sent per call: model id, the relevance_criterion, and for search up to 200 candidates of {relative file path, line number, snippet up to 500 chars}; for classify, up to 200 items of full text (<=8000 chars each) plus metadata, labels and instructions. Not sent: whole files, diffs, Claude's conversation, tool outputs from other tools. But it does send code lines and file paths from personal AND client repos to a third party (OpenRouter + TypeSafe), which matters for client NDAs; secret filtering is regex-based only. Sending is entirely model-initiated (the model decides to call the tool).
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. Missing key -> JevError -> status "fallback" with raw ripgrep hits (top_k, unranked, deterministic pattern-count order) and fallback_reason. Per-request timeout 10 s (max 30 s), whole-tool deadline 30 s (config.ts:34-35), 2 attempts with 250 ms backoff on 429/5xx/timeout/transport (jev.ts:109-122). Schema mismatch -> fallback. Caveats: a slow Jev can stall a Claude turn up to ~30 s; rg failure or missing rg, secret-like patterns, or workspace-root failure throw a hard tool error rather than fallback; classify fallback returns items with no label so Claude has to classify itself. Unverified live contract means a wrong payload shape would silently degrade to fallback every time (fail-open masks breakage; only visible via fallback_reason).
entries.contextCost: 2 tools. Model-visible definitions: search_and_rank description ~250 chars + 6-param schema with constraints (~700 chars), classify_items description ~215 chars + nested item/label schema (~900 chars), titles ~90 chars; total roughly 2.2k chars, about 550-700 tokens (outputSchema is not typically sent to the model). No MCP server-level instructions. Plus the skill: only name + description (~430 chars, ~110 tokens) always loaded; SKILL.md body (~1.7k chars, ~430 tokens) loaded when invoked. No hook-injected text. Total always-on about 700-800 tokens: small. Note the user already runs Playwright and GitNexus MCPs, so this is marginal.
pros: Genuinely uses Jev via OpenRouter today: hard-coded openrouter.ai/api/alpha/decisions with OPENROUTER_API_KEY and model typesafe/jev-1.13 (jev.ts:135, config.ts:24-25), matching the user's provider choice; model overridable to ~typesafe/jev-latest.
Uses Jev's actual strengths correctly: typed Noul per candidate and Choice with confidence/probabilities, with no free text, and thresholds (0.5 drop, 0.8 include) exposed via env.
Explicitly ships a Claude Code plugin (.claude-plugin/plugin.json bundling skill + MCP) and Claude Code install docs; roots-based workspace detection works in Claude Code.

Well-designed safety: fail-open fallback to raw rg hits, per-call ($0.01) and daily ($0.25) spend caps, request and tool timeouts, retry with backoff, no shell (spawn args array), path traversal guard, secret-regex screening, metadata-only local telemetry, MIT license.

Tiny and readable (about 600 lines src, 52 KB total incl. tests): auditable in minutes; only 2 tools so about 700 tokens of context; no hooks that would interfere with the existing secret-guard/GitNexus hooks.
Good reference implementation of the Decisions API request/response shape (state + questions -> answers) that could be lifted into a custom hook or MCP.
cons: Very young and unproven: created 2026-09-24 (6 days old), 4 commits, 0 stars, no releases, no CI, one human author plus an AI-authored commit; README admits the live OpenRouter API path is not verified against a real key.

Solves a niche problem: re-ranking large ripgrep result sets and bulk English classification. Claude Code's Grep already caps output and the main model reads ~20 hits cheaply; the token saving is small and the value for daily coding (edit/debug/refactor/review) is low. Jev is not used for the decisions that matter in coding (which file to edit, does this diff break X, routing to model tiers).

Not automatic: pure model-discretion tool + skill trigger. The model must guess before searching that the result set will exceed 20 hits, and it will keep defaulting to native Grep/GitNexus. The user's requirement (no prompting, Claude Code uses it when needed) is not met deterministically.

Overlaps with and is weaker than existing tooling: GitNexus already provides graph/semantic context; ranking by a literal-pattern rg pass plus a per-line-snippet Noul (snippet only, max 500 chars, no surrounding code) has limited semantic power and relevance judged from one line is noisy; a wrong 'no' silently hides real matches (results below 0.5 dropped), a risk for refactors.

Sends code snippets and file paths from client repos to OpenRouter/TypeSafe; heuristic-only secret filter with gaps (.npmrc, .netrc, kubeconfig, JWTs, DB URLs); the model, not the user, decides when data leaves. Problematic for client NDA projects without a per-project opt-out beyond the prompt phrase 'local only'.

Fail-open masks breakage: because the Decisions API contract is unverified, a schema mismatch just returns 'fallback' raw hits every call, adding up to 10-30 s of wasted latency with no ranking benefit. Latency added per call ~0.5-2 s versus instant native Grep.

Codex-centric leftovers: telemetry path ~/.codex/state/..., .codex-plugin, openai.yaml, .mcp.json with Codex-only keys (env_vars, tool_timeout_sec); Claude Code would ignore those so the 10 s startup and 4096 output limits are not applied; plugin.json has no env passthrough config (relies on inheritance).

Manual build step (git clone, npm ci, tsc; dist not committed, no npm package), unpinned upgrade path, and running npm ci pulls unusual pinned versions (typescript 7.0.2, vitest 5.0.1) that should be reviewed.
entries.verdict: Real, clean, OpenRouter-native Jev integration, but a narrow 2-tool MCP (grep re-ranking and bulk classification) that is model-discretion only, six days old, with an unverified live API path; it does not deliver automatic Jev use in Claude Code. Worth reading as a reference for the Decisions API payload and safety patterns, not worth installing as the main integration; install at most as an optional low-priority extra after verifying with a live key, and skip on client repos.

entries.name: jev-dev-harness
entries.what: TypeScript/Node stdio MCP server plus CLI (jev-dev) that wraps Jev-style Noul/Score/Choice calls into 5 dev-workflow tools: context ranker (per-file relevance scoring), tool-manifest pruner, shell-command guard (regex classifier, Jev only for unknown commands), git-diff patch reviewer, and semantic linter. It also ships a git pre-commit hook, an opt-in local reverse proxy that can inject tool hints into Anthropic API requests, a telemetry dashboard, and rule files (CLAUDE.md etc.) telling agents to call its tools. Despite the README's "hooks" talk there are NO Claude Code PreToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks, only a git pre-commit script. Automatic invocation relies entirely on the model reading instruction text.
interface: CLI jev-dev setup / provider / doctor / compare / dashboard / update / uninstall
CLI jev-dev context rank / guard check / patch review / lint semantic / tools rank / proxy
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tools, nudged by prose rule files (CLAUDE.md / SKILL.md). The only deterministic pieces are a git pre-commit hook and an opt-in Anthropic reverse proxy (hint injection, not a real tool call). There are no Claude Code PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks. This does NOT meet the user's requirement that Claude Code use Jev automatically without prompting, unless the user adds their own hook wrapper around the CLI (`jev-dev guard check`) or a CLAUDE.md instruction, which still depends on the model complying.
security: Repo is 9 days old (created 2026-09-21), 0 stars, 0 forks, 1 contributor (55 commits), 17 npm versions in 4 days (0.1.0 to 0.2.7). Not vetted by anyone else.

API key is stored in plaintext in ./.env in the CURRENT project directory and in ~/.jev-dev/config.json (cli/setup.ts:215-250). On client projects that risks committing the key, and the wizard does not add .env to .gitignore.
typesafe-client.ts:21 calls process.loadEnvFile() on import, so it loads whatever .env sits in the cwd of the MCP process, i.e. every project's secrets.

MCP server config written by setup places the key in an `env` block (visible in the config file, not argv). Recommended launch is `npx -y jev-dev-harness`, which runs unpinned latest code from npm on every session start, so a supply-chain risk given a single-maintainer, 9-day-old package.

No npm postinstall script (package.json scripts: build, prepublishOnly, dev, test). No curl|sh installer. `jev-dev update` runs execSync `npm install -g` (cli/index.ts:517). git is run via execSync with string-built args (diff-extractor.ts:123): check for injection through commitRange, which the model controls via MCP args.

Prompt-injection surface: tool results (JSON) embed `instructionForAgent` text ('OBRIGATORIO: ...present the block') that steers the main model (mcp/server.ts:234,316). The README-mandated Portuguese efficiency footer would be added to every answer. File snippets and diffs go to the Jev model, and their content could try to manipulate scores.
entries.dataEgress: To the Jev provider only, redacted by regex: (1) jev_rank_context sends the task text, plus for each candidate file its relative path, extension, size, matched symbols and up to 1200 chars of the file snippet, one request per candidate, concurrent via Promise.all; (2) jev_guard_check sends the command string and task, only for commands the regex classifier could not classify; (3) jev_review_patch and jev_lint_semantic send diff content and the task; (4) the proxy sends the last user message (800 chars), the tool names and 150-char descriptions to the Jev provider. On OpenRouter with the default config, this code goes to whatever deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash provider OpenRouter routes to, not to TypeSafe. Also sent: HTTP-Referer 'https://github.com/marcelo/jev-dev-harness' and X-OpenRouter-Title headers. Local: telemetry.jsonl with commands and tasks. npm registry: version check.
entries.failureMode: Fail-open by design. SafeJevClient.systemOne() catches every error and returns {ok:false,fallback:true} (typesafe-client.ts:514-524). Default timeout 15000 ms (JEV_TIMEOUT_MS, :119), the proxy uses 4000 ms, and the SDK path does 1 retry. The context ranker falls back to heuristics only (stage-c-jev.ts:153-160). The guard falls back to the regex classifier, and unknown commands then require confirmation. The proxy passes the request through unchanged. With no key it silently runs in offline heuristic mode. Downside: a slow API can stall a tool call for up to 15 s, and a wrong OpenRouter model name silently degrades to DeepSeek or heuristics with no loud error. The MCP server is a stdio child of Claude Code, so if `npx -y` cannot fetch the package at startup, the server fails to connect.
entries.contextCost: 5 MCP tools (jev_rank_context, jev_rank_tools, jev_guard_check, jev_review_patch, jev_lint_semantic). The TOOLS array is about 4,850 chars, roughly 1,200 tokens of tool definitions, and the server sets no `instructions` field (mcp/server.ts:169-179). Each tool call returns pretty-printed JSON (JSON.stringify(..., null, 2)) plus an efficiencyReport with a long Portuguese instructionForAgent, adding several hundred tokens per call and pushing the model to add a footer to answers. No Claude Code hooks are installed, so hooks inject nothing. The proxy appends a ~60-char hint to the last user message only when the proxy is used. The CLAUDE.md/skill files, if copied in, add about 500-1,000 tokens to every session.
pros: Real code that calls the OpenRouter Decisions API (/api/alpha/decisions) with typesafe/ or ~typesafe/ model slugs (typesafe-client.ts:266-292, 449-455), so real Jev on OpenRouter works with a single env var change (OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13).

Wraps Jev in sensible, well-structured Noul/Score/Choice question sets (file relevance, command destructiveness, patch risk, tool routing) and shows how to compose all three primitives. This is a good reference for writing our own hook.
Fail-open everywhere with timeouts, a redaction pass before egress and result caching, so it will not block work when Jev is down.

Tool-guard's deterministic regex classifier (classifier.ts, 270 lines) runs locally and only escalates unknown commands to Jev; the design fits a PreToolUse Bash hook, and the CLI (`jev-dev guard check`) could be called from a hook script.

MIT licence, only 4 runtime dependencies (MCP SDK, @typesafe-ai/sdk, commander, ignore), no postinstall. 142 vitest tests across 22 files exist (tests/), including mcp server, hooks, redaction and typesafe-client error tests, though I did not run them.
Small MCP surface (about 1.2k tokens) which is cheap in context.
cons: Not automatic in Claude Code: no PreToolUse/PostToolUse/UserPromptSubmit hooks, no plugin.json or marketplace, setup does not register with Claude Code (only Claude Desktop, Cursor, Codex etc.). It relies on the model choosing to call the tools, which is the opposite of the 'never prompt to use jev' goal, and with Opus 5.5 in bypass mode a tool the model doesn't need simply gets ignored.

OpenRouter default is an emulator: the default model is deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash via chat completions with a made-up JSON schema, so the returned 'probabilities' are not calibrated Jev outputs. Any 400 from the typesafe/ slug silently falls back to DeepSeek (typesafe-client.ts:462-470). Provider auto-detect prefers TYPESAFE/Vercel keys over OpenRouter, and OPENROUTER_API_KEY alone yields DeepSeek, not Jev.

The tools duplicate what Claude Code already does well. The context ranker sends a Jev call per file (N calls, 1200-char snippets of possibly client code) to save tokens Claude already saves with Grep/Glob/GitNexus; the guard duplicates the user's existing secret-leak and permission setup and is advisory only; and in bypass/auto mode it never gates anything.

Jev is a poor fit for the large-text jobs: the patch reviewer and semantic linter feed diffs (32k context limit, no reasoning trace) to a beta System One model; the false-positive/negative rate is unmeasured, and the README numbers (92.4% token cut, 5x faster, $15,500/yr) are simulator constants, not benchmarks.

Tool results force a Portuguese 'Eficiencia Jev' footer onto every reply via instructionForAgent, which is intrusive noise and a prompt-injection-style side channel into the main model. It is bad for client-facing sessions.

Very immature and single-author: created 2026-09-21, 0 stars, 1 contributor, 17 releases in 4 days, CI only for a lint workflow (no test CI), and server version string hard-coded '0.1.0'. Running unpinned `npx -y` from it on client projects is a supply-chain risk.
Setup writes the API key to ./.env in the project dir and process.loadEnvFile() ingests project .env files, which is unsafe for client repos; the wizard does not gitignore it.

The proxy mode would sit in front of the Anthropic subscription/OAuth traffic, forwarding all headers, and adds a Jev round trip per turn plus a hint suffix that could disturb prompt caching; the user's setup (OAuth login) makes ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL routing awkward and risky.
entries.verdict: Not a good primary integration: it is an alpha, single-author MCP toolkit whose 'automatic' behaviour is just prose telling the model to call its tools (no Claude Code hooks), and its OpenRouter path defaults to a DeepSeek chat emulator rather than real Jev. Its value is as a reference for the Jev question designs and OpenRouter Decisions API call shape (with OPENROUTER_MODEL=typesafe/jev-1.13), not as something to install.

entries.name: xerify-cli
entries.what: Node/TypeScript CLI, library and stdio/HTTP MCP server for cross-provider claim verification. Three MCP tools: xerify_ask, xerify_verify, xerify_capabilities. Jev is one built-in verify-only backend next to codex, claude, cursor, openai-api, anthropic-api, openai-compatible and generic command adapters. A verify call sends {claim, context} as the Jev state with one fixed 3-way Choice question (confirmed/refuted/unclear); Jev probabilities/confidence are thresholded (p>=0.90, conf>=0.80, no tie, else 'unclear'). It is a claim-checker, not a general Jev decision gateway: no Noul, Score or arbitrary typed questions. The model must decide to call the MCP tool itself; nothing is automatic.
interface: xerify health / doctor / providers list|probe / config show|validate
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. The tool descriptions are generic ('Verify a claim with an invocation provider different from its author'), and the bundled SKILL.md is not a Claude Code skill and does not enforce anything. There is no hook and no proxy. Claude would have to be prompted (CLAUDE.md rule) to call xerify_verify, which needs the from provider (anthropic:claude-opus-5) and a hand-built claim and context, and the skill text demands per-call user approval. This does not meet the requirement that Claude Code uses Jev automatically without prompting.
security: API key read from env var (default TYPESAFE_API_KEY) or an optional literal apiKey in config. Only sent in the Authorization header via fetch (jev.ts:152-162), never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. Configs with a literal key or explicit endpoint must be chmod 600 (config/resolve.ts:56-62). Endpoint URLs are redacted in diagnostics (config/redact.ts).
For the MCP server, the key must come from the env block of the mcpServers entry in ~/.claude.json or from the shell environment. The tool does not read .env automatically (docs/jev.md).
No telemetry or analytics: grep of src/ finds no outbound URLs except the provider endpoints in schema.ts and openai-api/anthropic-api.

Prompt-injection surface: the claim and context are model-supplied and go to Jev as untrusted state. Prompt text tells Jev to ignore embedded instructions (jev.ts:40-58), but Jev's output is a typed enum plus probabilities, and Xerify never executes output. The injection risk is low; the main risk is a wrong verdict, not code execution.
Shell execution: process adapters use shell:false with an env allowlist, but they are irrelevant to the Jev path, which is pure HTTP fetch.

Supply chain: the postinstall is guarded and writes only .xerify/ files, no network. Published with npm provenance; CI actions are SHA-pinned; there is a secrets:check gate against .env leakage. Single maintainer, 0 stars, first release 12 days before the audit date, so trust is limited.
entries.dataEgress: Only for a verify call routed to Jev: the JSON body {model, state:{claim, context}, questions:{verdict: fixed instructions and criteria}} goes over HTTPS to the configured endpoint (TYPESAFE by default, OpenRouter if overridden). claim is written by Claude and context is whatever Claude pastes in (code, diff hunks, logs, file contents, tool outputs, up to about 1 MiB by default via maxInputBytes). It is not automatic, since the model chooses what to send. Nothing else leaves the machine and there is no telemetry. If OpenRouter is used, the content also passes through OpenRouter and its logging/data-policy settings. The docs and skill say to get user approval per call, which conflicts with a fully automatic workflow.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed per call, not blocking overall. On timeout, HTTP error, invalid JSON or schema mismatch, the tool returns a typed error (isError with TIMEOUT / PROVIDER_FAILURE / AUTH_UNAVAILABLE / INVALID_PROVIDER_RESPONSE) and Claude proceeds normally. Default timeout is 120000 ms (config/schema limits.timeoutMs, http.ts:39), far above Jev's claimed 70-500 ms, so a hung endpoint can stall a tool call for up to 2 minutes unless limits.timeoutMs is lowered (max is per request via limits). No retries and no fallback (docs/jev.md). Low-certainty output becomes 'unclear'. There is no risk of hooks blocking work, because it is a normal MCP tool.
entries.contextCost: 3 MCP tools. Estimated 3.5k-4.5k tokens of tool definitions per session: inputSchema plus outputSchema are exported as JSON Schema (schemas/ask-request 2.0 KB, verify-request 2.1 KB, ask-result 3.0 KB, verify-result 6.4 KB, plus a small capabilities schema and short descriptions, about 14-15 KB, /4 = about 3.6k tokens). The verify-result schema is large because it carries findings/evidence/decision fields Jev never fills. No MCP server 'instructions' string is set (server.ts:98-101). No hooks and nothing injected per turn. Does not use Claude Code's deferred tool loading unless the user's tool search does.
pros: Real, non-toy Jev integration: correct Choice-question payload, strict Zod parse of answers.verdict.probabilities/confidence, tie and threshold abstention (jev.ts:137-204). Directly reusable as a reference for the System One request/response shape.
Endpoint and key env var are configurable (schema.ts:77-82), so pointing at OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone with OPENROUTER_API_KEY is plausibly a config-only change; it would work without forking.
Key never appears in argv; no telemetry; HTTP-only Jev path with bounded output, timeouts and abort support (http.ts); no shell, no eval of outputs.
MIT, CI matrix on 3 OSes, about 196 tests, provenance-signed npm release, SHA-pinned actions, thoughtful SECURITY.md and exit-code contract.
Small tool surface (3 tools, about 3.6k tokens), no per-turn hook injection or latency; fail-soft: errors return typed tool errors and do not block Claude.
Fits a legitimate Jev use case: a calibrated second-opinion gate ('does this diff satisfy this claim?') with a probability threshold for abstention.
cons: Not automatic: model-discretion MCP tool, with no hook, and the shipped SKILL.md is aimed at Codex and demands explicit user approval per live call. It would need CLAUDE.md nudges, which is exactly what the user wants to avoid.

Narrow: only a fixed confirmed/refuted/unclear verify question. It cannot do Noul/Score, routing, permission triage, commit-type choice or any other typed decision, so it captures little of Jev's value for coding.

Jev is fed only what Claude writes into claim and context, so accuracy depends on Claude's summarization and there is no independent evidence collection. Jev is a no-reasoning classifier; a 'confirmed' on a diff gives false assurance (authors admit thresholds are uncalibrated and accuracy unmeasured).

Requires a declared 'from' provider and a different 'to' provider; the code hard-codes the Jev provider as 'typesafe' and the shorthand as typesafe:jev-latest, awkward with an OpenRouter model id. The OpenRouter response shape is untested.
Default history captureInput='full' writes every claim and context (code, diffs) to .xerify/runs in the working directory: undesirable for client projects unless disabled.

Very young single-maintainer project (0 stars, 33 commits, one dev, first published 2026-09-18, 'first signed release' not yet cut); postinstall script exists; the 120 s default timeout is too long for a 70-500 ms service.
Adds the tool schemas (about 3.6k tokens) to every session for a capability the model will rarely use unprompted.
entries.verdict: Well-built, safe-ish claim verifier with a config-overridable Jev endpoint, so OpenRouter should be reachable without code changes. But it is a model-discretion MCP tool for one narrow question type, not an automatic integration, so on its own it does not deliver 'Claude Code uses Jev without being asked'. Useful mainly as a reference implementation of the System One request/response parser; a custom hook or thin MCP tool is the better route.

entries.name: frostney/clean-code-review
entries.what: A Next.js + eve (Vercel agent framework) web app, deployed publicly at clean-code-review.vercel.app, that judges every code file of a GitHub PR/diff/paste against ~Clean Code question set using Jev (via Vercel AI Gateway, model id typesafe-ai/jev, AI SDK experimental_evaluate), then has a second LLM (Luna, openai/gpt-5.6-luna-fast) write prose review and approve/comment/request_changes decision. It also exposes a hosted, anonymous stateless Streamable-HTTP MCP endpoint (https://clean-code-review.vercel.app/api/mcp) with two tools: review_pull_request and review_pasted_code. It is a demo/showcase app, not a Claude Code integration or a reusable Jev client library.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. Claude Code would call review_pull_request only if the model judges the tool description relevant (e.g. user asks for a PR review); no deterministic hook, no skill trigger, no proxy. Not an automatic Jev integration.
security: Hosted MCP is anonymous, no sign-in (README:49-50): no key ever touches the client, but also anyone can use/abuse the shared budget; IP-based throttles 10 calls/10 min, shared $ hourly/daily budget, so it can be refused when budget is spent (mcp-server.ts RETURNS text).
review_pasted_code sends your code to a third-party Vercel-hosted service (Vercel AI Gateway -> TypeSafe/Jev, and OpenAI-hosted Luna); unsuitable for client/NDA code without a contractual basis.

Prompt-injection surface: the submitted code/PR description flows into Jev (typed output, low risk) and Luna (free-text; tool result explicitly says read as advice, not authorization). Tool output returned into Claude Code context is model-written prose shaped by untrusted code.
Vercel Analytics and Speed Insights on the web page (package.json); results cached for one hour in Vercel Runtime Cache shared across callers (mcp-server.ts RETURNS).

No curl|sh installers; postinstall is `test -e .git && lefthook install || true` (self-host only, benign). Self-hosting would need a Vercel AI Gateway key via .env.local; the API key would not be in argv (bun --env-file).
entries.dataEgress: With the hosted MCP: full PR contents (fetched server-side from public GitHub) or the entire pasted diff/files (up to 1M chars; 24 files x 64k judged) leave the machine to clean-code-review.vercel.app, then to Vercel AI Gateway -> TypeSafe Jev and to Luna (openai/gpt-5.6-luna-fast, first 300 chars/file excerpts plus Jev's findings plus PR title/description). Results cached 1h server-side keyed by content. Caller IP used for rate limiting. Nothing else from Claude Code (no prompts/tool outputs) unless Claude chooses to paste them.
entries.failureMode: Only a model-discretion MCP tool, so nothing fails closed on Claude Code's normal flow. Server-side: per-attempt Jev timeout 12 s with one retry (judge.ts:26-29,367; withOneRetry), overall judging deadline and review deadline (returns partial results; mcp-review.ts), function maxDuration 120 s (mcp-facts.ts:28). If the shared budget is exhausted or IP throttled the tool returns isError with reset time. If the Vercel-hosted service is down, the tool call fails and Claude continues; MCP connect failure just leaves the server disconnected.
entries.contextCost: 2 MCP tools; tool descriptions are long: RETURNS description alone ~1,435 chars plus CAPS ~452 chars plus paste-input description, roughly 4-6k chars total (~1,000-1,500 tokens) for names+descriptions+schemas. No server-level instructions seen; no hook-injected text. Each call returns a large structured result (per-file answers to ~20 questions + prose), potentially several thousand tokens per PR.
pros: Real, working, well-tested (25 test files, CI) end-to-end example of using Jev for structured code judgments: shows the question/answer design, probabilities for yes/no smells and scored scales, per-file fan-out and caching (agent/lib/judging/judge.ts, questions.ts).
Zero-install: one `claude mcp add --transport http` line gives a PR-review tool with no API key and no local process (README:49-54).

Useful reference for prompt/state schema when building a custom Jev hook: judge.ts:31-46 shows the exact evaluate() payload (state: code/diff/path + typed questions) and resilience patterns (12 s timeout, one retry, windows of 16k chars, concurrency tuning at judge.ts:281-290).
MIT licensed; the hosted tool description explicitly frames output as advice, not authorization.
Cost per review claimed ~$0.02 for 24 files (README:118).
cons: Not an integration into Claude Code: no hook, skill, plugin or proxy; the only Claude Code surface is a third-party hosted MCP endpoint that Claude uses only when it decides to, contrary to the user's requirement of automatic use.

Hard-wired to Vercel AI Gateway (typesafe-ai/jev); no OpenRouter or TypeSafe-direct support anywhere in code, and the hosted endpoint's provider cannot be changed by the client, so it does not use the user's OpenRouter-hosted Jev or key at all.

Sends client/personal code to an anonymous public Vercel deployment and onward to Vercel, TypeSafe and OpenAI; unacceptable for client projects; shared, publicly budgeted service ($15/week gateway cap, 10 calls/10 min/IP) can refuse calls at any time and has no SLA.

Wrong task shape for daily coding: a batch PR-level Clean Code lint plus an LLM-written review (Luna); doesn't expose Jev's Choice/Noul/Score primitives for arbitrary routing/decisions inside Claude Code turns; adds a second LLM and its prose to context.
Very young and single-maintainer (created 2026-09-17, 121 commits, 1 contributor, 12 stars, version 0.0.0, no releases); relies on experimental_evaluate from ai 7 and eve 0.x, so breakage likely.
Tool descriptions are verbose (~1-1.5k tokens) and results large, costing context for a tool that fires rarely; 2-60 s latency per call.
entries.verdict: A polished Jev showcase and a good code reference for the evaluate() payload, but not a Claude Code integration: it is a Vercel-AI-Gateway-only hosted demo whose MCP tool is model-discretion and ships your code to a third-party public service. Do not install for client work; at most mine judge.ts/questions.ts for ideas when building your own OpenRouter-backed hook.

entries.name: thienle99-dev/typesafe-mcp-server
entries.what: Small Node/TypeScript MCP server (7 tools) that wraps the official @typesafe-ai/sdk and calls POST {baseURL}/v1/systemone. Each tool sends a client-supplied payload (diff, error text, issue, file list) plus one hard-coded Jev choice question (or one noul per test group for select_tests) and returns an envelope with the chosen label, confidence, probabilities, a template "reason" string and needsHumanReview (true when confidence < 0.97 by default). It runs as a standalone Express HTTP/SSE server on port 3000. It has no stdio mode, no hooks, no skill and no plugin manifest. The "hooks" claim in the discovery summary is false.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool only. There is no hook, skill, CLAUDE.md snippet or plugin. The one-line tool descriptions give Opus no trigger guidance and no reason to prefer them over its own reasoning, so it would rarely or never call them unprompted. Making the calls automatic would need a separate CLAUDE.md rule or hook layered on top by the user, i.e. the integration the user wants is not provided by this repo.
security: Unauthenticated network listener: app.listen(port) (src/server.ts:71) has no host argument, so it binds all interfaces on 0.0.0.0/::. There is no auth, no Origin/Host validation and no CORS handling. Anyone on the LAN, or a DNS-rebinding web page, can call the tools and spend the user's OpenRouter or TypeSafe credit.

The API key lives in the server's environment or .env, not in Claude Code argv, so it is not visible in the client's process list. It is visible in /proc/<pid>/environ to the same user. .env is gitignored. No key is logged; the SDK redacts authorization headers (index.mjs:285).
Throws at startup if no key is set (src/jev.ts:96), which is fail-fast.
No shell execution, no filesystem access, no postinstall in the repo. The dependency tree is standard, and the SDK is MIT with a publish-time check script and no install scripts.
No telemetry in the repo. I did not audit the SDK beyond grep, and TypeSafe or OpenRouter may log requests.

Prompt-injection surface is small. Jev returns typed labels only, but the labels are advisory and a poisoned diff or error text could steer merge_gate to 'pass'. merge_gate accepts arbitrary model-provided strings.
entries.dataEgress: Everything the tool arguments contain is sent to the endpoint (OpenRouter then TypeSafe, or TypeSafe directly). That means full unified diffs (classify_change, review_risk), file paths and symbol names, commit messages, issue text, repoContext, full compiler, test and runtime error output, command lines, test/lint/security result strings, and dependency reasons. Claude must copy all of it into the tool call, so it also becomes Opus output tokens. Nothing is read from disk by the server. For client projects this means client source diffs leave the machine to a third-party beta model. The 32k-context limit truncates or rejects large diffs.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed at the tool level, with no fallback. The SDK timeout defaults to 10s (TYPESAFE_TIMEOUT_MS) with 3 retries (TYPESAFE_MAX_RETRIES), so a hung Jev could block one tool call for roughly 40s or more plus backoff. After that, errors propagate as an MCP tool error and Claude just continues without it. Malformed responses throw (src/jev.ts:245,275). The server is a separate process. If it is not running, Claude Code shows the MCP server as failed and the tools are simply absent. It does not block a session, because nothing is a hook. The confidence gate defaults to 0.97, so most non-trivial decisions come back needsHumanReview=true, which is noise. If the server lacks a key at boot it exits, so it never registers.
entries.contextCost: 7 tools. Descriptions are 4-8 word one-liners ("Classify a code change"), and the zod schemas have no .describe() text. I estimate the tool names, descriptions and JSON schemas at about 2,000-2,800 chars, roughly 500-700 tokens (more if Claude Code tool-search defers them). There are no MCP server 'instructions'. No hook injects any text. Each call adds the diff twice to context (the tool-call args and the JSON envelope result, which is small).
pros: Uses the official @typesafe-ai/sdk (MIT, from TypeSafe's org) with an env-configurable baseURL, model, key, timeout and retries. Pointing it at OpenRouter should need only env changes: TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api, key = OpenRouter key, model = typesafe/jev-1.13.

Correct use of the Jev primitives: choice for categorical decisions, and one noul per test group with a P>=0.5 threshold. Probabilities and confidence are passed through, and reasons are honestly labelled as adapter-generated rather than Jev explanations.
Small (about 28 KB), fully readable in minutes, with no shell/fs access and no postinstall. It is easy to fork and audit.
Zod input validation and a configurable confidence threshold (DECISION_CONFIDENCE_THRESHOLD).
Low static context cost, about 600 tokens for 7 tools.
cons: Discovery claim of 'hooks' is false. The repo has no hooks, no skill and no plugin. Nothing makes Claude Code call it automatically, so it fails the user's core 'no prompting' requirement. Only the model's discretion triggers it, and the 4-8 word descriptions are unlikely to trigger it.
Brand-new and abandoned-looking: 0 stars, 1 author, 3 commits pushed within seconds on 2026-09-23, no release, no CI, no license, package.json private:true, and README written in Vietnamese only.

Hard-coded questions are weakly designed for the task. select_tests' fallback choice question ('Which test group is highest priority?') is mismatched with the noul flow. Priority is derived from the count of selected groups. confidence for a noul is max(p,1-p). merge_gate takes free-text, model-written summaries, so it is garbage-in/garbage-out. The 0.97 default threshold flags most results as needing human review.

The tasks it covers (classify diff, triage error, route task, pick tests) are things Opus 5.5 already does inline with full repo context. Using this server forces Claude to re-emit whole diffs as output tokens (slow and expensive) for a label that Claude must then still verify. Net latency and token cost are a loss.

Network exposure: an unauthenticated Express server on all interfaces, port 3000, using the deprecated SSE transport. The user has to run and supervise it manually, and one shared credential-bearing process is exposed to LAN or DNS-rebinding abuse.

Sends full client-project diffs and error logs to OpenRouter and TypeSafe beta, a data-governance risk for client work, with no allow-list, redaction or size cap other than 2 MB. It sits alongside the existing secret-guard hook, which does not cover MCP tool arguments.

OpenRouter compatibility is unverified at the schema level, and default retries of 3 x 10s allow long stalls. No stdio option, so it cannot be launched via a simple 'claude mcp add -- npx ...' command.
entries.verdict: Not recommended as the Jev integration. It is a thin, 3-commit proof of concept whose advertised 'hooks' do not exist. It only offers seven model-discretion MCP tools that Opus is unlikely to call unprompted, and it exposes an unauthenticated SSE port. Its only real value is as a reference for how to map Jev choice/noul questions onto coding decisions, and as a config-only OpenRouter patch (TYPESAFE_API_URL=https://openrouter.ai/api plus typesafe/jev-1.13). For real automation, build a small stdio MCP server or hook that reuses these question definitions.
entries.license: None declared (licenseInfo null, no LICENSE file), so legally all rights reserved. package.json has private:true.

entries.name: typesafe-tpm-mcp (geronimo-deploy-cloud)
entries.what: Small Python MCP server (stdio, mcp v2 MCPServer) that gates work-ticket quality. It sends a structured ticket (title, goal, description, acceptance criteria, scope lists) plus 11 Jev primitives (Noul/Choice/Score) to TypeSafe System One in one batched typesafe_sdk call. Routing (ready_for_execution / needs_revision / needs_human_scoping / blocked_on_dependency), hard gates and fix hints are computed in local Python. It is a ticket/issue-template reviewer for an agent-orchestration workflow, not a general coding aid.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion: a skill description trigger (SKILL.md 'Trigger whenever writing a new ticket or issue, or when handed a ticket to implement') plus a model-discretion MCP tool whose docstring says not to implement unless ready. No hook, so nothing is deterministic. It only fires when the agent recognises a ticket-shaped task, so it is not automatic for general coding.
security: README instructs passing the key via `claude mcp add --env TYPESAFE_API_KEY=your-key-here`. This stores it in plaintext in ~/.claude.json, but it is not in argv of the server. `uv ... run` inherits the env. The README's own recommendation is fine, but the key is on the `claude mcp add` command line once.

No shell execution, no subprocess or eval, no telemetry, no npm postinstall or curl|sh installer in the repo. Tiny code surface (about 450 lines) that is easy to audit. Dependencies are the pinned uv.lock set (mcp 2.x, typesafe-sdk 0.7.0, httpx2).

Prompt-injection surface is small: tool output is only fixed-vocabulary routes/fixes computed locally, and free-text is never returned by Jev. Ticket text is passed as JSON state to Jev. The SKILL.md makes the route 'binding', which is a benign instruction but could stall an agent on a false negative.
No LICENSE means legal ambiguity for use on client projects (cannot legally be copied or modified without permission). Repo owner is a small org account (geronimo-deploy-cloud) with a single author.
SDK logs redact exceptions (transport.py imports redact_exception; SECRET_HEADERS in _core/constants.py:21), so key leakage in logs is unlikely.
entries.dataEgress: Only the ticket fields the agent passes to review_ticket_quality (title, goal, description, acceptance criteria, in/out-of-scope lists, file path lists, context references). These go as JSON `state` plus the 11 question definitions to {TYPESAFE_BASE_URL}/v1/systemone (default https://api.typesafe.ai; would be OpenRouter if repointed). No file contents, diffs, transcripts or tool outputs are sent unless the agent pastes them into a ticket field. Client project details would leak if the agent drafts tickets about client work, and with OpenRouter this transits OpenRouter too. Nothing is sent at startup or by the other two tools.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed by design (README, server.py:91-98). If TYPESAFE_API_KEY is missing it returns an error dict without a route. On any exception it returns error plus route=needs_human_scoping and reason=review_unavailable. SDK default timeout is 10 s per HTTP operation (constants.py:21) with tenacity retries (retry policy not inspected in detail), so a hung Jev could block a tool call up to ~10 s or more per attempt. The sync call blocks the stdio server. Because SKILL.md says never to implement unless ready_for_execution, an outage would stall ticket-based agent work until the user intervenes. This is intentional but hostile to a fail-open daily workflow.
entries.contextCost: 3 tools. Approx tokens for names, descriptions and schemas: get_ticket_template ~60, review_ticket_quality ~350 (9 params, docstring with the DO NOT implement warning), explain_primitives ~50, so about 450-550 tokens. No MCP server `instructions` field is set. The skill adds only its ~90-token description to the listing until triggered, and about 1.2k tokens when loaded. No hooks, so no per-call injected text.
pros: Genuinely a real Jev integration: batches 11 Noul/Choice/Score questions in one system_one call (schema.py:59-129,165), the closest thing to a worked example of Jev used as a typed classifier with local threshold-based routing.

OpenRouter switch needs only env vars, no code change: SDK reads TYPESAFE_BASE_URL and TYPESAFE_DEFAULT_MODEL, and posts to /v1/systemone with Bearer auth, matching OpenRouter's /api/v1/systemone path.
Very small (about 450 lines), no shell execution or telemetry, pinned lockfile, so it is easy to audit and fork.
Cheap in context (~500 tokens, no server instructions, no hooks) and zero per-turn latency, so it is safe to leave installed.
Good design pattern to copy: routing thresholds in code (TQ_* env overrides), hard gates that ignore confidence, and fail-closed handling.
cons: Wrong domain: it reviews issue/ticket text against a specific template (Goal / Not In Scope / Do Not Touch, with a hardcoded 'ask Chris'). It never sees code, diffs, or Claude Code tool calls, so it does nothing for edits, commits, permission decisions, or test selection.
Only triggers if the agent is drafting or handed a formal ticket, which a senior dev doing interactive coding rarely does. It is not automatic in Claude Code's general loop.
No hooks, so the invocation is up to the model's discretion, contrary to the user's requirement of deterministic automatic use.
Fail-closed plus 'binding route' in SKILL.md would block work on any Jev outage or false negative. This is the wrong default for daily coding in bypass/auto mode.

Maturity: 5 commits in one day, 1 contributor, 0 stars, no tests, CI or releases, no license (unusable legally on client projects without permission), and it needs a manual clone plus a manual skill copy. The README references a missing .env.example.
Untested against OpenRouter: the SDK's strict response parsing may not match OpenRouter's System One schema.
Tickets sent to Jev may contain client project details and would pass through OpenRouter.
entries.verdict: A well-built proof of concept for a single narrow use, ticket pre-flight review, that does not help everyday coding in Claude Code and has no license, tests or hooks. It is worth reading as a pattern (batched Jev primitives with local routing, and OpenRouter reachable via TYPESAFE_BASE_URL), but not worth installing for this user's goal of automatic Jev use.
entries.license: None (no LICENSE file; GitHub reports licenseInfo null, so all rights are reserved by default)

entries.name: teempai/jev-in-codex
entries.what: A Codex plugin plus stdio MCP server (TypeScript, Node 22+) with ONE tool, jev_label. It reads a JSONL file of {id,text} records (1-256 records, 1 MiB max) inside a configured workspace root. It sends them to TypeSafe System One as 'choice' questions, 8 questions per request, and writes a new id/label JSONL file. It returns counts and the original text of records with confidence below 0.8. The earlier versions had three tools (capability selection, context search, output triage). The author removed them in v0.3.0 (2026-09-20) because benchmarks showed no useful gain. Today it is only batch text classification, not the tool/skill selection or context search in the discovery summary. The discovery summary is out of date.
entries.autoInvocation: Model-discretion MCP tool. In Codex the skill description acts as a trigger. In Claude Code you would only get the MCP tool, and its description says 'Label id/text JSONL text records'. Claude will rarely pick it, because a Claude Code session almost never has a labelling job with a JSONL file. There is no deterministic hook.
security: API key: read from the TYPESAFE_API_KEY env var and sent only in an Authorization header (labelling.ts:53). It is never in argv, so it does not show in the process list. The bundled README config uses env_vars passthrough.
Redirects rejected (redirect:'error'). Provider error bodies are not exposed. The server logs nothing and has no telemetry and no cache (README, and confirmed by reading the 225 lines of src).
No shell execution and no child processes. The old ripgrep dependency was removed.

Filesystem: workspace-root confinement with realpath and O_NOFOLLOW. It excludes .git, node_modules, .ssh, .aws, .gnupg, .env*, *.pem, *.key and similar (workspace.ts:5-6). The write uses flag 'wx', mode 0600, and no overwrite. Exclusions are filename-based only; the README admits there is no secret detection.

Prompt injection: records are marked untrusted in the instruction. The model returns only a constrained enum label, so an injection cannot direct actions. The returned review text is original file content that goes back into Claude's context.

Supply chain: private:true (not on npm); it must be cloned and built locally. Two runtime deps (@modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0, zod 4.6.5). CI uses 'npm ci --ignore-scripts' and there is no postinstall. Installation is by cloning and building, or via the agent-driven docs/INSTALL.md prompt. That needs a manual review before use.
entries.dataEgress: Every record's full text in the JSONL file, plus the question and criteria, goes to api.typesafe.ai/v1/systemone. It only sends what the model chose to put in a JSONL file inside the workspace. It does not send prompts, diffs, tool outputs or the repo automatically. Up to 256 records, 6,000 characters each. The bearer key goes to TypeSafe only.
entries.failureMode: Fail-closed, but harmless because it is an opt-in tool call. On a missing key, an HTTP error, a malformed answer or an incomplete batch it returns isError with 'No output was created; use ordinary tools or retry later' and creates no file (labelling.ts:49, 75, 85, 88-91). Per-request timeout is 8 s, total deadline 20 s, and the MCP tool timeout in config is 90 s. It never fabricates local labels. It cannot block other Claude Code work, since nothing is intercepted.
entries.contextCost: 1 MCP tool (jev_label). The tool description is about 470 characters and the input schema with the policy union is about 900 characters. Server instructions are about 330 characters. The total is roughly 400-500 tokens. There are no hooks and no injected text. The bundled SKILL.md is about 3 KB (about 800 tokens), but the skill only loads in Codex, and its description is about 550 characters.
pros: Small, readable code: 225 lines of TypeScript in 5 files, easy to audit and to fork.
Careful hardening: the key is passed by env and not argv, redirects are rejected, there is a workspace jail with O_NOFOLLOW, no overwrite, and no shell or telemetry.
Fails closed and never makes up labels.
Only one tool, so a context cost of about 500 tokens.

It really does use Jev's Choice primitive with per-option probabilities and confidence (labelling.ts:55-57, 76-83), so it is a useful reference for the wire format of /v1/systemone: {model, state, questions:{qN:{type:'choice', instructions, criteria}}} -> answers.qN.{choice, confidence, probabilities}.
Honest about limits: the author removed tools that lacked a benchmark gain and states it is synthetic data and alpha.
MIT licence, CI on Node 22 and 24, unit and e2e tests using a loopback simulator.
cons: The discovery summary is wrong. The 'tool/skill selection, context search, output triage' tools were removed on 2026-09-20. What remains is batch JSONL text labelling. That does nothing for daily coding in Claude Code.
Built for Codex: .codex-plugin/plugin.json and a Codex-format .mcp.json (env_vars, tool_timeout_sec). There is no Claude Code plugin or hook config.
No OpenRouter support: URL, model ID (jev-1.13.0) and env var (TYPESAFE_API_KEY) are hard-coded with no override. A fork is needed, and the OpenRouter schema is unverified.
Can't be automatic: model-discretion tool only, with no hook. Claude would rarely have a 1-256 record JSONL file to label, and the author's own skill says to avoid it for small batches.
Requires a clone and a local build (private:true, not on npm), with no release or version pinning by tag.
Very immature: 6 stars, 7 commits in 2 days of activity (2026-09-19 to 2026-09-21), no releases, and gains are measured only on 64-record synthetic sets with paired runs of n=4.
Sends full record text to a third party; embedded secrets are not detected. That matters for client projects.
The tool writes files, so it would go through permission prompts unless bypass mode is on.
entries.verdict: Not suitable. After v0.3.0 this is a Codex-only batch JSONL labelling tool, not tool/skill selection or context search, and it has no hooks, no OpenRouter support and no reason for Claude Code to invoke it on normal coding turns. Only useful as a small, clean reference for the System One choice-question wire format (a fork to OpenRouter would take 3 lines, but the tool would still be unused).
